US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
October 27, 2026
The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.
Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.
The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.
What are the latest allegations against James Comey?
The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.
The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.
Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.
According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.
However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.
Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.
A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.
How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?
The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.
Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.
Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.
Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.
"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
What other criminal cases does James Comey face?
The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.
A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.
In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.
Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.
Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?
Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.
His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.
Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.
Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.
The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.
The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’
Trump pushes unsubstantiated claims about Brazil’s presidential vote but says he ‘didn’t take sides’ in the race.
The political party of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has acknowledged the result of Brazil’s presidential run-off, despite the right-wing candidate pledging to annul the outcome.
On Monday, Valdemar Costa Neto, the leader of the right-wing Liberal Party, issued a statement saying his political group had accepted the outcome of the vote.
Still, he echoed Bolsonaro’s concerns about the circumstances surrounding the election.
“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
On Sunday, Bolsonaro was defeated by left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by a margin of more than 4.4 million votes.
Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede. In a post-election speech, he called the election results “unacceptable”, citing a last-minute extension to voting hours.
“We will take legal action,” he told supporters. “I will request that these elections be annulled.”
An extension to Sunday’s vote had been sought by the campaigns of both candidates — but for different reasons.
Bolsonaro’s camp had pointed to inclement weather that impeded some voters from reaching polling stations. Parts of southern Brazil, considered a right-wing stronghold, had experienced heavy rains on Sunday.
Lula’s campaign, meanwhile, pushed for longer voting hours after it accused some cities of limiting public transportation on election day.
The left-wing leader’s allies framed those reductions in service as an attempt at election interference, aimed at preventing Lula’s working-class base from voting.
Media reports indicated that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, was arrested on Sunday over the matter.
In response to the petitions, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin agreed to extend voting by two hours.
Whereas polls across the country had been slated to close at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT), Zanin’s order allowed those that had not already closed to remain open until 7pm (22:00 GMT).
Following his loss, Bolsonaro cried foul, saying that the justice’s decision had disadvantaged his voters.
He pointed to Zanin’s relationship with Lula as support: Lula had appointed Zanin to the high court in 2023, and Zanin had formerly served as the left-wing politician’s personal lawyer.
“With a simple stroke of a pen, at the request of a former partner, [Zanin] changed the rules of the game mid-match,” Bolsonaro said in his address on Sunday night.
But experts signalled they were sceptical of Bolsonaro’s claims of malfeasance.
An analysis by Pedro Burgos, a professor at the Brazilian educational institute Insper, found that the extension resulted in 35,000 additional votes across the country, less than 0.03 percent of the total.
That amount was far short of Lula’s 4.4 million vote advantage. The incumbent won more than 64.25 million votes, compared with Bolsonaro’s 59.83 million.
Still, some right-wing allies rallied to Bolsonaro’s support. US President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Lula in the past, told reporters that the vote seemed “rigged”.
“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump said on Monday. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly.”
Still, Trump stopped short of suggesting that he would get involved on behalf of Bolsonaro, saying instead he “did not take sides” in the election.
Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept his loss has raised concerns about whether he will abide by the democratic process or follow in the footsteps of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023.
After his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, the ex-president refused to acknowledge the outcome.
Instead, he and his allies sought to overturn the results, including through a legal challenge, and prosecutors accused him of plotting a coup to prevent the legal transfer of power.
Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence on coup-related charges.
Separately, he was also barred from serving in public office for eight years, after a court found he had misused his public office to spread misinformation about the election.
Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his siblings, has sought to have his father released. The family has denounced the elder Bolsonaro’s trial as a case of political persecution.
Still, it is unclear whether Flavio Bolsonaro will continue with his legal challenge over Sunday’s election.
The Brazilian news outlet Folha de S Paulo reported on Monday that legal advisers and political allies have convinced Bolsonaro to abandon his quest to have his loss annulled, citing the large margin of Lula’s victory and its validation by the Supreme Court and election authorities.
Bolsonaro also announced on Monday that federal police asked him to hand over his passports amid speculation that he could leave the country following his loss.
He said that he would comply with the order and had no plans to leave.
“To withstand the chaos, I’m going to organise the opposition,” the right-wing politician said.

Ukraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:30:27 UTC
10:30:27 KST

- Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded eight, with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying medical facilities and an intensive care unit had been damaged in the late Monday attack. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a ballistic missile attack had struck the grounds of a university campus in the Ukrainian capital. “The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media.
- The strikes on Kyiv came hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was due to start, after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages. The truce, aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into Oleshky, was to begin at 3am local time (0100 GMT). No end date for the truce has been provided. The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces. Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US has said who would monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it. The Russian defence ministry said on Friday it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire. Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied.
- Before the latest strikes on Kyiv, Zelenskyy highlighted Ukraine was still waiting for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on critical missile supplies. “We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again,” he said on X.
- Romania said on Monday that a network “coordinated” from Russia was involved in starting a fire near an arms factory. The fire broke out on 14 September near an arms factory in the central city of Brasov and two Belarusians and a Ukrainian – residents in EU countries – were involved, authorities said. Two of them were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offences”, the office for organised crime said. The third is at large in Poland, it added. Russia’s embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations.
- The attack in Brasov is the latest in a string of similar incidents in Europe, with Nato and the EU grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv. Over the past three weeks, at least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coast of Nato members Romania and Bulgaria. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing.
- Ukraine’s military has begun using specialised aerial rescue drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield, carrying two stranded troops to safety near the Russian border in the first such operations. The newly developed StarGate drone, a six-rotor aircraft fitted with an enclosed evacuation capsule, was used in two separate missions over the past week, the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, an elite unit, said on Monday. Developed by Ukrainian technology company SkyFall, the drone is intended to reduce rescue times from hours to minutes, reaching hard-to-access combat zones currently served by unmanned ground vehicles.

Hong Kong wants to be a regional hub for Halloween. Why not?
Some aren’t thrilled that Hong Kong is becoming the Spooky Administrative Region, but there is no reason not to join a multibillion-dollar trend
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
A journalist for more than 30 years, Cliff Buddle began his career as a court reporter in London and moved to Hong Kong in 1994 to join the SCMP. 
Hong Kong’s determination to become a hub for everything – innovation, finance, trade, culture and sport – appears to know no bounds. Now, Halloween has been added to the list. The city is aiming to become Asia’s premier destination for the annual spookfest.
Of all the regional hubs Hong Kong wishes to become, this is one of the more unlikely. But with Beijing urging the city to ensure “tourism is everywhere” and draw ever more visitors, Halloween, falling between the National Day “golden week” holiday and Christmas, offers an opportunity that cannot be missed.
This year, the city’s Tourism Board has, for the first time, extended the celebrations beyond the traditional October 31. “Hong Kong Halloween Month” is well under way.

Australia to host USS Colorado as first US nuclear submarine under Aukus pact

The Pentagon has assigned the USS Colorado as the first US nuclear-powered attack submarine to join a rotating force to be based in Western Australia.
The 115-metre (380-foot) Virginia-class submarine, armed with land-attack missiles and sophisticated torpedoes, would sail to the new Australian base in late 2027, officials said on Tuesday.

Russian forces introduce ceasefire in Kherson direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:24:15 UTC
10:24:15 KST

MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces introduced a ceasefire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) to prepare for a humanitarian operation near Alyoshki, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"As part of preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, the Russian Armed Forces ceased fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27," the statement reads.
Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that the Russian Armed Forces would cease fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to allow for a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the Kiev regime has been shelling roads leading to Alyoshki and extensively using drones to destroy vehicles. Ukrainian forces have also been using unmanned aerial vehicles to lay mines along roads to prevent civilian evacuations and impede the delivery of foods, medicine and other essential supplies to Alyoshki.
Over the past week alone, the Kiev regime carried out 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone strikes on Alyoshki and main roads in the area, while Russian troops devised over 300 landmines and other explosive devices.
On September 21, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the situation in Alyoshki as critical, saying that food and medicine could not be delivered there amid ongoing Ukrainian shelling and drone attacks. Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a phone call on October 9. Putin said the parties had agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in constant contact with US First Lady Melania Trump's office.
Peskov pointed out on October 26 that the agreement to conduct a humanitarian operation in Alyoshki could set a precedent for similar missions in other areas. He particularly highlighted the United States’ direct and constructive role in coordinating the process. Peskov added that Russia hoped Ukraine would honor all agreements concerning the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.

In Islamophobic rant, Trump seeks to stir Republican base in Michigan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:20:00 UTC
10:20:00 KST

In Islamophobic rant, Trump seeks to stir Republican base in Michigan
David E. Sanger and Bayliss Wagner
- Trump used Islamophobic claims at a Michigan rally to attack Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and boost Republican turnout.
- He called El-Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” and questioned his loyalty, while praising Republican rival Mike Rogers as “apple pie”.
- The race is close and important for Senate control, but Trump’s low approval in Michigan may also hurt Republicans, despite strong crowd support.
AI generated
PORT HURON, United States – US President Donald Trump turned to Islamophobic stereotypes to motivate Michigan Republicans on Oct 25, claiming at a rally that Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee, if elected, would bring a wave of jihadis to the country.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump told more than 4,000 supporters gathered in Port Huron, a working class, waterfront city in a deep-red congressional district about 95km north-east of Detroit.
Trump called El-Sayed, 41, whose family emigrated from Egypt, a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” – a baseless claim.
He then contrasted El-Sayed, a Muslim who was born in the US, with his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, who is white and also born in the US.
“I call him apple pie,” Trump said of Rogers, who is 63. “He’s like, perfect, this guy. He’s like central casting. He’s what your state is all about.”
Trump’s comments, coming in a key midterm battleground nine days before the elections, underscored the dark themes and personal vilification he and his allies have embraced as part of their closing pitch.
And, while he has often used crude and racist language, Trump’s message in Michigan seemed aimed at overtly stoking a fear of Muslims to get voters to the polls.
But a broader question about Trump’s rally here – which followed several in North and South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, among other stops – is whether his presence helps or hurts Republican turnout in a year when polls show deep dissatisfaction with the president.
His audience in Port Huron seemed enthusiastic, and thousands strained to take Trump’s picture as he took to the stage. But he held the rally in a conservative district of a state that pollsters believe is swinging back to Democrats.
Trump’s deep unpopularity has complicated Republicans’ path to victory.
While Trump carried Michigan by 2 points in 2024, just 34% of likely voters now approve of him, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.
Polls indicate that El-Sayed has a narrow edge over Rogers in a race that will be pivotal to determining control of the Senate.
Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed on Oct 25, questioning his loyalty to the United States, began before he got on Air Force One outside of Washington and accelerated after he landed in Michigan.
Speaking in a town on the Canadian border, Trump did not dwell on his battle with Prime Minister Mark Carney, one of the few world leaders who has directly confronted him on tariffs and other issues, and he did not repeat his frequent call for Canada to give up its independence and become the 51st state.
Instead, he focused on El-Sayed, his religion and his relatives. Trump also disparaged Jewish voters who were considering voting for El-Sayed.
“Any Jewish person who supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump said, adding that he “cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy”.
Hundreds of Jewish voters in Michigan publicly announced they were backing El-Sayed, while others have said they are voting for Rogers or threatened to withhold their support.
Trump made the statement after claiming that El-Sayed’s half sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Oct 7, 2023, massacre of Israelis by Hamas fighters.
She posted a video on the first anniversary of the attack that said that “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner”, but did not mention the massacre directly and did not celebrate the violence.
El-Sayed’s campaign told Fox News that he disagreed with her “on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use”.
El-Sayed has repeatedly disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, and has said comments about his name and faith are attempts to distract from voters’ economic woes. His aides have said claims of ties to overseas terrorist groups are racist and Islamophobic.
But his opponents have raised an open letter he signed in 2012, when he was a medical student.
It was addressed to Mohammed Morsi, then the new Egyptian president, from a party that represents the political wing of the Muslim Brotherhood.
It asked him to “purge the media and police” of loyalists to the government that was overturned during the Arab Spring.
El-Sayed has not discussed the letter. But his spokesperson, Cole Wozniak, said, “Abdul remains laser-focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington”.
“Michigan knows Trump is on the ballot on Nov 3,” he added, “and they will vote like it by rejecting Trump’s rubber stamp Mike Rogers and sending Abdul to the Senate.”
Trump deepened his critique as the day went on, saying that someone with El-Sayed’s background “would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane”.
“They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate,” he added.
He also said that El-Sayed should not be given access to classified information.
At his own rally on Oct 25 in Grand Rapids, El-Sayed said the Republican strategy was “to point at me and my name and my faith”.
“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” he said.
In Michigan, Trump also veered into a discussion of Greenland. He insisted, “Oh, you know we did get Greenland”, suggesting that it was now owned by the US.
In fact, Trump was forced to drop that demand and instead signed a new treaty with Denmark, which handles Greenland’s foreign affairs, that envisions opening two new US bases on the island and bars similar arrangements with foreign powers, notably China. But it does not change Denmark’s sovereignty, as Trump initially insisted.
He also drew cheers when he insisted Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, and vaguely said the war with Iran would be resolved soon.
But he largely steered clear of discussing how his decision to attack Iran led directly to high gas and diesel prices.
Rogers has sought distance from the war, calling for it to “end quickly”, and from the President’s tariffs on Canadian goods, saying “Canada is not our enemy” in a campaign ad. He has also backed a one-year moratorium on data centres, creating a contrast with Trump’s support for them.
Like other Republicans, Rogers has largely avoided talking about Trump in ads and on the campaign trail.
Speaking at the rally in Port Huron, Rogers again accused El-Sayed of having family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. He said that watching El-Sayed try to tell the truth is like “watching an octopus put his socks on in the morning”. And he said the country “can’t risk his extreme ideology and thinking”.
On NBC News’ Meet The Press on the morning of Oct 25, Rogers did not endorse Trump’s baseless claim that El-Sayed is “a terrorist”, but did not condemn it outright.
“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers said of El-Sayed.
El-Sayed has become a central villain in Republicans’ narrative of the midterms.
In western Iowa on Oct 22, more than 1280km from Port Huron, Trump railed against El- Sayed, drawing some of the loudest applause of the night. He did the same in North Carolina and Ohio last week.
After holding forth on the potential demise of the nation in Michigan on Oct 25, Trump spent five full minutes admiring the body and physicality of Senator Jon Husted, the Republican running for re-election in Ohio, and rapper Nicki Minaj, who traveled with Trump to the rally.
“I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before – Nicki Minaj,” Trump said. “Hard to miss it.”

Russia announces ceasefire in frontline town
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ceasefire takes effect in frontline town – Russia
A temporary ceasefire around the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region has taken effect to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians, the Russian Defense Ministry has announced.
According to a brief statement by the ministry, the ceasefire began at 4am Moscow time (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday “in preparation for a humanitarian operation.”
General Valery Gerasimov, Russia’s chief of the General Staff, said last week that military engineers would conduct reconnaissance and ensure “the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy” into the town. The Ukrainian General Staff also confirmed last week that it would observe the truce.
Russian authorities estimate that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians remain trapped in Alyoshki, on the left bank of the Dnieper River opposite the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson. The town has been largely cut off from supplies for months, with Ukrainian shelling and drone strikes preventing regular aid deliveries, according to Russian officials.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing civilians from leaving the embattled town. However, residents who managed to escape told RT earlier this month that Alyoshki was effectively under siege by Ukrainian forces, which they said were carrying out constant attacks.
Between October 19 and 26 alone, Ukrainian forces carried out 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone strikes on Alyoshki and its main access roads, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.

Teen arrested in Florida shooting will be tried as adult, US officials say
Billy Witz
- A 15-year-old, Anthony Rivers III, will be tried as an adult after an Oct 24 Tallahassee shooting left 11 people shot and six in hospital, one critically ill.
- Police said the gunfire followed a fight between people who knew each other, and none of the victims seemed to be intended targets. More arrests may follow.
- Prosecutor Jack Campbell said the case is severe, with 11 attempted second-degree murder charges and one firearm charge. He also linked the decision to Rivers’ past arrests.
AI generated
Tallahassee, Florida - A 15-year-old boy who was arrested in the shooting of 11 people after a college football game in Tallahassee, Florida, will stand trial as an adult, a Florida prosecutor said on Oct 26.
The teenager, Anthony Rivers III, was ordered to remain in custody at a juvenile court hearing on Oct 26 after his arrest the day before. The shooting took place in a crowded, closed-off street on Oct 24 about an hour after Florida A&M University’s homecoming game. A crowd of just over 20,000 attended the event.
The shooting left six people hospitalised as of Oct 25, one of whom was in critical condition. A spokesperson for the Leon County School District said four of its students were wounded, including the one in critical condition.
Six of the 11 people shot were minors, the Tallahassee Police Department said. A 12th person was injured but not shot, officials said.
Lawrence Revell, chief of the Tallahassee police, said at a news conference on Oct 26 that the shooting appeared to have stemmed from a physical altercation between people who knew one another and that none of the victims appeared to be intended targets. He said more arrests were possible.
Judge Andrew Sheeran, who presided over the hearing on Oct 26, said he would grant the request of the top prosecutor in Tallahassee to try Rivers as an adult, which Florida law allows in certain cases. He will be charged with 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, officials said.
“It’s our discretion because of the severity of the offence,” said the prosecutor, Jack Campbell.
In a phone interview, he added that he had discussed the decision with juvenile-case prosecutors before asking his prosecutors to review the case. “Ultimately, it was my decision,” he said.
Rivers, dressed in a white T-shirt, grey gym shorts, sandals and his hair pulled up into a bun, stood quietly at the hearing on Oct 26 with his hands clasped behind his back, as the public defender who is representing him addressed the court.
The public defender said she had previously represented Rivers. Her office did not reply to a request for comment. Efforts to reach relatives of Rivers were not immediately successful.
According to court records, Rivers has been arrested previously on charges including burglary and theft of a gun, but it was unclear what the outcome was. He was arrested on Sept 6 for violating his probation and had been sentenced to a juvenile home.
According to a police affidavit, Rivers was arrested after surveillance cameras and an ankle monitor he was wearing identified him at a Tallahassee mall where gunfire had erupted in an underground parking lot.
The police identified another 15-year-old who was with Rivers as the shooter, according to the affidavit. Nobody was injured in the shooting, which occurred after an altercation in the mall.
Campbell declined to discuss anything about Rivers’ criminal record. But he said if someone was a repeat offender, “that’s something we consider” when determining whether to charge a juvenile as an adult.
The shooting echoed others in Tallahassee in recent years. Nine people were shot – one fatally – outside a liquor store in 2022 that Campbell said was connected to a homecoming event at Florida A&M.
In 2025, two people were killed and six others were wounded in a shooting at Florida State University, which is adjacent to Florida A&M.
Campbell is seeking the death penalty against the shooter in that case, Phoenix Ikner, who has pleaded not guilty and is awaiting trial.
The shooting on Oct 24 could have been much worse, Campbell said.
It happened on Perry Street, a residential street that runs alongside Bragg Memorial Stadium, where the football team plays. The street was blocked off for vendors selling food and T-shirts, and it is a popular place to tailgate before and after games.
“If you go to FAMU, you’ve spent time on Perry Street,” Campbell said. NYTIMES

Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged', defeated Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:10:22 UTC
10:10:22 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's surprise win in Brazil's presidential vote "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro, has refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party's head, Valdemar Costa Neto.
"We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
"I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange."
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded."
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
Markets roiled by Lula win
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil's real BRL= fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
"The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

Israeli man arrested in Thailand on suspicion of drugging women, secretly filming sex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:10:20 UTC
10:10:20 KST

Bangkok police arrested a 54-year-old Israeli man last Friday on suspicion of meeting women through dating apps, inviting them to his apartment, and serving them cakes suspected of containing drugs before having sex with them and secretly recording the encounters.
According to a police statement, officers searching his apartment seized methamphetamine, drug-packaging equipment, and a mobile phone containing numerous intimate videos. Investigators also discovered that the Israeli had stayed in Thailand without a valid visa for 2,095 days, or nearly six years.
Thai media identified the suspect as Tomer Kahiri. He was reportedly known in Thailand as “Tom,” “Tommy,” or “Tom Yum Kung,” after the popular Thai soup.
He was arrested at an apartment building in Bangkok’s Huai Khwang district in a joint operation involving the capital’s narcotics suppression unit and immigration police. A 44-year-old Thai woman was arrested with him.
Investigation followed tip to Thai narcotics authorities
According to the police statement, the investigation began after information was received by the hotline of Thailand’s narcotics suppression authorities. The informant described an Israeli man with an eagle tattoo on his left arm who allegedly contacted women through dating apps and invited them to his home.
According to the tip, the women experienced hot flashes and increased sexual arousal after eating cakes he had prepared for them. They subsequently had sex with him, which police suspected was recorded without their knowledge.
Police suspected the cakes contained drugs, but laboratory test results confirming their contents had not been made public.
The investigation was led by Major General Teeradet Thamsuthee, deputy chief of Bangkok police responsible for narcotics suppression. With assistance from immigration police, investigators discovered that the suspect’s visa had expired 2,095 days earlier.
During surveillance, officers observed numerous women entering and leaving his apartment. Police said the suspect did not have regular employment and spent most of his time at home, but had enough money to support himself.
Drugs, cakes and intimate videos found on phone
During the raid, police seized 15 grams of crystal methamphetamine, 50 bags used for packaging drugs, an electronic scale, a tray of cakes suspected of containing drugs, and a mobile phone.
According to police, an examination of the phone revealed messages concerning the purchase of drugs for resale, along with numerous videos showing sexual encounters with different women on a sofa in the apartment. The encounters were allegedly filmed without the women’s knowledge.
The man denied that the seized drugs belonged to him.
According to the police statement, he claimed during his arrest that he had connections to an influential person who could secure his release within two hours. He demanded the names of the officers involved in the raid and threatened to have them transferred or fired. Police also alleged that he threatened to kill one of the officers involved in the operation.
The Israeli man was accused of possessing a dangerous drug, overstaying his visa, refusing to undergo a drug test, and disobeying law enforcement officials. The Thai woman arrested with him was suspected of possessing and using methamphetamine.
The police statement did not say that the Israeli had, at that stage, been formally charged with drugging women or secretly recording intimate encounters without their consent. Both suspects and the seized evidence were transferred to Huai Khwang police station for further legal proceedings.
According to Thai media reports, the Israeli denied all the allegations against him. He reportedly described himself as a former Israeli soldier and businessman involved in textile exports. He also said he had two children and had moved to Thailand after separating from his partner because he loved the country and found its residents friendly.

Jordan bombs Syria after deadly church attack
Jordan carried out airstrikes on what it described as terrorist sites in neighboring Syria on Monday following a deadly attack on a Christian church last week. The Syrian government condemned the operation.
According to the Royal Jordanian Air Force (RJAF), fighter jets targeted “hideouts of terrorist organizations in southern Syria.” It added that “several terrorists” were killed or wounded and unspecified equipment was destroyed.
Although the RJAF claimed it had acted in coordination with Syrian authorities, the government in Damascus denied receiving advance notice of the strikes. The Syrian Foreign Ministry said it had informed Jordan of its “objections to operations on Syrian territory without prior coordination.”
Khaled al-Omeian, director of health in Syria’s Daraa province, told SANA that seven civilians, including three children, were killed in the strikes and three others were injured.
“We affirm our support for the affected Syrian families and our full solidarity with them in this tragedy,” the Syrian government said in a statement.
Jordan vowed retaliation after gunmen opened fire on mourners attending a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, in Jordan’s Karak governorate, on Friday, killing nine people and wounding more than 40.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. Jordanian police arrested three suspects during a raid on a compound in Hamoud. Roya News, citing a source, reported that one of the suspects remained in critical condition following a shootout with police.

Ex-FBI chief Comey faces third prosecution attempt by Trump Justice Department
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:10:03 UTC
10:10:03 KST

The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday.
The case was revealed in a court document known as a "criminal information" that the Justice Department said it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.
The document filed in Washington federal court charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from the New York Times in October 2016.
Comey said in an Instagram video that "they're back again" and referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. "I'm still innocent," he added. Comey's lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.
The new case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening US President Donald Trump in a social media post. A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats case remains pending.
Comey did not commit crimes, lawyer alleges
Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that the document "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit." The criminal information was filed on October 5, but was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey's lawyers.
A Justice Department spokesperson described the maneuver to halt the statute of limitations as a "widely recognized practice in federal court."
"This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Kyiv • UNN
As of 03:00, Ukraine halted fire in the occupied city of Oleshky to deliver aid and ensure the safe movement of civilians. The General Staff urged people to trust only official information.
In the occupied city of Oleshky, Kherson region, Ukraine introduced a ceasefire regime starting at 3:00 a.m. to conduct a humanitarian operation. This was reported by Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets, UNN writes.
Details
According to him, the ceasefire is intended to create conditions for delivering humanitarian aid to residents who remain in the city, as well as for organizing the safe movement of civilians.
The main goal of the operation is to help people living under occupation, ensure their safety, and create conditions for their rescue.
General Staff issues an important warning
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine called on citizens to rely exclusively on official statements regarding the humanitarian operation.
The military stressed that spreading unverified information about the routes, times, and locations of movement of civilians and humanitarian convoys is unacceptable.
Such information could endanger people’s safety and the conduct of humanitarian activities.
Information about the further course of the operation and the possibility of civilians leaving safely should be obtained only from official sources.

PASIGHAT/ITANAGAR: A 12-hour bandh against a proposed hydropower project in Arunachal Pradesh’s Upper Subansiri district turned violent Monday, with mobs damaging vehicles and NHPC equipment and wounding two security personnel as anti-dam protests spread from Siang basin to Subansiri valley, report Kangkan Kalita and Joken Ete.The latest flashpoint was Daporijo town, 220km west of Pasighat by road. NHPC equipment, a company vehicle and two police vehicles were damaged during the bandh called by All Tagin Students’ Union and other organisations against Menga dam, part of the proposed 1,605MW Subansiri Upper Hydroelectric Project. Police conducted a flag march in Daporijo and appealed for peace.
Remove central forces, say protesters; depends on restoration of peace: Government
Constable-driver Hibu Lasha and a CRPF man were wounded. Both were shifted to Ziro for treatment,” Upper Subansiri SP Pawan Kumar Yadav said.The bandh began at 5am over opposition to the proposed Menga dam and an alleged attempt to detain ATSU president Tadak Pakba. Backed by student unions and community groups from the Subansiri basin, the agitation grew out of fears that the project would threaten their land, livelihoods, and future.Earlier, Pasighat recorded widespread arson, vandalism and clashes with security forces when protesters laid siege to the East Siang district headquarters from Friday night to early Saturday over the proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP), with its main reservoir planned near Geku village, about 35km downstream from Upper Siang district headquarters Yingkiong.
The Siang flows from Tibet into the ancestral land of the Adi community inhabiting Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang districts, while Upper Subansiri is home to the Tagin community. The Adi and Tagin people are closely related.Tension continued in Upper Siang, where protesters demanded the release of people arrested for the violence and four activists placed under preventive detention. They also demanded the withdrawal of central security forces and an immediate halt to the pre-feasibility survey for the project.
Upper Siang DC Ashok Tajo said govt was examining their cases, but release of those detained required further approvals. Protesters had set Sunday as the deadline. He said pulling out central forces from affected areas would depend on restoration of peace. “We are ready to facilitate talks between the villagers and govt,” Tajo said, urging villagers to nominate representatives to begin dialogue.

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:01:53 UTC
10:01:53 KST

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
US appeals court blocks government effort to stop California from tabulating ballots from list of alleged non-citizens.
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.
In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.
But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.
In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.
The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.
The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.
Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.
California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.
The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.
The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.
Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.
But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.
It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.
But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.
The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.
Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.
In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.
Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.
Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.
Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.
Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.
But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.
Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.
In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

CAR: Special Criminal Court, the last hope of justice for thousands, on the brink of collapse – new report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

- Special Criminal Court at risk of closure by 2028 with thousands of victims awaiting justice
- Other than the UN and the EU, no state providing financial support to SCC at the moment
- ICC closed investigations; National courts lack resources and independence to take on SCC cases
Suspected perpetrators of crimes under international law in the Central African Republic (CAR), including some of the country’s highest-ranking officials, are at risk of escaping justice unless the Special Criminal Court (SCC) receives the funding it requires to continue investigating and prosecuting cases, Amnesty International said in a new report.
“The perpetrators are still here” – The Central African Republic’s Special Criminal Court on borrowed time, as victims await justice examines the progress and challenges faced by the SCC, which has tried six cases since its inauguration on 22 October 2018, resulting in 19 people being convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity. However, victims of the most serious crimes committed during some of the bloodiest periods in CAR’s history, including during the 2003 coup led by François Bozizé and the 2012–2014 internal armed conflict, are still waiting for all perpetrators in positions of high authority to be prosecuted.
Yet the court, which relies solely on voluntary contributions from states and international organizations, is at risk of closure by 2028. After an initial sense of hope, survivors and victims are beginning to lose faith.
“Victims’ right to justice, truth, and reparations must not depend on the shifting priorities of donors. Thousands of civilians were killed, raped, abducted, maimed, injured, displaced, or had their homes burned down during waves of violence and armed conflict over the last 25 years. Each one of them deserves justice,” said Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa.
“Amnesty International calls on the Central African authorities, the United Nations, the European Union, and all partner states to provide – or continue to provide – financial support to the Special Criminal Court to meet its operating budget.”
The Special Criminal Court was established at the request of the Central African people and civil society. If the court does not receive the resources it needs to continue its essential work, it will fail them.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
‘Victims want justice [to be done]’
Of the six cases tried by the SCC, verdicts have been handed down in the first four at least in the first instance, resulting in the conviction of 19 people for war crimes and crimes against humanity. In one case, victims also received reparations. The verdict in the fifth trial relating to attacks in Guen, western CAR, in 2014, is expected next December, while the Bossembélé trial, which lists former president Bozizé among the accused, is currently underway.
Despite the remarkable progress in fighting impunity in the CAR, numerous grave crimes still remain unpunished. These include widespread campaigns of murder, rape, and looting committed in 2002–2003, in particular by security forces of former president Ange-Félix Patassé and fighters from Jean-Pierre Bemba’s armed group that he enlisted to try to crush François Bozizé’s coup; as well as many crimes of killings, rapes, torture, and enforced disappearances committed between 2012 and 2014, in the context of conflict between Seleka and Anti-balaka armed groups.
Despite a significant improvement in the enforcement of arrest warrants issued by the SCC in the last few years, dozens of individuals are currently still wanted, and significant obstacles to their arrest remain. François Bozizé resides in Guinea-Bissau, while other suspects subject to arrest warrants are in Chad.
The SCC has tried a number of individuals, such as Bozizé, in their absence, but these in absentia trials significantly undermine the process and defence rights, and fall short of victims’ needs.
“Victims want justice [to be done]. When their perpetrators are brought to justice their hearts will be at peace, when they see them in prison,” said a representative from a Central African organization that supports victims. Other victims said they are satisfied with judgments in absentia.
An unprecedented financial crisis
In 2025, the United States withdrew its financial support for the SCC, leaving it to face an unprecedented funding crisis with more than US$4.15 million in commitments that remain unpaid. The United Nations and the European Union are currently the sole financial contributors to the court.
Funding cuts forced the court to lay off a quarter of its staff, including foreign experts, between August and September 2025. Its witness protection unit has lost more than half of its staff, which has the potential to compromise its ability to limit reprisals against witnesses. Due to the lack of staff and resources, the Office of the Prosecutor can no longer open any new investigations, while cases before the various Chambers suffer delays.
To the best of Amnesty International’s knowledge, with the exception of the UN and EU, no state or organization has committed to future voluntary financial contributions to the SCC, raising the prospect of the SCC’s closure at the end of its mandate in 2028.
States and international organizations must providing urgent funding, preferably through multi-year commitments, so that justice can be served as long as it is necessary.
Marceau Sivieude, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for West and Central Africa
No alternative for trying the worst crimes in the CAR
Despite progress, CAR’s national courts currently lack the human and material resources, as well as the necessary independence, to handle cases currently before the SCC. “If the cases are transferred to the national courts, it will mean that they will be before our judges, and their superiors will influence them,” a representative of victims said.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) also has jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in the CAR since 2002. It has opened two investigations at the request of the Central African government. However, in December 2022, the ICC Prosecutor’s Office announced that it was closing its investigations.
An essential jurisdiction amid persistent conflict
In the CAR, the intensity of the violence has decreased since its peak in 2021, but all parties to the conflict continue to commit serious human rights violations and crimes under international law in the northeast and southeast of the country.
“The SCC was established at the request of the Central African people and civil society. If the court does not receive the resources it needs to continue its essential work, it will fail them and embolden those who continue to commit atrocities today,” said Marceau Sivieude.
“The Central African authorities must support and protect the SCC, and extend its mandate beyond October 2028 until the Court’s mission has been accomplished. They must help to secure additional funding for its budget.”
“States and international organizations must fully cooperate by executing the SCC’s arrest warrants and providing urgent funding, preferably through multi-year commitments, so that justice can be served as long as it is necessary.”
Background
This report builds on the research work that Amnesty International has been conducting for a decade on issues of justice, truth and reparation for crimes under international law in the CAR. For this report, the organization conducted a mission in April 2026 to Bangui, the capital, and interviewed 63 people. It also reviewed court decisions, legal texts, reports from international organizations, NGOs and donors, academic works, official statements, and news articles.
The report’s findings were shared with the Central African authorities on 6 October 2026. Amnesty International had not received a response at the time of publication.
The SCC has a mandate to investigate and prosecute crimes under international law committed during conflicts in the Central African Republic since 2003. It is a hybrid court supported by the UN, composed of Central African and foreign prosecutors and judges. It began its second five-year term on 22 October 2023, due to end in October 2028.

Taiwan is developing an AI-powered system to coordinate drone fleets for maritime surveillance and countering “grey-zone” activities, with researchers completing a simulation involving 20 aircraft, according to the island’s Ocean Affairs Council.
The system, which is funded by the council, would allow different types of drones to autonomously divide tasks, plan routes and coordinate their movements while providing wide-area, persistent surveillance for coastguard operations.

'I felt like I had Jew stamped on my forehead': BBC settles antisemitism dispute with producer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:58:35 UTC
09:58:35 KST

The BBC has agreed to pay more than £400,000 (about $534,000) to Jewish producer Lucie Kon, who alleged that she faced antisemitic remarks from colleagues and was pushed out of her job after complaining about the treatment of Jewish employees following the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023. The settlement was reached without an admission of liability by the British broadcaster, after Kon threatened legal action over alleged discrimination and unfair dismissal.
Kohn, 57, worked at the BBC for 22 years and was involved in documentary productions that won prestigious awards. She was among the executive producers of "We Will Dance Again," a documentary about the Hamas attack on the Nova music festival, and "Mr. Nobody Against Putin," which won this year's Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature.
In an interview with The Telegraph, Kon said her Jewish identity had never been an issue at work for many years, but that the atmosphere changed dramatically after October 7. She described a conversation with a colleague in which she said Hamas terrorists were evil, only to receive the response, "So are Zionists." On another occasion, she said, a colleague told her to consider what had driven Hamas to carry out the attack.
"I really did feel like I had Jew stamped on my forehead," Kon said, describing the change she experienced. According to her account, instead of being regarded as a journalist and producer who happened to be Jewish, she began to feel that colleagues viewed her primarily through her Jewish identity and the political positions they attributed to her.
One of the central disputes involved Kon's efforts to advance a documentary about the Hamas attack at the Nova music festival. She said there were demands for the film to present the events in a broader context and examine the reasons behind the attack. Kon alleged that her ability to cover the subject objectively was questioned because she was Jewish, and that she was told she could not oversee the project because she was biased.
Kon also recalled a colleague telling her that if she wanted to describe Hamas members as terrorists, she should apply the same label to Israel. Following these and other remarks, she said she raised concerns about the treatment of Jewish employees with BBC management and established a support group for Jewish staff members.
In January 2024, Kon filed a formal internal complaint. After an investigation lasting approximately five months, she was informed that her complaint had not been upheld. Her subsequent appeal was also rejected.
Kon said the stress later affected her health, forcing her to take sick leave. The broadcaster subsequently informed her that her position was at risk because of organizational restructuring. Her employment with the BBC ended in April 2026, shortly after a documentary she had helped produce won an Oscar.
Kon pursued legal action alleging discrimination, harassment and unfair dismissal. The BBC ultimately agreed to pay her more than £400,000 but did not admit liability for her allegations. According to reports, the settlement also included a correction concerning how her name appeared in the credits for "Mr. Nobody Against Putin."
Kohn also sought a formal apology and a meeting with the BBC's new director-general, Matt Brittin, but said both requests were rejected.
A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster does not comment on individual personnel matters and that antisemitism of any kind is not tolerated within the organization.
In a separate statement cited in reports, the BBC said its internal investigation had not upheld Kon's allegations of antisemitism, but acknowledged that the handling of the matter had revealed shortcomings and had a personal impact on her. The broadcaster also expressed appreciation for her years of service and contributions.
Kon stressed that she does not believe the BBC as a whole is antisemitic. However, she argued that antisemitism and groupthink remain problems within the organization, making it difficult for employees to express views that differ from those prevailing in their workplace.
She said that even after leaving the BBC, she had spoken with Jewish employees who continued to feel uncomfortable and were afraid to speak openly about their Jewish identity or identify themselves as Zionists.

MOLD punctures terracotta-colored greek island ‘M residence’ with seven open-air courtyards

Unknown Publisher

MOLD punctures terracotta-colored greek island ‘M residence’ with seven open-air courtyards
curved passages and planted courtyards create a sheltered interior within the rose-colored home on serifos.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a solid square carved open to the sky
On the Greek island of Serifos, Athens-based MOLD Architects shapes its M Residence around seven open-air courtyards carved into a square volume. From above, the terracotta-colored home looks almost like a diagram. Its flat roof is punctured by irregular openings, revealing planted gardens and shaded passages within the building’s compact outline. The residence occupies an exposed site in Lia, where its geometric silhouette stands against the dry, rocky hills overlooking the Aegean Sea.
The project has an unusually long history. Architect Iliana Kerestetzi first developed the design in 2011, during the early years of her practice, though it remained unbuilt for more than a decade. When new owners revived the scheme, the architect returned to the original drawings with a different perspective. The central concept remained, while the rooms opened more generously toward the courtyards and the material palette grew warmer. Completed in 2026, the house retains the graphic strength of its original design, with a more fluid layout inside.
seven courtyards shape the interior
MOLD Architects’ M residence takes its exterior form from the enclosed architecture of Cycladic monasteries, whose solid walls shelter spaces within. The team combines this reference with the cubic buildings of traditional island settlements and the softer geometry of rural stone structures. The house maintains a strict square perimeter, though inside, curved walls bend around the rooms and connect a sequence of seven courtyards. Each opening introduces a different relationship with the landscape, bringing daylight deep into the plan.
Moving through the house, enclosed rooms give way to pockets of open sky. Some courtyards become small gardens planted with grasses, while others offer shaded places to sit with views toward the Aegean. Broad passages connect these spaces beneath the continuous roof, whose irregular cutouts form curved edges overhead. The sea appears between the walls, disappears around a corner, and returns through another opening.
a pink monolith hovering above the rocky terrain
From the surrounding hillside, the house presents a very different character. Its exterior walls are largely solid, interrupted by recessed windows and occasional perforated brick screens. The entire volume sits on a raised plinth, with a narrow shadow line separating the terracotta-colored mass from the uneven ground. A rectangular swimming pool extends beyond the building’s footprint which introduces a long, straight edge alongside the more irregular geometry of the roof.
The warm plaster continues throughout the residence, covering the walls and ceilings in earthy pink tones. Inside, rounded corners soften the transitions between spaces, while pale wood cabinetry brings a change in texture. The kitchen faces the water through a broad opening, and large sliding glass panels connect the rooms to their neighboring courtyards. Even the bedrooms and bathrooms maintain a close relationship with the surrounding terrain, where windows frame glimpses of the sea.
shifting light across the curved walls
Across the courtyards, the architecture changes considerably with the movement of the sun. Roof openings cast broad shadows that travel over the rounded walls, while the perforated screens filter daylight into smaller patches. The planting adds another layer of texture against the plaster surfaces. In some spaces, the architecture almost entirely frames the sky, leaving the surrounding coastline momentarily out of view.
The residents have already begun making their own additions. Beneath one of the roof openings, they have suspended a piece of white fabric that filters the sunlight and moves with the breeze. It is a small intervention within an otherwise strongly defined composition. For a house conceived around a single geometric figure, M Residence contains a surprising variety of places to occupy, each shaped by the changing light and its particular opening to the outdoors.
project info:
name: M Residence
architect: MOLD Architects | @moldarchitects
location: Serifos, Greece
lead architect: Lia, Serifos Island, Greece

Collingwood's AFLW coach Sam Wright will leave his post at the end of the season.

What's next?
Collingwood faces Essendon in the final round on Sunday, with both sides on the bottom of the ladder.
Collingwood's AFLW crisis has deepened, with coach Sam Wright another casualty in a horror season.
Wright will leave his position after the Magpies' final-round match against Essendon at Windy Hill on Sunday, ending a three-season campaign.
The Magpies have managed just one win from 11 games to anchor the AFLW ladder alongside the Bombers and St Kilda.
The match will also be the last for Essendon coach Natalie Wood, while St Kilda is already looking for a replacement for Nick Dal Santo.
Tarni White, Lauren Butler, Bri Davey, Sarah Rowe and Mattea Breed are all out of contract, while vice-captain Jordyn Allen is contracted but is expected to seek other opportunities.
Players and staff are reportedly frustrated with list management, development coaching, and medical treatment at the powerhouse AFL club.
Wright backed Collingwood's commitment to the women's football program.
"I look forward to coaching the group this Sunday and I wish them all the very best for the future — I leave knowing Collingwood is committed to driving its AFLW program forward," he said in a statement on Tuesday.
"It has been a privilege to serve the AFLW program at Collingwood.
"I will always look back on my time at the Pies with gratitude, and I want to thank every player, coach, staff member and supporter I've shared this journey with.
"While these decisions are never easy, I know it is the right one for my family and the football program as we move forward."
The Magpies haven't made the AFLW finals since 2022 when they were semifinalists, after ending the regular season sixth.
Despite their resources, they have finished outside the top 10 in each of the following seasons.

Russian air attacks struck Kyiv late on October 26, hitting a university dormitory and other civilian sites, leaving at least one dead, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Ukraine's partners to provide the "proper tools" for the country to defend itself.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least 10 people were injured in the strikes, "most of whom were students from a university dormitory."
The strikes come just before a US-negotiated cease-fire is to start in the eastern city of Oleshky, and efforts by a bipartisan group of US lawmakers for the White House to step up efforts to defend Ukraine.
"It is precisely under such circumstances, when the threat is constant, when strikes can come at any moment and target cities and villages directly, that artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.
"It is important that our partners understand that Ukraine needs the proper tools to destroy Russian ballistic missile launchers. This would be the most effective way to save lives. It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war. "
US lawmakers have been challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they have said in recent days that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
For several months, Zelenskyy has also called on the US and other allies to step up supplies of critical defense systems such as Patriot missiles amid almost nightly barrages of Russian ballistic missiles and drones.
He said last week that Ukraine was still waiting for previously agreed deliveries of interceptors for Patriot air-defense systems.
Despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, Russian officials deny targeting civilian infrastructure in the conflict, which has raged since the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
The university hit in the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), one of Kyiv's largest schools with more than 15,000 students.
