Daylight Saving Time Ends This Week. Here’s How to Best Prepare Yourself for the Time Change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:25:08 UTC
07:25:08 KST

The clocks in most of the U.S. will fall back an hour this weekend as Daylight Saving Time once again comes to an end.
Early Sunday morning, most of the country will switch back to observing Standard Time, resulting in earlier sunrises and earlier sunsets. The looming clock change comes as some lawmakers, with the backing of President Donald Trump, have been trying to push a bill through Congress that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent and end the biannual time change. But the bill has been met with pushback from other lawmakers and sleep experts.
Here’s everything you need to know about the clock change this fall, and the state of the bill that’s trying to put a stop to the cycle of changing the clocks twice a year.
When do the clocks fall back in 2026?
Daylight Saving Time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m. local time. At that time, the clocks will fall back an hour, to 1 a.m. local time.
How can I prepare for the clock change?
Dr. Alex Dimitriu, a psychiatrist and sleep medicine physician, likens the practice of changing the clocks twice a year to “an hour of jet lag,” adding that it can be an adjustment for many people. But the transition to Standard Time also means that people will gain an extra hour of sleep.
“Typically, moving to Standard Time is actually in sync with our circadian rhythm,” says Dr. Andrea Matsumura, a sleep medicine physician and spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. “Most people have a fairly easy transition into Standard Time; it’s the Daylight Saving Time that you have to do a lot more work to adjust [to] losing an hour of sleep.”
In the days leading up to the start of Daylight Saving Time—which will happen next March—Matsumura typically advises that people start going to bed a little earlier to help make the time change “a little less painful.” But there’s less preparation needed in the days leading up to Standard Time; in fact, Matsumura recommends that people simply stick to their regular sleep schedule ahead of Nov. 1.
Matsumura does suggest that people continue to take steps that normally help improve sleep, such as getting some daylight when they wake up in the morning and not drinking caffeine too late in the afternoon. Similarly, Dimitriu recommends that people do some physical movement in the morning, such as going for a walk, and avoid eating food too late in the evening.
What’s the status of the bill that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent?
Most states in the U.S. change their clocks twice a year: once in March as Daylight Saving Time begins, and again in November for Standard Time. Under the current federal law, states are permitted to opt out of Daylight Saving Time and remain in Standard Time year-round. Hawaii and most of Arizona have chosen that option, and so observe Standard Time throughout the year. Federal law does not, though, allow states to remain in Daylight Saving Time year-round.
A bill known as the Sunshine Protection Act, if passed by Congress and signed into law by the President, would change that. The measure would result in the country observing Daylight Saving Time year-round, though individual states could choose to forgo that path and instead stay in Standard Time permanently.
The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House with bipartisan support in July. But the measure is facing an uncertain fate in the Senate. Earlier this month, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told POLITICO that “there’s no clear path forward or consensus” on the bill yet.
Some lawmakers in the upper chamber, such as Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, have criticized the proposal. Critics have argued that permanent Daylight Saving Time would mean much later sunrises in some parts of the country, resulting in people going to school and work in the dark.
Sleep experts, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have also objected to the bill because they say that Standard Time aligns better with people’s circadian rhythms.
Still, Trump has slammed critics of the Sunshine Protection Act and continued to push for the bill. At the beginning of October, he accused Cotton of “holding up” the bill, and urged his followers on Truth Social to “call Tom on his cellphone” to express support for the Sunshine Protection Act.

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:18:34 UTC
07:18:34 KST

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As young people protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living across Europe, misleading videos are spreading online. Footage from Poland in 2017, military preparations in Portugal and a protest in Argentina have all been falsely presented as recent demonstrations in Europe, painting a misleading picture of unrest. Vedika Bahl fact-checks three viral videos to uncover what they really show and how old footage is recycled to spread misinformation and attract clicks.
As young people take to the streets across Europe to protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living, misleading videos circulating online regarding the demonstrations.
Footage from Poland, Portugal and Argentina has been falsely presented as evidence of recent unrest in Europe, with some posts suggesting the continent is descending into chaos. Others may be seeking to attract clicks and engagement.
One viral video, viewed more than a million times on X, appears to show enormous crowds gathered in Poland. Social media users claimed it depicted millions of people taking part in recent protests. But the footage is nearly nine years old. It shows Poland’s annual Independence Day march and was already circulating online in 2017.
The video has repeatedly resurfaced with misleading captions over the years. It was also previously shared as footage of unrest in France and was debunked earlier this year by FRANCE 24’s fact-checking service, The Observers.
Another video has been used to spread false claims about protests in Portugal. Posts on social media claimed the country had deployed its army to suppress demonstrations, warning that Portugal was on the “brink of social explosion”.
The footage shows military vehicles driving through the streets of Porto, accompanied by dramatic music. While the video was indeed filmed in the Portuguese city - with the famous Chapel of Santa Catarina is visible in the background - it does not show troops being deployed against protesters.
Instead, the footage shows preparations for Army Day, held from October 20 to 25. According to the city’s official website, thousands of soldiers arrived in Porto for a multi-day programme of events showcasing the military.
There have been no credible reports of the army being deployed to quell the recent protests. Demonstrations, including those calling for more affordable housing, have been handled by police. On Sunday, police dismantled housing protest camps in Porto and Lisbon, with more than 30 people arrested.
The same military footage has also recently circulated on TikTok with a different false claim: that it shows French police being deployed against protesters in France, despite Portuguese architecture being visible in the video.
A third video was shared by an account known for spreading false information, allegedly showing Italian protesters tearing down a US flag as onlookers cheered during a demonstration against rising fuel prices.
However, a reverse image search revealed that the footage dates back to August and was filmed in Buenos Aires, Argentina.The video shows the American flag being removed from the facade of a hotel near Argentina’s National Congress during a protest linked to a law introduced by President Javier Milei concerning private property.
The footage has no connection to protests in Italy.

Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal 'remains null and void,' Greek foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:10:23 UTC
07:10:23 KST

The joint statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 memorandum.
Greece's foreign minister said on Monday that a 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal remained "null and void" as he delivered a joint statement on behalf of Greece, Egypt, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union.
"The memorandum in question remains null and void and without legal effect, runs counter to international law and cannot serve as a lawful basis for the delimitation of maritime zones, nor can it produce legal consequences for third states," Giorgos Gerapetritis said.
The statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 Turkish-Libyan memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean, which, it said, "raises serious concerns for regional security and stability."
The statement also highlighted a broader challenge to the international legal order, namely "the need to ensure that arbitrary bilateral agreements do not undermine the established rules of international law or prejudice the rights of third states."
Gerapetritis underlined that international law and, in particular, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), as well as customary international law, provide the legal framework for the delimitation of maritime zones.
These rules, he said, are "of fundamental importance for safeguarding predictability, legal certainty and peaceful relations among states."
He also warned that accepting bilateral agreements that disregard the applicable rules and principles of international law "would create a dangerous precedent, undermining the international legal order and the principles on which the peaceful settlement of disputes is based."
According to the statement, the memorandum violates these fundamental principles as it "ignores the geographical reality and the rights of all the coastal states involved over maritime zones, including the rights of islands in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea."
"The subsequent decision of Libya's House of Representatives does not alter this legal reality," it added.
The signatories reaffirmed their commitment "to the reunification of Libya's institutions and to the prospect of a united and prosperous Libya," while stressing that a stable Libya, engaging actively in regional cooperation, was essential for peace and security in the Mediterranean.
They also said that the country's political transition and its relations with its neighbours "must be governed by respect for international law and good-neighbourly relations."

Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:07:08 UTC
07:07:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week
Ukrainian troops evacuated two seriously wounded soldiers from the battlefield using the StarGate unmanned aerial CASEVAC platform after ground vehicles could not reach their positions, according to footage and information published online by the 475th Separate Assault Regiment CODE 9.2.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign “Izium,” and 24-year-old Artem, call sign “Kolobok,” suffered severe limb injuries while positioned in a gray zone about five kilometers from the Russian border.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian FPV drones made evacuation by ground transport impossible, leaving an airborne extraction as the only available option.
Over the course of one week, CODE 9.2 planned and completed two separate evacuation missions with support from SkyFall, the Ukrainian defense technology company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units, additional personnel and equipment, and fire support. Ukrainian forces used heavy Vampire strike drones to suppress Russian positions during the evacuations.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers to reach the wounded soldier and another 30 kilometers back with him onboard.
Russian forces were actively using electronic warfare in the area in an attempt to suppress GPS navigation completely. Despite the interference, StarGate continued flying using its onboard AI-based navigation system and was able to complete the mission.
The regiment now plans to turn the experience into a permanent capability.
“Going forward, we plan to make changes to the organizational structure of our regiment and create a separate air ambulance section within the medical company,” CODE 9.2 commander Oleksandr Nastenko, call sign “Flint,” stated.
“It will specialize directly in evacuating wounded personnel from the battlefield by air transport,” he added.
StarGate is Ukraine’s first specialized unmanned aerial platform developed specifically for battlefield CASEVAC missions. SkyFall designed the system for situations in which conventional vehicles cannot reach wounded troops or where sending ground transport would be too dangerous.
The drone can carry up to 150 kilograms and reach speeds of up to 105 kilometers per hour. Its evacuation module is based on certified medical stretchers, while onboard AI, navigation, and redundant communications systems allow it to continue operating when GPS is jammed or communications are lost.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces evacuated a soldier who had survived 491 days in an isolated frontline position and lost both feet after being wounded by Russian drones. Conventional ground evacuation was impossible because of mines and intense drone activity, prompting several Ukrainian units to adapt a heavy hexacopter to carry him out.

Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Hasn’t Left Port in Five Months, Firing Kalibrs From Novorossiysk
Unknown

22:07:03 UTC
07:07:03 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Hasn’t Left Port in Five Months, Firing Kalibrs From Novorossiysk
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet has avoided open waters for five consecutive months, launching Kalibr cruise missiles directly from its base in Novorossiysk, Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk reported on October 26, according to NV.
Speaking on Ukraine’s national television, Pletenchuk explained that Russian commanders likely fear losing their warships at sea. As a result, they have opted to conduct missile launches from their own naval base, despite the potential dangers of such operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It’s better to launch missiles from their own harbor, even though if something detonates there, everyone nearby will be in serious trouble. So yes, they decided to stay home,” Pletenchuk explained.
However, the restrictions on Russian naval movements have not eliminated the threat of Kalibr missile strikes against Ukraine. Pletenchuk noted that Russian submarines face greater operational limitations because they do not launch missiles from inside the harbor and have also stopped venturing into open waters.
Kalibr is a family of Russian sea-launched cruise missiles deployed aboard surface warships and submarines. Its 3M-14 land-attack variant has an estimated range of 1,500 to 2,500 kilometers and carries a warhead weighing approximately 450 kilograms, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The missile’s long range allows Russian warships to strike targets across Ukraine while remaining in port. This enables Moscow to maintain a naval missile threat without exposing its surface vessels to the same risks of operating in open waters.
Meanwhile, Russian military aviation continues to operate over the Black Sea around the clock, conducting patrols and strikes both day and night. Russian drones also remain active in the area.
Pletenchuk emphasized that Russian aircraft and helicopters maintain a distance of at least 100 kilometers from Ukraine’s coastline.
He recalled that Ukrainian forces had previously used naval drones to shoot down Russian aircraft and helicopters, demonstrating the expanding capabilities of Ukraine’s unmanned maritime systems.
Earlier, on September 9, several branches of Ukraine’s security and defense forces struck the naval base in Novorossiysk, hitting military harbor facilities, warships, and Kalibr missile carriers, along with a terminal involved in oil shipments.
At the port’s fuel oil terminal, a commercial logistics hub with an annual throughput capacity of 4 million metric tons, at least one petroleum storage tank was set ablaze.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:04:11 UTC
07:04:11 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud will send workers to document Israeli Arab voters on Election Day, and may use the footage as false evidence for a conspiracy theory that the election was rigged, Haaretz has learned.
Likud over the past few weeks has set up unofficial teams to "observe" voters in Arab communities, sometimes citing voter fraud. These teams are designated to stand outside polling stations in Arab communities, document voters and report back to headquarters in real time.
Concurrently, Likud officials are preparing to launch a postelection campaign centering on voter fraud in the case that Likud suffers major losses.
Likud members have discussed and planned scenarios of major election losses, a source close to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said. Some are pushing for a "stolen election" campaign that echoes U.S. President Donald Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election.
There is no information to suggest that the prime minister attended these meetings. At this stage, senior party officials are seemingly planning the campaign as a possibility for after Election Day.
Other sources close to Netanyahu say that several party officials are pressuring the prime minister to implement the plan, and that Netanyahu is considering the matter.
This is not the first time Likud planned to use a "rigged election" conspiracy theory to curry favor among voters and sow distrust in the electoral process. Likud's Yoav Kisch claimed there had been voter fraud on election night in 2022 when he spoke to Channel 14.
"I appeal from here to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee: We have dozens of cases of fraud, of harm to voting at polling stations in the Arab community," he said then. But Likud won the most seats in the election, and the claims were short-lived.
"2022 was a trial run for the current election," a senior Likud official involved in Election Day operations says, referring to claims of fraud and other matters.
The Likud system to document Arab Israeli voters at polling stations could be used to disseminate the voter fraud conspiracy theory.
The system is one of the party's largest investments this election campaign, standing at an estimated cost of millions of shekels. All team members were recruited and will be paid.
The system, which first took shape in the previous election, is unofficial and will not use the Likud representatives who work inside polling stations. Therefore, it is not subject to the Central Elections Committee's strict regulations.
"Suppose a woman comes to vote wearing a burqa," a Likud source said, "and then a few minutes later another woman arrives wearing a burqa – perhaps it's the same one? We will try to check and verify this." The teams, however, have no legal authority to verify voters' identities.
According to Likud sources, it is not unlikely that the videos from Election Day will be distributed as false evidence that the election was rigged. Since the videos will not feature the inside of polling stations, it will be difficult to legally oppose their distribution.
In addition to the dedicated teams, other Likud observers across the country will report any unusual incidents to the party, as is customary for every party in every election campaign. However, these reports are also meant to be forwarded to an established "fraud war room."

Former FBI director James Comey hit with third set of charges under Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:03:26 UTC
07:03:26 KST

Former FBI director James Comey hit with third set of charges under Trump
Comey, who was fired during Trump’s first term, has been accused of unlawfully divulging national security information.
James Comey, the former director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), is facing a third set of criminal charges under the administration of United States President Donald Trump.
On Monday, sealed documents came to light showing that the Trump administration has accused Comey of two counts related to the unlawful dissemination of “information related to national defence”.
Comey, a high-profile Trump critic, has not been indicted in the case. He has denied any wrongdoing.
But it is the third time the Trump administration has sought to level criminal charges against the former FBI director since the president returned to office in January 2025.
In an October court filing, prosecutors accuse Comey of ordering his FBI colleagues to leak information to the news media.
“The defendant [Comey] through one or more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication,” the court filing reads.
In a video published on the online platform Substack, Comey once again denounced the Trump administration’s attempts to prosecute him as a campaign of political retribution.
“Well, now they’re back again. It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said.
“Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent, and I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
Comey also noted that Trump is only midway through his second term, and he hinted that he expects more criminal charges to come his way.
“The next couple years are going to be hard for all of us,” Comey added. “It’s really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America.”
The latest charges pertain to a New York Times article from October 5, 2016, which describes how the email platform Yahoo was ordered to scan traffic on its site for a specific computer signature allegedly tied to a “terrorist” organisation.
Prosecutors have accused Comey of directing sensitive information to be disclosed to the reporter on that story, Charlie Savage.
In a statement released to news media, Comey’s defence lawyer Pat Fitzgerald framed the charges as feeble, claiming that the government had already investigated the matter twice before.
“Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone,” the statement said.
Fitzgerald pointed out that government prosecutors had not sought an indictment, which involves presenting charges to a grand jury that must then choose whether to approve the criminal charges.
Instead, they are seeking to charge Comey through a process called a “criminal information”, which allows prosecutors to bypass a grand jury.
“Ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury,” Fitzgerald said. “It purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit.”
Federal Judge Trevor McFadden, from the US District Court in Washington, DC, is overseeing the case. He is a Trump appointee.
Trump has long sought the prosecution of Comey, whom he fired from the role of FBI director in 2017, during his first term as president.
Comey had been FBI head since 2013. But his dismissal came as the FBI investigated the possibility of collusion between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, a probe that Trump has repeatedly denounced as a “hoax”.
Following Trump’s second inauguration in 2025, his administration has sought the prosecution of several of the president’s critics, including Comey.
In September 2025, Trump appeared to request that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi look into Comey and other perceived political adversaries.
“Nothing is being done. What about Comey, Adam ‘Shifty’ Schiff, Leticia???” Trump wrote to Bondi in a social media post, referencing the former FBI director, a Democratic senator and New York Attorney General Letitia James. “They’re all guilty as hell, but nothing is going to be done.”
Trump concluded his post by telling Bondi not to “delay any longer” before pursuing the three critics.
“JUSTICE MUST BE SERVED, NOW,” he wrote.
Five days later, on September 25 of that year, Comey was indicted on charges of lying to Congress and obstructing a legislative proceeding.
The case was ultimately dismissed on the basis that the prosecutor in charge, Lindsey Halligan, was unlawfully appointed.
A second indictment came on April 28. In that case, the Trump administration accused Comey of threatening the president by posting a photo on social media of seashells, arranged to form the message “86 47”.
Forty-seven is a reference to Trump, the 47th president, and “86” is a rhyming word for “nix”, common in the service industry as code for throwing out a dish or customer.
The Trump administration, however, has argued that “86” implies violence. That case is ongoing.
Earlier on Monday, before the third set of charges was revealed, a federal judge in a separate case ruled that Comey’s daughter, former assistant US attorney Maurene Comey, had been unlawfully fired last year under Trump’s second term.
The younger Comey has maintained her termination was retaliation against her father. The court determined she was entitled to “retroactive reinstatement” and backpay.
James Comey has denied all accusations of criminal wrongdoing, and his legal team has sought to have the latest set of charges dismissed.

New Delhi: No one will be prosecuted for using Form 6 to re-enter their name in electoral rolls, the Supreme Court verbally assured electors on Monday. It allayed fears that use of Form 6, which asks applicants to declare they are fresh voters, for re-inclusion in draft electoral rolls could invite prosecution for false declaration.The statement came from a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohan while hearing a PIL against large-scale exclusion of names from Maharashtra’s draft electoral roll and as a response to senior advocate Aravind Datar’s plea that using Form 6 for re-inclusion would amount to lying under oath.
Will grant time to genuine voters to submit papers if out from final list: SC
The bench also said that if it found there were genuine voters whose names could not be included in the final electoral list, to be published on Nov 6, it could grant them more time to submit their documents for the purpose. A similar concern was raised by advocate Prashant Bhushan 10 days earlier while questioning the EC’s directive that voters whose names were deleted from Delhi’s draft electoral roll during SIR exercise use Form 6 to restore them in draft rolls.Datar said that with two crore voters excluded from Maharashtra’s draft electoral roll, including 1.22 crore on grounds of logical discrepancy, and the deadline for claims and objections ending on Oct 26, many voters who were removed on flimsy and non-existent grounds would have little chance of getting names restored.
The senior advocate requested the bench to extend the Oct-26 deadline for those seeking inclusion of their names in the electoral roll. The bench asked the EC to file its response to the PIL by Nov 5 and said it would examine on that day whether extra time would be required for those seeking inclusion of names.
Datar said, “In Maharashtra, 33% of voters have been deleted. In Mumbai, 40% of the voters have been excluded. What is happening is people are asked to fill Form 6, which is meant for fresh voters. There is no provision for a person who had voted in the last three or four elections to get his name restored in the voter list. If he fills Form 6, which is meant for registration of fresh voters, then he would face prosecution for false declaration.”However, the CJI allayed these fears and said, “No one will be prosecuted for filling Form 6 seeking re-entering of their names in voter lists.” Datar said that since there was no imminent election in Maharashtra, the SC could direct EC not to finalise the electoral roll for the state on Nov 6 and postpone the schedule to enable genuine voters to re-enter them in voter lists. The bench also said, “If we find, even after the publication of the final electoral roll, that there are people who are genuine voters but still excluded, we can extend time for them to submit documents for the purpose of re-entering their names in voter lists.”

Air Force Launches ARRW, Its First Hypersonic Weapon, into Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:54:59 UTC
06:54:59 KST

The Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract to produce its first-ever hypersonic missile, the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, the service announced Oct. 26.
The decision advances ARRW from testing into production, a major milestone for a long-sought capability. The Air Force, citing operational security concerns, withheld details on how many it ordered or when they must be delivered.
Budget documents describe ARRW as a standoff weapon and “a lethal capability against high-value time-sensitive
targets.” It is too large to go on most fighter jets and will initially be fielded on the B-52 and has also reportedly been tested on the B-1. A multistage boost-glide weapon, it uses a rocket booster to accelerate to hypersonic speed, when the booster separates and falls away, leaving a glide vehicle that can maneuver to its target at five times the speed of sound. or greater—at least 3,800 miles per hour or just over a mile per second.
“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink in a statement. “By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems.”
ARRW development began in 2018 when the Air Force signed Lockheed to a design contract worth up to $480 million. The program built on the joint DARPA-Air Force X-51, and sought to deliver a prototype capability by 2021.
The Air Force conducted captive carry tests in 2019 and that same year awarded Lockheed a $988.8 million contract modification for critical design review. The first operational flight test was planned by the end of 2020, with initial operational capability projected in 2022.
But the first launch test, delayed to April 2021, failed and two more failures followed. The first successful test came in May 2022—at which point funding became a problem. In 2021, Congress stripped funds for 12 ARRW missiles from the fiscal 2022 budget plan, and the Air Force zeroed out funds for 2023.
In March 2023, the Air Force’s top civilian acquisition executive, Andrew Hunter, said the program would end without purchases. Air Force leaders said they would focus instead on the smaller Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile and other reusable hypersonic systems.
In 2025, however, then-Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. David Allvin told Congress the Air Force would buy ARRW, and the fiscal 2026 budget allotted $362 million for that purpose. The contract was awarded Sept. 29, 2026, but the decision was not announced until a month later.
The Air Force’s 2027 budget request included $452 million for ARRW production. That budget is currently stalled in Congress, and the Pentagon is operating under a continuing resolution based on 2026 funding levels. The Future Years Defense Plan projects procurement from 2028 to 2031 to range from $556 million to $621 million per year. Quantities are dubbed “controlled unclassified information,” and not publicly released.
“Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world,” Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach said in a statement. “This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments.”

A cooling-off period for MPs, MLAs who quit? SC to decide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:54:43 UTC

SC agrees to examine whether MPs and MLAs who resign voluntarily should bear by-election costs and face a five-year cooling-off period before contesting again.
NEW DELHI: In a development that could impact politics of shifting loyalties, SC Monday agreed to examine whether an MLA or an MP who contests a by-election caused by their voluntary resignation should be made to bear the entire expenses incurred by Election Commission in conducting the previous poll.Senior advocate Shoeb Alam told a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that six persons elected on AIADMK tickets to the Tamil Nadu assembly had resigned in May and June after declaration of results and defected to TVK. Two of them resigned, causing by-elections which they went on to win, this time as TVK candidates.Appearing for petitioner K Suthan, Alam said the court was required to examine whether a person who voluntarily resigned as an MLA or MP should be barred for five years from contesting a state or parliamentary election. SC issued notices to Centre, EC and the six AIADMK MLAs who resigned and defected.The trend of lawmakers crossing over to the party in office and quitting their seats to avoid disqualification has caught on. The petitioner has sought legislative or regulatory measures “to create a mechanism for ensuring financial accountability of elected representatives who prematurely resign from their seats without legally recognised compelling circumstances, including introduction of an ‘Election Expenditure Security’ to recover cost of resultant bye-elections”.
He has requested the court to direct Centre and EC to examine and initiate “necessary legislative and/or regulatory measures to introduce a statutory disqualification or a reasonable cooling-off period to prevent elected representatives who voluntarily and prematurely resign from contesting subsequent polls”. Suthan has suggested a five-year cooling-off period.The petitioner contended that none of the vacancies in the six seats was caused by death, permanent disability, disqualification or other compelling circumstance warranting a bypoll. “Public shouldn’t be made to pay twice for polls to the same constituency because of an individual’s personal or political choice to resign,” he said.Refusing to entertain Suthan’s petition, a Madras HC bench led by CJ S A Dharmadhikari had said, “We are being asked to design a punitive and financial regime that would operate as a fresh disqualification under Constitution and would curtail statutory right to contest election.
In our opinion, the same is a matter of legislative policy, not of judicial direction.”“Right to resign a legislative seat is itself a facet of the constitutional scheme governing membership of a House and cannot be burdened with extra-statutory conditions by judicial order, however sound the underlying concern may be,” the HC had said while refusing the plea to impose a five-year cooling-off period on MPs and MLAs who voluntarily resign from their seats in the House concerned.

Frontex set for new powers to deport beyond EU borders in latest overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:50:19 UTC
06:50:19 KST

The logo of Frontex is pictured at the headquarters of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency in Warsaw on September 17, 2026. | Roland Schlager/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The European Commission will unveil a sweeping overhaul of EU border agency Frontex on Oct. 27, turning it into a fully-fledged “European return agency,” according to two EU officials familiar with the proposal.
The legislative proposal, which will revamp the Warsaw-based agency’s mandate, will focus on three key areas: strengthening its role in deportations, improving its ability to anticipate and respond to border crises, and boosting its operational capacity without poaching border guards from countries.
At the heart of the reform is an ambition to give Frontex a much more prominent role in returning people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory, said the officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss information not yet in the public domain.
Advertisement
The push comes just months after EU lawmakers approved a new “return regulation” aimed at accelerating deportations and allowing member countries to establish controversial deportation hubs outside the EU.
With the legal framework largely agreed, Brussels is now turning its attention to enforcement — and to the agency expected to help make the new rules work in practice.
Political pressure has also been mounting. In June, the leaders of 19 EU countries urged the Commission to support the establishment of return hubs outside the bloc, including through EU funding, as first reported by POLITICO.
The proposed Frontex overhaul, which is on the College of Commissioners’ agenda and is expected to be approved by the EU executive on Oct. 27, would help put that broader shift into practice by giving the agency more resources, greater operational flexibility and an expanded role in carrying out returns beyond EU borders, including transfers between third countries.
Emergency response
But deportations are only part of the equation.
The Commission also wants to transform Frontex into a force that can intervene in border emergencies within 24 hours, according to the two officials.
Brussels wants to ensure that a similar crisis doesn’t catch the EU off guard again. Under the plans, Frontex would be given a stronger mandate to monitor potential flashpoints, particularly on social media, and improve early warning capabilities and identify emerging threats before they escalate.
The agency would also be better equipped to respond swiftly once a crisis happens, with personnel and equipment available for deployment on short notice rather than relying exclusively on existing arrangements with national governments.
Staffing questions
Another central question is how big Frontex should become.
The agency had around 7,800 personnel in its Standing Corps in early 2026 and is working towards a target of 10,000 by 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has previously called for tripling that figure to 30,000 European border and coast guards.
The Commission’s proposal is expected to seek a compromise between the competing ambitions for expansion and the practical constraints facing national governments.
Advertisement
Rather than relying entirely on a substantially larger permanent force, Brussels is considering a sizeable reserve that officials say could be mobilized when needed. That would help address countries’ concerns that an expanded EU-level force could pull their border guards away at a time when national authorities are already under pressure.
The approach would allow Frontex to increase its deployable capacity while keeping more personnel available for national duties when they are not needed for European operations.
Beyond staffing, the two people expect the Commission to put forward measures to give the agency better equipment and more agile operational procedures, particularly for deportations.
The reform is also likely to reopen debates over the agency’s accountability and human rights of migrants and asylum-seekers, especially as the EU moves towards more deportations to third countries.
Frontex did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Serbia’s elections: 'Tracking fraud for sure had an impact on the results'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:49:17 UTC
06:49:17 KST

Serbia’s elections: 'Tracking fraud for sure had an impact on the results'
On October 25, Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in parliamentary elections, defeating outgoing President Aleksandar Vucic's party. Supporters of the student list explained to FRANCE 24 how they mounted a massive mobilisation to fight electoral fraud and monitor the electoral process inside and outside the polling stations.
Serbia’s parliamentary elections on Sunday, October 25 delivered a political earthquake. The Student List movement challenged the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) which had dominated Serbian politics for 14 years, led by outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic.
The result marked a historic turning point: the Student List won 52.45 percent of the vote, securing 138 seats in the National Assembly, while the Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia list received 39.2 , earning 103 seats.
The student movement emerged in the aftermath of the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, a tragedy that claimed 16 lives and triggered nationwide protests against corruption. Initially non-partisan, the movement gradually gained widespread public support before deciding to field its own electoral list. Rather than running for office themselves, the students chose to nominate highly qualified individuals with no prior political experience, selected through a democratic process organised within universities.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'We trained at least 16,000 people to become official controllers'
Petar Botoski, an agricultural student supporting the Student List, was in Novi Sad, a city located in the northern part of the country, when Aleksandar Vucic acknowledged the defeat of his party.
 "It was the most challenging moment. We expected to win, but we did not know what would happen next. When the announcement came, I was in shock, everyone was cheering. At that time, the votes were still being transferred and being counted."
He explained that the student movement prevented much electoral fraud during the day.
 “The whole day we reported to authorities incidents such as the finding of parallel lists or the detection of carousel votes.”
Both are practices that can facilitate voter pressure or manipulation of the voting process. The parallel list is an unofficial list of voters used alongside the official register to manipulate or falsify voting records, while carousel voting is a form of electoral fraud in which a voter is given a ballot that has already been marked, takes it into the polling station and deposits it in the ballot box. The voter then brings the unmarked ballot they received as proof that he or she voted as “required”.
Petar Botoski goes on:
 “For a year and half, since we decided to propose a student list for the legislative elections, the student movement spent a lot of time and resources to create connections between people and to teach them how to prevent electoral fraud.
We trained at least 16,000 people to become official controllers, two for each polling station. Then we trained about five people per polling station to be part of mobile teams. Their mission was to detect fraud outside the polling stations, such as the use of parallel lists, carousel vote, pay[ing] for voters and intimidations. [Tracking] fraud had for sure an impact on the results.”
Turnout reached 69 percent, with more than 4.4 million citizens casting their ballots. This represents a significant increase compared with the 55.5 percent turnout recorded in Serbia’s December 2023 parliamentary elections.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'We ensured that it was harder for them to fraud'
Janko Sikosek, a member of the movement “Bikers with Students”, was among the volunteers that assisted in monitoring polling stations and helping to ensure a fair and transparent electoral process.
 “I went out to vote early in the morning; the line was already forming before the polling station opened. At this moment, I felt very optimistic. People were looking at each other and smiling. The line was so long, I waited for an hour and a half to vote.
Then I joined my mobile team. Only in my municipality (Vozdovac), there were 14 mobile teams, each one composed of 3 people.
We were there to record, to observe, to be present. We ensured that it was harder for them (SNS supporters) to fraud.
The job of my team of bikers was to help mobile teams that got in trouble. One mobile team discovered vote-buying headquarters in Ovca, in the north of Belgrade. A guy of the mobile team was hit on the head, the other two escaped, but their car was trapped. When we intervened, a couple of our guys got hurt. One received a strike on the head with a rock and the other had his arm broken. But we managed to get the mobile team out of there.”

The incident involving Sikosek’s team was not isolated. Several other incidents were reported throughout election day, both inside and outside polling stations. For example, a group of masked men attacked election monitors from the Student List in Pancevo using pyrotechnic devices. Several of them were struck in the head.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Moreover, an observer from CRTA, a Serbian democracy watchdog, was harassed by a group of people in Zemur.
There were also reportedly some tensions inside the polling stations.
Marko, a student in Novi Sad, was an official controller. He reported some tensions between the controllers from SNS and the ones from supporting the Student List. He said the SNS controllers tried to obstruct some people from voting, notably younger ones, pretending “they don't look like their ID photo".
In some places, there were tensions about voting booths. Voting booths with curtains were introduced in Serbian elections for the first time in this election. According to the student supporters, this increases the risk of taking pictures of ballots. This is reportedly done by people who were paid to vote to support the ruling party or who received pressure over their vote because they work in public administrations.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
According to CRTA, the most frequently observed irregularity was the photographing of ballot papers, reported at as many as 50 percent of the polling stations monitored. Voters take pictures of their ballots when they are paid for or when they receive pressure from their employers.
An investigation published by Balkan Insight on October 20, based on more than 150 testimonies, describes pressure exerted on public sector employees to give their electoral support to the ruling party and to participate in its political rallies.
A few days before the election, Rasa Nedeljkov, the program director of CRTA, told the FRANCE 24 Observers team about some worrying observations:
 “The CRTA found that 7 out of 18 lists that were going to be on the ballot were basically completely unexisting phantom fake lists. Through these fake lists, the ruling political party had the additional votes in the electoral commissions at local and national level.
We also noted that in the past 90 days, there were 14,100 new voters. This is something which is again strange and odd. We had addresses with a high number of completely new voters and multiple voters registered in one address.”
'The polling boards were filled with well-prepared representatives for the very first time'
Nedeljkov said at a press conference the day following the elections:
 “Manipulation was prevented by the fact that a large number of Serbian citizens attached importance to election rule and got involved in the implementation and the control of election at polling stations. The polling boards were filled with well-prepared representatives for the very first time.”
'It was a historical moment'
Until Vucic announced his defeat, many student list supporters were quite worried about possible tensions and clashes with SNS supporters.
Sikosek, from Bikers with Students, reported his concerns a few minutes before the announcement:
 “When the dark came, the police were fortifying the center of the city, there were some incidents. We were thinking that he is going to come out and say that he won. Suddenly he said that he got defeated. We were all euphoric. It was a historical moment.”
Botoski, the agricultural student, said that students will continue to monitor their elected representatives:
 “We expect that the people we’ve chosen to represent the student list in parliament will do their job with care and dignity. We expect them to work on reforming the institutions and eradicate corruption from this country.”
In less than two years, Serbian students built a grassroots movement that won widespread public support and defeated a party that had been in power for 14 years. Through peaceful and democratic means, they turned public discontent into political change. The next challenge for the students and their supporters will be the presidential elections which will be held in December 2026.

Europe can be forgotten — Russians promised visa-free travel to Ethiopia
Kyiv • UNN
Russia and Ethiopia are discussing the gradual abolition of visas for tourists and businesspeople. The timeline for introducing visa-free travel has not yet been announced.
While Russia continues its war against Ukraine and remains under international sanctions, its citizens are being promised new travel prospects. However, instead of European resorts, Russian diplomacy is suggesting that attention be turned to Ethiopia, with which Moscow is discussing the gradual easing of visa requirements. This is reported by The Moscow Times, writes UNN.
Details
Russia's ambassador to Ethiopia, Yevgeny Terekhin, said that the countries could gradually ease entry rules for tourists and businesspeople. However, the diplomat did not name specific deadlines for introducing a visa-free regime.
The issue of further phased liberalization of the entry regime will be decided depending on the growth of mutual tourist flows and bilateral business contacts
Russia's new tourist horizons
For now, Russians still need a visa even to travel to Ethiopia. A 30-day permit costs $62, while a 90-day permit costs $152.
Despite the high-profile talk about new opportunities, Ethiopia remains far from the most popular destination among Russian tourists. In 2025, 23,400 Russians visited the country, and it ranked only 24th among foreign tourist destinations.
Moscow and Addis Ababa are also discussing an increase in the number of flights. Currently, Ethiopian Airlines operates 6 flights per week between the capitals of the two countries.
Notably, Ethiopia is one of the poorest countries in the world. The average salary there is about $60, while GDP per capita is approximately $994.
At the same time, following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia faced the closure of EU airspace to Russian airlines and other restrictions.
Thus, while the Kremlin talks about new international opportunities, one of the diplomatic achievements for Russian tourists may be the prospect of eventually visiting Ethiopia without a visa. And even that is only a promise for now.

The Second Western District Military Court has sentenced Yuri Belenky, a 49-year-old IT specialist, to 13 years in prison for financing terrorism, the human rights group Department One reported.
Belenky will serve the first three years in prison before being transferred to a high-security penal colony. The court also fined him 500,000 rubles and ordered the confiscation of another 126,000 rubles.
News of Belenky’s detention emerged in late 2025. He had lived in Bulgaria since 2015 and regularly visited Russia. He was detained at Sheremetyevo Airport in September 2025, initially jailed for the administrative offense of petty hooliganism, and then charged with financing terrorism.
The case stemmed from donations to an account whose details blogger Arkady Babchenko had published. Russian investigators were able to prove that the transfers took place “thanks to a detailed report that the cryptocurrency exchange Binance sent in response to a request from the Investigative Committee,” Department One said.

Africa food security under threat due to Iran war, trade officials warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:42:18 UTC
06:42:18 KST

Africa food security under threat due to Iran war, trade officials warn
The US-Israel war on Iran is driving fuel and fertiliser costs across Africa, threatening food security, trade officials tell Al Jazeera.
Doha, Qatar – African countries are feeling the economic fallout from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with rising fuel and fertiliser prices threatening to drive up food costs, according to trade ministers from the region and the United Nations’ top trade official.
The crisis around the Strait of Hormuz due to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran needs to be resolved “sooner rather than later”, Luz Maria de la Mora, director of the Division on International Trade and Commodities at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), told Al Jazeera at the World Investment Forum on Monday. She warned that soaring fertiliser prices could affect harvests next year.
“Prices of fertilisers have risen dramatically … so many countries have decided to reduce the use of fertilisers, which will have an effect next year in terms of crops,” she said.
“It may have an effect on availability of food and prices of food.”
The US-Israel war on Iran has highlighted the world’s heavy reliance on the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade previously passed.
Against this backdrop, Doha hosted UNCTAD’s World Investment Forum on October 25 and 26, bringing together heads of state, policymakers, CEOs and investors to discuss global investment and sustainable development.
The Strait of Hormuz’s disruption has rippled through African economies. In Zimbabwe, rising fuel and fertiliser prices are a critical concern in a country where more than 70 percent of the population depends on agriculture, Monica Mutsvangwa, the country’s minister of women affairs, community, small and medium enterprise development, told Al Jazeera.
Uganda, another heavily agrarian economy, has also been hit, with fuel prices more than doubling, Sanjay Tanna, the country’s minister of trade, industry and cooperatives, told Al Jazeera.
The impact extends beyond the immediate cost of energy. Rising oil prices have disrupted supply chains, with effects lasting longer than anticipated, according to de la Mora.
“The effects are lasting longer than we would have expected or would have wanted,” she said.
‘Friend to all, enemy to none’
The shock has also exposed differences in how African economies weather global disruption.
Uganda’s reliance on subsistence farming has helped cushion the impact, with domestic food production offering some protection from international market volatility, said Tanna.
But the country has not been insulated from financial pressures: its currency has lost 10 percent of its value against the US dollar, the minister said. The Ugandan shilling has steadily declined since mid-2026.
For Zimbabwe, the crisis has reinforced the importance of attracting investment while maintaining economic ties across geopolitical divides.
Amid the simmering trade war between the US and China, Harare considers itself a potential partner to investors from either side, Mutsvangwa said.
“We are a friend to all and an enemy to none,” she said.
“Money has no color … If we get an investor who comes into our country, follows the rules and regulations of the country, makes his money, and Zimbabwe develops, that’s what we want.”
The official pointed to Zimbabwe’s deposits of more than 60 critical minerals, including lithium and graphite, as well as its tourism potential.
Trade in an unequal system
But attracting foreign capital remains a challenge for developing economies, with investment concentrated in a relatively small number of countries.
That concentration is “very understandable”, de la Mora said, arguing that investors need confidence that their money will generate returns.
“Capital is risk averse. Capital needs to have certainty that its investment is going to yield returns and it’s going to come to fruition,” she said.
Governments can help build that confidence through transparent institutions, the rule of law and investment in infrastructure, including reliable electricity, energy supplies and digital connectivity, she added.
The question of whether the international trading system treats all countries equally prompted a more blunt assessment from Uganda’s trade minister.
“Of course not,” said Tanna. “The world cannot be equal … It’s unfair, but we believe that, within the space that we are in, we are in a good space.”
Uganda was well placed for the future, he argued, because it produces its own food – an advantage at a time when international supply chains are under pressure.
For both Uganda and the Republic of Congo, building resilient economies also means investing in younger generations.
The Republic of Congo’s Deputy Prime Minister for Coordination, Development Infrastructure and Land Planning, Jean-Jacques Bouya, said the country had aligned its national development plan, Vision 2063, with the African Union’s broader development ambitions.
Connectivity – through electricity, digital infrastructure and physical links – is central to that strategy, he told Al Jazeera.
The Republic of Congo also wants to expand local processing so that more value from its natural resources remains within the country.
“Africa can no longer be a reservoir of raw materials, and neither can Congo – a place where raw materials are extracted, taken elsewhere, processed and then sold back to us at a much higher price. We cannot go on like this,” Bouya said.

Inside Russia’s shadow oil trade: WSJ examines how a failed business partnership led to multimillion-dollar lawsuits and allegations of threats involving Chechen fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:36:34 UTC
06:36:34 KST

Inside Russia’s shadow oil trade: WSJ examines how a failed business partnership led to multimillion-dollar lawsuits and allegations of threats involving Chechen fighters
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian oil came under sanctions, and little-known intermediaries using shell companies and a shadow fleet of tankers took over a large share of its exports. A network of companies linked to Azerbaijani businessmen Tahir Garayev and Etibar Eyyub became one of Rosneft’s main oil traders. They are now in a legal battle with former Rosneft executive Igor Soglayev, who sought to make money reselling Russian diesel in Brazil. Documents from the litigation reviewed by The Wall Street Journal offer a glimpse into how Russian oil and petroleum products have been exported since the war began.
Soglayev is a former Deutsche Bank executive in Russia and former head of SamaraNefteOrgSintez, a petrochemical company that Rosneft bought in 2015. After the acquisition, he headed Rosneft’s petrochemicals department and, according to the Journal, also served as an adviser to its chief, Igor Sechin. In 2017, he left to pursue private ventures in the petrochemical industry.
After the war began, Soglayev decided to make money selling Russian diesel in Brazil. He wanted to act as an intermediary for buyers worried that, because of sanctions, dealing directly with Russia could cause problems with their banks. He planned to buy diesel in Russia and resell it at a markup to Brazilian distributors. In preparation, he leased fuel storage capacity at Brazilian ports.
According to Soglayev, his suppliers were oil traders known as the Coral network. The network took its name from Coral Energy, a company established in Singapore in 2010 to trade Azerbaijani oil. Its former executives, Garayev and Eyyub, became two of the leading sellers of Rosneft’s crude in 2022. Companies controlled by the two businessmen assembled most of the shadow fleet used to export Russian oil.
Soglayev founded a firm called Dia33 in Dubai and bought Russian diesel from another Dubai firm in late 2023. He alleges that the firm’s head, Andrey Romanovskiy, was linked to the Coral network and that the two men even discussed the possibility of Dia33 becoming Coral’s Brazilian division. But the relationship soured when a Brazilian port turned away an aging tanker carrying tens of millions of dollars’ worth of diesel. The ship waited for several weeks to be unloaded before another port accepted it.
The Journal does not specify whether the diesel reached the final buyer. Either way, the fuel sellers, allegedly linked to the Coral network, accused Soglayev of misappropriating the cargo. They filed a lawsuit in Dubai, resulting in an order requiring him to pay $42 million. He responded with lawsuits of his own in Dubai and Brazil, alleging that Coral had used the prospect of a partnership as a pretext to gain access to Dia33’s internal information and poach its clients. He estimated his lost profits at more than $500 million.
Soglayev said he also received threats. In particular, he took it as a death threat when Eyyub called and told him he had discussed their dispute with a “Chechen warlord,” the Journal reported.
The litigation is ongoing. In the summer of 2026, a Dubai court barred Eyyub, Garayev, and 13 other individuals and companies from disposing of assets worth up to $700 million as an interim measure in Soglayev’s lawsuit. The judge later questioned whether he had jurisdiction to hear the case. Soglayev appealed the judge’s decision, and the asset freeze remains in effect.

interview: aron sanchez-baranda finds otherworldly forms in marine life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:35:14 UTC
06:35:14 KST

interview: aron sanchez-baranda finds otherworldly forms in marine life
the artist invites viewers to reconsider how they perceive nonhuman life, embracing the unfamiliar and the uncertainty of encountering other species.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
aron sanchez-baranda on observing life beyond the human
Aron Sanchez-Baranda observes life beyond our own species, a practice that offers a way to reconsider the assumption that the world exists primarily around human experience. Through photographs and videos of marine organisms along the Californian coast, he documents biological forms that appear at once familiar and alien, shifting attention away from identification and toward the sensations of encountering something we do not fully understand. The California-based artist allows the presence, movement, and material qualities of these organisms to take precedence through his photographs, inviting the audience to reconsider how they perceive life beyond human.
His relationship with observation began long before he developed a conscious understanding of humanity’s place within the natural world. ‘Observing them has always focused the entirety of my attention from my earliest memories onward, it’s relaxing,’ he explains during our interview. Over time, this instinctive fascination has developed into a broader questioning of human primacy. As he has considered his place within a larger system, the idea of humanity occupying a central position has seemed ‘counterintuitive or at least confusing,’ he tells us. Sanchez-Baranda is interested in the moment before an encounter becomes knowledge, when an unfamiliar organism can provoke curiosity, discomfort, or fascination without settling into a single interpretation. His images create space for viewers to experience its forms without immediately placing them under familiar categories.
encounters beyond explanation
Sanchez-Baranda’s creative process begins with openness. He might walk through an area until something catches his attention or return to photographs and videos he has already recorded. From there, he develops what he describes as ‘a series of concentric experiments’, which may lead to one idea or, ideally, several. Some images begin with a clear internal vision that he gradually shapes through the material, and others emerge through the act of making, becoming recognizable only over time, ‘through a sort of automatism’. Sanchez-Baranda traces his interest in how images affect the viewer to childhood experiences of cinema and music that both engaged and unsettled his developing sense of reality. He has continued trying to recover something of that early uncertainty, describing his interest as ‘the abstraction of sensory responses’. For him, the significance of an encounter lies partly in its resistance to immediate understanding, in the way a sensation can remain unresolved even after the experience has passed.
The biological forms he documents often prompt viewers to ask for specific information about what they are seeing. Sanchez-Baranda does not dismiss this curiosity, but questions the assumption that an image of an organism must necessarily come with an explanation. Such expectations, he suggests, can distract from the experience he is trying to convey. ‘The lack of certainty and ultimate permeability of those early sensations persist in my work,’ the artist tells designboom. ‘They’re what I’m pursuing.’ Identifying an organism can provide useful knowledge, but it does not exhaust the experience of encountering it. By allowing uncertainty to remain, Sanchez-Baranda challenges the expectation that looking should lead directly to classification and understanding and asks instead whether we can attend to another form of life without making its meaning, usefulness, or relationship to ourselves the primary concern.
the limits of a human-centered world
For the LA-based artist, this way of looking also responds to the conditions under which people experience the world today. The continuous availability of information, analysis, and distraction can fragment attention, often making it difficult to remain with a single experience. ‘I think we increasingly overlook singular activity,’ he shares. Human access to information, he argues, can have ‘a fragmentary effect on perception’, while the ways people understand time and memory become shaped by the data available to them. The collection and application of this information can undermine what he calls a ‘natural’ human perspective.
His photographs and videos propose a kind of attention that’s grounded in observation rather than facts. The camera becomes a means of sharing, however incompletely, the experience of encountering an organism in person. ‘For me the act of observing them is enough,’ Sanchez-Baranda comments. ‘The work I produce endeavors to impart some fraction of that sensation I receive encountering the subjects I photograph in person.’ He recognizes the limits of this translation. An image cannot fully reproduce the experience of being in the presence of another living organism, and the viewer remains separated from the original encounter by the conditions of documentation. Yet this partial reproduction is itself meaningful. Sanchez-Baranda believes it ‘emphatically suggests an alternative to a world organized around human experience’. The organisms Sanchez-Baranda documents are not imagined inhabitants of a distant future. They exist alongside us, following their own rhythms and occupying environments that do not depend on human recognition to have value.
Becoming more familiar with these forms of life has enriched Sanchez-Baranda’s own experience. He hopes that ‘we can collectively benefit from examining what feels familiar as we continue to deal with human impact on Earth’.
imagining a future with less
Sanchez-Baranda’s vision of a future shaped by greater awareness of nonhuman life is notably unsentimental. Asked what such a future might look like, he imagines one with ‘seemingly limited choices compared to what many are used to’. The reduction of human consumption, he argues, is a necessity if any extended future is to exist. Learning to perceive other forms of life differently does not, by itself, resolve the environmental consequences of human activity. A shift in perspective must also confront the systems of consumption that shape how people inhabit the planet and use its resources.
Sanchez-Baranda does not offer a detailed blueprint for an alternative society, nor does his work claim to resolve the contradictions of a human-centered world. Its proposition is to make room for forms of life that do not need to justify their existence through human needs and to recognize that our own experience is only one among many ways of inhabiting the Earth. Sanchez-Baranda’s work encourages viewers to pause before identifying, explaining, or assigning value, allowing the encounter itself to become a form of attention.

artist: Aron Sanchez-Baranda | @waterbod

Hollywood’s Secret Romances – It Has Become Known Who Tom Cruise, Scarlett Johansson and Madonna Dated
Kyiv • UNN
Entertainment Weekly compiled 16 little-known Hollywood romances. Among them are Cruise’s relationship with Cher and Madonna’s with Tupac Shakur.
The personal lives of Hollywood celebrities are constantly under public scrutiny, yet some star romances remained little known for years. Tom Cruise dated Cher, Scarlett Johansson was in a relationship with musician Jack Antonoff, and Madonna kept her romance with rapper Tupac Shakur secret. Entertainment Weekly reports on this in a roundup, writes UNN.
Details
The publication collected the stories of 16 unexpected celebrity couples whose relationships either failed to attract significant attention at the time or were later almost forgotten.
They included both brief flings and romances that lasted several years. Some celebrities spoke about their former partners only decades after the breakups.
Which celebrity romances surprised fans

US judge says firing of daughter of former FBI director unlawful
NEW YORK – A US judge ruled on Oct 26 that the firing of former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, the daughter of Donald Trump foe James Comey, was unlawful and she should be reinstated.
Comey, whose father briefly served as FBI director during Trump’s first White House term, was summarily dismissed in July 2025 as an assistant US attorney in Manhattan.
Comey filed suit against the Department of Justice in federal court claiming she had been dismissed “solely or substantially” because of her father’s criticism of Trump or “because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs”.
In ruling against the Department of Justice, District Judge Jesse Furman said Comey, an assistant US attorney (AUSA) in the Southern District of New York, had been deprived of her due process rights.
“Yes, the Attorney-General is authorised by law to remove an AUSA,” Furman said. “But the Attorney-General... is also limited by law... to do so only in a particular manner and only for certain reasons.”
Comey was involved in a number of prominent cases while serving as a prosecutor in Manhattan, including those brought against music producer Sean “Diddy” Combs and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
She also prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell, the only former Epstein associate who was criminally charged in connection with his activities. Epstein died in prison before coming to trial in what was determined to be a suicide.
Since taking office, Trump has taken a number of punitive measures against his perceived enemies, purging government officials deemed to be disloyal, targeting law firms involved in past cases against him and pulling federal funding from universities.
James Comey, an outspoken critic of Trump, was indicted in April for allegedly threatening the Republican president in an Instagram post that showed the numbers “8647“ spelled out in seashells.
The Trump Justice Department has claimed that “8647“ constitutes a threat to the president – “86“ meaning to kill and “47“ a reference to Trump being the 47th president. Comey has denied threatening the president’s life.
Trump fired Comey in 2017 as the then-FBI chief was leading an investigation into whether any members of the president’s campaign had colluded with Moscow to sway the 2016 election, in which the Republican beat Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton. AFP

How Hong Kong’s 5-year plan can fuel its financial clout
Rather than chase new instruments, the city is refining the ecosystem that powers them – upgrading infrastructure, securing liquidity, and drawing in capital
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Dr Stephen Wong is head of the Chief Executive's Policy Unit. 
Finance ministers from 21 Asia-Pacific economies recently met in Hong Kong, the first time the city has hosted them. A practical question sits one level down.
Picture the treasury team of a company running its regional business from Hong Kong. It arranges funding in several currencies, pays across markets and manages the risks that follow. Its question is: how can Hong Kong’s services help it operate more efficiently and at lower cost?
Those needs are a practical lens for reading the five-year plan and the chief executive’s policy address. The plan sets the direction; the address puts dates on it. In our research exchanges with think tanks on the mainland and in Hong Kong, the same concerns come up: not more products but what makes products usable – settlement, term funding and collateral. The plan’s mention of “a capable government working in tandem with an effective market” frames market development as a shared endeavour.

Canadian pension giant takes stake in La Trobe Financial
Canadian public pension fund OMERS has taken a minority stake in La Trobe Financial, one of Australia's largest non-bank lenders, from Brookfield.
The Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System (OMERS) is one of Canada's largest defined benefit pension plans.
La Trobe did not disclose the price or the size of the stake but Brookfield said it will remain majority shareholder and OMERS will sit alongside Brookfield and Axight as an institutional investor.

Key Event
Directors of 1 in 5 companies going into liquidation have been there before
The corporate regulator has released a review on business liquidations that gives us an insight into how often directors of one company that goes under have been there before.
ASIC's review says there were 26,664 grouped appointments — 7,023 court liquidations and 19,641 creditors' voluntary liquidation (CVLs) — for the period from July 1, 2021, to June 30, 2025.
It found that roughly one in five involved a company with at least one director who had previously been a director of another company when it entered liquidation.
Many companies in the review were small in financial and operational scale, with limited assets available by the time they entered liquidation.
The median age of a company entering liquidation was seven years, with 60.9% of appointments involving companies aged six years or more.
About half of all liquidations realised no more than $10,000 in assets, and about one-quarter realised no assets.
About 69% reported liabilities of less than $1 million and 89.6% had five or fewer employee creditors. Liabilities reported by companies entering liquidation remained relatively stable across the review period, with median liabilities ranging between $410,000 and $530,000.
Limited assets also affected the work and remuneration of liquidators. In 88.1% of finalised liquidations, no dividend was paid to ordinary unsecured creditors and either no remuneration was approved or remuneration paid to the liquidator was less than the amount approved. This indicates that unrecovered remuneration was likely common.
"Directors should closely monitor their company's financial position and seek advice early when financial difficulties arise," ASIC Commissioner Kate O'Rourke said.
"Taking action early gives a company more options to address financial difficulties. The longer action is delayed, the fewer options may remain to restructure the business, preserve value or limit further losses to creditors."
Key Event
Federal Reserve expected to leave rates on hold, but it's 'tactical'
The US Federal Reserve will meet this week to decide whether to raise interest rates for the second time this year in a bid to tackle inflation.
Most economists and Wall Street analysts expect the Fed to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4% when officials release the latest policy statement on Wednesday US time.
Wolfgang Bauer, fund manager at Royal London Asset Management, says "this should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than the end of the renewed tightening cycle".
"Growth and employment remain resilient in the US, inflation is still well above target, and Fed Chair [Kevin] Warsh recently described financial conditions as difficult to characterise as restrictive," he said.
"As further inflation data will only be published after the meeting, the Fed has good reason to wait without thereby adopting a softer monetary policy stance."
He adds the key question will be whether "Warsh maintains his assessment of financial conditions and clearly keeps a December rate increase open as an option".
"In our view, the most likely scenario is therefore a rate pause with a restrictive undertone: no change this week, but equally no signal that interest rates have already reached their peak," he said.
