The Foreign Affairs Ministry on Monday called the report from a United Nations commission accusing Israel of genocide a "propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel’s right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
The UN commission released a report Monday accusing Israel of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza.
The report also mentioned wrongdoings by the Palestinian Authority, claiming that it had pushed for arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
In contrast, Hamas is named exactly twice, and neither mention accused Hamas of committing a crime or other wrongdoing.
The UN reported an increase in the number of Palestinian deaths in the West Bank, with almost 500 Palestinians killed annually in the West Bank since 2022, which were the highest numbers recorded since the UN started collecting data on the topic in 2005.
The report also claimed that Israel is continuing to commit “genocidal acts” with the “intent to destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part” in spite of a ceasefire agreement that went into effect in October 2025.
The report focused on Palestinian casualties in the West Bank due to Israeli military action and settler violence, as well as analysis of elected MKs and senior military officials.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, an Indian jurist who currently serves as the chair of the Commission of Inquiry.
Report cites increase in West Bank airstrike deaths
The Commission reported a sharp increase in Palestinian deaths caused by airstrikes in the West Bank since October 7, 2023. Six Palestinians were killed by airstrikes between 2008 and October 6, 2023, compared with 254 between October 7, 2023, and September 30, 2026, according to the commission’s findings.
It said airstrikes had become more frequent following the launch of Operation Iron Wall in January 2025, particularly in refugee camps and areas around Jenin, Tulkarm, Tubas and Nablus.
The Commission described the operation as a shift toward widespread destruction of Palestinian housing and infrastructure and the clearing of refugee camps. It cited the IDF's stated aim to “dismantle and restor[e] the operational freedom of action for IDF forces”, while reconstruction of the infrastructure is considered to be “endangering the citizens of the State of Israel and the military forces”.
Commission's analysis of statements by Israeli officials
The commission also cited statements by Israeli officials including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and IDF Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth in assessing Israeli military conduct and the intentions behind operations in the West Bank.
Smotrich referred to “two million Nazis” in the West Bank in November 2023, citing a poll on Palestinian support for the October 7 Hamas massacre. In November 2024, he said “The only way to remove the danger of a Palestinian terror state from the agenda is to apply Israeli sovereignty to Jewish settlement in the entire Judea and Samaria,” he said.
In January 2025, he wrote that Fondouk, Nablus and Jenin should “look like Jabalia,”.
The Commission also highlighted a reported May 2026 statement by Bluth that Israeli soldiers were “killing like we haven’t since 1967.”
Report alleges sexual violence against detainees
The Commission said it had verified four additional cases of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees since its March 2025 report on gender-based violence. Two victims were from the West Bank. The cases included alleged gang rape, genital violence, groping, threats of sexual violence, forced nudity, and searches conducted without an apparent security justification.
One case involved a male detainee at Megiddo Prison in 2025. He was allegedly blindfolded, forced to remove his lower garments, and repeatedly raped with objects during interrogation.
The Commission alleged that guards mocked and photographed him, threatened to mutilate his genitals and threatened sexual violence against his family and colleagues. The detainee reportedly suffered serious injuries, including rectal bleeding, without receiving medical treatment.
The Commission claimed that the cases it investigated involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence were not isolated incidents. It alleged that these acts formed part of a broader attack against the civilian population and concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed crimes against humanity involving torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence.
Israel has rejected previous allegations by the Commission of Inquiry that its forces systematically used sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinian detainees, describing the claims as unfounded and disputing the Commission's verification methods. In a March 2025 response, the Foreign Ministry said the IDF had rules prohibiting such misconduct and mechanisms for investigating allegations.
Commission also reports abuses by Palestinian Authority
The report also accused the Palestinian Authority of suppressing political dissent through arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and the targeting of journalists, activists and human rights defenders.
It cited reports of excessive force during West Bank protests in October 2023, when at least two men, a boy and a girl, were killed in Ramallah, Tubas and Jenin. The PA accepted responsibility for the death of the boy, who was run over by a security forces vehicle during clashes with protesters.
The Commission also investigated the December 2024 killing of a Palestinian journalism student in Jenin refugee camp who had documented alleged abuses by Palestinian security forces. Witnesses said a security force member had threatened to shoot her the previous day. She was killed by a single shot to the neck near her home.
The report said information conflicted on whether clashes were underway at the time. Palestinian security forces had a significant presence in the area, and their spokesman blamed the killing on “outlaws,” saying the case was under investigation. The Commission said key witnesses had not been asked to testify.
It also reported cases of arbitrary detention, including instances in which the PA allegedly ignored court orders for detainees' release.
The Commission concluded that the PA had violated the right to life and the right to security of person and had failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into killings or provide effective remedies to victims and their families.

Israel’s moment of truth: Knesset election pivotal to future US-Israel relationship - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:18:24 UTC
05:18:24 KST

The upcoming election in Israel will likely prove pivotal in determining whether the ongoing erosion in support for Israel in the United States devolves further into a full rupture that makes both Americans and Israelis less secure.
As Americans, we are not interested in picking winners and losers. Israelis should decide such things, but our friends there should understand the consequences of their decisions.
Our colleague Mark Dubowitz has recently warned of possible American financial warfare against Israel. Some of this risk is linked to a growing campaign of antisemitism and anti-Zionism that has exploded since the October 7 terror attacks plunged the Middle East into conflict. But some of this is also linked to senseless violence in the West Bank and other concerns.
If the next government in Israel, regardless of who leads it, fails to punish and end lawlessness and cruelty by anarchists in the West Bank, there could be painful consequences.
We firmly support Israel’s right to exist and defend itself and believe that America is safer, and US interests in the Middle East are more secure, when a strong Israel works closely with Washington. We are proud that America and Israel have fought together to defend common interests and to counter common enemies.
Enemies of US engaged in unprecedented cooperation, understand value of partnerships
America’s enemies – namely the Axis of Aggressors, consisting of China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea – are engaged in unprecedented cooperation. Our foes understand the value of partnerships.
America needs partners, too, especially capable and motivated partners like Israel. We need Israel’s muscles in the Middle East so we can focus more on deterring and defeating aggression by Beijing, Moscow, or Pyongyang. Americans also benefit from Israel’s defense-technology expertise and defense-acquisition agility, which can help ensure American warfighters wield the best weapons.
But we are witnessing a sad paradox with Israel. On one hand, Israel has demonstrated that it is the most powerful military in the Middle East, worthy of closer cooperation with the United States. Israel has battled back and gained the upper hand in a regional war that it neither started nor wanted. And yet, in the United States, Israel is more unpopular than it has been in years. This is clear in recent polls from Pew, Gallup, and the Ronald Reagan Institute.
This is a strategic liability for Israel. A steep decline in approval could lead the next Congress and US administration to adopt policies that undermine our bilateral relationship, including defense cooperation. That would materially damage the security of both the US and Israel.
Some in Israel may respond by shrugging and saying, “Fine, Israel will just become independent and self-sufficient in its defense production and arm itself.”
But that is not possible. Israel is heavily reliant on major American-made platforms and will remain so for decades.
True defense production independence doesn’t just require assembly lines in Israel. It also requires suppliers and raw materials in Israel. Many of the inputs for Israeli-produced weapons are imported, meaning a hostile administration could try to block them.
Israel’s enemies are actively working to drive a wedge between Washington and Jerusalem. The goal is to slowly but surely deprive Israel of the means to defend itself. Unfortunately, those enemies are capitalizing on some Israeli unforced errors.
It is certainly true that some of the withering criticism of Israel will continue regardless of the country’s policies. It is also true that enemies are increasingly well-organized and funded, and they are conducting information warfare against the United States and Israel.
But explaining the negative shift in opinion in America solely through those dynamics is simply unrealistic. Such efforts ignore the agency of the Israeli government and encourage a dangerous apathy in terms of undertaking necessary reforms. The rule of law and the distinction between combatant and noncombatant are a primary difference between defenders of Western civilization and the terrorists who murdered innocents on September 11, 2001, and October 7, 2023.
US-Israel security cooperation needed more than ever
As threats to Americans grow, we need US-Israel security cooperation more than ever. And Israel needs continued American diplomatic and defense cooperation. But this could prove difficult if some Israeli policies continue.
Battles against the terrorist regime in Iran and its proxies will continue, as will the fight against disinformation and blind hate that unfairly targets Israel. But that does not absolve Israel from making some crucial decisions about its own conduct. The fate of the US-Israel alliance could hang in the balance.
Bradley Bowman is senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD). Jonathan Schanzer is executive director at FDD.

Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:17:16 UTC
05:17:16 KST

French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.
“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”
More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.
High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.
Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.
The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.
Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.
The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.
The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.
Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

A Russian television production designer arrested after returning from Kyiv to renew his passport has died in a Moscow hospital, the rights group First Department reported Monday, Oct. 26.
Aleksandr Kondratov, 52, was transferred from a pretrial detention center to Botkin Hospital on Oct. 23, the group said in a Telegram post.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The cause of death has not been disclosed. First Department said his death was at least the 11th this year among defendants in cases it considers politically motivated.
Kondratov had lived in Kyiv since 2012 and returned to Russia to replace his passport, according to rights monitors. He was subsequently held through repeated administrative arrests before authorities opened a treason investigation.
Passport trip leads to months in detention
Kondratov was detained at Moscow’s Vnukovo airport on May 5.
Before the criminal case was opened, he spent more than 70 days under successive administrative arrests for alleged petty hooliganism, OVD-Info said. Such repeated short sentences are commonly described by Russian rights monitors as carousel arrests.
The treason case was opened Aug. 5 and investigated by the Federal Security Service’s (FSB) directorate for Moscow and the Moscow region.
Mediazona reported from a Moscow City Court hearing in September that his lawyer, Natalia Tikhonova, said the case concerned “at least six publications” online. She did not disclose their contents.
The court rejected an appeal against his detention. The publicly reported details do not establish what the posts said or how investigators argued they constituted treason.
12-Year-Old Boy Dies After Weeklong Fight for Life Following Russian Strike on Nova Vodolaha Park
Kondratov was best known for his work as production designer on “Likvidatsiya” (“Liquidation”), a 2007 crime drama set in postwar Odesa. He received Golden Eagle and TEFI awards for his work on the series. His other credits included Odesa-Mama and Return My Love.
Rights group records at least 11 deaths this year
First Department’s death count covers those among individuals prosecuted in politically motivated cases. It is a rights-monitoring assessment, rather than an official Russian category or a finding that all the deaths had the same cause.
The Moscow Times reported that Kondratov was the third such defendant whose death became known in October.
The other two were Igor Yakovenko, 52, who died in a Krasnodar detention center, and Rustam Khalikov, 49, who died in a penal colony in the Penza region. Both had been convicted on terrorism-related charges that their defense teams disputed, according to the outlet.
The newspaper said that eight of the 11 people in its tally had entered custody aged 50 or older. It described complaints about detention conditions, pressure from prison administrations, and difficulties obtaining medical treatment.
Those broader allegations do not establish the circumstances of Kondratov’s death. The reports announcing it did not identify a medical cause.
Campaigners warn prisoners may not survive their sentences
Kondratov’s death follows renewed appeals by Russian human rights campaigners for international attention to those imprisoned in politically motivated cases.
Earlier in October, Memorial estimated that more than 1,800 people in Russia were recognized as political prisoners. Its broader estimate of individuals imprisoned or facing politically motivated prosecution was approximately 5,700.
At an event in the French National Assembly on Oct. 7, Memorial co-chair Oleg Orlov urged European lawmakers to prioritize prisoners whose health and circumstances put them at particular risk.
“While there is still a chance, we must save at least some of those who will not survive imprisonment,” he said.
Orlov asked lawmakers to follow individual prisoners’ cases, speak about them publicly and maintain scrutiny of their treatment. His appeal focused on securing releases while prisoners could still benefit from them, warning that some might otherwise die before completing their sentences.

Govt allows registration of flex-fuel vehicles running on 85% to 100% ethanol-blended petrol (file photo)
NEW DELHI: Paving the way for roll out of flex fuel vehicles (FFVs) that can run on up to E100 — nearly 100% pure ethanol or about 93-95% ethanol-blended with petrol — road transport ministry Monday modified changes in Central Motor Vehicles Rules.This comes barely months before some car manufacturers launch their E100 models.FFVs with an internal combustion engine can run on petrol, biofuels like ethanol or methanol, or any mixture of both stored in a single fuel tank. E100 fuels are “intended only for vehicles designed and certified to use it”.Officials said this is not applicable for other vehicles.“Vehicles that use E20 or normal fuel can’t use E85 or E100 fuel. Hence, the notification doesn’t require owners of existing vehicles to switch to these fuel categories or modify their vehicles now or in the future,” said a transport ministry official.TOI has learnt that the change in rules was essential for type approval and registration of FFVs on E100 considering that vehicle manufacturers are ready with their products.
Depending on the vehicle’s design and certification, the range of blending may extend to E85 or E100, a fuel predominantly consisting of ethanol.Flex fuel technology is used in countries such as Brazil and the US.
Ethanol has a lower fossil carbon footprint than conventional petrol and the use of higher ethanol blends can help reduce tailpipe emission of carbon monoxide (CO) and certain hydrocarbons. Greater ethanol use will also reduce dependence on import of crude oil.While govt notification will enable OEMs to manufacture FFVs, this won’t be enough to push adoption of these vehicles, experts said. This is evident as even after almost seven months of the launch of E85 cars, only 17 such vehicles have been registered.Industry players called reduction in GST on FFVs from 28% to 5% (on par with EVs) to bring down vehicle cost for buyers and compensate for mileage loss, which is about 27% while using E100 fuel.Besides, they sought a reduction in fuel cost to around Rs 75 a litre.But a bigger problem is availability of E100 given that there are only a handful of pumps, although it can run on other grades of ethanol-blended fuel.

Serbia may halt arms exports to Ukraine - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
"Student List" plans to halt arms exports to war zones and not join EU sanctions against Russia.
The political movement "Student List," which won Serbia's parliamentary elections on October 25, advocates halting arms exports to war zones, including Ukraine, and also does not plan to join the European Union's sanctions against Russia. Reuters reports this, UNN writes.
Details
As the publication notes, the "Student List" will have to navigate a complex energy and foreign-policy context in relations with Serbia's traditional ally—Russia.
In particular, party representatives said they did not intend to join the EU or impose sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government will have to rely on an exemption from U.S. sanctions to maintain oil imports while the sale of Russia's stake in the energy company NIS, which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to the Hungarian company MOL is being finalized.
The article notes that the Russian company "Gazprom" is Serbia's largest gas supplier. It delivers about 2.2 billion cubic meters per year at prices below market rates. The "Student List" party stated that this energy dependence is not a geopolitical choice but an acute economic dependence.
In addition, leading candidates from the "Student List" stated that the future government would halt all arms exports from Serbia to areas of military conflict, including sales to Western intermediaries who transfer weapons to Ukraine.

Gyurov Accuses Radev of Campaigning for Yotova Through Government Channels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

05:07:31 KST

Bulgaria's PM Congratulates Serbia’s Student List on Election Victory
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev congratulated Serbian citizens on their participation in the democratic process and the “Student List” on its election victory
Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov accused Prime Minister Rumen Radev of using the Council of Ministers’ official channels to promote Iliana Yotova and attack her political opponents, warning against the use of state institutions for election campaigning.
“Mr. Radev, you hold an absolute majority and bear full responsibility. Leave the choice to the citizens,” Gyurov said in response to messages disseminated through the government’s official channels in support of Yotova.
Gyurov called the incident a dangerous blurring of the boundaries between state authority and the election campaign. He said the problem was not the prime minister’s political position itself, but its promotion through an institution financed by all Bulgarian citizens.
“This is not the opinion of a commentator, nor is it a speech by a party leader in a public square. This is the official voice of the state, funded by the money of all taxpayers - including those who do not support the current government,” Gyurov said.
He noted that the Council of Ministers controls the state budget, the administration and the executive branch, arguing that this authority carries a particular obligation to prevent public resources from being used to benefit a single candidate.
“The Council of Ministers is not an election campaign headquarters. The state is not the property of a political party. And no Bulgarian citizen should be cast as an adversary simply because they vote differently,” the presidential candidate said.
Gyurov defended the right of every citizen to choose politically without being subjected to labels or division. He argued that people who back another candidate are not enemies but equal citizens entitled to the same treatment by the state.
“Yesterday, one in three voters chose us. These people are not some hysterical mob. They are teachers, doctors, entrepreneurs, pensioners, and young families. They are Bulgaria. And I will not accept anyone dividing them into 'ours' and 'yours.'” Gyurov said, adding that he would take the same position if a prime minister used official state channels to campaign for him.
He insisted that election rules must apply equally to everyone, including those in power, or they would have no meaning.
Gyurov also opposed efforts to portray the presidential election as a division between citizens deemed “the right kind” and “the wrong kind.” He said all sides wanted peace and framed the central question as whether those in government would serve the public or use state resources to influence voters.
According to Gyurov, one of the presidency’s main roles is to act as an independent check on concentrated power and defend the rules regardless of who governs.
“I want a president who stands between those in power and the citizens. Someone who upholds the rules even when it is inconvenient for the powerful. Someone who does not resort to intimidation or division, but instead demands that the institutions do their jobs. Bulgaria needs a state that its citizens can trust,” he said.
“Mr. Radev, govern. That is your responsibility. The choice of a president belongs to the Bulgarian citizens,” Gyurov concluded.

A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:07:00 UTC
05:07:00 KST

A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
October 26, 2026
Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.
"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.
Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.
"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.
Controversial ban
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.
"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."
Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.
The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."
A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Bad omen?
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?
Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.
Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.
All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers
Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.
Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.
In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.
Gender stereotypes
"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."
The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.
"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."
But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"

First US submarine to be deployed for WA rotational force
The US Navy has identified which of its submarines will be deployed to Australia first for the "rotational force" being established under AUKUS.
AUKUS proponents in Washington say it's proof the US is moving "full steam ahead" on the plan to arm Australia with nuclear-powered submarines, despite the concerns around shortfalls in the US's own fleet.
Fast-attack submarine USS Colorado will be part of Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) from late next year, the Pentagon says.
The Virginia-class boat will be the first of up to four American submarines to rotate through HMAS Stirling, near Perth, under SRF-West. One British boat is also expected to be part of the rotation.
The rotational force is aimed at helping Australia prepare to operate its own nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines down the track.
USS Colorado joined the US Navy fleet in 2018. It is crewed by 134 personnel.
"The activation of SRF-West puts Australia one step closer along the Optimal Pathway to Australia operating its own nuclear-powered submarine capability," said congressman Joe Courtney, who co-chairs Congress's Friends of Australia caucus.
"The combination of US and UK attack submarine rotations and Australian nuclear-powered submarines will transform allied naval posture in the Indo-Pacific."
USS Colorado completed a six-month deployment to waters off Europe in December 2023.
The following year, it was moved to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, for a two-year maintenance period. In June, the US Navy announced its return to its fleet after maintenance finished a month ahead of schedule.

Australia's cyber-spy agency is warning the country to prepare for disruptions to everyday life, as it deals with a surge in AI-driven cyber attacks.
The Australian Signals Directorate's latest report found a 20 per cent jump in incidents.
Defence Minister Richard Marles attributed this to malicious actors using AI to help them exploit vulnerabilities in systems.
"What we're saying to people right now is if you've got old systems, you've got to get rid of them. If you've got an old system which is connected to the internet, that's a gateway for a malicious actor," he tells ABC's News Breakfast.
"You've got to take time to harden your networks even if that means bringing them down for a couple of days to do that and you need to use AI yourself.
"There's a lot of AI products out there. Use them."

Big mining boss brought in to fix Australia’s Defence buying system
The way Australia buys weapons and defence gear is getting a major overhaul, with former Rio Tinto chief Kellie Parker hired to run the country's new Defence Delivery Agency.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy will announce today that Parker will become the new National Armaments Director — effectively making her Australia's chief weapons buyer.
For decades, defence procurement has been bogged down by massive budget blowouts and severe delays. To fix this, the Albanese government is transforming its purchasing division into an independent agency — known as the Defence Delivery Agency — starting July 2027.
By hiring a veteran mining executive accustomed to delivering complex, multi-billion-dollar infrastructure under strict commercial pressures, the government is hoping to inject real-world business discipline into the ADF.
Parker takes on the role in November 2026 before the agency goes fully live in July 2027.

NACC holds off on decision over controversial grant scheme inquiry
The NACC says it has not ruled out an investigation into a contentious government grant scheme that saw a golf club in the PM's electorate get $6 million dollars, but is putting any decision on hold until other parliamentary inquiries into the program conclude.
Appearing before Senate estimates, National Anti-Corruption Commission acting commissioner Kylie Kilgour confirmed the agency had received referrals regarding the $560 million Local Community Infrastructure program.
The scheme has faced intense scrutiny after analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity found it heavily favoured Labor electorates.
Kilgour said the scheme had "piqued" her interest but ultimately the watchdog would wait on the outcomes of a parliamentary inquiry and a potential audit by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) before taking further action.
"If you've got another integrity agency conducting a process, it's not necessarily appropriate for us to come in," Kilgour noted, adding that the NACC was "not there yet" in determining whether it holds statutory jurisdiction.
During the hearing, Kilgour also paid tribute to independent MP Helen Haines — a prominent critic of the grant scheme and a key architect of the NACC. She remains in hospital after being attacked outside her electorate office last week.
Key Event
Snowy 2.0 boss defends project progress since 2023 reset
Snowy Hydro made a late appearance at yesterday's Senate estimates, where company representatives were grilled over the latest cost blowout for Australia's biggest renewable energy project.
It was revealed last week that the Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro project would cost $22 billion-$25 billion and be delayed another year.
The cost has doubled since a 2023 project reset, where Snowy Hydro and the contractor building the project moved to a revised contract; which includes penalties for poor performance relating to cost and schedule.
Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes says the increase in cost was mainly due to flaws in the initial design and that there had been significant progress since the new contract model was adopted.
"In 2023, the advice of myself and the Snowy board … was to reset this contract to an ITC model, get progress moving again and we saw progress did double over that period," he said.
Barnes also said the federal government would need to contribute a "substantial proportion" of the extra $10b required to complete the project but that discussions around exactly how much were still underway.
New election funding system ready to go for 2027
The new election funding regime previously had its start date delayed because the Australian Electoral Commission said getting it up and running was a complicated task.
And little wonder: it's a whole new system, with donations to be disclosed in close to real time, and with caps now to apply to candidates, parties and donors.
But in what AEC commissioner Jeff Pope says is a "near miracle", the complicated technical system to make all of that work is now ready to roll from its mooted start date of January 1, 2027.
The next step will be to work with political parties and candidates to make sure they understand how to use the new system. Liberal senator James McGrath, a keen follower of electoral matters, sounds doubtful that it will all be so seamless. But in theory at least, it should be full steam ahead.
Nine politicians to get electorate office security upgrades after Haines attack
The AFP held a security briefing for politicians just two days after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, and it seems tangible outcomes are already afoot.
Nine electorate offices are now having security concerns actioned after they were raised last week, according to the Department of Finance.
In a late-night Senate estimates hearing, Finance secretary Matt Yannopoulos explains how the system works.
The AFP handles threat assessments and security details, Home Affairs does home security for those eligible, and Finance handles offices and transport. All three co-ordinate and share information.
"Where there's an ask for something to be upgraded, we go about that as quickly as possible, and indeed from the discussions that occurred last week there are nine different offices that are raised and we are dealing with those," Yannopoulos tells the committee.

Trump says Brazil election looked ‘rigged’, defeated Bolsonaro’s party recognises Lula win
- Trump said Lula’s Brazil win “looked like another rigged election”, but Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party later said it recognised the result and wanted the issues clarified.
- Lula won by over 4 million votes, and the extra two hours added by the Supreme Court brought fewer than 35,000 votes, making the result hard to overturn.
- Lula’s victory shook markets, with the real falling 8.1% and stocks dropping sharply, while he now faces a Congress full of Bolsonaro allies.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - United States President Donald Trump said on Oct 26 that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote “looked like another rigged election”, although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in the presidential election on Oct 25, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Oct 26, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Oct 26 he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded”.
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
Markets roiled by Lula win
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right. REUTERS

Trump offers $1 million for tipoffs that lead to voter fraud convictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:05:44 UTC
05:05:44 KST

Trump dangles US$1 million reward for reporting voter fraud
Tyler Pager
WASHINGTON – As US President Donald Trump has implored voters to support Republicans in November’s midterm elections, he has frequently dangled financial incentives and issued unfounded warnings about voter fraud.
On Oct 26, he married those two passions.
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid US$1 million (S$1.28 million) upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Trump wrote on social media.
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about where the money would come from for the ostensible rewards or how Americans are supposed to report fraud accusations.
The announcement reflected another step in Trump’s gathering campaign to use the powers of his office to influence the outcome of the midterms.
For years, the President has attacked the integrity of US elections, and in his second term, his administration has tried to assert more control over the voting process, which is overseen by states.
Earlier in October, Trump moved to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate loses.
The President and his Justice Department have also leaned on expansive but unsupported claims of voter fraud in trying to force states like California to set aside thousands of mail ballots they claim were sent to non-citizens.
At the same time, Trump has stepped up the financial incentives for voters as Republicans face increasingly steep odds of keeping control of Congress.
A national poll from The New York Times and Siena University found Trump’s approval rating hit a new low in October, with just 36% of likely voters saying they approved of his job performance.
Likely voters said they preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points in their congressional districts.
Over the past two months, Trump has signed pardons at campaign rallies, sent US$500 Obamacare “refund” checks and issued US$90 direct deposits to seniors to offset Medicare premiums.
The central reward, though, is the so-called “Trump Dividend”, which Trump announced at the Republican gathering he insisted his party throw in September in Dallas.
Trump has promised US$5,000 for every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, a proposal that has drawn bipartisan criticism and would cost more than US$1 trillion. It would also likely require congressional approval.
In October, Trump announced a new US$25 million whistleblower incentive programme to provide information to combat fraud.
There are already multiple avenues for reporting fraud to the federal government, and the new programme raised concerns because Trump said he would personally determine who received the money. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:05:24 KST

Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
Serbia will maintain its longstanding ties with Russia and will not impose sanctions on Moscow despite EU pressure, a representative of the winning Student List movement has told RT Balkan.
The student-led opposition secured 52.73% of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election, according to the latest preliminary results, defeating the coalition of former President Aleksandar Vucic. He conceded defeat but warned that Belgrade could abandon its resistance to EU pressure and sanction Russia within months.
The movement emerged from nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Speaking on Monday, Jovo Bakic, a university professor and Student List representative, said: “We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.”
“There will be no changes in that regard,” he added.
Recalling the harsh UN sanctions against Yugoslavia in the 1990s, when Serbia was one of its constituent republics, Bakic said restrictions imposed by “small Serbia” would have little effect on Russia but would be “symbolically very bad” for Belgrade.
🇷🇸 Jovo Bakić za RT Balkan: Studentska lista neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji ▪️Predstavnik "Studentske liste", profesor Jovo Bakić ponovio je da nova vlada Srbije neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji, uprkos tvrdnjama bivšeg predsednika Aleksandra Vučića da će se to dogoditi za nekoliko meseci. "Mi Rusiju poštujemo i kao veliku silu i kao našu istorijski važnu partnerku i u mnogim slučajevima zaštitnicu. Tu (u spoljnoj politici zemlje) neće biti nikakvih promena", izjavio je Bakić gostujući u emisiji "Srbija bira" na TV RT Balkan.
— RT Balkan (@rtbalkan) October 26, 2026
Under Vucic, Serbia resisted EU demands to adopt the bloc’s restrictions on Russia over the Ukraine conflict, despite pursuing EU membership. The Student List campaigned primarily on domestic reforms, leaving several contentious foreign policy questions unaddressed.
According to Reuters, leading candidates of the victorious movement have said the incoming government would halt arms exports to conflict zones, including sales to Western intermediaries that subsequently supply weapons to Ukraine.
Vucic previously said European buyers could decide how to use Serbian ammunition, including whether to send it to Ukraine, although Belgrade has denied supplying Kiev directly.
Energy ties present another major issue for Serbia’s incoming government. Russia remains the country’s dominant gas supplier, accounting for roughly three-quarters of its needs. In March, Vucic said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to maintain deliveries on favorable terms, at prices far below those in most of Europe. The agreement was subsequently prolonged through the end of 2026.
Serbia also faces uncertainty over its oil supplies due to US sanctions on NIS, the majority Russian-owned energy company that runs the country’s only oil refinery. Hungarian energy group MOL is seeking to acquire the Russian stake, while the current US waiver allowing NIS to continue business expires on October 30. The company has requested another extension to avoid disruptions to fuel supplies.
Unlike Serbia, the EU has sought to phase out Russian fossil fuel imports and secure alternative suppliers since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Asked about pressure to abandon Russian energy supplies, Bakic said: “We are not here to satisfy foreigners, but to act in our national interest.”
The Kremlin said on Monday that it hoped to maintain mutually beneficial relations with Serbia. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic’s contribution to bilateral ties and added “As you know, it takes two to tango.”

SC restores Karnataka land, says government can acquire only for public purpose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:01:59 UTC
05:01:59 KST

NEW DELHI: Holding that govt can acquire land from citizens only for public purpose and not for the benefit of some person or organisation, Supreme Court Monday quashed a 1988 acquisition of about 59 acres of land near Bengaluru by Karnataka govt for a cooperative housing society and restored the land to its owners after 38 years.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran held that the whole process of land acquisition is indicating “the fraud played on unsuspecting citizens”. It said that illegal acquisitions were made through fraud and undue influence and directed the state govt to pay Rs 50,000 to all litigant landowners who had challenged the process.
“Condemnation of privately owned land for public purpose can only be with authority of law and with just compensation being paid. That such authority of law can be exercised only for public purpose is without cavil, with just compensation being an ancillary right, which does not by itself justify an acquisition. However just the compensation be, if the authority of law is lacking or the public purpose is absent, there can be no eminent domain exercised,” the court said.
SC upheld the single-bench HC order,which said that it was at the instigation of middlemen that the state employed its machinery to acquire land for the society.

Can Serbia's student movement now govern the country?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:01:37 UTC
05:01:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Serbia's student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's election, Serbia's student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now comes the gritty business of governing, something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience with.
Tens of thousands took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine Serbia's political stability, its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.
The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement's limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
Winners, but can they stick together?
The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024, and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Without a figurehead, the students won widespread support before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list give an idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.
It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia's former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia's accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.
Prominent figures include the head of the students' candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic; former central bank governor Dejan Soskic; and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students after their victory.
But it is uncertain whether any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
"(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts," said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
"We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system."
Reforming public institutions
Under Serbia's constitution, candidates for the government have 90 days to form a government once parliament convenes after the state election commission announces the final results.
Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid rising public and private debt, while any attempt to end corruption will require overhauling the police and intelligence services and reforming the judiciary.
State institutions require "detoxification" after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
International relations
In Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.
"We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector," Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia's RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia's foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia's four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country fight corruption.
"I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms," said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.

Women reach orgasm more often alone, but partnered orgasms are more closely tied to sexual satisfaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:00:47 UTC
05:00:47 KST

Women tend to reach orgasm more often during solo sex than with a partner, but a new study suggests that partnered orgasms are the ones more closely tied to overall sexual satisfaction. The survey of nearly 28,000 users of a period-tracking app, published in Archives of Sexual Behavior, also found that a wider variety of partnered activities was linked to greater satisfaction, while variety in solo sex showed no such benefit.
Sexual satisfaction refers to a person’s overall evaluation of how fulfilling and pleasurable their sex life is, a measure closely tied to overall health and quality of life. Past research has consistently linked women’s sexual satisfaction to how often they reach orgasm and to sexual variety, which is the number of different sexual behaviors a person engages in. For instance, a 2017 national survey of U.S. adults found that people in long-term relationships who incorporated a wider range of intimate behaviors and had more frequent orgasms tended to feel more satisfied with their sex lives.
Reaching orgasm with a partner, however, is far less consistent for women than reaching orgasm alone, a disparity examined in a 2024 review of the partnered orgasm gap. That review noted that 38 to 92 percent of women usually or always climax when masturbating, and that women’s orgasm rates rise sharply when sexual activity includes direct stimulation of the clitoris, a small, highly sensitive organ at the top of the vulva. During partnered sex with men, routines often center on vaginal penetration alone, leaving many women without the stimulation needed to climax.
Because solo sex is such a reliable source of orgasms, one might expect frequent masturbation to boost sexual satisfaction, yet prior research has yielded mixed results. Among studies of women in a 2024 systematic review, 40 percent found no link between masturbation and sexual satisfaction, a third found a negative link, and about a quarter found a positive one.
The review’s authors argued that negative links may arise when masturbation compensates for unfulfilling or absent partnered sex, but they found that for women, masturbation more often seemed to complement partnered sex rather than replace it. The context of solo activity may also matter: a study covered by PsyPost in 2020 indicated that women who used vibrators both alone and with a partner reported higher sexual satisfaction than those who used vibrators only alone.
Most earlier studies examined only a narrow set of partnered behaviors or treated masturbation as a single category without comparing specific solo and partnered activities side by side. To explore how distinct behaviors, variety, and orgasms relate to satisfaction across both contexts, Yella Hewings-Martin and Adam C. Cunningham of Flo Health UK Limited and their colleagues surveyed users of the Flo health app to test whether solo orgasms and variety relate to overall satisfaction the same way partnered ones do.
The researchers recruited participants between April 11 and May 5, 2024, via in-app messages shown to adult English-speaking Flo users. From 70,424 initial responses, the team excluded users who did not complete the survey, lacked a valid app ID, or failed two attention-check questions, leaving 27,931 participants with an average age of 28 years. Nearly all respondents were biologically female (98.9 percent) and identified as women (96.4 percent); 70.7 percent identified as heterosexual, 23.1 percent as bisexual or pansexual, and 81.3 percent had a male partner.
Respondents reported on their sex lives over the previous six months, rating their overall sexual satisfaction on a five-point scale and their orgasm frequency from never to almost always. They also rated how often they engaged in 13 partnered and 13 solo sexual activities, including vaginal penetration, clitoral stimulation by hand or vibrator, watching erotica, and role-play, and how often each behavior led to orgasm. Multiplying activity frequency by orgasm frequency yielded weighted orgasm scores for solo and partnered contexts. Those who climaxed more often in one setting than the other selected up to three reasons from 22 options to explain why.
Across the full sample, 56.2 percent of participants were moderately or very satisfied with their overall sex life, while 19.5 percent were moderately or very dissatisfied. Roughly 36.9 percent reached orgasm almost always or always, and 22.9 percent did so most of the time, whereas 20.6 percent climaxed less than half the time or never. Overall orgasm frequency had a moderate positive correlation with sexual satisfaction (r = 0.38, on a scale where 1 would be a perfect match): 61.2 percent of very satisfied respondents reached orgasm almost always, though 19.5 percent of very dissatisfied respondents also climaxed almost every time.
The data showed a difference between the behaviors performed most consistently at every encounter and those practiced by the widest share of women overall. Vaginal penetration without other stimulation was the partnered behavior most consistently performed every time (39.7 percent), but clitoral stimulation by a partner’s hand, mouth, or tongue was the most widespread partnered activity overall (90.2 percent at least sometimes), followed closely by vaginal penetration paired with other body stimulation (90.1 percent) and by vaginal penetration paired with clitoral touch (90.0 percent).
The authors noted that clitoral stimulation topping the list of widespread partnered behaviors contrasts with older surveys where vaginal intercourse was most common. They suggest this likely reflects their more detailed questions about a six-month period, though they also speculate that it could partly reflect a younger sample (38 percent of respondents were aged 18 to 25).
In solo sex, clitoral stimulation by hand was both the most widespread behavior (84.6 percent) and the most consistent (44.5 percent every time), while only 5.5 percent practiced solo vaginal penetration alone every time. Across all 13 paired comparisons of similar activities, women reached orgasm more frequently when alone than with a partner, with differences ranging from small to moderate. Overall, 47 percent of participants reported reaching orgasm more often during solo sex, compared to 21 percent with a partner and 27 percent who reported no difference.
In solo sessions, clitoral stimulation with a vibrator or dildo, watching erotica, and clitoral stimulation by hand were linked to the highest orgasm rates. During partnered sex, the highest orgasm rates came from using sex toys together, combining vaginal penetration with clitoral stimulation, and masturbating with a partner present, while vaginal penetration alone and anal stimulation were linked to the lowest rates in both contexts.
Participants’ own explanations pointed to both psychological and physical factors. Women who climaxed more often alone most commonly cited inadequate stimulation from a partner, an absence of pressure to perform, reduced body image self-consciousness, and feeling safer to let go because they controlled the stimulation. Many also pointed to partnered obstacles such as a partner finishing too soon, difficulty communicating preferences, life stress, or painful intercourse. By contrast, those who reached orgasm more often with a partner emphasized emotional intimacy, adequate partner stimulation, and heightened arousal from attraction to their partner.
To examine how solo and partnered experiences predicted overall sexual satisfaction, the authors analyzed the 19,469 respondents who had engaged in partnered sex during the past six months. Partnered orgasm frequency was the strongest positive predictor of sexual satisfaction, whereas solo orgasm frequency showed a tiny negative association in initial models and was not statistically significant in the final model. Participants averaged 7.79 of the 13 partnered activities and 6.45 of the 13 solo activities; greater partnered variety predicted higher satisfaction, while greater solo variety was weakly associated with lower satisfaction. Together, these factors accounted for about 16 percent of the differences in satisfaction between participants.
In a separate model of 20,805 partnered-sex participants controlling for relationship status, being in a relationship and engaging in greater partnered variety both predicted higher overall orgasm frequency, whereas solo variety was not statistically significant. That model accounted for about 7 percent of the differences in orgasm frequency between participants.
The positive tie between partnered climax and satisfaction aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2018, which examined heterosexual newlywed couples rather than a broad sample of female app users and similarly found that a woman’s partnered orgasm frequency is positively linked to her sexual satisfaction. At the same time, the findings on solo sex and variety stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which linked frequent masturbation in women to higher sexual satisfaction alongside frequent intercourse and variety. That earlier study, however, looked at overall masturbation frequency across a broad adult population, whereas the new study specifically evaluated solo orgasm frequency and sexual variety among female app users.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the survey captured data at a single point in time, it cannot establish cause and effect: women who already feel happy and secure in their relationships may simply feel more comfortable exploring a wider variety of activities with their partners, while women experiencing an unfulfilling partnered sex life may turn to solo masturbation and try more solo techniques to compensate. In addition, sexual satisfaction was measured with a single question about a respondent’s overall sex life, which many people may naturally judge based on their partnered relationships rather than their solo habits. The large sample size also makes it possible to detect tiny statistical differences that have little practical impact in daily life.
The sample consisted of English-speaking users of a health tracking app who were mostly young, White, and heterosexual, and about half held a bachelor’s degree or higher. Because participants volunteered for a study described as being about female orgasms, they may be more comfortable discussing sex, or more sexually active, than women in general. Four of the authors are employees of Flo Health with equity in the company, and the other three are consultants for it.
The authors suggest that bringing elements of solo sex into partnered encounters, such as open communication about preferences and less pressure to perform, could help narrow the gap between solo and partnered orgasms. Future research tracking couples over time could help explain how emotional closeness, trust, and communication interact with physical stimulation to shape sexual fulfillment.
The study, “Sexual Satisfaction and Orgasm Experiences During Partnered and Solo Sex Among 27,931 Users of the Flo App,” was authored by Yella Hewings-Martin, Adam C. Cunningham, Jordan Rullo, Karen L. Blair, Carley Prentice, Anna Klepchukova, and Liudmila Zhaunova.

Israel committed extermination in West Bank, genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, says UN inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:00:24 UTC
05:00:24 KST

Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the occupied West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in besieged Gaza, United Nations-mandated investigators said.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said on Monday that Israeli occupational troops had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
The commission first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts.
In a new report, which comes the day before Israel's general election, the investigation found that in the occupied West Bank, through military incursions reinforced by sustained illegal settler attacks, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.
"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.
The three-member investigative UN team was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
South African former High Court judge Navi Pillay, who chaired the investigation until November 2025, won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier this month.
The commission's new report focused on killings and bodily and mental harm caused by Israeli forces since October 2023.
It found that the situation in the occupied West Bank has deteriorated gravely since 2023.
'Unliveable' conditions
The commission found that the Israeli authorities "intended to collectively punish" occupied West Bank civilians due to the October 7 blitz.
"The targeting of Palestinian civilians across different locations in the West Bank indicates a high level of coordination and organised planning and is the product of state policy," the report said.
The conduct of Israeli authorities indicates that "they knew and intended settler violence" to be part of the widespread and systematic attack in the occupied West Bank, it added.
"The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel's persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable," said commission chairman Srinivasan Muralidhar.
"Attempting to equate Palestinian statehood with a threat to the existence of Israel is blocking any viable attempts to realise Palestinians' right to self-determination," the Indian judge said in a statement.
The report cited cases where the commission concluded that Israeli forces intended to seriously harm and kill civilians, in acts which amount to war crimes including willful killing.
Military incursions since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
Findings on genocide
Since 2023, Israel's military has uprooted nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
However, experts and studies indicate that the death toll is an undercount, with the actual figure potentially reaching 200,000 in Gaza, 60 percent of which remains under Israeli occupation.
"The cases investigated for this report show that the Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza," the report said.
The inquiry urged Israel to "end the commission of genocide in Gaza" and act immediately on "obligations to prevent and punish genocide and incitement to genocide".
Israel should "immediately end the unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory", and remove all settlers and settlements.
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.
It said the "Yellow Line" which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial invasion of Gaza.
