FBI arrests CIA contractor for allegedly leaking secret defense, Middle East intel to journalist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:00:09 UTC
05:00:09 KST

A US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) contractor with Top Secret security clearance was arrested by the FBI on Friday for allegedly leaking classified defense and Middle East-related information to an individual who published the information online, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ).
The contractor, 42-year-old Ian Brinksman, worked for a US government agency based in Virginia since 2020 before being hired by a contractor to the same agency in 2022. Throughout his employment, Brinksman held the Top Secret security clearance with access to Sensitive Compartmented Information.
In a statement about the arrest, CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman provided services to the CIA as a contractor.
Brinksman accused of leaking information for use in publication
The criminal complaint against Brinksman alleged that he had an ongoing personal relationship with a person the DOJ identified as “Individual 1,” who claimed to have published reporting based on classified government intelligence assessments.
An affidavit for the arrest included an email Brinksman sent to a friend in which he stated that he had recently begun seeing “a lady” who worked as a journalist and wrote articles on the online publishing platform Substack.
Brinksman told the friend that the lady’s work focused on foreign policy and that he was “helping her get that off the ground.”
Brinksman’s workplace, a facility that stores and processes classified information, does not allow employees to bring cellphones or personal electronics into the facility for security reasons.
According to the DOJ, Brinksman was documented on multiple occasions entering his workplace, accessing specific Top Secret reports, then exiting the facility and speaking to Individual 1 on the phone.
Shortly after speaking with Brinksman, Individual 1 posted Substack articles containing classified information related to the Top Secret reports Brinksman accessed.
According to the affidavit, Brinksman is accused of sharing information from at least five Top Secret intelligence reports, including material that “reasonably could be expected to cause exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the US if leaked. None of the reports Brinksman allegedly leaked fell within the scope of his work.
Affidavit details align with Substack articles published by American journalist
The DOJ and FBI did not identify Individual 1 or her Substack, but The Jerusalem Post’s analysis of the details of the affidavit found that the information may align with American journalist Aida Chavez and articles written by her for Substack publication Capital & Empire.
Reports from both Ynet and the New York Post also connected Chavez to the information released by the DOJ, but Chavez has not been charged with any offenses related to the investigation into Brinksman or officially linked to the case.
The affidavit notes multiple dates on which Individual 1 is alleged to have published articles containing classified information leaked by Brinksman.
Articles published by Chavez on corresponding dates cite sources including a “confidential US intelligence assessment,” a “classified CIA assessment,” and a “classified CIA analysis.”
Many of the articles alleged to contain leaked confidential information discussed Israel, US-Israel relations, and the ongoing war with Iran.

French student leaders vowed to go on protesting despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, stokes unrest and deepens the economic damage.
The measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes; €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans for renovating schools; and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system students see as socially unfair.
"Not all our demands were met. We'll go on for as long as it takes," Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said as he and fellow student leaders emerged from a meeting with government officials in Paris.
The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and yellow-vest activists, known for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Macron's minority government.
The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120% of GDP, while the turmoil is boosting support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen ahead of next year's presidential election.
The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
"It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.
Protests show little sign of easing after nine days of violence
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday's protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centers.
Candidate Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year's presidential election, has benefited from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
An opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Over 1,400 arrested during protests on Saturday
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organized far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
"We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralized, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique.

'We do whatever they say': Yeshiva students defer to rabbis over response to IDF draft enforcement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:59:57 UTC
04:59:57 KST

Yeshiva students attending a massive United Torah Judaism election rally in Bnei Brak on Sunday told The Jerusalem Post that whether they would leave Israel, stay in the country, or enlist in the IDF if the next government stepped up draft enforcement would depend on their rabbis’ instructions.
The rally, held two days before Israel’s election, drew tens of thousands of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Jews under the slogan “Gather and Stand Up for Our Lives.” Central to the gathering was military conscription for haredi yeshiva students, regarded as a red line by much of the haredi community but widely supported among Jewish Israelis. An October Israel Democracy Institute survey found that 72% of Jewish respondents supported legislation requiring young haredi men to enlist.
Speaking at the rally, Rabbi Dov Landau, a leading haredi rabbinic authority, urged supporters to defend Torah study.
“Never have yeshiva students and kollel scholars been persecuted as they are being persecuted now,” Landau said.
The yeshiva students interviewed by the Post likewise described deferring to their own rabbis when asked how they would respond to draft enforcement.
“If my rabbi says to leave (the country), I’m going to leave,” Reuven, one of the students attending the rally, told the Post. When asked whether he would stay or enlist if his rabbi instructed him to do so, he replied that “of course” he would.
‘We would go through fire and water’ for our rabbis, yeshiva student says
Dovid, another young haredi man at the rally, said that he and others like him would “go through fire and water” for their rabbis.
“In our culture, we listen to whatever our rabbis say. If our rabbis will tell us to go, then we’ll listen to them,” he said. “We’re going to listen to them until the end.”
Shmuel, a fellow yeshiva student, emphasized that Torah study was his highest priority and that he would leave Israel if staying meant he could no longer continue his studies.
“If I need (to leave), that’s what I’ll do,” he said. “What’s more important for us is that we need to learn. And, if we can’t learn here, then we’ll learn in a different place. We’re not going to serve in the IDF because this learning is the most important thing in the world.”
Chaim, another of the students interviewed, also expressed a commitment to rabbinic authority, but argued that “the Jews doing Torah and mitzvot, to them, God gave Israel.” If the government enforced the draft, he believed the response should be to “fight it.”
Student emphasizes desire to stay despite saying he will obey rabbi if instructed to leave
Avi, another young man at the event, emphasized his desire to remain in Israel.
“We will stay (in Israel) because we believe it’s our country and Hashem will help us,” he said. Still, if his rabbi instructed him to leave, he would comply, “because he’s our rabbi, and we do whatever he says.”
Despite broad agreement about following their rabbis, the students appeared to hold differing personal views about military service.
When a group of young men was asked whether some yeshiva students wanted to enlist but refrained because their rabbis forbade it, several agreed, with one answering, “of course.”
One of the students, speaking anonymously, expressed frustration over the situation. He feared arrest at the airport over his draft status if he tried to travel abroad, and questioned why young yeshiva students were being targeted for draft evasion rather than the rabbis whose directives they were following.

“Coordinators in the Russian Federation assigned [the group] a wide range of targets in the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as other sites of military and industrial interest,” the Romanian Intelligence Service said in a statement published on its website.
The Bucharest Court of Appeal has issued European Arrest Warrants for all three suspects, with the ruling made in their absence. Romanian authorities have requested their extradition and are taking steps to bring them to Romania, BTA reported.
Investigations conducted this year have also uncovered other attempted attacks against sites in Romania, including international military facilities and locations used to train the Ukrainian Armed Forces. The operations were intended to intimidate, damage defense capabilities and undermine the contribution of targeted countries to European and regional security, Digi24 reported.
Russia has repeatedly denied allegations that it carries out sabotage operations in Europe, Reuters reported.

Digital News Publishers Association is set to move the Supreme Court challenging provisions of the DPDP Act and Rules, alleging they violate free speech and threaten journalistic activity. (file photo)
NEW DELHI: Challenging the constitutional validity of various provisions of Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and subsequent rules framed by govt, Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) is likely to move Supreme Court, alleging that they were violative of the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression and threatened the full spectrum of journalistic activity.“It is prayed that sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37, 44(3) of DPDP Act and Rules 16, 17, and 23 of DPDP Rules framed under Section 40 be declared void to the extent they are in contravention of fundamental rights of the Constitution,” said the petition of the association, representing 21 of India’s leading media organisations.“The sections mentioned above fail to provide any exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class of processing, entitled to constitutional protection under Article 14 and 19(l)(a) of the Constitution and threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, RTI activists, and other stakeholders, and strikes at the core of our democratic framework and runs contrary to the basic tenets of the Constitution.”It said publishers, editors, reporters and correspondents will be brought within a regime of notice and prior consent, compelled erasure and verifiable consent, obligations that cannot be reconciled with the ordinary functioning of the press. DPDP Act creates restrictions on the fundamental right to free speech and expression in relation to the dissemination of news,” the petition added.

Police stepped up surveillance in neighbouring districts, particularly Villupuram, where several of the fugitives are believed to hail from. Vehicle checks were intensified across Villupuram district amid concerns that the inmates could attempt to return to their hometowns.The escapees were identified as Lingam, Raja Singandhar, Karuppasamy, Silambarasan, Thirupathi, Menjisundaram, Sabari, Pon Muthu, Nijanth, Karthik Raja, Mugilan, Selva, Tarun, Rajkumar, Praveen, Muthu Ilango and Rajuveen.Senior police and prison officials are investigating possible security lapses and the sequence of events leading to the escape.Authorities have yet to disclose the condition of the assaulted guard, the offences for which the inmates were imprisoned or whether any of them have since been apprehended.Further investigation is underway.

Creation of a Coordination Center, new criteria and limits — the Cabinet of Ministers published changes to the reservation rules
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:48:05 EET
04:48:05 KST

Creation of a Coordination Center, new criteria and limits — the Cabinet of Ministers published changes to the reservation rules
Kyiv • UNN
The Cabinet of Ministers created a Coordination Center and introduced new criteria for the criticality of enterprises. A reservation limit of up to 95% was established for the defense industry and energy sector.
New rules for reserving conscripts in Ukraine are coming into force. They include, in particular, changes involving reductions in reservation limits for defense-industry and energy-sector employees, the establishment of new criteria for determining whether enterprises are critical, as well as the creation of a Coordination Center for Organizing Reservations. UNN reports this, with a reference to Government Resolution No. 1328.
Coordination Center for Organizing Reservations
According to the resolution, a Coordination Center for Organizing the Reservation of Conscripts for the Period of Mobilization and Wartime is to be established.
It will include:
-  the Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment, co-chair of the center; 
-  the Deputy Minister of Defense, co-chair of the center; 
-  the Deputy State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers; 
-  the Deputy Minister of Digital Transformation; 
-  the Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs; 
-  the Deputy Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport; 
-  the Deputy Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food; 
-  the Deputy Head of the Office of the President (subject to consent); 
-  the State Secretary of the Ministry of Energy; 
-  the Deputy Chief of the General Staff (subject to consent); 
-  the First Deputy Head of the State Border Guard Service; 
-  the Deputy Head of the National Police; 
-  the Deputy Head of the Pension Fund; 
-  the Deputy Head of the State Labor Service; 
-  representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the Main Intelligence Directorate (subject to consent); 
-  a representative of the Ministry of Economy.  
The Coordination Center has been assigned the following tasks:
-  facilitating coordination among central and local executive authorities, other state bodies, and state administration bodies on issues related to reserving conscripts for the period of mobilization and wartime;  
-  submitting proposals on ways, mechanisms, and methods for resolving issues related to reserving conscripts for the period of mobilization and wartime;  
-  considering proposals from state bodies to increase the number of conscripts reserved for the period of mobilization and wartime;  
-  considering proposals from state bodies concerning the designation of enterprises, institutions, and organizations as critically important for the functioning of the economy and ensuring the livelihoods of the population during a special period, and as critically important for meeting the needs of the Armed Forces and other military formations during a special period;  
-  monitoring information concerning conscript employees of enterprises, institutions, and organizations; 
-  providing state bodies with recommendations and proposals on canceling decisions designating enterprises as critical.  
The Regulation on the Center establishes clear procedures for the work of the advisory body. In particular, it sets strict deadlines for considering appeals from government bodies—no more than one month. Decisions designating enterprises as critically important remain within the competence of the authorized state bodies. At the same time, proposals from the Coordination Center are subject to consideration by central executive authorities and regional military administrations.
Determining critical status and reservation quotas
According to the resolution, within 10 days, state bodies and regional administrations must review the criteria for determining critical status and verify the enterprises that have already received this status. If the grounds for granting it are eliminated, the decision on critical status may be revoked ahead of schedule.
Decisions designating an enterprise as critical that are in force as of the date this resolution enters into force shall remain valid for the period for which they were adopted. The exception is decisions canceled as a result of the review of the criteria.
Decisions by the Minister of Defense to increase the number of conscripts reserved, adopted after December 8, 2025, shall also remain valid for the entire period of validity of the decision designating the enterprise as critical.
From now on, every decision designating an enterprise as critical must be preceded by a recommendation from the Coordination Center. The government body considers an appeal within up to 7 working days, the Center within up to 1 month, and the decision is then made within 3 working days.
The Coordination Center will approve increases in reservation quotas exceeding 50%.
Justified proposals to increase the number of persons liable for military service to be reserved are submitted to the Coordination Center by the relevant state body that made the decision to designate the enterprise, institution, or organization as critically important.
The grounds for the Coordination Center refusing to consider justified proposals to increase the number of reservations include, in particular, establishing facts of systematic violations by the head of a critically important institution of the legislative requirements governing the organization and maintenance of military registration, including the existence, within the past 12 months, of two or more documented instances of such violations and/or the head being held administratively liable for committing them.
New requirements are also being established for representative offices of donor institutions. In particular, the number of persons liable for military service who hold positions in representative offices of donor institutions and implementers of international technical assistance projects and who are subject to reservation must not exceed 50% of the number of employees liable for military service who are directly involved in carrying out the tasks of a single project, and must not exceed seven people.
The government has set a maximum reservation level of up to 95% of employees liable for military service for enterprises in the fuel and energy and defense-industrial sectors. However, this decision may be revised upward by the Coordination Center, although it may reject the proposal if facts are established of systematic violations by the head of a critically important institution of the legislative requirements governing the organization and maintenance of military registration.
Which enterprises may be recognized as critically important
Critically important status may be granted to enterprises, as confirmed by verifiable indicators, and to enterprises, institutions, and organizations in the humanitarian sphere, exclusively those that are critically important for ensuring the functioning of the state during a special period and whose continuous operation is necessary during a special period, including those operating in the following sectors:
-  defense-industrial sector; 
-  fuel and energy sector; 
-  housing and utilities; 
-  extractive industry;  
-  processing industry; 
-  agricultural production, including ensuring food security;  
-  retail trade;  
-  construction;  
-  transport and logistics;  
-  information technology;  
-  banking; healthcare;  
-  communications;  
-  carrying out emergency rescue and other urgent work (emergency rescue services).  
Other sectors qualifying as critical for enterprises will be determined only with the Center’s approval. Regional administrations determine only sectors ranging from energy to transport. The defense industry, IT, banks, healthcare, and communications will receive this status only through a central body.

Age pensioners who want to keep working say system punishes them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:45:46 UTC
04:45:46 KST

Age pensioners say system punishes them for wanting to keep working
In short:
Australians who receive the age pension face strict income limits before the pension is reduced.
Some pensioners want to keep working for social, health and economic reasons.
Advocates and industry groups are supportive of relaxing some of the rules to unlock older Australians' participation in the workforce.
As Australia's population ages, it is expected more people will want to continue working beyond retirement age, whether for financial reasons or otherwise.
It has prompted renewed calls from advocates and industry groups to relax the rules around working on the age pension, which some say unfairly punishes them.
South-east Queensland 71-year-old Peter Gibney would go as far as to say the system is stacked against him and his wife continuing to work.
Having worked in retail for decades, he is not interested in slowing down.
"There's none of this airy, fairy stuff ... it's down on the ground dealing with customers and staff, training staff and getting the load done," he said.
Despite his enthusiasm for his job, Mr Gibney feels he is being unfairly punished. Both he and his wife, who works as a teacher's aide, receive part age pensions.
However, the more they work, the more of their age pensions they lose.
Without large superannuation balances and with a mortgage, they cannot afford to stop work.
Bringing in some extra money gives them additional financial security.
"It is freedom, to a degree. The downside is that it's stacked against us doing those things," Mr Gibney said.
Complex rules around pension and work
A Department of Social Services spokesperson said the rules around working on the age pension mean a single pensioner with no other income can earn up to $526 a fortnight before the pension begins to reduce.
That is because of a system called the work bonus, which disregards the first $300 of work income a fortnight from the income test.
A couple with no other income can earn a combined $996 a fortnight if both are eligible for the work bonus.
Council on the Ageing (COTA) Australia chief executive Patricia Sparrow has called for that system to be "simplified".
The Department of Social Services said age pensioners who worked kept more of their age pension now than four years ago.
A department spokesperson said the government was committed to reviewing the rate of social services payments in each budget.
There are overseas examples to look to. New Zealand has a system in which the pension (NZ Super) is paid on a universal rate.
Mr Gibney believes "the ideal situation would be the old age pension is for achieving an age ... it's payback for 40, 50 years of paying taxes".
More older Australians expected to keep working
According to COTA's latest State Of The Older Nation report, about 15 per cent of Australians aged over 67 continue to work, up from 11 per cent in 2021.
Almost 25 per cent are not opposed to returning to work in some capacity.
As the population ages, and more people begin to retire with mortgages or without a partner, those numbers are expected to rise.
"We're really urging government to look at the things we need to do right across the system to make sure that older people can continue to support themselves, contribute to the community," Ms Sparrow said.
Ms Sparrow said one of the main barriers keeping older Australians out of work was age discrimination, an issue she said needed to be addressed to ensure fair workforce participation.
Industry groups also want to unlock an older workforce to help boost productivity.
Productivity benefits touted
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said more needed to be done to encourage older Australians who wanted to continue to work without facing a "significant" penalty.
ACCI advocates for a "more flexible" system and a doubling of the work bonus to $600 a fortnight.
"[Older Australians] have experience. They have the skills. That's important," he said.
"There's a huge benefit for the economy if they want to continue in the workforce."
Mr McKellar said even part-time work could help alleviate productivity challenges in the economy, particularly in sectors that continued to struggle for staff.
And the benefits for people like the Gibneys go beyond the economic.
Mr Gibney believes it is important to stay connected to the community for the mental health and social benefits, and for him and his wife to continue to have separate interests.

Space Force Wants Cislunar Kit Ready to Launch by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:45:38 UTC
04:45:38 KST

For years now, Space Force officials have said the service is getting serious about defining its role and crafting an architecture for future cislunar capabilities. Now, the Space Force is taking steps to realize that vision, asking industry to rapidly invest and develop satellites and software that could be ready for operations as soon as 2029.
Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy—the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for advanced programs—said he’s seen the Pentagon’s posture toward cislunar operations and planning efforts change drastically over the past year.
“There was no talk of cislunar, and basically I was told, ‘Don’t talk about cislunar, and stop getting into it,’” Purdy said Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference.
Now, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine, and even a December 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump are emphasizing the importance of cislunar operations and advocating for more investment. The shift is in part linked to China’s lunar ambitions, Purdy said. Beijing has a cislunar roadmap of its own and has already landed several uncrewed spacecraft on the lunar surface. Now, it plans to launch a crewed Moon mission by 2030.
“I’ve got the Secretary of War and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs full on stating in public: ‘This is a warfighting domain,’” Purdy said, using the department’s secondary name. “And so, I would ask you all, please jump on my cislunar bandwagon because I need some more friends here, along with our deep, passionate crew that have been working on this for years.”
Cislunar space is the region beyond geosynchronous orbit extending to the moon and even farther to cover areas influenced by Earth and the moon’s gravity—hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and 1,728 times the volume of space contained within geosynchronous orbit. Purdy described the region as “painful” for satellite operations, as it is further from Earth and navigation is more of a challenge.
To date, much of the U.S. government’s cislunar planning and operations have centered on NASA and its plan to return astronauts to the moon through the Artemis program. The Defense Department has pursued research programs aimed at better understanding the vast expanse of cislunar space—including the Air Force Research Lab’s Oracle program, which plans to launch several cislunar space domain awareness satellites in the coming years. But the Space Force hasn’t dedicated much planning, funding, or personnel to those efforts.
That may be about to change. In April, the Space Force set up a new Cislunar Coordination Office, housed within Purdy’s portfolio and tasked with crafting a roadmap for cislunar technology and a future space architecture. Since then, that office – led by Jaime Stearns—has refined that roadmap and crafted strategies for various mission areas, like space domain awareness, communications, and lunar navigation.
The CCO has also drafted a list of high-priority but unfunded requirements, which Purdy said includes relatively low-dollar “ticky-tacky” efforts that can help the Space Force make real progress in this area.
The service is also pursuing multiple technology development and rapid fielding efforts, Purdy said. In partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory and the innovation arm SpaceWERX, it plans to launch an industry challenge called Lunar Prime to get after some of its more nascent technology and research needs. The effort has $30 million in funding and is targeting flight demonstrations within two years of contract award.
The Space Force also has two requests for information it plans to release “imminently,” Purdy said. The first will call for existing commercial technology that can be ready to launch by 2029.
“We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.”
The second request is for AI and autonomous processing capabilities for spacecraft operating in cislunar space. The goal is to have “a fully autonomous system out there at cislunar that’s able to handle all its hardware faults, all its processing, all the sensor activities,” Purdy said.

Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:43:54 UTC
04:43:54 KST

Israelis head to the polls Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long rule or leave the country facing another political deadlock, with neither major bloc projected to secure a governing majority, Anadolu reports.
The vote will be Israel’s first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip, as well as military confrontations with Lebanon and Iran.
It will also be the first Israeli general election held on schedule since 1988, following decades in which successive governments collapsed before completing their four-year terms.
Around 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). Election day is a public holiday.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing for seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
Under Israel’s proportional representation system, voters choose parties rather than individual candidates. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter parliament.
No party has ever won an outright Knesset majority, making coalition negotiations decisive in determining who becomes prime minister.
Eisenkot’s party leads final polls
Final surveys published by Israel’s three main television broadcasters put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud.
Yashar is projected to win 22 to 23 seats, compared with 19 to 21 for Likud.
The B’Yachad, or Together, alliance led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid is projected to finish third with 14 or 15 seats.
Other opposition parties include the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
The three surveys project Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc winning 50 seats, while the opposition bloc is forecast to secure between 52 and 56.
Palestinian-led parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
The figures suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.
Winning the largest number of seats does not automatically determine who becomes prime minister.
President Isaac Herzog will consult the elected parties before assigning the task of forming a government to the lawmaker considered most likely to command a parliamentary majority.
READ: Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday’s parliamentary vote
Netanyahu fights for political survival
Netanyahu, 77, is seeking another term after serving as prime minister for more than 18 years across three separate periods.
His campaign has focused heavily on national security, portraying his experience and military policies as essential to confronting regional threats.
However, he faces criticism over his government’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, its handling of subsequent conflicts and its opposition to establishing an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures.
Netanyahu is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
His potential coalition partners include far-right parties led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alongside the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, rejected Palestinian statehood and encouraged Palestinians to leave Gaza.
The ultra-Orthodox parties have meanwhile faced mounting criticism over demands to preserve military-service exemptions for religious students as the Israeli military struggles with personnel shortages after years of conflict.
Eisenkot offers change in leadership, no major shift in security issues
Eisenkot, 66, served as chief of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and joined Netanyahu’s emergency government following the Oct. 7 attacks.
He later left the government after criticizing Netanyahu’s management of the Gaza offensive and the absence of a clear political strategy.
His son was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in December 2023.
Eisenkot has campaigned on government accountability, political stability and restoring public confidence in state institutions.
He supports establishing an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures and ending broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Despite positioning himself as an alternative to Netanyahu, Eisenkot maintains similar positions on several major security issues.
He opposes establishing a fully sovereign Palestinian state under current conditions and says Hamas’ military capabilities and rule in Gaza must be dismantled.
The election therefore presents voters with competing approaches to leadership, governance, judicial independence and relations with far-right parties, even as the two leading candidates share positions on key security issues.
OPINION: Israeli elections and the limits of change
Arab parties could hold balance of power
The Joint List and Ra’am, the principal parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, could play a decisive role if neither major bloc secures 61 seats.
Polls project the Joint List winning around nine seats and Ra’am securing between five and seven.
An Eisenkot-led government could require support from one or both Palestinian-led parties, either through formal coalition participation or outside parliamentary backing.
Such an arrangement would face political obstacles.
Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while other opposition figures have been reluctant to commit to such an agreement.
Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked the possibility of Palestinian-led parties influencing the next government to mobilize right-wing voters.
Coalition scenarios, possible deadlock
Several possible outcomes could emerge from Tuesday’s vote.
Netanyahu could form another government if his bloc secures enough additional seats or attracts lawmakers from outside his existing alliance.
An Eisenkot-led coalition would likely depend on an agreement involving Palestinian-led parties, defections from other camps or difficult compromises among ideologically divided opposition leaders.
A unity government involving Likud and major opposition parties is another possible arrangement, although Eisenkot and several allies have ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
If neither side assembles a majority, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister during prolonged coalition negotiations, potentially leading to another election.
The performance of smaller parties polling near the 3.25% electoral threshold could prove decisive. Parties that fail to meet the threshold win no seats, potentially weakening their political allies and shifting the balance of power between the competing blocs.
Exit polls are expected immediately after voting ends at 10 pm local time Tuesday.
Initial official results will begin emerging overnight, although counting ballots from military personnel, hospitals, prisons and other special voting arrangements could take several days.
Official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, after which coalition negotiations could continue for weeks.

Kharkiv under sustained attack
The Novobavarskyi strike was one of at least four attacks on Kharkiv on Monday evening. Earlier, Russian drones hit the city’s Kholodnohirsky district around 4:40 p.m. local time, and again at 5:49 p.m.
Hours before the evening attacks, Syniehubov released a report showing that Russian forces had hit 113 settlements across the region over the past week, killing 12 people and wounding 148.
Among those, two children were killed, and 11 injured.
During that period, Syniehubov said, Russian forces used 27 missiles, eight guided aerial bombs (KABs) and three MLRS across the region.
They also launched nearly 880 drones, including 19 Shahed-type Geran-2s, three Lancet loitering munitions, 19 Molniya drones and 50 first-person-view (FPV) drones, as well as 786 other drones whose type is still being identified.
In Kharkiv alone, last week’s attacks damaged seven apartment buildings, 16 private homes, seven businesses, power lines, two gas stations, a hypermarket, the city circus, railway infrastructure and about 50 private cars.
Separately on Monday, it became known that a 12-year-old boy, Artem Koval, died in the Kyiv hospital from injuries sustained in a Russian drone strike that targeted a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha.
The same Oct. 19 strike killed his eight-year-old sister Ariana, along with five other civilians, including an infant killed in her stroller and her mother.

A year's salary buys a bathroom: Demographic crisis grips one of Europe's youngest countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:40:23 UTC
04:40:23 KST

Slovakia is facing a deepening demographic crisis, with births falling to a historic low of just over 42,000 in 2025, while the population aged 65 and older reached 1.03 million, accounting for 19% of residents. According to Slovak news outlet Pravda, the trend is placing growing pressure on public finances and essential services, raising concerns about the country's ability to support an increasingly elderly population.
Despite the alarming figures, Slovakia remains relatively young by European standards. The average share of residents aged 65 and older across Europe is 22%, and only four European Union countries have younger populations than Slovakia. Italy leads the continent, with 24.7% of its population aged 65 or older, followed by Portugal at 24.3%, Bulgaria at 24%, Greece at 23.7% and Finland at 23.6%. Germany, Europe's largest economy, stands at 22.7%.
But projections suggest Slovakia is rapidly catching up. The number of elderly residents already exceeds the number of children under 15, and the share of people aged 65 and older could reach 30% by 2050 and stabilize at around 33% between 2060 and 2080. Meanwhile, annual births are projected to fall below 35,000 by 2060 and remain between 32,000 and 33,000 through 2080.
The financial consequences are already becoming apparent. The report cites projected annual pension spending of 13.7 billion euros, alongside a planned 3.5% increase in benefits from January. The average monthly old-age pension was estimated at 703 euros at the end of 2025. Slovakia's fiscal watchdog has warned that age-related spending could gradually increase by the equivalent of 3.8% of GDP by 2060, while domestic and European Union assessments have identified significant risks to the pension system's long-term sustainability.
A year's salary buys barely enough space for a bathroom
The demographic crisis is closely intertwined with Slovakia's increasingly unaffordable housing market. The country's average annual gross salary of 23,500 euros is enough to purchase just 8.1 square meters of residential property. In the capital, Bratislava, where average annual gross earnings reach 30,000 euros, an entire year's salary buys only 6.8 square meters, roughly the size of a bathroom. Only 16 Slovak cities offer more than 14 square meters for the equivalent of one year's salary, most of them in the Nitra and Banská Bystrica regions.
Financial pressures are also keeping older Slovaks in the workforce. According to data from Eurostat, the European Union's statistical agency, 24.7% of Slovak retirees continue working or earn supplementary income, nearly twice the EU average. Of those, 18.3% continue working without changing their schedules, while 6.4% switch to adjusted working hours.
For many, the decision is driven by financial necessity rather than personal fulfillment. Some 30.3% of working retirees describe employment as an economic necessity, while 31% say continuing to work is financially worthwhile. Relatively few cite enjoyment or social connections as their primary motivation, placing Slovakia among the EU countries where retirees report the lowest levels of work-related enjoyment.
The healthcare system faces mounting pressure as the number of elderly patients with complex medical needs grows alongside persistent staffing shortages. The problem is particularly visible in residential neighborhoods built during the housing boom of the 1970s and 1980s, where large concentrations of elderly residents now live after younger families moved to suburban areas.
Pensions, healthcare and long-term care are competing for limited public funds alongside education, defense and infrastructure. At the same time, young households struggling with housing prices are finding it increasingly difficult to save for mortgage down payments, particularly without financial assistance from relatives. Many are postponing starting families, creating a cycle in which unaffordable housing contributes to declining births, leaving fewer young workers to support an aging population.

Europe's five NATO powers vow greater defence role while keeping US close
Unknown

04:39:17 KST

Europe’s five leading NATO members have pledged to take greater responsibility for the continent’s security while maintaining the United States as an indispensable ally, seeking to strengthen Europe’s role within the military alliance amid uncertainty over Washington’s future military presence.
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, known as the E5 group, made the commitment after talks in Paris on Monday, stressing that Europe must shoulder a greater share of the burden while preserving close coordination with Washington and other NATO members.
“We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition,” the ministers said in a joint statement.
“The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO,” they added.
E5 seeks a stronger Europe within NATO
French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin said the five countries had agreed to pursue “a stronger Europe within an equally stronger NATO” through a coordinated plan developed in “full transparency” with Washington.
The group’s next meeting will take place in Rome in March 2027, Vautrin said.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who attended the meeting, also called for further investment in Europe’s military capabilities.
“We must continue to modernise our forces and capabilities to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” Kallas said.
Poland was represented by Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski.
Planned US troop reduction raises coordination concerns
The talks come as Washington plans to withdraw around 5,000 troops from Germany, roughly 15 percent of the approximately 36,000 US troops stationed there.
The Pentagon announced the planned reduction in May, catching European allies off guard. Washington said the withdrawal would take place over six to 12 months.
Zalewski said he was confident that any agreement on the US military presence would be coordinated with allies to avoid gaps in deterrence or military capabilities.
The E5 statement sought to balance calls for greater European responsibility with an acknowledgement that continued US engagement remains central to NATO’s collective defence.
European ministers reaffirm support for Ukraine
The five countries also reiterated their commitment to supporting Ukraine, although they announced no new financial or operational assistance following the meeting.
British minister Wes Streeting said European support would continue for as long as necessary, warning that the Russian threat was “of a kind we haven't seen since the end of the Cold War”.
At the same time, Streeting stressed that the allies were not seeking a direct confrontation with Moscow.
“None of us seek war with Russia. And we certainly have no quarrel with the Russian people,” he said.

From Iran to Gaza: What are Netanyahu, Eisenkot and Bennett’s competing visions for Israel’s security?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:38:11 UTC
04:38:11 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel Elections
- Israel without Netanyahu: Still a nation at war
Israel without Netanyahu: Still a nation at war
Netanyahu’s rivals promise to repair Israel after three years of war. But both of his main opponents back a hard military line, similar to that of Netanyahu
Two days before Israel’s election, Benjamin Netanyahu shared a post with an AI-generated image of a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a warning that choosing a leader incapable of confronting Iran could expose Israelis to a “second Holocaust.”
Gadi Eisenkot, his leading challenger and a former IDF chief of staff, accused him of threatening voters with mass destruction after failing to achieve his own war aims. “Netanyahu, you’re hysterical,” he wrote.
Netanyahu says only he can finish the job. His opponents say his leadership is endangering Israel. But replacing him would not necessarily bring the country’s wars to an end.
“The way Israel is being led today is dangerous,” Eisenkot told a party conference.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett offers an equally blunt promise: “The October 7 government destroyed, and the October 27 government will repair.”
Both challengers support confronting Iran and removing Hamas from power.
Their differences with Netanyahu concern what military force should achieve, how long Israeli troops should remain deployed — and which agreements could follow.
Iran: What counts as victory?
“I am personally committed to finishing the job,” Netanyahu said earlier this month. “Finishing the job means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran.”
Eisenkot argues that regime change must come from the Iranian people rather than being imposed militarily. His priorities include eliminating Iran’s nuclear weapons potential and cutting its support for Hezbollah.
That distinction affects how a war is fought, says military affairs analyst Yaakov Lappin.
“If the regime is to be toppled, resources have to be allocated to that, for example within Mossad. If the air force also has the regime as a target, it has to hold bombs in reserve for that. The objectives determine how resources are distributed.”
It also changes the finish line. Weakening Iran’s military capabilities would fall short of a declared objective to bring down its leadership.
But any government would inherit the same regional threats — and a military that has already changed its approach since October 7.
“Over the past three years, the Israeli military has formulated a new doctrine. It is still being adjusted, but the broad outlines are fairly clear, and the military will press hard for the next government to follow it,” Lappin says.
The principle is to confront threats before they become attacks, rather than simply contain them. A different prime minister would still face pressure to act.
Gaza: The Road to Removing Hamas
“From the moment I enter the Prime Minister’s office, within 18 months, Hamas will no longer rule the Gaza Strip,” Eisenkot has pledged.
He leaves open both Trump’s Gaza framework and military force. Bennett would maintain the yellow line separating Israeli- and Hamas-controlled areas until Hamas disarms, while seeking a central role for Egypt — one Cairo has not agreed to assume.
Lappin, meanwhile, expects military operations to continue under any government.
“All the candidates will face the same difficulties, both militarily in removing Hamas from power and politically in finding a new leadership that can actually take over governing Gaza.”
But a change of government could affect the extent and duration of Israel’s military presence, he explains.
“It remains an open question whether a center-left government would be more inclined to withdraw the army more quickly from more areas of Gaza than a Netanyahu government. That is very possible. But who knows how access to all the intelligence would change that assessment?” Lappin says.
West Bank: Partial crackdown, but continued support
Lappin expects a different government to act more quickly and forcefully against the growing wave of attacks on Palestinians by violent settler groups. Something the international community has criticized Netanyahu's government for failing to do. But it will likely not be easy nor quick, since both Eisenkot and Bennet do not want to get into a broader confrontation with the settler community as a whole.
In addition, the existing power dynamics between the PA and Israel in the West Bank will likely not change overnight - and the major threats will not disappear. Meaning Israel’s room for maneuver is rather limited, says Lappin.
A Different Way?
But one man does promise change. Yair Golan, the former deputy military chief who leads the left-wing Democrats, proposes a more explicit diplomatic approach: a new, long-term nuclear agreement with Iran under intrusive inspections; replacing Hamas with a Palestinian technocratic administration in Gaza, backed by regional and international support; and halting annexation moves in the West Bank while strengthening security coordination with the Palestinian Authority and cracking down on violent settlers.
How much of that program he could advance would depend on negotiations with the other parties needed to form a government.
Netanyahu as a barrier
Abroad, Netanyahu’s departure could create an opening even where Israel’s security interests remain unchanged.
He has become the face of the Gaza war. A government without him and his far-right partners could give European and Arab leaders political space to rebuild ties, negotiate over Gaza’s future and pursue regional cooperation.
Some cooperation already takes place away from public diplomacy. The Jerusalem Post reported on October 22, citing a defense official, that Israel was providing intelligence through US mediation to help Saudi Arabia counter the Houthis. The arrangement shows how common threats can bring the countries together without formal diplomatic relations.
Lappin sees a change of government as a possible opening for more public ties, rather than a prerequisite for all cooperation.
“Another government could make it easier to have a more open relationship. Saudi Arabia is clearly waiting for a new government. It looks very bad to be close to Netanyahu, especially in the Arab world. But the United Arab Emirates has maintained its position and its cooperation. It depends on each country’s interests.”
Moving from discreet security cooperation to normalization would still require political decisions. Saudi Arabia’s demand for Palestinian statehood remains at odds with the leading candidates’ positions. Netanyahu’s departure could remove one barrier without resolving that disagreement.
Israel without Netanyahu would still face the same enemies. And with the faces leading the opposition, it means it would still face a similarly hard line. What could change is how far it fights, what it considers victory — and whether a different leadership can turn military gains into agreements.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

How Ukraine's annual radio dictation brings a nation together, one word at a time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:33:01 UTC
04:33:01 KST

How Ukraine's annual radio dictation brings a nation together, one word at a time
People take part in the Radio Dictation of National Unity at the Odesa Regional Universal Scientific Library named after M.S. Hrushevsky in Odesa, Ukraine, on Oct. 25, 2024. (Viacheslav Onyshchenko / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
As it turns out, dictation exercises are not just for schoolchildren. On Oct. 27, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians — from diaspora communities abroad to service members on the front lines — will take part in an annual tradition: listening, writing, and testing their mastery of the Ukrainian language.
Organized by Ukrainian Radio since 2000, the annual Radio Dictation celebrates the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language, bringing participants together to transcribe a text broadcast live across multiple platforms. Those who wish to have their work assessed can submit it to a professional review panel.
For Ukrainian author and war veteran Artur Dron, who wrote this year's dictation, the invitation to craft a text that so many people would follow word by word was "daunting." Still, he didn't hesitate to accept.
"I've taken part in (the dictation) myself several times, and I see something truly special in it," Dron said.
"The fact that, even during the full-scale war, we're holding this initiative for the fifth time — that we continue to do so even under these circumstances, and that language still brings us together — means a great deal."
Yuliia Sheludko, an executive producer at Ukrainian Radio, told the Kyiv Independent that she believes the dictation serves as "a kind of anchor" for Ukrainians during wartime.
Bringing Ukrainians together around a shared love of the Ukrainian language also carries particular weight as Russia intensifies its attacks against the country.
"We know from history that the Ukrainian language was suppressed for many years, so we must value and protect it," Sheludko said.
Under Russian imperial rule, successive restrictions curtailed Ukrainian use in publishing and education, while Soviet authorities continued to subordinate Ukrainian to Russian, despite periods of official support for Ukrainian-language culture. Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and cultural figures were also persecuted, imprisoned, and even killed for their pro-Ukrainian stances.
The 2014 EuroMaidan Revolution helped accelerate a broader societal shift back to Ukrainian, which has gained further traction since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. For many, speaking Ukrainian has become one of the most powerful expressions of their national identity.
Despite its power to unite Ukrainians through a shared love of the language, however, the Radio Dictation also tends to stir up strong opinions.
Ahead of this year's event, volunteer and civic activist Dasha Astafieva received what she described as "an avalanche of hate" for being chosen to read the dictation alongside teacher Artur Proidakov, with people criticizing everything from her past as a Playboy model to her former use of Russian in public life.
Since 2022, Astafieva has worked to promote Ukrainian culture. She launched the audiobook app UnderBooks in 2023, and wrote on Facebook that "the hysteria over the fact that the dictation will be read by someone who narrates audiobooks marks a whole new level of absurdity."
Public debate isn't limited to this year's dictation. Actress Nataliia Sumska drew criticism in 2025 for delivering the dictation at what many felt was too fast a pace, with many participants saying that it left them scrambling to piece their sentences together.
The uproar grew when a longtime participant with a track record of top marks reportedly had her microphone switched off after she criticized the pace of Sumska's dictation and called author Eugenia Kuznetsova's text "silly."
In 2024, author Oksana Zabuzhko's text was so challenging that only one person in the country wrote it without any errors.
The disputes point to a tension at the heart of the dictation's mission: how to celebrate Ukrainian as a shared national language while navigating disagreements over who represents it and what mastery of it should look like.
The organizers, however, seem to take the controversy that comes with the Radio Dictation in stride, pointing out that when an event draws this much public attention, some people will always be dissatisfied.
As for the controversy surrounding Astafieva, Sheludko encouraged those who haven't heard her narrate audiobooks to do so, describing it as "something she does with real mastery."
Ukrainian Radio can't provide the exact number of people who take part in the Radio Dictation every year, but it can estimate participation in the hundreds of thousands based on how many people post about it on social media and submit their written work to the professional committee for review.
According to Sheludko, Ukrainian Radio received more submissions in 2022 than in any previous year — and encouraged people to keep doing so not only for the commemorative prizes given to those with top marks.
For all the arguments over who reads the dictation and how difficult the text should be, its enduring appeal lies in something simpler: the chance for Ukrainians, wherever they are, to take part in a shared cultural tradition.
"I believe that this year thousands of people will enjoy the text, the act of writing, and, above all, the sense of unity around the Ukrainian language," Sheludko said.

Russian sabotage network believed to have caused Romanian fire, prosecutors say

BUCHAREST, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Romania’s Intelligence Service said on Monday it had identified a sabotage network coordinated by Russia, which it believed was responsible for a fire in September at an industrial site in central Romania near a state-owned weapons company.
The European Union and NATO state shares a land border of more than 600 km (370 miles) with Ukraine, and centrist president Nicusor Dan has said it is the target of a hybrid war waged by Russia to destabilise nations that support Kyiv.
The attacks range from drone incursions into Romanian airspace to cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, acts of sabotage and attacks on cargo vessels near Romanian waters, Dan has said.
Russia’s embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment outside business hours but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations.

The Intelligence Service said all three were part of the network coordinated by Russia, whose coordinators had assigned it targets including “state and private weapons production facilities, as well as other objectives of military and industrial interest”.
A year ago, Poland and Romania detained eight people suspected of involvement in a Russian plan to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.
Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO’s eastern flank this month after a series of drone strikes on cargo vessels in the Black Sea.
At least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coast of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing.

UNICEF chief says children 'cannot wait another 30 years' for protection in war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:28:48 UTC
04:28:48 KST

Merve Aydogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
By Merve Aydogan
HAMILTON, Canada (AA) - The UN Children's Fund chief on Monday warned that children caught in today's conflicts "cannot wait another 30 years for the protection they have been promised," stressing that the reality for children living through war is becoming more dangerous.
"While the international community has built a strong framework to protect children in war, the reality for children living through conflict is increasingly dangerous," UNICEF chief Catherine Russell said at a UN Security Council briefing marking 30 years since a landmark report by Mozambican children's rights advocate Graca Machel on the impact of armed conflict on children.
"Since 2005, the United Nations has verified more than 430,000 grave violations against children in armed conflict — more than 38,000 were in 2025 alone," she said.
The highest numbers of violations last year were verified in the state of Palestine, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria, she said.
"And these are only the violations the United Nations was able to verify. The true scale is undoubtedly greater," Russell noted.
She said the UN has verified more than 44,000 incidents of denial of humanitarian access since 2005, including more than 8,000 in 2025 alone.
"At the very moment children most need protection, our ability to reach them is being undermined," she added.
Pointing to the use of explosive weapons in populated areas, she stressed: "More than 70% of verified child casualties in 2025 were caused by explosive weapons."
"These weapons do not only kill and injure children. They destroy schools, hospitals, water systems, and other infrastructure essential to children’s survival and development. The consequences can last long after the fighting has stopped," she said.
Describing it as "deeply alarming," Russel emphasized that such trends "are not inevitable."
 
Progress is possible given ‘political will’
"Three decades of experience have shown us that progress is possible when political will is matched by sustained engagement and concrete action by member states," she added.
Russel urged the Security Council to act immediately, saying that "the children caught in today’s conflicts cannot wait another 30 years for the protection they have been promised. We must act and we must act now."
Vanessa Frazier, the secretary-general’s special representative for children and armed conflict, told the council that decades of legal frameworks, advocacy, and engagement with parties to conflict had produced "concrete results."
"More than 40 action plans have been signed to date with parties to conflict, contributing to the release of over 220,000 children from armed forces and groups and their transfer to civilian child-protection actors," she said.
Noting the current violations, Frazier said: "In 2025, the UN verified 38,558 grave violations affecting 24,174 children. This is the highest number of children affected since this mandate was established."
She said government forces were responsible for the majority of verified grave violations for the first time in the mandate’s history.
"This is deeply troubling. I condemn all grave violations against children, in every situation and every conflict, irrespective of who commits them," Frazier said.
"No party is exempt from its duty to protect children or from scrutiny when violations are committed," she said.

ICC turning into an EU court – researcher (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) is increasingly becoming Europeans’ “own personal court” as the US expands sanctions on the institution, an expert has told RT.
George Szamuely, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute in Budapest, pointed out that major global powers such as the US, Russia, and China do not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction, leaving European nations as its main backers.
“So essentially the ICC is becoming a European project,” he said.
Szamuely argued that the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navi Pillay underscored Europe’s support for the court.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded Pillay the prize on October 9, just hours before Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution, expanding measures that had previously targeted individual officials.
The ICC is now becoming increasingly the tool of the Europeans.
According to Szamuely, European lawmakers sought to reaffirm their backing for the court despite mounting pressure from Washington.
“The European Parliament wanted to send a message to the Trump administration… to say: ‘we thoroughly endorse the ICC. The ICC does our work’,” he said.
Szamuely noted that Washington’s “war against the ICC really intensified” during President Donald Trump’s first term, when the US sanctioned several court officials, including then-chief prosecutor Fatou Bensouda.
“Now he has imposed much harsher sanctions against the ICC,” he said, arguing that the latest measures effectively impose secondary sanctions on “anyone who actually engages in any kind of dealings with the ICC.”

Fewer than half of Ukraine’s F-16s may be operational. Kyiv wants newer Block 70/72 jets to face Russia’s Su-35 fighters, Air Force says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:28:21 UTC
04:28:21 KST

Ukraine is remaking its air force on NATO’s model, down to the way its squadrons are organized and the aircraft they fly. The reforms are planned to be completed by 2035 and include modernizing its F-16s while pursuing the Swedish Gripen jets, Air Force Spokesperson Yurii Ihnat says, per Tse Baza.
Ukraine’s fighters are working hard against Russia’s air war, and in the previous month alone the Air Force faced around 3,500 jet-powered targets, with F-16s heavily used to intercept Russian drones. The new reform is meant to build an air force that can be sustained over the long term and can contest Russian jets and glide bombs, not only survive the next wave.
Wings and universal air bases
The central change, Ihnat said, is a move to the “wing” units that NATO air forces use. The first steps have already been taken: Ukraine has set up the 107th F-16 wing, which now has its own Facebook page and may publish material about its work.
Ukraine also plans to build universal air bases on the operational airfields it has used through the full-scale war. In the future, Ihnat says, those bases should be able to receive and service different models of combat aircraft, as NATO does.
A worn fleet, and the jets Ukraine wants next
Currently, the F-16s Ukraine flies are older Block 15 jets, used by other countries before they arrived, and intensive combat has left them in need of repairs, service life restoration, and upgrades.
Ukrainian officials discussed modernization with the American manufacturer Lockheed Martin, while Kyiv would prefer the newer Block 70/72 version, which Ihnat says would let its pilots stand up more confidently to Russia’s Su-35 fighters.
Keeping the current fleet flying has been hard: fewer than half of Ukraine’s F-16s may be operational, held back by slow maintenance abroad.
At the same time, Lockheed Martin and Kyiv are discussing a special F-16 variant for Ukraine, with a modern AESA radar, longer range, and a wider choice of weapons, though no firm deal exists yet.
Ukraine is also counting on Swedish Gripen fighters. Ihnat says Ukrainian pilots are drawn to them for their lower operating costs and simpler maintenance, with the country likely to receive older C/D models first, before the newer Gripen E that Saab is developing.
Ukrainian pilots have already begun their training on the Gripen, a jet seen as a counter to the Russian aircraft dropping guided glide bombs on the front, though delivery timing depends on further agreements.
