Exclusive: Russia significantly expands glide-bomb production, research shows
Russia is significantly expanding its glide-bomb production, indicating that Moscow has no plans to scale back its war against Ukraine, a new report by Kyiv-based think tank Center for Defense Reforms exclusively shared with the Kyiv Independent reveals.
"Given the role of guided aerial bombs in destroying defensive positions, isolating battlefields and facilitating ground advances, this provides a basis for sustaining high-intensity offensive operations over an extended period," the report concludes.
The report reveals that in 2025, the centralized procurement entity TRV-Engineering JSC obtained nearly 278,000 servo drives, used to control the flight surfaces of glide bombs — enough to manufacture 139,000 of the deadly munitions. The report identifies the key Russian supplier of servo drives, CED Sail LLC, which is currently not subject to any Western sanctions, and suggests this entity should be a "priority target" for sanctions designation.
"Russia is building the military-industrial capacity to continue waging wars even after the war in Ukraine ends. These are not the actions of a country preparing for lasting peace," Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Center for Defense Reforms and former chief adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, told the Kyiv Independent.
The report also identifies a network of interconnected Russian companies which are responsible for importing key components and raw materials essential for the production of UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits.
Russia converts older, unguided bombs into precision-guided weapons with these guidance kits, significantly increasing their range and accuracy. The increase in range allows Russian fighter-bomber aircraft to remain within Russian territory, out of range of Ukrainian air defenses, as they deploy their deadly payloads.
As with many other Russian munitions, both UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits are heavily reliant on foreign components for their manufacture.
Ukrainian military intelligence has repeatedly identified a range of foreign components in Russian glide bombs, including parts from the U.S., Japan, China, Switzerland, and Taiwan, among others.
The report also reveals the majority of entities and individuals involved in the production of Russia's glide bombs are currently unsanctioned, despite the munitions being a key part of the Kremlin's offensive airborne arsenal.
Out of 20 corporate entities involved in the manufacture of Russian glide bombs, only eight are subject to some level of Western sanctions or export restrictions. The "uneven sanctions coverage," the report assesses, allows Russia to continue to "procure necessary components without significant restrictions."
Four Chinese companies are identified as being critical to the supply chain, with some, such as Shenzhen Fire Power Control Technology Limited, not hiding the explicitly military application of their products. Only one of the four Chinese companies is subject to U.S. export restrictions, and none are sanctioned by the U.K. or the EU.
"Despite its repeated declarations of readiness for peace, Russia continues to dramatically expand the production of offensive weapons, particularly guided aerial bombs," Danylyuk said.

Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes
Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers.
Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant.
The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said.
Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems.

====================================================================================================

Mystery money from super PACs floods US midterm election campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:00:18 UTC
04:00:18 KST

With just over a week until voting day, the records in the notoriously expensive US election system have been shattered.
An AFP news agency analysis of federal data shows just five groups known as super PACs (political action committees) accounted for nearly a third of non-party spending in this election cycle as of October 25.
Significantly funded by dark money, they have poured more than $1 billion into the US midterm election campaign.
Three of the five groups skew Republican, and about two thirds of the billion dollars spent will benefit the Republican Party (GOP), fuelled by ultra-wealthy Republican-leaning donors like Elon Musk — a key ally of President Donald Trump.
Musk alone has put almost $450 million into Republican groups, including the biggest of the super PACs, the Senate Leadership Fund.
Meanwhile, Democrats have a fundraising edge when it comes to direct donations to candidates' campaigns and to the party's national committees.
Democratic candidates in competitive Senate and House races have consistently outraised their Republican counterparts.
That suggests smaller donors in the Democratic base are highly motivated.
But tortuous US election laws impose strict caps on how much individuals can give, while there is no limit — or really any control at all — on how much super PAC groups can throw at candidates.
Unlimited contributions
The six giant spenders in this cycle are technically a mix of super PACs and hybrid PACs, entities that didn't even exist before 2010.
They grew out of a Supreme Court ruling, known as Citizens United, which held that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.
A lower court decision ruled that these organisations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors.
The result was that big donors can funnel vast sums of money to try and influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organisations.
In contrast, direct contributions to a candidate's official campaign are limited to a mere $3,500, and donations to national party committees have a cap of $44,300.
The PAC spending sprees have surged ever higher during the Trump era, with Musk's mega-million donations encapsulating the new reality of pay-to-play politics.
Across the nation, super PACs have put far more of their money into Senate contests and spent it largely on attack ads.
The Texas Senate election tops the list in terms of expenditure. Democrat James Talarico has faced more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups as he attempts to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.
Second is Ohio's special Senate election, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has also faced extensive outside spending against him — nearly $170 million — as he tries to return to the Senate.

Air Force Plans $1 Billion Campus for Testing F-47 at Nellis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:56:52 UTC
03:56:52 KST

The Air Force is taking the first steps to build a $1 billion campus including hangars, laboratories, maintenance and training facilities, and more to test the F-47 at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev.—and the service plans to finish construction by 2031 as it moves quickly to field the upcoming sixth-generation fighter.
In a presolicitation notice posted Oct. 22, the Air Force said it is looking for as many as four qualified firms that can quickly work on a project to design and build the proposed F-47 campus. The entire project, including construction, design, security, and other expenses, will ultimately cost about $1.057 billion.
The project would include a nearly 117,000-square foot facility, largely on the east side of Nellis, combining flightline operations and maintenance. It would also have a specialized laboratory for reprogramming the plane’s systems, an aircraft apron with sunshades, and a nearly 41,000-square foot simulator facility.
The notice lists several other facilities that could be built later as “potential subsequent work,” including additional hangars for fuel system maintenance, corrosion control of its stealth coating, weapons load training, maintenance training, and other maintenance needs.
The Air Force plans to issue an initial award for the F-47 campus in February 2027, which would then kick off about nine months of design and preconstruction, and then about 40 more months of more intensive construction into early March 2031.
The presolicitation notice for the campus provides the latest window on how the Air Force is preparing to bring the Boeing-made F-47 into its fleet. It follows the Air Force’s 2027 budget proposal, which requested $730 million for hangars and other support infrastructure for the F-47 and revealed its operational testing will take place at Nellis.
The Air Force in March 2025 announced it had chosen Boeing to build the F-47, which will replace the F-22 Raptor sometime in the 2030s and eventually make up 20 percent of the Air Force’s fleet. It is expected to have advanced stealth, data sharing, and electronic warfare capabilities, and it will be able to direct semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in September 2025 that the first F-47 fighter was in the process of being built and would fly in 2028. Service officials have stuck to that schedule ever since and said its first flight will take place before the end of the Trump administration.
Allvin also said in a May 2025 social media post that the F-47 will be able to fly faster than Mach 2, or more than 1,500 miles per hour, and have a combat radius of more than 1,000 nautical miles, far more than the F-22 or F-35A Joint Strike Fighter. That expanded range would give the F-47 an advantage in a potential conflict with China, where aircraft will have to fly long distances over stretches of the Pacific Ocean.

Wheelaroos out to 'send a message' in pursuit of breakthrough World Cup title
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:54:08 UTC
03:54:08 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Breakthrough moment beckons for Australia's Wheelaroos at home Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
Australian wheelchair rugby league is poised for a breakthrough moment this week, with Wollongong, south of Sydney, hosting the nation's first World Cup since 2008.
Bundled in as part of the larger Rugby League World Cup, which also includes the men's, women's and physical disability tournaments, the wheelchair competition will benefit from free-to-air coverage in prime-time slots.
It is the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of, and Australia's Wheelaroos are well aware of the gravity of the moment.
"I think it's going to bring a whole different experience for wheelchair rugby league in Australia," Australia captain Bayley McKenna told ABC Sport.
"It's gonna bring people together, it's gonna bring people in to support our sport."
The Wheelaroos are currently ranked fourth in the world and are yet to claim a world title, with their game generally taking a back seat to the likes of wheelchair basketball and wheelchair rugby at a grassroots level in Australia.
But coach Brett Clark has told ABC Sport his charges are ready to take the rough-and-tumble sport into living rooms across the country.
"We know this is a quality game for all to play and this is the opportunity for us to show it at its top level," Clark said.
A unique kind of inclusion
Wheelchair rugby league, not to be confused with Paralympic favourite wheelchair rugby, is played on a basketball-sized court and with five athletes per side.
The sport replaces tackles with tagging like in Oztag and uses AFL-style handballing instead of kicking, but otherwise, remains relatively faithful to the running game.
Played across full-length 40-minute halves, it is a game filled with exhilarating chair skills, hair-raising collisions and retains much of rugby league's trademark physicality.
For Wheelaroos captain McKenna — who played the running game for years before joining the wheelchair sport — wheelchair rugby league's physicality is one of its biggest drawcards.
"In hindsight, I've had more injuries playing wheelchair rugby league than I did in the running game," McKenna said.
"You can hit people as hard as you want as long as you're going for the tag."
At 26, McKenna is a Wheelaroos trailblazer, being both the youngest and first non-disabled national team skipper.
Wheelchair rugby league is unique among international wheelchair sports in allowing teams to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.
This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from the grassroots all the way to elite competition, allowing for both non-disabled and disabled friends and family to share the same court.
McKenna, who began playing wheelchair sports alongside his disabled father, has seen the benefits of that inclusiveness firsthand.
"Being a non-disabled athlete in this sport is one of the most unreal things you can ever be a part of," McKenna said.
"The sport's so big, it's so broad, you can travel all across the world … it's so inclusive, because for me it gave me an opportunity to play a sport underneath my dad as a coach."
Wheelaroos squad member Liam Luff, living with hereditary spastic paraplegia, told ABC Sport the policy was an "incredible benefit".
"It just opens the doors to more and more people in our sport, which is what we need to grow awareness, get more people in chairs and show how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
The importance of the moment
Beginning on Friday, the 2026 World Cup will be just the fifth edition of the wheelchair tournament, with France and England having split the first four titles evenly.
With the sport having been first designed in France in the early 2000s, the two northern hemisphere titans have benefited from close contact and regular meetings.
In England, the sport experienced an explosion in popularity after the nation hosted the 2022 World Cup, which was also held alongside the men's and women's competitions. Grassroots participation saw a sharp uptick in the year after the event, while standalone international games have attracted audiences in the thousands since.
The Wheelaroos are now optimistic the 2026 tournament will have a similar impact in Australia, and Luff believes the sport is well and truly ready for it.
"I think more people are going to stumble across the game and find out about how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
Finding a way past France and England will undoubtedly be an almighty task for the Wheelaroos, who will play three group-stage games before the knockouts.
But the team is bullish on its chances in the Illawarra, and Luff is convinced the Wheelaroos are finally ready to take a seat amongst the world's elite.
"This is our biggest opportunity to really prove where the Australian Wheelaroos are in wheelchair rugby league," Luff said.
"We are gonna make sure we can prove ourselves taking on those top dogs … I think we're gonna really send a message about where we stand."

The Council of the EU allocates €4.7 billion in compensation to member states for supporting Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:53:40 EET
03:53:40 KST

The Council of the EU allocates €4.7 billion in compensation to member states for supporting Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Council of the EU approved €4.7 billion in compensation to states for military support to Ukraine. A further €230 million will be allocated to the EUMAM mission.
On October 26, the Council of the EU adopted a package of eight decisions enabling €4.7 billion from the European Peace Facility to be used for the EU member states providing support to Ukraine. This was reported by the press service of the Council of the EU, UNN writes.
Details
These decisions allow for partial reimbursement from the European Peace Facility for military assistance already provided by the member states, totaling €4.7 billion. They also provide additional funding for the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine, EUMAM, totaling €230 million.
These decisions are an important step toward implementing the political agreement reached by the EU member states on September 25, 2026, to mobilize €6.6 billion for Ukraine from the European Peace Facility. The agreement provided for €1 billion in new military assistance to Ukraine and further strengthening of EUMAM Ukraine in 2027
The adopted decisions increase the total volume of EU support for Ukraine under the European Peace Facility to €10.8 billion, including €9.9 billion to reimburse the cost of military assistance provided by the member states and €950 million for military training under EUMAM, the Council of the EU stated.
Background
The European Peace Facility was established in March 2021 to finance measures under the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) aimed at preventing conflicts, preserving peace, and strengthening international security and stability. In particular, the European Peace Facility enables the EU to finance measures designed to strengthen the capabilities of third countries, as well as regional and international organizations, in the military and defense spheres.

Sports commission urges kids not to specialise in sports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:53:34 UTC
03:53:34 KST

Australian Sports Commission urges young athletes to play range of sports
In short:
A new position statement by the Australian Sports Commission suggests kids shouldn't specialise in sports.
The statement says specialisation at a young age can lead to burnout and injury.
Australian fast bowler Kim Garth says she played multiple sports as a child.
Prior to becoming arguably the greatest tennis player in history, Roger Federer sampled a huge range of other sports.
"I had a flair for all different kinds of sports and tried skateboarding, basketball, table-tennis, badminton, football, wrestling, skiing, swimming," he said in a 2004 letter to his fans.
In a 2019 TV interview he urged kids to do other sports for fun.
"Go play squash, go ride your bike, go play basketball, go ski whatever it is," Federer said.
"If you only start focusing on just one sport only, I feel like you can get burned out."
The tennis great's words are echoed in an Australian Sports Commission (ASC) position statement.
The report said specialisation for children younger than 12 could result in reduced motivation, burnout, injury and psychological stress.
"What we don't want is kids specialising really early and losing their love for it and not partaking in sport at all in the future," Australian Institute of Sport director Matti Clements said.
"That's the worst thing we could hope for.
"There's got to be the enjoyment, the motivation to do it."
The ASC said there had been a trend towards youth athletes specialising at an early age.
The statement said specialisation had been viewed as a way to increase opportunities for selection, scholarships and progression to elite or professional sport.
"Often, unfortunately, mum and dads [are] getting misinformation around the value of early specialisation," Clements said.
"If you have someone saying you need to specialise early in this sport if you're going to make it … then of course you're going to listen to that."
She highlighted the the proliferation of private academies for certain sports, including soccer.
"I think that the establishment of academies that are a business model academy, they can often present a compelling message to a parent that their child should be in there early," Clements said.
"We all know an individual who was physically quite developed at a young age and therefore was absolutely smashing it out of the out of the park in a particular sport but, by just doing that sport, lost the enthusiasm for doing it."
That "burnout" can be seen in the figures provided the ASC's most recent survey into sport in Australia.
Participation in Australia's most-played sport, soccer, peaks for girls and boys between nine and 11 and then quickly declines.
That teenage dropout trend is evident in all the popular sports played in Australia, netball, cricket, Australian Rules, basketball, tennis and rugby league.
"Athletes who maintain broader sport participation until after age 12 and then specialise are more likely to succeed in their chosen sport," the statement said.
That rang true for Australian fast bowler Kim Garth, who played multiple sports when she was a kid.
"I played football in the winter, cricket in the summer, and then I played a fair bit of Gaelic football as well," the Irish-born cricketer said.
Garth chose Gaelic football over cricket in her final year of school, but cricket won out as she progressed to the Irish national team before transferring her allegiance to Australia in 2022.
"I couldn't speak more highly of trying to play as many sports as you can when you're younger," she said.
Clements said specialisation in and of itself was not necessarily bad, but depended on the individual and their development.
She hoped the position statement would help young athletes, their parents, coaches and organisations make considered choices about when children started to specialise.

Submarine Affair: Communications adviser Tzahi Liber convicted of brokering bribes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:54 UTC
03:52:54 KST

The Tel Aviv District Court on Monday convicted communications adviser Yitzhak (Tzahi) Liber of acting as a bribe intermediary in the Submarine Affair, finding that he received nearly NIS 94,000 from businessman Miki Ganor, intended for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former chief of staff, David Sharan.
Judge Dr. Shmuel Melamed convicted Liber of brokering bribes, money laundering and assisting in the preparation of false accounting records. The court found that the payments were disguised as fees for consulting services that were never provided.
The verdict concerns one part of Case 3000, the corruption affair surrounding Israel’s purchases of submarines and naval vessels from German shipbuilder ThyssenKrupp. Ganor represented the company in Israel, while Sharan held senior positions in the Prime Minister’s Office.
The court tried Liber separately from the defendants in the main case, including Ganor and Sharan, whose proceedings remain ongoing.
The court examined two payments from Ganor’s company: NIS 35,400 transferred in November 2014 to a company owned by Liber, and NIS 58,500 transferred in August 2016 to a company owned by his business partner.
Judge: Companies, false invoices used to conceal Ganor-Sharan financial connection
Melamed found that the companies and false invoices were used to conceal the purpose of the payments and the financial connection between Ganor and Sharan. The arrangement also allowed the payments to be recorded as business expenses.
Liber, a close friend of Sharan, denied wrongdoing and maintained that the money paid for genuine communications and strategic consulting work. His defense argued that he had not passed Ganor’s money to Sharan and that a separate payment of several thousand shekels to his friend was a gesture of thanks for introducing him to Ganor.
The court rejected that account, relying on Liber’s admissions during police questioning, statements Ganor gave investigators, and supporting financial and other records.
In his police account, Liber described receiving the money and passing it to Sharan in cash. He also acknowledged conveying information and requests between Ganor and Sharan concerning submarines, according to the verdict.
Both Liber and Ganor later withdrew their incriminating accounts. Melamed nevertheless found that their earlier statements were supported by evidence including payment records, a table of consultants maintained by Ganor, staff notebooks and communications data.
Liber’s explanation of supposed consulting arrangement made no commercial sense, judge finds
The judge also found that Liber’s explanation of the supposed consulting arrangement made no commercial sense. Among other difficulties, the parties exchanged unsigned draft contracts, and Liber could not adequately explain how the amounts and timing of the payments had been determined.
A substantial part of the verdict addressed the defense’s attempt to exclude Liber’s police admissions. His lawyers argued that investigators from the Lahav 433 National Crime Unit had pressured him improperly, interfered with his access to legal advice, and linked cooperation to release from detention.
Melamed rejected the request, finding that Liber retained control over what he said, chose when to answer questions and when to remain silent, and gave his central admission after consulting privately with his lawyer. The judge concluded that the admissions were voluntary and reliable.
Although the prosecution sought separate convictions for each payment, Melamed treated the transactions as one continuing course of criminal conduct. Liber was therefore convicted of one count of each of the three offenses.
Melamed took over the case following the death of Judge Benny Sagi, who had heard the evidence. He explained that his verdict rested on the existing record, after both sides asked not to add to the material presented before Sagi.

Civic responsibility and philanthropy strengthen Israeli society - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:45 UTC
03:52:45 KST

In the months prior to election day, public debate naturally focused on politics, parties, and the future direction of the country. Elections matter. They are one of the most important ways citizens shape the character and priorities of their nation. But democracy does not begin and end with voting.
If the events following October 7 taught us anything, it is that a healthy society depends not only on governments and elected officials, but also on ordinary people who choose to take responsibility for one another.
In those difficult days and months, countless volunteers, non-profits, and community initiatives stepped forward to support vulnerable populations and strengthen the country’s social fabric. They demonstrated that while governments govern, citizens build society.
Every one of us has opportunities to shape the world around us, not only through the choices we make at the ballot box, but through the causes we support and the people we help. Volunteerism and philanthropy allow us to transform our values into action.
However, we must not forget that government action alone is generally not enough. Reimbursements and public budgets often cover only part of what is truly needed to sustain essential human services, nurture community health, and support vulnerable groups.
Philanthropy and civic participation make it possible to bridge that gap, sustain essential care, and create opportunities where none existed before.
This spirit is embodied whenever dedicated volunteers and community partners give their time, energy, and financial resources – not for personal gain, but to ensure that members of our society facing extraordinary challenges receive the support they deserve.
These initiatives show what becomes possible when people refuse to be mere passive observers, and instead choose to become active participants in building their community.
For many active citizens, grassroots engagement represents an Israel they are proud to support: an Israel that respects the dignity of every human being, harnesses cooperation for the benefit of society, and builds shared resilience.
A clear reflection of this commitment can be seen in the upcoming Alyn Hospital Ride – “Wheels of Love.” The hospital’s annual event will take place from November 8 to 12 and includes hundreds of cyclists, hikers, and volunteers from Israel and around the world.
Former Alyn patients ride for others
All of them devote months to training and fundraising to ensure that children facing extraordinary challenges receive the care and opportunities they deserve. Among the most inspiring participants are members of The Swift & The Bold, a cycling team made up of former Alyn patients.
These children and teens are not merely beneficiaries of rehabilitation services; they are active participants in the ride itself as riders and fundraisers – a powerful demonstration of how civic action fosters independence and shared solidarity.
With election day behind us, dedicated volunteers, donors, and grassroots initiatives remind us that democracy is about far more than choosing leaders. It is about actively choosing values, taking mutual responsibility, and standing alongside one another.
A ballot may help shape the political direction of a nation, but it is our daily commitment to volunteerism, civic responsibility, and caring for others that truly defines its soul.
To learn more about the Alyn Hospital Ride or support its participants and the children of Alyn Hospital, visit www.Alynride.org
The writer is deputy director of resource development for Alyn Hospital Friends. Alyn Hospital Pediatric & Adolescent Rehabilitation Center in Jerusalem is a global leader in the active and intensive rehabilitation of children and adolescents with congenital and acquired conditions. Alyn Hospital Friends supports Alyn’s mission to maximize their abilities, foster their independence, and open the door to a life full of possibilities.

Legendary Jewish actor Walter Koenig, 'Star Trek's' plucky Chekov, dies at 90
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:26 UTC
03:52:26 KST

Walter Koenig, who brought humor and grit to the role of starship navigator Pavel Chekov on the classic 1960s sci-fi TV series "Star Trek" and seven subsequent feature films, has died at the age of 90.
"My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," George Takei, who starred alongside Koenig in the show and was a long-time friend, wrote on Facebook on Monday. Koenig died at his home in Los Angeles, the AP reported, citing his talent agent.
"Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry picked Koenig, who had played only a few prior roles on television, when he decided to add a Russian character to the crew of the fictional Starship Enterprise. The introduction of a Russian officer who worked harmoniously with a racially and culturally diverse crew came amid the real-world Cold War tensions of the era.
"We were stating tacitly that peoples of all races and creeds, nationalities could not only co-exist but care for each other deeply, and in doing so we were heralding a future that was very optimistic," Koenig once told a BBC interviewer.
While Koenig was the son of Russian Jewish immigrants, he used an inauthentic Russian accent that was sometimes played for laughs.
Walter Koenig's career as Pavel Chekov on Star Trek
The original TV series ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969. Koenig appeared on 36 episodes, and then in seven movies from 1979 to 1994.
"I was informed while I was still there at my audition that I had the role," Koenig told the Joplin Globe in 2008. "It seemed like an engagement that might work out over several episodes, but I had no idea that it would totally shape my career and my life."
The show remained popular in syndicated reruns and inspired several later TV series and a succession of films. It attracted a devoted worldwide fan base and earned an enduring place in pop culture.
Koenig's "Star Trek" fame was a blessing and a curse, as it was for cast mates such as William Shatner (Captain Kirk), Leonard Nimoy (Spock), DeForest Kelley (Dr. McCoy), Nichelle Nichols (Uhura), James Doohan (Scotty) and Takei, who played Lieutenant Sulu.
They were often typecast because they were so closely associated with "Star Trek."
"Most of the '70s, I didn't work at all, and I blamed it on typecasting," Koenig told the St. Petersburg Times in 1998.
Walter Koenig's life and career beyond Star Trek
He later landed a regular role on the 1990s sci-fi series "Babylon 5" and was an author, script writer and occasional director.
Koenig was born on September 14, 1936, raised in New York City and attended the University of California, Los Angeles, before beginning his professional acting career. He suffered a personal tragedy in 2010 when his son, actor Andrew Koenig, took his own life. Koenig married his wife Judy in 1965. They also had a daughter, actress Danielle Koenig.

====================================================================================================

'Lack of Jews hasn't meant lack of antisemitism,' Expert on Jews in Wales tells 'Post' - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:52:25 UTC
03:52:25 KST

"The absence of Jews in Wales hasn't meant the absence of antisemitism; it's actually the opposite," Bangor University Professor and expert in Welsh Jewry, Professor Nathan Abrams, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Abrams was born into a Jewish family in North London but has lived in Wales for twenty years and speaks Welsh fluently.
He recently published a book, Jews in the Welsh Imagination: Medieval Times to the Present, which explores the nation's attitudes towards Jews over the centuries.
“For most of Wales’s existence as an entity – for 15 centuries – there have been no Jews here. The fascination the Welsh have with Jews is inversely proportional to the numbers," he said. "So the absence of Jews hasn't meant the absence of antisemitism or similar attitudes. It's actually the opposite."
According to the 2021 UK Census, 2,044 people in Wales identified as Jewish by religion, representing approximately 0.07% of Wales's population of 3.1 million.
Most of Wales' Jews are located in Cardiff, where there are two synagogues: a Reform synagogue and an Orthodox synagogue. A Chabad synagogue also serves Llandudno, and small community-organized groups or individual Jews exist in other cities.
Antisemitism in Wales often overshadowed by wider UK statistics
Jews in Wales are not a commonly discussed topic in Jewish media, and reporting on antisemitism in the nation is often swallowed by wider UK statistics, which do not typically show breakdowns by country.
The latest Welsh policing figures show 6,157 police-recorded hate crimes across Wales between April 2025 and March 2026, including 4,098 motivated by race and 325 motivated by religion.
Of those, 325 had a religious motivation, down from 451; however, there is no breakdown of which religion was targeted, so it is not possible from these figures to determine the number of anti-Jewish crimes.
The UK's Community Security Trust, however, separately recorded 25 antisemitic incidents geographically associated with Wales during calendar year 2025, including 13 in North Wales, 8 in South Wales, 2 in Dyfed-Powys and 2 in Gwent.
Separately, a Freedom of Information disclosure from Dyfed-Powys Police shows the force recorded 17 crimes classified as anti-Jewish in 2025, up from 12 in 2024, an increase of about 42%.
The figures are for the Dyfed-Powys policing area, not all Wales. They also do not necessarily capture every antisemitic offense recorded under other categories. It also, of course, differs from the CST reporting, suggesting that on-the-ground figures may far exceed those ultimately reported to CST.
While the available national police statistics do not establish how many anti-Jewish crimes occurred specifically in Wales, the number is clearly high enough to be deemed serious, as the Welsh Local Government Association (WLGA) recently met with Jewish community representatives from across Wales to discuss tackling antisemitism.
During the meeting, Jewish community representatives spoke about growing anxiety about antisemitism, including routine verbal abuse, concerns about children in schools and people changing their behavior to avoid identifying as Jewish in public.
The South Wales Jewish Representative Council said: “The Welsh Jewish community is long-established and deeply rooted."
"We are a resilient community, but there is no doubt that the rise in antisemitism in recent years has left many people shaken and concerned."
Forms, sources of antisemitism in Wales
What forms does antisemitism take in Wales, and who does it come from?
"In a sense, it's a microcosm of England, and similarly a lot of the antisemitism is on social media," Abrams told the Post. "Obviously, a lot of it coalesces around the Israel-Palestine conflict."
Abrams referenced the phenomenon known as "ambient antisemitism," which speaks to the impact demonstrations, ripping down posters, putting up stickers, ripping down stickers, and the like have on creating an environment that is hostile to Jews.
"It's not specifically hurting Jews, physically, but it creates an environment in which Jews are not comfortable being themselves. And I think that's quite a good way to describe it here."
Abrams' experience of antisemitism, he continued, is shaped by living in the northwest of Wales, which is highly nationalist, Welsh-speaking and supportive of Plaid Cymru, the left-leaning Welsh nationalist political party.
Plaid Cymru's official stance is critical of Israel and very supportive of Palestine. It has long campaigned for Palestinian State recognition, and deems Israel's actions to be genocide. In September 2025, the party leader called for "harsh sanctions against the Israeli Government" in light of its actions in Gaza.
"Wales has always been a place where there's been eyes on Palestine. It fits in with the narrative that the Welsh Nationalists have of themselves. The first colony of the British Empire was the Welsh, so [they see themselves as] the Palestinians of the British."
"Because of this, the antisemitism here is kind of an obsession with Israel," Abrams continued. "You'll get the antisemitism that's expressed by people who don't think they're being antisemitic."
"The position I would take [in Wales] is that many people are well-meaning but cross the line into antisemitism through repetition of age-old tropes. They won't know that this emphasis on killing babies has been used throughout history."
Abrams also noted a class difference in Wales regarding who cares about Israel-Palestine and who does not.
"If you're working class, you probably don't care; you probably hate the demonstrators more. Whereas the middle-class protesters are kind of indistinguishable from the academic antisemitism."
"A lot of it is not expressed in front of Jews, because Welsh society is polite. Older, middle-class Brits, right, aren't so vulgar as to be openly racist."
"So I would say across Wales, outside of the metropolises, it's older white people, do-gooders, right thinking, wrong application."
As discussed in his book, Welsh attitudes towards Jews started with Israel and now, 1600 years later, have returned full circle.
"The complexity of Jewishness is still reduced to the Middle East conflict," Abrams concluded.

France: Lawmakers must reject regressive “Rioters Pay” bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:50:43 UTC
03:50:43 KST

France’s proposed bill to make demonstrators pay for damage caused to property by acts of violence in street protests, even if they did not directly cause it themselves, will have a chilling effect on freedom of peaceful assembly and must be rejected by lawmakers, Amnesty International said ahead of a two-day debate in the Senate.
This bill threatens to further deter people from exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly
Nathalie Godard, Amnesty International France
If passed, the legislation commonly referred to as the “Rioters Pay” bill, could hold individuals liable for acts they did not personally commit, provided they ‘knowingly’ participated in a gathering where acts of violence, theft, destruction, or property damage took place. A protester could be liable to pay up to 10,000 euros; in addition, social benefits could be seized if compensation is not paid, which risks plunging already marginalised families further into poverty. Parents may also be held civilly liable for acts that their children did not commit.
“This bill, coming on the back of a series of legal amendments to restrict the right of protest in France, threatens to further deter people from taking to the streets to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” said Nathalie Godard, Director of the Action Department at Amnesty International France.
“Holding protesters responsible – and making them pay – for acts committed by others creates a risk of arbitrary punishment and would be contrary to France’s international obligations. If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step, and it must be categorially rejected by lawmakers.”
Under international law, those participating in demonstrations may only be held responsible for their own conduct and any such responsibility must be based on evidence of individual culpability.
If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step, and it must be categorially rejected by lawmakers
Natalie Goddard, Amnesty International France
Under current French law, family social security allowances and housing benefits are generally protected from seizure to recover debts. The bill introduces additional exceptions to this protection, allowing these benefits to be seized to recover compensation. This would include where damage is caused by children and would reduce the financial support available to families to meet their essential needs and costs. The bill further allows for the possibility of seizing payments from the Active Solidarity Income (Revenu de Solidarité Active), a benefit designed to provide a minimum income for people who would otherwise have no or very low income.
“Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people, impacting their ability to access an adequate standard of living for themselves and their families,” said Natalie Goddard.
The proposed bill also expands the scope of the penalty of exclusion from French territory for people who are ‘foreign nationals’ and who have been found guilty of certain serious offences committed during public gatherings. These include attacks against the physical integrity of others, serious damage to property, such as arson, and aggravated theft or looting.
Amnesty International calls on the lawmakers to ensure that in no case should the penalty of expulsion from French territory result in the violation of the principle of non-refoulement, which is absolute and prohibits the expulsion of anyone, regardless of status, to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or human rights violations.
“Existing law already allows for the penalty of expulsion from French territory. We are therefore deeply concerned that this amendment may introduce xenophobic rhetoric into the legislative debate, and further fuel the scapegoating of refugees, migrants, asylum seekers and minorities,” said Nathalie Godard.
Background
The bill is due to be debated by the French Senate on 27 and 28 October.
The French government announced the proposed bill titled “Compensation for damage resulting from violence or property damage in public spaces and the recovery of damages” in the summer of 2026, following the incidents of violence and property damage during the UEFA Champions League final in May 2026. The French authorities put this bill on the parliamentary agenda and initiated an accelerated procedure for its consideration in the context of the ongoing protests in France, which started on 31 August 2026 in the overseas territories and from 18 September in Metropolitan France.

As artificial intelligence pioneer Anthropic prepares to go public, the company has warned users—including scientists—on Monday that advanced models may be delayed because of cybersecurity and safety threats that risk eclipsing the models’ benefits.
In documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission ahead of Anthropic’s expected initial public offering, the AI lab vowed to weigh the effects of its models on the public good before issuing any new products.
“Moving quickly brings AI’s benefits sooner, but moving too quickly could outrun the world’s ability to make AI systems safe,” the company wrote.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In the filing, Anthropic acknowledged that its future relies on outpacing its competition in developing increasingly capable and complex large language models. But it also raised the risk of its AI being used for harmful purposes, such as developing biological or chemical weapons.
“We deploy technical safeguards, including automated classifiers, specifically intended to detect and block these categories of misuse,” the company warned. “But such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented.” The comments reflect a debate among AI experts over what adequate safety testing looks like in light of repeated AI breaches and hacks.
Still, Anthropic highlighted the potential for new discoveries in biology and medical sciences as a key pathway to profitability—the company currently runs at a loss in the billions of dollars. Anthropic cited its life sciences laboratory, which recently discovered a segment of DNA that bears some resemblance to CRISPR, as an example of how it could access new markets. Even that expansion presents dangers, the company acknowledged, because more traditional science and research is outside its current area of expertise.
“These activities expose us to categories of liability, including for workplace injury and environmental contamination, that differ from those associated with our core business,” the company acknowledged.
Anthropic also warned investors that the company will like make investments into compute power that could appear “irresponsibly large at first glance.” Those vast sums of money are part of a bet that AI will have “wild exponential” growth.
“In order to fully capture the opportunity in front of us, we need to invest more aggressively than would a business that operates in a more slowly changing technological regime,” the company wrote.

Google Fitbit Edge Review: I Still Prefer the Air (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:49:49 UTC
03:49:49 KST

The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
TIRED
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.
Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.
At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.
A Screen Has Its Perks
The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.
As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.
I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.
The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.
I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.
Two Steps Forward, One Step Back
The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.
Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.
Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)
The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.
Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.
The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.
The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.
Boutayna Chokrane is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering consumer wearables, wellness tech, and online trends. She specializes in smartwatches, fitness trackers, beauty tech, and more. Before joining the Gear team, she was a music editorial fellow at Pitchfork. She also worked as a freelance journalist, covering fashion, ... Read More

U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jet to get hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:46 UTC
03:47:46 KST

- Castelion received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic missile onto the F-16.
- The company did not disclose the value or timeline, and the U.S. Navy has already ordered 444 Blackbeard missiles for production.
Hypersonic missile startup Castelion has received a contract modification from the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin integrating its Blackbeard hypersonic weapon onto the F-16 fighter jet, the company announced on Oct. 26, bringing the missile one step closer to the U.S. Air Force after earlier work for the U.S. Navy and U.S. Army.
Castelion did not disclose the value of the modification, how long the integration work will take, or when the first test launch from an F-16 could happen, and the U.S. Air Force has not commented on the award.
“Castelion has been awarded a contract modification to its existing work with the Air Force Research Laboratory to begin Blackbeard integration activities with the F-16. We are grateful to the Air Force for their trust,” the company wrote on X.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering inside the atmosphere, which makes it harder to intercept than a ballistic missile on a predictable arc, and Castelion has built the program around producing it cheaply and in large numbers. The company, founded in 2022 by former SpaceX engineers and based in Torrance, California, is building a factory campus in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, aimed at turning out 500 weapons a year.
The Air Force Research Laboratory added $16.4 million to an existing Castelion contract in September, raising its total value to $37.2 million, for work on a low-cost, mass-producible long-range strike weapon running through June 2028. Castelion described the F-16 award as a modification to its existing work with the laboratory, though it did not say whether it falls under that same contract.
The U.S. Navy is furthest along with the weapon. It awarded $105 million in April to integrate Blackbeard onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and carry out live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific, ordered 50 early operational capability weapons in June, and in August awarded nearly $90 million to move Blackbeard toward a formal program of record, including features meant to speed sales to allies. In September, the Navy placed a first production order worth up to $200 million for 444 missiles. The U.S. Army received an integration award in October 2025 for a ground-launched version compatible with the HIMARS rocket launcher.
Putting Blackbeard on the F-16 would give it a launch platform far more common than the Super Hornet. The F-16 remains the most numerous fighter in the U.S. Air Force and flies with more than two dozen other countries, although Castelion has not said whether the integration work covers export versions of the jet.

Ukraine Extends Martial Law and Mobilization Until Jan. 29
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:47:02 UTC
03:47:02 KST

Ukraine has extended martial law and general mobilization for another 90 days, until Jan. 29, 2027, as Russia’s full-scale invasion continues in its fifth year.
Since February 2022, both measures have been renewed every three months. On Monday, Oct. 26, President Volodymyr Zelensky signed laws No. 5029-IX on martial law and No. 5030-IX on mobilization after they were approved by the parliament on the same day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Both laws take effect on Oct. 31, when the current extension expires, Ukrinform reported.
Decrees cite ongoing Russian aggression
The laws Zelensky signed approve two presidential decrees; No. 1060/2026 on extending martial law and No. 1061/2026 on extending general mobilization, which required parliament’s consent to take effect.
The martial law decree points to Russia’s continuing large-scale armed aggression against Ukraine as the reason for the extensions.
It was issued on a proposal from the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC), under Article 106 of Ukraine’s Constitution and the law on the legal regime of martial law. The decree amends Article 1 of Decree No. 64/2022 of Feb. 24, 2022, which first introduced martial law nationwide.
Parliament backs extension
According to Ukrinform, lawmakers approved both measures earlier on Monday, after parliament’s committee on national security, defense and intelligence had endorsed them.
Bill No. 16182, approving the martial law decree, received 293 votes, while Bill No. 16183, covering mobilization, passed with 281 in favor.
Trump’s Diesel Scam Backfires
Speaking in parliament ahead of the vote, NSDC Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine Ihor Klymenko said the extension would help Ukraine take “adequate measures to counter armed aggression.” The move would also safeguard the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, he argued.
According to Klymenko, the extension also keeps in force the special powers held by state authorities, the military command, military administrations and local governments, which they need to repel the invasion.
Deferment rules tightened days earlier
The extension comes days after Prime Minister Serhii Koretsky’s government finalized an overhaul of Ukraine’s worker deferment system on Oct. 23, effectively ending automatic exemptions from mobilization for defense and energy companies.
Unless they qualify for a deferment due to health-related issues or work, Ukrainian law requires men aged 25 to 60 to serve in the military. Under the previous rules, most critical companies could defer up to 50% of their draft-age employees, while defense and energy firms have been allowed to defer up to 100%.
The latest overhaul ends automatic 100% protection and aims to create fair rules for those working away from the front, and, above all, for soldiers who have been fighting for nearly five years and need a realistic chance to return home.
“Unconditional full deferment is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to misuse,” Koretskyi said earlier, adding that some companies had been set up purely to obtain deferments and that “it became a business.”
The new approach makes full protection conditional – companies can keep their entire workforce only in case they contribute to the military on a rotating basis.
“The ultimate goal is that no one has to search for anyone on the streets,” Koretskyi said, in an apparent reference to recruiters forcibly detaining men in public.
Defense manufacturers have already lobbied against the new measures, noting that lowering the quota, even to 85%, could halt production lines, delay weapons deliveries and expose companies to penalties for missing state contract lines.
Speaking at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Monday, Koretskyi reiterated that Russia could mobilize another 300,000 to 500,000 people. Without planning ahead, he argued, Kyiv could again be forced into unpopular emergency decisions.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree No. 700, increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel, marking the fourth time such a decree was signed in 2026 alone.
Around the same time, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia had already begun additional mobilization, including the expansion of foreign troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.

tactile contours and weighted bases shape ergonomic chess set in white oak and walnut

tactile contours and weighted bases shape ergonomic chess set in white oak and walnut
lucy aboonour develops flora, a chess set milled from american white oak and walnut featuring low-center-of-gravity weighting and ergonomic contours optimized for tactile recognition and pinch-grip play.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
CHESS SET designed FOR TACTILE RECOGNITION AND PINCH-GRIP PLAY
Designed by industrial designer Lucy Aboonour, Flora is a tactile chess set engineered to be recognized, grasped, and maneuvered primarily through touch rather than sight. Developed over a four-year period of observational research across New York City parks and chess clubs, the project addresses common ergonomic shortcomings in contemporary minimalist sets, where visual abstraction often impedes rapid piece identification and tactile handling during competitive play.
full set – top view | all images ©Lucy Aboonour
CONVEX OAK AND WALNUT PROFILES INTEGRATE PINCH-GRIP CONTOURS
Each of the six piece typologies features a wide footprint, a tapered silhouette, and a weighted base configured with an intentionally low center of gravity to prevent tipping. The piece profiles incorporate convex curvatures calibrated specifically for a two-finger pinch grip, distributing fingertip pressure to maintain hand stability during quick movements. Following iterative 3D printed prototyping in recycled PLA and wood composites between 2021 and 2025, the final set was milled in contrasting American white oak and American walnut. Extending beyond terrestrial gameplay, Designer Lucy Aboonour’s ergonomic research examines how tactile recognition, haptic feedback, and grip dynamics perform in microgravity environments, considering applications for hand-operated interfaces and instrumentation on orbital stations.

Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:44:31 UTC
03:44:31 KST

Microsoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce.
This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally.
Some of Microsoft’s most recognizable divisions – including Xbox, Windows and Copilot, its AI tool – will be participating in the offer, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Employees in certain divisions, including in cybersecurity, datacenters and marketing, would not be eligible for the offer, it said.
“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said in a statement. The company did not respond to a request for comment on further details about the offer.
Multiple tech companies have announced layoffs due to the rise of AI and increased investment in the technology this year. Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, announced plans in April to cut 10% of its personnel, or about 8,000 employees, to boost efficiency. Amazon has made several cuts to its workforce, most recently in its retail division. And in June, Oracle shed its workforce by nearly 13%, cutting 21,000 jobs, as a result of AI.
But it’s unclear whether these workforce-reduction measures have translated yet into greater efficiency, and some companies, including Meta, have scaled back their layoff plans. A top leader of Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky, recently complained about “AI slop” in the workforce on social media.
The National Bureau of Economic Research also recently published a working paper which found that among the 9,000 senior executives it surveyed from around the world, 90% said AI had yet to result in greater productivity at their companies.

Economy Ministry begins developing Ukraine's industrial strategy through 2030, plans to present it in three months
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:43:53 EET
03:43:53 KST

The Ministry of Economy and Environment has begun developing Ukraine's industrial strategy through 2030 and plans to present a draft for discussion with the professional community over the course of three months, Deputy Minister Vitaliy Kindrativ said.
According to him, the Federation of Employers of Ukraine (FEU), the Institute of Economic Modeling, relevant industry associations, and experts are involved in drafting the document.
"Our priority today is, on the one hand, to support the domestic manufacturing industry, and on the other hand, to help it enter foreign markets," the deputy minister emphasized during the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) titled "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" on Monday in Kyiv, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Kindrativ said the strategy will focus on sectors with high added value and the potential to enter foreign markets, particularly in mechanical engineering, the manufacturing sector, and agricultural processing.
He said that once work on the document is completed, it will be discussed with relevant business associations, whose input will form the basis for its final approval by the government. Furthermore, in his view, a clear definition of priority sectors and government support programs will serve as an important signal for attracting foreign investment and capital into the Ukrainian economy.
For his part, CEO of the Federation of Ukrainian Industries (FUI) Ruslan Illichov said the document must be based on the real needs of domestic businesses.
"This strategy must be built, first and foremost, on an understanding of the perspectives of the industries operating in Ukraine. We must take our most competitive existing industries and ask what they need to scale up," the FRU head said.
Illichov added that key components of the document should also include maximizing localization in large government and infrastructure projects and coordinating a common industrial policy with European partners to integrate Ukraine into EU markets.

The Verge reported that the program would allow Microsoft to reduce its workforce without another round of layoffs, months after the company cut 4,800 jobs, primarily in Xbox and commercial sales.
The outlet also cited a Fortune report that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma was planning further layoffs.
The new initiative follows a voluntary retirement program earlier this year that covered approximately 9,000 US employees whose combined age and years of service totaled at least 70, according to The Verge.

Ukrainian forces evacuate 2 severely wounded soldiers from battlefield using drone, video shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:42:57 UTC
03:42:57 KST

Ukrainian forces evacuate 2 severely wounded soldiers from battlefield using drone, video shows
Ukraine's 475th Separate Assault Regiment Code 9.2 evacuated two severely wounded soldiers from the battlefield using a domestically developed aerial evacuation drone, StarGate, the unit reported on Oct. 26.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign "Izium," and 24-year-old Artem, call sign "Kolobok," had suffered severe limb injuries and were stranded in a contested area about five kilometers (three miles) from the Russian border.
Ground evacuation was impossible due to difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones, the regiment said.
The two evacuation missions were carried out over the course of a week in cooperation with SkyFall, the Ukrainian company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units and fire support from heavy Vampire attack drones to suppress Russian positions.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers (20 miles) to reach a wounded soldier and approximately the same distance back with him aboard.
Russian electronic warfare systems attempted to jam satellite navigation signals in the area, but the drone completed the evacuation using its AI-based navigation system and the pilots' skills, according to the regiment.
Oleksandr Nastenko, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, said the unit plans to use the experience to train additional crews and make aerial evacuations a regular practice.
The operations come a week after Ukrainian forces reported what they described as a first-of-its-kind aerial evacuation of a severely wounded soldier who had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position, using a drone.

UN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after truce
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:41:52 CET
03:41:52 KST

GENEVA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Israel continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, a UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel dismissed as part of a “misinformation campaign”.
The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel examined violations against Palestinian children since the start of the war between Israel and Hamas on October 7, 2023 up to September this year.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”, and that the situation had also continued to deteriorate in the occupied West Bank.
Another report by the commission in September last year found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts — accusations that Israel called scandalous.
The Israeli mission in Geneva said the latest report was part of a misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel.
“The attempt to destroy the Jewish state … continues today through efforts by actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself,” Ambassador Daniel Meron said in a statement.
HEAVY MUNITIONS HIT POPULATED AREAS, COMMISSION SAYS
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.
It said the “Yellow Line” which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
In its report to the UN Security Council, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and October 6, 2023, to 254 between October 7, 2023 and September 30, 2026.
Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank formed part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.
Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and human rights defenders had been killed and injured.
(Reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin, writing by Kirsti Knolle)

Australian billionaire James Packer paid at least $1.25 million – 1.78 million Australian dollars or 3.85 million shekels – to the law firm of Amit Hadad, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's attorney, the Australian newspaper The Age reported Monday.
Packer is also a witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial, in which Hadad represents the prime minister.
The investigation, published on the eve of Israel's election, uncovered a trail of monthly bank transfers of $50,000 over the past two years, from a bank account controlled by Packer's company to the account of the law firm representing Netanyahu.
On the same day the investigation was published, Hadad filed a motion on behalf of Netanyahu's defense team requesting that Packer and two of his employees be allowed to testify from abroad, with their testimony broadcast by video link to the judges in Israel.
According to the investigation, the first monthly payment was made on September 23, 2024, from a Citibank account belonging to Packer's legal firm to an account held by Hadad, Roth, Shenhar at Mizrahi Tefahot Bank. A source familiar with the details reportedly said the payments urgently needed to be investigated to determine whether Netanyahu had received an undisclosed benefit from Packer.
Packer insisted that the bank transfers to Netanyahu's lawyers were payments for work carried out on his behalf, including "deal finding" in Israel, where he has business interests, and that they were unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
The Australian newspaper also reported that a Netanyahu spokesperson asked for comment replied: "I couldn't give a monkey's about your questions. We are very busy. We have an election on right now."
Packer did not deny making the monthly payments but declined to comment. Hadad also declined to comment.
Packer's representatives responded that the law firm represents him in his "personal and business affairs." "Any claim that I paid even a single cent toward the legal defense of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is false. Anyone who claims otherwise risks being sued."
Packer was expected to testify as a key prosecution witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial in Case 1000, in which he and businessman Arnon Milchan are alleged to have provided Netanyahu and his wife with gifts and other benefits worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.
Packer gave a statement to police during the investigation, but in February 2024, prosecutors announced that they would not call him to testify at the trial. During the phase of the trial devoted to prosecution witnesses, prosecutors were unable to contact Packer to arrange for him to travel to Israel.
Meanwhile, attorney Amit Hadad filed a motion on Netanyahu's behalf Monday requesting that Packer and two of his employees, Ben Tilley and Guy Jolland, be questioned abroad. The defense requested that their testimony be broadcast by video link to the judges in Jerusalem, as was the testimony given by Arnon Milchan from England during the trial.
During the cross-examination of Hadas Klein, Packer's former personal assistant in Israel, the defense submitted letters from Tilley and Jolland challenging her testimony that most of the champagne and cigars purchased for Packer went to Netanyahu and his wife.
In the motion, Hadad stated that he represents Packer in Israel on matters unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
In the letters, the two described their visits to Israel between 2013 and 2016, when they were members of Packer's staff. Tilley testified that he smoked a cigar every evening during each of the 83 days he spent in Israel, as did Ian Morris, another Packer employee.
Jolland described the hospitality at Packer's properties, including a suite at the Royal Beach Hotel in Tel Aviv and a villa he purchased in Caesarea. He claimed that the properties were always stocked with food and wine for entertaining guests, including a supply of rosé champagne, and that Packer himself regularly drank rosé champagne.
Hadad is seeking to call Packer, Tilley and Jolland as defense witnesses to challenge the testimony of Klein and driver Yonatan Hasson regarding the quantities of cigars and champagne transferred from Packer to the Netanyahu family.
Hadad explained that the defense has no way to compel the witnesses, who live abroad, to testify in Israel because they refuse to travel there. However, they have indicated that they would comply with any lawful court order issued by the courts in their countries of residence.
He attached a letter written by Jolland on Packer's behalf, stating that Packer refuses to come to Israel because of the treatment he received from law enforcement authorities.
Netanyahu had a close personal relationship with Packer, which also involved attempts to advance business and media interests. Packer, who came to Israel in 2013 through businessman Arnon Milchan, grew close to Netanyahu and admired him.
One of the clearest signs of their relationship was Packer's purchase of a villa next to the Netanyahu family home in Caesarea, after Netanyahu encouraged him to buy it. The Netanyahu family treated the property almost as their own home. Family members had dinner there and sometimes took boxes of cigars and cases of champagne from the house. Netanyahu also regularly swam in his neighbor's pool.
Packer also developed a friendship with Netanyahu's son Yair, who frequently stayed at Packer's properties, including the Royal Beach Hotel, a penthouse at Robert De Niro's hotel in New York, a villa in the ski resort town of Aspen, Colorado, and a yacht moored in Ibiza.
Testifying at his trial last year, Netanyahu confirmed that Milchan had introduced him to Packer at a dinner. "My impression of him was positive, and I think it was mutual," Netanyahu said. "We developed an emotional connection. I'm good at reading people, as I always have been, and I could see that he was genuinely someone who, I would say, had no ulterior motives. What he wanted was closeness."
Netanyahu also claimed that Packer had told him he was the most impressive person he had ever met.
