====================================================================================================

Childcare is undergoing a 'reckoning' but safety gaps remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:11 UTC
03:30:11 KST

Australian child care is undergoing a reckoning, but some centres remain unsafe
When Christina Spark toured Little Zak's Academy in the Sydney suburb of Gladesville early last year, it seemed like the perfect place to enrol her one-year-old.
"The playground was shiny, they had soccer and yoga and swimming," she said. "I was pretty blown away and amazed."
Within weeks, Spark started to notice hygiene issues, dietary instructions not being followed, her little boy's milk bottle coming home unused and babies sitting in soiled nappies.
"The underlying problem was just a lack of supervision … and not enough people," she said.
Then the incidents started to pile up. One bite turned into two and by October her child, now 19 months old, had been bitten five times.
After months of mounting concerns, Spark pulled her son out and used her skills as an auditor to dig into the centre and the chain behind it.
"If I [had] just looked up who owns the centre, done a little bit of digging, realised the number of enforcement actions, realised the level of profits being generated, I wouldn't have sent him there, but I just didn't know," she said.
Little Zak's is one of the country's fastest-growing childcare chains, generating $142 million in revenue and $17 million in profit in 2025.
The family-owned business also has the highest proportion of centres subject to enforcement action among the country's 26 largest long daycare operators.
'It's child abuse'
At the Little Zak's centre at Shellharbour, two hours south of Sydney, the warning signs had been building for months.
Leigh Cotter said he initially blew off the incidents as kids being kids, but when they started to escalate, he raised concerns.
"I said, 'Look, you guys really need to do something about the safety of kids, because if you don't, something serious is going to happen.'
"A month later, my son broke his leg in daycare, and I don't think they were completely honest about how it happened."
Cotter said the centre told him his son was wearing socks indoors and had slipped and hit his head and left ankle just before pick-up.
When he took him to the hospital, the doctors discovered a spiral fracture on the other leg, running from his ankle towards his knee.
Cotter said an educator later told him his son had been screaming in another room much earlier in the day, but staff had not realised he was seriously injured.
"Six hours of walking on a broken leg — it's child abuse," Cotter said.
Four Corners put the claims to Little Zak's but it did not comment for privacy reasons.
Since Cotter pulled his son from Little Zak's Shellharbour in May 2023, the centre has faced repeated parent complaints and regulatory action.
In the past two years alone, it has been subject to four enforcement actions, including an emergency action notice over staffing ratios, which is the minimum number of educators legally required for the children in care.
In August, regulators issued a further compliance notice.
The centre has also been downgraded from Meeting the National Quality Standard to Working Towards, which means it is no longer meeting the nationally agreed standards for child care.
Gabrielle Meagher, an emeritus professor at Macquarie University, has spent decades researching privatised social services including child care.
Her analysis of the country's 26 largest long-daycare providers found the proportion of Little Zak's centres subject to enforcement action was 10 percentage points higher than the next highest, Edge Early Learning, which entered voluntary administration in August.
Meagher says 56 per cent of Little Zak's centres are recorded on Starting Blocks as having been subject to enforcement action in the past two years.
She says the chain has experienced rapid expansion. The company grew from 16 centres in 2021 to about 43 today.
A deeper analysis of regulatory records reveals the regulator confirmed almost 600 breaches at Little Zak's centres between 2020 and September 2025.
Of these, 181 were linked to inadequate supervision, inappropriate discipline and failures to protect children from harm and hazards.
At September 2025 staff turnover was 79 per cent, which is equivalent to almost eight departures for every 10 employees in its average workforce over the year.
Childcare sector faces 'reckoning'
But the problems uncovered at Little Zak's are not isolated.
Four Corners has analysed thousands of regulatory records from across the sector, examined internal company documents, spoken to parents and educators and obtained CCTV as part of an investigation into child safety across Australia's $23 billion childcare sector.
It has uncovered serious failures at some major operators and examined the gaps that remain despite sweeping government reforms.
ABC Investigations has been uncovering systemic failures in child care for the past 18 months.
Early Childhood Education Minister Jess Walsh says those stories have had a profound impact on the sector.
"There has been a reckoning in this system over the past 12 months, and it is changing in no small part because of the way in which you have shone a light on the problems in early learning," she said.
The revelations have triggered a series of reforms including tougher penalties, mandatory child-safety training, a national worker register, tighter Working With Children Check requirements, greater powers for regulators and new powers to cut Commonwealth childcare subsidies to poorly performing providers.
"The reforms that we have put in place are the right reforms," Walsh told Four Corners.
"They are on track, and we are seeing the results of those reforms."
So far, 120 services with a history of failing to meet quality and safety standards have been put on notice to improve or risk losing access to Commonwealth subsidies. To date, funding has been withdrawn from 12.
More than 1,300 childcare services are currently failing to meet the national quality standards, accounting for around 48,000 childcare places. About 350 have failed twice in a row and can go on average more than three years between assessments.
"Around half of the services that we have put those conditions on have turned around and have met the quality standards," Walsh said.
"That is what we would like to see, but where they fail to do that or refuse to do that, we are clear that there is no place for those services in early learning."
But a year into the funding crackdown, some big operators with regulatory issues have not been caught by it.
None of Little Zak's centres are on the list, despite a regulatory record spanning dozens of centres and hundreds of confirmed breaches, including failures involving supervision, staffing ratios and protecting children from harm.
Little Zak's said it had restructured its executive management team, including replacing its CEO, and that its focus was the health, safety and wellbeing of children in its care.
It said notifiable incidents and compliance breaches were down following increased investment in staff training and more open communication with families.
"Our focus is on quality and safety in our existing services, not on growth," it said in a statement.
Only About Children (OAC), which is owned by US-listed Bright Horizons, isn't on the list either. In the past two years, more than one in four of OAC's centres have been subject to enforcement action, including for inadequate supervision of children.
In April, OAC's Mosman centre on Sydney's north shore entered into an enforceable undertaking after a child was subjected to inappropriate conduct.
In August, enforcement action was also taken against two OAC centres in Victoria. Brunswick West was cited for inadequate supervision and failing to protect children from harm and hazards.
Coonans Hill was cited for a much broader range of breaches, including inappropriate conduct, inadequate supervision, staffing arrangements, protecting children from harm and hazards, interactions with children, and safety and record-keeping requirements.
"They've got 78 services, and of them, 21 have had enforcement actions against them in the last two years, which is 27 per cent of them, more than a quarter of their services," Meagher said in September. One centre has since been closed.
"That's quite a high number, and it's more than twice as many as the largest not-for-profit."
The public record tells only part of the story.
Four Corners has seen previously secret regulatory records, parent complaints and internal documents detailing thousands of incidents across its centres, including children going missing, serious injuries, failures of supervision and allegations of children being grabbed, dragged and forcibly restrained.
OAC's Williamstown centre in Melbourne's inner west has its own troubling history. Alleged paedophile Joshua Brown, who was committed to trial on 156 charges, worked there in 2020 and 2021, and police have since identified alleged victims from his time at the centre.
In the past two years, Williamstown has also faced two enforcement actions. In July, it was breached for failing to protect children from harm and hazards, as well as breaches of health, hygiene and safe food practices. In September, its quality ratings were slashed from exceeding to "working towards", which means it failed to meet the national quality standards.
The Williamstown centre is slated to close next year and its website says it is not taking any new enrolments.
OAC said in a statement that child safety was its highest priority, that it had a strong reporting culture and acted quickly when problems were identified.
It said more than 97 per cent of services were meeting or exceeding the standards. Services facing enforcement action were down 20 per cent.
For-profit providers still dominate
The Commonwealth has begun using its new powers against some major operators. One is Edge, which has 59 centres across Australia.
"We had very serious safety concerns about that provider," Walsh said. "Since then, we know that Goodstart Early Learning, which is a large quality not-for-profit provider, is in discussions with the administrator to take over some of those services. We're supporting them in that," she said.
Walsh said the Commonwealth had also stopped two large providers from expanding until safety concerns were addressed. One was Edge. She would not name the other.
While experts and advocates say the reforms will make child care safer, they warn they won't fix the deeper structural problems in a sector dominated by for-profit operators.
Georgie Dent, from parent advocacy group The Parenthood, says until the funding model is addressed, little will change.
"I think if we look at the money that is being spent on early education and care from taxpayers via the childcare subsidy to the tune of $16 billion a year … and you look at the out-of-pocket costs that parents are contributing, which is billions and billions of dollars, and you think for the exponential increase in investment, what are we getting?" she said.
"Are we seeing better outcomes for children? Are we seeing better access? Are we seeing better quality services? The answer is no, we're not. Not at scale, not across the board."
She says the problem is not educators or every childcare service, but a funding model that she argues creates the wrong incentives.
"It means our system is not delivering on the objectives of best meeting the needs of children and enabling parents to participate in the workforce," she said.
"Providers have set up in areas where they can charge higher fees. They are far less likely to go and set up in a regional town."
The Commonwealth is trying to change that. Its $1 billion Building Early Education Fund will support up to 160 new or expanded services, with a focus on not-for-profit provision in areas where child care is scarce.
"We do want to see more quality not-for-profit services out there and we're backing that to happen," Walsh says.
But in a sector plagued by childcare deserts, with one in four Australians living in areas where demand outstrips supply, rolling out 160 new or expanded centres will hardly make a difference.
Dent argues a much bigger shift is needed.
"Over 70 per cent of long daycare in Australia is now delivered by for-profit organisations, and that has come at the expense of not-for-profit and community organisations, notwithstanding the fact we know that not-for-profit and community services tend to have higher quality ratings," she said.
In Melbourne's north, parents are fighting to save Merrilands Uniting Early Learning, a not-for-profit long daycare centre that signalled it would close before the end of the year after three for-profit centres opened in the area since April.
"There are [now] six for-profit centres in the area and another one being built that's due to open next year," said one mother, Erica. Another mother, Etta, said one of the reasons she sent her child to Merrilands was that staff had been there for a long time.
"A lot of them [have been there] decades," she said.
"It was just full of heart. There was a lot of warmth in all the staff," said Nikolas, the father of another child.
Non-profit childcare services operate under a different model with any surplus reinvested back into the centre. They are generally cheaper for families, employ more highly qualified staff and perform better on national quality standards. But they are losing ground as for-profit child care expands.
One of the parents who sends their child to Merrilands said the difference could be as much as $70 a day.
"The financial impact is … huge," said one mother, Eman.
For Eman, however, she chose a community-run centre mainly for reasons of safety.
"For me, the deciding factor … was about the lower incident rate. I'm a survivor of child sexual abuse myself, so it was really important to find somewhere where my daughter will be safe," she said.
Walsh says safety is the priority.
"The reforms that we're making are really putting children first. We have made child safety and wellbeing the paramount consideration in early learning as it should always have been," she said.
Putting children first may now be written into law. But in a sector dominated by large for-profit operators, including private equity-backed and listed companies, ensuring children come first will not be easy.

How a shocking death led to the downfall of To Catch a Predator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Explain The Internet: How To Catch a Predator trod the line between justice and entertainment
Welcome to Explain the Internet, where we break down the noise on the World Wide Web with the help of experts.
"Why don't you take a seat right over there?"
It's a question asked by journalist Chris Hansen of dozens of men caught with their metaphorical, and in some cases literal, pants down by the news reality show To Catch a Predator.
Running from 2004 to 2007, the hidden camera show became such a cultural touchstone that it was parodied in the cold open of the 2006 Emmys, with Conan O'Brien playing the part of a distressed accused sexual predator confronted by Hansen in a rented house masquerading as a family home.
A ratings juggernaut for US network NBC, the show ended following a high-profile suicide after one of the program's sting operations.
Almost 20 years later, the program and its host are being put under the microscope by documentarian Lance Oppenheim in his directorial narrative debut, Primetime.
The 30-year-old, whose next project is the highly anticipated Nathen Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, grew up watching To Catch a Predator.
"I'd never seen anything before that had mixed truth and fiction in the way the show had. Hiring adult actors pretending to be children … these houses that would be turned into sets," Oppenheim tells ABC News.
"All of this artifice would collide with the very real high-stakes situation of getting an attempted child predator into the house.
"There was something so odd about the mixture of real-life horror with this sort of surrealist absurdity that came from Hansen."
What is To Catch a Predator?
To Catch a Predator premiered in 2004, originally as a part of NBC's Dateline news program.
A typical segment would include production working with private investigation organisation Perverted-Justice, whose volunteer decoys would pose as children to chat with potential predators.
The decoys would then invite them to a house leased by production with the promise of meeting and sexual activity. After being initially greeted by hired actors playing tweens, Hansen would emerge, questioning the men and revealing the hidden cameras. The men would then be allowed to leave, only to be arrested by local law enforcement. All of which was recorded and broadcast.
To Catch a Predator soon outgrew Dateline, with episodes featuring the segment attracting 13 per cent more audience than those without. By 2006, the show was moved to its own prime time slot on US television, directly competing with ratings juggernaut Lost. This is also around the time To Catch a Predator brought law enforcement officers into the co-ordination of the stings.
Men caught by the program included firefighters, teachers, religious and government workers.
In 2006, a To Catch a Predator sting in Murphy, Texas netted 25 arrests from men arriving at their decoy house. Perverted-Justice volunteers had one more man marked, soon revealed to be local assistant district attorney Louis William "Bill" Conradt.
Production was unable to lure Conradt to their Murphy house, so in coordination with local law enforcement, the decision was made to confront Conradt at his home. After a multi-hour sting, local police sent in a SWAT team to arrest Conradt, who killed himself.
Following the incident, legal issues were found with all arrests made in Murphy, including insufficient evidence and lack of active warrants. In June 2007, a Texas district attorney refused to prosecute any of the 24 men arrested in the sting.
A month later, Conradt's sister brought a $US109 million wrongful death lawsuit against NBC Universal. Although the network initially announced to be fighting the claims, in June 2008 the suit was "amicably resolved" with an undisclosed settlement amount.
To Catch a Predator was cancelled shortly after.
What is Primetime about?
Primetime chronicles the period of time leading up to Conradt's death, loosely based on the 2007 Esquire article Tonight On Dateline, This Man Will Die.
Some characters, like Robert Pattinson's Chris Hansen and Perverted-Justice founder Xavier Von Erck (Matthew Maher), are based on real people. Some, like Merritt Wever's stern producer and Skyler Gisondo's starry-eyed "Decoy Dan" are an amalgamation of several real people involved in the story.
And some like Jeff Zucker, the former NBC Universal CEO who moved To Catch a Predator into its prime-time slot to compete with Lost, simply play themselves.
"I liked this idea of being able to mix truth and fiction in a way that almost was an homage to the show and the way the show created almost this reality-distortion field," Oppenheim says.
"When people would enter it, they would no longer be a part of the world we all exist in. They were a part of Chris Hansen's world."
Oppenheim paid particular care to the characters playing "predators": young men; older men; a rabbi who demands to know who gave Hansen permission to conduct the sting; a man with cerebral palsy.
"It was interesting to present the predators in a similar way to how Chris Hansen would experience it, to how his crew would experience it," Oppenheim says.
"The attempt to sort of deny any form of humanity to these people and see them as almost a form, a token of entertainment. They almost became commercial objects in this sort of space race against Lost."
How to keep children safe
Hansen has condemned Primetime as "detached from reality", going so far as to buy ad space before US screenings to promote his streaming service TruBlu, where he still conducts predator investigations.
In Australia, child safety in online spaces remains an issue, with a 2025 eSafety report revealing one in four girls experience online sexual solicitation by an adult before they turn 18.
Cybersecurity and privacy expert Joel Scanlan is the academic co-lead of the CSAM Deterrence Centre, working with the technology industry and other stakeholders to prevent the access and sharing of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).
"To Catch a Predator did raise awareness of this harm occurring, and that is great, because the awareness of the level of harm that's occurring online is actually pretty low," Scanlan says.
"However, it is doing it for entertainment. The motivations aren't there. So many of those cases got thrown out or overturned. What if it had just been law enforcement in the first place and not all those other elements?"
Scanlan says there needs to be a "generational shift" in how we view online safety for children and that the solution lies in robust prevention, including education, deterrence messages, legislation like Australia's social media delay and higher expectations of online companies.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $23.6 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial.
"To stop this kind of crime that's happening at this large a scale, we need five or 10 different approaches as there is no quick fix," he says.
Scanlan points towards the Stop It Now! Australia program, Australia's first national child sexual abuse offending prevention service, as an effective tool for harm prevention.
Launched locally in 2022 by Jesuit Social Services, the program includes a free phone helpline and resources for anyone concerned about their own sexual thoughts or behaviours toward children, or about the behaviour of someone else.
The program received federal funding in April 2026 as a part of the National Strategy to Prevent and Respond to Child Sexual Abuse 2021-2030.
"People ask, 'Why are you sympathising with them?' But I do work in this space. I see the horrific scale of the problem. We need to have less harm happen," Scanlan says.
"If that means we need to get people in therapy, let's do it. That's it. That's literally abuse prevention."
Primetime will be in Australian cinemas from October 29.

Why a big discount during Black Friday sales isn't necessarily a great deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Why a big discount during Black Friday sales isn’t necessarily a great deal
This year Black Friday falls on Friday, November 27.
Cyber Monday, which typically marks the end of the sale period, is on November 30.
It is becoming hard to miss in Australia, with competing offers vying for our attention in emails, texts, app notifications and shop windows.
Black Friday sales originated in the United States as a way for retailers to make money after Thanksgiving Day, says Sara Quach Thaichon, an associate professor in marketing at Griffith University on the Gold Coast/Yugambeh language region.
But it has now become part of the Australian retail calendar and November is "almost a whole sale season" with deals beginning weeks in advance, Dr Thaichon says.
You can expect retailers to promote offers of "up to 50 per cent off" and "up to 70 per cent off", but most discounts fall closer to 20 or 30 per cent off, she says.
Mark Serrels, the editorial director at consumer group Choice on Gadigal land in Sydney, says the Black Friday "behemoth" is expanding every year.
But before tapping a card or clicking "buy", Mr Serrels and Dr Thaichon recommend considering the value of the purchase to you, its quality and how much you're spending — rather than just how much you are saving.
Why percentage discounts can be deceiving
While there are savings to be made, Mr Serrels says, there are "a million different ways retailers are using Black Friday to their advantage".
"[For example], they're trying to get rid of stock. They're trying to get rid of older models. They're trying to get you hooked into giving your details so they can reach out and sell more things down the line."
Sometimes products are advertised as 50 per cent off the recommended retail price (RRP) during a promotion period, but it might normally be 40 per cent off anyway.
"You've got to be wary of those markdowns," Mr Serrels says.
Dr Thaichon says the percentage discount can make us feel like we've scored a bargain but "doesn't actually tell us whether the final price is good".
If it's an inferior product or something you simply don't need, you've wasted money buying it, even if it was 70 per cent off, she says.
Mr Serrels says that an expensive pre-sale RPP price does not equate to quality.
"Sometimes you might think, 'oh great, that TV is 50 per cent off', but it's a shit TV, so don't buy it," he says.
"We've had coffee machines that cost $200 that outperformed $2,000 [machines in testing]."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Finding a good deal
Dr Thaichon recommends focusing on how much you're spending and what you're getting for that money.
"Instead of looking at percentage, compare the final price across different retailers, think about the quality of the product, how long it will last and how often [you will] actually use it," she says.
Research the product and compare prices before sales begin, particularly when it comes to white goods and electronics, Dr Thaichon says.
When we don't know much about "big ticket" products we tend to use price as an indicator of quality, she says.
Electronics and appliances tend to be the "most heavily promoted categories", Dr Thaichon says, and major retailers have previously offered discounts of as much as 70 per cent off on some specific products.
Mr Serrels says you should decide on the exact product you want to buy — such as the model of TV — beforehand.
This gives you the opportunity to check reviews and the product's historical pricing.
Recognising scams
Slowing down is "key", Dr Thaichon says.
Mr Serrels says to try to avoid the influence of time pressure when shopping during sales, such as "you've got four minutes to complete this transaction" or "this sale only lasts for 12 hours".
"Worst case scenario it's a scam. Best case scenario you're getting bullied into buying something you're not really 100 per cent sure you actually need."
A spokesperson for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission's Moneysmart program says to check who you are buying from.
"With an unfamiliar online retailer, look for independent reviews and make sure you are using the genuine website rather than a look-alike site," they say.
How to prepare and shop during Black Friday
Ahead of Black Friday, Moneysmart also suggests:
- Making a list before you start shopping
- Setting a spending limit
- Shopping around and comparing prices
- Checking the full cost of an item, factoring in additional costs such as delivery and international transaction fees.
- Being careful with buy now, pay later services and making sure you can afford repayments
Mr Serrels cautions against embracing sales with unbridled "consumer lust".
"Don't feel like you have to buy [a product] right now. There's always another sale around the corner," he says.

Trump faces private citizens lawsuit over limiting White House media access

Unknown Publisher

Trump faces private citizens lawsuit over limiting White House media access
The plaintiffs argue they are losing access to vital information media outlets covering Trump used to provide.
A group of private citizens has sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over its restrictions on news outlets covering the White House.
“All of the Plaintiffs rely on the White House press corps for independent reporting about the president and his administration, and all of them use that reporting in a variety of ways in their scholarship, teaching, journalism, or advocacy,” says the lawsuit, filed on Monday in a federal court in New York.
The lawsuit is the first lodged not by the news outlets being banned, but by those who consume the news and rely on it for their work.
The plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a media watchdog, a university history professor, a high school teacher, a legal journalist and a student journalist.
Each argues they need unbiased, diverse media reporting from the White House to do their work.
“I’m gravely concerned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on White House reporters are cutting off access to crucial information,” Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a high school social studies teacher in New York City, said in a statement.
“I joined this lawsuit because my students deserve to know what’s happening in their government and to hear from a free and independent press.”
Trump already faces several legal challenges to his practice of banning journalists from outlets he dislikes from accessing the White House.
Last month, he banned journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from attending news conferences at the White House. A federal judge later ruled the order was unconstitutional, a violation of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press, and ordered access be restored. However, the Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.
Last week, Trump dismissed reporting that he planned to evict journalists from the White House press briefing room and restore a swimming pool that was housed there starting in 1933. But he said he is still considering moving the press out of the briefing room.
“I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space,” Trump said in a social media post.
Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said the restrictions on press access were familiar postmarks in countries whose leaders have become authoritarian.
“Worldwide, I have seen how governmental leaders’ efforts to penalise independent journalists are a prelude to the rise of autocracy,” he said in a statement.

Brazil’s real sinks after Lula’s re-election victory
Investors react to Lula’s election victory with a sharp decline in the Brazilian real and concerns over increased spending and fiscal challenges.
Brazil’s real dropped against the United States dollar on the heels of Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s unexpected re-election after right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led in the first round of voting earlier this month.
Brazil’s currency dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading. Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15 percent on Monday.
“I’m not surprised the real is sinking sharply; traders are covering their bets that assume a Bolsonaro victory and tighter fiscal policy,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
Brazil’s stock exchange halted trading for 30 minutes. The Bovespa index fell 10 percent from its previous close, triggering a circuit-breaker safety mechanism and reversing a rally earlier this month amid expectations of a shift to the right after Bolsonaro won the first round.
Ziemba says Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede the election has driven some financial uncertainty.
“The market pressure is also amplified by the objections raised by Bolsonaro, but the scale of the victory suggests that the result will stand,” she said.
Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under Bolsonaro would allow borrowing costs to decline.
“They [investors] assume more domestic spending and higher rates in Brazil. However, the real is still likely to be supported by strong commodity revenues,” Ziemba noted.
Stocks closed on Friday almost 7 percent above their level before the first round, while the Brazilian real was nearly 5 percent stronger against the US dollar.
Interest rate futures are up 3.1 percent, rising sharply after President Lula’s win. Interest rate futures had previously reflected a tighter fiscal policy amid expectations that Bolsonaro would oust the incumbent and that he would allow borrowing costs to decline.
Lula faces an increase in Brazil’s debt and will be challenged with protecting both social programmes and investment, with investors looking for signs of whether his gradual fiscal approach can bring borrowing costs down.
Lula’s team aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030. That would leave money to cover part of the interest bill, reducing the need for fresh borrowing. But public debt already exceeds 82 percent of GDP, while pensions and other legally required spending limit where savings can come from.
“Lula’s policies have talked about spending cuts, but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look,” said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital.
Attention will now turn to Lula’s choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach.

UN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after truce

HEAVY MUNITIONS HIT POPULATED AREAS, COMMISSION SAYS
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.
It said the "Yellow Line" which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
In its report to the UN Security Council, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and October 6, 2023, to 254 between October 7, 2023 and September 30, 2026.
Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank formed part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.
Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and human rights defenders had been killed and injured. REUTERS

María Corina Machado seeks talks with Delcy Rodríguez after return from exile

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:25:15 UTC
03:25:15 KST

After a year in exile, Venezuela's opposition leader returns, ready to negotiate with the government. The EU welcomes her and calls for free and fair elections.
María Corina Machado says she is willing to talk with Delcy Rodríguez after returning to Venezuela.
Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado said on Monday that she is ready to meet the country's interim president following her unexpected return from exile.
Machado landed in Caracas on Sunday after almost a year in exile, where she was greeted by a crowd of supporters in a direct challenge to the US-backed government.
Thousands of people gathered along roads, toll booths and streets in the capital, waving Venezuelan flags and shouting "Freedom!" as a smiling Machado entered Caracas accompanied by a convoy of cars and motorbikes.
Dressed in her usual white T-shirt and jeans, she leaned out through the sunroof of a vehicle to greet the crowd and shake hands with her supporters.
On Monday, Machado reached out to the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, and signalled her willingness to engage in talks with the former vice-president of her main political rival, Nicolás Maduro, prior to his capture by the United States.
Machado "has said she is willing to sit down not only with Delcy (Rodríguez), but with whoever she needs to sit down with, before the country, with full transparency and with an agenda", her spokesperson Claudia Macero told local broadcaster Unión Radio.
The European Union welcomed her return: "We trust that the Venezuelan authorities and all political actors will seize this opportunity to move towards an inclusive dialogue, led by Venezuelans themselves, that leads to free and fair elections," said the EU foreign affairs spokesperson, Anouar El Anouni.
Finally back home
Machado's return once again places the most influential figure in Venezuela's opposition at the heart of the country's turbulent politics.
"María, if you come back, my daughter has to come back too!" a supporter shouted on Sunday, referring to one of the millions of Venezuelans who have left the country to escape repression and a stagnant economy.
Machado slipped out of Venezuela clandestinely last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending almost a year in hiding.
Since then, the 59-year-old leader had tried to return to the country at least seven times without success, according to party sources. She is now coming back to a very different Venezuela.
Nine months ago, Maduro was captured in an extraordinary US military operation and imprisoned in the United States. Yet, to the disappointment of the democratic opposition, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, took over as interim president with Washington's backing.
From her exile in Panama, Machado had been forced to follow from afar the US-backed talks on political transition, in which she did not take part. The interim government has promised to hold elections, although it has not yet set a date.
Machado has repeatedly praised US President Donald Trump for ordering the risky military operation, and even gave him the medal from her Nobel Prize.
Trump, for his part, has repeatedly voiced his satisfaction with Rodríguez, who is meeting key US demands, especially regarding access to Venezuela's oil.
On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of Machado's return, but added: "I think she is a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so what else can I say?" "We are doing very well in Venezuela," he said.
Huge oil reserves
Last week, thousands of people demonstrated in Caracas and other cities to demand Machado's return and the holding of elections.
Many leaders of her party, Vente Venezuela, have also recently returned from exile, to which they were driven by the post-election crackdown that left 28 people dead and more than 2,400 detained, including dozens of Machado's associates.
Her party is calling for elections to be held in 2027 and for Machado to be allowed to stand as a candidate, something she was barred from doing in the last presidential election.
Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves. Yet current output, at one million barrels a day, is far below the three million it was pumping decades ago, after years of corruption and mismanagement.
Rodríguez has granted Washington access to a significant share of the country's crude reserves and has signed agreements with foreign companies to explore, produce and export oil and gas.

French firm launches mine-hunting underwater drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:25:15 UTC
03:25:15 KST

- French company SEABER launched RAVEN, a 13 kg underwater drone for mine hunting and seabed survey that a single operator can deploy.
- SEABER says RAVEN matches high-end mine-hunting drones at one-third of the price but did not disclose its price or customers.
French underwater drone maker SEABER has launched RAVEN, a compact autonomous underwater vehicle for hunting naval mines and surveying the seabed that weighs 13 kg (29 pounds) and can be launched by a single operator, and the company says it will offer performance comparable to high-end conventional mine-hunting drones at about one-third of their price, SEABER announced on Oct. 26.
The company, based in the Brittany port of Lorient, did not give a price for RAVEN, name any launch customers or say when deliveries will begin, and it did not identify which competing vehicles it used as the benchmark for its cost claim.
RAVEN is 131 to 137 cm (about 4.5 feet) long with a diameter of 12 cm (4.7 inches), can dive to 300 meters (985 feet), travels at 3 to 6 knots, and can run for up to eight hours. Every version carries a side-scan sonar, which paints an acoustic image of the seabed to spot mine-like objects, and the vehicle comes in two configurations: the SCAN-MAG adds a magnetometer to detect and locate metal objects such as naval mines and shipwrecks, while the SCAN-LUMEN adds a high-definition camera and a 24,000-lumen lighting system so operators can visually inspect a contact.
Navigation is the part of the design SEABER is emphasizing most. The vehicle relies on LYNX, the company’s own optical-based inertial navigation system, which SEABER says drifts by less than 0.2% of the distance traveled on straight runs and does even better on the back-and-forth lawnmower patterns used to search an area, combined with a Doppler velocity log that measures speed over the seabed. Accurate navigation matters for mine hunting because a detected object is only useful if divers or a neutralization drone can find it again later.
Before diving, RAVEN fixes its position with a dual-antenna satellite navigation receiver that SEABER says resists jamming, an issue for navies operating in waters where GPS signals are deliberately disrupted, as has happened widely in the Baltic and Black seas.
Underwater, operators can send commands and track the vehicle in real time through an acoustic modem at ranges of up to 2 to 3 km (1.2 to 1.9 miles) using SEABER’s SEAPLAN software. At the surface it communicates by UHF radio at up to 5 km (3 miles) and by Iridium satellite, and it carries infrared lights visible only through night-vision equipment so crews can find and recover it at night without giving away their position.
“With RAVEN®, our ambition is simple: to deliver the performance of the best conventional AUVs at one-third of their price. Thanks to our LYNX® navigation technology and the integration of advanced inspection and detection capabilities, we believe RAVEN has the potential to fundamentally change the rules of the market,” said Vidal Teixeira, president of SEABER.
RAVEN moves SEABER up from the micro-AUV segment, where it built its YUCO range of small underwater drones that it has supplied to European navies for mine countermeasures work. The company says it has sold more than 200 AUVs internationally through a worldwide distributor network.

From emergency repairs to resilience in the housing sector: How Transitional Development Assistance contributes to Ukraine's social recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:23:55 UTC
03:23:55 KST

From emergency repairs to resilience in the housing sector: How Transitional Development Assistance contributes to Ukraine's social recovery
Representatives of the six housing pilot cities of the Strengthening of Urban Resilience in the Areas of Supply Infrastructure and Housing (SUR) project visit a construction site during a housing conference in Zhytomyr, Ukraine, on May 6, 2026. (SUR)
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Iryna Simakina was in Enerhodar, a city in southern Ukraine, home to Europe's largest nuclear power plant.
As Russian forces advanced on the city, staying became increasingly dangerous. Simakina, who uses a wheelchair because of a disability, eventually left her home behind, uncertain whether she would ever return.
Simakina found refuge in Zhytomyr, northwestern Ukraine, in 2023, where she initially stayed with a friend. In December 2025, she received a call that changed her life.
"I didn't believe it and didn't dare to hope. And I received a call: 'Come pick up the keys,'" she said.
Simakina was one of 15 new residents to receive an inclusive apartment for use through a partnership between the Zhytomyr authorities and the Strengthening of Urban Resilience in the Areas of Supply Infrastructure and Housing (SUR) project, implemented by Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH.
SUR is part of Germany's Transitional Development Assistance (TDA), a flexible crisis-response instrument of the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) that bridges the gap between short-term humanitarian relief and long-term development cooperation. TDA operates in line with the U.N. 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, while aligning its work with EU priorities on local resilience, crisis prevention, and the Humanitarian–Development–Peace (HDP) Nexus.
About 10.8 million people in Ukraine need humanitarian assistance, 6.4 million needing water and sanitation services, 5.6 million needing shelter, and 4.5 million needing health care, according to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, nearly 4.7 million people have been registered as internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Ukraine, according to the Social Policy, Family and Ukraine's Unity Ministry. The actual number remains difficult to determine, while Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has warned that the figure has not been updated for nearly two years, with a flawed system for identifying and counting IDPs.
The scale of displacement, even if difficult to measure precisely, places enormous demands on the state to provide housing and to help people settle into new communities.
The pressure is compounded by continued Russian attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure, particularly the power grid. The impact is especially severe in winter, when hours-long blackouts, disrupted water supply, and homes without heating threaten Ukrainians nationwide.
"If there is anything I would describe very much in the spirit of TDA, as our truly fundamental principle, it is the commitment to be guided by the most urgent needs of our Ukrainian partners," Erik Schweikhardt, the SUR project director, told the Kyiv Independent.
From immediate action to lasting vision
The broader aim of SUR is to help Ukrainian cities withstand the impacts of Russia's war and prepare for future challenges, while supporting the most vulnerable groups, including internally displaced people and returnees. Operating in more than 100 cities, primarily in eastern and central Ukraine, the project helps war-affected municipalities maintain and restore essential services, including electricity, heating, water supply, and housing, while strengthening local disaster risk management.
In wartime, decisions often need to be made quickly. At the same time, communities need long-term solutions that can be adapted to similar ongoing and future challenges. This approach helps communities stabilize during emergencies, strengthen their resilience, and better prepare for future shocks.
“Reconstruction should go beyond restoring what was lost and be embedded in long-term urban planning and development.”
"Within the framework of TDA, reconstruction should go beyond restoring what was lost and be embedded in long-term urban planning and development, guided by these principles," Schweikhardt said.
In this way, the project addresses urgent needs while helping people maintain their daily lives. Access to clean water is one example. Mykolaiv, a city in southern Ukraine with roughly 460,000 residents, has been without a centralized drinking water supply since Russian forces destroyed a key water pipeline in 2022. To address this ongoing challenge, the project is supporting a decentralized network of public drinking-water points, helping ensure that residents have access to clean, safe water.
At the same time, the project is investing in the long-term resilience of urban water infrastructure. It supports risk assessments in the water sector and helps cities develop resilience plans for their local water utilities. These efforts aim to establish more sustainable and reliable water services that can better withstand current and future threats.
Supporting municipal energy systems is another key area of SUR's work. The project helps municipalities maintain electricity and heat supplies by providing essential equipment, including cogeneration units, mobile boiler houses, battery storage systems, and hybrid generators. This support is particularly critical during the harsh winter months, when attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure threaten essential municipal services.
"Housing should be viewed as part of the city's overall development."
To help municipalities maintain reliable electricity and heating supplies, more than 450 energy units have been supplied and commissioned, including 118 combined heat and power plants. The equipment has benefited more than 4.5 million people. The support was provided in part through the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ)'s "Winter Aid 2024/2025" initiative and in cooperation with other GIZ projects.
In addition to providing decentralized heat and energy to help mitigate outages caused by damage to centralized municipal systems, SUR supports cities in modernizing their heating infrastructure. These systems remain vulnerable to external shocks, including large-scale destruction, and are heavily reliant on carbon-intensive energy sources.
In Kryvyi Rih, a city located roughly 70 kilometers (nearly 40 miles) from the front line and frequently targeted by devastating Russian attacks, the project is supporting the development of a district heating strategy that integrates urban resilience and disaster risk reduction while aligning with the EU's long-term decarbonization goals.
SUR has also supported municipal hospitals in Kryvyi Rih by upgrading their heating networks. Hospitals are particularly vulnerable to energy disruptions, as life-saving equipment and medical procedures depend on a reliable power supply. To strengthen their energy resilience, the project has developed plans for three municipal hospitals to establish a stable, decentralized energy supply that can operate independently of the grid. These plans also integrate project-provided boiler houses into the hospitals' energy systems.
In nearly three years of operations in Ukraine, SUR has supported the restoration of municipal supply and waste management infrastructure in war-affected regions, benefiting more than 2 million people.
In the housing sector, SUR has so far contributed to restoring more than 800 homes since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, enabling Ukrainian families to remain in their communities rather than face displacement. The project focuses on rehabilitating war-damaged private homes, developing and piloting rehabilitation approaches for damaged multifamily residential buildings in cooperation with local authorities, and helping homeowners' associations access funding for repairs.
"At the same time, it would be misleading to describe the project as simply something that acts quickly and locally," Schweikhardt said. "In line with TDA, its interventions are also designed to build structures and capacities that remain valuable beyond the immediate crisis."
Blueprint for the cities of tomorrow
The shortage of affordable housing, compounded by the precarious living conditions many internally displaced people continue to face, underscores the need for effective, long-term municipal housing strategies.
In cooperation with the Housing Initiative for Eastern Europe (IWO) e.V., SUR is supporting six pilot cities — Zhytomyr, Poltava, Kremenchuk, Bila Tserkva, Mykolaiv, and Kalush — in conducting a diagnostic analysis of the housing sector, including an assessment of local housing needs. Based on the findings, concepts for municipal housing strategies aligned with Ukraine's national housing strategy and the requirements of Reform 7 under the Ukraine Facility, "Ensuring Access to Housing for People in Need," are being developed.
"Ukraine's housing policies have long addressed the consequences of deeper structural issues rather than their root causes," Yuliia Popova, project director at the Housing Initiative for Eastern Europe (IWO) e.V., told the Kyiv Independent.
“Ukraine's housing policies have long addressed the consequences of deeper structural issues rather than their root causes."
At the heart of the problem is an incomplete privatization model. Mass privatization transferred individual apartments to residents but left buildings without the legal, financial, or institutional mechanisms needed to manage and maintain them as shared property. The state also failed to deliver on its promise to finance the first round of major repairs, leaving a growing backlog of renovations.
Meanwhile, housing policy largely ignored the rental market, leaving it poorly regulated, while privatization steadily depleted the municipal housing stock.
As demand for rental housing grows, most of Ukraine's rental market remains informal, operating outside the formal housing system. IDPs, who make up a significant share of renters, face not only high housing costs but also legal uncertainty because of informal rental agreements. War-related destruction has deepened these challenges, compounding longstanding structural problems. Addressing both the immediate consequences of the war and the housing sector's deeper flaws requires fundamental changes in how housing is provided and managed. Reform is no longer optional, but a structural necessity.
Municipalities must balance three competing priorities: meeting the immediate housing needs of displaced and vulnerable residents, repairing and renovating existing homes before they deteriorate beyond repair, and rebuilding housing destroyed by the war.
All three demand the same limited municipal resources, staff capacity, and political attention. At the same time, cities must align their efforts with national reforms and seek funding from a fragmented donor landscape.
"The local housing strategies we are developing with the pilot cities within the SUR project take a bottom-up approach to build a comprehensive picture of local housing conditions. They bring into municipal planning perspectives that have often been overlooked: housing market monitoring, assessments of existing housing stock, analysis of needs across population groups, including IDPs, and structural problems in housing stock management," Popova said.
The diagnostic process and subsequent recommendations for housing strategies translate competing needs and priorities into a structured, evidence-based plan of action. They provide a basis for inclusive local debate and help bring fragmented resources and capacities together around shared goals. Zhytomyr, Kremenchuk, and other cities participating in the SUR project are demonstrating that this is possible even under current conditions.
Kremenchuk has been cooperating with GIZ for several years, Maletskyi said, with housing policy now among its main priorities. The issue is particularly urgent given that more than 31,000 IDPs are currently registered in the city. At the same time, Maletskyi said the development of municipal housing should also benefit families who cannot afford to buy a home.
Svitlana Olshanska, deputy mayor of Zhytomyr, said housing remains an urgent issue for the city as well, and that Germany's approach offers a model Ukraine could learn from.
"When the full-scale war began, Ukraine found it difficult to respond to the challenges of providing housing," Olshanska told the Kyiv Independent. "At the same time, many Ukrainians who relocated to Germany saw similar situations addressed."
"We cannot provide affordable housing even to those who need it because we do not have a housing stock for crisis situations," she added.
Like Kremenchuk and other pilot cities, Zhytomyr, together with GIZ, is developing strategies to address the housing crisis. Olshanska said a long-term strategy is important not only for residents, who need a clear understanding of how their city will develop, but also for partners, donors, and potential lenders.
Maletskyi also stressed that affordable housing and broader development strategies should be centered on the needs of the local community, which should benefit from such initiatives and play a role in the city's future.
"One of the key takeaways for us is that housing should be viewed as part of the city's overall development. If a person has a job but cannot find decent, affordable housing, it will be difficult to keep that person in the community," Maletskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
Affordable housing, including municipal housing, is in high demand among large families, people with disabilities, older people, orphans, and low-income households. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, however, IDPs are one of the largest groups in need of housing, with their numbers continuing to grow as Russian forces continue their assault.
For people like Simakina, who was forced to leave her hometown and move to another city, securing accessible housing can be life-changing, providing the stability to remain in Ukraine, support her community, and build a new life away from home. At the same time, her dream remains unchanged.
"My plans are to go back home (to Enerhodar)," Simakina said. "I really want the war to end soon so I can go back home as soon as possible."
Next step
Ukraine is gradually updating its housing policies at both the national and local levels. Yet, governing during wartime comes with significant constraints — from the legal and time limits imposed by martial law to supply-chain disruptions, permitting delays, data security challenges, relentless Russian attacks, and corruption risks.
Mariia Kostenko, GIZ project adviser for housing and urban planning, said that a shortage of staff is one of the key bottlenecks in some communities. Employees often juggle multiple roles, leaving them with limited capacity to focus on longer-term strategic and conceptual goals. Another challenge is the sheer volume of urgent tasks, risks, and threats competing for their attention due to constant attacks on the Ukrainian cities.
"Sometimes we can make plans and agree on things, and then we get a call saying, 'We've been attacked.' For the next few days, local authorities are completely focused on dealing with the aftermath," Kostenko told the Kyiv Independent.
Despite these challenges, Schweikhardt said municipalities continue to move the work forward.
"I'm continually struck by the dedication and resilience of our Ukrainian partners," Schweikhardt said. "Even under tight constraints, we continue to work together constructively and proactively."
"The project is not operating in isolation; it is part of German-Ukrainian cooperation and Germany's broader civil and development support to Ukraine," he said. "We have established communication channels and, perhaps most importantly, a level of trust. For me, this is one of the project's major achievements and a very strong basis for continued cooperation."
Deeper cooperation between Ukrainian and European municipalities could open up new opportunities for peer learning and collaboration. At the same time, work on initiatives already underway — including resilience strategies and universal reconstruction mechanisms — should continue.
"The demand is still enormous," the project director said.

BLADE wins deal to build decontamination system for special forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:22:21 UTC
03:22:21 KST

- BLADE, formerly HDT Global, won a contract to advance the large variant of a decontamination system for U.S. special operations forces.
- The system cleans chemical and biological agents from sensitive equipment so it can be reused, but the contract value was not disclosed.
BLADE, the Ohio-based defense contractor formerly known as HDT Global, has won a contract to continue developing the large version of the Critical Equipment Decontamination System, a transportable system that cleans chemical and biological warfare agents off sensitive equipment used by U.S. special operations forces so the gear can be put back into service instead of thrown away, the company announced on Oct. 26.
BLADE did not disclose the value of the contract, how long it runs, or how many systems it covers, and it did not say whether the award moves the program toward production or keeps it in development.
The program, known as CEDS, is run by the Joint Project Manager for CBRN Special Operations Forces under the Pentagon’s Portfolio Management Executive for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense, and is meant to give special operations units a way to decontaminate low-density, high-value equipment in austere and contested locations far from a depot. BLADE said the large variant is intended to reduce the logistical burden of replacing contaminated gear and to get mission-essential equipment back to operators faster.
“This award underscores our commitment to delivering innovative solutions that protect warfighters and enhance mission readiness,” said Tim Stickler, senior director of CBRN integrated protection and bio and chemical security at BLADE.
CEDS comes in two versions. The small variant is an inflatable, soft-walled shelter developed by Integrated Solutions for Systems of Huntsville, Alabama, while the large variant, which resembles a medium-sized metal shipping container, was developed by the company’s former HDT Expeditionary Systems unit in Fredericksburg, Virginia, the U.S. Army reported. Equipment that goes through the system is meant to come out clean enough to be reissued without troops having to wear extra protective gear.
Prototyping began in fiscal 2022, and the program has been tested with real chemical and biological agents on actual equipment at the Czech military’s research institute, known as VVU, rather than relying on simulants. The small variant completed operational testing there in December 2024, and the large variant was scheduled to follow in 2025, with U.S. Special Operations Command units targeted to receive the first systems in fiscal 2027.
“Through the CEDS program, we are advancing critical decontamination capabilities that enable Special Operations Forces to recover essential equipment, sustain operations and maintain their advantage in contested environments. We are proud to support this mission and provide the reliable solutions our warfighters depend on,” said Tim Stickler, senior director of CBRN integrated protection and bio and chemical security at BLADE.
Special operations forces are also receiving a separate decontamination system, the Forward Area Mobility Spray System, which comes in backpack and vehicle-mounted versions for washing down contaminated vehicles and equipment in the field. Its man-portable version reached full operational capability in May 2025, nearly three years ahead of schedule, and all three variants are due to be fielded by fiscal 2028.
BLADE, headquartered in Solon, Ohio, has operated as HDT for nearly 90 years and builds robotic systems, shelters and infrastructure, environmental control and CBRN protection equipment for the U.S. military. The company has not said when the large CEDS variant will begin production or reach special operations units.

AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion

AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion
October 26, 2026
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic on Monday filed paperwork to make its stock market debut in what analysts say could be one of the biggest in history.
The initial public offering (IPO) could happen as early as November, reports say, with analysts putting the company at a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
What did the Anthropic founders say about the IPO?
The seven co-founders of the company, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, outlined their vision for the future of AI in a letter to potential investors.
"We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," they said.
The AI startup behind Claude also addressed the societal risks of AI as they have done before, writing that the company's leadership might have to take unusual decisions to slow down the pace of development, even if that meant falling behind competitors.
The filing toward an IPO represents a major milestone for a company that was founded just five years ago.
Money raised at the IPO could provide the company with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.
What do we know about Anthropic's IPO?
Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."
But the company is yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell and what price, leaving that space blank in its paperwork filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.
Anthropic filed confidentially with the SEC in June and that gave the agency time to go over the company's financial credentials before they were made available to the public and potential investors.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters.
Anthropic debut follows SpaceX IPO
The San Francisco-based company was founded by members who defected from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2021.
OpenAI, Anthropic's main rival, is also set to debut on the stock market next year.
Both IPOs are taking place amid growing concern about AI and the race to develop AI infrastructure, including data centers that consume vast amounts of energy.
The document filed by Anthropic shows that the company has seen massive revenue growth but is yet to turn a profit, much like its AI rivals.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, the company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30.
And as for money raised at the IPO, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX that ultimately raised $86 billion in what was the biggest IPO on record to date.

Details

Senators seek details on 23,000-strong National Guard riot force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:18:24 UTC
03:18:24 KST

- Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly asked the Pentagon and National Guard Bureau to explain the command and legal authority of new Guard quick reaction forces.
- The senators asked whether the forces could be used around elections and set an Oct. 28 deadline, one week before the midterms.
Two Democratic senators with military and national security backgrounds, Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and Mark Kelly of Arizona, have asked the Department of War and the National Guard Bureau to explain who commands the National Guard’s new “quick reaction forces,” under what legal authority they would deploy inside the United States, and whether they have been prepared for use around elections, setting an Oct. 28 deadline for answers one week before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
In a letter announced on Oct. 26, the senators said President Donald Trump’s executive order directing the Pentagon to make Guard troops available nationwide to help law enforcement with civil disturbances and public safety, and to stand up a force able to deploy rapidly anywhere in the country, leaves the most important legal question unanswered.
“The memo provides no clarity on whether this force would operate under state or federal authorities, or whether they operate under a dual-status commander. The distinction is critical and legally consequential to preventing the National Guard from being used to abuse the constitutional or civil rights of Americans or to circumvent existing legal limitations,” wrote Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly.
The distinction matters because Guard troops serving under a governor’s control can perform law enforcement duties, while troops called into federal service are generally barred by the Posse Comitatus Act from policing American civilians unless the president invokes a legal exception such as the Insurrection Act. A dual-status commander is a single officer who can lead both state and federal troops during the same operation.
The forces trace back to an executive order Trump signed on Aug. 25, 2025, as part of his declared crime emergency in Washington, which directed the Pentagon to create Guard units “available for rapid nationwide deployment.” National Guard Bureau memos signed that October by Maj. Gen. Ronald Burkett, the Guard’s director of operations, ordered every state and territory to form a quick reaction force, typically of 500 troops each and more than 23,000 nationwide, The Associated Press reported at the time, with a quarter of each force ready to move within eight hours and the rest within a day. The units were to be operational by Jan. 1, 2026, and the troops received extra training in crowd control and nonlethal weapons, including batons, body shields, Tasers and pepper spray, Task & Purpose reported, with each state receiving 100 sets of crowd control equipment from the Guard Bureau.
When the memos became public, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth declined to discuss their particulars but said the country has “multiple layers of National Guard response forces” that can be used under federal and state authorities.
The senators also asked about a second unit, the National Guard Response Force, and pressed the Pentagon on how many troops are assigned to each force, where they are based and who commands them, what would trigger a mobilization and how governors would request or activate the troops, how the forces are funded, and what notice Congress would receive before or after any domestic deployment. They also asked whether there are plans to detail Guard troops to support the Department of Homeland Security or the Justice Department in law enforcement roles within the next 100 days.
Elections are the central concern of the letter. The senators asked whether the Pentagon or the Guard has considered using the forces to respond to an election-related civil disturbance and requested all training materials that reference elections. Federal law prohibits stationing troops at polling places unless it is necessary “to repel armed enemies of the United States,” with violations punishable by up to five years in prison.
“This administration must make clear that our troops will not be used to interfere with Americans’ lives or to meet some political end. The use of military personnel in connection with elections raises additional legal concerns, including the risk of violating federal restrictions on troops at polling places, interference with election officials, and voter intimidation,” wrote Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly.
The letter noted that Mark Ditlevson, the Pentagon’s assistant secretary for homeland defense, and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, have acknowledged that risk in responses to Congress, and that the department has repeatedly confirmed that no election threat exists that would require federal forces to secure polling places. In April, Gen. Steven Nordhaus, chief of the National Guard Bureau, told a House Appropriations subcommittee that the Guard “always follows the Constitution, law, policy and guidance” when asked about troops at the polls, Florida Phoenix reported.
The administration has defended its use of the Guard at home as a response to crime and threats to federal personnel and property. Trump deployed Guard troops to several Democratic-led cities in 2025, in some cases federalizing them over governors’ objections, before withdrawing them after the Supreme Court left in place a lower-court ruling that blocked a deployment in Chicago. Nearly 2,500 Guard members remained deployed in Washington as of April.
Slotkin, a former CIA analyst and Pentagon official, and Kelly, a retired U.S. Navy captain and former astronaut, both serve on the Senate Armed Services Committee, and both appeared in a 2025 video urging troops to refuse illegal orders that drew an administration investigation.
“The future of our democracy and the prosperity of the Americans we all serve depends on maintaining our military’s nonpartisan tradition,” wrote Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly.

Govt establishes Coordination Center to organize registration of those subject to military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:17:07 EET
03:17:07 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has established a Coordination Center for the Organization of Reservist Enlistment during Mobilization and in Times of War.
Specifically, in accordance with Resolution No. 1328 of October 23, the government approved the composition and regulations of the Coordination Center for the Mobilization of Conscripts.
The Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment and the Deputy Minister of Defense have been appointed as co-chairs of the Coordination Center.
The Coordination Center also includes: the Deputy State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers; the Deputy Ministers of Digital Transformation, Internal Affairs, Infrastructure, and Agrarian Policy and Food; the State Secretary of the Ministry of Energy; a representative of the Ministry of Economy; the Deputy Head of the President's Office of Ukraine (subject to approval), the Deputy Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces (subject to approval), the First Deputy Head of the State Border Guard Service, the Deputy Head of the National Police, the Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Pension Fund of Ukraine, the Deputy Head of the State Labor Service, a representative of the Central Directorate of the State Security Service of Ukraine (subject to consent), a representative of the Foreign Intelligence Service (subject to approval), and a representative of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defense (subject to approval).
The main tasks of the Coordination Center are: to facilitate the coordination of actions by central and local executive authorities, other state bodies, and public administration bodies whose jurisdiction extends to the entire territory of Ukraine, regarding the reservation of conscripts for the period of mobilization and during wartime; providing proposals on the approaches, mechanisms, and methods for resolving issues related to the reservation of conscripts; coordinating criteria and, if necessary, providing recommendations for their refinement; reviewing proposals from state bodies regarding increasing the number of conscripts reserved for the mobilization period; reviewing proposals from state bodies regarding the determination of the criticality of enterprises; monitoring, through the Unified State Register of Conscripts, Persons Subject to Military Service, and Reservists, the Pension Fund's e-services web portal, and the Unified State e-services web portal, information regarding employees subject to military service of enterprises that have applied for critical status; providing state agencies with recommendations and proposals regarding the revocation of decisions designating enterprises as critical, particularly in response to relevant requests from law enforcement agencies.
In accordance with its assigned tasks, the Coordination Center: analyzes the current state of affairs and the causes of problems arising in the process of reserving conscripts; reviews the performance of state agencies, local government bodies, enterprises, institutions, and organizations on matters within its jurisdiction; coordinates the criteria for determining critical status; reviews proposals from state agencies regarding an increase in the number of conscripts reserved; reviews proposals regarding the designation of enterprises as critical and provides relevant recommendations; and provides recommendations regarding the revocation of decisions designating enterprises as critical.
The Coordination Center's recommendations and proposals are considered approved if more than half of the members and representatives of state bodies present at the meeting and invited to participate in the meeting vote in favor of them. In the event of a tie, a recommendation or proposal may be approved only if supported by both co-chairs.
The timeframe for the Coordination Center to issue recommendations and proposals based on the review of requests from government agencies may not exceed one calendar month from the date of receipt of the request.
