Published 26 Oct, 2026 18:09 | Updated 26 Oct, 2026 19:10
MOSCOW, OCTOBER 26, 2026 — The media forum “Russia–Africa,” organized by RT alongside the Sputnik and TASS news agencies, takes place in Moscow from October 26 to 29 as part of the “Russia–Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.” Descendants of prominent African leaders, politicians, media executives, and bloggers with millions of followers are set to attend the event.
The media forum is expected to gather over 200 participants from 46 African countries. Leading experts from the regional media community and political figures, including Gregoire Ndjaka, Director-General of the African Broadcasting Union; Evariste Ngamana, Minister of Communications and Media of the Central African Republic; and Badr Shneba, Director of Foreign Media Department in the Libyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, will participate. Also, prominent bloggers and descendants of esteemed African leaders such as Nelson Mandela, Patrice Lumumba, Samora Machel, and Gamal Abdel Nasser will take part in the event.
The key focus of the media forum will be the role of media in the development and unification of the African continent, as well as in shaping its identity and image abroad. On October 26 and 27, RT will hold sessions featuring leaders of major African television channels and influential bloggers.
On October 28, a plenary session of the media forum will take place, featuring Elizaveta Brodskaya, RT First Deputy Editor-in-Chief; Dmitry Kiselev, Director General of the Rossiya Segodnya media group; and Andrey Kondrashov, Director General of TASS, along with representatives from ministries and media regulatory authorities in both Russia and Africa.
On the final day of the forum, a session organized by RT will include descendants of legendary African leaders who inspired RT’s program “Africa: Legacy of the Great Leaders.” The session will feature Juliana Lumumba, daughter of Patrice Lumumba; Ndileka Mandela, granddaughter of Nelson Mandela; Gamal Abdel Nasser, grandson of Gamal Abdel Nasser; and others.
Throughout the business program, attendees will not only participate in the media forum but will also conduct joint broadcasts with Russian media and sign several cooperation agreements with their Russian counterparts.
The international RT television network includes news channels in English, Arabic, Spanish, German, Serbian, and French, as well as the RTD documentary channel in Russian and English. RT also operates online portals in ten languages and the global multimedia agency RUPTLY, which supplies exclusive content to broadcasters worldwide. RT is available 24/7 to more than 950 million viewers in over 100 countries.
Africa is one of the key regions for RT’s operations. The channel is expanding its partnership network with new media corporations and enhancing cooperation with existing partners. Currently, RT has eight bureaus across Africa. Additionally, RT conducts training programs for African journalists and co-hosted the African Media Awards ceremony in Ethiopia in 2025, which is the largest media event of the year for the continent.

Przemyśl suspended cooperation with Lviv over the decision to declare 2027 the Year of the UPA, Shukhevych, and Olzhych. It may be restored after the decision is revoked.
The city council of Przemyśl, Poland, unanimously decided to suspend its partnership cooperation with Lviv, which had continued since 1995. The city’s mayor, Wojciech Bakun, announced this, UNN reports.
Details
The reason was the decision by the Lviv Regional Council to proclaim 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), Roman Shukhevych and Oleh Olzhych.
According to Bakun, after an extended discussion, the councillors agreed that joint activities with Lviv should be suspended until a clear position is received from the city authorities regarding the commemoration of historical figures and organizations whose activities are considered anti-Polish in Poland.
As PAP reports, Przemyśl councillors recognized that the decision of the Lviv Regional Council of October 20 insults the memory of Polish victims of crimes committed by the UPA and contradicts the establishment of relations based on historical truth and mutual respect.
The resolution obliges Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun to take legal measures aimed at terminating the 1995 cooperation agreement.
At the same time, it stipulates that cooperation between the cities will be restored if the Lviv Regional Council finally cancels or officially withdraws the resolution and the Lviv authorities clearly distance themselves from initiatives that "glorify structures responsible for crimes against the civilian population."
The mayor must inform Lviv’s local authorities of this position and provide the Przemyśl city councilors with information about the measures taken and the deadline for terminating the agreement.
"After a lengthy discussion of this issue, all the councillors unanimously decided that until the Lviv authorities clearly determine their position on promoting ideologies directed against Poland and Poles, we are suspending all joint activities. For my part, I thank the councillors for this position and for demonstrating that we will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions!" Bakun wrote.

MFA on UN Commission of Inquiry's report: As another winter approaches, these findings particularly important
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:06:26 EET
03:06:26 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) welcomes the presentation of the report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on violations in Ukraine to the Third Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
"Ukraine highly values the independent and impartial work of the Commission, which consistently documents violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The Commission is establishing the circumstances of international crimes and gathering evidence to hold those responsible to account," the MFA said in a statement.
The ministry said the Commission's findings regarding Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure are of particular importance. The Commission has recognized such targeted attacks as war crimes, and the large-scale and systematic strikes that caused severe suffering to civilians as crimes against humanity.
Indeed, the Commission established that for over four years, Russian strikes on energy infrastructure deprived millions of Ukrainians of electricity, heat, and water.
"Of fundamental importance is the Commission's conclusion that these attacks were intentional and consistent with the state policy of the Russian Federation. The aim of this policy was to deprive civilians of vital energy supplies and to inflict suffering upon them. Russia has deliberately turned cold and darkness into weapons against Ukrainian civilians. As winter approaches, these findings are particularly important. They serve as a reminder to the international community that Russia continues to systematically destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We cannot allow the lives of millions of people to be threatened once again by cold and darkness," the MFA said.
The statement notes that the Commission's findings regarding how Russia recruits citizens of other states into its armed forces through deception and coercion warrant the strongest possible international response. The Commission found evidence of such practices involving citizens of 29 countries and classified the actions of the Russian authorities as human trafficking. People were lured to Russia with false promises of work and sent to fight in the war against Ukraine. Many of them were killed, wounded, or went missing.
"We call on the states whose citizens have been victimized by these criminal practices to strengthen cooperation in order to dismantle the recruitment networks and hold those responsible to account. We believe that the Commission's findings should be used to ensure that accountability for international crimes committed during Russia's aggression against Ukraine becomes inevitable," the statement reads.
The MFA also called on the international community to strengthen its support for Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, and to facilitate the effective investigation of crimes and the prosecution of those responsible.
"Behind every documented crime lie human lives and destinies. These crimes cannot go unpunished. Justice and accountability are essential conditions for a just and lasting peace," the ministry said.
Earlier, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine stated in its new report to the UN General Assembly that Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts, by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The Commission also concluded that Russian authorities recruited men who were victims of human trafficking in various countries into their armed forces, which constitutes a violation of international human rights law.
The Commission investigated the impact of the Russian armed forces' large-scale attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure on the civilian population, particularly during the difficult winter of 2025-2026, as well as the cumulative effects of these attacks since the fall of 2022.

Russia drops out of top three global exporters of non-coking coal as shipments fall by nearly 19%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:05:19 UTC
03:05:19 KST

Russia has fallen from third to fourth place among the world’s largest exporters of non-coking coal, according to data from analytics firm BigMint. From January through September 2026, Russian exports in the category fell by 18.6% to 42.5 million metric tons, the steepest decline among large suppliers.
Russia ceded third place to South Africa, which increased shipments by 8% to 52.1 million metric tons. Based on BigMint’s published figures, The Insider calculated that Russian shipments fell by about 9.7 million metric tons from the same period in 2025.
Overall, global trade in non-coking coal declined by 3.2% to 602.5 million metric tons, a drop of about 19.9 million metric tons. That means the decline in Russian exports accounted for roughly 49% of the overall contraction in global trade in the category as tracked by BigMint. Russia’s share of that market fell from about 8.4% to 7.1%.
Indonesia remained the world’s largest exporter despite a 10% decline in shipments that lowered its output to 240.3 million metric tons. Australia ranked second after increasing exports by 2% to 151.2 million metric tons.
Among major suppliers, Mongolia recorded the strongest growth, with exports rising 73% to 24 million metric tons.
The biggest declines in Russian exports were to China and Turkey. Shipments to Turkey fell 32% to 15.7 million metric tons, while exports to China dropped 26% to 15.1 million metric tons.
India was the only major destination in where Russian companies managed to increase sales, rising by 63% to 9.6 million metric tons and surpassing the 7.4 million metric tons Russia shipped to India during all of 2025.
Analysts interviewed by the Kremlin-aligned newspaper Kommersant attributed the decline in Russian exports to weaker demand for power-station coal in Turkey, high fuel inventories in China, and growing competition from Mongolia. Russian suppliers also face additional pressure from the cost of rail transportation, shipping, and vessel insurance. Companies were able to increase sales in India by offering discounts, analysts said, although higher logistics costs could make Russian coal less attractive in that market as well.
BigMint’s figures should not, however, be treated as a measure of Russia’s entire coal export sector. According to data from Kpler, Russian seaborne exports of all types of coal rose 7.25% from January through September, reaching 135.86 million metric tons.
The two estimates cover different product categories and use different methodologies.
Nearly two-thirds of Russian coal companies are unprofitable
The deterioration in Russian exporters’ position comes amid a prolonged crisis in the country’s coal industry. According to official data from Russia’s state statistics agency Rosstat, coal-mining companies posted a combined net loss of 178.2 billion rubles ($2.2 billion) from January through July 2026. Profitable companies earned 45 billion rubles ($556.9 million), while total losses among the rest reached 223.2 billion rubles ($2.8 billion). Overall, 64.5% of companies in the sector were unprofitable.
The situation is particularly severe in Kuzbass, Russia’s largest coal-producing region. According to data from the regional Coal Industry Ministry, 20 of the region’s 93 underground mines and open-pit operations were not operating as of August 2026. Employment in the coal sector fell from 103,000 to 97,300 workers over the course of a year.
Russia’s Energy Ministry, however, says the industry has passed the worst stage of the crisis. Deputy Energy Minister Dmitry Islamov said recently that prices had begun to recover, although the situation remained difficult. The ministry estimates that the industry’s losses for all of 2026 will be as high as 310 billion rubles ($3.8 billion).
As The Insider previously reported, among suppliers to the Chinese market Russia fell from second to third after being displaced by Mongolia. In August, Mongolia exported 9.81 million metric tons of coal to China, compared with Russia’s 9.2 million metric tons.
Experts cited Chinese import duties of 3% to 6% on Russian coal — tariffs from which Russia’s main competitors are exempt — as well as rising transportation costs as being among the reasons for Russia’s declining position.
In June, The Insider also reported on a Green Think Tank study that concluded redirecting exports to China had failed to compensate Russian coal companies for the loss of the European market. The initiative’s researchers estimated that the industry’s combined financial losses during the years of the full-scale war exceeded 2.5 trillion rubles ($30.9 billion). For Russian coal companies, maintaining export volumes has become increasingly dependent on government benefits, tax deferrals, and state support for rail transportation, rather than on actual market mechanisms.

Feed recommendations are the most common way teens encounter self-harm content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:48 UTC
03:00:48 KST

An analysis of data from the 2025 OxWell Student Survey found that about a third of 11- to 18-year-old students in England had come across self-harm content online in the past month. Most of these encounters were unintentional, and about two-thirds of exposed students said the content had appeared in their social media feeds or been suggested while they were browsing. Students who were lonelier, had experienced other online harms, or had poorer mental health were more likely to report exposure. The paper was published in Nature Mental Health.
Social media has become an integral part of young people’s everyday lives. It provides wide opportunities for communication, entertainment, self-expression, and social connection. Platforms such as TikTok and Instagram offer an almost endless stream of content, much of which is selected by recommendation algorithms that personalize what users see based on their interests and online behavior.
While this personalization can help users discover content they enjoy, it can also expose them to potentially harmful material. One particular concern is content related to self-harm, which can range from personal stories of recovery and supportive discussions to graphic images and videos that portray self-injury in a positive or encouraging way.
Research suggests that repeated exposure to such content may increase emotional distress and the risk of self-harming thoughts and behaviors, particularly among vulnerable adolescents. However, the effects are not always negative, as some online communities that discuss self-harm also provide emotional support and encourage young people to seek help.
Adolescents also do not need to search for self-harm content to encounter it, as recommendation algorithms may place it in their feeds without them seeking it out. Their interactions with such content may then lead algorithms to recommend more similar material, potentially creating a cycle of repeated exposure.
Study author Holly Bear of the University of Oxford and colleagues examined how often adolescents in England reported coming across self-harm content online in the past month and the routes through which this happened. They were particularly interested in whether exposure was passive (unintentional) or active, such as searching for the content or having it shared with them, and how these different routes related to students’ demographic characteristics, social experiences, and mental health.
The researchers analyzed data from the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, a school-based survey of young people in England run by researchers at the University of Oxford. The analysis drew on 32,102 students in school years 7 through 13 (ages 11 to 18) at 49 secondary schools and further education colleges, mainly in Liverpool and Oxfordshire, who completed the survey between February and May 2025.
Students were asked whether they had come across content about self-harm on online platforms in the past month and, if so, how. They also answered questions about loneliness, bullying, online aggression and coercion, and symptoms of anxiety and depression. A total of 28,797 students answered the question about exposure, 14,083 of whom were girls.
Of these students, 9,940 (34.5%) reported encountering self-harm content online in the past month. Most of them (55%) had seen it once or twice, while 26.5% had seen it a few times and 18.5% several times.
Among exposed students who described how they came across the content, 66% said it had appeared in their feed or been suggested while they were browsing, and 24% said it was embedded within other, unrelated content. Fewer said they had accidentally encountered it (12%), searched for it (8%), or had it shared with them by someone else (8%), and 15% reported some other route.
Based on these answers, the researchers sorted students into groups. Nearly three-quarters (73%) had been exposed only through passive routes, 12% through a mix of routes, 9% only through “other” routes, 3% only by having the content shared with them, and 3% only by searching for it.
How often students saw the content depended on how they encountered it. Most students exposed only passively (59%) or only through content shared by others (62%) had seen it just once or twice in the past month, compared with about 30% of those who had only searched for it or who were exposed through a mix of routes. The authors note this is consistent with a feedback loop in which actively engaging with self-harm content leads algorithms to show more of it.
Each exposure route was associated with higher levels of loneliness, online harms, anxiety, and depression compared with students who reported no exposure, though the patterns differed across groups. Girls had higher odds than boys of passive-only exposure but lower odds of having content shared with them, and trans and gender-diverse students had elevated odds across most routes, particularly searching for the content.
Black students and students from mixed ethnic backgrounds were more likely than white students to have only searched for the content, as were students who often went to bed hungry compared with those who rarely did. Searching was most strongly linked to depression, while having content shared by others was more closely tied to receiving aggressive or threatening messages online. Students exposed through a mix of routes had some of the most pronounced risk profiles, with especially strong links to online aggression and coercion.
“Exposure to online self-harm content is widespread and shaped by distinct pathways that differ according to adolescents’ wider vulnerabilities, social environments and digital behaviors. Around one-third of our large community sample reported recent exposure, underscoring the need for interventions that account for diverse exposure experiences, from passive, algorithmically driven delivery to more intentional searches and peer sharing,” study authors concluded.
The authors call for a public health approach that combines regulation to reduce self-harm content in feeds, efforts to direct young people who search for it toward supportive resources, and digital literacy education for adolescents and their parents.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of how adolescents encounter self-harm content online. However, it should be noted that the survey was cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether loneliness, online harms, and mental health difficulties make exposure more likely, result from exposure, or both. The researchers also did not ask what kind of self-harm content students saw, which could range from graphic material to recovery stories and peer support.
In an earlier wave of the survey, about two-thirds of students who had actively sought out self-harm content cited potentially positive motivations, such as finding support or connecting with others with similar experiences. The data were self-reported and came mainly from two regions of England, and the wording of the exposure question, which asked whether students had “come across” such content, may have led some who sought it out to underreport.
The paper, “Algorithmically driven exposure to online self-harm content and its association with broader psychosocial risk in 32,000 adolescents,” was authored by Holly Bear, Emma Soneson, Galit Geulayov, and Mina Fazel.

US midterm elections 2026 in maps and charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:07 UTC
03:00:07 KST

US midterm elections 2026 in maps and charts
On November 3, Americans decide which party controls the US Congress for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency.
On November 3, about 210 million registered voters will decide how much power Donald Trump has for the rest of his US presidency.
Trump is not on the ballot, but control of the United States Congress is. Made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate, Congress writes the country’s laws and controls federal spending.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down how the elections work, which races matter and what the results could mean for either party.
What happens in the midterm elections?
Held halfway through a US president’s four-year term, midterm elections decide the makeup of Congress.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested, including special elections in the states of Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.
House members represent one congressional district each and serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.
Midterm elections are also widely considered a referendum on the sitting president’s performance.
Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 seats in the House and a handful in the Senate in midterm elections, according to Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.
Beyond Congress and governors, voters will also elect state legislators and local officials.
Nadia Brown, a professor of government at Georgetown University, said that while national elections get most of the attention, “It is important to remember that local politics is where most Americans interact with government.”
She added that “It is the local propositions or referendums on ballots [that] will impact the everyday lives of people.”
What is at stake in the House and Senate?
Republicans hold majorities in both chambers. Losing either would give Democrats the power to block legislation and launch investigations into Trump’s administration.
Democrats need to gain three seats in the House and four in the Senate to take control. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control, because Vance can cast tie-breaking votes.
Belt said a Democratic victory could significantly limit Trump’s ability to pursue his domestic agenda.
“If Democrats take one chamber, all non-government funding legislation will grind to a halt,” he told Al Jazeera.
How do House elections work?
The House of Representatives is the lower house of the US Congress.
Its 435 members each represent one local district and serve two-year terms, so every seat is contested every two years.
Seats are divided among the states by population, based on the US Census conducted every 10 years. California, the most populous state, has 52 seats, while the least populous, such as Wyoming and Vermont, have one each.
A party needs 218 seats for a majority.
Republicans currently control the House, with 218 seats to the Democrats’ 214, and one independent sits with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant, one last held by each party.
The new House will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
The House races to watch
Each district elects its own representative, and the party that wins 218 seats takes control, so a few narrow wins in close districts can decide the majority.
Belt estimates that about 35 House races could decide the majority. He predicts Democrats could gain about 15 seats, despite Republican redistricting that he says has given the party an advantage in nine additional districts.
“People generally vote straight ticket, meaning they will vote for all the candidates of one party, so this is likely to affect down-ballot races [as well],” he said.
A battleground district is a seat either party could realistically win. The graphic below highlights 12 of these key races to watch.
How do Senate elections work?
The Senate is the upper house of the US Congress.
Its 100 members, two from each state regardless of population, are elected statewide and serve six-year terms, with about a third of seats contested every two years.
This year, 33 seats are being contested in regular elections, alongside special elections in Florida and Ohio. Those two contests will fill the remaining two years of terms previously held by Marco Rubio and JD Vance.
Of the 35 seats being contested, Republicans hold 22, and Democrats hold 13.
Republicans currently have 53 senators. Democrats have 45, and two independents sit with them, giving the Democratic bloc 47 seats.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and take control. Republicans can keep control with 50 because Vice President Vance can break tied votes.
The new Senate will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
The Senate races to watch
To win the Senate, Democrats must hold the 13 seats they are defending and flip Republican-held ones.
In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff faces Republican Mike Collins. Michigan’s open seat pits Democrat Abdul El-Sayed against Republican Mike Rogers, while Democrat Chris Pappas faces Republican John Sununu for an open seat in New Hampshire.
Republican-held seats offer Democrats opportunities elsewhere. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced primary winner Graham Platner after he withdrew in July. North Carolina’s open seat pits Democrat Roy Cooper against Republican Michael Whatley.
Ohio, Alaska and Iowa are also competitive, while Texas and Kansas have drawn growing attention as Democrats look for more routes to a majority.
Although Democrats face a more difficult path to a Senate majority than to control of the House, the growing number of competitive races has increased their chances of winning the chamber, according to election analysts.
What are the key election issues?
The cost of living tops voters’ concerns, with rising petrol prices, housing costs and healthcare coverage squeezing household budgets.
Reproductive rights remain a major issue, while immigration and the state of US democracy are also on the ballot.
The US-Israel war on Iran and the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI)` and data centres have raised further questions about security, jobs and energy costs.
Who votes in the midterms?
About 210 million Americans are registered to vote, nearly eight in 10 US residents aged 18 or older, according to USAFacts, a nonpartisan organisation that compiles government data.
California has the most registered voters, with 23.2 million, followed by Texas (17.4 million) and Florida (13.6 million). Together, they account for about 26 percent of all registered voters.
Wyoming (278,468), Vermont (459,455) and Alaska (603,310) have the fewest.
How different groups plan to vote
A Pew Research Center survey conducted from September 28 to October 4 found that 44 percent of registered voters backed the Democratic candidate in their district, compared with 36 percent for the Republican. Five percent support another candidate, and 15 percent are unsure.
Men are evenly split, with 42 percent backing each party, while women favour Democrats by 45 percent to 31 percent.
The graphic below shows how voting preferences differ by gender, race, age, education and party affiliation.
US election voter turnout
Fewer Americans vote in midterms than in presidential elections. Since 1944, average turnout has been about 42 percent in midterms, compared with 58 percent in presidential races.
What happens if Republicans lose the House?
A Democratic House could block Republican legislation and use its committees to investigate the Trump administration. It would also hold the power to impeach the president, which only the House can do.
Control would also give Democrats leverage over government funding. Every bill needs approval from both chambers, so a Republican Senate could not pass laws on its own.
Belt expects a Democratic-controlled House to lead to more confrontations over federal spending, including the 12 annual bills needed to fund federal agencies. That raises the possibility of further government shutdowns, when funding lapses and many federal services stop.
Belt also believes that Trump could turn increasingly to foreign policy if his domestic agenda faces opposition in Congress.
“Traditionally, presidents facing divided government in their last two years pivot to foreign policy almost exclusively. I think the same will be true for Trump,” he said.
What happens if Republicans lose the Senate?
A Democratic Senate could block legislation and reject presidential nominees, including federal judges, Supreme Court justices, cabinet officials and ambassadors.
That makes Senate control consequential beyond the next two years. Federal judges serve for life, shaping rulings long after a presidency ends.
The Senate also holds the trial if the House impeaches a president. Removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority, a threshold neither party is likely to reach.
Would winning both chambers give Democrats full control?
No. Trump would remain president and could veto legislation, and overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
Senate rules also require 60 votes to end debate on most legislation, though some budget bills can pass with a simple majority. A narrow majority therefore does not guarantee a party can pass its programme.
A Democratic House could open impeachment proceedings against Trump, who has already been impeached twice. However, removing a president from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Belt considers another impeachment unlikely.
“There will definitely be investigations,” he told Al Jazeera, but added, “There will not likely be another impeachment because Democrats tried that twice and Republicans rallied behind Trump.”
When will we know the results?
Results will begin emerging after the first polls close at 6pm Eastern time (23:00 GMT) on November 3, but some close races could take days to resolve.
Election night results are preliminary. Final tallies can take days or sometimes weeks as officials count mail-in, provisional and other outstanding ballots before certifying the results, and the pace varies by state.
“In some states, it may take up to a week or more,” Belt said.
Some contests may go further. In Georgia, if no Senate candidate wins a majority, the race goes to a run-off election on December 1.
Belt warned that early results could give a misleading picture of the outcome. Because Republicans have historically been less likely than Democrats to vote by mail, some states could initially appear to favour Republican candidates before later-counted ballots narrow or reverse their leads. This is known as the “red mirage”. In states that count mail ballots first, the reverse can happen.
A delay in counting or a change in which candidate is leading does not, by itself, indicate electoral fraud.
The vote will decide who writes legislation, scrutinises the administration and controls federal spending, setting the balance of power for the rest of Trump’s term.

Why the manosphere sees 'desperate young men as moneybags'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Young men open up about looksmaxxing, toxic influencers and being a good man
It seems like the manosphere is lurking behind every corner.
From alarming headlines to documentary deep dives, what was once a fringe ideology has come full thrust into the mainstream.
And with young men shown toxic content within 23 minutes of creating a social media account, it's becoming an inescapable part of growing up in the internet age.
We asked young men what they're seeing online and how it's shaping their concept of masculinity.
Jak, 18, Melbourne
For me, it started with workout videos. It was generic stuff, like encouraging men to go to the gym, showing them proper form, that kind of thing.
Typically, you'd see a video of a guy, shirtless, ripped, big muscles, with electronic music playing in the background, saying, "You need to go to the gym. You need to lock in. You need to be strong and become the man you should be."
At first I thought, "Hell yeah." The message seemed to be that you need discipline and strength.
But I realised that the main idea is often that you're not good enough in various ways, and in order to be better you have to do X, Y and Z.
Over time, my algorithm became filled with people pushing peptides and steroids. Any influencer I watched long enough eventually started selling a course, supplements, or some kind of product.
A lot of it was saying that if you get big muscles you'll get women, and if women don't want you after you've built your body, then they're stupid.
I never tried to seek out the misogynistic side of these videos; it just came to me.
I was just thinking, "How did I go from gym videos to this?"
A lot of this content paints the idea that the world is out to get men, and I think some of that has bled into the real world.
Things that wouldn't have seemed normal before now feel normalised.
A couple of years ago, making fun of women wasn't really OK. Now you can be watching videos with friends, and if a woman starts speaking, someone says, "Shut up," and everyone laughs.
Recently, I worked on a Year 12 project about the manosphere. I learned a lot about how it can affect your mental wellbeing without you even realising.
Since doing that project, I've hopped off most social media.
At first, my friends thought I'd died. Then everyone thought I was crazy. A lot of people wanted to know what I actually do with my time.
But since leaving social media, I've just spent more time doing things I actually enjoy. I feel more confident and more present.
I wish people understood that no young man goes online intending to become misogynistic. A lot of it happens subconsciously and over a long period of time.
The core ideas are usually self-improvement — the ideas themselves are positive.
It's the way those ideas get twisted that becomes harmful.

Top cyber spy braces for more AI-powered hacking attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Disruptions 'inevitable' as AI-powered cyber threats grow, Australian Signals Directorate says
In short:
The Australian Signals Directorate says more disruptions to essential services are likely as AI increases the risk of cyber attacks.
AI is turbocharging the number and potency of cyber threats Australia faces from criminal networks and state-aligned operators, the agency says.
The ASD has also revealed previously secret details of its offensive operations, including the targeting of criminals hoarding and selling personal data on the dark web.
Australia's top cyber spy is warning the country to prepare for more frequent disruptions to everyday services amid a surge of AI-powered cyber attacks.
Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) director-general Abigail Bradshaw said artificial intelligence frontier models had "redefined" the threat facing Australia.
"What is inevitable is that with each capability increase, we are likely to see more disruption," she said.
"Disruption can look like what we've seen over the last few weeks, with websites that require patching having to be taken down in order to be secured.
"Disruption could look like data breaches. Disruption could look like service disruption.
"Virtually any service that you rely on in your life today is enabled in some respect by a digital network."
The warning comes just days after a number of government websites, including the ASD's, were brought partially offline after vulnerabilities were found.
Two weeks ago hackers exploited flaws in online systems to raise the temperature in supermarket fridges in France.
Today the ASD is publishing its annual cyber threat report, which details a 20 per cent jump in cybersecurity incidents the agency was required to respond to last financial year.
But Ms Bradshaw said the defining event of the past year was the release of frontier models such as Anthropic's Mythos.
Models such as Mythos were touted as being too dangerous to release publicly due to their capability to find vulnerabilities in cyber defence systems.
A swarm of AI agents was responsible for breaching Australian health data security, in what was described as the first autonomous hack of a government website.
Ms Bradshaw said that incident led to a reworking of the relationship between agencies such as the ASD and the massive American companies at the forefront of the technology.
She said the ASD had worked "very quickly" to set up protocols to act as an "early warning system" with AI companies, including OpenAI.
"These protocols have been shared with all of the labs, and all of the Five Eyes [intelligence agencies]," she said.
"We now have an equal expectation about the sorts of things that agencies like ASD need to be engaged on ahead of model testing."
Dismantling dark web operators
Responding to cyber incidents makes up a large portion of the ASD's work, but the agency is also keen to talk up the success of its offensive operations.
It revealed details of a recent effort to take down criminal groups selling and operating a piece of malware known as Amadey.
Hidden inside free software, Amadey steals the personal data or login details of its victims and transmits it back to criminal groups, where it is then sold on the dark web.
The ASD said in one case, it was found hidden in a free, illegitimate version of Photoshop editing software.
It also found evidence of the software being sold on the dark web for about $US500 ($712).
ASD operators were able to access the back end of Amadey's operation and found the criminal network had access to 180,000 computers across the globe, including in Australia.
"The next steps that we took were to disconnect that Amadey controller from all those victims," ASD acting deputy director-general of intelligence Tauri Gregory said.
"And so, effectively, that cyber criminal can no longer access those 180,000 computers and no longer steal data from all those people.
"If ASD had not acted here, you'd have 180,000 businesses or individuals whose data was being stolen and be either sold on the dark web or monetised in other ways, or used to inform follow-on crimes such as fraud and identity theft."
In another case, the ASD was tipped off to the sale of 5 terabytes of data stolen from a business that was unaware it had been hacked.
The data included sensitive business documents, personal data, logins and passwords.
Mr Gregory said the agency was able to break in and destroy the data before it could be sold.
"To give some context, we think there are about 4.8 million files which were stolen from Australians, which we destroyed in that operation, as well as hundreds of thousands of files from other victims around the world," he said.
Mr Gregory said AI was increasing the scope and scale of attacks, but it was also an enormous asset to those trying to defend against them.
"We are using AI to generate software capabilities much more quickly, and so we use it to support our software engineering and development of new tools and capabilities directly," he said.
An accelerating threat
The agency has previously joined international partners in warning of Chinese-aligned actors building hidden networks of hijacked devices that can be used for espionage or offensive operations.
It has also warned that some state actors want to maintain access to essential services and infrastructure that could be disrupted if conflict were to break out.
Ms Bradshaw said strategic tensions in the region would increase that threat.
"The natural progression of this is, as the world becomes uncertain, of course nation states will try to reduce that uncertainty by obtaining more information," she said.
"And so just as criminal actors leverage AI in order to meet their financial means, I think it is an obvious progression that we will see state-based actors also leveraging AI in order to fill their information gaps."
Ms Bradshaw said there was a huge amount of work to do in both corporate and government systems to better prepare for and defend against cyber threats, particularly in replacing vulnerable "legacy" systems.
She said it also meant learning how to best use AI as a defensive tool.
"There is much more that we need to do and, in the current context, that is now a matter of urgency," Ms Bradshaw said.

Labor MPs turn to AI to combat online abuse as thousands of threats flagged
In short:
Social media companies are facing calls to take greater responsibility for online safety after new data exposed the extent of abuse aimed at politicians.
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments were directed at a sample of 22 Labor MPs and senators trialling a new AI moderation tool in the past three months.
What's next?
MPs are demanding tech giants do more to tackle online abuse and threats.
Almost 5,000 threats and violent comments have been flagged on the social media accounts of 22 Labor politicians in just three months as MPs have turned to technology to combat online abuse.
New data from an AI tool being trialled by some senators and MPs has exposed the scale of hostility elected representatives face, with about half of the more than 460,000 comments analysed between July and October classified as abusive.
About 190,000 of the screened comments were personal attacks, with gender-based abuse, racism and transphobia the categories most commonly identified by an AI-powered plug-in, called Areto.
There were 2,497 threats and 2,487 comments using violent language, with examples including "someone shoot this dopey b***h" and "you need to be hung for treason".
In one post, an MP was called a "brain dead b***h", while in another comment a person said they "prefer assassinations".
Labor MPs using Areto told the ABC the tool protected both staff and community members, with abusive content clearly differentiated from genuine political criticism.
The safety of politicians has become a focus in the wake of the attack on Indi MP Helen Haines, for which the motive remains unknown.
Senior public servants have also warned that social media clips of various parliamentary committee hearings were fuelling abuse towards bureaucrats.
Abuse has 'chilling effect' on community
A few female Labor members began experimenting with Areto, which uses AI to identify and hide abusive and threatening comments, earlier this year before a trial was then extended to others in the caucus.
Analysis of the results for 22 parliamentarians using the tool in the past three months found high-profile accounts typically received more attacks, with one MP recording 57,522 abusive comments.
Facebook carried about 94 per cent of all comments, of which 51 per cent were abusive, compared with 42 per cent of the small number of comments on Instagram and 21 per cent of the comments on TikTok.
Finance and Women's Minister Katy Gallagher, who has started using Areto, said the volume of abuse online was "extraordinary".
"It is having a chilling effect on genuine community engagement," she said.
"For women, the abuse is usually sexualised, a lot about physical harm that will be done to you or your children."
Senator Gallagher said the automated AI tool was not filtering critical comments about the government or policy, but was giving her staff and others "respite" from abusive content.
"It's not a perfect solution, and I don't think anyone expects it to be, but the platforms themselves are not dealing with this," she said.
Minister told 'you're next' after Haines attack
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said the behaviour of the social media platforms was "pitiful", accusing them of prioritising profits over safety.
"These platforms are profiting off people treating each other with disrespect, anger, aggression and abuse. Then they play dumb at the devastating social effects that are happening across the country," she said.
Ms O'Neil said the fact that Areto existed was a "tragedy", but it was essential in helping to manage the mental health of her team.
"Female MPs shouldn't have to have a program that screens for death and rape threats, but that's where we are,"
she said.
Ms O'Neil said the majority of public interactions she had as an MP were respectful, but she sensed the "online environment is seeping into the way people behave in real life".
"No-one should feel sorry for us; that's not what this is about," she said.
"Politicians just happen to be in the public conversation right now, but it doesn't matter if you're an AFL footballer or a nurse working in a hospital, or a retail worker … Anyone who interfaces with the public is feeling this declining respect."
Ms O'Neil said the abuse directed at politicians went beyond the "democratic process" of "people being upset with government and wanting to convey that".
"I don't see a straight line between that and, 'You're next s**t,' being written on my social media wall two days after Helen Haines [was attacked]."
MP's children the target of racist abuse
Bonner MP Kara Cook has been trialling Areto for the past six months. She said as someone who did most of her own social media, she had noticed a vast improvement.
"For me, having a safe space for people locally to be able to genuinely express their views has been positive because I want to hear those," she said.
Areto has hidden 15,244 comments, mostly on Ms Cook's Facebook page, which were identified as "abusive", with racism, gender microaggression and transphobia the most common categories of attack.
Ms Cook, who has three First Nations children, said posts about her family often attracted "overwhelmingly racist comments".
"I've never hidden who I am as a person from my community … and I don't want that to change, but I also want to protect my family from that abuse," she said.
The first-term MP, who was a domestic violence lawyer and has previously served as a local councillor, said the day after she was elected to federal parliament, her home address and pictures of her house were published online.
"From that moment it was very clear to me that I'd entered a very different environment to any other workplace I'd ever been in," she said.
Ms Cook also said tech companies had an "obligation" to stop threatening and racist abuse appearing on their platforms.
She said the attack on Ms Haines needed to be a "pivotal moment" when Australia changed its approach to the safety of everyone, particularly women.
Public service hits out at 'ridicule' and 'vile abuse' of officials
At a Senate estimates hearing on Monday, top public servant Steven Kennedy said officials were also subject to increasing abuse online, and that parliamentarians were partly to blame for sharing "misleading" clips.
Those concerns were first aired in September when a senior defence official told a committee she did not want her answers clipped up for social media.
That request was rejected, with opposition and crossbench parliamentarians outraged by the idea.
But Mr Kennedy, who heads the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, said while he did not propose censoring footage, the "health and safety" of officials was a concern.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.
"Evidence has been edited [for social media] in ways that invite ridicule, hostility or abuse directed at individual public servants … Unfortunately, some public servants have been the subjects of vile abuse."
Mr Kennedy urged parliamentarians to moderate comments on their social media posts and to delete abuse directed at officials.

Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Volcanoes lurk behind the scenes of human history
Cold spells after eruptions may have spurred famine, disease, revolt and religious changes
“The bright sun was extinguish’d … and the icy earth swung blind and blackening in the moonless air.” These words from Lord Byron’s 1816 poem Darkness evoke a hellish apocalypse. But Byron may have been inspired by the fallout of a real cataclysm — one that happened half a world away.
Mount Tambora, in present-day Indonesia, blew its top in 1815. More than 71,000 people in the vicinity died. And climate-cooling aerosols from the eruption ushered in extreme weather the following years in far-flung places. Cold weather in the summer of 1816, sometimes with frosts and snow, destroyed corn in New England, rice and buckwheat in China and wheat, oats and potatoes in Ireland. In some places, the rising cost of bread sparked protests and riots. The circumstances may have helped spread typhus. Some called 1816 “the year without a summer,” others “the year of the beggars.”
Like Tambora, volcanoes, and the cooling they cause, may be an underappreciated geologic force at times moving behind the scenes of human history.
“These climatic impacts of the Tambora eruption were recorded without any knowledge that this had anything to do with an eruption,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge.
While Tambora is the most well-studied eruption in history, others have also rattled the planet. Oppenheimer and his colleagues analyzed 38 large eruptions in the 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Their work pulled together studies linking the geologic events and their effects on climate with their potential societal fallout in food systems, the economy, unrest, culture and religion. The locations and exact timing of the eruptions that spurred some notable cold spurts aren’t known. But understanding how the events impacted the climate, environment and society can offer clues to the past, including how people coped with climate stress.
“Volcanic eruptions, they are kind of this like hammer blow to the climate system,” says Heli Huhtamaa, a climate and environmental historian at the University of Bern in Switzerland. Volcanoes may offer lessons about resilience for modern societies in a warming world, she says.
Volcanic gases create a chilling effect
Volcanoes spew sulfur-containing gases. Over weeks, those gases react in the atmosphere to form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. Paintings from years after eruptions show bloodred sunsets or landscapes shrouded by hazy skies.
Because no two eruptions are exactly alike, it takes work to grasp each one’s impacts on weather and climate. “If we understand the climate response of one [eruption], that does not mean that we understand the climate response of another,” says Ulf Büntgen, a paleoclimatologist at the University of Cambridge.
Up in the air
A volcano’s explosivity impacts how high it shoots its gases and where they travel. Over time, those gases form particles that block sunlight. The particles can stay aloft for many months, riding jet streams to encircle the globe. In this computer model of a 1991 eruption, colors represent how high particles are in the atmosphere. Red is high and blue is closer to Earth’s surface.
Researchers find the traces of past eruptions in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. Scientists try to nail down the date on a sulfur-loaded ice core layer and compare it with tree ring data, a logbook of sorts for summer growing conditions since temperatures impact how trees lay down their wood each year. Scientists can pull together tree ring records from far-flung places and use statistics to work out annual temperatures in a hemisphere.
Cold spells sometimes jump out from tree ring records. For years when cool summers impeded the final stages of wood formation, a chemical method used to estimate temperatures turns wood layers blue. Büntgen and colleagues saw two blue rings around 1345. “And that is very rare. We never saw that two years in a row,” he says. The rings coincided with the timing of the Black Death’s spread in Europe, the team reported in 2025 in Communications Earth & Environment. The researchers traced the connections between chilly summers, poor grain harvests in the Mediterranean and shipping records showing how Italian city states imported flea-ridden grain from the Caucasus.
Oppenheimer, Büntgen and their colleagues broadened the detective work for their 2026 review. The team studied Northern Hemisphere temperature responses to the 38 largest eruptions between A.D. 1 and 1900. On average, each volcano caused about 0.5 degrees Celsius of cooling in the year after the eruption. Recovery to normal temperatures was slower for eruptions that occurred in times that were already colder on average, Büntgen says. In some periods, large or successive eruptions may lead to an elevated amounts of particles in the atmosphere for a long time. The team’s calculations show that high aerosol levels concur with some of the past two millennia’s coldest spells, such as the one preceding the Black Death.
Human agency factors into eruptions’ outcomes
Those cold snaps often had dire consequences. Out of 17 large-scale famines in Europe from 1300 to 1800, 11 followed major eruptions. In addition to faltering crops and famines, the most frequently societal responses described in studies collected by the review authors were disease outbreaks, political turmoil and migration.
The societal circumstances surrounding eruptions are as important as the amount of cooling, Huhtamaa says. She and her colleagues studied crop failures and farmstead desertion in three different volcanic eruptions that impacted Ostrobothnia, in what is now Finland. During the 17th century, Ostrobothnia experienced cooling from three sets of eruptions at different time periods.
Although the latest eruption event, in 1695, was the coldest of all, peasants fared better than they had after eruptions earlier in the century, Huhtamaa and colleagues reported in 2022 in Climate of the Past. Though people still starved, only around 7 percent of peasants lost their farmland, compared with 20 percent in the other periods. This was because the crown provided tax relief, Huhtamaa says. This wasn’t humanitarian aid, as it was meant to preserve the tax base and prevent possibly decades of lost revenue.
“When there is a climatic shock, it doesn’t matter if it’s 0.5 or 1.5 degrees cooler, because what really matters is the societal vulnerability,” Huhtamaa says.
Studies like Huhtamaa’s reveal how societies can tick on in spite of climate disasters. But historians haven’t always been keen to look to climate for clues to explain history. Human agency has often been considered the only reasonable explanation for human affairs, Huhtamaa says. “And climate explanations sounded lazy.”
Investigating societies’ preconditions and responses to the climate change caused by volcanoes could help people prepare for a now warming world. A recent report from the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, noted that not enough research had been done on responses, Huhtamaa says. Researchers could examine one place’s response to different events, as in Huhtamaa’s work on Ostrobothnia, or parse different locales’ responses to the same event. Meanwhile, greater use of insights from ecology, agronomy and economics, for instance, can help with this detective work that reveals how humans respond to climatic events beyond their control.
Those responses appear in religion, too. For instance, lines in the famed 10th century poem Vǫluspá seem to reference the 939 eruption of Iceland’s Eldgjá volcano, with high-flying flames and blackened sun beams. “It’s like an eyewitness description of a phenomenal lava flood,” Oppenheimer says. The poem foretells a fiery end to pagan gods, such as Odin, who are replaced by one god. Vǫluspá, which explained the eruption in terms of divine displeasure,may have contributed to the island’s Christianization around 1000, Oppenheimer and colleagues suggest.
Famines, riots, disease, migration. The widespread climatic effects of volcanoes across the ages may be subtler than the hellscapes conjured by poets but more tangible in the marks they’ve left on history.

Israel’s democracy faces its greatest test as Netanyahu clings to power - opinion

2026-10-26
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

As Israel’s elections draw closer, the Israeli government has once again reaffirmed its illiberal orientation and embarked on a troubling escalation, with a series of controversial decisions affecting civil liberties and the rule of law.
Two journalists, one German and the other Italian, who had come to cover the election, were denied entry visas to Israel, for no apparent reason. And no explanation was provided for the suspension of the aliyah process for two young left-wing Jews, which was forcefully condemned by Labor Party lawmaker Gilad Kariv.
This arbitrary decision, which runs deeply counter to the very idea of Zionism, follows the expulsion of two Jewish women from Israel for their own activism in support of Palestinians, along with a 10-year ban on entering the country.
In another display of demagoguery reflecting his authoritarian drift, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to identify the soldiers who testified anonymously in the film NAZA and bring them to justice, after reiterating his call to strip the film’s directors of their citizenship.
This threat against the film’s witnesses retrospectively vindicates their decision to remain anonymous, a practice criticized by those who have attacked the film. The documentary is certainly not beyond reproach, particularly because of its analogy with the Holocaust. Yet its critics have failed to take sufficient account of the authoritarian drift of Israel’s current government.
As with the two young Jews whose aliyah process has been suspended and the journalists denied entry visas, the real objective of these maneuvers is not necessarily to target the individuals concerned. Rather, it is to create a climate of fear and intimidation that encourages others to think twice before speaking out or taking action.
This well-established method in authoritarian regimes applies, for example, to future young left-wing Jewish activists who might one day consider immigrating to Israel and who could be deterred from doing so by the prospect of being targeted.
These reprehensible intimidation tactics also serve populist and electoral demagoguery. Netanyahu is capitalizing on Israelis’ sense of isolation and of living in a besieged fortress – a feeling he has helped foster – and turning it into electoral fuel by dismissing all critical voices as “hostile.”
When the government itself is not making threats, far-right thugs, often affiliated with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, regularly disrupt public meetings and leaflet distributions organized by Yair Golan’s party, the Democrats.
They use hooligan-style tactics all too familiar to Palestinians in the West Bank, who are attacked by violent settlers, a journalist from The Washington Post, or European diplomats, while the authorities look on with culpable indulgence.
All these incidents reflect tensions within Israeli society, but also the nervousness of a prime minister clinging to power.
Opposition fears election interference
Attacks by the Right on expatriate voting, the Likud’s efforts to ban Arab parties, threats to bomb Iran before the elections that could lead to their cancellation, and the party’s allegations of possible foreign interference, intended to cast doubt on the election’s legitimacy, help explain the fears expressed by opposition figures.
They are also wary of Netanyahu’s political exploitation of security concerns.
Netanyahu is so attached to power that it is difficult to believe he would accept the ballot box’s verdict if it went against him, much like his “friend,” US President Donald Trump, who has just endorsed him.
These warning signs could help pave the way for such a scenario. This volatile situation, combined with the prime minister’s cynicism, explains Golan’s recent remarks in which he warned of a scenario resembling January 6, 2021, when Trump’s supporters stormed the Capitol.
In 1999, shortly before suffering a resounding defeat, Netanyahu repeatedly said of his opponents, “They are afraid,” in an attempt to dispel his own fears.
Today, as then, Netanyahu is afraid. Of judges. Of critics. Of voters. Of defeat. That fear makes him unpredictable and dangerous, ready to do anything to remain in office.
Israeli democracy is rightly a source of national pride. A small country under threat, Israel has never abandoned the practice of holding elections despite geopolitical tensions and a wartime atmosphere, and no election in its history has ever been contested. It will face its greatest test on October 27 and in the days that follow.
The writer, who was born and raised in France, is the correspondent of French Jewish radio, Radio J, and of the French paper librejournal.fr in the US, where he has been living for 16 years. He also holds US and Israeli citizenship. The opinions expressed are his own.

Hind Rajab Foundation files UK criminal complaint against Israeli soldier over Gaza war crimes

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has filed a criminal complaint with UK authorities against Israeli soldier Lidor Dafna over alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide committed in the Gaza Strip.
The foundation said in a statement Sunday that Dafna, a reservist serving as a D9 armored bulldozer operator in the 603rd Combat Engineering Battalion of the 7th Armored Brigade, participated in military operations in Gaza and Lebanon from November 2023 onward.
The foundation said it has reason to believe he is currently in the UK.
The complaint focuses on the destruction of Great Ocean Mills, an industrial flour-producing facility in the Morag Corridor between Khan Younis and Rafah, on May 25, 2025.
According to the foundation, footage posted by Dafna on social media shows a bulldozer demolishing the facility's wheat silos.
The foundation said Israeli forces subsequently occupied the building, converted it into a military base and reportedly used it to shoot Palestinians seeking food aid at a nearby Gaza Humanitarian Foundation site.
The foundation said the destruction occurred when Israel had sealed Gaza to food, fuel and medicine, with flour reportedly selling for as much as $70 per kilogram and half a million people facing starvation.
The foundation also said that the 603rd Battalion carried out more than 60 controlled demolitions of buildings, including mosques and residential blocks, and contributed to widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure and agricultural land during the establishment of the Morag Corridor.
The foundation said its investigation indicates that Dafna may be criminally responsible for extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity, intentionally targeting civilian objects, using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, extermination as a crime against humanity and genocide.
The foundation called on British authorities to open an investigation, arrest and question Dafna, citing Article 146 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which requires states to search for individuals alleged to have committed grave breaches of the convention.
Dyab Abou Jahjah, the foundation's director general, said: “Lidor Dafna filmed himself destroying one of the last remaining food production facilities serving a starving population, then posted the footage on social media as a trophy.”
“The United Kingdom now faces a simple test: will it arrest and prosecute a man, who remains an active soldier of an army carrying out such crimes, or once again permit a perpetrator of genocide to walk freely on its soil and return to Gaza to continue committing his crimes?” he added.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday.

Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future.

Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:49 UTC
02:56:49 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel entered an election silence period Monday ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary elections, with restrictions on campaign activities taking effect at 7 pm local time (1700GMT), an Anadolu correspondent reported.
Under Article 129 of the Knesset Elections Law, campaigning at gatherings and marches, through loudspeakers, and on radio and television is prohibited from 7 pm on the eve of the election and throughout polling day, according to the Knesset's official website.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) Tuesday and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). In communities with no more than 350 eligible voters, voting will take place from 8 am (0600GMT) to 8 pm (1800GMT).
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm, when Israeli media outlets are also expected to release exit poll results, according to Israel's Channel 12.
Under Article 11 of the Basic Law: The Knesset, the Central Elections Committee has eight days after election day to publish the official results in the official gazette, setting a deadline of Nov. 4.
 
More than 7.3 million eligible voters
A total of 37 parties and electoral alliances are contesting seats in the 120-member Knesset, with 13 projected to secure parliamentary representation.
The main contenders include Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and Yashar, which is contesting its first election under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Opinion polls suggest Yashar could emerge as the largest party, challenging years of Likud dominance.
According to the Central Elections Committee, 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in elections for the 26th Knesset.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide and around 100,000 personnel working on election day.
Of the polling stations, 6,209 will be accessible to people with disabilities.
Twenty regional election committees will oversee preparations and voting operations in their respective jurisdictions.
To facilitate access to polling stations, 660 intercity public transport routes and all Israel Railways services will operate free of charge on election day, according to the committee.
 
Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Forming a government requires the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset.
The previous Knesset dissolved on July 17, paving the way for the Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has led the current government since December 2022, heading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel's history.
He is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
The International Criminal Court has also issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu over war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:31 UTC
02:56:31 KST

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Chilean studio Paralelo Transversal has designed a rectangular house with a large hip roof and a terrace that cantilevers over a ravine in Puerto Varas, Chile.
Completed in 2025 on a 1.2-acre site near Lago Llanquihue, the 155-square-metre house, known as Casa Ensenada, was oriented around its roof.
“In southern Chile, rain is not an exception but part of everyday life, so we wanted the roof to become more than a protective element,” architect Sebastián Silva of Paralelo Transversal told Dezeen.
“It creates a place beneath the rain, extending daily life beyond the enclosed rooms while bringing the different parts of the project together under one continuous gesture.”
The roof serves as the organising element for the program, circulation, relationship to the landscape and the home’s structure.
“Its section thickens toward the center while remaining remarkably thin at its perimeter,” Silva said.
“This allows it to be perceived as a light, continuous sheet while providing the structural depth required for long-span trusses capable of resisting both Chile’s seismic conditions and the strong winds of Patagonia.”
The house sits on a sloped site with a stream. Residents and visitors approach along the stream before the access ramp turns towards the house, where they enter at the junction of public and private zones.
The narrower side of the plan contains a large, open kitchen, dining and living room that bleeds onto the cantilevered terrace.
Oriented toward the northeast to capture winter sunlight, the house opens its living spaces to the landscape – the valley of Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park on one side and Calbuco Volcano on the other – through floor-to-ceiling windows with thin black frames.
The other side of the house widens to hold three suites. On either side of the house, the perimeter wall pushes under the roof canopy to form a covered bench and a planted garden.
The warm, contemporary material palette continues across the exterior and interior with exposed concrete slabs, large spans of glazing, tongue-and-groove timber and standing-seam metal roofing.
The concealed joints allowed the roof to be precise while reducing the visual impact of construction tolerances. The team collaborated closely with engineers and local builders to achieve its long spans and thin edge.
“Looking back, we believe the project fulfilled its original ambition of integrating architecture and landscape without compromising comfort, construction logic or budget,” Silva said.
“More importantly, it reinforced our belief that a project becomes stronger when one clear architectural idea is capable of organizing structure, climate, materiality and space simultaneously.”
Previously, Paralelo Transversal created a sail-like skylight that brought sun, shadows and air into a home on the outskirts of Santiago.
Other homes recently completed in Chile include a mass timber forest hideaway by Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos and a seaside home with stacked terraces by Croxatto and Opazo Architects.
