Award-winning producer receives £400,000 payout from BBC over workplace antisemitism claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:52 UTC
02:39:52 KST

An Oscar- and Emmy-winning producer has received a payout of more than £400,000 from the BBC after claiming she was victimized and forced out of the corporation following the October 7 attacks.
Lucie Kon left the broadcaster in April, just 19 days after winning an Oscar for her work, following a dispute over antisemitism in the workplace. Having built a stellar career on major programs including Panorama, Today, BBC Breakfast, and Storyville, her commissioned and produced films have earned an Emmy, an Oscar, a BAFTA, and many other prestigious industry honors.
Speaking to The Telegraph on Sunday, Kon alleged that her professional treatment shifted rapidly after the October 7 attacks in Israel. As footage and news of the atrocities emerged, she had messaged a colleague on WhatsApp asking if they had seen what was happening in Israel and remarking that Hamas were evil. In response, the colleague told her that “Zionists” were evil.
“I was like, ‘What?’ And she went, ‘Evil Hamas, evil Zionists,’ a bit like it was a joke, like they were the same and they’re not the same, and that was a particularly tasteless thing to say at that particular moment in history,” Kon said.
Later, when Kon sought to raise concerns about the treatment of Jewish staff and insisted that staff should at least be able to describe Hamas as committing acts of terror, another colleague told her that if she wanted to refer to Hamas as terrorists, she was required to call Israel a terrorist state as well.
Kon helps set up WhatsApp group for Jewish BBC employees
Pushed by the worsening workplace environment, Kon helped set up an internal WhatsApp group for Jewish employees at the corporation and wrote to then-Director General Tim Davie to raise concerns.
Shortly afterward, as more footage of the atrocities emerged, Kon proposed producing a film about the events of October 7 to a colleague who had previously made inappropriate remarks. When she mentioned the idea, the colleague dismissed it, saying they had already made enough films about Israel, but Kon’s manager later called her over to discuss the project.
“She said, ‘Lucie, we probably will do the Nova film,’” Kon recounted. “And she said to me, ‘But if we do it, we need to contextualize why Hamas did what they did.’”
When Kon questioned this requirement, explaining that the project was intended as a straightforward account of what happened that day rather than a deep dive into the historical and political context of the region, her manager’s manager informed her that she could no longer oversee the film. When Kon asked why, the manager told her it was “because you’re Jewish” and stated she was partial.
Kon noted that the manager then stated the person who was going to look after the film instead was the very same colleague who had previously told her that if Hamas were terrorists, the Israelis were terrorists too. An arrangement was later reached where Kon could oversee the film, but only under the strict supervision of someone else to ensure she remained impartial.
Kon subsequently raised a formal grievance. News of the grievance quickly reached the colleague who had made the remarks about Zionists, and that colleague wanted nothing more to do with Kon. This meant the two could no longer attend meetings together, and Kon was instructed not to come into work.
Six months later, she received the outcome. “It wasn’t upheld,” Kon said. “I was told that a lot of the things that I’d said people didn’t remember saying. And I was told that I’d been told - that I hadn’t been told I couldn’t work on the Nova film because I was a Jew - that they were worried about my mental health.”
When she appealed the decision, that appeal was also unsuccessful. At the time of her appeal, the BBC moved her colleague away from the Strand to work elsewhere, while Kon was told she could no longer travel, commission, or speak on behalf of the BBC because it would be unfair to her colleague.
Kon continued working from home while her appeal was considered, but by December, the stress took a toll, and her health began to deteriorate. After submitting a doctor’s note for stress-related sick leave, she was called into a meeting where she was told her job was being put at risk of redundancy. Having returned from sick leave, she applied for a newly created position but was rejected and made redundant in April.
BBC refuses to apologize, call Kon victim of antisemitism
According to The Telegraph, she brought unfair dismissal proceedings against the BBC, which agreed to pay her substantial compensation, partly funded by the license fee, without admitting liability. The corporation refused to apologize or admit she was a victim of antisemitism.
The Telegraph noted that she is the first person known to have been given a settlement by the BBC after alleging antisemitic behavior among colleagues. Speaking about the broader climate for staff after her departure, Kon reportedly told The Telegraph that other Jewish colleagues are still being bullied and abused, adding, “I know that nothing has changed because I’ve spoken to quite a few people since I left. Friends who are still struggling, still suffering, who feel embarrassed to say that they’re Zionist or that they’re a Jew.”
“I went from being a journalist and commissioner at the BBC who was Jewish to being a Jewish journalist at the BBC,” Kon said. “It was like I had Jew stamped on my forehead. I think I became a problem. I think I made too much of a noise about being a Jew inside the BBC.”
Kon added, “A colleague of mine said to me a while ago that if you say you’re a Zionist at the BBC, you might as well say that you were the person who had their foot on the neck of George Floyd. You’re a murderer. You’re an evil colonialist. You are a racist, and I’m not any of those things, and neither are the other people I know who are Zionist.”
“I stood up for who I was,” Kon said. “I stood up for what I believed to be right. The BBC says, ‘Bring your authentic self to work.’ And I did, and I lost my job as a result.”
A BBC spokesperson said in a statement, “We are grateful that Ms. Kon acknowledges that the BBC is not institutionally antisemitic. The BBC processes did not uphold any of Ms. Kon’s allegations of antisemitism. However, the outcome acknowledged shortcomings and the personal impact on Ms. Kon. We would like to acknowledge that Ms. Kon was a valued member of staff with many years of dedicated service to the BBC.”

They will serve out their terms under Israel’s next government.
Israel and Rwanda established relations in the early 1960s, but severed them in 1973. Decades later, in 1998, Israel and Rwanda renewed their relations, which have remained cordial. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Rwanda in 2016, and Rwanda President Paul Kagame visited Israel in July 2017 in return.
Since taking office in the immediate aftermath of the Rwandan genocide, Kagame has spent the past 26 years rebuilding his country and forming strong international partnerships. Israel and Rwanda cooperate on many levels, including innovation, technology, agriculture, and security. Rwanda and Israel signed several bilateral agreements earlier this year when Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe visited Israel.
Bayingana said that he would work to further expand the relationship between the two countries.
Neither Herzog nor Parisot tried to pretend that relations between France and Israel were rosy. However, Parisot noted that, despite their diplomatic challenges, the people-to-people relations and cultural ties between France and Israel remained strong.
Herzog and Parisot also discussed the chaos and unrest that have overtaken France in recent weeks. Herzog recalled how different Champs-Élysées had felt when he accompanied his late father, then-president Chaim Herzog, on a state visit to France in 1988.
Herzog recalls time of 'amazing' French-Israeli relations
Herzog also recalled a time when relations between France and Israel were so positive they were “amazing.”
Parisot later wrote in the guest book that he would devote all of his energy to improving relations between the two countries.

He was born in Haifa; he left the country as a child, and returned some 20 years ago as a spokesman for the Austrian embassy. Michal Herzog, the president's wife, seldom sits in on the presentation of diplomatic credentials. This time, however, she attended the meetings with both the French and Austrian ambassadors and joined the ensuing conversations.

But he also expressed concern over the discourse emanating from Holland and some of the government’s own negative comments. He warned that Israel and Holland’s relations were currently under strain. Rubacic replied that she was happy to be in Israel and stressed the importance of highlighting the good relations between the two countries, which are based on shared values.
The significance Israel attaches to its ties with the Netherlands was evident in the brief, closed-door tete-a-tete Herzog had with the ambassador after the formalities concluded.
Most African countries with which Israel has diplomatic ties are proud of their culture and heritage. Ghana is no exception. Ofosu-Amable and her entourage arrived at the President’s Residence in national dress. Herzog was struck by the swell of colors and commented on it. He also noted that Israel’s relations with Ghana span seven decades, dating back to when former premier Golda Meir made her historic visit to Africa.
Israel trained Ghanaian soldiers early in relationship
In the early years of their relationship, Israel helped to train soldiers in Ghana’s army. Ghana stands out for the confidence it places in its women. Many of the country’s diplomats and high-ranking officials are women, and the ambassador is among them.
Where Israel and Ghana differ is their stance on a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Ghana’s President John Mahama told Ofosu-Amable that she must remember that her mission is to uphold Ghana’s longstanding commitment to the two-state solution.

Form a government, you can hate each other on your own time - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:47 UTC
02:39:47 KST

Before casting his vote in Israel’s first national election, Rabbi Moshe Yekutiel Alpert told off the polling committee.
Its chairman was two minutes late.
On January 25, 1949, Alpert got up at 5:35 a.m., put on his Shabbat clothes, and headed for a Jerusalem polling station. His home in the Beit Yisrael neighborhood had been damaged by shelling; he was staying elsewhere while it was being repaired. He carried his Israeli identity card, he wrote, with the same joy of carrying a Torah scroll during Simchat Torah celebrations.
He arrived at 5:50. The chairman appeared at 6:02. Alpert reminded him that proceedings were supposed to begin at six. The man apologized.
As the oldest person present, Alpert was invited to vote first at that station. He received “voter number one,” said Shehecheyanu, the blessing of gratitude for reaching a special occasion, and cast his ballot.
His father and grandfather had never had the same opportunity.
I shared the story this week. The Jewish state was eight months old, and Alpert already expected it to run on time.
It’s a familiar mix of reverence and impatience. Israelis can be fiercely attached to their country and furious with it, often in the same conversation. People expect a great deal from a place their families have paid a great deal for. From abroad, the anger can be easier to hear than the attachment.
Today, Jewish and Arab Israelis will again choose the people who govern them. I hope we allow ourselves a little of Alpert’s pleasure before we begin arguing about the exit polls. The ability to vote a government out is worth appreciating, including when a government we favor loses.
Israel needs several years where its citizens can make plans again
What I want from this election is a few years in which Israelis can make plans again.
Three years after October 7, consider what that would mean for a reservist trying to keep a business alive. Someone has to cover the work while he is away. His spouse has to rearrange work and childcare. Eventually, decisions about next month become decisions about whether the business has a future.
Families rebuilding their homes need to know that funding and official attention will last until the work is finished. They should be able to plan around a budget that survives the next coalition dispute.
I believe only a broad Zionist government can give this country the political stability it needs for that work. Likud, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, and other Zionist parties should negotiate an agreement to govern together for several years.
That will require leaders to sit with people they have spent the campaign attacking and explain the arrangement to voters who believed those attacks.
Some will have to accept a job smaller than the one they wanted. They should tell us which demands they are prepared to set aside. I would find that interview considerably more useful than another account of why everything is someone else’s fault.
There is a reason these concessions are so hard. In Israel, a political allegiance often comes with a family history. It may include a grandparent’s experience of immigration, a parent’s sense of being looked down on, or a lasting belief that people like us were denied a fair hearing. Calling an entire camp ignorant or dangerous reaches well beyond the politician at its head.
An election settles who has the votes to govern. People still have to live together afterward. A citizen should be able to lose an election and feel at home in their country. Leaders who want a broad coalition will have to show they understand one another’s voters.
Start the negotiations by asking what 70 or 80 percent of Israelis could support. I would begin with security preparedness, restoring damaged communities, and arrangements that let reservists serve without ruining their livelihoods. Agree on what can be done, how much it will cost, and who is responsible. Give ministers enough time in office to be judged on whether they delivered.
A coalition agreement might even contain a deadline unrelated to the next leadership rotation.
Independent October 7 commission must be part of coalition agreement
An independent, credible examination of October 7 must be part of that agreement. Families deserve to know how the state failed them. Officials and commanders need to answer for their decisions. A coalition assembled to restore public trust will have to accept findings that may be uncomfortable for its own members.
Before accepting another promise, I want to know whom that candidate appointed, what improved while they were in office, and what they did when something went wrong. The politician I like deserves the same questions. Newcomers can be judged on their experience and the seriousness of their plans.
Theodor Herzl, the founder of modern political Zionism, described Zionism in 1904 as “a never-ending ideal.” Even after the Jewish people obtained a homeland, he wrote, the pursuit of “ethical and spiritual fulfillment” would continue.
In our time, that responsibility includes a government office being responsible for treating a bereaved family, the education available to a child far from the center of the country, and the willingness of a prime minister to accept scrutiny.
The late chief rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook approached the problem from another direction. He wrote about the religious, national, and universal human concerns within Jewish society, arguing that each had value and could restrain the others’ excesses. He also understood how hostility between camps could consume them.
A religious minister and a secular mayor can have different ideas about the purpose of Jewish sovereignty and still agree on how to get a school built. They can resume the philosophical argument after the classrooms open.
The Jewish Agency’s Board of Governors has been meeting in Israel this week. The gathering brings Israeli leaders and Jews from abroad into the same room on the eve of the election.
Having spent years covering Jewish life abroad, I wish more Israelis were interested in what those communities are trying to achieve.
A minister visiting a Jewish school should ask how it keeps tuition affordable and what its pupils know about Israel. There is a great deal to learn from people who have to persuade families to choose a Jewish education.
We Israelis often ask Diaspora Jews to understand the pressures we live under. We should also be equally willing to learn about the pressures they face. The government answers to Israel’s citizens; its decisions can still affect a Jewish family thousands of miles away.
The next prime minister should put regular consultations with Jewish communities abroad in the diary and give the relevant ministers responsibility for following up. The Jewish Agency and other communal bodies can bring in voices from beyond the familiar leadership circles. Publish the commitments, then report what happened to them.
I would put affordable opportunities to study and spend time in Israel high on that list. Help young immigrants find their feet here. Give young Israelis more chances to encounter Jewish life abroad. A friendship formed over a semester has time to develop beyond the positions people take in an argument about the news.
A Jewish child abroad should be able to cultivate a relationship with Israel that lasts through several changes of government. She ought to have friends here, places she wants to revisit, and enough knowledge to form her own opinions.
I want my own children to make their lives here, and I want them to be able to plan beyond the next emergency. They will have plenty to complain about. I would like them to grow up expecting a government to finish the work it starts.

The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:41 UTC
02:39:41 KST

Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question.
Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed.
Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name.
The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once.
The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like.
 
Terry Barker
 
Honorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East Anglia
Your report that Andy Burnham has instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest.
The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds.
We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors.
The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options.
No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest.
 
James Wallace
 
CEO, River Action
If Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers.
There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs.
 
Philip Clayton
 
London

Bigger does not always mean better in hospital care | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:24 UTC
02:39:24 KST

The closure of maternity units is always a temptation when the NHS runs into staffing problems, largely of its own making (Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns, 19 October).
In my area the quality of care has already been called into question at the largest local unit, and directing mothers to chance their luck there seems to be an undeserved reward. Likewise a nearby large trust has had the quality of its neonatal care called into question. Closing small units is unlikely to provide the quality gain that is sought.
The problem for the NHS is that there is a freedom of ability to employ consultant staff. If you have the money, get on and advertise. This means that the supposedly better, larger units will be able to hoover up all the people they want. The smaller units don’t get a chance.
The reason people want to work at big centres is because for the same pay they don’t have to work so hard, or have the same level of responsibility. Government policy has created specialist units in large centres with the belief, promulgated by the medical profession, that bigger means better.
When I was appointed as a consultant in 1988, before trusts were invented, the regional health authority made the appointments and made sure that senior medical staffing was fairly spread. You could not have 20 specialists in one district general hospital (DGH) and none in the next.
Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations. If a DGH loses its obstetrics department, paediatrics would be immediately under threat. It would mean more children would have to travel. Accident and emergency departments would lose specialist support from paediatricians and gynaecologists. Fine if you have a broken arm, not so fine if you have meningitis etc.
So, when reviewing the future of obstetrics and midwifery, how about considering the people who live in the area and not just the needs of professors?
How about planning to relatively overstaff small units to make sure that they can provide for the needs of the population they serve, and ensuring that the newly qualified are directed towards these posts? After all, the NHS is paid for by everyone, so everyone should get a decent quality of care, without having to travel 50 miles in the dead of night.
 
Dr Paul Godwin
 
Keighley, West Yorkshire

With all due respect to Polly Toynbee, why do we assume that we would need another referendum to return to Europe (Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet, 19 October)? The last one didn’t work out too well. Asking the electorate to vote a simple yes or no on such a complex and multifaceted deal was never going to be the right approach; nor will it be to go back in.
Call it what you will – Brejoin, Bre-entry, Brehabilitation – it shouldn’t be an all-or-nothing deal. The one thing that Brexit has given us is the opportunity to cherrypick the elements of a relationship that are of mutual benefit to both parties. How about approaching it on a piecemeal basis, processing it through normal parliamentary procedure? No buses required.

France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:10 UTC
02:39:10 KST

I’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed.
Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.
Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality.
If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion.
 
Muriel E Cockcroft
  
Duclair, Normandy, France

Now home, Venezuela opposition leader Machado walks tightrope with supporters, Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:35:46 UTC
02:35:46 KST

Now home, Venezuela opposition leader Machado walks tightrope with supporters, Trump
CARACAS/BOGOTA, Oct 26 - Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned on Sunday after nearly a year away, will walk a tightrope as she seeks the elections her supporters want without running afoul of a US-backed negotiation process between the interim government and other opposition groups.
Machado's return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with US President Donald Trump's administration. Washington has said she has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado's Vente Venezuela movement.
The talks, which have continued this month, would remake the electoral council and top court ahead of eventual elections. Both bodies are staffed by ruling party loyalists and backed ousted President Nicolas Maduro in a disputed 2024 presidential election, despite tallies published by Machado's movement that showed her candidate had won. The US military captured Maduro in January.
Machado supporters, tens of thousands of whom swarmed her caravan between Barquisimeto and Caracas on Sunday, waving flags, chanting her name and festooning her with rosaries, are eager for elections and call her the next president. She has said a presidential vote should happen in 2027.
Machado's team did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked whether Machado would participate in the negotiations, Rodriguez said she hopes the dialogue will lead those who called for sanctions against the country — a common ruling party critique leveled at Machado — to feel remorse. Rodriguez added that the talks offer a chance for all voices to be heard.
“I hope both the dialogue and the program for democratic coexistence and peace can provide a space where all voices can be heard, where voices seeking the good of the country can be heard," the acting president said during a visit to a military hospital in Caracas, where she urged politicians to concentrate on serious issues and not put on a "show."
Though Machado cultivated Trump as an ally for years, he said last month it was too soon to consider democratic elections. On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of her return plans, though a person briefed on her movements disputed that.
RISK OF SHORT CIRCUIT WITH WASHINGTON
Machado's eagerness for a vote could "short-circuit" the relationship with the US and its three-phase stabilization, recovery and transition plan for Venezuela, said Ricardo Rios, head of Poder y Estrategia, a political risk consultancy.
"The idea (at the negotiations) is to hold a regional election before a presidential election. She will probably push for electoral guarantees and for a presidential election to be held as soon as possible," Rios said.
But much remains to be defined before voters cast ballots.
“What guarantees does the ruling sector have to leave power (if it is defeated)?" Rios asked. "That still needs to be defined in order to make this viable, because otherwise, no matter how popular she is, it complicates matters."
US AND EU URGE DIALOGUE
Machado's safe return was a direct outcome of the negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a longtime champion of Machado, said on Sunday, adding he expects all political actors to support the talks.
Venezuela's electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held, he told reporters on Monday. He did not provide an estimated date for elections.
"I think we're making real progress in that regard," Rubio said. "But if anybody tries to derail that process, they're doing a great harm to Venezuela."
The EU echoed that sentiment, saying on Monday authorities and all political actors should advance "an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue towards free and fair elections."
The negotiations will lead to a top court being in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
"The reception (Machado) got yesterday will only reinforce the tendency to demand instant results," said Phil Gunson, senior analyst for the Andes region at the International Crisis Group think tank. "Not only might that provoke a reaction from government hardliners, but it could — if successful — produce a political rupture instead of a peaceful transition, with inadequate post-electoral guarantees and a potentially ungovernable country."
The opposition included in the talks, led by Dinorah Figuera, a lawmaker elected in 2015 to the last Venezuelan legislative body recognized by the US, said Machado's return was a significant step in the US plan.
“Her role is also tied to how she interprets the signals from the United States, which has called for reconstruction and reconciliation. She has to be an ally in the negotiations," said Oswaldo Ramirez, managing director of ORC Consultores.
"Rubio sent a clear message," he added. “I don’t see her trying to torpedo the negotiations. She can’t stray outside the lines.” REUTERS

Britain sanctions Sudanese commanders over weaponised rape
Sanctions issued over mass killings and widespread sexual violence against civilians during the fall of el-Fasher.
The United Kingdom has sanctioned 15 Sudanese military commanders, militia leaders and security officials from both sides of the ongoing civil war accused of committing war crimes during the fall of the city of el-Fasher.
Commanders from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces were sanctioned for sexual violence, torture and attacks on civilians. The measures include travel bans and asset freezes, with the wider aim of ensuring that “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”, the UK Foreign Office said.
The announcement came after the release of UK-funded reporting by the Centre for Information Resilience, which revealed a campaign of “systematic starvation and conflict-related sexual violence against civilians in Sudan”, the Foreign Office added.
On Monday, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said those who perpetrated crimes against humanity “must be held accountable and support from all external backers to the warring parties must end”.
The move comes one year after the fall of the city of el-Fasher, which became a focal point of Sudan’s war last year as civilians faced a prolonged siege, reported mass killings, widespread sexual violence and attacks on hospitals.
According to Miliband, “The war in Sudan has created a humanitarian catastrophe.”
“A year on from the atrocities in El Fasher, UK-funded investigations have shown that rape and starvation are still being weaponised against the people of Sudan,” he said.
Sanctions were announced against Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege of el-Fasher, and Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as “al-Qubba”, who was identified as present and playing a prominent role in besieging and attacking the city, the Foreign Office added in the statement.
It added that the UK has allocated five million pounds ($6.6m) to support survivors of sexual violence in Sudan and another 10 million pounds ($13.3m) in humanitarian aid.
Tens of thousands of civilians have been killed and 14 million people displaced since the war broke out in April 2023, according to Amnesty International.

Oil at $117 exposes Trump’s illusion
In its analysis, Kayhan discussed Iran’s position on international affairs and its influence over key strategic and economic routes. According to the newspaper, oil prices reaching $117 per barrel sends a clear message to policymakers in Washington and Tel Aviv: Iran has the ability to influence major economic and vital waterways, making the threats issued by Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu increasingly difficult to carry out.
Netanyahu continues to speak of the possibility of toppling Iran’s government, while Trump still claims he can bring the Iran issue to an end. Such statements, the article argued, are driven less by realities on the ground than by domestic pressures, political rivalry, and internal challenges. It concluded that Iran would not remain passive in any future confrontation but would seek to reshape the balance of power in its favor through new military capabilities and strategic doctrines.
Shargh: Waiting and maintaining readiness
Shargh examined how electoral considerations in Israel and the United States may influence the policies of Netanyahu and Trump toward Iran. Citing university professor Ali Asghar Zargar, the newspaper argued that upcoming elections have not yet reached a stage where they can be regarded as the decisive factor in determining whether conflict with Iran could resume. According to Zargar, Tehran is pursuing a strategy of buying time while preserving its readiness and strategic capabilities. Iranian policymakers are monitoring developments closely and intend to adjust their decisions according to future circumstances. Zargar noted that Iran is not currently in a position to launch preemptive military action against either Israel or the United States. Moreover, such action could bring serious regional and international consequences. It might also encourage regional actors and Washington to adopt tougher positions and continue pressure on Iran. As a result, he believes that Iran’s current circumstances leave little alternative but to maintain a policy centered on patience, caution, and preparedness while awaiting further developments.
Khorasan: Elections under the shadow of war
Khorasan reviewed developments taking place ahead of elections in Israel and their possible connection to regional tensions. The newspaper argued that several indicators, including a notable rise in oil prices, a decline in global gold prices, the departure of some American diplomats from regional countries, and security reports published by US media outlets, could be interpreted as signs of an approaching conflict. At the same time, even if war does not occur, the effort to create a more security-focused atmosphere may itself serve political objectives. According to the analysis, Washington’s actions could be intended both to influence Iran’s calculations and to help Netanyahu politically. Concerns about security may encourage Israeli voters to support Netanyahu’s continued leadership. It further suggested that even if confrontation does not emerge before the election, the possibility remains afterward. In that scenario, Netanyahu may continue emphasizing security threats in order to strengthen his position, preserve his government, and manage political challenges from rival coalitions and opposition groups.
Resalat: Iran counts down to revenge
In an opinion piece, Resalat explored the contrasting views of Iran and its enemies regarding the possibility of military action. Iran’s adversaries believe an attack could weaken Tehran’s influence and restore conditions in strategic waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz. However, Iran views the prospect of such an attack very differently, seeing it as an opportunity to retaliate. According to Resalat, those considering action against Iran seek to weaken the country’s determination and reduce its impact on global markets. Yet the paper argued that Iran remains committed to responding forcefully if attacked. It portrayed Iran not simply as a geographical territory but as a historical force shaped by centuries of conflict, foreign pressure, occupation, and political challenges. The article concluded that this experience has repeatedly enabled the country to emerge from crises with a renewed capacity for resistance and endurance.
Arman-e-Melli: Proposal to leave NPT will favor US
Arman-e-Melli addressed proposals by some domestic hardliners calling for Iran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). According to the newspaper, advocates of withdrawal have promoted the idea for years, including before the recent conflict, without fully considering the consequences it could create. The article argued that Iran’s continued membership in the NPT has complicated Washington’s efforts to build a broad international consensus against Tehran. It added that the United States has already faced criticism regarding its policies and actions toward Iran. In this context, leaving the treaty could increase pressure on Iran and narrow its diplomatic options. The newspaper argued that such a move could prove particularly costly at a time when the country is already facing multiple political, economic, and international challenges. It concluded that any decision regarding withdrawal from the NPT should be based on a careful assessment of the likely costs, risks, and long-term consequences rather than short-term political considerations.

Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo draws early complaints of the screen cracking

Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo draws early complaints of the screen cracking
- Apple’s new foldable iPhone Duo is facing early screen crack complaints, with users hearing a “crunching sound” and seeing cracks or display faults after hours or days.
- Apple says it is “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units” and tells affected users to contact AppleCare for a replacement.
- The fault is an embarrassing setback for Apple’s first foldable phone, and experts say it shows how hard foldable design is, with iFixit blaming a hinge part rather than the screen itself.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The iPhone Duo, one of Apple’s biggest new products in years, is drawing a growing number of complaints from customers who say the foldable display cracked after just hours or days of use.
In these cases, customers reported hearing a crunching sound when unfolding the phone, followed by a large crack forming along the centre crease. Some users also experienced a white patch or other display malfunction on the right side of the screen.
Reports of the problem first surfaced on Reddit and other social media sites. Bloomberg News has since independently verified the issue with more than half a dozen customers, who provided photos showing damage to their devices or evidence of their support conversations with Apple.
“I went to unfold it and it felt stuck/harder/slower to open than usual. And when I opened it it had the lines on the screen,” Tom Battle, an Apple customer from San Diego, told Bloomberg. “You could feel a bump or loose piece under the display.”
Apple acknowledged the issue in a statement, saying it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units”.
“If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” the Cupertino, California-based company said. Most Duos aren’t affected by the problem, and the units that are impacted exhibit the defect quickly, Apple said.
Venture capitalist Jonathan King had a similar experience, saying he heard a crunch-like sound when opening his device on Oct 26.
“I had all intent to post a positive review of my Duo experience today, until it happened to me,” King said. “The smaller outer screen works just fine, but the inner screen is now unusable,” he said, adding that the device thinks he is touching the inner screen when he is not.
While the problem appears to affect only a subset of units, it represents an embarrassing setback for Apple, which spent more than a decade developing the device and touted its superior durability, hinge design and display technology.
The Duo, which went on sale Oct 23, represents the company’s first foray into foldable phones – and the biggest-ever design change to the iPhone, Apple’s largest source of revenue. Like other foldable phones, the device has a smaller screen on its outer surface and can be opened to reveal a larger display.
Chief executive officer John Ternus previously dismissed competing Android foldables as “cheap and crappy”, while the company’s head of hardware engineering, Tom Marieb, encouraged customers to hold Apple “accountable” for the screen crease’s durability.
During the phone’s development, Apple worked to reduce the visibility of the crease in the middle of the opened display – a problem that has plagued previous foldables.
Bloomberg didn’t encounter the issue on one review unit provided by Apple or another device purchased independently.
“I was reading Apple News and decided to open the display to enjoy it, and that’s when I saw the crack line and bruising,” a user who goes by Centrino31A told Bloomberg. “There is no damage to the outside of the phone nor to the inner display surface. It is pristine. The issue is the underlying display.”
The customer said his local Apple retail store in Richmond, Virginia, called the issue a defect that required a replacement, but the location had no Genius Bar customer-support appointments available. Apple then sent him to another store, which conducted testing to confirm there was no accidental damage. But that location had no inventory, so he is still waiting for a replacement device.
Centrino31A said he understands that first-generation devices can have unexpected issues, but that it was “extremely frustrating” that stores didn’t have separate inventory for addressing manufacturing problems, particularly for a device that starts at US$1,999 (S$2,559).
In all cases, users said they felt a bump under the display near where the crack started. Repair platform iFixit, which disassembles products to study their components, said it believes the issue is caused by a piece of the hinge failing and cracking the screen, rather than a problem with the display panel itself.
The company has faced issues with new iPhone hardware in the past, including the iPhone 6 Plus in 2014, which would bend easily, and the iPhone 4 in 2010, which sometimes lost reception when users touched the antenna cutout around the device. In both cases, the company emerged from the problems relatively unscathed.
The latest difficulties show that “even a company with Apple’s engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables”, according to IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo.
Samsung Electronics, which pioneered the foldable field, also had problems with its first Galaxy Fold in 2019, Jeronimo noted. “It also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category,” he said, adding that Apple’s move on Oct 26 to send users to customer care is “the right first step”.
Vishnu Rajkumar, an Apple customer who said he has used previous foldable phones from OnePlus and Samsung, also experienced the Duo issue. “I was setting up my apps and wanted to check how Outlook works in the wider inner screen,” he said. “I tried opening the screen and found an unusual tightness.”
After applying a bit more pressure, “the screen started bleeding”, he said. “Initially the line was small, and it increased further after multiple folds.”
Rajkumar, who lives in Chennai, India, was able to locate a replacement device at an authorised reseller and said that model hasn’t had any issues during his first 24 hours of use.
Another user, Surya Mangi of Allen, Texas, said the inner screen cracked after about 30 hours of ownership during normal opening of the display. “Trying to replace but no Apple Store around so asking me to send in and be phoneless for over a week,” he said. Apple is ultimately shipping Mangi a replacement by express mail.
Apple employees said the company hasn’t provided any official guidance so far to its retail stores or customer service agents about the problem, but a team is investigating the issue. In some cases, Apple engineers are trying to obtain affected devices for analysis.
One customer, Justin Lokos, said Apple did what is known as an Early Field Failure Analysis on his device. “I gave as much detail as possible,” he said in a note. “All of the employees in store were very intrigued (imagine I was the first person there to have this issue).” He received a replacement at Apple’s Fifth Avenue store in New York.
Lokos said he was sitting on his living room couch using the iPhone Duo to order Grubhub, but the experience wasn’t ideal on the outer screen because the app isn’t yet optimised for the new design. He thought it would work better unfolded, but when he opened the device, he heard a crunching sound and the display cracked.
Another user, Jainam Shah, said his iPhone Duo’s hinge felt perfectly normal until one particular unfolding, when it suddenly became noticeably stiffer. “I continued opening it, heard an audible crack and immediately noticed the bright vertical and horizontal lines across the inner display.”
Shah said there had been no drops, impacts or unusual pressure on the phone. “Took it straight back to the Apple Store, where the employees were just as surprised,” he said. “They replaced it immediately and asked if I’d be comfortable having engineering reach out to understand what happened.” BLOOMBERG

Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:30:46 UTC
02:30:46 KST

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak.
It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons.
Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse.
In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes.
Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak.
The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months.
“Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said.
“It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene.
“It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been.
“Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.”
Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct.
The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid.
Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice.
“Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said.
“We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for.
“Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have.”
Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the court of appeal on 5 November.
Kiran Kaur, Digwa’s mother, was also jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son. The knife was found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons.

Tehran designates emergency shelters across capital for wartime conditions
TEHRAN – Tehran Municipality spokesman has announced that specific locations across the capital have been designated as emergency shelters for use in wartime conditions.
Abdolmotahar Mohammadkhani, the spokesman, said on Monday morning that the municipality is pursuing both emergency measures and long-term plans to provide sheltering capacity in line with the current situation.
"Tehran Municipality is pursuing emergency actions and long-term programs to provide shelter capacities in accordance with the existing conditions," Mohammadkhani said, referring to the urban management's efforts to secure shelter spaces.
He added: "In the short-term section, Tehran's Crisis Management Organization has identified a number of metro stations, commercial complexes, schools and government buildings for use in emergency situations. The available capacities in different districts and neighborhoods have also been reviewed and their locations have been marked on the map."
Pointing to the municipality's long-term plans, Mohammadkhani said the construction of multi-purpose subsurface structures is among the programs to be pursued in the coming years. These spaces, in addition to being usable in critical conditions, will also have applications in normal times, with parts of them usable as underground commercial and office complexes.
Referring to Tehran's comprehensive subsurface plan, he added that building multi-purpose spaces requires time, and it is not possible to construct structures solely for wartime use in proportion to Tehran's population, which is why the use of multi-purpose capacities has been put on the agenda.

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure a war crime: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:27:34 UTC
02:27:34 KST

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure a war crime: UN
UN commission notes Russian weaponisation of cold in nearly five years of attacks on heating plants and power lines.
Russia’s persistent attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constitute war crimes as they weaponise the cold of winter, a United Nations commission has said.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine laid out in a report submitted to the UN General Assembly on Monday years of Russian attacks on heating plants, power lines, gas facilities and other infrastructure since the autumn of 2022.
The report was issued as Russia has stepped up its attacks on such civilian targets. Moscow has sought every year since its full-scale invasion in February 2022 to inflict suffering on Ukrainian citizens with an apparent ambition of draining the country’s will and ability to continue to defend its territory.
The commission said it has investigated the impact on civilians of large-scale attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and their cumulative effect since 2022.
“The frequency, intensity and geographic range of systematic waves of attacks with hundreds of drones and missiles at a time have increased over the years and inflicted significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector,” the report noted.
In particular, the report focused on the Russian attacks during the severe winter of 2025–2026, when temperatures dropped to minus 21 degrees Celsius (-5.8 degrees Fahrenheit). That left millions of people in Ukraine facing lengthy outages of heating, electricity, water and gas, and forced them to cope with intolerable living conditions, it said.
The commission assessed that the Russian commanders ordering the attacks knew that the heating facilities they targeted were indispensable to the civilian population.
“Russian authorities have made official declarations concerning further attacks and referred to a plan to carry them out. The commission concluded that they committed war crimes of intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects,” the report concluded.
Erik Mose, chair of the commission, noted that as the cold season approaches, “the attacks have intensified once again, raising serious concerns about the threats to civilians’ lives and health”.
Russia and Ukraine have continued their daily attacks on one another as winter approaches, with little indication that a ceasefire might be in sight.
On Monday, a Russian strike on Ukraine’s southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured four people overnight, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Telegram.
The Ministry of Defence in Moscow accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week.
The UN commission, which was set up by the Human Rights Council, in its report also accused Moscow of human trafficking in connection with the recruitment of foreign fighters into the Russian armed forces “in violation of international human rights law”.
“The majority of those recruited have been killed, went missing, while others have also been injured or captured,” the report read.
For instance, there have been numerous reports during the nearly five-year war of men from India having been duped into fighting on the front lines.

Breadcrumb
'Destruction of truth': UN report finds Israel's mediacide in Gaza seeks to bury evidence of genocide
Israel is attempting to "systematically eliminate" journalists in occupied Palestine in a bid to cover up evidence of genocide and war crimes, according to a UN report.
The paper, authored by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, says that "destruction of truth" has been integral to the assault on Gaza, and describes Israel's attempts to control information as "mediacide".
Israeli forces have killed hundreds of journalists in the occupied territories since October 2023 while most of Gaza's infrastructure lies in ruins.
Albanese will present her findings to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday.
The report identifies three ways in which Israel and its supporters attempt to destroy or hide evidence of crimes committed in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
These include the systematic targeting of journalists and communications infrastructure, and the Israeli government's attempts to censor and manipulate information.
It also highlights the complicity of Western news organisations and technology platforms, which it accuses of promoting Israeli narratives and suppressing Palestinian voices.
"These practices have not merely accompanied genocide but have facilitated its commission and obstructed accountability," the report reads.
The UN documented the killing of almost 300 Palestinian journalists between October 2023 and February this year. Hundreds of others have been wounded or unlawfully detained by Israeli authorities.
Some were killed in indiscriminate attacks while at least 70 are known to have been deliberately targeted.
Israel has replicated its assault on Palestinian journalists in its other conflicts in Lebanon, Yemen and Iran, where dozens of other media workers have been killed in airstrikes.
The report says that the Israeli military has wiped out more than 80% of Gaza's communications infrastructure and damaged another 12%. By October 2025, Israeli forces had destroyed 125 media offices and institutions, including news agency headquarters, broadcast towers and radio stations, it says.
Blackouts caused by the damage have prevented local journalists from broadcasting events and people outside the strip from verifying information.
The destruction has gone hand-in-hand with the Israeli government's media restrictions, which have prevented foreign journalists reporting from Gaza and censored thousands of articles related to the war.
"In the ongoing genocide, the systematic elimination of media witnesses and the destruction of the means of documentation are probative of genocidal intent," the report says.
"They reveal an effort not only to destroy a protected group, but also to destroy the conditions in which that destruction can be seen, documented, remembered and ultimately adjudicated," it continues.

Milan event commemorates child victims of Gorla, Minab and Gaza

Milan event commemorates child victims of Gorla, Minab and Gaza
TEHRAN- Italian artists and activists have commemorated children killed in wars in the country’s Gorla district, Iran’s Minab and the Gaza Strip, marking the 82nd anniversary of the bombing of an elementary school in Milan during World War II.
The commemorations took place on October 20, the anniversary of the 1944 Gorla massacre, which claimed the lives of 184 children and 19 school staff members when an Allied air raid struck the Francesco Crispi elementary school in northern Milan.
This year’s anniversary carries additional significance following the Italian parliament’s approval of a law establishing October 20 as a national day of remembrance for the child victims of the Gorla massacre and children killed in all wars. The legislation, Law No. 85 of May 6, 2026, aims to preserve the memory of the victims and promote a culture of peace.
During the recent commemorations, participants drew parallels between the Gorla tragedy and the deaths of children in the Israeli-American attack on a school in Minab, southern Iran, as well as the killing of children in Gaza.
Media activist Zio Filippo took part in the activities, accompanying his public outreach with music videos as he moved from Piazza della Repubblica toward Piazza Venezia, according to reports on the event.
Italian artists have also released a song titled “Gorla, Minab, Gaza” to honor children killed in armed conflicts and highlight the shared tragedy of civilian victims across different historical and geographical contexts.
The song links the memory of the children killed in Milan during World War II with that of children who have lost their lives in more recent conflicts, including those in Iran and Gaza.
The Gorla massacre occurred on October 20, 1944, when American aircraft taking part in an Allied bombing operation over Milan targeted industrial facilities in the surrounding area. A bomb struck the Francesco Crispi elementary school, killing 184 children and 19 members of the school staff.
The tragedy became one of the most painful episodes in Milan’s wartime history and a lasting symbol of the devastating impact of aerial bombardment on civilians.
On February 28, the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan province, became the site of a devastating massacre as the United States and Israel initiated their strikes against Iran.
While dozens of girls and boys aged between 7 and 12 were beginning their lessons, the school was targeted by a missile strike that caused the building to collapse, trapping children and teachers beneath the rubble. Iranian authorities confirmed a final death toll of 168 people, with at least 95 others wounded, marking one of the most harrowing incidents of the conflict's opening day.
Despite attempts by US and Israeli authorities to distance themselves from the carnage as images of the tragedy spread across social media, detailed forensic and digital investigations have painted a starkly different picture.
An analysis by Al Jazeera’s digital investigations unit, utilizing over a decade of satellite imagery and recent video clips, revealed that the school was a clearly distinct civilian facility, separated from any adjacent military sites for at least ten years. Furthermore, witness accounts and satellite-based analyses confirmed that the school was triple tapped by three separate, deliberate strikes, leaving no doubt about the nature of the attack.
The international community has faced mounting evidence regarding the responsibility for this atrocity, with investigations from major global outlets including The New York Times, BBC Verify, CBC, and NPR all concluding that the United States was responsible for the strike.
These findings have raised fundamental questions about the intelligence used to justify the bombing, as the patterns of the strike suggest a direct targeting of a civilian educational institution. The Minab school tragedy now stands as a somber testament to the immense human cost of the aggression and a focal point for those demanding international accountability.

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:24:43 UTC
02:24:43 KST

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
TEHRAN – The Persian translation of the book “Freshwater: A Comedy” written by Virginia Woolf has been released in bookstores across Iran.
Yousef Najafi Jablou is the translator of the book that has been brought out by Tagh Publication, ISNA reported.
“Freshwater: A comedy” is a play written and produced by Virginia Woolf in 1935, and the only play she wrote. Although only performed once in her lifetime, it has been translated into many languages and produced in many countries since. Alfred Lord Tennyson appears as a character in this play.
Virginia Woolf researched the life of her great-aunt, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, publishing her findings in an essay titled “Pattledom” (1925), and later in her introduction to her 1926 edition of Cameron's photographs.
The play is named after Freshwater, Isle of Wight, where Julia Margaret Cameron lived in a somewhat bohemian atmosphere at her home, Dimbola Lodge, surrounded by a number of artists and literary figures, including George Frederick Watts and Tennyson in the 1860s.
Tennyson's nearby home, Farringdon, was another artistic center. The plot revolves around the attempts by the young actress Ellen Terry to escape from her marriage to the much older Watts, partly family history, partly mocking the conventions of the Victorian times that the Bloomsbury group had fought to escape.
The Camerons are set to embark for India, while both Mrs. Cameron and Watts are intent on portraying Ellen in their respective media. Ellen, on the other hand, views a young naval lieutenant as her escape, with an offer to escape to Bloomsbury. This collapses a number of historic events into a single afternoon.
Although a slight work not intended for publication, and easily dismissed as frivolous, it has been given a larger meaning when placed in the broader context of Woolf's work and views. For beneath the comedic elements, there is an exploration of both generational change and artistic freedom. Both Cameron and Woolf fought against the class and gender dynamics of Victorianism, and the play shows links to both “To the Lighthouse” and “A Room of One's Own” that would follow.
Virginia Woolf (1882 – 1941) was an English writer and one of the most influential 20th-century modernist authors. She helped to pioneer the use of stream of consciousness narration as a literary device.
Woolf began publishing professionally in 1904 and rose to prominence during the interwar period with novels including “Mrs. Dalloway” (1925), “To the Lighthouse” (1927), and “Orlando” (1928). She also wrote the influential feminist essay “A Room of One's Own” (1929), followed by “Three Guineas” (1938), which explores the roots of fascism in society. Her work became central to 1970s feminist criticism and remains influential worldwide, having been translated into more than 50 languages.

Baran Auction to showcase Iranian calligraphy, miniatures
TEHRAN – The fifth edition of Baran Auction, specializing in Iranian and Islamic art, will be held in Tehran on Friday, October 30, featuring works of traditional calligraphy and Persian miniature painting, including “The Third Feather” by the late Iranian master Mahmoud Farshchian.
The event will take place at 5 p.m. at the Raizan International Conference Center, IRNA reported on Monday.
A public exhibition of the selected works will be held at the same venue on October 28 and 29, offering art enthusiasts, researchers and collectors an opportunity to view the pieces before the sale, the report added.
The upcoming edition continues Baran Auction's focus on preserving and promoting Iran's calligraphic heritage while expanding its presentation of traditional visual arts. Alongside calligraphic works, this year's selection includes pieces from the country's miniature painting tradition, highlighting the historical connections between the two art forms.
Among the featured works is “The Third Feather” by Farshchian, whose paintings frequently draw on Persian literary, spiritual and mythological themes. According to the organizers, the work evokes the mysterious feather of the Simorgh, the legendary bird associated with wisdom and spiritual discovery in Persian literature. They describe it as a symbol of awareness, hope and renewal, reflecting the enduring power of Iranian cultural thought.
Calligraphy remains central to Baran Auction's identity. Previous editions have featured works associated with major figures in the history of Iranian calligraphy, including Mir Emad Hassani, Darvish Abdolmajid Taleqani and Mirza Gholamreza Esfahani, alongside works by contemporary artists.
The fourth edition of Baran Auction, held in 2019, demonstrated the market appeal of Iran's traditional arts, with five folios from a rare copy of Ferdowsi's “Shahnameh”, written in the nastaliq style during the Timurid period (1370–1507), selling for more than $2.1 million.
The auction, held at Tehran's Raizen International Conference Center, presented 94 works and generated more than $6 million in sales, although 25 lots failed to attract buyers.
Other notable sales included a miniature portrait of Princess Navab Akbari Beigom, created by an Indian artist during the Zand dynasty (1751–1794), which fetched more than $1.3 million, and a cylinder inscribed with a Persian translation of the Cyrus Cylinder by calligrapher Hossein Niktalab, which sold for approximately $930,000.
The results underscored the commercial potential of traditional Iranian and Islamic art within the country's art market.
By bringing together calligraphy and miniature painting, the fifth edition aims to present a broader view of Iran's artistic legacy while providing a platform for the appreciation and circulation of works rooted in its cultural traditions.
Founded by Mahbubeh Kazemi Dulabi in 2016, Baran Auction specializes in calligraphic paintings and works of calligraphy.

Iran-Pakistan border trade serves mutual interests: ambassador
TEHRAN– Iran’s Ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri-Moghaddam, has stressed that cross-border trade is an integral part of high-level bilateral agreements and serves the mutual interests of both neighboring countries, while attributing the failure to implement the Islamabad understanding to 'US breaches of commitments.'
In remarks on Sunday, the ambassador addressed reports in Pakistani media about the status of trade across the shared border, emphasizing that disruptions to commercial exchanges under the current circumstances would serve neither country’s interests.
“There are currently no restrictions imposed by Iran on the export of Iranian goods, including liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), to Pakistan,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, adding that Iran’s borders with all its neighboring countries remain open.
He explained that difficulties affecting traders transporting goods from Iran to Pakistan stem from the implementation of an “E-Form” procedure by the Pakistani side for imports from Iran. Consultations are underway between the two sides to resolve the issue and facilitate the movement of goods.
The ambassador also acknowledged reports that several hundred LPG tankers had crossed the Gabd-Rimdan border into Pakistan but had yet to be unloaded or cleared. The situation, he said, had complicated the movement of goods and disrupted the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
Amiri-Moghaddam emphasized that Iran had consistently worked to facilitate and strengthen cross-border commerce and remained committed to cooperating with Pakistani counterparts to overcome existing obstacles and expand economic ties.
Border trade, he noted, is a vital component of economic cooperation between the two neighboring countries and benefits both nations and their peoples.
Pakistani media have meanwhile reported that the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has resumed operations, with commercial transport moving again on both sides of the border.
US breaches are behind stalled Islamabad understanding
Separately, Amiri-Moghaddam addressed speculation in Pakistani media about Tehran’s position on the future of negotiations with Washington, stressing that decisions and official announcements concerning whether talks will take place fall within the remit of Iran’s senior political authorities and Foreign Ministry.
Speaking to IRNA in Islamabad on Sunday evening, the ambassador said Iran remained committed to the Islamabad understanding, arguing that its implementation had been obstructed by the US side’s failure to honor its commitments.
He said that, during a recent meeting with think-tank figures and media representatives in Islamabad, he had reiterated Iran’s continued commitment to the understanding.
“The person who declared the Islamabad understanding over and violated it was US President Donald Trump,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, according to IRNA.
He added that Washington’s actions had created conditions in which understanding could not be implemented in practice.
The ambassador said Iran’s repeated emphasis on honoring the understanding reflected its respect for commitments and agreements undertaken within the framework of international law. He drew a parallel with Washington’s unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), arguing that Trump had similarly failed to implement the Islamabad understanding he had signed.
Amiri-Moghaddam stressed that any decision or announcement concerning the holding or cancellation of negotiations would be made by Iran’s senior political authorities and the Foreign Ministry in Tehran, with official information conveyed through the spokesperson for the Iranian negotiating team and official media outlets.
Tehran says diplomacy remains open as Iran stresses readiness to defend itself
The ambassador’s remarks come as Iranian officials have reiterated that diplomacy remains an option while emphasizing the country’s readiness to respond to any hostile action.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei, speaking to German public broadcaster ARD, said the United States continued to insist on unilateral demands in negotiations. He stressed that Iran was keeping the door to diplomacy open while remaining prepared to defend the country against any aggression and deal with every possible scenario.
Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, speaker of Iran’s Parliament and head of the Iranian negotiating team, also addressed the issue in remarks at the beginning of a parliamentary session held in person and online.
Qalibaf said Iran was prepared to deliver a response beyond its adversaries’ expectations to any act of aggression against the country’s territorial integrity. He added that threats of a wider war or assassination would not force the Iranian nation to abandon its rights and interests.
The statements underscore Tehran’s position that diplomatic engagement must be accompanied by respect for commitments and Iran’s national interests.
For Iran and Pakistan, maintaining the smooth operation of border crossings remains important to bilateral commerce and regional economic cooperation. Resolving the outstanding administrative obstacles would help restore the uninterrupted movement of goods and strengthen trade ties between the two neighboring countries.

Araghchi: Iran-Russia coop can strengthen global gas market stability
