====================================================================================================

Israel election: How it works and what it means for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:35:53 UTC
00:35:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel election 2026 explained as Netanyahu faces key vote
Israeli voters head to the polls on Tuesday in a closely fought election that will determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and the direction of Israel's policies towards Palestinians.
The vote pits a coalition of opposition parties led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot against the far-right bloc led by Netanyahu, whose opponents accuse him of undermining Israel's democratic institutions.
It is the first Israeli election since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 and Israel's subsequent genocidal war on Gaza, which has been followed by wider regional conflicts involving Lebanon, Iran and Yemen.
While much of the campaign has focused on Netanyahu's leadership, the war and domestic divisions, the outcome will also affect millions of Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank who have no vote in the election.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, meanwhile, could play a decisive role in determining the balance of power in the Knesset, even as the main Jewish-led political blocs remain reluctant to cooperate with them.
How will the vote work?
Polling stations will open at 7am on Tuesday and close at 10pm.
Major Israeli news organisations will publish exit polls shortly after voting ends, with counting beginning the same evening.
More than three dozen parties are contesting the election, with around 7.4 million people eligible to vote at polling stations across Israel.
Israel uses proportional representation, meaning voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate. The 120 seats in the Knesset are allocated according to each party's share of the national vote.
Candidates enter parliament according to their positions on their party's electoral list.
Parties must win at least 3.25% of the vote to enter the Knesset, equivalent to four seats.
No single party has ever secured an outright majority, meaning Israeli governments have always depended on coalitions.
When will the results be announced?
The official results must be declared by 4 November, although the likely distribution of seats should become clear as early as Wednesday morning.
Attention will then turn to coalition negotiations, with parties seeking to assemble a parliamentary majority of at least 61 seats.
After the official results are announced, President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions before selecting a Knesset member to attempt to form a government.
These negotiations could take weeks, particularly if neither of the main blocs wins enough seats to govern.
What are the polls saying?
The final opinion polls suggest that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition coalition led by Eisenkot is on course to secure a majority.
Surveys published over the weekend put the opposition on 54 to 56 seats, compared with around 50 for Netanyahu's Likud-led alliance.
Eisenkot's Yashar party was projected to become the largest party with 22 to 23 seats, ahead of Likud on 19 to 21.
The polls also pointed to gains for the far right, with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party projected to win eight seats.
But the remaining seats could prove crucial.
Parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel were projected to win between 14 and 16 seats, potentially leaving them with considerable influence over whether a government can be formed.
Eisenkot has previously ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian-led parties, leaving questions over how the opposition could secure the parliamentary support it needs.
Could Palestinian voters decide the election?
Palestinian citizens of Israel account for a substantial share of the electorate, but their political representation has long been constrained by divisions between parties, low turnout and the reluctance of major Jewish-led parties to include them in governing coalitions.
This election could nevertheless give their parties considerable influence over whether Netanyahu remains in power.
The two main Arab-majority electoral lists are Ra'am, also known as the United Arab List, and the Joint List, bringing together Hadash, Balad and Ta'al.
Their performance will depend partly on turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes could influence both the number of seats won by Arab-led parties and the overall balance of the Knesset.
In an interview with The New Arab, Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh highlighted the importance of Palestinian voters in an election where neither main bloc appears assured of a majority.
The campaign has also been marked by attempts to exclude Palestinian-led parties and candidates.
Israel's Central Elections Committee voted in September to bar the Joint List and Ra'am from contesting the election, but the Supreme Court overturned the decision.
The court nevertheless upheld the disqualification of Abu Shehadeh over an article in which he described the 7 October attacks as an important historical event.
The episode has renewed questions about the political rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the limits placed on their participation in Israeli politics.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly portrayed the possibility of opposition cooperation with Arab-led parties as a campaign warning, seeking to pressure his rivals into ruling out such an arrangement.
What about Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank?
Millions of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip cannot vote in the election that will help determine the policies governing their lives.
The next Israeli government will have a major influence over military operations, movement restrictions, settlement expansion and the future of Gaza.
In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians face an expanding network of military checkpoints, road closures and settler attacks.
Israel has also announced the closure of land crossings into the West Bank for election day, adding to restrictions that have intensified since October 2023.
In Gaza, the central questions include whether Israel will ease its blockade, withdraw troops from occupied areas, allow displaced Palestinians to return home and permit reconstruction after three years of devastating war.
However, Netanyahu's principal challengers have offered little indication that a change in government would bring a fundamental shift in Israeli policy towards Palestinian statehood or the occupation.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state, while other prominent opposition figures have supported Israel's military campaigns and taken hardline positions towards Gaza.
Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, whose party is part of the opposition coalition, has criticised Netanyahu for being too soft on Gaza and called for the Palestinian Authority to be dismantled.
Meanwhile, far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have advocated annexing Palestinian territory and ethnically cleansing the Palestinians.
The election could therefore change Israel's leadership without necessarily bringing major changes to the policies Palestinians face.
What are the main election issues?
Netanyahu's opponents have sought to make the vote a referendum on his leadership, focusing on the security failures surrounding the 7 October attack, his long-running corruption trial and Israel's growing international isolation.
According to the Israel Democracy Institute, the October 2023 attack is expected to play an important role in the voting decisions of more than two-thirds of the electorate.
Other major issues include military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and Netanyahu's attempts to overhaul the judiciary in 2023, which sparked widespread protests.
The election also comes after years of Israeli military operations in Gaza and regional conflicts involving Hezbollah, Iran and the Houthis.
Yet there is considerable overlap between the main Jewish-led parties on questions relating to Palestinian rights, the occupation and Israel's military operations.
While opposition politicians have criticised Netanyahu's handling of the wars and the diplomatic damage caused by his government, few have advocated a fundamental reversal of settlement expansion or a renewed peace process leading to Palestinian statehood.
The most explicit calls for annexation and Palestinian displacement have come from the far right, particularly Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
What happens if coalition talks fail?
If neither bloc can assemble 61 seats, Israel could face prolonged negotiations over a possible minority government or another election.
A minority government would need support or abstentions from parties outside the governing coalition to survive key parliamentary votes.
That could make Palestinian-led parties particularly important, even if they are excluded from formal coalition agreements.
If negotiations fail altogether, another election could be called in 2027, with Netanyahu potentially remaining as caretaker prime minister until a new government takes office.
The result could therefore leave Israel facing continued political deadlock, with Palestinian parties holding potentially important seats but little guarantee of a role in government.
For Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, the immediate consequences will depend less on which party wins the most seats than on the policies the next government adopts towards the occupation, military operations, settlements and displacement.

Nearly 30,000 excess cancer cases linked to inequalities across EU countries: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:35:27 UTC
00:35:27 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The incidence of nearly 30,000 additional cases of lung and cervical cancer was estimated across EU countries in 2024 due to disparities in cancer incidence rates, with some countries seeing rates more than seven times higher than others, according to a study presented Monday.
The findings were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress in Madrid by Italian epidemiologist Diego Serraino, the ANSA news agency reported.
Based on European Cancer Information System estimates, the study identified 29,412 excess cases in countries where incidence exceeded the EU average.
For lung cancer among men, incidence ranged from 38 cases per 100,000 people in Sweden to 130 in Hungary, with 11,105 excess cases seen across 12 countries.
Among women, Denmark saw 83 lung cancer cases per 100,000 compared with 20 in Lithuania, contributing to 13,441 excess cases across 11 countries.
Cervical cancer showed even greater disparities, with Romania seeing 36 cases per 100,000 women compared with just five on the island nation of Malta.
Of the 4,866 excess cervical cancer cases identified across 10 countries, Romania accounted for 2,475.
Researchers emphasized stronger anti-smoking measures to reduce lung cancer risks, alongside human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, and regular screening to prevent cervical cancer and detect precancerous lesions early.

Mecca pact countries in Iran in bid to stop war restarting

- Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from resuming.

Israel prepares to vote as Netanyahu faces a tight fight
Campaigning and ballot preparations mark the lead-up to Israel’s election Tuesday, widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job".
"US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday night.
"He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me."
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Monday that a vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq, without specifying the cause of the incident or the status of the crew.
"UKMTO has received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire, 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq," it said.
"Crew status, damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at time of report," the agency added.
Al-Faw is a port town that sits on the Gulf, neighbouring Kuwait and Iran.
Syria closes main border crossing with Jordan after strikes
Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions due to developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.
The closure came after Jordan's air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria, saying suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
The Nassib border crossing is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.
Syria says Jordan did not coordinate before strikes
Syria's government said Monday that Jordan did not coordinate with it before launching deadly strikes on the country's south in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week.
A Syrian government statement carried by state news agency SANA said "no prior coordination with the Syrian side was carried out concerning the military operation" by Jordan, adding that authorities were investigating the strikes and discussing them with Amman while stressing the need for joint security coordination in border areas.
Syria says death toll in Jordan strikes rises to 8
Syria said the death toll in Monday's strikes in its south had risen to eight, as Jordan said it had targeted "terrorist organisations" after a deadly jihadist attack on a church.
Health officials said "hospitals in Daraa province have received eight victims, including an elderly man and three children", in addition to four wounded, raising an earlier toll of five dead.
Jordan strikes militant groups in Syria after church attack
The Jordanian military said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings.
It said air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack.
Syria's state news agency SANA, citing a local health official, said the strikes across Daraa province in the country's south had killed five civilians, including women and children.
Iran security chief says 'very good discussions' held
Iran's security chief said on Monday he held "very good discussions" with the three member nations of the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, after their first meeting in Tehran.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television after the meeting with top officials from the three countries. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen."
The meeting, proposed by Pakistan, brought together senior officials from the three countries and Iran for talks in the Iranian capital.
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said earlier Monday that the meeting aimed to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis".
UN probe accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit "genocide" against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed "genocide" in the war on Gaza.
In a new report, which comes the day before Israel's general election, the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a "widespread and systematic attack" against civilians.
"The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core," it said.
Iran says agreed with Mecca pact countries on security
Iran said Monday it had agreed with three countries party to the Mecca pact, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan, that regional security should be ensured by countries in the region itself and not by foreign actors.
"The outcomes we agreed on were that security in the region where we live should be endogenous, meaning it should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention in this region," Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said after the meeting.
Israel dismisses UN-backed probe's report on genocide
Israel on Monday dismissed as "propaganda" a new report issued by UN-mandated investigators accusing it of committing the crime against humanity of extermination in the West Bank and genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
The Israeli foreign ministry said on X that the investigators' finding "is not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens".
At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the Gaza Strip since the so-called ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025.
UN raises 'ethnic cleansing' concerns over Israeli operation
Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, launched after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, raises serious concerns of "ethnic cleansing", the United Nations warned Monday.
Israel's "aggressive operation" has already resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely", UN rights chief Volker Türk said in a statement.
"The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force, which must end."
He said the lockdown was confining many to their homes and immediate neighbourhoods.
Gaza truce has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday. They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.
In response, Israel's mission in Geneva called for the commission's dissolution and said on X the report marked an example of the body's “misinformation campaign to demonise the state of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal."
Israel has long criticised the commission's output and denied accusations of genocide in Gaza and sexual assault by its forces.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has called for a just settlement of the Palestinian issue and comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council during talks with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Guterres welcomed Egypt's efforts to consolidate the Gaza ceasefire agreement, praising Cairo's role in facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid and ensuring it reaches those in need.
"Lasting peace in the region could not be achieved without a just settlement of the Palestinian issue," Guterres said, stressing that it would remain the central issue in the Middle East until a final resolution is reached.
The UN chief also expressed deep concern over developments in the occupied West Bank and urged the international community to fulfil its responsibilities by taking action to halt violations against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.
Putin to meet Qatar's emir, Iran's president in Moscow
Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday, as diplomatic efforts intensify to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.

India-US trade deal stalled over tariffs and politics – media

India-US trade deal stalled over tariffs and politics – media
India’s interim trade deal with the US remains stalled as New Delhi reportedly refuses to accept a proposed 18% tariff rate and weighs politically sensitive agricultural concessions ahead of next month’s US midterm elections.
India wants to retain the current additional 10% levy on covered exports and could reassess negotiations after the November 3 elections, the Hindu BusinessLine reported on Sunday, citing sources familiar with the talks.
Under a framework agreed in February, Washington proposed reducing tariffs on several categories of Indian goods to 18%, from penalties of up to 50% imposed last year. In return, India agreed to lower duties on US industrial goods and selected agricultural products.
However, the negotiating landscape changed after the US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs later that month. Washington subsequently imposed a separate additional 10% duty on covered Indian imports under Section 301 of US trade law.
Around 55% of India’s exports to the US are subject to the additional levy, while products including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones remain exempt, according to India’s Commerce Ministry.
New Delhi is seeking assurances that future US tariffs will not leave its exporters at a disadvantage to competitors in Vietnam, Bangladesh, and Indonesia, the BusinessLine reported. India also wants protection against further duties after an agreement is signed.
Agricultural market access remains another obstacle to finalizing the deal. Washington is seeking concessions on American farm products, including those from Republican-leaning states, while India has sought to protect sensitive sectors such as dairy, poultry, rice, and wheat.
Granting such concessions while accepting higher tariffs would be difficult to defend domestically, sources told BusinessLine. New Delhi is therefore reportedly inclined to wait until after the US elections before deciding how to proceed.
The deadlock comes despite US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying last week that 99% of the agreement was complete and that a deal could be finalized within weeks.
Trump also described the negotiations as “pretty close,” even as Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar cautioned that the remaining stages could prove difficult.
Trump waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs earlier this month, easing a major obstacle to the negotiations. However, a separate US investigation into alleged industrial overcapacity remains unresolved, leaving uncertainty over possible future duties on Indian goods.

Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:30:57 UTC
00:30:57 KST

Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees.
The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020.
The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result.
The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses. Sources close to the claim estimate that it could be worth about £5bn, based on the number of businesses allegedly overcharged between 2020 and 2026.
A spokesperson for Mastercard defended the interchange fees, saying the potential group claim was “speculative” and part of a “growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation”.
The case is being funded by Bench Walk Advisors, a London-headquartered firm that launched in 2017 and makes money from backing lawsuits. It is being led by Stephen Allen, a British businessman and former travel sector executive who has been pursuing Visa and Mastercard through a number of group legal actions since 2021.
If the application is successful, an estimated 1m UK-based businesses, organisations and charities with less than £100m in revenues will be automatically included for compensation, unless they opt out. Their claims could be worth several thousands of pounds each.
Larger businesses would have to actively opt in to be included in the claim, and could be due tens of millions over the claim period.
However, it could take years for the case to reach a conclusion. Visa and Mastercard last year agreed to pay a combined $167.5m to settle a class action lawsuit in the US which accused the two companies of conspiring to keep ATM access fees artificially high. That lawsuit was originally filed in 2011.
Commenting on the latest group claim application, a Mastercard spokesperson said: “We strongly disagree with the basis of this claim. Interchange plays a vital role in supporting the UK payments ecosystem, and ensures people and businesses can pay and get paid quickly and securely.
“This speculative claim does nothing to support UK businesses or consumers and instead reflects the growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation. It is exactly the type of claim the UK government’s recently announced proposed opt-out class action reforms [put out for consultation this summer] are directed at preventing.”
A Visa spokesperson said: “Visa continues to believe that interchange is a critical component to maintaining a secure digital payments ecosystem that benefits all parties, including consumers, merchants and banks.”

How is the Muslim world reporting on Israel’s election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:30:07 UTC
00:30:07 KST

The upcoming election is drawing attention across the Arab world, with regional media examining the political contest, its implications for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s future, and what a change in government could mean for the future of Palestinian statehood and the two-state solution.
Beyond speculation about Netanyahu’s political future, several Arab media outlets have focused on the potential influence of Arab voters and Arab-led parties on the election outcome, particularly the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad, and Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party. With neither major political bloc guaranteed a parliamentary majority, many Arab outlets have focused on the parties’ electoral performance’s significance in determining the next government.
Egypt’s Alghad TV reported on remarks made by Hadash politician Shadi Shweiri on Sunday, highlighting the influence of the Arab vote and what he described as a unique opportunity for Arab citizens of Israel to advance their national demands through the electoral process. The report referred to Arab citizens of Israel as “Palestinians in the country” and emphasized that Arab parties should not support just any candidate seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but one willing to halt Israel’s military operations in the region and improve economic opportunities for Arab citizens.
Shweiri accused the current government of racism and of committing crimes against Palestinians in Gaza. He also argued that Arab citizens’ right to vote should not be viewed as evidence of goodwill on Israel’s part, but as a right secured through international pressure.
Shweiri: Choice for Israel's Arabs 'between the bad and the worse'
“Our situation is that we are being asked to choose between the bad and the worse, rather than between the good and the better,” Shweiri said. “I want to emphasize something for our brothers and sisters in the Arab world who hear and see Israel described as a democratic state that gives equal voting rights to Jewish and Arab citizens. This was not an act of goodwill by the Zionist movement or the Israeli government. It was a fundamental condition for Israel’s acceptance as a member of the United Nations in 1948 and as part of the international community.
“They cannot take this right away from us, although, as Netanyahu does, they can act outside the bounds of legitimacy.”
Meanwhile, Iranian officials have downplayed the significance of Israel’s election, which is taking place amid continued tensions between the two countries following years of confrontations and conflict involving Iran-backed groups.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at a press conference on Monday that the outcome of Tuesday’s election “makes no difference to us.”
“I do not agree with elections in the occupied territories at all; there is competition between different gangs to commit more evil,” Baghaei said. “Their most important slogan is that ‘I can commit more crimes than you.’ It makes no difference to us in such an environment who becomes the helm of a regime that has achieved nothing but killing and genocide.”
Despite Baghaei’s assertion that the candidates’ identities make no difference to Tehran, Iranian state-affiliated media, including the Tasnim News Agency, have reported on multiple polls examining Likud’s chances of winning the election.
The London-based Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, owned by Qatar’s Fadaat Media, reported on Monday on fears of a potential “political stalemate” that could leave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu leading a caretaker government.
In an analysis by Qatar-based Palestinian journalist Beirut Hammoud, the outlet framed the election as taking place after three years of what it described as “genocide” and “ethnic cleansing” across the Palestinian territories, including east Jerusalem.
After examining polls measuring Netanyahu’s chances of electoral success, Hammoud highlighted what she described as declining international support for Israel. She argued that even opposition politicians differed little from the prime minister, whom she accused of leading a “government of ruin.”
“They differ from him only in their methods of managing the conflict,” she claimed.
Pro-Hezbollah outlet accuses Netanyahu of portraying Arab vote as liability
Meanwhile, the Lebanon-based, pro-Hezbollah media outlet Al-Khanadeq published an analysis on Monday alleging that Netanyahu had manipulated the political landscape by portraying the Arab vote as a liability.
The article pointed to AI-generated campaign material associated with Netanyahu’s camp depicting political figures, including Gadi Eisenkot, alongside Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas.
“Portraying Eisenkot as a hostage of Arab politicians specifically targets the ‘soft right,’ which might distance itself from Likud. Thus, the campaign’s impact extends beyond weakening the Arab vote; it also reaches Jewish voters who want Netanyahu gone but are hesitant about a government based on Arab partnership,” the author argued. “The incitement works in two directions: it redistributes seats and raises the cost of utilizing them after the election.”
The analysis also cited efforts by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify Arab-majority parties and alleged attempts to deter Arab citizens from voting through the deployment of 2,000 activists. The author presented these developments as evidence of what they characterized as Netanyahu’s attempts to evade the consequences of the electoral process.
The Palestinian news site Al Quds, based in east Jerusalem, paid special attention to the timing of Israel’s elections around the United States’ midterms, noting that the result of both could reshape the region.
Written by Dr. Ahmed Youseff, a former senior adviser to assassinated Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, the article argued that Eisenkot’s victory could reopen the door for Israel’s international diplomacy efforts and for accountability for Israel’s security failures, but it would necessarily “dismantle established political systems or guarantee a shift in positions.”
“The hopes are clear: that Netanyahu and his allies will lose, that Israeli society will have an opportunity to reassess its policies of war and extremism, that the language of threats and incitement will subside, and that those responsible for failures and violations will be held accountable,” he wrote. “The American vote should also curb Trump’s drive toward confrontation and empower Congress to hold the administration accountable and push for a political path that spares the region a wider war.
“However, a realistic assessment requires us not to confuse hopes with certain outcomes…the true value of these elections will be measured by the opportunities they offer for accountability, pressure, and policy change, and by whether the voters’ voices translate into concrete steps that curb war and extremism and restore respect for rights and justice.”

Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul, eventually saving $5b a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul, eventually saving $5b a year
- The Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs through an AI-led overhaul, aiming to save €900 million a year by 2027 and €3.5 billion by 2035.
- State Secretary Eric van den Burg said the state must be “simpler, smarter, and smaller”. The Cabinet will present AI plans early next year.
- Ministries, inspectorates and agencies will be hit hardest, while police and defence are exempt. The cuts link to a drive to remove 500 rules a year and use Dutch and European suppliers.
AI generated
The Dutch government aims to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive targeting annual savings of €3.5 billion (S$5 billion).
The central government wants to save €900 million a year by 2027, rising to €3.5 billion from 2035. That amounts to around 25,000 jobs, spread over several years, according to a government statement on Oct 26. The Cabinet will present plans for deploying artificial intelligence to work more productively in early 2027.
“We cannot keep doing what we have been doing,” State Secretary for Effective Government Eric van den Burg said. “That is why we are going to make tough choices for a central government that really works: simpler, smarter, and smaller.”
The number of government officials surged to a record 160,000 at the end of 2025, up 41% compared with 2018, despite pledges by previous Cabinets to scale back headcount.
The Dutch government budget deficit is already one of the smallest in the European Union. Yet the figure and its long-term outlook still raise concerns in the Netherlands, which has a reputation for being fiscally conservative.
The cuts will not hit equally hard everywhere, with police and defence among exempted areas.
Ministries, inspectorates and implementing agencies will be most impacted, according to a letter van den Burg sent to Parliament. Departments there could face “significant staffing implications” of reductions of 45% or even 60%.
Van den Burg emphasised that the reductions go hand-in-hand with government ambitions to cut red tape. Its flagship programme to scrap 500 unnecessary or overly bureaucratic rules per year should make the organisation “fundamentally more simple” and lessen the need for more staff.
Promising technological developments are also paving the way for fewer external hires and a smaller administration. Various AI initiatives have already been launched in recent years in different parts of the government and the goal is to “apply AI even more broadly” to increase productivity, van den Burg says.
He cited a string of non-binding motions passed by Parliament calling on the Cabinet to increase government productivity by 20% through AI as a reason for the cuts. He also said that the push aims to work as much as possible with Dutch and European suppliers to avoid getting dependent on non-European technology. BLOOMBERG

Kanyshai Butun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Ukraine and Moldova signed a military-technical cooperation agreement Monday to strengthen joint efforts to counter “Russian threats,” said Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi.
On US social media platform X, Koretskyi said he met with Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan in Kyiv, where they discussed EU integration, regional security, and economic cooperation.
Koretskyi said Ukraine and neighboring Moldova are pursuing EU membership together, adding that their coordinated integration would strengthen security and economic ties.
He said Kyiv is ready to extend joint border controls to two additional crossing points with Moldova, with an agreement expected to be signed soon.
Koretskyi also highlighted energy cooperation, including gas transit through the Trans-Balkan Corridor and the use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Moldovan firms.
Tofan said the two countries reaffirmed their commitment to deepening practical cooperation, accelerating key transport and energy infrastructure projects, strengthening regional resilience, and streamlining border crossings.
“Ukraine and Moldova stand united in our pursuit of peace, security, and a shared European future,” he wrote on X.
Separately Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting with Tofan to discuss bilateral issues, infrastructure projects, and European integration.
“Moldova and Ukraine are certainly stronger when we move forward on this track together. And it is important that we carry on together, because it is fair,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
He said the two also discussed the issue of Transnistria – a breakaway region of Moldova, bordering Ukraine, with a Russian military presence – and strengthening military cooperation.

AFRL Moves Cargo Through Space with SpaceX Demonstration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:25:51 UTC
00:25:51 KST

Editor’s Note: This story was updated Oct. 26 with additional information from the Air Force Research Laboratory.
When a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket took off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Fla., on Oct. 20, it didn’t only carry the usual mix of micro-satellites and cubesats built by a wide range of companies. Also catching a ride into orbit was a capsule containing, among other things, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear, and emergency medical equipment.
That capsule wasn’t bound for the only humans in space on the International Space Station; it was a test of a capability that could one day get critical supplies to U.S. forces around the globe.
The Air Force Research Laboratory launched its Rocket Cargo initiative in 2021 to explore the idea of moving large amounts of cargo through space, a process that would both be faster and allow the Pentagon to more easily reach remote or contested areas.
SpaceX, which has demonstrated the ability to return its rockets to Earth and safely land them, was the first company to get a contract under the program in 2022, when AFRL awarded the firm a five-year, $102 million contract.
Other companies, including Blue Origin, Sierra Space, and Rocket Lab, have since signed on as well, but AFRL never announced any experiments or tests for the project—until now.
In a release, AFRL said the Oct. 20 mission “used a SpaceX capsule with instrumentation to measure temperature, shock and vibration; it carried agile cargo pod designs built for various delivery loads.”
The lab did not specify how many pods or how much equipment were included in the test and did not immediately respond to a query. But in a subsequent social media post Oct. 26, the lab said it recovered the pods after they splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. Each pod had equipment and sensors to monitor the payload’s status as it launched and then reentered the atmosphere.
“Researchers paid special attention to the electronics equipment, including a satellite communication-enabled tracker, batteries, a reverse osmosis desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment,” the release states.
The SpaceX capsule used in the test is called Starfall. Back in May, the Federal Aviation Administration released an environmental assessment for Starfall operations in the Pacific Ocean, describing it as a “cylindrical shaped capsule” with these dimensions:
- Approximately 0.75 meters (2.5 feet) tall
- A diameter of 3.1 meters (10.2 feet)
- A weight of 2,100 kilograms (4,600 pounds)
- Capable of carrying 1,000 kilograms (2,200 pounds) of payload
- Total weight of 3,100 kilograms (6,800 pounds)
In June, SpaceX launched what it called a “Starfall Demo Mission,” ending with the capsule splashing down into the Pacific.
In a statement, AFRL’s Technology Transition Office director Adam Remaly touted the most recent test as a success.
“This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the future force,” Remaly said. “The cross-discipline collaborations and ability to unleash the speed of our defense industrial base are key to maximizing capability and winning the future.”
AFRL’s release noted that engineers also “measured the capsule to potentially include a life raft in future tests” on Oct. 20.
Rocket Cargo could one day deliver supplies “to contested environments and austere sites without access to runways and roads, including contested logistics, expeditionary operations, rescue operations, disaster relief and response to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear hazards,” the release states.

Italy-Japan: Forum on Economic and Financial Cooperation Held in Tokyo
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:24:50 CET
00:24:50 KST

The Italy-Japan Economic and Financial Cooperation Forum was held today at the Italian Embassy in Tokyo, organized in conjunction with the visit to Japan by Giorgio Mulè, Vice President of the Chamber of Deputies. The event brought together institutions and professionals from the financial sector of both countries to discuss investment tools and prospects, with the initiative promoted by the embassy in collaboration with the ICE office in Tokyo, the Bank of Italy, Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, and SACE. The proceedings were opened by Italian Ambassador Mario Vattani and Japanese Deputy Minister of Finance Atsushi Mimura. The roundtable discussions included top executives from Japanese public financial institutions such as the JFSA, JETRO, JBIC, and NEXI, as well as representatives from major banking groups, including MUFG Bank, SMBC, Nomura, and Crédit Agricole. Private equity firms were also present, including the FSI Fund and Investindustrial. In total, more than 50 representatives from the banking, insurance, and asset management sectors participated, along with major industrial groups.
                                    
The program was divided into three sessions. The first session focused on the macroeconomic landscape of the two countries; the second on financial and insurance instruments to support businesses; and the third on investment opportunities, both bilateral and in third countries. The organizers’ stated goal was to define new co-investment strategies in the Italian and Japanese markets.
                                    
In his remarks, Vattani described the economic and financial dialogue as “a fundamental pillar” of the Special Strategic Partnership between Rome and Tokyo, at a time he characterized as one of “profound transformation of global markets.” According to the ambassador, the participation of high-profile institutions and operators attests to “the strength of the diplomacy of growth” pursued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Italian economic system. The forum, he explained, provided an opportunity to present to Japanese partners and Italian companies the tools available to support investments, commercial opportunities, and industrial synergies. The meeting is part of the initiatives marking the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan, which will be celebrated in 2026.

Gustav Klimt landscape expected to fetch up to $80M at New York auction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:23:44 UTC
00:23:44 KST

Halis Sunnetci
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
A landscape painting by Austrian artist Gustav Klimt is expected to fetch between $60 million and $80 million at a Christie's auction in New York next month, nearly three decades after setting an auction record for the artist.
The painting, titled Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), will headline the auction house's 20th Century Evening Sale on Nov. 17, Christie's announced Monday.
The work last appeared at auction in May 1997, when it sold for $14.7 million at Sotheby's in New York, setting an auction record for Klimt at the time.
Commissioned by Austrian banker and art patron Otto Primavesi, the painting depicts a brewery and inn on the northern shore of Lake Attersee in Austria, where Klimt spent many summers between 1900 and his death in 1918.
The landscape features dense green foliage and shimmering reflections on the water, combining the artist's decorative painting technique with elements of abstraction.
The work was previously owned by art dealer and collector Serge Sabarsky, co-founder of New York's Neue Galerie, and has been on long-term loan to the Leopold Museum in Vienna in recent years.
Klimt's current auction record stands at $236.4 million, set in November 2025 when his Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer sold at Sotheby's in New York.
Another Klimt landscape, Birch Forest, fetched $104.5 million at Christie's in 2022.
Ahead of the November auction, Litzlbergkeller will be exhibited in Hong Kong from Oct. 27 to 29 before going on display at Christie's Rockefeller Center galleries in New York starting Nov. 7.

Rogue Claude AI tapped into US voter data – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:22:11 UTC
00:22:11 KST

Rogue Claude AI tapped into US voter data – Axios
Anthropic’s Claude AI model went rogue and broke past a paywall to obtain voter data in the US state of Georgia, Axios reported on Sunday. The intrusion heightens concerns about developers’ ability to control increasingly autonomous AI systems.
The incident occurred during an internal statistics project involving public information. Anthropic said the model obtained aggregate voter counts but did not access Georgia’s voter registration system, retrieve individual voter records or alter any data.
The company confirmed the incident on Sunday, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“Without being asked to, the model requested a token to query a dashboard that contained information normally available for a fee,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios. Claude had learned from an archived government webpage that the dashboard issued digital access keys to visitors. It was able to request a key and retrieve the information without paying.
Georgia Deputy Secretary of State Jordan Fuchs confirmed to Fox Business that the data came from a public information service but insisted that Claude “did not get into the voter registration system.”
Anthropic described the incident in an October 9 report but did not name Georgia. According to Axios, it notified state officials and the White House weeks ago. A source told the outlet that administration officials had urged Georgia to disclose the incident publicly sooner, but those requests went unheeded.
The case is among several instances Anthropic has disclosed of models finding unintended ways around restrictions instead of stopping. Other incidents included a false homicide tip submitted to Philadelphia police and incomplete applications filed on the US State Department’s visa website.
On Friday, Anthropic also revealed that a model had impersonated a human during a cybersecurity exercise, attempting to persuade an unrelated software developer to accept malicious code. The developer rejected the request and the attempt failed.
Other developers have tightened controls following similar incidents. OpenAI said Friday that it was keeping its most powerful models’ training offline after agents escaped restricted environments. In July, its agents bypassed safeguards and accessed systems belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets.
Anthropic said it has moved some evaluations offline, restricted internet tools and introduced systems to detect unauthorized actions. It said those systems blocked each of the disclosed cases when tested against them.

"Martial law required quick and flexible decisions on staff appointments. But emergency decisions must not become permanent practice. Changes to animal protection are being prepared in Ukraine - will punishment for cruelty become more effective
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:18:08 EET
00:18:08 KST

Changes to animal protection are being prepared in Ukraine - will punishment for cruelty become more effective
Kyiv • UNN
The ministry has established a working group to bring animal protection in line with EU standards. Only 5% of those convicted of cruelty received actual prison sentences.
The Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine has established a working group tasked with preparing proposals to strengthen the protection of animals from cruel treatment. In Ukraine, animal abuse is punishable by up to eight years in prison, yet only a handful of offenders receive actual prison sentences.
UNN found out what the authorities are proposing and what animal-rights advocates are demanding.
What the Ministry of Economy decided
The ministry announced the creation of the working group on October 26. It consists of about 30 participants and is headed by Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Krasnolutskyi. The participants will identify problems and prepare proposals in the area of animal protection.
The issue concerns the protection of domestic, stray, and wild animals. The goal is to bring Ukrainian regulations closer to EU law and improve interaction between the authorities and the public
What the working group will focus on
The tasks include analyzing current legislation, preparing recommendations for its improvement, and reviewing the practice of responding to cruel treatment. They also plan to strengthen coordination between the police, local authorities, and animal-rights advocates, since even strict prohibitions do not protect animals when the police fail to respond to reports or collect evidence. It is not yet known whether the group will propose new sanctions or powers for oversight bodies.
Why the animal-protection system in Ukraine raises questions
According to estimates by Opendatabot based on prosecutor's office statistics, 386 proceedings under Article 299 of the Criminal Code were recorded in Ukraine from January to May 2025. This is 3.7 times more than during the same period in 2024. At the time of the study, approximately 80% of the cases had resulted in charges being brought, while about 4% had reached court.
UAnimals lawyer and analyst Anastasiia Hevchuk explained the increase in the number of registered cases as resulting from a more active stance by citizens.
This is not about an increase in violence, but about less silence
However, registering a case and punishing the perpetrator are different stages. In November 2025, NGL.media analyzed 148 guilty verdicts handed down after liability was strengthened in 2021. Actual imprisonment was imposed in only seven cases, or approximately 5%. In 129 cases, the convicted persons were released from serving their sentences on probation; in 11 cases, fines were imposed, and in one more case, community service was ordered.
What punishment for cruel treatment of animals is provided for by law
Under Article 89 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses, abuse that causes an animal pain or suffering but does not result in bodily injuries, mutilation, or death is punishable by a fine of 3,400 to 5,100 hryvnias. If the offense is repeated within a year, committed by a group of persons, or involves several animals, the fine ranges from 5,100 to 8,500 hryvnias. Administrative arrest for up to 15 days is also possible. If the owner poses a threat to the animal, confiscation is possible.
Article 299 of the Criminal Code establishes liability for cruel treatment of vertebrate animals under circumstances specified by law, in particular if the actions result in mutilation or death. The basic sanction is restriction of liberty for one to three years or imprisonment for two to three years. Such actions committed in the presence of children are punishable by three to five years in prison, while particular cruelty, repetition, or the commission of the crime by a group of persons carries a sentence of five to eight years.
European animal-protection rules: what is already in force and what still needs to be changed
Ukraine has already become a party to the Council of Europe's European Convention for the Protection of Pet Animals: it entered into force for the country in 2014. In January 2026, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 11328 at first reading. Among other things, it proposes clarifying the concepts of abandoning animals to their fate and proper conditions of keeping, as well as strengthening the role of communities in information and educational programs.
In August 2026, EU Regulation 2026/1818 on the welfare of dogs and cats and the ability to trace their origin entered into force. It establishes common requirements for breeders, shelters, the keeping, identification, and sale of animals. The main provisions will begin to apply in August 2028, while certain registration requirements will be introduced gradually at a later date.
What animal welfare advocates propose changing
The animal welfare organization UAnimals is already insisting on changes concerning stray and wild animals, the operating conditions of breeding facilities, the keeping of animals in captivity, and liability for cruelty. The law protects both domestic and stray animals equally.
UAnimals lawyer Alina Soroka emphasizes: photos and videos may constitute grounds for opening a case; however, for a person to be served with a notice of suspicion, there must be a body of material evidence. Therefore, the specialist advises witnesses to document the circumstances of the incident, record the contact details of eyewitnesses, and submit written statements to the police. This will help challenge possible inaction by law enforcement officers.
Some activists are calling for harsher sentences. In particular, at the beginning of 2026, the initiator of a petition to the government, Lyudmyla Tsaryova, advocated stricter criminal penalties, a ban on convicted individuals keeping animals, and a register of people punished for such crimes.
Stray animals in Ukraine and the challenges of war
The full-scale war has added evacuation, treatment of injured animals, and the search for foster homes and shelter places to the challenges of protecting animals. Because of hostilities and the evacuation of people, some animals are left without care.
According to a UAnimals report, in September 2026 alone, the organization evacuated 145 animals from 13 settlements in four regions, helped improve the conditions in which 550 animals were kept in shelters and rehabilitation centers, and sterilized 871 animals. Its team also contacted the police regarding 13 cases of possible cruel treatment. This is the data of just one organization.
For communities, sustainable programs for sterilizing, vaccinating, housing, and rehoming stray animals are particularly important. Rules are needed regarding the removal of animals, their transfer to shelters, and the financing of their care.
In addition, cases of cruel treatment of animals have increased because of internal migration and Ukrainians leaving for other countries. Within the country, animal owners leaving dangerous regions cannot find housing because landlords refuse to rent them apartments and houses. Even attempts to pay a large deposit and a willingness to compensate for material damage if it is caused by a pet do not help. Moreover, according to the OLX platform, where internally displaced persons most often try to search for housing, in some cities (such as Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, and Kryvyi Rih) there are no housing offers at all for pet owners. As a result, some owners leave their cats and dogs outside or even resort to killing the animal.
In situations involving leaving the country, matters are even more complicated. To legally take an animal out of the country, veterinary documents, a microchip, and valid vaccinations are required. All of this costs money and takes time (on average, from one month to several months). Far from everyone has the financial means and time to meet all the requirements. In addition, not all countries can accept people traveling with a pet. For example, red-eared turtles cannot be taken to France because the country's law prohibits it. Therefore, instead of looking for foster care or new owners for the animal, some people simply abandon it.
Animal protection in Ukraine: should we expect real changes
For now, the new working group has an advisory mandate: to prepare proposals that could become the basis for legislative decisions. The creation of the group itself does not change sanctions or owners' obligations. The transparency of its work will also matter: publicly available proposals will make it possible to assess which proposals officials supported and which were left without progress.
The result can be assessed by concrete steps: whether the amendment texts and timelines for their consideration will appear, whether the police and communities will receive clear response procedures, whether there will be more properly investigated cases and court decisions, and whether animal-keeping conditions will improve.

Swedish government blocks ChatGPT and Claude. Here’s why

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:18:02 UTC
00:18:02 KST

The ban on employees using browser-based versions of ChatGPT and Claude took effect on Monday 26 October amid security concerns over data processing.
Swedish government employees can no longer use browser-based versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude on their work computers following security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data.
The decision comes following a review of AI tools used by workers at the Swedish Transport Administration earlier this year that found “problematic” uses of the AI platforms in carrying out government work.
Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training.
The use of platforms not regulated or protected by such agreements, also known as shadow IT, could bring “consequences for our information security”, said Mikael Wettercrantz, director of digitalisation at the Government Offices of Sweden.
Microsoft’s Copilot, which has passed a security screening process and is covered by a security agreement between the US company and the Swedish government, is being recommended as an alternative.
While government workers will still be able to use AI to help them carry out their tasks, they will do so under tighter security controls and with just a limited number of employees permitted to continue using ChatGPT and Claude but only through a special platform for AI assistants developed by Swedish authorities.
According to the Swedish public broadcaster Sveriges Radio, restrictions on the use of ChatGPT and Claude have also been put in place at the Swedish Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care. The Swedish Enforcement Authority is currently reviewing the issue.
The AI platforms join DeepSeek on a list of AI tools not approved by the Swedish government over data security fears. Last week, the US announced it was banning all products and services from the Chinese AI company.

How birds can quietly spread a severe form of pneumonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:17:59 UTC
00:17:59 KST

Birds are everywhere. They perch on rooftops and windowsills and sometimes share our homes as pets. But they can also carry dangerous germs, even when they appear healthy.
In a recent case report published in Frontiers in Medicine, a 43-year-old man presented with a persistent fever of 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius), fatigue and muscle pain but few respiratory symptoms. Several courses of antibiotics failed to bring down his fever.
Doctors detected abnormal breath sounds, and a scan revealed a round blotch in his right lung—a sign of blood, pus, fluid or tissue—but tests for common pathogens came back negative. Suspecting a more unusual infection, they tested samples from his lungs and identified the culprit: Chlamydia psittaci, a bird-borne bacterium.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The finding was key: the man switched antibiotics and recovered.
The likely source of the pathogen was a visit to a zoo, where the man had had direct contact with parrots about 10 days before his symptoms began. The infection, known as psittacosis, or parrot fever, can spread from many different birds, however, including poultry and pigeons.
Another case report describes a 16-year-old boy who developed pneumonia from a C. psittaci infection after he cleaned his dormitory, including by dusting windowsills and ventilation systems—despite the fact that he had no known direct contact with birds.
These cases show how everyday activities can expose people, sometimes unknowingly, to bird-borne diseases.
“Psittacosis is a respiratory disease mainly spread through inhaling the dust of bird droppings. You need to breathe in the bacteria to get infected,” says Brian Labus, an infectious disease epidemiologist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that there is no evidence that C. psittaci spreads through preparing or eating poultry products, though other case reports raise this possibility.
One, published in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases, described a chef who may have contracted psittacosis through handling poultry. Another, published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases, involved a man who developed fever and severe diarrhea after eating undercooked pigeon meat. The same bacterial strain was detected in the patient and in pigeons from the source of the meat, raising the possibility of foodborne transmission. But the exact routes of transmission in these cases remains unclear.
Psittacosis can be difficult to recognize because its symptoms resemble those of other respiratory illnesses.
“There are no unique symptoms that can make you suspect psittacosis as the cause of a respiratory illness, and doctors can’t tell without laboratory testing,” Labus says. He recommends that people with symptoms tell their doctor about any bird-related exposures, including caring for pet birds or cleaning up after wild birds.
According to the CDC, fewer than 10 cases of parrot fever are typically reported in the U.S. each year. Psittacosis may be more common than reported figures suggest.
“Many infections probably go undiagnosed and are simply classified as community-acquired pneumonia without identifying the underlying causative pathogen,” says Daisy Vanrompay, a professor at Ghent University in Belgium. She directs the country’s national reference laboratory for human C. psittaci infections.
While some infections are mild, others can cause severe pneumonia and, in rare cases, damage to organs such as the heart, liver and brain.
Severity depends on the amount of bacteria that’s inhaled, the strain that’s involved and individual susceptibility, Vanrompay says. Labus adds that young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems or underlying lung conditions may be at greater risk of severe illness.
To reduce exposure, both experts recommend wetting bird droppings before removal rather than dry sweeping or vacuuming them and wearing a well-fitting respirator when cleaning contaminated areas.

Disgusting or scary? What an aversion to clusters of holes tells us about the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:17:40 UTC
00:17:40 KST

Since childhood, clusters of circles have made me queasy—especially holes. Just thinking of honeycombs or lotus seed pods makes my stomach churn and skin crawl. My affliction has a name: trypophobia. By some estimates, trypophobia affects roughly one in six people. But its rise is sometimes put down to an online meme—an aversion to holes had a moment on the mid-2000s Internet. The condition is no joke, however: it can be debilitating, causing panic attacks and nausea—in extreme cases, people stop driving, miss work or avoid nature for fear of confronting upsetting stimuli.
Researchers first described trypophobia in a 2013 paper and argued that it may be a primitive fear response to venomous animals. Other, more recent theories include that it’s a disease-avoidance instinct that makes us recoil from anything resembling skin lesions or parasites, a form of cortical hyperexcitability where clusters of holes trigger a neural response—a visual equivalent to nails on a chalkboard—or simply a condition that caught on because it was a meme.
Now scientists may finally be closing in on an answer. Geoff Cole—the British scientist who originally pitched the evolutionary fear of venomous animals theory in 2013—recently looked back at the evidence and made a new conclusion. In a 2026 paper, Cole and his co-authors came down in favor of the disease-avoidance theory. Reviewing experiments that tested people’s reactions to triggering images, he concluded that trypophobia is primarily driven by disgust, not fear.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Disgust is the mechanism with which we can detect things which carry disease,” says Cole, a researcher at the University of Essex’s Center for Brain Science in England. “It’s clear that the evidence, when you stack it up, is more in favor of the disease-avoidance hypothesis.”
In one experiment, for example, college students were shown trypophobic images, typical fear-inducing pictures—such as those of snakes and spiders—and control images. Participants’ pupils constricted more when they saw the trypophobic images than any of the others—a sign that the parasympathetic nervous system, which is linked to disgust, was activated. Fear, by contrast, is linked to the sympathetic nervous system, which dilates the pupils.
Other research suggests trypophobic people find hole clusters as unpleasant as pictures of skin disease and that people with a history of skin problems may find hole clusters particularly uncomfortable to look at.
That’s not to say fear has no role in trypophobia. Last year a French-led team concluded that while disgust is the “dominant emotion” for trypophobes, “fear is also not negligible.”
To fully settle the question, scientists would need more “hard evidence,” says Christopher DiMattina, a psychology professor at Florida Gulf Coast University. For example, people could be put in an fMRI machine to track their brain activity, then be shown trypophobic and control images. Amygdala activation would suggest fear, while responses in the insular cortex would suggest disgust, he says.
Clinically, phobias are considered anxiety disorders, but some researchers believe that everyone is a little trypophobic. Some people, like me, are bothered by such images but can mostly ignore them. Trypophobia isn’t an official diagnosis—but someone with it could be diagnosed under the term specific phobia if they have severe reactions that interfere with their daily life, according to Kevin Chapman, a clinical psychologist and director of the Kentucky Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders.
“You can technically be phobic of anything,” Chapman says. “There are certain phobias that load more with what we call disgust sensitivity, versus, say, anxiety sensitivity.”
There is little research on effective treatments for trypophobia, and scientists have called for more investment in potential therapies that target disgust. Most people with trypophobia are offered exposure therapy—a form of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) that aims to gradually desensitize someone to the phobic trigger by exposing them to low-level versions of it in controlled settings.
In a handful of published case reports, treatment, including CBT, seems to reduce people’s fear-related symptoms, but it hardly affects their disgust response. That could be because disgust is “generally more resistant to exposure than fear,” according to researchers at Macquarie University in Australia. Just as important as exposure, they argue, is counterconditioning, in which the upsetting stimulus is paired with something positive, such as a good experience or relaxation exercises.
The Australian team put that to the test in a small trial that aimed to alleviate both fear and disgust in nine trypophobic people. The participants underwent a one-session treatment that condensed key CBT principles into a single three-hour session—and was modified to include counterconditioning and other techniques to help them adjust their thinking. A month after the session, most participants reported significant improvements in both disgust and fear.
Chapman says treatment should be tailored to the trypophobic patient based on whether they experience more disgust, fear or anxiety. He recommends a combination of exposure therapy and cognitive restructuring, another CBT-based technique that aims to replace irrational thoughts with neutral, realistic alternatives.
“Particularly when disgust sensitivity is high, you’ve got to really identify what they’re concerned would happen if they encounter it,” he says.
If a person is worried about vomiting, for example, Chapman will work with them on applied muscle tension—a CBT-related technique—to tense up their core so they don’t actually puke. Applied tension is often used to help people with phobias related to needles or blood avoid fainting. Other individuals simply need help learning to tolerate the discomfort of seeing trypophobic images.
“Learning history does matter,” Chapman says.

Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran, sources say
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:16:47 CET
00:16:47 KST

By Laila Bassam and Maya Gebeily
BEIRUT, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The group, founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.
Invading Israeli forces now occupy its heartland of villages in southern Lebanon, and political pressure has built up in Beirut for its disarmament.
It nevertheless remains committed to fighting Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the group received from Tehran to aid displaced families in its Shi’ite heartlands, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group’s operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah’s media office said Israel’s occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right. It rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
Israel’s military declined to comment. Iran’s permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters questions.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah’s finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
HEZBOLLAH ON ALERT
Hezbollah’s effort comes amid continued tensions in the wider Middle Eastern conflict ignited by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.
Hezbollah opened fire in support of Iran on March 2, triggering an Israeli offensive that killed more than 4,000 people and uprooted a quarter of Lebanon’s population, mostly members of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituency.
Hostilities largely abated over the summer as an interim Iran-US deal included a Lebanon ceasefire and Washington mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel. Full-scale hostilities have not resumed in Lebanon despite the collapse of the US-Iranian deal, though Israel continues deadly strikes in the south.
Hezbollah is on alert for a possible US-Iran escalation, potentially reigniting the Lebanon front.
The sources told Reuters the group had not yet managed to fully prepare its stockpiles or fighting force.
Hezbollah is still restocking, acknowledging this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to it and were intended for use against Israel. A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters they were specifically for its explosive drones.
ISRAEL’S REMOTE WARFARE PROVED A CHALLENGE, SOURCES SAY
The group will also need to repair command-and-control capabilities after losses on key fronts, including the flashpoint town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, according to one of the Lebanese sources and three security officials.
They said Hezbollah’s tactic of operating in small units and rationing the use of anti-tank rockets left some units isolated on those fronts, struggling to confront Israel’s remotely operated systems including weaponized drones and armed remote-controlled vehicles.
The Israeli military told Reuters it uses remotely-operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce troops’ threat exposure.
Hezbollah has not explicitly said whether it would take part in the eruption of fresh hostilities, but its media office said it was wary of giving Israeli leaders any justification to escalate in Lebanon, particularly as the group was concerned about its constituents being displaced once more.
(Additional reporting by Steven Scheer and Pesha Magid in Jerusalem, Olivia Le Poidevin in GenevaWriting by Maya Gebeily and Tom PerryEditing by Peter Graff)

Kenya releases first Ebola contacts from quarantine, milestone in containment efforts

00:16:23 KST

NAIROBI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Kenya on Monday released from quarantine the first group of people who came into contact with its index Ebola patient, a milestone in its efforts to contain cases to a single infection cluster.
The 20 people released completed 21 days of monitoring without developing Ebola symptoms and are in good health, the director-general in Kenya’s health ministry, Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.
Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases so far, two of whom have died. The remaining seven patients are stable and receiving treatment, Amoth said, adding that 98 others still in quarantine would be released in four waves beginning on November 3.
“This is a milestone worth celebrating,” Amoth said. “It is also a reminder that the work is not yet done.”
Kenya’s first case died in a hospital in Nairobi on October 5, after which eight others fell ill while in quarantine. It announced on Friday that a second person had died.
Ebola’s spread from Congo, where the outbreak was declared in mid-May, to Kenya has raised concerns about lapses in border screening.
Nigeria has said its first Ebola case in more than a decade, which it reported last week, appears to be closely related to Kenya’s index case, citing genomic analysis. The two cases both flew out of Uganda’s Entebbe airport on the same day in early October.
Amoth said those leaving quarantine posed no risk to their families or communities where they live and urged Kenyans to welcome them home. “We cannot afford to drop our vigilance,” he said.
