Russia-Ukraine war reaches orbit: What a close satellite encounter means for space operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:57:28 UTC
23:57:28 KST

In mid-October, a Russian military satellite in low-Earth orbit came dangerously close to a commercial US spacecraft reportedly serving Ukrainian military needs.
The approach was so extreme that the two spacecraft may have been “just a few meters” away from each other at one point.
Satellite trackers called the non-consensual manoeuvre a “worrisome cat-and-mouse game” in space between Russia and Ukraine, the two countries at war since February 2022.
Experts say the incident is an indication that space is increasingly turning into the final frontier for drawn-out geopolitical wars that countries can’t settle using conventional tools.
Russia’s Kosmos-2612 moved dangerously close to ICEYE-X36 equipped with a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) – a technology that can see through clouds during both day and night to create two-dimensional images of objects on Earth.
The satellite is owned by ICEYE US, an American subsidiary of Finland-based ICEYE. Analysts say ICEYE-X36 is likely used by Ukraine for satellite imagery. Kiev has formal access to data collected by the Finnish company’s constellation of SAR satellites.
ICEYE has been supplying satellite data and images to the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022.
Ukraine relies heavily on satellite networks such as Starlink, Starshield, and ICEYE to monitor Russian troop movements and run drones that both intercept missiles and strike targets.
Any disruption in the satellite network by Moscow would substantially degrade Kiev’s ability to launch precision weapons and execute interceptions.
Ukraine’s dependence on its so-called eyes-in-the-sky was on full display last week when Elon Musk’s SpaceX imposed speed restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade Starshield service.
US President Donald Trump had to intervene on Ukraine’s behalf as Musk restored internet speeds to previous levels.
Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in the department of space engineering at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, tells TRT World that the encounter was unusual in its closeness.
“We have never seen two satellites coming so close without cooperation between the operators of both satellites,” says Langbroek, who first reported the close encounter.
Earlier uncooperative approaches in space had taken place at distances of tens of kilometres, rather than a few hundred metres, he says.
Langbroek links the episode to a broader pattern that includes Russian satellites approaching other countries’ satellites apparently for eavesdropping, reported hacks of satellite feeds, on-orbit exercises involving close approaches, and tests of anti-satellite weapons.
“Space is quickly developing into a potential battlefield,” he says.
No wonder the language around space operations has also become militaristic of late: the US Space Force now treats space as a “battle domain” and has acknowledged possessing “space weapons”, he says.
Modern military operations now depend heavily on space-based communications, live data streams, including from drones, and satellite intelligence.
In the same vein, civilian life has also grown equally dependent on space-based communications, Langbroek says.
The result is heightened vulnerability for everyone, he adds.
“This is not just a military threat. It is a threat to us all,” he says.
Langbroek notes that the traditional divide between military and civilian satellites has blurred of late.
Commercial systems, such as those operated by ICEYE and Starlink, now support military tasks, he says.
Russia already considers any commercial satellite used by Ukraine as a legitimate target.
Consequently, satellite systems that multiple countries and ordinary users rely upon can become targets, potentially harming states that are not parties to the conflict, he says.
Militarisation of Earth’s orbits
Mark J Sundahl, director of the Global Space Law Centre at Cleveland State University, tells TRT World the stalking of satellites in space is on the rise.
The phenomenon is fanning global concerns about the growing militarisation of Earth’s orbits, he says.
“All kinetic warfare that could result in the creation of massive debris clouds that will stay in orbit for hundreds of years must be prohibited,” he says.
Sundahl says such action is already inconsistent with Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which requires states to exercise “due regard to the corresponding interests” of other countries.
Generating debris clouds that threaten civilian satellites would constitute a “clear violation” of that obligation, even though he notes that not everyone shares this interpretation of the law.
“The common orbital infrastructure that we all share for purposes of telecommunication, navigation, and other daily needs cannot be put into danger due to terrestrial conflicts,” Sundahl says.
Ilyas Golcuklu, head of the private international law department at Altinbas University in Istanbul, tells TRT World that the non-consensual close approach between a military and a commercial object in space is no longer a hypothetical exercise.
“Space has already become a new frontier for geopolitical conflict,” he says.
With the growing volume of objects in orbit, distinguishing commercial from military assets will become harder, he notes.
“The escalation of national rivalries into space is a justified concern for all humankind,” he says.
Lack of established norms
Clear and widely accepted norms for uncoordinated proximity operations in space remain mostly non-existent.
Langbroek attributes this mainly to the opposition by major space powers, which have resisted rules that might constrain their own extraterrestrial activities.
In wartime, rules of conduct are often the first to be broken, he says.
“Any form of uncooperative proximity should not be performed, because of the risks involved. Yet, it happens,” he says.
Golcuklu notes that space approaches conducted for peaceful purposes – such as refuelling, repairing a component, or removing space debris – rely on technologies that are essentially identical to those needed to spy on or disable a rival satellite.
Distinguishing legitimate activity from hostile intent – and closing the regulatory vacuum – has become increasingly challenging, he says.
“Minimum safe distances” or “keep-out zones” must be devised as quickly as possible by the UN before the risks become too big to handle, he adds.
For example, experts consider the risk of a minor miscalculation resulting in collisions and creating space debris as serious.
Langbroek notes that a kinetic attack – whether by collision or by a projectile – would generate large amounts of on-orbit debris that endangers satellites belonging to countries uninvolved in any conflict.
Even non-kinetic methods, such as disabling electronics with an electromagnetic pulse, would leave the targeted satellite itself as debris, adding to collision hazards, he says.
During close approaches, the risk of an unintended collision is real: if the operator of the approached satellite becomes nervous and attempts an evasive manoeuvre, the geometry can become hazardous, he says.
Even controlled approaches in space can go wrong.
“It really is a risky thing to bring your satellite so close to another satellite, especially without coordination with the owner of that satellite,” Langbroek says.

Ukraine Plans Draft Reform to End Street Conscription
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:56:39 UTC
23:56:39 KST

Ukraine aims to develop a new mobilization arrangement with businesses by Dec. 1 that would provide predictable military enlistment and remove the search for eligible men on the streets, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Monday, Oct. 26.
Speaking at the Kyiv International Economic Forum, Koretskyi proposed linking company access to worker deferments with commitments to help replenish the armed forces, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If such a solution could be found, there would be no need to look for people on the streets,” he said.
Koretskyi described the proposal as an ideal model that would require agreement with employers. He said the government must balance enlistment needs, the functioning of the economy and the need to rotate soldiers already serving.
Full worker deferments would come with conditions
The proposal builds on changes outlined by the government on Friday, Oct. 23.
Under the planned mechanism, companies could qualify for full workforce deferments if they regularly help some employees volunteer for military service. Koretskyi said those joining the armed forces should know where they would serve and for how long, while retaining their jobs and salaries.
The Defense and Economy ministries are to develop the terms together with businesses, according to a government statement.
The arrangement is intended to give serving troops confidence that replacements will become available. However, the announcement did not specify service periods, the proportion of employees companies would need to recruit or a guaranteed timetable for soldiers to return home.
Vučić Out, Students In: Still, No Sanctions Against Russia
Dec. 1 is the government’s target for approving the mechanism, rather than an announced date for ending street conscription.
Koretskyi warns Ukraine must prepare for Russian mobilization
Koretskyi warned that Russia could mobilize another 300,000-500,000 people and said Ukraine must prepare for that possibility.
Without advance planning, he argued, the government could again be forced to make unpopular decisions on an emergency basis. He presented the figure as a potential scenario, rather than announcing a confirmed Russian mobilization campaign.
The prime minister also said tougher accountability for people evading military service remained on the agenda. His forum remarks did not set out specific new penalties or an implementation date.
Koretskyi cautioned that changes to mobilization and deferments would not deliver a dramatic result on their own. One immediate objective, he said, was to stop the continued growth of deferments obtained through questionable arrangements.
Reform faces pressure from defense manufacturers
The government’s broader deferment overhaul targets companies allegedly created or expanded primarily to shield workers from mobilization.
Koretskyi has argued that high salaries and the absence of tax debts do not, by themselves, establish that a business is critical. The government plans to assess companies’ actual contribution to defense and essential services.
He has also said unconditional 100% deferments should end, while companies needing additional protection to maintain operations could submit a justified request to a coordination center.
Defense manufacturers have warned that reducing deferments could disrupt weapons production. Industry representatives say losing a small number of specialist engineers or welders can interrupt an entire production line, while replacements may require months or years of training.
They have called for targeted inspections of suspected abuse while preserving the workers needed to fulfill military contracts.
The debate comes as President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine needs a large, sustainably funded military as a central security guarantee.
In an interview broadcast Sunday, Oct. 25, Zelensky said he wanted to maintain a military force with 800,000 personnel if sufficient financing were available. He rejected externally imposed limits on Ukraine’s armed forces and said funding and long-term security guarantees remained key questions in negotiations with partners.

'No fuel to keep babies warm': shortages push hospitals in Yemen's Taiz to brink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:55:34 UTC
23:55:34 KST

'No fuel to keep babies warm': shortages push hospitals in Yemen's Taiz to brink
GENEVA, Oct 26 - Fuel shortages in Yemen's besieged city of Taiz have forced one hospital to cut the number of incubators it can operate from 40 to 10, putting newborn babies at risk as weeks of fighting choke off vital supplies and deepen a humanitarian crisis affecting hundreds of thousands of people.
"There's no oxygen, there's no fuel to run the incubators, to keep the babies warm," said Nada Ahmed, a nurse in the neonatal unit of the Yemeni-Swedish Hospital for Maternity and Childhood.
Nawal Najeeb, a supervisor in the neonatal unit, warned the facility could be forced to halt operations if fuel supplies do not arrive.
"It will be a catastrophe for the babies, a catastrophe of deaths and disabilities."
Taiz has been largely isolated since October 3, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering and civilians from leaving, following an escalation in clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
FUEL PRICES SURGE
Key supply routes, including the Taiz-Aden corridor, have been blocked by Houthi forces, worsening shortages of water, food and fuel. The city hosts nearly half of the 250,000 people displaced by the latest fighting, according to the United Nations.
In Taiz city, 42 health facilities are reporting acute shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said.
Fuel prices have surged to 2,000 Yemeni rials per litre, driver Abdullah al-Radfani told Reuters.
Oxfam Yemen's policy, advocacy and media manager, Fatma Jaffar Shotah, described one dialysis patient who has to spend two nights at a healthcare centre rather than travelling home between sessions because regular journeys have become unaffordable, the cost rising from half a dollar to around $10.
"Fuel shortage inside the city is having catastrophic impacts on people's lives," she said.
The strain is being felt beyond Taiz. Aid group Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said fuel shortages were causing power outages at hospitals and primary healthcare centres in the southern governorates of Aden and Lahj, affecting operating theatres and intensive care units.
HUNGER AND MALNUTRITION
UN agencies and aid groups also warned of worsening hunger and malnutrition. The World Food Programme says that more than 800,000 people have been cut off from food assistance in Taiz and surrounding areas.
UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said 52,000 of the 168,000 children screened in Taiz so far this year are acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
Although UNICEF has put in place nearly 8,000 cartons of life-saving therapeutic food, enough to sustain treatment services for around three months, Pires warned that worsening insecurity and movement restrictions could hamper future deliveries and prevent families from reaching treatment centres.
MSF said growing displacement was aggravating child malnutrition in southern Yemen, an area which has already faced a long-standing hunger crisis, as families flee fighting in the north and along the west coast.
Between September 15 and October 22, MSF screened 299 children under 5 at its mobile clinics in Aden and Lahj. Forty-four children, or 14.7%, were suffering from moderate acute malnutrition, while 28 children, or 9.4%, were severely malnourished and in need of hospital care.
"In each location we go, on a daily basis, we see at least one or two children who are in severe acute malnutrition," said MSF's mobile health activity manager, Sara Ghanem. REUTERS

Israel Police race to stop election disinformation as voting nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:51:40 UTC
23:51:40 KST

Israeli police are intensifying efforts to combat domestic disinformation campaigns ahead of Tuesday's national election, targeting fake social media accounts, artificial intelligence-generated videos and coordinated influence operations aimed at manipulating voters.
The operation, led by a specialized police intelligence unit known as Matzpen, will reach its peak on Election Day and continue until polling stations close at 10 p.m.
While the Shin Bet domestic security agency has spent recent months tracking foreign influence operations intended to affect the election's outcome, police investigators are focusing on individuals and groups operating inside Israel.
Matzpen, which operates within the Israel Police Intelligence Division and the national cybercrime unit of the Investigations and Intelligence Department, has been monitoring online activity for six months in an effort to identify and disrupt attempts to undermine the integrity of the vote.
Police announced Sunday that the unit had secured the removal of two networks engaged in what authorities described as improper activity on X and Facebook.
Separately, the Yashar! party, led by former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, filed a complaint after unidentified individuals allegedly forged a public message purporting to come from the party.
Fake profiles, AI videos and coordinated manipulation
According to police, domestic actors are employing an increasingly sophisticated range of tactics to influence voters, including creating fictitious social media profiles, impersonating real individuals and circulating posts that either promote or attack political candidates.
Other methods include spreading fabricated news about political parties, impersonating candidates and publishing statements in their names, and distributing AI-generated videos designed to mislead viewers.
Authorities have also identified coordinated efforts to flood social media posts with favorable or defamatory comments, creating the appearance of public support or opposition.
The techniques can make it difficult for voters to distinguish genuine political debate from organized manipulation.
Police warn that social media users should approach election-related content with caution, particularly when its source or authenticity cannot be verified.
Despite the extensive monitoring operation, investigators acknowledge that they can identify and disrupt only a small proportion of the individuals and networks engaged in such activity.
Police officials say the practice is unlikely to diminish significantly unless those responsible recognize that they could face substantial fines or prison sentences.
Police prioritize disruption over identifying operators
Police say impersonation, fraudulent accounts and automated networks designed to manipulate public opinion can constitute criminal offenses involving impersonation or forgery, depending on the circumstances.
However, investigators acknowledge that their immediate priority is stopping harmful online activity rather than identifying and prosecuting every person behind it.
"We are currently focused on monitoring the internet to identify and thwart activity across the various online platforms," police said.
That approach means authorities are concentrating on detecting coordinated campaigns and securing the removal of offending content before it reaches more voters.
Under normal circumstances, Matzpen primarily monitors social media for incitement against the State of Israel and incitement to terrorism.
With the election approaching, however, the unit has shifted significant resources toward protecting the integrity of the democratic process.
Six months of monitoring ahead of Election Day
A senior official in Matzpen, which operates within the police Intelligence Division, told ynet that investigators have been preparing for the election for approximately six months.
"We have been involved in safeguarding the integrity of Israel's elections for six months now," the official said.
"We are confronting domestic actors who are trying to undermine the integrity of the elections, and we are working around the clock to monitor the internet and identify influence operations aimed at promoting or discrediting a candidate or political party."
The official said the intensity of the operation has increased as Election Day approaches.
"Our work is becoming increasingly intensive as we get closer to Election Day," the official said. "Tomorrow will be our busiest day, and until the polls close, we will work to thwart online activity by bots seeking to smear a rival party or promote a candidate or political party."
Investigators are also targeting accounts that impersonate real people or fabricate political identities.
"We are also disrupting the activity of online impersonators and fictitious personas that publish posts, tweets or TikTok videos containing fake news or impersonating candidates running in the election," the official said.
Working with social media companies to remove content
When investigators identify suspected coordinated manipulation, they work through the cyber department of the State Attorney's Office to request the removal of offending content.
The requests are directed to operators of major social media platforms, including X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook.
"When we identify such activity, we contact the operators of Twitter, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook through the cyber department of the State Attorney's Office and ask them to remove activity that we have been able to establish is improper," the senior official said.
The process requires investigators to establish that the targeted activity violates applicable rules or laws before seeking its removal.
Police have not disclosed how many individuals are suspected of operating the networks or whether the two networks removed from X and Facebook were connected to particular political parties or candidates.
The operation comes amid broader concerns about efforts to manipulate Israel's election through both domestic and foreign influence campaigns.
For police, the immediate challenge is the speed at which misleading content can spread across social media, particularly in the final hours before voting ends.
Authorities say they will continue monitoring the platforms until the last polling stations close Tuesday night, seeking to prevent coordinated disinformation campaigns from influencing voters before ballots are cast.

Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.
According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.
“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”
The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.
While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.
“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the US government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.
In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran, sources say
BEIRUT, Oct 26 - Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The group, founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.
Invading Israeli forces now occupy its heartland of villages in southern Lebanon, and political pressure has built up in Beirut for its disarmament.
It nevertheless remains committed to fighting Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into Israeli positions, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the group received from Tehran to aid displaced families in its Shi'ite heartlands, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office said Israel's occupation of Lebanese land made any resistance to it a legitimate right. It rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
Israel's military declined to comment. Iran's permanent mission to the United Nations in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters questions.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
HEZBOLLAH ON ALERT
Hezbollah's effort comes amid continued tensions in the wider Middle Eastern conflict ignited by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.
Hezbollah opened fire in support of Iran on March 2, triggering an Israeli offensive that killed more than 4,000 people and uprooted a quarter of Lebanon's population, mostly members of Hezbollah's Shi'ite Muslim constituency.
Hostilities largely abated over the summer as an interim Iran-US deal included a Lebanon ceasefire and Washington mediated talks between Lebanon and Israel. Full-scale hostilities have not resumed in Lebanon despite the collapse of the US-Iranian deal, though Israel continues deadly strikes in the south.
Hezbollah is on alert for a possible US-Iran escalation, potentially reigniting the Lebanon front.
The sources told Reuters the group had not yet managed to fully prepare its stockpiles or fighting force.
Hezbollah is still restocking, acknowledging this month that explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to it and were intended for use against Israel. A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters they were specifically for its explosive drones.
ISRAEL'S REMOTE WARFARE PROVED A CHALLENGE, SOURCES SAY
The group will also need to repair command-and-control capabilities after losses on key fronts, including the flashpoint town of Bint Jbeil and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, according to one of the Lebanese sources and three security officials.
They said Hezbollah's tactic of operating in small units and rationing the use of anti-tank rockets left some units isolated on those fronts, struggling to confront Israel's remotely operated systems including weaponized drones and armed remote-controlled vehicles.
The Israeli military told Reuters it uses remotely-operated systems to monitor southern Lebanon and reduce troops' threat exposure.
Hezbollah has not explicitly said whether it would take part in the eruption of fresh hostilities, but its media office said it was wary of giving Israeli leaders any justification to escalate in Lebanon, particularly as the group was concerned about its constituents being displaced once more. ====================================================================================================

Copy-paste from Brussels: The EU’s error-riddled new sanctions package was generated using an LLM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:50:28 UTC
23:50:28 KST

The European Union’s latest sanctions package, adopted Oct. 12, bears signs of having been generated by a large language model. The document contains numerous errors — including references to companies that have long since closed, individuals listed without birthdates, and pseudonyms used in place of real names. The package also omits Chinese companies entirely, despite China’s growing role in helping Russia evade sanctions aimed at hindering the work of Moscow’s military-industrial complex amid the war in Ukraine.
The EU’s latest sanctions package is riddled with errors that are striking to the human eye: the mixing of Latin and Cyrillic characters (as in the phrase «Акcionерное общество», or “Joint-stock company”), names listed without birthdates, actors’ stage names used in place of real surnames, and references to companies that ceased operating long ago. While technical mistakes are inevitable in a document covering 1,500 individuals and legal entities, the latest package stands out for the apparent lack of care in its preparation. One of the clearest signs is what appears to be the use of large language models (LLMs) in drafting parts of the text.
“Workslop” and copy-pasting instead of meticulous bureaucracy
At first glance, the use of boilerplate language may not seem significant. Council Decision No. 2026/2279 relies on just two standard phrases to justify sanctions against 1,569 individuals and organizations. That marks a clear departure from previous sanctions packages, which generally included a specific explanation for why each newly designated person or entity had been targeted.
Additionally, for the first time, the EU writes the names of all legal entities as literal transliterations from Russian rather than as they appear in Russia’s official register of legal entities. When Russian organizations are registered, the database typically includes both their full and abbreviated Russian names as well as the English-language name chosen by the organization itself. Some companies use a transliteration in that field, while others provide an actual translation.
In the latest sanctions document, however, company names appear to have been transliterated mechanically and with little quality control. Capitalization was omitted throughout. While similar formatting errors had appeared occasionally in earlier EU sanctions lists, in the latest package nearly every legal entity contains the same type of error.
The transliteration itself is also inconsistent. Different systems appear to have been used for different entries. In most cases, the latest package appears to rely not on a standard transliteration system for Cyrillic but on output generated by the Python library transliterate, with apostrophes subsequently removed. Names of individuals, meanwhile, were generally rendered using the British-American BGN/PCGN system, though not consistently and sometimes with further modifications.
The document is also inconsistent in deciding when to translate Russian names, when to transliterate them, and when to do both at once. One example is the address of Neva-Ferrit LLC. The original address — “198320, St. Petersburg, Krasnoe Selo, Svobody St., 50” — was rendered as “98320, city Sankt-Peterburg, city Krasnoe village, ul. Svobody, bld.50.”
The result mixes translation and transliteration in a way that makes little sense. The place name “Krasnoe Selo,” which should normally remain a proper name, was partially translated into English as “Krasnoe village,” while the street name “Svobody” was left transliterated rather than rendered as “Freedom Street” or “Street of Freedom.”
One possible explanation is that large language models were used to generate parts of the document. That could also account for the apparent use of a Python transliteration library — when asked to automate a task of this kind, an AI system may generate a script, and such a script would likely rely on an existing software library.
If a Python library was in fact used to transliterate company names, that would explain some of the unusual spellings. It would not, however, explain instances in which Latin and Cyrillic characters appear within the same word, such as in the name of the Kalinovsky Chemical Plant: «Акcionерное общество калиновский химический завод».
Similar errors have appeared in earlier sanctions documents, but those usually involved letters that look identical in the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets — such as A, B, T and E. In those cases, the mistake was invisible to the eye but detectable by software and most likely resulted from a person typing without switching the keyboard layout.
The latest document is different. The mixing of alphabets within a single word is more consistent with errors that occur in text generated by neural networks, especially when a task requires several languages to be handled at once.
Another example is the English-language address given for CJSC Tehkrim: “Address: 426063, Udmurtskaya Republic of …” A human translator or conventional machine-translation system would be unlikely to produce that wording, as the standard English form is “Udmurt Republic.”
While a human translator would be unlikely to translate the phrase with such an awkward rendering, a large language model, which does not translate strictly word for word but predicts the most likely sequence of words, certainly could. Because many Russian regions are rendered in English using the construction “Republic of …,” a model could plausibly predict that “of” should follow the name of a Russian republic even where that order is incorrect.
The careless transliteration appears to have affected website addresses as well. For example, the website listed for LLC NPO AMB — rendered by EU sanctions officials as “Obschestvo s ogranichennoj otvetstvennostju Nauchno-proizvodstvennoe obedinenie amb” — became https://www.licenzia-gos.rf. The problem is obvious: the top-level domain “.rf” does not exist. Nor does the listed website exist in that form, or even in the corresponding Cyrillic version, лицензия-гос.рф.
Factories of days gone by
A telling example of an anachronism on the list involves the imposition of sanctions on the Federal State Unitary Enterprise “Novosibirsk Experimental Plant of Measuring Instruments” (TIN / INN 5425100089) and its director, Aleksey Timofeevich Morozov (designation no. 2549, TIN / INN 542505153869). However, this legal entity no longer exists, as it was reorganised in 2021 through a merger with the Federal State Unitary Enterprise “National Testing Association ‘State Ammunition Testing Ranges of Russia’” (TIN / INN 5023002050). That organisation was also subject to sanctions, but its CEO, Stanislav Gennadievich Yuzov, was not included on the EU sanctions list.
It is possible to see how such an error arose. Many companies appear to have been added to the list on the following basis:
“The entities concerned appear in a list recently established by the Government of the Russian Federation that identifies them as belonging to the Russian military-industrial complex, and they are therefore entitled to receive subsidies from the Government of the Russian Federation.”
That suggests an AI model or Python script may have been given a source list that, while broadly reflecting the composition of Russia’s military-industrial complex, was not fully up to date. The resulting entries appear not to have been adequately checked by experts.
More importantly, even an up-to-date list would have limited value as a sanctions tool. Companies in Russia’s defense sector generally do not make foreign purchases directly, meaning sanctions against them may have little practical effect on procurement. Instead, separate intermediary firms typically acquire goods on their behalf — a practice The Insider has documented repeatedly, as have other researchers who study Russian military-industrial procurement.
Even a cursory reading of the latest EU package reveals at least 25 discrepancies in the names and legal forms of the organizations on the list, and numerous errors occur when it comes to naming the positions held by individuals coming under restrictions. In some cases, parts of company names are missing, and in most cases, the legal form is incorrectly stated.
For example, Nikolay Nikolaevich Grechushkin (designation no. 2224) was sanctioned as the CEO of Textile Trading Company LLC (TIN / INN 9701054138). However, that position is actually held by Anatoly Mikhailovich Trubin. At the same time, the list correctly lists Trubin’s INN as 592003498702. Grechushkin, for his part, serves as deputy CEO of the company, and his TIN is 253303297804.
Evgeniya Vladimirovna Kovalenko (TIN / INN 525714947515), is listed as the director of JSC “Himreaktiv.” However, the CEO of this company is actually Vladimir Nikolaevich Lyamkin, who holds TIN 525702072428.
OJSC “Radiodetal,” with TIN 1308038496, also appears on the sanctions list. This organization has a different legal entity and a different name — PJSC “Zubovo-Polyansky Radio Component Plant” — which again indicates that the data used is outdated.
The list also includes the “Federal State Institution Federal Scientific Center Research Institute for Systems Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences” (original spelling retained) with TIN 7727086772. This is also an anachronism. This institute was transferred from the jurisdiction of the Russian Academy of Sciences to the Kurchatov Institute Research Center on Feb. 7, 2023, by Decree No. 268-r of the Government of the Russian Federation. Its current name is “Federal State Autonomous Institution ‘Federal Scientific Center Research Institute for Systems Studies of the National Research Center “Kurchatov Institute”’.”
Sanctioning everyone with the same name — and missing the mark
As previously noted by investigative journalist Sergei Ezhov, EU officials failed to specify the patronymic, date of birth, or taxpayer identification number of Promsvyazbank CEO Mikhail Dorofeev when imposing sanctions against him, thereby creating risks for all people named “Mikhail Dorofeev” worldwide. When compiling the new list, the European Commission expanded this practice: in fact, in the case of the 743 individuals on the current sanctions list, none are supplemented with a date of birth or passport number. However, tax identification numbers (INNs) are listed — something that was previously rare on lists of sanctioned individuals.
The absence of birth dates and passport numbers significantly increases the risk of false matches or missed matches during automated sanctions screening. When processing a Schengen or other visa application, consular officials typically verify an applicant’s passport information and date of birth, but not a Russian taxpayer identification number. After all, if a person is not publicly linked to a Russian company as a founder or director, authorities may have no reliable way to match a TIN to that individual using open-source records, as such information is not generally public. (The same problem can arise in bank compliance checks, which typically rely on a person’s full name and transliterations, date of birth, passport details, address, job title and employer — but not a Russian TIN.)
The Insider has already seen the consequences of this approach: one of our employees was temporarily unable to receive their salary simply due to the fact that they share a surname with a person added to the latest sanctions list, prompting the bank to freeze the payment.
Previously, journalists had repeatedly pointed out factual errors made by European officials when compiling sanctions lists. For example, the EU imposed sanctions on comedian Mikhail Galustyan by using his stage name (the artist’s official name is Nshan). An error was also made regarding his date of birth: Galustyan was born in 1979, not in 1970, as stated in the EU Council’s implementing regulation. These errors have not been corrected a year and a half after the document’s publication.
These oversights may seem minor, but they can have serious legal consequences for EU authorities. In May 2025, for example, an EU court lifted sanctions against Andrei Kharkovsky, described as a “representative of the Cossack Union,” after Brussels failed to establish his connection to the organization. The sanctions listing did not include his date of birth or other identifying information sufficient to distinguish him unambiguously.
Documents such as the October package are examples of “Potemkin sanctions.” They create the appearance of intense activity, and the sheer scale of the lists might impress an outside observer. In reality, however, the latest package completely ignores the Chinese manufacturers and banks that continue to supply Putin’s war machine.
The elephant in the room: Brussels ignores China
Investigations by The Insider and other publications have repeatedly pointed to China’s leading role in the supply of critical goods to Russia. It is Chinese manufacturers and their affiliated Chinese banks — not intermediary exporters or importers — that represent the potential bottlenecks in Russian factories’ supply chains.
The Insider has identified several bottlenecks in a series of investigations related to long-range unmanned systems, such as the Geran attack drone and the Gerbera decoy drone, as well as the mass production of first-person-view (FPV) drones. Both are absolutely critical to the Russian war machine. About 70% of combat losses result from the use of FPV drones, while civilians and civilian infrastructure suffer the most from Geran drones.
Not a single Chinese company — neither manufacturers nor resellers — was included among the hundreds of companies listed in the latest round of EU sanctions. Given the documented role that Chinese products play in the Russian military-industrial complex, the absence of Chinese entities suggests that Brussels lacks the political will to address the driving force sustaining the Russian war machine: imports from Chinese suppliers.

Patriot missiles
Ukraine could have had enough Patriot air defense missiles to sustain its systems for several years if more interceptors had not been expended in the Middle East, Yuriy Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said on the RBC-Ukraine podcast.
Ihnat revealed that Ukrainian forces have developed tactics for using the US-made systems more efficiently during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Unlike crews that keep Patriots at fixed positions, Ukrainian operators can set up ambushes, engage targets, and quickly relocate to avoid detection.
Ukrainian crews have also learned to conserve expensive interceptors, typically using one missile per target. By contrast, air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at a single target, including relatively cheap Shahed drones.
A senior Ukrainian Air Force officer previously told The Times that Gulf forces were using excessive numbers of interceptors and that Ukraine’s battlefield experience had not been fully incorporated despite Kyiv sharing operational data with allies.
Ukraine’s missile shortages remain acute. Earlier, Zelensky said Ukraine received just 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over 90 days, despite needing around 350 per month to counter Russian ballistic attacks.
He has requested 300 interceptors from European partners for the winter, but efforts to secure missiles from existing European stockpiles have faced resistance, including from Greece.

Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:49:40 UTC
23:49:40 KST

Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown
Louis Gore-Langton
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Indians living in the Netherlands are protesting for political solidarity and media attention to the ongoing “Cockroach” protests sweeping India, which are being met with a brutal crackdown by state forces.
The protests erupted in the summer over suspected corruption in the education system and have since turned to focus on changes in the voting system. Young Indians say they are being denied their democratic rights – something protesters say particularly affects minority groups and women.
Indians are a significant part of the Netherlands’ international community, with the statistics office CBS counting about 54,500 Indian nationals in the country – roughly 3.2% of all foreign nationals.
The Progressive Indians Europe group, based in Amsterdam, gathered in The Hague recently to call for recognition of the injustices they say Narendra Modi’s government is inflicting on its people.
A spokesperson for the group told Dutch News that it was asking the Dutch government to publicly stand up for the democratic principles and human rights commitments it recognises in its own foreign policy.
“These developments directly affect people in the Netherlands,” they said. “Our families, friends and communities remain connected to India. What happens there has real consequences for the people we care about, while the precedent set by the erosion of electoral safeguards matters to democracies everywhere.”
The suppression of the Cockroach movement, the group says, which has seen thousands arrested, journalists detained, and reports of widespread police brutality, means people in the Netherlands should “examine the reporting, listen to affected communities and recognise the importance of independent investigations, transparency and accountability.”
The group stressed that it was not asking people to accept every allegation without scrutiny.
“We hope it encourages the Dutch public, media and policymakers to engage seriously with these developments and recognise that defending democracy is a shared international responsibility.”
A spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Dutch News: “The Netherlands follows the developments in India. As human rights and democracy are an important part of the Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands, the Netherlands and India discuss these topics regularly in diplomatic contacts and will continue to do so.”
Struck off
Some of the members said the situation abroad is significantly impacting their lives. Surabhi, from Amsterdam, said she takes her right to vote very seriously, both in India and in Dutch municipal elections.
“I am an Indian national and have always travelled back to India to vote,” she said. “Most recently, I voted in the national elections in 2024 and the municipality elections in Mumbai in January 2026.”
Her name, along with millions of others, has been removed during a revision of the electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India, which says it is improving the voting system by removing dead, duplicate and ineligible voters.
Another protester, Anubhav, described how he can only see the voting list on the Election Commission of India website by using a VPN. When he saw his name had been removed, he submitted a complaint, which was closed the very next day.
He says he is a “popular anti-BJP [the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party] guy on social media among my acquaintances. Is this just a coincidence? I don’t know.”
Cockroach movement
The Cockroach Janta Party, whose name plays on that of Modi’s BJP, started in May as an online satire account. It was a response to India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, describing some activists and unemployed young people as “cockroaches” and “parasites of society”. Kant later said his remarks had been misquoted and misrepresented.
In July, Modi’s education minister was forced to resign in the wake of street protests against leaked exam papers. Amnesty International found that police used pellet-firing shotguns, electric shock batons, tear gas and batons against demonstrators. Delhi police said more than 400 people, including officers, were injured.
The latest wave of protests that began on October 2 was a reaction to a nationwide revision of the voter rolls. According to reports, about 14% of the original names on the rolls – more than 133 million – have been removed since the process began last year. Protesters say eligible voters have been wrongly struck off in favour of the BJP.
The Indian electoral commission says voters removed in error can register again, and has said all its actions were lawful.
More than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition MPs, were detained in Delhi over the weekend of October 10 and 11. On October 13, Human Rights Watch said police had beaten protesters, dragged them through the streets, arbitrarily detained them and suspended mobile internet services.
Police have said protesters were uncooperative and that force was sometimes needed. The UN human rights office has called on the authorities to fully respect the right to peaceful assembly.
Dutch ties with India
Indians make up one of the largest groups of highly skilled migrants from outside the EU, according to statistics bureau CBS. Many work in IT, and more than 300 Indian companies now have a presence in the Netherlands.
The Netherlands is India’s third largest export destination worldwide, the largest in Europe, and the fourth largest investor in India. According to the Indian embassy, merchandise trade stood at $27.8 billion in 2024-2025.
In May this year, Modi visited the Netherlands and, at a roundtable with Dutch business leaders, spoke of a “new golden era in India–Europe relations”, following the conclusion of free trade talks with the bloc. The agreement “between the world’s two largest democratic and responsible powers will become a strong foundation for shared prosperity”, he said.
Before Modi arrived, prime minister Rob Jetten told reporters there were concerns in the Netherlands and other EU countries about developments in India. “It is not only about press freedom, but also about the rights of minorities, who are under severe pressure,” he said, according to de Volkskrant, adding that the concerns were “regularly raised” with India.
India’s foreign ministry later dismissed the remarks as showing a “lack of understanding”.

NEW DELHI, October 26. /TASS/. The Indian Ministry of Defense plans to modernize up to 80 Soviet-and Russian-designed T-72 and T-90 tanks in service with the Indian Army annually, starting in April 2028, according to The Times of India.
The government has allocated 4.6 billion rupees ($48.3 million) for the program to extensively modernize the armored vehicles. The work will be carried out at a defense enterprise in Jabalpur (Madhya Pradesh) using Russian technical documentation and expertise.
In March 2025, India signed a $248 million contract with Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport for the procurement of 1,000 HP engines for the T-72 tanks slated for modernization. The deal also provided for the transfer of technology to India’s manufacturer Armored Vehicles Nigam Limited (AVNL) for the integration and subsequent licensed production of the engines as part of the promotion of the Made in India initiative in the defense sector.
Soviet-and Russian-designed T-72 and T-90 tanks, in various modifications, form the backbone of India’s armored forces. In total, the Indian army operates up to 4,000 such tanks, most of which were assembled in India under license.

Kenya releases first Ebola contacts from quarantine, milestone in containment efforts
NAIROBI, Oct 26 - Kenya on Monday released from quarantine the first group of people who came into contact with its index Ebola patient, a milestone in its efforts to contain cases to a single infection cluster.
The 20 people released completed 21 days of monitoring without developing Ebola symptoms and are in good health, the director-general in Kenya's health ministry, Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.
Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases so far, two of whom have died. The remaining seven patients are stable and receiving treatment, Amoth said, adding that 98 others still in quarantine would be released in four waves beginning on November 3.
"This is a milestone worth celebrating," Amoth said. "It is also a reminder that the work is not yet done."
Kenya's first case died in a hospital in Nairobi on October 5, after which eight others fell ill while in quarantine. It announced on Friday that a second person had died.
Ebola's spread from Congo, where the outbreak was declared in mid-May, to Kenya has raised concerns about lapses in border screening.
Nigeria has said its first Ebola case in more than a decade, which it reported last week, appears to be closely related to Kenya's index case, citing genomic analysis. The two cases both flew out of Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day in early October.
Amoth said those leaving quarantine posed no risk to their families or communities where they live and urged Kenyans to welcome them home. "We cannot afford to drop our vigilance," he said. REUTERS

Head of Mexico's electoral authority resigns amid corruption allegations
MEXICO CITY, Oct 26 - The head of Mexico's National Electoral Institute will resign amid allegations of corruption, a decision President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Monday that she supports.
INE chief Guadalupe Taddei's resignation is the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum's two-year-old presidency.

Lawmakers later supported a narrower package of electoral changes.
"There couldn't be this shadow of a conflict of interest. It's good that she made the decision to step aside," Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference, while rejecting the notion that the resignation pointed to a political crisis.
Mexico's Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars.
"Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated," Taddei said in a Sunday statement announcing her planned resignation.
Taddei said her resignation aimed to protect the INE and allow it to fulfill its constitutional mission.
The 2027 elections are expected to be hotly contested, and the INE's credibility is essential to avoid conflict, said Antonio Ocaranza, a consultant who was a spokesman for former President Ernesto Zedillo. He called Taddei's exit "a necessary and timely correction."
Ocaranza said the case also poses a broader test for Sheinbaum, as there are already many cases of political families close to her political party, Morena, accused by local news outlets, and "the government has shown little desire to investigate and punish them."
Authorities are also investigating potential fraud linked to several contracts signed by other INE officials in which there may have been conflicts of interest.
Opposition party PRI's President Alejandro Moreno said Taddei's resignation should not be used to "impose another person close to Morena."
"Mexico cannot go into the 2027 elections with an electoral authority whose impartiality is in serious question," he added. REUTERS

Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:45:22 UTC
23:45:22 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous waters for commercial shipping, the Financial Times reported. At least 40 sailors have died there since the start of 2026, compared with 24 who died in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war the United States and Israel are waging against Iran has complicated shipping.
More than 570 ships have come under attack in the Black Sea since the start of the year, according to the maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization. Some ships were hit by accident, while others were deliberately targeted. Both Russia and Ukraine try to disrupt each other’s maritime shipping to reduce export revenues.
War-risk insurance for the Black Sea now costs as much as 15% of a ship’s hull value, almost twice the rate for ships in the Persian Gulf. Nearly the entire Black Sea is now classified in the highest war-risk category, except for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey.
Shipping oil from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz is now cheaper and safer by comparison. As a result, shipping companies increasingly refuse to operate in the Black Sea or use older vessels that are cheaper to insure.
Crews are recruited from Syria, Egypt, and Azerbaijan. The FT found that Syrian sailors earn about $800 a month working in the Black Sea. They are promised double pay for each day spent in the combat zone, and their families are to receive $25,000 to $50,000 in compensation if a sailor is killed.
Ukrainian forces struck more than 300 Russian vessels over an 11-week period, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said in September. The targets included sanctioned tankers as well as cargo ships carrying grain.
Russia has responded by stepping up strikes on ships entering Ukrainian ports. Russian attacks accounted for about 90% of strikes on commercial vessels over the past 45 days, according to Ambrey’s estimates.
The strikes are affecting global fuel and food supplies. Russian wheat exports fell 52% in September compared with a year earlier, while Ukraine is exporting only half its projected volume of agricultural products. Russian diesel exports fell by 467,000 barrels a day in September compared with a year earlier, according to Kpler.
The global effects of the war in the Black Sea are difficult to separate from those of the conflict in the Persian Gulf, Bloomberg reported. High global wheat stocks have kept disruptions in grain supplies from significantly affecting prices, while diesel fuel grew more expensive even before Russian–Ukrainian attacks escalated, because of the war the United States is waging against Iran.
The war in photographs
A family from Oleshky starts a new life in the Kyiv region
Vitaliy and Iryna fled the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in September with their 13-year-old son, Vlad, and their cat, Marsik. By then, residents had been left in complete isolation, without food, water, electricity, or medical care.
A drone damaged Vitaliy and Iryna’s home, prompting them to leave Oleshky and walk more than 20 kilometers (12 miles) along a mined road. The family traveled through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory and is now rebuilding its life in the Kyiv region.
Russia and Ukraine agreed last week to a ceasefire in Oleshky for the evacuation of residents. It is set to take effect at 4 a.m. on October 27.

14:43:27 UTC
23:43:27 KST

Journalists from 17 European public service broadcasters, coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) Eurovision News Spotlight network, published an interactive map on 23 October 2026. It documents hybrid incidents linked to Russia across 17 European countries between 1 April and 15 October. Journalists compiled a database of hundreds of reported incidents, categorizing each by type and the source and strength of its alleged links to Russia, then verifying them through open-source research.
The map comes as officials warn the campaign is growing. On 28 September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in Brussels that Russia was planning more acts of sabotage to divide societies and intimidate them into abandoning their support for Ukraine. The points on the map represent an incomplete list of publicly known cases attributed to Russia or suspected of being linked to it, the report states.
The map covers airspace violations, sabotage attempts, “disposable” agents with no formal intelligence training, migration used as a weapon, and Russian military activity near or across European borders. It excludes cyberattacks, influence operations, and espionage by trained intelligence officers.
The EBU calls the result a very conservative estimate, not an official tally. Russia has consistently denied responsibility for the incidents. Many single points represent several incidents of the same type in one area or in quick succession. In Moldova, for example, Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi said on 30 September that the government had recorded 84 drone incursions.
Four German incidents are on the map, out of many more
The map shows four incidents in Germany, according to BR.
- On 2 August, German authorities arrested a 33-year-old Ukrainian man in Thuringia on suspicion of photographing a Bavarian weapons manufacturer for a foreign intelligence service as part of an alleged sabotage plot.
- On 4 August, a drone carrying explosives and a detonator struck the wing of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport but failed to explode.
- On 3 September, attackers threw firebombs from a car onto a construction site next to defense firms in Munich, and German security authorities suspect Russian intelligence.
- On 14 September, investigators learned of a crashed drone found near the Bundeswehr’s Wunstorf air base.
Internal papers from the new Joint Hybrid Defense Center, seen by Correctiv, record 163 suspected sabotage cases in 2026 up to 19 August. The targets included rail lines, military facilities, substations, and radio masts. The same papers record 1,034 drone overflights of critical infrastructure, military sites, and defense companies, and 25 espionage investigations. The papers cover possible attacks by Russia, China, and Iran, and media did not report a breakdown of the sabotage cases by country.
European leaders sound the alarm over Russian hybrid attacks
On 15 April, Swedish civil defense minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin said pro-Russian groups had moved from denial-of-service attacks to attempts at destructive cyberattacks, including one on a Swedish power plant in 2025. On 1 September, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul named Russia as the perpetrator of the Leipzig attack and accused Moscow of “blatant hostility” toward Germany.
On 18 September, French President Emmanuel Macron said Russia’s hybrid attacks would not go unanswered and ordered a plan to protect France’s critical infrastructure. On 1 October, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany was preparing for new hybrid attacks, “including serious ones.” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on 14 October called the attacks a sign of Russian weakness at a press conference in Tallinn and said NATO would react where needed without being “rattled.”

Uzbekistan Wants Out of the Iran-US Social Media War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

On October 23, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Iranian ambassador in Tashkent in order to hand over a note of protest related to a recent slate of social media postings made by several Iranian diplomatic missions. The posts sniped at U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, using his recent visit to Samarkand as a touchstone.
“It’s great that you’re learning history! The place where you are standing is part of the Persian civilization and architecture. The same civilization you were babbling nonsense about last week at the Acropolis!” read a since-removed post on X from the Iranian embassy in Armenia.
In early October, Rubio delivered remarks during a visit to Greece that set off a history-based social media war that has now spilled over to Uzbekistan. With the ancient Acropolis as his backdrop, he mused on the meaning of Western civilization. Early in the speech he recounted the destruction of the Acropolis in 480 BCE by a Persian army.
“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon,” Rubio said before jumping ahead a 25 centuries to the modern era and the American obsession with antiquity.
Later in the speech, Rubio got the point: a rhetorical attack to match the physical war ongoing between the U.S. and Iran.
“It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country… This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.”
When Rubio landed in Uzbekistan two weeks later, Iran’s keyboard warriors were ready.
“At the Acropolis, you invoked civilizations. Samarkand invites you to a deeper conversation with history, in a city whose heritage is deeply interwoven with Iranian civilization,” the Iranian Permanent Mission to the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) stated in its post, which remains available as of publication.
On October 24, the Uzbek Foreign Ministry reported that it had summoned the Iranian ambassador, Mohammad Ali Eskandari, to complain about the posts, which it said in its own social media post, “interpret the historical and cultural heritage of the city of Samarkand for unilateral political purposes.”
“During the meeting,” the ministry said, “it was noted that the heritage of Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva, and other historical cities of Uzbekistan is an integral part of the rich and multifaceted historical and cultural development formed over many centuries.” The ministry demanded that the offending posts be taken down, and those posted the Iranian embassies in Armenia, China, and Zimbabwe have been.
“Uzbekistan values relations with Iran based on mutual respect and trust,” the Foreign Ministry stated. “At the same time, it maintains its principled position against one-sided interpretation of the historical and cultural heritage of our country.”
Of note: While a post regarding Tashkent’s summoning of the Iranian ambassador remains available on Instagram as of publication, there’s no trace of an earlier post on the Foreign Ministry’s website regarding the meeting – although a relic remains on Facebook.
Without recounting the entire history of Samarkand, it’s fair to say that the city’s history and culture is multilayered, with many empires having risen and fallen across (and from within) its territory. It has existed, in some form, since the 8th century BCE. In 329 BCE, Marakanda – as it was then known – was captured by Alexander the Great. It had been one of the most important cities for the Sogdian civilization; by the time of Alexander, Sogdiana was part of the greater Achaemenid Persian Empire.
The importance of Persian civilization to Central Asia is indisputable. What Tashkent took umbrage over, however, is the operationalization of the past into a weapon (albeit an online one) in a very modern, and very difficult, conflict.
To put it bluntly: Uzbekistan does not want to be invoked in the Iran-U.S. conflict, certainly not while it has tried to deepen relations with Washington while also maintaining ties with Iran.

A cargo ship became uncontrollable during a storm off the Netherlands; there are injuries

A cargo ship became uncontrollable during a storm off the Netherlands; there are injuries
Kyiv • UNN
The UHL Freedom, with 25 crew members on board, became uncontrollable due to the storm, the loss of its anchor, and engine problems. Three people were injured.
In the North Sea off the coast of the Netherlands, the cargo ship UHL Freedom lost its anchor during a storm and effectively became uncontrollable. There were 25 crew members on board, three of whom were injured. Two of the injured were evacuated by helicopter. Bild reports, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred on Sunday approximately 30 kilometers west of the German island of Borkum, near the Dutch island of Schiermonnikoog. Due to a storm reaching up to nine on the Beaufort scale, the vessel began drifting under the influence of the wind and current. Engine problems created an additional hazard.
Dutch rescuers and the German rescue cruiser Hamburg came to the crew’s aid. A helicopter brought medical specialists on board, who provided assistance to the injured. Emergency tugboats were also dispatched to the site of the accident.
The 150-meter-long and 26-meter-wide cargo ship sails under the flag of Portugal and is owned by the Hamburg-based company United Heavy Lift. It was carrying, among other things, wind turbine blades and was heading to the port of Emden in northern Germany.

Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:42:27 UTC
23:42:27 KST

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.
Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.
Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.
Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.
A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.
Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.
Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.
The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.
Its German factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.
Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.
The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.
