Serbia’s student victory raises hopes of an EU reset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:42:21 UTC
23:42:21 KST

The Student List’s election win ends Vučić’s 14-year rule and raises hopes of an EU reset, but its stance on Russia sanctions and Kosovo leaves Brussels cautious.
The Student List’s landslide victory in Sunday’s parliamentary elections has raised hopes that Serbia will mend ties with Brussels and relaunch its EU accession bid, but whether Belgrade will actually change its foreign policy remains unclear.
The movement born from months of student protest has secured an absolute majority in parliament, ending the 14-year rule of Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and fuelling expectations that the new government might seek closer ties with the EU.
“We are at the very beginning of the new path. But at least it’s a new path. We have no guarantees of anything. There’s just one guarantee that now we have the possibility, we have hope. And this is a huge achievement,” MEP Matjaž Nemec (Slovenia/S&D) told Euronews.
Protest movement
The Student List is the electoral arm of a student-led movement that grew out of a deadly disaster at a recently renovated railway station in November 2024, which raised questions about government accountability and corruption.
After nearly two years, the protests became a nationwide challenge to Serbia’s political establishment, demanding institutional reform and democratic accountability and marking a historic rupture with the SNS’s 14 years in power.
The movement has elected a mix of figures from outside the traditional political class, including students, professors, doctors, artists and businesspeople.
For Brussels, the new political class’s roots in a pro-democratic, anti-corruption movement are an encouraging sign that Belgrade could align with EU values and push through much-needed rule of law reforms.
At the same time, the student movement is also very heterogeneous, at times harbouring opposing views, meaning that, beyond opposing Vučić, it is still unclear exactly what it stands for.
"Ousting Vučić from power was the pre-requisite for Serbia's European future," Jelena Vasiljević, a senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, told Euronews. "Now I hope we will be able to have an open, democratic discussion on the EU accession path."
Democratic change
The movement’s door-to-door campaign centred on corruption and accountability, drawing parallels between Vučić’s defeat and the ousting of Viktor Orbán in Hungary after 16 years. Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar ran on a similar platform.
Magyar was the first foreign leader to call the Student List to congratulate it on its result. “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle,” he wrote on X.
The fair, competitive vote and the peaceful transfer of power, after Vučić conceded defeat, are seen as proof that Serbia’s democratic process is working.
Still, whether the change of government will translate into a broader realignment with Brussels, and into progress on EU accession, remains to be seen.
“It is not exactly clear what their take on foreign policy is. Many EU countries will be watching very closely,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, pointing to Serbia’s weak alignment with the bloc on foreign policy. “It remains to be seen if that will change.”
EU accession
Senior EU officials have welcomed the result. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos went as far as saying that “the door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.”
In July, the European Commission pushed to open Cluster 3 of Serbia’s accession talks, which have been stalled for years, but eight member states blocked the move citing democratic backsliding concerns and lack of alignment on foreign policy.
The programme the Student List published last month, however, focuses solely on domestic governance: public procurement, education, media freedom, judicial independence and health care.
Bojan Vranić, a political science professor at the University of Belgrade, cautioned EU officials against excessive enthusiasm, saying the change of government would hardly lead to a breakthrough in European integration.
“So far, the Student List has been very conservative when it comes to the European Union. They aim to, firstly, improve the system within. And once they, as they said, become a credible partner in a negotiation, then the European Union will be their partner,” Vranić said.
Proceed with caution
Optimism in Brussels is tempered by history. In 2003, Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić was murdered by former members of the country’s security apparatus for pursuing a pro-Western agenda of closer ties with Europe, economic reforms and a crackdown on organised crime.
The EU executive is due to publish its enlargement package next week, an annual report on the state of play in candidate countries that will offer a first sign of whether the bloc’s approach to Serbia is shifting, though the new Serbian government is unlikely to be in place before the reporting period ends.
Perhaps more telling will be the conclusions the Council of the European Union adopts on the package, which will show where member states stand and whether they want to encourage Belgrade.
A key test may be how the Student List-led government treats Montenegro, the frontrunner to join the EU. Vučić and the SNS tried to undermine its accession by sowing divisions based on identity politics.
“I firmly believe that a new chapter lies ahead for Montenegro and Serbia, based on respect and open dialogue, without unnecessary escalation of tensions,” Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić wrote on X.
Foreign policy
Russia sanctions are among the main sticking points between Brussels and Belgrade, which has refused to align with the measures the EU imposed after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“The Republic of Serbia will retain its principled stance on not introducing restrictive measures toward the Russian Federation,” the student movement wrote on X in September, citing Serbia’s historical experience with sanctions.
Beyond its heavy dependence on Russian gas, Belgrade relies on Moscow’s diplomatic backing to prevent international recognition of Kosovo’s independence, which the student movement openly rejected in a memorandum published in May.
The Student List itself is split between staunchly pro-European figures and others who back a traditional Serbian nationalist agenda. Which camp prevails will shape the country’s foreign policy.
“There are strong nationalist voices in Studentska lista who would want to keep Russia onside because of Kosovo. Energy ties will persist as well. China ties might be downgraded a bit, but foreign direct investments and economic links are already there,” said Dimitar Bechev, a senior fellow at the think tank Carnegie Europe.
Vincenzo Genovese contributed to the reporting.

Russia ready for further cooperation with Slovakia on nuclear energy — minister

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia is ready for further cooperation with Slovakia in the area of nuclear energy, including both large-and small-scale power generation, Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov said at the 22nd meeting of the Russian-Slovak inter-governmental commission for economic, science and technical cooperation.
"We attach particular importance to nuclear energy. Russian enterprises have been supplying nuclear fuel to Slovakia’s nuclear power plants for many years, conscientiously fulfilling their obligations. We are ready to discuss future projects, including those involving both large-and small-scale nuclear power generation," said Falkov who serves as Russia’s co-chair of the commission.
In addition to the energy sector, the minister pointed to the importance of further cooperation in agriculture, including genetics and plant breeding, as well as in environmental matters, specifically regarding air quality and waste management. In the humanitarian sphere, he expressed readiness for cooperation regarding the education of Slovak students at Russian universities, the study of the Russian and Slovak languages, and in the fields of sports and tourism. Moscow is prepared for a substantive dialogue that takes mutual interests into account, Falkov emphasized. "We are prepared to work toward gradually bringing other areas back to the agenda of the intergovernmental commission, including industry, finance, transport, healthcare, standardization, and metrology," he said.
The commission reconvened after a five-year hiatus, with contacts between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico playing a key role in the resumption of its activities, Falkov stressed. "Despite the challenging international situation, Russia and Slovakia managed to maintain cooperation in a number of key areas," he said. Among these areas he mentioned energy, both nuclear and oil and gas sectors, as the primary focus.
Following the meeting, a ceremony was held to sign the final protocol. The document was signed by Falkov and Slovakia’s Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanar.

Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:38:50 UTC
23:38:50 KST

Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions
Countering Houthi advances in Yemen will be a major focus for Saudi Arabia and its allies, though the regional picture remains complex and intertwined.
Tehran, Iran – Ministers and senior security officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – the three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – are in Tehran to discuss regional security issues amid threats of new US strikes on Iran.
Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and will discuss tensions with security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The meetings are among the highest-profile dialogues held in Tehran in recent months. While there is still little information on what might be discussed, the meetings come amid a flurry of diplomatic activity to deal with a new escalation between the United States and Iran.
“The Mecca pact’s 11th-hour visit to Tehran is an attempt to tip the balance in favour of those willing to compromise before the guns start blazing again,” said Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group.
“But unless they arrive with a credible formula to bridge the US-Iran divide, they may find themselves with little more than goodwill in a race against the clock.”
The talks are expected to address the waves of missile and drone attacks carried out by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who are allied with Tehran, on Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“I believe that parties to the Mecca agreement lack options of military engagement with the Houthis, but Riyadh is certainly asserting greater pressure for more, and its expectation of its partners has grown in parallel with the offensive from Yemen,” Ayesha Siddiqa, a senior research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
But despite the collective security arrangement in the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia’s allies Turkiye and Pakistan cannot “afford to commit troops on the ground” in Yemen, said Siddiqa.
The latest diplomatic push is likely linked to visits by Pakistani army chief Asim Munir to Saudi Arabia and Iran last week, Siddiqa said, and coincides with Islamabad’s restrictions on overland border trade with Tehran amid the US blockade on Iran.
Iranian authorities have said they favoured “security originating from within the region” as they prepared for the meetings.
Umer Karim, who researches Saudi foreign policy and its implications for regional security, said the Tehran meetings are unlikely to reduce the risk of a renewed war between Iran and the US, which would likely lead to more regional turmoil.
“Therefore, these talks perhaps are more concerned about the security of Saudi Arabia and involve an attempt by Turkiye and Pakistan to compel Iran to reach a compromise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sanam Vakil, the director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said she was “cautiously optimistic” about the impact of the immediate meeting, but “less positive” about a lasting breakthrough.
“Iran has strong incentives to avoid another major confrontation, and there may be room for limited understandings, particularly concerning Yemen,” she said. “However, the Houthis have their own calculations, and Iran’s influence over them is not absolute. Preventing renewed US-Israeli attacks will be even more difficult because the fundamental disagreements between Tehran and Washington remain unresolved.”
US President Donald Trump is said to be considering new attacks to break the diplomatic deadlock with Iran, which has refused to agree to any peace agreement with Washington unless several of its demands are met.
The US and regional powers want international shipping and transit through the Strait of Hormuz to resume without impediments or attacks. Washington also wants to rein in Tehran’s nuclear programme and bring in international inspectors to assess Iran’s highly enriched uranium. Israel says it wants to overthrow the Islamic Republic.
Tehran wants to lift the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, which has halted crude oil exports and disrupted most trade, and return to a memorandum of understanding agreed between the two countries in June.
The US has refused this, with President Trump saying he is left with a choice to “finish the job” by launching major strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure. This could prompt Iran to lash out at its neighbours, as it did earlier in the war with strikes on US bases in Arab states and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State issued an October 21 order for nonemergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia for their safety’s sake, given the Houthi threat.
As talks involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye continue in Iran, analysts say these Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signatories will likely try to minimise the impact on Saudi Arabia if war does break out again.
“However, since little has changed from an Iranian strategic calculus and the actors involved don’t have the kind of leverage needed to affect Iran’s strategic thinking, these negotiations are going to yield little,” Karim said.

Russian Economy Ministry expects services export growth to $59 bln by 2030

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Exports of services from Russia may reach $59 bln by 2030 with the average annual growth rates of about 5%, department director at the Russian Ministry of Economic Development Dmitry Nekrasov said.

Imports of services are growing quicker than exports and stood at about $95 bln, Nekrasov noted.
Travels and transportation services will provide for the bulk of incremental growth of exports by 2030 according to the forecast, Nekrasov said. They are expected to add about $4.3 bln in total.

UN-backed inquiry accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank

UN-backed inquiry accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank
An international commission of inquiry mandated by the United Nations accused Israel on Monday of committing crimes against humanity against Palestinians in the West Bank, including extermination, torture and persecution. It also upheld its allegations of genocide in Gaza.
Israel immediately rejected the report’s findings through its ambassador in Geneva, who denounced an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and to “deny its fundamental right to exist”.
Established in 2021, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded last year that Israel was committing “genocide” in Gaza – allegations which the Israeli authorities dismiss as “false” and “anti-Semitic”, as they do the new allegations of crimes against humanity in the West Bank.
More
Beneath Gaza’s rubble lie the missing – and possible evidence
In its new report, published just before the Israeli general election scheduled for Tuesday, the commission “concludes that the Israeli authorities and forces have committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence, as well as persecution, based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, at the heart of which lie nationality, race and ethnicity”.
Deteriorating situation in West Bank
On September 4, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights had already accused Israel of forcibly displacing more than 33,000 Palestinians from three camps in the West Bank in early 2025, raising the possibility of a crime against humanity and ethnic cleansing.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967. More than three million Palestinians live there, alongside 500,000 Israelis in settlements deemed illegal under international law, amidst a climate of heightened violence on both sides, which has become even more tense in the run-up to the Israeli general election.
Since the unprecedented fatal attacks carried out by the Palestinian group Hamas on Israeli soil on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war in Gaza, the expansion of settlement activity in the West Bank has been evident in the rapid increase in the establishment of “outposts”.
More
Why Switzerland joined Trump-friendly FIFA to fund mini pitches in Palestine
The UN commission highlights a sharp deterioration in the situation in the West Bank since October 7, 2023: while six Palestinians were killed by air strikes between 2008 and October 6, 2023, 254 were killed between October 7, 2023 and September 30, 2026.
‘Demonisation’
In Geneva, the Israeli mission to the UN condemned the commission’s report, stating that it constitutes “yet another manifestation of its disinformation campaign aimed at demonising the State of Israel and portraying its very existence as criminal”.
‘The attempt to destroy the Jewish state did not end in 1948. It continues today through the efforts of actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry, which seeks to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and to defend itself,’ said Israeli Ambassador Daniel Meron.
The Israeli mission is calling on the international community to demand the “immediate dissolution” of the commission of inquiry, whose former chair is the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, the South African lawyer Navi Pillay.
‘Collective punishment’
In its new report, the commission concludes that the Israeli authorities sought to “collectively punish” the civilian population of the West Bank in response to the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023.
According to the commission, Israel has since that date been conducting “a widespread and systematic attack against civilians, through military operations reinforced by persistent violence by settlers”.
More
Why Switzerland doesn’t recognise Palestine as a state
However, “the intentional killing and wounding of Palestinian civilians, as well as the destruction of homes in the West Bank, combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility, form part of a broader strategy aimed at exterminating and displacing Palestinians and imposing unsustainable living conditions upon them”, said the commission’s new chair, Srinivasan Muralidhar of India in a statement.
Deaths despite a truce
“At the same time, Israel’s expansion of its territorial control over Gaza continues to cause deaths and injuries amongst Palestinian civilians who approach or cross the yellow line [which marks the boundary of the area under Israeli military control],” he said.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, according to the Gaza Ministry of Health, which is under Hamas’s authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
In a landmark ruling in January 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) called on Israel to prevent any act of genocide in Gaza, warning of a “real and imminent risk” of “irreparable harm” to Palestinians.
The report also condemns the Palestinian Authority’s violence against members of rival armed groups and its repression of civilian and political opponents. It further criticises the Authority for failing to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into such acts of violence.

Yandex said Monday that all three of its supercomputers remained unharmed following a series of Ukrainian drone attacks against its data centers and have been moved to more secure locations.
“Once brought back online, the computers will rejoin Yandex’s service infrastructure,” the Russian tech company said in a brief statement. “They will also continue to be used for training foundation language models.”
It marks Yandex’s first comments about the three supercomputers — called Chervonenkis, Galushkin and Lyapunov — since Ukraine began launching air attacks against the company’s sites earlier this month.
The supercomputers, launched between 2020 and 2021, rank among the most powerful in the world. But as the global AI race has accelerated in recent years, their position on the list has gradually slipped.
Ukraine’s attacks against Yandex data centers have led to temporary outages of the company’s services across Russia, including ride-hailing apps, food delivery platforms and banking. Corporate clients on Yandex Cloud have also been impacted.
The Kremlin has said that, while it is too early to assess the financial losses, Yandex was taking steps to deal with the aftermath of the attacks.
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry said it helped Yandex migrate core systems to external backup servers.
The ministry has also approved recommendations for protecting data centers against Ukrainian drone attacks, the Kommersant business daily reported Monday, citing the document.
The measures include building the most critical facilities underground, installing structures capable of withstanding blast waves, deploying electronic warfare systems and maintaining backup copies of data. They also call for regular coordination with the military and National Guard.
President Vladimir Putin vowed retribution for the attacks and earlier ordered officials to improve Russia’s ability to protect its digital infrastructure. Ukraine said it was responding to Russian attacks on its own data centers.

Russia has increased diesel production due to sanctions relief, Reuters says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:33:00 EET
23:33:00 KST

Russia has increased diesel production due to sanctions relief, Reuters says
Russian refineries are increasing diesel output in October after the government granted them export quotas under a supply deal between the Kremlin and the United States.
Source: Reuters, citing industry sources
Details: US President Donald Trump said Russia must immediately deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel (about 2.25 million barrels), followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and then one million tonnes.
Since 1 October, the Russian government has introduced exemptions to the existing diesel export ban and allocated quotas allowing Russia to supply fuel under its deal with Trump.
The industry sources told Reuters that Russian diesel production fell to around 160,000 tonnes per day in the first half of October, down from 175,000 tonnes per day in September.
However, since the new export quotas were approved in mid-October, output began to rise, reaching 180,000 tonnes per day.
Domestic consumption typically stands at around 140,000 tonnes per day in October, owing to seasonal factors such as the end of the grain harvest and the summer travel season.
This leaves at least 40,000 tonnes per day, or more than one million tonnes per month, available for export. Neighbouring countries may need around 200,000-300,000 tonnes of this volume, the sources added.
They also expect the Russian government to keep the diesel export ban in place rather than lift it entirely. Instead, Russia is likely to use quotas to regulate exports while monitoring the domestic market and changes in production.
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on sanctions being lifted on Russian diesel fuel.
- Russia subsequently began resuming diesel supplies to Türkiye and Brazil.
- On 22 October, the first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel fuel departed for New York. The vessel is expected to arrive in the US on 7 November.

Dictionary.com names 'maxxing' its 2026 Word of the Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:32:17 UTC
23:32:17 KST

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Dictionary.com named “maxxing” its 2026 Word of the Year, highlighting a growing internet-driven culture focused on optimizing different aspects of life, the Guardian reported on Monday.
“Maxxing,” sometimes written as “-maxxing,” is short for “maximizing” and refers to doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible, according to the online dictionary.
The term gained popularity among Gen Z and Gen Alpha and has evolved into a flexible slang expression that can function as a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb.
Examples include “gymmaxxing” for optimizing workout routines, “healthmaxxing” for maximizing health and wellness practices, “sleepmaxxing” for optimizing sleep and “tokenmaxxing” for deliberately maximizing the use of artificial intelligence tools.
“Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains,” Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, which operates Dictionary.com, told CBS News.
The term has also appeared in political messaging, including the use of “homelandmaxxing,” while “cozymaxxing” has been used to describe efforts to optimize leisure and comfort.
Dictionary.com said its selection was based on an analysis of search data, social media trends and news coverage, as well as the word's cultural significance.
Johnson said the dictionary's lexicographers maintain a list of words to monitor throughout the year, examining their frequency and how they reflect broader cultural developments.
The choice marks a contrast with Dictionary.com's 2025 Word of the Year, “67,” a viral expression whose meaning often remained unclear to users.
 
Other 2026 finalists
Dictionary.com selected finalists from internet culture, politics, technology and wider media trends.
They included “affordability,” reflecting concerns over housing, groceries, childcare and other rising costs; “data center,” amid the expansion of infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence; “unc,” a Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang term for an older person perceived as uncool or out of touch; and “odyssey,” referring to a long and eventful journey that gained renewed cultural attention following Christopher Nolan's 2026 film adaptation of Homer's epic.

Macron promises 'concrete measures' to French students' demands

Macron promises 'concrete measures' in response to French students' demands after weeks of unrest
French President Emmanuel Macron said the government would announce "concrete measures" on Monday to address school students’ demands for more resources and better learning conditions, after weeks of class boycotts, blockades and demonstrations that have grown into nationwide unrest.
“I have asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement,” Macron said during a visit to the southern port city of Marseille, where protesters briefly stormed City Hall on 17 October.
“The prime minister and government ministers will announce several major, concrete measures this afternoon,” Macron said.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and other government officials were scheduled to meet with high school and university students later Monday.
Macron and his centrist government have faced criticism for failing to address students’ grievances since high school blockades began in mid-September. The protests have led to mass arrests and scrutiny of police riot-control weapons blamed for life-changing injuries suffered by some teenagers.
The 17 October demonstrations against rising living costs and poor school conditions descended into violence, with groups setting fires, storming public buildings, looting shops and clashing with police in France’s worst unrest in years.
Another round of nationwide demonstrations on Saturday saw less violence. Authorities estimated turnout at more than 400,000, while organizers put it at nearly 800,000.
The government is expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France’s national online university admissions platform, French media reported. The platform has been a focus of the protests, with students criticizing unclear selection criteria, unequal opportunities and barriers to pursuing their preferred courses of study.
Students are also demanding more teachers to cover staff absences, school renovations, changes to teaching hours and smaller classes. On 8 October, the government said it would deploy 3,000 additional substitute teachers to struggling high schools.
The demands for better-resourced schools, particularly in poorer communities, come as France grapples with record poverty and record public debt.

Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:31:30 UTC
23:31:30 KST

Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of students electing to train as Frisian language teachers has doubled this year, amid a historic drive to strengthen and revive the Netherlands’ only officially recognised second language.
More than 34 students signed up to take a Frisian teacher training course at Leeuwarden’s hbo college NHL Stenden, either as a minor or part-time element of their studies, according to Omroep Fryslân.
The change signals a growing revival trend as Friesland, often ranked the Netherlands’ culturally proudest province, fights to protect its linguistic identity. Only 10 years ago, experts warned the language was on the verge of extinction.
Geert Driessen, of Radboud University in Nijmegen, said in a 2016 study that it was the “eleventh hour” for the province’s mother tongue – especially in urban areas, where Dutch speaking newcomers increasingly mix with locals.
Between 1994 and 2014, he found, Frisian spoken outside family homes had halved. This led to the founding of Taalplan Frysk 2030, a government-backed scheme to protect the language through education and social initiatives.
The plan has received millions of euros in funding, much of which has gone to NHL Stenden. Recent studies show Frisian comprehension is rising, and since this school year all primary and secondary school pupils in Friesland are actively taught the language.
In September, the University of Groningen also launched the first standalone Frisian language degree in 15 years.

Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:27:33 UTC
23:27:33 KST

Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian
Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian over negotiations with the US.
As the threat of a new war with the United States looms, the Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, a hardline political faction also known as the Paydari Front, has asked the Iranian parliament and the Supreme National Security Council to initiate a withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
This move has been interpreted as a call for Iran to develop nuclear weapons, with the Paydari Front saying these military endeavours should happen “as quickly as possible”.
It is the latest bold and defiant message by Iran’s hardliners against Washington, after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28 on the pretext that Tehran was trying to develop nuclear weapons.
The war has seen the Strait of Hormuz largely closed to shipping, massive damage to Iranian and Arab infrastructure in missile and air strikes, and huge disruptions to global energy supplies.
The past eight months have also marked an ongoing existential power struggle between moderates and centrists, such as President Masoud Pezeshkian, who generally favour talks with the US, and hardliners in the Paydari Front who do not.
Ultimately, the moderate camp wants a swift end to the conflict to save Iran’s crumbling economy. Hardliners believe Washington only understands the language of force, so the war should continue until the US capitulates to Iran’s demands.
The domestic rivalry can be seen in the public squares of major Iranian cities, where for the past 200 days supporters of the hardline faction have rallied at night.
Initially, these gatherings were a way for people to express public support for the government and protest the unprovoked US war on Iran. Over time, they have evolved into highly organised political rallies where activists can publicly express their strong opposition to moderates’ efforts to end the war through diplomatic channels.
The hardliners’ slogans include “No compromise, no surrender – the fight against America” and “Negotiating with the enemy is a betrayal of the homeland”.
They also protested against President Pezeshkian’s return to Tehran from the UN General Assembly in September, where he condemned the US war but also extolled the virtues of diplomacy. The pickets were viewed as a way for their “anti-negotiation” message to be heard by the president.
This bloc has considerable power beyond these activist circles. Hardliners have a strong presence in Tehran’s municipal government, the parliament, among religious preachers and eulogists, and academia and the media.
Amirhossein Sabeti, a member of parliament aligned with the Paydari Front, said in a statement that negotiations with the US will not begin unless Washington’s siege on Iran’s southern ports or sanctions end.
“The enemy’s objective of destroying Iran has not changed. It is simply waiting for the right moment to launch another surprise attack. Those who thought negotiations could prevent war, or that the United States would lift sanctions through negotiations, did not understand how the world works and were deluding themselves,” he said. “The only language the world understands is the language of power.”
The political faction to which Sabeti belongs has filed a motion in the Iranian parliament to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, following his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Iran’s parliament is also considering a law to criminalise interviews with foreign media outlets, which would be another win for hardliners.
But as the impeachment motion against Iran’s foreign minister moves through parliament, the political camp supporting the government continues to advocate for a diplomatic solution to the current conflict.
Davood Heshmati, a journalist considered close to Pezeshkian, said there are signs that US forces have foregone the grand ambition of overthrowing the Iranian government and have instead opted for more modest aims, which makes a diplomatic solution more likely.
“There are several ways to achieve those other goals, one of which is war. But, in any case, to prevent a war, all alternatives to military action must first be tested. Negotiations and a diplomatic agreement are among those alternatives, and they should always take precedence over war,” Heshmati told Al Jazeera.
“Those who say the Strait of Hormuz must not be reopened are people who believe the war must not end. From the perspective of Iran’s anti-negotiation camp, the war between Iran and the United States has no end. What they do not explain is what outcome they expect from this war. They seem to believe that, after several rounds of fighting, the United States will simply walk away from the conflict. But that idea does not appear to be consistent with the logic of what we are witnessing.”
He indicated that for any war to end, there needs to be an understanding with the US that respects Iran’s territorial integrity.
“Those in Iran who support negotiations argue that a balance of power does not necessarily have to be achieved through war, although, given everything that has happened along the diplomatic path, the distrust that exists is understandable,” he said.
Political analyst Negar Mortazavi argues that hardline groups are a powerful domestic force, but they currently have limited influence over Iran’s foreign policy.
“Iran’s hardliners are not a marginal political force. They are a well-organised and deeply entrenched part of [Iran’s] political establishment. Their strength lies in their ability to mobilise supporters, shape political discourse, pressure the government, and raise the political cost of diplomacy,” she said.
“But political influence should not be confused with ultimate decision-making authority. Decisions about war, peace, and negotiations are made at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and national security establishment.”
Hardliners can continue to confront negotiators, threaten impeachments against those who propose talks with the US, and try to obstruct diplomatic endeavours, she said. But they cannot prevent an agreement being reached if it is backed by the country’s main powerholders, including Supreme Leader Mujtaba Khamenei and the Supreme National Security Council.
“The [hardliners] are powerful enough to complicate diplomacy, but not necessarily powerful enough to stop it. [They] are a highly visible and vocal political force, but they are not calling the shots,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.
“Throughout the war, Tehran has kept the door open to diplomacy, and the decision at the highest levels of leadership has been to pursue negotiations with the United States and seek an agreement. The hardliners have been unable to stop that. The real test of their power is that they could not stop the JCPOA [nuclear agreement] under [former President Barack] Obama, and they could not stop the more recent MoU [memorandum of understanding] with Trump. Ultimately, the decisions were made above their heads.”
Street rallies and television programmes opposing a peaceful solution to the US-Israeli war against Iran will continue. But the delay in scheduling the foreign minister’s impeachment hearing, alongside continued diplomatic engagement with mediators to end the war, suggests that the moderates are still a force to be reckoned with.

On Tuesday, October 27, the Round of 16 of the Ukrainian Football Cup begins and will run through Thursday. On Tuesday, Ukrainian fans will already be able to watch the first Ukrainian classic of the season, as Shakhtar Donetsk host the reigning Cup holders, Dynamo Kyiv, reports UNN.
Details
The first matches will take place on Tuesday, October 27. At 13:00, Livyi Bereh Kyiv and Veres Rivne will meet at the Arena Livyi Bereh stadium.
Then, at 18:00, the first Ukrainian classic of the season will take place, with Shakhtar Donetsk hosting the reigning Cup holders, Dynamo Kyiv, at Arena Lviv.

“Dynamo” is the winner of the Ukrainian Football Cup20.05.26, 20:33 • 81276 views
In cup competitions (the Ukrainian Cup + the Ukrainian Super Cup + European competitions), the teams have played 34 matches against each other: 11 Dynamo wins, 9 draws, and 14 Shakhtar wins.
On 8 occasions, the winner was decided in a penalty shootout, with complete parity here—four wins for each opponent. In two other cases, the winner was determined in extra time.
On Wednesday, October 28, Mayak Rivne will face Kharkiv at Sarny-Arena, while Chernihiv will meet Epitsentr from Kamianets-Podilskyi at Chernihiv-Arena.

The winners of the one-match Round of 16 ties will advance to the quarterfinals. According to the Ukrainian Cup regulations, in the event of a draw in regular time, a penalty shootout will take place immediately—without extra time.
The matches will be available to watch on the MEGOGO OTT platform and on the UPL TV channel.

First international flight arrives at the new Western Sydney airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:27:11 UTC
23:27:11 KST

Sydney’s new 24-hour airport has welcomed its first international passengers with the opening described as a ‘milestone that has been decades in the making’.
Australia’s first major new international airport for 50 years is now fully operational.
Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport (WSI) welcomed its first international passengers on 26 October, with Air New Zealand flight NZ165 touching down from Auckland.
The arrival came a day after the airport officially opened, with Jetstar launching its first domestic passenger services.
Located at Badgerys Creek, about 60 kilometres west of central Sydney, the new airport operates around the clock. That gives airlines greater scheduling flexibility than at Sydney’s existing Kingsford Smith Airport, where a curfew restricts take-offs and landings between 11 pm and 6 am.
“WSI is the most transformational piece of infrastructure our nation has seen since the Sydney Harbour Bridge,” said WSI CEO Simon Hickey.
“WSI's passengers will be able to enjoy access to more than 250 destinations around the globe just over a year from now – a remarkable start for Sydney’s new 24-hour gateway.”
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the opening of the new airport a “milestone” that has been “decades in the making”.
“With the opening of Western Sydney International, this will help drive the next chapter for the region,” he said. “This isn’t just about a new runway or terminal. This is about jobs, investment and delivering for one of Australia’s fastest-growing regions.”
The airport is officially named after Nancy Bird Walton, who was Australia's first female commercial pilot.
What can passengers expect at Sydney’s new airport?
Domestic and international gates share a single terminal, with automated check-in and baggage technology designed to make journeys smoother.
WSI initially has capacity for 10 million passengers a year. The airport says it could eventually become Australia’s primary gateway, with capacity for more than 80 million passengers annually.
Transport options include public buses, taxis, rideshares and rental cars, while drivers can reach the airport via the toll-free M12.
Flights to and from WSI
Singapore Airlines will launch daily Singapore services on 23 November, followed by Vietjet flights to Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam in January 2027, and Fiji Airways services to Nadi in March. Qatar Airways will connect Doha and WSI from 15 December 2027.
Domestically, Jetstar’s network covers the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane, with daily Gold Coast services, up to 14 weekly return services to Melbourne and three to Brisbane.
Qantas will join on 28 March 2027, operating four weekly flights on each of its Melbourne and Brisbane routes through QantasLink.

Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:24:22 UTC
23:24:22 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them
Europe’s answer to Russia’s growing jet-drone arsenal is taking shape around a simple idea: use AI to coordinate mass interceptions, then kill fast threats with cheaper missiles instead of burning through million-euro air-defense rounds.
European defense technology company Helsing has unveiled Contra, a new AI-controlled air-defense system built to counter large-scale drone and missile attacks, alongside two new interceptors designed to chase down fast jet-powered UAVs and cruise missiles, according to a press releaseHelsing shared with UNITED24 Media on October 26.
The system is particularly relevant to Ukraine, which is already facing a growing Russian arsenal of jet-powered Geran drones.
Helsing says recent intelligence assessments indicate Russia has sharply increased production of Geran-4 and Geran-5 systems, with output reportedly reaching as many as 4,000 units per month while Moscow expands the number of launch sites.
Built for the jet-Shahed problem
Contra is designed for exactly that kind of saturation threat.
According to Helsing, the system can detect and coordinate engagements against hundreds or even thousands of incoming drones and missiles at the same time by combining multiple sensors and weapons into a single air picture. Its sensor architecture can include radar, electro-optical, infrared, and acoustic systems, while the Altra command-and-control platform keeps human operators in control of targeting priorities and decisions.
The architecture is also intended to remain functional under battlefield disruption, including jamming, broken communications links, and the loss of individual nodes.
For Ukraine, that matters because Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran variants are substantially faster than conventional Shahed-type drones, increasing the pressure on both interceptor drones and traditional surface-to-air missile systems.
Two new interceptors for two different threats
At the center of Contra are two Helsing-developed interceptors.
The AD-1 Inferno is a jet-powered interceptor intended to fill the gap between slower electric or propeller-driven drone interceptors and traditional missiles that are too expensive to fire in large numbers. Helsing says AD-1 can loiter after launch, operate in swarms, and re-engage targets in flight while receiving midcourse updates from Contra ground radars.
Company specifications list a maximum speed above 700 km/h and an operating altitude exceeding 9,000 meters.
The AD-2 Ambush, meanwhile, uses a solid rocket motor and is intended for faster and higher-flying threats. Helsing says it is designed to defeat high-speed one-way drones and subsonic cruise missiles beyond AD-1’s reach.
In its announcement, Helsing said AD-2 can reach roughly Mach 2.5 and engage targets beyond 20 kilometers.
Both interceptors use onboard radar seekers for terminal guidance, allowing them to operate in darkness, cloud, and fog—conditions where cheaper optical or infrared seekers can struggle. Helsing’s technical brief specifically emphasizes that the radar seekers are intended to maintain performance when visibility is poor.
Built for mass attacks, not one-off shots
Helsing is positioning Contra as more than a closed missile system.
The architecture is designed to integrate third-party weapons—including other interceptors, anti-drone lasers, guns, and even net-based systems—within days.
That would allow operators to choose different weapons for different targets rather than firing an expensive missile at every incoming drone.
The same command architecture is intended to protect population centers, borders, military bases, and maneuvering forces, with the sensor and weapon mix changing depending on the mission.
Helsing says both AD-1 and AD-2 are intended for mass production through separate European supply chains, reducing dependence on a single production line.
Niklas Köhler, Helsing co-founder and president, framed the system around the cost problem now confronting Ukraine and Europe.
“Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets. Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2. With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high—affordable and at industrial scale,” he said.
Ukraine already fighting the threat Contra was built for
For Ukraine, that dilemma is no longer theoretical.
Russia is moving beyond slower propeller-driven Shahed-type drones toward faster jet-powered systems such as the Geran-4 and Geran-5, forcing Ukraine to field increasingly fast interceptor drones, fighter aircraft, surface-to-air missiles, and other layers of defense.
The challenge is not simply destroying one fast drone, but doing so repeatedly during mass attacks without exhausting expensive interceptor stocks.
Contra is Helsing’s attempt to turn those different defensive layers into one coordinated network—using AI to manage the air picture while cheaper, mass-produced interceptors take on threats that would otherwise consume far more expensive missiles.
If Russia continues scaling jet-powered drone production at the rate Helsing describes, that cost equation could become one of the defining problems for both Ukrainian and European air defense.
Earlier, German defense company Helsing’s Ukraine-proven HX-2 drone performed successfully during tests with US soldiers in Lithuania.

Russia Turns to Coup-Hit Madagascar to Recruit New Soldiers for Its War Against Ukraine
Russia has expanded its military recruitment campaign to Madagascar for the first time since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, opening a new recruitment channel in an African country that has recently strengthened ties with Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 26, citing a Ukrainian intelligence presentation, the recruitment effort follows Madagascar’s 2025 military coup and subsequent expansion of cooperation with Russia, including deliveries of military equipment and food supplies.
Following the change of government, Russian personnel began training Malagasy troops, while Moscow supplied weapons and military equipment. Madagascar’s leader, Colonel Michaël Randrianirina, also met Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Moscow in February 2026.
A separate investigation published by Le Monde on October 20 documented the death of a Malagasy national who had joined the Russian military and was killed on the Ukrainian front in August. His family said recruiters had promised financial compensation and Russian citizenship.
Madagascar’s inclusion is part of a broader recruitment campaign across Africa. According to the intelligence figures reviewed by Bloomberg, Ukraine has identified 5,451 African nationals among 45,959 foreigners from 151 countries who signed contracts with the Russian military.
Earlier, on October 19, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported that nearly 46,000 foreign nationals from 151 countries had signed contracts with Russia’s Defense Ministry. Moscow has reportedly set a target of recruiting 18,500 foreigners in 2026, with more than 16,000 already enlisted.

Ukrainian intelligence: Russia can probably add 10–15 Su-34 bombers a year, but no new Tu-95s or Tu-22M3s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:23:31 UTC
23:23:31 KST

Russia’s aircraft plants still turn out modern fighter-bombers and fighters, enough to partly cover its losses, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency HUR told Ukrainian news agency UNIAN, which published the reply on 23 October. Its older bombers are a different story. Russia has no serial production of new Tu-95s, Tu-22M3s, or Su-24s and keeps them flying through repairs and upgrades, so each one lost for good leaves a lasting gap, HUR said.
Ukraine’s Navy said its Neptune missiles hit six Su-34M bombers at Borisoglebsk airbase in Russia’s Voronezh Oblast overnight into 15 October. Zelenskyy later said four were destroyed and two damaged. The Su-34 is one of the jets that drop Russia’s glide bombs, heavy bombs fitted with wing-and-guidance kits, on Ukrainian positions and towns.
How fast Russia replaces its jets
Russia can probably deliver 10–15 Su-34s a year now, HUR estimated. Deliveries grew from eight in 2022 to 11 in 2023 and 12–14 in 2024. But the agency said that trend does not confirm the same pace today.
For the Su-35S fighter, HUR pointed to an average of about 11–12 a year in 2021–2025. It called that a rough benchmark, not an established 2026 output. Su-30SM2 and Su-57 production continues, but reliable rates cannot be determined. Su-30 figures also mix new builds with upgrades of older Su-30SMs, HUR noted.
What Russia had, and what it lost or saw badly damaged in 2026
By the end of 2025, Russia had about 125 Su-34 and Su-34M bombers, which HUR counts together. It also had 140–145 Su-30 jets of various versions, 135–140 Su-35S, and about 20 Su-57s, HUR estimated. These are only fleet estimates, not a guaranteed number of jets Russia can send on combat missions at the same time, the agency cautioned. Some are under repair or upgrade, and HUR is not disclosing the current fleet size.
HUR also named specific 2026 cases of Russian aircraft destroyed or critically damaged. A Tu-22M3 crashed in Irkutsk Oblast on 15 June. Strikes on Engels airbase on 17 July and 28 August hit two Tu-95MS. The first suffered critical damage to its tail section, and HUR treats the second as a probable irrecoverable loss.
The list also includes a Su-35 that Ukraine’s military says it shot down on 8 July, a claim backed by published materials showing debris. It adds a Su-57 crash in Moscow Oblast on 23 July and a collision of two Su-35S over Kursk Oblast on 7 September. Full official details on those two incidents are still missing, HUR noted. Strikes on several Su-57s and a Su-34 at Shagol airbase on 25 April, and on a Su-24 in Crimea on 7 September, were also reported, but the state of those jets is unknown, so counting them as destroyed would be premature, HUR said. The list, as published, leaves out the Su-34s at Borisoglebsk and the Tu-95MS that Russia’s defense ministry said crashed on takeoff in Amur Oblast in late September.

'Yes Bibi or No Bibi': Netanyahu's political future overshadows Israel's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:23:26 UTC
23:23:26 KST

Israel's upcoming legislative election could reshape the country's political future amid deep divisions over Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership. Former government spokesperson Eylon Levy tells Euronews what is at stake and why another war with Iran may be imminent.
As Israelis prepare to vote in Tuesday's parliamentary election, questions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future remain central to the campaign, alongside national security, accountability for the 7 October 2023 attacks and the consequences of three years of war.
Former Israeli government spokesperson Eylon Levy told Euronews that the debate over whether Netanyahu should remain prime minister has become the defining fault line in Israeli politics, making cooperation between parties increasingly difficult.
"The question of whether he should or shouldn't be prime minister has contaminated, frozen, poisoned Israeli politics for a decade now," Levy said.
"Like him or loathe him, he really is a once-in-a-century kind of leader," he added.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces questions over the responsibility for the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, while his ongoing criminal trial remains another source of political division.
Levy suggested that Netanyahu's eventual departure could fundamentally reshape the country's political landscape.
"The day after Netanyahu, whenever that happens, I think we can expect to see Israeli politics being realigned. Until then, the battle lines really are drawn around, yes Bibi or no Bibi," he said.
An election in the shadow of 7 October
The vote, Israel's first since the 2023 attacks, comes amid demands for a state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed Hamas to carry out the assault.
"These elections are taking place in the shadow of the October 7 massacre and that issue is absolutely everywhere," Levy told Euronews.
He identified three central issues: responsibility for the attacks, Hamas's continued rule in Gaza and the social and economic costs of the war.
According to Levy, the unresolved question of Hamas's future has fuelled public anger, with political parties competing over who can deliver lasting security for Israel.
Prospect of renewed war with Iran
Beyond domestic issues, Levy predicted that military hostilities with Iran could resume after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
"I think that a return to war in Iran is extremely likely after the midterm elections," he said.
Levy described the current standoff with Tehran as unsustainable, pointing to tensions over the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian military activity in the region.
He also suggested that US President Donald Trump was reluctant to resume hostilities before the midterms because of concerns about oil prices.
"President Trump has said he doesn't want to return to the war before the midterms, clearly worrying what will happen to oil prices," Levy said.
According to Levy, Netanyahu would be likely to seek a more decisive outcome from any future confrontation, including the removal of Iran's leadership.
Yet for Levy, the prospect of change extends beyond Israel's regional security policies. He argued that Netanyahu's eventual departure could allow political parties to cooperate across divisions that have shaped Israeli politics for years.

US singer Chris Brown spared jail for UK nightclub attack
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:23:15 CET
23:23:15 KST

By Sam Tobin
LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US singer Chris Brown was spared an immediate prison sentence in Britain on Monday for attacking a music producer with a tequila bottle in a London nightclub in 2023, with his fans cheering as the musician walked free from court.
Brown, 37, was given an eight-month suspended sentence at London’s Southwark Crown Court over the attack on Abraham Diaw at the Tape nightclub in February 2023 that lasted around 20 seconds.
Diaw was hit twice in the head with a bottle, which was then swung twice more at him in what prosecutors described as “a vicious and unprovoked attack”.
The R&B star and his vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, pleaded guilty to a charge of affray in July, having denied more serious charges of attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm and assault causing actual bodily harm.
NO SPECIAL TREATMENT
Judge Tony Baumgartner said: “This was serious, public violence. In your case, Brown, it involved the repeated use … of a bottle, including twice striking Diaw to his head.”
The judge told Brown: “Your fame, commercial success and professional standing do not entitle you to special treatment – the law applies equally to everyone.”
But Baumgartner said he could suspend Brown’s sentence for 12 months, meaning he will not go to prison unless he commits another offence in that period. Akinlolu was also spared an immediate jail sentence.
“Violence will not be accepted on the streets of London,” Detective Chief Superintendent Christina Jessah from the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. “Regardless of an individual’s profile or status, we will pursue those responsible and work tirelessly to bring them before the courts.”
BROWN’S FANS CHEER SUSPENDED SENTENCE
Brown, winner of Grammy awards for best R&B album in 2011 and 2025, has previously admitted other violent offences in the US, having been charged with assaulting his then-partner, singer Rihanna, in 2009, with a photo of her bruised face making headlines around the world.
Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe said Brown pleaded guilty to the 2009 assault of Rihanna and was sentenced to five years’ probation. He also admitted a 2013 assault on a fan he was accused of punching when he asked for a photograph.
Brown remains hugely popular and has sold tens of millions of records worldwide, with dozens of fans queuing outside court from around 0700 GMT, about an hour before the building opened.
His lawyer Sallie Bennett-Jenkins said Brown was profoundly sorry for the incident and described him as “a dedicated, loving and loyal father to four children”.
“This was an ugly and unattractive incident, we would be the first to accept,” she added. “It was, however, an incident that was very short-lived.”
Brown thanked the judge before leaving the dock and nodding towards about two dozen of his supporters in the public gallery.
Other fans who gathered outside the building cheered as Brown left and went into a waiting car.
Brown was arrested in May 2025 having returned to Britain for the first time since the attack and was initially denied bail, throwing his worldwide “Breezy Bowl XX” tour into doubt.
But Brown was eventually released after promising to pay a £5 million ($6.7 million) security fee, allowing the tour to go ahead.
($1 = 0.7487 pounds)

Russia against forced evacuation, hope for deal compliance: Alyoshki situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Russian Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova responded to Kiev’s statements by saying that forced evacuation of families with children from Alyoshki in the Kherson Region is unacceptable.
Russia hopes that Ukraine will fulfill all agreements on the humanitarian mission in the city, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
TASS has compiled the key facts known at the moment.
Implementation of the ceasefire plan
- The United States has prepared a detailed plan for how the ceasefire regime in Alyoshki will function down to the minute, said Marc Beckman, senior adviser to the First Lady of the United States, in a comment to Vesti.
- On October 24, Lantratova said that both Russia and Ukraine are fulfilling their commitments under the agreements on the humanitarian mission in the town of Alyoshki in the Kherson Region.
Russia not amenable to forced evacuation
- Lantratova responded to Kiev’s statements by saying that the forcible removal of families with children from Alyoshki is unacceptable.
- She pointed out that if Ukraine wants people to make an informed decision, it should give them that opportunity by allowing them to live in peace and ordering its military to stop daily shelling of the town and mining of the roads.
- The ombudsman noted that people "are capable of making informed decisions on their own."
- "Everything must be done voluntarily, taking into account their interests specifically, and not those of the Kiev authorities, who have suddenly become concerned about the people living there," she said.
- Lantratova reminded that Alyoshki is Russian territory, where only Russian laws apply, and references to Ukrainian legislation carry no weight there.
Fake concern about residents
- Kiev is claiming in Ukrainian media that it is concerned about the residents of Alyoshki, Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large on issues related to the crimes of the Kiev regime, wrote on Telegram.
- However, he said that on October 24 between 7:15 a.m. (4:15 a.m. GMT) and 8:30 a.m. (5:30 a.m. GMT) 28 mines were launched at Alyoshki; at night, Ukrainian drones continued to remotely mine the access routes to the town.
- The civilian population of Alyoshki did not receive humanitarian aid from Ukraine; all reports to the contrary are false, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated resident of the town, told TASS.
Reaction to the ceasefire
- Lantratova thanked US First Lady Melania Trump and all members of the negotiation group for their cooperation in organizing a humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres welcomed the agreement, according to a statement by his official spokesman Stephane Dujarric.
- Guterres also expressed hope that this and other steps will help improve the dire humanitarian situation in Alyoshki and will make it possible to immediately provide vital assistance, as well as to carry out a safe and voluntary evacuation of the city’s residents in strict compliance with international humanitarian law.
- White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the agreements an important step towards resolving the Ukrainian conflict.
- The humanitarian communication channel between Lantratova and Melania Trump’s team on Alyoshki will help convey the truth about the living conditions in the city, which remains under Ukrainian blockade, Miroshnik said.
- Konstantin Basyuk, deputy head of the Federation Council Committee on Defense and Security, expressed hope that the humanitarian corridor to the town would not be disrupted.
- Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow hopes that Ukraine will fulfill all agreements on the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki.
- In his opinion, the agreements on the humanitarian operation could set a precedent for missions in other areas as well.
Agreement between Moscow and Kiev
- The White House said on October 23 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to cease fire in Alyoshki starting on October 29, 2026.
- It was noted that the countries agreed to cease all hostilities in Alyoshki to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and to prepare for the evacuation of the civilians through a special safe corridor.
- Reports also indicated that an independent media organization from the United States would monitor and document the actions of Russian and Ukrainian groups on the ground throughout the entire process.
- Later, Chief of the General Staff, Army General Valery Gerasimov, said that Russia would introduce a ceasefire in the Kherson direction starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 to carry out the humanitarian operation.
- Ukraine’s General Staff said that it would observe the ceasefire starting from 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27 to carry out the humanitarian operation.
The situation in the city
- On September 21, Peskov described the humanitarian situation as critical.
- Kiev’s shelling and drone attacks made the delivery of any food or medicines to the town impossible.
- On September 1, a decisive attempt was made to break the blockade to deliver humanitarian aid, but Ukrainian militants fired on the convoy of vehicles and almost completely destroyed the cargo, said Miroshnik.
- Four vehicles loaded with ten tons of food were attacked at the entrance to the town.
- Residents of nearby settlements on the left bank of the Dnepr tried to deliver food to Alyoshki, but Ukraine prevented this, Svetlana Popova, an evacuated resident of the town, told TASS.
- Slightly more than 1,000 people remain in Alyoshki, Miroshnik said in a comment to Vesti.
- Previously, more than 20,000 people lived in the city, he said.
- Miroshnik noted that the situation deteriorated over the past four to five months.

Environmental activists protested at the KMSKA, Antwerp’s Fine Arts Museum, on Sunday. The protesters are unhappy about sponsorship of the museum by French oil and gas producer TotalEnergies. They call themselves the ‘Rubens-fans’ and sang protest songs. They believe the museum is helping the company to polish up its image. The museum says it needs sponsorship and that it does, in fact, adhere to a code of ethics.
“Look at this painting that’s been restored by Total – KMSKA, this really isn’t on,” several environmental activists inside the museum shouted on Sunday. They criticise the KMSKA for accepting money from TotalEnergies in order to restore paintings.
“In this way, the museum is allowing itself to be used to boost the oil giant’s dubious reputation,” they say. Among other things, they point out that TotalEnergies has been found jointly liable for global warming.
‘Bribery and negligent environmental policy’
‘For decades, the French oil company has been guilty of bribery and negligent environmental policy and has been convicted in court for these offences. Furthermore, TotalEnergies intimidates critics by taking legal action against them.’
‘For example, in 2023, the company took Greenpeace to court after the environmental organisation had revealed that in reports TotalEnergies systematically underestimated its own emissions. In October 2025, however, Greenpeace was vindicated and a French court found the company guilty of greenwashing on account of deliberately misleading consumers about its emissions and climate targets.’
Funding needed
“We have indeed been working with TotalEnergies and many other parties since 2023 to restore a fantastic masterpiece by Rubens,” says Carmen Willems, director of the KMSKA. “At present, the KMSKA receives no government funding for restoration projects. Nevertheless, we are carrying out a number of them, all of which are entirely privately funded.”
“It is already very difficult just to keep a museum running, and these pieces are really in need of restoration. That is why we have launched a major campaign in which we have asked a number of companies to support us in this endeavour.”
According to Willems, TotalEnergies also meets the criteria for sponsorship. “It is a listed company and is required to report transparently and openly on the impact of its activities on people and the environment. In international rankings, it scores significantly higher than its competitors in its sector in terms of environmental policy and climate targets.”
This was not the first time that campaigners had criticised TotalEnergies’ sponsorship. The museum invited the campaigners, as it had done previously, to a meeting. “We will clearly explain our considerations regarding sponsorship policy. As a museum, we adhere to the code of ethics on sponsorship. But the campaigners never accepted our invitation.”

2026-10-26
14:22:35 UTC

Breadcrumb
Israeli military advances west of Gaza's 'Yellow Line' in Deir al-Balah as 15 people killed
Several Israeli tanks and military vehicles advanced further west of the so-called 'Yellow Line' in central Gaza on Monday morning, sources told The New Arab, amid fears that Israel is seeking to expand its occupation of the besieged Palestinian territory.
This came as Israeli attacks continued to kill people across the Gaza Strip.
On Monday afternoon, two Palestinians were killed and another injured in an Israeli strike on a vehicle in Deir al-Balah.
Earlier on Monday, civil defence spokesperson Mahmoud Bassal reported that at least 13 people had been killed and 60 injured by Israeli fire and airstrikes across Gaza over the previous 24 hours.
Eyewitnesses reported hearing heavy gunfire in eastern Deir al-Balah at dawn on Monday, followed by the westward movement of Israeli military vehicles and bulldozers into an area home to hundreds of displaced families.
Osama al-Kahlout, a resident of Deir al-Balah, said the Israeli army had advanced west of the demarcation line several times over the past week.
"These movements have forced residents to flee their homes and shelters, only to return when the forces pull back, leaving families in a constant state of uncertainty and fear," al-Kahlout toldThe New Arab.
Residents, he added, were growing "increasingly concerned that these advances could be part of a gradual effort to reposition troops and expand the Yellow Line westward, rather than temporary military operations."
The so-called 'Yellow Line', marked by large yellow concrete blocks, delineates areas under Israeli military control.
Although the initial arrangement under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan was intended to be temporary and followed by a gradual Israeli withdrawal, the Israeli military has instead expanded its area of control. Estimates now suggest Israel controls nearly two-thirds of the besieged Palestinian territory.
Al-Kahlout said residents’ main fear was that Israeli forces would eventually reach Salah al-Din Street, a major road connecting northern and southern Gaza that lies well west of the current demarcation line.
Mustafa Ibrahim, a Gaza-based political analyst, told The New Arab that any westward expansion towards the road "could further fragment the Strip and increase the territory under Israeli control".
Monday’s advance comes just weeks after dozens of Palestinian families in Gaza City’s Shuja’iyya neighbourhood were forced to flee when Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks marking the line towards their tents without warning.
Military expansion ahead of elections
Ibrahim said the "repeated advances and withdrawals could indicate an attempt to gradually expand the area under Israeli control and establish new military positions."
"Maintaining Israeli military control over parts of Gaza and expanding the area under its control could serve the objectives of [Benjamin Netanyahu’s] far-right coalition, which opposes a full Israeli withdrawal and seeks to impose new realities on the ground," Ibrahim told The New Arab.
With Israel heading to the polls on Tuesday, Ibrahim argued that Netanyahu’s continued military operations in Gaza were closely tied to his political survival.
Netanyahu "seeks to project an image of strength and security to Israeli voters, particularly among right-wing constituencies that support maintaining military pressure on Hamas," he said.
The prime minister, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Gaza, also faces fierce criticism from opponents over the security failures surrounding the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
Gaza has seen an escalation in Israeli attacks in the week preceding the general election. The total death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal campaign has reached 74,555.
"Ultimately, the continuation of these operations risks deepening Palestinian suffering while leaving the political future of Gaza increasingly uncertain," Ibrahim said.

Lula’s comeback puts brakes on Latin America’s rightward surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:21:34 UTC
23:21:34 KST

Brazil’s re-elected leader now faces a hostile Congress at home and a Trump administration that had bet heavily on his rival.
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow victory in Brazil’s presidential run-off on Sunday has ended a run of seven consecutive conservative wins in Latin American presidential elections over the past 18 months.
The leftist incumbent beat Flávio Bolsonaro by 51.8% to 48.2%. Bolsonaro has said he will challenge the result and seek its annulment, after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Voters across the region, frustrated by organised crime and economic hardship, have increasingly backed hard-line candidates, from Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Chile’s José Antonio Kast. Washington has encouraged the trend with endorsements, bailouts and military aid.
“The US is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region,” Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University, told the Associated Press.
Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, would have been the biggest prize. Bolsonaro had pledged to join a US-led anti-cartel coalition and campaigned on his closeness to Trump.
Instead, Washington’s pressure may have helped Lula. The steep tariffs Trump imposed on Brazilian goods over the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro for a coup plot triggered a nationalist backlash, which Lula channelled into the slogan “Brazil belongs to Brazilians”.
“To the extent that the regional superpower becomes a threat to Brazil’s democratic institutions, defending Brazilian national sovereignty also becomes a form of defending Brazilian democracy,” Roberts said.
'Brazil has leverage'
Lula has refused to join the US-led Shield of the Americas coalition. “We don’t accept being treated like children,” he said in May, after Washington designated Brazil’s two largest gangs as terrorist organisations.
Brazil also holds valuable cards: the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and around 90% of global niobium output, both vital to defence industries.
"Brazil has leverage," said Monica de Bolle of the Peterson Institute for International Economics. “With Lula, the US is on shakier ground.”
Yet analysts warn against reading too much into one result. Conservatives strengthened their grip on Brazil’s Congress this month, leaving Lula struggling to pass reforms.
“Lula has his hands tied,” said Guilherme Casarões of Florida International University.
A setback for Trump
The defeat of a Trump-backed candidate comes just over a week before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
A CNN poll put Trump’s approval rating at a record low of 32%. An NBC News/Telemundo survey found 68% of Latino voters disapprove of his foreign policy, a significant shift among a group that helped return him to power in 2024.
Reaction split along party lines. Donald Trump Jr attacked the extension of voting hours, while Democratic congressman Ro Khanna urged the president to respect the result.
Both governments still have reasons to cooperate, with Washington seeking rare earths and Lula wanting tariff relief.
"Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration," said Will Freeman of the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros’ allies in Washington were likely to lose influence after the family’s second straight defeat.

Elvis Presley music rights holders sue Anthropic over AI training
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:21:20 UTC
23:21:20 KST

Efe Ozkan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The owners of rights to Elvis Presley’s music catalog have sued artificial intelligence company Anthropic, accusing it of using 274 songs recorded by the singer to train its Claude AI models without permission, The Guardian reported Sunday.
The lawsuit was filed Friday in the US District Court for the Northern District of California by a subsidiary of Authentic Brands Group, which acquired Presley’s intellectual property and trademark rights in 2013.
The plaintiffs include music publishers Raleigh Music Publishing and Abilene Music, as well as trusts linked to songwriter Luigi Creatore and the Aberbach family, whose publishing business controlled rights to songs recorded by Presley.
The lawsuit alleges that Anthropic copied the songs without a license or payment and retained the material in an internal repository for training future versions of Claude.
The catalog allegedly includes Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up, Don’t Be Cruel, A Little Less Conversation and Return to Sender.
The plaintiffs are seeking $150,000 for each of the 274 allegedly infringed songs, amounting to $41.1 million, with additional damages bringing their total claim to $48.6 million.
Lead attorney Richard Busch accused Anthropic of building its business on copyright infringement and said the plaintiffs were “deeply protective” of the songs.
Anthropic disputed the allegations.
“We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully,” the company told NBC News.
The case is among a growing number of copyright disputes between AI developers and the music industry and could have broader implications for how copyrighted music is used to train AI models.
