The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:57:55 EET
22:57:55 KST

The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian businesses are gradually developing practices for employing and adapting veterans — from preparing teams and retraining to creating specialized positions.
Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and reintegrating veterans. Businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, creating adaptation and retraining programs, while some companies are introducing dedicated positions to support veterans. At the same time, it is still too early to speak of mass employment. Tetiana Karelska, head of the HR and CSR division of the European Business Association, said this in a comment to UNN.
We are observing a moderate increase in engagement. We have not measured separate, precise statistics that would representatively demonstrate the dynamics of veterans’ employment in recent years—and objectively, such statistics do not currently exist because of the dynamics of the hostilities. However, we are tracking an increase in preparatory work within companies
According to her, among the Association’s member companies there are both businesses that already have systematic practices for engaging and adapting veterans and those that are only beginning to develop their own programs.
Tetiana Karelska noted that the Association is recording growing demand for team training, including specialized training—from basic communication etiquette and psychological literacy to the specifics of interacting with people who have combat experience, injuries, or experience of captivity. In addition, the EBA is recording positive dynamics in the creation of internal adaptation and retraining pathways.
Introducing a veterans’ affairs officer position—companies that have the necessary resources are creating dedicated positions (veterans’ affairs officer/CVO) responsible directly for veterans’ reintegration. On our side, we have a vision for creating a specialized training program for such professionals
Adapting workplaces and teams
Veterans’ adaptation involves both arranging a physical workplace in accordance with the employee’s individual needs and preparing the team for their return.
The first aspect—adapting the physical workplace—is always about additional funding. Not every employer is able to independently arrange a workplace according to the individual needs of an employee with a disability. The state provides substantial assistance here, in particular through compensation programs, but this sometimes remains a complicated process that requires time and knowledge
At the same time, team adaptation and psychological support depend on the company’s willingness to invest in employee training, engage external specialists, or develop its own educational programs. According to the EBA’s assessment, this does not always require substantial budgets, since free training programs developed as far back as 2014 are available publicly.
What obstacles remain
One of the key challenges for employers is the so-called "military-to-civilian translation."
Recruiters and HR professionals still find it difficult to properly assess candidates’ military experience and match it with civilian vacancies. This requires systematic cooperation with support services and directly with veterans
Other obstacles include insufficient staff preparedness, a lack of communication and management skills, as well as stereotypes about people with combat experience, experience of captivity, or disabilities.
We continue to work on stereotypes concerning interaction with people who have combat experience, experience of captivity, or a disability. This is a lengthy process, and it is not solely the responsibility of the employer or a matter of training within the company. It is a global task for the state and society to develop a culture of respect and gratitude toward every citizen, regardless of their experience
As noted by the EBA, more effective integration of veterans requires companies to have not only their own programs, but also coordinated state policy and access to the necessary support tools.
Businesses are currently creating numerous initiatives and programs at their own expense. The main expectation businesses have of the state is synergy instead of duplication, along with a reduction in the number of fragmented working groups. Instead, there is a demand for the creation of a single specialized structure (or coordination center) that would bring together all process participants and provide convenient access to analytics, methodological materials, grant programs, and state compensation in one place, so that employers would not have to collect information separately
Let us remind you
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is also working to support veterans. According to the words of FPU Chairman Serhii Byzov, the Federation’s sanatoriums provide medical rehabilitation services to military personnel, while the organization itself, together with specialized ministries and the National Health Service of Ukraine, is developing programs to support, socially adapt, and employ veterans. According to the FPU, more than 32,800 military personnel have undergone medical rehabilitation at its sanatoriums.

Consultant doctors in England to stage 2-day strike over pay, working conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Consultant doctors in England will stage a two-day strike on Nov. 25 and 26 over pay and working conditions, the British Medical Association (BMA) announced Monday.
Consultants will provide emergency cover during the walkout, with staffing similar to Christmas Day and significant disruption expected to routine appointments and planned procedures.
In a joint statement, BMA consultants committee co-chairs Dr. Helen Neary and Dr. Shanu Datta said they had attempted to negotiate with the government in “good faith,” but that “time-and-time again ministers have kicked the can down the road.”
“Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes,” they said.
Consultants received a 3.5% pay increase this year. However, the BMA argues that their pay has fallen by a quarter over the past 17 years when adjusted for inflation.
The union is also seeking a reduction in the standard working week from 40 to 35 hours, higher pay for out-of-hours work and changes to pension arrangements, including greater flexibility over when pensions can be taken.
The union said 76% of consultants who participated in the strike ballot voted in favor of industrial action, with just over half of eligible BMA members taking part.
The government said this amounted to around one in five consultants employed by the National Health Service (NHS) in England, noting that nearly half of consultants are not BMA members.
Health Secretary Yvette Cooper described the strike announcement as “disappointing,” saying the government had been engaged in “constructive discussions” with the union. She called the planned action “irresponsible” and warned it would place the health service under greater pressure.

Gyurov Files Complaint Accusing Radev of Using Government Resources to Campaign for Yotova

The Gyurov-Kandev Initiative Committee has filed a complaint with Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission (CEC), alleging that Prime Minister Rumen Radev used official government communication channels to campaign for presidential candidate Iliana Yotova, while We Continue the Change leader Asen Vassilev accused Radev of delaying the state budget and failing to take a consistent position on national security.
The initiative committee is seeking an urgent CEC ruling over two alleged violations of the Electoral Code involving campaign messages distributed through the Council of Ministers’ official channels.
According to the committee, the government has effectively become a press office for Yotova. In a statement on October 26, Radev appealed directly to voters, saying, “Let us vote for Iliana Yotova,” while also making accusations against Andrey Gyurov. The same content was then published through the Government Information Service, the official gov.bg website and the Council of Ministers’ Facebook page.
The committee alleges that the actions breached Article 182, Paragraph 1 of the Electoral Code, which prohibits election campaigning through state institutions, and Article 168, Paragraph 3, which prohibits the free use of public administrative resources for campaign purposes. It argues that government communication channels, civil servants and taxpayer funds were used to benefit one candidate.
The complaint sets out six requests to the CEC: establish whether the violations occurred; order the immediate removal of the posts and stop campaign activity through official government channels; document the published content; identify the officials who drafted, approved and published the messages, as well as who instructed them to do so; take steps to issue administrative violation citations against Radev and any officials found responsible; and refer the materials to the National Audit Office for assessment within its jurisdiction.
“We are referring this matter to the CEC: the posts must be taken down immediately, and those responsible must be held accountable,” Gyurov said.
The initiative committee has called for the complaint to be considered urgently, within the prescribed 24-hour period.
Separately, Vassilev accused the government of postponing the presentation of the state budget, preventing citizens from examining its financial parameters before the elections. He said that if the National Council for Tripartite Cooperation does not meet this week, the Public Finance Act will be violated and the budget will not reach Parliament before October 31.
“I have just learned that there will be no tripartite meeting this week; this means the Public Finance Act will be violated, and the budget will not be submitted to Parliament before October 31. What are you hiding, Mr. Radev? What is in this budget that you do not want to show the Bulgarian citizens before the elections this coming Sunday?” Vassilev said.
He argued that the main budget parameters were already known and indicated that incomes would deteriorate in real terms.
“For the first time, you have officially included in a budget the fact that Bulgarian citizens will become poorer. Their incomes will grow at a slower rate than inflation. But what else have you hidden in this budget, and on what else are you spending money—to the point where, even with this impoverishment, you still cannot manage to stay within a 3% deficit?” the PP leader asked.
Vassilev urged voters to back Gyurov, arguing that he could scrutinize executive decisions and veto measures that harmed citizens or violated the Constitution. He said Yotova would not be able to perform that role.
The PP leader also sharply criticized Radev and Yotova over national security, accusing Radev of taking inconsistent positions on Russia, Ukraine and Bulgaria’s European allies.
“Let him, once and for all, take a firm, sensible stance - instead of saying one thing here and something else in Brussels, spinning around like a top wherever the wind blows,” Vassilev said.
He argued that protecting Bulgaria’s maritime and air borders required a clear position toward its allies and readiness to respond to violations. Effective defenses against drones and maritime threats, he added, required cooperation with Romania and other allies.
Vassilev also questioned the country’s defense preparedness, noting that Radev had served as president and commander-in-chief for nine years. He asked why Bulgaria still lacked a sufficiently developed system for countering drones and modern radar capabilities.
“I have done my job as Minister of Finance. I provided the funding, securing it within the 3% deficit limit, without taking anything away from pensioners or cutting salaries. What have they done since then?” Vassilev said.
He also challenged political allegations concerning “dependencies” and backroom deals, disputing Radev’s claims about links between political and economic circles. Vassilev said the president should be chosen by voters rather than through arrangements negotiated in party headquarters.
“The country’s President must be elected by the Bulgarian citizens,” he said.

A Movement’s Promise: The Making of Contemporary Palestinian Theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

When Palestinian negotiators returned from the Madrid peace talks in the early 1990s, they briefed the press at a theatre in East Jerusalem. It seems an odd setting for news of talks that held the world’s attention, until you discover the role theatre had played in Palestinian life since the Nakba.
A burned-out cinema until 1984, the Palestinian National Theatre was where the negotiator Hanan Ashrawi and the Jerusalem leader Faisal Al-Husseini accused Israel of ignoring its commitments. It also hosted a festival for local schools and a literary festival marking twenty years since Ghassan Kanafani’s assassination. In Al-Saber’s words, the theatre “stepped into the role of an acting ministry of culture”.
That a theatre could take on such a role says a great deal about what it had come to mean for Palestinians. The mass displacement of 1948 scattered the artists, troupes and audiences of pre-war Palestine. In the years that followed, Palestinian culture survived inside Israel under military rule, which lasted until 1966, and in the West Bank under Jordanian rule.
After the 1967 war and Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza, a generation of young people in Jerusalem and Ramallah turned to the stage.
Writing from exile in Lebanon, the Jerusalem writer Mahmoud Shqair observed that the theatre movement “became the most conspicuous artistic phenomenon on our occupied land. None of the other arts matched it in drawing and influencing the audiences.”
Al-Saber explains why. Under an occupation that restricted Palestinian assembly, attending a play was a social activity and a political act at once. In his words, theatre had become “a site for free thought and a battleground that did not require forbidden arms”.
Read: Theatre community slams Israel lobby attack on touring Palestinian play
A Movement’s Promise tells how that movement, known to its members as Al-Haraka Al-Masrahiyya (the theatre movement), came into being and grew into the theatre industry Palestinians have today.
Al-Saber assembled this history from scattered records and the recollections of the people who made it. “Due to the absence of a Palestinian state,” he writes, “Palestinian theater history has not been collected into a centralized archive.” During fieldwork between 2009 and 2023, he interviewed theatre artists and gathered material from their personal collections: reviews and interviews cut from period newspapers, posters, photographs, brochures and actors’ copies of scripts.
Further material came from the archive of El-Hakawati (The Storyteller), the Jerusalem company founded in 1977 whose theatre later became the Palestinian National Theatre, and from the papers of its founder, François Abu Salem. Records of the Israeli censorship board, held in the Israel State Archive, show how companies dealt with the censors.
El-Hakawati’s satire Mahjoub Mahjoub (1980), about a hapless Palestinian everyman under occupation, shows how artists slipped their plays past Israeli censors, and how censorship backfired.
To obtain a performance permit, El-Hakawati’s co-founder Jackie Lubeck sent the censors an English summary that made the play sound harmless. In one scene, Mahjoub is interrogated for wearing clothes in the colours of the Palestinian flag, which was then illegal. In Lubeck’s summary, this became simply: “Mahjoub is questioned about the outfit he wears to work one day.” The censors saw nothing political, and the play was approved in December 1980.
The following month, the authorities stopped a performance in Nazareth, claiming El-Hakawati had departed from the approved text. The audience turned the evening into a protest, and the actors improvised a new scene, sitting on stage tied to their chairs with their mouths taped. The novelist Emile Habibi condemned the ban, and the play went on to tour Europe.
Episodes like this lead Al-Saber to argue that Israel “inadvertently and unknowingly promoted Palestinian theater” through its efforts to suppress it. Censorship taught artists to say things indirectly, and every ban or arrest only drew more attention to their work.
Al-Saber concentrates on East Jerusalem and its close ties with Ramallah, from 1967 to the Oslo Accords. The two cities worked as a single cultural centre, linked by family, social and professional bonds, and most of the pioneering artists lived and worked in one or both.
Al-Saber wants readers to understand Palestinian theatre through the people who made it. Occupation shaped their working lives, but so did artistic ambition, friendships, rivalries and the effort to build an audience. As he explains, accounts centred on the “conflict” too often leave Palestine’s story existing only in relation to Israel. His approach stresses “the right of Palestinian theater makers to exist on their own merits, without being subsumed by crisis narratives or orientalist motifs”.
Balalin (The Balloons), the first independent Palestinian theatre company formed in the West Bank after the 1967 occupation, showed how theatre could rally an audience without saying a single forbidden word. In its best-known production, Al-‘atma (The Darkness, 1972), a young troupe sets out to perform a play, but the lights fail and the actors ask the audience to help repair them.
Many spectators believed the blackout was real, and electricians sometimes climbed onto the stage to offer help. As Al-Saber explains, “the struggle to end the darkness and perform the play represents the Palestinian struggle to fix its internal conflicts and end the occupation.” When the eager carpenter Adel dies at the lighting board, the cast carries him out on their shoulders as Palestinians carry their martyrs. “It was truly a call for an uprising, but using symbols,” recalls Emile Ashrawi, a founding member of the company.
Obliterated: Theatregoers’ dreams of seeing Palestinian play in London
Fifteen years later, El-Hakawati turned to the memory of the Nakba. By then it had become, in Al-Saber’s words, “a de facto representative of the Palestinian theater” in the international media. The Story of Kufur Shamma (1987) follows Walid, a young man who returns from studying abroad to find his village deserted. Kufur Shamma is fictional, but it stands in for the hundreds of Palestinian villages destroyed in 1948. With the village fool, Walid sets out to bring its scattered people home, tracking them across the diaspora, only to return and find the village erased.
Telling the story of 1948 met resistance well beyond the occupied territories. At a festival in Acre in 1987, a mixed Palestinian and Jewish city inside Israel, supporters of the Jewish extremist group Kahane Chai stood up in the front row, raised an Israeli flag and chanted “Death to Arabs”.
Two years later, Joseph Papp, one of America’s leading theatre producers, cancelled the play’s booking at New York’s Public Theater for fear of offending his audience, many of them Jewish and, in his words, “very sympathetic to Israel”. Each time, El-Hakawati performed anyway: the actors in Acre returned to the stage to applause, and weeks after Papp’s decision the play opened at another New York theatre to warm reviews.
The movement’s divisions run through the book as strongly as its achievements. Factional loyalties split ensembles, and the row over who controlled El-Hakawati’s theatre ended with its founders leaving the building they had rebuilt. Yet Al-Saber sees this constant breaking and re-forming as the movement’s strength: a “self-sacrificial” process that kept making way for new companies and artists.
After Oslo came new pressures. Foreign donor money professionalised the theatres but turned a collective movement into separate organisations competing for grants. At the same time, the Separation Wall, military checkpoints and expanding settlements cut East Jerusalem off from the West Bank.
Within a few years, most West Bank Palestinians could no longer enter Jerusalem without a permit. The Palestinian National Theatre lost its largest audience, and Jerusalem was separated from Ramallah, the city whose family, artistic and professional ties had given birth to the movement. Theatre-makers now had to tour to audiences trapped in their own cities, and artists with West Bank identity cards could rarely work across the new lines.
Al-Saber closes by asking whether the movement still exists. He believes it does, carried in the stories that two generations of theatre-makers still tell one another. “Even during war, genocide, and uncertainty,” he writes, “the movement is alive in its lore and lineage, promising and delivering a richly diverse theater industry.” If at times it seems dormant, “its history has shown that it may simply be under the radar”.

Von der Leyen’s big Commission shake-up moves a step closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:29 UTC
22:56:29 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen’s push for a sweeping overhaul of the European Commission moved closer to fruition on Monday, as a group of external advisers handed over a report that will help shape the institution’s biggest administrative shake-up in two decades.
The report, drawn up by a high-level group led by former Commission Secretary-General Catherine Day, marks a new stage in the so-called large-scale review — an exercise intended to make the Commission more efficient, streamline its sprawling bureaucracy and turn it into a more attractive employer.
“Now we’re reaching the second phase,” von der Leyen said at the handover, referring to the conclusion of an initial phase that involved 15 internal workstreams and contributions from thousands of Commission staff.
Advertisement
“We need to be able to act effectively and to act quickly,” she said about the needed changes in the EU Executive’s machinery. “That means simpler procedures, clearer structures, better cooperation across departments so that our colleagues can focus their efforts where it makes the greatest difference.”
The external group, consisting of Day and eight other experts with experience in national administrations and international organizations including the OECD and OSCE, put forward nine interrelated recommendations aimed at making the Commission more agile and better equipped to adapt to future challenges.
Among its main proposals is a shift away from working in siloed departments toward greater collaboration across directorates-general, including through cross-DG portfolios.
This part of the exercise is politically sensitive. Behind the push to modernize the Commission lies the prospect of a far-reaching reorganization of its departments, potentially redrawing the responsibilities of powerful directorates-general that oversee billions of euros in EU spending.
As POLITICO first reported, several major Commission departments face an uncertain future under plans to overhaul how the bloc manages and distributes EU funds, raising the prospect of mergers or other structural changes.
Among the departments potentially affected is the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO), which oversees cohesion policy funding, accounting for almost a third of EU spending. Other departments facing uncertainty include the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI), responsible for Common Agricultural Policy money; DG EMPL, which oversees employment and social funding; DG MARE, which handles fisheries funding; and DG RTD, responsible for research and innovation.
Advertisement
The group also called for a stronger Secretariat-General to act as a strategic center driving results, and for a human-centered approach to artificial intelligence to simplify administrative processes and modernize the institution’s operations.
But the release of the report on Monday does not mean that any restructuring decisions have been taken. Day’s report will feed into a wider review overseen by Budget and Public Administration Commissioner Piotr Serafin, who is tasked with presenting final recommendations to von der Leyen by the end of 2026.
Catherine Day, Chair of the High-Level Group on the Future of the Commission’s Civil Service gives a press statement in Brussels on October 26, 2026. | Dati Bendo/European Commission Audiovisual Service
Serafin said at the handover that the external assessment, combined with feedback from Commission staff, provided a “mandate to go for far reaching changes.”
Day, for her part, said the Commission had already demonstrated a willingness to reform, pointing to the wealth of ideas emerging from within the institution.
“The work done on the large scale review has shown that there is a broad coalition for change right across the Commission,” she added.
A separate internal process produced an initial set of recommendations in July, drawn up by Commission officials. Those proposals were intended to kick-start a broader discussion within the institution rather than serve as final decisions.
Advertisement
Any major reshuffling of the Commission’s structure, however, is likely to take considerably longer.
Speaking in July to a small group of journalists, including POLITICO, Serafin acknowledged that structural reforms would be closely tied to negotiations on the EU’s next long-term budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, which will determine how EU spending is organized from 2028 to 2034.
He indicated at the time that he did not expect decisions on major structural changes before those budget negotiations are concluded.
For now, Day’s findings will provide another input into Serafin’s final proposals, bringing von der Leyen one step closer to deciding how far she wants to go in reshaping the institution she leads.

In Odesa, firefighters were tackling a blaze at a private industrial facility when Russian forces struck the same location twice more, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. Emergency crews remained at the impact sites on Monday morning to extinguish fires, assess structural damage and restore services

Geneva to offer free home delivery of groceries to elderly
Following a trial phase, the Swiss city of Geneva is making its free home grocery delivery service a permanent feature for people aged 65 and over. This service will now also be available to recipients of a care allowance.
These people can enjoy free delivery of their shopping once a week. Launched in the summer of 2025, the pilot scheme for free home delivery of groceries has been a resounding success, with an average of 260 deliveries made each month, the Department for Social Cohesion and Solidarity (DCSS) said on Monday.
The beneficiaries, currently numbering 300, have an average age of 79.
Building on this positive outcome, the DCSS has decided to make this initiative a permanent service, whilst expanding the group of beneficiaries. The aim remains the same: to promote independence, mobility and social connections, while making everyday shopping easier.

Deliveries are made by electric bicycle by the Genèveroule association. Purchases can be made at all food markets as well as in all Migros supermarkets located in the city. Deliveries are available from Monday to Saturday, limited to two bags weighing a maximum of 20 kilos.

France: Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

Macron vows 'strong measures' to combat protests that rocked France
October 26, 2026
The French government is set to announce a series of "strong measures" to assuage protests which have rocked France in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
Speaking in the southern city of Marseille, Macron warned that fresh demonstrations planned for this coming Saturday were "risky" and said that protest routes would remain outside city centers in order to protect public order.
France braces for 'lively' Halloween
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told broadcaster BFM that he was expecting further disturbances on October 31.
"Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively," he said. "We expect it to be complicated again."
Prior to Macron's arrival in Marseille, the Elysee Palace said the president intended to "pay tribute to and thank the internal security forces that helped restore republican order" in France's second-largest city where protesters briefly stormed the city hall on October 17.
He acknowledged that French authorities had "not anticipated at all" the scale of demonstrations which descended into widespread violence in looting in several major cities, leading to suggestions the state had lost control of the streets.
Macron: 'Social media is damaging our democracies'
The French president also highlighted the role of social media in the protests, saying the online networks were "damaging our democracies" by "bringing young and not-so-young people to places where criminal acts, attacks and looting were taking place."
He described social media as "tools for mobilizing the worst impulses."
While Macron admitted that French security forces underestimated the extent to which "extreme left forces" would meet up "so early in the day" on October 17, Interior Minister Nunez highlighted the phenomenon of organized far-right mobs confronting left-wing activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out to defend businesses," he told BFM.
"In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organized formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A presidential aide said Macron wanted to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect."
The president said that curfews enabled relative order to be maintained during last Saturday's protests (October 24), when authorities also deployed 70,000 police officers across the country, making 1,435 arrests.
"The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong," government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio.
France: Macron acknowledges 'legitimate' student demands
Nevertheless, President Macron also said he had instructed his government, led by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, to "respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement."
He said the government will soon announce several "concrete and huge" measures aimed at addressing student concerns over education and university admissions, following a nationwide consultation with high school and university student representatives.
"There are demands that must be heard and answered," confirmed government spokeswoman Bregeon.
"But to answer them, there is a prerequisite: a return to calm. We cannot have a functioning social dialogue in a climate of violence such as the one we experienced a week ago."
Edited by: Alex Berry

Elections in Israel: Can Netanyahu Hold on to Power?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:51:21 UTC
22:51:21 KST

Israelis will elect a new parliament next Tuesday. The main issues in the campaign are foreign and security policy, mistakes regarding the 2023 Hamas attack, military service for ultra-Orthodox Haredi Jews, and high inflation. The right-wing religious bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the more moderate forces led by former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces Gadi Eisenkot are neck-and-neck in the polls.
Opposition overtakes PM on the right
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Many of Netanyahu’s opponents share his worldview, political scientist Sergei Medvedev explains on Facebook (Russia) :
“The opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot has a slight lead in the polls. ... Nevertheless, the election is taking place on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s terms. The key leaders of the opposition bloc have adopted Netanyahu’s worldview on a number of key issues and have even shifted further to the right than he has. ... The majority of Israeli Jews now see the world as Netanyahu has long viewed it. This is Netanyahu’s great victory. But it is matched by his great defeat: much of the world now sees Israel as the residents of the Gaza Strip do.”
No healing without facing the past
To move forward, Israel must first come to terms with the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, La Libre Belgique (Belgium) argues:
“It is precisely in view of these painful wounds that Israeli voters will have to make their choice on Tuesday. Not in the hope of healing this or that wound by any means necessary, but in order to set their country on the path to genuine recovery. ... Three years on, Netanyahu is still refusing to allow a state commission to be set up to clarify political responsibility for the events of 7 October. ... Yet every Israeli has the right to know what led to that fateful day in October. No society can look calmly toward the future if it turns a blind eye to its past.”
Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
Display of direct access to Washington
According to military expert Alexandru Grumaz writing in Adevărul (Romania), Monday’s surprise visit by US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was aimed at helping Netanyahu score points with his voters:
“The fact that the US secretary of defence came to hold talks with him at a military base – eight days before the election – reinforces the image of a prime minister who has direct access to the decision-makers in Washington. For voters, the message is easy to understand: a change of government would also mean replacing the very person who maintains those relationships just when the country is in a dangerous phase. This is a powerful election argument, even if the partnership between two states should not depend on who is leading them.”
Even small changes are important
TVNet (Latvia) explains why a change of government does not necessarily mean a change of course:
“Overall, it’s clear that Netanyahu’s departure would not automatically mean that Israel is prepared to end the wars or support the Palestinians’ right to their own state. Many voters want a more responsible government but are still in favour of military operations. A victory for the opposition cannot therefore be interpreted as a clear demand for a change of course in relations with the Palestinians and other neighbours. Nevertheless, even small changes would be important for both sides.”
Last stop before the abyss
The Israelis must use their votes to stop Netanyahu, urges Le Temps (Switzerland):
“In recent years, Israel has undergone a fundamental transformation: it is a country governed by a prime minister who is under investigation by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity, and which finds itself in a state of open war with multiple neighbours in the region. ... Tens of thousands of Israelis have already fled the country. ... Netanyahu’s potential departure would certainly not be enough to change the country from the bottom up, however urgent that may be. But at the very least it could allow Israelis to halt their rapid descent into the abyss.”
Bellicose slogans poisoning the campaign
The situation may well deteriorate futher, El Periódico (Spain) de Catalunya fears:
“Israel’s founding Father David Ben-Gurion is said to have remarked: ‘The Land of Israel is our homeland, and we shall defend it with all our might.’ ... This bellicose mindset still prevails today – the idea that the first defeat will drive the Israelis into the sea, and it is poisoning the campaign slogans – against a backdrop of an exhausted Palestinian society, an uncontrolled energy crisis and uncertainty hanging over the entire region, from Egypt to Iran. ... This already toxic atmosphere could deteriorate further if the election result prolongs the formation of a government amid a sea of irreconcilable parties. Things are liable to get worse.”
Outcry of the ultra-Orthodox
According to the Kronen Zeitung (Austria), the compulsory conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews is making waves:
“With just under a week to go before the elections a campaign bombshell has exploded, stirring up emotions like hardly any other issue: the privileges enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox (known as Haredim), particularly when it comes to compulsory military service. Israel is at war and there is a shortage of soldiers. Now the army has made an example of them. It intercepted a flight bringing young Haredim returning home from New York at Tel Aviv airport. Two coaches were waiting outside: the one on the right to take them to collect their uniforms, the one on the left to take them to a military prison. An outcry from the Haredim ensued. For years their parties – as sought-after coalition partners – have been extorting precious privileges. ... The Haredim have become a test of faith in the truest sense of the word.”

Siher 'capable of developing revolutionary strategy'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:50:56 CET
22:50:56 KST

Youssef Siher, a 30.year-old 
Italian researcher and freelance journalist with Moroccan roots
who has been accused of being the mastermind behind the shocking
rioting and looting that took place in Milan on the weekend of
October 17, is capable of developing a revolutionary strategy, 
prosecutors said Monday in their arguments in favour of his
being remanded in custody at a hearing Tuesday.
                                    
Siher, detained by order of the Milan Public Prosecutor's Office
for allegedly being the mastermind behind the social media
channel 'Movimento 17 ottobre' ('October 17th Movement'),
reportedly possessed a level of technical expertise that would
have enabled him to "develop a revolutionary strategy."
This is one of the points highlighted by prosecutors in their
request to validate the detention and impose pre-trial
incarceration—a request based on the assessment that there is a
risk not only of the individual fleeing, but also of him
reoffending.
                                    
In the request to validate the detention and impose a
precautionary jail measure—filed by prosecutor Francesca Crupi
of the counter-terrorism department, who is coordinating the
investigation alongside Chief Prosecutor Marcello Viola—it is
noted that Siher holds a "prominent profile within activist
circles."
He demonstrated "particular skill" by managing, in just a few
days, to build a social media group with nearly 9,000
followers—most of whom are inclined to engage in "criminal
conduct against public order."
Furthermore, regarding the risk of reoffending, he reportedly
possesses a "command of digital tools capable of developing a
revolutionary strategy," including the drafting of statements
designed to "gather thousands of people in public squares."
The instructions provided to users point to a "clear strategic
design," as the designated meeting points were chosen
specifically "to evade law enforcement oversight."
On Saturday, following intervention by investigators, the social
media channels were shut down; consequently, the previously
announced "instructions"—which included the names of specific
squares in Milan where participants were to gather—were never
disseminated.
                                    
No trace of these instructions has yet been found during the
digital forensic searches conducted on Siher's laptop.

Sybiha criticizes idea of ​​nominating Orbán for UN Secretary-General
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:50:20 EET
22:50:20 KST

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha has criticized a proposal to nominate former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as a candidate for the position of UN Secretary-General.
"I am certain that Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions. We can share with the rest of the world our great experience of taking him out for coffee at the right moment," Sybiha said on X.
As previously reported, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump proposed that Orbán put forward his candidacy, anticipating support for this initiative from Russia and China. Sources within the U.S. State Department noted that the concurrence of the USA, Russia, and China within the UN Security Council would have a decisive impact on the selection process; however, the other two permanent members of the Security Council—the United Kingdom and France—might oppose this candidacy, as they also hold veto power.

Russia Says Ukraine Has Repeatedly Struck Oleshky With Artillery, Drones Ahead of Local Ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:50:09 UTC
22:50:09 KST

Russia's Defense Ministry on Monday accused Ukraine of repeatedly striking the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine with artillery and drones ahead of a planned local ceasefire this week, something it said had prevented the delivery of food and medicine and stopped people from leaving.
Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed to a ceasefire in Oleshky that would go into effect on Oct. 27, allowing for the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Russia's Defense Ministry said in a statement on Monday that Ukraine had struck the town 18 times with artillery fire and carried out more than 120 drone attacks on it and the main roads around it in the week since Oct. 19.
Reuters could not independently verify that assertion, and there was no immediate response from Ukraine, which has in the past accused Russia of not letting aid in or people out of the town.
Also on Monday, the Kremlin said that the local humanitarian ceasefire agreed for Oleshky with the United States' help could set a precedent for similar ceasefires elsewhere in Ukraine.
The ceasefire comes as residents of the town, controlled by Russian forces since February 2022 and located close to the front line, have reported a deepening food crisis, with both sides accusing each other of blocking supplies.

Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:50 UTC
22:48:50 KST

Egypt’s parliament has authorised the country’s military to provide support for Saudi Arabia’s defence, lawmakers and local media reported, potentially bringing Cairo closer to a regional conflict intensified by attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militia.
President Abdel Fattah el Sisi asked parliament last week to approve military assistance if Riyadh requests help defending itself against the Houthis, whose operations threaten Saudi territory and the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait, a vital shipping passage linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and access to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The parliamentary authorisation comes as attacks on Saudi Arabia have disrupted aviation and oil exports, raising concerns over regional security and international trade routes.
Cairo draws a line around its military role
Egypt has repeatedly condemned Iranian and Iran-backed attacks on Gulf countries but has not publicly joined direct combat in the current conflict.
Sisi has indicated that any Egyptian support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks inside Yemen.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh last Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Following the visit, Abdelatty said Cairo supported exploring “every opportunity” to resolve the Yemen conflict through diplomacy.
Egypt’s potential involvement would mark a significant development given its military capabilities and strategic position along the Red Sea.
The country has also been considering joining a mutual defence pact involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, signed in August.
Abdelatty said earlier this month that Egyptian membership remained “under serious consideration.”
A history of involvement in Yemen
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in March 2015, primarily as a naval partner tasked with protecting Red Sea shipping lanes.
Cairo sent warships, pledged air support and deployed around 800 ground troops, although its direct combat role remained limited.
The country has a difficult history of military intervention in Yemen, having suffered heavy costs during its involvement in the 1960s. It has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia remains a key political and financial partner for Cairo, providing billions of dollars in assistance, central bank deposits and energy supplies during Sisi’s presidency.
Red Sea security raises regional stakes
The latest escalation has added another volatile front to the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, have attacked targets including Riyadh’s international airport and Saudi oil giant Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The conflict also threatens maritime traffic through the Bab al Mandab Strait, a strategic chokepoint for shipping travelling between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Any sustained disruption could affect routes serving the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt have stepped up security discussions as the fighting intensifies. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea.
The extent of any Egyptian military support will depend on Saudi Arabia’s requests and how Cairo balances its security commitments with efforts to prevent further regional escalation.

Vučić’s Defeat Is Not Yet a Victory for Serbia’s European Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:30 UTC
22:48:30 KST

Aleksandar Vučić has lost the election, and Ukraine now has good reason to take a close look at who has won. For Serbia’s citizens, worn down by 14 years of rule under the former president’s Serbian Progressive Party, the Student List’s victory offers grounds for hope that they will finally be able to hold those who govern them to account.
For Ukrainians defending their country against Russian aggression every day, it also matters what the winners intend to do with the relationship Belgrade has built with Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
With 98.8 percent of votes counted, the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy (CeSID), an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, and Ipsos, the international polling company, project that the Student List will take around 140 of parliament’s 250 seats, enough to form a government on its own.
In a country where party membership has for years opened the doors of state institutions, that result matters enormously. The deaths of 16 people when the canopy of Novi Sad railway station collapsed turned a demand for accountability into a revolt against the way the country was governed. Citizens have every right to expect courts free from political pressure and close public scrutiny of how the state spends their money.
The scale of that change makes it all the more important to read carefully what the winners say about the world. The Student List brings together professors, doctors and other public figures chosen by students to represent them, yet there are no students among its candidates. Some very old political convictions sit alongside its youthful symbolism, particularly regarding Russia, Kosovo and Europe. That gives Moscow an opening to preserve its influence after the defeat of the man it has dealt with for so many years.
Serbia’s Student Movement Ousts Longtime Leader in Parliament Poll
In these pages in August, I strongly supported Vučić’s decision to receive Volodymyr Zelensky in Belgrade. I stand by that position after his electoral defeat. Ties with a country defending itself against aggression retain their value after the politicians who built them leave office. Were we to undo every sound decision a government had made simply because its author had lost an election, Serbia’s foreign policy interests would endure no longer than an election campaign.
Vučić and Zelensky established regular contact and a working relationship that allowed them to discuss practical cooperation despite the deep differences between Belgrade and Kyiv over Moscow. After Vučić’s visits to Odesa in 2025 and Kyiv in July this year, Zelensky was officially welcomed in Belgrade on August 8. Their talks covered energy, railways, trade and Ukraine’s reconstruction. Each endorsed the other country’s European aspirations, and Serbia reaffirmed its respect for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
Those talks have been accompanied by concrete aid. By February 2024, Serbia had allocated €3 million for Ukrainian children and €1.5 million for internally displaced people, sent 14 trucks carrying humanitarian aid and donated ambulances. It also sent equipment to help restore the electricity grid. In August this year, the Ukrainian presidency confirmed a further €2 million for the energy sector. For a country whose power stations and grid are under systematic Russian attack, such support has an immediate practical value.
There is also a military dimension, which Belgrade has spent years describing in guarded diplomatic language. As far back as June 2024, the Financial Times reported an estimate that around €800 million worth of Serbian ammunition had reached Ukraine through intermediaries since the invasion began. These were commercial exports via third countries. This year, Christopher Hill, the former US ambassador to Belgrade, described American support for the purchase of that ammunition and said those involved in Belgrade knew who the end user was.
Vučić’s policy towards Russia provided ample grounds for serious criticism, from his refusal to impose sanctions to his attendance at Putin’s parade in Moscow. His visit to Odesa ended with his refusal to sign a joint declaration calling for increased pressure on Russia. Even so, Ukrainian diplomacy managed to secure tangible benefits from that contradictory relationship. Zelensky had a duty to seek help wherever he could obtain it, including in Belgrade.
Parts of the Serbian opposition judged his visit chiefly by how much it might benefit Vučić. Srđan Milivojević, leader of the Democratic Party, which backed the Student List, argued that Vučić was using Zelensky to signal his usefulness to Berlin, expecting it in return to accept whatever election result he declared. This reduced the visit of a president whose country was under attack to a weapon in a domestic political feud, leaving Ukraine’s interests almost entirely out of the picture.
Milivojević is fully entitled to doubt Vučić’s motives. But I also expect a politician who presents his party as pro-European to recognize Ukraine’s needs. Zelensky is answerable to people who need ammunition, medicines and electricity, and every meeting that can secure such support is justified by his country’s needs. To demand that he tailor his diplomatic contacts to the mood of the Serbian opposition would reveal how little we understand the responsibilities of a president whose country is at war.
A protest letter signed by a hundred intellectuals in response to the visit displayed even more open hostility. Its signatories declared Zelensky chiefly responsible for the war, denied that Russia was the aggressor and warned that his visit threatened Serbia’s relations with Russia. That position effectively grants Moscow the right to decide whom Belgrade may receive. Appeals to Serbian dignity end, on this reasoning, in acceptance of Russian tutelage over Serbian diplomacy.
By that logic, the Ukrainian president should be held responsible both for the war Putin started and for the discomfort his visit causes Putin’s admirers. Ukrainians are expected to understand Serbia’s historical traumas, Russia’s security demands and other people’s electoral needs, while their own right to survive is subjected to endless political qualifications. It is hard to imagine greater moral arrogance than demanding that a people under bombardment spare the feelings of those who justify bombing them.
The Student List’s representatives must now show what approach to Ukraine they intend to turn into state policy. Their campaign statement of September 30 explicitly pledged that Serbia would continue to reject sanctions against Russia. University professor Radomir Saičić, a member of the Serbian Academy and one of the Student List’s most prominent figures, advocated “productive relations with Russia” during the campaign, invoking historical ties and energy needs. For Kyiv, those positions matter more than photographs of celebrations on Belgrade’s streets.
Historical ties deserve respect, and energy dependence demands serious efforts to reduce it. When used as permanent excuses for giving in to Moscow, they become instruments through which Russia maintains its advantage. The new government needs to explain what Serbia gains by making its European future dependent on the Kremlin’s mood, and how far it is prepared to limit cooperation with Ukraine for the sake of that relationship.
Invoking Kosovo makes that choice particularly difficult to defend. Ukraine has not recognized its independence, maintaining a position Belgrade regards as essential to its national interests. Russia, meanwhile, occupies Ukrainian territory and seeks to redraw borders by military force. Politicians who demand that the world respect Serbia’s territorial integrity have an added obligation to uphold the same principle for Ukraine, including Crimea and the other occupied regions.
The question for the winners is how much of the sovereignty they demand for Serbia they are prepared to recognize for Ukraine. The right to choose a government and determine a country’s future is the very basis of their electoral victory. Ukrainians are defending precisely that right against a state that denies their country’s existence. It would be a bitter outcome if politicians brought to office by citizens who had freed themselves from fear showed more sympathy for Putin’s demands than for the people he is subjecting to violence.
There is also a very practical question: who in the new majority will decide the course of those relations? Will ministers have the political backing to continue cooperating with Kyiv when the nationalist wing of their alliance objects? Will decisions on exports, humanitarian aid and diplomatic contacts serve Serbia’s interests, or the need to keep the peace among people who, until yesterday, were united by their opposition to Vučić?
The Kremlin can exploit precisely these divisions. All it needs to do is raise the political cost of every decision that helps Ukraine, present it as a betrayal of friendship with Russia and provoke disputes within the new government. Delaying contracts, halting deliveries or withdrawing from joint projects could then be presented as temporary concessions made to preserve unity. Ukrainians and Serbian citizens alike would bear the consequences, while Moscow secured the outcome it wanted.
For the pro-European members of the winning alliance, this is where they must face the responsibilities they could avoid during the campaign. They will have to state what cooperation with Ukraine they support and which decisions they regard as unacceptable. Invoking the movement’s diversity will quickly lose its force once they are voting on budgets, appointing ministers and making commitments to other countries. Every concession to Russian interests will then carry their names and be backed by their votes.
I expect Moscow to use Serbia’s relations with Ukraine to test how much influence it can exert over the new government in Belgrade. Serbia now has an opportunity to make a democratic change of government the basis for greater independence in its foreign policy, and its new representatives have a strong enough mandate to take responsibility for that choice.
Ukrainians deserve to see that independence exercised in Serbia’s dealings with them as well. Their president must be welcome in Belgrade even when his visit displeases Moscow and offers no electoral advantage to his Serbian hosts. If, after a victory won on the promise of a freer Serbia, the Ukrainian president finds his scope for cooperation with the country curtailed, Vladimir Putin will have won a share of that victory. Responsibility for that outcome will lie with those who promised their citizens a free country, then allowed a foreign regime waging a war of aggression to set the limits of its foreign policy.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Türkiye plans $100 billion investment in power grids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:07 UTC
22:48:07 KST

Türkiye’s National Energy 2040 strategy envisages about $100 billion in investment in electricity transmission and distribution networks, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said on Oct. 26.
The strategy will be unveiled in Istanbul on Nov. 5, Bayraktar told an electricity distribution industry event in Ankara.
He said the spread of electric vehicles, greater use of electricity in industrial production, and growth in artificial intelligence and data centers would increase electricity demand and change consumption patterns. Expanding solar and wind capacity would also require networks to adapt.
“We cannot assess the energy transition solely in terms of investment in power plants,” Bayraktar said.
Transmission and distribution networks, storage capacity, digital technologies and system management capabilities needed to be developed together, he added.
Bayraktar also called for wider use of domestically developed software in electricity distribution systems and stronger protection against cyberattacks.
Electricity now accounts for 21 percent of Türkiye’s final energy consumption, up from 15 percent in 2002, he said. Its share has reached 30 percent in industry and 33 percent in buildings.
Greater electrification would help improve energy efficiency, expand the use of domestic and renewable resources, and reduce dependence on energy imports, Bayraktar said.
Strengthening electricity grids will be a priority on Türkiye’s agenda for COP31, the U.N. climate conference in Antalya on Nov. 9–20. Bayraktar said Ankara would seek greater international cooperation on modernizing distribution networks, integrating renewable energy and financing grid investment.

Lithuania hopes Latvia government change will unblock Rail Baltica project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

Vilnius hoped a change of government in Latvia would help unblock the Rail Baltica railway project that has been plagued by delays, Lithuanian Transport Minister Juras Taminskas said on Monday.
"The Estonians are executing the project, and like us, they are keeping to the deadlines. We face more challenges with the Latvians, but I believe that with the change of government, and if this prime minister remains prime minister in Latvia, which seems likely, the project should move past the deadlock there," Taminskas told reporters in Vilnius on Monday.
Following an agreement among the Baltic states to extend the deadline for completing the first phase of Rail Baltica to 2034, Taminskas reiterated that Lithuania remained committed to its plan to finish the project by 2030.
"There is not much flawed work on the Lithuanian side. There are certain alleged violations in construction committed by contractors. Legal remedies are being addressed by LTG Infra, and whatever was improperly built will have to be fixed or rebuilt," Taminskas said.
The minister said rising project costs were not unexpected, as delays had turned it into a decade-long undertaking.
Two weeks ago, the leaders of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Poland urged the European Union to ensure adequate funding.
In Lithuania, 114 kilometres of the main line are under construction. Across the three Baltic states, nearly half of the railway line is either under construction or ready for construction. Poland recently approved the construction of an almost 95-kilometre section between Bialystok and Elk.
The first phase, which will connect the Baltic states to Europe with a single track, is estimated to cost 15.3 billion euros across the three countries. Installing a second track could raise the total project cost to 23.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica will connect Tallinn, Parnu, Riga, Panevėžys, Kaunas, Vilnius and Warsaw.
The railway line in Lithuania will stretch 392 kilometres.

With Regional Tensions High, Mecca Alliance Partners Meet In Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:43:05 UTC
22:43:05 KST

Iran and three members of a regional mutual-defense pact have agreed to continue talks after their first meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported.
Iranian officials met with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey, the signatories to the Mecca Defense Alliance on October 26, to defuse tensions in the region.
The sides “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation...including on regional peace and security,” state television said.
The meeting came as the US-Iran war and increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have left the region reeling and are impacting global flows of oil and other cargo.
'Last-Ditch Effort'
Ahead of the meeting, a senior security official in Islamabad told RFE/RL that one of the main points of the meeting was to try to convince Iran to use its influence over Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia. The official said the alliance countries were prepared to raise the prospect of closer Saudi-Israeli security cooperation as leverage.
“The key question is why Iran should comply? The answer is that Saudi Arabia may ask for support from Israel and that will potentially require them to join the Abraham Accords,” said the official.
The accords, signed in 2020, normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
“Since Turkey has already diplomatic relations with Israel, the trio might place this scenario on the table should Tehran refuse to rein in the Houthis,” said the official. While Iran may comply by using its influence over the Houthis, the official added that it is unlikely that the regime would soften its stance on negotiations with the United States over the war.
Islamabad-based analyst Azaz Syed said the US-Iran conflict would be just as important during the meeting amid fears Washington is preparing to renew its military attacks on Iran.
Pakistan's powerful army chief, Asim Munir, was in Tehran last week where he reportedly delivered a "last warning" to the Iranian government.
“Apparently, this was a last-ditch effort to convince the Iranians” to come to a negotiated settlement with the United States, Syed told RFE/RL.
“The three partners will ask for an end to Houthi attacks, of course, but the key message is the broader settlement.”
Hamidreza Azizi, senior analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, said that the meeting in Tehran was a last-minute attempt to prevent another escalation.
“The immediate priority seems to be finding a way to prevent the resumption of war between Iran and the United States,” Azizi told RFERL.
Azizi said the October 26 meeting was essentially a continuation of diplomatic efforts already under way, and the timing suggests that regional countries are increasingly concerned that these efforts may be running out of time.
The Houthis, allies of Tehran who primarily operate from Yemen, have intensified their missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil infrastructure at a time when energy transit in the Middle East has already been curtailed by the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that normally sees around one-fifth of the world's oil and gas flows transported through it.
Earlier this month, Houthi rebels attacked Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, killing 13 people and wounding more than 300. The rebels have also warned airlines against using Saudi airspace.
Saudi Arabia has in turn launched strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen.
The conflicts have shed light on the complex diplomatic relations between nations across the Middle and Near East.
The Mecca Alliance enshrines a collective security arrangement modeled on NATO's Article 5, stating that "any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all."
Iran-Pakistan Tensions
The meeting also came amid already heightened tensions between Iran and Pakistan after Islamabad closed two border crossings between its Balochistan Province and Iran’s Sistan-Baluchistan Province.
Pakistan has also introduced changes in its E-form procedure, a digital declaration authorizing the tracking of foreign currency remittances, for Iranian exports coming into the country.
Sources say Islamabad has also suspended operating clearance for Mahan Air, the Iranian airline believed to have links with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). Iranian and Pakistani authorities have neither admitted nor denied the reports.
The Iranian side, in reaction, stopped the export of Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) to Pakistan causing manifold increase in gas prices for domestic and commercial consumers. Pakistan imports around 7,000 metric tons of LPG every day from Iran.
"The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal," said Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly in a social media post.
Commenting on the closure of Iran-Pakistan border crossings, Tehran envoy to Islamabad Reza Amiri Moghadam said in a social media post that consultations with the Pakistani side are under way to address the issue of cross-border trade.
Moghadam said several hundred trucks carrying LPG have crossed the Rimdan border into Gabd on the Pakistani side. However, despite having remained there for several weeks, these trucks have yet to be unloaded or cleared up, further complicating the movement of goods and the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
Significant Step
Rabia Akhtar, a professor of international relations at the University of Lahore, said the immediate concern among the three partners was to prevent the current confrontation from escalating further.
“Nobody at that table really benefits from another regional war,” Akhtar told RFE/RL, who added that if the participants can establish some understanding on restraint -- particularly regarding Saudi security, the Houthis, and further escalation with Iran -- that would already be a meaningful outcome.
“So I would see this as an attempt at regional crisis management rather than the birth of a new security architecture. And in the present circumstances, even that would be quite consequential,” Akhtar said.
Azizi of the International Crisis Group said the meeting could help reduce tensions, at least temporarily, by keeping channels of communication open.
“But the main problem remains unresolved: Iran wants credible security guarantees against renewed attacks, while the regional mediators have limited ability to influence Washington's decisions.”

The data center in Sasovo housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which are used to train neural networks. The most powerful of the two, Chervonenkis, ranked 19th among the world’s top 500 supercomputers in 2021, according to the independent science-focused outlet T-invariant.

Minister: Defense plan decisions must be reviewed, light fighter jets eyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Minister: Defense plan decisions must be reviewed, light fighter jets eyed
Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) told ERR that Estonia's 10-year defense development plan needs improvements in air and maritime defense.
This includes weighing up the procurement of light fighter jets for the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF).
The latest status of the national defense development plan was that it had reached the Government Office for approval, but you nonetheless found some changes needed to be made. Is that right?
As far as I know, the 10-year national defense development plan was issued by the Ministry of Defense back in the spring, if not early spring. And during that time, there have indeed been some changes in air defense, which had already begun to emerge in the war in Ukraine last year; the picture is now likely clearer, and for that reason alone. This is not a question of my having reviewed anything, but rather the Defense Forces as a whole have become better informed, and some things have also developed further based on the example of the war in Ukraine. So these changes stem from that.
The latest status of the national defense development plan was that it had reached the Government Office for approval, but you nonetheless found some changes needed to be made. Is that right? As I understand it, the plan was in fairly final form at the Government Office, awaiting approval alongside the state budget strategy (RES), and upon becoming minister, drawing on the commander's advice, you reopened it and saw things needed to be added and changed?
As far as I know, the 10-year national defense development plan was issued by the Ministry of Defense back in the spring, if not early spring. And during that time, there have indeed been some changes in air defense, which had already begun to emerge in the war in Ukraine last year; the picture is now likely clearer, and for that reason alone. This is not a question of my having reviewed anything, but rather the Defense Forces as a whole have become better informed, and some things have also developed further based on the example of the war in Ukraine. So these changes stem from that.
So, keeping the shipping lanes in the Gulf of Finland open and procuring additional air defense capabilities – most recently, you spoke about the need to acquire light fighter jets. Is that right?
For us this is not just the shipping lanes in the Gulf of Finland, but the sea routes toward the west as a whole. The Gulf of Finland is actually a secondary issue in that respect. But without these maritime connections, we would certainly die out very quickly – 80 percent of our trade currently takes place by sea, and the same is true for the Finns. So we must look at this as a whole together with our allies, to ensure that these connections remain under our control at all times.
Now, as for air defense and air-to-air defense, meaning those same jet aircraft, what Russia has come up with over the past year is essentially cheap cruise missiles, or jet-powered drones. And one of the most effective means currently in use against them is aircraft, jet aircraft. Whether we take the route of acquiring light jets such as the Hawk, L-39 or something similar, or instead look toward unmanned jets, is another matter. But I do think we should consider how to bring our air-to-air defense capability into play, so to speak. However, resources are limited, and we have to consider what we would have to sacrifice to do all of this.
In your assessment, is acquiring light fighter jets a genuinely realistic prospect at present? Are you proposing that this be added to the national defense development plan and that the necessary funding be found?
I think that this is realistic. But it is not only realistic, it may also be needed. How else are we to counter such threats? However, to do that, we will first need to review the broader air defense picture. What do we want to develop there, what do we have, and how would these aircraft, however many there might be, fit into it? It also depends on the circumstances: imagine that we are in a full-scale war. What airfields or runways would we be able to use for this? Maybe at some point we would no longer have them, so then the question arises of where the aircraft would take off from, or whether we would have to use something else, some other locations. And finally, how many of these aircraft should there be, at what point would we use them, and where would they operate? All of this is not yet entirely clear to me.
When did the commander of the Defense Forces provide his additional input on the national defense development plan?
I think it was a few weeks ago. I cannot say exactly right now. But it was during my time as minister, meaning within the past month. And it was sent to the minister of defense, not the Government Office.
And what did he recommend? Is that a matter between the two of you, or can you make it public?
That is actually where the issue of jets comes from, at least in part. But it also touched on other matters.
And now, as I understand it, you are due to give a presentation on this to the National Defense Council, which reports to the president?
Yes, I will be discussing these issues at the National Defense Council. Not in the form of proposals yet, but I will raise the issues we are working on. That said, I am not ready to present concrete proposals.
When might those concrete proposals be ready?
I really cannot say right now, but sometime this year.

The signing ceremony was attended by Head of SIBAT Brig.-Gen. (res.) Yair Kulas, Ambassador to Cyprus Shuli Davidovich, Israel Shipyards CEO Eitan Zucker, and Rafael's Head of Naval Warfare Systems Directorate Ran Tavor.
"This agreement marks another important step in strengthening the operational capabilities of the Cyprus Naval Command and enhancing its capacity to respond to maritime security challenges," the ministry said.
"The new OPV, alongside the upgraded OPV IOANNIDES, will support expanded patrol, surveillance, and search-and-rescue missions."
The ministry added that the agreement reflected the two countries' commitment to regional stability.
Israel and Cyprus have expanded their defense cooperation in recent years, including naval security, military exercises, and defense procurement. Cyprus previously acquired the OPV Ioannides from Israel Shipyards, providing a foundation for the latest agreement, which includes upgrades to the existing vessel.
The two countries also cooperate with Greece on regional security matters, including exercises and military coordination in the eastern Mediterranean.
Cyprus received its first Israeli-built offshore patrol vessel, Commodore Andreas Ioannides, in 2018. The vessel was equipped with Rafael Typhoon naval weapon stations. Cyprus has also acquired Israeli defense equipment including the Barak MX air-defense system and Spike LR2 anti-tank missiles, according to a report by Cyprus Mail.
The value of the new naval agreement was not disclosed in the ministry's statement, although Calcalist previously reported that the proposed package was worth approximately $100 million.

Parliament authorized Egypt's military on Monday to provide support to help defend Saudi Arabia, parliamentarians said, and local media reported, a move that could push Cairo directly into the regional conflict that has expanded with intensified attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on the Gulf kingdom.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi had asked parliament last week to approve defending its Gulf Arab ally and the world's biggest oil exporter if Riyadh requests help against the Houthis, whose advances also threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait - a gateway to Egypt's Suez Canal.
Egypt has frequently condemned Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks on Gulf countries but has not publicly engaged in direct combat or joined the Mecca mutual defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey that was signed in August.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said this month that Egyptian membership in the pact remains "under serious consideration."
Egypt joined Saudi-backed anti-Houthi coalition in 2015
Egypt, the Arab world's most populous state with one of the region's largest militaries, joined the Saudi-led coalition in an earlier phase of Yemen's war in March 2015 mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes while pledging air support. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but played only a limited combat role.
Egypt was involved in a costly military intervention in Yemen in the 1960s and has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia is a major political and financial partner of Cairo, providing billions of dollars in aid, deposits at the central bank, and energy supplies under Sisi.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government and the Houthi militia, which controls the capital Sanaa, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming a volatile front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Houthis attack Saudi airport, energy infrastructure
The Houthis have attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports, while aid agencies have warned of worsening conditions in Yemen, already suffering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Abdelatty and Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad traveled to Riyadh on Wednesday to deliver a letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen. Abdelatty said after that visit that Cairo advocates exploring "every opportunity" to resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically.
The Saudi crown prince visited Sisi in Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea after the fighting in Yemen reignited.
