German business confidence rises in October despite global economic risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:41:37 UTC
22:41:37 KST

Germany's ifo Business Climate Index rose in October, driven by stronger manufacturing confidence, although higher energy prices and interest rates continue to pose risks to the economic recovery.
Germany's closely watched ifo Business Climate Index increased to 90.2 points in October, up from 89.9 points in September, according to data released on Monday.
The ifo Business Climate Index is a highly regarded early indicator of economic developments in Germany, published on a monthly basis by the Munich-based Institute for Economic Research.
"German economic resilience continues as the Ifo index has increased for the sixth consecutive month," wrote Carsten Brzeski, head of global macro at ING, in a research note.
Despite companies being slightly less satisfied with their current business situation, the overall outlook suggests that Germany's economic recovery is continuing.
Manufacturing sector sees improvement in confidence
In the manufacturing sector, the index rose significantly, with companies reporting substantial improvements in both their current situation and expectations.
Both indicators returned to positive territory for the first time in more than three years. Incoming orders increased, prompting companies to plan an expansion in production.
In the service sector, business confidence weakened as companies expressed less satisfaction with their current performance. However, expectations improved, with IT service providers performing particularly well.
In trade, the index remained unchanged. Companies were more pessimistic about their current situation, although expectations improved slightly. Overall, the wholesale sector performed better than retail.
In construction, the index rose, with companies reporting greater satisfaction with their current business conditions. Future expectations also improved slightly.
However, significant risks remain for Germany's economic recovery.
"Despite this hope, however, clear risks remain: war in the Middle East and the potential for further escalation after the US mid-term elections, with oil prices remaining at elevated levels (or worse), as well as the likely incoming shock of higher gas prices in the current heating season," Brzeski wrote.
Low water levels on key transport routes could also disrupt industrial supply chains and production in the near future.
"The more the economy defies short-term risks, the higher the chances of a surprise growth story are," Brzeski added.
While the latest figures suggest that the economy is showing signs of recovery, economists warn that longer-term growth will depend on addressing structural challenges, including bureaucracy, high energy costs and weak competitiveness.

Fatatu Forest, a hidden natural retreat in northern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:41:31 UTC
22:41:31 KST

Fatatu Forest, a hidden natural retreat in northern Iran
TEHRAN - Tucked away in the rural landscape of northern Iran, Fatatu Forest is a natural attraction in Khomam county, Gilan province, offering visitors a peaceful escape among lush vegetation, wetlands, rice fields and the landscapes of the southern Caspian coast. Recognized for its ecological importance and its surviving Hyrcanian forest vegetation, the woodland holds considerable potential for nature-based tourism, although limited visitor facilities remain a challenge.
Located near Fatatu village, the forest covers approximately 300 hectares. It is among the remaining examples of the Hyrcanian forests, a distinctive forest ecosystem extending along the southern shores of the Caspian Sea. The broader Hyrcanian forest region, which dates back millions of years, was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2019.
Fatatu Forest has also been registered on Iran's National Natural Heritage List, reflecting its environmental significance and the importance of protecting its vegetation and biodiversity.
A tranquil landscape of alder trees
One of the forest's defining features is its dense growth of alder trees, characteristic of the lowland woodlands found along the Caspian coast. Other tree species, including maple and oak, are found in forested areas around Khomam, alongside plant species adapted to the region's humid climate.
The dense vegetation, natural walking routes and quiet surroundings make Fatatu an appealing destination for visitors interested in walking, photography and experiencing the natural environment away from crowded tourist centers.
Seasonal changes add to its appeal. In spring and summer, the forest is marked by fresh foliage and abundant greenery, while autumn brings warmer shades of color to the landscape. The sounds of birds and the cool, humid atmosphere contribute to the area's tranquil character.
Beyond its scenic appeal, the forest serves an important ecological function. Its vegetation provides habitat for wildlife and helps sustain the natural balance of the surrounding landscape. Preserving this environment is therefore essential to any plan to develop tourism in the area.
A walking route towards the Caspian Sea
Fatatu Forest's location is another advantage for travelers. A natural walking route passes through the woodland and surrounding rice fields before reaching the Caspian Sea, offering an opportunity to experience several of Gilan's characteristic landscapes on a single outing.
The route combines the shade of forest trees with open views across rice paddies and the coastal environment. It offers a different perspective on Gilan, a province widely associated with its humid climate, agricultural traditions and green rural scenery.
Visitors can also explore Fatatu village and nearby settlements, where rice fields and traditional rural life form part of the region's appeal. Local products, including rice, tea and traditional foods, provide additional opportunities to experience Gilan's agricultural and culinary heritage.
Fatatu Forest can be incorporated into a broader visit to Khomam, a small town situated about seven kilometers from Rasht, the capital of Gilan province, and approximately 15 kilometers from Bandar-e Anzali.
The surrounding area offers a variety of rural and natural attractions. Nearby villages provide opportunities to observe traditional architecture, agricultural activities and local crafts. Fashtakeh, in particular, is known for its traditional mat-weaving heritage and was recognized as Iran's first national village associated with mat weaving.
The wider Khomam area also offers access to coastal scenery and wetlands connected to the Anzali Lagoon region. These landscapes complement the forest experience and make the district suitable for travelers interested in combining woodland walks with village visits and rural exploration.
Khomam's relatively short distance from Rasht makes Fatatu Forest a potential option for a day trip for visitors staying in the provincial capital or traveling between Rasht and Bandar-e Anzali.
Tourism potential and conservation challenges
Despite its natural assets, Fatatu Forest remains relatively little known as a tourism destination, and the lack of basic visitor facilities limits its readiness to accommodate larger numbers of travelers.
Speaking to IRNA, Mansour Hadipour, head of the Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism office in Khomam county, has described the forest as a valuable natural area with significant potential for environmental protection and nature-based tourism.
He has said that the local authorities intend to promote Fatatu Forest as a potential tourism investment opportunity at a Gilan investment conference. Possible development concepts include health-oriented tourism that makes use of the area's natural setting, provided such activities comply with environmental regulations.
Hadipour has also highlighted the area's historical potential, saying that modern archaeological studies could help identify previously undocumented evidence of its past.
For travelers seeking a quieter side of Gilan, Fatatu Forest offers an opportunity to experience the province's lowland forest heritage, rural landscapes and proximity to the Caspian coast. Its alder woodland, seasonal colors and walking routes provide a setting for a relaxed excursion, while nearby villages offer a glimpse of the region's agricultural and craft traditions.

From reserve duty to Knesset candidate: Meet B'Yachad's Amir Sturgo - interview
Unknown

2026-10-26

22:41:06 KST

The current Knesset elections are imminent, but with a new race and new parties come new names and faces.
Depending on how this election turns out, these newcomers of today could be the ministers of tomorrow and can help shape the course of Israeli politics going forward.
One such newcomer is Amir Strugo, a candidate on Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad list. What is his story? What brought him to politics?
Strugois the CEO of Aharai, an organization that promotes leadership skills in Israeli youth. A veteran of the Second Lebanon War, he saw combat during the October 7 massacre. Sturgo spent over 450 days on reserve duty.
Today, he lives in the Negev and helps lead B’Yachad party policies on combating crime, particularly in the region he calls home.
Shortly before the elections, we spoke briefly with him to hear his story.
What got you into politics?
After losing 66 Aharai alumni and serving over 450 days in the military reserves, I decided this must be my mission. I view my entry into politics as a continuation of the path I forged in the military, in education, and in civil society.
What made you want to run with B'Yachad?
I believe Bennett possesses the experience and skills required to lead Israel at this critical juncture. B’Yachad is the only party offering detailed action plans to address the root causes of the challenges we face - from the conscription crisis and the collapse of our education system to rampant crime and the erosion of governance (a reality my neighbors and I witness daily in the Negev), and more.
What do you think are the biggest issues in this election?
We must invest in Israel’s social, security, and economic engines of growth. In practical terms, this means implementing the "Revolution for Those Who Serve" - a policy we propose. When we invest in the segment of the public that serves and works, the nation becomes stronger, more secure, and more prosperous.
Conversely, when we invest in draft evasion and educational systems that fail to teach core subjects, the consequences for our national security and economy are predictable.
This is the choice before us.
Why do you think Bennett is the right person to handle them?
Throughout his tenure as minister of education, minister of economy, minister of defense, and prime minister, Bennett has proven his ability to focus on what truly matters and deliver tangible results on the ground - such as the "5-unit" (advanced-level) reform in education, achieving the quietest year in the south in terms of security, and driving down prices in the economy.
Judging by his track record, he has succeeded in every role he has held - both before entering politics, as a businessman and a commander, and since.
There is no substitute for this kind of experience. As someone who served as a military commander and chose to live in a community that integrates both religious and secular residents, unity is important to me - not merely as a slogan, but as a way of life. I see Bennett as a leader capable of uniting all segments of the nation and forging a shared Israeli narrative.
What advice do you have for anyone interested in getting into politics?
Follow your heart and your inner convictions all the way, and do not let peripheral noise hold you back.

UN probe accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:40:00 UTC

UN probe accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank
- UN investigators say Israel has committed “extermination” and other crimes in the West Bank, with “widespread and systematic” attacks on civilians and settler violence.
- The report says Israel still commits genocidal acts in Gaza, urges an end to the occupation, and calls for settlers and settlements to be removed.
- It also says the Palestinian Authority targets dissenters and fails to investigate killings properly, while Israel rejects the findings as “misinformation”.
AI generated
GENEVA – Israel has committed the crime against humanity of extermination in the West Bank, while continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said on Oct 26.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry said Israeli forces had also committed other crimes against humanity and war crimes in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.
The commission, which does not speak for the UN itself, first determined in a September 2025 report that Israel had committed genocide in the war in Gaza following Hamas’ deadly Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel – a finding Israel flatly rejects.
In a new report – which comes the day before Israel’s general election – the investigation found that in the West Bank, through military operations reinforced by sustained settler violence, Israel has waged a “widespread and systematic attack” against civilians.
“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” it said.
Israel’s mission in Geneva said the report was part of the inquiry’s “misinformation campaign to demonise the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.
“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” it said in a statement.
The three-member investigative team was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
South African former High Court judge Navi Pillay, who chaired the investigation until November 2025, won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier in October.
The commission’s new report focused on killings and bodily and mental harm caused by both Israeli and Palestinian security forces since October 2023.
It found that the situation in the West Bank has deteriorated gravely since the Palestinian Islamist group Hamas’s attack from Gaza that month.
‘Unliveable’ conditions of life
The commission found that the Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” West Bank civilians due to the Hamas attack.
“The targeting of Palestinian civilians across different locations in the West Bank indicates a high level of coordination and organised planning and is the product of state policy,” the report said.
The conduct of the Israeli authorities indicates that “they knew and intended settler violence” to be part of the widespread and systematic attack in the West Bank, it added.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unliveable,” said commission chairman Srinivasan Muralidhar.
“Attempting to equate Palestinian statehood with a threat to the existence of Israel is blocking any viable attempts to realise Palestinians’ right to self-determination,” the Indian judge said in a statement.
The report cited cases where the commission concluded that Israeli forces intended to seriously harm and kill civilians, in acts which amount to war crimes including wilful killing.
Findings on genocide
The Hamas attack in October 2023 resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.
Israel’s military offensive, in response, has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is under Hamas authority but whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
“The cases investigated for this report show that the Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza,” the report said.
The inquiry urged Israel to “end the commission of genocide in Gaza” and act immediately on “obligations to prevent and punish genocide and incitement to genocide”.
Israel should “immediately end the unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory”, and remove all settlers and settlements.
PA ‘targets’ dissenters
Turning to the Palestinian Authority, the report said that “Palestinian state violence has targeted and continues to target members of opposing Palestinian armed groups and repress Palestinian civil and political opposition”.
The Palestinian Authority struggles with credibility and legitimacy, and “targets Palestinians who voice dissenting civil and political views... resulting in killings”, it said.
“The Palestinian Authority has also failed to conduct prompt, effective and impartial investigations into incidents of killings.”
There was no immediate reaction from the Palestinian Authority.
The commission is due to present its report to the UN General Assembly in New York on Oct 26. AFP

Ebola: Uganda restricts travel as Nigerian case evacuated to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:39:59 UTC
22:39:59 KST

The Ebola outbreak that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo in May, now the fastest-growing and most widespread on record, has caused nearly 10,000 confirmed cases across Africa.
Nigeria’s only confirmed case in Africa’s latest deadly Ebola outbreak was flown from the capital, Abuja, to Switzerland on Monday. Uganda, which was declared free of the disease in August, tightened its border controls on Sunday in response.
The evacuated patient, a 42-year-old Swiss citizen and wife of an embassy worker based in Abuja, had travelled to Uganda with her husband before returning to Nigeria. She did not visit the DRC and is believed to have contracted the virus in Uganda, Switzerland’s Federal Department of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press on Friday.
Uganda’s Ministry of Health said on 23 October that the patient had no symptoms when she left Uganda, adding that investigations were ongoing to establish when her symptoms began and how she became infected.
Her condition was “much improved, stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline”, Nigeria’s health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said in a post on X. “This does not mean she is not still infectious,” he added.
Nigerian health authorities have identified 53 of the patient’s contacts, including health workers, relatives and household staff. On Sunday, they said they had widened the search for potential cases, tracing a further nine contacts. Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation.
Pate said on Friday that the woman’s infection appeared closely linked to Kenya’s first case, but cautioned that this did not necessarily establish the route of transmission.
This is not the first case where a patient is transported to Europe for treatment.
Since May 2026, three people infected with Ebola linked to the outbreak have been medically evacuated to Europe for specialised care: two to Germany and one to the Netherlands. All three were healthcare or humanitarian workers in affected areas of Congo.
In July, another person was evacuated to the United Kingdom following potential exposure to the virus while treating Ebola patients in Congo.
Travel restrictions in Uganda
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had both travelled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport on 3 October.
The country is reinforcing border controls to stop the spread of the virus and now requires citizens returning from neighbouring the DRC to spend 21 days in quarantine at their own expense, the ministry said.
Anyone who has been in the DRC cannot transit through Uganda, including on chartered flights. Under the new measures, non-essential Congolese travellers will be sent back through the nearest border crossing at their own expense, while those entering illegally face prosecution, the ministry said.
“The end of local transmission does not mean the risk has ended. We share a border with the DRC, where transmission continues, and our communities remain closely connected through trade, travel and family ties,” the Ugandan health ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
“The recent cases involving travellers from the region further underscore the need to remain vigilant.”
Uganda recorded 20 cases, including two deaths. The most recent was confirmed on 21 June. On 27 August, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the end of the Ebola outbreak in Uganda after 42 consecutive days without new cases.
Deadliest outbreak in Congo history
The outbreak that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in May has infected nearly 10,000 people and killed more than 4,700, according to the country’s latest data from 21 October, making it the fastest-growing and most widespread Ebola outbreak on record.
It is now the deadliest outbreak in the DRC’s history, with 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths.
The epicentre is Ituri province, in the north of the country, where 3,298 people have died. The virus has so far spread to seven other provinces.
The outbreak has outrun the response, which has been hampered by instability in the area and the difficulty of reaching some of the worst-affected communities.
The DRC has also reported growing violence against health workers, hindering efforts to slow the virus’s spread. In the latest incident, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured while responding to an Ebola alert, according to the WHO.
Cases have been reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola case at the end of the month and has since recorded two deaths, while seven other patients are being treated in isolation.

Israeli media highlights Egypt’s Rafale deployment as part of broader regional deterrence strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:39:37 UTC
22:39:37 KST

Israeli media have highlighted the deployment of Egyptian Rafale fighter jets on the eastern front, describing the move as part of a broader military strategy aimed at strengthening Egypt’s deterrence capabilities and maintaining operational readiness across multiple regional fronts.
The Israeli platform Ntziv.net reported that Egypt possesses an advanced network of modern airbases, challenging the assumption that its most sophisticated fighter aircraft are positioned toward Israel because of insufficient infrastructure elsewhere in the country.
According to the platform, Egypt’s deployment of modern combat aircraft, particularly the French-made Dassault Rafale, reflects a strategy of multi-front deterrence, strategic independence and regional power projection extending beyond its eastern border.
The report identified Gabal al-Basur Air Base, northwest of Cairo, as the principal operating base for Egypt’s Rafale fleet, noting that it is located well inside Egyptian territory, away from the Sinai Peninsula and the Israeli border.
It emphasised that the Rafale is a multirole fighter aircraft with an operational radius of approximately 2,000 kilometres, allowing it to conduct missions across several strategically important areas without requiring permanent deployment at forward bases.
These areas include Libya to the west, the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Sinai Peninsula.
The platform also pointed to Egypt’s extensive network of operational airbases, including facilities in Mersa Matruh and Sidi Barrani near the Libyan border, as well as Aswan in southern Egypt.
It noted that Cairo has invested billions of dollars in modernizing its air force infrastructure, including the development of Berenice Airbase on the Red Sea coast, a strategic facility designed to accommodate advanced combat aircraft.
The report argued that Egypt’s air force modernization should not be viewed exclusively through the lens of its military relationship with Israel, but rather as part of a wider doctrine of active deterrence and strategic autonomy.
It further suggested that Egypt has sought to diversify its military suppliers to reduce dependence on the United States, particularly given Washington’s restrictions on certain advanced weapons exports intended to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge.
According to the Israeli platform, Egypt’s acquisition of Rafale fighters from France has enabled Cairo to obtain advanced radar and missile capabilities outside the framework of US arms export restrictions.
The report concluded that Egypt’s Rafale fleet and expanding military infrastructure reflect a broader effort to maintain operational flexibility across several regional theaters while strengthening the country’s independent defense capabilities.

Ukraine raises its stalled Patriot request with Washington again after almost a month without Hegseth’s signature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:38:35 UTC
22:38:35 KST

Ukraine has waited almost a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 October. He ordered his team to raise it with Washington again. Two other US holds on Ukraine, on Starlink speeds and intelligence sharing, have been lifted, leaving the interceptors as the last one.
Russia keeps firing ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities and the power grid before winter, and Patriots are the only systems in Ukraine that reliably stop Iskander-M, Kinzhal, and Zircon missiles. Zelenskyy has told EU leaders Ukraine needs 300 interceptors to get through winter, diplomatic sources told Radio Svoboda. The holds came as Washington pressed Kyiv to stop striking Russian refineries, which Trump blames for high US fuel prices before the midterms.
Zelenskyy: almost a month waiting for Hegseth’s signature
Zelenskyy held a meeting on weapons supplies with Ukraine’s defense minister, foreign minister, and commander-in-chief. They reported on interceptors for air defense, above all for Patriot systems. Afterward, Zelenskyy wrote:
“We are working in several directions: with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. In particular, for almost a month we have been waiting for Mr. Hegseth’s signature on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I have instructed the team to discuss this with the American side once again.”
Talks with other countries continue, he added. The meeting also covered preparations for November’s Ramstein meeting of Ukraine’s allies, where Zelenskyy wants decisions already on the table carried out faster.
Allies’ missiles need US approval
Some of the transfers come from friendly countries and need Hegseth’s approval, because the US must sign off on any re-transfer of its missiles, a US official and three people familiar with the matter said on 19 October. Hegseth has neither refused nor approved them.
The Starlink hot potato: Musk points to Trump, Trump points to nobody, then credits Musk with the fix. The speed limit stays
A Ukrainian official said in mid-October that only “a couple” of interceptors were left. Hegseth has said the US wants “our guys” to have “the most possible” interceptors, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted nothing was “being deliberately denied to Ukraine.”
Two of three US holds lifted
In an interview aired on 25 October, Zelenskyy listed three problems from his Oslo talks with the Americans: air defense, Starlink limits, and limits on US intelligence sharing. Full Starlink speeds returned on 24 October, and missile warnings resumed after his 20 October call with Rubio. Progress on Patriot missiles is “very slow,” he said, “slower than the flight of Russian missiles.”
Kyiv has also tried to trade for the missiles. Zelenskyy told US senators he had offered US envoys a 30-day pause in strikes on Russian refineries in return for Patriot interceptors. The envoys showed no openness to the idea.
Trump has called those refinery strikes a disgrace that only pushes oil prices higher. He said it days after striking a deal with Putin to bring Russian diesel back to the US ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November.
Trump treats Ukraine as the weak link to squeeze and wants a visible win partly with US domestic politics in mind, Ukrainian diplomat Oleksandr Khara has argued.

US wants Orban to be next UN chief – WSJ

US wants Orban to be next UN chief – WSJ
The administration of US President Donald Trump is pushing for former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban to become the next UN secretary-general, the Wall Street Journal has reported.
Members of Trump’s team have already reached out to Orban, who is open to the idea but will only run if there is confidence that he can secure the job, the paper said in an article on Sunday.
The US believes that Russia and China would also support the former Hungarian leader, who would be seen as a joint candidate from the three countries, a State Department official told the outlet.
The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expires on December 31. AP reported last week that none of the seven candidates to replace him, including Costa Rica’s Rebecca Greenspan, Guyana’s Carolyn Rodriguez Birkett, and the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi of Argentina, currently have the required support of all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC): China, France, Russia, the UK, and US.
The Trump administration considers Orban to be “the dream MAGA-conservative candidate,” who has the right ideology and knows how to exercise authority, according to the WSJ’s sources.
Orban, who left office in Hungary after 16 years in power this May, used to describe his rule as an “illiberal democracy.” The 63-year-old politician has been a harsh critic of EU’s policies, repeatedly clashing with Brussels over his moves against mass migration, a clampdown on left-wing NGOs, resistance to the LGBTQ+ agenda, and other issues.
He was one of the few European leaders to maintain contacts with Moscow after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, insisting on Hungary continuing to purchase Russian energy and decrying Western sanctions as counterproductive. The former Hungarian leader also consistently advocated stronger economic cooperation between the EU and China.
Orban has called Trump a “good friend” and visited the US to back the Republican’s presidential campaign in 2024. The US president endorsed Orban ahead of this year’s Hungarian election and sent Vice President J.D. Vance to Budapest to campaign for him, although the move did not help to deliver victory.
A State Department official estimated that Orban would “comfortably” get eight votes in the 15-member UN Security Council, with two more also being within reach. Permanent members the UK and France, who could stand in the way of majority support for Orban, usually use their veto power cautiously, the WSJ stressed.
Trump has been increasingly unhappy with the UN during his second term, saying that the global body hasn’t come close to reaching its “tremendous potential.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last month that Moscow expects the new UN secretary-general to represent the interests of all mankind, not just a small group of Western nations as happened under Guterres. Lavrov also said several of the candidates possessed the qualities needed to be effective in the role.

Lula wins Brazil election but faces uphill battle to govern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:38:09 UTC
22:38:09 KST

Lula wins Brazil election but faces uphill battle to govern
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's narrow election victory on Sunday has dealt a blow to Brazil's far right, but deep political divisions remain. The newly re-elected president must tackle economic and security concerns at home while navigating international tensions with US President Donald Trump.
“Even if you're not a Lula supporter, what was at stake was democracy versus the far right.” In Rio de Janeiro's beachfront Botafogo neighbourhood, Katia celebrated Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's re-election on Sunday, as supporters took to the streets.
“I couldn't just sit on the sidelines,” she told FRANCE 24.
At nearly 81, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defied expectations by defeating far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro with 51.7 percent of the vote against 48.2 percent.
Read moreBrazil's Lula beats odds and seals re-election, rival Bolsonaro demands annulment
After trailing in the first round, Lula's campaign stepped up its efforts to reach young and undecided voters.
“The sense of urgency created by coming second in the first round triggered this fairly massive mobilisation in the second round, particularly on social media,” said Bruno Ronchi, a doctoral researcher in political science at the University of Rennes who specialises in far-right movements, particularly in Brazil.
The result does not, however, signal the end of Bolsonarism, the political movement built around former president Jair Bolsonaro and his ideas.
“Bolsonarism remains a major political force among conservative voters,” Ronchi said. “Flavio Bolsonaro's result was not exactly a humiliating defeat.”
Lula now faces the challenge of turning a victory built on broad mobilisation into a workable governing coalition, while contending with a powerful opposition at home and international pressure from Washington and neighbouring countries.
'Little room for manoeuvre'
Lula is set to govern without a majority in Congress. The Liberal Party, led by the Bolsonaro camp, won 121 of the 513 seats in the lower house and 28 of the 81 seats in the Senate in legislative elections held earlier this month.
“Lula will therefore have to govern with a Congress that is even further to the right and even more conservative than the one in 2022,” Ronchi said.
Ronchi said the president would have to work with centrist parties despite their limited alignment with his agenda.
The president will depend on the Centrao, a bloc of centre-right parties that typically backs governments in exchange for political concessions and access to public resources.
“I genuinely believe Lula will have very little room for manoeuvre,” Ronchi said, predicting a government that would be “very moderate, perhaps even more moderate than his previous governments”.
Purchasing power and public security
Economic concerns will be one of the main priorities. Rising fuel prices and inflation have squeezed household budgets, while the government faces pressure to balance public spending with its commitment to welfare programmes.
“Purchasing power is undoubtedly one of the main issues, as it is in many countries around the world,” Ronchi said.
He noted economic indicators during Lula's first term had been relatively positive, with Brazil close to full employment.
Lula must also contend with questions over institutional stability. Flavio Bolsonaro has called for the election's second round to be annulled, citing delays in decisions over requests to extend voting hours.
He compared it with Jair Bolsonaro's refusal to accept his defeat after the last elections. On January 8, 2023, just a week before Lula took office, a mob of Bolsonaro's supporters stormed Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace in Brasilia, seeking to overthrow the government.
Public security is also expected to remain a contentious issue. Accused by his opponents of being too soft on crime, Lula will face pressure to tackle criminal groups and militias that control territory in several cities.
During the campaign, he said he would support lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for heinous crimes, while the political right wants to reduce it to 14.
A counterweight to Trump?
Lula's victory also carries implications beyond Brazil. The country's re-election of a left-wing leader challenges the growing influence of right-wing governments across Latin America that have aligned themselves with US President Donald Trump.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Trump imposed tariffs on Brazil last year in retaliation for legal proceedings against his ally Jair Bolsonaro, followed by an additional 25% tariff on some products this year. Lula campaigned on defending Brazilian sovereignty in the face of US pressure.
Ronchi said Lula's victory sent a message to other countries in the region, where political shifts are often portrayed as an inevitable swing between left and right.
“This election shows that these trends are not inevitable,” he said.
He pointed to pressure from Washington, including efforts by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to secure a stronger American sphere of influence across the Americas.
Read moreRubio kicks off tour in Latin America as US vies for regional influence
“This victory shows that there are ways to counter this American ambition to assert its power across the continent,” Ronchi said. “It also demonstrates that left-wing movements can mobilise and reorganise themselves.”
But there again Lula's ability to act as a counterweight to Trump will depend on his room for manoeuvre at home.
‘A bulwark’
For Armelle Enders, a professor of contemporary history at Paris 8 University and director of the research laboratory at the French Institute of Geopolitics, Lula's victory has significance beyond Brazil.
“This is a victory for democrats around the world,” she told FRANCE 24. “He represents a bulwark and that is very important.”
Ronchi said the election results reflected a broad mobilisation against the risks posed by Bolsonarism to democratic institutions, rather than the disappearance of the movement itself.
“There was also a kind of broad democratic front that came together, highlighting the distrust of Bolsonarism and the risks it poses in terms of breaking with democratic institutions,” he said.
For Katia, the prospect of renewed political tensions remains a concern.
“The coming days are going to be intense. It will be just as intense as the last election [in 2022, editor's note], when they attempted a coup. And Bolsonaro is not going to accept having lost the election,” she told FRANCE 24.
“I think we can expect anything from them. These are people who are absolutely not democratic. Something is brewing.”
Lula has won another term, but his ability to govern will depend on whether he can bridge Brazil's political divide and deliver on voters' concerns.

Meta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:37:26 UTC
22:37:26 KST

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta has announced plans for $95bn (£71bn) of fundraising to cover its AI expenditure, even as Elon Musk warned that funding for smaller players in the sector was drying up.
The owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is a leading investor in AI and is ploughing multibillion-dollar sums into datacentres, the central nervous systems of the technology.
Meta’s announcement on Monday came after Musk added to the pressure on “neocloud” datacentre providers – which lease computing power to AI companies – by saying the sector faced “death and consolidation” amid concerns over the sustainability of their funding.
The Meta fundraising will come in two parts. In the first, the company plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock. This has some big-name backers, with chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom all showing interest, Meta said. These “cornerstone investors” could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.
In the second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” to sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future. That offering involves selling Meta’s new class C stock, which it announced it was creating last week. These class C shares do not have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting Zuckerberg’s control of the company.
The Silicon Valley company said these plans would support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.
Meta’s announcement came as other companies in the AI sector came under fire from Musk on Monday.
The tech entrepreneur said more than 200 neocloud firms were in trouble, which led to shares in Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren dropping in premarket trading on Monday. However, Iren and CoreWeave stock later recovered their losses, with Nebius closing more than 3% down.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” the world’s richest person wrote in a post on X on Sunday.
Drawing an analogy with the survival prospects of the guppy fish – which has a reputation for struggling to thrive in domestic fish tanks – Musk added: “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.”
The chief executive and largest shareholder of Tesla and SpaceX – which also owns and operates datacentres – was responding to a post by the venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, who had written on the Musk-owned platform that neoclouds were “disorganized and poorly capitalized”.
Fears over the financial stability of neocloud businesses are focused on their high levels of borrowing – approximately $35bn at CoreWeave, for example – and whether the AI market will grow fast enough to service it.
Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Musk’s comments “underscore the fears that there is just way too much debt” in the AI sector.
“Meta’s not going to struggle to service debts and can lean on equity raises to minimise debt, too. This is kind of exactly the point Musk made about SpaceX having all its earnings and is investment grade, which the neoclouds don’t have,” he said.
SpaceX reported on Monday that it had entered a $40bn deal with Apollo Global Management to lease chips to power AI datacentres.
CoreWeave’s chief executive, Michael Intrator, reportedly sent an internal memo to employees this month saying that some investors had not understood the $30bn company. The firm’s stock has declined in value by more than a third over the past month.
“When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally,” he wrote, according to Bloomberg.

Restoration of Isfahan’s Chehel Sotoun palace awaits UNESCO funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:37:19 UTC
22:37:19 KST

Restoration of Isfahan’s Chehel Sotoun palace awaits UNESCO funding
TEHRAN - Restoration of Iran’s UNESCO-listed Chehel Sotoun palace and garden is awaiting additional funding from the government and UNESCO, as experts assess structural damage to the Safavid-era monument following a 40-day war with the US and Israeli forces, the site’s director said.
Most emergency measures to prevent further deterioration have been completed, but major restoration work, including repairs to the palace’s columns, roof structures and decorative features, cannot proceed without sufficient funding, Mostafa Hadipour, director of the Chehel Sotoun World Heritage site, told IRNA news agency on Monday.
Hadipour said the estimated damage to the complex stood at about 1.5 trillion rials ($56 million), adding that funds allocated by the government and Isfahan province for restoration planning and maintenance of the garden’s approximately 67,000 square meters of green space were insufficient to cover major restoration contracts.
He called for urgent intervention by the government and UNESCO, arguing that the international organization had a responsibility to support the protection of properties inscribed on the World Heritage List, including in circumstances involving armed conflict.
“We are waiting for the allocation of funds promised by UNESCO and the government for this World Heritage site,” Hadipour said.
Without the necessary financing, he said, essential work such as scaffolding the palace’s porticos, repairing roofs, restoring muqarnas decorative elements and rebuilding wooden structures could not be undertaken.
Emergency measures have so far focused on both structural stabilization and decorative features. They include covering vulnerable sections with plastic sheeting, installing temporary supports and treating doors and equipment to help protect them through the winter. Specialists have also carried out reinforcement work on the palace’s double-roof structure.
Technical assessments have identified several columns in the palace’s portico that have shifted from their original alignment, as well as displaced structural beams. A consulting company is conducting further studies to determine the appropriate repair methods.
One option under consideration is to reinforce the affected columns with steel elements and return them to their original alignment. Another is to stabilize them through engineering measures while retaining their current positions. Hadipour said no final decision had been made.
The damage to the columns has been tentatively linked to blast waves from attacks on the Isfahan provincial governor’s office within the historic Safavid Government House complex during the 40-day war. The reported damage affected the protected surroundings of Chehel Sotoun and other historic monuments in the city.
However, the precise cause and extent of the structural deterioration have been subjects of differing assessments. Some heritage specialists have questioned whether the blasts alone could explain the columns’ condition, noting that reinforcement work was reportedly carried out on the portico columns in earlier decades. Accounts differ over which restoration specialists undertook the work and whether all the columns were reinforced with steel.
Hadipour said detailed technical studies were continuing and that the consulting company was preparing the necessary implementation plans. Large-scale restoration can begin once the plans are approved and the required funding secured.
The attacks also damaged other historic buildings in Isfahan’s Safavid Government House complex, including the Ali Qapu Palace, the Talar-e Ashraf, the Timurid Hall, the Jabeh Khaneh building, which houses the Museum of Decorative Arts, and the Rokib Khaneh building, home to the Museum of Contemporary Art, according to IRNA.
The complex forms part of Isfahan’s historic urban landscape, which includes Naqsh-e Jahan Square, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Damage was reported to monuments in the square’s protected surroundings following attacks on March 8, with further damage reported after the provincial governor’s office was bombed on March 9.
Chehel Sotoun, meaning “Forty Columns” in Persian, is one of the principal surviving monuments of Safavid Isfahan. The 17th-century pavilion was developed under Shah Abbas II for royal receptions and diplomatic gatherings. Its name refers to the reflection of its 20-columned entrance portico in the long pool in front of the building.
The palace is renowned for its historic paintings and decorative interiors, including works associated with the Safavid artistic tradition. Its surrounding garden is one of nine Iranian gardens collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2011 as the Persian Garden, recognized for their distinctive design and influence on Persian landscape architecture.
The latest damage has heightened concerns over the conservation of Isfahan’s architectural heritage, while the delay in securing adequate funding threatens to postpone major repairs to one of the city’s most prominent historic landmarks.

Russia Builds Deadly Iskander and Kinzhal Missiles Using US, German, and Chinese Technology
Russian defense manufacturers continue to rely on foreign industrial equipment to produce ballistic missiles and their components, including Iskander-M and Kinzhal weapons, despite efforts to replace imported technology with domestically manufactured alternatives.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) disclosed details of 30 pieces of foreign-made manufacturing equipment used by Russian defense enterprises, publishing the findings on its War&Sanctions portal on October 26.
The equipment originates from seven countries—the United States, Germany, China, Taiwan, Türkiye, Switzerland, and Italy—and supports the production of missile components, including guidance-related electronics, gyroscopes, aerodynamic control surfaces, and altimeters.
Among the identified systems is a GX-650 five-axis machining center manufactured by China’s Hyper Machine Tool. According to HUR, the equipment is used at Russia’s Votkinsk Plant, which manufactures 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system and missile sections for the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile.
Ukrainian intelligence also identified Chinese-made Shtral turning and milling centers operating at PEMZ Molot, a Russian enterprise responsible for manufacturing electronic equipment modules used in Iskander-M missiles.
Another facility, UPKB Detal, reportedly uses measurement equipment produced by German manufacturer Rohde & Schwarz. The Russian company manufactures altimeters for Zircon hypersonic missiles.
HUR highlighted the growing presence of Chinese industrial machinery at Russian defense facilities, particularly advanced five-axis machining centers used for precision manufacturing. However, the intelligence agency noted that Chinese-made equipment frequently incorporates components manufactured elsewhere, including in Europe, Japan, and Taiwan.
These components include computer numerical control systems, servo drives, precision spindles, bearings, measurement devices, rotary systems, linear guides, and temperature-control equipment.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russia’s continued use of such machinery demonstrates the country’s dependence on international manufacturing technologies, particularly in industries requiring high-precision production capabilities.
Earlier, on October 12, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate revealed that 58 Russian companies were involved in producing Kinzhal missiles, including 22 that remained outside international sanctions. HUR also reported that approximately 90% of the Kinzhal’s components are shared with the Iskander-M ballistic missile.

Dictionary.com reveals 2026 Word of the Year - and it's a depressing one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:35:12 UTC
22:35:12 KST

The internet slang term / suffix "Maxxing" has officially been selected by Dictionary.com as its 2026 Word of the Year.
It's that time of the year again, when Words of the Year are selected to represent the most important term or expression in the public sphere.
First out of the gate is Dictionary.com. Following their pick of "6-7" last year, the online dictionary has chosen another Gen Z / Gen Alpha slang term by announcing its 2026 Word of the Year as "Maxxing".
Short for "maximizing," the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible," according to Dictionary.com.
The term's origins can be drawn back to the expression "maxing out a credit card" (exceeding assigned credit limit) and video game culture.
In the 2010s, it spread throughout manosphere and incel subcultures via the term "looksmaxxing", which means to maximise phycial attractiveness through fitness routines and physical grooming. It was usually used in the context of failed relationships and romantic rejection.
The term grew more popular with the rise of controversial manosphere influencers like Braden Peters, aka: Clavicular - the livestreamer promoting extreme devotion to male beauty who was accused of sexually assaulting a young woman in 2025. He pleaded not guilty last week.
Many have attempted to move the term away from its toxic reputation and its associations with aggressive masculinity. It has been embraced by Gen Z and Gen Alpha on social media, with searches for the word exploding in August.
"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," according to Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group at IXL Learning.
"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," said Johnson in a statement. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."
He added: “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI during the workday, cozymaxxing on a Friday night."
Other variations of maxxing are the likes of "hardmaxxing" (extreme dieting, facial reconstruction surgery or even bone smashing), "softmaxxing" (similar to the term "glow-up" - a new haircut, for example) or "jestermaxxing" (using humour to gain social acceptance or clout) and "sleepmaxxing" (increasing one's quantity and quality of sleep).
However popular the term may be, there's no escaping the rather depressing implications of this word, how it reflects an increasingly online society, and its expanded connotations. Case and point with “tokenmaxxing”, referring to businesses encouraging employees to use AI tools as much as possible.
Other words that were shortlisted for Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year include "Affordability"; "Data center"; "Odyssey" (a choice no doubt fuelled by the explosion in online searches and interest in Homer following the release of Christopher Nolan's hit blockbuster The Odyssey); and "Unc" - the shortened version of "uncle," used by Gen Z and Gen Alpha to describe an older person who is seen as out of touch or uncool.

The reflection on the creativity of words continued with a reading from Gianni Rodari’s *Grammar of Fantasy*, which served as a starting point to invite the audience to “explore,” with wit and vivacity, to explore rare and obsolete words, discovering in the richness of the Italian language an inexhaustible source of creativity and knowledge.

False DMCA claims leave Helsinki Times and affiliated sites invisible in Google Search for months
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:32:13 EET
22:32:13 KST

By Editorial Staff
Helsinki Times
Try searching Google for some of Helsinki Times’ in-depth consumer guides and specialized reporting today, and you might come up empty-handed. Where original articles once stood, readers are instead met with a quiet, sterile disclaimer tucked away at the bottom of the search page:
“In response to a complaint that we received under the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act, we have removed results from this page.”
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The articles haven’t been retracted, nor did our newsroom violate anyone's intellectual property. Instead, we have been erased by phantom copyright strikes - spurious takedown notices filed under United States law by anonymous actors using demonstrably false claims.
Even more alarming than the ease with which our journalism was knocked offline is what followed: months of dead silence from Google. Despite submitting comprehensive, legally sworn counter-notices complete with proof of authorship, our appeals have vanished into an automated void. Across our newsroom and affiliated digital properties like Stadtgame, original reporting has been held hostage in Google's unyielding "in queue" status since June.
Our experience is far from isolated. It reflects a growing, systemic crisis in digital journalism - one laid bare by UK media monitor Press Gazette, which documented how US copyright law has been systematically weaponised by commercial rivals and rogue operators to censor legitimate reporting and manipulate the web.
The Weaponisation of a 1998 Law
Passed nearly three decades ago, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) was built to protect musicians, filmmakers, and writers from early internet piracy. Under its "safe harbor" clause, tech giants like Google are shielded from massive copyright liability as long as they act swiftly to remove content flagged as infringing.
On paper, the bargain sounded reasonable. In practice, it has created a structural loophole that bad-faith actors exploit with impunity:
- Shoot First, Ask Questions Never: Google’s automated processing treats takedown complaints as guilty until proven innocent. To maintain immunity, the platform de-indexes reported URLs almost instantaneously - without demanding verifiable proof that the claimant actually owns the copyright, or even checking whether they are a real person.
- Fabricated Infringements: Anyone can claim ownership of an article by linking to a disposable web page, a backdated blog, or completely irrelevant media.
- Broken Reinstatement Clocks: Under the DMCA, when a publisher files a formal counter-notice swearing under penalty of perjury that the content is original, platforms are legally expected to restore the page within 10 to 14 business days, unless the challenger takes the serious step of suing in federal court.
In reality, that statutory 14-day timeline has become fiction. For independent publishers without a direct bat-phone to Google executives, counter-notices don’t lead to restoration; they lead to an automated processing limbo with no end date.
From Unrelated YouTube Links to the "Mixed-Case URL" Exploit
The tactics used to scrub legitimate journalism border on the absurd, yet Google’s automated filters repeatedly fall for them.
When Press Gazette saw spurious copyright claims wipe its investigative stories off Google, the challengers falsely claimed the journalism had been copied from an unrelated Reddit post. When leading search industry publication Search Engine Land reported on that exact takedown, Google removed Search Engine Land's article too - approving a bogus complaint from an anonymous entity calling itself "US Webspam," which claimed the outlet had stolen text and proprietary images from a 2024 Verge story, even though the Search Engine Land article didn't contain a single image.
Across Helsinki Times and Stadtgame, the attacks have been just as brazen. Entries logged in Harvard’s Lumen Database - the public repository tracking legal removals - reveal that rogue actors used a single, completely unrelated YouTube video as the alleged “original source” to strike down 18 different Stadtgame articles spanning wildly divergent topics.
Even more telling is a technical fingerprint left across the complaints targeting our network: randomized URL capitalization. In the notices filed against Helsinki Times and Stadtgame, attackers submitted URLs with bizarre, alternating uppercase and lowercase letters (such as /uK/nOnGAmStOp-oNline-cAsino-uk/ or /NeWs/wEttanbieter-ohne-lugas-paysafecard/).
In September, investigative outlet TheHolyCoins exposed this exact mechanism after noticing the same capitalization anomalies in the Press Gazette and Search Engine Land takedowns. When TheHolyCoins tested fake DMCA complaints against its own pages by pairing standard URLs with mixed-case variants, Google’s automated system approved three out of four bogus requests within hours - and in one instance, even reported removing a misspelled URL that had never existed.
Months in Limbo: From Helsinki to Stadtgame
While high-profile trade outlets covering Google sometimes see their articles restored after public outcry on social media, our publishing network has been met with months of bureaucratic paralysis:
- Helsinki Times: In June and July, in-depth reports and consumer analysis published on our domain were summarily scrubbed under complaints like these Case References (documented in Lumen notices 88288664 and 92160491). Counter-notices demonstrating our editorial provenance were filed immediately. Months later, the pages remain invisible in search results.
- Stadtgame.com: Our gaming and tech sister site has been battered by waves of mass takedowns since mid-June. A comprehensive appeal filed in August received an automated acknowledgment stating the matter was "in queue." Follow-ups in September triggered the exact same auto-reply. In late October, a third detailed counter-notice covering 11 core URLs was met with the identical canned response: waiting in line, no timeline given, no case officer named. Nearly two dozen additional Stadtgame guides and game reviews remain de-indexed.
- Network-Wide Suppressions: Across multiple other affiliated sites in our network, original editorial work has been stuck in the same queue since June. Every appeal ends up in a holding pattern instead of undergoing human review. Even on the rare occasion a page is verified and restored, bad-faith actors simply fire off a fresh, mixed-case strike days later - resetting the clock and forcing our teams back to square one.
The Algorithmic Black Box: Manual Contact Is Impossible
What turns an operational headache into an existential crisis for digital publishers is the total absence of human accountability.
Manual contact with Google representatives to resolve these false takedowns is utterly impossible.
Outside of the generic legal web forms - which do nothing but churn out the same hollow queue confirmations - Google provides no direct email, no dedicated partner support, and no human appeal desk for verified news organizations. Support queries sent to general company addresses are instantly bounced back by bots directing publishers to self-help forums. The door is firmly shut.
As former Google Search quality specialists and digital rights advocates have repeatedly pointed out, the modern DMCA ecosystem has evolved into a lucrative negative-SEO weapon. Shady reputation agencies and competitors can hire mass-takedown mercenaries on freelance job boards for as little as €20 per link. Armed with automated scripts and capitalization tricks, they blast search engines with hundreds of spurious claims at zero financial risk.
While falsely claiming copyright is technically a felony perjury offense under US law, anonymous operators hiding behind shell names never face prosecution. Instead, the entire cost - lost search visibility, decimated advertising revenues, and months of wasted editorial labor - is borne solely by legitimate publishers.
A Call for Accountability
Search engines are not merely private advertising businesses; they are the primary gatekeepers of the digital public square. When an opaque, buggy copyright filter allows anonymous bad actors to erase verified news outlets using random YouTube links and mixed-case URL tricks - and an unresponsive appeal system traps counter-notices for months - the platform becomes an active participant in censorship.
Helsinki Times calls on Google to address these structural failures immediately:
- Honor the 10–14 Day Rule: Restore legitimate content within the statutory DMCA window once sworn counter-notices with evidence of ownership are filed, rather than parking appeals in indefinite queues.
- Fix the Filter: Patch the system bugs that allow mixed-case URL exploits and unrelated video links to trigger automatic takedowns of original text journalism.
- Provide Human Escalation: Give accredited publishers a direct, human-staffed channel to contest fraudulent strikes and break free from endless automated loops.
Until Google fixes its broken takedown machinery, no digital newsroom is safe. Any publisher’s voice can be switched off with a single bogus form - leaving original reporting buried, while an automated queue politely thanks you for your patience.

Germany's Merz heads to Asia as security issues loom large
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

Germany's Merz heads to Asia seeking closer security ties
October 26, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz kicked off a five-day tour of Asia on Monday, traveling to Singapore before his scheduled visits to Japan and South Korea. Merz is accompanied by an entourage of 30 senior businesspeople, including representatives of Germany's industry, tech and defense companies, and energy suppliers.
At the same time, Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is visiting China.
While the trips are not officially related, they both seem aimed at boosting Berlin's economic and security relationships at a time of geopolitical instability, which threatens global supply chains.
Japan needs close allies
In Singapore, Merz is set to deliver a major foreign policy speech and meet Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. He will then travel to Japan on Wednesday to meet with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and take part in the German-Japanese Business Summit.
Merz's visit "will be very much welcomed in Tokyo," said Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Tokyo's Waseda University.
"For more than a decade, Japan has been looking to generate new security allies and closer trade partnerships," he told DW.
"This greater outreach was started under Prime Minister [Shinzo] Abe, but Takaichi is very much following that blueprint because of the growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific region and the greater uncertainty around the second administration of [US President] Donald Trump," he added.
Germany and Japan face different, but connected threats
The challenges posed by an increasingly expansionist China in the region are of deep concern to Tokyo, particularly as Beijing is forging closer ties with both Russia and the unpredictable regime in North Korea. China and Russia have conducted joint military exercises off Japan, and Beijing is resolute in its insistence that Taiwan be brought under the control of the mainland.
Ascione points out that any conflict over Taiwan, the disputed islands of the South China Sea or territorial claims elsewhere in the region would have a major impact on global trade. Such disruptions would also impact Germany.
"Japan and Germany have different primary security threats at the moment, with Germany focused on the Russian invasion of Ukraine and Japan keeping a close watch on China, North Korea and Russia, but I do believe that Germany has come more into line with Takaichi's perception of the security threat that is posed by China," Ascione said.
"Takaichi is going to underline the importance of a rules-based order and the policy of a free and open Indo-Pacific at a time of such geopolitical uncertainty," he added. "Japan has in recent years moved towards greater resilience building, supply chain resilience and more and deeper security partnerships."
German military assets welcome in Japan
According to Ascione, Japan would also "welcome" Germany deploying its military assets to the region, following its Bayern frigate docking in Tokyo in 2021 and its fighter jets conducting air drills with Japanese fighters in 2024.
The frigate Bayern became the first German Navy warship to dock in Tokyo in 20 years in May 2021 and went on to conduct air and maritime exercises with Japanese units. In July 2024, German Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft similarly carried out air drills with Japanese fighters over northern Japan.
Merz and Takaichi are expected to exchange views on responding to geopolitical threats.
This would include ensuring supply chain resilience, protecting strategically important industries and ensuring access to technologies and components, such as the rare earths that are critical to a range of advanced technologies but remain largely controlled by China.
European nations 'irritated' by Seoul's outreach to North Korea
Merz is then scheduled to visit South Korea, where he will meet with President Lee Jae-myung and open the 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul. He is also due to visit the Demilitarized Zone that marks the border between North and South Korea.
Security issues will again dominate discussions in Seoul, believes Saeme Kim, a research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies.
However, the German leader could voice concerns about South Korea's perceived "outreach" efforts towards North Korea and, by extension, Russia.
"There has been discussion recently about exports of petroleum to Russia, although Seoul says it has not breached sanctions," she said.
South Korea is trying to set up a way to communicate with Pyongyang, according to the expert, despite the regime of Kim Jong Un sending troops to the conflict in Ukraine.
"It's not just Germany, I think a lot of European countries will be irritated by the Lee administration trying to improve relations with North Korea and Russia," Kim said.
The South also continues to provide humanitarian assistance to North Korea, even as the regime forges ever closer economic ties with China and Russia.
"The government needs to keep in mind that some of these policies are going to be damaging to South Korea's own interests over the long-run," she said.
Can South Korea learn from Germany's history?
At the same time, Merz could also offer insight into two Koreas trying to work with one another, drawing on the German experience of reuniting in 1990.
"There are lessons that South Korea can learn, of course, but there are a lot of differences," Kim said. "The two Koreas are still technically at war and Seoul has to deal with an aspiring nuclear power on its border."
Merz will have the opportunity to see the North at a distance when he visits the DMZ. His visit to the border, however, could also be canceled due to lingering tensions over the North Korean mine injuring three South Korean soldiers last month. Pyongyang has accused the South of staging the incident.

The Verkhovna Rada has reinstated competitions for civil service positions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:31:13 EET
22:31:13 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has reinstated competitions for civil service positions
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported Draft Law No. 13478-1 on bringing back competitions for civil service positions. The selection process will be restored in stages through the Diia portal.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted in the second reading and as a whole a bill providing for the resumption of competitive examinations for entry into the civil service and the improvement of the procedure for serving in it. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Draft Law No. 13478-1 "On Amendments to Certain Laws of Ukraine Regarding the Resumption of Competitive Examinations and Improvement of the Procedure for Entering, Serving in, and Terminating Civil Service" was supported in the second reading and as a whole by 247 members of parliament.
The document proposes a phased return of competitive selection, which was restricted during the period of martial law. The resumption of competitive examinations is planned in three stages: first for Category A positions, then for Category B positions in government-controlled territories without hostilities, and at the final stage for Category C positions under the same conditions.
The bill allows appointments without a competitive examination to positions in areas where hostilities are ongoing, and also grants managers the right to retain employees appointed without competitive examinations in their positions in order to preserve staffing capacity.
As Olena Shulyak, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on the Organization of State Power, Local Self-Government, Regional Development and Urban Planning, reported, competitive examinations for Category "A" positions and in local self-government bodies will resume immediately after the law enters into force, while the transition period for Categories "B" and "C" will be one and two months, respectively. Those appointed without a competitive examination during the war will be able to continue their service without a new selection process, provided they receive positive results in their annual evaluation.
According to her, civil service vacancies and documents for participation in competitive examinations will be submitted through the Diia portal, where announcements, selection results, appointment information and competition statistics will also be published. This will make the procedure more accessible and transparent for candidates.
Shulyak outlined specific steps for veterans. These include an internship in a government body for up to six months and representation of veterans' associations on the Commission on the Higher Corps of the Civil Service. Candidates will also be able to indicate their veteran status when submitting their documents.
The member of parliament added that civil servants with outstanding annual evaluation results will be able to move to a higher position without a competitive examination, while Category "B" and "C" positions may be filled based on the results of a simplified internal competition.

IMD, during the meeting, informed the NCMC that the cyclone ‘Arnab’ is likely to cross Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam as a “very severe cyclonic storm” with a maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 kmph gusting to 140 kmph by the forenoon of Wednesday.
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Monday reviewed preparedness for the impending cyclone - named ‘Arnab’ - and directed agencies to “ensure zero loss of life and minimise damage to property and infrastructure”.In the review meeting of the National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC), chaired by cabinet secretary TV Somanathan, it was emphasised that essential services should be restored in the shortest possible time in the event of any damage.Somanathan also directed that eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar should be suitably alerted as these two states are also expected to receive high rainfall in addition to Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana, Chhattisgarh and Puducherry.IMD, during the meeting, informed the NCMC that the cyclone ‘Arnab’ is likely to cross Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam as a “very severe cyclonic storm” with a maximum sustained wind speed of 115-125 kmph gusting to 140 kmph by the forenoon of Wednesday.
Cyclone Arnab map. Credit: IMD
The name of the cyclonic storm, ‘Arnab’ (pronounced as ‘Ornab’), is given by Bangladesh in the list of tropical cyclones. The list carries 52 names, given by 13 countries including India, which were adopted by WMO panel member countries in April 2020 for naming of tropical cyclones over the North Indian Ocean, including the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
The Committee was informed that the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) has deployed teams in the states, with additional teams on standby. “Rescue and relief teams of the Army, Navy, Air Force and Indian Coast Guard, along with their ships and aircraft, have been kept ready. Indian Coast Guard has so far shepherded multiple ships/boats to jetties/shore, and the remaining ships have been alerted to return to the coast,” said the govt in a statement.
Sharing the progress of the cyclone before it makes landfall on Wednesday, IMD told the Committee that the deep depression over the Bay of Bengal intensified into cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ on Monday. It is very likely to move west-northwestwards, intensify further into a “severe cyclonic storm” over the west-central Bay of Bengal and then into a “very severe cyclonic storm” over the same region on Tuesday.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.
