MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Europe needs to keep open channels of communication with major energy producers, Slovak Parliament Deputy Speaker Tibor Gaspar said in an interview with TASS.
"Slovakia’s interests lie in ensuring sufficient energy supplies, maintaining the competitiveness of its industry, and protecting households from excessive price increases. Therefore, when making decisions in the energy sector, it is important to consider not only political goals but also real economic consequences for the population, as well as technical capabilities of individual states. In the long term, it is in the interest of both Slovakia and Europe to maintain open channels of communication with major energy producers and to seek solutions that help strengthen energy security, price stability, and the predictability of supplies," he said when asked whether Europe still needs Russian energy resources.
The current situation in energy markets demonstrates that energy security, the availability of raw materials, and price stability remain critical issues for all leading global economies, Gaspar noted. "According to reports from October 2026, US President Donald Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions, allowing for the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the American and global markets. Subsequently, American administration granted the necessary authorization for conducting such operations. The agreement drew criticism from a number of European officials pointing to its potential implications for the effectiveness of the sanctions policy," he stated.
"This situation indicates that certain states may prioritize different instruments and interests when addressing energy and economic issues. For countries with high energy consumption, it is essential to ensure stable supplies at economically acceptable prices, whereas the sanctions policy also pursues broader foreign policy goals and security objectives. For the Slovak Republic, this issue is of particular significance, given its geographical location, energy infrastructure, and long-standing historical relationships with energy suppliers," the politician emphasized.

Serbia’s Vucic Loses Vote, Predicts Sanctions on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

21:56:00 KST

Serbia’s former president Aleksandar Vucic conceded his coalition’s defeat to a student-backed opposition movement on Sunday, Oct. 25, and predicted that the incoming authorities would impose sanctions on Russia within months.
Speaking at his Serbian Progressive Party’s headquarters in Belgrade, Vucic said preliminary estimates showed the Student List winning 135-140 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with around 105 for his United Serbia coalition.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” he said, acknowledging that final results were not yet available. A parliamentary majority requires 126 seats.
The defeat marks a major setback for one of Moscow’s closest political partners in Europe. Under Vucic, Serbia maintained ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while continuing to pursue EU membership.
Vucic predicts sanctions, but winners pledged otherwise
Vucic accused his opponents of implementing an agenda devised abroad and alleged that unnamed European countries and an “American deep state” opposed to President Donald Trump had supported their victory.
“By March or April, you will have sanctions imposed on the Russian Federation,” he said, according to RFE/RL. However, his prediction conflicts with the Student List’s stated pre-election position.
In a foreign-policy platform published in September, the movement said Serbia would continue opposing sanctions against Russia. N1 reported that the statement cited Serbia’s own experience and history with sanctions, indicating that such restrictive measures do not help resolve political and security disputes.
Bulgarian Presidential Election Exposes Split Over Ukraine War
The election outcome therefore does not establish that Belgrade will change its sanctions policy. Vucic’s remarks were a forecast about his opponents’ intentions, rather than an announcement by the projected winners.
Student protests become an electoral challenge
The opposition movement emerged from protests following the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Demonstrators demanded accountability over suspected corruption and construction failures. The protests developed into a nationwide challenge to Vucic’s political dominance, with students organizing a parliamentary slate drawn from outside the established governing parties.
Supporters celebrated in Belgrade, Novi Sad, and other cities after Vucic conceded. The movement’s leading candidate, cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, said its next task would be building a state governed by the rule of law.
Vucic had resigned as president on Sept. 27 to contest the parliamentary election, hoping to return as prime minister. He previously held that position before becoming president in 2017.
His resignation left parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić serving as acting president pending a separate presidential election. Sunday’s vote concerned control of parliament and the formation of the next government.
Serbia’s balancing act between Moscow and Kyiv
Serbia’s relationship with Russia extends beyond sanctions. Belgrade has relied on Russian energy supplies and Moscow’s diplomatic support over Kosovo, whose independence Serbia does not recognize.
At the same time, Serbia has supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity, received Ukrainian refugees, and provided humanitarian and financial assistance. President Volodymyr Zelensky visited Belgrade in August for talks on bilateral cooperation and European integration.
Serbia had provided roughly €60 million ($69 million) in nonmilitary assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, according to earlier reporting.
The EU remains central to Serbia’s economic interests, accounting for nearly 60% of its foreign trade. But maintaining Russian ties while seeking deeper European integration has complicated Belgrade’s foreign policy. The next government will inherit that balancing act alongside the student movement’s central domestic promises to tackle corruption and restore public institutions.

The Haifa Magistrate's Court on Monday ordered the immediate release, without bail, of two German tourists arrested overnight Saturday on suspicion of espionage after photographing the exterior of Damon Prison on Mount Carmel, where security prisoners are held. 
Judge Orit Kantor said she could find no provision in Israeli law prohibiting photography of a prison from outside its grounds and wrote: "I found no evidence whatsoever supporting the suspicion."
On Saturday night, prison guards at Damon spotted the two men standing outside the facility and photographing its entrance. Officers from the nearby Nesher police station were called to the scene and arrested them. An Israel Prison Service official claimed that photographs of "security facilities and security-related activities" had been found in their possession. However, the Shin Bet security agency quickly concluded that the incident did not constitute an espionage case and left the investigation to the police.
Kantor criticized the decision to arrest the tourists, writing: "I believe discretion should have been exercised, especially when Israel's public diplomacy is not at its best these days."

Kyiv • UNN
The Russian attack on October 24 destroyed the last «Epicentr» in Kharkiv. Over the course of a week, the city experienced 36 shellings, and three people were killed.
Russian forces destroyed the last "Epicentr" in Kharkiv. This was reported on October 26 by the city's mayor, Ihor Terekhov, on social media, UNN writes.
On their third attempt, the Russians destroyed the last "Epicentr" that continued to operate in Kharkiv. Over the past two months, they attacked this hypermarket three times. After the first two strikes, it was possible to restore it and resume operations. But on October 24, a series of strikes by jet-powered drones caused an excessively large fire. The blaze instantly engulfed all the sales areas and warehouses
What this means for the city
The mayor noted that "for Kharkiv, this is not simply the loss of a large retail facility." "First and foremost, it means hundreds of jobs. In addition, this was where residents came after their homes had been shelled to purchase repair materials under the state-run 'eVidnovlennia' program and use certificates from charitable foundations to buy the essentials for their homes and everyday needs," he said.
"We are in constant contact with the store's management. For its part, the city is ready to provide the necessary municipal and operational-technical support - to help clear the area, remove debris, and organize the site. Preserving jobs and supporting economic activity remain critically important to us," he emphasized.
How many Russian strikes hit Kharkiv in a week
"Last week, Kharkiv endured another series of brutal enemy attacks - in total, the city suffered 36 strikes. Unfortunately, three people were killed. Another 28 Kharkiv residents sustained injuries of varying severity, including three children," Terekhov said.
Of the 36 recorded strikes, according to the mayor, 28 were carried out by the aggressor using jet-powered "Shaheds." The occupiers also used "Bandеrol" drones, FPV drones, UAVs of an unidentified type, and "Tornado-S" multiple-launch rocket systems.
Six districts of the city came under fire: Osnovianskyi, Novobavarskyi, Industrialnyi, Slobidskyi, Kholodnohirskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi. "The private sector was severely affected, and high-rise buildings were also damaged. The enemy targeted civilian industrial enterprises, warehouses, offices, the television tower, and railway and energy infrastructure facilities. Blast waves damaged the Kharkiv circus," Terekhov said.
"The enemy's treacherous and risky tactic is to launch repeat strikes at locations where emergency services are already working. On October 24, while fires were being extinguished in the Osnovianskyi and Industrialnyi districts, State Emergency Service personnel came under enemy fire - three emergency responders were wounded. At one of the sites, a fire engine tanker was completely destroyed," he said.

The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) chairman, Brijesh Goyal, said the traders would write to leaders of all parties in the INDIA bloc, besides Congress president Kharge and Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, asking them to defer the rally."We will write to leaders of all the parties in the INDIA bloc, urging them to hear our sentiments and postpone the rally," Goyal said.He expressed concern over the Congress's claim that around 10 lakh people could attend the rally, arguing that the gathering could severely affect wholesale markets around Ramlila Maidan."Business will be heavily impacted because, as reports suggest, 10 lakh people might gather at Ramlila Maidan, whereas its actual capacity is around 50,000," Goyal said.He cited a gathering at Jantar Mantar on October 10, claiming that the presence of around 2,000 to 4,000 people had led to metro station closures, barricading and restrictions. More than 20 major markets were forced to shut down, he alleged.According to Goyal, a rally of the anticipated scale could affect more than 20 wholesale hubs within a 5-km radius of Ramlila Maidan. These include Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazar, Khari Baoli, Naya Bazar, Chawri Bazar, Daryaganj and Kashmere Gate.He said road closures could prevent three to four lakh buyers from outside Delhi, who visit the capital daily, from reaching the markets. Local customers could also stay away because of traffic restrictions.
Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, responded to the traders' concerns in a post on X on Monday, saying the protests would "stop in 30 seconds" if they asked Modi to sack chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the "vote chori" issue.
Paramjeet Singh Pamma, president of the Sadar Bazar Bari Market Trade Association, also appealed to the Congress leadership to postpone the rally. He said the festive season was crucial for traders to recover their business across the year.Pamma warned that restrictions around major wholesale markets, including Sadar Bazar, Chandni Chowk, Khari Baoli, Fatehpuri and Azad Market, could cause losses worth crores of rupees, as traders and buyers from Delhi and other states flock to these areas during the festive season.The traders have urged the Congress to hold the rally after Diwali to avoid disrupting business during one of the busiest periods of the year.

‘Enough for Years’: Ihnat Says Patriot Missiles Used in Middle East Could Have Protected Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:52:50 UTC
21:52:50 KST

Ukraine could have had enough Patriot air defense missiles to sustain its systems for several years if a significant portion of the interceptors had not been expended in the Middle East, Yuriy Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said.
Speaking on the RBC-Ukraine podcast Tse Baza (“This Is the Basics”), Ihnat said Ukrainian forces had adapted their tactics for using the US-made Patriot systems throughout Russia’s full-scale war, learning to employ them in different combat scenarios while conserving expensive interceptor missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s approach differs significantly from that of other countries, Ihnat said. Ukrainian crews can deploy Patriot systems for ambushes rather than keeping them at fixed positions, such as airfields or military bases, and then relocate after engaging targets.
“For instance, rather than using the Patriot as a stationary asset – the way the Americans typically deploy it at airfields or bases – it can be used, in a sense, as a ‘roving’ system: set up an ambush, shoot down five aircraft, and then withdraw safely,” he said.
Ihnat also pointed to an incident in Russia’s Bryansk region as an example of the capabilities Ukrainian forces have demonstrated with the system.
Another key difference, he said, is ammunition use. Ukrainian crews have learned to use a single interceptor against a single target, while air defense forces in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at one target.
‘Interceptors Still Not Coming’ – Zelensky Says US Has Yet to Authorize Patriot Deliveries
The Patriot system has three operating modes: automatic, semi-automatic and manual. Ihnat said that in automatic mode, the system can launch multiple interceptors at once.
Without sufficient combat experience, crews could end up firing an entire salvo from one launcher at a single target, including a relatively inexpensive Shahed drone.
“Because of this lack of experience, they might have fired an entire salvo of interceptors from a launcher at a single Shahed drone or a single ballistic missile,” Ihnat said.
He estimated that the number of interceptors expended in the Middle East could have kept Ukraine’s Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years.
“That is why we now find ourselves in the current crisis; the ammunition expended in the Middle East would have been enough to keep our Patriot systems operational in combat for several more years,” Ihnat said.
Notably, in March, a senior Ukrainian Air Force officer speaking to The Times criticized Gulf forces for using excessive numbers of expensive interceptor missiles against relatively cheap Iranian Shahed drones, saying Ukrainian crews typically use one or two missiles even against more complex targets.
Ukrainian officers said their battlefield experience has not been fully incorporated despite sharing operational data with allies.
They also described the March 1 incident in which Kuwaiti air defenses shot down three US F-15E fighter jets as “clear negligence,” arguing that better coordination could have prevented the friendly-fire incident.
During the first four days of the Iran war, the US and its allies reportedly fired more than 800 Patriot missiles – more than Ukraine received over three years of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has received just 24 Patriot air defense missiles from the US over the past 90 days, despite needing around 350 interceptors per month to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with ABC News.
Zelensky contrasted the limited deliveries to Ukraine with the roughly 2,000 partner-supplied interceptors fired during the first 84 hours of fighting in the Middle East.
Ukrainian officials have warned that the allocation of US-made Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles to the region is affecting supplies available to defend Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
On Oct. 16, Zelensky asked European leaders to provide 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter, warning that deliveries of just two to four missiles every few months were insufficient to counter Russian attacks.
He proposed that European countries with existing Patriot stocks help bridge the gap until new procurement arrangements and defense projects become operational.
However, efforts to secure missiles from European stockpiles have faced resistance. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Athens would not transfer PAC-2 missiles if doing so compromised Greece’s own defense capabilities in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:52:39 UTC
21:52:39 KST

Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.
Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.
Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.
NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.
Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.
While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.
A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.
“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”
Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.
After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

A Jordanian court on Sunday sentenced seven leaders and members of the banned Muslim Brotherhood, including the group’s General Supervisor Murad Al-Adayleh, to prison terms ranging from six months to three years in a case involving illegal fundraising and money laundering.
According to Jordanian media reports, the verdicts are subject to appeal within one month.
Al-Adayleh and fellow Brotherhood leader Tariq Al-Raqab were each sentenced to six months in prison after being convicted of the misdemeanour of illegal fundraising.
Al-Adayleh was acquitted of charges related to violations of Jordan’s Anti-Money Laundering Law.
Five other Brotherhood leaders and activists received three-year prison sentences, including Ahmed Al-Zarqan, who was responsible for overseeing the organization’s financial affairs.
Al-Zarqan was convicted of violating the Anti-Money Laundering Law and engaging in illegal fundraising.
Four other defendants—Aref Hamdan, Ibrahim Hijazi, Mohammed Alayan and Omar Yassin—were also sentenced to three years in prison in connection with the same case.
During the proceedings, prosecutors alleged that funds collected by the defendants were not intended to support Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, despite claims associated with the fundraising activities.
The prosecution also alleged that some of the donations had been deposited into bank accounts through non-transparent financial arrangements, raising concerns about compliance with anti-money laundering regulations and the potential misuse of collected funds.
The verdicts come after Jordanian authorities banned the Muslim Brotherhood in April 2025.
All seven defendants retain the right to appeal their sentences within the legally prescribed period.

Russian-installed governor and two school staff members suspected of illegally transferring children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea
Volodymyr Saldo, the Russian-installed "governor of Kherson Oblast", and two staff members of the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum (specialised secondary school) have been served with a notice of suspicion over the illegal transfer of three children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea under the pretext of "recuperation".
Source: Office of the Prosecutor General; Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: The teenagers have since been brought back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
In October 2022, Saldo ordered the occupation administration's so-called "Ministry of Education" to arrange the transfer of children from Kherson Oblast to Crimea under the pretext of "recuperation".
The "ministry" issued an order for school holidays, and heads of educational institutions were instructed to arrange "recuperation" for students.
On 7 October 2022, three minors from the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum were taken to Crimea. The school's director prepared the documents, while a vocational training instructor accompanied the children. Their parents had not consented to the "recuperation".
The children were placed at the Druzhba children's camp in Yevpatoriia. They were later transferred to another camp. After the "holidays", they did not return home. Instead, in January 2023, they were enrolled at the Kerch Maritime Technical College without their parents' consent.
"The teenagers were involved in military-patriotic activities, exposed to Russian propaganda and had a Russian identity imposed on them," the Prosecutor's Office said.
One of the children had a severe form of diabetes and was admitted to intensive care in Yevpatoriia because of an insulin shortage. He spent about three weeks in hospital.
All three children have now been brought back to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Saldo, the deputy director and the vocational training instructor at the Kherson Professional Shipbuilding Lyceum have been served with a notice of suspicion of violating the laws and customs of war, committed by a group of people acting in prior collusion (Articles 28.2 and 438.1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). They face up to 12 years in prison.
Background: Five children and young people were recently brought back from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.

Iran seeks to ease economic pressure from US sanctions through inflation control, food subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:51:56 UTC
21:51:56 KST

Sahin Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Iran is seeking to ease economic pressure from US and Western sanctions by slowing inflation and increasing food voucher allowances for households, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Monday.
Speaking to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency, Mohajerani said inflation was rooted in broader macroeconomic conditions and could not be addressed through short-term measures.
“We are trying to counter the economic pressure imposed on us by the West and the US by controlling the pace of inflation on the one hand and taking measures to improve people’s livelihoods, including increasing food voucher allowances, on the other,” she said.
The government is seeking to expand its electronic food voucher program, known as Kalabarg, which provides eligible households with subsidies to purchase essential food items.
Iran’s economy has faced mounting pressure from US sanctions, currency depreciation and rising consumer prices.
Washington launched a new economic pressure campaign, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, in August, targeting Iran’s oil exports, financial transactions and access to international markets.
The US also restored its naval blockade against vessels traveling to and from Iranian ports in July, further restricting Tehran’s oil trade.
Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in August that the country’s oil exports had fallen to zero amid the conflict and sanctions.
The International Monetary Fund projected in August that Iran’s economy would contract by 6.1% in 2026, with average annual inflation reaching 68.9%.
The economic difficulties have been compounded by the military conflict between Iran and the US, which began in February, and continuing disagreements over sanctions relief and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brazil’s Lula hangs on, but his final term promises to be toughest yet

- Fiscal policy is his biggest challenge. High debt, high interest rates and rising spending could block welfare promises, wage rises and tax changes.
- Congress may slow key appointments and reforms. Bolsonaro’s allies may also fight Lula and the courts, raising political tension and even impeachment risk.
AI generated
BRASILIA – Brazil’s octogenarian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva faces an uphill battle from day one of his final term, analysts say, with his plans hemmed in by economic headwinds and a right-wing Congress.
Already the country’s oldest president, Lula overcame a first-round loss to pull off a surprise run-off victory against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Oct 25, securing 51.8% of votes and a record fourth term just two days before his 81st birthday.
He will take office on Jan 5, 2027 after winning what he has said was his last election, hanging on to power in a country that has swung dramatically to the right since his first electoral victory in 2002.
Fiscal policy ‘his biggest challenge’
“Lula has shown that he still is the dominant political figure of his era, but he is weaker,” said Michael Ahn Paarlberg of the Center for International Policy think tank.
Brazil’s incoming Congress is its most conservative since the country’s return to democracy in the 1980s, with Bolsonaro’s party and its allies enjoying majorities in both chambers.
“He’s likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, an international relations professor at Sao Paulo’s Getulio Vargas Foundation, who predicted Lula would struggle to build a coalition to pass much of his agenda.
As of the morning of Oct 26, Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, had yet to concede, and Lula faced the prospect of adversaries in Congress who do not recognise his win, analysts said.
In addition, Congress has amassed significant power over government spending in the past decade, which could frustrate Lula’s promises to maintain his signature welfare programmes.
His government forecasts meagre 2.3% economic growth in 2027, adding to fiscal challenges worsened by high interest rates and public debt that has grown past 82% of gross domestic product, the highest since the Covid-19 pandemic.
“On the broad macroeconomic outlook, things are not looking great,” said Monica de Bolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
A hostile Congress “will make it very hard to push any reform through Congress and even try to manage the budget”, she said.
Lula’s promises to ensure minimum wage increases remain above inflation are among those that clash with growing pressure to get debt under control.
Lula’s aides have signalled that he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.
“Fiscal policy remains Lula’s biggest economic challenge,” said Andres Abadia, chief Latin American economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, as growing mandatory spending and high interest costs leave little room to cut deficits.
Analysts said an economic crisis could even spur Lula’s impeachment, with some drawing comparisons to Brazil’s 2014-2016 crisis, which preceded the impeachment of Lula’s ally Dilma Rousseff.
“I think the campaign for Lula’s impeachment begins now,” said Paulo Kramer, a political scientist who worked on former president Bolsonaro’s first campaign and has spoken to people close to his son.
Investors reacted nervously on the morning of Oct 26, sending Brazilian assets sharply lower as markets reassessed the country’s fiscal outlook under Lula.
Senate stumbling block
Congress is likely to block or slow Lula’s appointments to key roles in institutions such as the Supreme Court and the central bank, analysts say.
For the first time since Brazil returned to democracy, the executive branch will be clearly at odds with the Senate, said Lucas de Aragao, a partner at Brasilia-based consultancy Arko Advice.
“Lula will have some room to negotiate in the lower house by giving centrist parties more space, but in the Senate, he will have to bargain issue by issue and adjust his legislative agenda to fit what the opposition wants,” Aragao added.
Bolsonaro’s allies in the incoming Senate have also vowed to impeach Justice Alexandre de Moraes, escalating their long-running fight with a powerful judiciary that has often aligned with Lula, blocking key right-wing legislation and shaping policy on everything from Indigenous rights to the internet. What the US Spends on Patriot Missiles in the Middle East Could Defend Ukraine for Years

What the US Spends on Patriot Missiles in the Middle East Could Defend Ukraine for Years
Patriot interceptor missiles expended during US and allied air defense operations in the Middle East could have supported Ukraine’s air defenses for several years, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to RBC-Ukraine on October 26, Ihnat made the assessment during the outlet’s “TSE BAZA” podcast, highlighting differences in how Ukrainian forces and other Patriot operators use the American-made air defense systems.
Ihnat explained that Ukrainian crews have developed tactics to conserve expensive interceptors while maintaining their effectiveness against Russian missiles and aircraft.
One major difference involves the number of missiles launched against individual targets. Ukrainian operators have learned to engage certain threats with a single interceptor, while air defense crews in the Middle East have reportedly fired as many as eight missiles at one target.
Patriot systems can operate in automatic, semi-automatic, and manual modes. According to Ihnat, automatic operation can result in multiple interceptors being launched against a single threat, particularly when crews lack extensive combat experience.
He argued that the volume of Patriot missiles expended in the Middle East could have sustained Ukrainian Patriot operations for several years, contributing to concerns over interceptor availability.
Ukraine has also adapted how Patriot batteries are deployed. Rather than keeping the systems in fixed defensive positions near military installations, Ukrainian forces have used mobile tactics to intercept Russian aircraft before relocating.
Ihnat cited a May 2023 operation in Russia’s Bryansk region, when Ukrainian Patriot crews reportedly shot down five Russian aircraft—including two fighter jets and three helicopters—in just five minutes. The operation demonstrated Ukraine’s ability to use Patriot systems for mobile air defense ambushes rather than relying exclusively on fixed defensive positions.
The comments come amid growing concerns over Ukraine’s limited access to Patriot interceptors as Russia continues launching ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously stated that Ukraine receives approximately 12 Patriot interceptors per month, roughly four times fewer than during former US President Joe Biden’s administration. Zelenskyy also said that some interceptor shipments already financed by Ukraine’s international partners have yet to receive authorization from Washington.

Germany Moves to Buy Ukrainian-Made Bars Missiles for Bundeswehr in Historic First
Germany is preparing to purchase Ukrainian-developed Bars cruise missiles for its armed forces, potentially marking the first time the Bundeswehr has acquired an offensive weapon designed in Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 26, citing people familiar with the plans, Berlin could finalize an agreement for an initial batch within weeks. The missiles would undergo technical testing in early 2027, with successful trials potentially leading to an order of several hundred units.
The Bars is a jet-powered cruise missile capable of striking targets up to 1,000 kilometers away and carrying a warhead of up to 105 kilograms, depending on the variant. Ukrainian officials sometimes classify it as a drone-missile, while Germany considers it a low-cost cruise missile.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously identified Bars among the weapons used to strike Russian military bases and energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that Bars missiles are already being manufactured in Germany through a Ukrainian-German joint venture established under the Build with Ukraine initiative. The first German-funded batch was delivered to Ukraine in October 2026.
The planned Bundeswehr purchase would expand the venture’s production beyond supplying Ukraine, reflecting growing European interest in Ukrainian defense technologies developed and tested during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Germany is also seeking more affordable alternatives to American Tomahawk cruise missiles, which cost approximately $4 million to $6 million each and are unlikely to arrive before the 2030s because of production constraints.
According to the Financial Times, Bars missiles cost even less than the US-developed Anthem cruise missile, which is priced at roughly one-tenth of a Tomahawk. Berlin plans to test both systems, while a potential purchase of Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missile has been postponed.
The procurement plans form part of Germany’s broader €780 billion rearmament effort over five years, aimed at expanding military capabilities and strengthening European deterrence against Russia.
Earlier, in September, a European joint venture began producing Ukraine’s Bars jet-powered drones, with initial deliveries scheduled for October. The system can reach speeds exceeding 700 km/h and strike targets up to 1,000 kilometers away. Its modular design allows developers to adjust payload capacity and range depending on operational requirements.

The new sites were identified through satellite imagery analyzed jointly with OSINT researcher jembob.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators found that the 16 towers were constructed in October within roughly 50 kilometers south of the residence—the direction facing Ukraine.
The new structures appear to form an additional outer air-defense ring and are expected to host Pantsir gun-and-missile systems, Tor surface-to-air missile systems, or similar equipment.
No corresponding new positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the outer ring, although investigators said additional construction could follow.
The new defensive belt passes through Khotilovo military airfield and the area around the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
Khotilovo is used for Putin’s travel, and a dedicated railway line connects the airfield area with his Valdai residence. One air-defense tower at the base had already been constructed by March 2026.
Several additional positions have appeared around the reservoir, including near Lisiy Island. Russian forces have built a laboratory complex there that, according to an earlier RFE/RL investigation, may be connected to Russia’s biological weapons research program.
Construction of two air-defense towers near that facility began in early September, roughly when the investigation into the laboratory became public.
The latest expansion pushes the number of known air-defense positions around Valdai above 50.
That figure is particularly striking when compared with Moscow. Russia has built roughly twice as many air-defense positions to protect Moscow and the surrounding region since the beginning of the full-scale invasion—but Moscow and its suburbs are home to more than 20 million people.
Fewer than 100,000 people live in Valdai, the surrounding district, and nearby territory within roughly 50 kilometers.
Previously, Russian leader Vladimir Putin signed an order to expand the core personnel of the Federal Protective Service, marking the fourth increase since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Serbia’s student-backed opposition has defeated Vučić at the ballot box. He says the winners will impose sanctions on Russia — but they say otherwise.
Serbia held snap parliamentary elections on October 25. Among the candidates was former president Aleksandar Vučić, who had resigned just a month earlier but was hoping to return to power as prime minister.
Aleksandar Vučić served as president of Serbia for six years, becoming the country’s head of state in May 2017 and winning reelection to a second term in 2022.
Serbia has seen continuous protests demanding Vučić’s resignation for the past two years. They began after a concrete canopy collapsed at a railway station in the Serbian city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Vučić called early elections to the National Assembly, Serbia’s parliament, in early September 2026 and resigned on September 27, saying he would take part in the upcoming vote “as an ordinary citizen.”
Vučić ran at the head of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party. His main challenger was the Student List, a leaderless movement formally established just a month earlier but rooted in the mass protests that began in 2024.
The movement’s candidate list, registered with the election commission, included 250 people. None of them were students. Instead, the list included scientists, university professors, experts, and athletes. Cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the University of Novi Sad, topped the list.
Movement representatives described how they built the list:
We weren’t looking for people who would look best on billboards, and we weren’t looking for those who have known for years how to negotiate a spot on an electoral list. We were looking for people who, in our view, are capable of entering government institutions, doing their jobs responsibly, and not forgetting why they’re there.
The Student List’s 11-point platform was organized into three main sections. The first, titled “Serbia or the Mafia,” focused on stepping up the fight against corruption; the second addressed adapting the education system to modern needs; and the third covered socioeconomic issues.
Polling stations across Serbia closed at 8 p.m. local time. Less than two hours later, Vučić spoke at Serbian Progressive Party headquarters and conceded defeat.
“We don’t have final results yet. Based on a stratified sample, it’s clear that we lost this election. Student List has won: they will have between 135 and 140 seats, and we will have 105,” Vučić said. After Vučić conceded, people poured into the streets across Serbia to celebrate the Student List’s victory.
According to the latest election commission data, the Student List received 52.54% of the vote, while Vučić’s list got 39.29%. Turnout was a preliminary 68.78% — higher than in any parliamentary election over the past decade, when turnout never exceeded 60%. The highest turnout on record came in Serbia’s first multiparty elections in 1990, when 71.49% of voters cast ballots.
Ilija Srdanović, who leads the Student List, said Serbia had won, adding that he was proud of the people who had managed to say “no” to a tyrant. “We are moving toward a civilized and better Serbia,” he said.
Who will seek the post of prime minister remains unclear. Dejan Šoškić, a Student List candidate for parliament and former governor of the National Bank of Serbia, said before the vote that the makeup of the future government would be discussed after a possible election victory.
Whether Serbia will change its foreign policy toward Russia remains a separate question. Less than a week before the election, Vučić gave an interview to Ksenia Sobchak, saying that if his party lost the election, “within 10 days of the new government’s formation, we would see sanctions being imposed against Russia.”
“But I don’t want to talk this way in front of Russian media, because it comes across as if I’m speaking badly about someone from my own country,” he added. Vučić repeated his warning about possible sanctions even after his election defeat, saying he expected them to take effect by March or April 2027.
In their foreign policy platform, released in late September, representatives of the student movement said Serbia would maintain its principled position against imposing restrictive measures on Russia.
Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal confirmed this position during preelection debates in mid-October. “We have taken the position that sanctions against Russia will not be imposed; on the other hand, there is a need to coordinate foreign policy [with the European Union], but, I repeat, all of this is a matter of negotiation,” he said.

Study in Switzerland finds over half of participants see fake news as 'major' social issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:48:10 UTC
21:48:10 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
More than half of research participants in Switzerland consider disinformation a "major" social problem, expressing concern over misinformation, according to a study released Monday.  
The findings were published in the University of Zurich's Research Centre for the Public Sphere and Society 2026 Quality of the Media Yearbook, Swissinfo reported.
Some 56.5% of the participants view "fake news as a major social problem," the report noted. 
The latest percentage represents a "significant" increase compared with five years ago, it added.
The study found that more than half of respondents regularly encounter misleading information, particularly through social media, video-sharing platforms, and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Some 42% were classified as "news-deprived," referring to people who rarely follow current affairs or rely on fragmented information from social media, making them more vulnerable to conspiracy theories.
Researchers found that relying exclusively on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram offered no greater protection against conspiracy theories than avoiding news altogether.
While overall news quality remained stable in 2025, media diversity declined, with 44.7% of national political coverage appearing across multiple German-language publications.
The study also found that 57.7% of respondents considered public broadcasting important or very important.
Meanwhile, technology platforms captured up to 2.5 billion Swiss francs ($3 billion) in annual advertising revenue, while domestic media revenues fell to 1.94 billion francs ($2.3 billion).
The researchers called for countermeasures, such as media vouchers for young adults.

Russia promises “favorable conditions” to European firms a month after seizing control of Nestlé and Auchan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:47:13 UTC
21:47:13 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed Russia is trying to create “favorable conditions” for European companies that stayed in the country, The Moscow Times reported. He said it on state TV weeks after his decrees put several of the largest Western businesses in Russia under Kremlin-appointed managers. Meanwhile, Russia’s own government expects investment to fall at the fastest pace in over a decade.
To keep paying for its full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia has drained reserves, borrowed more, and raised taxes. Its war spending will still rise by 27% next year, as the EU moved this month to adopt its largest sanctions package against Russia’s war industry. Fresh foreign money could ease that squeeze, and the Kremlin keeps scaring it away.
Putin: Europe’s companies left Russia in tears
Putin made the claim in an interview with Kremlin propagandist Pavel Zarubin, which Russian state outlet Vesti published on 25 October. He claimed Russia has “many friends in Europe,” but European governments forced their businesses out:
“When some companies were leaving us under pressure from Western European governments, our friends from these countries nearly cried… Some of them, by the way, are working, and we are trying to create appropriate favorable conditions for them.”
He also attacked Western sanctions, calling it stupid to ban “everything that comes from Russia.”
The decrees came first
On 17 September, Putin’s decree handed the Russian assets of Nestlé, Auchan, and the former Leroy Merlin chain to a firm run by an Interior Ministry major general. US packaging maker Aptar and German wholesaler Metro followed. In mid-October, Russia seized French flooring maker Tarkett and four more foreign-owned firms.
“A warning to companies that remain”: Russia takes control of Nestlé and Auchan’s assets – companies that stayed in Russia following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine
The Kremlin claimed their home countries are “actively involved” in fighting Russia, and Putin cited his 2023 decree on retaliating for Western moves against Russian property. Since the full-scale war began, Russia has put 135 foreign-linked firms under such management. Asked which European companies could be next, a senior Russian official said: “Let them be scared.” Metro reportedly asked to be taken over itself, hoping to keep more control over its fate.
“We don’t steal,” Putin said three weeks earlier
In early October, Putin denied that the takeovers amounted to seizures. At the Valdai Discussion Club on 1 October, he claimed: “We take nothing from anyone, we don’t steal, and we don’t nationalize… Yes, we place some enterprises under external management.”
Russia’s investment drop is the worst since 2015
Putin has demanded an urgent new “investment cycle.” Instead, his economy ministry expects investment to shrink by 5.4% this year. Russian authorities have seized assets worth 7.6 trillion rubles (about $95 billion) from their owners during the war, law firm NSP estimates. More than half of large Russian companies ended 2025 with lower profits and cut or froze investment projects.
Two rubles for the army for every one on welfare, schools, and hospitals: Russia’s 2027 wartime budget
Ukrainian long-range strikes add to the risk of building anything in Russia. Overnight on 26 October, drones attacked a Voronezh aircraft plant that makes parts for Russia’s military transport planes. A day earlier, drones reportedly hit a titanium plant in Perm Krai, and Storm Shadow missiles reportedly struck a battery plant in Yelets supplying Russia’s missiles and glide bombs.

French student representatives hail govt's ‘concrete measures’, call for protests to continue
Representatives from French high school student groups on Monday hailed the government’s first measures to calm the crisis over ongoing unrest linked to their protest movement, including a gradual replacement of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup, but called for “continued mobilisation” after their meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Read about the day’s events as they unfolded on our liveblog.
This page is no longer being updated. For more of our coverage, click here.
'The success of our young people must not depend on their social background,' PM Lecornu says
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu posted on X, "The success of our young people must not depend on their social background, their high school, or the area in which they grow up."
He added, "In recent weeks, high school students and college students have expressed strong expectations. The national consultation of high school students... has brought their concerns and proposals to light."
New government measures proposed to quell high school student unrest
- Reform of the Parcoursup admissions system in 2027, ahead of its full replacement in 2028
- Creation of 15,000 additional higher education places
- A cap of 28 students per class in the "seconde" (first year of high school)
- A €5 billion low-interest loan for the renovation of educational infrastructure (€4 billion towards secondary schools, €1 billion for universities)
- 500 additional teaching positions
- Adjustment to student grants, bringing them in line with inflation
No 'empty promises', education minister says
France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray stated on Monday that "none of the decisions" made in response to the crisis involving high school students "are empty".
"Everything we say will be done and will be honoured within specific timeframes and with clear, quantifiable targets," he declared during a press conference, following a meeting held on Monday – alongside Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu – with high school and student organisations.
French student union leaders call for 'continued mobilisation' after meeting PM
The French government met student representatives on Monday following weeks of unrest. Students who had been demanding a meeting for weeks hail progress. Nonetheless they are now calling for fresh demonstrations next Saturday (October 31) to press for further measures.
Details by FRANCE 24’s French Politics Editor Marc Perelman.
Major evolution to Parcoursup admissions platform proposed
French Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste has announced that there will be a "major evolution" of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup in 2027, followed by its "replacement in 2028".
The system that has faced significant criticism from high school students since the onset of the crisis.
During a press conference, Baptiste explained the need for a "two-stage" transition by noting that Parcoursup "is anchored in law".
He stated, "Consequently, certain parametres of Parcoursup can only be altered if the law itself is changed."
Consultations with school, student groups to commence, education minister says
"Starting tomorrow, we will launch a consultation process with high school students and staff trade unions to examine the role of continuous assessment in high schools and for the baccalaureate." – Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray
Classroom cap
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray says tenth-grade classroom sizes will be capped at 28 pupils within two years.
Funds for renovation of education facilities
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray pledges a €4 billion budget to be made available for catchment areas to continue, scale up, and complete building renovation projects.
Issues raised by students
Among the main issues raised by high school students are:
- imbalanced school scheduling
- ill-suited school facilities
- subsitution issues when replacing absent teachers
- overcrowded classrooms
- challenges related to classroom atmosphere and mental health
- pressure surrounding academic orientation and the Parcoursup admissions system
- high school voices not being sufficiently heard
Education ministers to hold press conference at 7pm
Minister of National Education Édouard Geffray and Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste plan to hold a press conference at 7pm to provide details of various measures to assuage the demands of protesting high schoolers.
The ministers spent the afternoon meeting with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, as well as high school and university organisations.
Louis Létoublon, vice-president of prominent French high school union Les Lycéens! called for seeing things "through to the end", urging further mobilisation next Saturday and on November 5 – a date designated by trade unions for a general strike.
"The government is afraid; it has clearly shown that it is disoriented by everything that has been happening. This fear gives us an opening – a breach we can exploit to secure as much as possible in defence of high school students' rights."
Macron promises 'concrete measures' in response to French students' demands
French President Emmanuel Macron said the government would announce “concrete measures" on Monday to address school students’ demands after weeks of unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was scheduled to meet with students later Monday. FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago reports from the ground.
High school student representatives welcome 'concrete announcements' but call for 'continued mobilisation'
Speaking to FRANCE 24, Clément Vieillot, co-founder of the “Cachan 94” collective, said that the measures announced by the government are “not enough”.
“The announcements from the Lecornu government are woefully inadequate. The government is offering a €4 billion loan to the regions; not only is this insufficient for infrastructure, but it also means the regions will have to repay it.”
Furthermore, “we were asking for 250,000 additional spots in higher education, yet we’re only getting 4,000. This is completely absurd,” he continued, calling for “the movement to continue until our demands are heard and implemented”.
National Assembly debate on Parcoursup to be held at 5pm
The French government will hold a non-binding National Assembly debate at 5pm on the future of high-school orientation and the placement of students in higher education, following President Emmanuel Macron’s pledge to overhaul admissions portal Parcoursup.
The debate will be held under Article 50-1 of the Constitution, meaning politicians will be allowed to present proposals without involving any voting. The government plans a two-phase replacement of Parcoursup this academic year and next, amid the ongoing student protest crisis.
Amnesty International calls on French government to 'abandon' 'Make Rioters Pay' bill
Human rights organisation Amnesty International is urging the French government to "abandon" its plans to introduce a "make rioters pay" bill, which it claims could potentially "violate France's obligations under international human rights law".
"The government must abandon this new, rights-infringing bill, which poses a serious threat to the right to protests, by exposing all demonstrators to the risk of financial penalties," wrote Nathalie Godard, Director of Action at Amnesty International France in a press release.
Deemed "absolutely essential" by French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, the legislation will be debated in the Senate starting Tuesday just over a week after looting and violence marred peaceful demonstrations across France on October 17.
Higher education admissions platform Parcoursup could be replaced by end of next academic year
The government plans to replace admissions platform Parcoursup in two phases over the course of this academic year and the next, according to the education-focussed social media influencers who met with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday at midday, ahead of his meetings with youth organisations.
The higher education admissions platform has faced heavy criticism from high school students since the start of the current protest movement.
Minister of Education Edouard Geffray and Minister of Higher Education Philippe Baptiste are set to unveil "concrete" plans at 5.30pm during a press conference.
More than 400,000 protest across France Saturday
Saturday’s demonstrations across France were largely peaceful, easing fears of a repeat of the violence seen the prior weekend.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets to demand action on the rising cost of living and more funding for public services, with students, workers and retirees marching side by side.
Many say their anger shows no sign of fading. The government put turnout at 410,000 nationwide, while the CGT union – organisers of the authorised demonstrations – estimated the figure was almost twice as high.
FRANCE 24's Jack Pownall shares more 📺.
Shopkeepers fear ongoing impact to trade
"There’s no such thing as a business without customers; the clientele needs to return."
Between precautionary shop closures and a drop in footfall, shopkeepers grow increasingly concerned about the impact that Saturday social protests are having on their sales – against an already gloomy economic backdrop.
The year's final quarter is typically a crucial period for businesses in the run-up to the holiday season.
And while Saturday’s day of protest was calmer than expected – despite some clashes and isolated incidents of looting in several cities – "the fact remains that we didn't do any business this weekend," laments Virginie Grimault, General Delegate of the Federation of Grocery and Local Convenience Stores (FECP), in an interview with AFP.
October 24 protests: 267 police officers and 150 protesters injured, including three seriously
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while the activity on October 24 in general was kept under control, "we observed a very high level of violence directed at internal security forces," with "267" police officers and gendarmes injured, he told network RMC/BFMTV.
"An estimated 150" protesters were injured" – three of them "quite seriously" in Toulouse, Reims, and Clermont-Ferrand – the minister announced, noting that the injuries occurred "during police operations, given the context of extreme violence."
He added that "investigations by the IGPN" – the national police oversight body – "are underway, as is the case every time".
🗣️ 'Not normal' for France to be in turmoil so close to election, says Macron
Macron says it is "not normal for France to be in such "turmoil" six months from the election – according to reports by AFP.
He called for the type of unrest seen on October 17 to "never" happen again.
"We will continue to hold the line," Macron told security forces on a visit to Marseille. "If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

====================================================================================================

Beyond the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia’s Strategic Footprint in PNG Grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

Last week Australia’s foreign and defense ministers, Penny Wong and Richard Marles, travelled to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea (PNG) to lead Australia’s delegation to the 32nd Australia-Papua New Guinea Ministerial Forum. The meeting was the first since the Pukpuk Treaty, which established PNG’s first formal defense alliance with another country, entered into force in July. The forum focused on turning the treaty’s commitments into practical initiatives for defense cooperation, infrastructure, recruitment, and new technologies.
The headline agreement was a new rotation of Australian defense personnel to PNG. A new combat group of 130 Australian Defense Force (ADF) personnel will be based in PNG on three month rotations. The deployment, known as the Magani Rotation, is intended to deepen military cooperation and increase familiarity between the two forces.
A rotation offers greater advantages over occasional military exercises. It allows personnel to develop more consistent working relationships, become familiar with how each defense force works, and be able to coordinate activities over longer periods. For PNG, it provides greater access to Australian military expertise, while for Australia, it strengthens its ability to operate alongside a neighbor whose geography makes it important to the defense of Australia’s northern approaches.
Alongside this, the two governments also announced a $77 million infrastructure investment fund for the PNG Defense Force. This funding is intended to upgrade PNG’s military facilities to be better able to house, train, and sustain additional personnel.
While the Magani Rotation may be a significant step in advancing the integration of the two defense forces, the more radical idea is the opening up of Australian military recruitment to eligible Papua New Guineans. Applications for the first intake will open on November 16, with an initial pilot program starting in 2027. The first two cohorts will comprise roughly 50 recruits each, with candidates initially sought from the University of Papua New Guinea, Pacific Adventist University, and the University of Technology in Lae. The program is intended to expand over time, although the initial recruitment numbers are modest.
In order to address recruitment shortages, Australia has already expanded ADF recruitment to Australian permanent residents from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada who are on the pathway to citizenship. However, the new PNG recruitment is different – it has been established under the Pukpuk Treaty and will allow eligible PNG citizens living in PNG to apply directly.
The initial rationale is similar – to overcome persistent personnel shortages – but it comes with a broader strategic goal. These recruits will train and serve alongside Australians, creating personal, cultural and institutional links as part of a longer-term alliance-building objective. Australia citizenship will be an eventual requirement, but this will come via the conventional permanent residency and citizenship application processes.
At the ministerial forum, Australia and PNG also formalized a partnership covering digital governance, network security, and emerging technologies. The agreement builds on a Telecommunications Blueprint designed to improve PNG’s connectivity and digital infrastructure. For Australia, the partnership has strategic as well as economic significance: secure telecommunications networks are essential to military coordination, government resilience, and the protection of critical infrastructure. It also gives Canberra a greater role in shaping the systems connecting PNG to the outside world, while helping the country strengthen its own digital capabilities.
Australia’s alliance with PNG builds on an existing security program. Since 2023, Canberra has committed AU$200 million under the bilateral security agreement to support PNG’s police and justice institutions, including upgraded training facilities, police helicopters, and a National Forensic Science Center. A second phase of support is planned after the current program ends in 2027. Though separate from the Pukpuk Treaty, this work strengthens PNG’s capacity to maintain internal security and exercise authority across its territory.
The challenge for both Australia and PNG is to turn these commitments into lasting capabilities. Australia is investing serious capital in PNG – including across issues like health and other social infrastructure – and hopes to gain a return for its investment. This return for Australia is PNG’s ability to develop its defense, economic, and social capabilities, and to be better equipped to contribute to its own security and regional stability. This also comes with the caveat that it keeps PNG within Australia’s orbit of influence. For Port Moresby, the objective will be whether its alliance with Australia actually increases PNG sovereign capabilities and improves its development objectives, rather than simply accommodating Australia’s strategic priorities.

Jordan says three family members behind Karak church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:44:22 UTC
21:44:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Jordan says three members of one family behind Karak church attack
Jordanian authorities on Monday identified three suspects arrested at dawn over last week's deadly church attack as members of the same family.
"The perpetrators of the attack on the church were two brothers and the third was their relative by marriage," Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said at a press conference. He named the three as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.
The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, in Karak governorate, killed nine people and wounded 34 others during a funeral service.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya and Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani, the security chief described the suspects as extremists who had adopted an extremist ideology.
He said the three men lived near Hamoud village and had acted without prior planning.
According to the security chief, the suspects were following the funeral procession when they decided to carry out the attack, a decision he attributed to their extremist beliefs.
He said the three men had developed the idea together while following the procession, rather than preparing the assault in advance.
Following the shooting, the suspects fled the scene in a single vehicle, which was later recovered by investigators.
Security forces also seized firearms and a large quantity of ammunition following their arrest.
Suspects arrested after shootout
Jordanian authorities announced early on Monday that they had arrested all three suspects following an armed confrontation at an abandoned house in the village of Al-Jadida, approximately five kilometres from Hamoud.
The Public Security Director said security teams had spent three days searching designated areas before narrowing their operation to a number of abandoned buildings.
Shortly after midnight on Sunday night, officers divided part of Al-Jadida into sectors and identified several abandoned houses for inspection.
The operation led security forces to the building where the suspects were hiding.
According to the Public Security Directorate, the men refused to surrender and opened fire on officers, prompting an exchange of gunfire.
All three suspects were wounded before being taken into custody and transferred to hospital. No members of the security forces were injured during the operation.
The security chief said investigators had pursued two lines of inquiry immediately after the attack.
The first focused on criminal investigations, intelligence gathering and collecting evidence from the scene.
The second involved emergency response measures, surveillance operations and tracking the suspects' movements and escape routes.
No evidence of links to wider groups
Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said investigators had found no indications that the suspects were connected to other extremist cells or organisations.
He stressed, however, that the investigation remained ongoing and that authorities would pursue anyone found to have helped plan, encourage or facilitate the attack.
Al-Faraya described the killings as the product of an extremist ideology that was alien to Jordanian values and traditions.
He said tackling terrorism required more than arresting those responsible, calling for efforts to address the roots of extremism, hate speech and incitement.
The minister also referred to King Abdullah II's visit to survivors in hospital, during which the monarch pledged a firm response against those responsible for the killings.
Al-Faraya said the successful arrest operation demonstrated the authorities' commitment to protecting citizens and ensuring accountability.
Jordan warns against sectarian divisions
Government Communications Minister Mohammad Al-Momani urged Jordanians not to allow the attack to fuel religious hatred or divisions within society.
He described the killings as a turning point in the country's efforts to confront extremist and takfiri ideology, announcing that the government would continue working to combat radicalisation across different sectors.
Al-Momani said royal directives had called for a review of policies aimed at countering extremist thought and addressing its underlying causes through a systematic national strategy.
He stressed that confronting extremism was a shared responsibility involving government institutions, religious authorities, schools, the media and wider society.
Protecting the public, he argued, required challenging not only acts of violence but also the ideas and rhetoric used to justify them.
The minister also warned against misinformation and rumours, saying misleading information could spread fear, undermine public confidence and encourage incitement during times of crisis.
He urged the public to avoid discussions that could deepen religious or social divisions, stressing that the actions of extremists should not be used to blame entire communities.
"We must not allow terrorism to achieve through words what it failed to achieve through crime," Al-Momani said.
He added that Jordanian citizenship was not determined by religious or social identity and that no citizen should have to prove their belonging to the country.
The government would not allow extremist ideology to redefine relations between Jordanians or undermine the shared national identity that united them under the rule of law, he said.
Al-Momani also praised the solidarity shown by Jordanians towards the families of those killed, describing it as a demonstration of the country's rejection of hatred and division.
"This solidarity embodies our belief that the suffering of any Jordanian is the suffering of us all, and that our national unity is firmly rooted and cannot be undermined by terrorism," he said.
The attack on St George's Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud took place during a funeral service, leaving nine people dead and 34 others injured.
Authorities have pledged to continue investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings and bring anyone involved to justice.

New free email service against phishing: “Protecting people with less digital literacy”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:42:42 UTC
21:42:42 KST

A suspicious email sent to his mother gave Jany Ertveldt an idea. The Fleming developed a free service that analyses suspicious emails within minutes and explains whether they are safe. The aim is to better protect people with less digital literacy, in particular against online scammers.
New free email service against phishing: “Protecting people with less digital literacy”
The idea came about a few weeks ago when Ertveldt’s mother received an email purporting to be from a parcel delivery service. She was asked to pay €1.99 to receive her parcel and wasn’t sure whether the message was genuine.
“As it happened, my mum had just ordered something online,” says Ertveldt. “She asked if I could have a look to see if the email was genuine. Because of my work, I could tell straight away that it was a typical phishing email. But not everyone recognises it that quickly.”
According to Jany Ertveldt, such messages are sent to hundreds or even thousands of people. “Some of them fall for it, and that’s how scammers make money.”
Simply forward a suspicious email
With info@checkmijnmail.be Ertveldt aims to make the process as simple as possible. Users do not need to install any app or software. They simply forward a suspicious email and receive an analysis back within a few minutes.
“You can see straight away what’s suspicious about the email,” he says. “If it concerns a perfectly normal advertising email. Even then, the system explains exactly what’s going on.”
The system checks the sender, the domain behind the email address, links in the message and even QR codes. It also checks how long a website has been in existence.
“Fraudsters often use domains that have only recently been created,” explains Ertveldt. “That can be an important warning sign.”
Database containing hundreds of suspicious websites
The email service compares emails against a database of more than 600 domains. This database is updated every week with new reports and warnings.
“We’re expanding the system every week,” says Ertveldt. “We monitor reports of online fraud and add new information. This makes the system increasingly smarter.”
Since its launch, he has noticed that more and more people are using the service. “At the moment, dozens of users have already had an email checked. We’re seeing growing interest.”
Privacy must continue to be guaranteed
According to Ertveldt, privacy has been a key priority from the outset. That is why the service does not store forwarded emails.
“As soon as someone has received the analysis, the email is deleted,” he says. “At the end of the day, we also delete all log files. We do not keep any records of the user.”
Dream of collaborating with the government
The service is free, and Ertveldt wants to keep it that way. His ambition is to reach even more people and further expand the system.
“I want it to remain as simple as possible,” he says. “Ideally, in the future we could collaborate with the government or with cyber safety agency Safeonweb. That way, we can help even more people recognise phishing for free.”
