Kiev loses 1,285 troops along engagement line in past day – latest figures
The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,285 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 300 troops and 19 motor vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, more than 220 troops and three jamming stations in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and over 185 troops and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost roughly 340 troops and three armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 210 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and about 30 troops and a counterbattery radar station in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 300 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 300 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 19 enemy motor vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Podsredneye, Prikolotnoye, Doroshenkovo and Fyodorovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.
In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of a mechanized brigade, an airmobile brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Khoten, Barilovka and Nikolskoye in the Sumy Region, it said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 300 personnel, 19 motor vehicles and three electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 220 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 220 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy jamming stations in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Lesnaya Stenka and Donetskoye in the Kharkov Region, Raigorodok, Cherkasskoye and Bogorodichnoye in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 220 personnel, 20 motor vehicles and three electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 185 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 185 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, an airmobile brigade, a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Kramatorsk, Slavyansk, Druzhkovka and Kondratovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 185 personnel, two armored combat vehicles, 33 motor vehicles, an artillery gun and four electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts 340 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted roughly 340 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, an assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and three National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Stepanovka, Krinitsy, Belozerskoye, Shilovka, Starovarvarovka and Malotaranovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 340 personnel, three armored combat vehicles, eight motor vehicles, a US-made 155mm Paladin self-propelled artillery system and two electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 210 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 210 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Gavrilovka, Vsesvyatskoye and Pokrovskoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Volnyanka and Vasilevskoye in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 210 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, seven motor vehicles and a counterbattery radar station in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 30 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 30 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy counterbattery radar station in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on formations of a mechanized brigade and a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Dimitrovo and Preobrazhenka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 30 Ukrainian military personnel, 12 motor vehicles and a counterbattery radar station were destroyed," it said.
Russia strikes storage sites for Ukrainian army’s ground robotic platforms in past day
Russian forces struck storage sites for the Ukrainian army’s ground robotic platforms and long-range unmanned aerial vehicles and enemy deployment areas over the past day, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck military-industrial enterprises, energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, ammunition depots, workshops producing and sites storing ground robotic platforms and long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 151 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses intercept 581 Ukrainian UAVs, two cruise missiles over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 581 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and two Storm Shadow cruise missiles over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down two guided aerial bombs, two British-made Storm Shadow airborne cruise missiles and 581 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 271,778 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,406 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,792 multiple rocket launchers, 36,815 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,658 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

‘More they do it, stronger PDA gets’: Akhilesh Yadav alleges 'misinformation campaign' against SP-Congress alliance
Unknown

21:42:05 KST

NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Monday alleged that efforts were being made to spread misinformation about the party’s seat-sharing negotiations with the Congress but maintained that such attempts would only strengthen the alliance’s support base among the “PDA” communities.The term “PDA”, coined by Akhilesh Yadav, stands for “Pichhda, Dalit and Alpsankhyak”, referring to Other Backward Classes, Dalits and minorities. These groups form a key focus of the SP’s political outreach.
Addressing a press conference at the SP headquarters in Lucknow, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister questioned who was putting up the posters and "funding" the campaign. He was referring to a recently installed hoarding in the state capital featuring Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, with the message: “200 seats are our right; UP trusts Rahul Gandhi.”“These objectionable posters have not appeared for the first time. Who is putting them up? Who is spending money on them? Who is running this racket?” Akhilesh Yadav asked.He added that such campaigns would only strengthen the PDA, saying, “The more they put up such posters, spread misinformation and insult others, the stronger the PDA will become.”The Congress has reportedly shared with the SP a list of 175-200 seats it wants to contest in the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections scheduled for February-March 2027.
Responding to questions about the SP’s alliance with the Congress, Akhilesh Yadav stated that his party's leaders have experience in bringing political parties together and managing alliances.“Samajwadi Party and all our leaders know how to bring people together. We all have experience in managing alliances. We will strengthen our alliance ahead of the Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections,” he remarked.
The SP and Congress contested the 2017 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections in alliance but suffered a setback, with the Akhilesh Yadav-led party winning just 47 of the 403 seats as it was voted out after a single term. The Congress fared worse with only seven seats, while the BJP came to power with a sweeping victory, winning 312 constituencies.In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP won 255 seats, while the SP secured 111. The Congress managed only two seats, with the SP and Congress contesting separately.However, the two parties reunited for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning a combined 43 of Uttar Pradesh’s 80 seats. The SP won 37 constituencies and the Congress six, while the BJP’s tally fell to 33, down from 71 seats in 2014 and 62 in 2019.(With PTI inputs)

U.S. Air Force trains with heavy drone hunter with net gun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:35:16 UTC
21:35:16 KST

- The U.S. Air Force trained with Zone 5 Technologies’ Paladin counter-drone multirotor at MacDill Air Force Base on Oct. 8.
- The drone carried a Gen12 launcher that fires net rounds to entangle and bring down hostile drones.
The U.S. Air Force has put the Paladin, a heavy counter-drone multirotor built by California-based Zone 5 Technologies, through training with Joint Interagency Task Force 401 at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida on Oct. 8, with the drone carrying a Gen12 counter-drone launcher that fires net rounds to entangle and bring down hostile drones, according to photos and captions released by the base.
Photos from the training show the compact, magazine-fed launcher mounted on a stabilized gimbal beneath the six-rotor drone, with net rounds and a deployed net laid out beside the aircraft. The base said the system uses a net round to bring down drones, giving MacDill an additional option for protecting personnel and infrastructure as part of a layered defense, but the Air Force did not say how many systems took part, whether any live intercepts were carried out, or whether the base plans to buy the Paladin.
Net rounds work by throwing a net into the path of a target drone so that it wraps around the rotors and stops the aircraft from flying, an approach that suits bases and other sensitive sites because it avoids sending bullets or explosive fragments into the area below. MacDill hosts the 6th Air Refueling Wing as well as the headquarters of U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command.
The Paladin is a multi-mission drone that Zone 5 describes as a fully autonomous wingman integrated with the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK) mapping and command software used across the U.S. military. It uses a quick-swap payload system, so operators can change it in the field between the counter-drone launcher, a munitions drop, a 7.62 mm (.308-caliber) rifle, and a loudspeaker and spotlight.
Zone 5 markets the counter-drone version as a Low Collateral Effects Interceptor, and the Paladin was the first drone of its kind added to the Department of War’s Blue UAS Cleared List, which approves drones for use across the U.S. military. The company also selected Echodyne’s EchoFlight radar to give the interceptor its own real-time picture of the airspace and the ability to track target drones autonomously.
The training at MacDill also featured the Bumblebee V2, a separate counter-drone system that intercepts hostile drones by ramming them, which the 6th Security Forces Squadron received as a low-cost option for its layered defense.
Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which Secretary of War Pete Hegseth established in August 2025, is the Department of War’s lead organization for countering small drones and has been testing and fielding systems at U.S. installations to protect them from drone incursions, which have been reported over military bases at home and abroad.
Zone 5 Technologies, founded in 2011 and based in San Luis Obispo, California, also develops the White Spike low-cost interceptor missile for counter-drone and precision strike missions, and the Air Force has not said whether the Paladin will be fielded at MacDill or other bases after the training.

Israeli elections: Will Trump’s endorsement help or hurt Netanyahu?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:35:09 UTC
21:35:09 KST

US President Donald Trump's endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could prove a double-edged sword ahead of Tuesday's election, with analysts saying it may help the embattled leader consolidate support but is unlikely to sway many voters and could even backfire.
Trump publicly backed Netanyahu on Sunday for the second time in a week, urging Israelis to re-elect the prime minister and linking his leadership to Washington's campaign against Iran.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump reiterated his support for Netanyahu, whom he had described a week earlier as a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a key partner in confronting Tehran.
The endorsement came as polls suggested Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc could struggle to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman said Trump's intervention was unlikely to significantly influence the outcome.
"Trump's pledge will have little impact on the Israeli voters; it was more of a desperate attempt by Netanyahu, who begged Trump to give him an endorsement, to get some support from his friend, at a time when in Israel the opposition parties seem, at least according to recent polls, to do quite well."
Axios reported Sunday, citing US and Israeli sources, that Netanyahu had personally pressed Trump for additional public support last week, even suggesting specific language for the endorsement.
Netanyahu's Likud party denied the report, although Trump had told Newsmax earlier this month that people in Israel had asked him to intervene on Netanyahu's behalf.
Bregman, a senior teaching fellow at King's College London, warned that the intervention could backfire among Israelis who resent foreign involvement in domestic politics.
"Trump's endorsement might even cause damage to Netanyahu, as many Israeli voters, including from Likud, hate this external intervention in domestic Israeli politics," he said.
Israelis head to the polls Tuesday to elect all 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in a pivotal election that will decide the country’s political direction amid the Gaza genocide and the war with Iran.
Netanyahu's bloc faces a challenge from opposition parties, including one led by Gadi Eisenkot, as both sides seek a path to forming the next government.
A recent Channel 12 poll suggested Trump's endorsement had done little to boost Netanyahu's prospects. Some 64% of respondents said it would not influence their vote, while 17% said it made them less likely to support Netanyahu.
Only 12% said the endorsement strengthened their support for his Likud party.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the RANE Network, said the endorsement could matter even if it fails to change many voters' minds.
"I don't think it'll change too many minds that are already made up, but Israel is such a fractious political environment, you don't need to change that many minds for it to necessarily be a decisive outcome."
Bohl suggested Trump's backing could discourage some traditional Likud voters from switching to rival right-wing parties, including those associated with opposition figures such as Avigdor Lieberman.
For center-right voters increasingly dissatisfied with Netanyahu, the endorsement could reinforce the argument that he is best placed to manage relations with Washington.
"I think for the center-right kind of national conservative voters that are traditionally go with Likud, who are getting sick of Netanyahu, I think this is a reminder to them that Netanyahu is, at least for the near term, at least for this presidency, indispensable."
Bohl said the endorsement could also strengthen Netanyahu's position in post-election coalition negotiations, particularly if neither bloc secures a clear majority.
Netanyahu could use his relationship with Trump to attract smaller parties or individual lawmakers during coalition negotiations, arguing that his ties with Washington give him an advantage on issues including Iran and the occupied West Bank.
Trump's endorsement marks an unusual intervention in Israeli politics, departing from the longstanding practice of US presidents avoiding explicit support for candidates in Israeli elections.
"I think it's unusual because American presidents don't usually endorse," Bohl said, describing the move as "very Trumpian."
He said the intervention comes as some Israelis question whether their country's close relationship with Washington can be sustained in the long term.
Netanyahu, however, could use his close relationship with Trump to argue that he is best placed to maintain strong ties with Washington, Bohl said.
But an endorsement from Trump does not guarantee electoral success.
Bregman pointed to Trump's backing of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who lost his country's parliamentary election in April.
“An endorsement from this guy in the White House is not necessarily a recipe for electoral success,” Bregman said.
He also questioned whether Trump's backing came without expectations in return.
Bregman raised similar questions about what Netanyahu might have offered in exchange for the endorsement.
“You don’t get a free meal from Trump,” he said. "What exactly did Netanyahu promise in return? I'm not sure. Perhaps Netanyahu pledged not to attack Iran before the Israeli elections and the American midterm elections."
The endorsement comes amid growing debate in the US over support for Israel following the wars in Gaza and Iran.
Bohl said declining support for Israel among some Americans could create political challenges for politicians closely associated with the Israeli government.
“Israel is becoming more and more unpopular in the United States,” Bohl said.
He pointed to changes in the political environment surrounding the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), including shifts in campaign spending and the use of new political action committees.
Bohl also contrasted Trump's intervention with US Vice President JD Vance's decision not to endorse Netanyahu.
He argued that Vance was mindful of growing criticism of Israel among both left-wing voters and younger conservatives, a constituency that could matter if he seeks the Republican presidential nomination in 2028.
The distinction was particularly striking given Vance's decision to campaign for Hungary's Viktor Orban ahead of April's election.
"He knows Israel is a liability for both his party and for the United States writ large, and he's trying to keep himself distant from it," Bohl said.
Beyond its potential electoral impact, Trump's endorsement could also have implications for Israeli policy toward Iran and the Palestinians if Netanyahu remains in office.
Bohl said Netanyahu's close relationship with Trump could give him greater freedom to pursue a hard-line regional agenda, although domestic and regional constraints would still limit Israel's ability to escalate conflicts on several fronts simultaneously.
He argued that Netanyahu has demonstrated an ability to persuade the Trump administration to support Israeli military action despite the political costs in the US.
Bohl said reports of possible further Israeli strikes on Iran illustrated how the relationship could shape future decisions, although the timing and likelihood of another attack remain uncertain.
A new Netanyahu government could also have implications for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, where movement restrictions and threats against Palestinian communities have raised concerns.
Bohl said Trump's backing could give Netanyahu greater room to pursue policies Washington might otherwise resist, provided they did not directly embarrass the US president.
"If Netanyahu is able to get through as the next prime minister, he will have a close enough relationship with this White House" to pursue policies including further military action against Iran and expanded Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon, he said.

By Gopal Sharma
KATHMANDU, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A German climber died after a fall while descending from the summit of a Himalayan peak in northeast Nepal, a hiking company official said on Monday.
The climber, who had topped the 6,814 metre (22,256 ft) Ama Dablam peak on Sunday, fell some 1,500 metres (4,920 feet) on his way back down from the summit and died on Monday, Gokul Thapa, head of the Real Himalaya Pvt Ltd company, which provided local logistics to him, said.
“His body was recovered by a search team today itself,” Thapa told Reuters from Lukla, gateway to the mountainous region.
Ama Dablam is a popular mountain among climbers in Solukhumbu district, home to the world’s tallest peak, Mount Everest.
Last week, two Japanese climbers died on another peak in west Nepal.
Thapa said the body of the German climber had been picked up from the mountain and would be carried by a helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu for a post mortem examination.
More than 300 mountaineers have received permits to climb Ama Dablam during the current September-November Autumn climbing season.
Earlier this year, 10 climbers including a noted Nepali-British climber died on a mountain in Pakistan.

Kremlin hails defeated Serbian ally Vucic as student election win adds to its geopolitical woes
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:33:37 CET
21:33:37 KST

By Andrew Osborn and Dmitry Antonov
MOSCOW, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Aleksandar Vucic’s crushing election defeat by a student-backed protest movement has cast gloom over Moscow, which has lost another important partner in Europe just six months after ally Viktor Orban was ousted in an election in Hungary.
Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow who had been prime minister or president since 2014, suffered a defeat on Sunday that prompted nationwide celebrations, although few had any idea of how the Balkan country’s new student-backed leaders would govern.
Russia saw Vucic’s Serbia as a crucial ally in Europe, and as a bulwark against what Moscow has cast as the European Union’s aggressive attempts to contain and punish it over its war in Ukraine.
Serbia buys large quantities of gas from Russian energy giant Gazprom, and although it has aspirations to join the European Union, it has not signed up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Instead, under Vucic — who enjoyed close ties to President Vladimir Putin — it continued to develop close economic, political and military links to Moscow.
The Kremlin put a brave face on Vucic’s defeat, saying it had taken note of the result and that Vucic — whose contribution to bilateral ties it warmly praised — was moving into opposition.
“As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
“For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango.”
GEOPOLITICAL SETBACK
Russia can still count EU member Slovakia, under Prime Minister Robert Fico, as a friendly country. It has also been closely watching unrest in France, where far-right politician Marine Le Pen has said she would cut financial aid to Ukraine if she won next year’s presidential election.
Recent regional electoral successes for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have been welcomed in Russia, where Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has begun to speak about the possibility of one day reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia which were blown up in 2022.
But for now at least, the potential loss of Serbia as a close ally — after setbacks to Russia’s geopolitical influence in the South Caucasus region and parts of Central Asia — is being seen as a serious blow in Moscow by Kremlin-aligned politicians, media and analysts.
Before Sunday’s election, the Student List party said it would not introduce sanctions on Russia over Ukraine, that it would retain Serbia’s military neutrality, and that it would not seek to join NATO.
Vucic has cast doubts on those pledges, suggesting the party would renege on them and impose sanctions on Moscow as soon as March or April.
Jovo Bakic, a representative for Student List and university lecturer, on Monday denied his party would U-turn.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector. There will be no changes there (in the country’s foreign policy),” Bakic told Russia’s RT Balkan TV outlet.
Members of Russia’s political elite fear Serbia’s EU aspirations could see it put under serious pressure to align itself more closely with EU foreign policy however and that Moscow could find itself betrayed by a traditional ally in the process.
“Brussels, for its part, is keen to see Belgrade align itself more closely with the common European position on Russia. The main indicator of Serbia’s actual course will not be Vucic’s statements or his opponents’ electoral pledges, but rather the first decisions taken by the new cabinet,” said the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper.
Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of the influential Russia in Global Affairs journal, said it was clear that a new political era was under way in Serbia that could sharply reorient the country towards the EU, in the same way that Orban’s loss of power in Hungary saw Budapest and Brussels become much closer.
“In this sense, the Hungarian case is quite telling,” said Lukyanov. “And Russia has nothing good to look forward to.”
(Reporting by Reuters in MoscowAdditional reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic in Belgrade Writing by Andrew Osborn Editing by Keith Weir and Sanjeev Miglani)

Can GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate who's bucked Trump, keep his Pennsylvania swing seat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:33:16 UTC
21:33:16 KST

Over nearly 10 years in Congress, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has cultivated an image as a middle-of-the-road GOP lawmaker who operates above the partisan fray and is willing to buck President Donald Trump.
It's a formula that has allowed Fitzpatrick, who is among the most moderate lawmakers on Capitol Hill according to his hometown newspaper, to win swing voters and consistently outperform his party in a highly competitive district that opted for Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. But in a year when Republican candidates across the country are being weighed down by Trump, Fitzpatrick is facing a stiff challenge from Democrat Bob Harvie in Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, and testing whether his personal brand can carry him in a difficult national political environment.
"Brian Fitzpatrick is Brian Fitzpatrick. I'm not Donald Trump. I'm not anybody else. And that's the way voters should approach this," Fitzpatrick told CNBC. "I'm not happy with [Trump]. I'm not happy with his tone. I don't think he's done a sufficient job. I think leaders are supposed to unite our country, unify people. He has not done that."
The battle between Fitzpatrick and Harvie comes as Trump's approval rating craters, the Iran war drags on and consumer prices rise. The contest is one of the approximately four dozen House seats considered in play in the Nov. 3 election that will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's term. Pennsylvania voters are often an indicator of how the country will swing overall, and because the state is on the East Coast, Fitzpatrick's district is one to watch as returns come in.
Democrats are on offense and spending money in districts previously thought out of reach — including Fitzpatrick's, in a race that could signal Democratic success outside of just the most vulnerable seats.
But Harvie, a former high school social studies teacher and county commissioner, is still a long shot to win. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted the race in Democrats' direction, from "Likely R" to "Lean R," earlier this month. Erin Covey, who leads coverage of House races at the Cook Report, called Fitzpatrick Democrats' "white whale."
As part of Democrats' final push to unseat Fitzpatrick, Harvie was joined earlier this month by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for a rally in Bucks County.
"This is an incredibly important state," Jeffries told reporters after the rally. "The commonwealth is a big swing state, and Bucks County is a big swing county. And so this is a critically important race."
Fitzpatrick grew up in Bucks County, which makes up much of the district, and is a former FBI agent who succeeded his brother, Michael, in 2017. He's a co-chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus and, according to a recent Philadelphia Inquirer analysis of his voting record, has voted against the White House and his party this Congress more than any other House Republican. The paper endorsed Harvie earlier this month.
Fitzpatrick is also part of a bipartisan group that's been outspoken as the White House has taken a more conciliatory tone toward Russia in recent weeks. He led a bill last week that would undo Trump's recent authorization of the U.S. purchase of Russian diesel. And he signed a bipartisan letter urging the Department of Defense to restore Ukraine's access to satellite communications that are critical to the country's defenses, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the services were downgraded. Fitzpatrick threatened to pursue the firing of U.S. officials responsible for the slowdown, The New York Times reported.
Fitzpatrick is seeking his sixth House term and for much of his career has easily warded off Democratic challenges. Christopher Nicholas, a Republican consultant based in Pennsylvania, said Fitzpatrick "has been the most moderate member of the House."
"If they are able to beat him this cycle, it is definitely going to be a great night for Democrats," Covey said.
Harvie casts Fitzpatrick as a rubber stamp for Trump and questions the claims of bipartisanship. While Fitzpatrick was one of only two Republicans to vote against the final version of Republicans' 2025 signature tax and spending package, he voted in favor of an earlier iteration in the House that sent the measure to the Senate and set it on a path to passage. Fitzpatrick has said he supported the initial draft of the bill, but opposed cuts to Medicaid that were added in the Senate.
Harvie also called out Fitzpatrick's mixed record on tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted to overturn Trump's tariffs on Canada, but has also sided with most Republicans on procedural votes to limit Congress' ability to challenge some of the president's tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted in favor of a controversial, Trump-backed election bill, dubbed the SAVE America Act, which would require identification to cast a ballot and proof of citizenship to register to vote. And he backed a controversial GOP immigration proposal and Trump's bid to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America."
"When it comes to our economics in this country, people are suffering," Harvie, a Bucks County native, told CNBC. "The government is one that is totally detached from the people it's supposed to serve. Internationally, we've never been weaker and more isolated … and all of that is because of Donald Trump and because of people like Brian Fitzpatrick, who are just letting him run amok."
Fitzpatrick is still favored to win. But Brit Crampsie, a Democratic strategist based in Pennsylvania, said Democrats have a stronger candidate in Harvie than they have in past cycles.
"Bob Harvie, from his time as a school teacher to a local official, has deep ties to this community, and he's very representative of this community," Crampsie said. "He understands Bucks County and has high name ID."
In addition to Trump's low favorability and voters' economic concerns, Fitzpatrick and other Pennsylvania Republicans must also contend with one of the most popular governors in the country at the top of the ticket. Shapiro is expected to win reelection easily, according to recent polling. In Fitzpatrick's district, Shapiro is predicted to coast to victory by double digits, Covey said.
Pennsylvania also has three other neck-and-neck races that together could decide control of the House. Two Republican incumbents, Reps. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District and Scott Perry in the 10th, are seeking reelection in races labeled "Lean D." Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, in Pennsylvania's 8th District, is in a "toss up" race, according to the Cook Report.
Fitzpatrick, however, noted he won nearly 55% of voters in his district in 2022, even as Shapiro won 59% of the vote in the district, evidence to him that his constituents are more than willing to split their tickets.
Independent public polling on the race for the district is sparse, though a recent internal survey conducted by Global Strategy Group for the Harvie campaign showed him and Fitzpatrick tied. A September poll conducted by Public Opinion Strategies for the National Republican Congressional Committee and Fitzpatrick's campaign had the incumbent up by 9 percentage points. A poll released Sunday by The New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University found Harvie with a narrow 48% to 46% lead over Fitzpatrick — within the poll's margin of error.
Recent outside spending paints a competitive picture.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has committed more than $1.5 million to TV ads in the district since the start of October, while House Democrats' main super PAC has pitched in more than $7.5 million, according to AdImpact data. Before this election, neither group had bought TV ads in the district since 2020.
Republicans are also shelling out to shore up Fitzpatrick. The House GOP's main super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, and the NRCC have committed just under $5 million and just over $1 million, respectively, to ads in the district, according to AdImpact. And Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., recently purchased $100,000 in ads in the district opposing Harvie, according to an Oct. 12 Federal Election Commission filing.
"Here's how you know where his loyalties lie," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale told CNBC. "Donald Trump and MAGA Inc. coming in to spend $100,000 to bail him out because they know when push comes to shove, he'll be loyal to them."
Fitzpatrick has a significant cash advantage, with more than $709,000 in his war chest as of Oct. 14 according to FEC filings, compared with Harvie's just over $409,000 in cash on hand.
Reilly Richardson, a spokesperson for the NRCC, pointed to this fundraising disparity, saying Harvie had "a stagnant campaign" and "a significant cash disadvantage."

Swiss court finds Belarusian man guilty over disappearance of Lukashenko opponent
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:33:13 CET
21:33:13 KST

By Marleen Kaesebier
ST GALLEN, Switzerland, Oct 26 (Reuters) - A Swiss court on Monday found a former Belarusian security officer guilty over the abduction of businessman Anatoly Krasovsky, an opponent of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko.
Yuri Harauski, who has admitted involvement in the abductions more than two decades ago of three of Lukashenko’s opponents who were later killed, was however acquitted over the kidnapping of former Belarusian Interior Minister Yuri Zakharenko.
Harauski now faces two years on probation in Switzerland, a sentence that was reduced because of his cooperation and comprehensive confession, the court said.
Rights groups say the ruling is the first conviction anywhere of a member of Belarus’ security forces. It came after the daughters of two of the victims appealed his 2023 acquittal.
Harauski had originally confessed in a Deutsche Welle interview in 2019 that while he was working in a special police unit called SOBR in Belarus in 1999, he had been involved in the abductions of three people.
A Swiss court had ruled three years ago that Harauski’s alleged role had not been legally proven because he had made contradictory statements over time.
The court said on Monday that Harauski’s confessions were credible and in the case of Krasovsky, his intent and knowledge of the violent abduction and subsequent killing were clear. In the case of Zakharenko this intent could not be established, it said.
FIRST SUCH CONVICTION
“Even if it’s a partial victory, it’s the first conviction anywhere in the world of a member of the Belarusian security forces,” said Philip Grant, founder of rights group Trial International, which had supported the daughters of Krasovsky and Zakharenko.
The case is the first in which the Swiss courts, applying the principle of universal jurisdiction, have tried charges of enforced disappearance or alleged crimes committed in Belarus.
Lukashenko’s government has rejected criticism of its human rights record from the UN and rights groups, and denies holding political prisoners.
“An accountability gap has been closed,” said Severin Walz, lawyer for the daughters of Zakharenko and Krasovsky. ”My clients feel very relieved.”
There was no comment on Monday from Harauski’s lawyer.
The verdict could be appealed one more time, which would take the case to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court.
(Reporting by Marleen Kaesebier, editing by Linda Pasquini and Keith Weir)

Explainer-Serbia’s new leaders face host of tough challenges
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:32:53 CET
21:32:53 KST

BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Serbia’s student-led protest movement won a historic victory in Sunday’s parliamentary election, ending the long rule of Aleksandar Vucic and sparking mass celebrations. But their yet-to-be named leaders face a long list of issues.
Here are a few of them:
KOSOVO
The Student List believes that Kosovo, which declared independence from Belgrade in 2008, remains an integral part of Serbia. During their campaign, the students’ candidates said that Kosovo is a temporarily occupied territory which could be reintegrated into Serbia through peaceful means, diplomacy and dialogue.
Their focus is preventing the exodus of the Serbian population in the north of Kosovo, and strengthening institutions funded by Serbia and operating under the Serbian legal system, such as healthcare and education. They want Kosovo’s Serb communities to operate autonomously, rejecting previous agreements with the ethnic Albanian-led government in Pristina, such as those on energy, vehicle licence plates and the use of the dinar currency.
FRAYED EU RELATIONS
With Serbia’s European Union accession talks largely stalled by a lack of necessary reforms, the Student List campaign deliberately avoided such polarising foreign policy issues.
Prominent candidates, including former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, have said the government must first focus on domestic reforms and close all EU negotiating clusters before asking the public to cast a definitive ballot on membership of the bloc.
The Student List position on Kosovo is also at odds with membership of the EU, which requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc stood ready to support reforms including on the rule of law and media freedom, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the EU.
COMPLEX RUSSIAN RELATIONSHIP AND US SANCTIONS AGAINST NIS OIL FIRM
The Student List must navigate an intricate energy and foreign policy web with traditional Serbian ally Russia. The students have said they have no plans to align with the EU and impose sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government would be reliant on US sanctions waivers to maintain crude imports while it waits for the sale of Russia’s stake in energy company NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery, to Hungary’s MOL.
Russia’s Gazprom is also Serbia’s biggest gas supplier, delivering around 2.2 billion cubic meters a year at below-market pricing. The Student List said this energy reliance was not a geopolitical alignment, but an acute economic dependency.
The Student List’s top candidates have said a future government would end all arms exports from Serbia to war zones, including sales to Western intermediaries who pass weapons to Ukraine. Vucic cultivated strong personal ties with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
CORRUPTION
The Student List’s anti-corruption program centres on institutional overhauls, such as the creation of an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors rather than the Interior Ministry and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime or violent crackdowns on protests.
They want a ban on the appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies in favour of transparent, merit-based hiring. Financial accountability and fiscal oversight would include a strict asset origin law allowing the state to audit, seize and return illegally acquired wealth from officials to the state budget.
Convicted officials would be barred from holding public office. The students’ anti-corruption program also envisions public scrutiny of all major state infrastructure contracts and the creation of independent oversight bodies to curb the misuse of public funds.
Vucic, the SNS and the authorities repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
ECONOMY
Serbia’s economy is deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows.
The IMF has forecast Serbia’s economic growth at 3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027. Inflation in September stood at 4.1%, almost double August’s 2.2%, while the central bank has maintained a 5.75% benchmark rate since 2024.
The Student List’s economic platform shifts Serbia’s growth model away from state-backed infrastructure projects and cheap labour to domestic market security and labour rights.
Central to the plan is a campaign against retail monopolies to lower food prices, coupled with a tax overhaul that raises levies on wealthy citizens and cuts them for lower-income groups.
The movement has pledged to sharply lower the maximum allowed duration for temporary work.
Fiscal sustainability would rely heavily on anti-corruption savings and rigorous state oversight. Social spending would be focused on curbing a youth exodus through an affordable housing initiative for young couples, teachers and healthcare staff, alongside guaranteeing free school textbooks and cheaper, state-subsidised medication.
(Reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — An AI system will be tested in Taiwan to identify roads where wildlife collisions are most likely, as about 3,000 animal-related traffic accidents are reported annually, CNA reported Monday.
The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network’s AI model will draw on existing records of roadkill, wildlife sightings, and traffic accidents to identify areas where collisions are likely to occur. It will also factor in road conditions, surrounding land use, and weather to detect risks in areas not previously identified as hotspots.
The Formosan pangolin will be the first species covered in the pilot program. The network plans to expand the system to include leopard cats, land crabs, and reptiles.
Many animal-related collisions go unreported, the network said, making the actual annual toll difficult to determine. It estimates that collisions involving medium-sized and large mammals alone number 500,000 to 1 million annually.
Police data show that 25,345 people were injured in animal-related traffic accidents over the past eight years, with 95% of accidents involving motorcyclists. The network estimates annual related economic losses at NT$800 million (US$24.5 million) to NT$6.4 billion.
Since 2019, the network has worked with providers of in-vehicle warning systems and navigation services to issue voice alerts as drivers approach known accident hotspots. It has also developed a solar-powered LED warning device that detects nearby wildlife, with initial testing planned on roads managed by the New Taipei City Government.
The Taiwan Roadkill Observation Network was launched in August 2011 by the Ministry of Agriculture's Taiwan Biodiversity Research Institute. The citizen science project documents wildlife deaths caused by transportation infrastructure and related facilities to help reduce collisions.

On October 23, a storage, preparation, and launch site for attack UAVs in the Donetsk area was struck. Three buildings used for preparing and equipping attack UAVs and one launch rail were damaged.
The General Staff noted that this reduces the Russians’ ability to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure with various types of drones.
On October 24, the “Tolyattikauchuk” plant in the city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, Russian Federation, was struck. A process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units, and one rectification unit were damaged.
“This disrupts the production chain for solid rocket fuel used in tactical and ballistic missiles,” the General Staff emphasized.
The General Staff stressed that the Ukrainian Defense Forces are striking enemy military targets within the framework of the right to self-defense guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter.
“Operations against key enemy military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ceases completely,” the General Staff added.

Explainer-Oleshky: the occupied Ukrainian town for which Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:30:41 UTC
21:30:41 KST

Explainer-Oleshky: the occupied Ukrainian town for which Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire
Oct 26 - Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a localised ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, an arrangement that will enable aid deliveries and allow evacuations from a frontline town suffering acute shortages of food and medicine.
The agreement was announced on October 23 and brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo, as Washington seeks to revive broader peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
WHY ARE RESIDENTS OF OLESHKY AT RISK?
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since.
Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023.
The United States has said only a few thousand people remain in Oleshky, from a prewar population of 24,000. Residents and officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies.
WHAT DOES THE CEASEFIRE INVOLVE?
According to Ukrainian and Russian officials, the arrangement provides for a local halt in fighting, the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the evacuation of civilians who wish to leave the town.
The two sides said humanitarian corridors would be established to allow aid deliveries and the movement of residents.
WHO BROKERED THE DEAL?
The White House said Melania Trump helped secure the agreement after becoming involved in discussions on the humanitarian situation in Oleshky. The White House said the first lady and a representative worked with Russian and Ukrainian officials to agree the terms of the ceasefire.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets publicly thanked Melania Trump and her team for helping coordinate the talks. Russian officials also confirmed the agreement.
Pope Leo also played a role. He held a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the Vatican said, and urged Ukraine and Russia to cooperate to let aid and food in.
WHAT MIGHT HAPPEN NEXT?
The ceasefire is limited in scope and does not address the wider conflict, now in its fifth year. But it is a rare example of direct cooperation between the two sides since the start of the invasion.
The Kremlin said on Monday that the truce might serve as a precedent for similar localised ceasefires in the future. REUTERS

‘It killed us’: Fake US election polls infiltrate major media and damage campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:30:30 UTC
21:30:30 KST

A company that presented itself as a legitimate political polling firm has admitted fabricating election surveys that were published by major American news organizations and incorporated into influential polling averages, triggering a scandal just over a week before the November 3 midterm elections. One former Democratic Senate candidate says the false numbers helped destroy her campaign.
Wedgewood Polls, a relatively new firm that began publishing surveys earlier this year, acknowledged on October 20 that it had fabricated most of its results. The company insisted that the deception was part of an experiment designed to expose how easily unverified polling data could gain credibility with journalists, political analysts and election forecasters.
But the consequences may have extended far beyond embarrassing the media. The fabricated surveys reached major polling trackers, influenced political narratives and, according to candidates and campaign officials, contributed to decisions about donations, campaign strategy and whether to remain in electoral races.
More than a dozen Wedgewood surveys were included in polling databases maintained by leading organizations, including The New York Times and election analysis website FiftyPlusOne. The company also solicited donations to finance what it presented as legitimate polling operations.
The New York Times subsequently removed 15 Wedgewood surveys from its tracking project, while Decision Desk HQ removed 17 polls from its race-level lists and averages.
The admission came only after researchers at FiftyPlusOne began questioning the authenticity of Wedgewood's data and approached the company for an explanation.
In a statement posted on social media, which has since been deleted, Wedgewood described itself as an experimental project intended to demonstrate the weaknesses and lack of oversight in the modern political polling industry.
The company maintained that it had never intended to influence an election or permanently mislead the public.
Its social media account has since disappeared, and the polling operation appears to have shut down.
‘It killed us’: The Michigan candidate who says fake polling ended her campaign
One of the most prominent figures affected by the scandal is Mallory McMorrow, a Democratic state senator who competed for her party's U.S. Senate nomination in Michigan.
McMorrow had entered the race hoping to secure the nomination against two major rivals, former public health official Abdul El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens.
On June 29, Wedgewood published a survey showing McMorrow's support collapsing to just 9%, compared with 46% for El-Sayed and 39% for Stevens.
The findings appeared to suggest that McMorrow had little chance of winning the nomination. Six days later, on July 5, she suspended her campaign, a month before Michigan's Democratic primary.
After Wedgewood admitted fabricating its results, McMorrow publicly described the damage she believes the survey caused.
"It killed us," she said, explaining that the numbers contributed to an impression that her campaign was no longer viable.
In a post on X, McMorrow said donations dried up, volunteers became deeply discouraged and reporters repeatedly contacted her to ask whether she would withdraw.
She described the period as among the worst days of her campaign, particularly for her staff, whose morale suffered as the damaging polling figures spread.
Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic strategist who ran a political action committee supporting McMorrow, said several donors used the Wedgewood survey to justify withdrawing financial support.
According to Holdsworth, the funding losses were particularly damaging because McMorrow's campaign was already being outspent by approximately $80 million.
The significance of the alleged damage is difficult to establish conclusively. Other polling organizations also showed McMorrow trailing her rivals, and analysts caution that it is impossible to determine precisely how much one fabricated survey contributed to her decision to withdraw.
Nevertheless, McMorrow argues that the episode demonstrates how polling figures can become self-fulfilling political narratives, particularly when donors and campaign supporters begin making financial decisions based on them.
She has also called for greater transparency and reforms to the American campaign finance system.
The Mississippi poll that exposed the deception
The fabricated data did not appear only in Michigan. Wedgewood also published surveys involving other competitive races across the United States, including the Senate contest in Mississippi.
There, the firm released a poll showing Democratic candidate Scott Colom trailing Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just four percentage points, 48% to 52%.
The numbers suggested that a race in a traditionally Republican state could be considerably closer than previously expected. Colom pointed to the polling as evidence of growing momentum behind his campaign.
Democratic organizations were also increasing their attention to Mississippi, although there is no established evidence that Wedgewood's survey was responsible for their spending decisions.
The Mississippi poll ultimately became the key to exposing the company's operation.
Researchers at FiftyPlusOne were already suspicious of several newly established polling organizations that appeared to be publishing results without an established public track record.
G. Elliott Morris, a journalist and polling analyst at FiftyPlusOne, told TIME that the appearance of numerous unfamiliar polling companies had raised concerns among his colleagues.
After receiving a tip suggesting that Wedgewood's data might be fabricated, the researchers requested the underlying responses from its Mississippi survey.
Wedgewood supplied what it claimed was raw polling data collected through an online survey platform called Pollfish.
However, investigators noticed irregularities. The sample appeared unusually representative of Mississippi's electorate for a survey conducted through that method.
To investigate further, FiftyPlusOne commissioned its own Mississippi poll using the same platform and questionnaire.
The comparison exposed discrepancies in the technical identifiers associated with survey respondents and the timestamps recording when their responses were submitted.
The data provided by Wedgewood did not display the same patterns as the genuine responses collected through the platform, raising serious doubts about its authenticity.
On October 19, FiftyPlusOne contacted Wedgewood about the discrepancies. The following day, the company publicly acknowledged that its polling had been fabricated.
Rather than accepting responsibility for the political consequences, Wedgewood argued that the episode demonstrated how easily a fictional polling operation could win recognition from established media organizations.
How fake polls reached major news organizations
The scandal has also forced questions about the standards used by news outlets and polling aggregators when deciding which surveys deserve credibility.
Wedgewood argued that its experiment exposed a failure by major organizations to verify the identity, methodology and legitimacy of new polling companies.
However, both The New York Times and FiftyPlusOne rejected the suggestion that they had accepted its data without conducting any checks.
FiftyPlusOne said it had asked Wedgewood to identify its staff and explain its polling methods before including its results.
The company supplied the names of two purported polling professionals, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater, and provided methodological explanations that appeared consistent with industry standards.
Researchers also independently confirmed that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry.
The New York Times similarly said it had questioned the company about its staff, sampling methods and sources of funding before accepting its surveys.
The problem, according to the investigators, was that Wedgewood had presented convincing answers and supplied data that appeared credible until subjected to more detailed examination.
The episode illustrates how even organizations that attempt to verify polling firms can be vulnerable when those firms deliberately misrepresent their operations.
Another fake polling scandal just two months earlier
Wedgewood was not the first company to admit manufacturing political polling data during the 2026 election cycle.
In August, another organization, Median Strategies, acknowledged publishing fabricated surveys involving races in Wisconsin, Nevada and California.
Among the misleading results associated with that earlier operation was a survey suggesting that democratic socialist Francesca Hong was leading the Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin. Hong ultimately lost the contest.
Median Strategies also described its activities as an experiment intended to test whether journalists and polling organizations would accept unsupported data.
Unlike Wedgewood, however, its surveys were largely rejected by major polling aggregators.
The Wedgewood affair proved more consequential because the fabricated numbers entered established polling databases and became part of the information available to journalists, candidates, donors and voters.
The revelations have intensified concerns about the ease with which fraudulent information can enter political reporting, particularly as technological tools make it increasingly simple to generate convincing datasets and supporting documents.
With Americans preparing to vote on November 3, the scandal raises questions not only about the reliability of individual polls but also about the political consequences of publishing figures that have never been independently verified.
For McMorrow, the damage cannot simply be reversed by deleting the surveys or shutting down the company.
The fabricated numbers may have been presented as an experiment, but the campaign she believes they helped derail was real.

Europe can still shape the rules of AI
As Washington and Beijing race to supply AI systems, the EU can use its regulatory weight to influence how they are tested and deployed
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Hao Nan is a Susan Strange Associate Fellow with the Helsinki Geoeconomics Society, and a Nuclear Futures Fellow with Ploughshares Fund & Horizon 2045. 
In October, two technology executives offered Europe similar advice. In Turin, Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai urged European companies to use open-source models and their proprietary industrial data to build AI capabilities. In Berlin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang pressed German manufacturers to apply AI to factories, robotics and other physical industries. Both see opportunity in Europe’s engineering strengths, while their companies stand to benefit from supplying the technology.
Recent safety incidents and evaluations expose another dimension of the AI race: the difficulty of keeping increasingly capable AI agents under human control. During internal cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI agents bypassed isolation controls and accessed external systems beyond their intended scope.
In September, Reuters reported on documented cases of Chinese-model agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot displaying deception or evading constraints in controlled tests. In October, Tencent Holding acknowledged unintended browsing behaviour by agents evaluating third-party models. These cases range from controlled experiments to real security lapses. They underscore the need for better evaluation before wider deployment.

Resuming trilateral Ukraine talks does not restrict military operations: Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:29:50 UTC
21:29:50 KST

Elena Teslova
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that the decision to resume US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks on the Moscow-Kyiv conflict does not imply any restrictions on military operations.
Speaking at a news briefing in Moscow, Peskov said the territorial issue could be a topic of discussion during efforts to reach a peaceful settlement, along with other matters.
"The decision to resume trilateral negotiations does not imply any restrictions on military actions. You know that our armed forces continue the special military operation and continue to deliver massive and consistent strikes on Ukraine’s military complex, on military and quasi-military targets," he said.
"There will be a very serious conversation consisting of a huge number of details. We would not like to discuss these details publicly, because we believe it would harm the potential future peace process," Peskov added.
Asked about humanitarian efforts, the spokesman said they could set a precedent, citing the "very positive, coordinating involvement" of US negotiators and first lady Melania Trump.
"We highly appreciate these efforts," he said, adding that Moscow hopes Ukraine will fulfill all the agreements reached with the direct participation of negotiators.  
Kremlin's views on Serbian, Brazilian elections
Commenting on Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, the spokesman said Moscow highly values the contribution of Aleksandar Vucic to bilateral relations and expects him to remain on the political stage.
"Even in opposition, he will still contribute to the development of bilateral relations," he said.
He expressed hope that the new political force coming to power would act constructively and understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interest.
"We, for our part, intend to continue to promote the development of relations with Belgrade in every way, but, as you know, it takes two to tango," he added.
Serbia held an early election to the National Assembly on Sunday. With 96.47% of ballots counted, the Republican Electoral Commission said the “United Serbia” list of Vucic trailed the opposition “Student List,” with 39.27% against 52.57% of the vote.
Peskov also welcomed the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Brazil’s presidential election.
“We welcome the victory of Mr. Lula,” he said. Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier sent congratulations to Lula. 
Russia to host 2030 weightlifting championships
Peskov also welcomed the decision of the International Weightlifting Federation to hold the 2030 championships in the Russian capital, calling it an important step toward depoliticizing sport.
"Russia must return to the world sports family with full rights, because this family cannot live fully without Russia’s participation," he said.
On the Olympics, he said it was too early to talk about it.
"At the moment, not a very large number of countries are interested in hosting the Olympics. All the pros and cons must be weighed, of course. For now, this issue is not on the agenda," he said.

Macron vows ‘concrete’ measures to address student demands after unrest

French students vow to continue protests despite concessions from Macron govt
French student leaders on Monday called for more protests despite President Emmanuel Macron's pledge of "concrete and strong" measures to address their demands after weeks of nationwide unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu met with high school representatives alongside education ministers to announce follow-up action ranging from a total overhaul of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup to a cap on class sizes.
French student leaders vowed to go on protesting Monday despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, stokes unrest and deepens the economic damage.
Read moreFrench student representatives hail govt's ‘concrete measures’, call for protests to continue
The new measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes; €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans for renovating schools; and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system students see as socially unfair.
"Not all our demands were met. We'll go on for as long as it takes," Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said as he and fellow student leaders emerged from a meeting with government officials in Paris.
The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and yellow-vest activists, known for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Macron's minority government.
The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120 percent of GDP, while the turmoil is boosting support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen ahead of next year's presidential election.
The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
"It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday's protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.
Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year's presidential election, has benefitted from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
Read moreFrench far-right leader Le Pen seeks to leverage unrest in presidential campaign kick-off
An opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32 to 33.5 percent, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon on 17 percent. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Mélenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Far-right gangs confront far-left activists
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
"We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Smoking ban on outdoor terraces delayed: Council of State raises objections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:23:55 UTC
21:23:55 KST

The introduction of the smoking ban on outdoor terraces in the hospitality industry is being postponed, the office of Belgian Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke (Flemish socialist Vooruit) has confirmed. The Council of State, which vets Belgian laws before they come into force, has raised several issues. As a result, the planned start date of 1 January 2027 will not be met.
“The Council of State has asked us to amend certain measures, and we are currently working on this,” the statement from the health minister’s office reads. According to Vandenbroucke’s office, the government also wishes to give the hospitality sector sufficient time afterwards to prepare for the new rules, including the putting up of the necessary signage.
Consequently, the planned start date is being postponed. It is not yet clear when the long-awaited smoking ban will actually come into force. This depends on how quickly the amended measures are passed by parliament.
Stricter anti-tobacco policy
In September 2025, the federal government announced that smoking and vaping on and around hospitality terraces would be banned from 1 January 2027. The measure forms part of a broader tightening of Belgium’s anti-tobacco policy.
There will also be a ban on public smoking rooms, including those in hospitality venues and airports. These measures are intended to help achieve a smoke-free generation by 2040.
When presenting the plans, Minister Vandenbroucke stated that the number of smokers is falling, but that tobacco use still has a significant impact on health. According to recent figures, 12.8 per cent of Belgians smoke every day.
Hospitality federation Horeca Vlaanderen is not happy with the forthcoming ban. The federation fears it will have a negative impact on the sector.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is set to attend five international summits by the end of the year, including meetings in Türkiye, South Korea and Libya, as Ankara seeks to strengthen diplomatic and economic ties across Asia, Africa and the wider international community.
Erdoğan’s schedule includes an Organization of Turkic States (OTS) summit, a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the U.N. climate conference COP31, the Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit and the Group of 20 leaders summit, according to Turkish media reports.
The diplomatic tour will begin with the 13th OTS summit in Ankara on Oct. 30. Türkiye is expected to take over the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan at the meeting, which will be held under the theme “Turkish Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action.”
The summit is also expected to address the organization’s strategic priorities and the appointment of a new secretary-general.
Erdoğan is also scheduled to attend a meeting of the OIC’s Standing Committee for Economic and Commercial Cooperation in Istanbul before traveling to South Korea for a two-day visit. Talks there are expected to focus on strengthening the countries’ strategic partnership, trade, investment, defense industry cooperation and regional developments.
In November, Erdoğan is expected to attend COP31, which Türkiye will host in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya. The climate conference is scheduled to begin Nov. 9, with the Turkish president expected to participate on Nov. 11-12.
Climate action, the green transition, energy policy and climate finance are expected to feature prominently at the summit, which is projected to draw world leaders, ministers and thousands of delegates.
Erdoğan is then expected to travel to Tripoli on Dec. 8-9 for the fourth Türkiye-Africa Partnership Summit. The meeting aims to deepen strategic cooperation between Türkiye and African countries, with defense, energy, agriculture and transport links among the expected areas of discussion.
The president’s final summit of the year is scheduled to be the G20 leaders’ meeting in Miami on Dec. 14-15. Leaders of the world’s major economies are expected to discuss global economic challenges and reforms at the gathering.

Trump Officials Reportedly Push Orban for UN Chief

Trump administration officials are promoting former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban as a candidate for United Nations secretary-general, potentially with backing from the United States, Russia and China, the Wall Street Journal reported, although no decision has been confirmed.
According to the newspaper, sources in all three countries have indicated that the Trump administration supports Orban's candidacy and is seeking to make him a joint nominee of Washington, Moscow and Beijing.
Orban lost power in Hungary's parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar's Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of rule with an absolute majority.
His hard-right, strongly anti-migration and euroskeptic policies, alongside Hungary's democratic backsliding on the rule of law, strained ties with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. However, Orban maintained close relationships with US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Since the election, Hungarian authorities have opened fraud and corruption investigations involving several members of Orban's former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary's National Bank have been arrested, and investigators could also examine whether Orban was involved in the cases.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the proposal remains undecided. A US State Department official acknowledged that the idea might initially sound crazy but said previous discussions with Washington indicated that Russia and China also supported it. The objective would be to put forward Orban as a candidate backed by all three countries.
“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper.
The current secretary-general, António Guterres, is due to complete his second five-year term on December 31.
The White House, Moscow and Beijing have not confirmed the report.
Euronews has requested comment from Orban's spokesperson but has not received a response. The spokesperson previously rejected media reports suggesting Orban might seek the position of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.
In May, the investigative newsletter VSquare reported that a UN post could appeal to the former prime minister because the position carries diplomatic immunity.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Orban would only enter the race if his election were guaranteed, a prospect that currently appears unlikely. A candidate needs the support of at least nine of the 15 members of the UN Security Council, while any of its five permanent members can veto a nomination. The permanent members are the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.

IG Metall’s Benner said the Audi chief’s attendance at a political campaign event in the US blatantly violated Audi’s own guidelines, which explicitly require political neutrality in the run-up to elections.
She also criticized the hasty announcement of a US plant, stressing that any final decision to build a new factory requires approval from the relevant bodies, including Volkswagen AG’s supervisory board.
“For months, our employee representatives have been demanding job security for the German sites, alongside a clear North America strategy from Volkswagen and Audi,” she said.
“Our primary focus remains, at all times, on ensuring secure employment prospects for our colleagues at all of our local plants. This will continue to shape future discussions and decisions within the company’s governing bodies,” Benner added.

US holding up air defense missiles for Ukraine for nearly a month, Zelensky says
Ukraine has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 26.
The delay, first reported by the Kyiv Independent, affects missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for. Ukraine relies on Patriot systems to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to stop, making timely deliveries critical to the country's air defenses.
"I instructed our team to raise this with the American side once again," Zelensky said.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States, a senior Ukrainian military official said.
Zelensky has said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that the batch awaiting Hegseth's approval was "significant."
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Kyiv has also had problems with military-grade Starlink service, Starshield, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the use of interceptor drones to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as another example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.
