Japanese troops drill with new long-range ship-killer missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:56:09 UTC
20:56:09 KST

- Japan deployed its new Type 25 surface-to-ship missile to Nagasaki’s Ōnohara training area during Keen Sword 27 to rehearse anti-ship strikes.
- Crews practiced engaging sea targets using information from U.S. forces and higher headquarters, the Ground Self-Defense Force’s Western Army said.
Japan Ground Self-Defense Force troops deployed the new Type 25 surface-to-ship missile system to the Ōnohara training area in Nagasaki Prefecture and rehearsed anti-ship strikes using targeting information from U.S. forces and higher headquarters during Keen Sword 27, Japan’s largest joint field exercise with the United States, the GSDF’s Western Army said.
The Western Army said the training walked crews through the full sequence of an engagement against targets at sea, from receiving information supplied by the U.S. military and senior commands to carrying out the attack, with the aim of improving the units’ anti-ship combat capability. Units from the 4th Division and the 2nd Artillery Brigade, which commands the GSDF’s missile regiments in Kyushu, took part, although the Western Army did not say when the drill took place, how many launchers were deployed or whether any missiles were fired.
The Type 25 is the new name for the upgraded Type 12 surface-to-ship missile, a long-range cruise missile built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries that Japan formally designated and deployed with the 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment at Camp Kengun in Kumamoto on March 31, Naval News reported. Its range is reported to be about 1,000 km (620 miles), compared with roughly 200 km (125 miles) for the original Type 12, which puts targets across the East China Sea within reach of launchers based in Kyushu and makes the missile a central part of the “counterstrike” capability Tokyo adopted in its 2022 security strategy.
The truck-mounted system relies on outside sensors to find targets far beyond the horizon, which is why the drill focused on taking in data from U.S. forces and other units before firing. A ship-launched version is set to go to sea first aboard the destroyer Teruzuki, and an air-launched version is being tested on upgraded F-2 fighters, with both scheduled to enter service in fiscal 2027.
Keen Sword 27 runs from Oct. 19 to Oct. 29 at training areas, camps and bases across Kyushu and Okinawa, and the Western Army describes it as the largest field exercise held in Japan. Troops from the United States, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines are taking part alongside Japan’s ground, maritime and air self-defense forces, and the exercise opened with a ceremony at Camp Ishigaki on Oct. 19.
The Western Army said the exercise is intended to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance and cooperation with partner nations, and it has not said whether the Type 25 will take part in any further phases of Keen Sword before the exercise ends on Oct. 29.

Saldo has been served a notice of suspicion for the illegal deportation of Ukrainian children
Kyiv • UNN
Saldo and two other individuals have been served notices of suspicion for taking three children from Kherson to Crimea without their parents’ consent. All the children have been returned to Ukraine.
The so-called "governor of Kherson region," Volodymyr Saldo, was notified of suspicion of organizing the illegal transfer of three Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied Kherson to Crimea. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General on October 26, UNN reports.
Under the pretext of providing health improvement treatment, the minors were taken away without their parents’ consent and later enrolled in an educational institution controlled by the occupiers.
Details
According to the investigation, in October 2022, Saldo instructed the occupation "ministry of education" to organize the transfer of children from educational institutions in the Kherson region to Crimea. To this end, the occupation administration announced school holidays and ordered the heads of the institutions to ensure that students were sent on so-called vacations. In particular, on October 7, 2022, three underage students of the Kherson Vocational Shipbuilding Lyceum were taken to temporarily occupied Crimea without their parents’ consent. The children were initially placed at the Druzhba camp in Yevpatoria and later transferred to another institution.
After the holidays ended, the teenagers were not returned home. Instead, in January 2023, they were enrolled without their parents’ consent at the Kerch Maritime Technical College, which was under the control of the occupation administration. According to the prosecutor’s office, the children were involved in military-patriotic activities at the college, exposed to Russian propaganda, and subjected to the imposition of a Russian identity.
In addition, one of the boys, who had a disability and a severe form of diabetes, was admitted to intensive care in Yevpatoria due to a lack of insulin and the untimely provision of medical assistance. He remained hospitalized for about three weeks.
Eventually, all three children were returned to territory controlled by Ukraine במסגרת the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA, with the assistance of the public organization Save Ukraine.
The Office of the Prosecutor General noted that, in addition to Saldo, two other individuals were notified of suspicion: the acting head of the lyceum controlled by the occupiers and a vocational training instructor. All three are charged with violating the laws and customs of war, committed by a group of persons acting in prior collusion (Part 2 of Article 28, Part 1 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

In March 2026, the UN recognized Russia’s deportation of Ukrainian children as a crime against humanity.

UN-commissioned experts: Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
An alleged ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report Monday. They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the occupied West Bank.
The report has multiple graphic accounts of sexual assaults by Israeli prison guards and soldiers on Palestinian detainees since October 2023.
The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.
The report released on Monday said Israel was "continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza."
Much of the harm has come, the report says, from Israel’s expansion deeper into Gaza during that period. Since October 2025, when the US-brokered ceasefire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53% of Gaza to at least 60%, the commission said.
The report also accused Israel and members of its security forces of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and Gaza, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.
The commission says it drew its conclusions after investigating seven cases between November 2023 and June 2026, where Israeli forces caused bodily harm on Palestinians, often children, who did not appear to be posing a threat.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed over 75,000 Palestinians in Gaza—mostly women and children.

GMO Internet, a Japanese internet infrastructure company, will compensate customers for losses from unauthorised trading linked to a cyberattack on its cloud service, and will make a ¥5,000 (€28) goodwill payment to every customer currently using the affected service.
A Japanese internet infrastructure company is compensating customers affected by unauthorised transactions following a cyberattack on its cloud service.
GMO Internet announced on Saturday that it would cover losses from unauthorised trading linked to the attack and issue a ¥5,000 (€28) goodwill payment to all customers currently using the affected service, regardless of whether they had suffered financial losses.
The attack targeted Onamae.com Desktop Cloud, a virtual private server service used by customers to access remote desktop environments. GMO said customer information had been taken and some users had reported transactions in their trading accounts they did not recognise.
According to the company’s founder and CEO, Masatoshi Kumagai, the incident potentially affected 26,739 servers and involved unauthorised operations on trading accounts held with more than 70 securities and foreign-exchange firms in Japan and overseas.
GMO shares fell almost 16% on Monday to a four-month low. The company had a market value of around $2.6 billion at Friday’s close.
The company began investigating on 19 October after receiving a customer inquiry. It confirmed the installation of a malicious programme on some customer server environments on 20 October, suspended new applications and access to the service’s control panel, and began shutting down all servers the following day to prevent further damage.
In a blog post on Sunday, Kumagai apologised for the company’s response and acknowledged that security issues had been identified by its security specialists before the incident, but that the response had been insufficient.
GMO said it had received a ransom demand from a party believed to be behind the attack. In an update to his blog post on Monday, Kumagai said the attackers had demanded $50 million in cryptocurrency and threatened to disclose company and customer information. The company has refused to pay and is cooperating with the police and other authorities.
GMO will offer customers who wish to continue using a Windows desktop environment an alternative service on independent cloud infrastructure, free for six months. It also plans to overhaul its security architecture and investigate the cause of the breach with external experts.
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to strengthen its active cyberdefence measures, arguing that private companies cannot tackle sophisticated cross-border cyberattacks alone.
GMO has asked the authorities to consider applying the framework to the incident and has offered to share evidence and technical information with investigators.
The attack comes amid wider concerns over cybersecurity following the disclosure last week of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites and applications.
Security authorities warned that the flaws could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, prompting organisations around the world to patch systems or temporarily take services offline.
However, GMO has not publicly confirmed a link between the PHP vulnerabilities and the attack on its cloud service.
Separately, a Google Cloud outage in the UK disrupted online services last week, including those operated by financial technology company Revolut, showing the potential knock-on effects when digital infrastructure fails.

Germany’s elite special forces unit is preparing for a possible war with Russia - media
Kyiv • UNN
Germany’s KSK special forces unit has changed its training due to a possible conflict with Russia. The soldiers are training to operate against tanks, artillery and drones.
The German Special Operations Command (KSK) is reviewing its training program in light of a possible military conflict with Moscow. BILD reports, according to UNN.
Details
"We are very specifically orienting ourselves toward an adversary represented by Russia," KSK commander Andreas Kühne said in an interview with BILD.
According to him, operations used to be planned for approximately three days, but now the soldiers are preparing to remain in the field for much longer. In addition, the special forces are once again training to face an adversary equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare capabilities. They are also practicing operations in extreme cold: the KSK is preparing for conditions typical of the eastern flank.
The unit is based at the Zeppelin Barracks in Calw, near Stuttgart. Approximately 1,500 personnel serve in the KSK. However, only one-third of them are special forces operators; the rest are administrative staff. The selection process is extremely rigorous: only about 15% of candidates pass it.
Just a few years ago, the future of the most elite unit hung by a thread. Incidents involving far-right extremists, a Nazi salute and pig heads at a farewell party, missing ammunition, and the discovery of a weapons and explosives cache at a KSK soldier's home shook the unit. In 2020, one of the special forces unit's companies was disbanded.
We remind you
The President of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Martin Jäger, considers the threat of an armed confrontation between Germany and Russia to be real.

golem’s ariel andré on reimagining architecture beyond the human
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:50:57 UTC
20:50:57 KST

golem’s ariel andré on reimagining architecture beyond the human
in this guest essay for designboom, the architect explores how shifting perspectives toward animals, overlooked bodies, and other forms of life can reshape the way we design and inhabit space.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
IMAGINING AN ARCHITECTURE BEYOND THE HUMAN
As a child, whenever I woke from one of those recurring nightmares that haunt the little ones, I would close my eyes again and imagine myself as a bee asleep with its wet nose nestled among the pistils of a flower; a young bird huddled against its siblings in a nest of twigs lined with feathers from their father, tucked into the hollow of a tree trunk; a snake free of predators, slithering across a carpet of moss in a world it claimed as its own. To this day, no other thought experiment, glass of alcohol or pill, prescribed or otherwise, has ever given me that same intensity of pure pleasure and well-being, the kind that starts in the belly and spreads to the very tips of your hair.
Looking back, I am convinced that this was the beginning of my path towards architecture, a practice capable of giving physical form to a world of fantasy guided by pleasure. An alternative to the nightmare of the built world we are compelled to inhabit.
Indeed, from apartments designed to constrain souls according to the ideals of the society that builds them, to sofas that fix bodies in front of televisions and airports that process crowds as fluids to be channelled and travellers as commodities to be exploited, the built world dictates how we live, down to the dimensions that govern the standard furniture at which we eat and work and sleep. All this feels like a bad dream, a terror by night and day.
My escape-dream is that of a world built to adapt to those who inhabit it and not the other way around. Through architecture and design, I aspire to build the flower in which to fall asleep, the nest in which to huddle against one’s siblings, the carpet of lichen across which to slide. To give these imaginary realities physical form, where the widest possible range of beings can find pleasure and fulfilment.
The premise is simple: use architecture’s transformative potential to produce an alternative reality guided by pleasure. And the best path to somewhere else is to start from a different standpoint. Therefore, the strategy follows: change perspective to design a world beyond conventions, one shaped around the full expression of people’s lives in their singularities.
BROKEN HEARTS BAZAAR EXPLORES ARCHITECTURE THROUGH SCENT
Broken Hearts Bazaar offers a direct example of this approach. We designed and built it for the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, commissioned by Gayane Umerova and curated by Diana Campbell. Diana asked me to develop the Biennial’s entrance and the kiosks distributed across the city as a food market, making arrival a convivial experience pulling it away from the trade-show atmosphere that so usually greets visitors to traditional biennials.
Within Bukhara’s historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, I approached these kiosks from the perspective of those who do not see architecture: people who cannot see, and beings whose encounter with a building is free of our distinction between nature and culture (man-made) such as cats or wasps, of which the city is full. Smell became the starting point. An architecture to be discovered through the nose before it is seen.
The answer emerged from Uzbekistan’s Silk Road heritage: spice markets and their spice mounds. The conical timber kiosks echo these displays and their coloured finishes are made with actual spices: paprika for red, dill for green, black tea for dark tones and clover blossoms for pink.
The fruitfulness of this shift in perspective, made before even sketching, became tangible in the variety of visitors who enjoyed the kiosks. A blind passerby returned with fifteen companions to identify the cones by scent. A local guide used them to weave folk knowledge of medicinal herbs into her tours. Bees rested on clover blossoms. Cats waited for the visitors to leave at night to lick the paprika walls.
For GOLEM, this project gives concrete form to architecture’s capacity to expand who design is for. Starting from the standpoint of those usually overlooked opens up new forms and spaces, enriching the experience of life for everyone.
AMOREBA: FURNITURE INSPIRED BY MICROSCOPIC WORLDS
The same thought experiment extends to furniture. Amoreba is an organic surface that spreads through rigid interiors, transforming them into contemporary environments for non-conformists. In a curator’s apartment in Brussels, it takes the form of a conversation pit. Its design begins with a psychedelic fantasy: lounging among the soft, microscopic bumps of a forest mushroom colony. This time I imagined the surface from the perspective of a tiny creature slithering across this buoyant terrain.
Amoreba follows smooth curves, negotiates sharp angles and adapts to complex geometries. For each project, we shape its design around the interior and the social activities its future inhabitants imagine taking place in it, much as lichen spreads across stones and tree trunks on a forest bed. Again, starting from the standpoint of those usually overlooked, here, microscopic beings, allows us to create new forms and spaces that enrich the experience of life for everyone.
DESIGNING FOR DIFFERENT BODIES, CULTURES AND WAYS OF LIVING
Beyond these animal fantasies lies a necessary response to a broader condition: the world has been designed by a small minority whose imagination extends little beyond themselves. This calls for an architecture beyond the self. A practice of shifting perspectives and exercising empathy to create new forms that enrich the experience of being alive and together in shared spaces.
For the sofa inside the Public Program Building we designed for the Diriyah Biennale Foundation in Riyadh, commissioned by Aya Albakree and Sybel Vazquez, we documented a plethora of ways of positioning one’s body in public space across Saudi Arabia’s diverse communities. The result is a 24-metre-long sofa that operates as both furniture and public infrastructure. It brings different cultures, generations and bodily habits together, allowing each person to settle comfortably into their own posture and opening up conversations across ages and cultures.
Lamputée takes an aesthetic step sideways. Each lamp is unique, moulded from an amputated limb. When the form is literally turned upside down and abstracted from its familiar context, a shape that can provoke fear or discomfort from an unfamiliar viewer’s perspective, becomes a source of beauty and an asset as a collectible object.
Our responsibility as architects is to draw on the needs that bodies, in all their plurality, express in space. It falls to us to dream into existence the environments in which we can all flourish, nest, forage or slither.
Ariel André is an architect and founder of GOLEM, an architecture, design, and research studio based in Paris. His practice challenges standardized design conventions by drawing on overlooked perspectives, marginal aesthetics, and the narratives of underrepresented communities and non-human life. Before founding GOLEM, André worked at OMA in Rotterdam, where he led design teams across projects spanning retail, museums, offices, and urban development, and collaborated with architecture studios in Paris, Tokyo, Los Angeles, Amsterdam, and Rotterdam, as well as the government in Haiti. GOLEM’s work has been presented at international platforms including the Diriyah Biennale, the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah, and the Bukhara Biennial.
project info:
architect: Ariel André, GOLEM | @golem.digital
This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. These stories rethink our relationship with the planet through interspecies architecture, living materials, regenerative landscapes and emerging technologies – learn more here! She has instead pointed the finger at the central bank, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility watchdog, accusing them of working against her. Drone Designed to Counter Cruise Missiles: Helsing Unveils the AD-1 Inferno
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:48:11 UTC
20:48:11 KST

German defence company Helsing has presented the AD-1 Inferno jet-powered interceptor drone, designed to counter high-speed strike UAVs and cruise missiles.
Militarnyi reports this from a presentation by the company’s co-founder, Gundbert Scherf, in Berlin.
The AD-1 Inferno is powered by a jet engine and can patrol a designated area of airspace while waiting for targets, operate as part of a swarm, and make repeated interception attempts.
During the midcourse phase, the interceptor receives guidance commands from radar stations, then uses its own radar seeker to engage the target in the terminal phase.
According to the developers, this enables the interception of aerial targets regardless of weather conditions or time of day, including at night.
During the presentation, Helsing representatives emphasized that modern aerial threats require interception systems capable of operating at altitudes of up to 9–10 km.
AD-1 Inferno is container-launched. According to the manufacturer, a single container can hold around 20 interceptors.
Standard trucks or rail can transport these containers, which should simplify deployment of the air defense system.
The AD-1 Inferno is being developed as one of the components of Contra, a new autonomous air defense system that Helsing also unveiled on October 26.
The system uses artificial intelligence to fuse data from various sensors and coordinate effectors. According to the company, it is designed to track and intercept hundreds or even thousands of aerial targets simultaneously.
At the core of Contra is the Altra command-and-control platform, which automates system operations while allowing operators to retain control over decision-making and target prioritization.
Production is planned to be held at Helsing Resilience Factories. According to the developers, the interceptors are intended to be significantly cheaper than conventional SAMs.
Helsing is also the developer of the HX-2 AI strike drones. In February 2025, the company announced an order to produce 6,000 drones for Ukraine.

Could Syria help Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis without troops?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:46:52 UTC
20:46:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria denied plans to send troops to Yemen – but how could it still help Saudi Arabia?
Reports have continued to circulate about a possible deployment of Syrian fighters to Yemen despite Damascus' denials.
But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said such a move was unlikely given Syria’s own domestic security challenges, and suggested that any military support to Saudi Arabia against the Houthis could take other forms, without involving troops on Yemeni territory.
Citing unnamed Yemeni intelligence sources, Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar reported that Riyadh and Damascus had held talks on transferring up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to Yemen.
It said a Syrian military delegation had recently visited the Saudi capital and the kingdom’s southern regions to assess the proposed deployment.
According to the newspaper, Brigadier General Khaled Khattab, formerly leader of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and now commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army, spent four days in the southern Saudi regions of Asir and Najran, accompanied by Saudi officers. The delegation reportedly visited sites being prepared to receive Syrian fighters.
Meanwhile, Brigadier General Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army’s Third Corps and a former Hayat Tahrir al-Sham commander, was said to have met Saudi officers at the defence ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, benefits and their expected military role. Al-Akhbar said the delegation had finalised logistical preparations for the transfer.
The New Arab could not independently verify Al-Akhbar’s claims.
Could Syria support Riyadh without entering Yemen?
Muaz al-Abdallah, a Syria analyst at the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), told The New Arab that any Syrian military support to Saudi Arabia would not necessarily involve deploying troops inside Yemen.
He said one possibility was that Syrian forces could be sent to help protect Saudi Arabia’s southern border, rather than take part directly in the fighting against the Houthis on Yemeni territory. Al-Abdallah said this statement left open the possibility of military cooperation with Riyadh, even if Damascus maintained that it had not deployed forces inside Yemen.
"Damascus has said it has not sent forces to Yemen, while also expressing support for Saudi security and saying military cooperation would take place through official channels and bilateral agreements," Al-Abdallah said.
He added that deploying Syrian personnel to the Saudi side of the border would not necessarily contradict the government’s denial that it had sent forces to Yemen, but could instead represent another way of supporting Riyadh.
Al-Abdallah suggested that Saudi Arabia could increase its financial assistance and investments in Syria’s reconstruction in return for military support.
Syrian drone expertise could help Saudi Arabia
Al-Abdallah also pointed to the potential for Syria to offer expertise in drone operations, particularly given its forces' experience operating drones during the war against Bashar Al-Assad’s regime. He said drones had played an important role in the lightning rebel offensive that toppled Assad, giving Syrian forces considerable experience in their use.
That expertise could prove useful to Saudi Arabia amid its confrontation with the Houthis, particularly if cooperation were to involve training or the use of smaller attack drones.
Al-Akhbar also reported that Syrian drone specialists were already involved in training forces in Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and that Syrian operators had helped establish drone units within Saudi emergency forces. However, these claims have not been independently verified.
Despite the reports, Al-Abdallah said ACLED had not documented evidence of Syrian fighters currently operating in Yemen. The organisation had found no reports of Syrian casualties, captured fighters or funerals linked to a deployment there, he said, noting that such evidence had helped establish the presence of Syrian fighters in other conflict zones, including Libya.
Al-Abdallah also questioned reports, including those published by Axios, that Syria could send its 84th Division to Yemen. He said the division was deployed around Suweida, in southern Syria, which remains largely outside the central government’s control after last year's sectarian clashes.
"Given the situation there, and reports of heavy Israeli arming of the National Guard and a possible escalation with the Syrian government, I don’t see how this division would leave Suweida," he said.
Syria's unresolved issues make deployment unlikely
The prospect of Syria deploying fighters to Yemen remains unlikely given the transitional government’s security challenges at home, according to Benjamin Schmida, a Middle East researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Schmida told The New Arab that Saudi Arabia likely requested that Syria send forces to Yemen, but Damascus appears to have declined.
"It does not seem like these discussions proceeded very far beyond consulting CENTCOM," he said, adding that the Syrian government’s public rejection of the request suggested the talks had not continued.
Schmida said it remained unclear what forces Syria could realistically deploy, given the security challenges facing the country, including Kurdish areas in the northeast, Druze militia control over Suweida, sporadic Islamic State group attacks, and repeated Israeli incursions in the southwest.
He also cautioned against assuming that foreign fighters integrated into Syria’s military would be available for deployment abroad.
"Foreign fighters, such as Uyghur Turkistan Islamic Party fighters that are integrated into the Syrian Defence Ministry, represent some of Syria’s most elite units," he said.
"The Syrian government likely views integrated foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, as vital assets for Syria's defence and internal security that must remain in Syria in the event of a future crisis."
Would Syrian fighters change the balance in Yemen?
The possibility of transferring foreign fighters to Yemen was also raised in Al-Akhbar's report, which suggested that Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks, Afghans, and Chechens who joined Syrian opposition factions before Assad’s fall could be among those considered for deployment.
However, Schmida said the potential impact of any Syrian deployment would depend on the number of fighters sent and where they were integrated into the conflict.
Axios recently reported that Syria could send between 10,000 and 20,000 fighters. Schmida said this would represent a sizeable proportion of Syria’s total army manpower and could meaningfully bolster forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose forces he estimated at around 100,000.
But he noted that the Houthis are a much larger force, while government-aligned fighters remain spread across several frontlines, including Taiz, Marib, and Jawf.
More importantly, he said, sending additional fighters would not necessarily address the divisions undermining the Yemeni government’s war effort.
"Merely sending more fighters - though they may be experienced - is unlikely to solve one of the primary challenges for the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis: its own internal disunity," Schmida said.
He pointed to the political fragmentation and poor military coordination among government-aligned forces, warning that they could struggle to integrate Syrian fighters effectively, limiting their ability to change conditions on the battlefield.
Ultimately, Schmida said a meaningful Syrian deployment was unlikely "at this time or in the foreseeable future," as the government’s focus on domestic stability took precedence over Saudi requests.
While Riyadh could potentially use aid and investment to encourage Damascus to provide military support, he warned that doing so "could risk souring the Syrian-Saudi relationship and pushing Syria closer to Turkey or Saudi rivals like the UAE".

By Maayan Lubell and Michal Yaakov Itzhaki
BE’ERI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Gal Cohen walks along a memorial wall engraved with the names of the men, women and children slain in the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on his kibbutz. For him, the idea that the man leading Israel, then and since, may be re-elected on Tuesday is painful.
One-in-ten residents of his kibbutz, Be’eri, were among the 1,200 people killed in Hamas’ surprise attack. Dozens were among the 251 taken hostage to Gaza. It was Israel’s deadliest single day.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should have taken responsibility and stepped down, said Cohen, 61, and the fact that he has fulfilled a full term in office is a slap in the face. Tuesday’s election, he said, is critical for Israel.
“If this government will stay, many hearts and minds will be broken. It will be really hard to continue,” said Cohen.
Many of Netanyahu’s opponents see the election as an opportunity at last to deliver a long-postponed reckoning for the worst security failure in generations. But even if Israel’s longest-serving prime minister loses his majority, he could well escape the decisive verdict his foes are seeking.
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. He maintains that Israel’s wars against Hamas in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran will result in a more peaceful Middle East.
The task will be complete only with the downfall of Iran’s clerical rulers, Netanyahu has said on the campaign trail, and only he has the conviction and standing to deliver.
Opinion polls have for months predicted a sharp drop for Netanyahu’s Likud party. But a rival alliance of parties on the right, left and centre looking to unseat him also has no clear path to power, suggesting months of political stalemate with Netanyahu potentially at the helm of a caretaker government.
‘TWO CLICKS TO THE RIGHT’
In the days after October 7, Be’eri was crawling with Israeli soldiers patrolling through burnt and shattered homes, floors stained with blood, doors pierced with bullet holes. In some spots, the stench of dead bodies still hung in the air.
The sounds of shelling and Israeli war planes flying over Gaza were incessant.
Three years on, the kibbutz is up and running and the sounds of construction of brand-new houses are heard all around the leafy green grounds. Most members, now residing in another kibbutz, are expected to return by summer.
A collective community established in 1946, now with around 1,000 residents, Be’eri exemplifies the socialist values that dominated Israel’s politics in its early decades. Nearly all its votes went to the centre-left in the previous 2022 election, when only around 4% voted for parties in Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition.
The attack has made residents question longstanding views that there could be peace with the Palestinians in this generation.
“Everyone in Be’eri has made two clicks to the right. But I still think that most of us will stay with the opposition, the parties that want to replace this government,” he said.
Miri Gad Messika, 48, third generation in Be’eri, hasn’t yet decided how to vote. But it won’t be for Netanyahu.
“He failed as a leader so many times. And he shouldn’t be in politics anymore,” she said. “I’m looking for a leader. Unfortunately, it’s hard for me to see any leader in Israel at the moment.”
“I want to be optimistic,” she added, “and I can only hope for a better change.”
‘HOPE IS STRONGER THAN PAIN’
Through much of the past three years, opposition to the Netanyahu government gravitated around families of hostages taken to Gaza, some of whom accused the government of dodging responsibility and doing too little to secure their freedom.
A Tel Aviv open space came to be known as “Hostages Square”, site of constant rallies and vigils. Although the last of the hostages were released under a US-brokered ceasefire reached a year ago, the families are still among those most prominently calling for accountability now.
“I don’t see any legitimate reason why this government is running again for election,” said Ofri Bibas, whose young nephews, a 4-year-old and a 9-month-old, were slain in captivity in Gaza along with their mother. Their father, Ofri’s brother Yarden, was released in an early 2025 truce.
Bibas said her goal now is to make every Israeli remember October 7, “to take it with them to the day of the election and remember what happened here and who still hasn’t taken responsibility.”
On Saturday, thousands of Israelis rallied in Hostages Square. One of the speakers was Danielle Alony, who was kidnapped from Nir Oz with her 5-year-old daughter and freed from Gaza in a brief truce weeks later.
“Go vote,” Alony urged the crowd. “In three days we can start writing a new chapter for our children. One in which truth is stronger than fear, responsibility stronger than dereliction and hope is stronger than pain.”

Ukrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:46:37 CET
20:46:37 KST

KYIV, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Six weeks ago, Vitaly, his wife Iryna, their 13-year-old son Vlad and their cat left the besieged town of Oleshky in Russian-occupied Ukraine to escape what they feared was certain death by starvation.
Now back in Ukraine after a gruelling journey via Russia and Belarus, Vitaly views with deep scepticism a temporary ceasefire in his native town set to begin on Tuesday to allow evacuations and send in supplies.
Russia and Ukraine reached the agreement, announced by the White House on Friday, with the mediation of US first lady Melania Trump and after additional involvement from Pope Leo.
After more than four years living under Russian occupation in a town on the front line of fierce fighting with Ukrainian forces, Vitaly is not optimistic that the ceasefire can hold for long or the humanitarian situation significantly improve.
“Regarding the truce, I’m very sceptical about all this,” said Vitaly, 55, who declined to give his last name for security reasons because his relatives were still living in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
“I have a lot of respect for Melania Trump, but she does not influence dictator (Russian President Vladimir) Putin,” he told Reuters, sitting in a modern apartment in the Kyiv region where his family has temporarily settled.
He said many of those remaining in Oleshky are sick or elderly and it would be difficult for them to relocate.
Ukraine and Russia blame each other for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. Drones present the greatest threat to civilian life, and the town is within easy reach of unmanned aerial vehicles belonging to both armies.
Because supplies are running out and the route north is blocked by the Dnipro river, some residents have walked 20 km (12 miles) to the next village to stock up on food and water. The journey is fraught with danger and locals call it the “road of death”.
TEMPORARY CEASEFIRE AGREED
Ukraine and Russia agreed to a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky that is expected to begin on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (0100 GMT).
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that Kyiv hoped it would be possible to open up Oleshky, provide access for food and medicine and allow people to leave the area.
The Kremlin has said that all civilians wishing to leave Oleshky would be allowed to do so and that the evacuation was expected to take at least several days.
Oleshky, a small town across the Dnipro from Ukraine’s regional hub of Kherson, had a prewar population of some 24,000. It is still home to around 1,700 residents, including about 35 children, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
UNDER RUSSIAN CONTROL
Russian troops have occupied Oleshky since the first days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
It has been largely cut off from running water, electricity, gas and central heating since the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 and subsequent flooding of nearby areas.
As the war ground on, the humanitarian crisis deepened. By the middle of last year, the constant threat of drones choked off supply lines, causing food scarcity.
And from late May this year, the situation became severe, according to residents Reuters has spoken to.
Vitaly said his family survived for weeks by rationing a single cup of rice or buckwheat a day, occasionally adding a cucumber or tomato mixed with purslane, a common wild weed.
During the summer months, some residents could sell vegetables, but prices were unaffordable for most.
A kilo of tomatoes cost about 1,500 roubles ($18.50). To buy eggs, you needed to know the right people and 10 eggs would cost around 3,000 roubles, Vitaly recalled. No one was willing to sell potatoes.
After counting their meagre food stocks, and remembering last winter when the temperature in their apartment dropped to between 1 and 3 degrees Celsius (34 and 37 degrees Fahrenheit), they decided to leave.
“You look at what remained from your food supplies and realize that there is only one way for you — to go on foot or die of hunger,” Vitaly said.
Their home in Oleshky had been damaged by a drone, Iryna said, and they did not have anything left there.
ARDUOUS ESCAPE
On September 13, the family joined a small party of eight people and set out on foot. They walked for more than 20 km to the village of Radensk.
The road was heavily mined, and drones were flying overhead. Vitaly said they saw the body of a woman lying on the road as they passed by. They took with them only their autumn clothes, Vlad’s teddy bear, the cat and a handful of family photos.
They travelled from Radensk by bus deeper into Russian-occupied Ukraine, crossed into Russia after lengthy questioning by authorities at the border, and finally Belarus before returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory on September 17.
The family has spent the past several weeks settling into a new routine in the Kyiv region.
One of their first purchases was a bag of potatoes, bought to cook mashed potatoes for their son.
“The kid will be in school. We will be working. My wife needs to get her health back on track a bit,” Vitaly said.
As for his own future: “I will either join the army or will try to find a position somewhere here with weapon producers to help our country defeat its enemies.”
(Reporting by Olena Harmash; Additional reporting by Katerina Besedina, Editing by Mike Collett-White and Alexandra Hudson)

By Makini Brice and Inti Landauro
PARIS, Oct 26 (Reuters) - French student leaders vowed to go on protesting despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, stokes unrest and deepens the economic damage.
The measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes; €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans for renovating schools; and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system students see as socially unfair.
“Not all our demands were met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes,” Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said as he and fellow student leaders emerged from a meeting with government officials in Paris.
The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and yellow-vest activists, known for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Macron’s minority government.
The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120% of GDP, while the turmoil is boosting support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen ahead of next year’s presidential election.
The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
“It’s clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday’s protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.
Candidate Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, has benefited from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
An opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32% to 33.5%, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon on 17%. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Melenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
FAR-RIGHT GANGS CONFRONT FAR-LEFT ACTIVISTS
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
“We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses,” he said. “In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement.”
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody’s on Friday refrained from downgrading the country’s sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
“We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce,” he told Radio Classique.

Kremlin hails defeated Serbian ally Vucic as student election win adds to its geopolitical woes

Gloom in Moscow as Vucic's defeat in Serbia deprives Russia of an ally
MOSCOW, Oct 26 - Aleksandar Vucic's crushing election defeat by a student-backed protest movement has cast gloom over Moscow, which has lost another important partner in Europe just six months after ally Viktor Orban was ousted in an election in Hungary.
Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after Vucic, a frequent visitor to Moscow who had been prime minister or president since 2014, suffered a defeat on Sunday that prompted nationwide celebrations, although few had any idea of how the Balkan country's new student-backed leaders would govern.
Russia saw Vucic's Serbia as a crucial ally in Europe, and as a bulwark against what Moscow has cast as the European Union's aggressive attempts to contain and punish it over its war in Ukraine.
Serbia buys large quantities of gas from Russian energy giant Gazprom, and although it has aspirations to join the European Union, it has not signed up to EU-backed sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Instead, under Vucic — who enjoyed close ties to President Vladimir Putin — it continued to develop close economic, political and military links to Moscow.
The Kremlin put a brave face on Vucic's defeat, saying it had taken note of the result and that Vucic — whose contribution to bilateral ties it warmly praised — was moving into opposition.
"As for the new political force that will come to power as a result of the elections, we wish to express our hope that its actions will also be constructively directed towards the further development of relations, and that these new political forces will understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests, because it benefits Serbia," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
"For our part, we intend to continue to do everything we can to foster the development of our relations with Belgrade. But, as you know, it takes two to tango."
GEOPOLITICAL SETBACK
Russia can still count EU member Slovakia, under Prime Minister Robert Fico, as a friendly country. It has also been closely watching unrest in France, where far-right politician Marine Le Pen has said she would cut financial aid to Ukraine if she won next year's presidential election.
Recent regional electoral successes for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have been welcomed in Russia, where Putin's special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has begun to speak about the possibility of one day reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Germany and Russia which were blown up in 2022.
But for now at least, the potential loss of Serbia as a close ally — after setbacks to Russia's geopolitical influence in the South Caucasus region and parts of Central Asia — is being seen as a serious blow in Moscow by Kremlin-aligned politicians, media and analysts.
Before Sunday's election, the Student List party said it would not introduce sanctions on Russia over Ukraine, that it would retain Serbia's military neutrality, and that it would not seek to join NATO.
Vucic has cast doubts on those pledges, suggesting the party would renege on them and impose sanctions on Moscow as soon as March or April.
Jovo Bakic, a representative for Student List and university lecturer, on Monday denied his party would U-turn.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector. There will be no changes there (in the country’s foreign policy),” Bakic told Russia’s RT Balkan TV outlet.
Members of Russia's political elite fear Serbia's EU aspirations could see it put under serious pressure to align itself more closely with EU foreign policy however and that Moscow could find itself betrayed by a traditional ally in the process.
"Brussels, for its part, is keen to see Belgrade align itself more closely with the common European position on Russia. The main indicator of Serbia's actual course will not be Vucic's statements or his opponents’ electoral pledges, but rather the first decisions taken by the new cabinet," said the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper.
Fyodor Lukyanov, editor-in-chief of the influential Russia in Global Affairs journal, said it was clear that a new political era was under way in Serbia that could sharply reorient the country towards the EU, in the same way that Orban's loss of power in Hungary saw Budapest and Brussels become much closer.
"In this sense, the Hungarian case is quite telling," said Lukyanov. "And Russia has nothing good to look forward to." REUTERS

"The terrorists in Lavi Prison sat and hoarded what little food they had, a spoonful of jam here, a slide of bread there, day after day," he wrote in a social media post.
"They did this for several days, all so they could make an improvised cake and celebrate if I am not elected," he continued.
המחבלים בכלא לביא ישבו ואגרו מהמעט מזון שיש להם. כף ריבה ועוד כף ריבה, פרוסת לחם ועוד פרוסת לחם, כך במשך כמה ימים, הכל כדי להכין עוגה מאולתרת ולחגוג ביום שלישי, במידה ולא אבחר. אלא שנציב שב״ס המצוין ואנשיו איתרו את העוגה, והאסירים הועמדו לדין משמעתי, והועברו לצינוק. הם כבר תכננו את החגיגות, אבל אצלנו נגמרה החגיגה. ביום שלישי אסור לתת להם לחגוג, מצביעים ב׳ בקלפי!

Ben-Gvir, who leads the Kahanist Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power party, has attempted to make conditions for Palestinian inmates as unbearable as possible since taking control of Israeli prisons in 2022.
He has also personally taken part in the abuse and humiliation of Palestinian prisoners, as well as captured activists from the Gaza Freedom Flotilla.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem has described Ben-Gvir's prison system as a "network of torture camps" that subjects Palestinians to physical and psychological abuse, starvation and inhuman conditions.
Ben-Gvir also led efforts to introduce the death penalty for Palestinian prisoners.
Otzma Yehudit is expected to gain seats in the Knesset following Tuesday's vote, profiting from the growing radicalisation of young Israelis.
Polls tracked by The New Arab project the party to pick up eight seats and become joint fifth-largest party in the assembly.
In 2022, the party was only able to make it into the Knesset by forming a joint list with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and another small far-right group.

2026-10-26
11:42:48 UTC
20:42:48 KST

Zelenskyy said the planned visit would gather Ukraine, the US, EU and NATO in high-level talks on security guarantees and diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's planned visit to Brussels this week for high-level talks with the US, EU and NATO has reportedly been cancelled.
Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's communications adviser, told reporters on Monday that Kyiv could no longer confirm the visit because of changes to the American side's plans.
Speaking to Ukrainian media on Sunday, Zelenskyy said the talks were being planned for 27 or 28 October, bringing together representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU, as well as NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
Asked by Euronews about the planned talks, the European Commission said it remained engaged in diplomatic efforts but offered no further details.
"The Commission continues to participate in talks and efforts with allies and partners to achieve a just and lasting peace for Ukraine," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
"At this stage, we have no further information to share."
The Brussels meeting was intended to follow a series of diplomatic discussions in Oslo last week, including talks between Zelenskyy and US special envoy Steve Witkoff attended by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
According to Zelenskyy, wider discussions also involved security advisers to the leaders of Britain, France and Italy, alongside Björn Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The US subsequently briefed its partners following Witkoff's talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, Zelenskyy said.
"We had a briefing from the Americans, and now they want not just a briefing, but to discuss security, guarantees, the EU and its involvement more broadly," Zelenskyy said.
"They want a meeting in Brussels this week. The Americans, Ukraine, the EU at presidential level and NATO at secretary-general level. I don't know whether anyone else will be part of this group in Brussels."
The development comes ahead of another round of negotiations between Ukrainian, American and Russian teams, which Zelenskyy said was being planned for the first half of November.
Abu Dhabi has been mentioned as a possible venue, although the date and location have yet to be confirmed.

Ukraine Wants EU Representative at Russia Negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:40:38 UTC
20:40:38 KST

Ukraine is seeking to move up planned trilateral negotiations with the United States and Russia by at least a week and bring an EU representative into the talks, Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing sources close to the negotiation team.
The next round of discussions between Ukraine, the US and Russia is tentatively scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on November 10, after the US congressional midterm elections. Kyiv and Washington are working to persuade Moscow to agree to meet at least a week earlier.
A source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's team told Ukrainska Pravda that the timing was critical because of the coming winter. “in December, every week will be important. When you have no power, water or heating, every single day plays a role”, the source said.
As of the evening of October 25, Moscow had not provided final confirmation of a change to the date.
Kyiv does not anticipate a breakthrough at the initial meeting, believing that several rounds of negotiations will be needed to reach substantive agreements. A source from the President's Office said Moscow still believed it “will be able to break us this winter”.
A member of Zelensky's team who has taken part in similar negotiations said the delegations might change, meaning the first meeting would be used to familiarize the participants with one another. “We have a feeling that there will be updates to the composition of the groups. Therefore, at the first meeting, the new delegations will get used to each other. At the second, substantive work will begin. And somewhere around the third, there may already be some real decisions,” the source said.
Ukraine also wants the sides to begin by discussing what peace should look like after the war, rather than immediately negotiating which villages should belong to each side.
A source close to the negotiation team told Ukrainska Pravda that Kyiv wanted to outline a future security arrangement for the region, including how Ukraine would be protected and what cooperation with NATO or other partners might entail. The source also pointed to low public confidence in the US president. “In Ukraine trust in Trump is only 6% higher than trust in Putin. Nobody here is going to do anything purely on Trump's assurances,” the source said.
Kyiv continues to push for European partners to participate in the negotiations despite resistance from Russia and, frequently, the United States.
Sources in Zelensky's diplomatic team told Ukrainska Pravda that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had conveyed to Russian President Vladimir Putin the idea of discussing a new security model, and that Putin had reportedly agreed.
Over the past two meetings, a potential EU representative has also emerged: Björn Seibert, head of cabinet and close aide to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to a source cited by Ukrainska Pravda, Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, told US officials that any final peace arrangement must be acceptable to people living in Kharkiv and Dnipro. “After Donbas, they are next, and if the residents of these regions look at our 'peace formula' and say, 'Okay, this suits us,' then that will truly be a work in progress,” the source said, relaying Arakhamiia's message.
US government sources have said the next round of talks involving American, Ukrainian and Russian delegations could take place in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Russian leader's aide Yuri Ushakov has said Moscow is ready to resume trilateral negotiations on ending the war after November 4.
Zelensky has said Ukraine will not accept restrictions on the size of its armed forces or neutral status under any potential peace agreement.

Ukrainian regulator stalling EBRD-backed capital market plan – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:40:21 EET
20:40:21 KST

Implementation of an integrated capital markets infrastructure model, developed jointly by the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), the Ministry of Economy and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), is currently being held up by the position of the head of the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC), NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"We are being asked what is happening with the capital markets. We explain the capital markets infrastructure model that has been developed jointly by the NBU, the Ministry of Economy and the EBRD. Unfortunately, its implementation is currently being held up by the position of the head of the NSSMC," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
In the NBU governor's view, the proposed model takes the state's interests into account in building a vertically integrated system, and therefore confidence in it should not be undermined.
"The key idea is to bring the entire capital markets infrastructure chain together under a single holding company. The strategic investor in this infrastructure holding company should be an entity trusted by global private capital: Deutsche Börse, Euroclear, Clearstream… Naturally, it should be selected through a competitive process. But in the current circumstances, national security requirements must also be taken into account. Our model provides for all of this. So why is the process being held up?" Pyshnyy concluded.
As reported, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso expressed hope at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group that Ukraine would pay greater attention to the capital market development project.
"Despite all the short-term challenges, we have indeed managed to move this process forward, and I hope this issue will soon become a priority," she said.
In July last year, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Rome by the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance, the NBU, the NSSMC and the EBRD on supporting integrated capital markets infrastructure in Ukraine. Its signing was preceded by the Financial Stability Council's approval of a plan for the practical implementation of the target capital markets infrastructure model.
In early September 2025, the National Bank announced the launch of the memorandum's implementation. The first stage involved optimizing the ownership structure and corporate governance of the National Depository of Ukraine (NDU) by transferring management of the state-owned stake, previously managed by the NSSMC, to the NBU.
The next stage envisages the creation of a holding company involving a reputable international strategic investor selected through an open tender, an operator of trading and post-trading infrastructure, international financial institutions, local market participants, and the state and state-owned banks. The holding company, in turn, will establish a new stock exchange in Ukraine, which will become the majority owner of the Central Counterparty Clearing Institution, the Settlement Center (SC), replacing the National Bank in that role. In addition, the exchange will own a minority stake in the NDU, while the National Bank will hold a majority stake.
The final stage is to consolidate depository services under the NDU, which is to operate as a single central securities depository, by transferring to it the functions of recording and servicing the circulation of government bonds from the National Bank.
In early June this year, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a bill on establishing a capital markets infrastructure holding company with the participation of a foreign strategic investor. However, due to a change of government, the document was submitted to the Verkhovna Rada only on September 4. The NSSMC subsequently proposed substantial amendments to the government's bill, including tightening the conditions for attracting a foreign strategic investor.
In addition, an alternative bill (No. 16038-1) was registered on September 21. Its authors include 12 members of parliament, among them Serhiy Taruta, first deputy head of the Verkhovna Rada's economic committee; Andriy Nikolaienko, head of the capital markets subcommittee of the parliament's finance committee; Oleksandr Fediyenko, head of a subcommittee of the parliament's security committee; and Anton Yatsenko.

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Despite growing interest in engineering, Estonia faces a shortage of more than 800 young engineers in the next decade as 40 percent retire. Changes to math teaching may help.
Interest in engineering has grown sharply, but according to OSKA, the Estonian Qualifications Authority's labor market forecasting system, the sector will still be short more than 800 young engineers over the next decade as 40 percent retire. There are no quick solutions, but efforts are being made to alleviate the shortage by changing how mathematics is taught.
Interest in studying at Tallinn University of Technology's (TalTech) School of Engineering has increased by 25 percent over the past three years. According to Fjodor Sergejev, dean of the School of Engineering, students are enrolling in a variety of programs, from energy and construction to mechanical and industrial engineering, but there will not be enough graduates to fill the gap.
"We need replacement workers because many engineers from previous generations are retiring and need to be replaced, but we also need to ensure the development of the sector, and for that we need even more engineers. Even the substantial demographic support we currently have is unfortunately unable to meet all our needs, because the replacement demand is indeed very high, in some fields even numbering in the thousands."
Cathy-Liis Põlluveer, president of the Estonian association of engineers (Eesti Inseneride Liit), also acknowledged the shortage: "We currently have a situation where it depends somewhat on the field, but when an engineer, particularly an experienced engineer, is being sought and a recruitment competition is held, there is practically no queue of applicants or diversity among candidates. Instead, engineers are being sought like needles in a haystack."
According to Anneli Leemet, an analyst at OSKA, demand will grow most for electrical and energy engineers, mechanical engineers and electronics engineers. Leemet said the issue is not only meeting the numerical demand but ensuring engineers have a diverse range of skills.
One possible solution experts see is strengthening mathematics education in basic schools (grades 1–9) — making mathematics teaching more relevant to everyday life, more integrated with other subjects, and delivered in a way that supports all children's motivation to learn. According to Tiina Kraav, a lecturer in mathematics education at the University of Tartu, there are no quick solutions, but mathematics teaching is being continuously developed.
"Making mathematics more interesting to learn, making mathematics learning more visible, making mathematical thinking more visible to students, making mathematics learning more creative, improving how problem-solving skills are taught in the classroom, getting students to talk about what they think and how they think when solving mathematics problems – all of this will certainly help in the longer term," Kraav said.
Põlluveer believes subjects that help connect natural sciences and mathematics could be beneficial.
Priit Laats, a teacher of technology education, arts and technology at Tartu Raatuse School, confirmed that schools are increasingly moving toward theme-based learning: "For example, in the first stage of basic school, there is integrated learning. It is theme-based, with Estonian, mathematics, nature studies and creative subjects all together all the time. In fact, other grades should already be structured in a similar way. But again, who is going to develop all of this? It is a huge amount of work. If I take how I, in turn, support mathematics, we introduce 3D modeling as early as fourth grade: the spatial world, shapes, symbols, symmetry, reflection, all the faces and planes – it is all mathematics all the time, and we do this right through ninth grade."
OSKA will publish a new cross-sector study of labor and skills needs in engineering in early November, which will show that competition for hybrid competencies is increasing in the labor market. This means engineers must have in-depth specialist knowledge combined with digital, data analysis, artificial intelligence, business or management skills.

Italy sees progress in well-being indicators, but poverty remains above EU average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:35 UTC
20:38:35 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Italy has made progress in several areas of equitable and sustainable well-being, including health and the environment, but continues to face challenges related to poverty, disposable income and households’ ability to make ends meet, according to the latest report by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT).
The report, which examines 132 indicators of equitable and sustainable well-being, found that 54 indicators improved, 55 remained stable and 23 deteriorated.
Despite the overall progress, Italy’s at-risk-of-poverty rate remains 2.3 percentage points above the EU average.
Compared with the EU, Italy performs better in health and safety, while significant challenges persist in education and training, employment, work-life balance, and innovation, research and creativity.
More than 5.4 million people were living in absolute poverty in Italy in 2025, with large families and households with at least one minor child facing particularly difficult conditions.
According to the report, 8% of households were living in absolute poverty, affecting 9.3% of the country’s population.
The incidence of individual absolute poverty remained highest in southern Italy, although it declined to 11.5% in 2025 from 12.5% in 2024.
In northern Italy, the rate fell to 8.5% from 8.8% a year earlier, while central Italy continued to record the lowest incidence, at 7.4%, down from 7.6% in 2024.

How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:32 UTC
20:38:32 KST

Article
Presidential election 2026
How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Monday 26 October 2026 14:05
Monday, 26 October 2026, 14:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The boundary between geographical distance and national identity often fades on election day. For our compatriots living thousands of kilometres from their homeland, presidential elections are not merely an administrative procedure, but an expression of belonging, hope and the desire to have their voices heard. How do Bulgarians around the world view the role of the head of state, and what makes them feel close to their homeland despite the physical distance?
Principles, Unity and International Standing: What matters most in a President
The question of whether the head of state should primarily uphold principles, unite the nation or defend the country’s standing on the international stage prompted a range of nuanced responses in our conversations with fellow Bulgarians on election day on October 25. For many, however, these three roles are inseparable.
40 thousand Bulgarians abroad register to vote in presidential election
“Personally, I think that if one person embodies all three of these qualities, that might sound a little utopian, but it would be the best possible outcome,” says Marina Tomova, who lives in Nettuno, Italy. “The president is the face of a country. We Bulgarians would identify with this representative figure in a number of ways: how they present themselves on the international stage and how they defend Bulgaria’s interests. At the same time, the president should serve as a unifying figure and a corrective force in both domestic and foreign policy.”
“People want to see a president who stands up for Bulgaria’s interests and is not afraid to take a position. They also want someone who protects their interests, is educated and well-informed, can speak eloquently at international events and is not afraid to express their views clearly and openly.”
Estela Encheva, from Munich, Germany, emphasises the importance of international law and domestic dialogue.
“For me, it is also important that the president respects international law and insists that our country abide by it, while also bringing the nation together. We live in a time when society is so divided that political measures alone can hardly bridge the divide. In our particular situation, it is important for the president to be able to act as a check on those in power.”
Marin Kachamakov, from Geneva, Switzerland, stresses that the head of state should unite people around moral principles and integrity, while also having the strength and voice to hold those in power to account.
“I believe the president should unite fellow Bulgarians around integrity and a shared moral compass, and help ensure that Bulgaria is not seen as a country that disregards principles, a country where anything goes and where signed treaties are not honoured. In short, the president should bring people together, set a moral example and ensure that the agreements and treaties signed by the state are respected.”
Milena Baeva, from Kuwait, says that, for her, it is equally important for the next presidential ticket to unite people in Bulgaria and defend the country’s interests:
“I imagine them as people whose actions, both at home and on the world stage, will make me proud to be Bulgarian.”
Viktoria Vlahovska, from Reading, United Kingdom, points out that Bulgarians abroad want a steady hand as commander-in-chief and a representative figure they can be proud of.
Adriana Dimitrova, from Berlin, Germany, sums up her expectations by saying she wants a competent leader who can hold their own with dignity on the world stage, someone Bulgarians will not be ashamed of.
When do Bulgarians abroad feel represented and heard?
For Bulgarians living outside the country to feel represented by the presidential institution, they need genuine attention, not merely formal gestures.
The role of the presidential ticket is to seek common ground and represent all Bulgarian citizens, regardless of their political beliefs or place of residence, stresses Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia:
“I would feel represented if the president regarded Bulgarians abroad as an integral part of the nation. This is not just about official visits or statements, but about genuinely understanding the problems faced by Bulgarian communities around the world and the contributions they make. What matters is that people abroad know their voices and experiences also count in shaping Bulgaria’s future,” says our compatriot from the other side of the world.
Martina Shopova-Yanev, from Vienna, Austria, is adamant that she has yet to see genuine concern from the presidential institution for the problems faced by Bulgarians abroad, and hopes this will change:
“I hope for a president and vice-president who will be present in the lives of Bulgarians abroad, not just on paper or during election campaigns, and who will help address our problems. These often concern the exercise of our right to vote and making voting easier. We hope the next presidential ticket will take a more active approach in this regard and demonstrate genuine interest, rather than merely campaigning for support.”
“I think the president should visit as many different countries as possible and make time for Bulgarians abroad,” suggests Marin Kachamakov from Geneva. “Although there are only 24 hours in a day, the president should also try to listen to the views of these Bulgarians. Let us not forget that some of them left Bulgaria not because they wanted to, but because they decided they could build a better life abroad, or because they were driven out of the country. I am referring to the period before 1989-1990.”
Marinela Koleva, from Kraków, Poland, proposes a concrete way to show support: the president could serve as patron of initiatives organised by Bulgarians abroad, demonstrating through action and policy that their concerns matter.
Ties to the Homeland and Faith in the Power of the Vote
Despite the distance and fluctuations in voter turnout, the bond with Bulgaria remains strong. In Melbourne, for example, 77 people voted, compared with 149 in the previous parliamentary elections in April 2026. Bulgarians abroad continue to express a desire for change in their homeland. This is reflected in the decisive victory of the Andrey Gyurov-Georgi Kandev presidential ticket among voters abroad, while in Bulgaria the advantage went to incumbent head of state Iliana Iotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev.
Gyurov wins 45.79% of overseas vote, well ahead of Iotova
“Wherever we live, we always feel close to our homeland,” says Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia.
“We keep ourselves informed through social media and the news, and we watch Bulgarian television. We will always remain Bulgarians, no matter how far away we are from our homeland. Every one of us cares deeply about Bulgaria, which is why you see such strong engagement abroad. People vote, they take an interest and they are not indifferent to what is happening, because we all care about Bulgaria.”
The organisation of polling stations abroad demonstrates the strength of the community and its commitment to developments in the homeland. In this sense, voting is not simply a civic duty, but a powerful expression of an enduring connection with Bulgaria. This is also evident in a video sent to us by Nadia Ullman from the Bulgarian Centre in Boston, USA. Voter turnout in New England was lower than in the previous vote in April 2026, but for her, taking part in the electoral process is a personal mission.
“As the mother of two grown-up children who have attended Bulgarian school in Boston for years, I see it as my mission to raise them as informed and engaged Bulgarian citizens. I teach them to love Bulgaria and value their right to vote. By actively participating in the life of the Bulgarian community abroad, they are learning to preserve their roots and traditions. I believe that this is how we raise responsible individuals who will always carry Bulgaria in their hearts and contribute to its future.
For me, voting is not simply an obligation, but a way of helping shape a better and more prosperous Bulgaria. Every vote cast from abroad sends a clear message that Bulgarians living outside the country are not indifferent to what is happening at home. The organisation of polling stations demonstrates the strength of our community and our desire to make Bulgaria a more attractive place for us and our children to return to.”
The conversations conducted by the Radio Bulgaria team with Bulgarians living in different parts of the world make one thing clear: liviging at a distance from Bulgaria does not diminish their expectations of the country’s institutions. Bulgarians abroad want their president to act as a check on those in power, unite the nation and serve as an authoritative representative of the country on the international stage. They want a leader who shows genuine concern for Bulgarian communities around the world and makes them proud of their origins.
