PKK-linked group in Iraq’s Sinjar begins disarmament, integration process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:23:30 UTC
20:23:30 KST

Iraqi security forces on Oct. 26 have taken control of key military positions held by the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS), a group affiliated with the PKK terrorist organization, as the group prepares to disarm and integrate into Iraq’s security institutions.
The handover is part of a broader process to bring the group’s members, weapons and military positions under state control, according to statements by Iraqi authorities.
Iraq’s Security Media Cell announced that the transfer of military positions in the Sinjar district began, confirming that Iraqi security forces took over several key sites previously held by the YBS. Additional positions were expected to be handed over later on Oct. 26.
A ceremony scheduled for Oct. 26 on Mount Sinjar will mark a new phase in the process, with around 2,000 YBS members expected to lay down their arms.
A further 3,000 to 4,000 members are expected to disarm in subsequent stages, while YBS personnel will be distributed among the Iraqi army, police and the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi, an Iraqi state-sponsored paramilitary umbrella organization.
Sabah al-Numan, military spokesman for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, said the process would also involve reorganizing the group’s military ties with Iraqi security forces and transferring responsibility for security on Mount Sinjar to the relevant federal authorities.
Al-Numan said the initiative was part of the government’s policy to bring all weapons under state control, adding that Iraq’s Constitution prohibits the formation of armed groups outside the country’s official armed forces.
The developments come amid broader efforts by Ankara and Baghdad to strengthen state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of unauthorized armed groups.
Türkiye and Iraq agreed on Sept. 23 to restore full state authority in Sinjar and end the presence of banned foreign armed groups, according to a joint statement issued after Turkish President Recep Tayyip 
Erdoğan met Iraqi al-Zaidi on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Under the agreement, Turkish forces are to gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan military compound to Iraq’s federal government, in line with progress on Baghdad’s security measures and an agreed mechanism and timetable.
The move also comes as Türkiye continues its “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, aimed at ending the PKK’s terror in the country. While the disarmament process is ongoing, Ankara has called for a broader regional approach, urging that all groups affiliated with the PKK across the region should lay down their arms.

Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

British premier says revising UK’s Brexit deal with EU could ‘bring people together’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:22:23 UTC
20:22:23 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
British Premier Andy Burnham has said that revising the UK’s relationship with the EU could help bring people together, while insisting that any decision to rejoin the bloc would be for the British public to make.
Speaking in an interview on Monday on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, hosted by Susanna Reid and Richard Madeley, Burnham said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime but stressed that he would not impose his personal views on the public.
“I’ve said – I’m going to be honest – in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the British public are the bosses here,” he said.
Asked whether he saw himself as the prime minister destined to take Britain back into the EU, Burnham replied: “Honestly, I don’t.”
He said his priority was to take a pragmatic approach to the country’s challenges, adding: “I see it as my job to be pragmatic about the whole situation. Can I make it work better? Can I add growth to the British economy?”
Burnham rejected suggestions that he was reopening the Brexit referendum debate in breach of a promise made during the Makerfield by-election campaign.
Instead, he reiterated his argument that the UK should reconsider its post-Brexit arrangements with the EU, saying the current settlement was not working.
He also argued that a more practical and open discussion about Brexit could help bridge political and social divisions that have persisted since the 2016 referendum.
“And [to] go back to Brexit, by just talking about it in a more practical way, by being honest about it … that can start to bring people together who voted in different ways,” he said.
“The divides that we’ve lived through in the last decade really do need to end, and we need to pull people together …”
Burnham said addressing the UK’s relationship with Europe was necessary to provide the country with a clear direction.
“I’m trying to give the country a direction and there is no way I can do that without coming back to the relationship with Europe and saying, ‘Look, here are some options as to how we got this right.’”
He again ruled out seeking to rejoin the EU before the next general election.
 
Rules out early election
During the interview, Burnham also dismissed speculation about an early general election, saying there would be no election “anytime soon.”
Asked whether he was preparing the public for an early election, he replied: “No, I’ve ruled that out.”
Pressed on whether that was definite, Burnham said he had made his position clear before the Labour Party conference.
“I just don’t think people want another backward-looking squabble. I think they want me to get on with the job,” he said.
Reid returned to the issue towards the end of the interview, prompting Burnham to reiterate that an early election was not on his agenda.
“My mind is not on that [an early election]. I don’t know if that is coming over here, but it genuinely is not on that. There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well just put that out of their mind,” he said.

Agricultural Year Recap and Spring Planting Scenarios: UCAB to Host #DoAgro26 Conference
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:22:21 EET
20:22:21 KST

On December 4, the 18th International Conference “Agribusiness in Ukraine” (#DoAgro26) will take place in Truskavets (Lviv Oblast). The event will be attended by government officials, market leaders, and leading agricultural producers.
This was reported by the press service of the organizers—the “Ukrainian Agribusiness Club” and the UCABevent agency.
This year, the event is completely revamping its format and usual location to take stock of the past year and develop a roadmap for the upcoming season.
This isn’t about monologues or dry reports—those are a thing of the past. What lies ahead is the search for new operating models: open dialogue with government officials, collective brainstorming, and making strategic decisions right here and now. The main goal is to find effective operating models under the new rules of the game.
Participating in #DoAgro26 means:
- Pre-conference fireside chat: an evening meeting with a guest expert, an informal conversation, and quality networking on the eve of the conference.
- Open agropolitical debates: no imposed topics or pre-written scripts. Participants themselves choose the direction of the discussion and the most pressing issues right here and now.
- Collective brainstorming and roundtables: a format where everyone becomes a co-creator of the event, joins the discussions, and collaboratively shapes effective strategies.
- Direct access to solutions: the opportunity for open dialogue with government officials and market leaders.
The program will focus on key issues:
- 2026 in Review: How the agribusiness market (did NOT) adapt to challenges.
- Checkmate to the season’s challenges: scenarios for the 2027 spring planting season and strategic moves for agribusiness.
- A macroeconomic overview above and below the line—from global trends to the financial realities of agribusiness.
The “Agribusiness in Ukraine” conference will be held in cooperation with the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and in partnership with the Ministry of Finance of the Czech Republic. Valtra, part of AGCO Corporation, is the exclusive technical partner, and Credit Agricole is the gold financial partner.
Agricultural producers and participants in previous UCAAB events are eligible for a 20% discount off the base price, while association members receive special terms.
For more information about the event, follow the links: https://cutt.ly/9yQmTlnY
Interfax-Ukraine is the conference’s media partner.

Engagement Altitude of Up to 9 km: Helsing Unveils AD-2 Ambush Counter-UAS Interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:21:38 UTC
20:21:38 KST

German company Helsing has presented the new AD-2 Ambush interceptor missile, designed to engage high-speed and low-observable aerial targets.
Militarnyi reports this from a presentation by the company’s co-founder, Gundbert Scherf, in Berlin.
The AD-2 Ambush is primarily designed to neutralize high-speed threats that exceed the capabilities of standard counter-drone systems.
“Thanks to rocket motors, an affordable all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, these interceptors deliver autonomous fire superiority at altitudes of up to 10 kilometers, at an affordable cost and on an industrial scale,” company president Niklas Köhler reported.
The interceptor is equipped with a solid-fuel rocket motor that lets it reach speeds over Mach 2.5. Its combat radius exceeds 20 km.
The AD-2 Ambush has a maximum target engagement altitude of over 9 km. This allows it to intercept objects flying at altitudes beyond the reach of most low-cost air defense systems.
For target guidance, the missile uses an onboard radar seeker with artificial intelligence capabilities. During the midcourse phase, ground-based radar stations correct its trajectory with commands.
The missile can effectively engage targets at night and in adverse weather conditions.
The seeker is designed for mass production without relying on exclusive components.
The AD-2 Ambush launches from dedicated transport-launch containers, each holding 20–40 missiles. They can be mounted on vehicles or railway platforms.
Helsing will manufacture the missiles at its Resilience Factories.
In July, Helsing announced that Andrii Shevchenko would head the company’s office in Ukraine.

Drone strikes cut power across southeast Sudan, operator says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:20:31 UTC
20:20:31 KST

Drone strikes cut power across southeast Sudan, operator says
CAIRO, Oct 26 - Paramilitary drone strikes hit power stations in southeast Sudan on Monday, cutting power across the region, the state electricity company said.
The operator accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces — which have been fighting a civil war with the army for around 3-1/2 years — of knocking out power in four states, which cover about half the territory currently held by the military.
The Rapid Support Forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the account from the Sudan Electricity Holding Company.
Power was cut in Sennar, Al Qadarif, White Nile and Gezira states, threatening the stability of the whole national grid, the operator said.
The attacks hit stations in the towns and areas of Sinja, El Hawata, Al Fao and Mashkour, as well as Al-Junaid in Gezira State, causing "severe damage" and "major destruction" to equipment, it added.
The United Nations has warned that attacks on power infrastructure threaten health and other services for millions of people already hit hard by the conflict.
Sudan's army has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, when the two fell out over issues including how to integrate their forces in a planned transition to civilian rule.
Both sides have stepped up drone strikes, with a series of attacks on Nyala, held by the RSF, and Khartoum airport, held by the army, this month. REUTERS

Koretsky: government must deliver new mobilization social contract by Dec 1
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:19:28 EET
20:19:28 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky predicts that following changes to the reservation system, over 90-95% of employees in the fuel-energy and defense-industrial complexes will be re-reserved.
"We are separating the concept of criticality from economic reservation criteria. This is very important. Why? Because salary and the absence of tax debt are not the same as an enterprise's criticality. This is important, it indeed brings transparency, cleanup, and additional revenues, but it does not equal criticality. Critical means energy, the defense-industrial complex, communications, housing and communal services, pharmacies, groceries, logistics, and so on. But there are enterprises, a large number already, that got there largely due to salaries and a lack of tax debts. Therefore, we are separating criticality from the economy," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
He emphasized that workers currently in the energy sector or the defense-industrial complex have nothing to worry about, as over 90-95% will be re-reserved.
"However, creating a large number of enterprises, whether IT or conditionally defense industry, where three drones are made and hundreds of people are reserved – I am conditionally simplifying, hyperbolizing in a certain sense, but that is how it is. And there are very many such cases. Contracting organizations. And it grows, grows, grows," he added.
According to the Prime Minister, changing the rules is designed, on the one hand, to cut down on unfair reservations without letting the economy collapse, and on the other hand, to give active military personnel a clear understanding regarding rotations.
"To say that these mobilization and reservation rules will produce a super-effect – no, there is no such thing, but we are at least stopping the endless growth of sometimes unfairly reserved individuals. And now, most importantly, what I am appealing to enterprises, business, and the economic sector about: we need to jointly come up with a new social model where, even if everyone is reserved, enterprises provide predictable mobilization of people into the army. This is an idealistic model. If such a solution could be found, the need to search for people on the streets would disappear. And if a business, entrepreneur, manager, or head takes on such a commitment – then nothing else is needed at all, this is a new social contract. But not thinking about it, not preparing for it, is a super-strategic mistake," Koretsky stated.
He stressed that failing to prepare in advance for a potential tightening of mobilization in Russia, which could reach 300,000–500,000 troops, would mean being forced to make unpopular decisions in manual mode once again.
"Then it won't be about reservations, or percentages. The issue is the survival of the state, and therefore this must be taken into account. Seeking to increase accountability for those who hide is also on the agenda – this is all a comprehensive story. By December 1, we must deliver a new social contract," he added, announcing a meeting with businesses on this issue.
As reported, on October 23, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky stated that the Cabinet of Ministers had finalized changes to the reservation system – an enterprise's criticality is being separated from its economic indicators, sectoral and regional criticality criteria will be updated, and enterprises will be checked for abuses.
The second change is that the maximum reservation level, particularly for the energy sector and defense industry, will no longer be 100% (dropping to 95%). The government will not weaken the work of those manufacturing weapons or maintaining critical infrastructure, and if uninterrupted operation requires reserving more, the enterprise can submit a justified appeal to a special Coordination Center.
The third change involves the Ministry of Defense strengthening liability for draft evasion. The fourth is the preparation of a mechanism for 100% reservation provided mobilization obligations are fulfilled: an enterprise will be able to fully reserve employees if it regularly and voluntarily recruits a portion of them for military service.
The Cabinet has also initiated a review of sectoral and regional criticality criteria, taking into account new requirements within 10 days.

Spanish airline Volotea cancels flights in France amid soaring fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:16:02 UTC
20:16:02 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Spanish low-cost airline Volotea has canceled more than 10% of its winter flight capacity in France amid soaring jet fuel prices and mounting financial pressures, leaving passengers scrambling for alternatives, according to a report Monday.
The carrier, which operates many domestic routes in France and connects medium-sized European cities, is struggling with rising kerosene costs and €250-300 million ($280-336 million) of debt accumulated during the COVID-19 pandemic, BFMTV reported.
Consumer association UFC Que Choisir criticized the airline's handling of cancellations, citing passenger complaints about delayed refunds and inadequate assistance with alternative travel arrangements.
Under EU regulations, airlines must offer passengers either refunds within seven days or alternative transportation when flights are canceled.
Volotea said refunds were being processed within seven days, while reimbursement requests for alternative travel expenses would be assessed individually.
According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, the airline has eliminated over 10% of its capacity between November and February.
Bordeaux has reportedly experienced the sharpest reductions, with cancellations reaching 35% year-on-year.
Volotea also plans to reduce its fleet from 44 aircraft to approximately 30-35, focusing on larger planes to improve revenue per seat.

Ukrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:15:51 UTC
20:15:51 KST

Ukrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism
KYIV, Oct 26 - Six weeks ago, Vitaly, his wife Iryna, their 13-year-old son Vlad and their cat left the besieged town of Oleshky in Russian-occupied Ukraine to escape what they feared was certain death by starvation.
Now back in Ukraine after a gruelling journey via Russia and Belarus, Vitaly views with deep scepticism a temporary ceasefire in his native town set to begin on Tuesday to allow evacuations and send in supplies.
Russia and Ukraine reached the agreement, announced by the White House on Friday, with the mediation of US first lady Melania Trump and after additional involvement from Pope Leo.
After more than four years living under Russian occupation in a town on the front line of fierce fighting with Ukrainian forces, Vitaly is not optimistic that the ceasefire can hold for long or the humanitarian situation significantly improve.
"Regarding the truce, I'm very sceptical about all this," said Vitaly, 55, who declined to give his last name for security reasons because his relatives were still living in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
"I have a lot of respect for Melania Trump, but she does not influence dictator (Russian President Vladimir) Putin," he told Reuters, sitting in a modern apartment in the Kyiv region where his family has temporarily settled.
He said many of those remaining in Oleshky are sick or elderly and it would be difficult for them to relocate.
Ukraine and Russia blame each other for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky. Drones present the greatest threat to civilian life, and the town is within easy reach of unmanned aerial vehicles belonging to both armies.
Because supplies are running out and the route north is blocked by the Dnipro river, some residents have walked 20 km (12 miles) to the next village to stock up on food and water. The journey is fraught with danger and locals call it the "road of death".
TEMPORARY CEASEFIRE AGREED
Ukraine and Russia agreed to a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky that is expected to begin on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time (0100 GMT).
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that Kyiv hoped it would be possible to open up Oleshky, provide access for food and medicine and allow people to leave the area.
The Kremlin has said that all civilians wishing to leave Oleshky would be allowed to do so and that the evacuation was expected to take at least several days.
Oleshky, a small town across the Dnipro from Ukraine's regional hub of Kherson, had a prewar population of some 24,000. It is still home to around 1,700 residents, including about 35 children, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
UNDER RUSSIAN CONTROL
Russian troops have occupied Oleshky since the first days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
It has been largely cut off from running water, electricity, gas and central heating since the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 and subsequent flooding of nearby areas.
As the war ground on, the humanitarian crisis deepened. By the middle of last year, the constant threat of drones choked off supply lines, causing food scarcity.
And from late May this year, the situation became severe, according to residents Reuters has spoken to.
Vitaly said his family survived for weeks by rationing a single cup of rice or buckwheat a day, occasionally adding a cucumber or tomato mixed with purslane, a common wild weed.
During the summer months, some residents could sell vegetables, but prices were unaffordable for most.
A kilo of tomatoes cost about 1,500 roubles ($18.50). To buy eggs, you needed to know the right people and 10 eggs would cost around 3,000 roubles, Vitaly recalled. No one was willing to sell potatoes.
After counting their meagre food stocks, and remembering last winter when the temperature in their apartment dropped to between 1 and 3 degrees Celsius (34 and 37 degrees Fahrenheit), they decided to leave.
"You look at what remained from your food supplies and realize that there is only one way for you — to go on foot or die of hunger," Vitaly said.
Their home in Oleshky had been damaged by a drone, Iryna said, and they did not have anything left there.
ARDUOUS ESCAPE
On September 13, the family joined a small party of eight people and set out on foot. They walked for more than 20 km to the village of Radensk.
The road was heavily mined, and drones were flying overhead. Vitaly said they saw the body of a woman lying on the road as they passed by. They took with them only their autumn clothes, Vlad's teddy bear, the cat and a handful of family photos.
They travelled from Radensk by bus deeper into Russian-occupied Ukraine, crossed into Russia after lengthy questioning by authorities at the border, and finally Belarus before returning to Ukrainian-controlled territory on September 17.
The family has spent the past several weeks settling into a new routine in the Kyiv region.
One of their first purchases was a bag of potatoes, bought to cook mashed potatoes for their son.
"The kid will be in school. We will be working. My wife needs to get her health back on track a bit," Vitaly said.
As for his own future: "I will either join the army or will try to find a position somewhere here with weapon producers to help our country defeat its enemies." REUTERS

The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) Executive Committee on Sunday firmly rejected any plans to lay off large numbers of staff at the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), calling on donor countries to provide adequate and sustainable funding.

The committee said UNRWA staff formed the backbone of the agency and that laying them off would not resolve the financial crisis. Instead, it would threaten the continuation of education, healthcare, relief and social protection services provided to millions of Palestinian refugees.
It warned that cuts to these services would increase the humanitarian and social burden on refugee camps, threatening regional stability.

Frozen Russian assets key to covering Ukraine's 2027 financing needs – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:13:04 EET
20:13:04 KST

The issue of immobilized Russian assets is being discussed in the context of the need to find confirmed sources of financing to cover the "gap" in the state budget for 2027, which Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky estimated at $32.6 billion at the Ukraine Ministerial Roundtable on October 14 during the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"Currently, the IMF chief [Kristalina Georgieva] has confirmed the need for assurances from partners regarding coverage of this 'gap,' which has been verified by the IMF. The IMF is also considering, in this context, the use of immobilized assets in a way that European partners would consider acceptable to them, in order to ensure that Ukraine receives the necessary amount of financing," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings.
According to him, the IMF always discusses this issue very cautiously, recognizing that its mandate and influence are limited.
"But the IMF is involved in discussions on the format for accessing immobilized assets. For example, the Fund may recommend paying attention to a factor such as debt sustainability, so that the use of immobilized assets does not create additional interest-rate pressure for Ukraine. As for how exactly this will be structured, that will be determined by the European bureaucracy," the NBU governor explained.
He said he was optimistic about the possibility of continuing to use immobilized Russian assets to finance Ukraine and mentioned the evolution of the IMF's and the European Central Bank's positions on the issue.
"This issue requires complex, comprehensive communication on the part of the president, the government and the National Bank. You have seen how many meetings I have had here: over these past few days, I have held dozens of discussions with partners. This issue remains one of our priorities," Pyshnyy said.
As reported, in 2024, the G7 established the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) mechanism, providing Ukraine with $50 billion in unconditional, non-repayable financing based on discounting future cash flows from the further investment of Russian assets immobilized in Europe, primarily at Euroclear, totaling approximately EUR 200 billion. Most of the $50 billion is scheduled to be disbursed in 2025–2026, while only $1.4 billion is allocated for 2027.
In addition, after the idea of a EUR 140 billion reparations loan for the EU backed by the same proceeds from frozen Russian assets fell through in autumn 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan (USL), a EUR 90 billion mechanism for 2026–2027 to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine. This is also non-repayable assistance to Ukraine; however, the allocation of part of the funding for budget financing is tied to Kyiv's fulfillment of reform conditions.
The 2027 state budget currently provides for $52.6 billion in external financing, of which only approximately $20 billion comes from confirmed sources. In mid-October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, taking defense spending into account, estimated Ukraine's total additional financing needs for 2027 at EUR 70 billion while in Brussels.
As part of efforts to secure these funds, according to available information, consideration is being given to launching ERA-2 and/or USL-2 mechanisms by continuing to discount future cash flows from Russian Federation assets immobilized for a longer period or investing them in higher-yielding assets.

Trump officials back Orbán bid for UN secretary-general, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:11:58 UTC
20:11:58 KST

Trump administration officials are reportedly floating former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for UN secretary-general, potentially backed by the US, Russia and China, though nothing is confirmed and his selection remains uncertain.
Officials in the Trump administration are advocating the nomination of former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for the post of UN secretary-general, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.
The newspaper reports that Orbán could be a joint American, Russian and Chinese candidate, and that sources in all three countries have confirmed the Trump administration is backing his bid.
Orbán lost power in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar’s Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of governing with an absolute majority.
His hard-right, fiercely anti-migration and eurosceptic policies, together with the rule of law backsliding in Hungary, strained relations with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. Nevertheless, Orbán maintained close ties with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Since the election, Hungarian authorities have launched fraud and corruption investigations into several members of Orbán’s former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary’s National Bank are under arrest, and authorities could also examine Orbán’s potential involvement in those cases.
According to the WSJ, no final decision has been taken on the plan. A US State Department official admitted that the idea sounds crazy at first, but said previous talks with Washington suggest Russia and China also support it. The aim is for Orbán to be the joint candidate of the three countries.
“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper. The second five-year term of the current secretary-general, António Guterres, ends on 31 December.
The White House, and Beijing have not confirmed the information.
According to Russian deputy foreign minister Aleksandr Alimov, the US, China or Russia will not nominate Orbán, as permanent members of the UN's Security Council can not do so.
"Neither Russia, the United States, nor China will nominate Orbán because we are permanent members of the UN Security Council and we do not nominate anyone for the position of UN Secretary-General," Alimov told the Interfax news agency, adding that if press reports are true, those behind the idea need to find a nominating country.
"We will discuss all the people officially nominated for the post of Secretary General" Alimov noted.
Euronews has contacted Orbán’s spokesperson for comment but has not yet received a response. The spokesperson previously dismissed press reports about Orbán’s candidacy for the post of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.
In May, the VSquare investigative newsletter reported that a UN position could be important for the former prime minister because of the diplomatic immunity attached to the role.
According to the WSJ, Orbán would only run if his victory were assured, a scenario that currently seems unlikely.
A candidate must secure the support of at least nine of the 15 Security Council members, while any of the five permanent members can veto the nomination. Besides the US, Russia and China, France and the United Kingdom are also permanent members.
Two European governments have already spoken out against the idea of putting forward Orbán as a potential candidate.
"I do not foresee Poland supporting Viktor Orbán's candidacy for UN Secretary-General," Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said in a social media post.

Israel, but not in Palestine?

Argentina, 1896
In ‘The Jewish State’, Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, proposed Palestine and Argentina as possible locations for a Jewish state, citing Argentina’s fertile land and Palestine’s historical significance to Jews.
Cyprus, 1901–1902
Herzl and other Zionist leaders explored establishing a Jewish settlement in then British-controlled Cyprus, but the idea never became an approved proposal.
Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, 1902–1903
Herzl negotiated with British authorities to establish a settlement near El Arish. The plan depended on Nile water but failed to win Egyptian approval.
British East Africa, 1903
British Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain proposed territory in present-day Kenya. The Zionist Congress agreed to study the “Uganda Scheme”, but rejected it in 1905 after fierce divisions.
Angola, 1907–1913
The Jewish Territorialist Organisation, led by Israel Zangwill, explored alternatives to Palestine. Angola, then a Portuguese colony, was considered but the plan never materialised.
Palestine, 1947
UN Resolution 181 proposed dividing then British-ruled Palestine into Arab and Jewish states, with Jerusalem under international administration. Zionist leaders accepted the plan, while Palestinian Arab leaders and Arab states rejected it. Israel was declared a state in 1948.

Russia will not slow its offensive against Ukraine despite plans to resume US-brokered peace talks, but Moscow is open to localized humanitarian ceasefires, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday, Oct. 26.
Asked whether Russia would consider temporary truces along the front line, Peskov told reporters: “For humanitarian purposes, absolutely.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
His remarks come ahead of a localized ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region, intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The agreement, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, is scheduled to take effect on Oct. 29, according to the White House. Russian and Ukrainian officials are coordinating the operation.
However, Peskov made clear that the arrangement would not signal a broader halt to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations,” he said.
“Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial complex,” he added.
Oleshky сeasefire aims to evacuate civilians
Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city on the left bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, has faced a worsening humanitarian crisis, with residents reporting severe shortages of food, clean water, and medicine.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, the city had a population of about 24,000. The White House estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 people remain, including elderly residents and around 50 children.
It’s About Security, Stupid!
The temporary truce is intended to allow humanitarian supplies into the city and establish a safe passage for civilians who want to leave. Residents will be able to choose whether to evacuate to Ukrainian-controlled territory or Russia, according to the White House.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who led Kyiv’s negotiating team, confirmed the agreement and said the operation would be implemented in stages.
Melania Trump said she worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to coordinate the arrangement. Her involvement builds on previous efforts to reunite Ukrainian children separated from their families during Russia’s war.
Russia intensifies attacks as talks approach
The latest diplomatic push follows meetings between US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
The envoys had held consultations with Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo the previous day.
On Sunday, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US after Nov. 4, following Russia’s National Unity Day holiday.
“After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, according to Russian state media.
He cautioned against expecting an immediate breakthrough, describing the next round as an opportunity to explore the parties’ positions rather than reach a final agreement.
Working-level delegations could meet in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland to prepare for further discussions.
Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to bring the sides closer to a settlement. Moscow continues to demand additional Ukrainian territory and sweeping restrictions on Kyiv’s military and political independence.
Ukraine and its allies have rejected those demands as unacceptable, warning that concessions imposed under pressure could leave the country vulnerable to another Russian attack.

International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of parcels sent from outside the EU dropped by one-third in the last three months, mainly as a result of tighter EU restrictions, postal service PostNL said in its latest quarterly report.
The company said the 32% drop mainly reflected a drop in packages being sent from Asia after the bloc imposed a €3 surcharge per product on July 1.
It follows a 15% dip in the second quarter of the year and PostNL expects the trend to continue after the import fees are raised by a further €2 from next month.
The impact was partly offset by a 40% increase in parcels within the EU compared to the third quarter last year as Asian websites lost trade to European rivals because of result of the new measures.
But PostNL said that growth was “more than wiped out” by the drop in deliveries from further afield.
Three-day deliveries
The company’s turnover increased in the third quarter by €6 million to €768 million after the government relaxed the rules on deliveries.
Since July PostNL has been required to deliver letters within two days rather than 24 hours and the deadline is due to be stretched to three days next July.
CEO Pim Berendsen said the move to three-day deliveries was an important “interim step” towards ensuring the postal service could survive in the long term, but also renewed his calls for the government to compensate the company’s losses in recent years.
“Until we have a future-proofed regulatory framework, the uncertainty for thousands of our postal workers, customers and consumers will continue,” he said. “This situation requires a structural solution.”

In a statement, the company said the strikes targeted substations in Singa, Al-Hawata, Al-Faw, Mashkur and Al-Junaid in central and southeastern Sudan.
“The attacks caused significant damage to components of the facilities and completely cut electricity from the southeastern grid, affecting Sennar, Gedaref, White Nile and Gezira states,” said the statement cited by local media.
It warned that the damage also threatened the stability of Sudan’s national electricity grid.
“Engineering and technical teams were dispatched to the affected substations to assess the damage and begin repairs aimed at restoring electricity and stabilizing the grid as soon as possible,” it added.

About 90,000 properties still without power after two storms strike Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:09:13 UTC
20:09:13 KST

A major clean-up operation was under way on Monday after weekend storms caused havoc, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come.
Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms, Austen and Boelo, struck parts of the UK, and there was widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations.
The Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power on Monday morning. That figure was later down to 39,000.
The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread, with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend.
He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen,” he said.
Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northern Scotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc,” Slade said.
The weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way and issued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times. The Met Office advised people to take care near cliffs and be aware of strong waves.
The second warning will be in place from 3am to 9pm on Tuesday and covers most of Scotland. Forecasters said winds of 50-60mph were likely to be quite widespread, with gusts up to 70mph in the far north. It warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and more power cuts.
The weekend storms led to two deaths, authorities said. A 60-year-old man was hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway, while a man in his 20s died in Finchley, north London.
The 60-year-old was named on Monday afternoon as Richard Baines, the curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Port Logan.
David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, said Baines would be remembered for his “passion and enthusiasm for plants … significantly increasing and expanding the plant collection at Logan”.
There was flooding in several parts of Scotland, with dramatic footage from Largs showing flood water cascading through the town centre. One resident said it was the highest she had ever seen in 36 years of living there.
Staff at the Thai restaurant Tha-Tien-Thai shared a video of their kitchen overrun by water with the desperate caption: “There is nothing left.” They said its doors would be closed for the foreseeable future “due to larger flood restoration than originally planned”.
Robyn Cryans, an executive assistant from Renfrew, is on holiday in Cyprus and woke to see pictures taken by a neighbour of her Nissan Micra Sport submerged back at home.
“It is very upsetting, a bit stressful,” she said. “It was unexpected considering we’ve got a £10m flood barrier literally just down the road which is supposed to activate if the Clyde bursts its banks.”
She is scheduled to fly back on Tuesday and fully expects to find her flat damaged. “I’m obviously very upset about it, but at the end of the day it’s material objects. It could have been a lot worse.”
In Aberdeenshire, 13 primary schools without power were shut on Monday, and Ellon academy was closed because of storm damage. Ten primary schools were shut in the Highlands.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency teams and forecasters on Sunday to discuss the ongoing response to the weather.
Emergency services were called to a flooded care home in Saltcoats, North Ayrshire, on Sunday evening. Police Scotland said everyone at the care home was accounted for, road closures were in place and officers were expected to remain on site overnight to assist.
There was also travel disruption, with flights diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford, England’s highest airport, and others cancelled. Most train services were getting back to normal but operators advised customers to check before they travelled.
The storms brought a number of event cancellations including the Sunday racing at Aintree, abandoned because of the high winds. The Guardian’s live blog of the terrible tea-time Sunderland v Leeds goalless draw summed up the action: “And the winner is … the wind.”

Jordan arrests three suspects over church attack in dawn raid: What to know

Jordan arrests three suspects over church attack in dawn raid: What to know
Jordanian authorities have not named the individuals or any group involved in the ‘terrorist incident’.
Jordanians mourn victims of deadly church attack
Jordanian security forces have arrested and identified three suspects in connection with an attack on a Greek Orthodox church on Friday.
At a news conference on Monday, the country’s public security chief said the perpetrators represent only themselves and come from one family.
Nine people were killed and at least 34 others wounded in the rare attack in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate, about 120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman. Authorities said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”.
Here’s what we know about the suspects.
What do we know about the operation to arrest the suspects?
Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin al-Farrayeh said on Monday that all three suspects were Jordanians and “were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them”.
They were hiding in an abandoned house in the village of al-Jadeeda in Karak, the Public Security Directorate said, adding that they refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three suspects.
They “put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries”, al-Farrayeh said.
He added that many locations were raided in efforts to apprehend the suspects, and the scope of the search was expanded until the suspects were surrounded during the final operation.
Al-Farrayeh said that investigations into the attack are ongoing, and added that “everyone who has been part of this terrorist act will be taken to justice”. He also said that Jordan is “adamant that an attack like this doesn’t take place again”.
The Public Security Directorate said the suspects were injured, including one critically, during the dawn raid in Karak on Monday.
“Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their “just fate”.
Security forces recovered firearms and ammunition at the suspects’ hideout, the state news agency Petra reported.
A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the gun battle to arrest the suspects lasted about three hours in the village of al-Jadeeda, a six-minute drive from Hamoud, where the church attack happened.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II ordered security forces to respond with an “iron fist” to the unprecedented attack on the Christian minority community.
Have the suspects been named?
Yes. The Jordanian Public Security Director Major General Obaidullah al-Maaytah said at a news conference on Monday that the three suspects belong to the same family and include two brothers.
“They are the two brothers Hazza, the planner and mastermind, and Mishal Zeidan Muhammad, and their relative Ahmed Sami Hussein,” he said.
Interior Minister al-Farrayeh said there was no indication that the suspects arrested have ties with other cells.
What happened during the church attack?
St George’s Church, which was attacked, is located in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, known for its medieval-era castle.
Armed men stormed the church compound during a funeral procession on Friday, killing nine people and wounding at least 34 others.
Security camera footage of the attack circulated online. Video broadcast by Al-Mamlaka TV showed three people shooting outside the church and running towards its entrance.
Other footage showed the attackers opening fire on a group of men trying to flee outside the building.
What has been Jordan’s response to the attack?
“We have apprehended the killers, we are examining all the circumstances that lead young people towards extremism, and we will hold accountable everyone found to have been involved,” al-Farrayeh said in an X post on Monday.
He called for citizens to remain calm and said the tragedy would result in practical measures to protect civilians, urging Jordanians to reject violence.
King Abdullah, who met with the victims, said during a National Security Council meeting on Saturday, “The security and safety of Jordanians are a red line … the hand of justice will reach every terrorist.”
A day earlier, he had said the shooting would be met with the “harshest retaliation” possible.
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered three days of national mourning, beginning last Friday, with flags flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.
Who were the victims?
Eight of the people killed were laid to rest in Karak on Sunday in a funeral that drew a huge crowd.
Their coffins were draped with Jordanian flags as they were carried through the gathered mourners amid a large security presence.
Karak is home to a significant minority Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up between 2 and 3 percent of the population.
Social media showed images of the victims, including Mohammad al-Qasous, a Christian.

A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:06:08 UTC
20:06:08 KST

A 2,700-year-old solar eclipse just revealed something surprising about Earth
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Nagoya University
- Summary:
- A solar eclipse recorded more than 2,700 years ago is revealing surprising secrets about Earth's rotation and the Sun's ancient behavior. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the location of an ancient Chinese capital, scientists were able to reconstruct a total solar eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and obtain more accurate measurements of how fast Earth was spinning at the time.
- Share:
An international research team has revisited one of the oldest precisely dated records of a total solar eclipse, uncovering new details about how Earth's rotation has changed over thousands of years. By combining historical geography with modern astronomical calculations, the scientists reconstructed an eclipse that occurred in 709 BCE and determined how it would have appeared from Qufu, the ancient capital of China's Lu Duchy.
The researchers also examined an early account that may describe the solar corona, the Sun's faint outer atmosphere that becomes visible to the naked eye during a total solar eclipse. Their analysis of its possible shape suggests that the Sun was returning to a more active phase following an extended period of unusually low activity.
Published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, the findings provide more precise evidence of Earth's rotation speed in ancient times. They also offer potential independent support for previous reconstructions of solar activity based on radiocarbon measurements.
An Ancient Chinese Eclipse Record Holds a Crucial Clue
On July 17, 709 BCE, observers at the court of the Lu Duchy witnessed a total solar eclipse. The event was preserved in the "Spring and Autumn Annals," a historical chronicle compiled approximately 200 to 300 years later. The original account stated that "the Sun was totally eclipsed."
An additional description appears in the "Hanshu" (Book of Han), which preserves a passage written about seven centuries after the eclipse. This later account contains an unusual observation that may refer to the Sun's corona.
"What makes this record special isn't just its age, but also a later addendum in the 'Hanshu' (Book of Han) based on a quote written seven centuries after the eclipse. It describes the eclipsed Sun as 'completely yellow above and below.' This addendum has been traditionally associated with a record of a solar corona. If this is truly the case, it represents one of the earliest surviving written descriptions of the solar corona," explained lead author Hisashi Hayakawa, an assistant professor at Nagoya University's Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research and Institute for Advanced Research.
Initially, however, the historical account appeared to conflict with modern astronomy. When the team calculated the eclipse's path using existing estimates of Earth's ancient rotation, their results indicated that a total eclipse should not have been visible from the previously assumed location of the Lu court in Qufu.
The researchers traced the discrepancy to a mistake in the city's geographic coordinates. By examining archaeological excavation reports and historical geographic evidence, they determined that earlier calculations had placed ancient Qufu approximately eight kilometers from its actual location.
Correcting this relatively small error made it possible to reconstruct the eclipse more accurately and extract valuable information about Earth's rotation and the Sun's appearance.
"This correction allowed us to accurately measure the Earth's rotation during the total eclipse, calculate the orientation of the Sun's rotation axis, and simulate the corona's appearance," explained Hayakawa, who holds doctorates in solar physics and oriental history.
Why Ancient China Preserved Such Detailed Astronomical Records
The survival of this remarkable observation reflects the importance of astronomy in ancient Chinese society. Successive dynasties employed specialists to monitor celestial events because unusual phenomena in the sky were often interpreted as omens.
This practice, known as omenology, was closely connected to political beliefs. Eclipses, auroras, and other extraordinary astronomical events were sometimes considered warnings that an emperor had acted improperly.
As a result, court astronomers carefully documented changes in the sky. The records maintained across successive dynasties eventually became some of the world's most valuable historical sources for studying ancient eclipses.
Even so, the researchers emphasize an important distinction between the original eclipse observation and the later description of the corona.
The 709 BCE event is regarded as the earliest explicit written record of a total solar eclipse that can be securely dated. It may also be associated with one of the oldest surviving descriptions of the solar corona, but that interpretation remains uncertain because the relevant passage appears in a source written centuries after the event.
Although the corona account requires caution, the established timing of the eclipse provides a reliable basis for investigating Earth's historical rotation. The possible corona description also offers a valuable comparison with other studies of ancient solar activity.
How a 2,700-Year-Old Eclipse Reveals Earth's Faster Rotation
Earth does not rotate at a perfectly constant rate. Over long periods, its spin has gradually slowed, partly because of friction associated with ocean tides generated by the Moon's gravitational pull.
Consequently, Earth rotated slightly faster 2,700 years ago than it does today.
Using the revised position of ancient Qufu, the researchers obtained improved constraints on Earth's rotation during the period spanning the eighth through sixth centuries BCE.
Their calculations placed delta T (ΔT), a measurement used to describe variations in Earth's rotation relative to a uniform time scale, between 20,264 and 21,204 seconds for the eclipse of 709 BCE.
"This new dataset fixes coordinate errors in previous Earth rotation studies. Additionally, it improves the accuracy of dating and reconstructing historical astronomical events," said coauthor Mitsuru Sôma of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan.
These measurements help scientists better understand changes in the length of Earth's day over thousands of years. They can also improve calculations of when and where other ancient astronomical events would have been visible.
Evidence That the Sun Was Awakening From a Long Quiet Period
Beyond revealing Earth's rotational history, the eclipse may provide evidence of an important transition in the Sun's activity.
Scientists have previously reconstructed ancient solar cycles by studying radiocarbon preserved in tree rings. The possible corona description from 709 BCE offers another way to examine those findings.
"This unique historical addendum for the possible solar coronal structure is critical for providing a spot reference on solar activity reconstructions from tree rings and ice cores, as well as providing independent validation of solar activity models," explained coauthor Mathew Owens, a professor of space physics at the University of Reading.
Trees absorb carbon from the atmosphere during photosynthesis, including small amounts of radioactive carbon known as radiocarbon. Some of this material becomes locked into annual growth rings, creating a natural record that researchers can examine thousands of years later.
Radiocarbon levels are influenced by cosmic rays reaching Earth's atmosphere. When the Sun becomes more active, its magnetic influence generally reduces the number of cosmic rays that reach Earth, affecting radiocarbon production.
By measuring changes in radiocarbon concentrations across successive tree rings, scientists can reconstruct how solar activity varied long before modern instruments existed.
The Sun normally follows an activity cycle lasting approximately 11 years, during which the number of sunspots and the strength of solar magnetic activity rise and fall.
Occasionally, however, the Sun enters much longer periods of reduced activity called "grand minima." During these intervals, sunspots become exceptionally rare, and the usual cycle is much less pronounced.
One such interval, known as the "Neo Assyrian Grand Minimum" or "Homer Grand Minimum," lasted from approximately 808 to 717 BCE.
The eclipse of 709 BCE took place shortly after this prolonged quiet period ended.
According to the researchers, the possible description of the solar corona is consistent with a Sun that had resumed its regular activity cycles. Its apparent structure suggests substantial magnetic activity and indicates that the Sun may have been near the peak of its approximately 11-year cycle at the time.
This interpretation agrees with earlier solar activity reconstructions derived from radiocarbon measurements in tree rings, although the uncertainty surrounding the historical corona description means it cannot be considered definitive proof.
Ancient Astronomers Are Still Helping Scientists Understand the Universe
The findings demonstrate how observations preserved for thousands of years can continue to contribute to modern scientific discoveries.
By bringing together historical documents, archaeological evidence, geographic research, and sophisticated astronomical models, scientists can recover information that would otherwise be impossible to measure directly.
In this case, a correction of just eight kilometers helped transform an ancient eclipse record into a more precise source of information about Earth's rotation and a potential window into the Sun's distant past.
"Some of our ancestors were very skilled observers," noted coauthor Dr. Meng Jin of the Lockheed Martin Solar and Astrophysics Laboratory. "When we combine their careful records with modern computational methods and historical evidence, we can potentially find new information about our planet and our star from thousands of years ago."

Musk Fears Russia Could Target Starlink Satellites With Anti-Satellite Weapons

Musk Fears Russia Could Target Starlink Satellites With Anti-Satellite Weapons
Elon Musk has raised concerns that Russia could target Starlink satellites with anti-satellite weapons if the network is used to carry out offensive military strikes, warning that such attacks could generate dangerous debris and threaten other spacecraft in orbit.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a post on X on October 25, Musk argued that the possibility of retaliatory attacks is one of the main reasons Starlink should remain a civilian system rather than be directly involved in offensive military operations.
His comments came in response to a discussion about Russia’s ability to destroy satellites in orbit. The discussion referenced Moscow’s November 15, 2021, anti-satellite weapons test, during which a Russian Nudol missile destroyed a defunct Russian satellite in low Earth orbit.
Musk acknowledged that satellite communications can support military infrastructure but distinguished such activities from directly facilitating offensive strikes.
He warned that using Starlink for offensive operations could make its satellites targets for retaliatory attacks, potentially creating risks extending far beyond the immediate military consequences.
The destruction of satellites in orbit can produce thousands of fragments of space debris, threatening operational spacecraft and other satellites. Further collisions could generate additional debris, potentially triggering a chain reaction known as the Kessler syndrome.
Such a scenario could make parts of Earth’s orbit increasingly hazardous for satellite operations, affecting civilian communications, navigation, and other space-based services.
Musk’s latest remarks follow earlier statements opposing the use of Starlink to guide offensive drones intended to kill people. He previously alleged that Ukrainian forces had violated restrictions on the network’s use.
However, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president, disputed those allegations, explaining that technical limitations prevent commercial Starlink terminals from being used to conduct medium- and long-range drone strikes against targets inside Russia.
According to Beskrestnov, restrictions on terminal operating speeds and the absence of commercial Starlink coverage over Russian territory make such operations technically unfeasible.

PRESS REVIEW – Monday, October 26: Brazilian and international papers react to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's presidential election victory. Next: The New York Times warns that the war in Iran is entering a dangerous new phase. Also: cocaine consumption and cocaine-related crimes are surging across Britain. Finally, it turns out that wrapping children in cotton wool isn't the best parenting strategy.
Brazilian papers are reacting to Lula's tight re-election. "Following his victory, Lula says he will govern for all 215 million Brazilians," reports O Globo, explaining that it's a promise of reconciliation after a campaign that revealed a deeply divided country. In another article, the Rio-based paper reports a massive mobilisation in favour of Lula for the second round. The incumbent president secured more than 10 million additional votes compared with the first round. There was a fall in abstentions, and the number of blank and spoilt ballots reached their lowest levels ever recorded. Folha de São Paulo reports that after criticism, Lula is promising to "change" his way of governing. According to the newspaper, his re-election "confirms the status of the Workers' Party leader as Brazil's greatest popular leader of this century". But the paper says it is important "that arrogance does not prevent him from acknowledging the mistakes that nearly cost him the victory" – for example, the fact that "he resorted to a flagrant misuse of the state apparatus", according to the paper.
International papers are also reacting to the Brazilian election. The Washington Post writes that Lula's win is "halting Latin America's rightward shift" and keeping "Latin America's largest democracy from joining" that regional shift. Lula secured his re-election by campaigning against democratic backsliding and the erosion of civil rights. But after his inauguration, he'll be confronted by a right-wing Congress and more conservative governors. Spanish paper El País writes that "Lula wins, but the Brazil that made him invincible no longer exists". For the paper, this fourth term "paves the way for a leadership transition within the Brazilian left" and "forces it to respond to a sense of discontent".
Next, an article in The New York Times says that the war in Iran is entering a dangerous phase. The headline reads: "A new level of threat and fear risks pushing the US and Iran back to full war". The paper says that many factors are creating heightened levels of tension and risk – for example, the upcoming elections in the US and Israel, combined with US intelligence that Iran is planning to attack Americans. This situation is pushing all sides to seek a pretext for action. Experts who spoke to the paper are warning that this is exactly how countries can escalate into full-scale war.
Elsewhere, cocaine use in England is on the rise and so are cocaine-linked crimes. The Guardian looks into an analysis of wastewater in England that suggests that people there took around 2.5 billion lines of cocaine in one year. As consumption goes up, so are the crimes linked to it, such as assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving. The Guardian says that this rise can be explained by the historically low cost of cocaine – pushed by overproduction and high demand – combined with high purity levels. The drug is not considered middle class anymore, another article says. It has conquered pubs, festivals and even the workplace, as many turn it into an everyday habit. It's a "crime largely hidden in plain sight", the paper says, and many people don't even consider it a crime.
Finally, research suggests that giving kids more freedom and letting them do "risky play" is good for their physical and mental health, as The Times reports.

Japan’s Fighter Jet Scrambles Against Russian Aircraft Nearly Triple Over Past Six Months
Japan scrambled fighter jets 152 times in response to Russian military aircraft during the first six months of its 2026 fiscal year, more than 2.5 times the 59 interceptions recorded throughout 2025. The increased activity involved Russian Su-35 fighters, Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft, Tu-142 maritime patrol planes, and nuclear-capable Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 24, citing USNI News, Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force conducted 442 interception missions between April 1 and September 30, 2026, in response to Russian and Chinese military aviation operating near Japanese territory.
Chinese aircraft accounted for another 285 Japanese fighter scrambles during the same period, compared with 198 throughout 2025. Together, the figures indicate a substantial increase in military aviation activity around Japan.
Russian military aviation has operated both independently and alongside Chinese forces. Joint patrols have involved Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers and Chinese H-6 bombers, while separate Russian missions have included Il-20 electronic intelligence aircraft and Tu-95 bombers accompanied by Su-35 fighters.
On June 27, two Russian Tu-95 bombers, two Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft, and a Su-35 fighter joined Chinese military aircraft for a long-range flight across the region. Another Russian Tu-95 and Su-35 were documented flying over the Sea of Japan on July 21, according to USNI News.
Much of Russia’s military aviation activity has been concentrated around Hokkaido and northern Honshu, particularly over the Sea of Japan and the Pacific Ocean.
Japan’s Northern Air Defense Command, responsible for monitoring the country’s northern approaches, recorded 112 fighter scrambles during the six-month period, compared with 53 over the same period in 2025.
Defense Express assessed that the flights may serve as a demonstration of Moscow’s military cooperation with Beijing while increasing pressure on Japan. The activity is particularly significant because Russia continues to rely on Tu-95MS strategic bombers to launch long-range cruise missile attacks against Ukraine.
Japan warned in August that growing military cooperation between Russia, China, and North Korea posed increasing security risks. Tokyo also reported that joint Russian-Chinese bomber patrols had intensified, with recent flights heading toward the Japanese capital for the first time.

Lula wins presidential election in Brazil
Brazil's veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitterly fought campaign, beating his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro.

Key European defence ministers meet in Paris to discuss Ukraine support

European states pledge to boost air defence support for Ukraine
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK to discuss increasing military assistance to Ukraine.
Five major European countries have pledged to help strengthen Ukraine’s air defences as Russia intensifies its efforts to strike the country’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches.
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom met in Paris on Monday and promised to boost political, military and financial support for Kyiv.
In a joint statement, the group, known as the E5, also backed security guarantees to be provided by a coalition of Ukraine’s allies once a ceasefire or peace agreement is reached.
German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said the five countries have assembled winter aid packages and are working with Ukraine on building an air-defence system that will supplement existing defences, including United States-made Patriot missile systems, according to the dpa news agency.
Pistorius said the ministers would also try to ensure Washington continues providing military supplies, intelligence and satellite data.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting urged European allies to do more together, reiterating his country’s support for Ukraine “for as long as it takes”.
The ministers also committed to step up efforts to tackle Russia’s shadow fleet, a network of ships used to circumvent restrictions on its oil trade.
The pledge to provide Ukraine with additional air defence capabilities came as a United Nations-appointed commission of inquiry labelled Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as war crimes and crimes against humanity.
In findings released on Monday, it said Russian forces had deliberately struck facilities essential to civilians, with older people among those exposed to prolonged winter power and heating outages.
Russia has targeted Ukraine’s ability to operate heating for the civilian population since early in its war on its neighbour, which began with a full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Attacks across Ukraine and Russia
While Ukraine’s European allies were meeting, the results of Russia’s latest attacks were reported.
The Russian Ministry of Defence claimed its forces hit a power station in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, as well as a nearby warehouse, and a power station in the Khmelnytskyi region.
Port infrastructure in Chornomorsk in the southwest, and a cargo vessel en route to Odesa, which the ministry claimed was being used for military purposes, were also targeted.
A Russian strike on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured several people on Monday morning, according to regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin. A further two people were injured in the Chernihiv region, Ukraine’s emergency service said on Telegram.
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack on Voronezh in Russia killed two people and wounded 17, regional Governor Alexander Gusev said.
“A significant number of the injured, including two seriously wounded, were on a train that was moving in the left-bank suburb of Voronezh when debris from a UAV fell on it,” he said on Telegram.
The attack also caused fires at “a number of industrial businesses (without significant damage), a business centre in the central part of the city, and a residential building”, the governor added.
More than four and a half years into the war, attacks have been escalating between Ukrainian and Russian forces, with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries and Russian forces bombarding Ukraine with relentless air strikes.
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates in the first half of November.
In an interview aired on Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that for Kyiv to halt the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which US President Donald Trump has demanded, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure.
Zelenskyy said if the Russians continue to hit Ukraine’s power infrastructure, the US should be willing to allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect missile launch sites, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version, Starshield, were now fully functional after more than a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.

Vice speaker of Slovak Parliament opposes funding Ukraine with frozen Russian assets
Vice Speaker of the Slovak Parliament Tibor Gašpar has called the confiscation of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine's military needs unacceptable.
Source: European Pravda, citing Gašpar in an interview with the Russian agency TASS
Details: Gašpar said that regarding the issue of frozen Russian assets, Slovakia emphasises the need for a thorough legal assessment, caution and consideration of the long-term consequences of any decisions made.
Quote from Gašpar: "In November 2025, Prime Minister of the Slovak Republic Robert Fico expressed disagreement with the proposal to confiscate frozen Russian assets and use them to fund Ukraine's military needs. Such an approach towards confrontation and confiscation is unacceptable."
Details: As Gašpar recalled, Fico drew particular attention to possible litigation, the risk of retaliatory measures and the consequences of such a move for future peace negotiations.
Quote from Gašpar: "At the same time, he stressed that using these assets for the post-war reconstruction of Ukraine could be more appropriate than directing them towards the further funding of military operations. The Slovak Republic is interested in ensuring that any decision in this sphere has a clear legal basis, complies with international obligations and minimises the risk of further deterioration in international relations."
Details: Furthermore, according to Gašpar, it is necessary to seek sustainable solutions for financing Ukraine's reconstruction that will promote regional stability and create conditions for establishing long-term peace.
Background:
- Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever recently expressed confidence that the European Commission will not reopen discussions on using frozen Russian assets held in Euroclear to finance Ukraine.
- During the EU leaders' summit on 16 October, De Wever firmly opposed discussions on the idea of using frozen assets belonging to Russia's Central Bank.
- Meanwhile, Vsevolod Chentsov, Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration, proposed using Russian funds frozen in Europe for Ukraine's needs in phases – an idea that, in his view, could help shift Belgium's position.

Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:03:33 UTC
20:03:33 KST

Anthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.
The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a $1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.
“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said.
Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issued a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors. It then requested a token and gained access to the information.
The AI developer said it had since put in place guardrails to prevent similar actions happening again. The incident was first reported by the news website Axios.
Anthropic had pointed out the unauthorised behaviour earlier in the month when it said in a blogpost that it had found examples of Claude “working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee” and that some of these cases involved websites run by US government agencies. At the time, it said the incidents had “minimal real-world impact”.
The unintended actions flagged by Anthropic included a model submitting a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police department. The US state department also revealed this month that an Anthropic model had filed 19 visa applications in August.
Examples of unauthorised behaviour by AI agents – programs powered by AI models that carry out tasks autonomously – have been mounting since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, revealed in July that its bots had hacked an AI startup.
Since then, it has emerged that an OpenAI agent hacked the Australian healthcare system, and the UK’s AI security institute revealed that Anthropic agents had carried out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.
This month, the UK’s AI minister said he expected an AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the Australia hack, describing such an incident as likely, “if not inevitable”. Kanishka Narayan said the government would consider using the cyber security and resilience bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.
In the US, the White House’s newly formed Super Intelligence Force – a federal body overseeing AI development – is mandating that all AI companies report security incidents involving their technology.

Russia-Africa Media Forum kicks off in Moscow (PHOTOS/VIDEO)
