Russia-Africa Media Forum kicks off in Moscow (PHOTOS/VIDEO)
The Russia-Africa Media Forum has opened in Moscow, bringing together more than 200 participants from 46 African countries.
The gathering, which began on Monday, is being organized by RT in cooperation with the Sputnik and TASS news agencies. It brings together media executives, journalists, and experts from Russia and African countries. The four-day event will focus on media cooperation and the role of journalism in shaping Africa’s image abroad.
Speaking on the sidelines of the event, Sebastian Maganga, head of content at Tanzania’s Clouds Media Group, highlighted the importance of such gatherings, saying they allow media organizations to exchange stories and share their perspectives with international audiences.
“If you have forums similar to this, that’s when you get the opportunity to share our stories and get stories from Russia and other places respectively and package them,” he said.
The forum comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit, scheduled for October 28-29 in Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin will co-chair the plenary session on October 29 with Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the current chair of the African Union, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova.
Moscow will also host the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit on October 27, bringing energy diplomacy into the same week’s meetings. The gathering will address global market developments, energy security, and investment opportunities.
African leaders have begun arriving in Moscow ahead of the summit, including Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, and Mali’s transitional president, Assimi Goita. Ugandan Vice President Jessica Alupo has also arrived in the Russian capital, according to media reports.
Putin is also expected to hold bilateral talks with African leaders, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will meet his African counterparts on October 28. More than 2,000 guests are expected to attend the accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum, Zakharova said.
The economic forum will be held at Moscow’s Gostiny Dvor exhibition center. Its agenda covers trade, investment, energy, food security, digitalization, education, and technology.
The upcoming event follows two previous summits between Russian and African leaders. The first, held in Sochi in October 2019, attracted delegations from all 54 African countries, while the second, held in St. Petersburg in July 2023, brought together representatives from 48 African nations.

Parliament prolongs martial law and mobilisation for another 90 days
On Monday 26 October, the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian Parliament) voted in favour of bills introduced by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to prolong martial law and general mobilisation for another 90 days.
Source: broadcast of the Verkhovna Rada plenary session on 26 October
Details: A total of 293 MPs voted to prolong martial law, and 281 voted to extend mobilisation for another 90 days.
In addition, 280 MPs voted for the immediate signing of these bills by the chairman of the Verkhovna Rada and their submission to the president for his signature.
Currently, martial law and general mobilisation in Ukraine are in effect until 05:30 on 31 October 2026.
Zelenskyy proposed prolonging both periods for another 90 days, until 29 January 2027.
In December 2025, Zelenskyy stressed that the war with the Russian Federation will not end until Ukraine receives effective security guarantees and that martial law cannot be lifted until that point. When asked whether martial law could be lifted during a ceasefire, the president said:
Quote: "First of all, we all want the war to end, and only then will martial law be lifted – and that is the only way. Martial law will be lifted at the moment when Ukraine has security guarantees. Without security guarantees, this war will not truly end; we will not be able to recognise that it has ended, because there would remain a risk of renewed aggression from such a neighbour."
Background:
- Under previous decisions, martial law and mobilisation are in effect from 2 August to 31 October 2026.
- Martial law and general mobilisation have been in effect in Ukraine since 24 February 2022.

Kerr Kriisa plea deal caps US fraud sentence at 2 years, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Kerr Kriisa plea deal caps US fraud sentence at 2 years, lawyers say
Estonian basketball player Kerr Kriisa's court hearing in the United States is set for December 22, and his lawyers have been negotiating a plea deal for him.
Kriisa, 25, was arrested in the summer and charged with wire fraud stretching into the millions during his time playing US college basketball.
Under a plea agreement, the maximum sentence he can receive is two years, his Estonian lawyers told ERR — compared with the decades-long terms referred to when the case broke in July. Kriisa has admitted one count. If the court approves the deal, the remaining charges will fall away. His lawyers, Kati Reitsak and Tambet Toomela, say they are satisfied with the position and are working to bring him home to Estonia as soon as possible.
Kriisa was arrested in July and charged in connection with a fraud scheme that, according to the original indictment, defrauded victims of more than US$2.2 million. Under the agreement now before the court, the final sum will be determined by the judge. Kriisa has admitted guilt to a total of €9,000.
How is Kerr Kriisa doing at the moment? What is he doing — is he still involved in sport to some degree?
Toomela: Kerr is very much a sportsperson. He trains actively, both basketball and in the gym. He also plays basketball in an amateur league. The rest of the time he is actively working on his defense, together with us and our US colleagues. Generally the local population is very supportive, but of course this is not a pleasant experience for anyone. Kerr and we hope it will be over soon.
Kriisa was charged with five counts of internet fraud and has admitted one. Is this the only case currently pending against him in the US?
Reitsak: First, Kerr Kriisa has not been convicted of anything at this stage. To our knowledge, no other charges have been filed against him.
Please explain this agreement and how it came about.
Toomela: Some nuances need to be kept in mind here. In Estonia we are used to the state bringing charges and the person and their defense being taken through proceedings led by the prosecutor. But in America the system is built somewhat differently. From the moment a formal charge is filed, negotiations almost always begin. They are quite transactional: to summarize briefly what we and our American colleagues have been working on intensively for the last two or three months, it resembles transactional bargaining rather more than establishing what Kerr may have done or not done, the extent of the damage, and what penalty he should serve.
It has been a back-and-forth of several versions of an agreement with the prosecution, where we tried to put Kerr in the best possible position and the prosecution calculated its resources, its workload, and the need to safeguard justice as they saw it. We exchanged three or four versions and finally reached what could be called a balance point. If we were to give our own assessment, we are very satisfied with how we are positioned going into the December 22 hearing.
The initial estimates that went through the Estonian media — 20, 40, 60 years — were relevant in theory, but as a consequence of negotiations, we have reached a point where the maximum sentence the court can impose in December is now two years. That is the absolute maximum. Our work is very intensive now. We are certainly not aiming for two years; we are fighting for something else that would allow Kerr to come home. Again: it is a question of positioning, and we are satisfied with it.
Kriisa admitted one of the five counts but not the other four. What happens to those four? Is this now a plea deal that disposes of these?
Reitsak: Indeed, Kerr Kriisa has agreed to accept guilt on only one count, and it concerns a single request for €9,000. If the agreement reached is confirmed by the court, all the remaining allegations the prosecution may have had against Kerr fall away.
Why did you come down on the side of a plea agreement?
Reitsak: We have really had only one mandate from Kerr from the outset: to bring him home as quickly as possible. The aim is not to go to a foreign legal system demanding rights or justice. We have calculated our risks and opportunities quite precisely. As Tambet said, via negotiations, we tried to reach the point closest to our goal.
Will everything be finally settled on December 22?
Reitsak: It will likely be finally settled.
Two years is the maximum sentence and nothing more can come out of this agreement?
Toomela: No. It is the maximum, it is agreed, the court is bound by it, and Kerr will also have the right to speak at the hearing. The court will make the final decision based on all the materials, arguments and claims.
The figure that has been in the media is between $2 and $2.2 million. How large is the sum actually before the court, and will it have to be compensated in any case?
Reitsak: This is the peculiarity of the US system. Unlike in Estonia, the court has considerable discretion in such agreements. At present we can only say that the final sum will become clear in the judgment.
If Kriisa receives a real prison sentence, will it be served in Estonia or the US?
Toomela: First, let me say that our efforts are aimed at Kerr remaining at liberty. Naturally we want to bring him home, whether the sentence is custodial or suspended. There are international conventions to which Estonia and the US are party which allow for transfer regardless of the type of sentence. We are already examining these possibilities and, depending on the judgment, we will certainly try to bring him home.
Will that become clear on December 22 too?
Toomela: It may not become clear by December 22; it may become clear somewhat later, but in any case by sometime early next year.
Kriisa signed a contract with the Tartu basketball club before the season. Did he already know then that an investigation was underway against him, or was he not aware at that point?
Reitsak: It is known from public sources, visible to everyone, that in April 2026 a grand jury decided to charge Kerr. At that time he certainly did not know. He learned of it when he was arrested in July.
How often are you in contact with Kerr? What kind of advice does he receive from people in different fields — psychological, legal — as well as from family and friends?
Reitsak: We are in very close contact with Kerr, almost daily. Given the time difference between us, communication with both Kerr and his US representatives often happens late at night. In addition, Kerr actively attends meetings for gambling addiction treatment in various support groups and is doing everything possible to return to a normal way of life.
What does he himself think of all this? How has he put it to you?
Toomela: Kerr has deliberately opted to remain silent, to protect himself and his family, the people close to him. This is a difficult time. Kerr could have a lot to say. At some point he will open up; when that is, only he will decide. All things considered, his mood is positive, he is not despondent. He very much hopes to play basketball again and for that to happen as soon as possible. This turbulent time in his life has to be lived through. We hope the picture will be clear around Christmas, or at the start of the new year.
Reitsak: I would like to add, ultimately, that as far as we have spoken with Kerr Kriisa, it is clear that he is extremely grateful to those people who have stood by him through this crisis.
Background:
Kriisa signed with Estonian side Tartu Ülikool Maks & Moorits in early July, days before his arrest in the US. The Tartu club said at the time it hoped he could resolve his issues in America. He has not played competitively since. Before heading back to Estonia he had been due to join La Familia, a Kentucky alumni team competing in the summer basketball tournament, but the deal was rescinded by the team following his arrest.
Kriisa's last US team was the Cincinnati Bearcats of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), and the charges dated back to his time playing for West Virginia University (2023–2024). Prior to that, Kriisa played three seasons with the University of Arizona, then went to the University of Kentucky Wildcats for the 2024–2025 season, before joining Cincinnati.
Estonian basketball player Kerr Kriisa's court hearing in the United States is set for December 22, and his lawyers have been negotiating a plea deal for him.

Congress will hold ‘vote bachao, desh bachao’ rally on Nov 1 in Delhi, while Amit Shah will attend the ‘loktantra bachao, arajakta hatao’ padayatra on Nov 2 in Telangana
NEW DELHI: The Congress will hold a ‘Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao’ mega rally at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi on November 1, party president Mallikarjun Kharge said on Monday. The protest comes over the alleged vote theft, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an immediate halt of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).Meanwhile, Union home minister Amit Shah is also set to attend a BJP foot march in Telangana a day later, on November 2, to counter what the party calls the Congress's “false narrative” against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao announced Shah's participation in the November 2 ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao’ (save democracy, remove anarchy) padayatra on Monday.The announcement comes amid a political row over the SIR exercise, with the Congress accusing the Election Commission of large-scale electoral irregularities.“They (Congress) are trying to create anarchy in the state and country. Kharge announces mega rally at Ramleela Maidan

Long live the Constitution! Jai Hind!” he added.
BJP challenges Congress over SIR claims
Rao accused the Congress of spreading misinformation about the electoral roll revision and challenged Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy to identify voters whose names had been wrongly deleted.Observing that Congress was spreading lies over the SIR exercise, Rao said he was ready to visit the chief minister's native village, Kondareddypalle, to check how many voters' names had been removed from the rolls.He said genuine voters whose names were deleted had the option of getting them included again. Rao also asked Congress ministers in Telangana to identify at least 10 voters whose names had been deleted and explain the reasons for their removal.Responding to allegations that 13 crore voters had been removed during the SIR exercise, Rao claimed that they fell into the categories of 'Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate' (ASDD).Of these, he claimed, 2.8 crore were dead, three crore were absent or untraceable when booth-level officers visited them, 6.3 crore had permanently shifted and nearly one crore names were registered at multiple locations. Pointing to the impact of El Nino on water availability in Hyderabad, he said around 8,000 water tankers were being booked daily in the city. He urged Revanth Reddy to focus on addressing the water crisis instead.On the chief minister's recent pitch for Rahul Gandhi to become Prime Minister, Rao said the BJP's graph had risen since Gandhi began occupying leadership positions in the Congress.Taking a swipe at the Congress leader, Rao said, "you cannot market a failed product".

Why Israel’s wartime election isn’t just about the battle with Iran and Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:54 UTC
20:01:54 KST

From army exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox to a stalled 7 October inquiry, the issues splitting voters have little to do with Gaza, Lebanon or Iran.
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday in the country’s first national election since Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack, a vote that is shaping up as a verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Yet for a country that has spent three years fighting on several fronts, the campaign has been strikingly quiet on how those wars were fought.
Israel’s conduct in Gaza, which led to an international arrest warrant for Netanyahu, has barely been debated. Nor have its occupation of much of southern Lebanon and parts of Syria, or the two wars it launched against Iran. All enjoy broad support among Jewish Israelis.
The main contenders have instead argued over Netanyahu himself: his character, his responsibility for the security failures of 7 October, military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men and his 2023 attempt to overhaul the judiciary.
There is also little to separate the two main blocs on the Palestinian question. Both are dominated by parties that back Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank and oppose a Palestinian state, and no leading candidate is calling for a revival of the peace process.
The shadow of 7 October
Reminders of the war are everywhere. Stickers bearing the faces of fallen soldiers line train stations, alongside fading yellow ribbons for the hostages, the last of whom came home under a ceasefire deal last year.
According to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), a Jerusalem-based think tank, around 68% of Jewish Israelis say their views on 7 October are central to how they will vote. Among Arab citizens, the figure is 32%, with most naming crime as their main concern.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has pointed to military gains against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran while placing blame for the 7 October failures on the security establishment.
His critics say he has dodged accountability by blocking an official state inquiry. They also accuse him of delaying a hostage deal and of failing to secure a decisive victory on any front.
Who serves in the army?
The issue that has stirred the most anger is conscription. Military service is compulsory for most Jewish Israelis, but Netanyahu’s coalitions have long depended on ultra-Orthodox parties that insist yeshiva students be exempt.
Resentment has grown as reservists have been called up repeatedly and the army struggles with a manpower shortage. Around 13,000 ultra-Orthodox men turn 18 each year, but fewer than one in ten enlist.
About a quarter of Jewish voters told the IDI the issue would weigh on their choice. IDI president Yohanan Plesner said it was “probably the number one issue” for the anti-Netanyahu camp.
The IDI’s Tamar Hermann said many Israelis see military service as a “kind of permit to citizenship”.
Netanyahu’s main challenger, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to end the de facto exemptions. Eisenkot, a centrist, lost his son and two nephews in the fighting in Gaza.
Judicial overhaul fades as an issue
The judicial overhaul brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets in 2023 and left Israel deeply divided when Hamas attacked. Netanyahu cast it as a check on unelected judges. Opponents saw a power grab by a leader under indictment on corruption charges, which he denies.
After 7 October, much of that protest movement turned its energy towards demanding the hostages’ release. Today, only 18% of Jewish Israelis say the overhaul will shape their vote, a sign of what Hermann described as “public fatigue”. It matters more on the left, where 22.5% cite it.
A law passed last year giving the government more say in judicial appointments will only take effect once the next Knesset is sworn in. The opposition bloc has promised to scrap it.
Coalition arithmetic
Israelis vote for party lists rather than individual candidates, and no party is expected to come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The next prime minister will be whoever can assemble a governing coalition. If no one can, Netanyahu will stay on as caretaker until yet another election.
More than a quarter of Jewish voters say the party leader is a decisive factor. Netanyahu’s backers see a seasoned statesman who has stood up to US presidents and refused concessions they believe would endanger Israel. His detractors see him as corrupt.
Eisenkot’s supporters cite his decades in uniform and his personal losses. The son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, he would become Israel’s first prime minister of non-European heritage, though he has not campaigned on it.
The missing economic debate
Living costs are a major concern but have barely featured. Research by Sarit Menahem-Carmi of Reichman University’s Aaron Institute for Economic Policy found that Israel is now more expensive than wealthy European countries such as Austria, Denmark and Sweden.
The IDI found 38% of Jewish Israelis rank the economy as their first or second priority, rising to 46% among Arab citizens. Netanyahu credits his policies with fuelling growth and a thriving tech sector, while opponents say many have been left behind.
None of the leading candidates has put the cost of the wars at the centre of their campaign. Joseph Zeira, an economics professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, warned that heavy military spending cannot be ignored. “The cost of the conflict is tremendous,” he said.

Kremlin Signals Desire to Maintain Ties With Serbia After Vučić Ousted by Student Movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:37 UTC
20:01:37 KST

The Kremlin said Monday that it wants to maintain and develop ties with Serbia despite the defeat of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling coalition in this weekend’s parliamentary elections, while noting that building those relations will require effort from both sides.
“We deeply value the contribution that Mr. Vučić has made to the development of our bilateral relations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters at a daily briefing.
“We know that he will remain on the political stage, and we hope that even in opposition, he will continue to contribute to advancing our ties,” Peskov added.
Vučić, who dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade as prime minister and then later as president, conceded defeat on Sunday night following a historic snap election. The vote pitted his ruling coalition against a student-led movement that had spent months protesting against his government.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
The defeat followed Vučić’s resignation as president in September, a risky political maneuver intended to allow him to reclaim the prime minister post. It also came after nearly two years of anti-government demonstrations triggered by the November 2024 roof collapse at the Novi Sad railway station, an accident that killed 16 people and sparked widespread outrage over state corruption.
During his tenure, Vučić balanced Serbia’s candidacy for EU membership with a refusal to join Western sanctions against Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. He had remained one of the few European leaders to maintain direct contact with the Kremlin and make official visits to Moscow.
Peskov said Monday that Moscow hopes the incoming government in Belgrade will work “constructively” to preserve bilateral relations since, in its view, doing so would bring “tangible benefits to Serbia itself.”
“For our part, we intend to continue doing everything possible to foster our relations with Belgrade. But as you know, it takes two to tango,” he said.
Jovo Bakić, a representative of the Student List, told the Kremlin-backed broadcaster RT Balkan that the incoming government would not impose sanctions on Moscow or abandon Russian gas supplies despite pressure from the European Union.
He argued that sanctions imposed by a country of Serbia’s size would change little but would send a negative signal symbolically.
“We respect Russia as a great power and as a historically important partner, and in many cases as a protector,” Bakić said. “There will be no changes on this issue.”
Reuters and AFP contributed reporting.

Poland eyes more cooperation with Germany in space, Polish minister says
WARSAW, Oct 26 - Poland sees a lot of room to deepen cooperation with Germany in the space sector, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said on Monday, underscoring the need to possess sovereign technology in order to bolster security in the face of external pressures.
• "We need to invest in technologies ... that are not available right now in Europe, but are absolutely critical for our joint security," Domanski said, naming the space industry, during a joint panel with Germany's Economy Minister Katherina Reiche.
• "Together with our German partners I see lots of room for cooperation, thanks to which we'll be more resilient from some external pressure that can appear one day," he said, answering a question on how Poland and Germany could respond to competition from China and the U.S. in global trade.
• Domanski said security started in space and questioned how countries could defend themselves not having their own satellites, without which they were "blind".
• Domanski also said that Poland had decided to double its investment in the space sector.
• "We believe it's not only a very efficient way of spending money – from each euro invested you get 6-7 euros back, but that's also about our security and resilience. And we see room for further cooperation with German counterparts," Domanski said. REUTERS

Gyurov Sweeps Sofia and Most of Europe as Yotova Dominates Bulgaria's Provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

Andrey Gyurov leads in Sofia and among Bulgarian voters across most of Europe, while presidential candidate Iliana Yotova dominates in most Bulgarian provinces and Kostadin Kostadinov tops the vote in Russia, according to Central Election Commission (CEC) results from Bulgaria’s October 25 presidential election.
With 98.99% of polling station protocols processed by Regional Election Commissions, the results show that Yotova and Gyurov will face each other in a runoff in a week, following low turnout in the first round.
Yotova and running mate Kiril Valchev lead in the provinces, except for the 16th Multi-Member Electoral District, which covers the municipality of Plovdiv, where Gyurov and Georgi Kandev are in first place. Support for the candidates varies considerably from one region to another.
Gyurov leads in all three electoral districts of Sofia-City, with a substantial advantage over Yotova. In the 23rd district, he received 88,681 votes against her 35,767, while in the 24th district he secured 52,493 compared with 24,764 for Yotova. All protocols in both districts have been processed.
In the 25th district, where 99.81% of protocols had been counted at the time of reporting, Gyurov was also ahead, with 37,762 votes to Yotova’s 28,273.
The contest was much closer in Varna, where Yotova received 33,199 votes and Gyurov 31,364. In Plovdiv Province, Yotova led with 22,073 votes against 13,184 for Gyurov. The result was reversed in the municipality of Plovdiv, where Gyurov won 30,306 votes and Yotova received 24,608.
Yotova recorded a much wider lead in several other provinces. In Haskovo, she won 20,039 votes, compared with 7,768 for Gyurov. In Kardzhali, her total was 9,896 against his 4,953, while in Vratsa she received 13,242 votes to Gyurov’s 5,835. In Pleven, Yotova secured 18,274 votes, compared with 9,414 for Gyurov.
In Yambol, Yotova led with 8,886 votes. The battle for second place between Gyurov, who received 3,934 votes, and Kostadinov, with 3,354, was separated by less than three percentage points.
Among Bulgarian voters abroad, Yotova led in Turkey, receiving 3,933 votes against Gyurov’s 1,893. Turnout there was exceptionally low: around 7,000 people voted, compared with more than 27,000 in the parliamentary election less than a year earlier.
Yotova also led in Moldova, where she received 402 votes to Gyurov’s 216. She came first in Kosovo, Albania and North Macedonia, and won in Montenegro, where fewer than 20 people voted. Gyurov, meanwhile, led in Serbia and Romania.
Across most of the rest of Europe, Gyurov held a strong advantage. In Germany, with 99.84% of polling station protocols processed, he received 6,376 votes, compared with 2,630 for Yotova. In Spain, he won 2,521 votes against her 1,903.
Gyurov, who was backed by PP-DB, also led in France, with 1,469 votes to Yotova’s 417, and in Italy, where he received 1,254 votes against 521. In the United Kingdom, Gyurov secured 5,178 votes, while Yotova received 2,771.
Russia was an exception to the broader European pattern, with Kostadin Kostadinov taking first place in a vote in which approximately 200 people participated.
In the United States, Gyurov won 3,207 votes, far ahead of Yotova’s 871. Kostadinov placed third with 647 votes. Gyurov also led in Canada, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, China, Japan, Singapore, Kuwait, New Zealand and Australia.
The overall overseas results showed Gyurov and Kandev in first place, with 36,681 votes, or 45.61%, followed by Yotova and Valchev with 18,402 votes, or 22.88%. Their difference was 18,279 votes, close to 23 percentage points.
Kostadinov and Petar Volgin ranked third among overseas voters, receiving 9,352 votes, or 11.63%. Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva followed with 5,220 votes, or 6.49%, while Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov received 3,015 votes, or 3.75%.
The CEC figures for the overseas vote were reported as of 8 a.m. on October 26, with 99.35% of protocols from polling stations abroad processed.

stefan sagmeister’s artworks turn global data into good news at la gaîté lyrique

stefan sagmeister’s artworks turn global data into good news at la gaîté lyrique
finally, something good reframes metrics across health, democracy, and equality, inviting visitors to look beyond prevalent cynicism and view our era through data-driven optimism.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
‘FINALLY, SOMETHING GOOD’ FRAMES HARD DATA TO DRIVE OPTIMISM
Thirteen years after ‘The Happy Show’, Stefan Sagmeister returns to Paris’ La Gaîté Lyrique with his solo exhibition, ‘Finally, Something Good’, on view through April 18, 2027. Arriving at a pivotal moment marked by global pandemics, environmental crises, and political instability, the showcase directly confronts the relentless stream of short-term negative news and algorithm-driven outrage. Stepping back to examine broad historical patterns, Sagmeister uses visual design to demonstrate that human progress becomes undeniable when viewed across extended timeframes.
His work draws on centuries of data from the United Nations, the World Bank, and global archives. The empirical evidence reveals a clear trend: across health, democracy, and equality, global conditions have improved dramatically over time. Converting these complex datasets into tangible visual experiences, the exhibition invites visitors to shift focus away from short-term headlines and consider our era with fresh eyes.
STEFAN SAGMEISTER AND LA GAÎTÉ LYRIQUE LINK BEAUTY WITH ACTION
A two-time Grammy Award winner, the designer has long bridged graphic design, fine art, and human philosophy through album covers, public installations, and research on happiness and beauty. Guided by the belief that design should either inform or delight, he asserts that pairing aesthetic beauty with empirical data makes abstract statistics emotionally resonant.
‘There’s something almost perverse about being an optimist right now—the culture has decided that pessimism is the serious position,’ Sagmeister reflects. ‘I embedded these facts into 18th-century paintings because I think beauty and evidence, rarely combined, are more devastatingly strong together than either is alone.’ Hosted within La Gaîté Lyrique as part of its Factory of Our Times project, the exhibition aligns with the institution’s mission to address urgent cultural, democratic, and climate challenges through creative activism.
MATERIAL SYNTHESIS TAKES OVER TWELVE CHAPTERS
Spanning eleven thematic chapters across every floor of La Gaîté Lyrique, spilling into hallways and infiltrating even the restrooms, where no visitor escapes data-driven optimism, the exhibition transforms the venue into an immersive spatial takeover designed for active reflection. Sagmeister overlays historical 18th- and 19th-century oil paintings with bold geometric color fields, visualizing long-term metrics across conflicts, nutrition, healthcare access, climate, migration, and happiness. The showcase offers an essential opportunity to step back from the often exhausting nature of daily news, reminding us that social and political movements do change society over time, even if progress feels slow and indirect.
Beyond two-dimensional canvases, complex indices like the Gini Index and carbon reduction strategies are translated into physical forms using arranged produce, 18th-century Alpine sculptures, and monumental dark figures. Combined with projections detailing centuries of unfulfilled apocalyptic predictions and an engagement program co-developed with makesense and Studio 13/16, the project turns statistical evidence into a compelling material presence. Paralleling this artistic approach, the initiative aligns directly with La Gaîté Lyrique’s daily commitment to empowering new creative talents, breaking down barriers between disciplines and audiences, and building transformative cultural perspectives across Europe.
project info:
name: Finally, Something Good
exhibitor: Stefan Sagmeister | @stefansagmeister
location: La Gaîté Lyrique, Paris
date: until April 18, 2027

‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:42 UTC
20:00:42 KST

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.
In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”
Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.
These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.
Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.
Inflation
The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.
In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.
That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.
The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.
It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.
Gas prices
In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.
Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.
Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.
Monthly job figures
The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.
Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.
S&P 500
Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.
Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.
While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.
Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.
Interest rates
Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.
For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.
When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.
Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.
For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.
Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”
Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”
Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.
The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.
Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.
“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.
When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.
Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”
US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.
Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.
US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.
Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.
Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.
His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.
Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.
Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.
Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.
Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”
Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.
Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”
The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.
Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.
Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.
Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.
For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.
Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off? | Emma Beddington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:39 UTC
20:00:39 KST

Clips of the “epic conversation” (rambling, blokey chat) Rolling Stone orchestrated between Harry Styles and Thom Yorke keep appearing online, and none more often than the one in which Styles declared his laptop has been dead for about six years. “I don’t know where the charger is,” Styles laughed, prompting a predictable rash of “his computer is NOT OK” jokes from 6 Music dads everywhere.
Is this charmingly relatable, or … not? One personal finance influencer declared it “a deeply unlikeable clip”, seeing it as the kind of tech-free flex you can get away with only if you are rich and famous. It’s true that the ability to protect your peace by withdrawing from the brain-liquefying churn of online life is a privilege inaccessible to most people, who need tech to function and earn a living. Opting out means delegating digital drudgery to other people: Christopher Nolan’s determination not to have email must be a massive pain for his entourage. I bet Ed Sheeran not having a smartphone is extremely inconvenient, too – someone else must always have to put the hotel into Google Maps, arrange the Deliveroo dinner and order the Uber.
This dead laptop business does feel slightly disingenuous – Styles could have an entire Apple store delivered if he fancies a tech upgrade. But I’m inclined to feel more tolerant. He says he uses his phone to write songs, and maybe there is an element of overwhelm at play? I’m always losing cables and procrastinating over tech issues. “I don’t understand why you’re waiting for it to die when you’ll really be in trouble,” my husband said crossly to me this morning as I fought to turn off my ancient phone, which had decided once again that typing was forbidden. But I’m filled with dread and confusion at the thought of replacing it (what model, how many GBs, must I engage with the Cloud?) and my life isn’t too busy or demanding; I can’t imagine what it’s like when you are a global icon on a world tour.
So, in case he is floundering not flexing – Harry, check your sock drawer. That’s where I found my charger last time I lost it.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Political endorsements by scientific journals reduce public trust in research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:38 UTC
20:00:38 KST

When scientific journals publicly endorse political candidates, they risk lowering public trust in the scientific community, particularly among moderate and conservative Americans. These endorsements cause measurable declines in how people view the impartiality and societal value of science, though they do not appear to change whether people are willing to follow practical scientific advice. The findings were recently published in the journal Group Processes & Intergroup Relations.
Public trust in scientific institutions is an important factor in shaping how society responds to global challenges like pandemics and climate change. Historically, scientific organizations have sought to maintain an apolitical stance to preserve their reputation as objective arbiters of fact. In recent years, several high-profile scientific journals have broken from this precedent. Editors at these publications have published pieces endorsing Democratic presidential candidates or strongly criticizing Republican candidates, often framing these stances as necessary defenses of scientific integrity. Researchers wanted to understand how these explicit political stances affect how the American public views the scientific enterprise as a whole.
Stylianos Syropoulos, Kyle Fiore Law, and their colleagues set out to examine this phenomenon through the psychological framework of motivated reasoning. Motivated reasoning is the human tendency to process information in a way that confirms existing beliefs and political identities. When individuals encounter statements that conflict with their political views, they often scrutinize or reject the source of that information.
The research team suspected that political endorsements from scientific journals might trigger this psychological mechanism. They hypothesized that people who identify as moderate or conservative might question the objectivity of science after reading endorsements that clash with their political leanings.
To capture a complete picture, the researchers evaluated trust not as a single concept, but as a collection of distinct dimensions. These dimensions include perceived ability, which is the competence of scientists to provide accurate information. They also looked at integrity, which involves the belief that science is impartial and objective. Benevolence measures the perception that science serves the public good and lacks hidden agendas. Finally, behavioral trust reflects whether people are actually willing to follow scientific recommendations in their daily lives, such as adhering to public health guidelines.
In the first experiment, conducted shortly before the 2020 presidential election, researchers recruited a large sample of 3,081 participants online. They randomly assigned these participants to read one of two types of texts regarding prominent scientific publications, such as Science, The Lancet, or Scientific American. The control group read a brief, neutral description of the journal’s history and mission formatted like a news wire article.
The treatment group read the same background information, but with an added excerpt from an actual editorial published by the journal that endorsed Joe Biden or criticized Donald Trump. Following the reading, participants answered a series of questions measuring their trust in science and their intentions to comply with health guidelines.
The researchers found that reading the political endorsements caused a measurable drop in general trust in scientific institutions. Participants in the treatment group were more likely to report that science lacks impartiality, pointing to a decline in perceived integrity. This effect was largely driven by politically moderate and conservative individuals, who exhibited lower trust after exposure to the endorsements.
Among conservatives, the treatment also increased belief in conspiracy theories about science and the origins of the coronavirus, indicating a drop in perceived benevolence. However, the endorsements did not yield a statistically significant effect on behavioral trust. Participants exposed to the political messaging remained just as willing to follow practical public health recommendations as those in the control group.
To see if these results would hold up under different conditions, the researchers conducted a second experiment days before the November 2020 election. They recruited a sample of 1,056 participants, matched to national demographic quotas for age, gender, and ethnicity. The experimental setup mirrored the first study, with participants randomly assigned to read either neutral background text or a political endorsement from a scientific journal.
The results replicated the core findings of the first experiment. Exposure to the political messaging reduced general trust in science and increased the belief that science is biased, again driven by moderate and conservative participants. In this iteration, the treatment group also reported a lower likelihood of using scientific sources for coronavirus updates, which suggests a decline in perceived scientific ability or competence.
Just as in the first study, the political endorsements had no statistically significant impact on people’s willingness to comply with practical safety guidelines. The messaging also did not alter belief in conspiracy theories for this specific group.
A third experiment took place four years later, surrounding the 2024 presidential election. The research team recruited a large sample of 2,144 participants to read material from Scientific American, Nature, or The Economist. The Economist was included because it frequently covers science and technology for a broad audience. As before, participants read either neutral background descriptions or actual published editorials endorsing Kamala Harris or criticizing Donald Trump.
Because the pandemic was no longer a central issue during this later study, the researchers removed questions about the coronavirus. They added new measures to evaluate general perceptions of scientific objectivity and societal usefulness.
The results from the 2024 election cycle aligned closely with the 2020 data. Reading the political endorsements decreased general trust in science and increased the belief that personal and political values govern scientific research. Participants in the treatment group also reported lower confidence in the idea that science is objective and useful for society. Once again, the declines in general trust and perceived integrity were most pronounced among moderate and conservative respondents.
The study relies entirely on real-world editorials that endorsed Democratic candidates or criticized Republican ones. Because the researchers used actual published materials to ensure their experiment mirrored reality, they did not test how left-leaning individuals might react to a major scientific journal endorsing a conservative candidate. It remains unknown if political liberals would exhibit the same motivated reasoning and subsequent loss of trust if faced with scientific endorsements that opposed their own political identities.
The researchers note that while explicit political endorsements carry reputational costs, complete silence from the scientific community on policy matters might also negatively affect public perception. Choosing not to address political rhetoric that directly targets scientific funding or spreads false information could be viewed as a failure to defend the scientific enterprise. Future research will need to explore how scientific organizations can correct falsehoods or advocate for evidence-based policies without appearing overly partisan. Finding the right balance will help institutions maintain their legitimacy across the entire political spectrum.
The study, “Presidential candidate endorsements by scientific journals decrease trust in science especially for moderate and conservative Americans,” was authored by Stylianos Syropoulos, Kyle Fiore Law, Crystal Li, Bernhard Leidner, and Kevin L. Young.

AI Colonies Are Coming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

Each new release of a frontier AI model, such as Anthropic’s Mythos or OpenAI’s Astra, brings a new wave of speculation over how much closer this takes us to artificial general intelligence (AGI) and how much further that lofty goal remains.
But what if we’re overlooking something more important than an individual model’s supposed IQ?
OpenAI recently announced that an internal model, claimed to be “significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra,” solved Navier-Stokes, one of a handful of legendary math problems each carrying a million-dollar bounty. While mathematicians unpack what this means for the profession, and investors unpack what it means for OpenAI’s upcoming IPO, to me the biggest takeaway is that capability emerges from the collective. Just as it does in nature.
OpenAI didn’t crack Navier-Stokes by pointing its internal model at the problem. It pointed a swarm of 10,000 AI bots at it. These agents were encouraged to explore different directions and communicate promising leads with each other.
Think of what a lone honeybee or termite can accomplish compared to a colony of them. What a single person can accomplish compared to a nation of them.
In biology, a bacterial colony is a group of identical cells derived from the same mother cell. This, I would argue, is the most suitable analogy for the collective of agents that solved Navier-Stokes. It is many from one. Or, to paraphrase Walt Whitman: an AI that contains multitudes.
While OpenAI deployed its AI colony to solve a math problem that no human or individual AI agent could, Google DeepMind recently set an AI colony loose on math problems for a different purpose. It wanted to see what behaviors would arise within the colony. What it found was remarkable.
One agent discovered a way to cheat, convincing the examination software that it had solved math problems when it hadn’t. Rather than resting content with this small victory, it messaged other agents, telling them how to cheat. Some agents joined the unscrupulous agent and formed a sub-colony of cheaters. Others resisted and even formed a sub-colony of whistleblowers trying to out the cheaters.
As a math professor, I thought it was hard enough to keep students from using AI to cheat on exams. Now we have to worry about the AIs themselves cheating on math exams!
Which brings us to perhaps the most striking example of AI hive intelligence: the Hugging Face hack. OpenAI’s agents broke out of a sandbox environment and hacked into another company. Arguably, it was a felony offense—or rather, it would have been if a human were in charge. OpenAI’s agents coordinated their behavior in ingenious ways, including writing secret messages in a file system so that even when one AI colony was erased, a future colony could pick up the hack where the previous one left off.
Researchers have long known that complex behavior can emerge from simple computer systems. For instance, in 1970 the mathematician John Conway introduced the Game of Life, where an elementary set of rules governing the movement of pixels on a screen leads to remarkably rich ecosystems.
With today’s AI agents, we are going far beyond this by letting extremely sophisticated entities interact in sophisticated ways—using language, often hidden and coded.
This is why we must adopt a new mindset regarding AI capability. Testing a new AI model to see what it can do and how dangerous it might be by directly prompting it is like deciding how safe it would be to stick your head in a wasp nest by letting a single insect sting you.
Some developers and red-team activities do focus on AI colonies. The Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI trying to evaluate the cybersecurity capabilities of an AI colony. But the AI arms race between the U.S. and China, and between the competing companies within each country, has dangerously pushed our attention to what each individual model can do.
One model might top the leaderboards, but a thousand weaker models could wreak far more havoc. As calls to pace the frontier abound, let us not lose sight of the fact that the AI frontier isn’t what each model can do in isolation—it is what a colony of them can accomplish together.
