Israel's Choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

The Israeli settlement of Neve Daniel sits south of Jerusalem, atop one of the highest ridges in the West Bank, nearly 1,000 meters above sea level. The view to the east stretches to the mountains of Jordan, and to the west across the Mediterranean coastal plain—where most Israelis live. But the tranquility of the landscape belies the political fervor animating the Oct. 27 election, a contest with stakes as great as any in the 78-year history of the world’s only Jewish state. When I ask three residents what will ultimately determine their votes, one responds with particular ferocity.
“Seven hundred trucks were delivered to Hamas today by Israel,” says Barak Moore, who has lived in Neve Daniel for 14 years. He’s referring to commercial goods and international aid entering the Gaza Strip. “We’re paying a terrorist organization that committed the greatest atrocity against the Jewish people since Auschwitz.”
While much of the world has come to define Israel by its military actions in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, Moore’s views reflect the passions coursing through a society still traumatized by that day. Israelis tend to be less preoccupied by the nearly 75,000 Palestinian fatalities in Gaza since the war began, than by the 1,200 people killed in Israel and 251 hostages taken by Hamas—the women subjected to sexual violence, the children shot at point-blank range, the families burned alive in their homes. In a country so small and intimately connected, scarcely anyone was untouched by events that shattered the assumptions of a people whose nation was founded to give Jews a safe haven in their ancestral homeland.
Both the Hamas massacre and the wars that followed loom over a vote shaping up not only as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, but also the nature of the country that, as Israel’s longest serving prime minister, he has done so much to shape.
Arrayed against Netanyahu is a fractured field of challengers. There is Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief whose reputation for honesty, sobriety, and competence contrasts with Netanyahu’s polarizing leadership; Naftali Bennett, the right-wing former prime minister seeking a comeback; Yair Lapid, the centrist former premier who has spent years trying to dislodge Netanyahu; and Avigdor Lieberman, the hawkish secular nationalist who has become one of Netanyahu’s fiercest adversaries.
Also on the ballot: Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, far-right extremists whose parties made possible Netanyahu’s current coalition, and whose ambitions to annex the West Bank and resettle Gaza constrain his room to maneuver while damaging Israel’s standing abroad. The next government will either push Israel further down the path of religious nationalism, permanent conflict, and international isolation—or toward a new generation of leadership.
According to the polls, Netanyahu’s strongest challenger is Eisenkot, a soft-spoken, heavyset career soldier running as a centrist. His son, Gal, was killed fighting Hamas in Gaza, and one of his nephews also died in the war. Eisenkot is campaigning on a promise to restore public trust in government, rebuild Israel’s security, and heal the divisions that have fractured the country. “This election is about the identity of Israel,” Eisenkot told TIME in an interview on Oct. 20. “What will be Israel two weeks from now, 10 years from now, 20 years from now? This is the main question.”
Three years after Netanyahu’s political obituary was being written, pre-election polls show him running in a dead heat. On the eve of the vote, the nation is suffused with a sense of uncertainty; political analysts say almost anything can happen. Netanyahu and Eisenkot could form a unity government. Netanyahu could cobble together another right-wing coalition, dragging Israel further right. Eisenkot could join forces with Bennett, Lapid, and the Arab parties (20% of Israeli citizens are Palestinian) to oust Netanyahu, producing the closest thing Israel could muster to a center-left government. Or perhaps no bloc will manage to pull together the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority, plunging Israel into another round of elections and a reprise of the paralysis that produced five contests between 2019 and 2022.
“The most probable scenarios currently are either there will be some sort of unity government, which again is very complicated politically because all of the opposition parties swear they don’t want it under Netanyahu, and I don’t see how Netanyahu is going to sit under them,” says Nimrod Nor, an expert on Israeli politics at Hebrew University. “The other is we’re going to have another election after this one.”
According to two sources familiar with Netanyahu’s thinking, he would prefer to form a unity government with Eisenkot. One reason is legacy. He believes such an alliance offers his best chance to transcend the worst security failure in the nation’s history, and to be remembered not only as the leader who emerged from the slaughter of Oct. 7 to decimate Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon and persuade an American president to wage war against Iran, but also as the statesman who helped to reconcile a divided nation.
The other reason, the sources say, is personal. Netanyahu has little desire to form another right-wing coalition that would leave him beholden to the radical and uncompromising parties led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, both of which he brought into government four years ago to reclaim power. “He thought that he could control Ben-Gvir,” one Netanyahu aide says. “Now he knows that he can’t.”
That is precisely what the Israeli right fears he’s thinking, and what brought me to Neve Daniel. The settlement of capacious red-tiled homes is just across the Green Line that defined Israel’s borders before the Six-Day War of 1967. It was built on land that was a Jewish farm even before Israel was founded in the crucible of the 1948 war. Settler violence against Palestinians has risen sharply during Netanyahu’s tenure, but the militant settlers who make headlines by terrorizing their Palestinian neighbors tend to live on hilltops deeper into the West Bank than this.
But few, if any, of the 700,000 Israelis who live in settlements are leftist. Many regard Netanyahu as a cynical opportunist—a political chameleon who parrots their convictions but will do whatever it takes to survive. Among his many heresies, they say, is a long history of accommodating American presidents: signing the Wye River Memorandum under Bill Clinton to advance the Oslo peace process that aimed to create a Palestinian state; voting for the disengagement from Gaza under Ariel Sharon and George W. Bush; endorsing, at least rhetorically, a two-state solution and imposing a moratorium on settlement construction under Barack Obama; and, under Donald Trump, accepting a ceasefire and hostage-exchange agreement to end the war in Gaza.
Three people in Neve Daniel offer a revealing glimpse of the forces pulling Netanyahu rightward. Each plans to vote for a different party, but they all share an overriding objective: a right-wing government with Netanyahu at its center, constrained by allies who will keep him from drifting toward the middle.
Barak Moore is supporting Zehut, a libertarian nationalist party founded in 2015, whose eclectic platform combines tax cuts, the dismantling of monopolies, and cannabis legalization with an uncompromising vision of Israeli sovereignty and the removal of Palestinians from Gaza. It is something of a right-wing hipster party, blending free-market economics with religious nationalism.
Avi Abelow, 52, an activist who runs the website Pulse of Israel, is voting for Netanyahu’s Likud Party. His complaint is not that the prime minister has gone too far in Gaza, but rather that he has not gone far enough, hamstrung by a security establishment and governing coalition insufficiently committed to the nationalist cause. “We should have conquered all of Gaza and made sure it’s Jewish again,” he says.
The youngest of the three, Hershey Kellner, is a 19-year-old Orthodox Jew who moved to Israel from New Jersey just months before Oct. 7. He is supporting Otzma Yehudit, the far-right party led by Ben-Gvir, whose confrontational politics and open contempt for established norms have made him a hero to some of Israel’s most fervent ideologues. Helner admires Ben-Gvir’s push to expand civilian gun ownership, permit Jewish prayer on the Temple Mount, and introduce the death penalty for terrorists.
To explain his thinking, Kellner invokes one of the most consequential decisions in recent Israeli history: the 2011 deal that freed the Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit in exchange for more than 1,000 Palestinian prisoners. Among them was Yahya Sinwar, who would go on to mastermind the Oct. 7 massacre. Helner believes that sparing Sinwar’s life was a catastrophic mistake. “If you hanged him or put a bullet in the back of his head, not sure how the world would be now,” he says, “but it would definitely be better.”
For three years, Israel has been a nation at war, not only with its enemies but with itself. The extraordinary solidarity that followed Oct. 7 has given way to recriminations and ideological divisions, intensified by the trauma of war, the anguish of the hostage crisis, the pain of deepening antisemitism worldwide, and the unresolved question of who bears responsibility for such a stunning security lapse. Though Israel rejects the charge, critics accuse the country of committing a genocide in Gaza, where the dead include both uncounted Hamas fighters and 20,000 children—and of countenancing a thuggish brand of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. On Oct. 16, masked settlers were filmed attacking Palestinians and European diplomats in the West Bank, and injuring a Washington Post photojournalist.
The fault lines run through nearly every aspect of Israeli life. Secular and religious. Liberals and nationalists. Those obliged to serve in the military and the ultra-Orthodox who are not. Those who believe Israel must reach an accommodation with the Palestinians and those who want permanent Israeli control over the West Bank and Gaza. And, not least, those who regard Netanyahu as the indispensable guarantor of Jewish security and those who see him as the principal threat to the country’s democratic character and reputation abroad.
The fear increasingly voiced across Israel’s political and cultural establishment is that another Netanyahu victory could push those divisions toward a societal rupture. After Netanyahu’s coalition moved in early 2023 to restrict the power of the Supreme Court, the prospect of another government dependent on religious and ultra-nationalist parties has raised the specter of an exodus of young Israelis, who see the country’s liberal and democratic traditions slipping away. In a recent survey by the Agam Institute, an Israeli research firm, and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, 59% of Israelis said they believe internal threats are greater than external ones, while 64% said they were considering leaving Israel, citing insecurity, living costs, and political instability. In a nation of roughly 10 million, even the departure of tens of thousands of highly educated citizens could have consequences far beyond their numbers, draining the country of the talent and investment on which its economic and military strength depends.
There is a deeper irony. Israel was founded as a refuge, a place where a people long subjected to persecution and exile could finally determine their own destiny. Some Israelis now contemplate leaving, not because they have lost faith in the necessity of a Jewish state, but because they fear the political direction of the state created to provide one.
For those contemplating a future abroad, there is an unsettling question: Where, exactly, would they go? Antisemitism has surged across much of the world, with 2025 marking the deadliest year for Jews in the diaspora in more than three decades, according to Tel Aviv University. Israel has become increasingly isolated, condemned in international forums, denounced in the streets of European capitals, and regarded by many critics as a pariah state. The result is a profound paradox: Israelis who fear for their country’s future wonder whether they would be any safer, or more welcome, anywhere else.
It is this siege mentality, the sense of a small nation standing alone against a hostile world, that Netanyahu is counting on to sustain his political survival. He has spent much of his career presenting himself as a leader hardened by history, experienced in diplomacy, and ruthless in the exercise of power. His message: Whatever Israelis think of him personally, whatever blame they assign him for Oct. 7, the world is too dangerous to entrust their security to anyone else.
The chasm between how Israelis see themselves and how much of the outside world sees them has rarely seemed wider. In the new documentary NAZA, Israeli filmmakers draw on the anonymous testimony of 24 soldiers and intelligence officers to expose what they describe as the military’s systematic use of artificial intelligence to identify Hamas targets in Gaza, even when commanders knew that bombing them would kill women and children. Inside Israel, meanwhile, the fifth season of Fauda, the country’s enormously popular television thriller, recreates the atrocities of Oct. 7 in harrowing detail, immersing viewers once again in the terror, grief, and vulnerability of that day.
One production focuses on the suffering Israel inflicted, the other on the suffering Israelis endured. Together, they illuminate the competing narratives of a war that has left Israel increasingly estranged from the world, and many Israelis feeling more besieged than ever. Indications from polls and analysts are that even after voters have their say, no one bloc will have mustered a legislative majority. At that point the leading vote-getter will have weeks to try to gather a coalition, a test of the kind of political leadership at which Netanyahu has long excelled.
For nearly three decades, Netanyahu has been the dominant figure in Israeli public life, his political fortunes rising and falling with the country’s anxieties and ambitions. He has survived scandals, indictments, electoral defeats, and repeated attempts to engineer his ouster. The question is whether a political system he has spent so long mastering can produce a future that no longer revolves around him.
In a country not yet 80 years old, many are ready to chart a new era. “I think that Eisenkot is the one,” says Livna Savir, 72, at a rally for the challenger on a basketball court in Kibbutz Netzer Sereni, outside of Tel Aviv. “It’s a change of direction.” With her children living in the U.S., she laments the impacts of the last three years on a once unified group: “What happened now in our country—it’s not good for the family.”

World Philosophy Day this year is Thursday, November 19th, 2026.
World Philosophy Day, created by the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), celebrates “the enduring value of philosophy for the development of human thought, for each culture and for each individual.”
UNESCO’s theme for this year’s World Philosophy Day is “How can we coexist in a world in crises?”, with emphasis on issues related to migration, climate, artificial intelligence, and health.
Some philosophy departments take advantage of the day to promote philosophy, present interactive programs, or put on philosophy events (see the comments on this previous post, for example).
Is your department planning something to mark the day? If so, let us know about it in the comments—it’s not too late to provide inspiration for other departments looking for ideas.

In Maine, a Toss-Up Senate Race Is About the Incumbent and Not Much Else
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Susan Collins had just laid out her receipts.
The five-term Republican senator was standing on a debate stage in Portland earlier this month, explaining how she deserved credit for ensuring concrete and road salt were exempted from President Trump’s Canadian import levies. The move saved one small town in northern Maine $10,000, Collins said. It helped a concrete business owner avoid a $150,000 hike.
It was an updated version of the same argument Collins has been making for decades to win re-election in a state that hasn’t backed a Republican President since George H. W. Bush.
When it was her opponent’s turn to respond, Troy Jackson shrugged. What about everything else going up in price, he asked her, before adding, “We can’t eat road salt.”
For Jackson, the comeback was a hit. It sparked “let them eat road salt” memes of Collins depicted as Marie Antoinette and assuaged some fears among Democrats about how the last-minute replacement candidate would fare in the spotlight. The viral moment also brought into focus the race’s defining issue: Collins herself. Amid a handful of Senate races that will decide which party controls the upper chamber for the last two years of the Trump era, the race in Maine has emerged as the one most decisively about voters’ view of the incumbent.
“He’s got a unique challenge because this race really isn’t about him,” says Emily Cain, a former Maine legislator and Democratic political strategist in the state. “This race is about Susan Collins and asking the people of Maine whether or not it's time for change. He just happens to be the alternative.”
Given the candidate they ended up with, some Democrats are thrilled with this dynamic. Jackson became the nominee after a tumultuous summer in which the state’s Democratic primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race int he wake of being accused of sexual assault, which Platner has denied. While Platner and Jackson have nearly identical progressive, populist policy platforms, there’s a clear contrast between them in style. Platner is a charismatic, at times gripping, campaigner. Jackson is not. His speeches tend to be more subdued and matter of fact, and he often wears an expression of utter boredom despite being at the center of one of the highest-stakes contests in the country. His affect matches his typical attire on the trail—a Red Sox cap, a fleece vest, his cell phone on a belt clip.
“Troy’s a salt of the earth guy. His biggest strength is his authenticity,” says Toby McGrath, who ran President Barack Obama’s campaign in Maine in 2008 and 2012.
With polls showing Jackson ahead but within the margin of error, both sides have sharpened their attacks. Jackson has repeatedly highlighted a recent report that the FBI and Justice Department had previously sought to open a pay-to-play bribery probe into Collins, allegations, which she denied. And a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans released an ad calling Jackson a “freak” and a “creep” over his relationship with his second cousin, with whom he has two sons. Last week, Collins distanced herself from the ad and called for it to be taken down.
Yet it’s unclear if any of that is breaking through with voters in a race that could ultimately come down to how Collins ensures Maine isn’t forgotten by Washington. On the stump, she warns voters all that could all disappear if Jackson replaces her.
"He'll be 100 in seniority,” she told Fox News digital earlier this month, “And all of that essential federal funding targeted for the state of Maine, virtually all of it will go away."
Collins’ hold on Maine
For years, Collins has been the immovable stateswoman. She is both Maine’s longest-serving member of Congress and the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history. Astoundingly, she’s never missed a roll-call vote since taking office in 1997.
A self-described centrist, she has cultivated a deep connection with Maine’s independent-minded electorate. In 2020, she was reelected by 9 points as Joe Biden carried the state by the same margin.
Collins, 73, has increasingly found herself on the defensive over years of controversial votes, including those confirming Trump cabinet members like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She also cast votes elevating Justices Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. Her 2018 vote on Kavanaugh, in which she said she trusted he wouldn’t endanger the right to abortion access, became a flashpoint after the court overturned Roe v. Wade in in 2022. (Collins is also the only Republican senator to vote for all three Democratic-appointed justices currently on the court.)
Most towns in Maine have felt the benefit of Collins’ role as chair of the powerful Appropriations Committee, with which she has steered funding for community centers, railroad improvement projects and shipyards. Her campaign puts the total at $1.5 billion in congressionally directed spending and targeted investments since 2021.
“Even Democrats acknowledge her work to bring funding and support back to the state is just off the charts,” says Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. “So people are going to have to make a decision, ‘Do I hate Trump more than I appreciate and need the support Susan Collins has brought to the state over the years?’”
That argument faces more pushback this year given wider dissatisfaction with Republicans and the state of the economy. Jackson has capitalized on those economic anxieties. One of his final ads references high heating oil costs. It’s hitting airwaves just as residents fill their tanks for winter in the nation’s fourth-coldest state. He repeatedly points to Collins' votes related to the conflict in Iran for driving up fuel costs and her vote to advance the Big, Beautiful Bill, a major Republican budget and tax package, for slashing Medicaid in the state.
Last month introduced another chink in Collins’ armor, as a ProPublica investigation revealed that FBI and Justice Department agents sought to open a pay-to-play bribery probe into Collins related to allegations she’d rewarded a campaign donor with millions of dollars in federal naval defense contracts. Collins has denied the allegations, and no charges were ever filed against her or her campaign.
Several Republican and Democratic strategists told TIME they question how effective the corruption argument is landing in tight-knit Maine. “Susan goes to the grocery store, does her own shopping, doesn't live in a lavish house,” Dutson, the GOP strategist said. “People may disagree with her, but I think it’s a big stretch for almost everybody up here to get their head around her being corrupt.”
But the investigation cuts at the core of Collins’ Maine-first brand, McGrath argued, so even a small erosion of support could be the difference in a close race.
‘Troy is not a smooth talker’
As Jackson’s campaign keeps the spotlight on Collins, it’s kept its own candidate somewhat hidden away. Up until recently, Jackson had done very few on-camera interviews, and it was rare for him to take many unscreened questions at campaign events. Local and national campaign staff have feuded over how to showcase Jackson from the early days of the campaign, infighting detailed in an August New York magazine story.
“He has a nationalized campaign team, and these are folks who are generally only comfortable with smooth talkers, and Troy is not a smooth talker,” says a Maine Democrat who worked with Jackson in the state legislature. The Democrat, who supports Jackson, thinks there’s wisdom in trying to avoid gaffes that distract from Collins. Jackson has struggled at times to talk about foreign affairs or federal policy issues, like detailing how to pay for Medicare for All in a conversation with CNN’s Dana Bash in mid-October.
But other allies of Jackson say an overcautious campaign is impeding the Bernie Sanders progressive and stalwart labor champion from connecting with voters. “A lot of folks don’t know anything about him except that he’s a logger. He has a charming and funny side, and you don't get to see it,” says Betsy Sweet, an activist and political organizer who ran for U.S. Senate in 2020. “The D.C. folks are sure they know everything, and I feel like in so many of our national races they don’t listen to us and they screw it up.”
Jackson has a compelling working-class backstory. His mom was 16 when she had him in Aroostook County, on the rural northern tip of Maine. He grew up poor in Allagash, a frontier town near the Canadian border where he started logging at age 19, taking after his dad, his grandfather and his great-grandfather.
When Canadian loggers started crossing into Maine and taking work away from locals, he helped lead a blockade, driving his truck to the border to halt temporary workers from coming into the state. The protest made headlines but did little to change the situation, and a frustrated Jackson turned his attention to the state legislature. He first ran unsuccessfully as a Republican and eventually got elected in 2002 as an independent. He became a Democrat two years later and rose through the ranks to become Senate president.
Over decades in state politics, Jackson’s opinions on abortion and LGBTQ rights have evolved. Sweet, who lobbied for women’s groups, recalled pushing him to back abortion-rights legislation in the state. “I think it finally clicked for him after us telling him abortion is health care. It’s not whether women are gonna have one, it’s whether low-income women have the same access as rich women.”
His reputation for having a gruff demeanor, Sweet says, is accurate, but attack ads that portray him as antagonistic toward women go too far. “He will go toe to toe with you. He’s not genteel. You know where you stand with him, but you work it out.”
A shade of that temper came out in the final debate before the election. Jackson told Collins to “shut up” after she accused a protester of being one of his supporters. “It was a stupid thing for him to say,” the Democrat who worked with Jackson in the state legislature says of the debate moment. “Collins is known for her decorum, her civility. He’s courting 55- to 65-year-old women who are all about not being talked down to.”
Maine’s population is the oldest in America and the race will likely come down to older, moderate voters who have split their ticket in past elections. Collins' campaign has argued Jackson has run to the left of the electorate, drawing liberal figures like Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York to rally with him.
“That they are all campaigning in Maine for Troy Jackson tells voters exactly how he would govern,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said.
For all the debate about whether Jackson’s makeshift campaign has positioned him for victory, it will largely be Collins’ race to win or lose. A September CNN poll of voters backing Jackson found 29% said theirs was a vote for Jackson, while 71% said it was a vote against Collins. Her future in the Senate may not come down to Jackson at all but whether she gives voters enough confidence in what the next six years would look like.
“She’s got an amazing record in the past, but people need to hear from her what she’s gonna do in the future and what the game plan is,” Dutson, the GOP adviser, says. “They need to know, if we send Susan Collins back to Washington, how is that gonna help alleviate the anxiety this administration has been causing me right now?”

The Hottest New Side Hustle Is Stripping Copper Wire and Posting About It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

A woman wearing blue overalls and a pink tank top sits on a bench in a workshop lined with tools. Holding a broken copper wire in one hand and a small mechanical tool in the other, she looks at the camera and smiles. “Let’s make money stripping …” she says, pausing for effect. “Wire!”
This play on words is common in a specific corner of TikTok where users document the process of stripping copper wire in order to sell it for extra cash. Most of these creators don't appear to collaborate or use a common hashtag, and they haven’t coined a new term ending in -maxxing. But many of their videos have a similar, visually striking setup: A complex appliance is broken down into bits, or an industrial wire is split like ropes of licorice, and in the end, what’s left is a bundle of glistening amber.
The participants are diverse: Some are hobbyists or electricians looking for extra income. There are also people who claim to be saving for a big purchase, and others who appear to be cash-strapped teenagers. They speak a wide range of languages, including English, French, Spanish, German, and Romanian. At least one has an Etsy shop for selling hand-cast copper bricks, also known as ingots, which are made by pouring molten metal into molds.
Selling scrap copper is nothing new. The metal is relatively scarce, a strong electrical conductor, and fully recyclable—qualities that have made it a particularly valuable scrap metal for centuries. But copper prices reached an all-time high this year, making it an opportune moment for scrappers. In September, according to International Monetary Fund data, copper was worth about $14,473 per metric ton, or about $7.23 per pound, more than double what it was worth in September 2020.
While there’s no reliable data on how often people sell scrap copper, rates of copper theft—often involving metal taken from vehicles, plumbing, building roofs—may offer some clues. Craig Depken II, chair and professor of economics at the University of North Carolina, Charlotte, who has studied the phenomenon, says it tends to increase under two conditions.
The first is when the price of copper is increasing, much like it is now. The second is when people’s level of “economic distress” is high enough to make them believe the potential monetary benefits of stealing copper outweigh the risks of getting caught. (It’s legal to sell lawfully obtained copper everywhere in the US except Minnesota, which requires a state-issued license.)
On TikTok, it’s easy to find copper-themed accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers. On TikTok Shop, beginners can even buy their own wire stripper—the small tool that eats a cord and separates copper from its exoskeleton. The most popular option has sold more than 20,000 units globally at the time of writing.
Wire Transfers
The final price of recycled copper depends on a few factors, including its quality, grade, and whether it’s still “insulated” in plastic or rubber. Insulated copper can go for a fraction of the price of stripped copper, so many resellers remove it themselves to earn more. But even with a wire stripper, the process can be tedious. For some, sharing content about it appears to be a way to make the repetitive task more bearable.
People have posted about hosting a wire-stripping “girls night,” “movie night” and even “date night.” In one video from August, the creator @Payciencu.u strips wire on a bed near a man in a red sweatshirt. “How down bad are you?” reads the text overlay. “Well I’m stripping wire just to hang out with him sooo.”
Other creators treat copper scrapping as a full-on side hustle or hobby, posting time-lapses, tutorials, and lists of the “worst cables to strip for copper.”
Benjamin Stickle, a criminal justice professor at Middle Tennessee State University and author of the 2017 book Metal Scrappers and Thieves, identified three main types of legal scrappers: those trying to make ends meet, workers selling scrap metal they obtained on the job, and people raising money for a charitable cause.
Electricians, who are plentiful among wire-stripping TikTokkers, neatly fall into the worker category. Other creators are harder to classify, especially if they’re also earning money from TikTok itself.
The creator @Courtney2291, who did not respond to WIRED's inquiries, began documenting her efforts to strip enough copper to save $20,000 for a three-bedroom home earlier this year. She sourced wire and old machinery from family, her scrap yard, and Facebook Marketplace, stripping it almost daily. On October 10, a little over six months after she started, she announced she had reached her fundraising goal.
However, most of the money didn’t come from selling the copper itself. According to a scrap yard receipt Courtney shared, she earned just $99 selling 30 pounds of copper stripped over six months. One TikTok video, meanwhile, generated $1,446 after racking up 6.8 million views, according to an earnings screenshot she displayed in another video.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, Courtney says she plans to keep posting. “Once the house is mine, and it’s all set up and ready to be lived in, then I’ll continue pretty much the same kind of content,” she said. Her new goal will be to pay off the loan on the two acres of land where her home will sit.
Strip Tease
Other popular copper creators, including King of Copper and Queen of Copper take a different approach, emphasizing scale and spectacle over personal storytelling. Their videos show them buying crates and trunks with hundreds of pounds of old wire, and then, little by little, stripping every piece
Neither claims to be affiliated with the other, despite their similar names and videos, but they occasionally repost each other's content. Both have amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, though how much they earn from TikTok and YouTube is unclear.
King of Copper is currently more than 70 days into a self-described quest to obtain, strip, and sell 1 ton of copper. In early September, 44 days into his journey, he claimed to have collected 271 pounds.
In one recent video, King of Copper spent five hours stripping wire, melting the copper in a black furnace, and then pouring it into six-ingot molds, producing what he claimed was about $90 worth of metal. In another clip, he spent two hours meticulously dismantling a 110-pound air conditioner and extracted roughly 7 pounds of copper, which he valued at $47.
His videos are mesmerizing to watch, but it’s unknown how much he might earn from them, and King of Copper did not respond to inquiries from WIRED.
Strip Mall
Another way copper accounts can earn revenue is by marketing wire strippers and other goods for sale on TikTok Shop. When viewers purchase products through links in their videos, creators can earn a commission on each sale. Courtney, for instance, has advertised her own wire stripper. But many of these salespeople, like the creator @Dragonslayer_Industries, don’t speak much about copper outside of their ads.
“If you’ve got any scrap wire laying around, you need this wire stripper right here,” Dragonslayer Industries says in a January video before feeding a bright green wire through a machine linked for purchase. “This thing is basically just gonna print money for you. Probably pay for itself in the first hour you use it.”
“It's crazy, I only got this because my neighbor was stripping wire by hand,” he said in a June comment on one of his videos. “I got the free sample and thought l'd do 2 videos and give it to him. I thought it was such a niche thing that they probably wouldn't sell. It's been my biggest seller since l started doing affiliate videos. I can count on 5-10 of these a day selling.”
In May, he claimed to have helped sell thousands of wire strippers. It’s unclear how much he’s earned, since TikTok Shop merchants set their own affiliate commission rates. Dragonslayer Industries did not respond to WIRED's inquiries, but in a recent video he noted that it's not in his “best interest” to devote much time to wire stripping since he makes “more money” from doing other things.
But human salespeople like him face plenty of competition from AI-generated ads on TikTok Shop. Even in the specialized market for wire strippers, there’s a huge number of videos featuring AI-generated imagery and voice-overs, some using remarkably similar scripts about making “eight grand a week” from selling scrap copper.
Online, copper scrapping can seem like a solitary pursuit. Offline, however, scrappers sometimes form the kinds of communities that are less apparent on TikTok. Stickle tells WIRED that scrappers he spoke to often worked in small teams, split their profits, and looked out for one another. People struggling to get by, especially those who were experiencing homelessness, sometimes received donated metal from their fellow scrappers.
Stickle adds that they also would lean on friends who had trucks for help transporting large hauls. “If they came across a large amount [of metal] that they couldn't just dolly back to a place,” Stickle says, “they had somebody they'd call.”

After Vucic defeat, Serbia waits to see how student-backed leaders will govern
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:59:44 CET
19:59:44 KST

BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Serbia woke to a new era on Monday after a student-backed protest movement unseated longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a historic landslide election that sparked nationwide celebrations, although few had an idea of how they would govern.
Tens of thousands took to the streets of Belgrade and other cities and towns across Serbia after Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday, capping two years of peaceful anti-government protests calling for the populist ruler to step down.
With almost 99% of votes counted, the students’ candidates had secured a commanding 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Election Commission, versus 39.2% for Vucic’s Serbia Progressive Party (SNS)-led alliance.
That gives the students 139 seats in the 250-seat parliament, leaving the SNS alliance with 97, and the remainder held by minority parties. The constitution allows up to 90 days for the creation of a government, once the parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
“I thought it was unbelievable, I still do not believe it. It was too long, and (Vucic) was pressuring us for a long, long time,” said university administrator Marijana Radovanovic Pajovic.
Vucic dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president from 2014. But he was swept from power by a list of student-backed candidates born out of anti-corruption protests following the deaths of 16 people in the collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad.
PROFOUND POLITICAL SHIFT
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.
While the students’ candidates include university professors, actors and farmers, the movement is without a leader - a strategy employed during protests to avoid any smear attempts by the government. It is unclear who will become prime minister and assume other key positions in order to enact the students’ domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling, and manage the country’s place on the international stage.
“This corruption that has entered into all pores of our lives…of course it will change, we are hoping we will slowly go into that direction of a normal community,” said 60-year-old insurance worker Svetlana Karagkozidou.
Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory.
However, not everyone welcomed the change.
“Changing the country like that so suddenly and all at once, I don’t like it. I don’t even know who is standing behind, who those people are, who will be leading the country,” said 60-year-old civil worker Senka Radakovic.
Meanwhile, supporters of the student movement set about cleaning up a park near the parliament building in Belgrade that had long been used as a camp by Vucic’s supporters. They removed metal barricades and tents and cleaned stickers off children’s play equipment.
“I think it is one of Belgrade’s most beautiful parks, that they took from us for a year or a year-and-a-half, and this is the least we can do right now,” said one of the cleaning volunteers Filip Beselinovic.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
(Reporting by Jana Simovic and Anna Lubowicka; Writing by Kirsten Donovan; Editing by Edward McAllister)

LONDON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Britain on Monday sanctioned 15 military commanders, militia leaders and security officials from both sides of Sudan’s conflict, accusing them of waging sexual violence, torture and attacks on civilians linked to the fall of al-Fashir.

How Houthi attacks have grounded flights across Saudi Arabia
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:59:12 CET
19:59:12 KST

By Gianluca Lo Nostro
Oct 26 (Reuters) - Attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have nearly emptied the skies over Riyadh this month, aviation data showed on Monday, with cancellations grounding almost nine out of every 10 scheduled flights at the Saudi capital’s airport.
About 86% of scheduled flights at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, or 4,071 out of 4,736, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25, according to the latest data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia this month, targeting airports, ports and oil facilities with ballistic missiles and drones. Riyadh’s airport, the kingdom’s second-busiest after Jeddah, has been struck repeatedly, including an attack on October 10 that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Saudi authorities partially reopened the airport on Sunday after a halt that had started on October 10. Domestic flights resumed from Terminal 1, while national carriers were allowed to operate international services from Terminal 2.
However, the Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh’s airport again on Monday, calling it a “military target.” The attacks have prompted international airlines to suspend services to the Saudi capital into November, while Delta Air Lines has postponed the launch of its Riyadh route until next year.
The disruption has forced several events in Riyadh to be cancelled or postponed, including Saudi Arabia’s marquee investment conference, as flight cancellations hamper travel to and across the kingdom.
The upheaval also spread beyond the Saudi capital. More than 7,800 flights, or 45% of all scheduled departures from Saudi airports, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25, according to Cirium. The peak came on October 12, when cancellations exceeded 60% of scheduled flights nationwide.
Several major airports recorded severe disruption, including Riyadh at 86%, Dammam at 42% and Abha at 46.7%, where the Houthis have claimed strikes. A number of smaller regional airports saw the vast majority of flights cancelled, including Najran, near the Yemeni border, where all flights were cancelled.
(Reporting by Gianluca Lo Nostro; Additional reporting by Joanna Plucinska; Editing by Adam Jourdan and Xevi Fontdegloria)

• Ringqvist told reporters on Monday that there was no majority for a centrist government
• “There is a clear demand for solutions that can bring together a broader majority,” she said
• “However, the parliamentary situation makes it difficult at present to translate that support into a government,” she added
• Andersson earlier this month lost a parliament vote to form a government, as widely expected
• Speaker Norlen could now decide to schedule a new parliament vote for prime minister regardless, or hand the task of government formation to the leader of another party
• The centre-left opposition in September won 176 seats to 173 for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc

Restrictions on demining introduced near the front line and the border with Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:58:51 EET
19:58:51 KST

Restrictions on demining introduced near the front line and the border with Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Due to security risks, new operations near the front line and the border have been restricted in six regions. Ongoing demining will continue where possible.
Due to security risks, the planning of new humanitarian demining operations has been restricted in certain areas of six regions. This does not mean that demining has been halted. The Ministry of Defence stated this on October 26, UNN reports.
Details
"The decision of the National Mine Action Authority concerns certain areas in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv and Sumy regions within 20–50 km of the line of contact and the border with the aggressor state, where operations have not yet begun," the Ministry of Defence said.
According to the report, "where demining is already underway, the operations must be completed if the situation allows and they do not interfere with the tasks of the Defence Forces."
"Within the 50-kilometre zone, priority will be given to emergency response measures necessary for the evacuation of the population; emergency rescue operations; providing access to shelters; medical and humanitarian assistance; and responding to threats from explosive ordnance," the defence ministry said.
According to the ministry, the possibility of conducting unscheduled humanitarian demining also remains available upon justified requests.
"The decision will be reviewed depending on the security situation," the Ministry of Defence emphasised.
"Humanitarian demining remains a priority even in frontline areas. But we must act on the basis of a risk-oriented approach in order to find a balance between the safety of the people carrying out demining and the needs of communities in frontline areas," commented Vasyl Shkurakov, Deputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine .
The restrictions introduced do not provide for the cessation of humanitarian demining in frontline areas

Syria to launch first nationwide map of mine-contaminated areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:58:27 UTC
19:58:27 KST

Syria will soon launch its first map showing the distribution of mines across the country as part of a three-year strategy to address landmines and remnants of war, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al Saleh said on Monday.
“The National Mine Action Center is implementing the strategy to identify mine-contaminated areas and strengthen efforts to address the threat,” al Saleh said in comments carried by the ISNA news agency.
Mines and unexploded remnants of war remain among Syria’s most serious challenges because of their impact on civilians and children, as well as the obstacles they pose to reconstruction and the use of agricultural land, he said.
Al Saleh said his ministry continued to develop mine-clearance plans despite existing challenges, aiming to protect civilians and enable residents to use their farmland safely.
Syria is also working with Germany and Ukraine to exchange expertise and benefit from advanced demining technologies, he added.
Joint operations room with Türkiye
Separately, al Saleh said the ministry was working to establish a joint operations room with Türkiye to coordinate emergency response and disaster management on both sides of the border.
The mechanism is intended to speed up coordination and responses to fires, floods and other disasters, he said.
Syrian authorities regularly report deaths and injuries caused by explosions involving remnants of the war waged by the Bashar al Assad regime against civilians between 2011 and 2024.
The conflict killed and injured hundreds of thousands of people and caused widespread infrastructure damage before opposition fighters entered Damascus on December 8, 2024, bringing down the Assad regime.
Syrian authorities and international organisations, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, continue operations in several parts of the country to detect mines and unexploded ordnance left by the war.
According to Landmine Monitor data, unexploded ordnance in Syria has killed or injured more than 13,000 people since 2011.

Algeria to Deploy Troops Abroad for First Time Since 1973, Sending Forces to Niger

Algeria’s two parliamentary chambers approved on October 25 the deployment of the country’s armed forces to Niger to protect Algeria’s energy interests and honor bilateral agreements.
Algeria’s Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, made the announcement.
The decision was approved in closed-door sessions after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune submitted a request on October 22.
The lower house of parliament, the National People’s Assembly, also approved the troop deployment by an overwhelming majority.
According to an official statement by the Council of the Nation, the decision aims to protect Algeria’s energy interests and fulfill the terms of a bilateral agreement with Niger.
Algerian authorities have not yet disclosed the size of the military contingent, the exact deployment date, or the duration of the planned mission.
According to Reuters, one possible deployment site for Algerian troops is the Madama area in northern Niger, near the border with Libya.
Algeria has significant economic interests in Niger, particularly in oil production and the development of transcontinental energy projects.
The state-owned company Sonatrach is developing the Kafra oil project in northern Niger. In August 2026, its subsidiary ENAFOR was preparing to drill the Kafra Sud-Est 1 exploration well, approximately 85 km from the Algerian border.
Algeria, Niger, and Nigeria are also pursuing the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project, which aims to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria.
In June 2026, Sonatrach announced the start of construction on the pipeline’s Algerian section.
In August, Militarnyi reported that Algeria had deployed four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger following an attempted military coup in the country’s capital, Niamey.

South Korean firm signs air defence deals with four Lithuanian companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:58:00 UTC
19:58:00 KST

South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace has signed memorandums of understanding with four Lithuanian companies to cooperate on producing and integrating air defence systems, the companies and the Lithuanian Defence and Security Industry Association said on Monday.
The memorandums cover four areas of cooperation related to the 40mm wheeled anti-aircraft gun (WAAG) system.
Potential vehicle integration will be explored with KMT, turret hull and cable production with Cosmos Construction and T&G Lithuania, and the integration of command and control systems into NATO networks with Nortal.
The WAAG is a mobile air defence system designed to counter low-flying targets, including drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles. It combines automated fire control and target-tracking technologies with 40mm ammunition.
Robert Park, senior vice president of Hanwha Aerospace, said in a press release the company aims to build “long-term industrial partnerships” with Lithuanian companies, focusing on technology transfer, joint solution development and system maintenance throughout their lifecycle.
Park added that the company also aims to support Lithuania's ambition to become a regional hub for defence industry manufacturing and maintenance in the Baltic region.

====================================================================================================

November 2026 travel guide: Where to go, what to see and the new hotels to book in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:57:33 UTC
19:57:33 KST

From early Christmas markets in Vienna to late-autumn sunshine in the Canary Islands, November offers plenty of reasons to plan a European escape before the festive rush.
November can sometimes be an awkward month for travel. The days are shorter, the weather is less predictable, and much of Europe is firmly between autumn and winter.
However, that all tends to equal fewer crowds, plenty of cultural events and, by the end of the month, the first signs of Christmas appearing across European cities.
From early festive markets in Vienna to food and wine in Portugal, a major marathon in Athens and winter sun in Fuerteventura, there are still plenty of reasons to get away.
Here’s Euronews Travel’s guide for where to go, what to see and where to stay this November.
Destinations
Vienna, Austria
If you want to get into the Christmas spirit without waiting until December, Vienna is one of the best places to start.
The Austrian capital's Christmas markets begin opening early in the month, with both the Schönbrunn Palace and Stephansplatz markets opening on 6 November. The most famous market, Rathausplatz, follows on 13 November.
When you’ve had your fill of mulled wine and Christmas lights, November is a great time to explore Vienna's museums, grand coffee houses and palaces without the summer crowds.
Make sure to check out both the Belvedere and Hofburg palaces and head to the Kunsthistorisches Museum, which is filled with European old masters and Habsburg art treasures.
Fuerteventura, Canary Islands, Spain
For those who would rather avoid the cold altogether, the Canary Islands remain one of Europe's safest bets for some late-autumn sunshine.
Fuerteventura is particularly appealing in November, when its beaches, volcanic landscapes and enormous dunes can be explored without the intensity of the summer heat – and it’s one of the most affordable islands in the Canaries, too.
For those who suffer from seasonal depression, the sun sets in the Canary Islands later than in most places in mainland Europe, so it’s ideal for staying cheerful as the winter sets in.
There's also a new reason to stay here. The Elba Corralejo Resort & Spa is opening on 1 November, bringing with it 478 rooms, a staggering 20 swimming pools, restaurants and extensive wellness and family facilities.
Hotel openings
Casa Verbena Madrid, Spain
Hilton's new Outset Collection is making its European debut in Madrid with Casa Verbena Madrid.
The 45-room hotel is set on Calle de Preciados, a pedestrianised shopping street in the heart of the Spanish capital, within walking distance of Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor and the Royal Palace.
It is designed by Spanish interior designer Lorenzo Castillo, with boutique rooms drawing on Spanish architecture and culture.
Hotel Maastricht-Maas, Netherlands
Maastricht is getting a new four-star-plus hotel this November, with the Van der Valk Exclusief Hotel Maastricht-Maas celebrating its grand opening on the banks of the River Maas.
The 113-room property has a contemporary design with South American influences, alongside a restaurant, bar, meeting spaces and a fifth-floor panoramic wellness area.
It is also within easy reach of Maastricht's historic centre, making it a useful base for exploring the buzzy Dutch city.
Events and attractions
Berlin Science Week, Berlin, Germany
Germany’s capital gets particularly cerebral in early November, when Berlin Science Week takes place from 1-10 November.
This year's theme is “In Touch”, exploring how science affects everyday life through exhibitions, workshops, talks, performances and events across the city.
A public weekend from 6-8 November is one of the highlights, making this a good option for anyone who wants something a little different from the usual museum-and-gallery city break.
Athens Marathon The Authentic, Athens, Greece
November is a particularly good month to visit Athens if you like your city breaks with a bit of sporting drama.
The 43rd Athens Marathon, the Authentic, takes place on 7 and 8 November, following the historic route from Marathon to the Panathenaic Stadium.
Even if you're not running, it's a chance to see one of the world's most famous marathon routes and enjoy Athens at a time when summer's heat has disappeared.
International Hot Air Balloon Festival, Alentejo, Portugal
The Alentejo region of Portugal is set to gain tonnes of popularity next year, thanks to its appearance in countless travel experts’ trend predictions.
To experience it for yourself before it blows up as a destination, why not visit the International Hot Air Balloon Festival taking place there from 7-12 November.
The festival, which has been running since 1997, will feature balloon flights, public displays and opportunities to see the colourful aircraft filling the skies over the Alentejo landscape.
While you’re there, you could head to Borba, which will host its annual Vine and Wine Festival from 11-15 November, bringing together wine tastings, regional food, entertainment, crafts and local producers.
Planning ahead: Christmas markets, skiing and winter sun
November is also the month when Christmas travel starts becoming a much more immediate prospect.
If you want to visit some of Europe's biggest markets without the crowds of December, the final week of November is worth considering. Vienna starts early, while cities including Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Prague move into full festive mode later in the month.
It's also worth booking winter-sun trips now, with the Canary Islands and Madeira remaining as popular choices as temperatures fall across northern Europe.
Travelling over Christmas and New Year is notoriously tricky and sometimes pricey, so it’s best to book ahead to secure the best possible deals.
Finally, if you're thinking about skiing, November is the time to start looking ahead. A number of new Alpine hotels and lodges are opening for the 2026-2027 season, including The First Cortina in Italy, The Ski Lodge in Verbier and new properties in Morzine and Les Menuires.

France prepares for further unrest during weekend demonstrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:29 UTC
19:56:29 KST

French authorities are preparing for possible renewed violence during demonstrations planned for the coming weekend.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday would “definitely” be considered a high-risk day, according to Reuters.
He told French broadcaster BFM TV that curfews would probably remain in place in several areas to prevent vandalism and looting.
Trade unions and the Yellow Vest protest movement plan to continue street demonstrations during the coming weeks.
The protests began peacefully in late September over high living costs and conditions in French schools but have repeatedly developed into unrest.
More than 400,000 people participated in demonstrations Saturday.
Nuñez said 267 police officers were injured during the weekend, most of them lightly. Three officers sustained more serious injuries, while more than 250 protesters were estimated to have been injured.
The French government has blamed much of the violence on groups it describes as “ultra-left-wing.”
Education ministers will meet student leaders Monday to discuss their demands.
“We hope that the prime minister agrees to our demands,” said Louis Letoublon, a leader of high school student organization Les Lycéens!
Right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen promised Sunday to “restore law and order” if elected next year.
The next president will also inherit an economy in which public debt and the budget deficit exceed European Union limits.

====================================================================================================

German business sentiment improves in October on brighter outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:28 UTC
19:56:28 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Business sentiment in Germany improved in October, driven by more optimistic company expectations, the Munich-based ifo Institute said on Monday.
The ifo Business Climate Index rose to 90.2 points in October from 89.9 points in September, according to the institute's monthly survey of approximately 9,000 businesses.
While expectations climbed to 91.6 points from 90.4 points a month earlier, companies assessed their current business situation as slightly worse, with that subindex edging down to 88.8 points from 89.5 points.
"The economic recovery is continuing," said Clemens Fuest, president of the ifo Institute.
In the manufacturing sector, the index rose significantly to a seasonally adjusted balance of 1.2 points from minus 2.7 points in September.
Manufacturing companies rated both their current situation and expectations as substantially better, with both indicators returning to positive territory for the first time in more than three years.
Companies plan to expand production following an increase in incoming orders, the institute said.
In the service sector, the business climate suffered a setback, falling to minus 1.2 points in October from 0.7 points in September.
While service firms were less satisfied with their current performance, their expectations grew more positive, with IT service providers performing particularly well.
In the trade sector, the indicator remained unchanged at minus 17.2 points, as slightly improved expectations offset a more negative view of the current situation.
The wholesale sector outperformed retail, Fuest noted.
The construction sector index rose to minus 15.5 points from minus 17.0 points in September, as companies reported noticeably higher satisfaction with their current business situation alongside a slight improvement in expectations.

====================================================================================================

Power fault causes train delays and cancellations across Zealand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:23 UTC
19:56:23 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

ryue nishizawa places vivid orange peak against turquoise landfill in japan
against forested mountains and the vivid turquoise lining of a managed waste site, the sculptural platform turns the act of looking into a physical encounter with an industrial landscape.

ryue nishizawa designs landfill observation platform in japan
Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA with Kazuyo Sejima, creates an observation platform at Oono Development’s managed landfill. Part of Final Disposal Site – A Landscape Created by Nature, Industry, and People, the installation invites visitors into a working industrial landscape and makes a normally restricted site accessible as a place of observation. The project is presented as part of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, a decentralized festival that brings art and architecture into active industrial sites across Okayama and Ehime prefectures.
Curated by Kazuyo Sejima, the exhibition takes place within Oono Development’s integrated recycling complex, where a valley has been engineered into a vast basin for waste disposal. Separated from the surrounding ground and vegetation to prevent waste from mixing with the soil, the landfill is expected to fill over approximately 15 years. Its changing terrain forms the setting for an exhibition that directs attention toward the infrastructure and material processes often kept out of public view.
setouchi art and industry 2026 opens industrial sites to visitors
Visitors travel by bus toward the upper reaches of the site, wearing distinctive workwear in the same red-orange color as the installation, derived from a natural mineral produced in Ehime Prefecture. From the valley rim and its artificially formed hills, they look across the expansive landfill. Nishizawa’s observation platform provides a place to pause and take in the scale of the site, while the vivid orange surface contrasts with the pale ground, turquoise landfill lining, and surrounding green mountains.
Shingo Masuda and Katsuhisa Otsubo create gathering spaces and a bus stop, while Suzuko Yamada develops the bus and visitor workwear. Curated and supervised by Kazuyo Sejima, with Yuko Hasegawa, Yusuke Okura, and Atsuhiro Miyake as advisors, the exhibition integrates these elements into the visitor journey through the landfill.
The project is part of the inaugural Setouchi Art and Industry 2026. Organized by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation, the festival spans seven active industrial sites, including facilities connected to salt production, textiles, denim, shipbuilding, battery storage, and resource recycling.

Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll

Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week.
The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki.
🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz
— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026
In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health.
In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy.
Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases.
A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion.
The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%).
The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority).
One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand.
In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023
The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”.
Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”.
Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026
In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition.
However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.
After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment.
Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law.

Not just Iran: Netanyahu defies IDF chief over continuing Hebron operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:54:41 UTC
19:54:41 KST

The military operation in Hebron, launched after a deadly shooting attack near the West Bank city killed two IDF soldiers, has become another point of contention between the military leadership and Israel's political leadership, just a day before Tuesday's election. While troops from the IDF's 98th Division continue intensive operations involving searches for weapons, arrests of suspects, the evacuation of Palestinian residents and the demolition of unauthorized structures, military officials believe that the limited operational results so far warrant reassessing whether the operation should continue in its current form.
According to sources familiar with the discussions, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir presented his position during a meeting with the political leadership, attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, arguing that the time had come to end the operation. Netanyahu and Katz, however, rejected that assessment and instructed the military to continue. Ultimately, the chief of staff's recommendation was not accepted, and the decision was made to keep the operation underway.
The IDF has pointed, among other concerns, to the legal difficulties involved in keeping Palestinian residents away from their homes for extended periods, particularly when the operation is not producing significant military gains. So far, troops have made arrests and located a limited number of weapons, but have not uncovered unusual weaponry or large weapons stockpiles.
The political leadership, however, presents a different assessment. Officials argue that the two terrorists who carried out the deadly attack were armed with automatic weapons and substantial quantities of ammunition, making it necessary for the IDF to continue searching for additional weapons in the area. They also maintain that prolonging the operation will strengthen deterrence. Security officials explain that the very presence of large IDF forces operating inside Hebron creates a psychological impact among Palestinians, particularly because the troops have entered a major Palestinian city rather than refugee camps, as they did during previous operations in Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem.
The current disagreement recalls an IDF operation in the Qalandiya refugee camp in August. At the time, the military defined its objectives as targeting terrorist operatives and infrastructure. Katz also pushed for a large-scale operation and again raised the possibility of taking control of another refugee camp, similar to the operations carried out in Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams.
IDF officials said the military had operational plans for every refugee camp but had not mobilized forces to carry them out because there was no operational necessity. There was also tension over contingency planning for a scenario known in the military as a "turning of the guns," involving a possible armed escalation in which Palestinian security forces turn their weapons against Israel. Katz presented the IDF's extensive and aggressive plan for such a scenario, although intelligence assessments at the time did not indicate that an escalation of that kind was imminent in the West Bank.
It is important to note that the prolonged military operations in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, which Katz was among those pushing for and which were conducted under Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, led to a significant decline in terrorist activity in the area, according to Israeli security assessments. 
However, the Qalandiya operation ended after just two days and, based on the information available so far, did not produce significant operational results. Now, in Hebron, the question is once again whether continuing the operation is likely to yield further results or whether it has already achieved its main objectives.
But the debate over the Hebron operation is unfolding against a broader and more complicated security backdrop. The IDF is currently also focused on preventing the next attack, particularly attacks carried out by lone assailants inspired by previous incidents. Security officials are concerned about copycat attacks that could develop following exposure to incitement on social media and military activity on the ground. Central Command is therefore concentrating its efforts on identifying threats early, thwarting potential attackers and preventing an escalation that could emerge from several directions.
The IDF stresses that such conditions require precise, targeted counterterrorism operations, accompanied by constant assessments of their operational value and their consequences on the ground. The concern is that an escalation could develop rapidly, making it necessary to consider not only existing threats but also the reactions military operations themselves could provoke.
Against this backdrop, the Hebron operation illustrates the tension between the political leadership's demand to continue military activity in pursuit of deterrence and additional weapons discoveries, and the IDF's position that the operational benefits must be weighed against the consequences of prolonging the operation for the local Palestinian population.

The agency did not identify that person, but said alerting the authorities to a planned crime could exempt an informant from criminal liability.
The two suspects, identified only as foreign nationals from the Caucasus region, face up to 15 years in prison on terrorism charges.
Moscow is among the most heavily defended parts of Russia. During the record Ukrainian drone attack on the capital on September 19–20, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said more than 1,600 drones were intercepted across defensive lines, including 450 which were approaching the city.

Private technology companies are taking longer to go public, with the median age at listing rising from 6.9 years in 2014 to 11 years in 2025, according to figures cited by Revolut in an announcement released on Monday.
This means more of their growth takes place before shares become available on public markets and can be accessed by retail investors.

The new platform is expected to become available in 2027 and will be integrated into the Revolut app alongside existing investment options, including stocks, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bonds and money market funds.
The announcement follows the introduction of private market investment products in selected European Economic Area (EEA) countries in July 2026.
However, investments in private companies carry significant risks.
Unlike publicly traded shares, they are more difficult to sell and investors could lose a substantial portion or all of their invested capital.
The launch comes as Revolut continues to expand its operations, having secured full banking licences in the UK and France earlier this year.
The UK fintech, which is seeking to diversify its revenue streams, is also considering a dual stock market listing in London and New York, although no date has been confirmed.
