Eesti 200 preparing for 2027 Riigikogu elections
Eesti 200 Chairman Kristina Kallas said the party is preparing for the upcoming national election despite its low ratings and some members saying there is little point.
Junion coalition party Eesti 200 has polled below the 5 percent threshold for months in popularity surveys. This means the party is unlikely to be included in the next Riigikogu.
Eesti 200 parliamentary group member Ando Kiviberg and group chairman Toomas Uibo told ERR in mid-October that Eesti 200 should not run in the elections and that it would be more sensible to prepare properly for the 2031 parliamentary elections.
But Kallas is not giving up.
"We are currently preparing for the parliamentary elections and putting together candidate lists. That is the goal we are working toward," she told ERR.
The party has not yet chosen an advertising agency to run its election campaign, unlike some of its rivals whose posters can already be seen around the country.
"We currently have a so-called brief ready for advertising agencies, which we will use to start looking at agencies. We have not yet selected an advertising agency," Kallas said.
The chairman said the brief includes everything Eesti 200 would like to get from an advertising agency.
"We also have another option, which is to develop the creative solutions [election slogans and other content – ed.] ourselves. Because there have always been two options. In the previous parliamentary elections, we developed the creative solutions ourselves and only commissioned the work from an advertising agency," she said.
Kallas was unwilling to say how Eesti 200 would select an advertising agency or whether the party would hold a competition to find one.
"Look, this is a normal thing that parties do. It's a bit like explaining what goes on behind the scenes. I'm not going to explain how agencies are selected and on what basis. It's also something of a trade secret. I do not think it makes sense to explain that publicly," Kallas said.
The chairman said the party's candidate lists would probably be finalized in early January, as the deadline for submitting candidate lists is at the end of January.
Kallas said the party's election manifesto will start to be made public in the near future: "We will probably hold the election board meeting in early December, when the election promises will also be announced."
For now, Kallas was unwilling to reveal any election promises. "No. Absolutely not," she said.

Snakes that cartwheel, vultures that groan, and a Martian moon full of mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:26:38 UTC
19:26:38 KST

Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
Let’s start with some space news. Last week, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA for short, successfully launched a half-a-billion-dollar mission to land on Phobos, the largest Martian moon.
The Martian Moons Exploration spacecraft, also known as MMX, is expected to reach the vicinity of Mars in August of 2027. Once there, it will spend three years circling Mars in a path similar to Phobos’s orbit. One of its objectives is to find an ideal spot for landing on Phobos. In 2028 or 2029, MMX will send a rover down to the surface to spend 100 days observing the moon. That data will come in handy later in 2029, when MMX itself will attempt one or even two landings. If all goes well, MMX will return back up to orbit with 10 grams, or one-third of an ounce, of material from Phobos. It’s expected to make it back to Earth sometime in 2031.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
So, why all this effort to check out a lumpy little moon? Phobos may be just 14 miles wide, but it’s got a lot to say. With an orbit of just over seven hours, it’s closer to its planet than any other moon in our solar system. That orbit is also gradually shrinking, bringing it on a slow-but-steady collision course with Mars.
Then there’s the unknown origin of Phobos and its little sibling, the Martian moon Deimos. Scientists aren’t sure whether these wee moons were once asteroids that got too close to Mars or if they formed from debris after something collided with the red planet. When the MMX sample comes home, researchers will compare its composition against Martian material and asteroids to try to solve that mystery.
Speaking of weird little guys with adorably tiny orbits, our next story features a little snake that uses cartwheels as a strange evasive maneuver.
Now, I don’t know about you, but I find cartwheels hard enough with two arms and legs to support me. But apparently there are tiny little snakes that put my acrobatic attempts to shame with nary a limb in sight. Scientists first showcased this ability with the dwarf reed snake in 2023, but now they’ve identified that same cartwheeling behavior in two additional species of the same genus, Pseudorabdion. And what’s even better is that they caught the bizarre locomotion on video.
The snakes start out by making a tight little curve, kind of like the letter “C,” with its head up top, facing the direction it wants to go, and something like the middle of its body touching the ground. Then it reels forward until its tail is the part touching the ground, which gives it the momentum to launch itself into the air. While it’s airborne, the snake twists around until it gets itself into the position of the starting point of the next roll, and it alternates which side of its body strikes the ground with each rotation. And did I mention these snakes are tiny and adorable? I’m definitely not doing the footage of their limbless leaping justice, so you really gotta check the video out for yourself. We’ll link to that in our show notes!
Those aren’t the only animal showoffs we saw making headlines last week. In a study published last Wednesday, researchers shared the surprisingly complex range of sounds made by birds not generally known for their gorgeous singing voices: vultures.
When you think of a vulture, you probably picture a relatively solitary and silent bird, maybe like a few of them flying around in an ominous circle but not much more than that. But the thing is that some species are quite social—and, as it turns out, those more gregarious species can also be quite vocal. Rüppell’s vultures, which nest in colonies hundreds of birds strong, are known to follow a literal pecking order when it comes time to pick a carcass clean. Some experts think that social complexity fuels the evolution of complex communication. So, the set hierarchy that these vultures live by made scientists wonder how they might use sound to communicate.
Researchers captured 150 hours of noise from two groups of vultures in captivity, which contained something like 2,500 calls. When they analyzed qualities like pitch and length, they were able to distinguish 16 distinct call types, which could be double the average for birds in general, based on previous research.
If you’re wondering what those calls sound like, well lucky for you we have some examples. The study authors dubbed the most common call the “metallic groan,” and it generally came from birds who were on the receiving end of some kind of aggression. There were also specific brays that came from vultures trying to bully other birds for food, hisses made in response, hoarse mating groans, and special calls made by parents as they lovingly puked food into their babies’ mouths.
For our next story, you know those tabloid stories that show celebrities, like, grocery shopping and stuff with the headline “they’re just like us?” Well slap some Japanese macaques onto those glossy pages. Because according to a study published last week in Royal Society Open Science, these monkeys have a lot in common with humans when it comes to responding to disease outbreaks.
Not unlike the human tendency to stock up on hand sanitizer and wipe down groceries in the wake of a pandemic, the researchers say, primates who have survived life-threatening disease outbreaks remain more cautious about potential food contamination than their peers. That’s especially interesting given the fact that, for a macaque, there’s no public health agency announcing where a deadly ailment has come from. But even with no empirical knowledge of disease transmission, like literally these guys do not have germ theory, this study suggests that a brush with contagion inspires habits that limit exposure to new bugs.
The study looked at Japanese macaques at a primate sanctuary in southern Texas, where they’re grouped into several distinct enclosures. Three groups experienced an outbreak of simian retrovirus Type II, which can cause a sickness similar to AIDS, back in 2020. A fourth enclosure was completely spared, which provided a natural control group.
To test how that experience impacted pathogen avoidance, the researchers offered macaques food from visibly clean surfaces as well as ones seemingly contaminated by monkey poop, though covered by epoxy to prevent any actual disease risk. Previous studies have shown that this species will avoid some food with fecal contamination, but will risk it all for a favorite treat like a peanut. And, indeed, in this new study, monkeys ate from a seemingly dirty surface in 79 percent of trials. But in the groups that had survived an outbreak, monkeys went for the poop food less than half of the time. Even individuals who had not personally been sick were less likely to risk contamination.
Simian retrovirus Type II doesn’t actually spread through food, but via scratches and bites. But we know that disgust and pathogen avoidance are complicated—and not always actually very useful—in humans, too.
We’ll wrap up with a story about the funnest little animals of them all: preschoolers. Researchers were curious about why people seem to think that kids are more creative than adults, despite scientific evidence showing the opposite. In a study published last week in PLOS One, they had 92 preschoolers and 70 adults tackle three creative tasks: spending eight minutes drawing freely on blank paper with colored pens and spending eight minutes inventing and drawing a made-up animal. The study subjects were all asked about how much they enjoyed those activities, how anxious the tasks made them feel, and how confident they felt about the quality of what they’d come up with. Then their results were evaluated by five people trained in a system for rating creative work.
It turns out that, at least in this case, adults were objectively more creative than preschoolers, coming up with more original and effective ideas—but they also enjoyed themselves way less and felt worse about their work. So if you often find yourself wishing you could recapture the boundless creativity of your youth, maybe you should actually just work on your self-confidence. One time a lady in my ceramic studio looked at what I was making and said, “Wow, I wish I gave myself that much freedom.” And I have to tell you, at the time, it did not feel good. But now, I think I might have changed my mind.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to see how science is showing up in the midterm elections.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Sushmita Pathak, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Emily Makowski, Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Austrian chancellor threatens veto in EU budget dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:34 UTC
19:25:34 KST

Timo Kirez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker of the Austrian People's Party (OVP) threatened on Monday to veto the EU budget proposal.
Speaking to the German daily newspaper Die Welt, Stocker said, “There is a pain threshold for Austria. If this pain threshold is exceeded, I will not agree.”
Although Stocker did not specify exactly where Vienna’s “pain threshold” lies, he did point out that “a compromise will only be possible if the new proposal is realistic.”
Stocker specifically criticized the European Commission’s demand for 2,500 additional civil service positions as “completely unreasonable and out of touch with reality.”
“We are cutting 2,600 administrative positions in Austria,” the chancellor said. He expects EU institutions to do the same.
If bureaucracy is curtailed through future staff reductions, that would suit him just fine, Stocker continued.
Austria is currently subject to an EU deficit procedure and must consolidate its own budget. Therefore, Stocker said, he expects Brussels to exercise fiscal discipline and use its resources efficiently.
The EU's financial framework for 2028 through 2034 must be approved unanimously by the member states.
The European Commission had proposed a total budget of €1.985 trillion ($2.226 trillion) for the next seven years.
Opposition to this financial plan comes not only from Austria but also from Germany, the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, and Denmark.

Japan indicts U.S. Marine on murder charge over woman's killing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:09 UTC
19:25:09 KST

U.S. Marine indicted on murder charge over woman's killing in Japan
Japanese prosecutors have indicted a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering a woman on Okinawa, a court spokesman told AFP on Monday, in a case that prompted public outrage.
The alleged killing of the 39-year-old Japanese woman caused Japan's premier to slam the "heinous crime" and reignited controversy over the heavy U.S. military presence on the southern island.
"The case was indicted on October 25," said the spokesman for the court in Naha, confirming media reports that the suspect had been indicted on charges of murder and robbery.
Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha.
The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that, according to the indictment document, the suspect allegedly strangled the woman from Naha in a hotel with a telephone cord on Oct. 3.
He is also accused of stealing a backpack containing the woman's wallet and other belongings, the newspaper said.
The Marine denied the allegations at the time of his arrest but has now made statements that imply some involvement in the case, the Yomiuri and other media said, citing investigative sources.
Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions in the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi has said that officials were reviewing the off-base code of conduct for U.S. troops in Japan following the alleged killing.
The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said.
"We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States.
The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on U.S. military personnel drinking in public off base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours.
The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a month-long curfew.
Previous incidents have strained relations
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
In Japan, once a suspect is formally indicted, the conviction rate stands at more than 99%.
The justice ministry says the near-perfect rates are because prosecutors only pursue airtight cases, they are confident about winning.
Why are so many bases concentrated in Okinawa?
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today Okinawa hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 54,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today, despite comprising just 0.6% of Japan's landmass.
In the wake of World War II, Japan regained its sovereignty under the San Francisco Peace Treaty of 1952, but Okinawa remained under American control, making it a hub of U.S. military build-up.
The 1972 return of Okinawa's sovereignty to Japan did little to diminish the number of U.S. bases on the island, leading to the disproportionate burden it is saddled with today.

North Korea ‘Reaches’ Seoul in South Korea–U.S. War Games Simulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:08 UTC
19:25:08 KST

During the South Korea–U.S. joint command post exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield, North Korean troops breached defensive lines and advanced to the outskirts of Seoul in a simulation.
According to Chosun Ilbo, citing its own sources in military circles, the involvement of combined South Korean and U.S. forces did not prevent North Korean units from posing a critical threat to the South Korean capital.
The scenario accounts for the deployment of reinforcements, the operation of air defense systems, and ground maneuvers by both countries’ forces.
South Korean military officials suggest several possible reasons for the simulation’s unfavorable outcome.
These include coordination issues within the combined command and the significant transformation of North Korea’s military capabilities in recent years.
A key feature of the August exercises was assigning the main command-and-control functions for ground operations to South Korea’s Ground Operations Command. The Commander of the Combined Forces provided overall leadership.
This division of responsibilities rehearsed a scenario involving the future transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) from the United States to South Korea.
The simulation results indicate that South Korean forces have not yet achieved the readiness required to independently command a combined force.
South Korea’s reliance on U.S. intelligence systems remains another outstanding issue.
Without the U.S. constellation of satellites and reconnaissance aircraft, South Korean forces are unable to independently track the movements of North Korea’s mobile launchers.
Despite the simulation’s negative results, South Korean government officials reaffirm their intention to complete the transfer of OPCON during President Lee Jae-myung’s term in office.
Previously, North Korean self-propelled artillery systems, likely of 122 mm caliber, were spotted near the border with South Korea along the western front.

NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November, says BMA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:24:51 UTC
19:24:51 KST

England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”.
Consultant doctors, who earn an average of £152,000 a year inclusive of overtime and merit awards, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings.
On those days, hospitals will operate with consultants providing only emergency cover, in the way they do on Christmas Day, because most will withdraw their labour.
Consultants decided to strike after 18 months of talks with the government did not lead to agreement on key issues, including their call for action to address a 25% fall in the real-terms value of their salaries since 2009-10, the British Medical Association (BMA) said. The senior doctors also want a 10% cut in their working hours.
The BMA accused ministers of ignoring consultants’ concerns about burnout related to their workloads and said last week’s well-below-inflation pay offer of a 2.4% increase for next year was the last straw.
Consultants voted in July to take industrial action. The BMA said that since then, informal talks with the Department of Health and Social Care had produced no meaningful progress, only another cut to the value of their pay.
Ciarán Devane, the head of the NHS Alliance, which represents NHS leaders, said he was “astonished and dismayed” by the BMA’s move at a time when the health service was working to tackle a backlog of more than 6 million patients awaiting more than 7m treatments.
“NHS leaders will be both astonished and dismayed by the BMA’s decision to proceed with walkouts by consultants at a time when plans to restore waiting time targets hang by a thread and as teams make wider preparations for winter after a gruelling summer,” Devane said. “Any decision to down tools risks throwing these plans further off course and will once again disrupt patient care while severely hitting NHS finances.
“A consultant walkout will result in non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgeries and follow-ups being postponed or rescheduled. While [postponement] is needed in the interests of patient safety, it will potentially leave patients in unnecessary pain, discomfort, and inconvenience.”
The BMA’s decision presents the prime minister, Andy Burnham, with a considerable challenge as he grapples with tight public finances and Labour’s aim of improving access to NHS care.
In June, resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – accepted a deal to end a campaign of strikes that had lasted more than three years. Consultants last staged stoppages in 2023, when they walked out for nine days during four strikes.
“Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions,” said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee. “But time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes.
“Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough.
“Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.”
Ben Morrin, the chief executive of NHS Employers, which represents England’s 205 health trusts, urged the BMA to be realistic about what size of pay rise was affordable.
“We need to be honest and transparent about what the NHS can afford at this time. If that limit is reached and industrial action takes place, we owe it to patients to focus on delivering the safest care we can,” he said.
He added that the strike would “weaken the clinical teams in every NHS hospital, which are essential to delivering high-quality patient care this winter”.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, urged consultants to “not take irresponsible action that would place our health service under even greater pressure” during what would be a tough winter for the NHS.
A Department of Health and Social Care source said: “The BMA’s consultants committee is threatening strikes because they want a five-hour cut to the working week and to reduce the proportion of their week spent treating patients, changes that would cost taxpayers over £2bn. This is despite average earnings of £152,000 a year and a £25,000 increase to average earnings over the last four years.”

BJP protests across states over Kharge's 'baap' remark at PM Modi; demands apology

BJP protested nationwide, demanding Kharge apologise for his controversial remarks about PM Modi
NEW DELHI: BJP workers on Monday staged protests in Bihar, Jammu and Bengaluru against Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's controversial 'baap' remark against Prime Minister Narendra Modi, demanding an apology from the Congress chief.The protests came a day after Kharge, speaking at an event in Patna, responded to a person from the audience who said that PM Modi would not go anywhere. "Modi ka baap bhi jayega (Even Modi's father will have to go)," Kharge said, triggering criticism from BJP leaders.
The remark was made during a programme marking the 139th birth anniversary of Bihar's first chief minister, Shrikrishna Singh.
Delhi BJP workers hold protest outside Kharge's residence
Delhi BJP workers and leaders staged a protest near Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence on Rajaji Marg on Monday over his alleged disparaging remarks against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The protest turned tense as demonstrators attempted to break through police barricades and march towards Kharge's residence.Police stopped the protesters as they tried to march from Sena Bhawan circle towards the Congress president's residence. Around 2,000 BJP workers and leaders, including Delhi BJP president Harsh Malhotra, were detained, the Delhi BJP said in a statement.Amid heavy police deployment in the Sena Bhawan area, the detained BJP workers and leaders were packed into buses and taken to Mandir Marg police station.
They were later released, according to the party's statement.The BJP had called for nationwide protests over Kharge's remarks at an event in Patna, escalating its confrontation with the Congress over the alleged comments against the prime minister.
BJP leaders detained during Bengaluru protest
In Bengaluru, BJP leaders and workers staged a demonstration at Freedom Park, demanding an unconditional apology from Kharge over his remarks.
Police detained several BJP leaders, including Karnataka assembly leader of opposition R Ashoka and former minister CN Ashwath Narayan, during the protest.BJP leaders accused the Congress president of making offensive remarks against the Prime Minister and his family.
BJP workers burn Kharge's effigy in Patna
In Patna, BJP workers took out a 'Jan Akrosh March' under the leadership of Bihar BJP president Sanjay Saraogi.The protesters marched from the party headquarters towards Income Tax Golambar, raising slogans against Kharge and the Congress. They also burnt an effigy of the Congress president."Yesterday, all limits were crossed when the platform to celebrate the birth anniversary of Shrikrishna Singh, the architect of modern Bihar, was used to make abusive remarks about the late father of the Prime Minister," Saraogi said.He accused the Congress of making personal attacks against Modi out of political frustration and demanded an apology from Kharge and Rahul Gandhi."The Congress, Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi must apologise to the people of the country," he said.
Protests in Jammu, other districts
In Jammu, BJP leaders and workers staged a protest at Dogra Chowk, raising slogans against Kharge and the Congress. Led by BJP MLA Shagun Parihar and Bharatiya Janata Yuva Morcha's Jammu and Kashmir president Arun Prabhat, the protesters marched through Dogra Chowk, burnt posters of Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, and staged a brief sit-in on the road.Parihar condemned the remarks, saying they were disrespectful not only to the Prime Minister's late father but also to elderly people who had passed away."If they do not respect the prime minister's father, how will they respect the father of an ordinary citizen?" she asked. Protests were also reported from Samba, Kathua, Poonch, Udhampur, Rajouri, Doda, Kishtwar and Reasi districts. Similar demonstrations were held in Delhi and Lucknow as part of the BJP's nationwide protest against Kharge's remarks.
Congress defends Kharge's remarks
Meanwhile, the Congress defended its president, claiming that a BJP supporter had first insulted Kharge's father during the Patna event. Congress leader Pawan Khera said Kharge was referring to the RSS as PM Modi's "ideological father", rather than his biological father. RJD leader Bhai Virendra also defended Kharge, describing his remarks as a "slip of the tongue" and saying he did not need to apologise.
However, RJD MP Manoj Jha said such conduct was not expected from a senior leader like Kharge, while questioning what he described as selective outrage over remarks made by political leaders. Union home minister Amit Shah also criticised Kharge, accusing the Congress of repeatedly crossing the limits of political decorum by targeting PM Modi and his family.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh slammed Congress president
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Monday slammed Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his controversial remark about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father, saying the statement had left him shocked and hurt. He also criticised the Congress for defending Kharge’s comments instead of expressing regret over the controversy.

German intelligence agencies plan Google cloud system for secret data exchange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:22:58 UTC
19:22:58 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Germany's three main intelligence agencies plan to introduce a Google-based cloud system to exchange classified documents, public broadcasters WDR and NDR reported Monday.
The military intelligence service MAD, domestic intelligence agency BfV and foreign intelligence service BND intend to use an air-gapped version of Google Distributed Cloud, according to the report.
The system, known as "ND-Cloud," would operate autonomously with no direct connection to the internet, the broadcasters reported.
Data would be stored entirely within Germany, while Google would have no access to the information, according to sources cited in the report.
The platform would also operate as a separate, specially protected information technology network.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency BfV dismissed concerns that reliance on a US-based technology company could compromise security or conflict with the country's earlier preference for European technology providers.
In a statement to the broadcasters, the agency said European solutions remained a priority for strengthening resilience but stressed the importance of using the most advanced technologies available.
"The BfV's capacity for action and innovation depends directly on the availability of modern IT systems and technology platforms," it added.

Woman, 93, outwits would-be scammer, helps get him arrested, police say
A 93-year-old woman in western Japan outsmarted a suspected scammer by pretending to fall for the scheme and helping police arrest him at her home, a police official told AFP on Monday.
Japan has the second-oldest population in the world after Monaco, and senior citizens are often targeted by fraudsters, who last year collectively stole around 325.7 billion yen ($2.0 billion) from their victims.
The woman, who lives in the Shiga region, received telephone calls from Wednesday through Thursday last week from a man who claimed to be a police officer.
The caller falsely informed her that her bank account had experienced an unauthorized withdrawal.
The woman was told to give her ATM card to a man, posing as a police officer, who would visit her so authorities could verify her account.
Suspecting a scam, the woman consulted her son and the police as she waited for the man to visit her house.
"The person's family reached out to the police on Wednesday evening, and we were able to have officers at her house" before the scammer arrived on Thursday, a local police official told AFP on the customary condition of anonymity.
When a 47-year-old man appeared at her doorstep, waiting officers arrested him on the spot, the police official said.
"The person (the woman) is someone in good health and highly articulate," the official said, while urging other elderly residents to consult family members when they suspect fraud.

Oil plunges more than 6% from near wartime highs as diplomacy over Iran seemingly gathers pace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:18:53 UTC
19:18:53 KST

Brent crude fell more than 6% on Monday morning, retreating from its highest close since March, as regional mediators headed to Tehran and US President Donald Trump weighed a deal with Iran, while investors braced for a week packed with central bank decisions and earnings reports.
Oil prices tumbled on Monday morning as diplomatic efforts to calm the Iran war gathered pace and US President Donald Trump said he was weighing a deal with Tehran.
Brent, the global oil benchmark, fell more than 6% from about $117.4 per barrel at Friday’s close to around $110 at the time of writing, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate dropped about 2% to $101.5 per barrel.
Friday's close was Brent’s highest since 19 March and only about 2% below the $119.5 peak hit in early March, at the start of the Iran war. Before the conflict, Brent traded at around $72 per barrel.
Prices had surged last week after Yemen's Houthi rebels, an Iran-aligned armed group, attacked airports and energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter.
However, the mood shifted over the weekend.
Qatari mediators reportedly travelled to Tehran on Sunday in coordination with Washington, while Saudi Arabia's defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief were due in the Iranian capital on Monday for regional security talks.
In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump framed it as a choice asking, "do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?"
Supply risks have not gone away as the Houthis said they struck Saudi airports and energy sites again over the weekend, while Riyadh reported shooting down further missiles and drones.
Trump touts Hormuz flows
At a campaign event in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump defended his administration's reasons for starting the conflict.
Citing the Wall Street Journal, he also claimed that "oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz is now topping what it was before the war [...] our navy has been incredible."
The Strait of Hormuz carried about a fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
Gulf crude exports, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler, but around 40% of them now bypass the strait through pipelines, compared with 17% before the conflict.
Earnings and central bank week
Investors are also bracing for a busy week of rate decisions from the world's major central banks.
In Europe, both the pan-European Stoxx 600 and the Euro Stoxx 50 traded over 0.6% higher than Friday's close.
The UK's FTSE 100, Germany's DAX, France's CAC 40, Italy's FTSE MIB and Switzerland's SMI, all rose between 0.3% and 1% with the German index leading.
Spain’s IBEX 35 and the Netherlands’ AEX both traded flat.
French assets got some relief after ratings agency Moody’s unexpectedly kept France’s Aa3 rating on Friday evening.
In the US, futures on the S&P 500 were 0.3% higher and those on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 as well.
The week ahead is packed as the US Federal Reserve announces its decision on Wednesday, and is widely expected to keep rates at 3.75% to 4% before a possible hike in December.
The European Central Bank follows on Thursday, with France's bond market turmoil in focus, and the Bank of Japan on Friday.
Earnings season also peaks, with roughly one in three S&P 500 firms reporting, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon among them, while BP and Shell update investors in Europe.

Spain's Sanchez predicts election victory despite opposition lead in polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

19:18:12 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
- Prime minister pledges higher wages, stronger housing regulation, defends immigration policies ahead of Nov. 29 vote
- Sanchez rejects allegations against family, acknowledges former minister's corruption scandal as 'biggest mistake' of his 8 years in office
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has expressed confidence that his Socialist Party would win the Nov. 29 general election despite polls showing a substantial lead for the right-wing opposition, according to an interview.
"These elections can be summed up in one very simple idea: either the past advances or Spain advances," Sanchez told El Pais on Sunday, predicting a broader progressive parliamentary majority.
He dismissed surveys suggesting the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox could hold a lead of up to 15%, warning that a right-wing coalition would threaten social rights, including abortion and euthanasia.
"In a democracy, alternation is positive. But a PP government with Vox does not represent an alternation; it is a real regression. It means going back 40 years, 50 years at once," he said.
Addressing growing public frustration over housing affordability, Sanchez defended his government's record but called for stronger market regulation and expanded affordable housing, accusing conservative parties of blocking legislative measures.
He also pledged to raise the minimum wage before the election and urged employers to increase salaries amid inflation of 4.9%, which he largely attributed to the war in Iran.
On immigration, Sanchez defended his government's regularization policies, arguing that migrant workers were essential to sustaining Spain's welfare system amid demographic decline.
"The dilemma is whether we want to be an open and prosperous society or a closed and decadent one, without the capacity or manpower to sustain the current welfare state," the prime minister said, stressing "the migration must, of course, be orderly." 
Scale of deadly Ceuta crisis couldn't have been anticipated
Regarding the deadly July migration crisis in Ceuta, where 141 people died, Sanchez acknowledged that authorities had received warnings but insisted no security or intelligence service anticipated the scale of the tragedy.
He defended his government's response and rejected suggestions of Moroccan involvement without evidence, warning against escalating diplomatic tensions with a neighboring country based on assumptions.
"I cannot open a diplomatic escalation with a neighboring country simply based on assumptions," he said.
Asked about his brother David Sanchez's conviction and legal proceedings involving his wife Begona Gomez, Sanchez accused far-right associations and media outlets of targeting his family for political reasons.
"They are being tried for being the brother and wife of the prime minister," he said, insisting on their innocence and integrity.
"In these two cases, the red lines of a democracy have been crossed. First, because they are innocent. Second, because they are people of integrity," Sanchez said. "And third, because political attacks like those Begona and David are suffering from far-right associations and media should not be launched."
Sanchez also acknowledged corruption involving former minister Jose Luis Abalos as his "biggest mistake" during eight years in office.  
"The corruption of Abalos. For the double mistake of not having seen it and, of course, of it happening," he said.

Rahi’s granddaughter offering floral tributes to him
GHAZIPUR:Rahi’s work may have won hearts and acclaim in literary circles and Bollywood, but those in his native village feel he deserves more especially in the places linked to him.In Baghui Buzurg, the village where Rahi Masoom Raza was born, pride in his legacy comes with a wish for greater recognition.“This is Rahi’s maternal home. He was born in this very room,” said his nephew, Mohd Shakeeb, as he showed us around the house and the neem tree that Rahi personified in Neem Ka Ped to tell a larger story of ordinary lives, social change and a nation in transition. For the family, the house is more than a link to the past; it is a reminder of the place that shaped the writer and his imagination.
Raza's niece Samar Rizwi at Bashir Manzil - the house where Raza spent his early life. (2) Room where Raza was born
Preserving his memory, they believe, must go beyond remembering him on special occasions. His nephew Wasi Asghar feels the district should formally acknowledge Rahi’s contribution to literature.“Successive governments have yet to take an initiative to recognise his contribution to the literary world. The district could at least have a degree college dedicated to him,” he said. Such an institution, the family hopes, would introduce younger generations to a writer whose work drew deeply from the region and its people.
His daughter Mariyam has made a beginning of her own by setting up an English-medium school in his name. On Saturday, around 700 children at the school remembered Rahi.“Access to education was the foundation of his evolution as a person. So, we thought of making this humble beginning,” she said.The school is one way of keeping his name alive while extending the opportunity that helped shape his own intellectual journey.About 15 kilometres away, Gangauli, Rahi’s paternal village, shares this sense of belonging.“This is his dadihal (paternal home),” said Syed Abuzar Husain, a relative who looks after the family home, now an imambara that comes alive during Muharram. Visitors often come here to learn more about the writer, he said.But recognition remains uneven. Neighbour Anwar Ansari, a retired weaver who read Aadha Gaon and watched Neem Ka Ped out of curiosity, offered a less celebratory view.“People who love Rahi may be proud of him, but many locals, particularly those from his own community, are not. They resent him because he exposed them in his books,” he said demanding that at least a road in his name must be sanctioned. His observation points to a complicated legacy: the same writing that made Rahi an important chronicler of his society also unsettled people who saw themselves reflected in its unflattering portraits.
Students at Rahi Masoom Raza memorial convent school paying floral tributes to him.
At Peeli Kothi, also known as Bashir Manzil, where Rahi spent his early years, family memories offer a glimpse of the experiences that shaped his imagination. His niece Samar Rizwi recalled how polio restricted the six-year-old’s life for months.
His attendant, Kallu Kaka, kept him company with stories, including tales from Hindu mythology. “We believe those years came in handy when he later wrote dialogues for Mahabharat,” she said. Rahi also took to reading during this period.His nephew and filmmaker Asif Jah recalled that Rahi’s father, Bashir Saab, often hosted poets at home, exposing him to the literary world and nurturing his early interest in Urdu poetry. “People are taking up PhDs on his work even today which speaks volumes for his stature. He deserves more,” he said.

She keenly follows stories that celebrate hope and life in general.

Lithuania raises alarm over counterfeit cigarettes from Latvia as smuggling routes shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:17:27 UTC
19:17:27 KST

The smuggling of counterfeit tobacco products from Latvia into Lithuania is increasing after authorities stepped up efforts to curb cigarette smuggling from Belarus using weather balloons, Donatas Škarnulis, acting head of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, announced on Monday.
"The overall shift in trends shows that the share of tobacco smuggling from Belarus is declining. Looking at developments over several years, counterfeit tobacco products from Latvia are now becoming dominant, with a larger proportion coming from Latvia than from Belarus," Škarnulis told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
Škarnulis said that efforts to combat smuggling using weather balloons have been effective.
"Last year, approximately 200 people were held accountable in cases involving balloons alone. This year, we also have dozens of cases. This is our ongoing work, and it is certainly producing results," the acting border guard chief said.
"This year alone, the number of shipments transported by balloons is three times lower than last year, while the quantity of tobacco products brought in this way has fallen by approximately half," he added.
According to Škarnulis, these results have been achieved through preventive measures carried out by border guards, police and customs officers, as well as criminal intelligence operations and pre-trial investigations conducted by the State Border Guard Service and police.
Data published by Lithuania's State Border Guard Service last week show that Lithuanian authorities have intercepted 182 shipments of smuggled cigarettes transported from Belarus by weather balloons so far this year.
By comparison, 635 such shipments were intercepted last year, while 226 were recorded in 2024.
Border guards have also brought down 67 smuggling drones carrying illegal tobacco shipments from Belarus into Lithuania this year.
Last year, 59 such drones were intercepted, compared with 54 in 2024.
Lithuania has introduced a range of measures to combat smuggling, including declaring a national-level emergency and conducting law enforcement operations.
These operations have also uncovered suspicions that border guards and police officers may have been involved in smuggling activities.
Lithuanian leaders regard the airspace violations caused by smuggling balloons as a hybrid attack by the Minsk regime.

Lula wins Brazil presidential election as Bolsonaro refuses to accept defeat
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:15:44 EET
19:15:44 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office after defeating right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday's presidential election runoff, overturning his first-round defeat in a contest that ended with his opponent refusing to recognise the result.
Lula, 80, secured 51.79% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court. The president received 64.26 million votes, compared with 59.83 million for his challenger, a margin of more than 4.4 million.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The result makes Lula the first Brazilian president to win four non-consecutive terms.
Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, rejected the outcome and announced plans to seek annulment of the election.
He challenged a Supreme Court decision extending voting by two hours on Sunday following complaints about transport problems and weather conditions.
"It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.
Both campaigns had requested additional voting time. Lula's representatives cited transport shortages affecting voters in several cities, while Bolsonaro's campaign raised concerns about heavy rainfall in southern Brazil.
Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, a former lawyer for Lula, authorised the extension. The electoral court subsequently confirmed the result.
Electoral law specialists interviewed by BBC News Brasil said annulment was unlikely, citing Lula's margin of victory and the fact that both campaigns had sought extensions.
Lula's victory followed a reversal between the two voting rounds. Bolsonaro finished first on 4 October with approximately 47%, ahead of Lula's 45%.
The president subsequently increased his support through campaigning, social media mobilisation and efforts to encourage voter participation.
Lula gained ground across Brazil's north-east and overturned Bolsonaro's first-round lead in Minas Gerais. He also moved ahead in 211 municipalities, including Rio de Janeiro.
Thousands of supporters gathered in São Paulo to celebrate the result.
Speaking after his victory, Lula thanked voters and promised changes to his administration.
"No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," he said.
Lula previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010 and returned to office in January 2023 after defeating Jair Bolsonaro.
The former president is serving a 27-year sentence following his conviction for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
Despite Lula's victory, right-wing parties gained seats in Congress, leaving the president facing opposition to his legislative programme.
His campaign focused on poverty reduction, employment, social spending and environmental protection.
International leaders congratulated Lula, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
"Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil," von der Leyen wrote on X.
US President Donald Trump, whose administration supported the Bolsonaro political camp, had not publicly responded to the result as of Monday morning.
Lula's fourth presidential term is scheduled to begin on 5 January 2027 and run until 2030.

2.92 metres: German angler lands giant catfish from Polish reservoir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:15:10 UTC
19:15:10 KST

Oliver Schäfer from the Eifel and his fishing partner landed a 2.92-metre catfish at a tournament in Poland. The fish is already well known among anglers.
When Oliver Schäfer feels what is on the other end of his line, he quickly realises that this is no ordinary fish. The 34-year-old, from the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, is taking part in a predator fishing tournament in the southern Polish city of Rybnik in Poland, together with his Dutch fishing partner Kevin Cremers.
On 10 and 11 October, 70 teams with around 150 anglers from all over Europe competed there, according to the German newspaper Bild. Schäfer and Cremers had travelled specifically for the event. As Schäfer told the newspaper, the pair were fishing with a special rod designed for large catfish and a soft plastic lure.
Schafer only grasped how enormous his adversary was when the fish broke the surface for the first time. The fight lasted more than 30 minutes. Cremers kept the boat on course against the wind, while Schäfer held.
Measured and released again
Back on shore, judges measured the catfish at 292 centimetres. It was then returned to the lake, as tournament rules require. Schäfer told Bild that the fish are brought ashore on a tarpaulin so that their protective mucus slime layer is not damaged.
However, the catch alone was not enough to win the tournament, which was decided on total points. According to the Berliner Zeitung and the results list of the anglers’ association PZW Katowice published by the Katowice branch of the Polish Angling Association (PZW), the duo finished second with 28,930 points.
There are, of course, other impressive specimens in the lake as well. On Instagram, Schäfer reports that he and Cremers targeted zander at sunrise. Their catches, including a fish measuring 81 centimetres, earned them "a good number of points" for the overall standings.
Is it the same fish caught last year?
The catfish has a backstory. According to media reports, participants believe it is the same fish that was caught during the tournament in October 2025. On that occasion, Polish anglers Krzysztof Pyra and Adrian Gontarz landed a catfish that also measured 292 centimetres. The Berliner Zeitung reports that the fish has not grown any longer since, but has become noticeably more bulkier.
International Game Fish Association (IGFA), the sport’s global governing body, keeps catfish records by weight, and there is no official list based on length. According to the German daily Welt Die Welt, Italian angler Alessandro Biancardi landed a catfish measuring 2.85 metres from the River Po in 2023.
The Polish city of Rybnik in the Silesian Voivodeship is therefore regarded, especially among anglers, as the place where the longest known catfish has been caught.
Schäfer’s dream of a three-metre catfish remains alive even after this angling success. He told BILD he was now "just a hand’s breadth" away.
Europe’s largest freshwater fish
According to Germany’s Federal Agency for Nature Conservation, the European catfish is the continent’s largest native freshwater fish. It can grow up to three metres long and weigh as much as 150 kilograms. Striking features include its scaleless body, broad head and six barbels that help it find its way in murky water.
It feeds mainly on fish; larger individuals occasionally prey on small waterbirds or mammals. For 2026, the anglers’ association, the Federal Agency for Nature Conservation and the Ichthyological Society have chosen the catfish as fish of the year.
Thriving in warmer waters
Originally, the catfish was native mainly to the Danube and Rhine river systems. Stocking programmes dating back to the 19th century and waterways such as the Main-Danube Canal have since opened up many more habitats to the species, according to the agency.
Climate change is also helping. As a warmth-loving species, catfish benefit from rising water temperatures. Biologist Jürgen Geist told the German news magazine Focus that populations are increasing markedly, both in range and in density. By contrast, cold-water species such as the brown trout are among the losers.
Warmth also plays a role in Rybnik. The reservoir serves as a cooling basin for a coal-fired power plant, and the heated water is discharged back into it. Because fish feed more actively at higher temperatures, catfish, carp and zander grow faster there, according to Schäfer.
Experts say the fish pose little danger to humans. They have only small rasping teeth, and outside the spawning season there is virtually no risk. However, in June 2025, a catfish measuring around two metres in length bit several swimmers in Brombachsee in Middle Franconia, causing minor injuries.

Missiles Reportedly Hit Russian Factory Powering Iskander and Kinzhal Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category

Missiles Reportedly Hit Russian Factory Powering Iskander and Kinzhal Missiles
A missile strike reportedly hit the Energia plant in Yelets, Russia’s Lipetsk region, on October 25, targeting a facility that manufactures power systems used in Russian ballistic and cruise missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to footage published by the open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 25, several suspected cruise missiles struck the industrial facility, approximately 300 kilometers from Ukraine’s border. Videos circulating online showed smoke rising from the area following the reported impacts.
Lipetsk regional governor Igor Artamonov confirmed an attack on an industrial zone in Yelets. The Energia plant specializes in developing and manufacturing chemical power sources, including batteries and other electrical components used in Russian military equipment.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR), Energia is a strategically important supplier to Russia’s defense industry. Its products are used in several missile systems, including the Iskander-M ballistic missile, Iskander-K cruise missile, Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, and Zircon missile.
The facility also manufactures 9B280-1 power units for 9M727 cruise missiles launched by the Iskander-K system and 9B-287 batteries for UMPB D-30SN guided glide bombs.
Additional components produced by the plant are used in universal glide and correction modules (UMPK), which allow conventional aerial bombs to be converted into guided weapons, as well as Kh-35U anti-ship missiles.
The extent of damage to the facility and any potential disruption to production have not yet been independently verified.
The reported strike follows a series of Ukrainian long-range attacks against Russian defense-industrial facilities involved in producing components for missiles, drones, and other military equipment.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces targeted the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Orel, another facility associated with Russia’s defense supply chain. Such operations have increasingly focused on industrial infrastructure supporting Russian weapons production.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan hold security talks in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:14:39 UTC
19:14:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey agreed on Monday to continue security consultations and strengthen regional cooperation following high-level talks in Tehran, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A joint statement issued after the first meeting between Iran and senior representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement confirmed that the four countries had agreed to maintain dialogue and consultations, particularly on regional peace, security and stability.
The meeting was hosted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
The statement said the participants had agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation between their countries, but did not announce any specific security agreement or new joint mechanism.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also received the three visiting officials earlier on Monday, calling on regional countries to overcome their differences and work together to address common security threats.
Pezeshkian said historical and religious ties between Muslim countries should provide the foundation for closer cooperation, expressing hope that the meeting would help establish mechanisms for regional security based on shared interests.
He accused Israel, with US support, of committing widespread crimes in Gaza, Lebanon and other countries before extending its attacks to Iranian territory, including strikes that killed military commanders, scientists and civilians.
The Iranian president argued that military and economic pressure had failed to weaken Iran or force it to surrender, instead strengthening domestic solidarity and determination to defend the country's sovereignty.
He also urged regional governments to turn political understandings into practical measures rather than limiting cooperation to statements and agreements that remain unimplemented.
Pezeshkian called for stronger economic, scientific and cultural ties, as well as easier movement and exchanges between neighbouring countries.
He warned against attempts to inflame sectarian and political divisions, accusing Washington and Israel of seeking to weaken Muslim countries and deal with them individually.
Iran calls for regional security without foreign interference
Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the talks formed part of efforts to establish a regional security framework led by Middle Eastern countries rather than external powers.
Speaking to Iranian state television earlier on Monday, Bagheri Kani said the initiative had emerged during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when Iranian officials were informed of the three countries' intention to hold joint consultations.
He expressed hope that the discussions would contribute to regional stability and enable the participating countries to draw on one another's experience in addressing security threats.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the meeting would address developments in the occupied Palestinian territories and Lebanon, Israeli policies in the region and the consequences of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Baghaei described the talks as an opportunity to explore regional security arrangements based on the shared interests of neighbouring countries.
He said the initial consultations were intended to identify priorities and establish an agenda for further discussions.
Pezeshkian reiterates Iran's nuclear position
During his meeting with the visiting delegation, Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran was not seeking nuclear weapons and that its nuclear programme was intended for peaceful purposes.
He stressed Tehran's right to peaceful nuclear activities under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The Iranian president also criticised Washington's contradictory approach of expressing willingness to negotiate while threatening military strikes against Iranian facilities.
He argued that such threats undermined confidence in diplomacy and made it more difficult to reach lasting agreements.
Pezeshkian said Iran would continue defending its rights and interests under international law and urged regional countries to coordinate their positions to prevent further military attacks.
Saudi Arabia backs efforts to reduce tensions
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said the visit by Prince Khalid bin Salman and representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was part of continuing efforts to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
The ministry said the discussions supported mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan aimed at preventing another confrontation between Iran and the United States.
Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Raed Krimly also said the talks reflected the role the agreement's member states hoped to play in promoting regional stability through dialogue.
The diplomatic efforts come amid intensifying tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement, which has continued launching attacks against the kingdom.
The possibility of renewed US-Israeli military action against Iran has also raised concerns that another confrontation could spread across the region.
Qatar steps up mediation amid fears of renewed war
Monday's meeting followed the arrival of a Qatari delegation in Tehran on Sunday evening as part of Doha's efforts to prevent further escalation between Washington and Tehran.
A source familiar with regional mediation efforts told The New Arab that the visit was intended to build on continuing diplomatic contacts aimed at preventing the conflict from worsening.
The source said Iran had already communicated its positions and demands clearly to mediators.
Baghaei confirmed that the Qatari delegation's visit formed part of ongoing regional consultations, covering both bilateral cooperation and Doha's mediation efforts.
He said the exchange of messages and diplomatic initiatives between regional countries was important amid the current tensions.
Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States throughout the conflict.
Iran warns against another military confrontation
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday against renewed US military action, saying Tehran would maintain its regional policies regardless of whether another war broke out.
Araghchi said that although there was growing discussion of another conflict, he was already considering what would happen after it ended.
He argued that previous military confrontations had demonstrated the consequences of attempting to resolve disputes with Iran through force.
The foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's position that lasting regional security could only be achieved through cooperation between neighbouring countries without foreign interference.
He stressed that Iran remained prepared to work with Gulf states and other regional countries to establish a more stable security environment.

Breadcrumb
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey agreed on Monday to continue security consultations and strengthen regional cooperation following high-level talks in Tehran, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A joint statement issued after the first meeting between Iran and senior representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement confirmed that the four countries had agreed to maintain dialogue and consultations, particularly on regional peace, security and stability.
The meeting was hosted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
The statement said the participants had agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation between their countries, but did not announce any specific security agreement or new joint mechanism.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also received the three visiting officials earlier on Monday, calling on regional countries to overcome their differences and work together to address common security threats.
Pezeshkian said historical and religious ties between Muslim countries should provide the foundation for closer cooperation, expressing hope that the meeting would help establish mechanisms for regional security based on shared interests.
He accused Israel, with US support, of committing widespread crimes in Gaza, Lebanon and other countries before extending its attacks to Iranian territory, including strikes that killed military commanders, scientists and civilians.
The Iranian president argued that military and economic pressure had failed to weaken Iran or force it to surrender, instead strengthening domestic solidarity and determination to defend the country's sovereignty.
He also urged regional governments to turn political understandings into practical measures rather than limiting cooperation to statements and agreements that remain unimplemented.
Pezeshkian called for stronger economic, scientific and cultural ties, as well as easier movement and exchanges between neighbouring countries.
He warned against attempts to inflame sectarian and political divisions, accusing Washington and Israel of seeking to weaken Muslim countries and deal with them individually.
Iran calls for regional security without foreign interference
Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the talks formed part of efforts to establish a regional security framework led by Middle Eastern countries rather than external powers.
Speaking to Iranian state television earlier on Monday, Bagheri Kani said the initiative had emerged during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when Iranian officials were informed of the three countries' intention to hold joint consultations.
He expressed hope that the discussions would contribute to regional stability and enable the participating countries to draw on one another's experience in addressing security threats.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the meeting would address developments in the occupied Palestinian territories and Lebanon, Israeli policies in the region and the consequences of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Baghaei described the talks as an opportunity to explore regional security arrangements based on the shared interests of neighbouring countries.
He said the initial consultations were intended to identify priorities and establish an agenda for further discussions.

IN BRIEF: What is known about FSB’s thwarted attack on Moscow air defense site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:14:27 UTC
19:14:27 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained two men from the South Caucasus who, acting on orders from the Ukrainian State Security Service (SBU), were preparing an attack using FPV drones against one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility, the FSB press office reported.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Thwarting of terrorist attack
- The FSB thwarted the sabotage and terrorist activities of two men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, the press office reported.
- According to the Federal Security Service, the men were going to prepare attack drones obtained from hidden stashes, transport them to the Moscow Region for launch, and activate them before takeoff.
- It was specified that the drones were to be controlled remotely from Ukrainian territory.
- While preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electric power facility and one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system, the suspects were detained by FSB officers, the press office said.
- The FSB released a video showing the FPV drones that the two detainees, natives of the South Caucasus, were using, on orders from the SBU, to prepare an attack on one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility.
- A video provided by the FSB press office shows the suspects assembling the drones and getting them ready for use according to instructions from their handler.
- The video shows two drones, both disassembled and assembled, as well as the communication devices used by the agents and instructions for assembling the drones.
Recruitment
- According to the FSB, one of the detainees was recruited by an SBU officer. Acting on his orders and in exchange for a promised monetary reward, the detainee traveled to Russia to plan a terrorist attack.
- To this end, he enlisted the help of a close acquaintance. Together, they retrieved FPV drones and components for homemade explosive devices from hiding places in the Smolensk and Kaluga Regions.
- The FSB had prior intelligence indicating that individuals from the South Caucasus were preparing an FPV drone attack on air defense and energy facilities in Moscow on behalf of the SBU. These individuals were agents of the Ukrainian special services, just like their handler, an FSB officer reported.
- The operation involving the handlers is ongoing, he noted.
Investigation
- A criminal case has been initiated against the detainees under Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code (Participation in a Terrorist Organization).
- The court remanded them into custody.
- The Federal Security Service is conducting the necessary investigative and operational measures to establish all the circumstances of the suspects’ illegal activities and their possible connections, the press office noted.

Burnham wants UK back in EU within his lifetime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:13:20 UTC
19:13:20 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives to address a press conference with the German Chancellor at the Chancellery in Berlin on October 8, 2026. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Monday his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.
Asked by ITV's Good Morning Britain Monday whether he wanted to rejoin the EU, Burnham said: “I'm going to be honest and say, in my lifetime, I would like to see that happen but I am not going to move ahead of the public.
“I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the public, the British public, are the bosses.”
Advertisement
At the ruling Labour Party's conference last month, Burnham called for closer links with the EU.
He has yet to spell out precise details of the relationship he would seek — but the party's 2024 election-winning manifesto under Keir Starmer ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or accepting freedom of movement with the bloc.
Burnham said Monday that the promises of the 2016 referendum that took Britain out of the EU have not been delivered.
“We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign,” he said. “It's weakened our economy. It's also weakened our control of immigration and that might surprise people.”
But he said: “I'm not proposing rejoining in this Parliament. We're way, way away from that at this particular moment in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better than the arrangement we've got right now.”
The PM's remarks come after he told the Sunday Times that accepting freedom of movement with the bloc should not be off the table in future negotiations.
Advertisement
A U.K.-EU summit is scheduled for next month, although that is set to focus tightly on technical tweaks to the existing relationship rather than addressing bigger questions of Britain's future ties to the bloc.
Burnham's decision to reignite debate in Britain about the EU has already provoked a bullish response from some of Brexit's leading cheerleaders.
Speaking at a Westminster press conference Monday, Nigel Farage said rejoining the bloc would be “utterly moronic” and argued Brexiteers would win a referendum on reversing the result “very comfortably.”
“Listen, Brexit would not have happened if I had not been born — all right, simple as that," the Reform UK leader said Monday. "Yes, there were some Johnny-Come-Latelies. They came in at five minutes to midnight. Am I up for the fight again? You bet your blooming life I am.”

Syria to launch 1st nationwide mine map under 3-year clearance strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:12:36 UTC
19:12:36 KST

Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Syria will soon launch its first map showing the distribution of mines across the country as part of a three-year strategy to combat landmines and war remnants, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Monday.
“The National Mine Action Center is implementing the strategy to identify mine-contaminated areas and strengthen efforts to address the threat,” al-Saleh said in comments carried by the ISNA news agency.
“Mines and unexploded remnants of war remain among the most serious challenges facing Syria because of their direct impact on civilians and children, as well as their obstruction of reconstruction efforts and the use of agricultural land,” he said.
Al-Saleh said his ministry continues to develop mine-clearance plans and strategies despite existing challenges, with the aim of achieving tangible results that protect civilians and allow residents to make use of their farmland.
“Syria is also working to exchange expertise and benefit from advanced demining technologies in cooperation with Germany and Ukraine,” he added.
Separately, the minister said the ministry is working to establish a joint operations room with Türkiye for emergency response and disaster management on both sides of the border.
The mechanism is intended to spee coordination and response to fires, floods and other disasters, he added.
Syrian authorities regularly report deaths and injuries caused by explosions from remnants of the war waged by the Bashar al-Assad regime against civilians from 2011 to 2024.
The war killed and injured hundreds of thousands of people and caused massive destruction to infrastructure before opposition fighters entered Damascus on Dec. 8, 2024, leading to the fall of the Assad regime.
Syrian authorities and international organizations, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, continue field operations in several parts of Syria to detect mines and unexploded ordnance left by the war.
According to Landmine Monitor data, unexploded ordnance in Syria has killed or injured more than 13,000 people since 2011.

Jordan: 3 arrested over deadly church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria
October 26, 2026
Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.
Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.
Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.
But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.
A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.
Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province
Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.
Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.
"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."
He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.
"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.
Who carried out the attack in Jordan?
There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.
Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn and Wesley Dockery
