Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment in over 50 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:10:40 UTC
19:10:40 KST

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment in over 50 years
Algeria’s parliament on Sunday approved a resolution to send troops to Niger, making the first time Algerian soldiers will be deployed abroad since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including near its border with Algeria, and the deployment comes as Algiers and Niamey are building the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline after decades of delays.
Algeria on Sunday approved sending troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy facilities, according to statements from both houses of parliament, in what is the country's first foreign deployment of military forces since the 1970s.
The rare measure comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.
The overseas deployment will be a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The upper house approved the proposal, it said in a statement, with a legislator telling AFP it was approved by all 148 members in attendance.
The parliament's lower house said it also voted "by an absolute majority" to deploy the military unit in Niger, though it did not provide numbers.
Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher, before the official confirmation.
"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.
The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.
Read moreTrans-Saharan Gas Pipeline: an African dream that could reshape world energy markets
'Strong signal'
Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" – two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.
Read moreAlgeria cuts diplomatic ties with United Arab Emirates over 'provocative and hostile actions'
Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".
Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means – dialogue, international law, multilateral forums", Porter told AFP.
"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved towards more tangible means – actual physical presence."
"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."
Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.
"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on October 3. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."
"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."
The deployment of troops outside Algeria's territory required the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.
Gifted warplanes
The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.
A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.
The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.
Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.
Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.
The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.
Niger has been run by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a July 2023 coup that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Witness in MP Labaziuk’s case sentenced for remaining silent
Kyiv • UNN
Witness in the case of MP Labaziuk was convicted for refusing to testify. The court imposed a fine of UAH 3,400.
In Kyiv, a court handed down a verdict to a witness in the case of a member of parliament accused of attempting to bribe top officials in the reconstruction sector, for refusing to testify at the High Anti-Corruption Court. The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office reported this on October 26, UNN writes.
According to a source who spoke to UNN, the case concerns MP Labaziuk.
On October 26, 2026, the Solomianskyi District Court of Kyiv handed down a verdict against a person—a witness in the case involving a sitting MP and his accomplice, who were exposed while providing an unlawful benefit to the Deputy Prime Minister for Restoration of Ukraine—the Minister for Communities and Territories Development of Ukraine—and the Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine
Before beginning the witness's examination, as stated, "the court established that there were no circumstances that would make it impossible for him to testify." He was then sworn in and warned of criminal liability for refusing to testify. However, when the prosecutor began asking questions, the witness refused to testify.
In connection with this, the witness was notified of suspicion of refusing to testify. In February 2026, the indictment in the case was sent to the Solomianskyi District Court for consideration on the merits.
"Having heard the parties' arguments, the court found the person guilty of committing the offense provided for in Part 1 of Article 385 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and imposed a punishment in the form of a fine of UAH 3,400," the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office stated.
The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office noted that "the prosecutor is currently considering whether the punishment corresponds to the degree of gravity of the criminal offense and the personality of the accused."
Update
As UNN reported, in November 2023, MP Serhii Labaziuk of the "For the Future" group was notified of suspicion of providing a bribe to the then Deputy Prime Minister for Restoration of Ukraine—the Minister for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine (Oleksandr Kubrakov)—and the Head of the State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine (Mustafa Nayyem).

France Tests HELMA-P Laser Anti-Drone System Aboard Charles de Gaulle Aircraft Carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:10:30 UTC
19:10:30 KST

The French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle tested a laser anti-drone system during the La Fayette 26 mission.
The system was tested on the ship’s flight deck between June 4 and 8, according to the French Navy’s magazine Cols Bleus, as reported by Zone Militaire.
The experiment took place while the aircraft carrier was docked in the Gulf of Oman. A joint team of specialists from the Centre for Military Aviation Expertise (CEAM) and the ground-based air defense division was involved in deploying the system.
Installing the equipment aboard the ship took about four hours. The system comprises a camera turret, a LIDAR, a laser emitter, a cooling unit and a control console.
Although Cols Bleus described this as the system’s first shipboard test, the published photo shows the HELMA-P system in use.
In June 2023, the French military first tested the laser on the deck of the Forbin frigate. At the time, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces noted the laser’s high accuracy and effectiveness.
Development of the HELMA-P (High Energy Laser for Multiple Applications – Power) system began in 2017 by CILAS. The project is being carried out under the L2AD program to develop laser weapons for countering drones.
Before its sea trials, HELMA-P successfully completed ground tests in 2020 and 2021. The system was also deployed to provide security during the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris.
Technically, HELMA-P is a directed-energy weapon integrated with target detection and tracking systems. It is designed to neutralize small drones and other ‘asymmetric’ threats.
During operation, the laser uses a powerful beam to destroy the target’s structure within seconds.
The Charles de Gaulle is not the only aircraft carrier equipped with similar weaponry. In October 2025, the US aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush tested the LOCUST system and subsequently used it in the Gulf of Oman.

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:06:16 UTC
19:06:16 KST

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. Real-time observation of topological defect dynamics mediating two-dimensional skyrmion lattice melting. Nature Nanotechnology, 2025; 20 (10): 1405 DOI: 10.1038/s41565-025-01977-2

After Vucic defeat, Serbia waits to see how student-backed leaders will govern

After Vucic defeat, Serbia waits to see how student-backed leaders will govern
- Student-backed candidates won a landslide in Serbia, taking 52.7% of the vote and 139 of 250 seats, after two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
- Aleksandar Vucic, who led Serbian politics since 2014, conceded defeat after protests linked to the deaths of 16 people in the Novi Sad station canopy collapse.
- The win marks a major political shift, but the movement has no clear leaders yet, raising questions over who will govern and how it will fight graft and improve schools.
AI generated
BELGRADE – Serbia woke to a new era on Oct 26 after a student-backed protest movement unseated long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic in a historic landslide election that sparked nationwide celebrations, although few had an idea of how they would govern.
Tens of thousands took to the streets of Belgrade and other cities and towns across Serbia after Vucic conceded defeat late on Oct 25, capping two years of peaceful anti-government protests calling for the populist ruler to step down.
With almost 99% of votes counted, the students’ candidates had secured a commanding 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Election Commission, versus 39.2% for Vucic’s Serbia Progressive Party (SNS)-led alliance.
That gives the students 139 seats in the 250-seat Parliament, leaving the SNS alliance with 97, and the remainder held by minority parties.
“I thought it was unbelievable, I still do not believe it. It was too long, and (Vucic) was pressuring us for a long, long time,” said university administrator Marijana Radovanovic Pajovic.
Vucic dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014. But he was swept from power by a list of student-backed candidates born out of anti-corruption protests following the deaths of 16 people in the collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad.
Profound political shift
The students’ win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April.
It may also offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.
However, the movement, with candidates including university professors, actors and farmers, has no clear leaders, and it is unclear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions in order to enact the students’ domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling.
“This corruption that has entered into all pores of our lives...of course it will change, we are hoping we will slowly go into that direction of a normal community,” said 60-year-old insurance worker Svetlana Karagkozidou.
Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory.
However, not everyone welcomed the change.
“Changing the country like that so suddenly and all at once, I don’t like it. I don’t even know who is standing behind, who those people are, who will be leading the country,” said 60-year-old civil worker Senka Radakovic.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption. REUTERS

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Emir Yildirim
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan (BoJ) will make monetary policy decisions this week in the face of inflation risks and the ongoing Middle East conflict.
While investors are monitoring persistently high energy prices and their impact on markets amid mounting concerns over the profitability of massive artificial intelligence (AI) investments, the three central banks will announce their policy decisions.
Energy costs rose even further due to risks of renewed escalation in the Middle East.
The rise in energy prices is expected to reignite inflation, prompting central banks to keep rates high for longer.
The Fed will make its monetary policy decision on Wednesday.
The bank has the influence to guide other central banks, so the steps taken and the guidance provided by Chair Kevin Warsh will determine the trajectory of global financial conditions.
The Fed raised its policy rate by 25 basis points last month to a range of 3.75%-4%.
Persistently high inflation in the US limited expectations of monetary easing and reinforced estimates that interest rates may remain high for longer. Analysts are also monitoring the possibility of further tightening and its potential impact on the US dollar and Treasury yields.
The ECB will announce its policy decision on Thursday, when the inflation trajectory in the eurozone, the economic growth outlook and the potential impact of rising energy prices on price stability will be the main topics.
The bank previously raised its three key policy rates by 25 basis points in September. It is expected to maintain rates at its upcoming meeting, but expectations of rate hikes at subsequent meetings remain high amid elevated oil prices and inflation risks.
Escalating protests in France continue to threaten public finances, intensifying selling pressure on French government bonds.
France’s 10-year bond yield rose to its highest level since 2002 at 5.07%, surpassing that of the US 10-year Treasury bond for the first time since 2013.
Germany’s Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 1.9% month-on-month and 6.7% on an annual basis in September, above estimates and faster than in August. The annual growth was the fastest since March 2023.
Meanwhile, the BoJ will decide its monetary policy on Friday following a decision to hike its policy rate to 1.25% last month.
Rising oil prices due to tensions in the Middle East fuel energy and inflation concerns, particularly affecting Asian economies that depend on energy imports.
Japan’s annual inflation reached 2.1% in September, in line with estimates, while its core inflation rose above 2% for the first time in nine months, supporting hawkish expectations.
While Japanese exports surged 16.7% on an annual basis in September, they fell short of estimates and slowed compared with August.
Strong demand for semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) products drove Japanese exports.
The BoJ is expected to maintain rates this week, but it may hike rates in December.
The outlook for inflation, wage growth and economic activity will shape the bank’s monetary policy.

Mexico: spectacular Catrina parade brings the dead to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:03:31 UTC
19:03:31 KST

Wearing extravagant headdresses, glittering gowns and painted skull faces transformed Mexico City's Paseo de la Reforma into a colourful procession on Sunday, 25 October, as thousands took part in the annual Catrinas Parade.
Dancers, couples dressed as skeletal brides and grooms, and even costumed dogs made their way through cheering crowds. Some participants wore illuminated outfits, while others displayed elaborate embroidery and striking headpieces. Make-up artists worked behind the scenes to create the distinctive Catrina look, with full face designs taking between 20 and 40 minutes.
The parade celebrates La Catrina, a skeletal figure created by illustrator José Guadalupe Posada more than a century ago and later popularised by artist Diego Rivera. Once a satire of European-inspired fashion, she has become one of Mexico's best-known cultural symbols.
The event forms part of the build-up to Día de los Muertos, celebrated mainly on 1 and 2 November, when families honour deceased relatives with altars, flowers, candles and offerings.
Mexico City is preparing an even larger parade on 31 October, with more than 4,000 performers, 12 floats and two giant balloons expected. The capital's Zócalo will also feature a 32-metre Catrina surrounded by millions of marigolds.
The festivities combine music, creativity and remembrance, turning the commemoration of the dead into a celebration of life.

Oil spill off UAE widens, satellite images show, prompting more beach closures
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:54 CET
19:01:54 KST

By Vinaya K and Federico Maccioni
DUBAI, Oct 26 (Reuters) - An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union’s Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict’s environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
The images provided by the EU’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
“The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed,” Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Water Research Center, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice.
The UAE’s marine life “is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters,” including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.
(Reporting by Vinaya K and Federico Maccioni, Editing by William Maclean)

The Polish painter Tamara de Lempicka (1894-1980) was a defining figure of Art Deco: an aesthetic movement of the early 20th century that fused modernist geometry with excitement and glamour to capture a new faith in progress. Her paintings frequently convey unapologetic female autonomy and desire amid the Jazz Age. In this instalment of the YouTube series Great Art Explained, the curator and video essayist James Payne and the art historian Laura Beardsell-Moore explore how Lempicka’s life and times shaped her work – from her affluent upbringing and flight from the Russian Revolution to her experience in 1920s Paris. In particular, they dissect how her most famous painting, Autoportrait (Tamara in the Green Bugatti) (1929), depicted nothing less than a new, deeply modern conception of womanhood.

The hullaballoo contributed to his leaving Aligarh Muslim University, where he was working as a lecturer,” he said adding that he moved to Bombay thereafter.A former student Nadeem Adhami loved his teacher’s wit. “Unka andaz bada dostana tha,” he said adding, “he would crack jokes on himself which takes a big heart and an open mind.”
Rahi's student, Dr Nadeem Adhami
Citing a memory Adhami said: “Rahi used to limp because of the polio inflicted leg… but instead of being touchy about it, he said… Kaun Kehta hai ki rahi langda hai; jo Marris Road (where Aligarh Muslim University Women’s College is located) tak daud jaye wo langda ho hi nahi sakta.”Urdu enthusiast and former chief secretary Anis Ansari remembered how students were mesmerised by his handsome personality. “People felt that khuda ne unko fursat se banaya tha… He was hard to ignore in a room filled with 40-50 people,” he said.
Verse to prose.
Raza’s persona followed him to the Bollywood. Writer and film maker Amit Khanna admitted that in his early years, he was not fully aware of Rahi’s literary contributions to Hindi and Urdu but deeply felt his intellectual streak.“Urdu poet Majrooh Sultanpuri told me about his about Raza saab’s importance in literary circles… But there was something scholarly in his bearing and Tehzeeb dripped from his words,” he said.Not just in work, Raza left a lasting impression on people he met.“A true literary maestro, Rahi Chacha was in a league of his own in both Urdu and Hindustani. He did not merely play with words; he had an extraordinary understanding of human expression and emotion that gave dialogues a soul,” said actor turned politician Raj Babbar who often turned to him for clearing doubts and followed his advice even when they did not make sense to him.
Real to reel
Film maker Subhash Ghai also swears that he can never forget Dr Rahi. “A witty man, he was like family to me… So, he had to push his pen to write the dialogues of my first film production Karz. But all his work was better than Karz,” Ghai wrote.Calling Rahi his ‘Manas Pita’ and his visit to Ghazipur a pilgrimage, voice artist Harish Bhimani said: “like a father he envisioned the birth of Samay (the narrator in Mahabharat) and shaped him in every episode like a mother.”He also recalled how Rahi’s teaching never let success get into his head. “Once he told me apni avaz se nahi andaz se logon ko apna banao… and I follow this principle till date,” Bhimani said.
1959
To his niece Samar Rizwi, Raza is a jewel in her crown. “Some children are known by their family names while others became their family name. He is a jewel not just in the crown of our family but also that of Indian society who continues to sparkle,” she said.“Rahi’s writing combined Indianness with revolutionary thought and an uncompromising fight against casteism and communalism. He was deeply secular, and his command over Hindu mythology was remarkable,” said noted anthropologist Prof Nadeem Hasnain and close relative.
The love for Raza continues to linger, believes actor and producer, Rahul Mitra. “The most striking thing about him is that he called himself the son of three mothers – Nafisa Begum (his biological mother), AMU his alma mater and Ganga the great river along which he lived,” he said.
Asif Azmi, convenor Maati Foundation.
The programme concluded with attendees lighting earthen lamps in Raza’s memory, reaffirming their commitment to keeping his literary legacy alive. “Ideas don’t die when writers like Raza give them a life beyond their own,” said Asif Azmi, convenor of Maati Trust, which is organising 100 programmes to mark the occasion.Calling those who draw inspiration from Rahi’s work his “intellectual heirs”, Azmi said they had a responsibility to introduce his writing and ideas to the next generation.
Journalist with the Times of India since August 2004, Shailvee Sharda writes on Health, Culture and Politics. Having covered the length and breadth of UP, she brings stories that define elements like human survival and its struggle, faiths, perceptions and thought processes that govern the decision making in everyday life, during big events such as an election, tangible and non-tangible cultural legacy and the cost and economics of well-being. She keenly follows stories that celebrate hope and life in general.

Tainan to open second urgent care center in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tainan will open its second urgent care center on Nov. 1, expanding access to medical care for patients with minor illnesses and injuries on Sundays and national holidays, the city government said.
The National Health Insurance Administration launched the UCC program in November last year to treat patients whose conditions do not require hospital emergency care. The centers are staffed by doctors from local clinics on a rotating basis and provide internal medicine, pediatric, and surgical services when regular clinics are closed, according to CNA.
The program initially established 13 sites across Taiwan's six special municipalities. Tainan's first UCC, launched in partnership with Yongchuan Hospital, recorded 10,687 patient visits from November 2025 through September 2026, the highest total among all sites nationwide.
The center has averaged more than 100 patient visits per operating day. The city said it has also helped reduce the burden on hospital emergency departments.
To expand access to care, a second UCC will open in West Central District in partnership with Da-An Women and Children Hospital. It will draw on the hospital's pediatric and obstetrics and gynecology services, treating children with acute symptoms and women with common gynecological conditions.
Starting in November, both centers will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight on Sundays and national holidays.
Taipei is also planning to establish another UCC near National Taiwan University Hospital, though arrangements have yet to be finalized. Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said other cities and counties may also apply to establish UCCs based on local medical needs.

Scientists identify rare mutations in 36 genes that sharply raise the odds of OCD and tic disorders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:37 UTC
19:00:37 KST

A large-scale genetic analysis has identified 36 genes carrying rare mutations that substantially increase the likelihood of developing obsessive-compulsive disorder, chronic tic disorders, or both. By pinpointing specific biological pathways and brain regions where these genes are active, the research offers new insights into how these overlapping conditions develop. The study was published in Nature Neuroscience.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, commonly known as OCD, is a psychiatric condition defined by unwanted, intrusive thoughts or mental images, called obsessions, alongside repetitive physical behaviors or mental routines, called compulsions, that a person performs to ease their distress. Chronic tic disorders (CTDs), which include Tourette syndrome, involve persistent, involuntary motor movements or vocal sounds that are often preceded by an uncomfortable physical sensation or urge.
Both conditions affect roughly 1 to 2 percent of the global population and frequently appear together in the same individuals. About half of all people with chronic tic disorders experience obsessive-compulsive symptoms, while 20 to 30 percent of people diagnosed with OCD have a history of tics.
Because both disorders tend to run in families, scientists know they have a strong genetic component. Much of the inherited risk comes from common genetic variations that each contribute a tiny amount to a person’s overall susceptibility. For instance, a 2026 study of Korean participants found that genetic risk scores built from European data on OCD, schizophrenia, and anorexia nervosa were each modestly associated with having OCD. Alongside these common, small-effect variations, a smaller fraction of cases involve rare genetic mutations that have a large impact on individual risk.
Finding these rare, high-impact mutations is helpful because they allow scientists to trace direct biological routes from a specific disrupted gene to changes in brain development. Prior to this investigation, researchers had only confirmed four high-confidence risk genes carrying rare mutations for these conditions: two for OCD and two for chronic tic disorders.
Lead author Belinda Wang, an assistant professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at the University of California, San Francisco, who directs the Belinda Wang Lab, conducted the study alongside Gary A. Heiman, a professor in the Department of Genetics at Rutgers, the State University of New Jersey. They worked with a large international consortium of colleagues to expand this list by analyzing the protein-coding regions of the genome in a much larger group of patients, roughly doubling the sample sizes of earlier sequencing efforts.
“Many people with these disorders continue to experience debilitating symptoms despite treatment, and our limited understanding of the underlying biology makes it harder to develop more effective treatments,” Wang and Heiman told PsyPost. “By integrating data from the Tourette International Collaborative Genetics (TIC Genetics) study and the Foundation for OCD Research (FFOR) study, we identified substantially more genes contributing to the risk of both disorders than when each disorder was studied independently.”
To accomplish this, the researchers used a technique called whole-exome sequencing. While a person’s entire genome contains billions of DNA letters, only about 1 to 2 percent of that DNA actually provides the instructions for building proteins. Whole-exome sequencing physically isolates and reads just these protein-coding segments, known as the exome, where many large-effect disease mutations have been found. The team combined newly sequenced DNA samples with existing datasets to examine a total of 3,964 individuals diagnosed with OCD, chronic tic disorders, or both.
The patient sample was divided into two main groups based on family data availability. The first group consisted of 2,418 parent-child trios, which included an affected child and both of their biological parents, most of whom did not have either disorder. Studying complete trios allows scientists to spot “de novo” mutations, which are spontaneous genetic changes that appear for the first time in a child and were not inherited from either parent. The second group included 1,546 “singletons,” meaning affected individuals whose parents’ DNA was not available for comparison, all of whom had an OCD diagnosis and were of European ancestry.
For comparison, the researchers analyzed exome data from 1,734 control trios from the Simons Simplex Collection, consisting of unaffected siblings of children with autism and their parents, as well as 2,380 unaffected parents who served as singleton controls. When comparing the singleton groups, the researchers statistically controlled for biological sex and genetic ancestry to prevent population differences from skewing the results. Across all participants, the team looked specifically for two types of damaging genetic changes: likely gene-disrupting mutations, which prematurely cut short or scramble a protein’s blueprint, and severe missense mutations, which swap out a single amino acid in a way that is predicted to impair the resulting protein’s function.
The researchers first tested whether patients carried a higher overall burden of these damaging mutations than the unaffected controls, especially in genes that are known to be intolerant to mutation in the general human population. In the trio analyses, children with OCD or chronic tic disorders had higher rates of both spontaneous gene-disrupting mutations and severe spontaneous missense mutations compared to unaffected control children. By contrast, rare inherited variants passed down from parents were not more common in affected children than in controls, and the researchers found no differences between males and females in rates of spontaneous mutations.
Among the singletons, individuals with OCD also carried a higher frequency of rare gene-disrupting mutations in highly sensitive genes than the control group. Based on these comparisons, the authors estimated that roughly 7 to 8 percent of trio patients carry a spontaneous damaging mutation that contributes to their condition, while about 3 percent of singleton OCD patients carry a risk-contributing rare gene-disrupting variant.
Next, the scientists combined the evidence from both the spontaneous mutations in trios and the rare mutations in singletons to pinpoint specific culprit genes. The researchers labeled a gene high-confidence when the statistical evidence implied an estimated false discovery rate below 10 percent, meaning no more than about 1 in 10 genes on the list would be expected to be a false lead.
Analyzing the OCD cohort on its own yielded 12 high-confidence risk genes, while analyzing the chronic tic disorder cohort alone yielded 10. When the researchers pooled all the patients together into a single combined analysis, they identified 34 high-confidence risk genes, bringing the total number of distinct high-confidence genes identified across all analyses to 36. Four of these matched the genes known from earlier exome studies, and four, including one of those previously known genes, overlapped with genomic regions previously flagged in studies of common, small-effect OCD variants.
Mutations in these 36 genes were linked to large increases in risk. On average, carrying a damaging variant in one of these genes was associated with a 57-fold increase in the odds of having OCD or a chronic tic disorder, with individual genes ranging up to a 210-fold increase in odds compared to baseline expectations. Because these mutations are exceptionally rare in the general population, even a large relative increase means that only a small fraction of all people with OCD or tic disorders actually carry a mutation in any single one of these genes. Out of the 36 genes, 30 showed statistical support from both OCD and tic disorder cases, reinforcing the idea that the two conditions share biological roots.
“These are unusually strong genetic effects, giving us valuable clues about the underlying biology,” the researchers explained. “However, carrying one of these mutations does not make developing OCD or CTD inevitable.”
“Thirty of these genes had supporting evidence from both conditions, showing that studying genetically related disorders together can help us identify more of the genes involved,” Wang and Heiman added. “We are beginning to see evidence that these genes may affect some of the same biological processes. Understanding these shared processes could ultimately guide new treatments, potentially benefiting people beyond those who carry these particular genetic changes.”
The team also compared their newly identified genes against established genetic databases for other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions. The 36 genes showed substantial overlap with known risk genes for autism spectrum disorder, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and schizophrenia, but no overlap with genes tied to congenital heart disease.
To see where and when these genes operate, the researchers mapped them onto existing atlases of human and animal brain tissue across different stages of life. Like autism risk genes, the broader set of genes carrying spontaneous damaging mutations was especially active in the developing brain before birth. Unlike autism genes, however, the high-confidence OCD and tic disorder genes also showed elevated activity after birth, most strongly in the cerebellum and, more tentatively, in the striatum and thalamus.
At the cellular level, the genes tended to be most specifically active in excitatory projection neurons of the cortex and, more tentatively, in medium spiny neurons of the striatum. These specific cell types form the backbone of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit, a loop of brain regions that connects the brain’s outer layer, the cortex, to deeper structures involved in habit formation, movement control, and reward processing.
This aligns with a 2017 study covered by PsyPost, which found that eliminating specific synaptic receptors involved in the development of corticostriatal circuits caused mice to exhibit repetitive, OCD-like behaviors such as excessive grooming and continuous digging, though that earlier work relied on targeted genetic manipulations in animals rather than naturally occurring rare mutations in human patients.
A network analysis drawing on a database of known functional relationships between genes found that the 36 genes were more interconnected than expected by chance, with links to processes such as cell polarity, cilia, and the growth of nerve fibers. A separate database limited to direct physical contacts between proteins did not show the same pattern, which the authors suggest may reflect gaps in that resource.
“One striking finding was that these risk genes were more interconnected than expected,” Wang and Heiman noted. “Moreover, genes that interact with them also showed evidence of genetic risk for OCD or CTD. This pattern suggests that diverse genetic changes may converge on shared biological processes, although the specific mechanisms involved are still being elucidated.”
“We were also surprised to find that several of the risk genes encode proteins involved in the extracellular matrix, the material surrounding cells that helps organize their environment and shape brain circuitry and neuroplasticity,” the researchers said. “We are now investigating the proteins encoded by these genes to determine how their disruption may contribute to the development of OCD and CTD.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Whole-exome sequencing only examines the protein-coding portions of DNA, meaning the study did not capture mutations in the vast non-coding regions of the genome that regulate how genes are turned on and off, nor did it directly evaluate large structural deletions or duplications of DNA. The singleton analyses were also restricted to individuals of European descent to avoid statistical confounding, which limits how well those specific findings apply to other global populations.
In addition, among the parent-child families with OCD, tic status was unknown for 832, compared with just 36 confirmed to have no tics, which makes it harder to separate genes specific to one condition from shared ones. The authors also noted that incomplete clinical records prevented them from thoroughly testing whether specific mutations were tied to the exact age a patient’s symptoms began or to whether a person had both conditions.
“These findings do not mean that everyone with OCD or a CTD has a damaging mutation in one of these 36 genes,” Wang and Heiman emphasized. “Many different genetic and nongenetic factors can contribute, and much remains to be discovered. The findings also do not immediately change diagnosis or treatment, but they give us specific starting points for understanding the biology and working toward new, more effective treatments.”
Future research will need even larger and more ancestrally diverse patient cohorts to uncover the remaining genetic contributors, as statistical models in the paper estimate that roughly 550 genes contribute to risk for OCD, 1,100 for chronic tic disorders, and 760 when the conditions are combined. In the meantime, having a concrete list of 36 high-confidence genes gives neuroscientists a starting point for laboratory experiments. Researchers can now introduce these specific human mutations into cell cultures or animal models to observe how they alter brain wiring, which could help identify new biological targets for medications.
“We are moving in two directions: expanding our studies to find more large-effect risk genes, and understanding what these genes do and what goes wrong when they are disrupted,” the researchers told PsyPost. “To find more genes, we plan to recruit more individuals and families affected by OCD and CTD and sequence their DNA. In parallel, we are studying how these genes work together and how their disruption affects brain cells. Our long-term goal is to use that understanding to guide the development of new and more effective treatments.”
“This work depended on years of collaboration across the Foundation for OCD Research, Tourette International Collaborative Genetics, and many participating institutions,” Wang and Heiman concluded. “Perhaps most importantly, our conversations with individuals and families affected by these disorders continually remind us of why this work matters and of the hope that advances in genetics will lead to more effective, targeted treatments. While much work remains to be done, findings such as these bring us closer to that goal and provide a stronger foundation for understanding the biology of CTDs and OCD and, ultimately, improving care for those affected by them.”
The study, “Whole-exome sequencing in individuals with obsessive–compulsive disorder and chronic tic disorders identifies 36 large-effect risk genes,” was authored by Belinda Wang, Matthew N. Tran, Sheng Wang, Yuting Liu, Emily Olfson, George Wang, Nawei Sun, Jeanselle Dea, Charles Ochieng’ Olwal, Lyvia Bertolace, Michael H. Bloch, Carolina Cappi, Yi-Chieh Chang, Denise Chavira, Barbara J. Coffey, Martha J. Falkenstein, Adam C. Frank, Martin E. Franklin, Stephanie Garayalde, Helena Garrido, Marco Grados, Rami Hatem, Allyna-London Howell, Starlette Khim, Jennie M. Kuckertz, Mindy M. Le, Allison Libby, Ryan J. McCarty, Mary E. If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner Mueller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:28 UTC
19:00:28 KST

Whichever metaphor one prefers – landslide, earthquake, wave – it seems increasingly like the Democrats can expect a significant victory in the midterms.
As the joke goes, every gas station display of prices has become an ad for Democrats; what’s more, some of them have managed to connect the relatively abstract issue of corruption to the daily misery of many Americans.
But, in the end, no election outcome ever interprets itself; Democrats should not rest content with the conclusion that only what moderate leaders (and consultants) like to call kitchen table issues really mattered.
They have a historic opportunity to dislodge the image of the Republicans as the party of national security and the party best trusted with the economy.
After 2024, Republicans massively benefited from elite actors – Silicon Valley oligarchs, no less than many journalists – reading a globally important “vibe shift” into the presidential election outcome; we now know that what political scientists politely call “low-information voters” were simply fed up with inflation, as opposed to a large majority thirsting for a far-right agenda.
But Trumpists turned the perception to their advantage; and to be sure, successful politicians are entitled to interpret a vote as they see fit.
Democrats could stay relatively timid and read the outcome as simply a rejection of Donald Trump and the most egregious elements of his misrule since January 2025; they certainly should make the point that the spectacular cruelty of ICE and the incitement to hatred in which Stephen Miller and JD Vance regularly engage is deeply unpopular with the public. But it would be a mistake to see the outcome as only a referendum on Trumpism.
True, the US president’s catastrophic record in foreign policy is partly explained by conduct the old Republican establishment could never have imagined: recklessly alienating allies, with the result that the US may never be trusted by Nato countries again; massively destroying soft power by mistreating foreign students and undermining the capacity of American universities to attract talent internationally; blatant interference in elections to favor the global far right.
But the Iran war shows continuities with the George W Bush era that neoconservatives probably find uncomfortable to contemplate: an inability to think strategically and an apparent indifference to loss of human life. In fact, a line can be drawn from the torture memos to the murders at sea and the plans for a public execution under the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.
Yet the Republican party still lives off an image that the party of Ronald Reagan is supremely competent in matters of national security. The right response is not that Democrats should not enter a competition of how often they can use the word “lethality” in one sentence; they should simply point out how shameful it is that Republicans, some murmuring on the part of has-beens like Thom Tillis aside, have betrayed Ukraine; how damaging the loss of bases in the Middle East will turn out to be; and that, from the very beginning of Trump 2.0, it was a sign of deep unseriousness to put a second-rate TV host in charge of the world’s most powerful military force. There might be monuments to both Trump and Hegseth in Moscow and Beijing one day; after all, they effectively capitulated to the former and sped up the rise of the latter.
The Republican party has also long benefited from the notion that, as the party of business, they are best qualified to boost the economy (no doubt, some low-information voters still buy into the myth of Trump as the great entrepreneur).
The actual record has long shown something different: not just when it comes to Trump and his string of bankruptcies, but for the party as a whole. Since Trump engaged in policies so irrational and damaging that the old Republican establishment would never have contemplated them – tariffs being the obvious example – it is again easy to overlook continuities.
The party that claims to be deeply concerned about debt and deficits (one of Elon Musk’s disingenuous justifications for Doge’s chainsaw massacres) has given us Reagan, Bush and Trump – all of whom managed massively to increase the national debt. The reason is, of course, that they pushed through enormous tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy.
In the postwar period, economic growth, job creation and even stock market returns have on the whole been higher under Democratic administrations; it just seems that average gains are not enough for the uber-wealthy, who can buy themselves tax cuts by donating massively to Republicans.
Needless to say, as soon as Democrats are in charge, Republicans discover that the very debt they were instrumental in causing constitutes a national crisis and requires deep cuts to social security.
Conventional wisdom has it that the Biden administration overreached: too woke, too ambitious a Green New Deal, too harsh in its criticisms of Maga Republicans (with the next claim usually being that such overreach made a “backlash” inevitable and, so the implication goes, at least somewhat legitimate).
But what if the opposite is true? What if Joe Biden’s mistake was to assume that there were still many Republicans who cared about policy – as opposed to endless culture war performance a la Hegseth – and long-term success for the country?
What if Democrats seized the opportunity to discredit their opponents in the way Franklin D Roosevelt made the most of the Great Depression (as opposed to pining for bipartisanship); what if they showed people that all the Republicans who will soon be running away from Trump were not just complicit in the misrule, but that the misrule has been part of a larger story predating Trump?

If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:27 UTC
19:00:27 KST

After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.
I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.
Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.
Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.
This kind of talk isn’t cheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.
But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownership and investing on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.
Many of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures to provide breathing room in the face of the cost of living crisis.
Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.
So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the time John Healey finishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.
We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such as equalising income and capital gains tax.
The decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.
So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.
- Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

Carrying Iran’s flag at Youth Olympics a great honor, Faraji says
TEHRAN - Iranian table tennis sensation Benyamin Faraji has expressed his pride at being selected as Iran’s flagbearer for the Dakar Youth Olympic Games, while setting his sights on further success on the international stage.
Faraji and national futsal player Hadis Yari have been selected as Iran’s flag-bearers for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
The Youth Olympic Games will begin in Dakar on Oct. 30, with Iran set to compete across the event with 29 qualification places. Iran will look to make its mark at Dakar 2026, as its young athletes prepare to represent the country on one of the biggest international stages in youth sport.
Speaking after securing qualification for the World Table Tennis Championships in both singles and doubles, Faraji said he was delighted with his achievements, particularly given the tough competition.
“Thankfully, I managed to qualify for the World Championships in singles, and together with Arian Ghaffari, we also secured a place in the doubles event,” Faraji said.
“It was a major achievement, and I’m extremely happy. Considering the strong opponents we faced, I honestly didn’t expect us to qualify in doubles as well, but fortunately, we made it.”
The rising Iranian star also reflected on his recent performances at the Asian Games and Asian Championships, highlighting his victory over one of the world's top-ranked players.
“I performed well at the Asian Games and managed to defeat a player ranked 20th in the world, which was a fantastic result for me,” he said.
“I also delivered a strong performance at the Asian Championships, and I hope to maintain this momentum in upcoming competitions.”
Turning his attention to the Dakar Youth Olympic Games, Faraji insisted he is fully prepared for the challenge despite a demanding competition schedule that has left him with limited time for rest and recovery.
“I’m completely ready for the Dakar Games. Although I haven’t had much time to rest and recover, I’m determined to give my best and compete with everything I have,” he explained.
Faraji described his appointment as Iran’s flagbearer at the Dakar Youth Olympics as one of the proudest moments of his young career.
“Carrying Iran’s flag at the Dakar Youth Olympics is a tremendous honor, and I’m incredibly proud to have been given this responsibility,” he said.
“I hope to represent my country in the best possible way and make Iran proud through my performances.”
The talented paddler faces a busy period, with the Dakar Youth Olympics and the World Youth Table Tennis Championships in Istanbul both on his upcoming schedule.
“I have two major competitions ahead of me: the Dakar Youth Olympics and the World Youth Championships in Istanbul. My goal is to shine in both events,” Faraji stated.
“It’s going to be a challenging period because these major tournaments are taking place so close together. However, I’m ready for the challenge and determined to perform at my highest level.”
Despite already making a significant impact on the international table tennis scene at a young age, Faraji stressed that his ambitions extend far beyond his current achievements.
“I know I’ve accomplished some important things at my age, but this is only the beginning,” he concluded.
“I have much bigger goals in mind. I want to keep working hard, improving my game and achieving even greater success for myself and my country in the future.”

Why China’s heritage-listed Dog-Carrying Festival honours canines as sacred lifesavers

In a remote Miao village in southwestern China, dogs are honoured as life-saving heroes.
Every seventh month of the lunar calendar, residents of Jiaobang village in Jianhe county, Guizhou province, celebrate Tai Gou Jie, or the “Dog-Carrying Festival” – a unique folk tradition recognised as local intangible cultural heritage in 2015.
During the festival, villagers select a dog. Traditionally, it was a white female, but today adult males and native Xiasi dogs may also be chosen.

Politeness Has Changed. Our Language Shows How
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

The next time someone does you a favor, take a minute to note how they respond to “thank you.” You’ll likely find that the traditional “you’re welcome” is fast fading and being replaced by “no problem” or “no worries.”
We often treat politeness as a set of rules that people either follow or ignore. But the rules themselves are changing.
In the time of Old English (5th to 11th centuries), acting according to one’s rank and station was simply expected. Linguistic analysis shows very direct request forms, for example, “Thou shalt do X,” rather than the more modern, “Would you mind doing X?” And routine thanking, or saying “you’re welcome,” would have seemed odd in a time when people simply did what was required.
When Norman French started to enter English around 1066, the idea of courteous behavior also entered the language. An example would be the move toward switching between “you” and “thou” to appropriately show respect or intimacy, modeled on the French tu/vous distinction.
This concept of courtesy was central to how one expressed gratitude and, by the time we arrived in the early modern era (the time of Shakespeare), thanking was firmly established. However, routinely responding to those thanks was not common. If uttered at all, we’d more often hear something like a deferential, “I am but your humble servant.”
In the 18th century, elaborate complimenting routines became popular, and by the late 19th and early 20th century, English-speaking society had a greater focus on treating all people as equals. As a result, being aware of how one’s actions might impose upon others became increasingly important.
Requests that were once directly stated as imperatives were now couched with indirectness as merely suggestions or questions: “Shut the window,” became “Could you please shut the window?” And, in addition to saying “thanks,” responding with an acknowledgment of that thanks, such as “you’re welcome,” became routine.
This brings us to modern times. Today, “you’re welcome” is becoming less common. Instead, when someone says “thank you,” we reply with “not at all,” “no problem,” or “no worries.” This assures the person who expresses gratitude that no imposition was involved. In this way, we attempt to offset any social imbalance.
As a result, Americans who say “no problem” and those who always respond with “you’re welcome” can tend to believe the other camp sounds rude.
Those who prefer “no problem” often feel that “you’re welcome” has a condescending tone, while “you’re welcome” traditionalists feel like “no problem” suggests the favor could have been a problem. For instance, the sense that “you’re welcome” can have a bit of a smug, haughty tone has been played up by comedians like Will Ferrell in his 2009 Broadway show, You’re Welcome America, satirizing George W. Bush’s presidency.
Research confirms this shift toward expressions like “no problem” or “no worries” over “you’re welcome” is a generational one. In the norms of how we respond to thank you across generations, linguist Aaron Dinkin found that young Americans increasingly preferred “no problem” as the go-to polite response to “thank you.” Older speakers still felt “you’re welcome” was more appropriate, particularly when a favor required more than perfunctory gratitude.
So, the way someone responds to “thank you” is much more than a simple return on someone’s gratitude. These small words help us understand how politeness—and our expectations of one another—have changed over time.

Audi CEO's Trump rally appearance was with company's 'best interests in mind'
Audi on Monday issued a statement responding to "the current situation," as it coyly referred to the controversy following CEO Gernot Döllner's appearance with Donald Trump at an election rally in Georgia on Saturday.
Audi said that while a delegation was in Georgia for talks on its plans to open a production site in the US, "we were asked to present our plans publicly together with the President of the United States."
"We accepted this invitation solely with Audi's best interests in mind," the company wrote. "At the same time, we acknowledge that the circumstances surrounding the announcement may have been perceived as a political signal. We take this very seriously."
Audi said that it remained "firmly committed" to its values and principles but also said it had a "responsibility" to safeguard the company's economic future and believed these responsibilities went "hand in hand."
The company noted that it was currently not making a profit in the US, the second-largest premium car market on the planet, saying that producing in the country could help it rectify this and help secure Audi's "long-term success."
Despite expressing an intention to "provide context" on the decision and the approach taken, the statement neither named CEO Döllner or US President Trump, mentioned the upcoming US midterm elections, or spoke to the perceived poor judgment in Döllner appearing at a Republican Party campaign rally weeks before the vote.

Cruise captain investigated after Bremerhaven collision
German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven, forcing the cancellation of a 20-day voyage to the Canary Islands.
Police opened administrative offense proceedings to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. They have not specified the suspected lapse.
A gust of wind pushed the liner toward the container ships as tugboats assisted its departure on Sunday evening, police said. All three vessels were damaged, but none took on water and nobody was injured.

Germany's IG Metall union chief Christiane Benner has sharply criticized Audi CEO Gernot Döllner for appearing onstage at a campaign rally with US President Donald Trump.
Benner called the appearance "deeply embarrassing, politically unacceptable" and unworthy of Audi and its employees. She also accused Döllner of breaching the company's political neutrality rules.
Audi's code of conduct, published in April and signed by Döllner, bars public appearances with parties or politicians standing for election, and sponsorship of their events, during the three months before a vote.
Trump announced plans for an Audi factory in Georgia at Saturday's rally, with Döllner alongside him. The plant would produce around 200,000 vehicles annually, mainly large SUVs.
Benner stressed that the project still required approval, with the final decision "rightly and importantly" resting with Volkswagen's supervisory board, "with the full picture in mind."
She said employee representatives wanted safeguards for German sites alongside a clear North American strategy for Volkswagen and Audi. While acknowledging the US market's importance, she said IG Metall's priority was employment prospects in Germany.

Berlin Left leader says Dobrindt plan is unconstitutional
Berlin Left Party leader Elif Eralp has called Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt's proposal to restrict the socialization of property unconstitutional.
"You cannot use a federal law to make impossible what the Basic Law provides for and what Berliners voted for," Eralp told public broadcaster ZDF on Monday. She said the proposal had nothing to do with protecting investment and was aimed at Berlin's tenants.
Under Dobrindt’s plan, a state government would have to prove that socialization was unavoidable and that it had exhausted all alternatives, including investment in and support for new housing. Compensation would have to be paid immediately in cash and based on the property’s market value, determined by an expert assessment.
Eralp said that setting compensation at market value could make socialization impossible. "It is an attempt to prevent socialization," she said.
Eralp could become Berlin's first governing mayor from the Left Party. After winning the state election, her party is negotiating a coalition with the Greens and the Social Democrats. The parties plan to target private housing companies with more than 10,000 apartments and estimate compensation would cost €16 billion (about $18 billion), likely below the properties’ market value.
State premier criticizes Audi boss's Trump appearance
Lower Saxony premier Olaf Lies has criticized Audi CEO Gernot Döllner's appearance alongside US President Donald Trump at a campaign rally, saying he had become part of a political spectacle.
"A campaign rally cannot be the right place to announce an investment of this magnitude," said Lies, whose state is Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder.
Trump announced plans for an Audi factory in Georgia at Saturday's rally, with Döllner onstage alongside him.

German weightlifters question Russia's 2030 Worlds award
Germany's weightlifting federation says it will critically examine the decision to award the 2030 world championships to Moscow, while stopping short of an outright condemnation.
The International Weightlifting Federation becomes the first Olympic sports federation to award Russia a global sporting event since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The German Weightlifting Federation said it would assess the decision's political, ethical and international implications.
"The complexity of the situation must not mean that fundamental questions and the necessary critical examination of this decision are neglected," it told the SID sports news agency.
The championships will also serve as a qualifying event for the 2032 Olympics, adding to the significance of the decision.
Track worker killed after ICE train hits two in Essen
A track worker has died and another has been seriously injured after an ICE high-speed train struck them in the western German city of Essen.
The two were among six workers on a section of Deutsche Bahn track late on Sunday evening, the fire service said.
Emergency crews pronounced one worker dead at the scene. The injured colleague was lifted from the tracks to street level using a fire engine's aerial ladder and taken to hospital.
Police are investigating the cause of the accident.
The line between Gelsenkirchen's main station and Essen-Altenessen remained closed in the morning as cleanup work continued. The train had been removed, a railway spokesperson said.
Long-distance services were being diverted between Gelsenkirchen and Duisburg. Regional passengers were advised to check alternative routes.
German cruise ship cancels voyage after port collision
German cruise operator Tui Cruises has canceled a 20-day voyage to the Canary Islands after its cruise ship "Mein Schiff 3" collided with two container vessels in the northern port of Bremerhaven.
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship, carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members, leave port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
All three vessels sustained damage. One container ship suffered extensive damage to its port side, with several meters of its hull torn open above the waterline. The cruise ship also suffered significant damage, including to its lifeboats and bridge.
There were no injuries or water ingress on any of the vessels. All three ships have been temporarily prohibited from leaving port while investigations continue.
Tui Cruises said technical experts had inspected the vessel and determined that repairs at a shipyard were necessary, forcing the cancellation of the planned voyage.
The company described the cancellation as "the only responsible decision," stressing that passenger and crew safety remained its highest priority.
Merz and Steinmeier head to Asia on separate trips
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are departing on separate Asian tours to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties.
Merz will visit Singapore, Japan and South Korea on his longest overseas trip since taking office, accompanied by a high-level business delegation. He is seeking to broaden Germany's partnerships and reduce dependence on individual countries.
In Singapore, he will hold political talks and deliver a major foreign policy speech before traveling to Japan. In South Korea, he will attend an Asia-Pacific business conference and visit the demilitarized zone separating North and South Korea.
Steinmeier will make his second state visit to China, pressing for fairer trade relations and action to address economic imbalances, according to his office.
He is expected to speak at Peking University on Thursday and meet President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang on Friday.
Steinmeier also wants China to take greater international responsibility, including using its close ties with Moscow to help end Russia's war against Ukraine.
