Poland in talks with Vietnam on defence equipment sales
Poland is in talks with Vietnam on the sale of armoured personnel carriers, self-propelled howitzers, ammunition and coastal defence systems, Deputy State Assets Minister Konrad Golota told PAP.
Golota, who is accompanying Prime Minister Donald Tusk on his visit to Vietnam, told a briefing in Hoi An on Saturday that the talks marked the culmination of two years of close contacts between the state-owned Polish Armaments Group (PGZ) and its Vietnamese counterparts.
The discussions cover Rosomak armoured personnel carriers, Krab self-propelled howitzers, bridges, artillery ammunition and support vehicles, as well as radar and coastal defence systems. Poland is also offering communications and electronic components for combat platforms. The private WB Group is also participating in the visit.
Golota said that Vietnam had traditionally relied on Russian weapons but was now seeking to diversify its suppliers due to sanctions. Israeli, French and American companies are also strongly represented on the Vietnamese market, while Poland's advantage lies in its expertise in modernising post-Soviet equipment.
According to Golota, the two sides are discussing direct sales, the transfer of some production and technology to Vietnam, and maintenance and modernisation services, which he described as "very profitable financially".
Golota said it was too early to estimate the value of potential orders, explaining that Vietnam usually starts with small contracts that expand if the equipment proves successful. The two sides are expected to announce the main areas of cooperation on Monday, while commercial agreements could follow in December.
"We want to present specific contracts in December," he said, adding that this could happen at an arms fair scheduled to take place in Vietnam that month.
Golota also said he sees particular potential in coastal defence, which is a priority for Vietnam. Poland could offer radar and coastal surveillance solutions developed under the Digital Baltic programme. Furthermore, the Polish Naval Shipyard is exploring maritime support options, with talks covering rescue vessels and minehunters based on Poland's Kormoran-class design.
The discussions also extend to aviation maintenance services. Golota said that defence plants in Bydgoszcz could service transport aircraft, including C-130s, as well as post-Soviet aircraft from the Sukhoi (Su) family, provided that Vietnam supplies the necessary spare parts. (PAP)

Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank initiative
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:09:35 CET
18:09:35 KST

Oct 26 (Reuters) - Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to efforts to create the world’s first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The two countries instead said on Sunday that they would develop a framework for cooperation between their respective defence-funding initiatives, establishing two distinct but complementary institutions to support each other on investment opportunities and strategic challenges.
“We have been working closely to consider how the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) can best advance our shared objectives,” the statement said.
The two governments were unable to agree on key issues including the location of the headquarters of a joint institution, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, and the rules around new members, a second person said.
The MDM will focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement through financing, and bringing together demand across NATO allies to reduce procurement costs, while the DSRB will complement it by supporting investment in defence industries and supply chains, focusing more on single sovereign lending, the person added.
The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has faced challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project.
There were hopes Britain would reconsider its position under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team. Germany had previously declined to join. A spokesperson for the German finance ministry said Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB’s charter and is reviewing open questions.
Britain and Canada said the MDM and DSRB will be designed to work in close partnership, so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges.
AIMING TO RAISE BILLIONS
The DSRB has been aiming to raise around €100 billion ($112 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It will also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.
So far Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support, along with Canada.
Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the group would meet in Luxembourg on November 30 to sign articles of agreement establishing the bank.
“Membership (is) open to other allies and close partners who share the Bank’s objective,” he said in a statement.
Reuters previously reported that potential members had not joined because of concerns including whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments as well as the amount of capital countries would need to commit, the bank’s governance, and overlaps with existing initiatives.
Britain’s Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had recently described the DSRB as a “really interesting and innovative mechanism” and said that he did not see the proposed defence bank and MDM as being in competition.
Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. Reuters previously reported that Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM initiative with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during an August visit to Kyiv.
($1 = 0.8925 euros)

Nigeria’s Ebola patient medically evacuated from country, Arise TV reports

10:09:30 CET
18:09:30 KST

ABUJA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Nigeria’s Ebola patient left the country on a medical evacuation flight to Switzerland on Monday morning, the health minister said, adding that her clinical condition was much improved.
The patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is Nigeria’s first Ebola case in more than a decade.
The outbreak, which started in Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
The possibility that the Nigerian patient became infected in Uganda, where officials say she spent a two-week holiday before returning to Abuja, has fuelled concerns about undetected transmission in a country where the outbreak had appeared to be under control.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said in a post on X that the woman was “stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline” before her evacuation flight departed.
Her spouse has remained asymptomatic and left Nigeria on the same flight, Pate added.
The Swiss foreign ministry and Uganda’s health ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
SCIENTISTS INVESTIGATING HOW PATIENT CAUGHT RARE STRAIN
A team of leading Ebola scientists will travel to Nigeria to help investigate how the patient caught the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya told Reuters in an interview.
Switzerland said last week that she had not travelled to Congo, contradicting statements from Ugandan officials.
Her travel documents show she had not visited Congo, Kaseya said.
There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species, which has now caused almost 10,000 cases and more than 4,800 deaths in Congo, and spread to three other countries in Africa – Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
Kenya has reported nine cases and two deaths, all linked to a man who had travelled from Congo via Uganda’s Entebbe airport.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June but has not recorded any since and was declared free of the virus by the World Health Organization in August.
The WHO’s Africa director congratulated Nigeria’s government and health workers for stabilising the patient’s condition, allowing her to be evacuated.
“The Nigerian medical team successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilized her condition,” Mohamed Janabi said on X.

Starvation in Gaza becomes election campaign material in Israel as crises worsen Palestinians’ lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:09:22 UTC
18:09:22 KST

Hardline Israeli rhetoric toward Palestinians has increasingly become part of campaigning ahead of Tuesday’s Knesset elections, while humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip have worsened amid tighter restrictions and continued Israeli violations.
Last week, extremist Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir released an AI-generated campaign video depicting the Gaza Strip completely destroyed by 2030 as part of his far-right Jewish Power party’s election campaign.
Four developments have emerged among the most pressing crises facing Gaza: the loss of food assistance for half a million Palestinians, the threat of vital hospital services shutting down because of depleted generator fuel, the expansion of areas under Israeli military control, and rising numbers of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces.
The developments come amid continued Israeli bombardment, gunfire, and restrictions on the entry of supplies despite a ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025.
The following are four crises that have worsened in Gaza during Israel’s election campaign and their impact on Palestinians.
On Oct. 19, the World Food Program (WFP) said that it was reducing food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, leaving about 500,000 Palestinians without support and cutting the number of beneficiaries from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October.
The reductions included halving food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, as well as cutting quantities of wheat flour.
The WFP also reduced the number of hot meals it provides daily from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including those near the Yellow Line, now receive a meal every other day.
The UN agency attributed the measures to a funding shortage, saying financing for its operations in the Palestinian territories in 2026 had fallen to less than half the levels recorded in previous years.
It said it needs $450 million to continue operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank during the six months from October through March 2027.
Around 1.4 million Palestinians in Gaza, roughly two-thirds of the population, face high levels of food insecurity, according to the WFP.
Although the agency cited funding shortages as the reason for reducing assistance, Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and goods have further complicated efforts to meet humanitarian needs.
In a report published Oct. 19, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said aid deliveries into Gaza continued to face difficulties due to inspection procedures, limited crossing capacity and coordination requirements.
Gaza’s government media office warned the same day that aid cuts were accelerating famine conditions, accusing Israel of waging a “war of starvation.”
The Palestinian government also warned on Oct. 20 of rising malnutrition rates among children and pregnant women, calling for adequate funding for humanitarian aid and the opening of crossings.
On Oct. 21, Gaza’s Health Ministry said stocks of fuel needed to operate hospital electricity generators had run out, warning that the remaining generators could fail and life-saving medical services could be forced to stop.
Hospitals require more than 2,500 liters of fuel each month to keep generators running for extended periods amid a lack of electricity, the ministry said.
On Sept. 13, Mazen al-Araishi, director general of engineering and maintenance at the ministry, said the quantities of fuel allowed into Gaza were limited and insufficient to meet generator operations and maintenance needs.
The ministry did not say when the last shipment of fuel entered Gaza or how long the generators could continue operating.
Gaza hospitals have depended on generators since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023 and its sole power plant stopped operating after running out of fuel, while the war destroyed large sections of electricity lines and distribution networks.
The generators power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators and dialysis machines, making their failure a direct threat to patients’ lives.
The Israeli army has continued expanding the areas under its control in Gaza by moving “Yellow Line” markers westward, contrary to the gradual withdrawal outlined in the ceasefire agreement.
The “Yellow Line” marks the area to which Israeli forces withdrew during the first phase of the ceasefire agreement and separates territory under Israeli military control from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
When the agreement began to be implemented, around 53% of Gaza remained under Israeli control before the area gradually expanded.
On Oct. 11, Israeli forces advanced dozens of meters into the Shujaiya neighborhood east of Gaza City and moved concrete blocks marking the Yellow Line farther west, forcing scores of families to flee.
OCHA confirmed on Oct. 19 that markers near the Shujaiya junction had been moved and warned of the risk of further displacement in the area.
The expansion of Israeli-controlled areas prevents Palestinians from reaching homes, agricultural land and public facilities while making humanitarian relief operations more difficult.
On June 24, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the army controlled around 70% of the Gaza Strip. During a visit to the enclave on Sept. 2, he said Israel would not withdraw from the Yellow Line.
Netanyahu has linked further withdrawal to the disarmament of Hamas, while the Palestinian group says it is prepared to address the issue of its weapons alongside a gradual and organized Israeli withdrawal.
Alongside the expansion of Israeli military control, the number of Palestinians killed by Israel from Oct. 2-21 rose by around 40% compared with the same period in September, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry figures.
The data showed that 95 Palestinians were killed during that period in October, compared with 68 during the corresponding period in September, an increase of 27 deaths.
The number of Palestinians killed by Israel since the ceasefire agreement took effect reached 1,534 as of Oct. 21, according to Health Ministry figures.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed 74,494 Palestinians and injured 175,604 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Black Sea becomes most dangerous body of water for seafarers – FT
More seafarers have died in the Black Sea in 2026 than in any other body of water, outstripping fatalities in the Gulf, which has garnered more attention worldwide.
Source: Financial Times, citing shipowners and maritime organisations
Details: Crews on oil tankers, cargo ships and grain carriers entering the Black Sea close to EU and NATO territories must run the gauntlet of drone attacks. Some estimates put the number of attacks in the Black Sea as more than six times higher than in the Gulf.
"For me, the Black Sea and calling [at] Ukrainian ports is near suicidal," said Oleh Hryhoriuk, chair of the Marine Transport Workers' Trade Union of Ukraine.
Maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organisation report that over 570 ships have been targeted in the Black Sea this year, resulting in the deaths of at least 40 seafarers. In comparison, 24 fatalities have been confirmed in the Strait of Hormuz.
While some vessels were caught in the crossfire during port bombardments, others were intentionally targeted. Ambrey notes that the third quarter saw an average of over four attacks daily.
Driven by record-high freight rates, some shipping firms are willing to take the risk of transporting oil from the Middle East. However, shipping groups indicate that the majority are reluctant to send their fleets into the Black Sea, given the lower profit margins and significantly higher risks involved in trading there.
Background: Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu has stated that Russia is turning the Black Sea into a danger zone for civilian vessels.

Hundreds of animal lovers took part in the annual St Hubert’s celebration in Tervuren (Flemish Brabant) at the weekend. Visitors from Belgium and abroad came with their dogs and horses to take the traditional blessing. For many, it is a regular event. They reminisce about the past. Often several generations join up.
The lovely autumn weather drew a large crowd to Tervuren. Among those present were local residents, as well as visitors who had made the trip to Tervuren especially for the event.
Marie-Louise Selmans, a local resident, came mainly out of tradition and to spend time with her family. “I think it’s important to take part in local events, especially for the children and grandchildren, so that they realise how important it is.”
She had also brought her dog along for the blessing. “He’s part of the family, so why not?”
For many residents of Tervuren, too, the celebration remains a regular fixture. “This is an annual outing,” say a few friends from the town. “It’s a tradition in Tervuren.”
Blessing adds extra meaning
For some visitors, the blessing holds special significance. Sabine from Dendermonde drove to Tervuren with her Bernese Mountain Dog, Uta.
“I hope she’ll be with us for a very long time and doesn’t get ill,” she says. “And, in a way, I do believe that this blessing will help us.”
Visitors also emphasise the bond between humans and animals. Jolanders, who has recently moved back to Tervuren, explains that animals deserve an important place in our lives. “We must be open to animals. You get so much friendship in return.”
Memories of the past
For many visitors the St Hubert’s Festival brings back memories of their childhood. Lena has been coming to the event for 60 years.
“There used to be hundreds of horses here,” she says. “They used to gallop back then. That’s no longer allowed, and you do miss it a bit.”
Her husband Arri has also seen how tradition has changed over the years. “There are fewer horses than there used to be, but the atmosphere remains special.”
According to visitors, stricter safety regulations are the main reason why the famous horse gallop has disappeared. Nevertheless, interest remains high.
More than just a religious celebration
For many of those present, the day is not just about the blessing, but also about being together. After Mass, families and friends head into the village for a drink, a meal or a stroll.

Factbox-Battleground metros to watch in South Africa’s municipal elections
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:08:47 CET
18:08:47 KST

By Sfundo Parakozov
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 26 (Reuters) - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4 amid voter frustration over poor service delivery, unstable local government coalitions and rising costs.
Held every five years, the elections will be an important gauge of the political landscape ahead of the 2029 national vote, with support for the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela’s former liberation movement, continuing to erode.
Here are the key battleground metros:
JOHANNESBURG: THE PRIZE
Africa’s richest city has churned through seven mayors since the 2021 local elections as successive coalition governments have unravelled.
The pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) gained an early advantage by naming former Cape Town mayor and Western Cape premier Helen Zille as its mayoral candidate months ahead of its rivals. The 75-year-old political veteran has run an energetic campaign focused on deteriorating infrastructure and poor service delivery.
Recent polls put the DA above 30% and the ANC above 20%, raising the possibility of a coalition between the two parties, which have governed together nationally since the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024. Both parties could first seek deals with smaller parties rather than share power.
TSHWANE: ACTIONSA THE KINGMAKER
Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, underscores the importance of smaller parties in South Africa’s fragmented municipal politics.
The ANC governed the metro until 2016, when the DA captured it in a major urban defeat for the ruling party. Coalition politics subsequently proved volatile, and the DA lost power in 2024 after its coalition partner ActionSA backed an ANC-led no-confidence motion against its mayor.
Tshwane has since been governed by a multi-party coalition led by ActionSA. The party, founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, is a centre-right party that campaigns on anti-corruption and a hard line on immigration.
CAPE TOWN: DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE BASTION
The DA is heavily favoured to retain Cape Town, which it has governed since 2006 and where it has held an outright majority since 2011.
Polls suggest the party should remain above 50%, though some analysts expect a tighter contest as voters grapple with soaring property prices and persistent gang violence.
The DA is also targeting Nelson Mandela Bay, one of South Africa’s most turbulent coalition metros and currently governed by an ANC-led coalition.
ETHEKWINI: ZUMA WILDCARD
The economic hub of KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, could deliver one of the election’s biggest blows to the ANC, with former president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) threatening to displace it.
Zuma backed MKP after his bitter split with the ANC in 2023. Polls suggest the party could win 40% to 50% of the vote, while ANC support could fall into the low teens. MKP’s rise helped drive the ANC’s losses in the 2024 national election.
EKURHULENI: CORRUPTION TEST
Ekurhuleni, home to Johannesburg’s OR Tambo International Airport, could provide another measure of the ANC’s decline in Gauteng Province, where voters have cited concerns over corruption and crime.
Polls suggest ANC support could fall from 38% in 2021 to about 25%, leaving it neck-and-neck with the DA.
BUFFALO CITY AND MANGAUNG: LAST STRONGHOLDS OF THE ANC
Buffalo City, which includes KuGompo City in Eastern Cape province, and Mangaung, home to Bloemfontein in Free State province, remain the ANC’s strongest metropolitan bastions, making them important tests of how far the party’s urban support has eroded.
The ANC won 59% in Buffalo City and 51% in Mangaung in 2021, helped by deep-rooted loyalty to the former liberation movement.
(Reporting by Sfundo Parakozov; Editing by Bate Felix and Xevi Fontdegloria)

California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:08:42 UTC
18:08:42 KST

California’s billionaire tax faces a precarious road from rich opposition
Tech billionaires have raised more than $300m to oppose the billionaire tax proposal.
San Francisco, United States – University of California at Berkeley economics professor Brian Galle recently found a flyer in his mailbox about the proposed billionaire tax he helped write. But as he read it, Galle found things he hadn’t written, including that the tax can be on anyone and even on their retirement savings.
Californians have been getting such flyers and watching similar ads as they prepare to vote in the November 3 election on whether to impose the one-time tax of 5 percent on the assets of the state’s billionaires.
Spending by the billionaires to oppose the tax has made this the most expensive ballot measure ever and among the most expensive campaigns of this midterm, says David McCuan, professor of political science at Sonoma State University, who tracks state and local elections.
California’s celebrated tech billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Doordash founder Tony Xu, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Ripple co-executive chairman Chris Larsen and venture capitalists John Doerr, Michael Moritz and Vinod Khosla, are among those who have donated more than $300m to block the additional tax on their assets.
While Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg has not donated money to oppose the tax, Meta’s SEC filings revealed that he told the company’s board, which includes Xu and Collison, that he would buy a home outside California to avoid paying the tax. This could have affected Meta stock prices and the board created a new class of shares that Zuckerberg could use to pay the tax.
The billionaire fundraising has far outstripped that of the supporters, who only raised $32m. This has led to the ubiquitous ad campaign as well as outreach to voters.
“I feel like I am in an Alice in Wonderland alternate reality,” said Ashley Craig, a volunteer for Patriotic Millionaires, a group that supports the tax.
Craig has spent months door knocking and making calls to voters to campaign for the tax and often hears misinformation about it.
“They often tell me it has secret provisions allowing everyone to be taxed, which is not entirely true,” she said.
Any change in the tax would require a two-thirds majority in the assembly and would need to stay true to the spirit of the tax. But the prevalence of the ads has meant that voters often tell Craig the tax would soon include her – and them.
Making democracy more equal
“The irony is that Prop 40 [the billionaire tax proposal] is meant to make democracy more equal, but the billionaires are using their money to avoid that,” says Galle, the proposal’s coauthor.
The US Supreme Court’s judgement in the Citizens United v FEC case gave companies and special groups the freedom to spend freely in elections, he said.
“This has led to this situation where Sergey Brin has a lot more of a political voice,” says Francesco Trebbi, the BT Rocca professor of Business and Public Policy at the University of California at Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “It’s Sergey Brin v millions of Californians. This leads people to lose trust in the system ” .
Apart from the ad buys, Craig says she has also felt alone in the campaign arena. While the state Democratic party has endorsed the tax proposal, Craig says she hasn’t had ground support from the party. “We don’t have resources like social media, door knocking, phone banking and I would place the blame at the feet of the Democratic party.”
Sonoma State’s McCuan attributes this to the Democratic party’s internal rift between the progressives and moderates, with the former in favour of such a policy and the latter resisting it.
“This is a broader proxy test between the party’s progressives and moderates. If this works, progressive candidates could try such ideas in the 2028 presidential elections,” McCuan says, which the billionaires and moderates want to avert.
So while the party has endorsed the measure, California Governor Gavin Newsom has opposed it, as has Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor in the election and Katie Porter, a former congresswoman who also ran for governor.
Newsom, who is eyeing a 2028 presidential run, has opposed the tax, saying it is “poorly written. It would harm the state if its billionaires, who have an estimated wealth of 2.3 trillion according to the measure’s authors, move, as Zuckerberg has planned,” Newsom has said.
The tax’s opponents have also backed a ballot measure that prohibits any new state taxes based on personal property or imposed retroactively. Another asks state auditors to review any proposed tax measures for their financial impact before they are voted on. If these pass and get more votes than the billionaire tax, they could negate the billionaire tax, even if it is passed.
Only a third of citizen initiatives pass
The strong campaign opposing the billionaire tax may have impacted support for it. Voters support the tax by a small margin, but also the two measures that oppose it, according to a recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC).
“Only about a third of such citizen initiatives pass. So the burden is on the yes side,” says Mark Baldassare, statewide survey director and Miller chair in public policy at PPIC. “Support can decline if people don’t feel completely sure.”
But Suzane Jiminez, chief of staff at the SEIU health workers union, which has sponsored the billionaire tax measure, said, “We are feeling confident that we will have the votes. When voters see that billionaires are funding the ads, they see through them.”
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Congressman Ro Khanna of California rallied across the state to drum up support for the measure. Jiminez said that in the last few weeks, 3,000 volunteers have spread out to knock on doors and distributed flyers explaining the tax across the state. “The democratic figureheads do not represent the rank and file on this. They are supporting us,” Jiminez said.
It is unclear whether this will be enough, as the shortfall in funding means support for the measure remains precarious. Baldassare said he plans to do his poll again as voters read and receive the state’s voter guides explaining the ballot measures and make up their minds.
Sonoma University’s McCuan said that just the historic amount of money being spent on defeating the measure is a win in itself for the tax backers.
“Progressives can win by losing. They can say moderates sank us, use it as a morality play. They will attack big tech – as a bad bogeyman of US politics.”

Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado returns from exile, received by thousands of supporters in Caracas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Venezuelan opposition leader Machado returns from exile
October 26, 2026
Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas on Sunday after returning from nearly a year in exile.
Her supporters stood along highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting slogans like "freedom" as Machado made her way in a convoy of cars and motorcycles to the capital, Caracas.
Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned out of the sunroof and shouted "this country is giving lessons to everyone" as her convoy entered the capital.
In Guacara earlier, the AFP news agency reported seeing Machado singing the national anthem in a plaza packed with supporters, waving flags and cheering her return.
Venezuelan interim president responds unfavorably to Machado's return
Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, said in rare comments to reporters that Machado could have avoided the pomp and celebration that she chose to arrive with.
"The show could have been avoided—the airports are right here," Rodriguez said on state television.
Machado's spokesperson earlier said that she was willing to sit down with the Venezuelan regime to talk things through.
Why was Machado in exile?
Machado left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in promoting democracy in autocratic Venezuela.
Facing arrest by the regime of former President Nicolas Maduro, she sought refuge in the Argentine embassy in Caracas and was smuggled out of the country with assistance from the United States.
At first she was unable to return for fear of detention by authorities.
After the US-led ouster and arrest of Maduro, she gave her Nobel medal to US President Donald Trump.
However, her inability to return to Venezuela for so long was partly due to the Trump administration.
Instead of backing Machado, Washington decided to support Rodriguez.
Machado has said she faced travel restrictions and flight cancellations, partly due to Trump's worries that her presence in Venezuela could inflame tensions during a period of transition, and partly due to Rodriguez' interference.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

New power outages in six regions due to Russian attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:07:02 EET
18:07:02 KST

New power outages in six regions due to Russian attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Due to Russian attacks, new power outages were recorded in six regions. Hourly and industrial restrictions will remain in effect until the end of the day.
New power outages caused by Russian attacks have been recorded as of the morning of October 26 in six regions of Ukraine. The schedules remain in effect. This was reported by NEC "Ukrenergo" on Monday, UNN writes.
Enemy shelling
"Over the past day, the enemy continued to attack Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure. As a result, as of this morning, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Sumy regions," Ukrenergo reported.
As stated, emergency restoration work is already underway wherever security conditions currently allow. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power to all consumers who have been disconnected as soon as possible.
Schedules
"To prevent overloading equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, in some regions today until the end of the day, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to 2.5 rounds) for all categories of consumers will be applied as a necessary measure," Ukrenergo noted.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has decreased. Today, October 26, as of 09:30, it was 5.8% lower than at the same time on the previous working day—Friday, October 23. The reason for the change is the necessary restrictions caused by enemy attacks.
Yesterday, October 25, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 4.8% higher than the maximum recorded on the previous Sunday—October 18. This was caused by a drop in air temperature, prompting consumers to use electric heaters in the evening hours.
"Given the consequences of Russian shelling and the weather conditions, the need for economical electricity consumption during the evening hours remains. Please limit the use of powerful electrical appliances from 16:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo urged.

Ambassador Lener in Melbourne for the Eureka Democracy Award ceremony
Italy
Unknown Publisher

Nicola Lener, the ambassador to Canberra, spoke in Melbourne at the annual “Eureka Democracy” award ceremony, where this year’s prize was awarded to Antony Green, a former journalist with the public television network ABC who specializes in analyzing voter trends. The ambassador attended the event at the invitation of the “Stockade Australia” association, composed of descendants of the key figures in the failed Eureka Rebellion of December 3, 1854, remembered as one of the founding moments of Australian democracy.
                                    
In recent months, the embassy in Canberra had collaborated with the association to identify the location (the ossuary at the Verano Monumental Cemetery in Rome) where Raffaele Carboni is buried, a follower of Giuseppe Garibaldi who took part in the uprising and later recounted it in the book “The Eureka Stockade.” In his remarks, Ambassador Lener recalled the life story of Carboni, a follower of Mazzini and Garibaldi, who emigrated to Australia following the Roman Republic of 1849 and returned to Italy after being tried and acquitted for the Eureka Rebellion, and he highlighted the significance of the connection between the two countries centered on democratic ideals even before both achieved their independence. A deep connection, the ambassador emphasized, that predates the great waves of Italian migration to Australia and is being renewed today through the full alignment between Rome and Canberra on multilateralism and a rules-based international order.

Istanbul braces for new round of flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:06:16 UTC
18:06:16 KST

Istanbul is bracing for another round of heavy rainfall on Oct. 27, with Türkiye’s meteorological authority warning of possible flash floods and inundations in the city and other parts of western Türkiye, less than two weeks after torrential downpours killed eight people in Istanbul and the neighboring province of Kocaeli.
The Turkish State Meteorological Service forecast heavy showers and thunderstorms across western parts of the country throughout the week, with temperatures expected to fall below seasonal averages in some areas.
Abdullah Macit, a weather forecasting expert, said heavy rainfall was expected on Oct. 27 in the Marmara region, including Istanbul, Çanakkale, Tekirdağ and Bursa, as well as parts of the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts.
Rainfall is also expected to affect southern parts of İzmir, Antalya and Muğla, along with eastern areas of Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay.
Macit warned that the downpours could cause flooding and inundation, urging residents to take precautions. He said Istanbul was expected to remain dry on Oct. 26 and 28, but face heavy showers on Oct. 27.
Temperatures in Istanbul are forecast to drop to around 15 degrees Celsius on Oct. 27 before rising to approximately 19 degrees in the following days.
The meteorological service also expects heavy rainfall in parts of the Aegean and Mediterranean regions. Showers are forecast to be particularly intense in İzmir, Muğla, Aydın and western Antalya, with very heavy to torrential rain possible in parts of Muğla and Aydın.
The agency issued an orange-coded heavy rainfall warning, indicating a high risk of dangerous weather conditions for Aydın and Muğla, and a yellow-coded warning, signaling potentially hazardous conditions that require caution, for Antalya, Denizli and İzmir.
In the capital Ankara, showers and thunderstorms are expected from Oct. 27, accompanied by falling temperatures that could dip below seasonal norms in some areas.
The latest warnings come after torrential rainfall on Oct. 14 set an 84-year precipitation record in Istanbul, killing seven people in the city and one in neighboring Kocaeli. The downpours flooded roads, underpasses, homes and businesses, while vehicles were swept away by floodwaters.
Schools were closed from Oct. 15 as a precaution and reopened on Oct. 19, following the deadly flooding.
Authorities have advised residents in regions expected to see heavy rainfall to exercise caution against flash flooding and water pooling, especially in vulnerable urban zones.

Lula da Silva reelected Brazilian president: voting results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:05:47 UTC
18:05:47 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which carries out the functions of the Central Election Commission, has completed the vote count for the second round of the presidential election. According to the final results, with 100% of ballots counted, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has officially been reelected.
TASS has compiled the key information about the voting results.
Election results
According to the election authority’s final statistics, Lula da Silva, the candidate of the left-wing Workers’ Party, won with 51.79% of the vote, receiving 64,256,232 votes.
His rival, right-wing opposition Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, received 48.21%, with 59,826,041 people voting for him.
The total number of valid votes was 124,082,273.
Voter turnout in the second round stood at 80.78%, with 128,236,074 citizens taking part in the vote.
A total of 19.22% of the electorate, or 30,509,005 people, did not vote.
Invalid ballots accounted for 2.12%, or 2,723,305 ballots.
Another 1.12%, or 1,430,496 ballots, were blank.
A total of 158,745,502 people were eligible to vote in the election.
Records set
Lula da Silva set a new record by receiving the largest number of votes in the country’s history.
He also became the first politician in Brazilian history to hold the country’s highest office for a fourth time and set a record for the number of reelections since the rule allowing them was introduced in 1997. He has now been reelected twice.
In addition, Lula da Silva became the first candidate in the country’s history to win the election after finishing behind in the first round, when he received 45.16% of the vote against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 47.03%.
He will also become the oldest president in Brazil’s history.
According to CNN Brasil, the politician will be 81 years old when he takes office.
His fourth term as president will officially begin on January 5, 2027.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s position
Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing opposition candidate and senator who lost the second round of Brazil’s presidential election, refused to recognize the voting results and said they should be annulled.
He cited the judicial authorities’ decision to extend voting hours by two hours as the reason.
However, Bolsonaro’s campaign team, which refused to recognize the election results over the authorities’ decision to extend polling hours, had itself submitted a similar request, CNN Brasil reported.
According to the broadcaster, the campaign teams of both candidates had formally asked the courts to adjust voting hours.
Bolsonaro’s team requested an extension of voting in Sao Paulo state and several cities in the south of the country because of heavy rains that hit the region on the eve of and during the second round.
Meanwhile, the campaign team of incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s ruling left-wing Workers’ Party justified its request by citing a reduced bus fleet and transport problems in several states, including Sao Paulo and Bahia.
According to CNN Brasil, the Supreme Federal Court selectively considered the request submitted by the Workers’ Party’s campaign team.
The request was referred to Justice Cristiano Zanin, who ordered voting hours to be extended nationwide.

Türkiye services confidence falls in October, retail and construction sentiment improve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:05:24 UTC
18:05:24 KST

Türkiye’s seasonally adjusted confidence index fell in the services sector in October, while confidence improved in the retail trade and construction sectors compared with the previous month.
The services confidence index declined 2.4 percent month-on-month to 109.2 in October from 111.9 in September.
Readings above 100 indicate an optimistic outlook, while readings below 100 point to a pessimistic outlook.
Within the services sector, the business situation over the past three months index fell 3.1 percent to 106.8, while the demand-turnover over the past three months index declined 3.5 percent to 105.8. The demand-turnover expectation for the next three months edged down 0.7 percent to 115.0.
The retail trade confidence index increased 1.1 percent from the previous month to 112.5.
The business activity-sales over the past three months index rose 6.2 percent to 121.5, while the current volume of stock index increased 1.2 percent to 92.5. The business activity-sales expectation for the next three months, however, declined 3.4 percent to 123.6.
Meanwhile, the construction confidence index rose 0.4 percent month-on-month to 83.3 in October from 83.0 in September.
The current overall order books index increased 0.4 percent to 80.7, while the total employment expectation over the next three months index also rose 0.4 percent to 85.9.

Cruise liner hits container ship in Germany (VIDEO)
A cruise liner has collided with a container ship while departing Bremerhaven in northwestern Germany for a voyage to the Canary Islands.
The incident involving the Mein Schiff 3 occurred on Sunday in poor weather brought by storm Manja. Strong crosswinds appeared to overpower the tugboats assisting the 293-meter vessel down the Weser River. The collision was filmed from aboard the liner.
Hamburg-based operator TUI Cruises reported no injuries among the 2,428 guests and 922 crew members aboard the ship. The vessel was brought back to the pier for a damage assessment.
Media reports and footage indicate that at least three lifeboats were seriously damaged, potentially disrupting the voyage unless they can be replaced promptly. In similar cases, operators have negotiated cancellations with some guests to bring the number of people aboard into line with the remaining lifeboat capacity.
Die „Mein Schiff 3“ kollidiert beim Auslaufen in Bremerhaven mit einem Containerschiff. Aufnahmen zeigen die Wucht des Zusammenstoßes; mehrere Rettungsboote wurden offenbar beschädigt. Nach bisherigen Berichten gab es keine Verletzten. Die Unfallursache muss untersucht werden. Criminal case opened against editor-in-chief of Russian border-region outlet Pepel on charges of justifying terrorism
The Belgorod branch of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has opened a criminal case against Nikita Parmenov, editor-in-chief of the outlet Pepel, on charges of justifying terrorism, Fonar reported, citing a statement from the security service.
According to the FSB, Parmenov voiced support for the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion, both designated terrorist organizations in Russia.
The FSB’s press release does not include the actual statements, when they were made, or links to them, Fonar said. The security service did not name Parmenov but said the person named in the case has been designated a “foreign agent” and “is located in one of the South Caucasus countries.”
Pepel itself suggested the case was likely triggered by a livestream on the YouTube channel Vremya Nakazhet “Time Will Punish.” Asked by the host during the stream about his attitude toward volunteer units fighting on Ukraine’s side, Parmenov said he could not condemn Russians who join them. In the same stream, he also said he “unequivocally condemns” the actions of units that have shelled civilians in the Belgorod region.
The outlet said the pro-war Telegram channel Zapiski Veterana “A Veteran’s Notes” had previously written that Parmenov allegedly supports the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion. According to Pepel, the channel’s authors had edited the stream, cutting out the part where Parmenov condemns the units for shelling Shebekino.
Pepel launched in the fall of 2022. Its Telegram channel now has 170,000 subscribers, and the outlet covers the war and its aftermath in the Belgorod border region without censorship.

Crans-Montana first responders to receive first national ‘helping hand’ award
On December 8, the organisation helfen helfen Suisse will present the national Helfende Hand (Helping Hand) award for the first time. This inaugural ceremony, which will take place in the presence of Justice Minister Beat Jans and former Valais cantonal president Mathias Reynard, will pay tribute to the emergency and rescue services deployed during the fire in Crans-Montana.
With the Helping Hand award, helfen helfen Schweiz – a charitable organisation founded in Basel in 2017 – is establishing a national honour to recognise extraordinary achievements in exceptional emergency situations.
The ceremony will take place at the Bern Military Barracks, with the support of the Swiss Armed Forces. This initiative is backed by several sponsoring organisations, such as the Swiss Firefighters’ Federation, the Swiss Federation of Police Officers and the Valais Ambulance Workers’ Association.

Ukrainian drone strike on Voronezh kills two as Kyiv and Moscow prepare to restart talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:52 UTC
18:00:52 KST

Debris from a downed drone hit a moving commuter train, while Zelenskyy says territorial questions must be settled by leaders themselves.
A Ukrainian drone attack on the Russian city of Voronezh overnight killed two people and injured 17, many of them passengers on a commuter train, according to the regional governor.
Alexander Gusev said on Telegram that "more than 70 drones" had been shot down over the city between late Sunday and early Monday, describing the strike as a "terrorist attack".
A large share of the injured, including two people in a serious condition, were travelling on a train in Voronezh’s left-bank suburbs when debris from a downed drone fell onto it, Gusev said. He did not say where the two victims were killed.
Fires broke out at several industrial sites, a business centre in the city centre and a residential building, though the governor said the industrial premises had not been significantly damaged.
Voronezh, home to more than one million people, lies around 500 kilometres south of Moscow. Several faculties at Voronezh State University have temporarily moved classes online, a university spokesperson told the state news agency TASS.
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said that Russia had launched 140 drones and four missiles against the country. Ukrainian air defences shot down 112 drones and three Kh-59/69 missiles.
A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia injured four people. Local authorities reported damage to private houses, cars and a hotel building.
In the Chernihiv region, two people were wounded in a Russian strike. A hangar belonging to a private enterprise was hit, and a fire was also reported at a grain storage facility.
Emergency power cuts have been introduced in the Khmelnytskyi region: in the Kamianets-Podilskyi district, a Russian strike damaged an energy infrastructure facility.
Russian forces used guided aerial bombs in strikes on Izium. Three people were injured, and private residential houses and the building of an educational institution were damaged.
Talks back on the table
The strike comes days after Russia agreed on Wednesday to return to three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the United States in November. According to Moscow, the talks are due to take place in Abu Dhabi.
Direct talks between the two sides were held several times in 2025 but failed to produce a settlement, and have been frozen since the start of this year.
Speaking to Ukrainian television on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that a trilateral meeting would go ahead next month.
"We are ready to talk," he said. "If it’s a territorial issue, it must be addressed at a leadership level. Other issues fall within the remit of the technical groups."
Zelenskyy’s distinction suggests Kyiv wants the most contentious question in the war, control of occupied Ukrainian land, kept out of lower-level negotiations and reserved for direct talks between heads of state.
There have been tentative signs of de-escalation in recent days. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow agreed to a localised ceasefire around Oleshky, a heavily damaged Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region. The truce was brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Goldsmiths fine art students call for compensation over record tutor strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

Students arriving at Goldsmiths, University of London this autumn found a campus embroiled in a bitter industrial dispute that has upended timetables and disrupted courses.
“I was really excited to start my studies at Goldsmiths,” one international student told the Guardian at a gathering of unhappy students on Friday. “But when I first arrived, I was quite shocked because almost all the induction sessions seemed to turn into discussions about strikes.”
The international student was one of the unlucky ones, having enrolled on the master of fine art (MFA) course that has been among the worst affected, with 10 out of the 12 usual tutors on strike, and students now saying they want compensation from the university for their lost learning.
Florence Sweeney, a part-time student, said there had been “virtually no teaching” so far this term for many of the fine arts students, and that a group were seeking remuneration.
“Not only has it been a financial drain, but I can see my cohort are very distressed and anxious, and some are depressed by what’s going on,” Sweeney said.
“Some people have moved from the other side of the world, and for them it’s such a risk. To not even get welcomed or proper briefings, it’s really disappointing, especially for a place with such a good reputation for producing exceptional contemporary artists.”
Goldsmiths is famous for the stellar array of artists among its former students, including Steve McQueen, Sarah Lucas and Damien Hirst. But it has been financially squeezed in recent years by falling applications in its core humanities subjects and the erosion of domestic tuition fees, setting off what one staff member described as “non-stop” rounds of redundancies and restructuring.
Now entering its 21st week and with no end in sight, the current strike involving University and College Union (UCU) staff is the longest in living memory in British higher education, originating from a staff marking boycott in April over proposed job cuts.
Goldsmiths’ management responded firmly to the boycott by deducting 100% of pay from those involved. The union argued that amounted to a lockout and a formal ballot followed, so that since early June a group of UCU members at the south-east London university have been on indefinite strike.
Joe Newman, a Goldsmiths UCU branch co-president, said: “We’ve resisted as much as we can over the last two rounds of restructuring and redundancies. But right now, the scale of the action that we are taking is in response to the unprecedented scale and speed of the cuts management are pursuing.”
Newman said students were largely supportive because they “have more in common with staff on precarious contracts than with senior managers on six-figure salaries”, who he said wanted more savings despite earlier cuts.
“When we talk to the students about why we are on strike, of course there are a range of opinions, but overwhelmingly they are just aghast,” Newman said. “The students who have been here longer have seen the impact of previous cuts and seen how things have only got worse. Students who are new can’t believe that management is about to launch an incredibly messy redundancy process.”
The university said only “a small portion of our staff – around 8.5%” were on strike, leaving most students unaffected, and that it had offered significant compromises to the union, including a pause on compulsory redundancies. But it was not prepared to scrap the 100% pay deductions for the marking boycott, saying it had spent significant amounts to ease the impact on students.
“Like many UK higher education institutions, Goldsmiths faces significant financial challenges, which need to be addressed to ensure its future sustainability,” a spokesperson for the university said.
“We recognise colleagues’ right to take industrial action, but continued disruption risks further impacting students’ education and the university’s hard-earned reputation as a world-renowned academic institution in the long-term.
“We are doing everything we can to monitor and mitigate disruption, and are supporting students on courses affected by this strike action, including offering students’ regular updates, meetings with their schools and other appropriate support as needed.”
MFA students said they had been disappointed by the impact on the two-year course, which charges nearly £15,000 a year for full-time UK students and £33,000 for international students.
John Carver, a part-time student in his second year, said he had decided to suspend his studies after attending a “dismal” departmental meeting at the start of term.
“I’m a mature student, time matters to me, and I would be going into a chaotic situation where tutors have been on strike for so long. There wasn’t any light at the end of the tunnel,” Carver said.
“The tutors at Goldsmiths are fantastic, and the way they interact in tutorials, when you do get them, it’s as good as it gets, you build relationships with all the tutors. But what’s going on now is that [replacement] tutors are being brought in who don’t know the students and it’s not as impressive, to put it politely.”
James Evans, an international student from the US, said visa and funding restrictions meant he had to stick with the MFA course despite the disruption.
“Towards the end of last year, in the first days of the strike, I never received marks back, the end-of-term show wasn’t graded. The marks aren’t the important part, but the dialogue is, and there were very important fixtures for the year that went without any discussion. It was a bit frustrating. But this year it’s been worse,” Evans said.
“Our fees went up this year, [and] as an international student they were exorbitant to begin with. There’s still no feedback on projects from last year, but beyond that there’s no structure, barely any communication. We’ve been left to our own devices. It’s been difficult to navigate.”

‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

During lockdown, Charlotte and her ex-partner would spend evenings cooped up in their flat, listening to music, watching YouTube videos and chatting until the small hours. Those nights would be fuelled by alcohol and lines of cocaine.
“I wanted to be loved, and when he told me he loved me like nobody ever would and nobody ever will, I drank the Kool-Aid,” Charlotte says. “I wanted to believe that. And there’s a point when you’re with somebody and you’re drinking, you’re doing coke, where you think you have this bond, you think it’s just you two in the world.”
But that emotional high would be fleeting. “Without a doubt, without any exception, it would never end peacefully. My ex-partner would get so ridiculously paranoid once he was using cocaine. It was just crazy,” she says. Charlotte’s partner would accuse her of taking more than him, messaging men and hiding things from him. When she denied it, he would subject her to brutal physical assaults.
“And then the next day it was all apologies and it’ll all be fine, it’ll all be different.”
Data suggests it is a common scenario. Home Office figures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.
It is not possible to see the whole picture, as some of the tests were carried out after the police suspected drug-taking, but it tallies with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.
A wider Guardian investigation has found that Britain’s record-breaking cocaine habit is also driving crimes from assault to dangerous driving. The stimulant is increasingly ubiquitous, fuelling situations ranging from fights on nights out to violence at football matches.
Cocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years. Victoria Thomas, a 45-year-old mother-of-two from Cardiff, was strangled to death by her husband, Alcwyn Thomas, who was “argumentative and moody”, having been filmed on CCTV taking cocaine shortly before he killed her on 19 August 2024.
On 13 June last year, 32-year-old Izzy Knight was murdered by her husband, Paul Knight, in the house they shared in Northamptonshire while their two daughters slept upstairs. In a note, he blamed “having an addiction to cocaine and spending money I don’t have”.
Both men were sentenced to life in prison.
Cat Chappell, a BACP-registered therapist specialising in domestic abuse who previously volunteered on the National Domestic Violence Helpline, says cocaine boosts confidence but increases paranoia, “and so much of abuse is around paranoia”. “It’s taking what’s already there, making it like 10 times worse,” she says.
It can also make it more difficult to leave, she says, because perpetrators will often offer to get help with their cocaine problem. “And [for victims], that’s what you want to hear in those moments.”
Charlotte and her ex-partner got together just before the pandemic and, though it was not the first time she had taken cocaine, it was not something she had done regularly. Her ex, on the other hand, was a habitual user.
“My ex was a really small man, and after cocaine use he’d be like 10 men. He was like the Incredible Hulk, it was like there was this beast in him and he would get this strength. And I can’t tell you where it was from. Then he would come at me and he would absolutely beat me to a pulp. It was absolutely terrifying,” she says.
He would routinely trap her in the bedroom. “I remember one night he got really paranoid that somebody was in the house and he brought knives upstairs. He would pace about all night. It was really, really horrific.
“For somebody who’s already [controlling and abusive] it’s like adding fuel to the fire, it really is, with coke.”
He often stole from her to fund his habit, using her phone to take money from her bank account, including times when he had knocked her unconscious.
Charlotte remembers police visited their flat about 19 times, as a result of her own calls and those made by neighbours, but she would always cover up her ex’s cocaine use.
“I would deny a lot of it because I didn’t want to say, ‘Yes, I’ve been doing it as well’, so you’re in this absolute no-win situation because you’re then sticking up for them all the time.”
She began to abuse alcohol to cope with the situation she was in. “I didn’t want to be there,” Charlotte says. “I was just drinking because I didn’t want to feel anything. I’d wake up, drink all day. I just wanted to feel numb, numb, numb, numb, numb.”
She was finally able to leave on Boxing Day in 2021 when her ex went out to score drugs and she wrote an email to her father asking him to pick her up. She has been free of alcohol and cocaine since.
After initially attempting to pursue her ex for knocking her teeth out, police later decided to take no action against Charlotte’s abuser. She fears he will go on to abuse someone else.
It was Women’s Aid that helped her get her life back on track and she is now an advocate for the charity in her home city of Leeds. She also works for another charity, Smart Works, which helps women get into employment.
Nik Peasgood, the chief executive of Leeds Women’s Aid, says Charlotte’s story is increasingly common. She thinks cocaine is having an effect on the levels of violence perpetrated by abusers and she is calling for more research to help understand the relationship between cocaine, domestic abuse and mental health.
“If they’re already abusive and the relationship’s abusive, [cocaine] might lower their inhibitions, it might make the frequency worse, it might make the severity worse, it might mean that they can’t control how they normally control the relationship and the situation. But it doesn’t make somebody abusive or violent if they’re not already. It’s not an excuse for that violence.”
Peasgood says that cocaine, unlike a lot of other drugs, is used by a broad range of people, including middle- and upper-class people and those who are well-respected within society and do not fit the stereotype of what people think domestic abusers looks like.
The drug can be a barrier to people seeking help, particularly for victims in professional jobs who feel they have a lot to lose if they are caught using illegal substances.
“[Contacting the police] has ramifications away from just the perpetrator when there are drugs involved, and [there is] fear around that,” says Peasgood. “Especially if people have got children, it’s something they wouldn’t necessarily want others to know about.”
Through her work, Charlotte has now met many others who faced similar situations. “I’m in recovery now and it’s alarming how many people tell the same tale of drinking, doing coke, and it just becoming an absolute explosion of rows and just horrific violence,” she says.
“I think it’s not a problem that’s actually going away. If anything, it’s getting worse. You only have to speak to people in the rehab or recovery world and they’ll tell you this is going nowhere. It’s really scary.”
She believes the figures don’t show the true scale of the issue. “I think this is much wider reaching than we realise, due to the stigma of reporting it and the shame of the victim using the drug.”
For many people, she says, cocaine use is “very much seen as our weekend thing”. “It’s very much behind closed doors and not spoken about. People would be gobsmacked at how many people actually do it. It’s so widespread, it’s unbelievable.”
- In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

What are the US midterm elections and why do they matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

Donald Trump will still be US president on the morning of 4 November. But he could be facing a very different political landscape, depending on the results of the US midterm elections held the previous day.
As the name implies, midterm elections fall nearly halfway through a president’s term. They are often a telling referendum on the sitting president’s performance, something Trump is actively encouraging by telling voters “pretend I’m on the ballot”. In this case, voters will decide whether Trump’s Republican party can retain its grip on Congress.
Democrats are hoping to capitalise on growing discontent with Trump to seize control of the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. Republicans are fighting to preserve their congressional majorities and prevent a fresh period of legislative paralysis and investigations into the White House.
What is being decided?
The US Congress in Washington has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. Both must approve federal legislation before it can become law and both play important roles in overseeing the executive branch.
The House is elected every two years, meaning all 435 voting seats are contested at every congressional election. The Senate has 100 members serving staggered six-year terms, so roughly a third of its seats are up for election every two years.
This year’s ballot includes:
- All 435 seats in the House of Representatives. Republicans are defending a narrow majority, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.
- 35 seats in the Senate. Thirty-three seats are up in regular elections, along with two special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the remainder of terms that were vacated early. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, against 47 held by Democrats and independents who caucus with them. Democrats need to gain four seats to secure a majority.
- 39 governorships. Voters will choose governors in 36 states and three US territories.
- Thousands of state legislative seats, as well as local offices, judicial contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules.
The elections for Congress will determine which party controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s second term. The governorships and state legislative contests will shape policymaking closer to home, from education and reproductive rights to taxation and the administration of elections.
Why do the midterms matter?
They have a long history of punishing the occupant of the White House. The president’s party has lost House seats in 18 of the past 20 midterm elections, a 90% rate of loss that stretches back to 1946.
The pattern is not inevitable. George W Bush’s Republicans gained seats in the 2002 midterms, following the September 11 attacks. But Barack Obama’s Democrats suffered a “shellacking” in 2010 and Trump’s Republicans lost the House in 2018.
Republicans enter this election with a narrow margin for error in the House and a more substantial advantage in the Senate. The RealClearPolitics average of national generic polls showed Democrats leading Republicans by 8.2 points in early October. Trump has been forced to hold campaign rallies in what should be safe Republican states.
But political polarisation and years of redistricting have reduced the number of genuinely competitive House districts, making it harder for either party to translate a national swing into a big change in seats. The Reuters news agency has estimated that only about 40 to 50 House races are truly competitive.
What are the races to watch?
Several Senate contests have emerged as key battlegrounds. In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to hold an open seat for Democrats after Gary Peters, the incumbent senator, decided not to seek re-election. In Georgia, Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator, enjoys a healthy poll lead over Republican challenger Mike Collins.
In Maine, a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, Susan Collins, the Republican senator, is defending her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson. Ohio offers another major test, with Democrat Sherrod Brown seeking to return to the Senate against Republican Jon Husted.
Texas has become especially closely watched. Democrat James Talarico is taking on Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general. Republicans have spent about $210m to help the scandal-plagued Paxton. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024.
Other contests in Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and New Hampshire could help determine which party controls the chamber (if there is a 50-50 split, JD Vance, the vice-president, a Republican, wields the tiebreaker vote). Latest polls show Democrats ahead in Maine, North Carolina and Kansas, and competitive in Alaska and Ohio.
In the House, the contest is spread across dozens of districts. Republicans are defending vulnerable seats in places including New York, Texas and Iowa, while Democrats are also fighting to protect members in districts made more difficult by redrawn congressional boundaries. Notable gubernatorial elections include Alaska, Iowa, Florida, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
What are the main issues?
The cost of living regularly tops opinion polls. Democrats are campaigning hard on affordability related to food prices, housing, fuel and healthcare. The war in Iran has added a further complication for Republicans.
Immigration remains another defining issue, with polls suggesting that many voters feel Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) hardline approach has gone too far. This could wipe out many of the gains that Trump made with Latino voters in 2024.
Datacentres, AI, tariffs, trade, abortion rights, voting rules and the future of democracy also remain important themes. Democratic socialists scored some notable victories in Democratic primaries, creating momentum on the left of the party.
But in closely fought races, personal credibility, local connections, the ability to appeal to independent voters and a blitz of TV advertising can outweigh the national party message.
Will the elections be free and fair?
The integrity of the midterms is under scrutiny, with concerns ranging from voter registration to the certification of results. Trump has sought to amplify these fears, putting forward a litany of misleading and false claims about threats to US elections.
The justice department has sued states for access to their unredacted voter rolls, seeking to cross-check them against a federal immigration database in an effort to identify ineligible voters. A federal judge ruled that the department’s policy was unlawful, citing limits on its authority and the risks of inaccurate data.
There are also concerns about the use of immigration-enforcement data in voter-fraud investigations, the administration’s efforts to change mail-voting rules and the prospect of federal election monitors at polling places. The NAACP has sued over the planned deployment of monitors, arguing that their presence could intimidate voters.
The risks do not end when polling stations close. Voting-rights advocates are also watching for pressure on local officials to certify results, mass challenges to ballots and legal disputes that could delay or undermine the transition of power.
What happens if Democrats win?
A Democratic victory in either chamber would significantly constrain Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda and hasten the president’s decline into “lame duck” status.
If Democrats take the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump.
The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.
Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.
Why do state elections matter?
Governors and state legislatures have influence over abortion access, education, taxation and voting procedures. State legislatures also play a central role in drawing congressional district boundaries, although the precise arrangements vary by state and some maps are subject to court challenges or independent commissions.
Voting rules are another source of contention. New restrictions on identification, registration and mail-in voting have taken effect in several Republican-controlled states. Supporters describe such measures as safeguards for election integrity; critics argue that they risk making it harder for eligible citizens to vote.
These disputes are especially significant in a political climate in which Trump has repeatedly questioned election procedures and the legitimacy of results he dislikes.
When will we know who has won?
Voting takes place on Tuesday 3 November, but the results may not be known that night. Close contests, different state rules for counting early and postal ballots, and possible recounts or legal challenges could delay the final outcome.
Once the dust has settled, there will be no respite in this – the land of the endless campaign. Attention will soon turn to the 2028 presidential election campaign, when both parties will seek to turn the results of this November into a foundation for the next fight for the White House.
