A New Way to Think About Women’s Heart Health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Women are speaking more openly about periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause, bringing once-taboo topics into public conversation. Clinicians and health systems need to now connect these experiences with what the science is telling us about how they influence a woman’s cardiovascular health throughout her life.
A woman may see a gynecologist for her irregular periods, a therapist for her depression, and a primary care doctor or cardiologist for her high blood pressure. Each clinician may focus on an important concern. But what is often missing is a shared understanding of how those concerns fit together and what that means for her lifelong cardiovascular health.
A narrow lens has too often been applied to women’s health, defining it as care of reproductive organs and pregnancy. Reproductive health is essential to a woman’s well-being, but women’s health is much broader. We now know that menstrual patterns, pregnancy, and menopause can provide important information about cardiovascular health. Our approach to care should reflect this.
These missed connections matter because cardiovascular disease is the greatest threat to women’s health today. Approximately 1 in 3 deaths in women are due to cardiovascular disease every year. Yet fewer than half of women knew that heart disease was the leading cause of death for women, according to a 2019 survey performed by the American Heart Association.
As a preventive cardiologist and epidemiologist, I study how women’s life events shape cardiovascular disease risk. We now know that unique signals of cardiovascular risk in women can be identified years and decades before heart disease develops. The challenge is making sure that this information changes the care women receive.
This is what led the American Heart Association to bring together the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. Our three-part series, published today in Circulation, establishes a new framework for cardiovascular health in girls and women. The papers and accompanying videos introduce the new Female Life Stage tool, provide clinical guidance, and outline how health systems can deliver coordinated care throughout life.
This framework gives clinicians a shared approach to cardiovascular disease prevention across specialties, interconnected areas of health, and life stages.
What one clinician learns should inform the care a woman receives in different settings and from different clinicians. For example, pregnancy can act as a natural stress test, revealing cardiovascular risks that may otherwise go unrecognized. A history of preeclampsia should inform cardiovascular preventive care long after delivery. The 2026 Cardiovascular Kidney Metabolic Syndrome Guideline now explicitly recognizes pregnancy complications, as well as premature menopause, as one of the factors that can inform personalized prevention.
Menstrual cycle patterns can also provide information relevant to cardiovascular care. A first period before age 10, irregular menstrual cycles, or menopause at a younger age can each serve as signals of higher cardiovascular risk. In a study of more than 10,000 women that my colleagues and I recently published, menopause occurring naturally before age 40 was associated with an approximately 40% higher lifetime risk of coronary heart disease.
Mental health is also linked to hormonal and cardiovascular health. Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) can frequently disrupt sleep, physical activity, and eating patterns, which are relevant to cardiovascular health. These symptoms are common, but being common does not make them inconsequential. Mood symptoms during the menopause transition likewise deserve assessment and treatment as part of comprehensive care.
A woman and her care team need to anticipate that her health needs will change from adolescence through older adulthood. The framework defines four Female Life Stages: the transition around the first period, the years of ovarian cycling (including pregnancy), perimenopause, and postmenopause. It gives clinicians and patients a shared language for recognizing changing health needs so everyone can know what to expect, identifying cardiovascular risk earlier, and guiding prevention across a lifetime.
Recognizing perimenopause as a distinct life stage acknowledges that its symptoms can disrupt daily life, persist for years, and deserve treatment. Hormone and nonhormonal treatments can help, with decisions guided by symptoms, age, cardiovascular and cancer history, and a woman’s preferences. The same visit offers an opportunity to assess cardiovascular disease risk and address changes in cholesterol and cardiometabolic health.
Women may spend nearly 40% of their life in the postmenopause stage. Yet conversations of hormonal health and their enduring impact often end with the last period. Hormonal health history should continue to inform cardiovascular care.
But documenting information in the medical record will not be enough. We also need to change how care is delivered.
An instructive historical example can be drawn from Vienna. In 1991, an art exhibition documented the daily lives of eight girls and women, including an eight-year-old, a student, a nurse, and a retiree. This resulted in the city incorporating women’s everyday needs into urban planning, including street lighting on walking routes for women’s safety.
Health care should apply this principle; women’s experiences should shape how care is organized and delivered. But this redesign must be paired with structural change that addresses the barriers, bias, and discrimination that contribute to symptoms being dismissed, delays in care, and unequal access to health care and treatment for women.
A shared framework—like the one we developed—can support implementation of existing evidence, but we also need better evidence for women. In 1993, the NIH Revitalization Act made women’s inclusion in NIH-funded clinical research a requirement. Yet underrepresentation in research persists. A 2025 systematic review of cardiovascular trials registered from 2017 through 2023 found that women comprised 41% of participants but only 22% in trials studying acute coronary syndromes, including heart attacks.
Women’s health research also remains underfunded, though there may be some recent signs of progress. In October, President Trump signed an executive order to create a new division for women’s health in the National Institutes of Health, but no funding has been allocated at this time.
These efforts are part of a larger movement that builds on decades of public advocacy for women’s health. Since its launch in 2004, the American Heart Association’s Go Red for Women campaign has helped bring women’s cardiovascular health into public view. Melinda French Gates’ investments through Pivotal are directing resources toward understudied areas in women’s health. Katie Couric and Dawn Porter’s forthcoming documentary “HORMONAL!” will add to this momentum by sharing women’s experiences.
Girls and women represent half the population, and every clinician, every specialty, and every health system has a role to play in their health. Women can do much to protect their health, but they should not have to connect the dots in their care alone.

Why Switzerland is voting on individual taxation again

This AI Radio Host Speaks Spanish and Backs Immigrants. It’s Winning Over Listeners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

As footage of ICE raids, deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.
At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.
“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”
After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco history, to the Iran war, migrant workers, racism, and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.
“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa. That's reality.”
Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”
Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera, living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa–a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.
“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”
Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.
“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.
The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.
Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.
It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “amigo inteligente” that eventually became Coyotec.
LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.
Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.
Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.
Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”
Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.
“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”
“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”
While Coyotec may be the first Latino AI radio host, it is far from the first amigo inteligente on the airwaves.
In June 2023, Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT. AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.
In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori, depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).
The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters. Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”
AI personalities are also popping up in televised news. Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.
Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human.”
But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.
Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.
Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.
Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.
A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.
"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."
Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative—a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."
While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”
She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities.
In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”
While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."
Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.
"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”
Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana. Make noise that matters.”

Apple Music unveils logo that was physically "made by sound"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Apple Music unveils logo that was physically “made by sound”
Technology brand Apple has revealed the first rebrand for its Apple Music service, which was made in collaboration with musician Fred Again by passing sound waves through a pool of oil.
Created as part of the service’s first rebrand since Apple Music launched in 2015, the logo has a wave-like aesthetic that was created through a physical process at a time when digital design and artificial intelligence are at the forefront of creative processes.
According to Apple, the core concept was to give Apple Music a distinctive sound and create a logo that was “made by sound”.
“For the rebrand of Apple Music, we wanted sound to create the visuals,” said Apple. “How do we take this idea of music and distill it into something visually beautiful?”
The creation process was revealed in a video released by Apple, which showed an application icon-shaped piece of plastic placed in a shallow pool of mineral oil.
Musical frequencies, created by Fred Again in collaboration with NEST Acoustics, were translated into physical vibrations using a transducer. These vibrations moved the oil to produce the wave-like effect on the logo.
“Essentially, the idea was to create the perfect sound wave,” said Apple. “We take a frequency and we play it through a rig. This rig then moves a large amount of liquid at the frequency of the notes.”
“We partnered with one of the world’s best music artists to create the notes for the final mnemonic,” it continued. “And then we used that sound to create the visuals.”
Along with the wave-like overlay, the typology of the Apple Music logo has been amended to align with wider Apple visual identities. Sat alongside the apple icon, the M in music has been made lowercase.
The typology was changed to a custom version of Apple’s SF Pro typeface in an entirely lowercase, bold letterform.
Apple unveiled the new logo last week along with an additional musical note icon.
The Apple Music identity was teased earlier in the month, when the company unveiled its Apple Music Hall venue in Battersea, London. The logo is placed on the wall within the venue, which has an industrial aesthetic to match the renovated power station it sits within.

Font size
Bulgaria's Central Election Commission has published the final results of the first round of the presidential election held on 25 October, with 100% of polling station returns processed.
Iliana Iotova and Kiril Valchev came first with 528,929 votes, or 34.76%, followed by Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev with 486,214 votes, or 31.95%.
Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin finished third with 190,894 votes (12.55%), while Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov received 70,118 votes (4.6%).
The remaining 23 presidential tickets each received less than 4% of the vote.
A total of 67,353 voters, or 4.43%, chose the "I support no one" option.
Voter turnout was around 22%.
The two leading tickets, Iotova–Valchev and Gyurov–Kandev, will face each other in the presidential run-off on 1 November.

Central Bank moves to support corporate bond market liquidity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:55:45 UTC
17:55:45 KST

Turkish Lira-denominated loans extended for the repayment of domestic debt securities issued by private sector entities other than banks and maturing by the end of the year will be exempt from credit growth limits, according to a Central Bank directive issued to banks.
With this regulation, the Central Bank aims to support macrofinancial stability and liquidity management.
Under the measure, the central bank seeks to prevent potential difficulties arising from credit growth limits in the access of highly creditworthy issuers to bank financing, while also facilitating issuers’ liquidity management. The exemption will apply to debt securities maturing by the end of the year.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Oct. 20 that the total size of the private sector bond market stands at 1 trillion liras, while only 26.5 billion liras of that amount is due to mature by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) has decided to raise the minimum financial asset requirement for qualified investor status from 10 million liras to 50 million liras, while increasing the minimum transaction volume criterion from 5 million liras to 25 million liras.
The decision comes after the troubles in the fund market, which affected 455,000 investors. Amid the problems, SPK in September ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds, with combined assets of more than 900 billion liras.

7-year-old girl among 4 Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:54:53 UTC
17:54:53 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Four Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl, were killed and 14 others injured in attacks by the Israeli army and Israel-backed gunmen in the Gaza Strip on Monday, amid daily violations of last year’s ceasefire agreement, a medical source said.
 
The source at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza told Anadolu that the bodies of two young men and a girl were brought to the hospital following an airstrike and gunfire in the Bir 19 area west of Khan Younis.
 
An Israeli drone carried out several strikes on Bir 19, an area housing tents for displaced Palestinians, killing a young man and moderately injuring four others, witnesses said.
 
Israeli military vehicles also opened heavy fire toward the displacement tents as Israeli-backed gunmen fired in the surrounding area, killing another young man and a 7-year-old girl, who was shot while inside her tent, they added.
 
Another Palestinian man was killed and four others were injured in an Israeli strike west of Khan Younis, the source said.
 
Local sources said an Israeli drone struck a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis.
 
Israeli artillery also shelled areas east of Khan Younis as military vehicles stationed east of the city opened heavy fire.
 
In central Gaza, a Palestinian woman sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire in the Ard al-Shawa area east of Deir al-Balah, another medical source said.
 
Israeli military vehicles made a limited advance east of Deir al-Balah amid heavy gunfire, witnesses said.
 
In northern Gaza, Israeli artillery shelled eastern Gaza City as tanks positioned behind the “Yellow Line” opened fire east of the Shujaiya and Tuffah neighborhoods, they added.
 
The “Yellow Line” marks the area to which Israeli forces withdrew during the first phase of the ceasefire agreement and separates territory under Israeli military control from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
 
Despite the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
 
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Estonian musicians refuse to perform alongside Chinese orchestra with Russia links

Estonian musicians refuse to perform alongside Chinese orchestra with Russia links
The Estonian Festival Orchestra canceled a concert last week in China after it was revealed that the local symphony orchestra had close ties to Russia.
The Estonian Festival Orchestra, conducted by Paavo Järvi, is on tour in China and was scheduled to perform at Wuxi Symphony Hall, in eastern China, with the local orchestra on October 23.
The Wuxi orchestra toured Russia last year as part of an official China-Russia Years of Culture event and has performed with the Russian National Orchestra.
After learning about their partner's background, the Estonian musicians refused to take part in the joint concert.
The cancellation could cost the Estonian Festival Orchestra hundreds of thousands of euros, although the exact amount is not yet known.
According to the Estonian musicians, going ahead with the concert would have conflicted with their principles and caused irreparable reputational damage.

Mandelblit resumes testimony as Netanyahu defense presses on investigation approvals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:51:58 UTC
17:51:58 KST

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit testified Monday that police questioning of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Case 1000 went beyond the warning given at the outset, and that the warning in Case 2000 did not match the suspicions being investigated.
His testimony at the Jerusalem District Court came as Netanyahu’s defense continued to challenge the scope and timing of his investigation approvals. The judges also pressed Mandelblit on when he authorized questioning Netanyahu as a suspect in Case 2000, and whether an earlier decision he recalled had been documented.
Mandelblit, who authorized the investigations and later approved the indictment, was called as a defense witness. His questioning by Netanyahu’s lawyer, Amit Hadad, has focused on what investigators were permitted to examine and what Netanyahu was told about the suspicions against him before being questioned.
Case 1000 concerns expensive gifts Netanyahu allegedly received from businessmen Arnon Milchan and James Packer, and actions he allegedly took to benefit Milchan. Hadad argued that the warning given to Netanyahu described suspicions concerning the rules on accepting gifts, rather than bribery or fraud and breach of trust.
Mandelblit said that, to the best of his recollection, he had not been involved in drafting the warnings. He agreed that questioning about Netanyahu’s relationship with Milchan went beyond the wording presented to him.
Hadad compares language used in Case 1000, 4000
Hadad also compared the language used in Cases 1000 and 4000. Mandelblit said the wording in Case 4000 was intended to preserve room to determine whether the suspicions amounted to bribery or fraud and breach of trust. Hadad challenged the consistency of that explanation with his earlier answers about Case 1000.
Much of Monday’s hearing concerned the decision to question Netanyahu as a suspect in Case 2000, which centers on discussions with Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in exchange for steps against rival newspaper Israel Hayom.
Mandelblit said recordings of the conversations established reasonable suspicion against Mozes, while he deliberated over Netanyahu’s position. He recalled testimony from former Netanyahu chief of staff Ari Harow as a development that led him toward approving questioning of the prime minister as a suspect.
The judges pressed him to distinguish that developing assessment from a formal authorization.
Asked about a decision preceding January 5, 2017, Mandelblit said he could not identify documentation of it. He described discussions with other officials rather than a formally recorded decision, and agreed that the actual approval was given on January 5, the day Netanyahu was first questioned in Case 2000.
Mandelblit maintains he intended to have Netanyahu questioned as suspect
Mandelblit nevertheless maintained that he intended to have Netanyahu questioned as a suspect, possibly as early as December 25, 2016, when arrangements for questioning in both cases were discussed. He said final approval may have awaited Mozes’s questioning on January 4.
Hadad argued that Netanyahu had initially been summoned without approval to question him as a suspect in Case 2000. Mandelblit rejected the suggestion that he intended Netanyahu to be questioned merely as a witness.
Mandelblit also agreed that the Case 2000 warning, which referred to requesting and receiving improper benefits from businessmen in connection with his position, did not fit the suspicions in that case.
Monday’s exchanges followed testimony on Sunday in which Mandelblit said he had ordered police to stop wiretapping Netanyahu confidant Natan Eshel. Although investigators had obtained a court warrant, Mandelblit said the operation should have been brought to him for approval beforehand.
Netanyahu’s trial began in May 2020. He faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in all three cases and a bribery charge in Case 4000, concerning alleged regulatory benefits for Bezeq in exchange for intervention in Walla’s news coverage. He denies wrongdoing.

Gokhan Ergocun

European natural gas prices rose 3.3% to exceed €97 ($108.8) per megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022 as the Middle East conflict continues to threaten supplies.
Intensifying conflict in the Middle East has sharply heightened concerns over winter energy supplies, particularly as liquefied natural gas (LNG) flows from the Persian Gulf — which previously accounted for nearly a fifth of global supply — remain down roughly 80% year-on-year.
European gas futures traded at €97.15 per megawatt-hour as of 0820GMT, up 3.3% from Friday's close and hitting their highest level since December 2022.

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained two individuals from the South Caucasus who acted on instructions from Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) to carry out an FPV-drone attack on a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system and an electric power facility.
"The Federal Security Service has thwarted the subversive and terrorist activities of two individuals from the Transcaucasus region, born in 1991 and 1998, who were acting as agents of the Security Service of Ukraine and were involved in preparing a terrorist act," the FSB’s Public Relations Center (PRC) said.
According to the FSB, the suspects were tasked with assembling strike-capable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) retrieved from hidden caches, transporting them to a launch site in the Moscow Region, and preparing them for launch.
"The drones were to be operated remotely from Ukrainian territory. FSB officers apprehended the individuals while they were preparing an attack on an electric power facility and a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system," the agency said.
The FSB reported that one of the detainees had been recruited by an SBU officer and traveled to Russia in exchange for a promised monetary reward to carry out the planned attack. He subsequently enlisted an acquaintance from his inner circle to assist him.
FPV drones and components intended for the manufacture of improvised explosive devices were recovered from caches in the Smolensk and Kaluga regions, the FSB said.
The FSB’s Investigative Department has opened a criminal case against the detainees under Part 2 of Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code, which concerns participation in a terrorist organization. A court has ordered both suspects to be held in custody.
A comprehensive set of investigative and operational measures is underway to establish the full circumstances of the alleged activities and identify any possible accomplices, the FSB added.
The agency also warned that Ukrainian intelligence services were seeking to recruit civilians for illicit activities intended to harm Russia. It emphasized that anyone assisting what it described as the adversary would be identified and held accountable, according to the FSB’s Public Relations Center.

Battleground metros to watch in South Africa's municipal elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:50:31 UTC
17:50:31 KST

Battleground metros to watch in South Africa's municipal elections
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 26 - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4 amid voter frustration over poor service delivery, unstable local government coalitions and rising costs.
Held every five years, the elections will be an important gauge of the political landscape ahead of the 2029 national vote, with support for the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela's former liberation movement, continuing to erode.
Here are the key battleground metros:
JOHANNESBURG: THE PRIZE
Africa's richest city has churned through seven mayors since the 2021 local elections as successive coalition governments have unravelled.
The pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) gained an early advantage by naming former Cape Town mayor and Western Cape premier Helen Zille as its mayoral candidate months ahead of its rivals. The 75-year-old political veteran has run an energetic campaign focused on deteriorating infrastructure and poor service delivery.
Recent polls put the DA above 30% and the ANC above 20%, raising the possibility of a coalition between the two parties, which have governed together nationally since the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024. Both parties could first seek deals with smaller parties rather than share power.
TSHWANE: ACTIONSA THE KINGMAKER
Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, underscores the importance of smaller parties in South Africa's fragmented municipal politics.
The ANC governed the metro until 2016, when the DA captured it in a major urban defeat for the ruling party. Coalition politics subsequently proved volatile, and the DA lost power in 2024 after its coalition partner ActionSA backed an ANC-led no-confidence motion against its mayor.
Tshwane has since been governed by a multi-party coalition led by ActionSA. The party, founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, is a centre-right party that campaigns on anti-corruption and a hard line on immigration.
CAPE TOWN: DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE BASTION
The DA is heavily favoured to retain Cape Town, which it has governed since 2006 and where it has held an outright majority since 2011.
Polls suggest the party should remain above 50%, though some analysts expect a tighter contest as voters grapple with soaring property prices and persistent gang violence.
The DA is also targeting Nelson Mandela Bay, one of South Africa's most turbulent coalition metros and currently governed by an ANC-led coalition.
ETHEKWINI: ZUMA WILDCARD
The economic hub of KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, could deliver one of the election's biggest blows to the ANC, with former president Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) threatening to displace it.
Zuma backed MKP after his bitter split with the ANC in 2023. Polls suggest the party could win 40% to 50% of the vote, while ANC support could fall into the low teens. MKP's rise helped drive the ANC's losses in the 2024 national election.
EKURHULENI: CORRUPTION TEST
Ekurhuleni, home to Johannesburg's OR Tambo International Airport, could provide another measure of the ANC's decline in Gauteng Province, where voters have cited concerns over corruption and crime.
Polls suggest ANC support could fall from 38% in 2021 to about 25%, leaving it neck-and-neck with the DA.
BUFFALO CITY AND MANGAUNG: LAST STRONGHOLDS OF THE ANC
Buffalo City, which includes KuGompo City in Eastern Cape province, and Mangaung, home to Bloemfontein in Free State province, remain the ANC's strongest metropolitan bastions, making them important tests of how far the party's urban support has eroded.
The ANC won 59% in Buffalo City and 51% in Mangaung in 2021, helped by deep-rooted loyalty to the former liberation movement. REUTERS

Slovakia seeks agreements with the Kremlin: Foreign Minister in Moscow for energy talks
Kyiv • UNN
A Slovak delegation has arrived in Moscow for talks on energy and Russian gas. Bratislava fears arbitration claims of up to €16 billion.
A Slovak delegation headed by Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanár has arrived in moscow to participate in a meeting of the intergovernmental commission. UNN reports this, citing Deutsche Welle and the Slovak Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The main topic of the talks will be Slovakia's energy security, in particular the supply of Russian gas.
"The absolute priority with which I am travelling to moscow is Slovakia's energy security," Blanár said.
Details
On Monday, October 26, the 22nd meeting of the Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission on economic and scientific-technical cooperation will take place in moscow. The commission last met in November 2021, before the start of russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The meeting will be co-chaired by Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár and Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education valery falkov.
The aim of the meeting is to determine the scope of cooperation with russia in areas of "common interest," the ministry said. At the same time, it clarified that Slovakia's obligations within the EU would be taken into account.
The parties plan to discuss issues in energy, including nuclear energy, agriculture, environmental protection, tourism, sports and culture. Negotiations are also planned on economic cooperation in areas not covered by European Union sanctions. According to Blanár, the main priority of his visit will be Slovakia's energy security against the backdrop of the EU's decision to gradually abandon Russian gas.
In particular, the Slovak state-owned company Slovenský plynárenský priemysel (SPP) has a long-term contract with the Russian "gazprom" that runs until 2034. The agreement provides for the take-or-pay principle ("take or pay"), under which the buyer is obliged to pay for the agreed volumes of gas even if it declines to receive them.
The head of the Slovak Foreign Ministry warned that an early termination of purchases could lead to arbitration claims from russia amounting to more than €10 billion. In his estimation, potential financial claims could reach €16 billion. At the same time, Blanár stressed that the European Union is ready to provide Slovakia with legal assistance, but does not guarantee compensation for possible financial losses.
According to Russian media, Blanár is already in moscow.
The Slovak delegation was also expected to include State Secretary at the Ministry of Economy Vladimir Šimonjak and Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the National Council Marián Kéry. Experts from the Ministries of the Environment, Economy, Agriculture, Culture, Tourism and Sports are also expected. In addition, representatives of the Slovak gas industry, the Slovak state-owned joint-stock company JAVYS, the Slovak Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the Slovak-Russian Business Council were expected to arrive in moscow.
The Slovak minister plans to hold separate talks with russia's Foreign Minister sergey lavrov. The parties will discuss bilateral relations, economic cooperation and international issues, including initiatives to end the war in Ukraine. Blanár said that, despite condemning Russian aggression and violations of international law, Bratislava considers it necessary to maintain contacts with moscow in order to protect its national interests.

Two dead, 17 injured: aftermath of Ukrainian attack on Russia’s central Voronezh Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

VORONEZH, October 26. /TASS/. Two civilians were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured in a Ukrainian attack on the Voronezh Region in central Russia, Governor Alexander Gusev reported.
According to him, many of the victims were on a train traveling through the left-bank suburbs of Voronezh when drone debris fell on it.
TASS has compiled the key information on the attack’s aftermath.
Scale
- On-duty air defenses shot down 113 Ukrainian drones over the Voronezh Region in central Russia overnight, with 70 of them directly over Voronezh, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on his Max channel.
Fatalities, injuries
- Two people were killed and 17 others, including a child, were injured as a result of the Ukrainian attack, the regional head emphasized.
- He specified that the deceased were two men born in 1960 and 1973.
- According to Gusev, many of the injured, including two with serious injuries, were on a train traveling through the left-bank suburbs of Voronezh when drone debris fell on it.
- At least five passengers on the Anapa-Moscow train were injured as a result of the drone attack in the Voronezh Region, Russian Railways reported.
- They are receiving the necessary medical assistance, the company added.
Aftermath
- According to Gusev, the Ukrainian attack caused fires at several industrial facilities, an office building in the city center, an apartment building, two suburban settlements, a school stadium, and a parking garage.
- Damage to building facades and windows has been reported in nearly all districts of the city.
Train service update
- Due to the drone attack in the Voronezh Region on the Tresvyatskaya-Somovo-Otroshka-Voronezh section, train service has been temporarily suspended, Russian Railways said.
- Repair crews are working to restore service.
- Russian Railways has warned of possible delays for southbound passenger trains and commuter trains.
- Service was later resumed.
- Eighteen passenger trains are delayed, Russian Railways specified.
- The company added that train crew members are providing comprehensive assistance and support to passengers.
- Russian Railways is taking all necessary measures to bring trains back on schedule.
Investigation and response
- The Voronezh Regional Prosecutor’s Office will monitor compliance with the rights of the victims and ensure they receive assistance following the Ukrainian attack.
- The Moscow Interregional Transport Prosecutor’s Office is conducting oversight activities in connection with damage to railway infrastructure in the Voronezh Region.
- The Transport Prosecutor’s Office is monitoring compliance with the rights of rail passengers.
- The Southern Transport Prosecutor’s Office has taken steps to ensure the rights of passengers on delayed trains on the Tresvyatskaya-Somovo-Otroshka-Voronezh route are upheld following damage to the railroad contact line caused by a drone attack, the press service said on its Telegram channel.
- Transport prosecutors are monitoring compliance with passengers’ rights.
- The Russian Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case over the terrorist attack under Article 205 of the Russian Criminal Code, Spokeswoman Svetlana Petrenko said.
- Investigators are establishing all the circumstances of the incident.

The Moelln Letters | Storyteller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:44:38 UTC
17:44:38 KST

[NOTE: The Moelln Letters available until December 23, 2026.]
In November 1992, racist arson attacks in the German town of Mölln devastated the lives of Ibrahim Arslan and his family. The 7-year-old boy survived the fire, but he tragically lost his sister, cousin, and grandmother. In the aftermath, the city received hundreds of letters of solidarity which were archived and forgotten about for nearly three decades.
Woven into Ibrahim's poignant journey of discovery and his encounters with three of the letter writers, these long-forgotten messages create a powerful visual bridge between past and present. The film follows Ibrahim and his siblings and offers a sensitive portrayal of the enduring trauma that still affects their lives today. By fighting racism and advocating for victims, Ibrahim has found a way to channel his pain, while his brother Namik still struggles with the emotional scars of the past.
The Moelln Letters not only amplifies the voices of survivors and victims, but also uncovers long-forgotten letters expressing support and sympathy. This film brings forth a new perspective on remembrance — shifting the focus to the stories of the survivors and ensuring they receive the space and recognition they deserve.
DIRECTOR STATEMENT
By Martina Priessner | Director
When I met Ibrahim Arslan in 2020, I already knew who he was. The racist arson attacks in Mölln had shaken me deeply when I was 23 years old. Racism, antisemitism, the persistence of right-wing terrorism in Germany, and the state’s and societal ignorance towards right-wing extremist networks have remained central concerns for me to this day.
Ibrahim is a significant voice in Germany, especially in encouraging victims to step forward and speak out. His powerful message — that those affected are the "primary witnesses of their own stories" and cannot be reduced to mere extras or objects — has played a crucial role in transforming the country’s culture of remembrance.
Ibrahim told me about the letters of solidarity. His disbelief and shock at the withheld solidarity were written all over his face. What he shared with me left a lasting mark. How could such an important expression of support never reach those it was intended for? And what does this say about how victims are treated?
I couldn’t shake Ibrahim's words from my mind: "When we tell our stories, our trauma dissipates, because our greatest longing is to tell our stories." A few days later, I called him and proposed making a film together. The many unheard, unseen, and untold stories from the perspective of the victims and survivors form the emotional core of this film. To ensure these stories are heard, we need the power and magic of cinema, in which I have unwavering faith.
At a time when democracy in Germany faces threats unparalleled in the past 80 years, the film asks crucial questions, gives space to the personal losses of the victims, and makes solidarity visible.

Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?

2026-10-26

Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?
After years of war, displacement and restrictions, Gazans ask whether Israel’s election will affect their future.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — After three years of genocidal war, Palestinians in Gaza are watching the upcoming elections in Israel with a mixture of fear and uncertainty.
Although the territory has been under a “ceasefire” since October 2025, Palestinians in Gaza continue to endure almost daily Israeli air strikes, dire living conditions, and a punishing siege that has caused shortages of basic goods.
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday to vote for their next government, in an election that has been shaped by the war on Gaza. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been strongly criticised for his handling of security before the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel. Members of his far-right government have called for a tougher line on Gaza, including the expulsion of its population.
The people of Gaza know this election will shape their future and many have been closely watching the campaign.
Mohammed Eliyan, 36, was displaced from Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza and now lives in Deir el-Balah with his five children. He hopes a change in leadership in Israel could bring relief to Palestinians who have endured repeated displacement and war.
“We follow the Israeli election to see who will win in the next phase. We hope there might be some easing for the Palestinian cause and for us, who have been displaced again,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eliyan hopes that Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military commander and Netanyahu’s main rival, will defeat the prime minister. He sees Netanyahu as more hardline and fears that if his Likud party and far-right allies win another term, it would mean more war and further displacement for Gaza’s people.
“We hope there will be changes after the election, and that someone other than Benjamin Netanyahu will win. What Netanyahu has done to the Palestinian people, before and after October 7, has not been a small thing,” he said.
But regardless of who wins, Eliyan does not expect a major shift in Israeli policy.
“They are still our enemy, and I don’t expect things to improve dramatically,” he said. “But we hope someone else might be less harsh than Netanyahu.”
He called on Israel’s next leader to end the war, prevent displacement and starvation, and ease restrictions at Gaza’s crossings.
“We want whoever leads Israel not to be hardline. End the war and let us live in peace,” he said.
Islam Salem, 41, is displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and has three daughters. He is following Israel’s election closely and believes the result could affect Gaza’s future and the lives of his children, likely for the worse.
“Politics is our livelihood. It is connected to everything in our lives, our living conditions and even the future of our children,” he said.
But he also believes that elections primarily serve Israeli interests, so even if there are new faces in the next government, the Gaza strategy will likely remain the same.
“Israeli policy will not change in any way. Whatever they take, they consider it theirs and a political gain for them, the gains of a war they have pursued for a long time,” Islam told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Israel’s continued control of about 65 percent of Gaza’s territory inside the “Yellow Line”. He also doubts whether reconstruction will begin soon in Gaza, where more than 80 percent of buildings have been damaged, and about two-thirds of those have been completely destroyed.
“I think reconstruction will be difficult. They do not want to give others any rights. They want their rights in full, and even more,” he said.
Years of war have left Salem struggling to imagine a future beyond his harsh daily reality.
“There is no future left for us to be afraid of. We live day by day. We have no idea what will happen next, and everything we feared has already happened,” he said.
Asked what he would say to Israel’s next prime minister, he spoke of how many in Gaza are feeling.
“If only a simple person could come and talk to him and say, ‘Leave us alone. Give us some breathing space and let us breathe.’ But he would not be convinced. What can I say to him?” he said.
Hanan Abu al-Maaza, 57, has been displaced more than 12 times during the war on Gaza. She fears Israel’s next government could bring more suffering to its people in the besieged enclave.
“We follow the election because of the fear and anxiety we are living with. We have been displaced more than 12 times, and we are afraid they will do even worse to us than before,” she said.
“We go to sleep without feeling safe, wondering what they might do to us next. The fear is still in our heads and hearts.”
Abu al-Maaza says if Netanyahu is defeated, there will be more chance that she can return to her home in Beit Lahiya.
“I hope someone else wins, so we can have peace of mind and feel safe, and return to our homes. That is what we wish for,” she said.
After years of destruction in Gaza, she hopes Israel’s next leader will show Palestinians more mercy.
“Maybe he will say that there is nothing left in Gaza, that they have done enough and should let people live. There is hardly anything left in Gaza for anyone to think about doing anything more,” she said.
Abu al-Maaza urged Israel’s next leader to end the war and stop the suffering in the territory.
“We have had enough of war and destruction. There is nothing left to destroy, yet the suffering continues,” she said.
Manar Owaida, 23, is originally from northern Gaza and is now displaced in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City. She is also keeping an eye on the Israeli election and considering its potential impact.
“I follow the election to know what they are saying and planning, and to understand what is happening around us and how the next Israeli government might affect the situation in Gaza,” she said.
Owaida hopes Gadi Eisenkot will replace Netanyahu, and sees the current prime minister as more extreme than his challenger. But she does not believe a change in Israel’s leadership would transform Palestinian lives, arguing that government policies have remained consistent for decades.
“Israel’s policy is one of crime, killing and destruction. Since 1948, it has been the same policy, the same killing and the same blockade,” she said.
Still, she hopes a new government could ease restrictions and killings and withdraw from areas beyond the “Yellow Line”, allowing life to gradually return to Gaza.
“There might be a change in Israeli policy if someone comes in place of Netanyahu and eases the blockade and the killing we are living through,” she said.
“There could be a withdrawal from the Yellow Line and life could gradually return to Gaza. But we are waiting with fear and uncertainty, alongside a little hope.”
Her greatest concern is that Netanyahu could launch a wider regional war to avoid domestic political pressure around the time of the vote.
Owaida said she wants Israel’s next prime minister to allow Palestinians to live without fear of further violence.
“We want to live in freedom and peace, away from killing and wars,” she said.
Mousa Ali, 33, was displaced from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza and is now in Gaza City with his four children.
He believes that the outcome of the election could determine whether displaced Palestinians can return to areas beyond the “Yellow Line”.
“For Palestinians, this election is critical, especially because of the Yellow Line. We hope the opposition will be better when it comes to allowing displaced people to return to their areas,” he said.
Ali mentioned Gadi Eisenkot as a possible alternative and hopes Arab parties will perform strongly so they have a role in the next government.
But he does not expect a new leader to bring major changes for the people of Gaza and fears that Israeli attacks will continue. He says a Netanyahu victory would prolong displacement and control over areas around the “Yellow Line”.
“Every day in Gaza, there is blood, there are people being killed, and there is bombing everywhere,” he said. “We hope this policy will end and that a new prime minister will stop this ongoing bloodshed.”

Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies at 46
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:42:46 UTC
17:42:46 KST

Dilara Hamit
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Eric Bauza, the Emmy-winning Canadian voice actor best known for voicing Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died Sunday at age 46, according to his family.
Bauza died at his home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records.
His family announced his death in a statement posted on his Instagram account Sunday.
“Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly,” the family said, adding that further details would follow.
Bauza was among the animation industry's most prolific voice actors, with more than 400 acting credits over a career spanning roughly 25 years.
Besides Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, he voiced several other Looney Tunes characters, including Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner and Charlie Dog.
His work featured in productions including Looney Tunes Cartoons, Space Jam: A New Legacy and the 2026 film Coyote vs. Acme.
Bauza also contributed to animated series including Avatar: The Last Airbender, Chowder, Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated, Fanboy & Chum Chum, Ben 10: Omniverse, The Adventures of Puss in Boots and Rick and Morty.
He received five Daytime Emmy nominations for his performances in Looney Tunes Cartoons, Muppet Babies and The Adventures of Puss in Boots.
Bauza also won three Children's & Family Emmy Awards for his work on Looney Tunes Cartoons, Bugs Bunny Builders and Teen Titans Go!
Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks Chairman Channing Dungey said Bauza brought “joy and laughter to millions around the world” during his 15 years with Warner Bros. Animation.
“He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc,” Dungey said, referring to the voice actor who originated many classic Looney Tunes characters.
Born in Scarborough, Toronto, on Dec. 7, 1979, Bauza began his animation career as a character designer before moving into voice acting.
His first credited acting role came in the Canadian animated series The Ripping Friends in 2001.
At the time of his death, Bauza was working on Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical, in which he was due to voice Daffy Duck, and The Dragon Masters, in which he was cast as the Shogun King.

Crown Princess Elisabeth thanks well-wishers for birthday greets (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:56 UTC
17:41:56 KST

Crown Princess Elisabeth of Belgium celebrated her 25th birthday at the weekend. To mark this festive occasion, the Royal Palace released a new photograph of the Belgian Crown Princess. The Royal Mint and postal services provider Bpost are also celebrating the birthday with a commemorative coin and a new postage stamp.
In a short video posted on social media, Elisabeth thanks everyone, in two of Belgium’s three national languages, for the many birthday wishes she has received through various channels. “It has warmed my heart” she said.
A year’s break after her student days
Crown Princess Elisabeth is the eldest child – and daughter – of King Filip and Queen Mathilde and will be the first woman to ascend the throne in Belgium. She has held the title of Duchess of Brabant since 21 July 2013.
In May, Elisabeth graduated from the Harvard Kennedy School in Boston, one of the most prestigious universities in the world, with a master’s degree in public policy.
She had previously completed a bachelor’s degree in ‘History & Politics’ at Lincoln College, a college that forms part of Oxford University in the United Kingdom.
In an interview on the day of her graduation, the Crown Princess left it open as to when she would start working full-time for the Royal Family. “My time at university was very intense; I threw myself into it completely. I’m now going to try to take a step back and lay a solid foundation for what lies ahead. Nothing in a hurry; everything in its own time” the princess said.
“I’d like to take a year or so to think about it. For the time being, I want to develop myself in a different way. How exactly? I don’t know yet.”
As Crown Princess, Elisabeth will in the future lead Belgian trade missions abroad. At present, this is still a job for Queen Mathilde. When Elisabeth takes on her role as active Crown Princess, she will also be given her own royal household and an allowance.
Commemorative coin and stamp
Both Belgium’s Royal Mint and postal services provider Bpost are honouring the Crown Princess with a special issue.
The Royal Mint is launching Elisabeth’s first commemorative coin. The euro coin, with a face value of 12.5 euros, is the only gold commemorative coin to be issued this year. Only 2,500 copies will be produced.
Alongside the portrait of the Crown Princess, the number 25 and her monogram, the reverse of the coin also features Elisabeth’s father, King Filip, together with the face value and ‘Belgium’ in the three national languages.
Bpost is issuing a stamp sheet featuring Elisabeth’s brand-new black-and-white portrait by photographer Bas Bogaerts. Only a limited edition of 41,970 sheets will be printed.
This is not the first time Princess Elisabeth has been honoured with her own stamp. This happened in 2002, on the occasion of her first birthday, in 2016 (featuring the whole family) and in 2019, to mark her 18th birthday. Her latest stamp will, however, be the first special self-adhesive stamp dedicated to a member of the Belgian royal family.

LUGANSK, October 26. /TASS/. The strike capability of the Ukrainian armed forces declined last week amid attacks by Russian forces on Ukrainian military facilities, including those located in the rear, military expert Andrey Marochko reported.
"Last week, the situation on the line of contact worsened for Ukrainian forces, largely as a result of rear logistics disruption and Russian strikes targeting the military-industrial complex facilities, logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure, weapons and military equipment production sites, military-technical equipment warehouses, as well as temporary deployment sites for Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries. On Friday, the Russian Defense Ministry reported that over the past week, the Russian military had launched three massive and 11 combined strikes on the enemy’s logistics centers, energy and transport sites. Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities were incapacitated.

Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:23 UTC
17:41:23 KST

Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin America
The outcome of Brazil’s presidential election demonstrates that the far-right tide in Latin America is not inevitable.
At 80, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has pulled off an extraordinary political victory. After losing the first round to Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, by 47 percent to 45 percent, Lula defied the odds to secure a stunning second-round victory, with 51.8 percent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.2 percent.
His triumph confounded every pre-election poll and crowned a dramatic campaign revival that few had anticipated.
Lula’s victory in Latin America’s largest country does more than halt the far right’s return to power in Brazil. It breaks a succession of right-wing electoral victories across the region and deals a major blow to United States President Donald Trump’s increasingly interventionist agenda in the Western Hemisphere.
When Bolsonaro unexpectedly defeated Lula in the first round, the result sent shockwaves across Brazil and beyond. For the government, the defeat was particularly startling given its strong socioeconomic record. What followed was an extraordinary three-week political mobilisation that transformed the sluggish first-round campaign of Lula’s Workers’ Party into an existential confrontation over the future of democracy and sovereignty in Brazil.
The economic record was hardly that of a government heading for defeat. Brazil’s economy grew by a cumulative 9.2 percent between 2023 and 2025, compared with an average of just 5.6 percent among its South American neighbours. Unemployment fell from 9.3 percent in 2022 to a historic low of 5.4 percent in 2026.
Brazil also exited the United Nations Hunger Map in 2025, after having returned to it under the Bolsonaro senior administration. In the Amazon, deforestation fell to its lowest level in decades, a sharp reversal of the trend under his predecessor.
Not everything has been rosy under the Lula administration. Millions of Brazilians have remained trapped in credit-card debt, struggling with extremely high interest rates, while an explosion of online gambling has devastated the livelihoods of families. The run-off result sent a clear signal that there was social discontent.
Lula responded with unusually bold measures: a sweeping debt-relief initiative and restrictions on online betting, as well as expanded social benefits, fuel subsidies, and the transition from a six-day to a five-day working week. These policies sought to reconnect the government’s macroeconomic achievements with the everyday economic anxieties of Brazilian voters.
Bolsonaro offered a radically different vision for Brazil: sweeping spending cuts, privatisations, lower taxes and, above all, an iron-fisted response to crime and insecurity. His proposals included building five maximum-security prisons modelled on El Salvador’s notorious penitentiary system and authorising lethal force against heavily armed criminals.
Bolsonaro also pledged to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years for plotting to overturn the 2022 election, and to grant clemency to those convicted over the January 8, 2023 assault on Brazil’s democratic institutions. For his supporters, this represented an opportunity to reverse what they considered judicial persecution. For his opponents, it threatened to rehabilitate the attempted coup and undermine judicial independence.
Lula’s campaign came back re-energised, with many young Brazilians mobilising at the grassroots level. The campaign was able to overcome even algorithmic bias by social media giants like Meta, which favoured Bolsonaro.
Ultimately, the election became a battle not only over Brazil’s democracy but also its sovereignty. Trump’s administration has intervened conspicuously in Brazilian politics throughout Lula’s term, imposing punitive tariffs, sanctioning a Supreme Court justice involved in Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and openly embracing his son’s candidacy.
In May, Trump received Flavio Bolsonaro in the Oval Office. Two days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio designated Brazil’s two largest crime organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a measure Flavio had publicly requested.
These designations carry implications extending far beyond electoral politics. They potentially open the door to US military operations on Brazilian territory under Washington’s expanding war on so-called “narcoterrorism”. The world saw how one such foreign terrorist designation enabled the US to intervene militarily in Venezuela and abduct its sitting president.
Whereas Trump seeks to draw Latin America’s largest country into Washington’s expanding system of hemispheric military dominance, Lula has defended Brazil’s strategic autonomy, insisting that cooperation against organised crime must respect national sovereignty.
He framed the election as a choice between a sovereign Brazil charting its own course and one subordinated to Washington’s geopolitical agenda. Sunday’s election result shows that the Brazilian people have made their choice.
Importantly, Lula’s victory may mark a turning point in Latin America’s rightward shift. Since Trump’s return to the White House, the right has scored a string of electoral victories in Honduras, Chile, and Bolivia, among others. But Lula’s re-election suggests that its momentum may be faltering.
The result comes just ahead of the US midterms and could deliver a significant setback to the strength of Trump’s leadership in the Americas. In Argentina, President Javier Milei — who regularly attacks Lula and threw all his weight behind Bolsonaro — has been sliding in the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. In Chile, President Jose Antonio Kast has suffered an even more precipitous collapse in public support.
Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum, for her part, has likely breathed a sigh of relief. A Lula defeat would have left her increasingly isolated in a region gravitating towards Mexico’s northern neighbour. Instead, Latin America’s two most populous countries and largest economies will remain firmly on the left for the foreseeable future.
It is too early to declare the region’s rightward turn over. But Lula’s victory raises the possibility that the wave has already crested. Brazil will not be joining Trump’s Shield of the Americas, and while the “Donroe Doctrine” remains a threat, its moment of greatest ascendancy may already be behind it.
Lula’s victory is a vindication of a lifetime spent fighting for society’s most marginalised and disenfranchised. And its significance extends far beyond Brazil’s borders. For defenders of democracy, multilateralism, international law, environmental protection and the sovereignty of the Global South, it sends a powerful message: the far right’s advance is neither inevitable nor irreversible. Not in Brazil. Not anywhere.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Sulina Canal capacity must be expanded to develop Ukraine’s Danube ports – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:41:00 UTC
17:41:00 KST

Sulina Canal capacity must be expanded to develop Ukraine’s Danube ports – expert
Vitalii Nikula, Director of Izmail Sea Commercial Port, made the comment to Ukrinform during the Rebuilding Ukraine Forum in Bucharest.
“We need certain agreements to increase the capacity of the channels connecting the Danube and the Black Sea. First of all, this is the Sulina Canal, which now plays one of the key roles and is the central entry route for vessels from the Black Sea to the Danube cluster,” Nikula said.
He noted the canal allows passage for vessels with a draft of up to seven meters, carrying both export and import cargoes such as fertilizers, construction materials and other goods needed in Ukraine. The main problem remains limited capacity, with work under way at the level of the relevant ministries in Ukraine and Romania.
“Work is being carried out by ministries of both countries and by our Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority, which is in constant contact with colleagues from the Sulina Canal,” Nikula said.
One expected step is the introduction of night navigation, which he believes would increase cargo handling volumes for both exports and imports.
“We hope night navigation will start soon. This will allow us to boost cargo turnover and process more shipments,” he added.
Another challenge for Danube ports is low water levels, which reduce transport efficiency.
“Ports are facing seasonal drops in the Danube’s water level. It is now catastrophically low. Barges that can normally carry 2,000–2,500 tonnes of grain are currently loaded with a maximum of 750–800 tonnes,” Nikula said.
He also stressed the need for investment in port equipment modernization. “As a state stevedore we maintain our handling equipment in proper condition, but investment in upgrading our fleet of machinery would improve efficiency,” Nikula concluded.
As reported, Ukraine exported 2.4 million tonnes of agricultural products in September, equal to 46% of the required potential volume.

"I actually came back to it this year. It was really nice," she said.

"It helps provide a great bit of grounding for me, especially when you go away playing cricket.
"You can think it is the be-all and end-all playing professional sport, but it is literally grounding seeing some real world problems."
Redmayne has been a great success at the top of the order for the Brisbane Heat and was the leading run scorer in three consecutive seasons from 2020-2022.
Grace Harris, her opening partner much of the time, topped the aggregates in 2023 and 2024. The Heat made the finals in all five of those years and were runners-up twice.
The Heat moved Redmayne down the order last season, but it did not work, so a return to opening with Harris would be a good place to start for the side to turn their form around.
"(Opening) is somewhere I really enjoy batting and where I would like to bat," Redmayne said.
"My favourite time playing cricket was always opening the batting with Grace. We had a couple of very successful seasons.
"Last year our order was very changeable. I started at number eight and ended up at number four.
"I don't mind where I bat, so long as we are winning games."

AI chip surge lifts South Korea to record surplus, behind only China
Soaring memory prices pushed quarterly earnings past Germany and Japan combined for the first time
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Park Chan-kyongin Seoul
South Korea earned US$116.63 billion more from the world than it spent in the second quarter of this year – exceeding the combined current account surpluses of Germany and Japan for the first time on record.
The current account measures a country’s trade and income with the world. It counts goods and services sold abroad, money earned on overseas investments and payments flowing the other way. A surplus means more foreign currency is coming in than going out.
Surging demand for semiconductors helped propel South Korea’s second-quarter surplus, with chip exports reaching US$113.89 billion in the three months to June, according to government figures – up 181.6 per cent from the same period last year.
Prices for memory chips have jumped in recent months amid the global artificial intelligence boom. In June, US manufacturer Micron Technology reported that its prices had risen by as much as 80 per cent quarter on quarter.

Israeli opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman on Monday demanded a criminal investigation into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of treason, accusing him of attempting to drag Israel into a war with Iran to avoid defeat in Tuesday’s general elections.
Lieberman, leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, submitted a formal request to Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported.
In his letter, Lieberman said that Netanyahu had been pressuring senior security officials over the past month to take steps that could trigger a military confrontation with Iran.
“Over the past month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pressuring the heads of the security establishment to take steps that could lead to a miscalculation with Iran,” Lieberman wrote.
He accused Netanyahu of attempting to involve Israel in another war because of concerns about losing the elections.
“Attempting to drag the State of Israel into war on the eve of elections, along with the willingness to sacrifice IDF (army) soldiers solely out of fear of electoral defeat, constitutes treason against the state, its security and IDF soldiers,” he said.
“I demand the immediate opening of a criminal investigation against Benjamin Netanyahu on suspicion of treason,” he added.
Earlier Monday, Lieberman made similar accusations during an interview with Israeli radio station 103FM, according to Israeli newspaper Maariv.
“Netanyahu is clearly betraying the state when he wants to drag us into war,” Lieberman said, accusing the premier of being willing to sacrifice soldiers’ lives because of fears of electoral defeat. 
Presure
The opposition leader also alleged unprecedented tensions between Israel’s political and military leadership.
“Never has there been such a strained relationship between the military and political leadership as there is today,” he said, attributing the situation to Netanyahu’s efforts to provoke a miscalculation with Iran.

Election tensions

Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israeli intelligence indicated Iran and its regional allies could launch attacks aimed at disrupting the elections.
He warned Tehran against such actions, threatening a severe military response.
On Oct. 13, Lieberman accused Netanyahu of preparing possible military action against Iran, Hamas or Hezbollah to remain in power, claiming that the prime minister was motivated by political survival rather than security considerations.
Netanyahu also unveiled a new national security doctrine on Oct. 18, identifying the overthrow of Iran’s government as a strategic objective and emphasizing preemptive military operations.
The latest accusations come amid continuing tensions between Israel and Iran following their military confrontation earlier this year.
