Address by CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov at the conference “Greater Eurasia: Institutions for the Development of Cooperation”
23.10.2026
An international scientific and practical conference entitled “Greater Eurasia: Institutions, Development, Cooperation” was held at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO) of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, jointly organized with the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences (ICCA RAS). CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov took part in the conference.
Address by CSTO Secretary General Talatbek Masadykov:
Dear colleagues,
The world is experiencing a transformation of the international relations system. In the 2025 Declaration of the Collective Security Council, the heads of CSTO member states noted the growing importance of collective efforts at the regional and global levels to prevent and resolve crises and conflicts. These efforts must be based on the guiding principles of the UN Charter.
Regional conflicts are intensifying, and new security threats are emerging, particularly near the borders of CSTO member states. External actors are attempting to influence developments in our region.
The leaders expressed concern over attempts to turn Eurasia into an arena of geopolitical confrontation and undermine established ties and processes of Eurasian integration. They also rejected unilateral coercive measures that run counter to the UN Charter and are used as instruments of political, economic and financial pressure.
This is a matter of fundamental importance for development institutions: sustainable cooperation cannot be built on pressure. It is essential to establish clear parameters.
The CSTO area of responsibility is clearly defined: it encompasses the territories of its member states. However, it is not isolated. It borders the Far East, the Middle East and the Near East, and is adjacent to the Caspian and Black Sea regions, Eastern Europe and the Baltic region. Developments in all these regions inevitably have repercussions within our area of responsibility.
The response of CSTO member states is to build a sustainable security architecture across Eurasia based on the principles of equality and indivisibility of security.
Our states have also supported the negotiation process on the Eurasian Charter of Diversity and Multipolarity in the 21st Century. We proceed from the premise that security and development are inseparable.
Central Asia provides a clear example. Just a few years ago, the situation in the region was difficult, with border disputes frequently escalating into armed clashes. Today, the situation has changed dramatically. This is the result of the political will of the leaders of the countries in the region, their personal commitment and their readiness to seek compromises at the negotiating table.
On March 13, 2025, the Treaty on the State Border between the Kyrgyz Republic and the Republic of Tajikistan was signed. On March 31, 2025, the presidents of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan signed the Treaty on the Junction Point of the State Borders of the Three Countries and adopted a Declaration of Eternal Friendship.
The heads of CSTO member states welcomed these historic developments, as they contribute to greater stability in the Organization’s area of responsibility. The experience of the region shows that even complex differences can be resolved when there is a willingness to engage in dialogue and respect one another’s interests.
Dear colleagues,
I would like to emphasize the importance of expert assessments. Decisions on security and development are made in an environment of uncertainty, and the cost of error is high. Sound expert assessments are no less important than political will. Threats can be prevented only if emerging trends are identified in advance. Analysis and forecasting are becoming integral components of the security system itself.
Expert platforms make it possible to compare assessments before decisions are made, identify common approaches and resolve misunderstandings. This work helps states make more balanced decisions and thereby strengthens trust.
The CSTO Secretariat consistently develops cooperation with research and expert communities, both in member states and in third countries. Analytical reports are prepared annually at our initiative.
This year, the report prepared by the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia focuses on CSTO cooperation with other organizations and institutions across Greater Eurasia.
At the Collective Security Council session in Bishkek, a proposal was made to establish an association of CSTO member states’ analytical centers specializing in international relations and security. We are ready to support its implementation. Similar ideas are also being discussed in Central Asia, where the inclusion of an expert forum in the regional cooperation framework is under consideration.
A broad community of experts from around the world is already taking shape around the CSTO. They share a common vision of the principles underpinning a new Eurasian security architecture: equality, indivisibility and consideration of the interests of all participants. We will continue to develop contacts with analytical institutions in different parts of Eurasia and strengthen the CSTO’s role as an open platform for substantive international discussions.
Expert work delivers results when it is matched by coordinated action among organizations. The heads of state have declared their readiness to expand CSTO cooperation with the CIS and the SCO, which share the common task of ensuring stability and security across Eurasia. The basis for this cooperation is the Road Map for Developing Cooperation between the CSTO, CIS and SCO for 2026–2028, signed by the secretaries general of the three organizations in Beijing on September 3, 2025.
Dear colleagues,
A new security architecture for Greater Eurasia cannot be built by any one country or organization acting alone. It requires the political will of leaders, coordinated efforts by institutions, and precise and impartial expert assessments. I am confident that we will achieve this through our joint efforts.
Thank you for your attention!

EU Offers Serbia Closer Ties After Student List Victory
The European Union has offered to deepen cooperation with Serbia after the “Student List” won the parliamentary elections, pledging support for reforms to strengthen the rule of law, media freedom and democratic institutions and fight corruption, DPA reported.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa congratulated the “Student List” on its victory and expressed their readiness to help Serbia advance toward EU membership.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos pointed to historically high voter turnout in the elections, which followed almost two years of protests defending democracy, the rule of law and efforts to combat corruption.

Zelensky: Ukraine Offered US 3 Ways to Stop Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries

Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries at the request of US President Donald Trump’s team, but only if one of three conditions was met, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with journalist Alla Mazur.
Speaking on the TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week) program, Zelensky said that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries could not have a significant impact on global prices, noting that Russia accounts for only 2% of global diesel exports, while the remaining 98% comes from other exporters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“How can one reach an ‘energy truce’ with the Russians? You might be hated, but you should at least be respected as an adversary. They must respect Ukraine – and our strength. He [Putin] inflicts great pain upon us, and we respond. It is a matter of justice,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine had proposed three possible ways to resolve the dispute to the American side. However, none of the proposals had been implemented, which is why Ukraine continues to strike Russian oil refineries, he said.
“I said: if you want us to stop hitting diesel facilities and refineries, then they [the Russians] must stop striking our power infrastructure. That is fair – an ‘energy truce.’ A second option: you enable Starlink coverage over Russia, and we show you the locations of their ballistic missile launchers. We want to destroy them.
Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine
“The third option is this: if you won’t enable Starlink for us – which is entirely up to you – and you’ve said that Musk doesn’t want to, then give us something that doesn’t depend on Musk or Putin: missiles for the Patriot systems,” Zelensky said.
He added that Ukraine had received none of the three proposed forms of support.
“That is why the reaction is what it is – we are fighting for our lives,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky warns against lifting sanctions before negotiations
Zelensky also said that lifting sanctions against Russia should be considered only as part of the process of ending the war, rather than as a precondition for negotiations.
“I would not want us to approach the meeting of the three leaders – Ukraine, the United States, and Russia – having already lifted all sanctions against the Russian Federation. This is a crucial point. Sanctions were imposed in response to aggression, not as a price for the mere opportunity to talk.”
He said he had conveyed this position to the American delegation, cautioning that Russia could benefit from sanctions relief before any agreement on ending the war had been reached.
He warned that once sanctions were lifted, restoring them could prove difficult, requiring Ukraine and its partners to rebuild international support for a new round of restrictions.
“Without sanctions, we could reach a point in the trilateral dialogue where the future remains uncertain, yet the sanctions have already been removed,” Zelensky added.
He said that the international community had adopted more than 20 separate sanctions packages against Russia and questioned whether the same political resolve could be mobilized again if Moscow failed to follow through on its commitments.
“I do not want us to find ourselves without any leverage – lacking sanctions, funds, or frozen assets – when we sit down with Putin. Because then, as Mr. Trump put it, we would truly have very few cards left in our deck,” Zelensky added.
Ukraine, US, EU and NATO plan security talks in Brussels
Zelensky also said Ukraine, the United States, the European Union and NATO planned to hold a broad meeting in Brussels this week to discuss security issues, guarantees and European integration.
According to the president, the format of the discussions had expanded following a visit by the American delegation to St. Petersburg and a preliminary briefing to Ukraine.
The talks had initially been limited in scope, but the Americans were now seeking a broader discussion, Zelensky said.
“The Americans [after Oslo] went to St. Petersburg; we received a ‘brief’ from them, but now they want more than just a ‘brief’ – they want a broad discussion regarding security, guarantees, the EU, and involvement,” he added.
The meeting was expected to take place this week, tentatively on Tuesday or Wednesday. Zelensky said the participants would include representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU at the presidential level, as well as NATO, represented by the alliance’s secretary-general.

MPs urged 'let light win' as cockatoo sits in for Helen Haines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:47:12 UTC
16:47:12 KST

A cardboard cockatoo sits in tribute for Helen Haines as MPs are urged to 'let light win over darkness'
Far from the gum trees of north-east Victoria where cockatoos gather in noisy flocks, an orange cardboard bird perched in the parliament on Monday, saving a seat for Helen Haines.
"How lonely it looks," Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said.
But cockatoos are not normally lonely birds, and Ms Haines has built her life in much the same way.
The Independent Member for Indi could be loud for those she cared about. She made sure her people were impossible to ignore, and was surrounded by her community, building her political career from a grassroots campaign run by locals.
And unlike the rest of parliament, loud and raucous, Ms Haines was calm.
A week ago, she was standing by the boot of her car outside her Wangaratta office when a man hit her with his own car in what police say was a targeted attack.
The injuries were so severe both of her legs were later amputated.
"This should not just shock us," Wentworth MP Allegra Spender said.
"It should change us."
As the parliament suspended normal business to make time for messages of support for Ms Haines and her family, it was hard to escape the feeling that something had shifted.
One after another, for hours, MPs stood up to speak in the House about Ms Haines's uncommon kindness, wisdom and respect for civility as a politician.
"These are the type of politicians we wish we had more of," friend and crossbench colleague Kate Chaney said.
Like a "trick the heart plays on the mind", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described finding himself looking across to where Ms Haines would normally sit, expecting to see her there.
"It is hard to think of anyone in this place with a more irrepressible twinkle in the eye," he said.
But the tributes were also threaded with another message: that the tenor of Australian politics must change, and that the country needed to find a better way to argue.
"And this is a moment for all of us to rise to the challenge," Speaker of the House Milton Dick said.
What Would Helen Do?
Members of the crossbench cried as they listened to messages of support for the woman they regard as the "matriarch" of Australia's independent movement.
Ms Haines was among the first wave of community-backed independents to reshape Australian politics, winning Indi after the retirement of fellow independent Cathy McGowan.
Community Strong MP Zali Steggall spoke of the role Ms Haines had played in helping shape the modern crossbench, guiding newly elected independents through the workings of parliament and teaching them how to advocate for their communities without the backing of a major party.
"There will be much discussion ahead about the need for better health and mental health services in the regions, our increasingly polarised political environment, harmful online debate and the need for greater civility in disagreement in parliament, in our media, online and in our communities," she said.
"So, Helen, I look forward to seeing you back here and getting on with the job. Let light win over darkness."
Independent MP Allegra Spender shared the first words Ms Haines spoke after the attack, as relayed by her husband, Phil Haines, who had met with parliamentarians earlier on Monday.
"Your first concerns were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders," she said.
"And that exactly speaks to the character of who you are."
But for all her decency, Ms Spender said, Ms Haines was not a "benign force wandering through the parliament".
"People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition," she said.
"What I will say is that you are also a force for change."
After winning Indi, voters have rewarded Ms Haines with two further terms, entrusting her with an electorate of mountains, rivers and fertile farmland, which was also acutely exposed to the effects of a warming climate.
After years of advocacy by Ms Haines, the federal government adopted temporary disaster roaming, an emergency system that allows mobile phones to switch to another carrier's network when their own service fails during a major disaster.
But few issues, her friends and colleagues said, animated her more than integrity in government.
Independent MP Andrew Gee was emotional speaking about the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which she is credited for establishing.
Several politicians chose to commit to a Civility Pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016. Ms Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge earlier this year.
MP Kate Chaney spoke about t-shirts printed for a Christmas party in her first year in parliament with the slogan: What Would Helen Do?
"I ask myself that question all the time," she said.
"Helen, please come back to us. We need you here more than ever".
The rage is getting worse, but we can get better
Mr Albanese said Australia had a proud tradition of disagreement but warned against confusing the vigour of democracy with "this rising tide of rage".
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop. We keep talking. We keep working towards something better," he said.
There was a shared disbelief in the chamber that someone like Helen Haines, among parliament's most respected and unassuming figures, had become a target.
She had been "so, so far down" his list of potential security concerns, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
Mr Burke said Phil Haines had earlier urged the parliament to think not only about the words they choose, but about who might hear them.
"It goes to not simply would I be capable of doing something horrific, but would my words, if heard by someone on the edge, potentially have an impact that I wouldn't want them to have,"
Mr Burke said.
A number of people also called for an honest conversation about mental health, including Liberal MP Dan Tehan.
Ms Haines is a former nurse and maternal health expert, and has long campaigned for additional support for regional services.
"We have to look at mental health services in and around regional and rural Victoria and across this nation," Mr Tehan said.
"We have to see whether we can do better."
As one man hurt Haines, others ran to help
Many MPs said they had spent the week hearing from Australians worried about a country growing more angry and more divided.
But in the same breath, they pointed to people like Ricky Jefferies, the local barber who ran towards danger when Haines needed help.
"One man drove at Helen, but others ran to her instinctively and courageously, and they saved her life," Independent MP Monique Ryan said.
"Our basic decency and our selflessness are there still, and we have to use those muscles, not the others."
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said Mr Jefferies knew most of the first responders because he cut their hair, "not because of social media networks".
"And there's something in that," he said.
"We thrive as a nation when we are in a community with our neighbours, when we are known by them and they are known by us."
He encouraged all politicians to behave better in parliament and online.
"We can all go better and we should strive to do better," he said.
"Lets play the ball, not the person and leave nasty personal politics of MAGA in the US."
Labor MP Ged Kearney broke down as she spoke about Ms Haines but said she had tried to honour her example by making herself as "visible as possible" over the weekend.
"I walked the streets amongst kids in Halloween costumes. I went to listen to music. I had lunch in a cafe, and visited a scouts party," she said.
"We all have fears and we do things differently now to assess risks … but at the end of the day, if I can't walk down High Street or Edward Street or Station Street and be with the people I represent, then well, what is this for?"
Parliament looks to the day it is made whole again
At a vigil held in Wangaratta to honour Ms Haines in the days after her attack, cockatoos wheeled overhead.
"They make a lot of noise, but they're very supportive of each other as a flock," former politician and friend Cathy McGowan told the ABC.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said when Ms Haines resumed her seat, it would be a "resounding moment for democracy".
"In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man's cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he said.
In her maiden speech, Ms Haines had reflected on the erosion of trust affecting democracies around the world.
Indi, she argued, offered a different lesson.
"Division and polarisation are not the inevitable outcome," she said then.

Gökhan Ergöçün
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Singapore and Saudi Aramco plan to store Saudi crude oil in the underground Jurong Rock Caverns starting in 2027 to boost energy security amid global supply disruptions.  
Tan See Leng, Singapore's minister for energy, trade and industry, announced the joint intention during the Singapore Energy Lecture 2026 on Monday.  
Tan said the arrangement would enhance the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain across Southeast Asia.
The minister noted that the initiative would also contribute to the city-state's energy security during supply emergencies.  
"Today, Saudi Arabia and Singapore are announcing our joint intent to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027," the minister said.
Saudi Aramco, the Energy Market Authority and JTC signed a memorandum of understanding to finalize the storage agreement.
Officials aim to conclude negotiations within a few months.  
The global energy landscape has faced significant challenges this year following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabian airports and energy infrastructure have further escalated the international energy situation.
Tan emphasized that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would not be the last supply disruption.
Singapore has established multiple lines of defense to mitigate the economic impact of sudden supply chain crunches.
The government requires electricity-generating turbines to run on either gas or diesel to draw on reserve fuels.
The country also plans to expand its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity by 50% with a second terminal by 2030.

US pushing Orbán for UN secretary-general, hoping for Russian and Chinese support – WSJ
The Wall Street Journal, citing sources, writes that the Trump administration is promoting former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for the position of UN secretary-general, counting on the support of Russia and China.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing its sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The WSJ notes that the US not only supported the former prime minister of Hungary in his decision to participate in the race but was the one who suggested the idea to him.
One State Department official under the Trump administration admits that at first glance this sounds crazy. However, judging by previous talks with Washington, Russia and China are believed to support the idea, and the plan is for Orbán to become their joint candidate.
Officials from the US and another country emphasised that when the US, Russia and China pursue the same goal in the UN Security Council, they generally achieve it.
A State Department representative counted eight votes in the Security Council for Orbán that would support him "comfortably" and another 10 votes out of the 15 Council members that could potentially be secured.
One American official stated that Orbán is "the dream MAGA-conservative candidate".
The WSJ writes that in many respects, this is down to his actions against mass migration, liberal NGOs and left-leaning courts and the press.
Furthermore, the WSJ notes that Orbán frequently clashed with the European Union while benefiting from it in the form of subsidies and his pro-China orientation never undermined his image as a defender of Western civilisation.
If Orbán puts forward his candidacy for the UN post, US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are expected to support him once again, although according to a source familiar with the process, the announcement is being held back until after the US midterm elections.
American officials primarily contacted Orbán to gauge his interest in the UN position. They found that he was positively inclined, albeit with caveats.
The remaining candidates for the position of secretary-general, according to a representative of the second country, are heavy on "secretary" – with experience in international bureaucracy or behind-the-scenes diplomacy. Orbán, on the other hand, would be a "general".
A State Department representative agreed with this, adding that Orbán adheres to the correct ideology, knows how to exercise power under hostile conditions and will not be intimidated by the establishment.
Background:
- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez recently stressed the need to reform the UN and strengthen accountability mechanisms to stop governments and forces that undermine international rules, unleash wars of aggression and cause suffering in the world.
- Calls to abolish the veto power in the UN Security Council have been made for a long time, especially in connection with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In particular, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan also called for removing the veto power in the UN Security Council.
- In spring, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticised the UN Security Council for its inability to make decisions due to the vetoes of individual members.

Secondary schools to be get new minimum targets: bar for Dutch and maths set high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:44:33 UTC
16:44:33 KST

After primary education, new minimum standards are also to be introduced in Flemish secondary education. The Flemish Government has approved the proposal put forward by Education Minister Zuhal Demir (Flemish nationalist N-VA). The new minimum standards will come into force in September 2029: by then, the first cohort of pupils to have completed primary education under the new minimum standards will be moving on to secondary school.
Secondary schools to get new minimum targets: bar for Dutch and maths set high
The revised minimum targets for secondary education will be set on a subject-by-subject basis and will no longer be organised around 16 broad, cross-curricular key competences. The so-called ‘overlapping target frameworks’ will be phased out.
New minimum targets have already been introduced in primary education. There, the emphasis is more on knowledge and clear expectations for pupils. Particular attention is being paid to Dutch and mathematics.
The same priorities are also being emphasised in the revised minimum objectives for secondary education. The aim is to raise the standard of education once again. “We want to achieve a knowledge-rich curriculum for all pupils whilst significantly simplifying the educational objectives,” the people behind the project say.
Education Minister Zuhal Demir: “Education must form a single, coherent whole. What you learn in one year must form the basis for the next. So, when the first pupils enter secondary school in September 2029 with their new knowledge, secondary schools must be ready to build on it.”
Raising the bar for Dutch and maths
As with the revised minimum targets for primary education, there will be a greater emphasis on knowledge in secondary education. The various subjects will once again take centre stage.
The educational objectives centred on 16 broad key competences will be phased out, to be replaced by specific objectives for each subject area, such as Dutch, maths, history and science.
In addition, some general objectives, such as citizenship and financial literacy, will be retained. However, the foundation of these objectives is the knowledge that pupils need to build up across various subjects.
“We have sometimes made education a little too complicated. We talk about 16 key competences, whilst ultimately, it is about something very simple: what do our children need to know and be able to do in various subjects such as history, maths or Dutch? We are simplifying the rules, without lowering the bar,” says Minister Demir.
“Knowledge is not an outdated concept. Those who know a lot can understand things better, think more critically and make independent choices. That is exactly what we want to equip our young people with.”
The bar is set particularly high for Dutch and maths. By the end of the first grade, every pupil must achieve the set minimum targets for these two subjects, although the class council still has the final say.
For other subjects, schools must ensure that their pupils, as a group, sufficiently meet the minimum targets.

Jordan's security forces say three arrested for church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:43:38 UTC
16:43:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Jordan arrests three suspects over deadly Karak church attack
Jordanian security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox Church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.
The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects were arrested following a dawn shootout and that all three were wounded. No members of the security forces were injured in the dawn operation in Karak, south of Jordan's capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack on the Greek Orthodox Church in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.
There was still no claim of responsibility, and no armed group has been accused of the attack.
Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya identified the three men as those responsible for the attack.
"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," he said in a phone interview with state TV Al-Mamlaka. "They put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."
He added that there "are three individuals involved; they were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
King Abdullah II directed authorities to respond with "an iron fist" against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

Global markets open mixed amid ongoing tech selloff, Middle East risks

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

16:43:18 KST

Global markets ended the week of Oct. 23 on a negative note and opened mixed Monday, as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) financing, signals from corporate earnings and risks in the Middle East continued into the new week.
The potential for renewed US-Iran tensions after the November midterm elections continues to dampen risk appetite.
All eyes have turned to the Fed’s monetary policy decision this week, when the bank is expected to maintain its rates, but its forward guidance will be crucial in assessing the bank’s policy roadmap amid inflationary pressures.
US economic growth, personal consumption data and earnings from Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet will be on the agenda this week.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump is reportedly considering dropping “the mother of all bombs” on Iran. “It’s not nuclear at all, this is just an extremely large bomb — it’s like a tiny nuclear bomb,” the president said during an interview last week.
December-delivery Brent crude oil fell 1.9% to $114.50 a barrel after Qatari mediators reportedly traveled to Tehran to mediate talks with the US.
The 10-year US Treasury yield is down three basis points at 4.97% amid increased demand for safe-haven assets.

Japan cannibalizes P-1 maritime patrol planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:40:42 UTC
16:40:42 KST

- Japan’s Board of Audit found that spare parts shortages forced crews to cannibalize grounded P-1 patrol aircraft to keep others flying.
- Japanese reports put the fleet’s availability at roughly 20% to 30%, and the Defense Ministry aims to fix the parts shortage by fiscal 2027.
Posts on X lamenting the state of Japan’s Kawasaki P-1 maritime patrol fleet have drawn more than 100,000 views, as Japanese aviation enthusiasts urged the public to spread the word about the hardships facing Maritime Self-Defense Force units after reports that some newly delivered P-1s are arriving without their patrol equipment and are being stripped for parts to keep the rest of the fleet flying.
“It makes you kind of sad,” wrote X user Mendako_2654 on Oct. 24, in a post shared by Taizo Nakamura, a restorer of World War II aircraft who runs the Hokoku 515 museum, whose own response was viewed more than 105,000 times.
“The distinguished guests may not get the message, but let ordinary people keep spreading this, and even if our support is small, let’s make known the real hardships the units and their personnel are facing,” wrote Taizo Nakamura.
The posts follow a Sept. 19 report by Nippon Television, which said that of the roughly 40 P-1s in the Maritime Self-Defense Force’s inventory, only about 20% to 30% are able to fly missions, according to people familiar with the fleet. NTV reported that because of the parts shortage, new aircraft are sometimes delivered as planes that “can only fly,” without the equipment needed for patrol missions, and are then used as sources of spare parts, and that a reporter saw a P-1 with no engines at one Maritime Self-Defense Force base.
NTV said the fleet’s availability had not improved since a critical government audit because repair capacity has reached its limit, while replacing parts that can no longer be repaired has become difficult as prices have risen in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and general inflation, and as some components have gone out of production. The Defense Ministry is pursuing long-term comprehensive contracts that bundle parts, repairs, maintenance and supply, but crews are still removing parts from other aircraft, the broadcaster reported, and some people involved have argued that the ministry should focus on making the existing P-1s usable instead of buying new ones, or shift money toward drones.
The problems were first laid out in detail by Japan’s Board of Audit, which reported on June 27, 2025, that engine faults, malfunctioning mission electronics and long delays in obtaining replacement parts had left the fleet with very low availability, and that maintenance crews were routinely cannibalizing grounded aircraft, Japanese aviation outlet Aviation Wire reported. The auditors found that the aircraft’s IHI F7-10 turbofan engines suffered corrosion from salt in the air during low-altitude patrols, leaving a number of engines unusable, and that about 30% of replacement parts arrived more than a year after they were ordered as global supply disruptions, semiconductor shortages and suppliers leaving the program stretched lead times.
The P-1, built by Kawasaki Heavy Industries, is a four-engine jet designed from the start for anti-submarine and maritime surveillance missions and has been replacing the Lockheed P-3C Orion turboprop since entering service in 2013, with 61 aircraft planned in total. Contracts tied to the program reached ¥1.78 trillion (about $11.3 billion) between fiscal 1991 and fiscal 2023, and the unit price, originally expected to be about ¥10 billion (about $64 million), had climbed to ¥42.4 billion (about $270 million) by fiscal 2024, with the Defense Ministry requesting ¥47.3 billion (about $301 million) per aircraft for fiscal 2026.
The ministry said after the audit that it took the findings seriously and aims to resolve the parts shortage by fiscal 2027, and crews flying the aircraft have still performed well when the jets are available, with a P-1 unit from the 3rd Air Wing winning the U.S. Navy-led Sea Dragon 2026 anti-submarine warfare competition earlier this year.

As drone threat grows, Magos expands commercial security capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:40:37 UTC
16:40:37 KST

Israeli tech company Magos Systems is expanding its capabilities in drone detection, applying its commercial sector experience to the growing challenge posed by unmanned aerial threats.
Founded in 2010 by CEO Aviel Kisliansky and Amit Isseroff, Magos began by developing ground-based radar systems to detect perimeter breaches. While its business remains centered on commercial security, its technology is dual-use and it also serves military and defense applications.
The company’s strategy is built around the concept that security operators should be able to detect suspicious activity across large areas without having to replace their existing infrastructure or depend entirely on camera-based surveillance.
Magos operates in more than 70 countries, providing radar-based surveillance solutions for airports, ports, power stations, data centers, prisons, and other sensitive facilities. As drones become cheaper and more accessible, Magos is extending that approach to defense.
Radar designed for commercial infrastructure
The company’s radar systems are designed to detect and track moving objects and combines radar data with artificial intelligence and machine-learning-based object recognition to help operators identify potential threats and reduce nuisance and false alarms.
Its systems operate in varying weather conditions, and their integration capabilities allow customers to use existing camera equipment rather than commit to a single proprietary surveillance ecosystem. That flexibility is particularly relevant to commercial infrastructure operators, many of which already have extensive security networks and need to improve detection capabilities without undertaking expensive upgrades.
Additionally, MASS (Magos Area Surveillance Software) brings radar-based detection into a broader security-management environment.
The company’s radar portfolio includes several models designed for differing coverage requirements.
Its SR-150 detects people at distances of up to 150 meters and vehicles or boats at similar ranges. The SR-250 extends those distances to 250 m., while the SR-500 can detect people at up to 400 m. and vehicles or boats at up to 600 m.
At the longer end of the range, the SR-1000 is designed to detect people at distances of up to 800 m. and vehicles or boats at up to one kilometer.
The systems provide 100- to 120-degree azimuth coverage and 30-degree elevation coverage, depending on the model, with an accuracy of 0.1 m. across the portfolio, with its longer-range models offering azimuth accuracy of 0.7 degrees.
Extending detection to the drone threat
The same emphasis on detection and integration underpins Magos’ work in drone security.
Small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) can approach protected facilities at low altitude, creating challenges for security systems designed primarily to monitor ground-level or high altitude activity. For commercial operators, the first requirement is often to establish that a drone is present, track its movement, and assess whether it poses a threat in time.
Magos’ approach is to combine radar detection with camera-based identification, giving security teams a more complete picture of activity around a facility. And for those who need to protect large or geographically dispersed infrastructure, that flexibility can help them adapt surveillance to the layout and risk profile of each site.
The underlying capabilities of detecting movement, tracking objects, and combining sensor data have applications across both civilian and military environments.
In June, the company secured a NIS 21 million contract to provide hundreds of its radar systems to Israel’s Defense Ministry, which deployed them to the Lebanese border area to improve the detection and identification of Hezbollah’s fiber-optic drones.
As the security industry adapts to the growing use of drones, Magos’ accurate radar detection, integrated cameras, and flexible coverage are essential for both commercial and military uses.

Birthright Israel will host the inaugural Taglit Global Business Summit, “Shaping Our Future Together,” November 1-3 at the Hilton Tel Aviv.
The landmark event will bring together more than 350 prominent business leaders, investors, entrepreneurs, and philanthropists from Israel and around the world at a critical time for the country.
More than 100 participants will travel to Israel from over 15 countries, including Argentina, Australia, Switzerland, and the United Arab Emirates, joining leading Israeli executives and entrepreneurs in a major international gathering focused on business, innovation, philanthropy, and Israel's future
The first-of-its-kind summit marks a milestone in Birthright Israel's 26-year history, bringing its international network of supporters together in Israel to explore opportunities for business collaboration, strengthen global partnerships, and deepen their shared commitment to the country and the next generation.
Prominent participants include Dr. Miriam Adelson, a leading supporter of Birthright Israel; Meir Shamir, chairman of Birthright Israel's Israeli Board of Donors; and Josh Nash, international chairman of Birthright Israel and managing member of Ulysses Management. The summit will also bring together business leaders and entrepreneurs associated with companies shaping Israel’s economy, including NVIDIA, Wiz, Elbit Systems, El Al, and monday.com.
President Herzog expected to attend event, address participants
The three-day gathering will open on November 1 with a Gala Evening of Recognition honoring the leadership and philanthropy that have sustained Birthright Israel's impact, including Dr. Miriam Adelson's longstanding commitment to the organization. President Isaac Herzog is expected to address the gathering alongside leading supporters from Israel and around the world.
On November 2, the summit will feature prominent figures from technology, investment, finance, entrepreneurship, and public life. Speakers include Sir Ronald Cohen, a pioneer of impact investing and co-founder of Apax Partners; Dr. Miriam Adelson, a physician, media publisher, and prominent businesswoman known for her global philanthropy and investments; Eyal Waldman, founder of Mellanox; Yinon Costica, co-founder of Wiz; Sean Rad, founder of Tinder and a Birthright alumnus; Amit Krig, NVIDIA's Israel site leader; former Mossad director Yossi Cohen; investor and ICON founder Yasmin Lukatz; former Microsoft Israel CEO Shelly Landsmann; author and public intellectual Dr. Micah Goodman; real-estate developer and philanthropist Danna Azrieli Hakim; and Angela Homsi, co-founder and president of Ignite Power.
The program will also feature Birthright Israel alumni who have become entrepreneurs, business leaders, and investors, showing how a ten-day educational experience can create connections and opportunities that extend far beyond the trip itself.
Among the participants will be Avinatan Or, an NVIDIA engineer who was abducted by Hamas from the Nova music festival on October 7, 2023, and released after 738 days in captivity.
Also among the participants will be Moran Samuel, an Israeli Paralympic basketball player and world champion rower who gives lectures to Jewish communities worldwide.
“For 26 years, Birthright Israel has connected the next generation of Jews to Israel while building an extraordinary global network of leaders who share a commitment to its future. The Taglit Global Business Summit is a natural extension of that mission. We are bringing this network together in Israel to turn shared values into action, foster new business partnerships, strengthen Israel’s economy, and invest in the next generation. At this moment, bringing global leaders to Israel is itself a powerful statement of confidence in its future,” said Gidi Mark, Global CEO of Birthright Israel.
The initiative builds on Birthright Israel's established Business Forum, which brings together nearly 60 Israeli companies, creating an additional platform for meaningful engagement between Israeli business leaders and their international counterparts.
“Trust is one of the most valuable assets in business, and Birthright has spent 26 years building it across borders,” said Ethy Levy, Vice President of Global Resource Development and Partnerships at Birthright Israel. “We are bringing that network into one room, giving people who share a commitment to Israel the chance to discover what they can build together. A conversation here could become a business partnership, a philanthropic initiative, or an investment in Israel's next generation.”
Program offers volunteer opportunities alongside current Birthright participants
On November 3, participants will move beyond the conference setting for curated visits to Israeli companies, innovation centers, and communities engaged in recovery and rebuilding. The program will also offer opportunities to volunteer alongside current Birthright Israel participants and to connect global business leaders directly with communities and initiatives the organization has supported since October 7.
The gathering reflects Birthright Israel's impact both on Jewish communities worldwide and on Israel's economy. Since 1999, nearly one million young Jewish adults from 70 countries have participated in Birthright Israel programs. The organization estimates that its activities have contributed approximately $2.6 billion to the Israeli economy over 26 years through travel, accommodation, and spending at local businesses.
A March 2026 study by Brandeis University's Cohen Center for Modern Jewish Studies further demonstrated the organization's long-term relevance. Among politically liberal young Jews surveyed, connection to Israel increased by 60% among Birthright Israel participants, compared with a 26% decline among applicants who did not participate. The findings highlight the lasting impact of firsthand experiences in Israel on Jewish identity and connection to the global Jewish community.

Thailand receives IWI's ARBEL anti-drone solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:39:59 UTC
16:39:59 KST

As Thailand approved a $104.4 million emergency defense fund to buy military equipment and reinforce defenses along the Cambodian border, IWI (Israel Weapon Industries) announced it delivered its ARBEL Anti-Drone System (ADS) to Thailand’s Defense Ministry.
Thai forces have integrated the platform into their existing rifles after troops received on-site training from company officials.
Developed by IWI after close to a decade of design work, the fire control technology transforms standard infantry rifles into precision-guided interceptors.
“Small tactical drones have become a direct and growing threat to soldiers on the battlefield. We developed the ARBEL ADS to give soldiers an effective means of defending themselves against this evolving threat, while providing armed forces with a critical tactical advantage in an increasingly complex battlespace,” said SK Group’s vice chairman Ronen Hamudot.
Integrated directly into the AR-15 platform and IWI’s own ARAD assault rifles and Negev machine guns, ARBEL allows soldiers to engage threats, including aerial ones, using their existing weapons, optics, and ammunition with no additional gear required. Depending on the selected firing mode, it can hit targets up to 450 meters away using standard 5.56 mm ammunition.
With electronic sensors and gyros, it simplifies the shooting cycle after the initial shot and enables effective target engagement within a window of opportunity of several seconds, typical of real combat situations. According to IWI, it significantly improves efficiency and lethality by increasing hit probability for static and moving threats by two to three times.
Depending on the platform, the ARBEL system can be integrated into the lower receiver of the A-15 or mounted as an external unit on the grip of the Negev machine gun. The system adds only 900 grams to the weapon and meets MIL-STD-810 military standards, ensuring reliability under extreme environmental conditions.
The Thai forces chose to integrate the system onto their existing rifles, which, according to the company, “enables militaries to upgrade their existing platforms locally without replacing their rifle inventories or procuring entirely new weapons.”
Battery-operated, ARBEL’s power supply allows for 50 hours of continuous operation. It’s optic-agnostic, mission-configurable, and its built-in fire control system releases rounds when the shooter is stable on the target, depending on the operational scenario. IWI told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post that the system compensates for and mitigates shooting errors typical of combative scenarios such as heavy breathing, fatigue, and stress.
“As Southeast Asian militaries place greater emphasis on counter-drone capabilities, Thailand’s adoption of ARBEL ADS reflects this growing operational priority. We see rising demand across the region for solutions that can help soldiers meet this challenge,” said SK Group vice president Doron Korol, who oversees the Asia-Pacific region.
According to the company, Thai military officials are in discussions with IWI about an additional order for the ARBEL ADS, and several other countries are at various stages of the procurement process. The company expects to announce additional deployments of the solution in the coming months.
Modernization plans
Earlier in October, local media reported that Bangkok approved emergency defense funding to repair combat-damaged gear and purchase new weapons, including long-range Rampage standoff missiles manufactured by Elbit Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), along with bunker-buster bombs and High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) artillery upgrades.
According to a report in The Nation, the Royal Thai Air Force’s procurement plan includes 20 Israeli Rampage missiles, with an estimated value of approximately $30 million (1.04 billion baht), for use with the country’s F-16 fighter aircraft along with Elbit’s MPR-500 penetrating bombs and Lizard III laser guidance kits.
Under the modernization plan, the Royal Thai Army will procure HIMARS and M777 howitzers to replace older artillery, along with Stryker armored vehicles.
Thailand has been acquiring Israeli defense technology since the 1970s, and the relationship has only grown stronger with the transfer of knowledge to locally manufacture and produce certain weapons systems.

‘Within 96 hours’: US ready for major Iran strikes if Trump gives order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:39:09 UTC
16:39:09 KST

American forces in the Middle East are prepared to launch a major new military offensive against Iran within 96 hours of receiving an order from President Donald Trump, two U.S. officials told CNN in a report published Monday. The necessary forces are already deployed in the region, but Trump has not made a final decision on whether to authorize the operation. 
The potential campaign would be considerably broader than the limited strikes carried out against Iranian military assets in recent months. U.S. Central Command and the Pentagon have developed an extensive list of possible targets, including nuclear facilities, military installations and energy infrastructure.
Unlike earlier operations focused on missile launchers, radar installations and other equipment that Iran could replace relatively quickly, the new plans envision a more substantial campaign against the Iranian regime's military capabilities and infrastructure.
"It will be a big effort," one American official said.
Current and former U.S. officials familiar with the planning believe Trump could order renewed large-scale operations before the end of the year, with several considering an attack after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections the more likely scenario.
However, the president has not committed to military action. Officials cautioned that Trump has previously appeared close to approving major operations before reversing course.
The White House declined to comment on the report. A senior Pentagon official emphasized that developing military options is part of the department's responsibility and does not, by itself, indicate that the president has ordered an attack.
Trump rejected Netanyahu's push for strikes before Israeli election
The American military preparations are unfolding against the backdrop of a disagreement between Washington and Jerusalem over the timing of renewed attacks on Iran.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pressing for additional military action against Tehran, but senior American officials, including Trump, have urged Israel to postpone its plans until the two countries are prepared to conduct coordinated operations, according to two U.S. officials and an Israeli security source.
An Israeli security source said Netanyahu had sought Trump's approval for a joint attack before Israel's October 27 election, but the president refused.
According to that source, one factor behind Trump's decision was a warning from IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir to Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Zamir reportedly warned that an attack at such a sensitive moment could provoke Iranian retaliation, disrupt the Israeli election and potentially force its postponement.
Israel had been preparing for possible additional strikes over the past week and sought American assistance to support those operations. But officials in Washington reportedly instructed Israel to hold off, indicating that a joint offensive could follow after the U.S. midterms.
Israel appears to have accepted the delay for now, partly because of its dependence on American missile defense assistance. Israeli interceptor supplies have come under considerable strain during the conflict, and any renewed confrontation with Iran would likely trigger another wave of missile attacks.
The reported disagreement also comes amid growing scrutiny of Netanyahu's intentions regarding Iran. Recent U.S. intelligence assessments suggest that the prime minister and his allies have not established a clearly defined strategic objective beyond continuing to weaken the Iranian regime and demonstrating military progress, according to a source familiar with those assessments.
Netanyahu, however, has publicly articulated a more ambitious goal. Speaking at an IDF officers' graduation ceremony last week, he said he had instructed the military, Mossad and other security agencies to work toward overthrowing the Iranian regime.
Intelligence warns of immediate Iranian retaliation
American intelligence assessments indicate that both Iran and the Houthis in Yemen are taking the possibility of renewed U.S. and Israeli attacks seriously.
According to sources familiar with the assessments, Tehran and the Houthis would likely respond quickly to a new offensive by attacking American military personnel and facilities across the Middle East, potentially extending their operations beyond the region.
Intelligence officials do not currently believe Iran or the Houthis are likely to launch a major preemptive attack against American forces or Israel. However, they assess that both would be prepared to retaliate if Iran came under attack first.
An unclassified October 23 memorandum from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Iran had intensified efforts to target American personnel. The intelligence assessment indicated that some Iranian plots had reached advanced stages, including in countries outside the Middle East.
The growing threat is already affecting the American diplomatic and military presence in the region.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been placed under an ordered departure for certain personnel, and officials expect additional diplomatic missions to face similar restrictions or reductions in staffing.
Meanwhile, nonessential American military personnel who were expected to deploy to the Middle East as part of upcoming troop rotations have reportedly been told their assignments have been canceled.
The measures reflect concern that any new confrontation could quickly extend beyond Iranian territory and place American personnel across the region at risk.
The Strait of Hormuz adds pressure for military action
Another factor influencing Washington's calculations is the increasingly difficult situation in the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with international shipping routes.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, visited the strait Sunday as American forces continued enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and assisting commercial shipping through the area.
Cooper flew over the waterway by helicopter to assess conditions and met service members involved in clearing Iranian naval mines.
Although more oil tankers have begun passing through the strait, energy prices remain elevated, partly because of continuing concerns about Iranian attacks on shipping.
One American official described the existing situation around the strait as unsustainable over the long term. Without a diplomatic breakthrough, restoring more predictable maritime traffic could become another reason for Trump to authorize renewed military operations.
Yet significant uncertainty remains about what a new offensive would accomplish. Iranian forces have gained experience with American tactics, potentially complicating efforts to destroy intended targets. U.S. officials also acknowledge unresolved questions about Washington's broader strategy for ending the conflict.
For now, the military preparations continue while the political decision remains outstanding. Israel has reportedly delayed its immediate plans, Iran is preparing for possible renewed attacks, and American forces are positioned to act within days if Trump gives the order.
The timetable is therefore not a countdown to war. It represents the military's readiness to carry out a presidential decision that has yet to be made.

INTERVIEW - Yemen’s foreign minister sets out 5 conditions for peace, calls for Houthi disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:38:44 UTC
16:38:44 KST

Mahmut Geldi, Zahir Sofuoğlu and Tarek Chouiref
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba outlined five conditions for peace, saying the Houthis must surrender their weapons and join the political process.
Speaking to Anadolu during an official visit to Türkiye, al-Zouba said a settlement also requires rebuilding state institutions, ensuring the group can no longer carry out what she described as terrorism in Yemen or the region, and implementing agreed frameworks for peace.
Those frameworks include UN Security Council Resolution 2216, the outcomes of Yemen’s National Dialogue Conference and the Gulf Cooperation Council initiative, she said.
Resolution 2216 calls on the Houthis to withdraw from areas they seized, including Sanaa, hand over weapons taken from military and security institutions, and facilitate humanitarian access.
 
Peace talks used to rearm
Al-Zouba accused the Houthis of exploiting successive rounds of peace talks to build up their arsenal.
“We went through the peace process repeatedly, moving from one round of negotiations to another,” she said.
She argued that the government and international community had long pursued negotiations in the belief that a peaceful settlement was possible, but the Houthis had used those efforts to acquire weapons and expand their military capabilities.
She said she believed neighboring countries and international partners increasingly recognized that the group “was not a genuine partner for peace.”
The top diplomat said Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” launched by Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi on Oct. 5, aimed to end Houthi control, restore state authority and return Yemen’s sovereign decisions to the government.
Fighting has intensified in Yemen since July in the sharpest escalation since the relative calm brought by a UN-brokered truce in April 2022.
 
Iranian support
Al-Zouba accused the Houthis of seeking to turn Yemen into a base for attacks on neighboring countries, citing their strikes on Saudi Arabia and threats to shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
She described the group as a threat to regional and international security and accused it of cooperating with armed groups in the Horn of Africa.
Iranian expertise had helped the Houthis develop their arsenal since seizing Sanaa in 2014, including the ability to manufacture some weapons components and assemble weapons inside Yemen, she said.
Al-Zouba also said she believed the group was beginning to develop the ability to train others, including Somalia’s al-Shabaab, to use certain equipment.
“The Houthis are using the power they have acquired through Yemen’s resources against Yemenis, neighboring countries and the world,” she said.
 
Siege restricts supplies to Taiz
Al-Zouba said continued Houthi shelling and a partial siege were restricting access to essential supplies in southwestern Taiz province, home to roughly 4 million people.
Taiz has resisted years of Houthi attempts to bring it under their control, she said, but residents continued to face barriers to obtaining water, food, medicine and fuel.
The province has been a major front in the latest fighting. Government forces and their allies have announced gains near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and in Dhubab district, while Houthi advances in rural areas have tightened pressure on the city.
Taiz connects northern and southern Yemen and includes a strategically important stretch of Red Sea coastline, making it vital to transport and supply routes.
 
Türkiye’s regional role
Al-Zouba praised Türkiye’s political and diplomatic initiatives, describing Ankara’s role in regional security as “pivotal and strategic.”
She said the two countries shared longstanding historic ties and welcomed Türkiye’s efforts to promote stability.
“We believe Türkiye has a pivotal and strategic role in maintaining the region’s security and stability,” she said.

Europe weighs €10bn plan to launch its own astronauts ahead of Rome space summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:37:41 UTC
16:37:41 KST

Europe is seeking to boost its presence in space and cut technological dependence on other states. The 15 December ESA summit in Rome will shape choices on astronauts, cargo and investment.
Europe wants to stop depending on others to send its own astronauts into space. The next key date for deciding how to do that is 15 December in Rome, when the member countries of the European Space Agency (ESA) will meet to discuss the future of space exploration. On the table are multi-billion-euro investments, new technologies and one strategic issue: ensuring that Europe can reach Earth orbit with its own means, without relying exclusively on services provided by foreign companies.
The summit, officially the Intermediate Ministerial Meeting 2026, comes at a time of transformation in the sector. Member states will have to assess proposals to strengthen Europe’s role in low Earth orbit, prepare for the post-International Space Station era and build the continent’s presence on the Moon, while also looking towards Mars. The aim is not to abandon international cooperation, but to take part in it with greater autonomy.
Ten billion euros to send European astronauts into space
The most ambitious challenge concerns human spaceflight. Today, Europe does not have a fully autonomous system to launch astronauts and bring them back to Earth: for crewed missions to the International Space Station it depends on capabilities developed outside the continent, in particular in the United States.
ESA’s director general, Josef Aschbacher, has proposed investing around €10 billion over ten years to develop a European system capable of carrying astronauts into space and returning them safely. According to the estimates he presented, continuing to buy services from foreign providers could cost European taxpayers about €5 billion over the same period.
These are projections, not funds already allocated: the political and financial decision rests with the member states. The choice, as Aschbacher frames it, is between building up Europe’s own industrial capabilities or continuing to buy services from other operators, with costs and availability that also depend on the commercial decisions of those suppliers.
What is at stake goes beyond transporting astronauts. An autonomous capability would keep a larger share of investment within Europe’s space industry, drive the development of reusable technologies and strengthen the continent’s bargaining power in international programmes.
Ariane 6 and Vega-C: Europe’s renewed access to space begins with its launchers
Autonomy also depends on having reliable rockets that can be launched frequently enough to meet demand. In this field Europe can count on Ariane 6, the heavy launcher developed for institutional and commercial missions, and on Vega-C, designed to place lighter satellites into orbit.
The two launchers are key components of independent access to space. Vega-C, for example, put the FLEX and Sentinel-3C satellites into orbit in September 2026 as part of Europe’s Earth observation activities. The goal is to consolidate launch capabilities and widen opportunities for both public and private customers.
Competition, however, is global. SpaceX has built a model based on frequent launches and reusable rockets, securing a central role in the international market. For Europe, therefore, it is not enough simply to have its own launchers: they must also be competitive in terms of cost, availability and turnaround times.
The challenge also involves new commercial operators. German company Isar Aerospace took a step forward on 5 September 2026, when its Spectrum rocket reached space for the first time, placing five small satellites and an experiment into orbit. The first test flight in March 2025, by contrast, ended after about 30 seconds. The 2026 outcome shows the progress of a European sector in which start-ups are seeking to stand alongside established operators.
Cargo capsules and reusable technologies: the race among European companies
Another piece of the puzzle is the transport of goods to space stations and their possible return to Earth. On 10 September 2026 ESA awarded The Exploration Company a contract worth a total of €760 million for the next phase of the ALADDIN programme, dedicated to developing the Nyx capsule.
The agreement provides €310 million for a demonstration mission and includes a further €450 million for two additional missions, which still have to be confirmed. The aim is to prove Europe’s ability to carry cargo to low Earth orbit and bring it back, starting with a mission to the International Space Station.
The programme marks an important step towards a European commercial service: ESA is not only funding technological development, it is also becoming a key customer for a private company.
At the same time, industry is working on reusable rockets, a technology that can help cut the cost of access to space. This is the context for programmes run by European companies such as France’s MaiaSpace and Italy’s Avio. For the latter, the development of new propulsion and launcher-recovery solutions remains an area to watch, but the results of individual demonstrators and their timelines must be assessed on the basis of official updates.
Italy, the States General to organise the Space Economy
For Italy, the Rome summit comes as the country seeks to strengthen coordination between businesses, research and institutions. The space sector involves major industrial groups, specialist firms, start-ups, universities, research centres and financial operators: a complex value chain in which the ability to work together can make the difference in accessing European programmes and international markets.
In June 2026**,** the cross-party parliamentary group on space chaired by Andrea Mascaretti, launched the States General of the Space Economy. The programme includes twenty events in sixteen Italian regions, with the aim of showcasing aerospace clusters and gathering input from the national production system.
The initiative aims to help define strategic guidelines for the sector. The issue is not only the ability to build satellites or launchers, but also to connect industrial expertise, attract investment and turn innovation into services and economic opportunities.
Life after the International Space Station and the challenge of the Moon
The timetable for European decisions is also linked to changes in human exploration. Under current plans, the International Space Station is due to end operations by 2030, while commercial projects for new low-orbit infrastructure are taking shape. For Europe, securing a role in this scenario means being able to continue carrying out scientific experiments, developing technologies and taking part in future missions without depending entirely on the choices of external partners.
The Moon is the other major objective. The ESA wants to strengthen Europe’s presence through international cooperation and the development of targeted capabilities, viewing Earth orbit and lunar missions as stepping stones towards the exploration of Mars.
On 15 December in Rome, European governments will be asked to discuss the options prepared by the space agency. No single summit is expected to resolve all the sector’s vulnerabilities, but it will be an important step towards understanding which goals states are willing to fund, and on what timescale.

Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.

Trucks stuck as partial Iran-Pakistan trade resumes
Thousands of trucks remain stranded on both sides of the Iran-Pakistan border despite the resumption of limited overland trade between the two countries, southwest Pakistan business representatives told AFP on Monday.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the chamber of commerce for Gwadar city on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast, said the frontier with Iran was "only partially open" to trade, with a vast backlog of vehicles at the border.
There were "three to four thousand trucks on the Iranian side and two to three thousand trucks on the Pakistani side", Kalmati said.
Only certain vehicles were being allowed across the border to clear the backlog after a week-long closure, he said.
Iran's ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said on X on Sunday there were no restrictions on the Iranian side, including for the export of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).
He blamed the closures on "changes in the implementation of Pakistan's E-Form procedure for imports from Iran", which he said "have created a situation in which traders are effectively and literally unable to dispatch cargo from Iran to Pakistan".
UN probe accuses Israel of 'extermination' in West Bank
Israel has committed the crime against humanity of "extermination" in the West Bank, while continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, United Nations-mandated investigators said Monday.

Jordan's Director of General Security announced that the suspects in the Karak church attack "are from one family—two brothers and their brother-in-law," adding that "they live near Hammoud village."

"We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli airstrike targeting a camp for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Yunis," Bassal told AFP.
Israel's military told AFP it was "not aware" of any military activity in that area on Monday.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Yunis confirmed the three deaths.
"Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile," the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.
The hospital identified the deceased as Hossam al-Zamli, Tamer Abu Sneima, and Jouri al-Soufi, a young girl. The Gaza education ministry gave her age as seven.
Gaza's civil defence said a fourth person was killed in an airstrike on a tent housing displaced Palestinians near Khan Yunis.
In Gaza City's Rimal neighbourhood, a third airstrike killed one and injured three, according to the city's Al-Shifa hospital.
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir visiting Tehran: military
Pakistan's powerful army chief Asim Munir travelled to Iran on Monday, the Pakistani military said, after Tehran announced talks in the Islamic republic on regional security.
"Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir ... is visiting Tehran, Iran for an official visit," the Pakistani military's media wing said in a statement without elaborating on the purpose of the trip, one of several made by the army chief to Iran since Pakistan became a mediator in attempts to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said an operation in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage facility.
Spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X that the operation also aimed at cutting off the Houthis' supply lines between areas under their control and targeted rebel fortifications and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen.
Al-Malki said the coalition would continue to use "deterrent operational measures" to protect against the Houthis' "brutal attacks" inside the kingdom and in Yemen.
Oil spill off UAE widens, prompting more beach closures
An oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated October 24 show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is reaching close to the shores of the northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along its coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.

"The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X, insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two.

Brazil heads back to the future as Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to recognize Lula win
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:34:09 CET
16:34:09 KST

By Oliver Griffin and Eduardo Simões
SAO PAULO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote ”looked like another rigged election,” although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in Sunday’s presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded.”
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.
(Reporting by Oliver Griffin, Luciana Magalhaes, Gabriel Araujo, Eduardo Simoes, Lisandra Paraguassu and Andre Romani in Sao Paulo, Ricardo Brito in Brasilia, and Trevor Hunnicutt and Costas Pitas in Washington; editing by Brad Haynes, Gabriel Stargardter, Andrea Ricci, Rosalba O’Brien and Lincoln Feast.)
