Officials from Mecca pact states to hold talks in Iran amid regional tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:33:47 UTC
16:33:47 KST

Iran says Mecca pact states agree to boost cooperation
Iran and the three Mecca alliance countries have their first high-level contact since Houthi rebels escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Iran has said it will continue discussions with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye amid escalating tensions that have threatened regional stability and shaken the global economy.
The announcement came as top Iranian military officials met with senior Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials on Monday in what Iranian state television described as their first joint meeting.
Pakistan and Turkiye are strong allies of Saudi Arabia and have pledged military support to Riyadh as part of their new mutual defence pact, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The meeting in Tehran was held after Saudi Arabia faced weeks of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are fighting forces with the country’s internationally recognised and Saudi-backed government.
The meeting, which focused on “peace and security in the region”, was hosted by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
A statement issued by Iranian officials after the meeting said participants “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation between the four regional countries”, according to Iran’s Fars news agency.
Saudi Arabia and its allies have not commented on the meeting or reported agreement.
Rayed Krimly, the Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, said earlier today that the visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement allies “for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions in support of the mediation efforts carried out” by Qatar and Pakistan.
“The visit underscores the pivotal role of Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries in reinforcing regional security and stability and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he wrote on X.
Turkiye’s state news agency Anadolu reported that Kalin will attend the meeting in Tehran, citing Turkish security sources.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and the three members of the alliance since Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi armed group escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia last month.
Pakistan’s Field Marshal Munir last week visited Tehran, where he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials.
During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with the United States about ending the US-Israel war on Iran until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan has been a key intermediary between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel launched the war in February.
Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks later.
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.
Ministers from the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli war on Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August. Under it, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and internationally recognised borders, according to the text publicised at the time.
Efforts by Turkiye’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

Report: Cost of living pressures driven up by high oil price
Phillip Inman
Pressure on John Healey to provide more support at the budget to the most vulnerable in society is only going to become more intense with the price of a barrel of Brent crude still above $110.
A new report from a longstanding study of the impact of cost of living pressures on low income families, shows that parents struggle to pay the costs of transporting disabled children to school and health appointments.
Those in employment are also affected getting to and from work in a car when petrol is above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre. It can mean that work doesn’t pay, says the report by RuthPatrick, a professor in social and public policy at the UniversityofGlasgow.
Patrick runs the changing realities project that follows 100 low income families.
Rosie L, who lives in a couple household in rural Scotland, said:
“... it’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car, we live rurally. Absolutely have to have a car and public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are ... Not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly, as my children are disabled.”
The latest report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants of which 67 shared strategies taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
It found:
“Nearly three-quarters (73%) had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold. More than two-thirds (68%) had gone without buying something they needed for their children, such as new shoes or a winter coat. Just over half (51%) had visited a food bank or used other forms of charitable food provision, while 40% had borrowed money from family and friends. Almost half of parents (49%) had also said no to their children’s requests for educational or after-school activities.”
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities, so far, did not match the scale of the problem.
“The Budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’. Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of Child Benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”
Brazilian stock market plunges 17% after Lula's win
Stocks are plunging on the Brazilian stock market, as investors react to leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory over his far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro in last weekend’s presidential election.
The Ibovespa share index, of leading companies listed in Brazil, has tumbled by 17% in a chaotic start that saw trading briefly halted.

“Lula’s re-election could keep Brazilian stocks and the currency under pressure in the near term, but the sharp sell-off may also create opportunities for investors. Markets had largely expected a Bolsonaro victory, so part of the reaction reflects investors rapidly reversing their positions rather than a sudden deterioration in Brazil’s economy.”
Investors had expected a Bolsonaro victory, and some are concerned that Lula is less likely to try to rein in Brazil’s borrowing.
Viktor Szabó, investment director for emerging market debt at AberdeenInvestments, says:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has completed one of the most remarkable comebacks in Brazil’s democratic history. Three weeks after finishing second in the first round, he won Sunday’s run-off with 51.8% of valid votes against 48.2% for Flávio Bolsonaro. He is the first candidate since the return of democracy to win the presidency after trailing in the first round, and the first Brazilian to be elected president four times. His new term begins in January.
Markets will take a very different view. Brazilian markets had not opened when this article was written, but a strong negative reaction is expected. Investors had leaned heavily towards a change of government: the Ibovespa rose more than 8% in early trading after the first round and long-term interest rates fell sharply on hopes of a shift in fiscal policy. Much of that move now looks set to reverse, and the burden of proof sits squarely with the re-elected president.

Although Anthropic wants to sell some of its shares to the public, its founders aren’t planning on losing control.
The company has devised a “Founder Voting Structure” which will give its seven co-founders majority voting control over the company, under a plan outlined last month.
Anthropic explains:
We believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.
Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members (the “Founder LLC”).
Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.
Anthropic’s IPO filing thrown a light on the company’s financial performance – where revenues and losses have both been growing at a remarkable rate.

That jump in losses was mainly due to a rise in the fair value of convertible notes, which can be converted into stock.

On a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor may have dreamed of, pedestrians walked freely through the temporary bollards onto a green welcome banner rolled along the tarmac, declaring Oxford Street traffic-free.
SadiqKhan said it was a “momentous day”, with almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street now pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with the private car.
After decades of discussion, the closure to traffic has come into effect in time for the busy Christmas shopping period, although the bigger transformation of the street, a £150m project including trees, seating and level “plazas” for events, will start taking shape from spring 2027.
Speaking on Monday morning in the John Lewis department store, Khan said he was proud to be “finally unlocking a new era”, noting that the first action plans to pedestrianise the street started in 1971 “when I was literally in nappies”.
The mayor, whose first jobs were in retail in stores in the street, said:
“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street and the capital. We want high quality shops that will atrract people here but also culture, hospitality, leisure, and people going to and from the office having a good experience and I’m confident we’ll get that.”
He added:
“We’ve seen over the last couple of decades this street in decline… Pedestrianising the street with great public transport links, more greenery, more seating, will link to a better experience all round.”
The permanent plans will depend on feedback in the first phase and testing, and Khan said London “would be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”.
He added: “I want this to be a proof of concept – that investing in people rather than traffic leads to better footfall and spend.”
About half of the 1.2 mile street is now vehicle-free, roughly from Oxford Circus station to close to Marble Arch.
Many of London’s double-decker buses have traditionally run the length of the street and will now be diverted into neighbouring roads.
Claire Mann, chief operating officer at TransportforLondon, said there would still be “plenty of capacity for passengers” and it should not affect reliability. She said:
“People have said for some time it’s an unpleasanat environment to walk along, narrow and busy – the main movement through Oxford Street is pedestrians so this is us enabling people to make that journey in a nicer way. We’ll be monitoring to see if it does have an impact on ridership – but Bond Street and the Elizabeth Line does give you a way to arrive in style.”

South Korea bans missile maker LIG D&A from bids over bribery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:31:02 UTC
16:31:02 KST

- South Korea’s DAPA barred LIG D&A from government bidding for two years over a bribery and cost fraud case, the maximum penalty allowed.
- Prosecutors say a DAPA official received 460 million won in money and benefits, and LIG D&A has asked a court to suspend the ban.
South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) has barred LIG Defense & Aerospace, the maker of the Cheongung air defense missile formerly known as LIG Nex1, from bidding on government contracts for two years after prosecutors accused the company of paying a DAPA official hundreds of millions of won in bribes during weapons development tenders, the maximum penalty allowed under the country’s State Contracts Act.
DAPA’s defense procurement contract review committee, a 20-member panel that includes outside experts, approved the 24-month ban at a meeting at the Government Complex in Gwacheon on Oct. 20, South Korean daily Kyunghyang Shinmun reported, citing the agency. The committee said it chose the harshest sanction because the case involves the largest bribe since DAPA was founded in 2006, deliberate misconduct including cost fraud carried out over a long period, and the damage such wrongdoing does to national security and public trust in defense procurement.
The ban takes effect five business days after the company is notified, and from Oct. 29 LIG D&A will be unable to take part in new bids by DAPA or other public institutions, The Asia Business Daily reported, keeping it out of new domestic tenders until October 2028. Existing contracts and export deals are not affected, but the company relies heavily on its home market, which accounted for 72.1% of its revenue in the first half of 2026.
The case stems from an investigation by the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office, which said on Aug. 20 that a grade-five DAPA civil servant who sat on proposal evaluation panels for six defense projects worth a combined 91.5 billion won (about $69 million) between 2021 and late 2025 had received 460 million won (about $348,000) in money and benefits. Prosecutors said the official took 320 million won in cash, the right to recommend a subcontractor for a 2.2 billion won (about $1.7 million) service contract, and 140 million won in fees for selecting subcontractors, with the money allegedly routed through sham service and consulting contracts. The official and an LIG D&A executive were both detained and indicted, along with others accused of helping launder the money.
The sanction approved on Oct. 20 covers only one of the six projects, a counter-small-drone system, together with the cost fraud tied to that contract, and DAPA said the other five projects will also be reviewed, leaving open the possibility of further penalties. The agency weighed a two-year ban for the bribery and a six-month ban for the cost fraud and, under its rules, applied the heavier of the two.
LIG D&A said it regretted that DAPA had imposed an administrative sanction based only on an indictment while legal proceedings were still under way, and announced that it would seek a stay of enforcement and file a lawsuit to have the ban overturned, filing the request for a stay with a court on Oct. 22. The company has also said it will take every step to keep its programs on schedule.
Lawmaker Chun Ha-ram of the Reform Party responded that both the DAPA official who received the bribes and the subcontractor representative who passed them on have admitted the charges. At the first hearing of the case at the Suwon District Court on Sept. 29, four defendants, including the DAPA official, acknowledged the allegations in the indictment, while LIG D&A has disputed the prosecutors’ findings.
The ban could also affect major upcoming programs. LIG D&A was ranked first for system integration in the roughly 1.9 trillion won (about $1.44 billion) program to develop a long-range air-to-air missile for the KF-21 fighter, and industry observers have raised concerns that the sanction may leave the program to a single company. DAPA has also asked the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy to revoke LIG D&A’s designation as a defense contractor for the counter-small-drone system, a step that would limit its access to negotiated contracts as well.

66th Brigade Commander Krot: I don't want some latte-swilling guy judging my actions in front of the whole country
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:30:00 EET
16:30:00 KST

66th Brigade Commander Krot: I don't want some latte-swilling guy judging my actions in front of the whole country
On 15 September, after several months of keeping it quiet, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps announced Operation Vivaldi, a major offensive operation on the Lyman front.
The operation involves mopping up Russian troops that have infiltrated deep into Ukrainian positions and cutting off a sizeable Russian salient west of the Chornyi Zherebets River.
The salient had been expanding for two years, gradually encircling Lyman and looming over Sviatohirsk. Allowing it to keep growing would have put several areas at risk – the town of Izium in Kharkiv Oblast and the Kramatorsk agglomeration, widely regarded as Ukraine's last "fortress belt" in Donetsk Oblast.
One of the brigades involved in the initial stages of Operation Vivaldi was the 66th Separate Mechanised Brigade named after Mstyslav the Brave.
The 66th advanced from west to east and liberated at least two settlements that have been publicly confirmed – Serednie and Shandryholove (we don't yet have the complete list).
Interestingly, the brigade did not simply storm the two villages head-on. Serednie was partially blockaded before being mopped up. Shandryholove was encircled and brought under complete fire control, and it was only after a period of siege had demoralised the Russian troops that Ukrainian forces moved in to mop it up.
A few days ago, Ukrainska Pravda had an exclusive opportunity to work on the Lyman front, where we spoke to Rostyslav "Krot" ("Mole") Sylivakin, commander of the 66th Brigade.
In this interview with Ukrainska Pravda, Sylivakin explains how his brigade managed to retake one settlement without suffering a single casualty, whether Operation Vivaldi is really changing the balance of forces in Donetsk Oblast, how the 3rd Army Corps treats his brigade despite it not being one of the corps' original units, and why he hates giving interviews, yet still spent two hours with Ukrainska Pravda journalists at his command post.
Secrets of Operation Vivaldi
Your brigade has been deployed on the Lyman front since 2022 – longer than any of the brigades currently operating here. Can you take us back a year or two and explain what was happening here before Operation Vivaldi? Where was the line of contact?
At the start of the operation, the official front line ran near Serednie – a village we later liberated. But Russian groups had penetrated even further. They had infiltrated as far as the outskirts of Korovii Yar [5 km north-west of Serednie – ed.]. So during the preparatory stage of the operation, we had to mop up those infiltrating groups, stabilise the situation, and prevent the Russians from capturing Korovii Yar. We succeeded.
We then seized the high ground overlooking Serednie, followed by the northern part of the village and then its centre, effectively encircling the Russian troops inside the settlement. That enabled us to eliminate all the Russian troops who had infiltrated onto our side of the Nitrius River.
We then began offensive operations to capture Shandryholove, which is across the river from Serednie. We crossed the Nitrius, established a bridgehead on the high ground north of Shandryholove and continued advancing through the strips of forest [the brigade continued advancing further east – ed.]. It was only after moving further forward that we began mopping up Shandryholove.
Why did you leave Shandryholove before it had been mopped up and continue advancing? Was that the plan?
It was. We had neither the time nor the personnel to mop up the village at that stage. We needed to wear the Russians down and demoralise them. And it worked: nine Russian soldiers surrendered, around 15 were killed, and another two, according to the POWs, died of starvation.
A few months ago I was working on a piece about an offensive operation by Ukraine's Air Assault Forces on the Oleksandrivka front, and I can tell you that they used similar tactics. But they ran into problems: Russian troops would emerge from their shelters and attack Ukrainian soldiers as they made their way through the forest strips that hadn't been mopped up yet…
I'm not saying this tactic would be effective on every part of the front. But storming well-fortified positions, and especially mopping up settlements, even small ones, requires far more forces, resources and personnel than simply blocking them and continuing to advance.
It was better for us to first block the enemy and cut them off from the rest of their units so they were unable to bring ammunition and supplies into Shandryholove, and then keep them under observation and fire on them with drones and artillery.
Every time the enemy came out from their cover, we were able to hit them, force them back, and make them feel their situation was hopeless. In time they realised that no one was coming for them – there would be no food or ammunition. We also dropped leaflets on them and played audio recordings over loudspeakers offering them the chance to surrender.
And it worked. An enemy that was prepared to defend their positions just a month earlier eventually breaks and becomes willing to surrender. Especially after eating nothing but roots, clay and worms for four or six weeks...
If we'd tried to mop up Shandryholove without blocking it first, we would have lost a lot of our people.
In your interview with Anna Kaliuzhna, you said you liberated one settlement without suffering a single casualty. Which settlement was that, and how did you manage it?
It was the village of Serednie. We were able to do it first and foremost because of the training our people had received. We were helped enormously by the fact that in February or March 2026 we were given permission to conduct basic combined military training at our own military unit. Because when we got people who'd done their basic training at training centres, they were just as strange to us as those who'd come straight from the enlistment offices. We had to spend time giving them additional training.
Do you remember when fair and regular replenishment of personnel was introduced at the end of 2025?
But they promised 50 people per brigade, didn't they? That's not many.
It isn't, but under those circumstances it was enough for us to prepare people for offensive operations. It gave us some certainty. Based on the battlefield situation and the fact that we would receive 50 people, we decided that we would conduct offensive operations [at the start of Operation Vivaldi – ed.] using small infantry groups of two or three people. A group like that is harder to detect and hit, and it's easier for them to find or dig shelter.
Groups of two or three assault troops? Wait, how many people did you actually have retaking Serednie?
Up to 30 people in total [an astonishingly small number for an offensive operation – UP]. But you can't say it was just those 30 people, because capturing a settlement involves a whole range of measures. To liberate Serednie, we had to capture the strongpoints overlooking the river, establish a safe route to the village, and so on.
We weren't able to block Serednie in the same way we later blocked Shandryholove because the Nitrius River runs along its eastern side. At the time we couldn't cross the river and seize the opposite bank, but we did manage, to some extent, to isolate the village using drones and minimise the number of enemy personnel that went into it.
Did the Russians not engage your men in small-arms combat in Serednie at all? Given that you suffered no casualties there.
Of course they did. There were about 20 enemy troops there. But when planning the operation, we were counting on the element of surprise. Basically our infantry shot the f**kers while they were asleep or resting in their dugouts and completely unaware of what was coming. Of course there were some cases where the enemy put up resistance, but thanks to our training, every small-arms engagement ended in our favour.
Am I right in thinking that this is the second time the Ukrainian army has liberated villages on the Lyman front? Didn't the first offensive operation sweep through here in 2022?
Yes. These territories were liberated, roughly all the way up to Ploshchanka, in autumn 2022. Then, from spring 2024 onwards, we began losing these territories. The enemy's 20th Army launched a large-scale offensive here, and our forces were weakened and stretched thin because everyone was fighting on higher-priority fronts – in Bakhmut, near Avdiivka.
Serednie and Shandryholove, the villages we're talking about, were lost in the autumn and winter of 2025.
A Ukrainian tank in a liberated village on the Lyman front in autumn 2022. Photo: Dmytro Larin
There was a whole combination of reasons why we lost those territories, ranging from incompetence on the part of individual officers at the commander level to decision-making at the group level.
In my view, another major factor was the mixing of units. In summer 2024, the 66th Brigade's sector was 38 km long [this is a huge sector – UP] and in addition to five of our own, 15 other attached battalions were fighting in it. For a single brigade, that's far too many attached units – untrained, understaffed, and originating from various structures ranging from Territorial Defence to border guards.
"I don't like it when every commander who gets an interview talks about how great he is"
You've emphasised several times that you aren't particularly keen to give interviews. I've heard a lot of military personnel say that. Why is that?
I don't like it when every commander who gets an interview talks about how great he is, giving expert assessments of what other commanders or other units have done without having the relevant experience to do so. And then there's the principle that the more frequently a person is interviewed, the faster they're made a Hero of Ukraine.
In normal armies in the rest of the world, it doesn't work like that. Press officers comment on events, not commanders. The commanders lead the troops.
From my point of view, I have to say that for us as journalists, it's an immense privilege to be able to speak with commanders directly and not just with press officers.
In our country and in our army, it's something we have to do, because service members and the Armed Forces as a whole have had a pretty poor reputation since 2014. There's a widespread stereotype that commanders are butchers, bribe-takers and incompetent fools and every other soldier is an alcoholic or a drug addict. So we need to promote the army and improve our reputation.
But some commanders exploit this carte blanche they have in terms of interviews and media exposure to satisfy their personal ambitions and become famous. From a professional standpoint, this is inappropriate. It leads to a situation where any young lad in this country can sit in front of a camera and deliver expert evaluations of decisions made by generals and colonels.
Personally, I don't want my actions and decisions to be judged later by some latte-swilling fella who's never been in my shoes.
I don't think that General Syrskyi deserves to have his decisions and actions judged by a generation this young, privileged and superficial – people who have experienced little beyond lattes, consumerism and sexual experimentation. Still less does he deserve to be judged publicly, before the whole of Ukraine.
Or even those colonels who've made sure they get interviews but have never served as group commanders – they sit there and criticise decisions made by Syrskyi or Zaluzhnyi, and in the future they'll criticise Drapatyi's decisions. Assessment and criticism should only come from people who have the necessary competence, relevant experience and level of training.
Remember Oleksandr "Henii" Shyrshyn – in the summer of 2025, when he was serving as a battalion commander in the 47th Brigade, he posted on Facebook saying the tasks set by the top leadership were "idiotic"...
Henii was criticising a specific situation and tasks in which he was directly involved. Henii was not criticising the commander-in-chief's overall activities across the Armed Forces or decisions made with regard to other sectors and other commanders.
So that form of criticism is acceptable?
The reason that criticism was expressed publicly was because it hadn't worked at the level where Henii initially raised his concerns and proposed alternative courses of action – it had been ignored.
I know Henii as a completely capable and effective commander.
Personnel audit, relationship with 3rd Army Corps and expectations of Drapatyi
When you took over in 2024, the 66th Brigade was in a pretty bad way: exhausted, understaffed and suffering losses. How did you handle that situation? What advice would you give to those in a similar situation today or in the future, especially considering that new brigades continue to be created, such as the 167th?
First of all we had to figure out what kind of personnel we actually had and what we didn't. Remember, we had 15 attached units at the time and only a handful of them were fighting independently. Most had minimal training, lacked proper combat experience, and were fundamentally unable to fight independently. So step one was to determine the true state of the personnel.
Then we did a huge amount of work to form a good, effective team with the right moral values. Some unit commanders had to be removed.
What are the right values to you?
First, zero tolerance for corruption. Second, openness and honesty. And third, you could be melodramatic and say the value of human life, but to be honest, it's the pursuit of efficiency.
In any interview you listen to these days, all the commanders talk about human life being the top priority. That is undoubtedly true. But if the command is incompetent, it doesn't matter how much they value human life – they're not going to preserve it.
The only way you can value human life in the conditions of our war is through high-quality training, high standards and discipline. There is no other way. If you're constantly shielding the lives of your own soldiers, your neighbours to the left and right of you are going to suffer. If you protect your own people all the time, someone else is going to get killed. If we run away from every danger, then I'm sorry, but tomorrow the front line is going to be beyond the Dnipro.
I think the very fact that we took the decision, as a society and as a country, to fight and not surrender in 2022 means we fundamentally agreed that for us, Ukraine's existence stands higher than any single human life.
Putin said in an interview that he does not see a world without Russia – the same must hold true for Ukraine, for Ukrainians. There are no Ukrainians without Ukraine.
So first you conducted a sort of personnel audit, then you assembled a team with the right values?
Assembling a team is a lengthy process – it can't be done in a week or two. That process continues to this day and will continue for as long as I am in this position. I found all the battalion commanders right here within the brigade – I didn't bring anyone in from outside or pull in any friends or acquaintances. I observed them for six months and found them, and we are learning here together and developing our brigade.
I get a sense from your words that you're a supporter of the corps reform, even though your 66th Brigade is fighting in another corps. I'd like to ask: how does the 3rd Army Corps treat you as an attached brigade?
The 3rd Corps treats our attached brigade as if we were their own (smiling).
To put it in simple terms and briefly, to start with, the 3rd Corps helped us to complete missions with their own personnel so that we had time to train our new recruits and non-commissioned officers. This ensured that we didn't deploy them chaotically, but according to plan – so that people could first gain combat experience in defence, and then we could train specialised groups to eliminate infiltrated enemy forces and conduct assault operations.
[According to UP's information, Andrii Biletskyi ordered the allocation of well over a thousand soldiers from the 3rd Assault Brigade to reinforce the brigades that joined the newly formed corps and its operational control.]
Prior to the corps reform, those types of decisions didn't happen. If any units were sent to reinforce us, they were mostly understrength. Firstly, they couldn't really reinforce us much, and secondly, they'd arrive when it was already too late.
The 3rd Corps also evaluated our brigade's capabilities very quickly and objectively. Their groups visited our units and observed the commanders and our supply levels. They provided training wherever possible, helping us restructure our command and control system.
I understand that this includes introducing a role known as a "battle captain" – a dedicated person who directs combat operations in real time from the command post? I saw some last year at 13th Khartiia Brigade command posts, and it looked very unusual.
Yes, the 3rd Army Corps helped us introduce this system. Before that, the entire burden of managing ongoing combat operations fell on the brigade commander and his deputies. As a result, we were falling behind in every area of our work, particularly when it came to planning future operations. Now we have time to plan, develop our capabilities and so on.
So if you didn't have a battle captain now, we wouldn't be sitting here recording this interview? Would you be next door in the main command room, watching a live drone feed on a big TV and shouting "Open fire!" into the radio?
Yes. When I took command of the 66th Brigade, what it boiled down to was that either I or one of my deputies would be sitting in front of a screen shouting orders about who should fire where, which drone should go where, where to put the mortar and where to put the machine gun. This is called hands-on control or micromanagement, and it has never been effective anywhere. I knew perfectly well even then that this wasn't how things should work.
I'd been a company commander and a battalion commander. For example, at the 93rd Brigade, I was taught that every commander must make decisions within their own remit. When I was a company commander, I didn't tell section commanders what to do – I expected them to make decisions themselves. If I wasn't happy with their decision, I'd adjust it and guide them towards a better one.
At the 66th Brigade, we had to start from scratch and teach commanders to make their own decisions. I spent a lot of time on that.
By 2025, when the corps reform began, my battalion commanders had become fairly independent. I no longer needed to sit in front of a screen all the time shouting orders. But I didn't have a dedicated officer who could take over that role.
The 3rd Army Corps showed us how battle captains should operate. It sent its own battle captains to our command posts to train us and share their experience. That had a positive effect. Now, other brigades are coming to us to learn.
How did you let go of the need for constant control? I've written more than one article about what micromanagement in the military was like under Oleksandr Syrskyi. And as someone who has managed at least something in life – even a tiny team working on a tiny task – I understand how difficult it can be.
It's not a question of how I let go. I never intended to hold on to that kind of control in the first place. I'd been a company commander and a battalion commander; I'd had my fill of directing small infantry groups. I don't want to be doing the same things as a brigade commander that I did when I was a company commander.
It's simple: any reasonably sensible person will be too lazy to do someone else's job.
My job is to appoint effective leaders, train them, hold them to high standards and give them the autonomy they need to make decisions. I will only make decisions on their behalf if those decisions contradict my intentions or if, based on my experience and training, I can see that they won't lead to the task being carried out effectively. That's how it works.
The system should work, not rely on one person.
On the subject of micromanagement, our sources say the new commander-in-chief is trying to move away from this kind of command system. Have you noticed any changes in the military since Mykhailo Drapatyi took over?
I'd put it this way: it's too soon for anyone at brigade level to have felt the effects of the change of commander-in-chief. The appointment can't be evaluated solely on the basis that I've asked the commander-in-chief about a few specific issues and he's agreed to help me. [Our sources say that Sylivakin has a fairly good relationship with Drapatyi – UP.]
But I believe that over time our defence forces will undergo major systemic changes, particularly when it comes to micromanagement. I know that General Drapatyi wants to build effective teams at every level, made up of competent people and officers, and root corruption out of the Armed Forces.
"There will be no wars without living people taking part"
How has Operation Vivaldi affected the defence of Donetsk Oblast as a whole? Has it really changed the situation fundamentally?
Operation Vivaldi will at the very least force the Russians to ease the pressure on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, because they will have to redeploy reserves from there [to the Lyman front] to stop us from advancing further.
Secondly, it's a massive blow to the Russians' illusion that they are already in the final stages of this war. Their media keeps claiming that Sviatohirsk has been captured, that Oskil [a village 10 km east of Izium] has been encircled, or that they are already storming Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. The successes of Operation Vivaldi are tearing their whole "victory" narrative to shreds.
It's unlikely, of course, but maybe some ordinary Russians will eventually realise that they are still a very long way from capturing Donbas.
They're a long way from capturing Donetsk Oblast at the moment, but could they still manage it?
We're fighting a huge country with an effectively inexhaustible pool of manpower for mobilisation. With those resources, the Russians can achieve anything they want. The question is whether they are capable of doing so with their current approach. I don't believe they are.
Personally, I don't think losing one territory or another would be a huge catastrophe for us. The war will go on for years, and the decisive factors in the final outcome will be things such as the combat effectiveness and technological development of the Armed Forces.
We may lose some territory, but if we preserve our combat effectiveness and develop faster than the Russians, we will be able to liberate that territory later.
Why are you confident that training and developing the Ukrainian Armed Forces can offset Russia's numerical superiority?
The clearest example is 2022, during this very war, when their numerical advantage was reduced to nothing because our units were more experienced. In 2022, Ukraine was technologically more advanced than Russia. Some of our companies already had Mavic drones and FPV drones, which had become available thanks to enthusiasts who had figured out how to use them on their own.
There will be many more technological innovations during this war. The question is which side will be quicker to adopt them and scale them up.
Like two-metre-tall humanoid robots?
That's possible too. When I was just beginning to gain combat experience, I couldn't have imagined that one day I'd be adjusting artillery fire with a drone and using that same drone for reconnaissance. Back then I had to go out on foot to see anything and gather information. And now warfare has changed so much…
There was a time when we couldn't even have imagined that you could kill an enemy by dropping a munition from a drone or evacuate a wounded soldier using a robot. Just six months ago our brigade wasn't using UGVs [unmanned ground vehicles] at all. Now we're consistently among the top 10 most effective units in terms of UGV use. And this month we even built our own UGV.
In the same way, five years from now, humanoid robots might be running through trenches and shooting. But the point is that they too are just a tool, a piece of technology, and they won't remain effective forever. As long as war exists, there will always be a place for ordinary infantry. There will be no wars without living people taking part.
Do you agree that the war has reached a stalemate?
In my opinion, the claim that the war has reached a stalemate is more political than military and isn't entirely accurate. From a military perspective, there are no dead ends in war. Sooner or later, one side will achieve a breakthrough.
If a ceasefire isn't reached politically, the war will continue until one side develops new technological solutions that give it a significant advantage. In the First World War it was chemical weapons and tanks. In the Second World War it was aircraft and new tactics for motorised and mechanised units. There will be something new in this war, too.
Olha Kyrylenko, Ukrainska Pravda

Planned Overflow: How Singapore Balances Floods, Canals, and Public Space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park in Singapore, a river does not occupy a fixed boundary. Under ordinary conditions, water moves through a naturalized channel bordered by grass, planting, and paths that bring visitors close to the river. During heavy rainfall, water spreads into the surrounding park, which is designed to accommodate flows beyond the capacity of the narrower channel. What appears to be a public landscape is also working infrastructure. Singapore's approach retains drainage engineering while assigning a wider role to the land around it.
For decades, Singapore's network of concrete canals has been central to managing stormwater in a densely developed city exposed to intense tropical rainfall. Their hard surfaces and defined channels were designed to convey water efficiently. These channels moved stormwater efficiently, but offered limited space for public access, planting, or other uses along the water's edge. Through its Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters (ABC Waters) Programme, launched in 2006, Singapore began integrating waterways with parks, ecological systems, and public spaces. The programme links stormwater management with the design of parks, waterways, and public spaces.
The transformation of the Kallang River at Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park offers one of the clearest examples of this approach. A 2.7-kilometer stretch of the former concrete canal was redesigned as a naturalized river, bringing the waterway into the surrounding park. The central design decision was to allow the park to function as a flood conveyance area. Under normal conditions, water occupies a narrower stream. During heavy rainfall, the flow can expand into the adjacent landscape. The park's ground is part of the flood conveyance system, not just the public space around it. Soil bioengineering and naturalized banks support this arrangement, combining hydraulic requirements with a more varied river edge.
Related Article
Rivers Before Roads: How Southeast Asia's Waterways Produced an Alternative Urbanism
At Bishan, the naturalized banks allow visitors to approach the water more closely. Compared with the former concrete canal, the naturalized river introduces gentler banks and stepping stones along the water's edge. PUB documents the park's dual role as a recreational landscape and a flood conveyance area. Sungei Tampines shows how naturalized banks can be introduced alongside measures to increase a canal's stormwater capacity.
In 2022, drainage improvements along a 1.4-kilometer section included widening the waterway by up to 4.5 metres and deepening it by 0.5 metres. These interventions increased its stormwater conveyance capacity by a reported 30 per cent. Approximately one kilometer of one bank was also naturalized using soil bioengineering techniques. A cantilevered park connector, lookout decks, and a bridge provide public access along the waterway.
A canal can be widened and deepened while sections of its banks are naturalized. The widened channel conveys stormwater, while selected sections of its banks accommodate planting, habitat, and public access. At Sungei Tampines, naturalisation is limited to sections of the bank while the main channel is enlarged to carry more stormwater. Channel dimensions, bank stability, water levels, and maintenance requirements continue to determine how these spaces operate.
At Sungei Ulu Pandan, the landscape also treats runoff before it reaches the canal. Here, the design incorporates features intended to treat runoff before it enters the waterway, making the landscape an active part of the drainage system rather than simply its visible setting. PUB's project documentation describes vegetated swales, sedimentation basins, cleansing biotopes, and habitat cells as components of this approach. Swales guide runoff while helping remove larger sediments. Sedimentation basins allow suspended particles to settle, while cleansing biotopes use plants and soil media to filter pollutants and absorb nutrients. Shallow, planted habitat cells along the canal edges provide shelter and feeding opportunities for wildlife.
The interventions were implemented in phases. An initial 600-metre section was completed in 2013, followed by works along a further 1.9 kilometers, completed in 2022. The phased works combined drainage improvements with runoff treatment and habitat features along the canal. The presence of these features alone does not establish their environmental performance. Research evaluating Singapore's ABC Waters Programme has found that some interventions perform well in removing suspended particles, while nutrient removal has been less consistent. Treatment performance varies with site conditions, including the characteristics of incoming runoff and the operation and maintenance of individual features.
At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park, the river forms part of a larger recreational landscape. At Sungei Tampines, bridges, lookout decks, and a park connector establish points of access along a more linear drainage corridor. In both projects, access is provided along waterways that continue to serve drainage functions. When a canal is accessible from everyday routes, it can become part of how residents experience their neighborhood. Paths, bridges, and places to stop along the water's edge allow residents to encounter the canal as part of everyday public space.
Research on the non-market value of Singapore's ABC Waters Programme found that residents valued its environmental and amenity features, although preferences varied between groups. They do not, however, establish that every project increases social interaction or provides equal access to public space. Those outcomes depend on how spaces are connected, maintained, and used by different communities.
Public access must be maintained alongside the operational requirements of the waterway. These landscapes must accommodate fluctuating water levels and intense rainfall, while planted and engineered systems require ongoing maintenance. Paths and public amenities must therefore remain compatible with changing water levels and flood conditions.
Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park, Sungei Tampines, and Sungei Ulu Pandan extend the role of drainage infrastructure in different ways. One integrates the river with a floodable park; another combines increased conveyance capacity with naturalized banks and public access; the third incorporates runoff treatment and habitat features into the waterway's landscape. Across the three projects, drainage remains the primary hydraulic function, while the surrounding landscape also provides flood storage, runoff treatment, habitat, or public access.
The long-term performance of the ABC Waters Programme depends on how its projects are monitored and maintained after completion. Monitoring is needed to assess environmental performance, while ecological features require maintenance. The benefits of public access also need to be evaluated through how people use these spaces. A greener canal is not, by itself, proof of improved water quality, restored biodiversity, or reduced flood damage. These outcomes must be established through evidence over time.
Singapore's waterways show why drainage infrastructure needs to be evaluated beyond its hydraulic capacity. Hydraulic capacity and the appearance of a natural river are insufficient measures of a waterway's performance. The surrounding landscape can provide space for floodwater, habitat for other species, and public access to the waterway. The canal remains a drain. Its banks and surrounding ground determine how much more the waterway can do.

Good morning. It’s Angela Skujins holding the newsletter pen for the entire week. On Monday’s agenda: Serbian elections serve as a death knell for long-time leader Aleksandar Vučić and his political party, while French fury continues to manifest through violent protest and a presidential bid.
While you were sleeping: Serbia’s longtime conservative politician Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat last night in a parliamentary election that pitted himself and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) against the left-wing Student List in the Western Balkan nation.
“It is clear that we have lost the election,” the former president of Serbia and prime minister hopeful said in a televised statement, with the votes paving the way for the student-backed political group to seize a minimum 135 parliamentary seats, while the SNS party is set to win around 105. The vote count, however, is not yet final.
Breath of fresh air: Bojan Vranic, a professor of political science at the University of Belgrade, just told Europe Today Student List’s victory is a “historic” moment for the country as it brings in a “new, fresh political elite”. Watch.
From the outside, it was expected the vote would impact Belgrade’s long-standing bid to join the European Union — a 14-year process that has been complicated by Vučić’s relationship with Russia and China, and his defiance against adopting certain foreign policy protocols.
Vranic believes, however, that the Student List movement is “very conservative” when it comes to inching Belgrade closer to joining the bloc, as the organisation is focussed on internal changes. “I would not be overly enthusiastic… of a miracle breakthrough in European integration,” he said. Watch.
Fourth time’s a charm: French political hopeful and far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen also officially launched her presidential candidacy on Sunday, at a campaign rally in the city of Orléans attended by thousands of Rassemblement National RN (National Rally) supporters. This is the fourth time she has attempted to snap-up the top job.
In a fiery speech, the dame of the ultra-conservatives promised the protection of public spaces so “that they can remain places full of life and mutual respect”. The pitch was in clear reference to the defiant protests that have transformed France over the last few weeks into a country gripped by looting, violence and thousands of arrests.
Anarchy in France: During her speech, Le Pen lamented the leadership of French President Emmanuel Macron during this period, stating that under his presidency, rule of law has become “too lenient”.
She also set out other major policies while at the podium, including her position on military conflict — vowing that France "will not send" its young people "to die in reckless or irresponsible military adventures, and even less in wars that are not ours" — as well as getting tougher on migration. The former will surely cause EU heads of state and allies in Kyiv a headache, but the latter could be a welcome reprieve from Macron’s centrist tendencies.
Election fever in Jerusalem: Former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert just said on Europe Today that the future of the country hinges on a crucial upcoming vote. Watch.
Olmert, a fierce critic of Israel’s incumbent head of state Benjamin Netanyahu, was speaking on the programme as just over seven million eligible Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday to cast their vote in arguably the country’s most important vote in recent history.
It will be the first national election since the deadly 7 October attack by Hamas, and is seen as a referendum on the leadership of the country’s far-right nationalist leader and the last three years of war.
The election comes as the occupied West Bank continues to be squeezed by the Israeli Defence Force, with soldiers displacing hundreds of Palestinians from their homes. The activity follows a gun attack last week, with two Israeli soldiers killed and more injured.
News from Brussels: The European Commission is proposing a bundle of reforms to the EU’s major border force agency, Frontex, this week. As my colleague Vincenzo Genovese reports, the EU’s border agency will have more personnel to deploy at the bloc’s borders and a “quick response force" could be activated in case of sudden arrivals of a large volume of migrants.
This is according to an EU official with knowledge of the matter speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity, who stated the reform is expected to be formally proposed on Tuesday by the EU executive.
‘Innovative solutions’: The proposal will also include an online surveillance unit to monitor social media and prevent large-scale movements. The goal is to avoid situations previously witnessed in the EU’s recent history, such as 80,000 migrants illegally entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta via Morocco in July, prompting a political firestorm among EU leaders, and triggering a crisis of confidence in leadership.
To associate or not: The concept of “associate membership” is at risk of disappearing from the declaration of this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal as member states butt heads over its inclusion, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
Ambassadors will gather today to discuss the content of the declaration, with some countries still unclear about what “associate membership” is as it has no precedent. They want the European Commission to provide clear answers before the summit takes place on Thursday. In a declaration of intent, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will travel to Montreal with 10 Commissioners by her side.
Time to pay up: The summit in Montreal will give von der Leyen the perfect opportunity to gently press Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to increase Canada’s financial support to Ukraine. As previously reported, the EU has committed to addressing Kyiv’s massive €70 billion shortfall for next year.
Officials and diplomats in Brussels all agree that the bloc should continue to provide two-thirds of support, which, in this operation, would amount to €50 billion, with other allies covering the remaining third.
However, this division of labour hasn’t worked. According to an internal document seen by Jorge, the EU is slated to provide 80% of Ukraine’s military and financial aid next year, a share that vastly exceeds the agreed two-thirds. Brussels has ratcheted up pressure on allies to first, make good on what they have already promised and second, ramp up their contributions for 2027.
Fighting an uphill battle: As Sasha Vakulina reports, officials in Moscow have said Russia is ready to resume trilateral peace talks with Ukraine and the US but only after 4 November — Russia’s National Unity Day.
What might happen before talks resume? Sasha expects more Russian attacks on Ukraine. Just over the past week, Russia launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Lithuania expects EU vote on ending seasonal clock changes in June 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:27:00 UTC
16:27:00 KST

Lithuania expects a vote in the EU on ending seasonal clock changes in late June 2027, the Transport and Communications Ministry said.
"In February 2027, we will discuss this issue at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers, and toward the end of Lithuania's presidency, in late June, a vote will be held. We will see what the decision will be," Deputy Transport Minister Lukas Paškevičius said.
Lithuania will hold the presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027. Paškevičius said ending seasonal time changes had been included in the proposed presidency agenda, pending final approval by the Lithuanian parliament.
"Our initial and most important plan was to get this issue onto the agenda, as we heard that a number of member states did not want to do so. [...] Currently, there is no opposition that would prevent this topic from being included in Lithuania's EU presidency agenda. That in itself is significant progress," the deputy minister said.
He added that Lithuania had discussed the issue with ministers from France, Spain, Germany and the Nordic countries, as well as with members of the European Parliament.
The European Union is awaiting a European Commission study, expected in February 2027, that will assess the potential impact of scrapping seasonal clock changes on the economy, agriculture, public health and other sectors, including in Lithuania.
According to Paškevičius, European Union member states have so far failed to reach a common position because of differing views on which time zone should be adopted permanently.
"Southern European countries share a similar view – they would also lean toward summer time, as it would mean longer, brighter evenings. The main challenges arise for the Nordic countries, especially Finland, where natural light is already scarce in winter. Choosing permanent summer time would make mornings there even darker," he said.
"Our goal is to abandon seasonal time changes altogether, regardless of whether summer or winter time is chosen. Surveys show that most Lithuanian residents prefer remaining on summer time," Paškevičius said.
According to the ministry, the European Commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes in 2018, and the European Parliament backed the proposal in 2019.
However, the process stalled because member states failed to reach a consensus.
Paškevičius added that if no agreement is reached during Lithuania's presidency, Vilnius would coordinate on the issue with Greece, which will take over the presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2027.
Clocks in Lithuania, as in the rest of the European Union, are currently changed twice a year. Over the weekend, clocks were turned back by one hour to switch to winter time.

Taiwan's Artery Technology posts record quarterly profit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:26:57 UTC
16:26:57 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Microcontroller unit (MCU) maker Artery Technology Corp. reported record quarterly profit in the third quarter.
Net profit rose 442% year-on-year to NT$179 million (US$5.5 million). Revenue increased 191% from the same period a year earlier to NT$1.12 billion, according to MoneyDJ.
For the fourth quarter, Artery expects revenue to decline 30% to 35% from the previous quarter, as some orders originally scheduled for the second half of the year were shipped ahead of schedule. Despite the anticipated slowdown, full-year revenue is still expected to double from 2025.
Artery specializes in 32-bit MCUs for mid- to high-end applications, while many competitors focus on 8-bit products. An MCU is a compact computer integrated into a single chip, according to Pocket Securities and LTN.
MCUs typically combine a processor, memory, and input-output controls to manage the functions of an electronic device. These chips are widely used in industrial equipment, motor control systems, and consumer electronics.
Artery sees robotics as a major source of future growth as the industry expands over the next three to five years. Five robotics customers have already adopted its products, with each robot estimated to require about 70 MCUs.
The company began volume shipments of MCUs for robotic joint motors in the third quarter and expects deliveries to exceed 1 million units next year. Several customers have also adopted its chips for dexterous robotic hands, with trial production underway.
MCUs designed for electronic skin applications are expected to enter mass production next year. Other robotic applications, including robot vacuum cleaners, floor scrubbers, lawn mowers, and pool cleaners, are projected to contribute about 7% to 8% of Artery's revenue this year.
Beyond robotics, the company expects the MCU industry to grow steadily as connected devices, smart home appliances, and industrial automation become more widespread. The expansion of artificial intelligence computing into additional applications is also expected to support growth.
Over the next two years, Artery sees further opportunities in millimeter-wave radar and 3D printing. Its products have been adopted by one of the world's three largest 3D printer manufacturers, while another customer has begun trial production.

Russia has lost 1,580,440 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 26.
The number includes 1,990 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,448 tanks, 25,609 armored combat vehicles, 167,240 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,632 artillery systems, 2,239 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,726 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,018 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

- A Myanmar resistance group destroyed several Chinese-made ZSL-92 armored vehicles of the Myanmar Army using FPV drones, analyst Jesus Roman reported.
- The strikes were attributed to Monywa Scout, a local armed group, but the exact number, date and location of the losses were not disclosed.
Fighters from a local armed group in Myanmar have destroyed several Chinese-made ZSL-92 infantry fighting vehicles belonging to the Myanmar Army using first-person-view (FPV) drones, open-source analyst Jesus Roman reported on Oct. 24, attributing the strikes to Monywa Scout, a resistance group named after Monywa, the main city of Myanmar’s Sagaing Region in the country’s northwest, though he did not say exactly how many vehicles were hit or when and where the attacks took place.
The ZSL-92, also known as the Type 92, is a Chinese six-wheeled armored vehicle that carries infantry and is armed with a 25 mm cannon in a small turret, and Roman noted that this version is seen less often in Myanmar than the WMA-301, a wheeled vehicle built on the same family of chassis and armed with a 105 mm gun, of which Myanmar’s armed forces operate about 100, according to Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi.
FPV drones are small, cheap quadcopters flown by an operator watching a live video feed through goggles or a screen, which lets them steer an explosive charge into a precise weak point on a target such as a vehicle’s roof, engine deck or open hatch, a tactic that became widespread during the war in Ukraine before spreading to other conflicts, including Myanmar’s civil war.
Myanmar’s resistance groups first used drones in combat in December 2021 in Pale township of Sagaing Region, less than a year after the military seized power in a coup, and the conflict monitor ACLED had recorded more than 2,100 drone strikes by resistance groups across more than 600 locations in the country by mid-2025, most of them carried out with commercial and agricultural drones converted to drop small explosives, although both resistance fighters and government forces have since adopted FPV drones.
Chinese-made armor has been a frequent target: in December 2023, Roman reported the destruction of a Chinese Dongfeng Mengshi armored vehicle belonging to the Myanmar Army during fighting in the north of the country, alongside BTR-3 and MT-LB armored vehicles, and earlier this year footage showed resistance fighters destroying a Myanmar Army WMA-301 that had been fitted with a metal grille, a type of improvised drone protection that also first spread during the war in Ukraine.
The drones are now reaching beyond the battlefield, as on Sept. 10 anti-junta fighters launched FPV drones at Myanmar’s Tada-U Air Base, about 35 km (22 miles) south of Mandalay, where video posted online showed one striking the nose of a Russian-made Yak-130 jet.

U.S. Prepares Bases for Three Months of Combat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:21:16 UTC
16:21:16 KST

The Pentagon has started preparing U.S. military bases to operate independently for at least 90 days in the event of a major war.
According to Fox News, the preparations are part of the FORTRESS military initiative, which aims to ensure that U.S. military bases can continue operating without relying heavily on civilian infrastructure.
Major U.S. military installations on the mainland must be able to meet their essential needs for electricity, water, fuel, and communications independently for at least three months.
To ensure energy independence, the initiative includes the use of portable small nuclear reactors, large-scale energy storage systems, and local power grids.
This will allow military bases to operate independently if civilian power infrastructure is disrupted.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell stated that the U.S. military can no longer rely solely on the protection provided by the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
“We do not want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to support our national defense. That is an unacceptable risk,” he emphasized.
Other aspects of the program include establishing strategic reserves of ammunition, fuel, critical minerals, electronics,spare parts, and medical supplies.
The Pentagon also aims to ensure at least two independent supply or production channels for the most critical defense components, so that the loss of a single factory or supplier does not disrupt military operations.
Particular attention is being given to preparing U.S. industry for large-scale wartime production. Through the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network, the Pentagon plans to identify civilian companies in advance that could quickly switch to manufacturing defense products during a war.
To achieve this, the military will need to coordinate technical requirements, contracts, production conversion procedures, and cybersecurity measures. The initiative also includes regular industrial capacity tests and exercises to practice mobilizing manufacturing capabilities.

India-China face-off: Beijing says it carried out normal activities in border areas
China's Foreign Ministry on Monday said it carried out normal patrol and control activities along its border with India, in response to New Delhi's claim that it deviated from established patrolling patterns leading to a tense military standoff in Arunachal Pradesh.
India's Foreign Ministry, on Friday, had said that the situation along the India-China border was periodically disrupted, blaming Chinese forces for "miscalculations" along the Line of Actual Control.
In response, Chinese diplomats said the country has consistently and strictly abode by the relevant agreements between the countries and conducted routine patrols and management activities in the region, as reported by Chinese Communist Party's Global Times newspaper
The nuclear-armed neighbors remain in communication through diplomatic and military channels, a ministry spokesperson said as per the report.

India has over the years reiterated that the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh is an integral part of the country, while China considers it to be a part of Tibet.
Gandhi acquitted in defamation case
An Indian court acquitted Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi in a defamation case on Monday, local media reported.
Gandhi was accused of calling India's Home Minister Amit Shah an "accused murder" during a state election campaign speech in 2018. The case was filed in Sultanpur town of Uttar Pradesh by a BJP member. Sultanpur is less than an hour away from New Delhi by road.
The remark related to when Gandhi's convoy reportedly got into a minor accident on the highway on the way to Sultanpur, when a vehicle in front slammed the breaks suddenly. The INC leader was unhurt.
The acquittal comes as Gandhi is leading a united opposition campaign against Prime Minister Narendra Modi and India's Chief Election Commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.
India hosts prince of Liechtenstein for state visit
Prince Alois of Liechtenstein arrived in Mumbai today, on the second day of his four-day state visit to India.
He was accompanied by his spouse, Princess Sophie, along with other officals and industry leaders.
Liechtenstein is an independent principality nestled between Austria and Switzerland. With a population of about 40,000 people, the country is about the size of the Indian city of Varanasi.
This is Prince Alois's second visit to India this year. Before that, he has visited the country in 2010 and 2018, India's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The prince is scheduled to attend an official banquet with India's President Droupadi Murmu and hold a meeting with India's Foreign Minister Surahmanyam Jaishankar.
"Prince Alois will hold bilateral meetings to discuss cooperation in various areas including trade and investment, science, technology and innovation and people-to-people exchanges as well as exchange views on regional and global developments," the statement said.

At least two bodies were recovered in northeastern Delhi on Monday morning after rescue workers conducted an overnight operation at the site of a collapsed house.

Authorities identified the deceased as 60-year-old Chanderpal and his 36-year-old son Vijay Kumar.
India's capital has seen a number of building collapses off late, as illegal constructions, lack of maintenance and unimplemented safety standards threaten lives. In September, a five-storey building housing paying guest students collapsed killing at least seven.

Indian Home Minister, and Prime Minister Modi's right-hand man, Amit Shah on Monday slammed opposition president Mallikarjun Kharge for making an "indecent remark" about the premier's late father.

Under Rahul Gandhi's leadership, the Congress party keeps crossing the limits of indecency every day," Shah said on X.
He claimed that the INC had taken to personal remarks in "desperation and frustration" over losing their political base.
BJP plans nationwide protest over Modi remark
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata party has called for a nationwide protest on Monday, over a prominent opposition leader's "indecent and offensive" remark about about Modi caused controversy.
BJP spokespersons and regional leaders said they were organizing protest rallies across the country, including some that plan to burn effigies.
What caused the controversy?
The incident occurred at an Indian National Congress (INC) party event in the eastern state of Bihar, where party president Mallikarjun Kharge was speaking about the controversial national voter roll revision.
The party has recently intensified its year-long campaign against PM Modi over claims of using the revision process to "steal votes." A recent news report over mass deletions of voter names and irregularities by India's election body have also led to major protests led by opposition parties, political pressure groups and student organizations.
At the INC event, Kharge claimed that all officials responsible for the voter roll irregularities, including Modi, would be sent to jail.
In response, an audience member reportedly shouted out: “As long as there is no rebellion, Modi won’t go anywhere,” news agency Press Trust of India reported. Kharge responded, saying "Modi ka baap bhi jayega."
That translates to "even Modi's father will go (to jail)."
While the terminology is a commonly used phrase in India, BJP leaders argued that it was deeply offensive to invoke the prime minister's late father over politics.
BJP accuses INC of 'cheap politics'
"Mallikarjun Kharge appears to have lost all sense of decorum. “Modi ka baap bhi jayega” — is this the language expected from the national president of a party that claims to uphold democratic values?," a BJP spokesperson wrote on social media.
"Oppose politically, but don't turn the respect for late parents into a weapon of your cheap politics. The country is watching everything. 140 crore Indians will never forgive those who insult their elders!" BJP's social media handle said. Crore is equivalent to 10 million in the Indian numbering system.
Meanwhile, INC leaders defended Kharge, saying BJP too had often made personal remarks targeting their party members at rallies.
