What will a pedestrianised Oxford Street mean for transport?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

Much of Britain’s most famous shopping street will be closed to traffic from Monday as the long-awaited pedestrianisation of London’s Oxford Street begins.
About half of the 1.2 mile street will initially be vehicle-free, after decades of planning and dispute over how to best use the street, an important transport thoroughfare and the home for flagship stores for big shopping chains.
Private cars have been barred for years but now all motorised traffic, including buses and black cabs, as well as bicycles, will be kept away.
For the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has targeted the switch as part of clean air plans throughout his tenure, it is a political victory, aided by the backing of central government to override local council objections.
While towns and cities around the UK have long pedestrianised their centres, the location, scale and notoriety of Oxford Street, attracting millions of foreign visitors each year, will make the £150m scheme’s outcome of interest to city planners around the world.
London has studied the pedestrianisation of central Sydney, and discussed the scheme with Barcelona, whose La Rambla is similarly viewed as shabbier than its renown deserves.
The big retailers, Transport for London and those who just want a pleasanter, green city centre will be hoping the changes live up to their promise. Here we unpack what is changing:
Where will be pedestrianised?
From 7am on 26 October, a stretch of nearly 0.6 miles (almost 1km) of Oxford Street, containing the most famous department stores including John Lewis and Selfridges, will be vehicle-free.
The junction with Orchard Street, near Marble Arch, to Great Portland Street, east of Oxford Circus Ikea, will be closed to all traffic between 7am and midnight on every day of the week.
Businesses will be able to make deliveries outside those hours via certain access routes, but vehicles will not be able to travel the length of Oxford Street.
What does this mean for transport?
Private vehicles, such as cars, are already forbidden to drive on the street between 7am and 7pm and this ban will now extended to 24 hours a day seven days a week and cover buses, black cabs and bikes too.
Vehicles will still be able to cross the pedestrianised stretch of street at several points including the major junction of Regent Street and Oxford Circus, and others including New Bond Street.
Bus routes including the numbers 7, 98 and 390 will now run along Wigmore Street, which runs parallel to Oxford Street.
There will be taxi ranks within 100m of the traffic-free area on Oxford Street and surrounding roads.
In contrast to some other traffic-free areas of London, cycles, e-bikes and e-scooters will not be allowed on the pedestrianised strip at any time.
What about disabled people and essential services?
Mobility scooters will still be allowed. Access for disabled people may prove easier than many other parts of London, with Bond Street and Tottenham Court Road stations, on the Underground and Elizabeth line, both step-free.
Emergency services will be able to access the entire area whenever required via the cross streets. Cargo e-bikes will be introduced to collect litter and enable street cleaning during pedestrianised hours.
What other plans are there for the street?
Khan has talked about making Oxford Street a public plaza with outdoor dining, and improved street furniture and lighting is coming.
Early next year, more trees and seating are due to be installed, while the road surface will be raised level with the pavements in places to create public squares and event spaces.
Will the rest of Oxford Street follow?
The pedestrianisation of this stretch of the landmark shopping street has repeatedly been described as the “first phase”, although plans for the rest of the thoroughfare are likely to depend on the success – or otherwise – of the scheme.

====================================================================================================

Stung with a parking fine for an 18-second airport stop to tackle a wasp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

I had to stop my car for 18 seconds in a red zone at Leeds Bradford airport to deal with a wasp. It was buzzing in front of my face and making safe-driving impossible.
The result was a £100 parking charge notice (PCN) sent to my wife (the registered keeper) by Vehicle Control Services (VCS).
I’ve explained the circumstances to VCS, whose CCTV footage shows I only stopped for seconds and never left the car, but it won’t listen. 
 
AW, Hebden Bridge
Its hearing improved when I contacted the airport, which ordered VCS to refund the charge as “goodwill”. The airport tells me that if you had contacted it directly, it would have intervened. However, it is evidently worried that its actions in this case will open the floodgates to wasp-ridden drivers.
“Stopping in this area remains enforceable,” it says sternly. “And due to the safety-critical nature of the road, we would not be able to consider cancellation of any future penalty notices for stopping in this area.” VCS did not respond to a request for a comment.
Parking operators are infamously ruthless when enforcing airport no-stopping zones. Drivers have been charged for stopping at temporary lights, or waiting in traffic queues.
By remarkable coincidence, SM of Pontyclun in Wales also stopped for 18 seconds in an airport red zone. She was billed £100 by VCS, via her husband, who is the vehicle’s registered keeper.
In her case, the airport was Bristol, and she stopped to read the terms and conditions on a sign planted in the no-stopping area.
“I had prepaid £103.60 for three days in the short-stay car park,” she writes. “At the entrance was a prominent sign stating that payment was on exit, and including several lines of information. Confused, I wanted to make sure I was at the right place.”
Her appeal was rejected by VCS, which argued that it is “the motorist’s responsibility to ensure they are familiar with the terms and conditions displayed on the signage” – which is ironic given that SM was doing just that.
It was also rejected by the Independent Appeals Service, which concluded that red-route restrictions prohibit stopping under any circumstances.
“Is it reasonable to expect a motorist to read a substantial amount of car park information while their vehicle is moving, particularly when that information is relevant to determining whether they are entering the correct car park?” asks SM.
There are 24 lines of information, in varying sizes of font, on the sign SM was studying.
Drivers enter a contract when using a car park and are assumed to have agreed the terms and conditions, or else risk a PCN. It was therefore imperative SM read the notice, and not unreasonable she stopped to do so safely.
Bristol airport says: “The customer did not contact us to make us aware of the situation and that she had pre-booked parking. After the circumstances were reviewed, the penalty charge was refunded by the enforcement company.” VCS was contacted for a comment.
In fact, neither AW nor SM were obliged to pay the charge because of a loophole in the law. Airports are “statutory land” governed by bylaws, and are not subject to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012, which governs private parking enforcement in England and Wales.
The act allows private parking operators to pursue the registered keeper of a vehicle for charges. There is no such keeper liability on statutory land, so if the keeper declines to confirm who was driving, the parking operator is powerless. Operators don’t, of course, want you to know this.
The clue is in the small print of PCNs sent to the spouses of AW and SM which “invite” them to pay up or name the driver. Anyone else in this situation should reply stating that as an airport is statutory land, they are not liable as the vehicle keeper and not obliged to name the driver.
Motorists penalised for reasonable stops on land that does fall under the act may have a future get-out clause.
The government’s newly announced crackdown on private parking charges means that when the new official code of practice takes effect (we don’t have a date yet), charges will be cancelled on appeal for things such as stopping briefly because of a medical emergency (potential wasp stings, hopefully, included).

‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.
A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.
Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.
As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.
Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.
“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”
At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.
The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.
“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”
By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.
“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.
By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.
“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

The UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Over the past few years, you can plot the plunge into global instability not only through the unchecked assaults on international law and civilian life, but through the decline and undermining of the authority and credibility of international institutions. The latest level in this spiral is the proposed appointment of Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the UN secretary general. Her bid has been rapidly gaining momentum and endorsements. And it has been met with outrage among the Sudanese.
Nusseibeh is the minister of state at the UAE and a former UAE ambassador to the UN. For the past three years, the country has been connected to – bear with me, this will be a long sentence – supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia in Sudan, facilitating mercenaries to fight alongside the militia (which is accused of ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity and sexual violence), and appropriating international aid infrastructure to smuggle weapons into the country.
The war between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) is an ongoing calamity of historic proportions. It is grinding and brutal, and has already resulted in hunger, displacement and a humanitarian crisis. Although it has drawn in external actors, multiple investigations and reports point to the UAE as the country that has in essence fuelled the conflict by aggressively sponsoring one side from the start. The result has been intractable conflict, unfathomable losses and relentless momentum fed by external supply lines.
The UAE’s role in Sudan’s war has been the target of years of media investigations, human rights activism and political condemnation. There were calls from two US congressmen to American media and sports organisations to end all associations with the UAE in response to its “abetting genocide” by “arming one faction”. In the UK, a complaint was submitted to the government demanding an investigation into the Manchester City owner and deputy prime minister of the UAE, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, due to the “abundance of evidence” of UAE involvement. Attention has been called to the well-established violations associated with the vastly wealthy and hitherto immune power, which has used that wealth to try to secure a toehold in territories in Africa with geopolitical significance. Sudan’s Red Sea coastline, its bountiful gold reserves and strategic location within the continent seemingly drew the Gulf power’s predatory eye.
In the face of all efforts to highlight the gravity and high stakes of the situation, the UAE has behaved with arrogance, dissimulation and, according to reports, the use ofmisinformation and digital propaganda. Wherever such prevarications were made, there was Nusseibeh, affirming the denial of “baseless allegations”, undermining the work of the international media and, in one instance that should surely be disqualifying, disputing the findings of a UN panel of experts.
In one instance, Nusseibeh was confronted by an indignant Sudanese man in Chad who rejected her whitewashing visit to his refugee camp, imploring her delegation to keep their aid and insisting that if the UAE wants to help, it should stop interfering and stoking the war. Another enraged refugee refused aid, saying the UAE killed her brothers. Against this backdrop, the appointment of Nusseibeh, who has been the face of the UAE’s Sudan strategy, would be a slap in the face to the millions of people suffering the horrors of war, a dereliction of duty towards those thousands who have already been killed, and a green light to the prolonging of conflict.
It has been a lesson, or I should say another lesson, about the extent to which so many of the pleas from those who purport to care about Sudan are performative. How so much of the rhetoric about Sudan or even cursory interest in it is a sort of box-ticking, name-checking exercise. Something to be put on the record – here is the official statement of concern for civilians, here is the pundit with their once-and-that’s-enough treatment, here is the post on X. Going beyond that, making the necessary links that render the conflict not just a sad clash of armed groups but a war in which powerful external parties have been allowed to play abjectly immoral and accelerating roles, is a step too far.
It has also been a lesson in how much a certain kind of Arab politics and mien goes a long, long way to securing consent and licence. Nusseibeh is an operator, that’s for sure, but she is also a beneficiary of a branding exercise that the UAE has been working on for a long time to ingratiate itself with western establishments. One pillar of that strategy has been presenting itself as a “moderate” Muslim country that is alive to the dangers of radical Islam (up to and including being allegedly linked to the funding and support of hard-right groups in Europe). The other is in the cultivation of close financial ties with the UK and the US, particularly with the Trump family, conjoining itself with political and business elites.
And it has understood that between the allied, the gullible and the ignorant, Nusseibeh can easily be presented as the obvious choice for the position as a Muslim woman with liberal credentials and a western education, regardless of the dark politics she advances and represents. It is hard for some to see beyond the facts of her CV – Wycombe Abbey, Cambridge University and, on top of that, of Palestinian origin, serving a country that has normalised relations with Israel. A high identity-politics jackpot.
All which makes Nusseibeh and the country she represents far more relatable and knowable to the world than the vastly weaker, poorer and underrepresented Sudanese people who have been victimised. The UAE, to put it simply, is seen as one of the club, its offences the private business of a country that is too wealthy to antagonise and too solicitous to spurn. Its rise speaks to this moment. At a time of big regional wars, multipolarity, energy crises and fraying norms, who better to become a global anchor than a country that is offering value-free transactional politics, is backed with sovereign wealth, and is expert in the opulent backroom gangsterism of the new world order.
Appointing a representative widely seen as one of the authors of Sudan’s tragedy to such a prestigious and influential post, one that only entrenches the UAE’s position and secures it even more wriggle room vis-a-vis its actions in Sudan, is not just another small way in which the business of international affairs is changing. It is a new chapter, one in which a perpetrator and its tribunes are not just not held to account, but crowned. The contempt is exceptionally bewildering even in an era of outrages. Nusseibeh’s appointment can only be secured by stepping over the dead, and turning backs on the living.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Everyone had their reasons for joining the trip. Louisa from south London was putting her life back together after a split from her partner; first-timer Tim was strapping on ski boots following years of hesitation; and Lexi from Bristol had a classic case of the non-skiing boyfriend.
I was there because I needed a ski gang. None of my friends ski, and my brother was out of action with an injury. Not only that, I needed a good night’s sleep. I love my two-year-old son dearly, but I have somehow spawned an insomniac – still waking four times a night. Weary from bedtime battles, Holly, my partner, bluntly pointed out we could both benefit from “a temporary break from family life”. In other words: separate holidays.
Holly arranged a walking trip with friends; I opted for a week’s skiing in the French ski resort of Les Deux Alpes with Friendship Travel, a specialist operator in solo travel for more than 20 years. They find a chalet, fill it with solo skiers, provide travel, most meals and group ski lessons – that’s the basic service.
We were staying in a comfortable, largeish chalet just back from the resort’s mile-long drag. Entering a group holiday with strangers is a leap into the unknown. I was greeted by Sam and Mike, our (thankfully) low-key hosts, shown to my private room (you can save by bunking up with a same sex stranger), then introduced to my fellow holidaymakers. It turned out that there were 17 of us – nine women, eight men – and we were whisked into the lounge for a briefing and welcome drink. The atmosphere was upbeat and easy, and we gathered round one large table for an excellent three-course dinner.
Most Friendship Travel guests are aged between 35 and 65, and our group was at the top end of that range. There was Vivienne, a retired nurse from Cumbria who had just lost her partner, and Adriana, a “silver splitter” relishing retirement. For a few – myself included – it was the first such holiday, but many were inveterate solo travellers, with Ivyon, a former production operator from Bridgend, clocking up more than 90 trips.
The first morning, we set off to our ski lockers at the bottom of the slopes (tip: I booked my equipment hire in advance, saving €40). The group naturally fragmented, allowing small cliques to form – people relaxed as they started to identify potential après buddies.
I skied with Elaine, Clemmie, James and our guide, Luke, in the “level 4 advanced” group (we were asked to rate our ability beforehand). The backbone of Les Deux Alpes, the new Jandri 3S cable car, whisked us up to an altitude of 3,200 metres in 17 minutes – instead of the previous 40. Above broken clouds, we paused to admire the astonishing jagged peaks of the Écrins national park.
We blasted down a mixture of broad blue and red runs, plus some not overly challenging blacks. Although none of us had met before, we quickly settled into a rhythm, looking out for one another as the snow fell softly. There’s safety in numbers, especially on the off-piste sections. “I’d never have tried that alone,” said Clemmie.
Afternoons brought more skiing, followed by hands-in-the-air après at Skandal – reopened in 2025 following an extension – with a DJ on a packed terrace. Around sundown, the chalet WhatsApp group would start to ping. “Polar Bear Pub, anyone?” would be a typical message, often sent by Mícheál from Armagh, a dependable partner for a pint.
Solo travel has undergone a perception shift in recent decades, according to Colum McLornan, who founded Friendship Travel in 1999. “Travelling alone was often seen as unconventional, and for many it carried a stigma. But travellers are increasingly seeking independence, flexibility and personal growth. What was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industry,” he said.
At times, group etiquette could be a minefield: nobody likes waiting for latecomers (me); is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast? (probably); is it OK to peel away from the group and ski by oneself? (up to a point); will I look like a skinflint if I buy my own wine? (absolutely, but life’s too short for plonk).
Honourable mention to Steve, a jolly retired doctor from north London. I enjoyed his vivid stories of cruising the Yangtze River, and skiing with his father in Austria during the late 1950s. Despite our age gap, we struck up a bond that lasted all week. Naturally, not all guests are interesting and fun. One seemingly endless dinner conversation about printer cartridges had me dreaming of Netflix in my room.
Then, suddenly, I found myself hugging my ski gang goodbye, bound for the train. Would I go solo again? Yes. Our hosts were helpful without being intrusive, the skiing superb (especially the high-altitude stuff on Glacier de Mont-de-Lans) and I met people I will stay in touch with. Best of all, I finally got some sleep.
The trip was provided by Friendship Travel. A seven-night package with a private room in a shared chalet, daily breakfast and afternoon tea, dinner with wine on five evenings, and six days of group ski lessons in Les Deux Alpes, costs from £1,820pp. Return rail travel from London to Grenoble was provided by Eurostar

Young people's household income in Europe: How does France compare?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:06 UTC
16:00:06 KST

Households with young people aged 18 to 24 generally have lower equivalised disposable income, but experts note that this may not show the full picture.
Protests have spread across several European countries over rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and pressure on public services in recent weeks. In France, students and young people have been at the forefront of the protests.
That has turned attention to Europe’s Gen Z.
Alberto Alemanno, EU law expert, believes framing protest as “teenage revolution” deeply misleading, and he emphasises that youth protests around Europe are multifaceted.
So, how does the household income of young people compare across Europe? What is the financial situation of their households? And how does France compare with other European countries?
While it does not show all the picture, the equivalised disposable income is one useful indicator. It is “the total income of a household, after tax and other deductions, that is available for spending or saving, divided by the number of household members converted into equalised adults,” according to Eurostat. This also includes social benefits.
Eurostat data are available for young people aged 18 to 24. The figures show the income of the households they live in, rather than what young people themselves earn.
Young people in France live in households with a median equivalised income of €23,850 in 2025, according to Eurostat. The EU average is €21,482.
Among 34 European countries, including EU members, EU candidate countries and EFTA members, France ranks 11th.
“In France, the indicator does not capture students living on their own or in collective housing such as university halls of residence (excluded from the sample),” Anne Brunner, director of studies at Observatoire des inégalités, told Euronews Business.
She also pointed out that the 18–24 age group is heterogeneous: it includes both students living with their parents and young workers, many of whom have few or no qualifications and are in precarious employment and at risk of poverty.
Switzerland has the highest median equivalised household income for young people at €52,206. Luxembourg (€43,028) and Austria (€37,299) follow it.
Among the EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies, Germany has the highest income at €26,330. Italy (€20,315) and Spain (€19,338) are below the EU average.
North Macedonia (€4,640), followed by Albania (€5,736) and Turkey (€5,987), has the lowest median equivalised income for people aged 18 to 24.
This figure is also less than half the EU average in Bulgaria (€8,680), Hungary (€8,576), Serbia (€7,754) and Romania (€7,237).
Data vs reality
The European Youth Forum secretariat noted that income is only part of the equation. In some countries, young people may look better off on paper because they stay in the parental home for longer. But behind those figures is a generation that cannot afford to move out, rent or buy a home, and build a life on their own.
“The paradox is that young people can look better off when they depend on their families for longer, and poorer when they go out on their own,” the secretariat told Euronews Business.
Young people fall behind in most countries
Comparing young people with the whole population in their own country shows whether they are falling behind. Combination of several factors has a role in this.
“Overall, less work experience and a lower level of education (often young people are still studying) than older adults. Additionally, being a student is often associated with a lower level of income. Also, housing arrangements can matter [as the Nordic countries],” Ilari Ilmakunnas, senior researcher at the Finnish Centre for Pensions (ETK), told Euronews Business.
In 28 of the 34 countries, young people live in households with a lower median income than the overall population.
Across the EU, young people have 93.6% of the median income of the whole population: €21,482 compared with €22,939.
In France, the figure is 90.1%. Young people live in households with a median income €2,609 lower than the national median: €23,850 compared with €26,459.
Where is the gap widest?
Finland has the widest gap. Young people there live in households with a median income of €22,277, compared with €29,740 for the whole population. That is 74.9% of the national median.
Denmark (78.3%), Norway (82.7%), Luxembourg (86.0%) and Sweden (88.2%) follow Finland.
Anne Brunner noted that public policy in the Nordic countries actively promotes the autonomy of young people, who consequently leave the parental home earlier and are far more likely to live independently.
“Their household income is then measured on their own, often modest, resources rather than pooled with that of their parents, which mechanically widens the gap with the overall population. A low ratio in these countries should therefore not be read as a sign of greater hardship,” she said.
In six countries, young people live in households with higher income than the whole population. In Croatia, young people’s households have a median of €15,921, compared with €15,057 for the whole population
Croatia leads at 105.7%, followed by Malta (105.5%) and Slovenia (105.4%). Lithuania and Austria are both at 102.1%. Switzerland is at 100.5%.
Austria leads in purchasing power
Price levels differ across Europe. Measured in purchasing power standards (PPS), the median equivalised household income of young people aged 18 to 24 is highest in Austria at 33,052 PPS. Luxembourg (32,391) and Switzerland (29,989) follow.
In PPS terms, France (21,446) ranks 13th, slightly above the EU average.
Germany (24,237) ranks higher, while Spain (21,272) and Italy (20,883) are below France, although the gaps are relatively small.
Albania (8,175), North Macedonia (8,994) and Montenegro (9,955) have the lowest figures.
Call for looking beyond income
The European Youth Forum calls for looking beyond just income and considering the idea of the social wage: the affordable housing, public services, education, healthcare and social protection that determine how far our incomes actually go.
“A decent life should not depend on a good salary alone, or on having family wealth to fall back on. It requires decent wages alongside strong public services that make the essentials affordable,” the secretariat said.

Kweichow Moutai Becomes Premier Partner of the Hong Kong Open 2026, Deepening Its Global Presence
In golf, you must hit one good shot after another while waiting for a rare hole-in-one. Moutai demands a parallel patience: perfecting every step of its craft and letting time do its work. From October 22 to 25, 2026, Moutai served as a Premier Partner of the Link Hong Kong Open, staged at Hong Kong Golf Club at Fanling, where it witnessed outstanding international players in action. One depends on probability, the other on time, yet both point to the same philosophy: bring every part of the process to its highest standard, and then wait for the result to come.

In golf, you must hitFrom the Chishui River to the Golf Course
Reframing Moutai’s Brand Narrative
For Moutai, waiting is not a metaphor, but part of the craft itself. Its production takes one year and eight months, followed by three years of storage, then blending and stabilization; from the start of production to release takes at least five years. Through years of maturation, its initial sharpness gradually gives way to greater mellowness, richness and complexity. The idea that Moutai “grows more fragrant with age” is more than a simple description; it is the physical trace that time leaves within the spirit.
When Moutai ventures overseas, it brings with it more than a product. It carries a philosophy of time and a set of values steeped in Eastern thought. These values happen to resonate with the spirit of golf: discipline, etiquette, patience and the pursuit of excellence.

It naturally brings together high-net-worth audiences who value quality living and social affinity. Through its partnership with the Asian Tour, Moutai is reaching this audience. During the Hong Kong Open, golf clinics and spectator engagement activities turned the brand from something simply seen into something that could be experienced and participated in. The sophistication of Moutai’s association with golf lies in the new associations the brand gains between each swing: “healthy social interaction” and “elegant living.”
From the Hong Kong Fairways to a Way of Life
A Shared Journey in Step with Time
There is a quiet composure within Hong Kong’s sporting culture that resonates deeply with golf. This time, as Moutai and the Asian Tour join hands again in Hong Kong, Moutai is moving from a “participant” in the tournament experience to a “companion” to the city’s sporting culture.

Anchoring Moutai’s Place on the Global Stage

From the banks of the Chishui River to the fairways of Fanling, from taking products global to taking culture global, Moutai is quietly deepening its international presence - one swing and one raised glass at a time.

Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda dies at 90: media

TOKYO, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda died of heart failure at a hospital in Tokyo on Oct. 22 at the age of 90, local media reported Monday.
Born on July 16, 1936, in Takasaki, Gunma Prefecture, Fukuda was the eldest son of former Prime Minister Takeo Fukuda and graduated from Waseda University.

After retiring from politics in 2012, Fukuda remained a committed advocate of China-Japan friendship and visited China many times. ■

Antonelli dominates U.S. Grand Prix but must wait to clinch F1 title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:52:00 CST
15:52:00 KST

Race winner Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli of Italy celebrates on the podium after the Formula One United States Grand Prix, in Austin, Texas, the United States, Oct. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Xiaoling)
by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli took another major step toward becoming Formula 1's youngest world champion with a commanding victory at the United States Grand Prix on Sunday, although the Italian must wait at least another week to secure the title.
Starting from pole position, Antonelli controlled the 56-lap race at the Circuit of the Americas, making a one-stop strategy work to claim his ninth victory of the season, finishing 13 seconds ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.
Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the podium in third, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and McLaren's Lando Norris.
The result extended Antonelli's championship lead over Mercedes teammate George Russell to 123 points with five races remaining. However, Russell's eighth-place finish and Hamilton's fourth place prevented the 20-year-old from securing the title in Austin.
Antonelli, who is in only his second F1 season, could now clinch the championship at next weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, potentially surpassing Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 when he became the sport's youngest world champion in 2010.
The Italian made a clean getaway from pole, while Leclerc and Verstappen battled behind him on the opening lap. Leclerc initially moved ahead of the Dutchman, only for Verstappen to reclaim second place before the end of the lap.
Their battle allowed Antonelli to establish an advantage of more than two seconds almost immediately, and the Mercedes driver steadily extended his lead as the opening stint progressed.
While most of his rivals opted for two pit stops, Antonelli made his medium tyres last before switching to the hard compound, allowing him to maintain track position and control the race without needing a second stop.
The strategy proved decisive as Ferrari and Red Bull were unable to mount a sustained challenge, with Antonelli managing his tyres effectively through the closing stages.
Behind him, Leclerc and Verstappen fought over second place, with the Ferrari driver eventually emerging ahead to claim his second consecutive runner-up finish.
Verstappen struggled with his Red Bull's performance during the race but held on to third, while Hamilton finished fourth to help Ferrari secure a strong points haul.
Russell endured a difficult afternoon in the other Mercedes, finishing eighth after struggling for pace and receiving a five-second penalty. His result effectively ended any realistic prospect of challenging Antonelli for the championship, although he remains mathematically in contention.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri finished seventh, behind Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, while Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson and Alpine's Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.
The race saw three retirements, with Haas driver Oliver Bearman, Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas all failing to finish.
Antonelli's victory also provided encouragement for Mercedes following an uncertain introduction to its latest upgrade package, which had initially struggled to deliver the expected performance gains at the previous two rounds in Malaysia and Singapore.
With 125 points still available over the final five races, Antonelli now needs only to avoid a substantial loss of ground to his closest rivals in Mexico to secure a historic first world championship. ■

Lula wins Brazil's presidential runoff; Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede defeat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:51:51 CST
15:51:51 KST

Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (C), candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, delivers a speech following his victory in the presidential runoff in Sao Paulo, Brazil, Oct. 25, 2026. Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court on Sunday night. (Photo by Paulo Lopes/Xinhua)
BRASILIA, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court on Sunday night.
With 99.99 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.79 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.21 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally.
Lula will be sworn in on Jan. 5, 2027, for a four-year term, his fourth as Brazil's president.
Speaking in a live speech in Sao Paulo following his victory, Lula vowed to work with the conservative Congress elected by the people and ensure greater public participation in the decision-making process.
He also stressed the need to strengthen digital regulation after defeating foreign interference through digital platforms, stressing that Brazil is no one's backyard.
Lula also pledged to strengthen public healthcare, improve care for the elderly, respect women and continue efforts to combat climate change.
"This election taught me many lessons. I want to say that we will change the way this country is governed. We will have the people participate more in our decisions," he said.
Meanwhile, Flavio Bolsonaro, speaking in the Brazilian capital of Brasilia, said it is "impossible" to recognize the results, and called for the annulment of the election, alleging unequal treatment of voters following an extension of voting hours.
Earlier on Sunday, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered polling stations nationwide to extend voting by two hours in response to disruptions caused by public transport stoppages and heavy rain. The measure applied only to polling stations that remained open when the decision was communicated by the Superior Electoral Court; stations that had already closed were not reopened.
Bolsonaro argued that the decision had disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and that his legal team would challenge the results.
Under Brazil's electoral rules, if no presidential candidate wins outright in the first round by securing more than half of the valid votes, the top two candidates advance to a runoff.
In the first round, held on Oct. 4, Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent.
Presidents from several Latin American countries congratulated Lula on his victory. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum hailed the result as a victory for the Brazilian people and democracy, while Uruguayan President Yamandu Orsi praised Brazil's electoral process as a celebration of democracy.
Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel called for stronger regional integration. Paraguayan President Santiago Pena emphasized cooperation with Brazil to promote regional integration and development, while Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz highlighted the countries' shared history and pledged to strengthen bilateral ties. Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino also congratulated Lula and expressed his commitment to continued cooperation. ■

Climate change threatens ecological balance of South Australia's coastal lagoon: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:51:50 CST
15:51:50 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Climate change could reshape phytoplankton communities and increase the risk of harmful algal blooms in the Coorong, a shallow coastal lagoon in the state of South Australia, a new study finds.
Led by Flinders University researchers and funded by the Goyder Institute for Water Research in Australia, the study examined phytoplankton across the Coorong, combining field samples from freshwater to salty habitats with 16 years of historical data, according to a university statement released on Sunday.
The researchers found that changes to salinity and water levels through variations in freshwater inputs to the Coorong had the most influence on phytoplankton abundance, diversity and community structure.
Freshwater and mildly salty habitats supported the greatest number of species, while extremely salty habitats had fewer species and were dominated by diatoms and dinoflagellates, two major groups of single-celled phytoplankton, the study published in Continental Shelf Research found.
The researchers also found that while the levels of harmful bloom-forming species in the Coorong are low overall, there are more than 80 phytoplankton species capable of producing toxins. ■

AI model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available US state of Georgia aggregate voter counts without human authorization, Anthropic said in a statement on Sunday.

The attack, which was described by the AI Security Institute (AISI) as a "supply chain attack," attempted to disrupt a public code repository on the GitHub platform by creating fake inquiries, introducing corrupted data, and even demanding changes by creating false accounts on the platform.

Will 70,000 Israelis returning from abroad for Election Day tip the political balance? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:23 UTC
15:47:23 KST

An estimated 70,000 Israelis living abroad have returned or are expected to return to Israel ahead of Tuesday's Knesset elections, potentially influencing the results if the race between the political blocs is close.
This begs the question: Could the Israelis arriving from abroad influence the election results?
In the 2022 elections, approximately 36,000 votes were needed to secure one Knesset seat. Given population growth and an expected increase in voter turnout, estimates suggest that the threshold for a seat could rise to approximately 38,000 to 39,000 votes.
It is difficult to determine which parties most of the Israelis arriving from abroad will support. Some estimates suggest that many will vote for the change bloc, but there is no reliable measure of their political preferences.
Even if, for example, 60% support the change bloc, this would add at most one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
These figures, however, remain estimates. The election results will reveal whether Israelis living abroad have tipped the balance in the event of a close race between the political blocs.
Election Day boosts hotel occupancy by 23%
The vast majority of Israelis arriving from overseas are combining family visits and vacations with Election Day. Most are staying with relatives or friends, or in apartments they own in Israel that are currently vacant.
However, some have chosen to stay in hotels.
Africa Israel Hotels reported an approximately 23% increase in hotel occupancy during election week. Although the comparison is with October of last year, when the security situation was more complicated, the increase appears significant.
"We are seeing an increase in occupancy at Africa Israel Hotels properties across the country ahead of Election Day. We are seeing more Israelis choosing to combine exercising their democratic right with a short vacation, taking advantage of the opportunity to break from their routine and enjoy a hotel stay," said Alex Eliyahu, marketing director of Africa Israel Hotels.
"Alongside the increase in demand, the chain is offering particularly attractive promotions and accommodation packages for Election Day, allowing guests to enjoy vacations at a variety of destinations across the country at affordable prices."
Fattal Hotels also reported an increase in room occupancy at its properties, particularly in central Israel.
"We are seeing an increase in bookings compared with October of last year, apparently due to the elections," said Maya Shalev, vice president of marketing and sales at Fattal Hotels.
"Many Israelis are taking advantage of the day off to combine voting with a vacation. Accordingly, we have offered promotions of up to 30% off, along with an additional 10% discount for members of the 'Fattal and Friends' club between October 25 and 29. At the same time, we are seeing bookings made from abroad for these dates, which may indicate that Israelis are coming to Israel to vote."
'I came from Miami to vote': Israelis returning to the ballot box
Among the tens of thousands who attended the October Council rally at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday night were Israelis living abroad.
"I came from Miami to vote. I coordinated my vacation in Israel with Election Day, and I'm returning to the US at the beginning of November," said Judy, who has lived in the US for more than 50 years.
"Many Israelis living in Miami and Los Angeles tend to vote for the Right. I'm different, and I'm not alone."
Nurit, from the South Sharon area, attended the rally with her son-in-law and grandson, who had arrived from Canada.
"My grandson is voting for the first time. He's 18 years old. They're combining a family visit with voting in the elections. My daughter stayed in Canada to be with my younger grandson."
Ofer, who arrived from New York, also shared his experience.
"We came to Israel specifically to vote. We're returning to the US the day after the elections. We have family here, and it's an opportunity to see everyone."
Gidi, who arrived from Australia with his wife, is scheduled to fly out of Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday.
"We've already been here for three weeks. We've met with many family members and friends. And I'm going back on Wednesday because I have work commitments. My wife will stay here for another two weeks."
In contrast, Zehava, who arrived on a flight from New York, said: "I'm voting for Likud, and I came to visit family ahead of the elections. I planned it in advance."
Canceled flights leave some Israelis unable to vote
Some Israelis had hoped to travel to Israel but were left stranded abroad after flydubai canceled flights following an attempted terrorist attack.
"Flydubai's cancellation caused flight prices to the Far East to rise," explained a young man who had planned to travel to Israel ahead of the elections.
There are also Israelis who live in Israel but will be abroad on Election Day. However, their number appears to be lower than the number of Israelis arriving from overseas.
"I booked the flight tickets for a vacation with my husband in Vietnam almost a year ago, and we didn't know the elections would be held in October. This will be the first time I don't vote. It breaks my heart, but we're going ahead with the vacation we started planning a year ago," said Racheli from Ramat Gan.
"It's a shame that Israelis traveling abroad can't vote on Election Day."

Voices within US President Donald Trump's inner circle are advocating for the establishment of a broad and moderate Israeli unity government without National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, with some even floating the idea of a rotation agreement in which Benjamin Netanyahu would serve as prime minister first.
However, Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot and former prime minister Naftali Bennett remain opposed to serving under him, and American officials have yet to discuss the framework with them.
American billionaire Bill Ackman, a prominent supporter of Trump with close ties to his circle, publicly called on Sunday for the formation of a broad, moderate Israeli government that excludes Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In a social media post, Ackman argued that such a government would allow Israel to restore its international standing, expand the Abraham Accords, and improve relations with both major political parties in the United States.
Ackman, who heads the hedge fund Pershing Square, supported Trump in the presidential election and is considered an influential figure in US political and business circles. He criticized Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, stating that their presence harms Israel's global image and its ability to advance key diplomatic objectives. At the same time, he praised Netanyahu and his relationship with Trump. Ackman favors Netanyahu remaining in office, but with a different set of coalition partners.
Realizing Trump's Middle East ambitions requires a change in Israel's Knesset
Ackman is not the only figure in Trump's orbit holding this view. According to several sources, additional figures in Washington believe that over the remaining two years of the president's term, realizing his ambitious Middle East plans requires a change in the composition of Israel's government.
Foremost among these plans is the possibility of a historic normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia, a prospect difficult to envision advancing while Ben-Gvir and Smotrich sit at the cabinet table.
Several senior advisors to Trump believe an Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right partners would make it significantly easier to advance the president's regional policy.
This comes amid existing friction between Washington and Jerusalem: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are reportedly frustrated by the pace at which Netanyahu is advancing Trump's plan for Gaza; Special Envoy Tom Barrick disagrees with Israel's strategy regarding Syria; and officials around Secretary of State Marco Rubio seek to strengthen the Lebanese government while expressing frustration over insufficient action regarding Jewish violence in Judea and Samaria.
These officials place high importance on the composition of Israel's next government, which could impact Trump's chances of achieving major diplomatic breakthroughs before his term ends. A deal with Saudi Arabia, for instance, requires difficult Israeli decisions on the Palestinian issue and other regional matters.
A government reliant on Ben-Gvir and Smotrich could struggle to make such choices, even if Netanyahu himself were willing to do so. However, replacing coalition partners alone does not guarantee a deal: Riyadh maintains its own political demands, including tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
Trump's inner circles question viability of diplomacy with Netanyahu around
Some within Trump's circle even question whether a diplomatic breakthrough is achievable as long as Netanyahu serves as prime minister. Consequently, an idea has emerged within the president's team for a rotation-based unity government: Netanyahu would serve during the first year, after which another prime minister would replace him to lead negotiations with the Saudis before the conclusion of Trump's term.
Proponents of the idea believe this arrangement would maintain governance continuity in the first year while entrusting regional diplomatic efforts to a prime minister who is not dependent on Netanyahu's current partners. According to several Israeli and American sources, Netanyahu told Trump he wants to form a unity government and will work toward that goal after the election.
Israel's Ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, also publicly said Netanyahu wants a broad government. Leiter said Netanyahu prefers a national unity government over continuing with the current coalition makeup.
He also addressed Ben-Gvir's future, saying Netanyahu made it clear he would not serve as national security minister again. The comments drew a sharp reaction from Otzma Yehudit, whose officials fear Netanyahu is paving the way for a coalition with Eisenkot at the expense of his current partners. For his part, Ben-Gvir called on Netanyahu to form a right-wing government rather than one with Eisenkot.
Although the idea originated in his inner circle, Trump has not formally endorsed the initiative. The president publicly backed Netanyahu on October 18, even as several advisors expressed reservations. Vice President JD Vance did not join the public endorsement.
Furthermore, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee explicitly denied allegations of an American effort to push a unity government, clarifying that the administration does not intervene in Israeli elections or dictate actions to the prime minister.
Meanwhile, the proposals discussed in Washington remain far removed from Israel's political reality. American officials have not conducted a deep feasibility check with leaders of the change bloc, and no substantive talks have taken place with Eisenkot or other senior figures in the opposition regarding the proposed framework. Electoral scenarios also present obstacles for the initiative.
If Netanyahu's bloc secures 61 mandates, he is expected to receive the mandate to form a government, but it remains doubtful whether Eisenkot or Bennett would agree to join. Additionally, ultra-Orthodox parties demand the passage of the conscription bill as a precondition for coalition talks. Conversely, if the right-wing bloc fails to secure a majority, Netanyahu may not get the first chance to form a government.
Even in the event of a victory for the right-wing bloc, Netanyahu could find himself in a trap: his natural partners will demand the fulfillment of previous commitments, primarily the ultra-Orthodox demands regarding military draft legislation.
Reaching out to Eisenkot and Bennett would require offering them a partnership in a government they have pledged not to join. Even within the right-wing bloc, few believe Eisenkot or Bennett would consent to such a move.

Investors see economic upside for Israel if opposition beats Netanyahu in upcoming elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:14 UTC
15:47:14 KST

Israel's markets have soared despite three years of war and political turmoil, but some investors see further upside if the opposition defeats Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s election, potentially easing regional tensions and political risk.
Opinion polls point to a tight contest, with neither Netanyahu's ruling Likud bloc nor an opposition alliance centered on former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected to secure the 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset needed to govern.
That raises the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations or even another election, all at time when one of the key drivers of the Israeli market rally - the global frenzy around AI - has also started to splutter.
Since the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, the Tel Aviv stock market has soared 130%, far outpacing Wall Street's 80% gain, while the shekel has climbed 25%, one of the world's strongest currency performances.
Analysts attribute some of that strength to Israel's tech sector and the global AI boom, while defense spending, which has nearly doubled to around 8% of GDP, has also provided a boost.
With both Netanyahu and Eisenkot vowing to maintain pressure on Hamas and Iran, markets are focused on their broader policy differences. JPMorgan estimates the shekel could swing as much as 3% depending on the result.
Opposition victory could improve Israeli economic position
An opposition victory that improves relations with Western allies and halts a judicial overhaul that sparked mass protests in 2023 could strengthen the currency, JPMorgan said, while another Netanyahu-led government could weaken it.
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, while stopping short of backing a candidate, said a government without far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would signal that Israel was "turning a new page," potentially helping rebuild its international credibility and expand the Abraham Accords with its neighbors.
IBI Investment House also expects an opposition victory to lift the markets. "From a capital markets perspective, this would likely be reflected in a decline in Israel's risk premium, appreciation pressure on the shekel, and a positive reaction in the local market," IBI's Chief Economist Rafi Gozlan said.
According to prediction market Polymarket, close to 60% are betting on Eisenkot becoming the next Israeli prime minister, compared with 27% for Netanyahu.
"The most significant issue is what the result will mean for the region," said Equity Bank's chief economic adviser Charlie Robertson. "If Netanyahu is reelected, it might increase the chances of further escalation with Iran, whereas a defeat might be seen as lessening the tensions."
But the prospect of gains under an opposition government does not mean investors expect Israeli assets to suffer if Netanyahu remains in power. Stocks and bonds have proved remarkably resilient through years of war and political upheaval, and some investors remain confident in the economy regardless of the election outcome.
Union Investment's Sergey Dergachev has been buying Israeli bonds ahead of the election, betting the economy and companies he favors will remain fundamentally strong. "We are very constructive on Israeli credits going into the election," Dergachev said, adding that bonds were less prone to major swings and the region's intertwined conflicts should eventually ease.
Tel Aviv shares were up around 1% in the final session ahead of Tuesday's vote, taking their year-to-date gain to about 12%.
However, both they and the shekel have pulled back some 10% since May. Analysts again point to the strong link to tech, given global AI indexes have also been dropping, although there has been one nagging issue throughout the last three years.
Despite the rally, foreign investors remain cautious. Copley Fund Research data show the share of global funds holding Israeli equities is at a record low, having fallen sharply since 2023.
TS Lombard's Christopher Granville cited central bank estimates that the war had cost the economy more than $55 billion by last year, equivalent to 8.6% in cumulative lost GDP growth.
Public debt, budget deficit high amid Iran war
Israel's fiscal position is another focus. Public debt has risen to nearly 70% of GDP, about 10 percentage points higher than in 2022, while the budget deficit is expected to remain around 4.5% of GDP, up from less than 2% before the conflict.
Central bank head Amir Yaron stressed last week the need to "preserve adequate fiscal policy space" given the Iran war.
Like stocks, Israeli government bonds have rallied, returning about 30% over the last two years, more than double the main emerging market indexes.
The main risk for investors is an inconclusive result that prolongs political uncertainty, delaying budgets, reforms and investment, some investors believe.
That uncertainty can produce sharp short-term swings. Tel Aviv Stock Exchange research covering the last 10 elections found volatility in leading share indexes rose by as much as 45% in the weeks after voting compared with a typical week. But initial losses were typically recovered within a month, with the indexes posting an average gain of about 1.7%.
Over a longer horizon, the TA-125 returned an average 16.4% in the year following elections, compared with a long-term annual average of 11.5%, the research found. Political deadlock often weighed on stocks before voting, but the effects typically faded within months, said Nissan Avraham, an analyst at the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's research unit.
Israeli businesses continue thriving despite political, regional upheaval
That record supports the view that elections matter less for Israeli companies than many investors assume.
Lior Yochpaz, chief investment officer at insurance company Menora Mivtachim, said businesses have continued to thrive despite years of political upheaval, judicial overhaul proposals, and regional conflict, helped by a relatively business-friendly environment.
For some investors, however, the more attractive election trade lies outside Israel. TT International's Jean-Charles Sambor said an opposition victory or weakened Netanyahu government could ease regional tensions and benefit Lebanese bonds.
"The best way to play it for us is through other Middle East countries, and for us Lebanon is a good proxy," Sambor said.

Appeals court skeptical over Trump administration lawsuit against California mail-in ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:46:46 UTC
15:46:46 KST

A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on Sunday of a lawsuit filed by US President Donald Trump's administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead of midterm elections.
During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals sharply questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms.
The Department of Justice's lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump's administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.
Trump's Justice Department has warned election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.
Data shows ineligible voting in US exceedingly rare
California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department's assertions relied on suspect data.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit in federal court in Los Angeles on October 15. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots and not count them until it verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
Bennett, a Trump-appointed judge, said during Sunday's oral argument that the lawsuit could not be reconciled with a provision of the US Constitution known as the Elections Clause, which gives states the authority to set election processes.
"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," Bennett told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly. "How can we do that?"
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
California focal point of Trump's anti-immigration crackdown
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold, with 52 seats in the House of Representatives — more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through so-called sanctuary state policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has also long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of former president Joe Biden, said on Sunday that he was confused by the question of why the appeals court should have jurisdiction to rule at this juncture, noting that the lower court judge assigned to the case had already set a hearing for Tuesday.

Green light shining on Mount Olympos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:43:27 UTC
15:43:27 KST

The U.N. climate conference (COP31), which will be held in Antalya this November, has been making headlines lately. I’ve been spending more time in Antalya due to a small assignment I’ve taken on. While the climate summit may not be on many people’s radar, climate change inevitably affects everyone. Recent flood disasters have turned our lives upside down. I don’t know if COP31 decisions are as binding on governments as they used to be, but it’s important from our perspective that the summit is being held in Antalya. Antalya and its surrounding areas are among our leading agricultural regions. At the same time, the Bey Mountains, which form the city’s backdrop, are a unique natural treasure. Mount Olympos, just west of the Antalya Gulf, is particularly special because at the top of its Çıralı hill is an ever-burning flame called Yanar Taş, which simply means “The Burning Stone.” The local name of the hill indicates its never-dying spark of light, as “Çıralı” means “with kindling firewood.” According to mythology, the flames came from the mouth of the monster Chimera.
Çıralı Hill is rocky, but further inland, you will find yourself in a wonderland of amazing flavors and aromas. Deep in the woods, you can find wild honey and mushrooms, and the air in the forest is healing. Down from the village of Beycik is a small retreat called the Olympos Mountain Lodge. It has only a few rooms, all of which face the woods. When Mehmet Ali Börtücene, the chef at The Rabbit Hole at Olympos Mountain Lodge, called me and offered me the chance to escape to Olympos, I put all my plans on hold for a night.
My reason for escaping wasn’t just my love for Olympos, though. It was mostly curiosity. I was eager to meet the trio of chefs — three nature-loving chefs whose cuisine has intrigued me and whose work I’ve followed from afar: Mehmet Ali Börtücene of The Rabbit Hole, the host; Bahtiyar Büyükduman of Telezzüz in Istanbul; and Daniel Vidal of Baldío in Mexico City. I wanted to witness what they would create when they came together.
Arca Tierra-Baldío: Mexico’s green star
The concept of “zero waste” has been rising in popularity in recent years. Mexico City, one of the world’s most populous cities, is likely a prime candidate for this concept. Baldío, the city’s first and only restaurant with a Green Michelin Star, is an Arca Tierra project. The core idea is simple: Source all ingredients from small-scale farmers, waste nothing and use fermentation to transform materials destined for the trash into delicious meals. Of course, achieving this in a bustling urban environment is no easy feat. The collaboration between Baldío chef Daniel Vidal and Arca Tierra founder Pablo Usobiaga has made it possible to bring this mission to life. The source of the food is key to the endeavor’s success. The starting point is the chinampas, agricultural islands dating back two thousand years. These man-made, floating gardens are essentially islands. The restaurant sources its fresh ingredients from these islands. They also apply the zero-waste concept to the full, that’s why they are nicknamed the restaurant without a trash bin. This is precisely how Baldío earned its Green Michelin Star.
Different landscapes, shared mindset
How did this green connection stretching from Mexico to a mountain village in Antalya, Türkiye, come about? Thanks to Mehmet Ali Börtücene, who is well known in Ankara and is affectionately called “Mali” by his friends. His “rabbit hole,” an escape from Ankara, is the Olympos Mountain Lodge in Beycik village. The lodge offers a tasting menu that changes every night, providing a surprising adventure where you never know what you’ll encounter — just like falling down the rabbit hole in Alice in Wonderland. After Mali’s exploratory trip to Mexico, his like-minded Mexican friends followed him into this rabbit hole. Bahtiyar Büyükduman, the chef at Telezzüz — Istanbul’s go-to spot for plant-based cuisine and recipient of the Michelin Green Star — also joined them, contributing with finding a sponsor for the whole mission. His totally vegan restaurant is the only vegan fine/dining venue in Istanbul and as he is an archaeologist in origin, he likes to dig deep down in the history of dishes and ingredients.
These three like-minded chefs have prepared a special nine-course tasting menu. They are all committed to sustainability. They find joy in even the smallest things they forage and gather in nature. They don’t want to waste anything. Bahtiyar’s Ajo Blanco dish used zucchini stems and was inspired by the Mediterranean tradition of repurposing stale bread.
Daniel’s amazing white mole dish was straight out of the woods, featuring local wild mushrooms and pine nuts foraged from the forest and served with white mole sauce. Mali’s crispy chicken was blended with forest herbs, his butter spread was cedar-smoked and the olive explosion was straight from the olive tree in the garden, only a few meters away from the kitchen. Each flavor was a new discovery and an exciting surprise.
This culinary collaboration, shaped around the gastronomic heritage of Anatolia and Mexico, as well as a focus on sustainability and a zero-waste approach, brought together three different chefs not only at a shared table but also with a shared vision and a common goal. And that was what truly mattered. While Antalya was bustling with preparations for COP31, a quiet yet powerful voice emerged from the Olympos Mountain. The ever-burning flame of Yanat Taş, the burning stone, seemed to shine even brighter. The shared vision of these three eco-conscious chefs lit a green light for the future.

AA Photo
The capital Ankara is set to host the 20th Turkish History Congress from Oct. 26 to 30 at the Atatürk Supreme Council for Culture, Language and History campus, Turkish Historical Society (TTK) President Professor Dr. Haluk Selvi has announced.
Established in 1932, the landmark congress continues to illuminate research on Turkish history. It gained international prominence during its second edition in 1937, attracting scholars and participants from across the globe.
TTK President Selvi noted that they began preparations for the 20th conference approximately two years ago. He mentioned they have invited academics from both Türkiye and abroad to Ankara and have finalized the conference topics.
“The 230 papers selected through the academic selection process will be presented by 300 scholars from 30 different countries. At the conference, a wide range of topics related to Turkish history — from the earliest times to the present — across a broad geographical area stretching from Central Asia to the Balkans and from Crimea to Qatar will be addressed by an international audience,” he said.
Selvi explained that the purpose of the Turkish History Congress is to demonstrate the Turkish contribution to civilization through historical data in response to Western-centric claims, and announced that the papers presented will be published in a book.
As the conference runs through Oct. 29, a special panel will be held to observe Republic Day, Selvi announced. He also revealed that another special panel at the conference will focus on the role of institutes in historical writing, featuring the participation of scholars from the Turkic states and Italy.
Selvi stated their great honor in hosting the congress as the TTK approaches its 100th anniversary. “Throughout the five-day congress, sessions and special exhibitions will be held in five different halls. We invite history enthusiasts and history students from all over to our conference,” Selvi said.

Türkiye converts food waste into animal feed in 74 provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:43:07 UTC
15:43:07 KST

Food waste collected from public institutions and large-scale catering facilities is being converted into animal feed in 74 of Türkiye’s 81 provinces, with daily production reaching 31,274 kilograms, according to Interior Ministry sources.
The initiative is part of the Zero Waste Project, spearheaded by first lady Emine Erdoğan. Under the scheme, food waste collected through provincial governor’s offices and municipalities from student dormitories run by the Higher Education Credit and Hostels Institution (KYK), military units, hospitals, prisons, hotels and restaurants is processed into animal feed.
Machines and equipment for converting food waste into animal feed are available in 74 provinces, with a combined daily production capacity of 65,352 kilograms. However, actual daily output stands at 31,274 kilograms, indicating that existing facilities are operating below half of their total capacity.
Iğdır, Kahramanmaraş, Kırıkkale, Kocaeli, Kütahya, Samsun and Tunceli are the seven provinces without equipment to process food waste into animal feed.
An inspection report recommended that food products deemed unfit for human consumption but suitable for animal feed — including items ordered destroyed under insurance procedures or official inspections — be redirected to animal shelters and designated natural habitats where appropriate. The report also called for efforts to expand the use of food-processing equipment at animal shelters.
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said the government was pursuing a comprehensive approach to protecting, housing and caring for stray animals, while also seeking to use public resources more efficiently.
He said the Zero Waste Project had helped protect the environment and make better use of existing resources, adding that the government aimed to establish feed production facilities in the seven provinces currently lacking them through cooperation with relevant institutions and local authorities.
“On the one hand, we aim to bring food waste generated in public institutions, dormitories, hospitals, military units and mass-consumption facilities back into the economy; on the other, we seek to reduce feeding costs at animal shelters and in natural habitats as much as possible,” Çiftçi said.
He added that the ultimate goal was to establish a sustainable system in all 81 provinces that prevents waste, saves public funds and improves conditions for stray animals.

Brazilian voters have denied Latin America’s resurgent right its ultimate prize, snapping a streak of seven straight conservative presidential victories in 18 months.
The stunning triumph of leftist incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over Flávio Bolsonaro on Oct. 25, with 51.8 percent of the vote to 48.2 percet, limits U.S. President Donald Trump’s drive to tighten his grip on the Western Hemisphere and cements Latin America’s most populous country and largest economy as a counterweight to Washington.
