A Bolsonaro victory would have left Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum as the only progressive president among the region’s powerhouses.
For the Trump administration, which has wielded punishing tariffs, severe sanctions and military force to reassert its dominance in the region, Lula’s victory complicates its campaign to enlist Brazil in its military coalition against cartels and to gain preferential access to the country’s critical minerals, analysts say.
Yet both sides see reasons to cooperate. Washington wants access to Brazil’s vast trove of rare earths to reduce its defense industry’s reliance on China. Lula wants foreign investment and tariff relief for Brazilian exporters.
“Lula is pragmatic enough to work out some kind of modus operandi with the Trump administration,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, adding that the Bolsonaros’ allies in Washington would likely lose sway after the family’s second electoral defeat. Flávio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, lost to Lula in 2022.
“I’m not sure anyone in the Trump administration, beyond a few individuals, will want to keep making the Bolsonaros the central issue in the U.S.-Brazil relationship,” he said.
Across much of Latin America, voters fed up with organized crime and economic insecurity have rewarded presidential candidates promising to restore order. From Peru’s Keiko Fujimori to Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella and Chile’s José Antonio Kast, newly elected conservatives have courted Trump while taking their cues from El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, whose sweeping gang crackdown has sharply reduced homicides at the cost of mass arrests and suspended civil liberties.
Trump has reinforced that shift with electoral endorsements, financial bailouts and millions of dollars in military aid.
“The U.S. is certainly putting its finger on the scale to try to help the more hard-line right-wing elements in the region,” said Kenneth Roberts, a professor of government at Cornell University.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen on Oct. 26 hailed Lula’s victory as a win for “democracy and multilateralism.” She congratulated Lula on social media, adding: “Europe’s partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come. Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate.”
French President Emmanuel Macron on Oct. 26 congratulated his Brazilian counterpart, calling for efforts to “strengthen our strategic partnership.” “France and Brazil have much to build together,” Macron said X, saying their two countries should nurture their friendship “in the service of a fairer world”.
China also congratulated Brazil’s leftist President on his reelection. “Beijing is willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future,” Foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing.

Independent republics, castles and bagels: How to spend 24 hours in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:41:14 UTC
15:41:14 KST

From strolling around the UNESCO-listed Old Town to reading the constitution of the independent republic Užupis, Lithuania’s capital city is perfect to explore in just one day.
Back in 2018, Lithuania’s capital Vilnius marketed itself as the “G-spot of Europe”, claiming that “nobody knows where it is but when you find it, it’s amazing”.
While I can’t comment on improvements around sex education (except anecdotally), more and more people are finally discovering the joys of the Baltics with the rise of “coolcations”.
I visited both Latvia and Estonia in the summer last year, and this October, after a quick return to Riga and a detour to Sigulda, Latvia’s autumn capital, I made it down to Vilnius.
Amazing? With its UNESCO-listed baroque Old Town, its growing food scene, and fascinating museums, I’d say so.
If you only have 24 hours in Vilnius, here’s where to go and what to see.
Things to see and do in Vilnius
Climb up to Gediminas Tower
The best way to admire the city is from above, and there’s no better place for it than Gediminas Tower.
Located at the top of Gediminas Hill, the tower is what remains of the Upper Castle. Inside, you’ll find displays showing you what the castle looked like over its many iterations, starting from when it was first built by Gediminas, the Grand Duke of Lithuania who founded Vilnius.
The tower has long been a symbol of the city as the place where the tricolour flag was hoisted for the very first time in 1919 during Lithuania’s independence between the two World Wars, as well as the spot where it was rehoisted in 1988 during the independence movement during the Soviet era. This history is also explored through the Frequency of Freedom exhibition inside.
After exploring the exhibitions, you’re treated to an incredible view from the rooftop.
As an aside, if you do visit Vilnius during the warmer months, you can get an even better view by booking a hot air balloon ride over the city.
Visit the Vilnius Cathedral…
Just down the road from the castle complex you’ll find Vilnius Cathedral and its bell tower.
While its current form is neoclassical, the cathedral has been rebuilt several times following fires, with parts dating back to the 13th century in the catacombs.
Once used for the inaugurations of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, the cathedral is also home to the Chapel of Saint Casimir, the Patron Saint of Luthania. Born into the royal family, he was known for its devotion to God and was recognised by the Pope in 1602.
…and the Church of St. Anne
One of the most beautiful churches in Lithuania, the Church of St. Anne was built in a Gothic style in the late 15th century.
Such is its beauty that Napoleon apparently said he wanted to carry the church back home with him to Paris “in the palm of his hand”. Emphasis on apparently – it’s a legend rather than provable fact, although it is very pretty I must admit.
Wander around Bernardine Gardens
Behind the Church of St. Anne and the Bernardine Monastery are the Bernardine Gardens.
Cultivated by the Bernadine monks in the 15th century, this once swampy area was transformed into a collection of planted gardens with several ponds, and it even has a botanical garden.
Located right next to the river, it’s a peaceful spot for a stroll, particularly in the autumn sunshine.
Read the constitution of Užupis
Located across the Vilnelė River, the neighbourhood of Užupis declared independence in 1997.
It has its own flag, a national day (which falls on April Fools’), and embassies “among Canadian cats”, “in cheese”, “in pencils” and “in rock music”, among others.
You can read the 41-point constitution, which states important things like “everyone has the right to love and take care of the cat” while “a cat is not obliged to love its owner, but must help in times of need”, in nearly two dozen different languages.
Unsurprisingly for a republic founded by artists, Užupis is known for its creative scene, which you can explore at the Užupis Art Incubator.
Take a stroll down Literatai Street
Once the home of poet Adomas Mickevičius, Literatai Street is lined with plaques paying tribute to more than 200 notable Lithuanian writers.
The project was commissioned by the Modern Art Centre in 2008 ahead of Vilnius’ stint as the European Capital of Culture, which you can also visit here.
Explore the city’s museums
There are plenty of museums dotted around Vilnius, from the Toys Museum and Railway Museum to the House of Signatories and the Energy and Technology Museum.
If we had to narrow it down to just two, our picks would be the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights, and Castellan’s House.
The former is located within the former KGB headquarters and covers the history of Soviet repression while also briefly touching on the country’s Nazi occupation, while the latter forms part of the National Museum of Lithuania and explores Lithuanian identity through themes like religion.
Where to eat and drink in Vilnius
The oldest market in Vilnius – Halės – is an obvious choice, with dozens of choices from pastries and soups to tacos and Korean plates.
Hardly traditional, but I was a big fan of Beigelistai, which serves up Vilnius-style bagels. I couldn’t tell you the difference between Vilnius and New York-style ones, but I can tell you the bagel of the month for October (with fig jam, camembert, walnuts and cream cheese) was fantastic.
For a more modern option, head to Paupys Market. Again, the market has many different restaurants to choose from, but the potato pancakes and bao buns are real winners.
Next time I’ll visit Vilnius for…
If I’d had more time in Vilnius, I would have taken the advice of a friend who visited in April and headed to Trakai Castle.
Located on an island, the castle is about a 35-minute train journey followed by a 10-minute bus or a 40-minute walk. Just be aware that the trains aren’t super regular, so you should plan this out in advance.
How to get there
Vilnius International Airport is just under six kilometres away from the city centre, which you can reach in around 15 or 20 minutes by bus. There’s also a train which takes under 10 minutes, but they run less frequently than the bus.
The biggest airlines operating from the airport are airBaltic, Ryanair and Wizz Air. There are direct flights from cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona, London, Rome and Paris.
Alternatively, Vilnius is around a four-hour bus ride from Riga.

With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:38:39 UTC
15:38:39 KST

With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones
Anton, a soldier with Ukraine's 112th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, stands beside an Oktava electronic warfare system outside Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Jakub Laichter / The Kyiv Independent)
In a cornfield north of Kyiv, pieces of blackened metal are scattered among rows of dried stalks. They are all that remains of a Russian Geran attack drone, shot down by Ukrainian fighter jets as it flew toward the capital during one of Russia's mass aerial assaults.
"Last year we had so many of them," says Halyna Prykhodko, deputy director of the Branytsia division of the agricultural company Zemlya i Volya. "We found three, four, even five in the fields."
Above Prykhodko's land is one of the routes Russian drones take to approach Kyiv. Ukrainian forces try to intercept them over the countryside before they reach the capital and crash into homes and critical infrastructure.
Since late summer, Russia has been terrorizing Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.
Defending Kyiv requires a layered system of air defenses, from sophisticated missile systems and fighter jets, to mobile machine-gun and interceptor-drone units.
Over two days, the Kyiv Independent accompanied soldiers of the 112th Territorial Defense Brigade at several positions outside the capital, observing how their units hunt incoming Russian drones and adapt to Russia's evolving weapons and tactics.
read also
A Coordinated Effort
Radar stations and other detection systems are the first link in a wider system coordinating Kyiv's air defenses. They track approaching Russian drones, relaying information through command posts that direct the response of individual units.
"Every unit is subordinate to its own combat command post," says Senior Sgt. Serhii, who leads a mobile fire group. His surname is withheld for security reasons. "It gathers all the information from higher commanders and other groups, and issues orders to each group."
His three-man mobile fire group is armed with a truck-mounted Browning M2HB heavy machine gun, a SkyLock targeting system, and thermal-imaging equipment.
One soldier mans the machine gun, another commands the group and operates observation equipment, and a third covers them with an assault rifle.
When a drone approaches their sector, the soldiers receive information about its direction, altitude, and distance. They must then locate it using their observation equipment, adjusting for discrepancies between the target's reported and actual positions.
The crews operate within designated firing sectors, limiting where they can engage targets to avoid endangering civilians or friendly aircraft.
The gunner must account for the target's speed, distance, and direction of travel, calculating how far ahead to fire so that the bullets and aircraft arrive at the same time at the same point.
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is."
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is," explains Volodymyr, a soldier in the mobile fire group.
Repeated practice and experience are essential, he says, until judging a target's movement and calculating the necessary lead become almost instinctive.
Weather conditions, altitude, and speed further determine whether a target can be engaged. Thermal-imaging equipment helps soldiers detect drones at night, but cloud cover can obscure them, and faster, higher-flying jet-powered drones present greater difficulties.
"Within five seconds I have to engage it as much as I possibly can," says Volodymyr.
It's his birthday when the Kyiv Independent visits the mobile fire group. He spends it at the group's position, surrounded by fields.
"Grand celebrations," he jokes when asked how he plans to mark the occasion. "I've got these wide fields. I can walk over there, walk over here. Not many options."
Other crews use shoulder-fired missiles to engage targets beyond the reach of machine guns.
"Bodya," another soldier, operates a Soviet-designed 9K38 Igla man-portable air-defense system, which uses a heat-seeking missile to pursue aerial targets. Even with a guided missile, soldiers have very little time to engage a fast-moving target.
With conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones, Bodya explains, the sound of the approaching engine can provide some warning. Jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, however, travel much faster, and by the time crews hear one, it can be almost on top of them. Some targets pass through his unit's engagement area in as little as 20 seconds, he says.
Ukraine primarily uses systems such as NASAMS and IRIS-T against Russian cruise missiles, aircraft, and other aerial threats, but to intercept ballistic missiles, Ukraine has to rely on its scarce arsenal of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Interceptor drones have become another means of bringing down Russian targets, particularly conventional Shahed-type drones, without expending costly surface-to-air missiles.
A soldier with the call sign Gendalf shows the Kyiv Independent the Sting interceptor drones operated by his unit. Equipped with cameras, the interceptor drones transmit live video to operators who guide them toward incoming Russian drones.
But Russia's increasing use of jet-powered drones, some capable of flying at about 600 kilometers per hour, has created a problem for operators like Gendalf.
read also
Reaching about 320 kilometers per hour at full throttle, the conventional rotary-wing interceptors available to his unit struggle to match the jet-powered drones' speed, he says.
Beyond these different means of kinetic interception, electronic warfare provides another layer of defense by targeting the signals Russian drones rely on.
At an electronic warfare unit, Maj. "Secret," the brigade's head of electronic warfare and electronic intelligence, demonstrates a sensitive spectrum analyzer developed within the brigade. The device allows soldiers to detect and analyze radio-frequency signals, including those transmitted by Russian drones.
"Here we see all the signals that are nearby," he says, pointing to a series of transmissions appearing on the screen.
"First, we have to detect the signals and understand what we need to jam," Secret explains. "What matters is that there's data exchange," he says. "I can see the flow of data in real time."
Electronic warfare can disrupt an incoming drone in two main ways. First, jamming interferes with the signals it relies on, potentially severing its connection to an operator. Second, spoofing feeds the aircraft false information, potentially misleading its navigation or diverting it from its intended course.
But disrupting a communication link does not necessarily stop an attack. Some drones can continue toward preprogrammed coordinates without further instructions, meaning electronic warfare can only complement kinetic interception.
The Race to Adapt
One of the most significant developments since late summer has been Russia's growing use of jet-powered Geran drones. Some variants fly at altitudes of 5 to 6 kilometers, beyond the effective range of mobile machine-gun crews.
Soldiers defending Kyiv also describe Russian drones changing their routes and maneuvering when Ukrainian interceptors approach. Some newer Geran variants carry cameras and mesh radios that allow operators to receive a live video feed and redirect the aircraft during flight.
Ukraine is adapting its interceptors in response.
On Oct. 18, Andrii Hrytseniuk, then head of Brave1, Ukraine's government-backed defense innovation initiative, said seven types of Ukrainian interceptors had already successfully intercepted jet-powered Russian drones. Twenty-two teams joined the effort to develop high-speed systems, including models powered by miniature jet engines.
The government had ordered more than 1,000 of these new interceptors, but production is still being expanded, he said.
A similar race is playing out in electronic warfare.
read also
The electronic warfare unit studies the wreckage of drones brought down by Ukrainian forces and examines their electronics to understand how Russia is adapting its weapons.
"We dig around in these burned-out remains, looking at how everything is configured, what electronic components they use, which antennas, which parts," Secret says.
Russian forces continually modify the communications systems carried by their drones, forcing Ukrainian units to adapt the equipment used to detect and disrupt their signals, Secret says.
"They change the signal's form, and we adapt to that form," he says.
Equipment purchased just a year earlier may no longer be as effective against modified drones. But older systems cannot simply be discarded, since Russian forces can still use the technologies those systems were designed to counter.
Secret compares the process to constantly renovating an apartment without ever being able to remove the old wallpaper.
"Every six months, every three months, the fashion changes," he says. "And without stripping off the old wallpaper, you have to glue new wallpaper over it."
"And the wallpaper is, first of all, extremely expensive and very difficult to obtain," he adds.
Russia is also changing its tactics to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
"They're coming in from all directions," one air defense officer says, describing a hypothetical attack involving 15 drones.
Most might be shot down, but a handful could get through. He believes Russian forces study the results to identify routes for subsequent strikes.
"They're probing, feeling things out," he says. "Then, yes, everything's clear, a mass attack."
Meanwhile, the pace of attacks is placing a growing strain on the soldiers defending Kyiv.
"The tactic is constant exhaustion, non-stop," says Serhii.
During particularly intense periods, he says, his men have worked 20-hour shifts, leaving just four hours for sleep. And during the hours spent on alert, some targets remain beyond their reach.
One machine gunner recalls a jet-powered Russian drone passing so high overhead that he could barely make it out.
"I couldn't even see it with my eyes," he says.
But he knows how to calculate the lead needed to hit a moving drone.
"I'd tear it apart if it were lower," he says.

Ex-Japan prime minister Yasuo Fukuda dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

06:38:33 UTC
15:38:33 KST

Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, the Nikkei business daily reported on Monday.
Beijing expressed condolences over his passing.
The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become premier himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei said.
Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year – a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo's two-year stint.
A graduate in economics from Tokyo's prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company – including a two-year posting in the United States – before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became premier in 1976.
Elected to Japan's more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was chief cabinet secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not paying into the pension system.
Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments in which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped.
When Fukuda succeeded Abe he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming office given the divided parliament and opposition parties' ability to delay legislation.
Frustrated with the stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office.
Known as a diplomatic dove, Fukuda made several visits to China after leaving office in an effort to improve often fraught relations.
Speaking at a regular briefing on Monday, Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called Fukuda an old friend of the Chinese people who held the "correct view" of history.
Guo praised him for making significant contributions to the development of bilateral relations, citing the China-Japan Joint Statement on All-round Promotion of Strategic Relationship of Mutual Benefit that was issued in 2008 when he was prime minister.
Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister. (Reuters/RTHK)

Factbox-Who are the leading candidates in Israel’s election?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:38:13 CET
15:38:13 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long looked on course to lose power in Israel’s election, but the race has narrowed as the vote approaches and his rivals have no clear path to power.
Votes will be cast on Tuesday for parties, and seats in parliament will be allocated to individuals on party lists according to proportional representation.
Here are details of some of the leading candidates in Israel’s first parliamentary election since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that plunged the Middle East into turmoil, with Israel going to war in Lebanon and Gaza and launching airstrikes against Iran.
BENJAMIN NETANYAHU
In power for much of the time since 2009, after a first stint as prime minister in the 1990s, Netanyahu has become the face of Israel abroad and a polarising figure at home.
Supporters hail Netanyahu as “King Bibi” and see him as the strong leader Israel needs to defend itself in a hostile region. But, wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes in Gaza which he rejects and on trial in Israel on corruption charges which he denies, he is fighting for his political life.
Opinion polls have pointed to a sharp drop for his Likud party since the October 7 attack, which shattered Netanyahu’s security credentials. His government’s policies on matters of religion and state have also been unpopular among many Israelis.
But Netanyahu, 77, is a consummate political survivor. He has said he wants to form a “broad national” government after the election, if he wins. In the event of a stalemate, he could remain a caretaker prime minister for many months.
NETANYAHU’S TOP RIVALS
* Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who lost a son in Gaza combat. Eisenkot, 66, has projected an image as a political outsider, soldier and security hawk whose humble background and family sacrifices stand in vivid contrast to Netanyahu’s decades in high office and lingering corruption cases. He heads a new centrist party called Yashar, Hebrew for “straight” or “honest”.
* Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, 54, a right-wing former commando, former Netanyahu aide and high-tech millionaire who has joined forces with centrist former premier Yair Lapid. Their new party is called Together and its messages have focused on healing a traumatised nation and getting the country back on track. Their alliance, despite being on opposite ends of the political spectrum, ousted Netanyahu in a 2021 election.
* Former Defence Minister Avigdor Lieberman, 68, was once a close ally of Netanyahu. Even more hawkish than his former boss, Lieberman quit Netanyahu’s government in 2018, accusing the prime minister of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza, and has become one of Netanyahu’s sharpest critics. His party, Israel Our Home, draws much of its support from the country’s ex-Soviet immigrant community.
* Former general Yair Golan, 64, hailed for his rescue of people from one of the Hamas October 7 attack sites, leads the Democrats, founded on the moribund remnants of Israel’s historical Labour party and smaller left-wing Meretz.
CANDIDATES ON NETANYAHU’S SIDE
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, have both drawn intense international scrutiny for their far-right policies toward the Palestinians.
Smotrich has spearheaded Israel’s rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would ‘bury’ the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs, has promoted capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants, toughened prison conditions for jailed Palestinians and easier gun ownership for Israelis.
Both men have advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and Israel resettling the enclave.
ULTRA-ORTHODOX ALLIES
Netanyahu has relied on two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, for his political survival for years. Their demands for their community to be mostly exempt from compulsory military service, along with their low participation in the work force and reliance on state benefits, have angered many Israelis, all the more so at a time of war.
POTENTIAL KEY PLAYERS
Parties which are not clearly aligned with either side could tip the balance in favour of Netanyahu or his rivals. They include Raam and the Joint List, the two parties that represent Israel’s 20% Arab minority. Along with them are a new right-wing party called People of Israel and a centre-right party called The Reservists, both of which have been wavering in opinion polls.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

Trial by Fire: The 2025 Thai-Cambodian Border Clashes and the Royal Thai Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:34:00 UTC
15:34:00 KST

The long-simmering border conflict between Thailand and Cambodia erupted into a higher intensity military clash in July and December 2025, which saw the participation of the Royal Thai Air Force (RTAF) in a high-intensity conflict for the first time since World War II. During the conflict, the RTAF proved its status as a highly professional air force – one that belongs to the front ranks of Southeast Asia’s air forces.
This article uses available open-source information to assesses the RTAF’s air operations against the Royal Cambodian Army (RCA) during the July and December border clashes. It also discusses what the fighting revealed about the RTAF’s current capability today.
July 2025 – Operation Yuttha Bodin
Multiple clashes between Thai and Cambodian forces since the spring of 2025 led to a major escalation of hostilities on July 24, when Cambodia fired BM-21 rockets across the border, killing at least 11 Thai civilians and one soldier.
In response, the Thai military launched Operation Yuttha Bodin, a coordinated air and land assault, to defend Thai sovereignty, retaliate against Cambodian military actions along the border, and to reduce Cambodian military capability in order to preserve Thai state security and public safety.
On the first day of the operation, on July 24, the RTAF dispatched two missions totaling 10 strike sorties against RCA military command posts and army positions in the Ta Moan Thom temple area in Oddar Meanchey province.
During the five-day operation, the RTAF operated under a joint tactical plan, with Army Commander Gen. Pana Klaewplodthuk acting as the overall joint force commander. The RTAF provided direct support to a ground offensive by the Royal Thai Army (RTA).
The primary geographic focus of Operation Yuttha Bodin was on the disputed border area adjacent to Thailand’s Surin province and Cambodia’s Oddar Meanchey province (see Table 1). The RTAF provided support to the RTA, specifically in areas of active fighting, conducting air strikes to neutralize Cambodian C2 posts, troop strongholds and artillery positions, and weapons and ammunition supply depots.
Besides the Wing 1 F-16s in Korat, a major RTAF air force base located northeast of Bangkok, the 7 Wing, deployed its key assets from their home base in Surin to the base, including JAS39 Gripen fighters and Saab 340 Erieye AEW&C and Saab 340 ELINT aircraft to support the operation.
Together with the base’s 103 Squadron, 1 Wing, and 403 Squadron, 4 Wing F-16s, which had also dispatched aircraft to Korat from its base in Takhli, northwest of Bangkok, and the Gripen detachment, the three units represented the brunt of the RTAF’s offensive force.
The F-5TH and F-16s from the 21 Wing in Ubon Ratchathani, near the Thai-Cambodian border and the 4 Wing at Takhli executed all-important defensive counter air missions to protect critical military and civilian infrastructure.
The 702 Squadron’s Erieye aircraft flew day and night, providing a unified aerial picture, airspace management, and deconfliction between the different offensive and defensive assets in close coordination with the air force’s Air Command and Control System (ACCS) at Wing 6 Don Mueang base in Bangkok.
Critically, while the RTA led the overall joint force, the RTAF (through the ACCS) held control of all air assets and responded to requests from RTA for air support.
Other critical assets included the Sa Kaeo-based 3 Wing – the RTAF’s dedicated uncrewed aerial systems unit – which operated the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS, and 7 Wing’s Saab 340 electronic intelligence platform, which provided critical intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance, and targeting (ISTAR) and battle-damage assessment (BDA) support to the joint force during the operation.
In addition, the RTAF and the Thai Army deployed their ground-based air defense systems to provide additional cover for ground forces and forward bases against air-based threats.
During the operation, the RTA employed multiple types of uncrewed systems that ranged from bomb-dropping quadcopters dropping munitions on RCA trenches to larger DP-20 MALE UAS, which provided additional battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance support.
December 2025 – Resumption of Air Campaign
In December, in response to what Thailand described as the RCA’s continued provocations and movement of heavy equipment and combat forces into disputed border areas, the Thai military launched Operation Sattawat, which aimed to “penetrate and destroy the opposing side’s combat support structures and strategic supply routes.”
To support the RTA’s operation on the ground, the RTAF targeted Cambodian C2, drone control facilities, weapons and ammunition depots, logistics, and equipment that could pose a threat to “national security and civilian safety.”
In a major departure from the more geographically constrained operations against RCA forces and supplies adjacent to Surin province during Operation Yuttha Bodin, the December air campaign saw the RTAF expand its target list to encompass the entire length of the shared border (see Table 2).
In addition to the frequent close air support missions along the border, the RTAF carried out some deep strike operations to destroy selected bridges and weapons depots deep inside Cambodia. For example, on December 24, Thai fighters penetrated as deep as 100 kilometers into Cambodian territory in Battambang Province to hit a weapons depot there.
Although not publicly disclosed like the 1 Wing and 4 Wing F-16s and 7 Wing Gripens use in strike missions, visual evidence of bomb mission marking on other units and combat aircraft like the F-5TH “Super Tigris” and T-50TH from the 21 Wing and 4 Wing verify their active participation in strike missions as well.
Tempo and Targeting
During the July operation, the RTAF flew two to three combat missions daily, involving two to four combat aircraft per mission. On the first day of heavy fighting, larger formations (up to 10 combat aircraft in total) were involved in strikes in anticipation of a greater level of resistance (see Table 1). The lower-than-expected opposition allowed required sorties to be reduced to an average of four sorties or two two-ship missions per day. In total, RTAF conducted 28 strike sorties during Operation Yuttha Bodin.
Compared to July, it appears that the RTAF operated at a higher operational tempo in December, based on the known targets struck and the geographic spread of combat operations (see Table 2). For example, during the more active phase of ground fighting on December 18-19, the RTAF flew a larger number of sorties against RCA forces along the length of the shared border, including in Siem Reap, Oddar Meanchey, and Banteay Meanchey provinces.
Critically, the publicly released sorties only consider actual strike sorties. Several supporting sorties, including defensive counter air, airspace surveillance and strike coordination, reconnaissance and target acquisition, electromagnetic domain monitoring, and airlift sorties were carried out simultaneously, even if not publicly acknowledged.
The bombing effort was preceded and supplemented by an attempt to locate any ground-based air defense threats and eliminate them. To achieve this, RTAF deployed crewed and uncrewed ISTAR assets, including the 7 Wing’s Saab 340 ELINT was used to establish the Cambodian forces’ electronic order of battle along the key operational axes opposite Ubon Ratchathani, Buri Ram, Surin, Si Sa Ket, Sa Kaeo, and Chanthaburi Provinces.
The RTAF and RTA uncrewed ISTAR aircraft deployed the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS and Defense Technology Institute (DTI) DP-20 MALE UAS to reconnoiter the border area, locate RCA force disposition, and provide post-strike battle damage assessment.
To reconnoiter targets and provide precision-guidance for PGMs, RTAF combat aircraft employed Litening-III targeting pod (Gripen and F-5TH) and the Sniper ATP pod (F-16 and TA-50TH)—to find, fix, identify, engage, and BDA (battle damage assessment) targets.
Weapons Deployment
The RTAF dropped more than 30 tons of munitions on Cambodian positions during Operation Yuttha Bodin. Munitions employed included unguided general-purpose bombs (GPBs) and precision-guided munitions (PGMs), and direct attack and standoff weapons.
The most commonly employed munitions included the Mk. 82 high-explosive GPB and laser-guided 500-lb Lizard-III and/or GBU-12-kitted PGMs. Some 2,000-lb Mk. 84 high-explosive GPB and AGM-65 Maverick air-to-ground missiles were also employed against larger hardened targets and RCA armor.
In addition, the 500-lb Korean GPS-guided glide-bomb (KGGB) was used in combat for the first time. The KGGB was reportedly employed especially during the opening phase of the conflict to provide standoff range in the face of potential Cambodian deployment of its Chinese-made medium-range KC-1 surface-to-air missile system along the border.
Importantly, the RTAF sources many of these weapons from the United States and Israel, as well as South Korea. In addition, the Thai defense industry is thought to manufacture variants of the Mk. 82 bombs, which can be mated with the Israeli (Elta Lizard-III and GBU-12) and Korean (LIG Nex1 KGGB) precision-guidance kits. The diversified and largely non-U.S. supply of key munitions and their guidance kits make the RTAF more resilient against a potential U.S. arms embargo.
Pictures of RTAF fighters that have surfaced since the border clash show large numbers of sorties on individual aircraft. For example, an F-16B has been spotted with 63 bombing mission markings; T-50THs with 32 and 34 Mk. 82 bomb mission markings; an F-5TH with 20 Mk. 82 bomb mission markings; and a Gripen with seven GBU-12 mission markings. These indicate that the real sortie numbers may be higher than publicly reported. They also highlight the employment of all of RTAF’s primary combat aircraft in bombing sorties – something which has not been disclosed publicly.
In addition to aircraft delivered munitions, Thailand has also drawn lessons from recent conflicts by employing indigenous KB-5E and KB-10G long-range loitering munitions and one-way attack drones (OWADs) in combat for the first time. Thai forces deployed the capability alongside scouting drones, artillery and air support in a multilayered reconnaissance-strike complex.
Opposition and Losses
The RTAF’s losses during the July and December operations were very low. The Thai military is known to have lost at least two aircraft during December fighting. On December 17, a DP-20 UAV of the RTA was lost for an unknown reason. The second aircraft, an RTAF Aerostar BP UAV, was reportedly shot down over Cambodia’s Banteay Meanchey Province on December 21.
Importantly, enabling RTAF impunity of operations was the fact that Cambodia has no fast jet air power of its own. Despite having acquired Chinese-made KC-1 medium-range surface-to-air missile system and the very short-range QW-3 MANPAD, they posed little opposition to RTAF operations.
The Verdict
The July and December 2025 border clashes between Thailand and Cambodia were the first major conflict that saw a large-scale deployment of Thai air power in support of its ground forces. It was also the largest deployment of air power in Southeast Asia since the Vietnam War.
It employed and tested nearly all of the combat assets and enablers in the RTAF’s inventory, including both crewed and uncrewed tactical aviation.
Critically, the conflict successfully showcased results of the RTAF’s more than decade-long effort to create a truly network-centric force. It employed all key enablers in a demonstration of modern air power, using domestic datalink (the Link-T) to coordinate and communicate between C2 nodes, ISR assets, and strike aircraft.
The air force’s Erieye AEW&C platform provided effective airspace control, coordinating and deconflicting defensive counterair aircraft and ground-based air defenses from strike aircraft ingressing or egressing from target areas, while various crewed and uncrewed platforms provided effective tactical and strategic level ISR and targeting for the joint force.
The brief air campaign included many firsts. This was the first time the Swedish Gripen had dropped bombs in anger. It was also the first real-world test for the Korean KGGB glide bomb and the indigenous KB-series OWADs. The RTAF demonstrated that it has taken great strides in the integration of uncrewed platforms into the force.
Although Cambodia could not challenge RTAF in the air, the threat of “pop-up” air defense threats posed by the RCA’s VSHORAD and SHORAD systems and explosive-armed small drones remained real throughout the conflict.
Underlining its status as one of the region’s most professional air forces, the RTAF sustained only very limited losses, while meeting many of its stated objectives. These included reducing the threat posed by RCA heavy weaponry to the state and civilian population, and reasserting deterrence.

Türkiye expands automation in tax services

Unknown Publisher

06:33:43 UTC
15:33:43 KST

Türkiye’s Revenue Administration (GİB) has used automated systems to prepare and send more than 200,000 official letters without staff intervention, according to the Treasury and Finance Ministry.
The administration uses robotic process automation to handle routine transactions and correspondence around the clock. The tools also send taxpayers text reminders to help them meet their obligations on time.
Through its Digital Tax Office, taxpayers can make payments, file returns and submit applications without visiting a tax office. The platform offers 261 services and received around 18.3 million applications and written requests in the first nine months of 2026.
The platform has recorded more than 750 million logins since its launch. Around 13 billion financial documents, including invoices and receipts, were issued electronically in 2025.
A central monitoring system introduced in 2024 also oversees operations at 860 tax offices, generating about 56,000 reports each month. Follow-up procedures track whether the necessary work identified in those reports has been completed.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said digital services were simplifying tax procedures and speeding up transactions.
“These applications aim to improve access to services, shorten processing times, improve administrative efficiency and make better use of public resources,” he said.
Şimşek added that the changes also sought to protect taxpayers’ rights, reduce errors and improve service standards.

Lula promises a Brazil 'everyone dreams of' after historic comeback

15:30:49 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pledged to govern for all Brazilians, bolster the country’s international standing and advance an ambitious climate agenda after securing reelection on Sunday.
According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Lula won 51.79 percent of valid ballots, while Flavio Bolsonaro received 48.21 percent.
"No one is required to like the president-elect, but he must govern for everyone," Lula said as he addressed supporters, expressing gratitude to the Brazilian people and promising to respect citizens regardless of their political allegiances.
He also criticised his opponent Flavio Bolsonaro’s political camp, declaring "this was a defeat for denialism and lies."
Promising an ambitious agenda for his next term, Lula said: "I want to make a commitment: I will deliver the best term any president has ever served. I will dedicate myself 24 hours a day to making this the country that everyone dreams of."
He also emphasised national sovereignty, saying "in this election, we defeated the interference that was coming from the outside in."
"This country will not accept being anyone's backyard," he added.
Outlining his vision for Brazil's place in the world, Lula said the country should play a central role in international affairs and lead by example on climate policy.
"We want to be a central country, not a peripheral one. We are going to show the world how climate policies are handled in this country," he said.
A historic comeback
Lula's victory marked a historic comeback after he finished second in the October 4 first round, when Bolsonaro led with 47.03 percent of valid votes against Lula's 45.16 percent.
Lula became the first candidate in Brazil's democratic history to finish second in the first round and win the presidency in the runoff, according to Brazil's Chamber of Deputies.
His campaign mobilised supporters through street rallies and social media.
The victory gives Lula a fourth nonconsecutive presidential term following his wins in 2002, 2006 and 2022. He is the first Brazilian president elected to four terms by popular vote, according to the G1 news portal. His new term is scheduled to begin on January 5 2027.
The runoff recorded an abstention rate of 19.22 percent, down from 21.08 percent in the first round, according to reported figures from Brazil's Superior Electoral Court. Blank ballots accounted for approximately 1.12 percent of ballots cast and null ballots for 2.12 percent, bringing their combined share to 3.24 percent.
Lula's next administration is expected to face congressional opposition and pressure to balance public finances while expanding social programs.

Politecnica, Park Associati, and AMDL CIRCLE Win Competition for Cultural Hub in Italy’s UNESCO-Listed Valle Camonica
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

A team led by Politecnica Building for Humans, with Park Associati and AMDL CIRCLE as architectural co-leads and Studio Mattioli responsible for geology and archaeology, has won the competition for a new cultural hub in Ceto, Italy. The project will transform the former Società Filati Niggeler & Kupfer textile mill into a facility comprising exhibition spaces, research facilities, an auditorium, and visitor services. Located in Valle Camonica, an area known for its prehistoric rock engravings, the proposal approaches the site through the relationship between industrial heritage, archaeology, and the surrounding landscape.
Ceto is located at the southern entrance to Valle Camonica, in the province of Brescia, near Monte Concarena and Pizzo Badile Camuno. The valley is home to the Rock Drawings in Valle Camonica, which became Italy's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. Known as the Pitoti, the prehistoric engravings form an extensive record of early human expression, while the wider area has been part of the UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Reserve "Valle Camonica – Alto Sebino" since 2018.
The winning proposal places the landscape at the center of the site's development, identifying the relationship between cultural heritage, the natural environment, and the local community as a guiding principle. The traces carved into the rock inform an approach that considers the territory's material characteristics, geological conditions, and morphology. The project is also conceived as an open infrastructure intended to serve as a starting point for a network of routes connecting archaeological sites with the natural environment.
Related Article
From Aalto Works to Tashkent Modernism: Discover the 19 New Cultural Sites Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2026
The project is part of broader cultural initiatives in Valle Camonica, which has launched its candidacy for Italian Capital of Culture 2029. The year will mark the 50th anniversary of the Rock Drawings in Valle Camonica's inscription on the UNESCO World Heritage List. The cultural hub is intended to contribute to the region's cultural infrastructure by bringing together archaeological heritage, landscape, and community-oriented facilities.
The competition was launched by the Municipality of Ceto, with the Comunità Montana di Valle Camonica as a contracting authority and Imago, led by Luca Molinari, providing scientific coordination. Politecnica Building for Humans is responsible for project coordination, structural and building services engineering, sustainability, fire safety, acoustics, health and safety, and mobility. Park Associati and AMDL CIRCLE lead the architectural design, while Studio Mattioli oversees geology and archaeology. The project is listed as ongoing, with 2026 as its starting year.
In other heritage news, Design Museum Gent in Belgium reopened on October 3, 2026, after four years of renovation and expansion that combined historic building restoration with a new wing designed by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, along with restoration work by RE-ST architectenvennootschap. In Lima, Peru, the Red Lima Milenaria campaign is seeking public support for a future UNESCO World Heritage nomination of selected pre-colonial archaeological sites, with more than 600 sites remaining across the city. Meanwhile, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee added 25 sites to the World Heritage List during its 48th session, including 19 cultural properties, five natural sites, and one mixed property.

Political earthquake in Serbia: The end of the Vucic Era and the rise of the student list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:29:39 UTC
15:29:39 KST

This is not simply a change of government. It is the collapse of a political order that has defined Serbia since 2012.
Serbia's elections have produced a result that will almost certainly be remembered as one of the biggest political turning points in the country's modern history. The Student List has won a landslide victory and, with 140 of the 250 seats in parliament, secured an outright majority. The Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), until now the country's dominant political force, has won 104 seats and, for the first time in almost 14 years, is heading into opposition.
This is not simply a change of government. It is the collapse of a political order that has defined Serbia since 2012.
Since the Serbian Progressive Party came to power, Aleksandar Vučić and his political bloc have exercised almost complete dominance over Serbia's political life. The SNS controlled the executive branch, enjoyed large parliamentary majorities, dominated local politics and, through an extensive network of political and institutional alliances, largely determined the boundaries of political competition in the country. For more than a decade, opposition parties repeatedly tried to break that dominance, but without success.
The paradox of this political earthquake is that the SNS was not defeated by the traditional opposition.
It was defeated by students.
The Student List has transformed itself from a movement born out of months of student protests into the country's dominant political force, turning what began as a social revolt into electoral legitimacy. In doing so, the student movement has achieved what Serbia's traditional opposition parties failed to accomplish for more than a decade: it has directly broken Aleksandar Vučić's political monopoly.
The result should therefore also be understood as a referendum on 14 years of SNS rule.
A large part of the electorate clearly did not vote simply for a particular group of candidates or a particular programme. They voted against a model of government that had become synonymous with personalised politics, a strong concentration of power, political control over institutions, media and deep social polarisation. The student movement succeeded in bringing together different forms of dissatisfaction – from demands for institutional accountability and the rule of law to broader calls for political change.
The fact that no other small party managed to cross the three-per-cent electoral threshold makes the result even more dramatic. Serbia's traditional party landscape has effectively disappeared between two dominant political forces: the Student List and the SNS.
This is another indication of the scale of the earthquake.
Parties that had been a permanent part of Serbia's parliamentary life have been wiped out of the legislature. At the same time, the Student List has not merely emerged as the largest political force; it has won enough seats to govern alone.
The collapse of the old political geography of minorities
An equally important signal has come from Serbia's ethnic minority communities.
For almost a decade and a half, most minority political parties were among Aleksandar Vučić's most reliable political allies. The major exception was the Albanian political bloc, which never became part of Vučić's governing coalition. These elections, however, suggest that even this traditional political geography has been seriously disrupted.
The Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (SVM), a long-standing political partner of the SNS, won only three of the five parliamentary seats it could potentially have secured. This is more than a simple decline in parliamentary representation. It points to a significant shift in political sentiment among Vojvodina's Hungarian community and suggests that a substantial share of Hungarian voters may have supported the Student List rather than Vučić's traditional ally.
A similar signal has come from the Bosniak community. Only two Bosniak representatives will enter parliament – one from a political group that previously cooperated with Vučić and one from a movement that has traditionally remained in opposition. Here too, the previous pattern of political loyalty has been seriously disrupted.
The new parliament will also include two representatives of the Albanian coalition, a political community that has never collaborated with Vučić's government.
The old system of political alliances has therefore been fundamentally weakened.
For years, Vučić's political system relied partly on his ability to build a broad network of allies around the SNS – from minority parties to smaller coalition partners. That network has now either disappeared or been reduced to a minimum.
From Belgrade to Brussels: an international dimension
The scale of the political change was also reflected in the first international reactions to the result.
The Student List received congratulations from senior European figures, including Antonio Kosta, head of the European Council, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. Congratulations also came from other European politicians, including Péter Magyar, the Hungarian prime minister.
Those reactions carry considerable political weight.
For years, Brussels has closely followed Serbia's domestic political situation, particularly issues concerning the rule of law, the functioning of institutions, electoral conditions and the relationship between the government, opposition and civil society. The fact that senior European officials were among those congratulating the election winner therefore sends a significant signal that the Student List's victory is being viewed as the possible opening of a new political chapter in Serbia's relationship with the European Union.
The reaction from Péter Magyar is particularly symbolic. Hungary has been one of Aleksandar Vučić's closest political allies within the European Union under the rule of Viktor Orban who was defeted himself in Hungary i April this year. A new political reality in Serbia could therefore have consequences not only for Belgrade's relations with Budapest, but also for the wider political balance in the region.
In other words, the election result has already moved beyond being solely a domestic Serbian affair. It has acquired a clear European dimension.
Vučić warns of sanctions against Russia and investor uncertainty
Aleksandar Vučić's first reaction to the result also pointed to the potentially profound geopolitical and economic consequences of the change of government.
Vučić said he expected Serbia, under the new authorities, to introduce sanctions against Russia. Such a move would represent a major foreign-policy shift for Serbia, which has maintained close political, economic and historical ties with Moscow while simultaneously pursuing EU membership.
The outgoing president also warned that the election result could send a negative signal to investors.
That warning is significant because attracting foreign investment has been one of the central pillars of Vučić's economic policy. During his years in power, the government repeatedly presented Serbia as a stable and increasingly attractive destination for foreign companies and investors. A transition to a completely new political establishment could therefore raise questions among investors about political stability, economic policy, regulation and Serbia's future foreign-policy orientation.
At the same time, the Student List will inherit an economy deeply integrated with both the European market and international investment flows. Its challenge will be to demonstrate that political change does not mean economic instability.
A movement now facing the burden of governing
For the people behind the Student List, however, the significance of the election is about much more than simply replacing one government with another.
Dejan Šoškić, a professor at the Faculty of Economics and one of the prominent figures associated with the Student List, described the result in explicitly historic terms.
“I am proud of the students who have brought us to this historic situation in which Serbia has freed itself, in which Serbia has a chance to become a democratic and free society again,” Šoškić said.
The statement captures the broader meaning that the new governing camp attaches to the election.
Candidate of the “Student List – Students Are Winning”, academician and professor Radomir Saičić, said after the election victory was declared that the citizens of Serbia had demonstrated courage and a willingness for change, stressing that “serious work and the building of a new Serbia begin tomorrow.”
But winning an election is one thing; governing a country is another.
The Student List now faces the much harder task of transforming a protest movement into a functioning political establishment. It will have to form a government, rebuild institutions, establish its own political structures and formulate policies on the economy, foreign affairs, the European integration process, social policy and the rule of law.
Its victory is historic. But historic victories often mark the beginning of the most difficult phase.
For the SNS, meanwhile, this is much more than simply losing a government.
For the first time since 2012, the party will have to operate without control of the state apparatus and without the political privilege of organising Serbia's political life around itself. It will be the first real test of how strong the SNS is as a political organisation when it no longer controls the executive branch and when Aleksandar Vučić is no longer at the centre of government.
The political consequences could extend far beyond the immediate parliamentary arithmetic.
For years, Serbian politics revolved around one dominant question: whether a political force could challenge Vučić.
The answer has now been given.
It can.
And the force that did it was not one of the established opposition parties, but a student movement that only recently existed outside the traditional political system.
That is the real significance of these elections.
The traditional opposition has virtually disappeared from parliament. The minority parties that once formed part of Vučić's political support structure have lost influence. The SNS has been pushed into opposition after almost 14 years of uninterrupted dominance.

Netanyahu denies clash with IDF chief over Iran as mystery Iraq strikes raise tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:29:11 UTC
15:29:11 KST

The heightened military alert declared by IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir roughly a week and a half ago was driven by fears of a dangerous miscalculation involving Iran. His message to Israel's political leadership was clear: The military wants to avoid inflammatory statements and provocative operations that could trigger an Iranian response or convince Tehran that a U.S.-Israeli attack is imminent.
Such a misunderstanding could lead Iran to launch a preemptive strike, even if Israel and the United States had not yet decided to attack.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have continued issuing warnings to Tehran, raising concerns that Iranian leaders could conclude a joint U.S.-Israeli operation is approaching, potentially before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
The tensions between Israel's political and military leadership have now surfaced publicly, alongside reports of mysterious attacks on Iranian-supplied military equipment in Iraq.
The reported confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir
On Sunday, Channel 12 reported details of a serious confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir over an undisclosed military operation connected to Iran.
According to the report, Zamir recently received instructions from the political leadership but requested an extensive discussion before implementing them. He also sought formal, signed legal authorization from the political echelon for the proposed action.
A security source said the operation could trigger a rapid confrontation with Iran at an exceptionally sensitive moment, potentially resulting in precisely the kind of miscalculation the IDF chief has been seeking to prevent.
Two sources said the atmosphere at a meeting held Sunday at Palmachim Airbase was extremely tense.
Netanyahu denied that any confrontation had occurred.
"There is no clash," he told Channel 14. "Someone is trying to obscure the fact that the chief of staff himself said Iran is trying to interfere in the elections."
The prime minister's remarks referred to warnings by Israeli security officials about possible Iranian attempts to disrupt the Israeli election, scheduled for Tuesday.
The precise nature of the military directive at the center of the reported dispute has not been disclosed.
The mysterious attacks in Iraq
A separate development may help explain the broader strategic tensions surrounding Iran and Israel's military activities.
According to a report published Saturday by the Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat, Iraqi authorities suspect that two facilities storing air defense systems supplied by Iran to pro-Iranian militias were targeted in airstrikes last week.
The weapons reportedly included portable antiaircraft missile systems intended to provide an additional defensive layer in eastern Iraq.
The militias were apparently preparing to use these systems as a forward line of defense against Israeli Air Force fighter jets and drones in the event of another Israeli attack on Iran.
That would potentially complicate Israeli air operations by placing air defense assets outside Iranian territory, along routes that Israeli aircraft might use in a future operation.
According to the assessment presented here, an Israeli Air Force attack against such targets has already taken place in recent days, possibly using drones or precision-guided weapons launched from a distance.
Reports of the suspected operation appeared in a limited number of Arab media outlets. However, Israel has not officially acknowledged carrying out the strike, and the Iraqi government has neither confirmed nor denied Israeli involvement.
The identity of those responsible and the precise circumstances of the reported attacks therefore remain unconfirmed.
Why Netanyahu and Zamir see the risks differently
Netanyahu has sought to assist Saudi Arabia and Iranian Kurdish groups operating in northern Iraq through operations against the militias threatening them.
Both have come under attack from Iran-aligned armed groups, making the militias a concern not only for Israel but also for other regional actors.
Zamir, however, is understood to believe that Israel has already accomplished enough through previous operations, some conducted in cooperation with the Americans.
His concern is that further operations, or even public reports about them, could put pressure on Tehran to respond.
Iran's leadership may feel compelled to defend the Iraqi Shiite militias that remain loyal to it, particularly given the financial and operational support those groups have received from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force.
Iran has provided money to these militias, including funding that enabled the Quds Force to pay their personnel.
Any Iranian intervention on behalf of the militias could expand an otherwise limited confrontation into a wider conflict.
Iran's strategy after the US withdrawal
The regional situation has become more complicated since U.S. forces completed their withdrawal from Iraq at the end of September.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps is now attempting to exploit the new circumstances by positioning Iraqi Shiite militias as an additional defensive shield for Iran.
This involves developing air defense capabilities on Iraqi soil that could threaten aircraft approaching Iranian airspace.
The militias also serve another strategic purpose for Tehran: They can operate against Saudi Arabia in support of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
In this way, the Iraqi militias are becoming increasingly important to Iran's regional military posture, both as an additional layer of defense and as a means of applying pressure on neighboring countries.
The Asharq Al-Awsat report suggested that officials in Baghdad were examining intelligence assessments raising an even more consequential possibility: that the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran may already have resumed, not through direct attacks on Iranian territory but through operations targeting Iranian military assets and allied forces inside Iraq.
The October 17 explosion and unanswered questions
One incident being examined took place on October 17, when Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces, known in Arabic as Hashd al-Shaabi, reported an explosion at an ammunition storage facility at one of its bases in the Baghdad area.
The organization said a fire had broken out following an explosion in an ammunition depot and that its personnel had brought the blaze under control. Five people sustained minor injuries.
The Iran-aligned militia umbrella organization announced that an investigation was underway to determine the circumstances of the incident.
More than a week later, however, no findings had been publicly released.
The Saudi report raised questions about whether the incident could be connected to the suspected attacks on weapons facilities storing Iranian-supplied air defense systems. No confirmed evidence establishing such a connection has been made public.
The uncertainty surrounding the Iraq incidents illustrates the challenge confronting Israel's military and political leadership. Operations intended to weaken Iran's regional defenses may carry limited immediate risks, but the cumulative effect of military action, public threats and Iranian fears of an imminent attack could prove much harder to control.
For Zamir, that possibility appears to be the central concern: An operation intended to strengthen Israel's security could instead produce the rapid escalation that the military is trying to avoid, particularly in the politically sensitive days surrounding Israel's election.

Caribbean presses Britain for reparations ahead of King Charles tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:28:24 UTC
15:28:24 KST

King Charles III and Queen Camilla begin a nine-day Caribbean tour this week, arriving to demands for slavery reparations, a formal British apology and greater independence from London.
The Bahamas National Reparations Committee says it knows what the royal couple will find. It expects “schools emptied of children who will stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling.”
Charles is expected to visit the Bahamas on Tuesday to begin the nine-day trip to the Caribbean. His last official visit to the archipelago was in July 1973 as a prince who granted the Bahamas independence, ending 300 years of British rule. But the Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, along with six other Caribbean nations that recognise Charles as their king and head of state.
While in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to visit Clifford Park, where the archipelago’s black, turquoise and yellow flag was raised for the first time more than half a century ago.
His visit will raise important questions, said Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said.
A psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, Campbell-Dean said she recently mentioned Charles’ upcoming visit to her students, and they were not excited. She responded: “I know y’all might not care about this man who is coming, but here’s why this is of importance.”
Reparations push gains legal momentum
Caribbean leaders have long demanded an apology and reparations from Britain, which has consistently rejected both.
In early September, Jamaica took its reparations case to Charles. It has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the island, a move AP describes as unprecedented.
After three days in the Bahamas, Charles flies to Guyana, where thousands of enslaved people rose up in the 1823 Demerara rebellion, one of the region’s biggest slave revolts. It took place on a plantation owned by the father of former British Prime Minister William Gladstone. More than 200 people were killed, and several were decapitated, with their heads placed on poles.
President Irfaan Ali told ITV News that Charles has “rightfully recognised slavery as the darkest days in human history”. “Moving to the apology is the next step,” he said.
Reparations set to test Commonwealth summit
After two days in Guyana, Charles flies to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where he meets leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders say slavery reparations should dominate.
Jamaica, a regular stop for British royals, is not on Charles’s itinerary this time.
Steven Bennett, a 51-year-old Rastafarian, says that is for the best. “Until the British monarchy is ready to stand on Jamaican soil, look us in the eye, apologise, and talk about actual repair and restitution, he has no business here. We want justice, not a parade,” he says.
Hermine Reid, a 68-year-old retired civil servant, fondly remembers Queen Elizabeth II’s visits but accepts the change. “Jamaica is growing up and charting its own course, and the king clearly recognises that,” she says.

Bulgaria remembers the revolt of 1185 on St Demetrius’ Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:27:18 UTC
15:27:18 KST

Author
Ivo Ivanov
Bulgaria remembers the revolt of 1185 on St Demetrius’ Day
Led by brothers Peter and Asen, the uprising ended nearly two centuries of Byzantine rule
Monday 26 October 2026 07:10
Monday, 26 October 2026, 07:10
The Church of St Demetrius of Thessaloniki in Veliko Tarnovo, where historical accounts place the proclamation of the uprising led by the brothers Peter and Asen.
PHOTO BTA
Font size
In 1018, after half a century of warfare, the First Bulgarian Empire was conquered by Byzantium. Despite repeated Bulgarian uprisings, Byzantine rule lasted more than a century and a half. In the autumn of 1185 or early 1186, the local nobles Peter and Asen launched a new uprising in Tarnovgrad. After three years of fighting, Bulgarian independence was restored.
In 1185, the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos sought a marriage alliance with his strongest European neighbour, marrying the ten-year-old daughter of King Béla III of Hungary. Her dowry included the regions of Braničevo, Belgrade and the Morava valley, then inhabited by Bulgarians. But, as the senior imperial official Niketas Choniates writes in his chronicle, “being reluctant to pay for the wedding celebrations from the state treasury, he extracted the money from his subjects… and stirred up hostility among the barbarians around Mount Haemus, chiefly against himself and the Romans, who were formerly called Moesians and are now known as Vlachs and Bulgarians”.
“The Uprising of Asen and Peter” by Georgi Bogdanov, 1961.
PHOTO museumvt.com
“The instigators of this evil, who stirred up the entire people, were a certain Peter and Asen, two brothers,” Choniates continues. “What words could convey what these godless and impious men did to the Romans? What account could encompass these Iliads of misfortune?” he exclaims dramatically.
Bulgarian historian Professor Plamen Pavlov, citing fellow historians, points out that Bulgarians commonly call it the “uprising of Asen and Peter”, although the correct order is “Peter and Asen”. Until 1194, the leading figure was the elder brother, Theodore, who took the royal name Peter and provided the ideas behind the movement.
The uprising was proclaimed at the consecration of a church the brothers had built in Tarnovo, dedicated to St Demetrius of Thessaloniki. His feast day, 26 October, is therefore traditionally regarded as the date the uprising began.
PHOTO BGNES
“They persuaded these fervent people to proclaim that God had decreed freedom for the Bulgarian and Vlach peoples and had consented to their deliverance from the long yoke. That was why Demetrius, the martyr of Christ, had left Thessaloniki and his church there, abandoning the Romans, and had come to help and protect them in their undertaking,” the chronicler recounts.
Even after Bulgarian independence was restored, the first tsars of the Asen dynasty – the brothers Peter, Asen and Kaloyan – continued to fight Byzantium. Their struggle was long and hard, with many setbacks. It continued until the Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople in 1204, forcing the remnants of the once-great Eastern Roman Empire into exile. The Latin Empire established by the crusaders then attempted to conquer Bulgaria, but suffered a crushing defeat at Adrianople, present-day Edirne. The victory of Tsar Kaloyan, who ruled Bulgaria from 1197 to 1207, proved enough to deter the Latins for good.
Editor: Elena Karkalanova

PHOTO Facbook /Estela Encheva
Font size
There are nearly 420,000 Bulgarians living in Germany, and Munich is home to one of the country's largest Bulgarian communities. According to the city's official statistics office, more than 14,500 Bulgarians live and work in Munich.
By early afternoon on Sunday, around 550 people had cast their ballots at one of the three polling stations outside Bulgaria's Consulate General in Munich, our compatriot Estela Encheva told Radio Bulgaria in an interview. Voters were heading to the polls with a range of emotions:
“Some are quite desperate, but still hope that things will change. The prevailing emotion is one of sceptical hope for change. Many people are also angry, probably because of the situation in Bulgaria, but this sense of sceptical hope is what dominates overall.”
Encheva is studying law and has been living in Munich for nearly seven years. Her time in Germany has changed the way she sees Bulgaria:
“I came to Germany when I was very young. I had not even finished school, and when I moved here, I had a somewhat idealistic feeling about and view of the place I was going to. Once I arrived, I realised that both Bulgaria and Germany have their advantages and disadvantages, which made me look at things more realistically. Back then, I seemed to have greater hope that something would change in Bulgaria in the near future. Now, after all these years, although I still want change, I do not know whether it will happen.”
PHOTO Private archive
For Estela, it is important that the president stands by their principles, brings people together and safeguards Bulgaria's international standing.
“It is also important to me that the president respects international law and insists that our country abide by it, as well as bringing the people together. We live in a time when society is so divided that it is almost impossible to unite it through political measures.”
Last but not least, the president must also act as a check on those in power, our compatriot insists.

The Ankara meeting brought together Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, deputy defense minister in the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, and Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based Libyan National Army.
Al-Araby al-Jadeed, citing Libyan sources, reported agreement on Sirte as the joint command’s headquarters but said differences over political oversight had prevented a final deal. Al-Zoubi wanted the unified military to answer to the Defense Ministry, while Haftar favored the Presidential Council.
A draft described by the Libya Observer would replace the command structure headed by Khalifa Haftar with an army command council jointly chaired by al-Zoubi and Saddam Haftar, with equal representation from both sides.
The proposal also envisages a joint force operating in southern Libya under the defense minister and suspending the supreme commander’s role until elections.
Arabic Post had earlier reported that Saddam Haftar accepted prioritizing a military accord after receiving assurances from Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates that a political agreement would follow.
The talks came after the eastern-based House of Representatives approved the 2019 Türkiye-Libya maritime boundary agreement on Oct. 20, reversing years of opposition to the accord signed with the then-government in Tripoli.
Ankara has expanded contacts with eastern Libyan leaders while maintaining ties with the Tripoli government, which it supported against Khalifa Haftar’s offensive in 2019-2020.
Arabic Post also reported that parliament Speaker Al-Salihin Abdul Nabi would begin a three-day visit to Tripoli on Oct. 27 for meetings with Government of National Unity officials.
Separately, Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah told Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad that his government was ready to address Cairo’s concerns over Mediterranean maritime boundaries through dialogue, his office said on Oct. 24. Egypt has rejected the Libyan parliament’s approval of the agreement with Türkiye.

“Students won and with them also a hope that Serbia can be a country of justice, freedom and dignity.”
Voters cast ballots in huge numbers on Sunday, with the country recording its highest parliamentary election turnout in more than three decades.

Serbia Votes as Student Movement Mounts Major Challenge to Vučić
According to the country’s election officials, nearly 65 percent of its 6.4 million registered voters had cast their ballots by 6:00 pm (1700 GMT), two hours before polls closed.

-‘Dream has come true’ -

“A two-year-long dream has come true,” Mirjana Nikolic, a candidate on the Students’ List, said shortly after the win was announced.
-Political novices -
Most of the student list’s 250 candidates are experts from fields including academia and the arts with little political experience.
The movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.
It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.
Despite pushing back against the movement for almost two years, Vucic under mounting pressure, called the vote last month, citing “major turbulence on the domestic political scene”.
The right-wing populist leader resigned the presidency to run for prime minister.
Domestic and international observers were monitoring the vote, with students mobilising large numbers of volunteers to oversee the process.
