Brazil's incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won Sunday's presidential election runoff, according to the final election results.
With all votes counted, left-wing candidate Lula secured 51.8% of the vote, while right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro received 48.2%. Lula won approximately 4.4 million more votes than his opponent.
Lula, who will turn 81 on Tuesday, has served as Brazil's president since 2023 and previously held office from 2003 to 2010. He is due to be inaugurated for another four-year term in January.
Bolsonaro announced that he would challenge the election results in court after the Supreme Court extended voting hours nationwide by two hours at the request of Lula's campaign.
The request was based on delays in transporting voters to polling stations by bus in São Paulo and Salvador, two cities where Lula enjoys strong support.
Bolsonaro's campaign had also requested extended polling hours in several locations in southern Brazil, where flooding caused by heavy rainfall and power outages disrupted voting. Bolsonaro has stronger support in the country's southern regions.
Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as a senator since 2019.
His father, Jair Bolsonaro, was Brazil's president from 2019 to 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula.
Jair Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his electoral defeat and is currently under house arrest because of his health condition.
In the first round of the presidential election on 4 October, Flávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote, while Lula secured 45%.
The election campaign focused primarily on crime, the role of the state, the independence of the Supreme Court and Brazil's relations with the United States.
Lula, representing the Workers' Party, intends to continue his government's social programmes and public investment policies while maintaining a strong role for the state.
Flávio Bolsonaro, representing the Liberal Party, advocates reducing government services and adopting tougher measures to combat crime.

GPHG 2026: The 'Oscars of watchmaking' scraps gender categories for ‘a breath of fresh air’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:18:16 UTC
15:18:16 KST

Each year, the world's finest timepieces are celebrated at the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) award ceremony, which marks its 26th anniversary on Saturday 7 November.
The world of watchmaking is counting down to the 2026 edition of the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG), where the finest luxury timepieces compete for 19 coveted prizes.
The winners will be revealed at a glamorous award ceremony in Geneva on Saturday 7 November, and you can watch the event live on Euronews Culture.
Here, the time-honoured mastery and meticulous skill that define the industry will once again take the spotlight. This year, 84 watches and clocks vie for awards in 14 categories, including sports, calendar and astronomy, jewellery and mechanical exception.
The winners are decided by a jury of experts including watch collectors, watchmakers, journalists and auctioneers.
The top honour, known as the ‘Aiguille d'Or’ Grand Prix, is open to any watch across all categories. Last year, it was won by Breguet's Classique Souscription 2025 - a watch which only has one hand.
As Euronews Culture’s resident watch expert has shared, each of the shortlisted timepieces is truly remarkable. The nominees include a Moscow workshop taking on the Swiss giants, a wearable solar system, and a 10-kilo clock that winds your watch while you sleep.
GPHG awards scrap gender categories
For the 26th edition, GPHG has overhauled its traditional categories to “enhance its representativeness and align with new market dynamics”. This includes scrapping the usual gender-based (Men’s and Ladies’) categories and replacing them with new technical categories: Essential Watch and Complication Watch.
This is to “reflect changing purchasing behaviours and meet industry expectations”, according to the organisers. “This provides a competition platform more representative of a market featuring increasingly blurred traditional boundaries giving way to a more universal approach.”
There is a new category for 2026. Gemset will award watches set with a total of up to six carats of gemstones, leaving the Jewellery category for the most impressive exceptional pieces.
This year, the Iconic Watch Prize is open to the entire watch market. All timepieces released during the year offering a contemporary reinterpretation of an iconic model that has been exercising a lasting influence on the industry for more than 20 years are eligible – whether or not they are officially entered in the competition.
The Special Jury Prize has been expanded. It can now also recognise – alongside individuals and institutions – a brand (whether or not it is entered in the competition) for a significant watchmaking development or an exemplary approach to ethics and sustainability.
GPHG 2026: Independent watchmakers take the spotlight
The GPHG has also set out to open the competition to a wider range of houses, from a wider range of countries, with a growing contingent of independents. This includes Moscow-based Konstantin Chaykin, whose ThinKing Mystery is billed as the thinnest series-produced mechanical watch in the world.
Several legendary names, on the other hand, aren't competing at all. While Rolex has never participated, many of the missing brands are past winners: Patek Philippe, Cartier, Vacheron Constantin, F.P. Journe, Richard Mille, A. Lange & Söhne, Greubel Forsey, and Breguet, last year's 'Aiguille d’Or', barred from competing the following year under GPHG rules.
The Oscars of watchmaking are going ahead without several of their record-holding stars, which means there could be some surprises this year.

Russia-Africa 2026: From summits to strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:17:51 UTC
15:17:51 KST

Russia-Africa 2026: From summits to strategy
The Russia-Africa Summit taking place in Moscow on October 28-29 will be the third of its kind, and relations have undergone a great transformation since the first summit. Over the past seven years, permanent frameworks have been established, diplomatic presence has expanded, and trade turnover has grown.
This year’s summit will provide an opportunity to evaluate the results of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum Action Plan, which was adopted at the second summit. It contains 181 points covering politics and security, trade, investment, agriculture, energy, industry, transport, digitalization, science, education, and humanitarian cooperation.
Prior to 2022, expert discussions focused mainly on Africa’s place among Moscow’s foreign policy priorities. However, in the past four years, the practical importance of Russia’s relationship with the continent has surged.
African nations have become a higher priority for Russia in terms of diplomacy, business, foreign trade, and international coordination. Today, the primary focus is on the quality of cooperation.
From summits to permanent mechanisms
The first Russia-Africa Summit, held in Sochi in October 2019, brought together all 54 African nations, including more than 40 heads of state and government. Its most significant outcome was the establishment of a pan-African approach in Russian foreign policy. This set a framework for regular summits, the ongoing work of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum, and cooperation with the African Union.
The second summit took place in St. Petersburg in July 2023 and was attended by delegations from 49 African states, 17 of which were led by heads of state. A three-year Action Plan adopted there featured key topics such as financial settlements, banking ties, logistics, investments, information technology, industry, and transport. Following the summit, expert discussions increasingly focused on shipping, insurance, correspondent accounts, currency settlements, and project finance – that is, issues that directly impact corporate business activity and trade volumes.
Cooperation has since become multi-dimensional. In November 2024, the first Ministerial Conference of the Russia-Africa Partnership Forum took place in Sochi, followed by a second such conference in Cairo in December 2025. In July, African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held high-level consultations in Addis Ababa.
Russia’s diplomatic network has also expanded.There are currently 45 Russian embassies physically operating in African nations. Since 2023, embassies have resumed operations in Burkina Faso, Equatorial Guinea, Niger, and Sierra Leone, and a new Russian embassy was opened in South Sudan. The opening of embassies in the Gambia, Liberia, Togo, and the Comoros are next on the agenda. A separate Department for Partnership with Africa has been established within the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The developments are, step-by-step, reducing the extent to which the African agenda depends on meetings between leaders.
Politics outpaces economics so far
Russia’s political presence in Africa has been expanding faster than economic ties. At the same time, tangible progress has been made in commerce: trade turnover between Russia and Africa grew from $16.8 billion in 2019, when the first summit was held, to $27.1 billion in 2025.
However, a pronounced imbalance persists: in 2025, Russian exports accounted for $22.7 billion, while imports amounted to only about $4.4 billion. Much of the growth seen in recent years is linked to shifts in the external environment and the redirection of trade flows. Establishing a sustainable presence, however, requires direct supply channels, infrastructure, local partners, and financing.
The geography of economic ties is also uneven, with about 70% of total trade turnover still concentrated in North African countries. Food, fertilizers, fuel, and metals account for a significant portion of trade turnover. The modest scale of economic engagement becomes clear when compared to that of other major powers; for example, China-Africa trade reached $348 billion in 2025.
Moscow’s policy currently commands fewer financial resources. To make its presence in Africa more effective, Russia is focusing on the sectors where it possesses the necessary technologies and expertise, and where demand is stable. These include the agro-industrial complex, nuclear energy, the extractive industries, digitalization, information security, and education.
Food, fertilizers, energy, and education
Russia maintains a strong position in the food and fertilizer sectors. Following the 2023 summit, a pledge to provide free shipments of wheat to six African countries was fulfilled. In 2024, Russia delivered 200,000 tons of grain (valued at approximately $60 million) to Mali, Burkina Faso, Zimbabwe, Eritrea, Somalia, and the Central African Republic. The deliveries were made independently of any international organizations, which means Russia is establishing a sovereign infrastructure for food supplies to African nations and engages with importers directly.
The next phase of cooperation could focus on developing production capacities in African nations. The African Union’s agenda prioritizes fertilizer production, the storage and processing of agricultural products, mechanization, seed production, transport infrastructure, and enhancing local added value. Talks between Russia and the African Union in July 2026 addressed industrialization, the expansion of trade within the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and food security.
This approach aligns with the objectives of Agenda 2063 – the African Union’s development blueprint –which calls for the strengthening of national economies, fostering domestic production, creating jobs, and reducing reliance on external supplies. The AfCFTA, designed to dismantle trade barriers between the nations of the region and establish a unified market, supports these same goals. Within this framework, fertilizer production, raw material processing, the establishment of service centers, the assembly of machinery, and the training of local specialists help build a sustainable presence in markets.
Cooperation in the field of nuclear energy also offers long-term benefits. The construction of the El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant in Egypt is Russia’s largest infrastructure project on the African continent, generating long-term demand for technical support, fuel, personnel training, and maintenance services. In the humanitarian sphere, education plays a comparable role: tens of thousands of students from Africa are currently enrolled in Russian universities. Value is further amplified when educational programs are linked to specific economic projects.
African demand
The context for cooperation with Africa has also evolved. One of the most notable shifts has been the development of the AfCFTA. By 2026, 50 of the 54 signatory countries had ratified the agreement. The primary challenge now is to ensure that free trade becomes a practical reality. Participants have agreed to phase out tariffs on 90% of product categories – a process set to take five years for more developed economies and 10 years for the least developed nations.
Concurrently, the African Union has taken a more active role in coordinating relations with external partners. African governments are cultivating ties with China, the EU, the US, India, Türkiye, the Persian Gulf states, Japan, South Korea, and other countries. Such diversification has become standard foreign policy practice. For several nations, most notably those in the Sahel, Russia has emerged as a high-priority foreign policy partner.
The summit in St. Petersburg in 2023 demonstrated the autonomy of African diplomacy. Prior to the meeting, an African peace delegation visited Kiev and St. Petersburg, presenting their own proposals for resolving the conflict. African leaders raised concerns with the Russian leadership regarding food security and the impact of the hostilities on the continent’s economy. For Moscow, this may signal a need to engage with partners who maintain a broad range of foreign policy options.
The number of leaders attending the summit in fact only offers a limited perspective on the state of relations. A more meaningful indicator lies in the ongoing cooperation with the African Union Commission, the AfCFTA, regional economic communities, relevant government ministries, and private-sector companies.
What are instruments of sovereignty?
There are 54 countries in Africa, and all are very different. The pan-African format is most suitable for education and humanitarian cooperation, international coordination, and shared economic initiatives. Practical projects, however, are better implemented at the level of individual countries and sectors.
Russia’s experience in recent years highlights the value of stable regional powers with large economies and well-developed external ties – such as Egypt, Algeria, Morocco, South Africa, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and several others. Entering these markets, however, requires more thorough preparation and a solid understanding of local conditions. At the same time, the scale of these economies opens up opportunities for long-term projects. Such ventures can serve not only the market of a single country but may also supply neighboring states, gradually expanding the presence of Russian companies throughout the region.
Another promising direction is the exchange of experience in the field of technologies that expand the practical capabilities of the nation in management – generally referred to as “instruments of sovereignty.” In the agricultural sector, these are food reserve systems, the forecasting of climate risks and the storage and processing of products. In the digital sphere, it is data localization, government information systems, satellite communications and fiber optic infrastructure. In the extractive industry, it is geological exploration, personnel training, and regulatory instruments that stimulate the processing of raw materials in the country.
This approach is giving practical meaning to Russia’s rhetoric about sovereignty. Results can be measured by an increase in new capacities, trained specialists, a reduction in import dependence and an increase in the tax base.
What will the Moscow summit show?
The practical results of the summit may be assessed according to five parameters. First, the public assessment of the implementation of the 2023-2026 Action Plan (including by the African side) will reveal functioning aspects, delayed initiatives, and projects that require revision. Then comes the new 2027-2029 Action Plan: Its measurable objectives and realistic timelines will facilitate the work of relevant departments. Third is financial infrastructure: export lending, risk insurance, banking support, and working settlement mechanisms are important for business.
Another important point is deepening the economic presence: developing projects, service centers, processing, energy and digital infrastructure. Lastly there is country prioritization, which means that limited resources necessitate that projects be chosen with a clear economic or political effect.
The 2026 summit will essentially serve as an evaluation of Russia’s policy in Africa over the past seven years. This period allows us to separate functioning projects from initiatives that exist mainly as part of the public agenda. The next three-year cycle will show to what extent Russia can play to its strengths and build sustainable mechanisms for financing, trade, local production, personnel training, and constant interaction with African institutions.

Why Are Laws Vital to Ukraine’s EU Integration Stuck in Parliament as the Country Loses Money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:14:00 UTC
15:14:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky recently signed laws abolishing the VAT exemption for foreign parcels worth up to €150 ($168) and introduced taxation of income earned by users of digital platforms. All three documents returned to parliament with the president’s signature on Oct. 22 and all laws were adopted as part of the EU’s requirements. Their passage took substantial time due to being highly unpopular.
One such requirement was the taxation of parcels arriving from abroad. The problem is that such “parcels” often serve as a convenient way to ship large quantities of various goods from third countries, primarily China. Everything from drone components to cosmetics, clothing, children’s toys and auto parts was imported under the guise of parcels.
The law proved extremely unpopular, despite Ukrainians’ desire to join the EU. During wartime, as Ukrainians face enormous expenses on fuel, generators and any equipment that could help them cope with the war and Russian attacks, nobody wants to spend extra money. This is especially true in the case of taxes which, in the wake of recent corruption scandals, many people believe do not always go where they should.
This is only the beginning of a long and politically unpopular road for a government that is already struggling to secure public support and approval for its initiatives.
By the end of the year, the Verkhovna Rada must adopt around 32 more laws, while the government must meet more than 30 benchmarks. Key reforms being monitored by Ukraine’s partners are as follows:
It’s About Security, Stupid!
1. Reform of the State Bureau of Investigation (DBR) and the Security Service of Ukraine SBU) – two key state agencies involved in law enforcement and anti-corruption efforts and subject to the influence of the central authorities.
Draft Law No. 13602 concerns changes to the DBR’s head, the introduction of a transparent competition to select its director, the vetting of DBR employees, and the removal of several provisions that allow the President’s Office to influence the appointment of the agency’s head.
As for the SBU, the European Commission demands that it be stripped of functions that do not properly belong to a security service, particularly investigative powers, and that its activities focus on counterintelligence, counterterrorism, cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure.
2. Adoption of an anti-corruption strategy and reform of the High Anti-Corruption Court.
Draft Law No. 15230 is intended to close many loopholes that allow corruption suspects to manipulate proceedings before the High Anti-Corruption Court, including methods of deliberately delaying cases. The anti-corruption strategy, for example, envisages selecting the Prosecutor General through an open competition. At present, the president appoints the Prosecutor General.
3. Joining the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) – the EU’s integrated system for euro payments.
Draft Law No. 14327 explicitly provides for Ukraine’s accession to the single European payments area, which already includes 27 countries, including some that are not currently members of the Schengen Area.
Limited progress so far
The draft laws remain in parliamentary committees, and in some cases, one or two alternative versions have already been drafted alongside the original proposals.
European officials are losing patience.
For example, Ukraine reportedly risks losing a substantial amount of $29.5 billion in planned international aid financing if parliament misses deadlines for required legislation, according to Ukraine’s Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi.
The EU has moved to a new approach: no more advances. The law comes first, and the money follows. This applies to every required piece of legislation.
So, what is the problem if these reforms are intended to make Ukrainian state institutions more effective?
The reality is complicated so let’s examine the main reasons.
The draft laws are unfinished and poorly prepared
One reason is that some draft laws are still in a rough form and have not been adequately prepared. For example, the anti-corruption strategy was drafted by the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NACP), and some members of parliament have openly said it needs further work.
Some draft laws have been prepared by the government and still need to be brought into compliance with legislative requirements.
The three bills mentioned above are among the main priorities. And even the approximately 35 laws required by the end of the year are merely a warm-up. According to estimates by lawyers and members of parliament, between 9,000 and 11,000 provisions must ultimately be brought into line with EU legislation.
That is a huge amount of work in an environment where parliament is characterized by dysfunction.
Fear of the elites?
Strengthening anti-corruption efforts, eliminating procedural delays at the High Anti-Corruption Court, and joining the European payments system, are concerns for many members of parliament, influential financial and industrial groups, and their lobbyists.
Ukraine is a country with a transitional economy, moving from the Soviet command-and-administrative system to a market economy based on private ownership. Amid the chaos of this transition – accompanied by the deterioration of Soviet institutions and the weakness of the newly established state apparatus – large areas of economic activity were left without proper legal regulation, while others were subjected to excessive regulation. This has led to blatant abuses and chaos in the former case, and to the search for corrupt “loopholes” to resolve issues quickly in the latter.
Now, many people fear that past “sins,” income and payments could become a source of legal trouble.
The same problem arises in connection with the work of anti-corruption agencies. Ten years ago, converting commercial premises into an office or residential property without changing the designated use of the land or building was not a problem. Now it could be. Examples can be found everywhere, from villages to parliament itself.
Take lawmakers’ salaries, for example. Since Soviet times, these have been very low. In the USSR, members of parliament were largely nominal figures. The situation has remained much the same in independent Ukraine. No one has been eager to raise lawmakers’ salaries because doing so would be deeply unpopular, especially when pay does not increase significantly during wartime.
Yet lawmakers do not want to take responsibility for drafting laws worth billions for next to nothing. Alternatively, they may take on that responsibility but also expect “bonuses” for drafting such laws. These payments began to be made through political parties, in cash-filled envelopes.
Such practice constitutes a criminal offense, and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) has drawn up dozens of cases against members of parliament involving precisely this practice.
Yet the problem remains unresolved. Raising lawmakers’ salaries is politically unprofitable because it is unpopular, while they are unwilling to vote for government-backed bills for $1,000 – especially when those bills could potentially make their own lives more difficult.
A question of power and stability
Reforming the DBR, the SBU and the Prosecutor General’s Office runs up against rivalry among various law enforcement agencies. Through 35 years of independence, an informal division of responsibilities and a system of “checks and balances” have developed among them.
Any changes are interpreted by each agency as an attempt to increase or expand the powers of its “competitors.”
Adding fuel to the fire is the fact that both the DBR and the SBU fall under the president’s sphere of influence and strengthen his power. The president personally appoints the heads of these agencies. Critics argue that the DBR is sometimes used as an instrument of political pressure against the authorities’ opponents, since its jurisdiction includes top officials, members of parliament and judges.
Would President Zelensky want to relinquish his influence over law enforcement agencies? That seems unlikely, as this is not merely about maintaining control over the situation – from surveillance of journalists, as happened with the SBU in 2023, to carrying out the president’s instructions, particularly those of his inner circle.
It is also a question of state stability. With NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) outside the president’s direct sphere of influence, many people both on Bankova Street and in the Cabinet of Ministers fear that any redistribution of powers among the agencies could trigger another political crisis.
‘Europe does not want us, so why should we want Europe?’
One argument against these initiatives is Euroscepticism. Ukraine has long been “fed” promises of EU membership, with the prospect of accession repeatedly pushed further into the future. Meanwhile, some countries admitted to the EU between the late 1990s and the mid-2000s were in no better condition than Ukraine is today in terms of legislation and the effectiveness of their state institutions.
This fuels a sense among many Ukrainians that the EU is simply stringing Ukraine along with empty promises.
Kyiv Post once asked a member of the European Parliament, “When will Ukraine become an EU member?”
“Immediately after Turkey,” the lawmaker replied optimistically.
“And when will Turkey join?”
“Never!”
That was 20 years ago, and the situation has still not changed. As a result, many people from different social backgrounds believe that reshaping the country to satisfy the EU – which, in their view, Ukraine will not join anytime soon, if ever – may not be worth the effort.
Ukraine’s parliament will continue its work, yet – for now at least – not on the EU-needed Bills.

AI model uses face photos to estimate biological age, predict survival risk in cancer patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:12:21 UTC
15:12:21 KST

Patients in the highest AI-assessed risk group had more than three times the mortality risk of those in the lowest-risk group, study finds
NEW DELHI: A photograph of the face could one day help doctors assess how old a person appears biologically and estimate survival risk in cancer patients, according to a new artificial intelligence (AI) model developed by researchers and tested in separate groups of patients.The model, called Foundation Artificial Intelligence for Health Recognition-Face (FAHR-Face), was trained on more than 40 million facial photographs and adapted for two tasks — estimating biological age, or how old a person appears to be physically, and predicting the risk of death. The findings were published in The Lancet Digital Health in 2026.When tested on publicly available photographs, the AI model estimated biological age with an average error of about five years. Among 38,183 patients treated at six US centres affiliated with Harvard, those who appeared biologically older than their actual age tended to have poorer survival outcomes.A second AI model, FAHR-FaceSurvival, was trained on photographs of 34,363 cancer patients and tested on another 3,820. Patients classified in the highest-risk group were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest-risk group, even after researchers accounted for other factors, including patients’ clinical characteristics and demographic details.
The researchers also tested the models on 4,892 cancer patients treated in the Netherlands. The results suggested that the AI could help estimate survival risk in patients beyond the original US group.Dr Mandeep Singh Malhotra, director of surgical oncology at the CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said the approach was an interesting development, but its reliability in India needed to be established.“An important consideration is whether this facial recognition AI can deliver equally reliable results in the Indian population, given our distinct epidemiological profile and diverse facial features. This remains to be established,” he said.Malhotra said the technology could eventually complement precision oncology if combined with genomic testing and other diagnostic techniques, including liquid biopsy. Such an approach, he said, could potentially improve predictions of cancer survival, help detect recurrence earlier and enable timely intervention.
“Rather than viewing it as a standalone technique, its potential may lie in complementing established diagnostic approaches, including genomics and liquid biopsy, as part of a more comprehensive, personalised approach to cancer care,” he said.The two AI models appeared to identify different aspects of health-related information from facial photographs. Using them together improved the accuracy of survival-risk estimates, suggesting that facial analysis could eventually complement existing tools doctors use to assess patients and plan treatment.However, the model cannot diagnose cancer or predict an individual’s lifespan. Since the study mainly involved patients in the US and the Netherlands, its findings may not apply to other populations. Lighting, image quality and facial expressions may also affect estimates. Further validation is needed before the technology can be used routinely in clinical practice.

She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

The index has stayed below zero since the second quarter of 2025, hinting that lenders willing to tighten loan standards outnumbered those willing to ease them.
The index for large corporations dropped from zero in the third quarter to minus 8 in the fourth quarter, while the index for small firms was unchanged at minus 19.
The broad squeeze was driven by global macroeconomic headwinds and recent weakness in loan soundness.
The index for mortgage loans to households rebounded from minus 17 to zero in the cited period, but the reading for other loans to households, such as credit loans, recorded minus 8 in the fourth quarter.
The BOK delivered its back-to-back policy rate hikes in July and August to 3.00 percent, hinting at further monetary tightening later this year or early next year.
The credit risk index for households increased from 19 in the third quarter to 28 in the fourth quarter.
The index for big companies rose from 3 to 6 in the cited period, but the figure for small firms declined from 33 to 31. ■

Who are the leading candidates in Israel’s election on Oct 27?

AI generated
JERUSALEM – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long looked on course to lose power in Israel’s election, but the race has narrowed as the vote approaches and his rivals have no clear path to power.
Votes will be cast on Oct 27 for parties, and seats in Parliament will be allocated to individuals on party lists according to proportional representation.
Here are details of some of the leading candidates in Israel's first parliamentary election since the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, that plunged the Middle East into turmoil, with Israel going to war in Lebanon and Gaza and launching air strikes against Iran.
Benjamin Netanyahu
In power for much of the time since 2009, after a first stint as prime minister in the 1990s, Netanyahu has become the face of Israel abroad and a polarising figure at home.
Supporters hail Netanyahu as “King Bibi” and see him as the strong leader Israel needs to defend itself in a hostile region.
But, wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes in Gaza which he rejects and on trial in Israel on corruption charges which he denies, he is fighting for his political life.
Opinion polls have pointed to a sharp drop for his Likud party since the Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which shattered Netanyahu’s security credentials.
His government’s policies on matters of religion and state have also been unpopular among many Israelis.
But Netanyahu, 77, is a consummate political survivor. He has said he wants to form a “broad national” government after the election, if he wins. In the event of a stalemate, he could remain a caretaker prime minister for many months.
Netanyahu’s top rivals
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who lost a son in Gaza combat, heads a new centrist party called Yashar, Hebrew for “straight” or “honest”.
Eisenkot, 66, has projected an image as a political outsider, soldier and security hawk whose humble background and family sacrifices stand in vivid contrast to Netanyahu’s decades in high office and lingering corruption cases.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, 54, a right-wing former commando, former Netanyahu aide and high-tech millionaire, has joined forces with centrist former premier Yair Lapid.
Their new party is called Together and its messages have focused on healing a traumatised nation and getting the country back on track. Their alliance, despite being on opposite ends of the political spectrum, ousted Netanyahu in a 2021 election.
Former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman, 68, was once a close ally of Netanyahu.
Even more hawkish than his former boss, Lieberman quit Netanyahu’s government in 2018, accusing the prime minister of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza, and has become one of Netanyahu’s sharpest critics.
His party, Israel Our Home, draws much of its support from the country’s ex-Soviet immigrant community.
Former general Yair Golan, 64, hailed for his rescue of people from one of the Hamas Oct 7 attack sites, leads the Democrats, founded on the moribund remnants of Israel’s historical Labour party and smaller left-wing Meretz.
Candidates on Netanyahu’s side
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, have both drawn intense international scrutiny for their far-right policies towards the Palestinians.
Smotrich has spearheaded Israel’s rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs, has promoted capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants, toughened prison conditions for jailed Palestinians and easier gun ownership for Israelis.
Both men have advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and Israel resettling the enclave.
Ultra-Orthodox allies
Netanyahu has relied on two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, for his political survival for years.
Their demands for their community to be mostly exempt from compulsory military service, along with their low participation in the workforce and reliance on state benefits, have angered many Israelis, all the more so at a time of war.
Potential key players
Parties which are not clearly aligned with either side could tip the balance in favour of Netanyahu or his rivals.
They include Raam and the Joint List, the two parties that represent Israel’s 20% Arab minority.
Along with them are a new right-wing party called People of Israel and a centre-right party called The Reservists, both of which have been wavering in opinion polls. REUTERS

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a 72-million-U.S.-dollar financing package to help Cambodia strengthen rural farming and increase women's participation in agriculture, according to its press release on Monday.
The financing consists of a 57-million-dollar concessional loan and a 15-million-dollar grant, the press release said, adding that the Smallholder Resilient Economic Development Sector Project will enhance the resilience of about 200,000 smallholder farmers in disaster-prone communes.
"Investing in smallholder farmers, particularly women, is essential for boosting the rural economy and supporting poor communities that are most vulnerable to extreme weather events," said ADB Country Director for Cambodia Yasmin Siddiqi.
"By helping women lead and participate in local decision-making and development programs, this project will scale up inclusive agricultural value chains and strengthen food systems, while driving women-led businesses and supporting families to build healthier, more secure, and resilient futures," she added.
Overlapping natural hazards such as heatwaves, drought, and flooding acutely impact Cambodia's agriculture and food systems, damaging infrastructure, limiting market access, and exacerbating food insecurity, particularly in rural areas where 59 percent of the country's population lives, the press release said.
Women, representing 51 percent of Cambodia's agricultural labor force, remain among the most vulnerable as they face limited access to economic opportunities, support, and financing, it added.
The project will upgrade agricultural infrastructure and services across 186 communes in seven provinces severely vulnerable to natural hazards, it said, adding that it will modernize irrigation systems to serve an additional 7,000 hectares of farmland and rehabilitate 190 kilometers of access roads to connect farmers to markets, jobs, and opportunities.
"The project will provide farmers with technical support and training to upgrade their skills and adopt resilient practices in crop production, horticulture, poultry, insect farming, and aquaculture," the press release said. "It will offer grants to help farmers reduce dependence on imported fuel and fertilizers and boost their resilience to disasters and global shocks." ■

Cooler than Tokyo: Sendai named Japan’s most comfortable city amid record heat

2-MIN READ2-MIN

As days of dangerous heat become more frequent in Japan, Sendai has emerged as the most comfortable city, with a climate that is “not too hot and not too cold”.
The Miyagi prefectural capital, about 300km (186 miles) from Tokyo, has the best weather, according to the Asahi newspaper, with the lowest number of midsummer and midwinter days among 11 major cities in the nation.
Citing Japan Meteorological Agency data, the newspaper reported that Sendai had only 31 midsummer days and no midwinter days between September 2025 and August this year. Midsummer days are logged when the temperature goes above 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), while midwinter days are when it falls below 0 degrees.

France's debt woes in focus as ECB meets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:05:02 UTC
15:05:02 KST

European Central Bank (ECB) headquarters is pictured behind a construction site in Frankfurt am Main, western Germany, on October 23, 2026. (AFP Photo)
France's deteriorating public finances will take center stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.
The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Oct. 29’s meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fueled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading — but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded, "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at the Oct. 29 meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5 percent.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the U.S. central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, although closely watched core inflation — excluding volatile energy and food prices — hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task."
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.

Insurance company adds 'war risk' protection without customers' consent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:03:00 UTC
15:03:00 KST

Insurance company adds 'war risk' protection without customers' consent
Insurance companies have begun offering coverage for war-related risks, such as damage caused by drones or missiles, but in some cases, fees have increased without customers' consent.
Seesam Insurance customers recently received an unpleasant surprise when their home insurance premiums increased overnight.
For example, a customer insuring a 200-square-meter property received an offer requiring them to pay €245 a year instead of the previous €190 – an increase of nearly 30 percent.
The reason was a new charge for coverage against war-related risks.
Indrek Petter, head of the insurance department at Seesam Insurance, said coverage against war-related risks primarily protects people's homes against explosions caused by stray military drones, missiles, shells and mines.
He explained that the monthly premium is around €1 for smaller apartments and around €3 for an average detached house. "It depends on the size of the house," Petter noted.
Customers must opt out themselves
The change was introduced by default, without asking for consent. Customers must now notify the company themselves if they wish to opt out.
"We add it to the insurance offer. Generally, the customer reviews it and consults their account manager or salesperson," Petter said. He added that this should then lead to a discussion about whether the customer wishes to opt out of coverage against war-related risks.
The company began offering war insurance following events in the spring, when Ukrainian drones started appearing in Estonian airspace after being knocked off course.
But several other insurance companies are moving in the same direction.
Swedbank and Elama Insurance also offer compensation for war-related damage, but their customers do not have to pay an additional fee. The new terms will take effect this week.
Hardi Saarniit, head of home insurance products at insurance company If, said that average insurance premiums may eventually change, but the company does not charge extra for compensation for war-related damage.
Coverage does not apply during a state of war
He explained that their coverage is intended for the current situation, in which Russia and Ukraine are at war and drones also stray into Estonian airspace.
"If the situation were to change, for example, if a state of war were declared in Estonia, then this coverage would no longer apply," Saarniit noted.
The Estonian Insurance Association hopes prices will not rise with the new terms.
Lauri Potsepp, a board member of the Estonian Insurance Association, said that insurance is moving toward packages tailored as precisely as possible to customers' interests and needs.
"In other words, individual customers are offered coverage for the risks they are interested in, and this makes it possible to keep insurance prices under control so that insurers remain competitive," he said.
Insurance providers are not the only sector using war risks to push up prices. Last week, ERR reported that utility providers are also raising prices due to increased security risks.

First international flight takes off from new Sydney airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:01:34 UTC
15:01:34 KST

Passengers board an Air New Zealand aircraft operating the first international departure from the newly-opened Western Sydney International Airport in Sydney on October 26, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The first international flight took off on Oct. 26 from a new, multi-billion-dollar airport in the fast-growing western suburbs of Sydney.
After more than four decades of planning, Western Sydney International Airport offers the first alternative to the city's main airport, which has been operating for more than a century.
An Air New Zealand plane from Auckland landed and soon afterwards flew out of the airport in the morning, launching a three-flights-a-week service to Sydney's largely working-class western suburbs.
The new single-runway airport, Australia's first new major aviation hub in more than five decades, began domestic flights on Oct. 25, and freight operations in July.
Sydney's main airport, Kingsford Smith, is Australia's busiest, its three runways handling more than 42 million passengers last year.
Lying in Botany Bay just nine kilometres (six miles) from the city center, planes using the airport roar over many city homes, and a curfew bars passenger aircraft from operating during the night.
The new airport in western Sydney has no such restrictions.
Qantas' budget carrier Jetstar is now the main domestic carrier, flying to the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane.
The airport says other international carriers are coming, including Qatar Airways from December 2027, Fiji Airways from March 2027, and Vietjet Air from January 2027.
Built at a cost of AUS$5.3 billion ($3.7 billion), excluding surrounding transport works, the airport is reachable by road but is not expected to have a direct rail link until at least December 2027.

Demand for travel to Klaipeda remains strong in the off-season: Lux Express extends services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:44 UTC
15:00:44 KST

Lux Express is extending its Riga–Liepaja–Palanga–Klaipeda route until 3 January 2027 as passenger demand remains strong beyond the summer season. The route was initially planned as a seasonal service, but Lux Express data show that overall demand is currently at a similar level to May, while passenger numbers between Riga and Klaipeda have increased by 16%.
Steady demand has allowed Lux Express to extend the route for the second time. In August, services were extended until 25 October, and they will now continue until 3 January, providing connections over the year-end and New Year holiday period.
“After the summer season, we expected passenger numbers to decline, but the actual demand has been a positive surprise. It shows that interest in travelling to the Lithuanian coast does not end with the summer holidays. We have therefore decided to continue the service until early January, providing a convenient connection between cities in Latvia and Lithuania throughout the autumn and winter months,” says Aldis Ķibēns, Management Board Member of Lux Express Latvia.
Riga increasingly serves as a starting point for travel across the Baltics
While Latvian and Lithuanian residents continue to make up the largest passenger groups on the route, Lux Express is also seeing growing interest from international tourists. Travellers from Germany stand out in particular, with their number increasing by 8% this year compared with 2025.
“Our data show that Riga is increasingly becoming a starting point for international tourists who want to explore more of the Baltics. People arrive in the Latvian capital and then travel on to other cities, including Liepaja and Klaipeda. This change in travel patterns is a positive sign not only for transport operators but also for regional tourism, as it helps attract visitors beyond the traditional summer season,” says Ķibēns.
For now, Lux Express continues to operate the route as a seasonal service but, depending on passenger demand, does not rule out running it year-round in the future.
Services will continue on the existing timetable
The Riga–Liepaja–Palanga–Klaipeda route will continue to operate once a day in each direction, with the current timetable remaining unchanged.
From Monday to Saturday, buses depart Riga Bus Station at 7.00 and Liepaja Bus Station at 10.30. On Sundays, departures are scheduled for 11.30 from Riga and 15.00 from Liepaja. From Klaipeda Bus Station, buses depart at 12.55 from Monday to Saturday and at 17.10 on Sundays.
The journey from Riga to Klaipeda takes approximately 5 hours and 10 minutes, while the journey from Liepaja to Klaipeda takes around 1 hour and 40 minutes.
Tickets for travel until 3 January 2027 are already on sale, with ticket prices remaining unchanged. Tickets are available at luxexpress.lv and via the Lux Express mobile app.
About Lux Express
Lux Express Group is an international coach operator providing long-distance services to major cities across the Baltics and to Warsaw, as well as domestic passenger services in Latvia and Estonia. The company operates a fleet of 105 high-comfort coaches. Last year, Lux Express Group marked 30 years of operations in Latvia and is the international coach operator with the longest track record in the Latvian market.

'Having money is not enough': Why a job no longer guarantees access to housing in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:41 UTC
15:00:41 KST

House prices rose 84.6% between 2015 and 2025, against 27.85% for average wages. Lack of affordable housing, rent burdens and saving difficulties deepen the crisis as experts call for structural reform.
In Spain, having a job no longer guarantees being able to access housing. The increase in property and rental prices in recent years, far outpacing wage growth, makes it difficult both to pay a mortgage and to save up enough for a deposit.
This is a gap that particularly – though not exclusively – affects young people and low- and middle-income households and that, in recent weeks, has placed access to housing at the centre of social and political debate, to the point that Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opted to bring forward the general election after failing to secure approval in Congress for a set of urgent measures aimed at addressing the discontent felt on the streets.
"The problem is essentially structural," says Rafael Pampillón, professor of Applied Economics at San Pablo-CEU University in Madrid, who acknowledges that the current gap between wages and the high cost of rents and mortgages "makes it harder to access housing" and emphasises that "having money for the deposit is not enough".
According to data from the National Statistics Institute (INE), housing prices rose by 84.6% between 2015 and 2025, while average annual gross wages increased by 27.85% between 2015 and 2024, reaching 29,540 euros. Wages agreed in collective bargaining went up by around 27% over the same period.
The gap persists today. Housing prices climbed 12.2% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, compared with average wage increases of between 3% and 4%, according to figures cited by the Ministry of Labour. Housing is becoming more expensive at a pace that earnings from work cannot keep up with.
A recent study by Oxfam Intermón, presented last week, warns that housing costs have pushed the in-work poverty rate up to 15.49%, affecting around 770,000 people across the country. According to the report, one in three working people who rent at market prices falls into poverty after paying the rent. The rate stands at 34.08%, compared with 10.22% among those paying a mortgage and 7.95% among those who own their home outright.
"Evictions are the most extreme face of the housing crisis, but not the only one," argues Oxfam Intermón's head of housing, employment and social policies, Alejandro García-Gil. "There is another, less visible reality: people who are working and just about manage to pay for their home every month, but who, once they have done so, do not have enough income left to sustain a decent standard of living."
Rent, a cost that makes buying harder
The problem is not limited to purchase prices. According to the latest annual report from the Bank of Spain, four in ten households living in rented accommodation face an excessive financial burden, spending more than 40% of their income on rent. In major cities and areas most exposed to tourism, pressure on prices further aggravates these difficulties.
"These access problems are compounded by the fact that housing prices have risen more than household income, which has increased the effort required and tightened the conditions for buying a home in Spain to a greater extent than in the large European economies," the document notes.
Rent also creates a barrier for those hoping to buy a home. Although in some cases a mortgage instalment could be more affordable than a monthly rent payment, putting together the money needed to qualify for a loan becomes increasingly difficult when a substantial share of wages goes on rent, explains Pampillón, who reiterates that "having money for the deposit is not enough".
"A pay packet allows you to meet monthly payments, but buying a home requires a large upfront payment to purchase a flat, for which you need to have built up considerable savings," says the economist, who also holds a doctorate in Economic and Business Sciences from the University of Barcelona and an MBA from IESE. "The longer it takes to save up the deposit, the more years you continue paying rent."
With an average home price of around 200,000 euros, a buyer needs approximately 60,000 euros to cover the deposit and the costs associated with the purchase. Without the ability to save, Pampillón adds, family support is often the only way to "break that circle". "Those who do not have it have to travel a much longer road. In this way, family wealth – together with generous pensions – is playing an ever bigger role in shaping children's opportunities," he laments.
In this respect, the difficulty of leaving the parental home reflects a growing inequality between those who can draw on family resources and those who depend solely on their wages. Since 2008, the share of households that do not own their home has risen by 45%, according to the National Statistics Institute's Survey of Living Conditions.
A structural problem that goes beyond wages
The fall in pay during the financial crisis, slower wage recovery and the arrival of investment funds in the property market have all helped widen this gap. On top of that comes a shortage of supply: between 2021 and 2025 an estimated deficit of around 750,000 homes built up, according to the Bank of Spain. In 2025, around 225,000 households were formed, while some 92,000 new homes were completed.
Despite the impact of this divide, many experts warn that the mismatch between incomes and housing will not be solved by wage rises alone. "Employment has always been seen as the best tool against poverty, and this analysis shows that having a job is not enough," notes García-Gil, referring to the Oxfam Intermón study.
The European Commission is blunt in its assessment of the sector's situation: "The housing sector in Spain faces deeply rooted structural challenges. The Spanish property market shows a severe mismatch between supply and demand, coupled with a lack of a substantial stock of affordable and social housing, including social rental options."
Faced with the current situation, the trade unions CC.OO. and UGT have called a 24-hour general strike on 11 November, under the slogan "wages, housing, prices", with which they hope to channel the social discontent generated by this crisis in Spain, especially in the wake of the eviction – and subsequent death – of Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who died in early October after being forced out of her home days earlier.
"Under the current conditions there is no wage or collective agreement that can allow us to access housing," recently said the UGT general secretary, Pepe Álvarez, speaking to the media. "We cannot continue for much longer with a situation in which it is practically impossible for the vast majority of workers in our country – with the wages we have – to access housing, whether to rent or to buy."
Both unions are demanding at least a 7% increase in the statutory minimum wage in 2027, taking it above 1,300 euros in 14 instalments. However, Unai Sordo, the CC.OO. general secretary, acknowledges the limits of wage policies in the face of surging property prices.
"There is no wage policy in any country in the world capable of dealing with the outrageous situation of increasing housing prices by 12% year-on-year," the union leader stated in a statement dated 13 October.
The organisation proposes allocating at least 1% of annual gross domestic product (GDP) to public housing for a decade and is calling for measures to curb speculation and rein in rising property prices.
In this regard, Pampillón also calls for reforms that go far beyond a simple pay rise, which in the end would itself require "more productive companies, investment and jobs that generate greater added value", and he stresses that one of the main problems is that "housing demand is rising much faster than the time it takes to build".
"Economic policy must address wages, but above all the supply of housing," the professor argues. "We need to make it easier to build where there is demand: ensure land is available for development, speed up permits, coordinate infrastructure and cut procedures that add costs without providing effective protection."
In any case, if there is one point on which all those involved agree – the political class, unions, experts and, more broadly, most of the population – it is that Spain's housing crisis is a structural problem, with few short-term solutions and one that requires much broader long-term planning.

Higher training costs for older workers risks plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis.
The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead.
Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed.
The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country.
However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive.
“It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK.
“We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.
Calling on Healey to “break the cycle” of cutting and reallocating the apprenticeship budget in England, Halfon said the system was already struggling to deliver what businesses and young people need.
“If the government is serious about getting young people into good jobs and giving industry the skills it needs, it should use that opportunity to grow the number of apprenticeships available rather than restrict training elsewhere.”
Andy Burnham has placed youth jobs at the heart of his agenda, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and plans to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.
With over-25s accounting for more than half of new apprenticeship enrolments, ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the system towards supporting more younger people.
Under the latest proposal, which is yet to be finalised, employers would be able to fund the full cost of an apprentice under the age of 25 using the money they contribute to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn-a-year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system.
However, for an older worker, they would face a “co-investment rule” whereby levy funds would cover 75% of the costs. The rest would need to be covered separately.
Employers have for years been told they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
John Foster, the chief policy and campaigns officer at the CBI lobby group, said: “We can’t make skills a zero-sum game.
“While it is right to focus on supporting young people who are Neet into work, adult training also has a vital role to play in opening up entry-level opportunities and helping people adapt and update their skills mid-career, particularly as AI reshapes the workplace.”
Ben Rowland, the chief executive of the Association of Employment and Learning Providers, said: “The key to any further changes to the apprenticeship system is to bring employers on the journey. Anything that is too abrupt or too quick significantly endangers that.”
Business leaders have been pressing Healey to use Wednesday’s budget to provide support with soaring costs amid the war in the Middle East, and have urged the chancellor not to add to the pressure on firms after Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions.
Kate Shoesmith, the director of policy and insights at the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “At a time when businesses are under pressure to improve productivity and drive growth, employers need greater flexibility and support to invest in skills at every stage of a person’s career.
“The best way to encourage more youth apprenticeships is to make it easier and more affordable for firms to take on young people by reducing the wider costs of doing business, rather than creating new barriers to training.”
Labour has been told its youth skills strategy risks failure without reform, after just 160 young people were enrolled into its foundation apprenticeship scheme in the first eight months. Ministers have an ambition for 30,000 starts over the current parliament.
Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, said that while flexibility was important for business, the current system was skewed too heavily towards funding older, often already highly qualified workers.
“These will not be easy decisions, and some will be unpopular with businesses. But tackling youth unemployment means making difficult choices about where public funding is spent.”
A government spokesperson said: “It’s right that we focus on reversing the 40% decline in the number of young people starting an apprenticeship and give them the skills they need to succeed.
“That’s why we have reformed the system backed by £3.3bn to deliver 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people and support employers with a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16- to 24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn Review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report.
The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly.
Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead.
In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle. It is a significant safety concern because it can impair pilots’ judgment, slow their reactions, reduce alertness and impair responses to unexpected situations.
Under European aviation safety regulations, airlines are required to have systems in place to identify, monitor and manage crew fatigue.
The survey, conducted in August, found that three-quarters of respondents had experienced at least one microsleep – a brief, involuntary episode of sleep – while operating an aircraft in the previous four weeks.
Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta reported the highest levels of microsleeps. More than a third said they were not getting enough rest to prevent fatigue from building up over time.
Despite the prevalence of exhaustion, only one in three pilots said they usually reported themselves unfit for duty when fatigued. Half admitted they had operated a flight in the three months before the survey when they should have declared themselves too fatigued to fly.
Almost half of the respondents said they feared negative consequences from management if they reported themselves unfit because of fatigue, while just 11.9% trusted their airline’s fatigue reporting system.
Ian Holder, the managing director of the aviation safety consultancy Baines Simmons, said the results showed persistent differences in how airlines and national authorities manage fatigue. “This survey captures how European pilots experience fatigue risk management in practice,” he said.
He stressed that the findings represented pilots’ first-hand experiences rather than a direct measurement of aviation safety outcomes, but said the consistency of the results over three years highlighted areas requiring attention.
Holder pointed to Finland and the Netherlands as evidence that stronger fatigue reporting cultures were achievable.
Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear management reprisals and the least likely to trust the reporting systems.
The proportion of pilots who said they would fly when fatigued was higher in Spain, Ireland and France. Two in five of the pilots working for airlines based in Spain and a third of those working for Ireland- and France-based airlines said they usually fly when fatigued. That compares with only one in 10 of the pilots flying for an airline based in the UK.
Only 15.6% of pilots at low-cost carriers believed their airline managed fatigue risks well, compared with 18.6% at ACMI or wet-lease operators – companies that supply aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance to other airlines.
Almost two in five pilots said they had used commander’s discretion – allowing captains to extend crew working hours or reduce rest periods in exceptional circumstances – at least once in the month before the survey.
But nearly 70% expressed concern about refusing to extend their duty, suggesting that a measure intended for exceptional situations may be accompanied by significant pressure on flight crews.
Pilots at low-cost and wet-lease operators, as well as those working for airlines registered in Ireland and Malta, reported the greatest concerns.
Capt Tanja Harter, the president of the ECA, said airlines and regulators should take responsibility rather than leaving pilots to manage the risks themselves.
“This cannot be simply left to us – the pilots – to manage, while we are on the flight deck and expected to bring our passengers safely to their destination,” she said.
She urged the European Union Aviation Safety Agency to strengthen fatigue management rules and ensure airlines comply with requirements for non-punitive reporting and the proper use of commander’s discretion.
“Waiting for another three years to discover that nothing has changed is simply not an option,” Harter said.
“The problems are identified, solutions are there, and we as the European pilot community are ready to contribute. What is needed now is the political will to act.”

We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

At around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.
Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.
That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible 1% of the UK’s total economic output in 2022.
But in recent years this iconic street has started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.
If we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.
People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.
That’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.
And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.
Of course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.
Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.
- Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London
