Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:30:27 UTC
14:30:27 KST

Russia is escalating its confrontation with the West in orbit. Its satellites are pursuing spacecraft from companies helping Ukraine — and Starlink has been put on notice.
There has long been talk of “hunter” satellites and an intensifying confrontation in space between Russia and the United States. But this week brought an unprecedented escalation in the new “star wars.” On October 18, a Russian inspector satellite came closer than ever to a spacecraft operated by the Finnish-American company ICEYE. The company openly helps Ukraine, giving its armed forces access to satellite images of Russian military facilities, including airfields, naval ports, and oil refineries. Here’s what we know about the exceptionally close encounter, how Moscow is describing it, and why independent experts are alarmed.
Russian Kosmos satellites have pursued this spacecraft before, but never like this
Overnight into October 18, the Russian satellite Kosmos-2612 approached the radar imaging satellite ICEYE-X36 after a series of maneuvers that began four days earlier. The Ukrainian military uses data from the ICEYE satellite.
This was not their first close encounter. In the spring, four Russian spacecraft were “hunting” this same satellite: Kosmos-2612, 2610, 2611, and 2613 all approached it. Earlier, in February, news outlets reported on maneuvers by Luch spacecraft pursuing telecommunications satellites operated by Intelsat and Eutelsat.
This time, Kosmos-2612 came exceptionally close to its target: hundreds or even tens of meters away, rather than tens of kilometers as before. Observational astronomer Marco Langbroek estimates that at their closest approach, at 1:35 a.m. GMT on October 18, the spacecraft were between 26 and 470 meters apart. Measurement errors make a more precise estimate impossible. Bart Hendrickx, an independent researcher of Russia’s space program, told Meduza that he knew of no previous encounter at such close range in low Earth orbit. In earlier encounters, he said, satellites had remained at least several dozen kilometers apart.
He said the complexity and methodical persistence of the maneuvers by Kosmos-2612 and its fellow satellites, numbered 2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614, were also surprising. All these spacecraft, along with satellite 2609, were launched aboard a single rocket from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on April 16.
“The satellites used a considerable amount of fuel on these maneuvers. By May, it was already clear that these weren’t ordinary Earth-observation and communications satellites, which generally conserve their fuel. Perhaps [through this latest escalation] Russia is demonstrating its ability to change orbits quickly and unpredictably to threaten enemy satellites,” Hendrickx said.
Moscow calls these maneuvers “a tool of strategic deterrence” and a warning to commercial companies
The Russian military previously acknowledged launching inspector satellites but said their sole purpose was “monitoring the condition of Russian satellites” — and said they had carried out such monitoring. Now, following Kosmos-2612’s dangerous maneuvers, the government newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta has published an article by Yuri Knutov, a military expert, retired colonel, and director of the Air Defense Forces Museum in Balashikha, outside Moscow. The article says Russia’s actions “do not violate international law” and that the inspector satellites themselves are “a tool of strategic deterrence.”
“Russia is demonstrating its ability to ‘blind’ or at least identify sources of threats. The approach to ICEYE-X36 sends a clear signal: Any commercial company making its capabilities available for intelligence gathering against Russia must recognize that its spacecraft may be subjected to forced inspection in orbit,” Knutov wrote. He said both ICEYE satellites and the Starlink constellation, which is critical to Ukrainian military command and communications, had effectively become part of NATO’s intelligence apparatus.
Like analyst Georgy Trishkin, whose views we quoted here, Knutov believes the Kosmos maneuvers were intended to force the ICEYE satellite to take evasive action to avoid a collision and quickly use up its fuel, turning it into “a useless piece of metal that will eventually burn up in the upper atmosphere.”
Knutov said the Russian satellites were less vulnerable to such a tactic because modern inspector spacecraft have much larger fuel reserves than their predecessors. Earlier models could perform only two or three orbital maneuvers before running out of fuel, he said, whereas newer satellites can remain in orbit for extended periods, carry out complex close approaches, and track other spacecraft over long stretches.
This latest episode in the space cold war was clearly visible from Earth. On Monday, Spaceweather.com asked whether the close encounter between Kosmos and ICEYE would be visible through binoculars or a backyard telescope. By Tuesday, it had its answer: yes.
This image, taken by the Swiss company s2a systems, shows the encounter. The bright object in front is the ICEYE-X36 radar satellite. Its apparent magnitude is about 7, making it invisible to the naked eye but easy to see through binoculars or an amateur telescope. The fainter object behind it is Kosmos-2612.
Russia isn’t the only country with space programs like these
Other countries, particularly the United States and China, have their own programs to develop inspector satellites. These spacecraft are designed to approach other objects in space that aren’t built for such encounters — those without docking ports, for example. These approaches can have various purposes: intercepting radio transmissions, inspecting another spacecraft, diagnosing problems, or even destroying it.
Militaries initiated and funded nearly all of these programs, so the public first learned they existed from amateur astronomers tracking the strange behavior of uncataloged satellites. Since 2011, when these observers identified an American satellite nicknamed Prowler this way, dozens more inspector satellites and many cases of pursuit have been detected, most involving Russian spacecraft.
Russian satellite maneuvers are easier to track because of censorship in the Pentagon’s main space catalog
Unequal access to information partly explains this pattern of observations. The U.S. military maintains Space-Track, the main publicly accessible catalog of artificial objects in space. It withholds the full orbital parameters of some U.S. military and intelligence satellites or publishes them with a delay. Until 2018, the Pentagon even classified data on civilian spacecraft launched as secondary payloads alongside military ones.
The U.S. military does not conceal Russian satellites’ orbital data, so anyone with the relevant skills can use the available data to plot their movements rather than track them through a telescope.
In 2018, the State Department protested the “very abnormal behavior” of Russian satellites. The U.S. military has protested their “threatening” maneuvers and anti-satellite weapons tests (we wrote about these nesting-doll satellites). Then, in 2024, Washington accused Moscow of preparing to deploy nuclear weapons in space.
Yet the United States has operated GSSAP satellites since 2014. These are essentially the same kind of inspector satellites, used to monitor satellites in geostationary orbit. And in June 2026, the U.S. military launched Jackal, built by True Anomaly, and Puma, made by Rocket Lab, as part of the Victus Haze exercise to practice space “hunting” scenarios.
In September of this year, the Pentagon acknowledged for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space — both kinetic and nonkinetic. The next few years in Earth orbit will clearly be tense.
Inspector satellites are also being developed for entirely civilian purposes. One example is LINK, a spacecraft meant to attempt a rescue of the Swift space telescope, but its mission ended in failure.
It’s hard to predict what the Kosmos satellites will do next
What happens next depends largely on how much fuel the Russian satellites have left. They may continue maneuvering around ICEYE spacecraft. According to Langbroek, as of midday on October 21, Kosmos-2612 had stopped moving away from its target and was holding at a distance of 480 kilometers. Hendrickx cautioned that the pursuit might not be over: Kosmos-2612 could return if it had enough fuel. He also pointed to four other Russian satellites launched alongside it — Kosmos-2610, 2611, 2613, and 2614 — that operate in similar orbits and probably have the same mission. Both ICEYE-X36 and ICEYE-X37 could be targets, he said.

Stefano Boeri Architetti Selected to Transform Former Locomotive Factory into Green Neighbourhood in Tbilisi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The LOCO Alliance architectural competition in Tbilisi, Georgia, was organized to transform a 73,600 m² brownfield site, the former Soviet-era Tbilisi Electric Locomotive Manufacturing Plant in the "Temka" residential area, into a new green neighborhood and cultural destination called Loco Park. On October 18, 2026, LOCO Alliance officially announced Stefano Boeri Architetti's design as the selected project for the site's transformation, with the official masterplan images unveiled on October 23. The selected masterplan is designed to integrate the industrial heritage of the factory with contemporary architecture, dense green public spaces and community recreation hubs. The site is already hosting large-scale cultural events, organized in parallel with the formal masterplan competition.
Stefano Boeri Architetti's Loco Park masterplan transforms the 73,600 m² site in the Georgian capital, the grounds of a large Soviet-era locomotive factory, into an integrated network of homes, green spaces, services and community facilities, open to the city. The gross floor area is 120,000 m² across nine buildings, with different home typologies on the upper floors and services such as local shops, cafés and workshops at ground level. The buildings are surrounded by a sequence of open spaces, including a sports forest, parks, shared gardens and a linear boulevard. Shared spaces are continuous and walkable, and extend pedestrian connections to the surrounding neighborhoods.
To incorporate the site's industrial heritage into the new neighborhood's identity, the project uses brick to establish material continuity. Brick is also rooted in local building traditions and can take on the characteristic colors of Tbilisi's architectural legacy. Through photographic color mapping of the urban landscape, Stefano Boeri Architetti identified the dominant color families (blue-gray, terracotta, green, taupe and mineral white) and translated these shades into a brick palette for the facades. The buildings' roofs are shaped after the silhouettes of the factories and workshops historically located in the area. In a more contemporary approach, the roofs also accommodate greenhouses, terraces, photovoltaic systems, loft apartments and communal spaces for residents.
 The new Loco Park neighbourhood will combine the memory of the large Soviet-era locomotive factory with a vision of a contemporary, vibrant space that is green and open to everyone. The buildings of Loco Park will be islands in an urban archipelago, distinct yet connected by a network of tree-lined pedestrian public spaces for the whole city to enjoy ― Architect Stefano Boeri
Other projects announced this year by Stefano Boeri Architetti include a new affordable housing development in Ibiza, which proposes approximately 190 affordable rental apartments distributed across four timber volumes. Earlier this year, the Rome City Council approved a memorandum for the urban regeneration of the Depositi delle Vittorie in Piazza Bainsizza, a former ATAC depot in Rome dating back to the early 1900s. The firm will be in charge of envisioning the adaptive reuse of the former transportation infrastructure by introducing cultural, educational, commercial, co-working and leisure functions. Also in Italy, the office revealed a design for the new Ambrosian Monastery in Milan's MIND district, a project conceived as a space integrating worship, interreligious dialogue and educational activities.

Trump Administration backs Orbán for UN Secretary-General – media
Ukrinform reports this, citing The Wall Street Journal and The Jerusalem Post.

Washington believes Orbán’s previous contacts with Moscow and Beijing could help secure their support for the Hungarian politician, who is seen as pro-Russian. This could make Orbán a joint candidate backed by three permanent members of the UN Security Council.
A State Department official estimated that Orbán could secure the support of at least eight of the Security Council’s 15 members, and potentially as many as 10 if circumstances are favorable.
It remains unclear, however, whether the United Kingdom and France, which hold veto power on the Security Council, would be prepared to block his candidacy.
A State Department official described Orbán as a “MAGA conservatives' dream candidate,” citing his positions on mass immigration, liberal nongovernmental organizations, and established centers of influence in Hungary’s judiciary and media.
Orbán has repeatedly clashed with EU leaders while strengthening ties with China. His relations with Moscow and Beijing, as well as his domestic policies, could come under particular scrutiny if he is nominated.
U.S. President Donald Trump supported Orbán in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, while Vice President JD Vance personally took part in his election campaign.
Another informal vote is scheduled for Wednesday at the UN Security Council to gauge support for the candidates. It remains unclear whether Orbán’s name will be included in the ballot.
António Guterres’s term as UN Secretary-General ends on December 31. The next Secretary-General will be elected by the General Assembly following a recommendation from the Security Council.

Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:27:03 UTC
14:27:03 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections

Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.

Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:24:59 UTC
14:24:59 KST

Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by students
Serbia’s longtime leader concedes defeat to a student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections.
Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years.
After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years.
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List.
The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights.
During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.
Vucic referred to the demonstrators, who included university professors, doctors and workers, as “blockaders” and accused them of seeking to destabilise Serbia.
A former ultranationalist, Vucic cultivated an image of a pragmatic leader who maintained ties with the European Union, Russia and China as well as, increasingly, with Israel in recent years.
Born in Belgrade in 1970, the nearly 2-metre-tall (6.5ft-tall) Vucic graduated from the University of Belgrade’s faculty of law. He entered politics in 1993, joining the ultranationalist Serbian Radical Party led by Vojislav Seselj.
His political record during the 1990s was marked by nationalist rhetoric. One of his most remembered statements came in Serbia’s parliament in July 1995, nine days after the Srebrenica genocide: “Kill one Serb, and we will kill 100 Muslims.” Vucic made the comments during a debate on possible NATO strikes against positions held by the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Vucic’s political mentor at the time, Seselj, was sentenced in 2018 to 10 years in prison by the Appeals Chamber of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals for persecution, deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serbs during the wars in the Balkans in the 1990s.
Aleksandar Seselj, the son of Vojislav Seselj, was on Vucic’s electoral list in Sunday’s elections.
After a split within the Serbian Radical Party, Vucic and Tomislav Nikolic founded the SNS in 2008. The new party sought to move closer to mainstream European politics.
Safeta Bisevac, a Serbian journalist who has long followed Vucic’s political career, believes he was initially less popular than Nikolic, who appeared closer to common citizens.
“Vucic lagged far behind in popularity at the time and was essentially the organiser of the newly formed party,” Bisevac told Al Jazeera.
In 2012, the SNS came to power promising to fight corruption, organised crime and abuses committed under previous governments.
One of the most prominent cases was the December 2012 arrest of businessman Miroslav Miskovic and his son Marko on suspicion of financial irregularities and tax evasion. After years of legal proceedings, both were acquitted and the state paid them compensation.
Bisevac said the results of the fight against corruption remained modest while the authorities expanded their control over institutions, the media and political life.
Vucic served as first deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2014 before ascending to the post of prime minister in 2014. Three years later, he became president of Serbia and won re-election in 2022. His term was due to run until 2027.
Under pressure from the student-led protests, he resigned in September and called early elections. Although the Serbian presidency is constitutionally limited, Vucic has retained a dominant influence over his party and state policy.
“He made many promises and fulfilled few of them, but in the meantime, he established almost complete control over the state apparatus,” Bisevac said.
Economic growth and the debate over living standards
The Serbian economy has expanded significantly since Vucic took Serbia’s political centre stage in 2012. Unemployment dropped from 26 percent to 8 to 9 percent while nominal gross domestic product nearly tripled, reaching about 90 billion euros ($101bn), according to official data cited by the Reuters news agency.
Annual foreign direct investment inflows rose from about 800 million euros ($896m) in 2012 to a record 5.2 billion euros ($5.8bn) in 2024.
A network of modern motorways has also been built.
However, rising wages have not necessarily translated into a proportional improvement in living standards. The rising cost of living and public debt remain important elements of the debate over the government’s economic record.
Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said “the students simply gave a voice to the justified anger of citizens.”
Speaking to Al Jazeera about Vucic’s policies, Radosavljevic said the past decade was characterised by “systematic pressure and the destruction of social institutions”.
“State intelligence services have spent less time on their actual duties and more time monitoring political opponents while critical thinking has been pushed out of the public media,” Radosavljevic said.

Lula Wins Historic Fourth Term as Bolsonaro Seeks to Overturn Brazil Vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:24:24 UTC
14:24:24 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term with 51.76% of the vote, defeating right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who received 48.24%, while Bolsonaro rejected the result and vowed to seek its annulment, according to official election results.
With more than 99% of ballots counted, Lula defied expectations and reversed his second-place finish in the first round, becoming the first candidate since Brazil returned to democracy in the 1980s to win a presidential runoff after losing the opening round. The victory also interrupts a series of right-wing electoral successes across Latin America and limits US President Donald Trump’s prospects of gaining a stronger ally in the region’s largest economy.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, challenged the result over a Supreme Court decision to extend voting hours nationwide by two hours. Speaking to reporters after the electoral court declared Lula the winner, he said he could not accept the outcome and announced plans to take legal action.
“What happened today was not normal. It was unacceptable,” Bolsonaro said, arguing that the extension had undermined equal treatment between states. He described the decision as a “dirty trick” and said he would request the election’s annulment.
The extension, ordered by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, moved the end of voting from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. Lula’s campaign had requested additional time, alleging that public transportation had been reduced or obstructed in several states, making it harder for voters to reach polling stations. Lula’s team said the problem affected about nine states, while André Janones, the campaign’s head of social media, called the alleged restrictions a “coup attempt.”
Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought longer voting hours, but only in municipalities across five states, citing heavy rain, flooding and power outages. Campaign chief Rogério Marinho denounced the nationwide extension as “a judicial coup.” The last time voting had continued beyond the formal deadline was in 1994.
Lula said voters had turned out to defend democracy. In his first remarks after the result, he credited his campaign with convincing people that voting mattered, while his victory speech included a sharp attack on his opponent and a pledge to defend Brazil’s sovereignty.
“This country doesn’t accept being anybody’s colony,” Lula said, reiterating a campaign message directed against US influence. He also described the result as a “loss for negativity, lies” and thanked his campaign team and Brazilians, particularly young people who had taken to the streets to defend democracy.
Celebrations erupted in several cities after Lula’s victory was confirmed. Fireworks and vuvuzelas sounded in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of supporters dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, gathered in São Paulo. On Paulista Avenue, supporters chanted in celebration as the results showed Lula passing the 50% mark.
The result capped a difficult campaign for the 80-year-old left-wing leader, whose reelection had appeared uncertain as voters grew frustrated with his party following corruption scandals and rising prices. Critics also argued that the former metalworker and union leader was out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and the expanding informal workforce.
Lula’s political comeback followed his imprisonment from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned. He subsequently defeated Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. During his third term, his campaign said, poverty and inequality fell, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation reached record lows.
Pollsters attributed Lula’s victory in part to turnout that exceeded expectations. Leonardo Barreto, co-founder of the consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen a familiar political path over an uncertain alternative. Left-wing federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in São Paulo during the vote count, described him to Reuters as “a statesman, a giant.”
Throughout the campaign, Lula warned that Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, reverse social progress and surrender Brazilian sovereignty to Trump. The US State Department had led a campaign to bring the Bolsonaro family back to power, and Trump’s administration had imposed tariffs on Brazil, travel bans on government officials and sanctions against Zanin’s fellow Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes over what it called a political “witch hunt” against Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula made national sovereignty a central campaign theme, arguing that Brazil should defend its territory, natural resources, oil and Amazon. He also promised to regulate major technology companies after his campaign accused Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, of favoring Bolsonaro through algorithmic manipulation and suppressing Lula’s content.
Meta denied interfering in the election but acknowledged that some Lula campaign advertisements had been deactivated by mistake because of technical errors. Lula said after his victory that social media companies would need greater regulation.
The campaign’s online conflict also involved a WhatsApp group called “Lula’s army,” which had more than 10 million followers. The group was suspended twice after the head of Brazil’s electoral court, described as an ally of Bolsonaro, alleged that it contained misinformation. Fellow judges overturned both decisions.
Lula’s fourth term is expected to face serious legislative obstacles. Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since the return to democracy in the 1980s, with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and its allies potentially controlling more than 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 in the Senate.
“He is likely to be a lame duck from the start,” Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo, told Reuters. Stuenkel said the new legislature could further shift power toward Congress, leaving Lula with less influence over Supreme Court nominations, difficult party coalitions and even the threat of impeachment.
Economic pressures will add to the challenges facing Lula. His government forecasts growth of just 2.3% next year, while public debt has climbed above 82% of gross domestic product, its highest level since the pandemic. High interest rates have fueled concerns over public finances, although the bulk of the increase in debt has been driven by interest costs rather than spending, according to the supplied account.
Goldman Sachs expects Lula to make only modest progress in curbing expenditure during his fourth term, as he remains committed to a state-led economic model. Economists are also concerned about rising household debt. During the campaign, Lula introduced a provisional ban on online betting and announced a new debt-relief program.
The incoming right-wing Congress is expected to pursue structural reforms favoring businesses, a process that could lead to spending cuts and fuel social unrest. Lula will also need to balance debt reduction with the protection of social programs and investment over the next four years.
Ahead of the runoff, Lula offered a series of policy pledges, including free nationwide public transportation on weekends, a proposal that still requires formal submission to Congress, and a 15% increase in his flagship welfare program, which is already being implemented. He also backed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades and passed Congress with broad support.
The result was also a setback for Trump, who had sought to expand a growing bloc of friendly right-wing governments in Latin America that support Washington’s security and migration agenda. Former Brazilian Foreign Minister Celso Amorim told Reuters that Lula could help balance the region politically, saying the president-elect would be important in establishing such a counterweight.
Lula received congratulations from several regional leaders, including Chilean President José Antonio Kast and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, both close allies of Trump. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum congratulated Lula in a post on X, writing, “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won. Congratulations, President Lula!” The presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Panama and Bolivia also congratulated him on X, while Cuba’s president called Lula his “dear brother” and described the victory as a win for peace, sovereignty and social justice.
Lula’s win came against the backdrop of a broader political shift in Latin America, where right-wing candidates had prevailed in the previous seven general elections. The Brazilian result was closely watched by centrist and left-wing parties ahead of the US midterm elections and upcoming votes in Spain, France and Germany, where established political forces have faced pressure from a media-savvy far right.
Despite his victory, Lula will govern a deeply divided country. Nearly half of voters backed Bolsonaro, and political tensions are expected to persist across Brazil’s institutions. Bolsonaro’s campaign had centered on freeing his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after losing the 2022 election, and impeaching Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who convicted him.
Flávio Bolsonaro also promised that Brazil would join Washington’s Shield of the Americas initiative and take a tougher line on crime, supporting the US designation of two Brazilian gangs as terrorist organizations this year. Trump did not explicitly endorse either presidential candidate, although he described Flávio Bolsonaro’s narrow first-round lead over Lula as a “close, but a very, very big victory.”
The campaign also exposed divisions over foreign influence and social media. Lula’s supporters accused Meta of suppressing their content while boosting Bolsonaro’s, allegations the company denied. Veronyka Gimenes, director of the digital rights group Código Não Binário, which organized a protest outside Meta’s São Paulo office, said there was no proof the company was acting on instructions from the White House but argued that its interests aligned with Bolsonaro’s and Trump’s.
Lula is expected to maintain distance from Washington and strengthen relations with China, the European Union and Africa as a leader of the global South, according to Michael Ahn Paarlberg, a former Latin America policy adviser to Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign. Paarlberg described Lula as a symbolic barrier to the global shift to the right, particularly in Latin America, while noting that the political environment differed from the period when Lula first took office during the region’s Pink Tide.
Lula, who has said this will be his final term, turns 81 on Tuesday. He now faces the task of governing with the PL holding the largest bloc in Congress after the first round, giving the Bolsonaro movement unprecedented influence over the legislature. Reginaldo Lopes, a lawmaker from Lula’s Workers’ Party, underscored the likely tension between the branches of government when he told journalists at Lula’s campaign headquarters on Sunday that “Congress is an enemy of the people.”

Gyurov Challenges Yotova to Debate as Both Candidates Seek Runoff Backing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

14:18:30 KST

Andrey Gyurov called for an open debate with presidential runoff opponent Iliana Yotova and ruled out seeking endorsements from political parties, while candidates and party leaders began outlining their positions ahead of Bulgaria’s November 1 runoff.
Speaking shortly after polls closed, Gyurov thanked voters for their support and stressed that the campaign still had important work ahead. He said Bulgaria needed an active president who could explain decisions and bring citizens together rather than divide them.
“This is not the time for patting ourselves on the back. I believe Bulgaria needs an active president - someone capable of explaining decisions and uniting Bulgarian citizens, rather than dividing them,” Gyurov said.
He insisted that the runoff would be decided by voters rather than party leaders. “These elections will not be decided in party headquarters; we will seek support solely from the citizens,” the presidential candidate said.
Gyurov also invited Yotova to participate in a public debate. “I call upon Yotova to join me in an open, honest, and civilized debate, where we can present our respective positions,” he said.
His running mate, Georgi Kandev, said he would not debate Yotova’s vice-presidential candidate, Kiril Valchev, because the debate should involve the presidential candidates themselves. Kandev urged citizens to participate in the runoff and defend democracy.
The initiative committee backing Gyurov said the result had been anticipated. Aleksandrina Pendachanska, co-chair of the committee, said the campaign had shown that Bulgarians wanted a president capable of restoring the country’s dignity and strength. She called for support from everyone who opposed a return to governance by what she described as the ghosts of the past.
Democratic Bulgaria also appealed for greater voter mobilization. Radan Kanev of the Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria (DSB) called on people seeking a strong, European and democratic Bulgaria, with checks and balances and a counterweight to unchecked executive power, to support Gyurov.
Bozhidar Bozhanov of Democratic Bulgaria said the alliance had backed Gyurov because its voters wanted him as their candidate, adding that he had not personally requested their support.
Asen Vassilev of We Continue the Change said anyone was free to support Gyurov but warned against parties waiting to be asked repeatedly before offering their backing. Such an approach, he argued, could leave Bulgaria with a president beholden to others.
Yotova, meanwhile, did not request explicit endorsements from political parties or other presidential candidates after the first round. She thanked voters for their participation and emphasized her intention to address all Bulgarian citizens, maintaining the positive approach of her campaign.
She criticized low turnout, saying voters should not have been intimidated or pressured into staying home. Yotova also argued that meaningful change would be impossible without voting and called for Bulgaria to avoid returning to years of stagnation.
The presidential candidate stressed that, with war raging in Europe, peace remained central to her platform. She said security and prosperity were impossible without peace and called for Bulgarian flags, rather than foreign flags, to fly in the country’s streets, alongside citizens who felt secure and could focus on their future.
Asked whether she would seek backing from other presidential tickets or political parties without candidates in the runoff, Yotova said her message was directed at all Bulgarian citizens. She also rejected the prospect of Bulgaria once again being governed by “haphazard coalitions” or ad hoc political arrangements.
Yotova’s running mate, Kiril Valchev, said a woman was leading the presidential race for the first time in the country. He expressed hope that more voters would participate in the second round and that Bulgaria would elect a female president. Valchev also challenged Kandev to a debate.
The Yotova-Valchev initiative committee described the upcoming debate as decisive for the election but acknowledged weaknesses in their campaign. Hristo Pimpirev, co-chair of the committee, said the candidates had traveled across almost the entire country, but their appearances had sometimes seemed overly formal and official. He said the campaign could have been more spontaneous, with events in public squares and a more sincere, authentic approach.
Progressive Bulgaria admitted that it had underestimated its vote and failed to mobilize enough supporters, while expressing hope of gaining ground in the runoff. Petar Vitanov, chair of the party’s parliamentary group, said the movement had a much larger reserve of potential voters and expected higher participation. He also noted that some political leaders had explicitly called on people not to vote.
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) indicated that Yotova could count on its support in the second round. BSP leader Krum Zarkov congratulated her on a campaign he described as requiring considerable strength of character and encouraged her to continue through the decisive seven days ahead. An assessment of the campaign is underway alongside preparations for the runoff strategy.
The question of where supporters of candidates eliminated in the first round will cast their ballots remains unresolved.
Kostadin Kostadinov, leader of Revival, said other political forces would have to take his party into account. He argued that many voters who had supported Rumen Radev in previous elections had returned to Revival, demonstrating its importance in Bulgarian politics. Kostadinov said the party’s voters would play a significant role in determining the November 1 outcome.
He added that Revival would decide whether to endorse a candidate and, if so, whom to support, potentially using an internal poll to assess its members’ and supporters’ views. He also stressed that the party’s voters were independent and could make their own choices.
Kostadinov said any request for support had to be made first and emphasized that Revival would not compromise on its principles.
Radostin Vasilev, leader of MECH, urged voters to follow their conscience but explicitly told them not to vote for Yotova. He said her defeat would lead to a situation involving snap parliamentary elections.
Ivan Hristanov said he had not yet decided whom to support in the runoff and would make that choice during the week, taking recent developments into account. He said it was too early to give a definitive answer.
Ivelin Mihaylov did not comment on the first-round presidential results on election night.

The Gambia’s first blind magistrate tests a system built for the sighted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:18:00 UTC
14:18:00 KST

First visually impaired Gambian magistrate tests system built for sighted
For a decade, Muhammed Krubally has shown what is possible and what still needs to change.
Banjul, the Gambia – It is still early when Magistrate Muhammed Krubally arrives at the Banjul Magistrates’ Court.
Before the first case, his clerk goes over the day’s proceedings, running through the files and making sure everything is in place. Krubally listens, asks questions, and prepares to preside.
Then he enters a packed courtroom, where lawyers, witnesses and relatives have gathered for a criminal case.
The room falls quiet.
Krubally cannot see the people before him, but he can hear them. A lawyer rises. A witness speaks. Papers move across the room. His clerk is nearby.
At his desk, his computer speaks back to him.
Krubally uses JAWS, or Job Access With Speech, a screen reader that allows him to navigate his computer and read documents and judgements.
“This makes my job very easy,” he tells Al Jazeera.
He also uses AI-enabled smart glasses to access information and carry out tasks independently.
But technology is only part of how he works.
He listens for voices, remembers details and follows the rhythm of proceedings, building a picture of the courtroom through sound. When necessary, he relies on his clerk.
At 41, Krubally says he has presided over more than 1,000 civil and criminal cases since joining the bench.
In 2016, he became the Gambia’s first visually impaired magistrate. The Gambia Organisation of the Visually Impaired (GOVI) identifies him as the country’s first person with a visual impairment to hold the position.
For Krubally, this is not an experiment in what a visually impaired person might be capable of doing.
It is his profession.
And he has spent a decade doing it.
A determination shaped early
Long before he took his place on the bench, Krubally grew up in a village in the Gambia’s Central River Region, the second of nine children.
From an early age, he wanted to become a lawyer. Part of that ambition was personal: he wanted to defend his own rights. But he also wanted to advocate for others.
He wanted, he says, “to be the voice for the voiceless”, particularly people with disabilities.
The path was not straightforward.
From primary school through university, Krubally encountered limited resources and an education system that often left visually impaired students like him facing obstacles their sighted classmates did not.
He remembers being discouraged by fellow students and some teachers from pursuing the education he wanted.
Instead of making him abandon his ambition, he says, their doubts only strengthened it.
“Their discouragement kept me going. I knew what I wanted, and see where I am now,” he says.
Those experiences later shaped his decision to enter the judiciary.
“I became a magistrate to change the system, to make it inclusive,” he says.
But joining one of the country’s most important public institutions did not make those barriers disappear.
Rights on paper, barriers in practice
The Gambia’s Persons with Disabilities Act, passed in 2021, sets out principles including independence, non-discrimination, full participation, equality of opportunity and accessibility.
The law also contains provisions covering employment, public buildings and services, information and access to justice.
Yet putting those rights into practice remains a challenge.
The National Human Rights Commission has identified barriers affecting people with disabilities, including discrimination and difficulties accessing services, education and employment.
Al Jazeera contacted the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Welfare for a response on implementation of the act, including measures to improve accessibility, education and employment opportunities for people with disabilities. The ministry did not respond.
Krubally encounters those challenges not only as a judicial officer, but also as an advocate.
As president of the Gambia Federation of the Disabled, he speaks at events in the Gambia and beyond, pressing for greater recognition of the rights and potential of people with disabilities.
“I want to see a world for all; inclusion matters,” he says.
For Krubally, inclusion is not simply about opening the door. It is about having the means to participate once inside.
The barriers begin at school
For many people with disabilities, working towards full inclusion begins long before they enter a courtroom or parliament.
It begins at school.
Today, GOVI’s Resource Centre for the Blind provides specialist education for children with visual impairments before they transition into mainstream schools.
Forty-nine pupils aged between four and 14 currently attend the centre, Lamin Colley, its head of school, told Al Jazeera.
After completing their studies there, pupils are expected to enter mainstream schools, where special-needs teachers stationed across school clusters are meant to support them.
But that support is stretched.
Colley told Al Jazeera that limited learning materials and the size of the school clusters are putting pressure on the support available to students. A single special-needs teacher, he said, cannot maintain regular contact with all students across those clusters.
“The reality on the ground is that not much has changed after the disability act has been passed,” Colley says.
He attributes this partly to what he describes as insufficient government funding for disability issues in the national budget.
Colley remembers Krubally as a pupil who loved to read and could often be found in the library. He also remembers his determination to participate in activities alongside his sighted classmates.
Years later, Krubally’s journey carries a message beyond the school gates.
“Disability does not mean inability.”
But one person’s achievement does not erase the obstacles facing those coming behind him.
Entering an institution is not enough
Ndey Yassin Secka-Sallah knows what it means to enter a public institution without having the tools to participate independently.
She was nominated to the Gambia’s National Assembly and has long advocated for the rights of people with disabilities. GOVI describes her as the country’s only visually impaired parliamentarian.
She was also involved in advocacy around disability rights and the push for stronger legal protections.
Yet taking a seat in parliament did not make the institution accessible.
“I used to depend on my fellow colleagues to know what was being discussed,” she told Al Jazeera.
What she wanted was not special treatment, but independence.
“I would have loved to be independent, without depending on people for help.”
Five years after the disability law was passed, Secka-Sallah says implementation remains a major challenge.
She sees Krubally’s appointment to the bench as significant, but not as the end of the struggle.
“Inclusion is all we wish for,” she says.
Musa Barrow, another visually impaired professional, teaches media law and ethics to journalism students.
Like Krubally, Barrow has encountered assumptions about what a visually impaired person can do. Some students have questioned whether he can meet the standards they expect from a lecturer.
Technology has helped him work independently. He uses digital tools to read, write and prepare lecture notes.
“Technology has broken that barrier for me,” he says.
But students’ assumptions have not disappeared.
His response is direct.
“I can do more than what sighted people can do,” he says.
Barrow’s visual impairment has also shaped how he teaches journalism, particularly when discussing the media’s portrayal of disability.
The experiences of Krubally, Secka-Sallah and Barrow all point to the same gap: entering an institution is not the same as being equipped to participate fully in it.
What does the law look like in practice?
The scale of the challenge is difficult to measure.
The Gambia’s 2013 Population and Housing Census recorded a disability prevalence of 1.2 percent, representing 21,873 people, according to later analysis of the census data.
But that figure may understate the scale of disability in the country. The census used a narrower set of questions and did not use the Washington Group questions commonly used to measure functional difficulties.
The Gambia has since conducted a new population and housing census, with preliminary results released in September 2024. But the preliminary report did not include detailed updated national disability data.
That leaves an incomplete picture of how the country’s disability landscape may have changed over the past decade.
What is clearer is the experience of people navigating institutions that were not designed with them in mind: a parliamentarian depending on colleagues to follow proceedings, a lecturer being questioned about his ability to teach, or children entering mainstream schools with limited specialist support.
Krubally knows that journey personally.
He now mentors young people, many of them visually impaired. One is Modou Lamin Dampha, who describes Krubally as someone who encourages him to keep pursuing his ambitions.
“He advises and encourages me to keep going, that things are possible,” Dampha says.
For Dampha, Krubally is more than a magistrate.
He is evidence that professional ambition does not have to end with disability.
Has the courtroom changed?
Back inside the Banjul Magistrates’ Court, the case continues.
Krubally listens as the proceedings unfold, using voices, memory, technology and experience to follow what is happening before him.
His career raises a harder question: how much has the system itself changed?
The judiciary was asked what accommodations are available to Krubally, what accessibility measures are in place for judicial officers and court users with disabilities, and what changes it has made since the Persons with Disabilities Act was passed.
It did not respond by the time of publication.
Krubally has spent a decade adapting to the demands of the courtroom.
Whether the institution around him has also adapted remains an open question.
Asked what he sees when he looks to the future, Krubally says it is not about the obstacles he has overcome.
“All I see is possibility.”

'You won't hear us coming': Police surveillance is ramping up across Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:16:59 UTC
14:16:59 KST

in brief
- WA Police has expanded its automated drone response program in Perth.
- Rights groups say better legal protections are needed to ensure individual privacy.
WA Police is expanding Australia's first automated Drone as First Responder (DFR) fleet, aiming to fill the sky with remote aircraft dispatched from Perth's CBD to emergency scenes within seconds.
While police promote the rapid-response technology as a vital tool to catch criminals and protect officers, civil liberties advocates warn the rapid rollout risks allowing Australian aerial policing to outpace laws meant to protect individual privacy.
WA Police is also trialling artificial intelligence-assisted facial recognition cameras, and while its drone program is the most advanced in the country, similar programs are being used across Australia.
It's "pretty scary, dystopian stuff", Tom Sulston, head of policy at the digital human rights charity Digital Rights Watch, told SBS News about the direction policing technology is moving in Australia.
In announcing an extension of the drone program, WA Police commissioner Col Blanch said unmanned aircraft will not be patrolling or hovering passively over suburbs.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We don't do patrol, we simply do response," he told ABC News. "You ring 000, we come to help."
However, the commissioner also said he hopes the program will expand: "The aim is to have as many as possible out there so we cover maximum distance throughout the state."
WA Police Minister Reece Whitby went further, saying criminals "won't see us coming ... won't hear us coming, but we'll be there in the air watching your every move".
The DFR X program, which will initially operate across the southern Perth suburbs of Baldivis, Kwinana, and Rockingham, is the latest move by Australian police who are increasingly experimenting with drones.
Sulston said it is "inevitable" their use will increase among police forces and it's therefore essential Australia has the frameworks to ensure they are used responsibly.
"If you don't have good transparency legislation over the police to know what they're doing, then how are we holding them accountable?"
How does the WA police drone program work?
Many police forces across Australia have used drones for years in search and rescue or to monitor unfolding incidents, with their small size, rapid response, and low cost making them particularly attractive.
Unlike a traditional police operation, where drones are launched by officers at the scene, WA's DFR X system houses drones in docking stations atop police stations, ready to launch remotely from a central command centre in Perth.
Flying "beyond visual line of sight", the drones are designed to arrive on the scene of a Triple Zero call in less than a minute, feeding high-quality video back to headquarters before officers can arrive.
Police drones spreading across Australia
In north-west NSW, the state's police force has been conducting its own controversial and high-profile automated drone trial in the regional centre of Moree.
Officers stationed more than 600km away in Sydney have been piloting the aircraft to respond to property crime, break-ins, and vehicle theft.
In August, the Minns government moved to expand the trial, saying police surveys reported strong community support.
However, human rights organisations and legal advocates say the trial's results have not been made public and therefore its expansion is unjustified.
Australian Human Rights commissioner Lorraine Finlay warned NSW should halt any wider rollout until the civil liberties impacts of automated aerial policing can be properly addressed.
"While existing surveillance laws regulate some aspects of these activities, they leave important questions about permissible uses, data handling, transparency and independent oversight unresolved," she said.
"Effective policing and human rights should never be treated as competing priorities. We should expect both."
Deploying automated drones over regional towns, particularly ones with a significant First Nations population like Moree, risks establishing a regime of persistent overhead surveillance of already over-policed demographics, advocates say.
Timothy Roberts, president of the NSW Council for Civil Liberties, told SBS News his organisation is "deeply concerned about the lack of transparency about the evidence base for why these drones are needed".
"The selection of Moree, in particular as a target, given some of the vulnerable community demographics there, is a very concerning aspect of this."
Can police drones film in your backyard?
The shift from police helicopters to manually operated drones and automated suburban fleets raises legal questions, as it's unclear what happens when drones film private property while travelling to a callout.
Under Australian common law, property owners have limited rights to the airspace above their land and modern aerial imaging makes the distinction between public and private land difficult.
"If you're in private from street level, but you're publicly viewable from 200m up, is that a private or a public place?" Roberts said. "Those are largely legally untested questions.
"We have to have pre-existing transparency and reporting regimes so that we collectively can see what the police have been looking at and make a call on whether this is a reasonable thing for them to be doing."
In NSW, there are "no legislative protections around what police are doing with these drones", Roberts said, calling on police departments across the country to release internal policy documents on how officers are being instructed to use the technology.
"Who's reviewing the footage being captured? Where are the policy documents about how this is used? Can the community have oversight? " he asked.
"All of these protections are completely absent."
What happens to police drone footage?
The operation of drones beyond line of sight is regulated by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), which told SBS News it has "approved emergency service operators" for such use.
"CASA has worked closely with police and emergency service operators over many years to support the safe use of drones," a spokesperson said.
However, CASA does not regulate how drones are used or what footage they can collect, only their aviation safety.
Privacy protections are left to state and federal legislation, which often predates the use of autonomous robotics.
State police forces are largely exempt from the federal Privacy Act 1988 when carrying out law enforcement roles.
In WA, there is no comprehensive public-sector privacy regime and surveillance device laws are designed for much more primitive technology.
When asked about the retention of footage, WA Police told SBS News that video captured during drone flights is "retained in accordance with agency retention policy".
Asked what protections are in place to prevent private residences being recorded, SBS News was told that "all DFR X flights are in accordance with CASA Regulations and endorsed Operations Manual".
"This requires a pilot to navigate remotely whilst transiting to an incident, using the aircraft camera to scan to the horizon for aircraft and hazards.
"Only once a DFR X aircraft has arrived at the incident will the pilot use the camera to record information relating to the incident."
For Roberts, the discussion over the use of drones is "cart before the horse".
"Why are we having this conversation when these things are already out there flying around?" he said. "Yes, these are difficult times, but we do not have to take large steps because we have a fancy new technology without first considering some of the implications."
"There's no real rhyme or reason that's been provided by either [NSW or WA] police force as to why they need to move this quickly and at this alarming rate without these protections."

Israel’s election: Five key things to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:16:38 UTC
14:16:38 KST

Israel’s election: Five key things to know
High-stakes vote comes as Israel is embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening domestic polarisation.
Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday for legislative elections.
The vote, the first since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, is being called one of the most important in its history.
It will determine the direction of Israel’s government as the country remains embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening polarisation at home.
Here are five things to know about the upcoming election:
Which are the main parties and what do opinion polls suggest?
Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, whose term lasts four years.
There are two main blocs vying to lead the next government.
The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and joined by several far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These include United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas – both conservative religious parties – and Otzma Yehudi and Religious Zionism-Zehut, led respectively by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
The main opposition coalition comprises four Jewish-led opposition movements – the Yashar party, led by former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, the Democrats, led by former deputy military chief of staff Yair Golan, the Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by former Finance Minister Avigdor Lieberman and the Together alliance, led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and joined by Knesset opposition leader Yair Lapid.
The latest opinion polls published before a ban on new surveys took effect on Friday showed that neither bloc was on course to secure a parliamentary majority of 61 seats.
A poll by public broadcaster KAN projected that the opposition alliance would win 52 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s bloc, with the remaining seats going to unaffiliated parties, including the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, and the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al parties.
However, both the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs have effectively ruled out joining forces with the Arab-led parties for now.
The fractured landscape means Israeli parties could be in for tough post-election negotiations to cobble together a governing majority. If those efforts fail, Israel could end up with a minority government reliant on support from parties outside the governing coalition – or potentially head to another round of elections.
What are the key issues?
Israelis are grappling with a series of domestic and international crises this election cycle.
On the domestic front, there is growing demand for accountability for reported security failures, including those leading up to the October 2023 attacks, anger over the growing ultra-Orthodox community’s military exemption and concern over Netanyahu’s repeated efforts to push judicial reforms that critics say undermine Israel’s liberal democratic order.
“The secular and liberal opposition factions in Israel feel this election is the last chance to save Israeli democracy and restore the institutions that have eroded over Netanyahu’s successive terms,” Mairav Zonszein, an Israeli-American commentator who is a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.
A war-weary public is also weighing how Israel should proceed with its multiple military conflicts, with many voters seeking security and economic stability while remaining resistant to perceived concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.
What makes this election so important?
It is Israel’s first election since the October 2023 attacks and comes amid a surge in far-right attitudes and growing divisions over the direction of the country.
“Strains of Israeli society had always been given to violence and right-wing rhetoric, but the trends that had always been present had accelerated under the current government,” prominent Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani told Al Jazeera.
The election also comes as Israel’s international standing has deteriorated, with a host of Israel’s allies sanctioning its illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, and many other nations denouncing the country’s continued attacks in Gaza and Lebanon.
When Netanyahu addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 24, dozens of envoys from around the world walked out, some jeering and booing.
The outcome of the upcoming vote could determine whether Israel’s next government maintains its approach to the international community or seeks to repair ties.
What does it mean for Netanyahu’s political future?
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has led the country for more than 15 of the last 17 years, and a total of 19, faces growing scrutiny at home and abroad over alleged security failures leading up to the October 7 attack, as well as corruption charges he has been battling since 2019.
An electoral defeat would also leave Netanyahu more exposed to his ongoing corruption trial, which could ultimately result in a prison sentence if he is convicted.
A new government could also affect the prospects of a potential commission of inquiry into the October 2023 attacks and Netanyahu’s political standing as he faces an arrest warrant for war crimes issued by the International Criminal Court.
What about Palestinian citizens of Israel?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million.
Meanwhile, roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no say in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.
Recent polling suggested that the turnout among the Palestinian citizens of Israel could reach 60 percent, with the majority of the votes expected to go the Arab lists, which are the principal representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel. If turnout reaches 65 percent, these parties could potentially win as many as 15 seats in the Knesset. Campaigners are aiming for 70 percent turnout, which would be the highest in decades and raise the threshold, keeping smaller parties out of parliament.
Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the Joint List and Ra’am from the election.
Israel’s top court quickly reversed that decision, enabling the Arab parties to stay in the race. However, the court did force Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the race over an article in which he described the October 7 attacks as “an important historical event”.
The role of Arab parties is going to be significant. Both major coalitions have ruled out joining forces with them for now, but without them, neither coalition might be able to form a majority.
Netanyahu has repeatedly sought to portray his opponents as potential partners of the Arab parties, claiming that an opposition-led government will seek their support and that only his Likud party can prevent this.
Joseph Mansour, a former aide to Israeli Knesset member Ayman Odeh, said politically alienating Arab parties is part of Netanyahu’s political strategy, which could allow him to remain in office as a caretaker prime minister if neither coalition forms a majority.
“If Palestinian-led party support becomes politically toxic and the opposition falls short of 61 seats, the deadlock itself becomes the latest win for Netanyahu,” wrote Mansour for the Arab Center Washington DC.

95% of Votes Counted: Yotova Leads Gyurov by 2.56 Points in Bulgaria’s Presidential Vote
Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission (CEC) said that presidential candidates Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov are heading to a runoff on November 1 after 95.29% of polling station protocols had been processed, with Yotova holding a lead of 2.56 percentage points.
Interim results published on the CEC website as of 6 a.m. on October 26, 2026, put Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, in first place with 34.598% of the vote, or 506,628 ballots. Both were nominated by an initiative committee.

According to data on the commission’s website, turnout stood at 15.95% as of 4 p.m. on October 25. Of the 6,637,238 eligible voters, 1,058,669 had cast ballots.
Among ballots cast abroad, the Gyurov-Kandev ticket was leading with 45.225% based on 96.57% of polling station protocols processed. Yotova and Valchev were second with 23.143%.
The relatively low turnout has helped election commissions process and submit polling station protocols more quickly than in previous elections. More than 95% of the protocols had already been processed by the time of the CEC’s latest update, reflecting an unusually rapid pace of data processing on the commission’s website.

Bulgarians Mark St. Demetrius’ Day and the Traditional Start of Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:08:22 UTC
14:08:22 KST

The Bulgarian Orthodox Church celebrates St. Demetrius’ Day (Dimitrovden) on October 26, honoring the Holy Great Martyr Demetrius the Myrrh-streaming and the Venerable Dimitra of Dorostol, while Bulgarian folklore associates the feast with the arrival of winter.
According to popular belief, Saint Demetrius brings the first snow and opens the heavens on the eve of his feast. A traditional saying captures the seasonal change: “Saint Demetrius brings winter, while Saint George brings summer.” Folklore holds that the first snowflakes fall from the saint’s white beard and that the heavens open at midnight before the holiday.
Saint Demetrius was born in Thessaloniki in the 3rd century. After his father died, he became the city’s governor, but his open profession of the Christian faith led to his imprisonment and execution on October 26, 306 AD. He was subsequently declared a martyr and saint, and the people of Thessaloniki regard him as their patron.
In Bulgaria’s folk calendar, the holiday is also called Mitrovden or Razpus. It traditionally marked the end of seasonal employment for shepherds, cattle herders and farmhands hired for the summer. Employers would pay their workers, while negotiations over employment for the following year would begin.
The feast is linked to various folk beliefs. In some parts of the Balkan Mountains, people believe that if the first person to enter a home is good and prosperous, the coming year will bring health and abundance. Another tradition holds that a full moon on the eve of St. Demetrius’ Day means the beehives will be filled with honey.
The holiday also signals the start of the season for engagements and weddings. Traditional festive meals include a kurban, or ritual mutton offering, rooster stew, an apple-filled flatbread and assorted vegetable dishes.
Saint Demetrius also occupies an important place in Bulgarian history. On October 26, 1185, the feast day of the Church of St. Demetrius in Tarnovo, the brothers Asen and Petar declared an uprising against Byzantine rule. Their struggle led to the restoration of the Bulgarian state and the founding of the Second Bulgarian Empire.
The saint’s relics are preserved in the Basilica of Saint Demetrius in Thessaloniki, which welcomes pilgrims from around the world every year.
Churches throughout Bulgaria will hold festive liturgies for the occasion. People named Dimitar, Dimitrina, Dimo and Mitko, along with those bearing variations of these names, will celebrate their name day.

Semikin later updated the information, saying the number of injured had risen to two: a 30-year-old woman and a 61-year-old man. They are receiving medical treatment.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian forces launched 832 strikes on 55 settlements in the Zaporizhzhia region over the previous day, injuring four people.
