Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:02:00 UTC
14:02:00 KST

Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.
On Monday, October 26, she asked the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.
She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety, she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.
This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.
Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation, it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”
That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague – the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice – have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.
It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, Chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says, “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”
She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law,” she says. Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark, which also supports the case.
I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.
The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the U.N. on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.
The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.
Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.
The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest U.N. report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to be displaced, many of them several times over. A U.N. Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.
The violence is taking place on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar the fourth most deadly conflict in the world. Far from being a frozen conflict, this is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, which makes justice and accountability even more important.
What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.
Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.

Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, becoming the first Russian city awarded a global championship in an Olympic sport since Russia launched the war in Ukraine in 2022, the sport's governing body announced Sunday.
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) confirmed the decision alongside the selection of Ahmedabad, India as host of the 2029 championships.

‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

At Groot Constantia, the oldest wine farm in South Africa, the 450,000 visitors who pass through its gates annually can admire the picturesque vineyards sloping towards a bay ringed by mountains or enjoy a glass of sweet Grand Constance, reputed to have been Napoleon’s favourite wine.
Unusually among the region’s old vineyards, there is also a museum that includes the history of slavery, run by state body Iziko Museums. Panels display information about enslaved people – about 30 of whom lived on the estate at any given time from its founding in 1685 until slavery was abolished in 1834 by the British colonial government – detailing everything from their work to what they ate.
Two plaques list the names of people forcibly taken from Mozambique, Madagascar, India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. “Today we pay tribute and acknowledge the enormous contribution of these men, women and children in the success of Groot Constantia and also acknowledge their oppression and suffering under slavery and their resilience and courage,” the plaques read.
“We have accepted that it’s part of our history and we are actually grateful for what they have done,” said Groot Constantia CEO, Jean Naudé. “It’s sad that it was built on that unsound foundation, but the foundation is there and the least we can do today is to build something proper on that foundation.”
Although there is no complete data, historians agree that only a handful of estates explicitly acknowledge their history of enslavement, in an industry that sold R36.3bn (£1.65bn) of wine last year. Groot Constantia is also unusual in having been owned by the South African government from 1885 to 1993, then transferred to a not-for-profit trust.
Jan van Riebeeck established a colony for the Dutch East India Company in what is now Cape Town in 1652, and the first enslaved people were brought there within a few years to work in houses and on farms. By the 19th century, the 21 most prominent wine industry families owned 3,557 enslaved people between them, according to Wayne Dooling, a School of Oriental and African Studies lecturer.
“The wine industry was very dependent on enslaved labour,” said Kate Ekama, a historian at Stellenbosch University. By the 1820s, according to her research, about 80% of “coerced” workers were enslaved, with the remainder dispossessed Indigenous people.
“People don’t want to sully their legacy,” Linda Mbeki, the Iziko Museums curator at Groot Constantia, said of the absence of slavery memorials from most historic wine farms. “To acknowledge slavery history; to acknowledge culpability, if not directly, comes with privilege and generational wealth.”
Nonetheless, Groot Constantia still faces criticism from unions and workers’ rights groups who draw a line from slavery, through colonialism and apartheid, to the present conditions of wine farm workers, many of whom are descended from enslaved people.
At least 10 families, mostly of former workers, have been evicted from the farm since July, according to the Trust for Community Outreach and Education (TCOE), an NGO, and the Commercial, Stevedoring, Agricultural and Allied Workers Union (CSAAWU).
“You may want to claim the history of being the oldest wine farm, but at the same time those that have given their labour and that have built the sector can be easily dispensed of,” said Mercia Andrews, a TCOE director.
Naudé said that evictions did not take place without a court order and referred to comments he made about previous evictions in 2024, when he said: “As a responsible and progressive employer, Groot Constantia upholds fairness and complies with all relevant laws at all times for all employees … ensuring all policies are implemented consistently and equitably.”
Rico Basson, CEO of South Africa Wine, an industry body, acknowledged that slavery had “left deep social and economic inequalities”.
“These are serious issues that cannot be separated from broader conversations about dignity, opportunity and fair treatment in the workplace. Acknowledging our history and improving the circumstances of those who contribute to our industry today are both important,” he said.
One farm that has tried to acknowledge its history and redress inequality is Solms-Delta, in Franschhoek, 40 miles east of Cape Town. “It’s not just some abstract historical principle,” said neuropsychology professor Mark Solms, who bought the estate in 2001. “You live in a big house on a farm with a whole lot of poor people, who are there as a direct result of that history and are impoverished as a direct result of that history.”
Nico Jansen is the third generation of his father’s family living on Solms-Delta, which was founded in 1690. When he was appointed as estate manager in 2001, he initially didn’t believe Solms’ promises to renovate their houses or raise wages above those of neighbouring farms.
“I wanted to exploit him as much as possible … so he can’t take the houses back to the old days, so if he wants to leave, then we are already in a better place,” said Jansen, who identifies his heritage as indigenous Khoikhoi.
In 2005, Solms helped the workers set up a trust and take out a loan to buy a neighbouring farm for themselves. From 2004 to 2016, the farm employed a historian, Tracey Randle, who organised for archaeologists to carry out excavations, set up a history museum and helped the workers bring their musical traditions back to life.
However, the farm is not currently operating. According to Solms, in 2016 the government stepped in to take over the workers’ shares, but did not put in the promised financial contribution, pushing the indebted estate into a business rescue process.
A spokesperson for the department of rural development and land reform did not respond to a request for comment. A 2018 statement blamed Solms-Delta’s problems on “accumulated debt and poor management” at the time of the government takeover, adding: “The challenges that have arisen have forced the department to cease the continued funding of Solms-Delta in its present form.”
Tommy Hall, an American technology executive, has pledged to buy back the government’s shares for the workers and invest in the business. Negotiations with the government are ongoing, Solms and Jansen said, and they hope to reopen the farm and sell wine again in about a year.
Jansen noted that many other wine farms were evicting workers whose families had lived there for generations, often since the time of slavery. “We built this land with our blood and tears and sweat,” he said. “And now it’s being taken away.”

Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.
The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.
At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?
If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.
But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.
The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.
The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.
But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.
Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.
Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.
Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.
Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.
This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.
- Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

I saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

It was mid-April and after a month of deadly airstrikes across Lebanon, Israel agreed to a ceasefire. Much of the bombing had focused on southern Lebanon, where entire villages had been demolished. But with the truce, people were hopeful of being able to return to their homes or to see what remained.
Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old photojournalist, decided to join Amal Khalil, 42, a newspaper reporter in Lebanon, on a trip to an area in the south of the country to document the aftermath of war. The two had worked together on a number of assignments after Khalil had seen Faraj’s work on social media and contacted her.
“I expected it to be like every other time. Amal and I would go out, take some footage and then leave. I had absolutely no sense of fear. We could hear some gunfire and artillery, but as a videographer, you find those things important to document and capture,” says Faraj, who was freelancing alongside finishing her degree in radio and TV.
By the time they reached the village of al-Tiri on the afternoon of 22 April, Faraj began to look out the window and reminisce. She was born and grew up in the nearby city of Bint Jbeil. “My whole life revolved around this area. As we say, a fish suffocates when it’s taken out of water. That’s how we feel whenever we leave Bint Jbeil.”
Ahead of them was a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, 27, a municipal official in Bint Jbeil, and Mohammed Hourani, 37, a friend of the mayor. They had met them by chance earlier in the day at Tebnine governmental hospital, which had become a gathering point because people considered it relatively safe and would base their movements from there. Bazzi was due to sign a marriage contract that evening, but was still keen to join the trip.
Faraj says she did not hear the missile coming, just the sound of Khalil screaming and then the sight of the car in front of them on fire. The two women got out of their car.
“I do not know how I managed to stay so calm. The only thing I could think was: if I come closer, I will be able to see Ali. Maybe I will be able to pull him out.”
Khalil kept repeating: “Oh God, they’re gone.” Slowly, Faraj began to understand what was going on. “I could see their bodies torn apart.”
Then the drones appeared.
“When the drones came, my heart started pounding in a terrifying way. The drone started coming very close to my face. I tried to cover my face, but whenever I did, it would fly back up. That was when I really felt the real danger.”
The drones flew low and close as Khalil and Faraj frantically made phone calls to emergency services who repeatedly assured them that help was on its way. Faraj says the assurances were “like an anaesthetic”, something that briefly numbed the reality that no one was rescuing them.
One of the paramedics on a call told them to get into their car and try to drive back up the road, as ambulances were being preventing from driving to where they were. But as they tried to get into the car, it was struck by a missile.
Both of them were thrown backwards, with Khalil wrapping her arms around Faraj. As the drone continued to circle overhead, Khalil said she hoped it would “think we were dead”.
With the nearby car engulfed in flames, they decided to take shelter in a nearby house. Khalil had visible injuries, with blood on her face, hand and leg. Faraj says she sent her sister a last message before her phone died: “There’s no hope left. Forgive me.”
Inside, they sat on a bathroom floor. Khalil was unable to move, so Faraj says she crawled to a position from where she could watch the road. Suddenly a drone descended towards her.
“It had been high up and suddenly it came down. The way it descended was terrifying. My heart stopped.” Soon after this, Faraj says she came back inside and began to feel tired and detached from what was happening. “I felt alone.”
Then came the sound of a missile falling. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life. I’ve heard so many strikes and drones, but this was completely different. It was terrifying and Amal was screaming,” she says.
She does not remember what happened next, but when she opened her eyes an enormous weight was pressing down on her body. Everything was black and she could barely breathe. She was trapped underneath rubble. “I couldn’t bear the weight. It felt like something was pushing me down, crushing me. All I cared about was being able to breathe.”
Faraj says she then heard a voice and thought it was her father, but it was a paramedic who had managed to reach the scene of the attack. As he held her by the shoulders, Faraj says she instinctively clung to him and refused to let go. “I told him: ‘Don’t leave me. I’m afraid to stay alone.’” He stayed beside her while a second paramedic cleared the rubble.
As the sound of drones returned once more, the paramedics quickly pulled Faraj free as she screamed from the pain. At about the same time, Faraj says she heard a stun grenade dropped by the drone. As they drove away in the ambulance, she repeatedly mistook the sound of the vehicle for a drone. “They’re going to hit us. We’re not going to make it,” she says she kept repeating.
After they got to a hospital, Faraj says she started to ask about Khalil. At first the nurses tried to reassure her. But eventually, she says, they fell silent. “That’s when I knew she was gone.” Khalil is believed to have died about an hour before the paramedics had been allowed to return to the area again after rescuing Faraj.
The Israeli military justified their attack saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. However, human rights groups called it a war crime. As Khalil and Faraj took refuge in the building the Israeli military received repeated messages urging them to allow a rescue operation. A week before the attack, an Israeli military spokesperson shared a video of Khalil published by her newspaper and described it as “terrorist media”. Khalil had also received death threats from Israeli numbers.
Today, as Faraj prepares to return to university, she still struggles to walk properly and has visible injuries to a hand. An injury to her face has affected the movement of one eyebrow; others are hidden by her clothes and hijab. Her limp is especially hard to bear. “I was always on the move. I lost that. Even climbing stairs can be hard,” she says.
At first she was in shock, she says, but now more symptoms are starting to appear. She wakes at night screaming and buries herself in the pillows as if a missile is going to strike. The sound of drones and warplanes put her on edge.
Returning to frontline journalism feels uncertain and she says she is repeatedly haunted by the image of Hourani lying on the ground after the first missile attack. “His head was turned towards me. His eyes open and looking at me. That is something I will never get out of my head.”

Labour urged to plug predicted £400m shortfall in overseas aid funding in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.
Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.
The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.
However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.
Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.
Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.
The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.
The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.
The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.
Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.
She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.
“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.
“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”
Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.
The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.
The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.
The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.
The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.
“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

Roca releases innovative all-in-one Avant toilet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Roca releases innovative all-in-one Avant toilet
Spanish bathroom brand Roca has rethought conventional toilet design with Avant, integrating the cistern within the toilet itself.
For the Avant toilet, Roca designed the cistern to sit within the bowl, removing the external cistern on its floor-standing model and the concealed cistern and flush plate on its wall-hung version.
Avant’s cistern uses flushing technology based on the Venturi effect. Here, fluid pressure drops when liquid is funnelled from a larger pipe section to a smaller one.
This creates a powerful suction in the tank, which is needed for the flush. As the components are concealed within the wall, this gives Avant a more minimalist appearance but also offers benefits in space, aesthetics, installation and maintenance.
The integrated aesthetic also makes bathrooms more adaptable and practical for different design needs and interiors.
“The removal of an external cistern or the flush plate further enhances the overall aesthetic of the bathroom, and its neutral, minimalist design blends seamlessly into any bathroom style, adding a touch of modernity,” said Roca.
Another innovative element is that the Avant is also powered without electricity, but if water pressure or flow is insufficient in a building, the Avant-E model is best suited – an electric version suitable for a wider range of plumbing systems.
The Avant also features dual-flush options, side-mounted flush buttons, a soft-close seat and cover and Roca Rimless Vortex. According to Roca, it meets the highest hygiene standards and operates with splash-free, low-consumption flushing, reducing water consumption.
The toilet is also covered in Supraglaze, a custom finish that mitigates the build-up of dirt, germs and residue, making cleaning simple and further increasing hygiene.
The result is an efficient, minimalist toilet ideal for compact spaces, easy to install and maintain.
“Avant not only brings a modern aesthetic to the bathroom, but it also reduces flush noise, providing a quieter, more comfortable experience than conventional toilets,” said Roca.
Founded in Spain in 1917, Roca now operates in 170 countries, with a special focus on sustainability and craftsmanship.
The company produces high-end, design-forward bathroom appliances, including everything from toilets to sinks, hardware and faucets.
It recently released modular bathroom furniture that can be adjusted to fit different scales and colourful taps in collaboration with designer Inma Bermúdez, in bright green, blue and yellow finishes.
To learn more about the Avant toilet, visit Roca’s website.
The photography is courtesy of Roca.

Drone reportedly strikes business center in Russia's Voronezh as fires break out across city

Footage published by ASTRA appears to show a drone exploding at the Chizhov Gallery business center, a 25-story building in central Voronezh.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also published imagery of the reported attack.
ASTRA further reported fires in residential areas, having received eyewitness photographs and videos that identified locations near apartment buildings where explosions occurred.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev confirmed that Russian air defenses responded to a drone attack over Voronezh and its surrounding areas on the morning of Oct. 26.
According to ASTRA, a drone threat was announced at approximately 3 a.m. local time, followed by a missile warning about two hours later.
Reports mentioned numerous explosions across the city and thick smoke rising from several locations. Some residents told ASTRA that they had not heard air raid sirens despite the ongoing attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify the extent of the damage or whether the explosions near residential buildings were caused by direct drone impacts or falling debris. There were no immediately confirmed reports of casualties.
Voronezh Oblast directly borders eastern Ukraine, with the regional capital located about 200 kilometers (nearly 120 miles) from the nearest Ukrainian-held territory in Kharkiv Oblast. The areas has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian military and industrial infrastructure.
On June 22, Ukrainian forces struck the Voronezh Semiconductor Plant, a facility producing electronic components used in Russian missile and air defense systems, according to Ukraine's General Staff.

Taiwan startup develops rapid gene sequencing test for infections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:54:06 UTC
13:54:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Biotech startup Asia Pathogenomics has developed gene sequencing technology that can identify infectious pathogens in as little as 24 hours, CNA reported Monday.
The company, also known as APG, said a clinical study found its technology detected pathogens at more than three times the rate of conventional testing, helping doctors identify causes of infection and make treatment decisions faster. Since its founding in 2020, the company said it has helped clinicians diagnose and treat more than 10,000 patients with infections.
APG CEO Li Ting-huan (李定寰) said conventional tests require doctors to suspect a pathogen and test for possible causes one by one, while culture results can take days or weeks. Gene sequencing compares samples against thousands of pathogens at once, without requiring doctors to predict the cause in advance.
In a clinical study provided by APG, gene sequencing detected pathogens in 88% of patients with bloodstream infections, compared with 26% using conventional blood cultures. The Taiwan Society of Infectious Diseases incorporated gene sequencing into its clinical recommendations for identifying infectious pathogens in July last year.
APG was selected for the Industrial Development Administration’s Corporate Venture Capital Accelerates Innovation and Entrepreneurship Program this year, receiving about NT$19 million (US$580,000) in government-approved funding. TCI Co., Ltd. is its corporate venture capital partner, and the program aims to facilitate NT$200 million in investment.
The company plans to link sequencing results with clinical information using the health ministry’s data exchange standard and apply AI to help identify pathogens. It also plans to introduce a lower-cost test covering more than 100 common pathogens at prices 30% to 50% below those of existing tests, which cost NT$30,000 to NT$50,000 out of pocket.
Li estimated the annual market for tests related to severe infections could reach NT$1 billion. APG is expanding in Japan, where it plans to complete clinical validation within one to two years before seeking public health insurance coverage.

Indonesia Reduces Gas Supply to Singapore, Citing Domestic Energy Needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:53:00 UTC
13:53:00 KST

Indonesia on Saturday began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore in order to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs, the country’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
According to reports by Reuters and Channel News Asia, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto said that the diversion involves 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day, which would be redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan, and Sumatra. This comprises 15 million standard cubic feet of gas per day from Natuna and 16 million from Sumatra, which makes up around 9 percent of Indonesia’s total exports of natural gas to Singapore.
“In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously destined for Singapore are being redirected for domestic use,” Djoko said, as per Reuters.
The latest cut comes after a series of serious power outages in Indonesia, including a major blackout across at least six provinces in Sumatra in May and rolling outages in Java and Kalimantan in June and July. More recently, the island of Batam in Riau Islands Province was last week hit with a 16-hour power outage.
Singapore is highly dependent on imported gas for electricity generation, generating more than 90 percent of its power from this source. Last year, around 43 percent of the country’s imported gas was shipped by pipeline from Indonesia and Malaysia, with the remaining 57 percent made up of liquefied natural gas shipped by sea.
Despite Singapore’s reliance on Indonesian gas, the reduction is unlikely to have much impact on the country’s electricity supply. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said on Saturday that the reduction would amount to around 17 billion British thermal units per day over a period of 18 days. This, it said, equated to “less than 2 percent of our total daily gas demand.”
Tan See Leng, Singapore’s minister for energy, trade, and industry, said yesterday that Singapore has sufficient gas supply to meet its demand, and was seeking continuously to diversify its sources of gas to guard against any potential future shocks.
“In the short term, the prices would not really affect that much,” he said. “I would like to urge all of our fellow Singaporeans: keep calm and carry on. We have dealt seamlessly with such reductions in the past without any incident, and the government will continue to ensure the reliability and the resilience of Singapore’s energy supply.”
The gas supply cut is consistent with Indonesia’s long-standing policy of prioritizing the use of natural resources for its domestic needs. Under Jakarta’s regime of Domestic Market Obligations, producers of key natural resources and commodities are required to reserve a specific portion of their production for the local market at below-market prices, before being allowed to export the remainder. For instance, in January 2022, the Indonesian government banned coal exports for a month after supplies at domestic power plants ran low.
Indonesia has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy.
The gas cut was foreshadowed by Indonesian Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia, who told reporters on October 21 that Indonesia would not hesitate to prioritize natural resources for its own domestic needs and that President Prabowo Subianto had ordered Indonesia “to adopt a survival-oriented approach amid geopolitical tensions and global energy challenges,” in the words of the Jakarta Globe.
The following day, he said that the government might also cut off supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia.
“Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” Bahlil said, as per the South China Morning Post.
The minister’s remarks were cryptic, and he made no mention of Singapore, but they come at a time of growing friction between the two neighbors due to the toxic haze resulting from months of Indonesian wildfires, and the recent turbulence in the Indonesian stock market.
In recent weeks, Singaporean citizens have grown increasingly frustrated with the haze, a result of raging forest and peatland fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and the apparent inaction of the Indonesian authorities – a sentiment that has not been helped by the defensive statements of some Indonesian officials.
Singapore’s government, too, has begun to express its discontent with Jakarta over the haze, albeit in much more measured language. On October 15, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into Indonesian companies that could be responsible for the fires in Indonesia, and potentially take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on October 19 that Singapore will “sustain pressure” on these companies even after the haze passes. “If companies refuse to cooperate, regardless of whether they have a presence in Singapore or do not have a presence in Singapore, we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters,” he said.
There have also been tensions related to the recent threat of global index provider MSCI to downgrade Indonesia to “Standalone Market” status due to a lack of transparency in its stock market. The possible downgrade, which was announced on October 16, led to an immediate plunge in the Indonesian stock market, which shed 15 percent of its value over two days of trading.
In the aftermath, Indonesia’s former Trade Minister Muhammad Lutfi claimed on social media last week that the Singaporean state investment firms GIC and Temasek had pressured MSCI to downgrade Indonesia in order to suppress stock prices. The two firms have denied his claims. Prabowo himself responded to the downgrade threat with strident nationalism, claiming that MSCI “intended to intimidate us.”
Prabowo’s two years in office have been marked by increasingly strident nationalism and rhetoric about national self-sufficiency, which have resulted in ever-more overt state involvement in the economy. While this policy may serve to safeguard Indonesia’s domestic energy and food security in the short term, the longer-term impact will be to undermine business confidence and potentially to generate friction with Indonesia’s neighbors. In this particular instance, it is hard to see that Indonesia’s main regional economic partners will begin to look elsewhere for their energy supplies, as indeed, Singapore is already doing.

PROFILE - From prison to historic 4th term: Brazil's Lula extends extraordinary political career
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:51:32 UTC
13:51:32 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva secured an unprecedented fourth presidential term Sunday, defeating challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely contested runoff that marked another chapter in Latin America's largest country.
Lula won 51.78% of valid votes against 48.22% for Bolsonaro, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), with 99.98% of polling stations counted.
The victory extends the political longevity of the 80-year-old leader, who rose from poverty to become Brazil's first working-class president and later returned to power after serving time in prison on corruption convictions that were subsequently annulled.
Lula, the candidate of the Workers' Party (PT), entered the runoff after finishing second in the Oct. 4 first round, receiving 45.16% of valid votes against 47.03% for Bolsonaro, a senator.
His comeback made him the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy to win a presidential election after finishing second in the first round, adding another historic distinction to his political career.
Speaking after his victory in Sao Paulo, Lula pledged to govern for all Brazilians despite the country's political divisions.
"Nobody is obliged to like the elected president, but he was elected to govern for everyone," he said, emphasizing respect for the Constitution.
Lula’s reelection followed a campaign dominated by concerns over living costs, public security, corruption and the direction of Brazil's foreign relations, particularly its increasingly strained relationship with the US under President Donald Trump.
Born on Oct. 27, 1945 in the northeastern state of Pernambuco, Lula grew up in poverty before moving with his family to Sao Paulo, where he worked from an early age.
He received vocational training as a metalworker and lost a finger in an industrial accident, an experience that became part of his political identity as a representative of Brazil's working class.
Lula became involved in organized labor during the country's military dictatorship and rose to lead the metalworkers' union in Sao Bernardo do Campo, an industrial center outside Sao Paulo.
His leadership of major strikes in the late 1970s brought him national prominence. He helped establish the Workers' Party in 1980, combining trade union activists, leftist intellectuals and other groups opposed to military rule.
Elected to Congress in 1986, Lula made unsuccessful presidential bids in 1989, 1994 and 1998 before winning the presidency in 2002.
He took office in January 2003, promising to combat poverty while maintaining economic stability.
During his first two terms, which ended in 2010, Brazil benefited from rising commodity exports and economic growth, while social programs including Bolsa Familia provided financial assistance to millions of low-income households.
Poverty declined substantially, although his administration also faced corruption scandals involving senior officials and lawmakers.
Lula left office with high approval ratings and was succeeded by his political ally Dilma Rousseff, who was later impeached in 2016.
Lula's political career suffered a major setback during the sweeping Operation Car Wash corruption investigation, which implicated politicians and business executives in bribery and money laundering.
He was convicted on corruption and money laundering charges and imprisoned in April 2018, preventing him from contesting that year's presidential election.
He spent 580 days in prison before being released in November 2019.
In 2021, Brazil's Supreme Court annulled his convictions, ruling that the court which handled his cases lacked jurisdiction. The court also found that former judge Sergio Moro had been biased in one of the proceedings.
The decisions restored Lula's eligibility to seek public office.
He returned to the presidency after narrowly defeating incumbent Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election, winning approximately 50.9% of valid votes.
His inauguration in January 2023 was followed a week later by an assault on Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace by Bolsonaro supporters seeking to overturn the election result.
During his third presidency, Lula prioritized poverty reduction, social spending, public investment and environmental protection while seeking to maintain fiscal stability.
His administration expanded social assistance programs and pursued measures to strengthen wages and employment, but concerns over living costs, government spending and violent crime weighed on his popularity.
The government also faced difficulties advancing legislation in a Congress where centrist and conservative parties held considerable influence.
For his fourth-term campaign, Lula promised to maintain Bolsa Familia, expand affordable housing and strengthen public health care and education.
His economic proposals included higher taxation of high incomes, continued infrastructure investment, support for domestic manufacturing and further increases in the minimum wage.
Lula also championed legislation to reduce the standard workweek from 44 to 40 hours without cutting wages, a constitutional amendment enacted on Oct. 16 that will be implemented gradually over 14 months.
Environmental protection remained another priority, with Lula pledging to eliminate deforestation by 2030 while supporting continued oil and gas development.
However, his victory does not guarantee control of Congress, where conservative parties strengthened their influence in the October elections.
The composition of the legislature could complicate his efforts to advance tax reforms, social spending, public security measures and environmental legislation, forcing his administration to negotiate with parties outside his political coalition.
Internationally, Lula has pursued closer cooperation with emerging economies through BRICS, strengthened relations with China and advocated a larger diplomatic role for Brazil.
He has criticized Israel's military operations in Gaza, supported Palestinian statehood and called for negotiated solutions to international conflicts.
His relationship with Washington frayed as Trump imposed tariffs on Brazilian goods and publicly supported former President Jair Bolsonaro, although Trump stopped short of formally endorsing Flavio Bolsonaro in the 2026 election.
Lula criticized what he viewed as US interference in Brazilian affairs, making national sovereignty a central theme of his reelection campaign.
His latest victory comes amid a broader shift to the right across Latin America, where conservative governments have taken power in several countries including Chile, Colombia and Peru, some seeking closer ties with Trump.
The result leaves Brazil among the region's largest governments maintaining an independent diplomatic approach toward Washington and seeking increased cooperation with the Global South.
Lula's new four-year term will begin on Jan. 5, 2027, extending his presidential career across nearly three decades.

====================================================================================================

How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:41:20 UTC
13:41:20 KST

In December 2025, the US-sanctioned tanker Reef arrived in Myanmar waters with some 113,000 barrels of fuel backed by sham paperwork.
Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave ordered the shipment, agreeing in a sales contract inked with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel. But the $15.8 million agreement, which Reuters viewed, was a charade: there was no such trade between South Africa and Myanmar in 2025, according to data from the United Nations and Vortexa, a shipping and energy data provider.
In reality, Reef carried jet fuel from Iran to Myanmar, according to records of fuel shipments to Myanmar, as well as satellite images and analysis by SynMax Intelligence, which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.
The deception was needed because the US in 2023 imposed targeted sanctions on Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry. The US did so citing the deadly bombing campaign waged by the Southeast Asian country’s military on civilian targets as part of an effort to crush a rebel-led insurgency. All purchasers of Iranian oil and fuel are also exposed to sweeping American sanctions.
Details of how Myanmar disguised purchases of Iranian jet fuel, as well as the entities involved in the transactions, are reported here for the first time.
Myanmar’s military junta was involved in the ruse. Days before Reef arrived, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel,” according to a copy of the agency’s November 30 letter seen by Reuters. The document, which was provided to Reuters by the activist group Justice for Myanmar, did not explain the purpose of the mislabeling.
The letter from the regulator also authorized Dynamic Wave and its client, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Company, to pay Tawan for the shipment.
Neither Dynamic Wave nor its client, which is part-owned by Myanmar’s military-backed government, responded to questions about the fuel shipment.
Spokespeople for Myanmar’s military-backed government and foreign exchange regulator, as well as the Iranian foreign ministry, also did not return requests for comment.
Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025, with much of the trade carried out by the tankers Reef – since renamed Maris – and Noble, a Reuters report revealed in January.
The scheme uncovered by Reuters underscores both the reach and limits of Washington’s power. The lengths taken to disguise the trade suggest US sanctions are biting. But Iranian jet fuel has continued to flow, earning Tehran valuable foreign currency and providing Myanmar with the means to conduct both commercial aviation and air raids.
The US Treasury did not respond to questions about jet-fuel shipments between Iran and Myanmar.
Jet fuel, airstrikes, and civilian casualties
Myanmar’s generals seized power in 2021 from the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The coup sparked a civil war, during which the military has killed thousands – including many civilians – in aerial assaults, the United Nations said in August.
Myanmar’s foreign ministry said in response to the UN allegations that the military “exercises maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.”
Justice for Myanmar, which also shared the fuel sales contract with Reuters, published a report on Monday concluding that Myanmar’s junta was importing jet fuel mislabeled as diesel.
The organization, which supports further sanctions on Myanmar's jet fuel imports, said it obtained the documents from a junta-run server that was briefly publicly accessible.
Reuters found a dead link to one of the documents on the DuckDuckGo search engine, indicating it had once been hosted on that server. Delivery dates and fuel quantities in the documents also match Iranian jet fuel shipment records that were separately reviewed by the news agency.
Thai bank connection
The sales contract for Dynamic Wave's fuel shipment stipulated that the payment be transferred into Tawan’s account at Siam Commercial Bank (SCB), Thailand’s oldest bank.
Tawan was identified by UN experts in a 2024 report as a jet-fuel supplier to Myanmar’s military. The firm has not commented on those allegations.
SCB was described as a major facilitator of Myanmar military procurement in that report.
The bank said after the report’s release that it adheres to anti-money-laundering laws and that its Myanmar-related transactions were legitimate and not connected to the arms trade.
Reuters could not determine whether SCB was aware of the nature of Tawan’s business.
Thai regulators in 2024 ordered banks to closely scrutinize transactions involving Myanmar in order to comply with sanctions and anti-money-laundering laws.
SCB did not respond to repeated requests for comment about its commercial relationship with Tawan.
Tawan and the Bank of Thailand, which supervises the kingdom's financial industry, also did not respond to questions.
The December shipment was not the first time jet fuel arrived in Myanmar disguised as diesel.
Dynamic Wave in May 2025 agreed to buy from Tawan 202,000 barrels of what a second contract, also obtained from the junta server, described as South African diesel. The agreement stipulated that the diesel should arrive at Yangon within a month and that Dynamic Wave would pay $26 million into Tawan’s SCB account.
The invoice for that contract contained discrepancies suggesting the tanker actually contained jet fuel.
The density of the fuel listed in the document matched the specifications for jet fuel rather than diesel sold in Southeast Asia, according to Joshua Heyne, a jet-fuel expert at Washington State University, and data from Platts, the energy-industry information provider. In addition, the price of the fuel was more than 50% higher than a global diesel benchmark.
Noble called at Yangon on June 17 carrying just under 200,000 barrels of jet fuel earmarked for Dynamic Wave, shipment records show.
Like Reef's December shipment, Noble’s cargo was loaded at Iran’s Bandar Abbas according to SynMax’s analysis of satellite imagery. As it made its way to Myanmar’s commercial capital, Noble transmitted location signals that made it appear as though its destination was the port of Chittagong in Bangladesh, according to SynMax.
The manager of the Reef and Noble tankers did not respond to questions sent via its listed website.
Shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued this year, Reuters reported in October, citing SynMax analysis and satellite imagery.

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.

Unknown Publisher

04:40:10 UTC
13:40:10 KST

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
What A7 is and how it became the largest player in the shadow payments market
Sanctions against Russian banks and payment systems, along with their disconnection from SWIFT after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, gave rise to shadow intermediaries offering Russians cross-border money transfers. Many have offices in the capital’s Moscow City business district, the investigative outlet Proekt reported in spring 2026.
The largest is A7, a company owned by Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, who was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in Moldova. Shor owns a controlling stake; the remaining 49% belongs to Russia’s state-owned Promsvyazbank (PSB). In late 2019, PSB officially became the designated bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry and defense industry.
The state development corporation VEB.RF, headed by Igor Shuvalov, “provides support” to A7. Proekt’s journalists suggest that Roman Abramovich may play “an important but secret role in the company.” A source in the cross-border payments business described Abramovich to Proekt as A7’s “protector and sponsor.” In the source’s view, Abramovich began working with Shor because he valued Shor’s ability to “devise financial schemes.” Abramovich’s representatives deny that he is involved in A7.
How Abramovich is connected to A7
According to Proekt, Shor’s first flight to Russia after a Moldovan court ordered his arrest in absentia was aboard Abramovich’s plane, suggesting that the two knew each other well.
Igor Shuvalov, the head of VEB.RF, the state corporation that “provides support” to A7, is a longtime acquaintance of Abramovich’s.
In 2024, A7 rented offices in Abramovich’s Belye Sady and Skolkovo Park business centers. Two A7 subsidiaries still occupy offices owned by Abramovich.
“Another indication of the oligarch’s involvement is the enormous financial support A7 receives from businessman Viktor Kharitonin, whom the press has long called ‘Abramovich’s protégé,’” Proekt reported.
A business partner of Abramovich’s, who spoke to Proekt on condition of anonymity, estimated that A7 handles about 15% of all cross-border transfers in Russia. The company puts its share even higher, at 19%. “No one else even comes close to A7,” a source working in the market told Proekt. The outlet’s other sources agreed that A7 is the largest player in the industry.
Proekt obtained a list of all of A7’s clients. They included at least 25 Russian companies already under U.S. and EU sanctions. Five manufacture or supply combat drones used by the Russian army in its war against Ukraine.
Other A7 clients include Arkady Rotenberg’s tour operator Biblioglobus, the online marketplace Wildberries, cigarette manufacturer International Tobacco Group, the Sunlight jewelry chain, and industrial companies including Leonid Mikhelson’s natural gas producer Arctic LNG 2, AAEM Turbine Technologies, and S7 Engineering.
In late October, journalists from the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) expanded on Proekt’s investigation. After reviewing internal company documents and speaking with sources, they found that most payments entering A7’s network are funded by hundreds of metric tons of rubles in cash collected from individuals and companies at several Moscow wholesale and retail markets, including the largest, Sadovod.
Sadovod is known as a market where most transactions are conducted in cash, and many of its shop employees and owners are migrant workers from countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. “Sadovod is simply a big client base,” a source familiar with the situation told ICIJ, explaining A7’s choice of location.
How the scheme works
Before 2022, intermediaries at Sadovod were already converting cash into ordinary bank transfers or into cryptocurrency, which most often went to China. Western sanctions later disrupted this system by cutting Russian companies off from SWIFT.
A7’s improved system allowed a group of brokers at Sadovod to keep operating. They now accept bags of cash brought in by vendors and count the money, according to the documents. A7’s records refer to these initial cash collection points as “departments”; there are at least eight.
The brokers then pack the rubles into numbered bags. The bags are loaded into vans along with customers’ payment orders and sent to an A7 payment processing center elsewhere in Moscow. About 50 cashiers work there, recording the cash in A7’s counting system. The cash is then delivered to Promsvyazbank, which places it in a vault and credits A7’s accounts.
A7 then uses its shell companies registered abroad. Intermediary companies in Kyrgyzstan buy cryptocurrency through Grinex, a crypto exchange linked to A7. By this point, the money is no longer identified as originating in Russia, thanks to Kyrgyzstan’s permissive policies on cryptocurrency transactions.
PSB provides the banking infrastructure for transferring money to Kyrgyzstan, along with loans and guarantees when needed. From Kyrgyzstan, the money goes to intermediary companies linked to A7 in third countries, most often in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. They convert the cryptocurrency into local currencies and send the money to the end recipient.
“By the time [an A7 payment] is received, nobody in the chain, from the U.S. clearing bank to the Chinese supplier, knows where it came from,” said illicit finance expert Zachary Tvarozna, who co-authored an investigation into A7 conducted with the British nonprofit Open Source Centre. “Washington essentially created a market for A7 [by restricting legitimate transactions] and then did nothing about it,” he concluded.
The risks this scheme poses to the global financial system
From November 2024 to July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 metric tons of rubles in cash worth more than $14 billion, ICIJ and Proekt reported. The journalists were unable to trace the cash’s origins, but it is clear that most of it went to China, as before.
A registry of A7 promissory notes that leaked online and was reviewed by ICIJ shows that A7’s cash deposits at PSB rose in 2025, reaching 195 billion rubles ($2.3 billion) a month by April and 250 billion rubles ($3.1 billion) in June. At its peak, A7 processed at least 58 metric tons of cash a month.
On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 a “significant transnational criminal organization.” This means U.S. financial institutions will no longer be able to process transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents” — foreign shell companies through which the network routes payments for clients in Russia.
A7 “uses a modern, multilayered system of controls” and “was established to ensure uninterrupted payments in the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures,” the company said in a press release issued after the Treasury Department’s announcement. “All clients are screened to identify risks and prevent us from serving individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” the company insisted.
Just two years earlier, when it launched, A7 presented itself as a “sanctions-proof payment system.”
George Voloshin, a financial crime expert at the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists, told ICIJ that A7 “not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls” but “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime.”
International intermediary banks and beneficiaries effectively become complicit in these activities even though they do not know where the money comes from. The reason lies in the cash itself, Voloshin added:
Cash is considered one of the highest-risk payment methods because it is anonymous, can move across borders, and is not tied to a specific person or company.
The entire scheme “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” said Ilya Shumanov, managing partner of TriTrace Investigations, a Russian company specializing in financial market due diligence. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
According to documents reviewed by ICIJ, A7 received 314 payment requests totaling $76 million from brokers working at Sadovod in late 2024. All of the money was intended for the Hong Kong export company Yiton Trading Ltd.
A7 representatives did not respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.

SAO PAULO – Joyful cheers of “Let’s go, Lula!” rose from the jubilant crowd again and again as Brazilians paraded down Sao Paulo’s Paulista Avenue on Oct 25, celebrating the leftist leader’s improbable election win.
Thousands of people spilled onto the streets following President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory over his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
Lula, who turns 81 on Oct 27, joined the parade, leaning out of the sunroof of his car with a megaphone in his hand and his trademark rasp more hoarse than ever.
“I just had to tell you that I love you. Tomorrow, the fight continues,” he said.
He received 51.8% of the votes compared to 48.2% for former president Jair Bolsonaro’s son, who has refused to acknowledge the result.
“I feel so happy!” 43-year-old Anna Zanatta told AFP before bursting into tears of joy.
“Lula’s victory represents many things for us: freedom, our democracy, our history,” she said, waving a flag bearing the message “Antifascist Action”.
Zanatta viewed a hypothetical Bolsonaro victory as a “threat” to Latin America’s largest democracy.
“I was born under a dictatorship, and I promised my granddaughter that we Brazilians would never go through that again,” she said, referring to the military regime which ruled from 1964 to 1985.
Doorman Alfonso dos Reis, 64, carried a sign reading “Lula again with the strength of the people” alongside a photo of the President.
“We’re going to build a much better country,” he beamed.
Fireworks boomed and cars honked their horns as the crowd marched down Sao Paulo’s main avenue, which turned into a sea of yellow and green as the Brazilian flag covered every square inch of the place.
Lula appeared alongside lawmaker Andre Janones, who created the “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel which surged to 10.8 million followers during the second-round campaign.
Lula’s supporters attribute his comeback in part to the lawmaker’s digital battle.
“I owe this victory to the rebellious youth who rose up to defend democracy,” Lula said.
‘No amnesty!’
Mateus Freitas, a 33-year-old theatre actor, waved a flare that sent red smoke into the air, the colour associated with Lula’s Workers’ Party.
“No amnesty! No amnesty!” Freitas yelled at the top of his lungs.
He was referring to attempts to free Jair Bolsonaro, who governed from 2019 to 2022 and is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup following his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
His son Flavio had promised to liberate him if elected.
“We stopped a government that would have been a fascist government, led by militias, criminals, racists, homophobes,” Freitas told AFP.
“This is a victory for minorities, for the people, for Brazilian workers... Lula’s government is inclusive,” he said.
Sigh of relief
The leftist victory has swerved Brazil away from a rightward turn, unlike a recent string of wins championed by US President Donald Trump across Latin America.
Flavio Bolsonaro came out on top in the first round of presidential elections, and polls had given him a slight advantage ahead of the run-off.
Those indicators had concerned Felipe Rodrigues, a 53-year-old architect taking part in the celebrations on Oct 25.
“I’m very glad to see that, despite the risks of having a far-right government, which seems to be a global trend, here in Brazil we have a president who continues his efforts to improve the lives of the poor,” he said. AFP

Scattered rain, snow to hit northern, central, and southeastern Kazakhstan
Under the influence of a broad anticyclone, most of Kazakhstan will see clear, dry weather on Monday, the national weather service Kazhydromet said, Qazinform News Agency reports.
However, passing fronts will bring scattered rain and snow to northern, southeastern, and central regions.
Black ice is expected in the north. Patchy fog will develop across the country.
Strong winds are forecast for western, southern, eastern, and southeastern Kazakhstan. Dust storms are predicted in western and southern regions.
In addition, a high fire hazard warning remains in effect for the Mangystau, West Kazakhstan, Aktobe, Atyrau, Karaganda, Ulytau, Kyzylorda, Zhambyl, Kostanay, Zhetisu, Almaty, and Turkistan regions.

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
Judge questions the Trump administration’s efforts to exert greater influence over elections process ahead of the upcoming midterm vote.
A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.
“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.
It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely noncitizens”.
The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.
Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefitting from widespread voting by noncitizens.
California has long been one of the targets of his election misinformation.
Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.
“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.
He then announced that the state would be under investigation by the US Attorneys’ Office.
Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.
The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.
Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran.
Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of noncitizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.
In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting.
It also said the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.
“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

Israel must listen to its friends, not dismiss their warnings - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:21:47 UTC
13:21:47 KST

When one of Israel’s most outspoken American supporters says two ministers are damaging the country’s standing, the government should listen. Bill Ackman’s Sunday warning about Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich deserves attention because it comes from someone who wants Israel to succeed, has defended it publicly, and has praised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Jewish-American billionaire investor made clear in his post on X/Twitter that Israelis must decide who becomes their prime minister. But from his vantage point in America, the national security minister and finance minister, respectively, have caused Israel “enormous reputational damage,” their statements and actions presented internationally as expressing the will of all Israelis.
A government without them, Ackman argued, would signal a new beginning, help restore credibility, improve relations with Democrats and Republicans, and increase the prospects of expanding the Abraham Accords, which normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states.
His warning should not be dismissed as another intervention by someone hostile to the government. Ackman has praised Netanyahu’s leadership since October 7 while identifying the two ministers as a serious liability. His criticism cannot credibly be reduced to opposition to Netanyahu or indifference to Israel’s security.
That makes it politically uncomfortable and valuable. It asks government supporters to consider whether loyalty to particular coalition partners serves the country they intend to defend.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee offers another example. A longstanding supporter of Israel appointed by President Donald Trump, Huckabee told The Jerusalem Post in September: “I wish that they understood the damage they’re doing to the country they claim to love because it is not helpful.”
He was referring to violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, which he warned was damaging Israel’s reputation, including among Republicans. He also argued that condemning Palestinian violence while refusing to condemn Israeli violence would be hypocritical. His support for Israel did not prevent him from demanding accountability.
There is a moral obligation here, before any question of reputation. Violence and humiliating treatment deserve scrutiny because of the harm they inflict, regardless of the headlines they generate. Israel should demand standards of its representatives that it can defend openly before its citizens and its allies.
Recognizing that friendship doesn’t require silence when Israelis harm Israel’s interests.
These interventions differ in scope. Huckabee’s criticism of specific conduct is not an endorsement of Ackman’s proposed coalition arrangement. What connects them is the recognition that friendship does not require silence when Israelis damage Israel’s interests.
Jerusalem should be capable of hearing that distinction. Criticism must be judged on its merits, whoever delivers it. But when people who regularly defend this country describe the difficulties created by its ministers, their warnings deserve attention. They understand Israel’s arguments abroad because they have made those arguments themselves.
Nor can every damaging image be explained away as hostile coverage. Ministers hold public authority. Their words carry weight because of their offices, and the government cannot expect foreign audiences to treat them as private citizens whenever their conduct becomes embarrassing.
There are limits to Ackman’s prescription. Removing two ministers would not automatically restore Israel’s standing, resolve disagreements over the Palestinians, or secure additional normalization agreements.
Those outcomes require policy, diplomacy, and decisions by other governments. Changing ministers alone would not substitute for responsible policy and leadership.
The people entrusted with power nevertheless help define a government’s priorities and credibility. A prime minister who promises responsible leadership abroad must exercise it within his cabinet.
Coalition calculations cannot be the only measure of whether a partnership serves the national interest. That responsibility belongs to whoever forms the next government and chooses its senior ministers.
The test for any coalition should be whether it can protect the country while governing responsibly at home and maintaining credibility abroad. That requires leaders willing to confront damaging conduct among their allies, rather than dismiss every warning as disloyalty or leave accountability to those watching Israel from overseas.
Israel needs leadership that puts security, responsible government, and national cohesion first. Israelis alone will choose that leadership. They should do so with an honest accounting of the costs of political partnerships, including those identified by friends who remain committed to the country.
Listening to those friends is an act of responsibility. Their support should give their warnings weight, not excuse ignoring them.

Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:21:26 UTC
