Attackers kill nurse, injure health worker responding to DRC Ebola case
The attack in eastern DR Congo is the latest on health workers and responders to the deadly Ebola outbreak.
A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.
It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.
The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.
The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.
“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”
Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.
Widespread distrust
Data from the DRC’s Ministry of Health indicate that more than 9,800 cases, including more than 4,700 deaths, have been recorded since the start of the outbreak in May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.
The government’s handling of the outbreak, combined with chronic corruption, has sown widespread distrust, with some even dismissing Ebola as a hoax.
Responders say scepticism about the disease among communities has complicated their efforts, including in remote areas and emerging hotspots already facing shortages of medical supplies and healthcare workers.
Last month, a DRC politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response to Ebola. He had called on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand-washing, on a radio show.
In May, at the start of the outbreak, angry residents set alight two tents at health centres in two separate attacks in just one week.
Responders say some residents have held captive or threatened team members in designated health zones.
Spreading to other countries
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Sunday, Uganda’s Minister of Health Chris Baryomunsi announced that all citizens returning to the country with a history of travel to the DRC will be quarantined for 21 days.
Uganda says it is Ebola-free after declaring an end to its latest outbreak in July. But health experts remain on alert after two people who had recently passed through the country later tested positive in Kenya and Nigeria.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The strain responsible for the current outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
Symptoms can take up to 21 days to appear, according to the WHO. In an October 23 update, it urged stronger monitoring and cooperation across borders, while advising against restrictions on travel or trade with affected countries.

7 killed in road accident in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Seven people were killed when a passenger jeep plunged down a mountain slope on the outskirts of Muzaffarabad in Pakistan-administered Kashmir on Sunday, local officials said.
The accident occurred around noon when the jeep was travelling from one village to another in the mountainous area, covering only about three kilometers before the crash, according to police and administration officials.
The driver lost control of the vehicle while passing through a landslide-affected stretch of road, causing the jeep to plunge down the slope and roll over several times before coming to a halt, officials said.
The vehicle fell an estimated 1,000 to 1,500 feet below the road, killing all seven occupants at the scene, according to a police report.
Local residents retrieved the bodies, later joined by personnel of the Rescue 1122 emergency service, officials said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will pay a state visit to China from Oct. 27 to 31 at the invitation of Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Steinmeier was born in Detmold, North Rhine-Westphalia, in January 1956. He obtained his doctorate of law from the University of Giessen.
From 1999 to 2005, he served as chief of staff to then German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder. He was foreign minister from 2005 to 2009, and concurrently vice chancellor starting in November 2007.
From 2009 to 2013, he was chairman of the Social Democratic Party parliamentary group in the Bundestag. He served as foreign minister again from 2013 to 2017.
In February 2017, Steinmeier was elected the 12th president of the Federal Republic of Germany (the 16th Federal Assembly). He was re-elected to the post in February 2022. ■

BERLIN, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Bayern Munich returned to the top of the Bundesliga with a 3-1 victory at Freiburg on Sunday, overcoming the absence of head coach Vincent Kompany before surviving a late fightback from the host.
Assistant coach Aaron Danks took charge after Kompany collapsed on Friday and remained under medical supervision. Bayern was also missing several key players, including Manuel Neuer, Kim Min-jae, Aleksandar Pavlovic, Jamal Musiala and Luis Diaz, while Joshua Kimmich was unavailable following a family bereavement.
Despite its selection problems, the defending champion controlled proceedings from the outset and broke the deadlock through Dayot Upamecano in the 16th minute.
The French defender blocked Niklas Beste's attempt near his own penalty area before launching a counterattack. After exchanging passes with Konrad Laimer and Michael Olise, Upamecano continued his run and finished calmly past Freiburg goalkeeper Mio Backhaus.
Freiburg responded when Lucas Hoeler met Jordy Makengo's delivery, but Jonathan Tah intervened to deny the striker. Bayern maintained its attacking pressure, with Backhaus producing a fine save to keep out Nathaniel Brown.
However, the goalkeeper was beaten again in the 42nd minute when Serge Gnabry collected Brown's return pass and slipped his finish through Backhaus's legs, registering his 100th Bundesliga goal.
Bayern continued to dominate after the interval. Harry Kane headed over before Backhaus frustrated Ismael Saibari and later denied further Bayern opportunities.
Freiburg unexpectedly revived its hopes in the 82nd minute when Tom Bischof diverted Makengo's cross into his own net. The host then pressed for an equalizer, forcing Bayern goalkeeper Jonas Urbig into crucial saves from Igor Matanovic and Matthias Ginter.
Olise eventually settled the contest in stoppage time, capitalizing on a misplaced pass from Backhaus to score from distance into an empty net.
"I am very satisfied with the performance. We knew from the beginning that this would be a very difficult away game. They are a top team and currently in very good form," Danks said.
Bayern leads Borussia Dortmund on goal difference, with both sides on 17 points from seven matches. Freiburg remains third with 13 points.
Elsewhere, Hoffenheim defeated Bayer Leverkusen 3-0 through an Andrej Kramaric penalty and late goals from Alexander Prass and Max Moerstedt. Prass was subsequently sent off after receiving a second yellow card. Leverkusen remains fourth, while Hoffenheim climbs to 10th. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Raising the bar for CPC's self-governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:17:46 CST
13:17:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee has drawn close attention for its core agenda: strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance, with a landmark document tabled for deliberation.
As China enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), a critical stage in laying the groundwork for basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035, the CPC faces severe challenges: strengthening its governing capacity, staying connected with the people, guarding against complacency and resolutely combating corruption.
Only through strong Party leadership and unwavering commitment to full and rigorous self-governance can central leadership decisions be fully implemented and the country's long-term development stay on course.
For more than a decade, the Party has emphasized advancing this effort, calling for higher standards and more concrete measures to strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance.
In the implementation of the major decisions and plans of the CPC Central Committee, there must be no resort to empty rhetoric. Words must be matched by deeds.
Oversight must be enhanced in a more targeted, precise and regular manner on applying the new development philosophy, promoting high-quality development, and accelerating the efforts to create a new development pattern, among other strategic imperatives. It should also target key tasks, including developing a modern industrial system and fostering new quality productive forces in line with local conditions.
More scientific and effective efforts are required to confine power to an institutional cage. It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation through rigorous enforcement and binding constraints.
Compliance brooks no privilege, and enforcement permits no exceptions. The Party has made clear that laws and regulations must be strictly enforced, serving as high-voltage lines that must not be touched.
The fight against corruption remains arduous and complex, demanding greater sobriety and resolve. This high-stake struggle cannot be lost and requires sustained and uncompromising pressure.
Few observers can doubt the resolve and intensity of the CPC's anti-corruption drive, as shown by years of consistent action targeting senior officials, grassroots misconduct, and cross-border corrupt fugitives alike. Beyond investigating individual cases, the drive combines institutional fixes and education campaigns to demonstrate that the Party's self-governance is sustained and systematic, not a flash in the pan. This approach targets root causes to ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption.
For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability. By steadily tackling these problems, China is also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation. The "rigorousness" in official documents must be translated into a level playing field where merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery. It is hardly surprising that many foreign observers said the CPC's ability to reform itself is a key factor in its success.
The message is clear: Party self-governance is a continuous endeavor, with no finish line, only new starting points. The CPC will continuously strengthen its capacity to serve the people better. ■

From Budapest to New York: Trump eyes ousted Hungarian PM Orbán for UN chief, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:13:39 UTC
13:13:39 KST

After 16 years in power and an election defeat, Viktor Orbán could be headed for a new position, this time in New York. The Trump administration is promoting the former Hungarian prime minister's candidacy for UN secretary-general and is even considering putting him forward as a joint candidate of the United States, Russia and China. The White House is weighing the possibility of handing leadership of the organization to a politician who spent years clashing with the international establishment.
According to The Wall Street Journal, U.S. officials have already approached Orbán and invited him to enter the race. He has expressed interest but has yet to make a decision.
The move would mark a significant development in the race to succeed António Guterres, whose term ends Dec. 31. A State Department official acknowledged that the idea initially sounded almost far-fetched, but said previous discussions with Russian and Chinese representatives suggested that both Moscow and Beijing might support Orbán. The administration has even begun counting votes. The official estimated that he could secure eight votes on the UN Security Council relatively easily, and possibly as many as 10 of the 15. A candidate needs at least nine votes and no veto from any of the five permanent members. The question would then be whether Britain and France would agree to his appointment. Both have traditionally been cautious about exercising their veto power, but either could block the move independently.
The unusual proposal reflects Trump's search for a conservative leader capable of confronting the international establishment, prompting his aides to approach Orbán directly. U.S. officials described him as "the dream candidate for MAGA conservatives," noting that, unlike candidates whose careers have largely unfolded in diplomatic circles, Orbán has extensive experience leading a country and confronting political opponents. According to a source familiar with the discussions, a possible announcement of his candidacy has been postponed until after the U.S. midterm elections in November, in part because Orbán is unwilling to enter the race without assurances that he can win.
Orbán, 63, is one of the most prominent figures on Europe's nationalist right. During his 16 consecutive years in power in Hungary, from 2010 to 2026, he pursued hard-line policies on immigration, civil society organizations and liberal institutions, repeatedly clashing with the European Union over judicial independence, press freedom and the rule of law. Critics accused him of undermining democratic institutions and tightening his grip on the political system and media. Orbán, however, portrayed himself as a defender of national sovereignty and conservative values against what he called liberal interference from Brussels. His close relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, even after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, drew fierce criticism across Europe, while he was also regarded as one of China's most prominent allies on the continent.
Orbán's time in power ended in a crushing defeat in April. His Fidesz party lost to Péter Magyar's Tisza party, which secured a two-thirds majority in parliament. Trump, who publicly endorsed Orbán during the election campaign, also sent Vice President JD Vance to Hungary to support his reelection bid. The effort failed, and Magyar was sworn in as prime minister in May. Orbán remained leader of Fidesz but found himself in opposition.
Orbán is well known in Israel. Throughout his years in power in Budapest, he cultivated close personal and political ties with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and supported Israel during sensitive discussions within the European Union. He was among Netanyahu's closest European allies and, during the war in Gaza, backed him in his confrontation with the International Criminal Court. In April 2025, Orbán hosted Netanyahu in Budapest despite an arrest warrant issued against him by the court and announced that Hungary would withdraw from the institution. The court later ruled that Hungary had violated its obligations by failing to arrest Netanyahu, while Magyar's new government reversed the withdrawal plan. Orbán also blocked European sanctions for months against settlers and Israeli organizations accused of violence against Palestinians. Those sanctions were approved following the change of government. His appointment, if it materializes, would therefore carry particular significance for Israel, whose relationship with Guterres deteriorated sharply during the war.
The idea is not entirely new. In May, Hungarian media reported that figures in the MAGA movement were considering securing a senior UN position for Orbán, partly because of the possibility of diplomatic immunity amid threats of corruption investigations by the new government. In September, The Guardian reported that his name was being mentioned as a possible candidate for secretary-general, although there was no public indication that he intended to run. What is new now is the claim that the U.S. administration has approached him directly and is holding discussions based on the support it believes it can secure.
Meanwhile, the race itself remains deadlocked. None of the candidates has secured sufficient support in six rounds of secret, informal straw polls held by the Security Council. In the latest round, on Oct. 16, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan received nine votes in favor but also six against, including two from permanent members with veto power. Grynspan, who is Jewish and the daughter of Holocaust survivors, is still considered the frontrunner. She serves as secretary-general of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development and previously served as Costa Rica's vice president. She has close family ties to Israel, including a sister who lives in Mevaseret Zion and nephews who served in the IDF. Nevertheless, Republican officials in the United States have expressed reservations about her candidacy, arguing that she is too critical of Israel and too accommodating toward China. Other prominent candidates include Rafael Grossi of Argentina, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana.
The lack of a clear outcome prompted the White House to seek new names beyond the existing field of candidates. According to a Politico report, the Trump administration does not want another veteran diplomat who would continue running the UN as it has been managed until now, but rather someone who would lead a sweeping transformation of an organization facing both budgetary and political crises. Among the names considered was Feridun Sinirlioğlu, Turkey's former foreign minister and secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. He previously served as Turkey's ambassador to the UN and accused Israel of war crimes. Yet he was also the official who signed the 2016 reconciliation agreement with Israel on Turkey's behalf following the Mavi Marmara crisis.
Last week, a new official candidate entered the race: Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates, the country's former ambassador to the UN. Nusseibeh, 48, comes from a longstanding Palestinian family in Jerusalem, speaks Hebrew and holds a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora studies. Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, held talks with Moshe Dayan after the 1967 Six-Day War, while her uncle, Sari Nusseibeh, partnered with Ami Ayalon on an Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative. She condemned the Oct. 7 massacre and the abduction of Israelis by Hamas, but later criticized IDF operations in Gaza and opposed the annexation of territory in the West Bank. As ambassador, she played a central role in advancing a resolution to expand humanitarian aid to Gaza. Her candidacy has the backing of Gulf states but has drawn criticism over allegations that the UAE provided support to a militia implicated in atrocities in Sudan, allegations that Abu Dhabi denies. On Tuesday, Nusseibeh is scheduled to formally present her candidacy at a public UN hearing and answer questions from representatives of member states. The Security Council is expected to hold another round of straw polls afterward.

Incumbent President of Brazil Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won in the second round of presidential elections and was re-elected as the president of the country for the fourth term, the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court (TSE) reported.
 
According to the TSE, after 97.69% of the ballots in the runoff election were counted, Lula da Silva secured 51.74% of the votes, while his opponent, a right-wing opposition candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, was backed by 48.26% of the votes.
 
Lula da Silva is now the first politician in the present-day Brazilian history to win the presidential election after trailing in the first round of voting. The elected head of state will assume the office on January 1, 2027.
 
The voter turnout in the second round was reported at 80.79%, with 127,807,732 citizens participating in the voting. The rate of abstainers was reported at 19.21%, which corresponds to 30,081,854 voters. The share of blank ballots was at 1.12% (1,426,055 votes), while the share of invalid ballots was amounted to 2.12% (2,713,225 votes).

Brazil's Lula clinches election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:10:03 UTC
13:10:03 KST

Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-center presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America’s largest economy will likely continue defying Trump’s demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs.
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched a re-election victory with a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, giving him 51.8% of the total vote.
The 81-year-old leftist defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term, staving off a conservative wave that has seen numerous South American countries, such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru, all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.
Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.
The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country's last election in 2022.
Lula had requested the extension after he complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as "unacceptable" and a "dirty trick".
"It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections," he said in a brief speech in Brasília.
Comeback after first round defeat
After a first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and revamped their social media strategy.
No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country's military dictatorship.
The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 percent to 19 percent.
"People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country," Lula said in his first comments after the win.
Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula's Workers' Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.
Lula's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump's United States.
“Either the homeland remains free, or we die for Brazil,” he said. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard," he said as he addressed his supporters.
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the color of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.
Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.
He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.
Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges were annulled on procedural grounds.
In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime.
Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

Taiwan tracks 15 Chinese ships, 3 military aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:07:13 UTC
13:07:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked six Chinese naval vessels, nine official ships, and three military aircraft between 6 a.m. on Sunday and the same time Monday.
One aircraft crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait and entered the nation’s southwestern and eastern air defense identification zone. In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 166 times and ships 309 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

"As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."
This is not a quote from a famous figure. Rather, it was something a friend’s father said to us during the Iran-Iraq war, while on leave behind the front lines, in a discussion about Saddam. We, the sons of his friends, found it so striking that for a long time, we used to jokingly write it in beautiful Persian calligraphy and mount it on a wooden plaque in our bunkers before returning to the front.
Years after the war, when I had written an open letter to Trump warning him against going to war with Iran, Noam Chomsky gave me a fascinating response. He essentially said that while my letter was excellent, the problem was that Trump was too foolish to understand such advice. I later realized that Professor Chomsky’s brief observation was, in essence, a different translation of what my friend’s father had said during the war:
As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."

France works with 10 European nations to increase strength as nuclear deterrent - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:06:16 UTC
13:06:16 KST

France is working with 10 other European nations to expand its capacity as a nuclear weapons power on the continent and a deterrent to Russian aggression as Europe's faith in the US's commitment to its security wanes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday morning.
The 'forward deterrence' plan involves the creation of new infrastructure, communications, early-warning and intelligence-sharing links with France's allies as well as deployments of French nuclear-enabled Rafale jet fighters across Europe.
The UK, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have all joined the project with varying degrees of involvement since French President Emmanuel Macron announced it in March.
“We don’t have any plans to put nuclear weapons on Finnish soil in peacetime. But we do have plans for creating a strategic dilemma for Russia,” said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
“We felt it would be useful for our security to get information, to be involved in it. We don’t know where this is going to end, it’s probably a 10- to 15-years process.”
Instead of the countries all gathering together to work on the plan, France has been holding individual talks, leading European partner nations to constantly communicate with each other to compare what the French have told them, WSJ cited senior defense officials as saying.
European countries doubt US reliability
The plan comes as faith in the US's willingness to defend Europe wanes. Doubts over if the US would risk nuclear war over the defense of a European ally have increased as US President Donald Trump strikes energy deals with Russian President Vladimir Putin and puts increasing pressure on Ukraine, WSJ wrote.
France claims that the French program is more credible as the safety of European countries is of far more direct importance.
“There is one difference between France and the US–we share the same geography, we are part and parcel of the same continent, we have economic and sociological continuity with our neighbors writ large,” Chatel, Macron’s adviser, said at the Warsaw Security Conference.
In his speech announcing the initiative in March, Macron emphasized that France's vital interests were directly affected by its allies.
“Could we consider that the survival of our closest partners may be put at risk without it affecting our vital interests?” Macron said.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said that the plan was not intended to "replace anything. It supplements the nuclear guarantees that were already there" from the US.
Program under French control
Macron also announced that France would resume making nuclear devices for the first time in decades and that the size of its stockpile would become confidential. Despite the involvement of other countries, the nuclear force will be entirely under French control, WSJ wrote.
“The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” one government minister of another European nation said.
According to the WSJ report, the decision was made to make the forward deterrence strategy acceptable across the political spectrum, including to the far-right party of Marine LePen who is polling ahead in the race for the presidency in next spring's elections.

The FBI is investigating whether to pursue economic espionage charges against former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested earlier this month for allegedly planting a recording device in a restricted conference room at the artificial intelligence company, the Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
Investigators are examining whether Alfozan obtained confidential information to offer to the Saudi government, even without being recruited to do so, according to a law enforcement official cited by the WSJ.
Authorities are also considering potential trade secret theft charges, although the investigation may not result in additional prosecution.
Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and US permanent resident, allegedly concealed a small circuit board and microphone behind a television in a conference room primarily used by OpenAI executives.
He currently faces a federal charge of unlawfully intercepting communications, punishable by up to five years in prison. His next court appearance is scheduled for November 6.
His attorney, William Pernik, said he had received no indication that additional charges were being considered.
“We made it very clear that Mr. Alfozan will fight these charges and allegations in court, not in the press,” Pernik said.
Prosecutors examine ties to Saudi royal family
Prosecutors say Alfozan exchanged frequent WhatsApp messages with an unidentified member of the Saudi royal family in 2025 and 2026.
The royal family member allegedly sought to recruit him for a Saudi artificial intelligence initiative, writing, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!”
Alfozan reportedly responded, “100,” but indicated he intended to remain at OpenAI until his company shares had vested.
Prosecutors said their last known exchange occurred on October 5, the same day Alfozan allegedly returned to the conference room to retrieve the recording device. OpenAI security personnel had already discovered and removed it, subsequently notifying the FBI.
Planned departure, Saudi consulate involvement raise concerns
Prosecutors also disclosed that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for himself, his wife, and their three-month-old son. He was arrested three days before their planned departure.
His wife and son subsequently traveled to Qatar on business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, according to prosecutors.
Defense attorneys said the official was the wife's brother-in-law, that no military funds were used, and that Alfozan frequently booked one-way flights.
During an October 19 detention hearing, US Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse questioned a letter from the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles offering to cover Alfozan's entire bail bond.
“Even if I set it at $10 million?” the judge asked. “I find that problematic. Seems like a blank check. ‘We’re gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out.’ ”
Alfozan was denied bail after the judge determined he posed a significant flight risk.
OpenAI is examining what information the recording device may have captured and whether the incident involved corporate espionage or potential state-sponsored intelligence gathering, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

US military says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil
US Central Command says more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support.
US military forces have helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of oil since June, despite Iran’s efforts to control the critical waterway, according to US Central Command (COMMAND).
The US military command said on Sunday that more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support over the past six months.
It added that more than 95 percent of ships navigating the channel had sailed through safely in recent months despite Iranian threats, “clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway”.
CENTCOM announced the figures as Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made a visit to the region, during which he observed the “current operational environment” in the strait while flying in a US Army helicopter.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry,” Cooper said in a statement.
“This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Cooper said the primary transit routes for vessels in the strait were free of Iranian mines due to the “incredible efforts” of personnel who conduct mine clearance operations.
“We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry,” he said.
Crude oil flows have largely returned to levels seen before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, despite the ongoing threat of attacks on commercial vessels by Iranian forces.
At least 16.5 million barrels of oil per day left the region in September, equal to the pre-war average, excluding Iran, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Analysts have attributed the rebound to a combination of offshore ship-to-ship transfers, US military escorts, and increased use of oil pipelines.
However, oil prices remain far higher than before the start of the war.
Brent crude futures stood at about $114.50 a barrel on Sunday, after easing about 2 percent from last week’s nearly six-month high.
Brent settled at $72.48 per barrel on February 27, the day before the US and Israel began strikes on Iran.

Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan were due in Iran on Monday in a push to de-escalate the regional conflict now afflicting the Gulf kingdom, as Yemen's Houthis launched further attacks on Riyadh's airport and Saudi oil facilities.
The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations - which signed the Mecca mutual defense pact in August - since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was part of efforts to "de-escalate" and "promote dialogue and diplomatic solutions." It stressed the need to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation."
Saudi Arabia was being represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.
They were due to consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, its deputy secretary, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV.
Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. On Sunday, Qatari mediators were in Tehran, an official told Reuters.
Earlier efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June but fighting between Iran and the United States soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-backed Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front.
US, Iran threaten renewed attacks
The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, pushed up global oil and gas prices, left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new humanitarian crisis in Yemen.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. US President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran. Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again.
The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, has weighed on Trump's approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's discussions would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran".
Baghaei said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus of Monday's meeting was to build a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, the official said.
Iranian officials told Munir during that visit that there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands - which include ending the US blockade and lifting sanctions on Iranian its oil exports - were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan's military media wing and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Houthis strike Saudi airport, energy infrastructure
Saudi Arabia has intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. Houthi attacks have targeted Saudi airports, ports and oil installations.
On Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked East-West crude oil pumping stations in Saudi Arabia as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had resumed operations at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreementsays signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognized borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

North Korea-South Korea tensions high as letters lodged with UN, howitzer spotted

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
05:03:58 CET
13:03:58 KST

By Hongji Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are running high this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council, repeating accusations that Seoul fabricated a September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted close to the border.
A Reuters witness at an observatory in South Korea overlooking the heavily armed border on Monday confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery piece positioned in clear view near the frontier.
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency on Sunday identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border marked a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as about 20 to 30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ).
“It is highly unusual (for North Korea) to expose its self-propelled artillery so conspicuously,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
“By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signalling through action, not words, that it intends to enforce its border policy through force rather than dialogue or negotiation.”
It is also warning South Korea to exercise caution about escalating border friction, with the intention to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in the letter sent on Sunday, the country’s UN representative said Seoul was using the landmine incident to depict Pyongyang’s border construction as a military incursion.
North Korea warned in the letter that violations of its sovereignty could trigger self-defence measures and that South Korea would be “wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences.”
PHOTOS ALSO SHOW NORTH KOREAN DRILLS
The letter is a response to a South Korean letter to the Security Council last week, which said a September 21 blast in the DMZ was planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang has denied responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea’s Unification Ministry said on Monday that the North Korean letter appears to repeat North Korea’s existing position and seeks to justify its so-called border line marking work.
The ministry had no separate comment on the placement of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to defuse border tensions.
North Korea’s letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling that a violation of the UN Charter, which bars the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity.
Seoul has said its military issues warning broadcasts and fires warning shots to send North Korean soldiers back across the line when they cross the military demarcation line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ.
North Korean troops have been building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the MDL in recent years.
The Yonhap report cited photographs taken from an observatory in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appeared to show the howitzer as well as North Korean troops conducting drills on the coast of Kaepung county, about 1.5 km (1 mile) from the observatory.
In 2015, there was a similar incident in which South Korean troops were injured by North Korean mines. Then, Seoul resumed anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts across the DMZ, triggering a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.
(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Edwina Gibbs )

Trump dials up Islamophobia at Michigan Senate rally against Abdul El-Sayed

Trump dials up Islamophobia against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan Senate rally
Al Jazeera looks at the key takeaways from the US president’s campaign event in Michigan ahead of the midterm vote.
Port Huron, Michigan – United States President Donald Trump has sharpened his anti-Muslim attacks against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, going so far as to suggest that Christmas would be cancelled if the progressive doctor won.
Trump visited Michigan on Sunday to shore up support for Republican candidates in the Midwestern state ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.
But from his podium, he levelled unfounded allegations against El-Sayed, including calling him a “jihadist”.
“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said of El-Sayed.
“I want him to have a metal detector.”
The president, whose popularity has been slipping in part due to the US-Israel war on Iran, spoke for nearly two hours to hundreds of supporters.
His remarks largely focused on Michigan’s Senate election, which is one of only about seven toss-up races for the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed faces Republican candidate Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat, and the race is considered crucial for Republicans to retain control of the 100-member Senate.
If Rogers wins, he would flip a seat currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, leaving Democrats with the difficult task of flipping five other seats to regain control of the chamber.
Currently, Republicans have a 53-seat majority in the Senate. Only 35 Senate positions are up for election in 2026.
Here are five key takeaways from the Republican event.
Trump doubles down on anti-Muslim attacks
While Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed’s Muslim identity in recent weeks, including by misrepresenting the Democrat’s name as “Mohammed”, the US president took his rhetoric to new heights on Sunday.
Throughout the speech, Trump returned to themes related to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, falsely accusing the candidate of wanting to impose Islamic law in the US.
“So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness,” Trump said, apparently imagining El-Sayed being tried in a religious court.
Several times during the rally, some attendees blurted out “traitor” when El-Sayed’s name was mentioned.
“I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said.
El-Sayed is a US-born citizen and former public health official who has pledged to uphold the Constitution. There is no evidence that he was ever a member of the Muslim Brotherhood or any foreign organisation.
Since Trump first ran for president during the 2016 election cycle, he has weaponised anti-Muslim bigotry for political gain.
In 2015, for instance – near the beginning of his first successful campaign – Trump said he would support “a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States”.
Less than two years later, Trump used the presidency to sign a short-lived executive order barring travel from multiple Muslim-majority countries, what became known as the “Muslim ban”.
In Sunday’s speech, Trump appealed once more to fears of Muslim immigration.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump said.
El-Sayed has previously largely dismissed the anti-Muslim rhetoric against him as an attempt to create “distractions”, saying he is focused more on domestic issues, including lowering the cost of living and expanding access to healthcare.
Rogers embraces Trump
With Trump’s approval ratings plummeting, some Republican candidates in tight races have kept their distance from the president.
Rogers has previously called for an end to the Iran war and expressed reservations about Trump’s tariff campaign, urging an end to the trade war with Canada, which borders Michigan.
But Rogers attended Sunday’s rally and took the stage alongside Trump in a display of mutual support.
A survey by the research firm Marketing Resource Group suggested earlier this month that only 35 percent of voters in Michigan view Trump positively.
Rogers set the tone for the anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed earlier in the rally, also claiming the Democrat is connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, a political movement in Egypt designated as a “terrorist” group by the US this year.
As a congressman, however, Rogers voted in 2012 to continue US aid to Egypt under Muslim Brotherhood President Mohamed Morsi.
In Sunday’s speech, Rogers also tried to paint El-Sayed as part of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), but unlike other progressives, El-Sayed is not a member of the left-wing group.
“This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah,” Rogers said, without offering evidence.
All three groups are designated as “terrorist” organisations in the US, making it illegal to provide any material support to them.
Trump unapologetic about Iran
On Sunday, the average price of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol in Michigan was $4.83, up from $2.91 before the start of the war on Iran.
Tehran has restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the war, sending energy prices soaring.
Trump initially promised the conflict would only last four to six weeks.
But nearly eight months after the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, the conflict is showing no signs of concluding.
On Sunday, Trump said he has no regrets about the war.
“I made that decision, and I have no second guess,” Trump told the crowd.
He added that he thought petrol prices would have increased by much more than they had. He also defended his decision by referencing the threat of nuclear warfare.
“The number one state sponsor of terror is Iran by far, and we had to make sure they didn’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
Iran has denied seeking a nuclear weapon. It has long argued its uranium enrichment programme is for civilian energy production.
Before the war, Trump also argued that US strikes against Iran’s uranium enrichment facilities in June 2025 had completely “obliterated” the country’s nuclear programme.
‘We’re making a freaking fortune’
Despite the economic anxiety related to the cost of living and skyrocketing petrol prices, Trump bragged about the amount of profit US oil companies are making from the war.
Demand for energy products has increased globally in recent months, as supply chains tighten.
“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas, and they’re coming to Oklahoma, and they’re coming to Louisiana, and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. “They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars.”
Trump added that his advisers asked him not to bring up this issue because “people are paying a little higher” for petrol and gas.
“I could just see the fake headline: ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune,'” the US president said.
Trump can still mobilise Republican base
A line of Trump supporters stretched several blocks outside the rally on Sunday.
Attendees, dressed in Make America Great Again (MAGA) gear, filled the hockey arena where Trump spoke.
The crowd roared and laughed with Trump, with attendees frequently blurting out expressions of admiration for the president and insults against his opponents, especially El-Sayed.
Trump may appear politically on the back foot amid dwindling popularity and mounting anger over inflation and the Iran war.
But the president has highlighted his continued ability to mobilise his core MAGA base, often pointing to his crowd size as a metric for his success as a campaigner.
The audience remained engaged and seated throughout the speech on Sunday.
At one point, the address took a bizarre turn as the president spoke about the backside of Jon Husted, a Republican incumbent from Ohio competing in another tight Senate race.
“I looked at his a**, and I’ve never done that with a man before. Women? Yes. Men? No,” Trump said.
The US president also complimented the derriere of the rapper Nicki Minaj, one of his prominent supporters in attendance.
“By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful a** before: Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss,” Trump said.
