First time voters could determine as many as 12 Knesset seats with high turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:16:37 UTC
12:16:37 KST

On Oct. 27, Yael Chernyvsky, 18, from Ramat Hasharon in central Israel, plans to cast her ballot for the first time.
“I’m voting so we can change the future of this country,” the teen told Jewish Telegraphic Agency earlier this month. She was entering a Tel Aviv auditorium where some of Israel’s top politicians were about to address more than 1,000 first-time voters, including many in pre-military programs.
Chernyvsky, who is studying in an army preparation program in the Negev, blames the current right-wing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the country’s problems.
So she said she will vote for one of the opposition parties in the “change bloc,” which seeks to oust Netanyahu, who has been in office since 2009 except for a brief period in 2021-2022.
Chernyvsky had not decided which party she will vote for, but she said it will “probably” be either the Democrats led by Yair Golan or Yashar led by Gadi Eisenkot.
“We’ve basically had the same government for 20 years, and I genuinely think it’s corrupt. Why has this war been going on for three years? Why did it take two years to return the hostages? Why does the government give so much money to haredi Jews who don’t work and don’t serve in the army?”
Chernyvsky is one of the estimated 640,000 Israelis aged 18 to 22 eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI). Comprising nearly 10% of the electorate, their votes could determine as many as 12 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
High voter turnout expected
“Israel is a young country with a high birth rate,” said Tammy Hoffman, head of the education policy program at the IDI, which co-sponsored the young voter event with the Yigal Allon Center. “If their turnout is high, as our research suggests, first-time voters will make a difference.”
In May, Hoffman and her colleagues surveyed potential young first-time Jewish and Arab voters about their attitudes and political engagement. Across Israel’s population groups, 80% to 95% said they would “definitely” or be likely to vote. Secular Jewish youth expressed the highest level of certainty regarding participation, while 87% of Arabs said they intend to vote.
It’s a higher percentage than in the US, where the youth turnout in the 2024 presidential election was only 47%, according to the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement.
More than four-fifths of respondents to the IDI survey described the opportunity to vote as either “fairly meaningful” or “very meaningful,” with particularly strong responses among traditional and religious Jewish youth.
A separate poll of 18-year-old to 22-year-old potential first-time voters for the Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth news outlets also revealed high motivation: 67% of respondents said they were certain they would vote, while another 19% thought they would.
National security, cost of living highest priorities
In both polls, national security and the cost of living were top priorities for both Jews and Arabs. Hoffman wasn’t surprised.
"For the past several years, they’ve lived in an unstable environment during their adolescence. They were in junior high during COVID, they witnessed the judicial reform protests, and of course Oct. 7. They are worried about their future.”
While the Hamas attack affected every Israeli, the fact that so many first-time voters are either serving in the Israel Defense Forces or will do so in the near future could influence how they vote.
Jewish Israeli voters of all ages have moved rightward politically over the past couple of decades, Hoffman noted.
“But military service doesn’t necessarily lead you to a nationalist stance,” Hoffman emphasized. “It can do the opposite: It can bring up questions about the war and its goals.”
Arab Israelis, meanwhile, haven’t shifted rightward, but they are more eager to vote in this election than previous elections, reflecting their growing engagement in Israeli society, Hoffman said.
In a Sept. 23 N12 poll, 74% of young people described their political views as right-wing or center-right, while 23% identified as left-wing or center-left. If the election were held at the time the poll was taken, 16% of respondents would vote for Eisenkot’s Yashar party and 14% would vote for Netanyahu’s Likud party.
Despite the assumption that the majority of Jewish youth will vote for right-wing and far-right parties, Hoffman said, mock elections at high schools around the country show a different picture.
She said the majority of students voted for Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Beyachad, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid from the opposition Change bloc, and “some for Netanyahu’s [right-wing] Likud, but not a lot for [Itamar] Ben-Gvir,” who heads a far-right party.
Omer Gross from Jerusalem, who graduated from high school in June and is now in an army-prep program in the Golan, plans to vote for the Religious Zionist party led by far-right politicians Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin.
“I don’t really agree with what Smotrich has been doing in Gaza,” he said, referring to Smotrich’s objective to reestablish the uprooted Jewish settlements in Gaza and incentivize Palestinian emigration from the strip, “but I support what he does in the territories” – the West Bank. “We need a strong, secure Israel.”
Tomer Shiloh from Herziliyah, who attends the same Golan Heights program as his friend Omer, has different plans.
“I’m voting for the ‘Change’ bloc, for Gadi Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett,” the 18-year-old said.
If it were up to Shiloh, the next government would require Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, young men to serve in the IDF, as he will do next year. He wants the next government to lower Israel’s high cost of living.
“I want the people who run this country to have good values and to do what’s best for the country and not for themselves,” the teen said.
Sgt. M is a 22-year-old office worker doing his first stint of reserve duty following the conclusion of his mandatory army service. He says ensuring that all Israelis serve the country either in the IDF or through National Service is at the top of his election priority list. But he will be voting for the left-of-center Democrats party mostly for economic reasons.
“Did you know that most university students have to work while they study to pay for tuition, books, food and housing?” the reservist, who requested anonymity due to IDF regulations, said as he traveled home by train from his army base. “I wanted to start studying right after finishing the army, but between the cost and reserve duty, that’s impossible,” he said.
Speaking from his home in the northern Israeli city of Shef-Amra, Khalel Alaa Sabeh, 18, said he plans to vote for an Arab party that will prioritize addressing resource gaps in the Arab community.
“I want to see more money allocated to the Arab community,” he said, noting that historically, Arab municipalities have received less government funding than Jewish municipalities. “But most of all, I want our families to be safe. There’s a lot of crime in the Arab sector and the Netanyahu government isn’t doing enough to stop it.”
Sabeh, who plans to start university next year, said he is urging his friends to show up to vote on Oct. 27.
“I want to see change in this country, and if Netanyahu wins we’ll have four more bad years.” Yet whatever the outcome on Election Day, he said, “I won’t leave the country. This is my land, this is my home.”

Automated aged care algorithm needs a human override, ombudsman finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:08:00 UTC
12:08:00 KST

Aged care funding algorithm neither fair nor consistent, ombudsman finds
In short:
Use of automation in Australia's aged care system lacks safeguards and has led to unfair outcomes for elderly patients, the commonwealth ombudsman has found.
The ombudsman released his findings after an investigation into the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing's classification algorithm.
What's next?
Of the 10 recommendations made, six were accepted by the government and a further two, including instating a human override, were noted.
Commonwealth Ombudsman Iain Anderson has issued a damning report on the aged care algorithm, saying the government should amend the law to allow senior assessors to override its decisions when it gets it wrong.
In a scathing report of more than 100 pages, the ombudsman says the actions of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, in its administration of the assessment scheme and the algorithm, "have been unreasonable".
The report says the department put the classification algorithm in place "without any meaningful risk assessment, evaluation or analysis, despite the obvious risks that would arise with deterministic automated decision-making".
The classification algorithm was launched on November 1 last year as part of the government's "once in a generation" reforms to aged care and is used to assign people a level of funding to stay at home with support rather than go into a nursing home.
But it has been mired in controversy since its introduction, with hundreds of people appealing its decisions, a more than five-fold increase on appeals in the previous year.
In his report released today, Mr Anderson said: "A reasonable person would, in my view, lack confidence that the system is in fact fair and consistent."
In a response to the draft report, the department said it "does not accept this characterisation" that it didn't test the algorithm or validate it.
However, as revealed by Four Corners and by the ombudsman, tests were conducted on an original version of the algorithm created by a consultancy. The algorithm in place today was modified by the department and there was no external validation.
Audit recommended
Mr Anderson also recommends the Australian National Audit Office consider doing an audit of the implementation of the Single Assessment System and the Independent Assessment Tool, which is the questionnaire that drives the algorithm, "and in doing so, assesses whether the department's use of public resources was efficient, economical and ethical".
The ombudsman made a total of 10 recommendations, with six being accepted by the government. The first two recommendations, that legislation be introduced to allow override by a human and amending the aged care rules, have not been accepted by the department, and have only been noted.
However, the department has accepted the recommendation for a comprehensive review of the Aged Care Act in relation to the assessment process and algorithm to "identify legal defects, inconsistencies, ambiguities or unintended consequences" and address these issues in a timely way.
It has also accepted the recommendation that any amendment to the act be "preceded by and informed by meaningful consultation with the public".
Department 'incorrectly advising' assessors
Mr Anderson said the department had been wrongly telling assessors that the algorithm outcomes could be changed right up until the new legislation took effect.
This is despite the fact that there was no mechanism in the act or the rules to change outcomes.
"The department did not, and may still not, understand key components of the legal framework it created, nor did it understand what legal framework it was meant to create,"
Mr Anderson said.
The government has resisted calls to give blanket permission for delegates for assessment agencies to override the classification algorithm.
It instead passed legislation last week to allow an "escalation pathway" for appeals in exceptional circumstances.
In return for the Coalition's support in passing the legislation, it has commissioned a review into the assessment system and algorithm, with a report due in the first half of next year.
In a statement, Minister for Health and Ageing, Mark Butler, and Minister for Aged Care, Sam Rae, said: "The government will consider the ombudsman's report carefully as we continue to improve our aged care system, including the assessments system."
"We're already acting on many of the recommendations to ensure our aged care system is transparent and reliable, and we'll examine what further action we can take to give every Australian confidence in the system."
More than a million people, or 85 per cent of those using aged care, receive services through the home support system.

'Our motherland needs us': The Israeli expats flying home to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:04:29 UTC
12:04:29 KST

Thousands of Israeli expats, including Australians, fly home to vote in election
In short:
Political activists have mobilised to bring thousands of overseas Israeli citizens to the country to vote.
As many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, according to one non-profit organisation, with some estimating up to 1,000 could be coming from Australia.
Some travelling from Australia said they felt Israel's PM Benjamin Netanyahu had contributed to "division amongst the people".
Tens of thousands of Israeli citizens abroad, including estimates of hundreds from Australia, are travelling to Israel to vote in the country's most consequential election in decades.
Polling indicates Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could face a stiff challenge to hold onto power in a vote largely seen as a referendum on his leadership and handling of Hamas's October 7 attacks.
His main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who leads the newly established Yashar opposition party.
Political activists mobilised around the world to bring Israeli citizens overseas to the country to vote, given ballots can only be cast in person on election day, with exceptions for serving soldiers and diplomats.
The AID Coalition, a US-based non-profit that describes itself as non-partisan, estimates that as many as 67,000 voters are returning to Israel, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data gathered for its Fly&Vote initiative.
It says about half are flying in from the United States, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Among those who have travelled to Israel is Anat Dror, who has been living in Melbourne for almost five years and recently became an Australian citizen.
"The sentiment for us is that right now, voting is absolutely essential. It's something that absolutely comes from the heart and no-one would be able to talk me out of it," she told the ABC.
"I'm coming here at the very expensive cost of missing out on work days and paying for a very expensive ticket and missing my kids at home … all of these are not deterring any of us from coming here to vote.
"This is our motherland and our motherland needs us right now."
In September, the Likud party tried to block the AID Coalition's Fly&Vote initiative by lodging an appeal with the elections committee, but withdrew the case after reaching an agreement.
'I don't trust any of them'
The most recent data from Israeli television networks KAN, Channel 12 and Channel 13, released on Friday, put Mr Eisenkot's Yashar a few seats ahead of Mr Netanyahu's Likud.
After Tuesday's vote both parties will need to embark on complicated coalition negotiations to secure the 61-seat majority required to form government.
Ms Dror said Israel was still reeling from the trauma of Hamas's deadly assault on October 7, 2023, and the legacy of that day cast a long shadow over this election.
But she argued the broader societal challenges Israel is facing began emerging before the terrorist attacks, including intense cost-of-living pressures.
She said Mr Netanyahu's government needed to go, but did not want to publicly back a particular candidate in the so-called "change" camp: the anti-Netanyahu parties, including Yashar, trying to end his tenure.
"What one single politician, do I trust his words or her words? The answer is none of them. I don't trust any of them, nor should anyone ever trust politicians' words before elections," she said.
"They will say everything because they are indeed politicians.
"What I'm counting on isn't any one individual. I'm counting on the change bloc to have the ability to oversee differences, oversee personal gain for the sake of actually building a coalition that is diverse."
Ms Dror said she believed anywhere between 500 and 1,000 Israeli citizens from Australia were making the journey.
"We have a really big Israeli WhatsApp group in Australia, and we made a joke that maybe we should meet for coffee here in Tel Aviv instead of in Melbourne," she said.
Another Israeli citizen travelling to the country to vote, Guy Marom, moved to Australia with his family during the COVID-19 pandemic.
As he packed his bags in Sydney's north-east, he was also undecided on which candidate to back, but insisted one of the "change" parties would get his vote.
"Most of them, at least, have leaders that I consider trustworthy, and I hope they will shape Israel differently than what it is today," he told the ABC.
"I think [Netanyahu is] maybe not the single cause, but I think he's contributing to the division amongst the people."
ABC/Associated Press

Ukraine accuses Google of providing Russian search results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:02:27 UTC
12:02:27 KST

Ukraine accuses Google of providing Russian search results
Ukrainian language ombudswoman Elena Ivanovskaya has accused Google of not doing enough to promote the national tongue in the global digital environment. The US tech giant’s search engine often provides results to Ukrainians in Russian even when the queries are typed in Ukrainian, she told a local media outlet.
The government has been cracking down on the use of the Russian language in Ukraine since the 2014 Western-backed Maidan coup, using what Moscow has repeatedly denounced as discriminatory practices.
Former Ukrainian President Pyotr Poroshenko introduced restrictions on the import of books from Russia and Belarus in 2016, which became an outright ban in 2023. Kiev also purged Russian literature from state curricula and systematically removed cultural monuments, memorials, and inscriptions to remove historical links to Russia.
Kiev seeks to block access to Russian music on international streaming platforms inside Ukraine and prevent its performers from appearing in domestic popularity charts, according to Ukrainian Sanctions Policy commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk. More than 100 Russian performers have been blacklisted in Ukraine, and the list will be expanded, according to the official.
In an interview with the outlet Censor.net, Ivanovskaya stated that her office had filed a formal complaint with Google over its search algorithms. “For example, when a user enters a search query in Ukrainian, the system returns results in Russian – solely because of the user’s geographic location,” she stated, adding that her office asked the company to address the supposed lack of “accuracy of their search result algorithms.”
The Ukrainian authorities have banned the use of any language other than Ukrainian in the public sphere, including government, education, media, and customer service. Violations can result in administrative fines of up to $270.
Ivanovskaya has previously suggested increasing the fines tenfold and demanded Russian-speaking children and parents use Ukrainian during breaks and in conversations with teachers, arguing that both instances fall under the “public sphere rule” and could be punished with fines.
Despite the concerted persecution campaign, Russian remains widely used in Ukraine. According to Ukrainian polling data, as many as 46% of country’s nationals spoke Russian in everyday life before the conflict escalated in 2022. Another survey last year showed the number of Russian speakers had fallen to 30% since four former Ukrainian territories, including the Donbass republics and Kherson and Zaporozhye Regions formally joined Russia after a series of referendums.
Ukrainian Culture Minister Tatyana Berezhnaya said earlier this year that 71% of Ukrainians regularly consume Russian-language content, with nearly a quarter doing so every day.
Moscow has repeatedly denounced the discriminatory measures as “Russophobic censorship,” warning that attempts to “cancel” Russian culture will ultimately fail.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and wife Marie-France van Heel acknowledge delegates and supporters at the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 29, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
LONDON — Andy Burnham pledged to bring back hope when he entered Downing Street. Labour MPs are feeling it — for now.
The British prime minister is approaching 100 days in No. 10 this week with his party believing things are on the up.
Keir Starmer was toppled earlier this year after disastrous local election results precipitated a loss of confidence in his administration.
Advertisement
Disgruntled Labour MPs warned their new leader must show up, listen to them and accept some disagreement to avoid repeating his predecessor’s mistakes.
POLITICO sets out the four reasons Labour MPs are feeling more chipper under Burnham — but they still see potential pitfalls ahead.
Some of the dozen parliamentarians interviewed by POLITICO for this piece were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the internal party matters.
1) Disagreement is tolerated
MPs reckon Burnham’s administration is more willing to recognize different views within the broad church Labour Party.
Burnham himself told a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting that disagreement is fine as long as MPs speak to him about it, according to Simon Opher — a 2024-intake MP and member of Mainstream, the soft-left faction supported by Burnham when he was Greater Manchester mayor.
“It sounds weird, but that is a remarkable difference from what they had before,” Opher said, claiming he felt a “slight climate of fear” early in his political career.
Advertisement
Starmer infuriated MPs when weeks after taking office he suspended the whip from those who voted to scrap a two-child benefit cap — only to U-turn earlier this year.
By contrast, Kim Johnson, a member of Labour’s left-wing Socialist Campaign Group faction, points out she wasn’t sanctioned after abstaining on the government’s Courts and Tribunals Bill earlier this month because she believes it still weakens the right to trial by jury.
“You’re not feeling you can’t do that or risk losing the whip,” she said.
Burnham’s eyes are photographed as he delivers a speech at the Labour Conference in Liverpool on Sept. 29, 2026. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
Of course, Burnham’s appetite for disagreement hasn’t been fully put to the test.
He entered No. 10 at the start of the summer recess, when MPs were away from Westminster, and there was a month-long conference recess when they returned to SW1 in September.
And MPs don’t want a totally laissez-faire regime.
Advertisement
“I didn’t get into politics to sit in a room and just agree with each other,” said another 2024-intake Labour MP. “I don’t think you get good policy by just sitting around like nodding dogs.”
But they said they “genuinely believe in collective responsibility,” and are “quite relaxed” about the consequences of voting against the whip.
Another backbench MP warns Burnham’s lax approach can only last so long.
“Andy is riding high still, he is not in [Nigel] Farage or [Zack] Polanski territory, he can afford for people to go ‘I don’t like this.’ It’s when the shit hits the fan, and the public are saying they’re not happy, then you begin to find the political patience wears out,” that backbencher added.
Burnham may yet regret his promise that the whips office will act as an HR department, the MP said, “because you want them to come down like a clonking fist.”
2) Ministers are more visible
Burnham’s team is making itself seen, his MPs report.
Whips have been calling them to check in, and Burnham himself has attended PLP sub-group meetings. Cabinet ministers have also been available for meetings.
Advertisement
Though another Socialist Campaign Group MP admitted “it’s a very low bar” for improvement. “Under Starmer, there was very little in terms of consultations, any discussions about anything at all.”
Mainstream member Alex Sobel said: “I’ve had more meetings with No. 10 — I’ve been to No. 10 North — in these three months than the entire time of the previous administration.”
One MP said: “People feel warmly towards Andy, which is half the battle. I think they trust his good intentions.” | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images
Bill Esterson, who chairs the Energy Security Committee, said he had “regular conversations with No. 10” and that Burnham’s team had “engaged very fully” with committee chairs and the PLP more broadly.
A second 2024 intake MP said: “There’s definitely more of a concerted attempt for them to be reaching out and listening to us.” The days of being viewed “as the legal necessity to get legislation through” are over.
3) Burnham’s political instincts
MPs reckon they’ve had an upgrade when it comes to raw political instincts.
“There’s a feeling that we’ve got a guy up front who we can get behind,” said Opher.
Advertisement
“He understands how politics works,” he added, citing the decision to delay approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field until after the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Labour faced a challenge from the Greens. “Andy’s much more savvy on what he’s doing.”
Backbenchers also claim to feel more confident they won’t get caught in the Starmer flip-flop policy trap.
The unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP quoted above is still smarting over the “absolutely awful” two-child benefit cap vote, where rebels lost the whip only for it later to become government policy.
The first 2024-intake MP reckons Burnham is better able to communicate difficult trade-offs, like alteringthe triple lock to fund social care.
4) Voters are giving Labour another chance
It is ultimately Burnham’s popularity with the public that has fed into the positive mood.
Many Labour MPs “agreed with the punters on the doorstep” about Starmer’s inadequacies, Opher said. Data showing Labour has retaken the opinion poll lead from Reform UK has boosted their optimism. “It doesn’t feel like a party that is about to be ripped apart,” he added.
Advertisement
The first 2024 intake MP said: “It has given us the right to be heard,” said the first 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above. “People feel warmly towards Andy, which is half the battle. I think they trust his good intentions.”
MPs say Burnham’s administration is willing to recognize different views within the Labour Party. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
Some flashpoints ahead…
1) The budget
Burnham can only coast on the good vibes for so long, and the first test of tough political choices comes Wednesday in the budget.
MPs on the left see the economic statement as a “crunch point” that will show if the chancellor will put his money where the PM’s mouth is.
“If there’s an attempt to take money from ordinary people who’ve got nothing and no attempt to get finances from people who have got far too much, then probably there will be some sort of opposition”, said the unnamed Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted. They hope to see the already trailed bank tax confirmed, or a wealth tax.
They warned that any decisions on what to cut and where to spend will pose “challenges from both sides of the PLP.”
“The measure of Andy Burnham is how he deals with it,” they added.
Advertisement
2) Welfare
Burnham wants to avoid a repeat of the botched attempt at welfare reform which severely weakened Starmer’s authority.
A long-awaited review by former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (NEETs) will be published shortly with recommendations.
Milburn — alongside Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden — has been trying to ensure communication is better.
“Pat has done an excellent job at building a consensus, rolling the carpet, setting out the argument, setting out the moral case, but he was doing that before the change of administration,” a third 2024-intake Labour MP said.
The second 2024 Labour MP quoted above said most colleagues “feel like it’s a decent stab at it and it’s not come out of the blue.” Reasonable critics “were just getting stonewalled” last year.
Esterson, who’s served in parliament since 2010, said regular engagement means “it’s not surprising that you get the benefit of the doubt far more often than if you don’t.”
Advertisement
3) Europe
Burnham’s admission that a future Labour manifesto could commit to a referendum on EU membership is already opening old Brexit wounds — and not in the way Labour wants.
The Socialist Campaign Group MP previously quoted is uneasy about its potential to spark further division. “It nearly ripped the country apart and I’m not sure if it’s the right thing to do [to] reignite that horribleness in each constituency,” they said.
The third 2024-intake Labour MP quoted above concurred. While people want a closer relationship with Europe, they believe rejoining is a “different kettle of fish” and jars with constituents who want “better public services and more economic growth” rather than continental renegotiations.
4) Energy
Energy policy has already become a flashpoint. The decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field was met with some dissent. A decision about the larger Rosebank oil and gas field is still looming.
Sobel told POLITICO’s London Playbook it “won’t make an impact on global prices and will give mixed messages in terms of investment in terms of both renewables and decarbonisation of home heating.”
Left-wing Labour MPs also signed a letter to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh urging her to reject the licenses due to climate change. “Every second we continue pumping fossil fuels into the atmosphere makes the crisis more severe,” the letter organized by Chris Hinchliff said.
Advertisement
The second 2024-intake MP quoted thought ministers are acting in good faith.
“They’ve got one go at government and they seem to be doing their absolute best to give it a good whack,” they said.

SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. La chute de Philippe, relégué derrière Mélenchon

SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. La chute de Philippe, relégué derrière Mélenchon
SONDAGE CLUSTER 17 x POLITICO. L’ancien Premier ministre chute de 3 points par rapport à notre enquête précédente, tandis que Jean-Luc Mélenchon reste haut et Marine Le Pen monte.
Edouard Philippe, arrive désormais troisième dans tous les cas de figure, devancé par Jean-Luc Mélenchon. | Benjamin Vodant/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Mauvaise nouvelle pour Edouard Philippe : l’ancien Premier ministre n’avait déjà pas réussi à enclencher une dynamique dans sa campagne, il chute désormais dans les intentions de vote et se classe bon troisième, derrière Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
Le maire du Havre perd 3 points dans une nouvelle enquête réalisée par l’institut Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, du 19 au 20 octobre, passant de 19% à 16% des intentions de vote, par comparaison avec notre étude précédente réalisée les 15 et 16 septembre. Il est désormais nettement devancé par Jean-Luc Mélenchon, qui, lui, est quasiment stable à 18,5% (-0,5).
A ce stade de la campagne, l’Insoumis est donc le mieux placé pour se qualifier pour le second tour face à Marine Le Pen, quelles que soient les configurations.
Advertisement
La candidate du RN, elle, ne pâtit manifestement pas de la révélation par Mediapart fin septembre d’anciens écrits antisémites attribués à Jordan Bardella, et reste hyperfavorite du premier tour, avec 33% d’intentions de vote lorsque Philippe représente le bloc central, contre 31% dans notre dernière enquête.
A noter : fraîchement auréolé de sa victoire dès le premier round à la primaire du PS et de Place publique, Raphaël Glucksmann, lui, passe de 12% à 13% des intentions de vote, en légère dynamique. Dans le détail, selon Cluster 17, le social-démocrate récolterait 29% des voix des électeurs d’Emmanuel Macron en 2022, ce qui explique en partie pourquoi seuls 49% d’entre eux voteraient Philippe.
“Glucksmann progresse parce que Philippe ne s’adresse pas assez à l’aile sociale-démocrate de l’espace modéré”, note Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de Cluster 17.
Retailleau doublé par Lisnard
Quant au candidat des Républicains, Bruno Retailleau, il ne décolle toujours pas, mais se maintient avec 7,5%-8% des intentions de vote. Il a toutefois une nouvelle raison de s’inquiéter : lorsque David Lisnard, étiqueté Nouvelle Energie, est testé lui aussi, il atteint les 8%, grappillant des points à Le Pen (30,5%), Retailleau (7%), ainsi qu’Eric Zemmour (qui passe de 4% à 3,5%).
La cote du maire de Cannes, pourtant encore méconnu d’une partie des Français, s’explique parce qu’il “répond à une forte demande de libéralisme du centre et même de miléisme des très conservateurs”, commente Jean-Yves Dormagen, en référence au président argentin Javier Milei.
Testée également par Cluster 17, l’hypothèse d’une candidature de Gabriel Attal à la place de celle d’Edouard Philippe ne donnera guère plus d’espoir aux partisans du bloc central : le secrétaire général de Renaissance recueillerait 12% des voix aujourd’hui, contre 13,5% selon le même institut au mois de septembre. Dans ce scénario, Jean-Luc Mélenchon grimperait lui à 19,5% et Raphaël Glucksmann à 14%.
(*) Sondage réalisé du 19 au 22 octobre auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française âgée de 18 ans et plus grâce à la méthode des quotas. L’enquête a été réalisée via un questionnaire autoadministré en ligne. La marge d’erreur est comprise entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.

Brazil election results 2026: Key takeaways from Lula’s historic win
Lula wins a fourth term after a dramatic run-off marred by voting confusion and allegations of interference.
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has pulled off a political comeback that no Brazilian presidential candidate has managed in nearly four decades.
On Sunday, the 80-year-old leftist president won a record fourth non-consecutive term, overcoming a first-round defeat to right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula won more than 51 percent of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48 percent. Some 98.76 percent of the ballots were counted when electoral authorities declared him the winner.
Sunday’s results were far from certain, keeping Brazilians on edge until the very end. Bolsonaro and Lula had been virtually tied in the polls in the lead-up to the election.
A last-minute decision to extend voting hours sparked accusations of election interference and questions about whether the result could face legal challenges.
Already, Senator Bolsonaro has pledged to annul the vote, crediting the extended hours with sowing voter confusion.
Here are five key takeaways.
Lula makes history with an unprecedented re-election
Just three weeks ago, Lula looked like he was in trouble.
Bolsonaro had surprised many observers by beating the incumbent in the first round of voting on October 4, winning 47.03 percent of the vote to Lula’s 45.16 percent. The difference was 2.2 million votes.
But Lula spent the next three weeks trying to bring back voters who stayed home in the first round, while making a renewed pitch to those concerned about the cost of living and the future of his signature social programmes.
In the final days of the campaign, opinion polls showed the two candidates virtually tied.
Bolsonaro briefly took the lead as ballots were counted on Sunday evening. But Lula ultimately pulled ahead as results began arriving from the northeast, according to the Reuters news agency.
The northeast has long been a strong source of support for Lula and his Workers’ Party.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has large bases of support in the south and southeast of the country, as well as the centre-west.
For Lula, the victory means an unprecedented fourth term as president. For Bolsonaro, Sunday marks a defeat in his bid to return his family to the presidency.
No other candidate in modern Brazilian history has placed second in the first round of a presidential vote only to win in a run-off.
At age 80, Lula is also on track to beat his own record as the oldest Brazilian president to be sworn in since the country’s return to democracy.
Brazil’s last-minute voting extension sparks confusion
As the presidential run-off entered its final hours on Sunday, both campaigns were calling for voting to be extended.
Lula’s campaign accused local officials of deliberately reducing public transport services in several cities, making it difficult for lower-income voters to reach polling stations.
Bolsonaro’s campaign, meanwhile, requested more time for voters in areas affected by heavy rain and flooding.
In Minas Gerais, the regional electoral court reported that 349 polling locations had lost electricity, although voting machines continued operating on backup batteries, according to local media.
Originally, voting was scheduled to end at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT).
But faced with the two campaigns’ petitions for an extension, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered polling stations to remain open for another two hours, until 7pm (22:00 GMT).
The decision, however, came after some stations had already closed and shut down their electronic voting machines.
Zanin later clarified that polling stations that had already closed would remain shut. Only those that were still open could continue accepting voters until 7pm.
The result was confusion over who could still vote, with some Brazilians turned away despite the extension.
In a brief post-election address, Bolsonaro pointed to those issues as a reason to annul the vote. He also accused Zanin of judicial malfeasance.
“He changes the rules of the game mid-game,” Bolsonaro said.
Election interference allegations raise prospect of legal challenges
Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating alleged election-related transport disruptions in five states.
In Salvador, a court ordered the arrest of the city’s transport secretary over allegations he had directed cuts to bus services. Lula’s camp pointed to such incidents as evidence of election interference.
Bolsonaro levelled similar allegations against Zanin, pointing to his history as Lula’s personal lawyer. Lula named Zanin to the Supreme Court in 2023.
“It is impossible to recognise the results of the election,” Bolsonaro told his supporters, calling the circumstances “unacceptable”.
He is likely to pursue a court challenge in an effort to overturn his defeat. Already, some figures on the global right have signalled their support.
Donald Trump Jr, the son of United States President Donald Trump, voiced outrage over the decision to extend the voting hours.
“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” Trump Jr posted on social media.
The Trump administration has backed the Bolsonaro family, echoing its claims that Jair Bolsonaro, the former president, was subject to a political “witch-hunt” in the courts.
Flavio Bolsonaro has called for reforming Brazil’s courts in the aftermath of his father’s legal troubles. Earlier this month, Bolsonaro said that if he were elected, he would seek changes to Brazil’s Constitution to “re-democratise” the country.
Al Jazeera correspondent Monica Yanakiew signalled that the tensions between Brazil’s right wing and its court system are likely to re-emerge after Sunday’s election results.
“The judicial system itself is very divided,” Yanakiew said, pointing to rifts within the Supreme Court. “There will need to be a lot of political negotiation.”
Higher turnout may have helped Lula
Higher-than-expected turnout may have helped Lula win, according to Andrei Roman, the head of polling firm AtlasIntel, who cited a drop in voter abstention as one factor behind the president’s victory.
An estimated 33.4 million Brazilians stayed home during the October 4 first round, despite voting being compulsory for most adults. That amounted to about 21 percent of the electorate, the highest abstention rate in a general election since 1998.
The question now is how much of a difference those voters made. With more than 2.2 million votes separating the candidates in the first round, even a relatively small change in turnout could have mattered in the run-off.
The final turnout figures, particularly in each candidate’s strongholds, could help explain how Lula managed to turn the race around.
Lula also made last-ditch pitches in the final weeks of his campaign, designed to energise his working-class base. Among them was a promise to pursue free public transport on weekends.
Lula’s victory complicates Trump’s ambitions in Latin America
Lula’s victory comes amid a wave of right-wing electoral wins across Latin America, where Trump has sought to expand Washington’s influence.
The Bolsonaro family has long enjoyed Trump’s support. Reuters reported on Saturday that officials in Trump’s State Department had pushed for sanctions against Brazil as part of an effort to weaken Lula and return the Bolsonaro family to power.
Asked on Sunday whom he wanted to win, the US president would not name a candidate.
“I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching,” he told reporters.
Though Trump has been vocal in his support for other right-wing candidates in Latin America, he was relatively circumspect with regard to the Brazilian election, something critics have speculated was intentional.
While Bolsonaro has promised closer ties with the US, Lula made defending Brazil’s sovereignty and resisting foreign interference a central theme of his campaign.
He has often pointed to Trump’s aggressive tariff campaign and his public statements about the Jair Bolsonaro trial as evidence of foreign interference. Lula’s campaign has also clashed with US-based social media companies, prompting Trump to accuse his government of censorship.
In his victory speech, Lula described having to “overcome interference coming from the outside” in his bid for a fourth term.
“The election was a defeat for denialism,” Lula said on Sunday night. “It was a defeat for lies.”
He finished his speech by praising his “army” of supporters.
“I highly doubt that Russia, China, or the United States possess an army as victorious as the army of democracy in this country,” Lula said, thanking the voters.

Seoul ‘fabricated” landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter

Seoul ‘fabricated’ landmine blast, North Korea tells UN in letter
South Korea blames Pyongyang for September landmine blast, but North Korea says incident a ‘sinister obstructive move’.
Pyongyang has sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, according to North Korea’s Korean Central News Agency.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN wrote to the UNSC on Sunday regarding the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Tensions have intensified after South Korea blamed a September 21 explosion in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating the two countries on North Korean landmines. North Korea has rejected the accusations.
Pyongyang’s UN representative alleged the landmine incident was “a sinister obstructive move to brand as a ‘military invasion’”, adding that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
North Korea’s ongoing border fortification efforts were “a legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty going in strict conformity with the UN Charter”, the letter states, while also criticising South Korea for violating the charter by firing warning shots at soldiers in the DMZ.
South Korea has said it fires shots to make North Korean soldiers return to the north when they cross the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) that runs through the DMZ. In recent years, North Korean personnel have been building tactical roads and fences near the MDL.
The South Korean Unification Ministry said on Monday that Pyongyang’s letter aims to “justify its border fortification work” and serve as a “countermeasure” to Seoul’s message to the UN, the Yonhap news agency reported.
Last week, South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a letter to the president of the UNSC, casting blame on North Korea for the landmine blast and calling it a “clear violation of the armistice agreement”.
The United States-led UN Command also said mine placement by North Korea violated the Armistice Agreement, signed in 1953 to end hostilities in the Korean War.
Days before North Korea’s letter to the UN, South Korea’s Defence Ministry proposed military talks to Pyongyang to “mutually confirm the precise location” of their border to reduce the risk of accidental clashes.

Flavio Bolsonaro vows to seek annulment of Brazil runoff following narrow defeat to Lula
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:49:04 UTC
11:49:04 KST

Laura Gamba
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro announced late Sunday that his legal team will formally petition to annul the country’s presidential runoff election following his narrow defeat to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Addressing supporters shortly after the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) declared Lula victorious, the Liberal Party (PL) candidate launched a scathing attack against the Federal Supreme Court (STF) over its late decision to extend voting hours nationwide.
“We will engage our legal team and seek to have these elections annulled,” Bolsonaro said. “I will not accept that the rules of the game have been arbitrarily changed—once again—by Lula’s friends on the Federal Supreme Court.”
Bolsonaro focused his criticism on STF Justice Cristiano Zanin, who issued a last-minute ruling extending polling hours across Brazil until 7 pm Brasília time following emergency petitions regarding transport blockades and severe weather.
The defeated senator condemned the decision, pointing out that Justice Zanin previously served as Lula’s personal defense lawyer before his appointment to the high court.
Lula secured a historic fourth non-consecutive term with 51.76% of the valid votes (over 60 million ballots), edging out Bolsonaro, who received 48.24%.
The high-stakes election capped one of the most volatile campaign cycles in modern Brazilian history. Bolsonaro initially led the race on Oct. 4, taking 47% of the vote against Lula’s 45%. Lula’s runoff win makes him the first Brazilian presidential candidate to overcome a first-round deficit since the two-round electoral system was adopted in 1989.
The PL campaign's challenge is expected to trigger intense legal battles in Brasília as electoral authorities prepare to certify the final election results.

Brazil's Lula da Silva wins historic 4th term after defeating Flavio Bolsonaro
Superior Electoral Court (TSE) declared Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva the winner of Sunday's presidential runoff, securing a fourth nonconsecutive term after defeating Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely contested race, Anadou Agency reported.
With nearly all polling stations tallied, the TSE reported that Lula secured 51.76% of valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.24%, a margin of more than 4 million votes.
The result marks an unprecedented development in modern Brazilian political history. Since the introduction of the two-round presidential election system in 1989, Lula has become the first candidate to win a runoff after finishing second in the first round.
In the initial vote on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro finished ahead with 47.03% of valid votes, compared with Lula's 45.16%, setting the stage for three weeks of intense campaigning across South America's largest country.
The runoff outcome represents a setback for the Bolsonaro family. Flavio, a 45-year-old senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, had sought to return his family to the presidency.
The lead changed hands multiple times during the early stages of vote counting before Lula pulled ahead as more ballots were tallied, including returns from urban centers and the heavily populated Northeast.
Lula, who previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010 before winning another term in 2022, will begin his fourth term on Jan. 5, 2027.
As reported earlier, polls opened across Brazil at 8 am local time Sunday as voters started casting ballots in a closely contested presidential runoff between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and conservative Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Protests in Europe stem from instability on energy markets — Iranian top diplomat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:44:38 UTC
11:44:38 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Geopolitical tensions and disruptions in energy supplies have impacted the entire world and, among other things, resulted in protests across European countries and surging fuel prices, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was quoted as saying in an article published by Russia’s Vedomosti daily.
"Any disruption and confrontation entail consequences that go far beyond our region and affect energy security, market stability and the economic interests of producers and consumers around the world," he stated.
"Take a look at the ongoing protests across Europe and the rapid rise in inflation and fuel prices in Europe and America," Araghchi noted.
The military actions on behalf of the United States and Israel against Iran and the ongoing military threats have led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the disruption of global natural gas supplies, especially in Asia, the Iranian top diplomat stressed. He also pointed to a hike in gas prices in Europe and the low level of annual gas reserves required ahead of the coming winter.
Aragchi called on fuel producers to resort to stronger dialogue, diversify supply routes, protect vital infrastructure and create practical mechanisms in order to reduce the impact of geopolitical shocks on global energy markets.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
Nearly 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade are transported through the strait. The US administration then effectively indicated that it would stop using large-scale military force against Iran and instead seek to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

Norwegian parliament member Peter Frølich, together with his organization, illegally transported drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras to Ukraine. After this, Norway changed the rules, and now citizens can send civilian drones to Ukraine. This is reported by Aftonbladet, UNN reports.
Details
It is noted that Frølich, together with the organization "Free Ukraine," attempted to send a shipment of drones with thermal imaging cameras to Ukraine. However, Norwegian customs stopped the shipment: under a law adopted back in the 1950s, this was illegal.
Later, Frølich appealed directly to the government, emphasizing that the situation was urgent and that delays could cost the lives of Ukrainian soldiers
The organization nevertheless somehow managed to deliver the drones to Ukraine. The following day, the Norwegian government promised to expedite consideration of the issue. Eventually, the rules were changed, and now Norwegians can legally send civilian drones to Ukraine.
"Frølich does not regret breaking the law," the outlet adds.

SYDNEY, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Australia's first new major airport in over 50 years has officially opened to passengers, with the first international flight landing at Western Sydney International Airport on Monday morning.
Air New Zealand flight ANZ165 from Auckland landed at the airport at about 7:30 a.m. local time on Monday, one day after the airport opened for domestic services on Sunday.
The start of passenger services marks the opening of Australia's first new major international airport since Melbourne Airport opened in 1970.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, CEO Simon Hickey said that services from the airport will fly to 250 destinations by the end of 2027.
He said that the airport, which is located 45 km west of central Sydney, will accommodate an estimated 10 million passengers every year by the mid-2030s.
"We'll continue to grow from there. This airport is for the next century as well, and we can continue to grow into the coming years. We're ready to grow with that demand across Sydney and Australia," he said.
Unlike the existing Sydney Airport, which operates under a strict curfew from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. every day, the new airport will operate on a 24-hour basis.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a speech at an opening event on Sunday that the airport would drive economic activity, jobs and the future of western Sydney.
Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways, Fiji Airways and Vietjet Air have announced plans to start operating services to and from the new airport. ■

Asian University Basketball League to introduce home-and-away format in 2026-27 season
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:35:25 CST
11:35:25 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Asian University Basketball League (AUBL) announced on Monday that its 2026-27 season will introduce a home-and-away format.
Eighteen college teams from 11 countries and regions will compete starting in November, with the season culminating in Championship Week in August 2027.
The season will feature 54 games in total, the most in a single season since the league was founded. The regular season is divided into the Eastern Conference and Southern Conference, with the Eastern Conference using a home-and-away format and the Southern Conference using a single-site tournament format. Qualifiers from both conferences will meet at Championship Week in August 2027.
The Eastern Conference will run from November 2026 to March 2027. Its 12 teams are divided into four groups of three, with teams in each group playing one another twice, once at home and once away. Games will be held on university campuses in China, Japan, South Korea, Mongolia and the Philippines.
The top eight teams in the Eastern Conference regular-season standings will advance to Championship Week. Defending champion Shanghai Jiao Tong University has an automatic berth. If it finishes in the top eight, the spot will go to the ninth-placed team.
The Southern Conference will be held from April 7 to 11, 2027, in Hanoi, Vietnam. Its six teams will be split into two groups of three, with the top two from each group advancing to the Final Four. The top three finishers will qualify for Championship Week.
Championship Week will take place from Aug. 16 to 22, 2027. The 12 qualifiers will first compete in a group stage, followed by a single-elimination knockout stage to decide the champion.
"This is a landmark moment for university basketball in Asia," said Jay Li, CEO of AUBL. "For the first time, the continent's best college teams will be tested home and away, and that changes everything."
"This season will connect different cultures and styles of basketball, bring the game to more fans than ever and give student-athletes new opportunities to travel, compete and learn," Li said.
The new season will tip off at the Sangnoksu Kim Yeon-koung Gymnasium in Seoul, South Korea. Yonsei University will host Shanghai Jiao Tong University on Nov. 22 and face Tsinghua University at the same venue on Nov. 24. ■

One-third of Australian households experienced food insecurity in past 12 months: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:35:24 CST
11:35:24 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- One-third of Australian households have experienced food insecurity over the past 12 months, with those that have children among the hardest hit, according to a new report.
The report released by NGO Foodbank Australia on Monday revealed that 33 percent of households experienced food insecurity in the past 12 months, up from 32.8 percent in 2025 and 32.5 percent in 2024.
Among households with children, the report said 45 percent experienced food insecurity in the past 12 months, with 25 percent classified as being severely food insecure.
It found that 37 percent of middle-income households and 53 percent of low-income households experienced food insecurity.
"Foodbank research shows that hunger is no longer confined to the margins; it is impacting middle Australia. A wage used to be what kept food on the table, but for a growing number of working Australians their pay packet no longer stretches that far," Foodbank Australia CEO Kylea Tink said.
Of households that reported experiencing food insecurity, 85 percent said they were unable to afford balanced meals, and 69 percent said they experienced food insecurity for the first time in the past 12 months.
Over 50 percent of renting households experienced food insecurity compared to 12 percent of households that own their home outright.
"People should not have to choose between putting a roof over their head or putting food on the table. We're hearing of parents going without just to make sure their children can eat. This is unacceptable, and we must do something about it," Tink said.
The report called for federal, state and territory governments to establish a national breakfast program at every school by 2030 and to increase investment in food relief organizations. ■

Profile: Brazilian President-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:34:59 CST
11:34:59 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a comeback victory in Sunday's presidential runoff, defeating Liberal Party candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who led in the first round, to secure a fourth term in office.
Born in October 1945 in northeastern Brazil, Lula was the seventh child in a poor rural family.
In the early 1970s, Lula gradually emerged as a trade union leader, becoming known as a voice for the poor and a leading figure in the struggle against the military regime. In 1980, he co-founded the Workers' Party (PT).
After winning a landslide victory in the 2002 presidential election, Lula became Brazil's first president from a working-class background.
In 2006, Lula was re-elected. His flagship Bolsa Familia (Family Allowance) cash transfer program helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty.
In 2014, Brazilian judicial authorities launched a sweeping anti-corruption investigation known as Operation Car Wash. Lula was subsequently investigated, convicted and imprisoned. In March 2021, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court annulled all the convictions on corruption charges against Lula.
He returned to the presidential race in 2022 and defeated then-President Jair Bolsonaro, becoming the first Brazilian president to be elected to three terms by popular vote.
Lula advocates a greater role for the government, stronger social policies and enhanced protection of workers' rights. On foreign policy, he favors active engagement in international affairs, with BRICS cooperation and South-South cooperation incorporated into his updated foreign policy agenda.
Lula attaches great importance to relations with China and has actively promoted the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future for a more just world and a more sustainable planet.
Lula is scheduled to begin his fourth four-year presidential term on Jan. 5, 2027. ■

Anthropic’s Claude accessed Georgia state vote count data behind paywall
Artificial intelligence model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available US state of Georgia aggregate voter counts without human authorisation, Anthropic said in a statement on Oct 25.
“Claude didn’t access the state’s voter registration system or change or pull any voting records,” Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block these kinds of actions.
Anthropic said in a blog post earlier in October that it found examples of Claude “working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee” and some of these cases involved websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels.
The secretary of state’s office in Georgia did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
Axios first reported the unauthorised action by Claude. REUTERS

From affordability to AI, the Issues driving the US Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

From affordability to AI, the Issues driving the US Midterms
- Economic worry is the main issue in the US midterms, with many voters angry about prices, gas costs, healthcare, immigration and government corruption.
- The Iran war is also hurting Trump and Republicans, with low approval and some Republican candidates breaking with him over the cost and open-ended fighting.
- Big fights over democracy, AI data centres, transgender rights and Social Security could shape control of Congress, while Democrats are favoured for the House.
AI generated
Ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov 3, national polls show that most Americans are deeply dissatisfied with the direction of the country.
Economic anxiety is at the fore of voters’ frustration. Many Americans say they are struggling to afford basic living expenses.
Also weighing on voters is an unpopular war with Iran that has disrupted global oil supplies and driven up the cost of petrol, home heating and diesel.
Other top concerns include healthcare costs, data centres, immigration and government corruption.
The midterms, held halfway through a president’s four-year term, determine control of Congress.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of Senate seats are up for election.
Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers.
With President Donald Trump in the White House, his party has unified control of the federal government, which means it is likely to bear the brunt of voter anger.
This election cycle, spending on political advertising is projected to reach a record US$11.6 billion (S$14.8 billion), surpassing even the 2024 presidential election.
Republicans are outspending Democrats. Still, polls suggest Democrats are favoured to win control of the House and have a meaningful shot at the Senate.
Here’s a look at some of the top issues that are animating the elections.
Economy and cost of living
The economy is almost always the dominant issue in US elections.
About 84% of registered voters say the economy is “very important” to their midterm election vote, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted from Sept 28 to Oct 4.
By a 51%-45% margin, voters say they trust Democrats more than Republicans to do a good job handling the economy, according to a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in mid-September.
“Affordability” is a major buzzword of the 2026 election, and voters overwhelmingly view the national economy through the prism of household expenses.
Average petrol prices were US$4.29 a gallon on Oct 24, up from about US$3.06 in 2025; mortgage rates in September crossed 7% for the first time in almost two years and have largely continued to climb higher. Those costs are increasingly straining people’s budgets.
Democratic candidates blame Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war for rising prices and are campaigning to end both.
Republican candidates tout Trump’s 2025 tax-cut law, which granted tax breaks for tipped employees, overtime work and Social Security retirement income.
Iran war
About 65% of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of US military action in Iran, compared with 33% who approve, according to Pew, and Democratic candidates have blasted the war as unpopular, costly and open-ended.
The war has also created fissures within the Republican Party. Some Republican candidates have privately or publicly broken with Trump, who disappointed some supporters after campaigning for president on an “America First” platform and promising to avoid new military conflicts.
Texas Attorney-General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee in one of the most consequential Senate races, said in a leaked audio recording that the war and high prices were a drag on his campaign.
Other Republican candidates have called for the war to be brought to an immediate end.
“I have been one of the leading and deciding votes against the continuation of the war in Iran because I take that seriously,” Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, who is in one of the most competitive House elections in the nation, said in a campaign debate on Oct 6.
Government corruption
A deep distrust of government courses through the electorate.
A record-high 89% of US adults view government corruption as widespread, according to a Gallup poll released in early September.
The surge was particularly pronounced among Democratic voters: 91% said government corruption was widespread in 2026, up from 57% in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden, a Democrat, was in the White House.
Democratic candidates and some Republicans have linked government corruption to high costs, arguing that federal lawmakers and officials are elites enriching themselves at the expense of ordinary Americans struggling to make ends meet.
There are growing bipartisan calls to ban stock trading by members of Congress.
Other government accountability proposals offered by candidates include term limits for members of Congress and Supreme Court justices and limitations on members of Congress becoming lobbyists when they leave office.
Democrats have pointed to Trump’s stock trading and earnings from cryptocurrency-related ventures while in office as examples of the president using his position for personal financial gain.
Democrats and some Republicans condemned his Justice Department’s now-abandoned plan to create a US$1.8 billion “anti-weaponisation” fund to compensate victims who claim they were targeted by the Biden administration for political or personal reasons.
The Justice Department’s handling of files related to the late sex offender and financier Jeffrey Epstein angered victim advocates and sparked allegations that the Trump administration is protecting powerful individuals.
Democracy in the US
In a Pew survey conducted from Sept 28 to Oct 4, 85% of Democratic voters and 69% of Republican voters said the future of democracy was very important to their vote in the midterms.
Democratic leaders have repeatedly characterised Trump as an existential threat to democracy.
They have pointed to his repeated false claims that his 2020 presidential election loss to Biden was “rigged” and that voting by mail is riddled with fraud.
Party leaders accuse Trump of employing authoritarian-like tactics in intimidating political opponents and minority groups with hostile language on social media and at political events.
Individuals who leak government information to the media “should be shot”, Trump said on Oct 14 at a campaign rally in Arizona.
“Our President is shredding our democracy” and “Republicans in Congress simply sit idly by, and don’t stop the chaos”, California Democratic state Senator Mike McGuire, who is favoured to win a House seat on Nov 3, said at a campaign debate on Oct 6.
However, Democratic candidates in the most competitive elections have publicly downplayed a potential third impeachment of Trump and centred their campaign platforms on lowering costs.
“Any sort of corruption has to be rooted out,” Representative Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire Democrat running for the Senate, said on CBS’ “Face the Nation” programme on Oct 11. “But we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now.”
Healthcare
About six in ten voters are worried about healthcare costs, and about half say it is “extremely important” for candidates in the midterm elections to talk about that issue, according to a KFF Health Tracking Poll released on Oct 6.
That survey also found that voters, by a 42% to 22% margin, trust the Democratic Party to do a better job handling healthcare costs than the Republican Party.
That 20-point advantage for Democrats is a wider gap for the party than in a survey from KFF released in April.
Many progressive Democratic candidates have campaigned for a government-run, universal health insurance system that would replace private health insurance.
Some Democratic centrists seeking politically competitive seats, such as Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington state and former Representative Elaine Luria of Virginia, say that sweeping proposal is unrealistic.
They say the party should focus instead on incremental improvements to the Affordable Care Act, Democrats’ healthcare overhaul signed into law by then-President Barack Obama in 2010.
Democrats have campaigned against the Republican-led 2025 tax law’s reductions in spending on Medicaid, a joint federal and state programme that serves low-income and disabled Americans.
Republican candidates have focused more on targeting healthcare fraud. They describe a universal government-run system as tantamount to a government takeover of healthcare that would hike taxes.
Immigration and border security
A surge in migrant crossings into the US from Mexico during Biden’s presidency helped power Trump’s 2024 election victory over Biden’s vice-president, Kamala Harris.
But a sweeping federal immigration crackdown, including ramped-up deportations, in Trump’s second term triggered a public backlash and calls to abolish or scale back the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency – including in states and districts that favoured Trump in 2024.
In some of those districts, Hispanic voters, who shifted sharply towards Trump in 2024 but have since moved back toward Democrats, can swing election outcomes.
They overwhelmingly disapprove of Trump’s handling of immigration (by 69% to 30%) and border security (by 58% to 39%), according to an NBC News/Telemundo poll conducted from Sept 21 to 28.
Most Republican candidates have defended Trump’s immigration policies and warned voters that Democrats would return to Biden-era “open borders”.
Some Democratic candidates running in Republican-leaning districts have charted a moderate path on the issue, mixing support for strict limits on illegal entry with proposals to expand legal pathways for undocumented immigrants to achieve citizenship.
Adam Hamilton, a Kansas Democratic pastor vying to unseat Republican Senator Roger Marshall in an agricultural state that relies heavily on immigrant labour, called Biden’s border-security policies a “disaster”.
Representative Don Davis, a North Carolina Democrat seeking re-election in a district that favoured Trump by 12 percentage points in 2024, praised the President’s border enforcement policy but said the government needs to do more to increase screenings at ports of entry to detect fentanyl and other contraband.
Data centres and AI
AI data centres, the warehouse-like computing facilities that support artificial intelligence systems, have aroused intense opposition and become a bipartisan flashpoint in the 2026 election.
Many Americans express concerns about data centres’ energy, water and land consumption impacts.
Additionally, the broader public unease and pushback against AI often manifests as opposition to data centres.
Democrats are more likely than Republicans to be concerned about the role of AI in daily life and its potential to take jobs, according to Pew.
Trump supports the expansion of data centres and AI, arguing that the US needs to outpace China in an emerging technology that is reshaping society.
Many candidates for Congress from both major parties have emphasised their opposition to the construction of new data centres in campaign advertising.
They include former senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, the Democratic nominee in a Senate election that could sway control of the chamber.
Brown attacked incumbent Republican Jon Husted for helping lure data centres to the state with tax incentives when he was Ohio’s lieutenant governor.
Transgender rights
Transgender rights is a prominent wedge issue in the 2026 campaign, just as it was in 2024, when Trump’s presidential campaign benefited from targeting Harris’ support for transgender inmates having access to gender reassignment surgery.
“Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you,” was the tagline in a Trump TV ad that Democratic and Republican campaign officials said was effective.
Republican ads in the midterm elections emphasise opposition to transgender athletes’ participation in women and girls’ sports.
According to a Sept 18-24 survey from The 19th/YouGov, 45% of US adults are more likely to vote for a candidate who supports banning transgender athletes from women’s and girls’ sports teams, compared with 20% who favour candidates opposing bans.
Some Democratic candidates in culturally conservative areas have aired campaign ads stating their opposition to transgender athletes competing in women’s sports.
Social security
Older Americans vote in disproportionate numbers in midterm elections, and many of them are concerned about the stability of the Social Security social insurance programme, which provides monthly income to retired workers, surviving family members of deceased workers, and disabled individuals.
The main fund that pays for retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its accumulated reserves in 2032, and incoming tax revenue will only be able to pay 78% of benefits if Congress does not intervene.
Social Security is funded primarily by a compulsory payroll tax that applies to the first US$184,500 of workers’ earnings in 2026, and surveys show widespread public support for raising or eliminating that cap to shore up the programme’s finances. BLOOMBERG

Early voting opens in New Zealand for November 7 election with no clear frontrunner
Italy

11:19:58 KST

By Lucy Craymer and Renju Jose
WELLINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the national election on November 7 would be decided on economic issues, as early voting opened on Monday in a race that polls suggest will be closely contested.
With voters frustrated by a sluggish economy and persistently high inflation, the cost of living has emerged as a key election issue, prompting competing policy solutions from across the political spectrum.
Luxon said his National Party had “the best plan” to help the economy to grow and improve affordability.
“We’ve worked incredibly hard over the last three years … the plan is working, but we need more time,” Luxon said after casting his vote.
Opposition leader Chris Hipkins said he hoped to form a Labour-led government before Christmas and would move swiftly to ease cost-of-living pressures.
Ballot boxes will be open for nearly two weeks at shopping centres, transport hubs and community halls across the country ahead of election day.
Recent polls show no clear frontrunner under New Zealand’s mixed-member proportional system, where coalition deals are often needed to form governments.
A 1News-Verian poll published on October 20 put the ruling centre-right National Party at 32% and opposition Labour at 27%, while a Post/Freshwater Strategy poll published a day earlier had Labour narrowly ahead at 28.7% to the National Party’s 27.6%.
In both surveys, the smaller Opportunity Party was polling around or above the 5% threshold needed to enter Parliament, making it a potential kingmaker.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission said 207 voting places were open on Monday, with that number rising to more than 2,300 on election day. Overseas voting opened earlier, on October 21.
UNCERTAINTY FACTORS CONVERGE
Political commentator Gareth Hughes said the level of uncertainty surrounding the outcome of a New Zealand election at this stage was unprecedented.
“Multiple factors are converging to contribute to the uncertainty,” Hughes told Reuters.
These include the possibility that both left- and right-wing parties could face an overhang - where a party wins more electorate seats than its share of the party vote entitles it to, increasing the total number of seats in Parliament, he said.
Hughes added that the emergence of the centrist Opportunity Party had compounded the uncertainty, amid the unpopularity of the two main legacy parties - National and Labour.
Voting began just hours after enrollment closed at midnight on Sunday, a deadline that has become one of the campaign’s most contentious issues.
Critics say the earlier cutoff could deter participation, particularly among harder-to-reach groups. The Human Rights Commission said last year that ending election-day enrolment was likely to unjustifiably restrict participation and would disproportionately affect underrepresented groups.
(Reporting by Lucy Craymer and Renju Jose; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Thomas Derpinghaus)
