China’s Communist Party opens fifth plenum
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:19:49 CET
11:19:49 KST

BEIJING, Oct 26 (Reuters) - China’s Communist Party began a meeting of senior cadres on Monday aimed at tightening discipline and pressing officials to implement Beijing’s orders, paving the way for a leadership reshuffle next year expected to extend President Xi Jinping’s rule for another five years.
Xi briefed the party’s four-day Central Committee meeting on a draft document centred on “full and rigorous party self-governance” that state news agency Xinhua said addressed the challenges the party faced, including growing its governing capacity, as well as guarding against complacency and combating corruption, the president’s signature campaign.
The implementation of major decisions and plans of the Central Committee, the largest of its top decision-making bodies, must not be empty rhetoric, the Xinhua commentary read.
“It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation,” it said.
The Central Committee will convene in the closed-door meeting from Monday to Thursday — the fifth such gathering since the current cohort was formed in 2022 and therefore known as the “fifth plenum”.
Analysts say this could be the last major party gathering before its 2027 leadership reshuffle, when Xi is expected to hold on to the top job for a fourth term.
“The plenum will present Xi as in control, and able to continue his command,” said Kerry Brown, director of King’s College London’s Lau China Institute. “It is likely everything will be centred on him, to dispel any rumours or doubts about his physical fitness and ability to continue in his role.”
With substantive policy issues already largely set in previous gatherings, “this will be a plenum where appearances will matter as much, if not more, than substance,” Brown added.
ROOTING OUT CORRUPTION FOR MARKET PREDICTABILITY
Xi has overseen a vast anti-corruption campaign in recent years which has led to the purge of hundreds of senior officials and top generals, even the president’s one-time allies.
While some say the purges — particularly those targeting the highest ranks of the armed forces — are destabilising and undermine combat readiness, the party has portrayed the campaign as both necessary and regenerative, saying the military must undergo a phoenix-like rebirth and “bathe in flames and be forged anew.”
The Xinhua commentary presented the anti-corruption drive as a demonstration of “sustained and systemic” self-governance to “ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption”.
“For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability,” it said, arguing that China was also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation as merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery.
Typically seven plenums — each usually associated with a particular agenda — are held between major party congresses, which convene twice a decade. The party’s constitution requires at least one plenum to be held every year.
The fifth plenum usually deliberates the country’s strategic blueprint, the five-year plan, but an unusually late third plenum, delayed for more than half year until mid-2024, has disrupted the conventional scheduling.
(Reporting by Liz Lee and Beijing Newsroom; Editing by Tom Hogue, Raju Gopalakrishnan and Hugh Lawson)

For many Israeli voters, concerns over Israel's public image take a back seat in election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:18:13 UTC
11:18:13 KST

Over the past few months, Israeli media has been full of reports of Israeli holidaymakers in Europe, Asia and the Americas being harassed or physically attacked after being identified as Israeli.
In July, a group of Israeli tourists visiting Montenegro was reportedly confronted by a man and a woman, apparently locals, who asked, “Taking a break from genocide?” and told them to stay in Israel. In Greece, an Israeli woman said a restaurant refused to serve her after she told an employee she was from Israel.
In Thailand, a mother and daughter were allegedly beaten after they told a man they were from Israel, according to the mother’s account.. And in the US, an Israeli couple checking into a hotel in California were asked if they were “baby killers.”
These reports come as Israel’s image around the world has fallen to historic lows. A Pew poll conducted between February and May this year found that across 36 countries, a median of 67% of adults held an unfavorable view of Israel.
On the diplomatic front, hostility is also growing. Israel’s ongoing military action in Gaza has been termed “disproportionate” by a growing number of world leaders, and unchecked violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank – as well as Israeli government policy there – has prompted some countries, including some considered allies, to pull back or even impose sanctions.
Growing foreign hostility not among primary concerns for Israeli voters
Despite this hostility, the issue of Israel’s diplomacy, its image worldwide and who is to blame for its deterioration is barely factoring into the fast-approaching election on Oct. 27.
Yaakov Katz, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that there have been complaints about Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government not being effective at explaining Israel’s policies or actions to international audiences. Nevertheless, most Israelis see this as a problem beyond their control, he added.
“There is the argument that Netanyahu makes, which is that no matter what we do, the whole world’s against us, and no matter what we say, it’s antisemitism,” said Katz, co-author of “While Israel Slept: How Hamas Surprised the Most Powerful Military in the Middle East.” “People accept that argument, and to a large extent, they don’t push back on it. Why? Because part of it is true, right?”
Katz pointed out that many Israelis believe the sharp rise in antisemitism worldwide would keep happening regardless of what Israel does.
“In other words, Israelis believe that even if the number killed in Gaza was not 70,000 but 10,000, you still would have genocide claims; it makes no difference,” he said, adding that the average Israeli does not fully understand that declining support, particularly in the US, could eventually have “existential consequences for the country.”
“Most people here don’t think that far ahead,” Katz said. Instead, they take comfort in news such as President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu, he added.
Ofir Dayan, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University, said, however, that Israelis are painfully aware of what is happening abroad and are concerned about it. But she said there are other, more pressing issues in a country that has been grappling with more than three years of war.
“When people talk about the elections and what the Netanyahu government did right or wrong, they definitely look at this issue, and it is something they care about,” Dayan said.
However, she continued, most are unlikely to vote for a party or a candidate based on their position on this issue because it is just not a priority.
“Israeli voters are very much one-issue voters, and the issue in this election is security,” Dayan said. “We’re not remote enough from Oct. 7 for people to completely shift their vote and vote based on this idea.”
In addition to security and the questions surrounding the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led terror attack, Peter Lerner, the former Israel Defense Forces spokesman for the international press, told JTA that the “issue of Israel’s international standing is secondary to two things: Netanyahu or not Netanyahu, and the left vs. the right.”
“Obviously, each one of those comes with its own package of Oct. 7-related issues and the question of who is most suited to deal with the threats that are around us,” he said, adding, “you just don’t see very many talking about it and when they do talk about it, it is secondary to everything else.”
Most parties have not suggested public diplomacy plans
Of the dozen or so parties expected to win seats in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, only a few have referred to Israel’s negative global image or suggested ways to improve public diplomacy.
The B’Yachad Party, headed by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, is one of those discussing it as part of a plan to repair ties between Israel and world Jewry. Under this plan, the party hopes to elevate the importance of Diaspora Jewry, allowing a non-voting observer in Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, to focus on such issues.
Amcha Yisrael, a new right-wing party led by former IDF Brig. Gen. Ofer Winter, has two candidates on its list who are prominent public diplomacy activists – Yoseph Haddad and Fleur Hassan-Nahoum. Haddad has said multiple times that he would like to be Israel’s next minister for public diplomacy.
Journalist Eylon Levy, a former spokesman for the Israeli government, told JTA’s “Waiting for 61” podcast that public diplomacy, or hasbara as Israelis refer to it, “is not a goal in itself” for most of the candidates.
He said the discussion was more about “who can manage relations with the world so that we can achieve our national interests.”
Within that framework, Levy pointed out, there is a range of opinions. On the far right, the approach of the Otzma Yehudit Party, led by Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, is to make Israel look tough and “screw the woolly-hearted soft liberals if they don’t like it.”
On the left, “the position may be equally detached from reality,” Levy said.
“There is a belief on the left that if Israel starts behaving like a normal country and doesn’t have ministers who say aggressive nonsense, then Israel’s relations will snap back to normal,” he said. “I think there may be a denial there of how much public opinion has shifted against Israel and how much the expectations of policymakers have shifted as well.”
While Levy said he did not believe there would be a massive change in perceptions if a new government were elected on Oct. 27, he did believe it would be given a grace period, at least by Israel’s less-than-friendly allies.
“The question is whether an alternative government would suddenly magically boost Israel’s international standing; I don’t think it will,” he said. “But I do think a more moderate government will buy Israel some goodwill, definitely among those who say, in theory, we support Israel.”

Two storms slam northern Europe, cut power to 150,000 homes
Storms Boelo and Austen kill a man in Scotland and cut power to thousands of homes in the UK, France and Germany.
A pair of storms battering northern Europe have killed one man, cut power to more than 150,000 homes, and disrupted flights and phone networks.
More than 82,000 homes in the United Kingdom, nearly 60,000 in France, and at least 10,000 in Germany had no electricity on Sunday after storms Boelo and Austen passed through the region within 24 hours, according to authorities in the countries.
A falling tree killed a man, 60, in southwestern Scotland on Sunday, while another falling tree injured two women in central Scotland, the Press Association reported.
Winds of up to 135 km/h (84 mph) were recorded in the Argyll and Bute regions of western Scotland. Trees and power cables brought down by the storm blocked roads and rail lines across Scotland and northern England.
In Brighton, on England’s southern coast, Austen blew away an unused pier on Friday.
Authorities have warned of flood risk in regions of both Scotland and England.
The Met Office, the UK’s national forecaster, warned that Boelo would bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and said people should stay indoors as much as possible.
From France to Germany
Across the English Channel, Europe battled its first big storm of the autumn, with strong winds inflicting widespread power cuts.
French energy company Enedis said that at Austen’s peak on Saturday, some 288,000 homes had no electricity. Some 59,000 remained without power at midday Sunday, mainly in Normandy and Brittany.
A marathon runner in the midst of a race in northern France was lightly injured by a tree knocked over in strong winds.
In Germany, Austen cut power to 10,000 homes in and around the southwestern town of Freiburg-Breisgau on Sunday. The town’s main hospital said it had to limit service to emergency cases because of the blackout, which also cut the mobile phone network.
German police said two people were seriously hurt on Saturday by scaffolding blown away by Austen’s strong winds at a market in the town of Nastatten.
The storms also hit the Netherlands and Belgium, where falling trees injured four people in Brussels on Saturday.
In the Netherlands, north of the island of Schiermonnikoog, three crew members on board a freight ship were injured in the storms, according to the country’s coastguard. Two of them were winched off and taken by helicopter to a hospital on the mainland.
The storms caused hundreds of flights to be cancelled or diverted across northern Europe, including at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport, one of the continent’s busiest hubs.

The older we get, the faster time seems to pass. We usually attribute this change directly to age,…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:03:50 UTC
11:03:50 KST

The older we get, the faster time seems to pass. We usually attribute this change directly to age, thinking it has something to do with the way time is perceived after we have experienced more of life. But while this change is a matter of subjective experience, the speed of time’s passage has a different cause.
We are just as capable in old age of experiencing time as slowly as children do. We know this because time moves as glacially as it ever has when we are actively waiting for some particular event to occur. Time usually moves more quickly for us simply because we are enormously distracted. We have endless responsibilities and obligations to fulfill, and our preoccupation with these things causes time to fly. Genuine boredom is rarely experienced. Every minute of our day is accounted for with some task, even if the task is only to relax and consume media products.
Children are not nearly so preoccupied. They are largely free from the normative world of obligations, which means they are also more attentive to their own needs. This freedom means that children do experience boredom, and they respond to it in the only way appropriate: by creating new and more exciting forms of play.

He also thanked those who helped convince others that “voting was very important to protect the country’s democracy.”
He referred as well to the controversy involving Meta that reached the courts. “We had to overcome the external interference of digital platforms, which we are going to have to regulate,” Lula said. And he added that digital communications will be very important in his government—an essential point, since during the reelection campaign he doubled down on his efforts on social media.
Leftist former presidents congratulate Lula on his victory
Contrary to the trend set by recent elections in Latin America, the right did not win in Brazil. Various leftist former presidents from the region celebrated the victory of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
"Thank you, dear old friend, for never stopping the fight, for upholding the hope of a world," said Gabriel Boric of Chile. Meanwhile, Bolivian leader Evo Morales posted: "Your triumph renews the hope of the peoples who fight for social justice, dignity, and sovereignty."
Former Colombian president also congratulated Lula.
Abstention decreased in Brazil’s second round
Lula’s campaign focused over the last three weeks on winning new votes in order to come back from Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
In that effort, securing votes from those who had abstained was essential. In the end, abstention was three million votes lower than in the first round. Although not all of those can be attributed directly to Lula, the difference between the president and Flavio Bolsonaro was just over four million votes in the runoff.
According to the Superior Electoral Court, 33.4 million people abstained from voting on October 4, compared with 30.4 million abstentions in the runoff.
Lula surprises in the runoff and wins Brazil’s presidential election
Supporters of Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, react to early result during the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Amanda Perobell
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva went from losing in the first round with 45.16% of the votes to winning the runoff with a total of 51.79%, while right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro obtained 48.21%, according to the official count from the Superior Electoral Court.
It is the first time in Brazil’s history since the return of democracy that a candidate who lost in the first round manages to win the runoff and become president.
Lula widens his lead over Bolsonaro with 70% of the votes counted
Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, gather to wait for the results of the presidential runoff election, on the outskirts of Brasilia, Brazil, October 25, 2026. REUTERS/Diego Herculano
At this point, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.92% of the votes, while Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.08%.
During the count, the difference between both candidates did not exceed one percentage point, but that gap has now been surpassed and continues to grow in favor of the left-wing president.
This is how Lula’s surge in the vote count was experienced in Rio de Janeiro
Lula retakes the lead in the vote count with a minimal difference
When half of the votes have been tallied, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has 50.14% of the vote. Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has 49.86%, according to the Superior Electoral Court.
The difference between both candidates has not exceeded one percentage point during the count.
Lula to win Brazil election runoff, AtlasIntel CEO says
Although in the vote count President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is trailing by a narrow margin, the CEO of pollster AtlasIntel, Andrei Roman, predicts that Lula will be re-elected.
Roman spoke to Reuters and made his predictions based on the ongoing vote count in the presidential runoff against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
A slight lead for Flavio Bolsonaro with 20% of the votes counted
The senator has 50.41% compared to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s 49.59%, as the TSE reports 20% of the votes counted. It is a difference of less than one percentage point.
As in the first round, the states in northern Brazil support the outgoing left-wing president, while those in the south back the far-right candidate.
Flavio overturns the results and takes the lead over Lula
Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro waves as he arrives in Brasilia, Brazil, on the day of the presidential runoff election, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
Although President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva began ahead in the Superior Electoral Court’s count, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro now has 50.04% of the votes.
He began to lead the count from 13% of the votes tallied.
Lula holds a slight lead with 5% of the votes counted
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has 51.16% of the votes, which is just over two percentage points more than his runoff rival Flavio Bolsonaro.
The Superior Electoral Court begins by counting votes cast abroad, where Lula won in the first round.
Voting officially ends in Brazil and the counting resumes
At 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT), the polling stations that were still operating closed.
Now, the Superior Electoral Court is resuming the vote count that it had suspended after the Supreme Court ordered voting to be extended by two more hours.
The extension of voting in Brazil causes confusion at the polls
The Supreme Court’s decision came at around 5:00 p.m. Brasilia time (8:00 p.m. GMT), when the polls were supposed to close. Local media report that several polling stations had already shut down.
In response, the Superior Electoral Court stated that “the election continues in progress only in the locations where voting had not been concluded by 5 p.m.” Meanwhile, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Liberal Party called on its supporters to keep voting.
Supreme Court approves extending voting by two hours across Brazil
Cristiano Zanin is the Supreme Court justice who decided to extend voting in Brazil’s runoff on October 25. (AP Photo/Eraldo Peres)
At the last minute, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ordered that voting in the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday be extended by two hours, until 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time (10:00 p.m. GMT).
The decision grants a request from President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign. A similar petition was sent to the Superior Electoral Court, but it has not made any decision.
Meanwhile, the Superior Electoral Court has paused the counting of votes following the Supreme Court’s decision.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign also asked to extend the closing of the ballot boxes
Their request is to extend the voting period by two hours, so that it ends at 7:00 p.m. Brasilia time. The appeal was submitted to the president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, and they are asking for the extension to apply in 17 municipalities in the states of São Paulo, Paraná, and Santa Catarina.
Just like Lula’s Workers’ Party, the Liberal Party that supports Bolsonaro denounced delays in transportation. However, Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign says that the transportation delays are due to the rains and flooding affecting those states.

Bolsonaro refuses to concede, says he will seek annulment of Brazil vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
02:01:09 UTC
11:01:09 KST

Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father's lead by refusing to concede defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential election.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled.
"It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.
Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.
Still, Bolsonaro's refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say.
Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.
Lula defies expectations
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. The result will disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaro family to power.
Financial markets also expressed initial concerns at the shock result. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index 1325.T dived nearly 15% in Asian trading on news of Lula's victory, while analysts expected the Brazilian real to fall against the US dollar.
Lula had trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Speaking at a hotel in São Paulo late on Sunday, he took a conciliatory tone.
"I won’t speak of national unity, because that doesn’t always fit the reality of this country. No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," Lula said.
'Countless' challenges
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy, and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will have to work alongside a Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast Brazil's legislature in favor of the president's enemies.
“The challenges are countless,” said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper in São Paulo.

Chinese researchers have found that the Yarlung Tsangpo River – soon to host the largest mega dam in the world – may face increased run-off and flood risks over this century.

Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days: Defense secretary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
01:54:23 UTC
10:54:23 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Britain must be ready to fight and win a war within the next 1,000 days as hostile states expand their military capabilities, Defense Secretary Wes Streeting has warned.
Writing in The Telegraph on Saturday, Streeting said Britain's adversaries could be ready to attack by 2030, giving the UK and its NATO allies a little over three years to prepare.
"Our adversaries' willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030, their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack. That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win," he wrote.
"To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it. My defining priority is to make sure that this country is ready to fight and win a war," he added.
Streeting also warned of growing threats from hostile states, cyberattacks, organized crime and climate change, including risks to critical infrastructure. Speaking on the BBC, he said Britain faces a greater level of threat "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime."
The warnings coincide with the government's newly launched "Be Ready" campaign, which advises households to stock enough essential supplies to last three days during a national emergency.
The guidance recommends keeping bottled water, nonperishable food, cash and other necessities at home. The government said the initiative aims to strengthen national resilience rather than respond to any specific intelligence warning.
Streeting said terms such as "hybrid warfare" and "grey zone threats" did not adequately convey the risks posed by hostile states.
"It's really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?" he said, according to The Mirror.
"In the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defense," he added.
The government cited a recent PHP software security incident as further evidence of the need for preparedness. Vulnerabilities disclosed Wednesday prompted governments and businesses worldwide to strengthen their systems, triggered millions of hacking attempts and forced some services offline.
Streeting warned that cyber incidents could become more frequent as artificial intelligence makes it easier for attackers to bypass traditional defenses.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also called for a more proactive approach to emergencies. Speaking at a meeting on the response to wildfires, he said Britain had previously been "on the back foot" and announced a new wildfire response plan that includes deploying military aircraft.
"It's not about panicking. It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation," Burnham told the BBC.
The UK's advice echoes guidance issued by the European Commission in March 2025 urging EU citizens to maintain 72-hour emergency kits containing essentials such as food, water, cash and power banks.

Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged', defeated Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula win
Unknown

2026-10-27

10:10:22 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's surprise win in Brazil's presidential vote "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro, has refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party's head, Valdemar Costa Neto.
"We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
"I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange."
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded."
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
Markets roiled by Lula win
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil's real BRL= fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
"The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

Bangkok police arrested a 54-year-old Israeli man last Friday on suspicion of meeting women through dating apps, inviting them to his apartment, and serving them cakes suspected of containing drugs before having sex with them and secretly recording the encounters.
According to a police statement, officers searching his apartment seized methamphetamine, drug-packaging equipment, and a mobile phone containing numerous intimate videos. Investigators also discovered that the Israeli had stayed in Thailand without a valid visa for 2,095 days, or nearly six years.
Thai media identified the suspect as Tomer Kahiri. He was reportedly known in Thailand as “Tom,” “Tommy,” or “Tom Yum Kung,” after the popular Thai soup.
He was arrested at an apartment building in Bangkok’s Huai Khwang district in a joint operation involving the capital’s narcotics suppression unit and immigration police. A 44-year-old Thai woman was arrested with him.
Investigation followed tip to Thai narcotics authorities
According to the police statement, the investigation began after information was received by the hotline of Thailand’s narcotics suppression authorities. The informant described an Israeli man with an eagle tattoo on his left arm who allegedly contacted women through dating apps and invited them to his home.
According to the tip, the women experienced hot flashes and increased sexual arousal after eating cakes he had prepared for them. They subsequently had sex with him, which police suspected was recorded without their knowledge.
Police suspected the cakes contained drugs, but laboratory test results confirming their contents had not been made public.
The investigation was led by Major General Teeradet Thamsuthee, deputy chief of Bangkok police responsible for narcotics suppression. With assistance from immigration police, investigators discovered that the suspect’s visa had expired 2,095 days earlier.
During surveillance, officers observed numerous women entering and leaving his apartment. Police said the suspect did not have regular employment and spent most of his time at home, but had enough money to support himself.
Drugs, cakes and intimate videos found on phone
During the raid, police seized 15 grams of crystal methamphetamine, 50 bags used for packaging drugs, an electronic scale, a tray of cakes suspected of containing drugs, and a mobile phone.
According to police, an examination of the phone revealed messages concerning the purchase of drugs for resale, along with numerous videos showing sexual encounters with different women on a sofa in the apartment. The encounters were allegedly filmed without the women’s knowledge.
The man denied that the seized drugs belonged to him.
According to the police statement, he claimed during his arrest that he had connections to an influential person who could secure his release within two hours. He demanded the names of the officers involved in the raid and threatened to have them transferred or fired. Police also alleged that he threatened to kill one of the officers involved in the operation.
The Israeli man was accused of possessing a dangerous drug, overstaying his visa, refusing to undergo a drug test, and disobeying law enforcement officials. The Thai woman arrested with him was suspected of possessing and using methamphetamine.
The police statement did not say that the Israeli had, at that stage, been formally charged with drugging women or secretly recording intimate encounters without their consent. Both suspects and the seized evidence were transferred to Huai Khwang police station for further legal proceedings.
According to Thai media reports, the Israeli denied all the allegations against him. He reportedly described himself as a former Israeli soldier and businessman involved in textile exports. He also said he had two children and had moved to Thailand after separating from his partner because he loved the country and found its residents friendly.

Ex-FBI chief Comey faces third prosecution attempt by Trump Justice Department

The US Justice Department is attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey for a third time, the latest case accusing him of sharing sensitive national security information in 2016, according to court documents made public on Monday.
The case was revealed in a court document known as a "criminal information" that the Justice Department said it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.
The document filed in Washington federal court charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from the New York Times in October 2016.
Comey said in an Instagram video that "they're back again" and referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. "I'm still innocent," he added. Comey's lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.
The new case adds to the legal fights facing Comey, whom the Justice Department has already charged twice, accusing him of lying to Congress about media leaks and threatening US President Donald Trump in a social media post. A judge dismissed the false statements case, while the threats case remains pending.
Comey did not commit crimes, lawyer alleges
Comey's lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that the document "purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit." The criminal information was filed on October 5, but was unsealed on Monday at the request of Comey's lawyers.
A Justice Department spokesperson described the maneuver to halt the statute of limitations as a "widely recognized practice in federal court."
"This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," the spokesperson said in a statement.

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:01:53 UTC
10:01:53 KST

US court rules against Trump administration in California voting case
US appeals court blocks government effort to stop California from tabulating ballots from list of alleged non-citizens.
A United States appeals court has ruled against the administration of President Donald Trump in its bid to block the state of California from counting certain mail-in ballots this election cycle.
In a decision on Monday, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals denied a request from the government to sequester roughly 20,000 mailed ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm election.
The Trump administration had asserted that the ballots were sent to people who are “likely” non-citizens.
But it has not publicly revealed how it created its list or determined that the voters identified upon it were ineligible due to their citizenship status.
In a two-to-one decision, the appeals court said the Trump administration had not given lower courts enough time to review the case. It therefore declined to stop California’s ballot tabulation.
The court’s majority also underscored that election administration was the state’s responsibility under the US Constitution.
The Trump administration was asking “the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain”, Judge Gabriel Sanchez wrote in his opinion.
Sanchez also warned that granting the Trump administration’s petition would be “inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The Trump administration filed its lawsuit against California on October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm vote on November 3.
California is a Democrat-led state, and Trump, a Republican leader, has repeatedly made unfounded claims that the state is prone to “cheating” in its elections.
The case is currently being weighed in a lower court, with a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.
But the Trump administration sought an expedited decision from the appeals court, pointing to the looming election date.
The midterm elections are critical to determine which political party holds power in Congress.
Currently, the Republican Party maintains slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, but experts project the Democratic Party is on track to make significant gains, flipping one or both chambers.
In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has raised the prospect of non-citizen voting as a threat to election integrity.
But experts say such voting is rare. California officials have likewise cast doubt on the administration’s claims of 20,000 ballots going to “likely non-citizens”, and they framed the administration’s lawsuit as an effort to interfere in the voting process.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing on October 20. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Trump’s Department of Justice has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for complete access to voter rolls that include sensitive personal data.
It has argued that releasing such information is necessary to prevent alleged voter fraud.
But the department has lost 26 of those cases thus far, with opponents successfully arguing that such manoeuvres could scare away voters and interfere with state election administration.
The Trump administration has yet to win any of the 30 cases.
Despite claims to the contrary by Trump and his allies, cases of illegal voting, including by non-citizens, are few and far between. Non-citizens are barred from participating in federal elections in all 50 states in the US.
In July, an investigation by the news service Reuters found only 129 cases of noncitizens being charged by federal authorities with illegal voting since 1996.
Many of those cases involved mistakes, like administrative errors or individuals being uncertain of voting rules, rather than fraudulent intent.
Voting rights advocates have also pointed to flaws in how the Trump administration has identified potential non-citizen voting, signalling some eligible voters may be disenfranchised as part of its efforts.
Immigration agents under Trump have been assigned to ferret out non-citizen voters, in some cases knocking on doors to inquire about the citizenship status of the residents inside.
Last week, the administration charged 28 immigrants in California with illegally voting.
But reporting from the Los Angeles Times found that some of the accused reacted to the charges with confusion and maintained that they never registered to vote.
Trump has a history of promoting false claims of election fraud in order to justify greater federal influence over the voting process.
In 2020, he lost his bid for re-election to Democrat Joe Biden, but he denied his defeat, instead blaming vote “rigging”. That claim prompted some of Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2023, in an apparent effort to halt the election certification.

Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory

00:33:06 UTC

Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory
Authorities say the fire in Brasov in September is part of a broader Russian campaign against European countries that support Ukraine.
Romanian authorities say they have uncovered a network “coordinated” by Russia that they believe was responsible for a fire at an industrial site near a state-owned weapons factory in September.
Romania’s Intelligence Service said on Monday that the blaze in the central city of Brasov on September 14 was “part of a wider campaign of sabotage operations coordinated” by Russia amid its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The agency said the operations were aimed at arms manufacturers and “other targets of military and industrial interest”.
“These actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken the contribution of the targeted states to European and regional security,” it said in a statement.
There was no immediate comment from Russia on Romania’s claim. Moscow has previously repeatedly denied such accusations.
Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, said three people had been involved in the Brasov fire – two Belarusians and a Ukrainian, all living in European Union countries.
Two were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offenses”, the directorate said.
The third remains at large in Poland.
According to Romania’s Intelligence Service, recruits for such networks are often found on social media and are first offered money “for a seemingly harmless task”, such as “observing or photographing certain targets”.
Over time, “the tasks become increasingly serious, potentially involving acts of vandalism, arson or even murder”, it said.
‘Hybrid’ war
Romania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border of more than 600km with Ukraine.
Its centrist president, Nicusor Dan, has said the country is a target of a hybrid war that Russia is waging to destabilise nations backing Kyiv, citing drone incursions into Romanian airspace, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and sabotage.
Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said the fire in Brasov was “part of a broader campaign of sabotage across Europe” targeting military production.
“Hybrid attacks will not hold us back from strengthening our resilience and defense,” he wrote on X.
The accusation follows a string of incidents at defence sites across Europe in recent weeks.
In September, explosions and a fire erupted at an ammunition storage site in Bulgaria, weeks after a blaze at another munitions facility in the country. Both sites are operated by the Bulgarian arms maker EMCO, whose munitions are used in Ukraine.
That same month, firebombs were thrown near the offices of a defence company in Munich, and Romanian authorities said they had detained a Russian citizen accused of filming and photographing military sites in preparation for sabotage.
In August, a blast struck an ammunition factory near Rome in Italy operated by the arms maker KNDS.
At sea, at least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks, and about 34 sailors have been reported dead or missing.
Dan, the Romanian president, has called the attacks on ships in Romanian waters “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”.
A year ago, Poland and Romania also detained eight people suspected of taking part in a Russian plot to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.

More than 40 sets of World War II remains exhumed in Mlyniv, Rivne region
Oleksii Zlatohorskyi, director of the specialized institution “Volyn Antiquities” and an archaeologist, told Ukrinform about this.
“During search operations in July of this year, 15 coffins containing remains were discovered on the grounds of the Memorial of Glory in the center of the village. The Soviet monument itself bears the names of 347 people who are supposedly reburied there. These are not local residents, but Soviet soldiers who died during World War II, who were originally buried on the outskirts of the village and later reburied in the center of Mlyniv. However, this figure has not been confirmed. “Preliminarily, during the exhumation, we discovered 47–48 sets of remains. The final figure will be known after a more detailed examination,” the archaeologist said.
1 / 12
Zlatohorskyi is a member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. While on leave, together with his fellow archaeologists Artur Alyoshin, Nazariy Romanyuk, and Dmytro Demianchuk, he conducted the exhumation of this burial site at the request of the Mlyniv community leadership.
As the search team discovered, based on the accompanying documentation, it can be concluded that most of the remains belong to military personnel. In particular, the remains of six women were found among them. The remains of two children were also discovered.
"I suspect that, perhaps, while excavating World War II-era graves near the local cemetery, they unearthed remains from a civilian burial site. That is why children were found buried at the memorial. As for the women, according to the accompanying materials found, they were military personnel,” Zlatohorskyi said.
Along with the remains, archaeologists found spoons engraved with their owners’ initials. They say this usually indicated military status. They also found pieces of leather belts, boots, fragments of eyeglasses, and a razor. Materials that may be important for identification will be transferred to the Rivne Regional Museum of Local History after processing and cleaning. Samples were also collected during the examination of the remains for DNA analysis.
According to Zlatohorskyi, working during the exhumation in Mlyniv was difficult because, during the reburial, the remains of 10–15 people had simply been dumped into a coffin, covered with clay, and placed in brick-lined crypts.
“For the Soviet authorities, the ideological significance of this memorial was more important than respect for the people they supposedly wanted to honor,” the archaeologist added.
The remains exhumed in Mlyniv were reburied at the local cemetery.
Previously, the memorial in Mlyniv was included in the list of 100 monuments to be dismantled as part of the decommunization process by the “Decolonization. Ukraine” project.
Suspilne. Rivne reported that, in order to dismantle the sculpture of a Soviet soldier and renovate the complex, the village council appealed to the Ministry of Culture to have the memorial’s status as a historical monument revoked. Subsequently, in coordination with the Ministry of Culture, search operations were conducted to locate the remains of World War II victims for their subsequent reburial. After obtaining all necessary permits and completing the exhumation and reburial of the Soviet soldiers, the plan is to transfer portraits of soldiers from the Mlyniv community who died in the Russian-Ukrainian war to the memorial grounds.
As reported by Ukrinform, a Ukrainian expedition completed search operations in Laskowo, Poland, where the remains of more than 40 people were discovered.

A US federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s move to block California from counting the ballots of 20,000 registered voters that the justice department claims are non-citizens.
The court on Monday ruled 2-1 against Donald Trump’s justice department in the dispute, denying the administration’s demand that election officials segregate the thousands of ballots until people on the list could verify their citizenship. The justice department had given the California secretary of state 48-hours to carry out the order, which state election officials refused – leading to the lawsuit.
The decision by the San Francisco-based ninth US circuit court of appeals marks a setback in Trump’s attempts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the 3 November midterms. Voting rights groups and Democrats have criticized the effort, saying the Trump administration is attempting to create uncertainty around the upcoming election results as Republicans vie to retain control of Congress.
The ruling is also the latest development in a conflict between California and Trump’s justice department. The DoJ additionally filed criminal charges against 28 green-card holders in California earlier this month over alleged voter fraud – including several people who court papers suggested were confused about their eligibility and agreed to voluntary interviews with investigators.
There is uncertainty over how the justice department developed its list of 20,000 non-citizen registered voters and its accuracy. Court filings from last week showed that Los Angeles election officials analyzed a sample of 200 people on the list and found that a “high percentage” were born in the United States.
The justice department claims about non-citizen voting in California have also faced backlash from state officials, who have said that the DoJ has not provided data or methodology to back up its allegations. California secretary of state Shirley Weber called the department’s claims “vague and unsubstantiated” in a letter earlier this month. Weber also stated that the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year claimed that California had 190,000 registered voters that “may be” non-citizens, but provided no further details on how it reached that number.
California’s attorney general Rob Bonta touted Monday’s decision as a victory for voting rights and rejection of the Trump administration’s “unlawful overreach”, while Governor Gavin Newsom accused Trump of carrying out an “assault on democracy”.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the constitution and our country’s democracy,” Newsom said in a statement.
Trump has personally advocated for his supporters to seek out voter fraud in the midterm elections, posting on his Truth Social platform on Monday that he would issue a $1m reward for anyone whose report led to an arrest or conviction. He has long made unfounded claims that ineligible voting such as non-citizen voting is rampant, despite experts and data having shown it is exceedingly rare.

Explainer-Israel election: What happens after polls close?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
01:23:53 CET
09:23:53 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Israel holds a parliamentary election on Tuesday, its first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but it might take time before clear results are known.
WHEN WILL WE KNOW WHO WON?
It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear.
Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and ends at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT), when Israeli TV channels will air exit polls giving the first indications of the outcome. The election results will then start coming in.
A clear picture may emerge quickly but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.
The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
WHY IS IT SO COMPLICATED?
Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be held every four years but early elections have been frequent.
The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE RESULTS ARE PUBLISHED?
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

By Steven Scheer and Pesha Magid
JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel’s election on Tuesday, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel’s deepening international isolation.
Yet Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel’s fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.
Opinion polls show a close race between Netanyahu’s Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.
Netanyahu is campaigning on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran. Netanyahu said on Sunday that Trump was prepared to act again to “finally” remove the Iranian threat, but only if Netanyahu remained in power.
Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of “relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats,” and said he was confident Trump would work “in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people.”
Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to form a government. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next year.
Polls open from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. (0500 to 2000 GMT).
THE OCTOBER 7 RECKONING
The election follows one of Israel’s most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Israel’s subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing government.
For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel’s deadliest day.
Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and Eisenkot supporter, said “the most important thing is the establishment of a national inquiry because that’s where our healing will come from.”
Lisa Tortor said she hoped Netanyahu would go and “they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel’s image.” Bibi is Netanyahu’s nickname.
But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Netanyahu was to blame for October 7 and called him “the right man for the state of Israel.”
“Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way,” Gabay said.
THE WARTIME RECORD
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after October 7, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks killed 74,000 people.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year’s joint US-Israeli war.
Eisenkot has said Israel’s next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an “arrangement” such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.
THE COALITION MATH
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.
A high turnout among voters from Israel’s Arab minority, Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage, could help nudge Israel’s complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.
Though Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
“My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide,” said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.
(Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Howard Goller)

Russia committed war crimes in Ukraine by attacking its energy grid, UN-backed inquiry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
00:21:17 UTC
09:21:17 KST

Russia committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine by intentionally attacking energy infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity and heat in freezing temperatures, a U.N.-backed inquiry reported Monday.
The inquiry also found evidence that Russia recruited men from 29 countries into its armed forces “through deception or coercion” to fight in Ukraine in violation of international law. The men, age 18 to 60, “came mostly from vulnerable and marginalized communities, with a poor economic background and a low education level,” it said.
The independent commission of inquiry was authorized by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council to investigate human rights violations shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its report to the U.N. General Assembly’s human rights committee on Monday was its first focusing on the impact of Russia’s wide-ranging attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The electricity cuts have left millions of civilians suffering in frigid winter darkness, the elderly without elevators to get to shelters during missile and drone attacks, and hospital patients without critical devices to keep them alive, the report said.
The commission concluded that the attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constituted war crimes because they were intentionally directed against civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity for “inflicting great suffering to civilians,” commission chair Erik Mose said at a U.N. news conference, speaking by video.
Mose, a former Norwegian judge, said the intensifying attacks as this winter approaches raise serious concerns about the threats posed to civilians.
The commission said it based its findings on the accounts of 255 Ukrainians who endured winter conditions in Kyiv and eight other regions in 2025-26 as well as government officials, doctors and civic organizations.
Mose said the Russians have not responded to requests for comment on any of the commission’s reports, including this one.
Russia’s U.N. Mission said Monday that Russia does not recognize the mandate of the commission and claimed its findings were based on “falsified data.”
Throughout the war, Russia has consistently maintained that its forces are only striking military or military-related targets in Ukraine, or targets that are used in the interest of the Ukrainian armed forces, despite multiple reports and evidence indicating otherwise.
Russian authorities have been openly and actively recruiting foreigners into the army, offering perks such as accelerated Russian citizenship or making enlisting in the army mandatory for certain foreigners seeking permanent residency in Russia. Official rhetoric usually underscores the voluntary nature of such enlistments.
The report, however, said the men were recruited through deception and coercion in coordination with agents operating in other countries who presented themselves as legitimate and government-endorsed businesses.
The agents arranged visas and sometimes traveled with the men, who soon after arrival were forced to sign documents in Russian with the Defense Ministry that they didn’t understand, the commission said.
“The recruits were shocked to discover that they would be serving for the Russian armed forces,” it said.
The commission said it investigated the recruitment of nationals from 48 countries and found evidence that men from 29 countries were recruited into Russia’s armed forces as a result of deception or coercion. It named the 29 countries: Azerbaijan, Bangladesh, Belarus, Bolivia, Brazil, Botswana, Cameroon, Colombia, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Ghana, Honduras, India, Jordan, Kenya, Morocco, Nigeria, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Tunisia, Turkey, Uganda, Uzbekistan, Yemen and Zimbabwe.

Libya says international aviation restrictions lifted
Unknown

2026-10-27
00:20:23 UTC

Breadcrumb
Libya says international aviation restrictions lifted after 11 years
Libya's Ministry of Transport said on Monday that the UN's International Civil Aviation Organisation removed airspace restrictions it issued in 2015 during the country's civil war.
The ministry said ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar announced the decision, formally issued on 23 October, at the opening of a meeting of civil aviation officials from the Middle East in Doha.
"This measure comes as a result of the notable progress made and the confidence placed in the capabilities of the Libyan civil aviation sector in recent times," the Tripoli-based Ministry of Transport said in a statement on its verified Facebook page.
In a separate statement, the ministry said the North African country has received requests for permits to transit Libyan airspace, which it characterised as "unprecedented demand from international airlines".
"The total number of permits registered for 2026-2027 winter season has surged to 61,968 flights per month, effective from this November," the ministry said, calling it a significant jump from an average of 2,000 transit flights per month during the 2025-2026 season.
"Such an increase will generate substantial financial revenues using Libyan airspace," it added.
Libya slid into chaos after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011. Three years later, a civil war broke out between armed factions vying for power, dividing the country between eastern and western administrations.
The war caused damage to up to 20 aircraft, including Airbus models, at Tripoli International Airport in 2014.
Few airlines currently operate flights in and out of Libya, and they have long been limited to destinations such as Tunisia, Jordan, Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Sudan.
The ministry added that ICAO's decision would be circulated to all 193 member states for implementation.

Jordan launches air strikes in Syria in response to a fatal church shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
23:50:11 UTC
08:50:11 KST

Jordan strikes Syria after church attack, killing at least seven people
Syria closes border crossings with Jordan after air strikes kill seven people in Deraa and Suweyda, including children.
Jordan attacks Syria in response to Karak church attack
Jordan has carried out air strikes in Syria in “retaliation” for last week’s deadly church attack, with Syrian authorities saying the raids killed at least seven people, including three children and a woman.
The attacks on Monday prompted Syria to close its main crossing with Jordan.
Jordan’s Armed Forces said in a statement that it targeted “hideouts” of armed groups in southeastern Syria in response to the gun attack at a church in its Karak governorate on Friday. At least nine people were killed and dozens more wounded in the shootings.
The Jordanian military said the strikes on Syria were launched “in coordination with the Syrian government”.
It said the raids “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”.
Syria, however, denied any coordination with Jordan.
In a statement, the Syrian government said “the military operation was conducted without prior coordination or notification” and said it has launched an investigation.
Syria’s Civil Defence service said at least four sites in rural Deraa and Suweyda provinces were hit on Monday evening, and that its crews had recovered the bodies of seven people: three men, a woman and three children.
Five of the dead – a man, a woman and three children – were members of one family killed in a strike on a tent in the village of Al-Tai in Deraa Province, the service said. Three other family members, including a child, were wounded.
A second strike hit Al Shayyah, also in Deraa, killing an 80-year-old man. A third hit a residential building in Muzayrib, in the Ain al-Basal area of Deraa, causing no casualties.
A fourth struck a residential building in the town of Shahba in Suweyda province, killing a 60-year-old man.
After the strikes, Syria’s border authority closed the Nassib crossing, suspending traffic in both directions. Nassib is the only crossing for passengers and commercial goods between Jordan and Syria.
A Syrian Foreign Ministry official called the strikes a “treacherous attack” and told Al Jazeera that the ministry would try to manage the fallout in a way that preserved Syrian sovereignty.
Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law on suspicion of involvement in the church attack. The arrests took place in the village of Al-Jadeeda, after a shootout with authorities.
A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the suspects sustained serious injuries during the confrontation, which lasted for about three hours.
The arrests and air strikes in Syria come after Jordan’s King Abdullah II pledged a stern response to the church attack. During the incident, three gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90km south of the capital, Amman.
The king said those responsible would face the “harshest penalties” and ordered a review of the country’s security procedures.
Karak is home to a minority Christian population, which makes up about 300,000 of Jordan’s 11.5 million people.

The awards were presented at the 70th Ballon d'Or ceremony at the London Palladium, marking the first time the prestigious event was held in the British capital.
Kane, 33, claimed the award for the first time after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025-26 campaign, including 61 goals in 51 matches for the German side, which won a domestic double.
The England captain also scored six goals at the 2026 World Cup, helping his country finish third.
Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second in the Men's Ballon d'Or voting, while Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal took third place.
Kane became the fifth English player to win the award, joining Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen, who last claimed the prize in 2001.
He succeeded Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele, who won the award in 2025.
Meanwhile, Putellas, 32, claimed her third Women's Ballon d'Or following her previous victories in 2021 and 2022, equaling former Barcelona teammate Aitana Bonmati's record.
The Spanish midfielder captained Barcelona to a quadruple during the 2025-26 season, winning Liga F, Copa de la Reina, the Spanish Super Cup and Women's Champions League.
She was also named the Champions League Player of the Season and helped Spain win the Women's Nations League.
Putellas joined London City Lionesses in July after her trophy-laden spell with Barcelona.
- Other award winners
Barcelona and Spain winger Lamine Yamal won Men's Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year, while Barcelona forward Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second successive year.
Spain's World Cup-winning coach Luis de la Fuente was named Men's Coach of the Year, while Barcelona's Pere Romeu received the women's coaching award.
Athletic Bilbao's Unai Simon won Men's Goalkeeper of the Year, with Barcelona's Cata Coll claiming the women's honor.
Bayern Munich's Kane also received the Men's Striker of the Year award following his prolific campaign, while Mexican forward Charlyn Corral became the first Mexican to win the Women's Striker of the Year award.
Barcelona were named Women's Club of the Year, while Paris Saint-Germain claimed the men's club award.
Arsenal and England winger Bukayo Saka received the Socrates Award for his humanitarian work, including funding 120 medical operations for children in Kano, Nigeria through a partnership with charity BigShoe in 2022.

AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – A US appeals court on Oct 26 ruled against President Donald Trump’s administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely non-citizens.
The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in.
The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Oct 27 in the case.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike”.
The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged non-citizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election.
The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent votes from being counted by a state, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people allegedly registered to vote in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.
Justice Department officials said on Oct 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives – 52 – than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its so-called “sanctuary state” policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including non-citizen voting, is exceedingly rare.
A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which non-citizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots, and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
California says the state’s safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust, and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data”.
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in an October 20 court filing.
“At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinising state voter lists to identify non-citizens risk wrongly flagging naturalised US citizens for removal from the rolls.
The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has sued 30 states and Washington, DC, for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data, but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one.
“Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney-General Rob Bonta, a Democrat. REUTERS

SC to UP police: Educate officers on investigation
