Supreme Court slams UP police for "slipshod investigation", orders Rs 6 lakh compensation for man held six years without evidence.
NEW DELHI: In a severe indictment of Uttar Pradesh police for carrying out a “slipshod investigation” that resulted in a man being in custody for six years when there was no evidence against him, Supreme Court Monday said the state cannot shirk its responsibility to protect citizens and directed it to pay a compensation of Rs 6 lakh to him.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person’s life and liberty,” SC noted at the outset of its verdict.On Sept 30, in a separate matter, the top court had slammed UP police for not naming the accused in a road accident case.
Appalled at the way UP cops carried out probe: SC
It would be better if investigations in all criminal cases were handed over to CBI if the state police works with an agenda and does cover-up jobs, court had said, noting the accused had not been named despite the complainant catching him on the spot and handing him over to police.In the present case, a bench of J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said there was no evidence to implicate the person in a kidnapping and murder case. It noted he was never named in the FIR and police made him an accused on the basis that he was seen in CCTV footage. SC said it was “appalled at the manner in which investigation was carried out”. “It is unfortunate that despite no evidence against the petitioner, he was imprisoned for six years as an undertrial.
Based on a slipshod investigation, a haphazard prosecution was carried out, which resulted, fortunately, in the acquittal of the accused. We cannot but deprecate the manner in which the probe was carried out and prosecution conducted,” SC said. “State police would do well to educate their officers in the process of investigation.”
Making the state accountable for police’s misdeed, the court said six years have been erased from the man’s life on the strength of a concocted story built on mere surmises and conjectures, and the state has to pay compensation.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The investigation and prosecuting agencies exist not merely to, and by whatever means, bring in a conviction. They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured but also to the accused,” the SC bench said.

Russia increases diesel production after Trump deal – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:50:47 UTC
07:50:47 KST

Russia increases diesel production after Trump deal – Reuters
Russia has significantly increased production of diesel in the wake of an agreement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his American counterpart Donald Trump, Reuters has reported, citing industry sources.
Daily output rose from 160,000 tons in early October to 180,000 tons after the Russian government introduced new export quotas in mid-month, the agency said. Moscow has eased its restrictions on diesel exports, allowing Russian companies to ship up to 500,000 tons of fuel to international markets in October while ensuring domestic demand remains fully covered.
Exports of diesel, marine fuel, and gas oil had previously been banned until October 31 as the government sought to stabilize the domestic market, which had been suffering from increased seasonal demand linked to the harvest season.
According to the sources cited by Reuters, domestic demand in Russia is now expected to fall to about 140,000 tons per day as the harvest campaign is largely over. This would free up as much as 40,000 tons of diesel per day or more than 1 million tons per month for export, according to the news agency’s estimates. Between 0.2 and 0.3 million tons are likely to be purchased by Russia’s neighbors, the sources said.
Trump and Putin agreed on diesel supplies during a phone call on October 9. Following the conversation, the US president announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially further shipments depending on refining capacity. Washington subsequently issued a temporary sanctions waiver permitting Russian diesel imports, reversing restrictions introduced under former US President Joe Biden in 2022.
Last week, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak noted that Moscow had already dispatched three tankers carrying diesel to the US under the agreement. He also announced that Russia would “ensure additional supplies of diesel fuel to world markets and the United States” to help ease the global diesel shortage. Deliveries would continue on a regular basis, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also said at the time.
The diesel deal provoked tensions between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to stop attacking Russian refineries, accusing Kiev of exacerbating the worldwide diesel shortage and hurting American consumers and farmers hit by high fuel prices.
Zelensky hit back by blasting Trump’s claims as “totally false” and accusing the American leader of “deflecting the focus away from Iran.” He was referring to the American and Israeli military campaign against the Islamic Republic that, together with the Iranian response, led to severe shipment disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz – one of the key seaborne oil transportation routes.
Russia has historically been the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, behind only the US, accounting for roughly 10% of global exports. Disruptions to Russian supplies can drive up prices even in countries that do not directly import the fuel.

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:18:34 UTC
07:18:34 KST

Protests in Europe: Fact-checking viral videos amid claims of 'chaos'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As young people protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living across Europe, misleading videos are spreading online. Footage from Poland in 2017, military preparations in Portugal and a protest in Argentina have all been falsely presented as recent demonstrations in Europe, painting a misleading picture of unrest. Vedika Bahl fact-checks three viral videos to uncover what they really show and how old footage is recycled to spread misinformation and attract clicks.
As young people take to the streets across Europe to protest poor school conditions and the rising cost of living, misleading videos circulating online regarding the demonstrations.
Footage from Poland, Portugal and Argentina has been falsely presented as evidence of recent unrest in Europe, with some posts suggesting the continent is descending into chaos. Others may be seeking to attract clicks and engagement.
One viral video, viewed more than a million times on X, appears to show enormous crowds gathered in Poland. Social media users claimed it depicted millions of people taking part in recent protests. But the footage is nearly nine years old. It shows Poland’s annual Independence Day march and was already circulating online in 2017.
The video has repeatedly resurfaced with misleading captions over the years. It was also previously shared as footage of unrest in France and was debunked earlier this year by FRANCE 24’s fact-checking service, The Observers.
Another video has been used to spread false claims about protests in Portugal. Posts on social media claimed the country had deployed its army to suppress demonstrations, warning that Portugal was on the “brink of social explosion”.
The footage shows military vehicles driving through the streets of Porto, accompanied by dramatic music. While the video was indeed filmed in the Portuguese city - with the famous Chapel of Santa Catarina is visible in the background - it does not show troops being deployed against protesters.
Instead, the footage shows preparations for Army Day, held from October 20 to 25. According to the city’s official website, thousands of soldiers arrived in Porto for a multi-day programme of events showcasing the military.
There have been no credible reports of the army being deployed to quell the recent protests. Demonstrations, including those calling for more affordable housing, have been handled by police. On Sunday, police dismantled housing protest camps in Porto and Lisbon, with more than 30 people arrested.
The same military footage has also recently circulated on TikTok with a different false claim: that it shows French police being deployed against protesters in France, despite Portuguese architecture being visible in the video.
A third video was shared by an account known for spreading false information, allegedly showing Italian protesters tearing down a US flag as onlookers cheered during a demonstration against rising fuel prices.
However, a reverse image search revealed that the footage dates back to August and was filmed in Buenos Aires, Argentina.The video shows the American flag being removed from the facade of a hotel near Argentina’s National Congress during a protest linked to a law introduced by President Javier Milei concerning private property.
The footage has no connection to protests in Italy.

In Moscow, large-scale mobile internet restrictions will be introduced from October 27 to 29 due to international events involving Russian dictator Vladimir Putin. Details

Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal 'remains null and void,' Greek foreign minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:10:23 UTC
07:10:23 KST

The joint statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 memorandum.
Greece's foreign minister said on Monday that a 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime boundaries deal remained "null and void" as he delivered a joint statement on behalf of Greece, Egypt, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union.
"The memorandum in question remains null and void and without legal effect, runs counter to international law and cannot serve as a lawful basis for the delimitation of maritime zones, nor can it produce legal consequences for third states," Giorgos Gerapetritis said.
The statement responded to the recent decision by Libya's House of Representatives to ratify the 2019 Turkish-Libyan memorandum on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean, which, it said, "raises serious concerns for regional security and stability."
The statement also highlighted a broader challenge to the international legal order, namely "the need to ensure that arbitrary bilateral agreements do not undermine the established rules of international law or prejudice the rights of third states."
Gerapetritis underlined that international law and, in particular, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), as well as customary international law, provide the legal framework for the delimitation of maritime zones.
These rules, he said, are "of fundamental importance for safeguarding predictability, legal certainty and peaceful relations among states."
He also warned that accepting bilateral agreements that disregard the applicable rules and principles of international law "would create a dangerous precedent, undermining the international legal order and the principles on which the peaceful settlement of disputes is based."
According to the statement, the memorandum violates these fundamental principles as it "ignores the geographical reality and the rights of all the coastal states involved over maritime zones, including the rights of islands in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea."
"The subsequent decision of Libya's House of Representatives does not alter this legal reality," it added.
The signatories reaffirmed their commitment "to the reunification of Libya's institutions and to the prospect of a united and prosperous Libya," while stressing that a stable Libya, engaging actively in regional cooperation, was essential for peace and security in the Mediterranean.
They also said that the country's political transition and its relations with its neighbours "must be governed by respect for international law and good-neighbourly relations."

Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week

Ukrainian Troops Evacuate Two Wounded Soldiers by Air With StarGate CASEVAC Drone in One Week
Ukrainian troops evacuated two seriously wounded soldiers from the battlefield using the StarGate unmanned aerial CASEVAC platform after ground vehicles could not reach their positions, according to footage and information published online by the 475th Separate Assault Regiment CODE 9.2.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign “Izium,” and 24-year-old Artem, call sign “Kolobok,” suffered severe limb injuries while positioned in a gray zone about five kilometers from the Russian border.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian FPV drones made evacuation by ground transport impossible, leaving an airborne extraction as the only available option.
Over the course of one week, CODE 9.2 planned and completed two separate evacuation missions with support from SkyFall, the Ukrainian defense technology company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units, additional personnel and equipment, and fire support. Ukrainian forces used heavy Vampire strike drones to suppress Russian positions during the evacuations.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers to reach the wounded soldier and another 30 kilometers back with him onboard.
Russian forces were actively using electronic warfare in the area in an attempt to suppress GPS navigation completely. Despite the interference, StarGate continued flying using its onboard AI-based navigation system and was able to complete the mission.
The regiment now plans to turn the experience into a permanent capability.
“Going forward, we plan to make changes to the organizational structure of our regiment and create a separate air ambulance section within the medical company,” CODE 9.2 commander Oleksandr Nastenko, call sign “Flint,” stated.
“It will specialize directly in evacuating wounded personnel from the battlefield by air transport,” he added.
StarGate is Ukraine’s first specialized unmanned aerial platform developed specifically for battlefield CASEVAC missions. SkyFall designed the system for situations in which conventional vehicles cannot reach wounded troops or where sending ground transport would be too dangerous.
The drone can carry up to 150 kilograms and reach speeds of up to 105 kilometers per hour. Its evacuation module is based on certified medical stretchers, while onboard AI, navigation, and redundant communications systems allow it to continue operating when GPS is jammed or communications are lost.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces evacuated a soldier who had survived 491 days in an isolated frontline position and lost both feet after being wounded by Russian drones. Conventional ground evacuation was impossible because of mines and intense drone activity, prompting several Ukrainian units to adapt a heavy hexacopter to carry him out.

Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Hasn’t Left Port in Five Months, Firing Kalibrs From Novorossiysk

07:07:03 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Hasn’t Left Port in Five Months, Firing Kalibrs From Novorossiysk
Russia’s Black Sea Fleet has avoided open waters for five consecutive months, launching Kalibr cruise missiles directly from its base in Novorossiysk, Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk reported on October 26, according to NV.
Speaking on Ukraine’s national television, Pletenchuk explained that Russian commanders likely fear losing their warships at sea. As a result, they have opted to conduct missile launches from their own naval base, despite the potential dangers of such operations.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It’s better to launch missiles from their own harbor, even though if something detonates there, everyone nearby will be in serious trouble. So yes, they decided to stay home,” Pletenchuk explained.
However, the restrictions on Russian naval movements have not eliminated the threat of Kalibr missile strikes against Ukraine. Pletenchuk noted that Russian submarines face greater operational limitations because they do not launch missiles from inside the harbor and have also stopped venturing into open waters.
Kalibr is a family of Russian sea-launched cruise missiles deployed aboard surface warships and submarines. Its 3M-14 land-attack variant has an estimated range of 1,500 to 2,500 kilometers and carries a warhead weighing approximately 450 kilograms, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The missile’s long range allows Russian warships to strike targets across Ukraine while remaining in port. This enables Moscow to maintain a naval missile threat without exposing its surface vessels to the same risks of operating in open waters.
Meanwhile, Russian military aviation continues to operate over the Black Sea around the clock, conducting patrols and strikes both day and night. Russian drones also remain active in the area.
Pletenchuk emphasized that Russian aircraft and helicopters maintain a distance of at least 100 kilometers from Ukraine’s coastline.
He recalled that Ukrainian forces had previously used naval drones to shoot down Russian aircraft and helicopters, demonstrating the expanding capabilities of Ukraine’s unmanned maritime systems.
Earlier, on September 9, several branches of Ukraine’s security and defense forces struck the naval base in Novorossiysk, hitting military harbor facilities, warships, and Kalibr missile carriers, along with a terminal involved in oil shipments.
At the port’s fuel oil terminal, a commercial logistics hub with an annual throughput capacity of 4 million metric tons, at least one petroleum storage tank was set ablaze.

Frontex set for new powers to deport beyond EU borders in latest overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:50:19 UTC
06:50:19 KST

The logo of Frontex is pictured at the headquarters of the European Border and Coast Guard Agency in Warsaw on September 17, 2026. | Roland Schlager/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The European Commission will unveil a sweeping overhaul of EU border agency Frontex on Oct. 27, turning it into a fully-fledged “European return agency,” according to two EU officials familiar with the proposal.
The legislative proposal, which will revamp the Warsaw-based agency’s mandate, will focus on three key areas: strengthening its role in deportations, improving its ability to anticipate and respond to border crises, and boosting its operational capacity without poaching border guards from countries.
At the heart of the reform is an ambition to give Frontex a much more prominent role in returning people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory, said the officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss information not yet in the public domain.
Advertisement
The push comes just months after EU lawmakers approved a new “return regulation” aimed at accelerating deportations and allowing member countries to establish controversial deportation hubs outside the EU.
With the legal framework largely agreed, Brussels is now turning its attention to enforcement — and to the agency expected to help make the new rules work in practice.
Political pressure has also been mounting. In June, the leaders of 19 EU countries urged the Commission to support the establishment of return hubs outside the bloc, including through EU funding, as first reported by POLITICO.
The proposed Frontex overhaul, which is on the College of Commissioners’ agenda and is expected to be approved by the EU executive on Oct. 27, would help put that broader shift into practice by giving the agency more resources, greater operational flexibility and an expanded role in carrying out returns beyond EU borders, including transfers between third countries.
Emergency response
But deportations are only part of the equation.
The Commission also wants to transform Frontex into a force that can intervene in border emergencies within 24 hours, according to the two officials.
Brussels wants to ensure that a similar crisis doesn’t catch the EU off guard again. Under the plans, Frontex would be given a stronger mandate to monitor potential flashpoints, particularly on social media, and improve early warning capabilities and identify emerging threats before they escalate.
The agency would also be better equipped to respond swiftly once a crisis happens, with personnel and equipment available for deployment on short notice rather than relying exclusively on existing arrangements with national governments.
Staffing questions
Another central question is how big Frontex should become.
The agency had around 7,800 personnel in its Standing Corps in early 2026 and is working towards a target of 10,000 by 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has previously called for tripling that figure to 30,000 European border and coast guards.
The Commission’s proposal is expected to seek a compromise between the competing ambitions for expansion and the practical constraints facing national governments.
Advertisement
Rather than relying entirely on a substantially larger permanent force, Brussels is considering a sizeable reserve that officials say could be mobilized when needed. That would help address countries’ concerns that an expanded EU-level force could pull their border guards away at a time when national authorities are already under pressure.
The approach would allow Frontex to increase its deployable capacity while keeping more personnel available for national duties when they are not needed for European operations.
Beyond staffing, the two people expect the Commission to put forward measures to give the agency better equipment and more agile operational procedures, particularly for deportations.
The reform is also likely to reopen debates over the agency’s accountability and human rights of migrants and asylum-seekers, especially as the EU moves towards more deportations to third countries.
Frontex did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Serbia’s elections: 'Tracking fraud for sure had an impact on the results'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:49:17 UTC
06:49:17 KST

Serbia’s elections: 'Tracking fraud for sure had an impact on the results'
On October 25, Serbia's student-led protest movement won a historic victory in parliamentary elections, defeating outgoing President Aleksandar Vucic's party. Supporters of the student list explained to FRANCE 24 how they mounted a massive mobilisation to fight electoral fraud and monitor the electoral process inside and outside the polling stations.
Serbia’s parliamentary elections on Sunday, October 25 delivered a political earthquake. The Student List movement challenged the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) which had dominated Serbian politics for 14 years, led by outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic.
The result marked a historic turning point: the Student List won 52.45 percent of the vote, securing 138 seats in the National Assembly, while the Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia list received 39.2 , earning 103 seats.
The student movement emerged in the aftermath of the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024, a tragedy that claimed 16 lives and triggered nationwide protests against corruption. Initially non-partisan, the movement gradually gained widespread public support before deciding to field its own electoral list. Rather than running for office themselves, the students chose to nominate highly qualified individuals with no prior political experience, selected through a democratic process organised within universities.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'We trained at least 16,000 people to become official controllers'
Petar Botoski, an agricultural student supporting the Student List, was in Novi Sad, a city located in the northern part of the country, when Aleksandar Vucic acknowledged the defeat of his party.
 "It was the most challenging moment. We expected to win, but we did not know what would happen next. When the announcement came, I was in shock, everyone was cheering. At that time, the votes were still being transferred and being counted."
He explained that the student movement prevented much electoral fraud during the day.
 “The whole day we reported to authorities incidents such as the finding of parallel lists or the detection of carousel votes.”
Both are practices that can facilitate voter pressure or manipulation of the voting process. The parallel list is an unofficial list of voters used alongside the official register to manipulate or falsify voting records, while carousel voting is a form of electoral fraud in which a voter is given a ballot that has already been marked, takes it into the polling station and deposits it in the ballot box. The voter then brings the unmarked ballot they received as proof that he or she voted as “required”.
Petar Botoski goes on:
 “For a year and half, since we decided to propose a student list for the legislative elections, the student movement spent a lot of time and resources to create connections between people and to teach them how to prevent electoral fraud.
We trained at least 16,000 people to become official controllers, two for each polling station. Then we trained about five people per polling station to be part of mobile teams. Their mission was to detect fraud outside the polling stations, such as the use of parallel lists, carousel vote, pay[ing] for voters and intimidations. [Tracking] fraud had for sure an impact on the results.”
Turnout reached 69 percent, with more than 4.4 million citizens casting their ballots. This represents a significant increase compared with the 55.5 percent turnout recorded in Serbia’s December 2023 parliamentary elections.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'We ensured that it was harder for them to fraud'
Janko Sikosek, a member of the movement “Bikers with Students”, was among the volunteers that assisted in monitoring polling stations and helping to ensure a fair and transparent electoral process.
 “I went out to vote early in the morning; the line was already forming before the polling station opened. At this moment, I felt very optimistic. People were looking at each other and smiling. The line was so long, I waited for an hour and a half to vote.
Then I joined my mobile team. Only in my municipality (Vozdovac), there were 14 mobile teams, each one composed of 3 people.
We were there to record, to observe, to be present. We ensured that it was harder for them (SNS supporters) to fraud.
The job of my team of bikers was to help mobile teams that got in trouble. One mobile team discovered vote-buying headquarters in Ovca, in the north of Belgrade. A guy of the mobile team was hit on the head, the other two escaped, but their car was trapped. When we intervened, a couple of our guys got hurt. One received a strike on the head with a rock and the other had his arm broken. But we managed to get the mobile team out of there.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The incident involving Sikosek’s team was not isolated. Several other incidents were reported throughout election day, both inside and outside polling stations. For example, a group of masked men attacked election monitors from the Student List in Pancevo using pyrotechnic devices. Several of them were struck in the head.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Moreover, an observer from CRTA, a Serbian democracy watchdog, was harassed by a group of people in Zemur.
There were also reportedly some tensions inside the polling stations.
Marko, a student in Novi Sad, was an official controller. He reported some tensions between the controllers from SNS and the ones from supporting the Student List. He said the SNS controllers tried to obstruct some people from voting, notably younger ones, pretending “they don't look like their ID photo".
In some places, there were tensions about voting booths. Voting booths with curtains were introduced in Serbian elections for the first time in this election. According to the student supporters, this increases the risk of taking pictures of ballots. This is reportedly done by people who were paid to vote to support the ruling party or who received pressure over their vote because they work in public administrations.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
According to CRTA, the most frequently observed irregularity was the photographing of ballot papers, reported at as many as 50 percent of the polling stations monitored. Voters take pictures of their ballots when they are paid for or when they receive pressure from their employers.
An investigation published by Balkan Insight on October 20, based on more than 150 testimonies, describes pressure exerted on public sector employees to give their electoral support to the ruling party and to participate in its political rallies.
A few days before the election, Rasa Nedeljkov, the program director of CRTA, told the FRANCE 24 Observers team about some worrying observations:
 “The CRTA found that 7 out of 18 lists that were going to be on the ballot were basically completely unexisting phantom fake lists. Through these fake lists, the ruling political party had the additional votes in the electoral commissions at local and national level.
We also noted that in the past 90 days, there were 14,100 new voters. This is something which is again strange and odd. We had addresses with a high number of completely new voters and multiple voters registered in one address.”
'The polling boards were filled with well-prepared representatives for the very first time'
Nedeljkov said at a press conference the day following the elections:
 “Manipulation was prevented by the fact that a large number of Serbian citizens attached importance to election rule and got involved in the implementation and the control of election at polling stations. The polling boards were filled with well-prepared representatives for the very first time.”
'It was a historical moment'
Until Vucic announced his defeat, many student list supporters were quite worried about possible tensions and clashes with SNS supporters.
Sikosek, from Bikers with Students, reported his concerns a few minutes before the announcement:
 “When the dark came, the police were fortifying the center of the city, there were some incidents. We were thinking that he is going to come out and say that he won. Suddenly he said that he got defeated. We were all euphoric. It was a historical moment.”
Botoski, the agricultural student, said that students will continue to monitor their elected representatives:
 “We expect that the people we’ve chosen to represent the student list in parliament will do their job with care and dignity. We expect them to work on reforming the institutions and eradicate corruption from this country.”
In less than two years, Serbian students built a grassroots movement that won widespread public support and defeated a party that had been in power for 14 years. Through peaceful and democratic means, they turned public discontent into political change. The next challenge for the students and their supporters will be the presidential elections which will be held in December 2026.

Africa food security under threat due to Iran war, trade officials warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:42:18 UTC
06:42:18 KST

Africa food security under threat due to Iran war, trade officials warn
The US-Israel war on Iran is driving fuel and fertiliser costs across Africa, threatening food security, trade officials tell Al Jazeera.
Doha, Qatar – African countries are feeling the economic fallout from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with rising fuel and fertiliser prices threatening to drive up food costs, according to trade ministers from the region and the United Nations’ top trade official.
The crisis around the Strait of Hormuz due to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran needs to be resolved “sooner rather than later”, Luz Maria de la Mora, director of the Division on International Trade and Commodities at UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), told Al Jazeera at the World Investment Forum on Monday. She warned that soaring fertiliser prices could affect harvests next year.
“Prices of fertilisers have risen dramatically … so many countries have decided to reduce the use of fertilisers, which will have an effect next year in terms of crops,” she said.
“It may have an effect on availability of food and prices of food.”
The US-Israel war on Iran has highlighted the world’s heavy reliance on the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade previously passed.
Against this backdrop, Doha hosted UNCTAD’s World Investment Forum on October 25 and 26, bringing together heads of state, policymakers, CEOs and investors to discuss global investment and sustainable development.
The Strait of Hormuz’s disruption has rippled through African economies. In Zimbabwe, rising fuel and fertiliser prices are a critical concern in a country where more than 70 percent of the population depends on agriculture, Monica Mutsvangwa, the country’s minister of women affairs, community, small and medium enterprise development, told Al Jazeera.
Uganda, another heavily agrarian economy, has also been hit, with fuel prices more than doubling, Sanjay Tanna, the country’s minister of trade, industry and cooperatives, told Al Jazeera.
The impact extends beyond the immediate cost of energy. Rising oil prices have disrupted supply chains, with effects lasting longer than anticipated, according to de la Mora.
“The effects are lasting longer than we would have expected or would have wanted,” she said.
‘Friend to all, enemy to none’
The shock has also exposed differences in how African economies weather global disruption.
Uganda’s reliance on subsistence farming has helped cushion the impact, with domestic food production offering some protection from international market volatility, said Tanna.
But the country has not been insulated from financial pressures: its currency has lost 10 percent of its value against the US dollar, the minister said. The Ugandan shilling has steadily declined since mid-2026.
For Zimbabwe, the crisis has reinforced the importance of attracting investment while maintaining economic ties across geopolitical divides.
Amid the simmering trade war between the US and China, Harare considers itself a potential partner to investors from either side, Mutsvangwa said.
“We are a friend to all and an enemy to none,” she said.
“Money has no color … If we get an investor who comes into our country, follows the rules and regulations of the country, makes his money, and Zimbabwe develops, that’s what we want.”
The official pointed to Zimbabwe’s deposits of more than 60 critical minerals, including lithium and graphite, as well as its tourism potential.
Trade in an unequal system
But attracting foreign capital remains a challenge for developing economies, with investment concentrated in a relatively small number of countries.
That concentration is “very understandable”, de la Mora said, arguing that investors need confidence that their money will generate returns.
“Capital is risk averse. Capital needs to have certainty that its investment is going to yield returns and it’s going to come to fruition,” she said.
Governments can help build that confidence through transparent institutions, the rule of law and investment in infrastructure, including reliable electricity, energy supplies and digital connectivity, she added.
The question of whether the international trading system treats all countries equally prompted a more blunt assessment from Uganda’s trade minister.
“Of course not,” said Tanna. “The world cannot be equal … It’s unfair, but we believe that, within the space that we are in, we are in a good space.”
Uganda was well placed for the future, he argued, because it produces its own food – an advantage at a time when international supply chains are under pressure.
For both Uganda and the Republic of Congo, building resilient economies also means investing in younger generations.
The Republic of Congo’s Deputy Prime Minister for Coordination, Development Infrastructure and Land Planning, Jean-Jacques Bouya, said the country had aligned its national development plan, Vision 2063, with the African Union’s broader development ambitions.
Connectivity – through electricity, digital infrastructure and physical links – is central to that strategy, he told Al Jazeera.
The Republic of Congo also wants to expand local processing so that more value from its natural resources remains within the country.
“Africa can no longer be a reservoir of raw materials, and neither can Congo – a place where raw materials are extracted, taken elsewhere, processed and then sold back to us at a much higher price. We cannot go on like this,” Bouya said.

Berlin plans to buy ‘drone missiles’ from Kiev – media
Germany is preparing to buy a batch of low-cost cruise missiles from Ukraine to expand its long-range strike capabilities according to several media outlets, including the Financial Times and Bloomberg.
The deal could be finalized in the coming weeks, FT said, citing officials familiar with the matter. It would initially involve a small batch of missiles for testing by the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, early next year. If the tests prove successful, Berlin could reportedly place a follow-up order for several hundred missiles.
Dubbed ‘Bars’ – meaning snow leopard in both Russian and Ukrainian – the cruise missiles, sometimes referred to as “drone missiles” in Ukraine, are jet-powered weapons with a range of up to 1,000 kilometers and a payload of up to 105 kg.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars missiles in July 2026. Under that agreement, Berlin would finance production, with all the missiles produced being delivered to Ukraine.
The potential purchase comes amid a surge in German arms procurement as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government seeks to turn the Bundeswehr into Europe’s strongest conventional army, citing the threat of a potential conflict with Russia. Moscow has repeatedly dismissed such claims as “nonsense,” insisting that it has no intention of attacking any NATO member.
Armament drive
Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Berlin was planning to acquire “thousands of precision deep-strike weapons” from several European and American companies. One proposed contract with US firm Covenant for the delivery of thousands of ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles could be worth more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion), according to the report.
Berlin emerged as Kiev’s single biggest military donor after Washington drastically scaled back its aid under US President Donald Trump. Merz has prioritized military spending, including assistance to Kiev, despite acknowledging that Germany’s economy is in a “structural crisis.” His government amended the constitutional debt brake to fund the buildup and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion for defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Germany’s central bank has warned that the country is on course to record its largest budget deficit since reunification by 2028.
Cashing in on war?
Ukraine, in turn, appears to be actively seeking to cash in on weapons exports, including sales to its Western backers. In February, David Aloian, deputy secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council, told Reuters that the country expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue from it this year alone.
Kiev halted all weapons exports following the escalation of the conflict in 2022, but Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reversed that decision when he announced plans to open nearly a dozen weapons export centers across Europe in early 2026.
The plans have not stopped Kiev from seeking further financial and military assistance from Western nations. Last month, Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara suggested that Western donors supply Kiev with highly sought-after US-made Patriot interceptors from their own stockpiles, which would then be replenished with 1,000 missiles it plans to purchase with EU funds at some point in the future. In October, Zelensky himself lashed out at the country’s backers over their reluctance to cover a major budget shortfall.
Trump accused Ukraine in mid-October of selling American-supplied missiles on the black market. He also claimed that Kiev had failed to account for billions of dollars in American military and financial aid.
Ukrainian arms manufacturers have been implicated in some of the nation’s numerous corruption scandals. Fire Point – a defense contractor personally promoted by Zelensky during his visits to Western nations – was reportedly effectively owned by the Ukrainian leader’s longtime former business partner, Timur Mindich, known as ‘Zelensky’s wallet’ in Kiev. The businessman fled Ukraine last year after a major corruption investigation named him as one of its primary suspects.

More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed across the Occupied Palestinian Territory since Oct. 7, 2023, including at least 21,500 children and 11,000 women, Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar told the UN General Assembly.
Israeli forces continue to kill and injure civilians, including children, who approach or cross the Yellow Line in Gaza, the commission said in its latest report.
Despite a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
The situation in the occupied West Bank has also deteriorated sharply, with Israeli military operations and violence by Israeli occupiers forming part of what the commission described as a coordinated attack against Palestinians.
The report identifies the expansion of settlements, annexation of Palestinian territory and displacement of residents as objectives of these actions.
Israel has committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence, the commission said.
It also found that Palestinian children had been persecuted because of their age and that gender-based violence was being used to displace, subjugate and destabilize Palestinians.
The report also said Palestinian security forces had increasingly used unnecessary or disproportionate force against Palestinians in the West Bank since Oct. 7, 2023.
The Palestinian Authority has failed to conduct effective and impartial investigations into killings or provide remedies for victims and their families.

Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
22:15:21 CET
06:15:21 KST

By Jason Lange
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump’s public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week’s record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party’s majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a “generic ballot” question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.
That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS
Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.
It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.
The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.
Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.
The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters.
(Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone, Will Dunham and Sanjeev Miglani)

Why Africa needs Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:48:42 UTC
05:48:42 KST

Why Africa needs Russia
There were times, in the mid-to-late 20th century, when the Soviet Union was deeply engaged with Africa. It not only welcomed decolonization but actively promoted it and it supported national liberation movements from Algeria to Angola and from Guinea-Bissau to Zimbabwe. It assisted newly independent nations economically, helping them build factories, hospitals, and schools. A number of African countries became Moscow’s political allies and received arms and advisers to strengthen their security.
Having long since recovered from the collapse of the USSR, today’s Russia is again turning its attention to the African continent. Both Africa and Russia, however, are very different from what they were sixty or seventy years ago. Russia’s interest in Africa is largely an expression of its comeback as a world power. It also reflects Moscow’s recognition of African countries’ rapid economic and demographic growth, and their potential as an important component of the 21st-century multipolar world order, which encompasses not just states but civilizations.
Russia, however, is not looking to impose an ideology on its partners because it has no ideology to export in the first place. Nor does it go to Africa primarily in search of natural resources, which it possesses in abundance within its own borders. Russia doesn’t need military bases in Africa as part of its grand strategy, which remains firmly focused on its own neighborhood in Eurasia. Rather, it sees Africa as part of what it calls the Global Majority, the part of the world where it has partners with whom to cooperate, as opposed to the West, which has shut itself off from Russia.
What Russia has to offer could be of considerable interest to Africans, given Russia is among the world’s major producers of energy and food. Over the decades, it’s built a reputation as a reliable supplier of both, and neither global energy nor food security can be assured without Russia. Disruptions in these markets are the result of Western sanctions and other attempts to undermine Russia’s strength. One of Moscow’s major projects is the North-South Transport Corridor, which would link Russia, the world’s fourth-largest economy in purchasing power parity (PPP) terms, with India, the third-largest, via Iran. Once fully operational, this corridor would also provide Russia with a gateway to East Africa.
Russia has already established itself as a security provider for African countries facing serious challenges. Under the banner of the Africa Corps, Russian military advisers and specialists are working in several West African countries belonging to the Alliance of Sahel States (Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso), as well as in the Central African Republic. They have managed to thwart a number of large-scale coup attempts and military offensives masterminded and supported from abroad. Such security assistance is essential to upholding the sovereignty of nations that have requested it.
Russia, of course, is much more than a military power. Among other things, it is a leader in digitalization. Moscow is one of the world’s most advanced capitals in this field. Russia is ready to share its expertise in establishing and improving electronic government services. Since Soviet times, Russian scientists have conducted pioneering research into deadly viruses and vaccines to combat them. A vaccine against Ebola was developed in 2019 by the Russian research institute Vector, located in Siberia, while the Sputnik V vaccine, developed against COVID-19, proved highly effective in fighting the pandemic.
In 1960, Peoples’ Friendship University was founded in Moscow for international students. The following year, it was named after Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the independent Congo (formerly Belgian Congo). At present, some 35,000 young Africans study at Russian universities, mostly majoring in medicine, energy, and engineering – fields in which Russian universities have historically been particularly strong.
To date, three African countries – South Africa, Egypt, and Ethiopia – are full members of the 10-member BRICS grouping. This format offers a novel, non-hierarchical and genuinely consensus-based approach to addressing economic, financial, environmental, educational, and other global issues. The BRICS way of doing business supports sovereignty and rejects diktat. Russia, which helped initiate the formation of BRICS just over two decades ago, works to ensure that the group remains true to its founding principles.
Russia has never been a colonial power in Africa and has never attempted to plunder its resources. It regards Africans as partners and African civilization as an equal in the emerging world order. This week’s Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow will bring the two even closer.

20:44:44 UTC
05:44:44 KST

It had looked like goodnight Vienna for Alex de Minaur as he trailed Tomas Machac by a set, a break and 0-30 on his own misfiring serve.
Machac, a top 20 player last year, was fizzing winners onto the lines and Australia's number one seemed to have no answer to his excellence.
The Czech was six points from victory and de Minaur's chances of making the end-of-season ATP Finals were receding rapidly as a first-round exit loomed in the Austrian capital.
But Demon never quits. He won the next four points to hold, then broke Machac in a three-deuce game. He then survived a break point on his next service game, which lasted nearly nine minutes, then broke again to take the set.
Machac broke immediately in the third set but it was a last hurrah. De Minaur took the next five games before completing a near-two-hour 1-6, 6-4, 6-3 win with an ace.
De Minaur greeted Monday's victory with a roar of delight, relief and vindication. The 27-year-old has made a career out of comebacks but few have been such a turnaround as this.
"For three-quarters of that match it was very tough for me," he said. "I have dug deep, found a way to get a crucial break when I needed it, and the momentum changed."
Referring to his recent run to the final in Beijing, and a narrow quarterfinal loss to Alexander Zverev in Shanghai, he added: "The last couple of tournaments I've learned a lot about myself and was able to draw on those situations and come out with some big serves when I needed it."
De Minaur began Vienna's ATP 500 event tenth in the standings for the season's Turin finale and, with Jannik Sinner's competitive season over, needs to be in the top nine to qualify.

Poland says it will never accept return to ‘business as usual’ with Russia on energy dependence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:29:05 UTC
05:29:05 KST

Jo Harper
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said Monday that Poland would never accept a return to “business as usual” with Russia, including renewed dependence on Russian gas and raw materials, during the Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw.
The remarks came as the European Union continued to unwind its dependence on Russian energy following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. EU member states have sharply reduced imports of Russian pipeline gas since 2022 and have agreed to phase out the remaining supplies over the coming years as part of a broader effort to reduce Moscow’s energy leverage over Europe.
Poland has been among the strongest advocates of ending Russian energy imports and had already spent years diversifying its supply before the full-scale invasion. It has expanded liquefied natural gas imports through the Swinoujscie terminal and receives Norwegian gas through the Baltic Pipe, which began operating in 2022. Warsaw has repeatedly argued that dependence on Russian hydrocarbons created both economic and security risks for Europe.
Domanski’s comments came as Poland and Germany pledged closer economic and industrial cooperation at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum. The two countries are major trading partners, but Warsaw and Berlin have often differed over energy policy and how far Europe should maintain economic links with Russia.
The issue has also acquired a sharper political edge in Germany as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has called for restoring Russian oil and gas imports and reopening Nord Stream, arguing that cheap Russian energy is essential to German industry. AfD leader Alice Weidel has said she wants to rebuild German-Russian economic ties.

Ukraine’s Satellite Disruption Exposes a Central Risk of Modern Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:28:45 UTC
05:28:45 KST

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed over the weekend that the Ukrainian military had “violated” the terms of service for Starlink, the company’s commercial satellite internet network, which has become central to the country’s defense against Russia. Musk said SpaceX had restricted Starlink to prevent that alleged misuse. Ukrainian officials disputed his claim. His allegation came after over a week of uncertainty about why the services had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials reported on Oct. 14 that restrictions affecting SpaceX’s satellite communications were disrupting drone operations, blocking a key line of defense amid daily Russian air attacks. Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for frontline communications, drone capabilities, and reconnaissance; the throttled connection ultimately led to the cancellation of several missions, officials said.
The restrictions also affected Starshield, a military-grade satellite communications service that uses Starlink technology but is supplied through U.S. government contracts.
Over a week after the disruption began, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that both services had been fully restored. It reported that connections remained stable even when terminals were moving at speeds above 400 km/h.
At the time, the cause for the interruption had not yet been clarified, but Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara emphasized the importance of a strong and stable connection, calling it “vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications.”
Musk maintains that the United States government controls changes to Starshield, leaving questions about who authorized its restrictions—and why.
U.S. President Donald Trump declined to identify those involved in the decision, while a Reuters report from Oct. 15 cited multiple officials who said the order came from inside the White House. The sources did not identify who authorized or implemented the restrictions, but a senior U.S. official denied that it was Trump, the report said.
Experts say that the disruptions expose a growing vulnerability in modern warfare: military reliance on a single private technology supplier.
The company that controls the technology can ultimately wield significant influence over military operations, leaving governments dependent on decisions made by executives and billionaire owners outside traditional diplomatic channels, experts warn.
Why U.S. control of Starshield matters for Ukraine
Ukraine’s access to satellite communications depends on decisions made in Washington as well as at SpaceX. That leaves Kyiv navigating both a private supplier’s restrictions and a fraught relationship with the Trump Administration.
In recent weeks, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising global fuel prices and called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop those attacks—despite the fact that experts have primarily attributed the price surge to the U.S. war with Iran.
Trump said on Oct. 15 that Zelensky was “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin and on Oct. 19 suggested that it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”
Alex Crowther, an adjunct professor at Florida International University’s Jack D. Gordon Institute for Public Policy, says the Starshield dispute goes beyond Trump’s souring relationship with Zelensky to a more basic question: Who has the authority to restrict Ukraine’s access?
“Usually when [a foreign entity] signs a contract with an American company, it says who has the capability to turn this stuff on and off, and the circumstances under which they can turn it on and off,” Crowther says, questioning who has that authority over the services Ukraine relies upon. “Is it Starlink, which is private, or is it Starshield, which is an American government contract? Is it Musk? Is it Hegseth? Is it Trump?”
“Nobody knows the rules right now,” he says.
Lance Hunter, a professor of political science at Augusta University, tells TIME that this dispute exposes the potential issues of having three different actors—the Trump Administration, SpaceX, and Ukraine—with potentially incompatible priorities.
How dependence on SpaceX limits Ukraine’s military autonomy
Hunter says that what is unfolding in Ukraine underscores warfare’s growing dependence on digital technology. Beyond traditional “tanks, bombs, planes,” he says that includes factors like artificial intelligence, drones, and navigation jamming.
Reliance on ongoing technology services creates a different relationship from a traditional arms purchase, Hunter says.
He points to traditional arms deals in which a private company sells a government a set amount of missiles or interceptors.
“Let's say you purchase a piece of weaponry or vehicle or any type of object that helps you in the conflict: You own it at that point. You have control over it,” Hunter tells TIME.
The relationship between Ukraine and SpaceX, however, is different; purchasing the technology does not guarantee operational sovereignty.
“Ukraine has a lot of transmitters which interface with Starshield and Starlink, and they're very much dependent on SpaceX as far as allowing them to use those when they need to,” Hunter continues. “There's not just a one-time dependence buying the technology; it's continual now.”
That gives the company more “influence and leverage” over conflicts than it has before, he adds.
It shifts the way that countries like Ukraine need to think about who they are willing to work with and how they weigh the potential costs.
Why Ukraine cannot easily replace Starlink and Starshield
In a perfect world, Hunter says, Ukraine would diversify its technology suppliers to decrease reliance on Starlink.
The country has already been expanding its domestic weapons production, including interceptor drones. But it remains dependent on foreign suppliers for critical air-defense weapons like the U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles.
That dependence has left it vulnerable to shortages and delays. On Oct. 26, Zelensky said Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve supplies of missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air-defense systems.
But replicating satellite communications networks presents a different challenge. Starlink technology is not something a government can easily reproduce domestically, Hunter says, and few providers worldwide offer comparable capabilities.
“Starlink has a monopoly on that technology to a degree, as far as the speed, the availability, the flexibility,” he says. “It's not like they can just flip a switch and diversify that technology. It takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of resources. It takes a lot of effort, and also in Europe we don't see that same level of technology with some of the European countries and also with some of the private companies.”
In the end, he says that Ukraine is stuck between “a rock and a hard place” as the country tries to negotiate its relationships with the Trump Administration and, separately, with Musk.
“You're reliant on the politics of those bodies all matching up,” he says of Ukraine. “All of a sudden, you kind of lose that autonomy.”
“If they really push back against the U.S. government or SpaceX, they have the potential of receiving less of the technology and being cut off to a greater extent,” he adds. “But if they don't really push at all and advocate for their interest as well, then they could be in a weaker position as far as having leverage exerted over them.”
Why Ukraine disputes Musk’s Starlink claims
In a social media post on Oct. 24, Musk said that SpaceX had restricted Starlink access deliberately because Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in one post. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be.”
Musk explained that Starlink continues to be “critical to the defense of Ukraine,” but that it could not be used for offensive military operations.
Ukrainian officials promptly disputed Musk’s claims.
Defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote in a Telegram post that operational and speed restrictions are in place that make it “physically impossible” for the military to use Starlink for medium- or deep-range offensive strikes.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine,” he wrote. “Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia.”

Conflict-related sexual violence more than doubles as women's share of civilian deaths rises: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:27:00 UTC
05:27:00 KST

Diyar Guldogan
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Women and girls are facing increasingly deadly consequences of armed conflict, with their share of civilian deaths doubling since 2021 and verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence rising sharply, UN Women officials warned Monday.
Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda, UN Women's deputy executive director for normative support, UN system coordination and programme results, told reporters that women and girls were bearing a growing share of the human cost of wars that she described as "preventable."
More than 37,000 civilians were killed in armed conflicts in 2025, with women and girls accounting for one in four deaths, twice their share in 2021, Gumbonzvanda said.
She added that at least 25 women and girls were killed every day, while more than 750 million lived within 50 kilometers (31 miles) of an armed conflict.
"The conflicts that have disappeared from our screens, but not from the lives of women and girls enduring them. And for women and girls who survive, the burden is relentless," she said.
Gumbonzvanda also warned of a sharp increase in conflict-related sexual violence, saying the UN verified 9,788 cases in 2025, more than double the number recorded in 2024 and nearly four times the figure reported in 2022.
"Women are paying the price of war," she said.
Gumbonzvanda urged governments and the international community to end armed conflicts, protect civilians, uphold international law and hold perpetrators of abuses accountable.
She also called for women to be included as decision-makers in all peace negotiations and for greater funding for women-led organizations working to save lives and build peace.
 
Sarah Hendriks, director of the Policy, Programme and Intergovernmental Division at UN Women, warned that the growing number of conflicts worldwide was worsening conditions for women and girls.
More than 185 conflicts were recorded globally in 2025, including 65 state-based conflicts, Hendriks said.
"Wars are multiplying; the ways that wars are fought are changing, and it is women and girls who are paying the price," she added.

Rubio says Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure must be replaced before a vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
21:26:01 CET
05:26:01 KST

By Simon Lewis and Matt Spetalnick
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure was designed to rig elections and so must be quickly replaced before a valid election can be held.
Rubio spoke to reporters by phone a day after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela for the first time since the US captured the country’s then-President Nicolas Maduro in January and took him to New York for trial.
The US believes that talks currently underway between the interim government in Caracas and opposition politicians are expected to see a new supreme judicial tribunal in place by the end of this year and a new electoral council shortly thereafter, a senior US State Department official said earlier.
“I think we’re making real progress in that regard,” said Rubio, who has acted as US President Donald Trump’s point person on Venezuela. “But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing a great harm to Venezuela.”
Maduro’s government had set up the country’s electoral infrastructure to rig elections so must be quickly changed, Rubio added.
But Rubio stopped short of giving a target date for elections. Machado has said elections should be held by mid-2027, though Trump has previously said he did not believe Venezuela was ready for a nationwide vote.
Machado’s return to Venezuela after several failed attempts risks straining her ties with Trump’s administration.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Machado, who was prevented from challenging Maduro for the presidency in 2024, had been out of the country for 10 months and spent the previous year in hiding following the disputed election.
Washington has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but has praised acting President Delcy Rodriguez and supports a negotiation process between the Rodriguez government and opposition groups that do not include Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement.
Rubio said the only time he had “discouraged” Machado from going back to Venezuela was in the immediate aftermath of devastating earthquakes in the summer, because the country was grappling with a humanitarian crisis.
But Rubio said that weeks ago the US told Venezuela’s interim authorities that Machado “belongs in her country” and “should be allowed to return unperturbed,” and the government had agreed.
Asked about Machado’s criticism of an oil deal that Trump had struck with the interim rulers, Rubio insisted that the agreement was a good one for both countries but that she had a right to express her opinion on the matter.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Rodriguez, a former deputy to Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country.
But some critics have accused Trump of a neo-colonialist approach to Venezuela aimed at exploiting its natural resources.
A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Machado’s political movement.
(Reporting by Matt Spetalnick, Simon Lewis and Christian Martinez; Editing by Nick Zieminski and Daniel Wallis)

The political movement "Student List," which won Serbia's parliamentary elections on October 25, advocates halting arms exports to war zones, including Ukraine, and also does not plan to join the European Union's sanctions against Russia. Reuters reports this, UNN writes.
Details
As the publication notes, the "Student List" will have to navigate a complex energy and foreign-policy context in relations with Serbia's traditional ally—Russia.
In particular, party representatives said they did not intend to join the EU or impose sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The new government will have to rely on an exemption from U.S. sanctions to maintain oil imports while the sale of Russia's stake in the energy company NIS, which operates Serbia's only oil refinery, to the Hungarian company MOL is being finalized.
The article notes that the Russian company "Gazprom" is Serbia's largest gas supplier. It delivers about 2.2 billion cubic meters per year at prices below market rates. The "Student List" party stated that this energy dependence is not a geopolitical choice but an acute economic dependence.
In addition, leading candidates from the "Student List" stated that the future government would halt all arms exports from Serbia to areas of military conflict, including sales to Western intermediaries who transfer weapons to Ukraine.

Gyurov Accuses Radev of Campaigning for Yotova Through Government Channels

Bulgaria's PM Congratulates Serbia’s Student List on Election Victory
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev congratulated Serbian citizens on their participation in the democratic process and the “Student List” on its election victory
Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov accused Prime Minister Rumen Radev of using the Council of Ministers’ official channels to promote Iliana Yotova and attack her political opponents, warning against the use of state institutions for election campaigning.
“Mr. Radev, you hold an absolute majority and bear full responsibility. Leave the choice to the citizens,” Gyurov said in response to messages disseminated through the government’s official channels in support of Yotova.
Gyurov called the incident a dangerous blurring of the boundaries between state authority and the election campaign. He said the problem was not the prime minister’s political position itself, but its promotion through an institution financed by all Bulgarian citizens.
“This is not the opinion of a commentator, nor is it a speech by a party leader in a public square. This is the official voice of the state, funded by the money of all taxpayers - including those who do not support the current government,” Gyurov said.
He noted that the Council of Ministers controls the state budget, the administration and the executive branch, arguing that this authority carries a particular obligation to prevent public resources from being used to benefit a single candidate.
“The Council of Ministers is not an election campaign headquarters. The state is not the property of a political party. And no Bulgarian citizen should be cast as an adversary simply because they vote differently,” the presidential candidate said.
Gyurov defended the right of every citizen to choose politically without being subjected to labels or division. He argued that people who back another candidate are not enemies but equal citizens entitled to the same treatment by the state.
“Yesterday, one in three voters chose us. These people are not some hysterical mob. They are teachers, doctors, entrepreneurs, pensioners, and young families. They are Bulgaria. And I will not accept anyone dividing them into 'ours' and 'yours.'” Gyurov said, adding that he would take the same position if a prime minister used official state channels to campaign for him.
He insisted that election rules must apply equally to everyone, including those in power, or they would have no meaning.
Gyurov also opposed efforts to portray the presidential election as a division between citizens deemed “the right kind” and “the wrong kind.” He said all sides wanted peace and framed the central question as whether those in government would serve the public or use state resources to influence voters.
According to Gyurov, one of the presidency’s main roles is to act as an independent check on concentrated power and defend the rules regardless of who governs.
“I want a president who stands between those in power and the citizens. Someone who upholds the rules even when it is inconvenient for the powerful. Someone who does not resort to intimidation or division, but instead demands that the institutions do their jobs. Bulgaria needs a state that its citizens can trust,” he said.
“Mr. Radev, govern. That is your responsibility. The choice of a president belongs to the Bulgarian citizens,” Gyurov concluded.
