A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:07:00 UTC
05:07:00 KST

A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
October 26, 2026
Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.
"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.
Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.
"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.
Controversial ban
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.
"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."
Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.
The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."
A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.
Bad omen?
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?
Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.
Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.
All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.
The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers
Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.
Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.
In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.
Gender stereotypes
"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."
The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.
"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."
But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"

The rotational force is aimed at helping Australia prepare to operate its own nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines down the track.

USS Colorado completed a six-month deployment to waters off Europe in December 2023.

Big mining boss brought in to fix Australia’s Defence buying system
The way Australia buys weapons and defence gear is getting a major overhaul, with former Rio Tinto chief Kellie Parker hired to run the country's new Defence Delivery Agency.
Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy will announce today that Parker will become the new National Armaments Director — effectively making her Australia's chief weapons buyer.
For decades, defence procurement has been bogged down by massive budget blowouts and severe delays. To fix this, the Albanese government is transforming its purchasing division into an independent agency — known as the Defence Delivery Agency — starting July 2027.
By hiring a veteran mining executive accustomed to delivering complex, multi-billion-dollar infrastructure under strict commercial pressures, the government is hoping to inject real-world business discipline into the ADF.
Parker takes on the role in November 2026 before the agency goes fully live in July 2027.
Key Event
NACC holds off on decision over controversial grant scheme inquiry
The NACC says it has not ruled out an investigation into a contentious government grant scheme that saw a golf club in the PM's electorate get $6 million dollars, but is putting any decision on hold until other parliamentary inquiries into the program conclude.
Appearing before Senate estimates, National Anti-Corruption Commission acting commissioner Kylie Kilgour confirmed the agency had received referrals regarding the $560 million Local Community Infrastructure program.
The scheme has faced intense scrutiny after analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity found it heavily favoured Labor electorates.
Kilgour said the scheme had "piqued" her interest but ultimately the watchdog would wait on the outcomes of a parliamentary inquiry and a potential audit by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) before taking further action.
"If you've got another integrity agency conducting a process, it's not necessarily appropriate for us to come in," Kilgour noted, adding that the NACC was "not there yet" in determining whether it holds statutory jurisdiction.
During the hearing, Kilgour also paid tribute to independent MP Helen Haines — a prominent critic of the grant scheme and a key architect of the NACC. She remains in hospital after being attacked outside her electorate office last week.
Key Event
Snowy 2.0 boss defends project progress since 2023 reset
Snowy Hydro made a late appearance at yesterday's Senate estimates, where company representatives were grilled over the latest cost blowout for Australia's biggest renewable energy project.
It was revealed last week that the Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro project would cost $22 billion-$25 billion and be delayed another year.
The cost has doubled since a 2023 project reset, where Snowy Hydro and the contractor building the project moved to a revised contract; which includes penalties for poor performance relating to cost and schedule.
Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes says the increase in cost was mainly due to flaws in the initial design and that there had been significant progress since the new contract model was adopted.
"In 2023, the advice of myself and the Snowy board … was to reset this contract to an ITC model, get progress moving again and we saw progress did double over that period," he said.
Barnes also said the federal government would need to contribute a "substantial proportion" of the extra $10b required to complete the project but that discussions around exactly how much were still underway.
New election funding system ready to go for 2027
The new election funding regime previously had its start date delayed because the Australian Electoral Commission said getting it up and running was a complicated task.
And little wonder: it's a whole new system, with donations to be disclosed in close to real time, and with caps now to apply to candidates, parties and donors.
But in what AEC commissioner Jeff Pope says is a "near miracle", the complicated technical system to make all of that work is now ready to roll from its mooted start date of January 1, 2027.
The next step will be to work with political parties and candidates to make sure they understand how to use the new system. Liberal senator James McGrath, a keen follower of electoral matters, sounds doubtful that it will all be so seamless. But in theory at least, it should be full steam ahead.
Nine politicians to get electorate office security upgrades after Haines attack
The AFP held a security briefing for politicians just two days after the attack on independent MP Helen Haines, and it seems tangible outcomes are already afoot.
Nine electorate offices are now having security concerns actioned after they were raised last week, according to the Department of Finance.
In a late-night Senate estimates hearing, Finance secretary Matt Yannopoulos explains how the system works.
The AFP handles threat assessments and security details, Home Affairs does home security for those eligible, and Finance handles offices and transport. All three co-ordinate and share information.
"Where there's an ask for something to be upgraded, we go about that as quickly as possible, and indeed from the discussions that occurred last week there are nine different offices that are raised and we are dealing with those," Yannopoulos tells the committee.

Trump says, without citing evidence, that Brazil election looks 'rigged'

Trump says Brazil election looked ‘rigged’, defeated Bolsonaro’s party recognises Lula win
- Trump said Lula’s Brazil win “looked like another rigged election”, but Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party later said it recognised the result and wanted the issues clarified.
- Lula won by over 4 million votes, and the extra two hours added by the Supreme Court brought fewer than 35,000 votes, making the result hard to overturn.
- Lula’s victory shook markets, with the real falling 8.1% and stocks dropping sharply, while he now faces a Congress full of Bolsonaro allies.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - United States President Donald Trump said on Oct 26 that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote “looked like another rigged election”, although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in the presidential election on Oct 25, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Oct 26, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Oct 26 he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded”.
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
Markets roiled by Lula win
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right. REUTERS

Trump offers $1 million for tipoffs that lead to voter fraud convictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:05:44 UTC
05:05:44 KST

Trump dangles US$1 million reward for reporting voter fraud
Tyler Pager
WASHINGTON – As US President Donald Trump has implored voters to support Republicans in November’s midterm elections, he has frequently dangled financial incentives and issued unfounded warnings about voter fraud.
On Oct 26, he married those two passions.
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid US$1 million (S$1.28 million) upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Trump wrote on social media.
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about where the money would come from for the ostensible rewards or how Americans are supposed to report fraud accusations.
The announcement reflected another step in Trump’s gathering campaign to use the powers of his office to influence the outcome of the midterms.
For years, the President has attacked the integrity of US elections, and in his second term, his administration has tried to assert more control over the voting process, which is overseen by states.
Earlier in October, Trump moved to pre-emptively challenge the certification of Alaska’s Senate election if the Republican candidate loses.
The President and his Justice Department have also leaned on expansive but unsupported claims of voter fraud in trying to force states like California to set aside thousands of mail ballots they claim were sent to non-citizens.
At the same time, Trump has stepped up the financial incentives for voters as Republicans face increasingly steep odds of keeping control of Congress.
A national poll from The New York Times and Siena University found Trump’s approval rating hit a new low in October, with just 36% of likely voters saying they approved of his job performance.
Likely voters said they preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points in their congressional districts.
Over the past two months, Trump has signed pardons at campaign rallies, sent US$500 Obamacare “refund” checks and issued US$90 direct deposits to seniors to offset Medicare premiums.
The central reward, though, is the so-called “Trump Dividend”, which Trump announced at the Republican gathering he insisted his party throw in September in Dallas.
Trump has promised US$5,000 for every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, a proposal that has drawn bipartisan criticism and would cost more than US$1 trillion. It would also likely require congressional approval.
In October, Trump announced a new US$25 million whistleblower incentive programme to provide information to combat fraud.
There are already multiple avenues for reporting fraud to the federal government, and the new programme raised concerns because Trump said he would personally determine who received the money. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:05:24 UTC
05:05:24 KST

Serbia will not impose Russia sanctions – election winner’s rep to RT
Serbia will maintain its longstanding ties with Russia and will not impose sanctions on Moscow despite EU pressure, a representative of the winning Student List movement has told RT Balkan.
The student-led opposition secured 52.73% of the vote in Sunday’s parliamentary election, according to the latest preliminary results, defeating the coalition of former President Aleksandar Vucic. He conceded defeat but warned that Belgrade could abandon its resistance to EU pressure and sanction Russia within months.
The movement emerged from nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Speaking on Monday, Jovo Bakic, a university professor and Student List representative, said: “We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector.”
“There will be no changes in that regard,” he added.
Recalling the harsh UN sanctions against Yugoslavia in the 1990s, when Serbia was one of its constituent republics, Bakic said restrictions imposed by “small Serbia” would have little effect on Russia but would be “symbolically very bad” for Belgrade.
🇷🇸 Jovo Bakić za RT Balkan: Studentska lista neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji ▪️Predstavnik "Studentske liste", profesor Jovo Bakić ponovio je da nova vlada Srbije neće uvoditi sankcije Rusiji, uprkos tvrdnjama bivšeg predsednika Aleksandra Vučića da će se to dogoditi za nekoliko meseci. "Mi Rusiju poštujemo i kao veliku silu i kao našu istorijski važnu partnerku i u mnogim slučajevima zaštitnicu. Tu (u spoljnoj politici zemlje) neće biti nikakvih promena", izjavio je Bakić gostujući u emisiji "Srbija bira" na TV RT Balkan.
— RT Balkan (@rtbalkan) October 26, 2026
Under Vucic, Serbia resisted EU demands to adopt the bloc’s restrictions on Russia over the Ukraine conflict, despite pursuing EU membership. The Student List campaigned primarily on domestic reforms, leaving several contentious foreign policy questions unaddressed.
According to Reuters, leading candidates of the victorious movement have said the incoming government would halt arms exports to conflict zones, including sales to Western intermediaries that subsequently supply weapons to Ukraine.
Vucic previously said European buyers could decide how to use Serbian ammunition, including whether to send it to Ukraine, although Belgrade has denied supplying Kiev directly.
Energy ties present another major issue for Serbia’s incoming government. Russia remains the country’s dominant gas supplier, accounting for roughly three-quarters of its needs. In March, Vucic said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to maintain deliveries on favorable terms, at prices far below those in most of Europe. The agreement was subsequently prolonged through the end of 2026.
Serbia also faces uncertainty over its oil supplies due to US sanctions on NIS, the majority Russian-owned energy company that runs the country’s only oil refinery. Hungarian energy group MOL is seeking to acquire the Russian stake, while the current US waiver allowing NIS to continue business expires on October 30. The company has requested another extension to avoid disruptions to fuel supplies.
Unlike Serbia, the EU has sought to phase out Russian fossil fuel imports and secure alternative suppliers since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Asked about pressure to abandon Russian energy supplies, Bakic said: “We are not here to satisfy foreigners, but to act in our national interest.”
The Kremlin said on Monday that it hoped to maintain mutually beneficial relations with Serbia. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic’s contribution to bilateral ties and added “As you know, it takes two to tango.”

SC restores Karnataka land, says government can acquire only for public purpose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:01:59 UTC
05:01:59 KST

NEW DELHI: Holding that govt can acquire land from citizens only for public purpose and not for the benefit of some person or organisation, Supreme Court Monday quashed a 1988 acquisition of about 59 acres of land near Bengaluru by Karnataka govt for a cooperative housing society and restored the land to its owners after 38 years.
A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran held that the whole process of land acquisition is indicating “the fraud played on unsuspecting citizens”. It said that illegal acquisitions were made through fraud and undue influence and directed the state govt to pay Rs 50,000 to all litigant landowners who had challenged the process.
“Condemnation of privately owned land for public purpose can only be with authority of law and with just compensation being paid. That such authority of law can be exercised only for public purpose is without cavil, with just compensation being an ancillary right, which does not by itself justify an acquisition. However just the compensation be, if the authority of law is lacking or the public purpose is absent, there can be no eminent domain exercised,” the court said.
SC upheld the single-bench HC order,which said that it was at the instigation of middlemen that the state employed its machinery to acquire land for the society.

Age pensioners who want to keep working say system punishes them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:45:46 UTC
04:45:46 KST

Age pensioners say system punishes them for wanting to keep working
In short:
Australians who receive the age pension face strict income limits before the pension is reduced.
Some pensioners want to keep working for social, health and economic reasons.
Advocates and industry groups are supportive of relaxing some of the rules to unlock older Australians' participation in the workforce.
As Australia's population ages, it is expected more people will want to continue working beyond retirement age, whether for financial reasons or otherwise.
It has prompted renewed calls from advocates and industry groups to relax the rules around working on the age pension, which some say unfairly punishes them.
South-east Queensland 71-year-old Peter Gibney would go as far as to say the system is stacked against him and his wife continuing to work.
Having worked in retail for decades, he is not interested in slowing down.
"There's none of this airy, fairy stuff ... it's down on the ground dealing with customers and staff, training staff and getting the load done," he said.
Despite his enthusiasm for his job, Mr Gibney feels he is being unfairly punished. Both he and his wife, who works as a teacher's aide, receive part age pensions.
However, the more they work, the more of their age pensions they lose.
Without large superannuation balances and with a mortgage, they cannot afford to stop work.
Bringing in some extra money gives them additional financial security.
"It is freedom, to a degree. The downside is that it's stacked against us doing those things," Mr Gibney said.
Complex rules around pension and work
A Department of Social Services spokesperson said the rules around working on the age pension mean a single pensioner with no other income can earn up to $526 a fortnight before the pension begins to reduce.
That is because of a system called the work bonus, which disregards the first $300 of work income a fortnight from the income test.
A couple with no other income can earn a combined $996 a fortnight if both are eligible for the work bonus.
Council on the Ageing (COTA) Australia chief executive Patricia Sparrow has called for that system to be "simplified".
The Department of Social Services said age pensioners who worked kept more of their age pension now than four years ago.
A department spokesperson said the government was committed to reviewing the rate of social services payments in each budget.
There are overseas examples to look to. New Zealand has a system in which the pension (NZ Super) is paid on a universal rate.
Mr Gibney believes "the ideal situation would be the old age pension is for achieving an age ... it's payback for 40, 50 years of paying taxes".
More older Australians expected to keep working
According to COTA's latest State Of The Older Nation report, about 15 per cent of Australians aged over 67 continue to work, up from 11 per cent in 2021.
Almost 25 per cent are not opposed to returning to work in some capacity.
As the population ages, and more people begin to retire with mortgages or without a partner, those numbers are expected to rise.
"We're really urging government to look at the things we need to do right across the system to make sure that older people can continue to support themselves, contribute to the community," Ms Sparrow said.
Ms Sparrow said one of the main barriers keeping older Australians out of work was age discrimination, an issue she said needed to be addressed to ensure fair workforce participation.
Industry groups also want to unlock an older workforce to help boost productivity.
Productivity benefits touted
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said more needed to be done to encourage older Australians who wanted to continue to work without facing a "significant" penalty.
ACCI advocates for a "more flexible" system and a doubling of the work bonus to $600 a fortnight.
"[Older Australians] have experience. They have the skills. That's important," he said.
"There's a huge benefit for the economy if they want to continue in the workforce."
Mr McKellar said even part-time work could help alleviate productivity challenges in the economy, particularly in sectors that continued to struggle for staff.
And the benefits for people like the Gibneys go beyond the economic.
Mr Gibney believes it is important to stay connected to the community for the mental health and social benefits, and for him and his wife to continue to have separate interests.

Space Force Wants Cislunar Kit Ready to Launch by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:45:38 UTC
04:45:38 KST

For years now, Space Force officials have said the service is getting serious about defining its role and crafting an architecture for future cislunar capabilities. Now, the Space Force is taking steps to realize that vision, asking industry to rapidly invest and develop satellites and software that could be ready for operations as soon as 2029.
Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy—the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for advanced programs—said he’s seen the Pentagon’s posture toward cislunar operations and planning efforts change drastically over the past year.
“There was no talk of cislunar, and basically I was told, ‘Don’t talk about cislunar, and stop getting into it,’” Purdy said Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s Space Industry Days conference.
Now, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine, and even a December 2025 executive order from President Donald Trump are emphasizing the importance of cislunar operations and advocating for more investment. The shift is in part linked to China’s lunar ambitions, Purdy said. Beijing has a cislunar roadmap of its own and has already landed several uncrewed spacecraft on the lunar surface. Now, it plans to launch a crewed Moon mission by 2030.
“I’ve got the Secretary of War and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs full on stating in public: ‘This is a warfighting domain,’” Purdy said, using the department’s secondary name. “And so, I would ask you all, please jump on my cislunar bandwagon because I need some more friends here, along with our deep, passionate crew that have been working on this for years.”
Cislunar space is the region beyond geosynchronous orbit extending to the moon and even farther to cover areas influenced by Earth and the moon’s gravity—hundreds of thousands of kilometers in distance and 1,728 times the volume of space contained within geosynchronous orbit. Purdy described the region as “painful” for satellite operations, as it is further from Earth and navigation is more of a challenge.
To date, much of the U.S. government’s cislunar planning and operations have centered on NASA and its plan to return astronauts to the moon through the Artemis program. The Defense Department has pursued research programs aimed at better understanding the vast expanse of cislunar space—including the Air Force Research Lab’s Oracle program, which plans to launch several cislunar space domain awareness satellites in the coming years. But the Space Force hasn’t dedicated much planning, funding, or personnel to those efforts.
That may be about to change. In April, the Space Force set up a new Cislunar Coordination Office, housed within Purdy’s portfolio and tasked with crafting a roadmap for cislunar technology and a future space architecture. Since then, that office – led by Jaime Stearns—has refined that roadmap and crafted strategies for various mission areas, like space domain awareness, communications, and lunar navigation.
The CCO has also drafted a list of high-priority but unfunded requirements, which Purdy said includes relatively low-dollar “ticky-tacky” efforts that can help the Space Force make real progress in this area.
The service is also pursuing multiple technology development and rapid fielding efforts, Purdy said. In partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory and the innovation arm SpaceWERX, it plans to launch an industry challenge called Lunar Prime to get after some of its more nascent technology and research needs. The effort has $30 million in funding and is targeting flight demonstrations within two years of contract award.
The Space Force also has two requests for information it plans to release “imminently,” Purdy said. The first will call for existing commercial technology that can be ready to launch by 2029.
“We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-developmental solutions, hardware with actual relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and ground systems,” Purdy said. “This isn’t a four- or five-year science project. This is about getting capability out soon.”
The second request is for AI and autonomous processing capabilities for spacecraft operating in cislunar space. The goal is to have “a fully autonomous system out there at cislunar that’s able to handle all its hardware faults, all its processing, all the sensor activities,” Purdy said.

Russia has accused Ukraine of intensifying attacks on the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and the nearby city of Enerhodar.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova on Monday criticised international organisations, particularly the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), for what she described as a restrained response to Kiev’s “provocative actions”.
“We are compelled to note that international bodies, first and foremost the IAEA, have responded with great restraint to Kiev’s provocative actions,” she said, accusing them of failing to explicitly identify Ukraine as responsible.
Zakharova claimed that Ukrainian forces had targeted civilian facilities earlier in the week, including an art school and a fire and rescue station operated by Russia’s Emergencies Ministry.
“Unable to strike the ZNPP directly, the Kiev regime continues its futile attempts to destabilise the plant’s operations by intimidating its personnel,” she said, alleging that Kiev sought to increase casualties and create a radiation-contaminated zone in the Zaporizhzhia region.
She also criticised Western support for Ukraine, saying it was creating radiological risks in Europe and endangering its own citizens.
Zakharova said Moscow was informing the international community about Ukrainian attacks and taking measures to protect the plant, its personnel and Enerhodar residents.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns about a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kiev frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility in south-eastern Ukraine.
IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant since September 1 2022. Russia has controlled the facility since March 2022.

Israel votes Tuesday in closely contested election as Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:43:54 UTC
04:43:54 KST

Israelis head to the polls Tuesday in a closely contested parliamentary election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long rule or leave the country facing another political deadlock, with neither major bloc projected to secure a governing majority, Anadolu reports.
The vote will be Israel’s first general election since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip, as well as military confrontations with Lebanon and Iran.
It will also be the first Israeli general election held on schedule since 1988, following decades in which successive governments collapsed before completing their four-year terms.
Around 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). Election day is a public holiday.
Thirty-seven parties and electoral lists are competing for seats in the 120-member Knesset, where a governing coalition requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
Under Israel’s proportional representation system, voters choose parties rather than individual candidates. Parties must secure at least 3.25% of valid votes to enter parliament.
No party has ever won an outright Knesset majority, making coalition negotiations decisive in determining who becomes prime minister.
Eisenkot’s party leads final polls
Final surveys published by Israel’s three main television broadcasters put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party narrowly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud.
Yashar is projected to win 22 to 23 seats, compared with 19 to 21 for Likud.
The B’Yachad, or Together, alliance led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid is projected to finish third with 14 or 15 seats.
Other opposition parties include the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, and former Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
The three surveys project Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc winning 50 seats, while the opposition bloc is forecast to secure between 52 and 56.
Palestinian-led parties are projected to win a combined 14 to 16 seats.
The figures suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.
Winning the largest number of seats does not automatically determine who becomes prime minister.
President Isaac Herzog will consult the elected parties before assigning the task of forming a government to the lawmaker considered most likely to command a parliamentary majority.
READ: Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday’s parliamentary vote
Netanyahu fights for political survival
Netanyahu, 77, is seeking another term after serving as prime minister for more than 18 years across three separate periods.
His campaign has focused heavily on national security, portraying his experience and military policies as essential to confronting regional threats.
However, he faces criticism over his government’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, its handling of subsequent conflicts and its opposition to establishing an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures.
Netanyahu is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
His potential coalition partners include far-right parties led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, alongside the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism parties.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have advocated expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, rejected Palestinian statehood and encouraged Palestinians to leave Gaza.
The ultra-Orthodox parties have meanwhile faced mounting criticism over demands to preserve military-service exemptions for religious students as the Israeli military struggles with personnel shortages after years of conflict.
Eisenkot offers change in leadership, no major shift in security issues
Eisenkot, 66, served as chief of the Israeli military from 2015 to 2019 and joined Netanyahu’s emergency government following the Oct. 7 attacks.
He later left the government after criticizing Netanyahu’s management of the Gaza offensive and the absence of a clear political strategy.
His son was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in December 2023.
Eisenkot has campaigned on government accountability, political stability and restoring public confidence in state institutions.
He supports establishing an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 security failures and ending broad military-service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Despite positioning himself as an alternative to Netanyahu, Eisenkot maintains similar positions on several major security issues.
He opposes establishing a fully sovereign Palestinian state under current conditions and says Hamas’ military capabilities and rule in Gaza must be dismantled.
The election therefore presents voters with competing approaches to leadership, governance, judicial independence and relations with far-right parties, even as the two leading candidates share positions on key security issues.
OPINION: Israeli elections and the limits of change
Arab parties could hold balance of power
The Joint List and Ra’am, the principal parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, could play a decisive role if neither major bloc secures 61 seats.
Polls project the Joint List winning around nine seats and Ra’am securing between five and seven.
An Eisenkot-led government could require support from one or both Palestinian-led parties, either through formal coalition participation or outside parliamentary backing.
Such an arrangement would face political obstacles.
Lieberman has rejected joining a government dependent on Palestinian-led parties, while other opposition figures have been reluctant to commit to such an agreement.
Netanyahu has repeatedly invoked the possibility of Palestinian-led parties influencing the next government to mobilize right-wing voters.
Coalition scenarios, possible deadlock
Several possible outcomes could emerge from Tuesday’s vote.
Netanyahu could form another government if his bloc secures enough additional seats or attracts lawmakers from outside his existing alliance.
An Eisenkot-led coalition would likely depend on an agreement involving Palestinian-led parties, defections from other camps or difficult compromises among ideologically divided opposition leaders.
A unity government involving Likud and major opposition parties is another possible arrangement, although Eisenkot and several allies have ruled out serving under Netanyahu.
If neither side assembles a majority, Netanyahu could remain caretaker prime minister during prolonged coalition negotiations, potentially leading to another election.
The performance of smaller parties polling near the 3.25% electoral threshold could prove decisive. Parties that fail to meet the threshold win no seats, potentially weakening their political allies and shifting the balance of power between the competing blocs.
Exit polls are expected immediately after voting ends at 10 pm local time Tuesday.
Initial official results will begin emerging overnight, although counting ballots from military personnel, hospitals, prisons and other special voting arrangements could take several days.
Official results are scheduled to be published by Nov. 4, after which coalition negotiations could continue for weeks.

A year's salary buys a bathroom: Demographic crisis grips one of Europe's youngest countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:40:23 UTC
04:40:23 KST

Slovakia is facing a deepening demographic crisis, with births falling to a historic low of just over 42,000 in 2025, while the population aged 65 and older reached 1.03 million, accounting for 19% of residents. According to Slovak news outlet Pravda, the trend is placing growing pressure on public finances and essential services, raising concerns about the country's ability to support an increasingly elderly population.
Despite the alarming figures, Slovakia remains relatively young by European standards. The average share of residents aged 65 and older across Europe is 22%, and only four European Union countries have younger populations than Slovakia. Italy leads the continent, with 24.7% of its population aged 65 or older, followed by Portugal at 24.3%, Bulgaria at 24%, Greece at 23.7% and Finland at 23.6%. Germany, Europe's largest economy, stands at 22.7%.
But projections suggest Slovakia is rapidly catching up. The number of elderly residents already exceeds the number of children under 15, and the share of people aged 65 and older could reach 30% by 2050 and stabilize at around 33% between 2060 and 2080. Meanwhile, annual births are projected to fall below 35,000 by 2060 and remain between 32,000 and 33,000 through 2080.
The financial consequences are already becoming apparent. The report cites projected annual pension spending of 13.7 billion euros, alongside a planned 3.5% increase in benefits from January. The average monthly old-age pension was estimated at 703 euros at the end of 2025. Slovakia's fiscal watchdog has warned that age-related spending could gradually increase by the equivalent of 3.8% of GDP by 2060, while domestic and European Union assessments have identified significant risks to the pension system's long-term sustainability.
A year's salary buys barely enough space for a bathroom
The demographic crisis is closely intertwined with Slovakia's increasingly unaffordable housing market. The country's average annual gross salary of 23,500 euros is enough to purchase just 8.1 square meters of residential property. In the capital, Bratislava, where average annual gross earnings reach 30,000 euros, an entire year's salary buys only 6.8 square meters, roughly the size of a bathroom. Only 16 Slovak cities offer more than 14 square meters for the equivalent of one year's salary, most of them in the Nitra and Banská Bystrica regions.
Financial pressures are also keeping older Slovaks in the workforce. According to data from Eurostat, the European Union's statistical agency, 24.7% of Slovak retirees continue working or earn supplementary income, nearly twice the EU average. Of those, 18.3% continue working without changing their schedules, while 6.4% switch to adjusted working hours.
For many, the decision is driven by financial necessity rather than personal fulfillment. Some 30.3% of working retirees describe employment as an economic necessity, while 31% say continuing to work is financially worthwhile. Relatively few cite enjoyment or social connections as their primary motivation, placing Slovakia among the EU countries where retirees report the lowest levels of work-related enjoyment.
The healthcare system faces mounting pressure as the number of elderly patients with complex medical needs grows alongside persistent staffing shortages. The problem is particularly visible in residential neighborhoods built during the housing boom of the 1970s and 1980s, where large concentrations of elderly residents now live after younger families moved to suburban areas.
Pensions, healthcare and long-term care are competing for limited public funds alongside education, defense and infrastructure. At the same time, young households struggling with housing prices are finding it increasingly difficult to save for mortgage down payments, particularly without financial assistance from relatives. Many are postponing starting families, creating a cycle in which unaffordable housing contributes to declining births, leaving fewer young workers to support an aging population.

Europe's five NATO powers vow greater defence role while keeping US close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:39:17 UTC
04:39:17 KST

Europe’s five leading NATO members have pledged to take greater responsibility for the continent’s security while maintaining the United States as an indispensable ally, seeking to strengthen Europe’s role within the military alliance amid uncertainty over Washington’s future military presence.
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, known as the E5 group, made the commitment after talks in Paris on Monday, stressing that Europe must shoulder a greater share of the burden while preserving close coordination with Washington and other NATO members.
“We are determined to work in close coordination with the United States and all Allies in order to implement this concrete ambition,” the ministers said in a joint statement.
“The United States is and will remain an indispensable Ally, and continued United States engagement in European security is essential to a strong and credible NATO,” they added.
E5 seeks a stronger Europe within NATO
French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin said the five countries had agreed to pursue “a stronger Europe within an equally stronger NATO” through a coordinated plan developed in “full transparency” with Washington.
The group’s next meeting will take place in Rome in March 2027, Vautrin said.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who attended the meeting, also called for further investment in Europe’s military capabilities.
“We must continue to modernise our forces and capabilities to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” Kallas said.
Poland was represented by Deputy Defence Minister Pawel Zalewski.
Planned US troop reduction raises coordination concerns
The talks come as Washington plans to withdraw around 5,000 troops from Germany, roughly 15 percent of the approximately 36,000 US troops stationed there.
The Pentagon announced the planned reduction in May, catching European allies off guard. Washington said the withdrawal would take place over six to 12 months.
Zalewski said he was confident that any agreement on the US military presence would be coordinated with allies to avoid gaps in deterrence or military capabilities.
The E5 statement sought to balance calls for greater European responsibility with an acknowledgement that continued US engagement remains central to NATO’s collective defence.
European ministers reaffirm support for Ukraine
The five countries also reiterated their commitment to supporting Ukraine, although they announced no new financial or operational assistance following the meeting.
British minister Wes Streeting said European support would continue for as long as necessary, warning that the Russian threat was “of a kind we haven't seen since the end of the Cold War”.
At the same time, Streeting stressed that the allies were not seeking a direct confrontation with Moscow.
“None of us seek war with Russia. And we certainly have no quarrel with the Russian people,” he said.

Netanyahu election win could spell early exit for IDF chief Zamir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:22:34 UTC
04:22:34 KST

Major disagreements between IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz during a meeting Monday at Palmachim Air Base could raise questions about Zamir's continued tenure and potentially cost him a fourth year in the post.
During the meeting, Zamir opposed a directive from the political leadership to continue IDF operations in the West Bank city of Hebron following Friday's attack, in which two soldiers were killed. Zamir argued that the operation had run its course militarily, partly because no weapons had been found. He also maintained that residents evacuated from their homes during the operation should be allowed to return on legal grounds.
In line with the chief of staff's position, the IDF halted the operation. Netanyahu and Katz ordered it resumed Monday, directing the military to maintain the cordon around Hebron as a measure of deterrence and to impose a cost for the attack.
Katz explained his position by saying the investigation had not yet been completed.
"Beyond the clear considerations of deterrence and imposing a cost, the investigation into the attack has not yet been exhausted," Katz said. "We still do not know who among the terrorists' associates knew or did not know about the attack. Therefore, it is inconceivable to end the operation just one day after it began."
The sequence of events means the military did not carry out the political leadership's initial directive to continue the operation, requiring another order Monday to resume it.
The confrontation illustrates the depth of the crisis in relations between the chief of staff and the political leadership, particularly Katz. The tensions did not emerge in recent days, but they have reached a new peak in recent weeks.
With polls set to open Tuesday, the election results could also affect Zamir's future. His relationship with Netanyahu, and especially Katz, has reached a low point. According to current assessments, if the two remain in power, they could move to end his tenure.
At the Palmachim meeting, Zamir argued that the immediate operational objectives in Hebron had already been achieved and that there was no justification for continuing a broad offensive operation in the city's densely populated neighborhoods.
He also presented intelligence suggesting that the attackers may have been directed from abroad, including by Hamas operatives in Turkey, and argued that the military should conclude the operation and redirect its forces and attention to other areas.
Zamir's position was reinforced by commanders on the ground.
Commanders in the Hebron sector said the operation had exhausted its military purpose after troops searched the area without locating weapons. They argued that keeping forces deployed in the city without additional findings would provide no operational benefit and would not advance the mission's objectives.
Their assessments supported Zamir's argument that a distinction should be made between the need for a forceful response to the attack and the continuation of military activity that was no longer producing operational results.
Beyond the operational and legal considerations, Zamir was concerned about the risks to soldiers' lives, unnecessary operational friction and the possibility that prolonging the operation would increase the danger of escalation.
The political leadership, by contrast, viewed maintaining the cordon and keeping residents out of their homes as part of the necessary response to the attack.
The disagreement escalated into a heated exchange in the presence of several senior generals. Ultimately, the decision was made to continue the operation.
Disagreements over Iran
Differences also exist between the chief of staff and the political leadership over Iran, although the dispute is not necessarily about whether Israel will need another round of fighting. Rather, it centers primarily on timing and how Israel manages its confrontation with Tehran.
As previously reported over the weekend, senior IDF officials have made clear that there is no reason to attack Iran before the elections unless intelligence indicates that Tehran is preparing to strike Israel.
The military is monitoring developments and preparing accordingly, but commanders want to avoid a situation in which heightened military alertness escalates into war because one side misreads the other's intentions.
IDF officials are also concerned about the conduct of the political leadership.
While the military seeks to maintain a high level of readiness without sliding into escalation, Netanyahu and Katz have continued making public statements about the possibility of an Israeli attack.
Zamir has warned about the potential consequences of those statements, which could heighten Iranian suspicions that Israel is preparing to strike and lead to a miscalculation.
Under such circumstances, the two sides could become trapped in a dangerous cycle of actions and reactions.
Israel might detect Iranian military preparations and raise its alert level, while Iran could interpret Israel's heightened readiness as preparation for an attack and respond accordingly.
A misunderstanding of the other side's intentions could trigger a confrontation that neither side necessarily planned.
That is the danger Zamir is seeking to avoid on the eve of the elections.
The intelligence involved is highly sensitive, making it difficult to provide a complete picture. Nevertheless, current assessments suggest Iran continues taking steps that could eventually require Israel to enter another round of fighting.
Netanyahu and Katz denied reports Monday evening that they intended to dismiss Zamir, calling the claims false.
"I recommended Zamir's appointment as IDF chief of staff," Katz said. "We are working together for the security of the State of Israel, with unprecedented historic achievements, and that is how I intend to continue working in the future."

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

British F-35Bs flying from HMS Prince of Wales and Norwegian F-35As have escorted a United States Air Force B-52 over the High North during Exercise Global Thunder, the American nuclear readiness exercise, according to a post by Defence Operations.
The post said: “UK F-35Bs & @RoyalAirForce Voyager, with @Luftforsvaret F-35As, escorted a @usairforce B-52 on Exercise Global Thunder. Above @RoyalNavy & @Forsvaret_no vessels including @HMSPWLS. Operating together to defend @NATO’s northern flank.”
An RAF Voyager tanker supported the formation. HMS Prince of Wales is in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest, accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and operating under NATO command, a deployment this publication covered as the ship sailed.
United States Strategic Command describes Global Thunder as an annual exercise involving personnel throughout the strategic enterprise, including its own components and subordinate units, and says the purpose of Global Thunder 27 “is to enhance nuclear readiness and ensure a safe, secure, effective and credible strategic deterrent force.”

Britain’s part in the American nuclear exercise comes as the country prepares to take on a nuclear role of its own in the air again. The Defence Investment Plan confirmed the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear task to the Royal Air Force for the first time since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998. RAF Typhoons also escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike over the Mediterranean last week on Exercise Rummy, the first British participation in a French nuclear exercise.
Norway operates fifty two F-35As from Ørland and Evenes and has become one of the closest partners in British operations in the High North, hosting Royal Marines for Arctic training and working alongside the carrier group through the Firecrest deployment.

Why Catholic Bishops Are Apologizing Over 'Exploited' Trump Meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:18:02 UTC
04:18:02 KST

A video of Catholic bishops praying around President Donald Trump during a meeting at the White House last week has sparked debate, with some bishops claiming their attendance was “exploited” for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections.
The 12 clergymen joined Trump on Thursday in the Oval Office, for what Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee has said was intended to be a private meeting to discuss matters such as immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, and human dignity. But in a “public apology” issued Sunday, Grob expressed deep regret over the meeting that he suggested was used as a "political photo opportunity” after White House officials shared images and footage of a moment of prayer. The video, which Grob claims was posted without the bishops’ consent, has been viewed over 1.8 million times on X alone.
Grob said he had received “many questions” over the encounter and wanted to emphasize that the meeting “was in no way an endorsement of the President, his policies, or his party.” He said his invite to the meeting had been extended by Heritage Foundation, the think tank behind the conservative policy playbook Project 2025, and that he had been informed ahead of time there may be an opportunity to pray privately with the President. “Several photos were taken and we were ushered out [after the prayer]. Unbeknownst to the group of bishops, a video was also taken. But permission for the public distribution or posting of either the video or photos was not given by the bishops,” he claimed, insisting the bishops “should never have been put in that position by the White House.”
The White House did not directly respond to questions over whether permission was obtained from the bishops prior to the video and photos being shared. Spokesperson Taylor Rogers told TIME “there has never been a greater President for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it,” citing the pardoning of “pro-life activists” as one such example.
Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines also issued a statement suggesting that the meeting had been ”exploited.” Acknowledging that “there are many things tied to this present [Trump] Administration that are blatantly at odds with our Catholic faith,” Joensen said he attended the gathering as the advance communication he had received “indicated that we were to have a conversation and that key officials would be interested in hearing our perspective.”
“None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election,” he said. “Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate.”
He added: “I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes. I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.”
Archbishop James Golka of Denver, who led the prayer in the Oval Office, has also addressed the matter after people raised questions over the timing of the video.
“I understand that many people saw the video, posted by the Administration twelve days before an election, as an endorsement. That was never my intention,” Golka told Denver Catholic magazine. “The bishops of the United States teach that the Church cannot champion any candidate or party. I hold to that.”
He continued: “I’ve had a lot of people, really good friends, ask me, ‘What were you doing?’ ‘Why did you do that?’ I just answer: ‘I was being a Catholic priest. We pray for people.'”
Other clergymen in attendance included the former Archbishop of Kansas City Joseph Naumann. In a statement to TIME, his successor, Archbishop Shawn McKnight, said Naumann’s presence at the White House “was in his own individual capacity” and that “his actions and presence at that event were not on behalf of, or representative of, myself or the Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas.”
A separate statement from Archbishop Emeritus Naumann’s office said of the event: “The bishops were assured that no photographs would be made public. They came to have a discussion on important policy matters. As Catholic bishops, they pray with everyone, but do not endorse candidates or political parties.”
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB), meanwhile, has distanced itself from the gathering. A spokesperson for the group told TIME that “the meeting was not organized by the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops” and emphasized it was “not affiliated” in any way.
Trump described the meeting as “really good” when speaking with reporters Friday, calling the bishops a “nice group of people” who “mostly prayed” in the Oval Office. Amid the online discourse, White House Faith Office director Jenny Korn defended the gathering, describing it as “not politics,” but “policy in action ending with meaningful prayer with, and for, the President.
The controversy comes as the Trump Administration seeks to maintain support among Catholic voters ahead of the midterms. According to data circulated by the Pew Research Center in 2025, 20% of U.S. adults describe themselves as Catholic. Trump's approval rating among Catholics has fallen to 30% as of October 2026, compared to the 47% he held when he returned to the White House in January 2025, per the D.C.-based think tank.
When asked about the drop in support from Catholic voters in an Oct. 22 interview, Vice President J.D. Vance, a Catholic convert, said that while he believes Catholics, and Americans in general, are not “displeased with the direction” of the country, he acknowledges that “a lot more work needs to happen.”
“The Catholic vote is absolutely critical in electoral politics in the United States, and particularly in the midterms,” says David Gibson, director of the Center of Religion and Culture at Fordham University. He adds that while certain religious groups may stick more with a particular political party, the “Catholic vote can shift between Republicans and Democrats much more easily than any other religious bloc.”
Trump won a majority of Catholic voters in the 2024 Presidential election, taking 55% of the Catholic vote to former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 43%, according to the Pew Research Center. With Republicans attempting to retain control of both chambers of Congress amid tight races, Catholic voters could prove an important voting bloc.
Yet the Administration has also faced growing tensions with Pope Leo XIV in recent months. Trump and the first American-born Pope have repeatedly clashed over policy disagreements, particularly Leo's opposition to the Administration's immigration crackdown and the Iran war.
“The dynamics are shifting. For the past few years, the white Catholic vote was very solidly with the Republicans and with Trump, but Catholics are growing disaffected with him,” says Gibson. “Now you have an American Pope, from Chicago, the Midwest, and he is widely popular. American Catholics identify with him, and Trump has not ceased picking fights with the Pope, and American Catholics [could be] getting kind of fed up with it.”
American Catholic leaders have raised concerns over Trump's policies
In January, three Catholic Cardinals issued a “rare joint statement on the morality of U.S. foreign policy.”
Archbishop of Chicago Blase Cupich, Archbishop of Washington Robert McElroy, and Archbishop of Newark Joseph Tobin said the “events in Venezuela, Ukraine, and Greenland have raised basic questions about the use of military force and the meaning of peace.” They argued that the “building of just and sustainable peace” is being “reduced to partisan categories that encourage polarization and destructive policies.” The statement bolstered remarks Pope Leo had made earlier that month, in which he warned against a “diplomacy based on force.”
Trump’s war with Iran has prompted further warnings from American Catholic leaders.
Archbishop of Oklahoma City Paul Coakley, who serves as president of the USCCB, earlier this year joined Pope Leo in urging Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement to the war.
The Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement practices have also prompted debate. Upon returning to the White House, Trump rescinded previous government guidance that restricted immigration arrests in sensitive locations, including schools, churches, and hospitals. Immigration enforcement efforts subsequently intensified, with arrests reported outside churches, drawing backlash from religious leaders.
In November 2025, the USCCB approved a special message opposing indiscriminate mass deportations by an overwhelming vote of 216 in favor and five against. The bishops also raised concerns about detention conditions, family separation, the loss of legal status, and “the lack of access to pastoral care.”
The message was later echoed by other Catholic leaders across the country. In December 2025, the Catholic bishops of Wisconsin issued a statement that expressed “strong concern” over what they referred to as “the indiscriminate nature of the current federal immigration enforcement.”
Gibson says that although the USCCB used to have a somewhat friendly relationship with the Republican party, particularly on the pursuit to overturn Roe v. Wade, relations have grown increasingly frayed during Trump’s return to the White House. He points to the USCCB’s argument that the Administration has denied visas for priests and bishops, and the announced cuts to the resettlement of refugees for Catholic charities.
However, Catholic bishops have diverse views on politics and the Trump Administration.
Last year, Bishop Robert Barron was among those selected to serve on Trump's Religious Liberty Commission.
The 2025 National Study of Catholic Priests found that from a sample of 1,164 priests, 30% identified as somewhat to very liberal, 36% as moderate, and 34% as somewhat to very conservative.

The Air Force unit tasked with training Tactical Air Control Party Airmen has halted all rope training events after one of its instructors was killed Oct. 17 in a rappelling demonstration in front of thousands of spectators at a college football game.
Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson of the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, died Oct. 17 from injuries he suffered from rappelling rapidly from the 180-foot ceiling of Alamodome, failing to stop before his body crashed into the field below. Patterson was participating in a pregame event before the University of Texas-San Antonio played Navy as part of its Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans night.
It’s unclear when the service will complete the investigation into the cause of Patterson’s fatal accident, a spokesperson at the Air Force Warfare Center at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., said.
Detachment 2 of the 6th CTS teaches rappelling and other skills TACPs need to embed and operate with Army and Marine units while coordinating and deconflicting all surface and air fires on the battlefield. But less than a week after Patterson’s death, the unit “paused all rappel and ropes training and demonstrations,” according to the spokesperson, who added that it’s unclear how long the pause will stay in place.
Other media outlets previously reported the unit’s pause in training.
Military units specializing in rappelling have frequently put on demonstrations at the Alamodome. In 2013, instructors from the Army’s 101st Airborne Division Air Assault School from Fort Campbell, Ky., conducted a pregame rappelling demonstration inside the stadium before the U.S. Army All-American Bowl game.
But the Alamodome’s ceiling is much higher than most service members are used to, measuring more than double the height of most military rappel towers.
Rappelling from such heights can cause increased friction to build up, radiating intense heat even through rappelling gloves. While practicing for the 2013 event, 101st instructors “complained about their hands feeling pretty warm, despite wearing gloves,” according to an Army release from the time. After their first practice rappel, the Soldiers added special inserts into their gloves to protect their hands from the heat buildup.
It’s unclear if Patterson had practiced rappelling from the stadium’s ceiling before the event. But the native of Fort Stewart, Ga., received recognition for his skill during his 15 years of service, including being named as the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level, according to an Oct. 18 press release.
