Exclusive: Russia significantly expands glide-bomb production, research shows
Russia is significantly expanding its glide-bomb production, indicating that Moscow has no plans to scale back its war against Ukraine, a new report by Kyiv-based think tank Center for Defense Reforms exclusively shared with the Kyiv Independent reveals.
"Given the role of guided aerial bombs in destroying defensive positions, isolating battlefields and facilitating ground advances, this provides a basis for sustaining high-intensity offensive operations over an extended period," the report concludes.
The report reveals that in 2025, the centralized procurement entity TRV-Engineering JSC obtained nearly 278,000 servo drives, used to control the flight surfaces of glide bombs — enough to manufacture 139,000 of the deadly munitions. The report identifies the key Russian supplier of servo drives, CED Sail LLC, which is currently not subject to any Western sanctions, and suggests this entity should be a "priority target" for sanctions designation.
"Russia is building the military-industrial capacity to continue waging wars even after the war in Ukraine ends. These are not the actions of a country preparing for lasting peace," Oleksandr Danylyuk, chairman of the Center for Defense Reforms and former chief adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, told the Kyiv Independent.
The report also identifies a network of interconnected Russian companies which are responsible for importing key components and raw materials essential for the production of UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits.
Russia converts older, unguided bombs into precision-guided weapons with these guidance kits, significantly increasing their range and accuracy. The increase in range allows Russian fighter-bomber aircraft to remain within Russian territory, out of range of Ukrainian air defenses, as they deploy their deadly payloads.
As with many other Russian munitions, both UMPK and UMPB glide bomb kits are heavily reliant on foreign components for their manufacture.
Ukrainian military intelligence has repeatedly identified a range of foreign components in Russian glide bombs, including parts from the U.S., Japan, China, Switzerland, and Taiwan, among others.
The report also reveals the majority of entities and individuals involved in the production of Russia's glide bombs are currently unsanctioned, despite the munitions being a key part of the Kremlin's offensive airborne arsenal.
Out of 20 corporate entities involved in the manufacture of Russian glide bombs, only eight are subject to some level of Western sanctions or export restrictions. The "uneven sanctions coverage," the report assesses, allows Russia to continue to "procure necessary components without significant restrictions."
Four Chinese companies are identified as being critical to the supply chain, with some, such as Shenzhen Fire Power Control Technology Limited, not hiding the explicitly military application of their products. Only one of the four Chinese companies is subject to U.S. export restrictions, and none are sanctioned by the U.K. or the EU.
"Despite its repeated declarations of readiness for peace, Russia continues to dramatically expand the production of offensive weapons, particularly guided aerial bombs," Danylyuk said.

Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes
Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers.
Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant.
The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said.
Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems.

Mystery money from super PACs floods US midterm election campaigns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
19:00:18 UTC
04:00:18 KST

With just over a week until voting day, the records in the notoriously expensive US election system have been shattered.
An AFP news agency analysis of federal data shows just five groups known as super PACs (political action committees) accounted for nearly a third of non-party spending in this election cycle as of October 25.
Significantly funded by dark money, they have poured more than $1 billion into the US midterm election campaign.
Three of the five groups skew Republican, and about two thirds of the billion dollars spent will benefit the Republican Party (GOP), fuelled by ultra-wealthy Republican-leaning donors like Elon Musk — a key ally of President Donald Trump.
Musk alone has put almost $450 million into Republican groups, including the biggest of the super PACs, the Senate Leadership Fund.
Meanwhile, Democrats have a fundraising edge when it comes to direct donations to candidates' campaigns and to the party's national committees.
Democratic candidates in competitive Senate and House races have consistently outraised their Republican counterparts.
That suggests smaller donors in the Democratic base are highly motivated.
But tortuous US election laws impose strict caps on how much individuals can give, while there is no limit — or really any control at all — on how much super PAC groups can throw at candidates.
Unlimited contributions
The six giant spenders in this cycle are technically a mix of super PACs and hybrid PACs, entities that didn't even exist before 2010.
They grew out of a Supreme Court ruling, known as Citizens United, which held that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.
A lower court decision ruled that these organisations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors.
The result was that big donors can funnel vast sums of money to try and influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organisations.
In contrast, direct contributions to a candidate's official campaign are limited to a mere $3,500, and donations to national party committees have a cap of $44,300.
The PAC spending sprees have surged ever higher during the Trump era, with Musk's mega-million donations encapsulating the new reality of pay-to-play politics.
Across the nation, super PACs have put far more of their money into Senate contests and spent it largely on attack ads.
The Texas Senate election tops the list in terms of expenditure. Democrat James Talarico has faced more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups as he attempts to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.
Second is Ohio's special Senate election, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has also faced extensive outside spending against him — nearly $170 million — as he tries to return to the Senate.

Air Force Plans $1 Billion Campus for Testing F-47 at Nellis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:56:52 UTC
03:56:52 KST

The Air Force is taking the first steps to build a $1 billion campus including hangars, laboratories, maintenance and training facilities, and more to test the F-47 at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev.—and the service plans to finish construction by 2031 as it moves quickly to field the upcoming sixth-generation fighter.
In a presolicitation notice posted Oct. 22, the Air Force said it is looking for as many as four qualified firms that can quickly work on a project to design and build the proposed F-47 campus. The entire project, including construction, design, security, and other expenses, will ultimately cost about $1.057 billion.
The project would include a nearly 117,000-square foot facility, largely on the east side of Nellis, combining flightline operations and maintenance. It would also have a specialized laboratory for reprogramming the plane’s systems, an aircraft apron with sunshades, and a nearly 41,000-square foot simulator facility.
The notice lists several other facilities that could be built later as “potential subsequent work,” including additional hangars for fuel system maintenance, corrosion control of its stealth coating, weapons load training, maintenance training, and other maintenance needs.
The Air Force plans to issue an initial award for the F-47 campus in February 2027, which would then kick off about nine months of design and preconstruction, and then about 40 more months of more intensive construction into early March 2031.
The presolicitation notice for the campus provides the latest window on how the Air Force is preparing to bring the Boeing-made F-47 into its fleet. It follows the Air Force’s 2027 budget proposal, which requested $730 million for hangars and other support infrastructure for the F-47 and revealed its operational testing will take place at Nellis.
The Air Force in March 2025 announced it had chosen Boeing to build the F-47, which will replace the F-22 Raptor sometime in the 2030s and eventually make up 20 percent of the Air Force’s fleet. It is expected to have advanced stealth, data sharing, and electronic warfare capabilities, and it will be able to direct semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in September 2025 that the first F-47 fighter was in the process of being built and would fly in 2028. Service officials have stuck to that schedule ever since and said its first flight will take place before the end of the Trump administration.
Allvin also said in a May 2025 social media post that the F-47 will be able to fly faster than Mach 2, or more than 1,500 miles per hour, and have a combat radius of more than 1,000 nautical miles, far more than the F-22 or F-35A Joint Strike Fighter. That expanded range would give the F-47 an advantage in a potential conflict with China, where aircraft will have to fly long distances over stretches of the Pacific Ocean.

“I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen,” said the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council.

Prince Khalid, Pakistan’s powerful army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Rezaei.

Andreas Krieg of the London-based risk consultancy MENA analytica said Prince Khalid’s presence in Tehran was “hugely significant”, calling him the “strategic mastermind of Saudi Arabia”.
Prince Khalid, brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto ruler, has emerged as one of Saudi Arabia’s key diplomatic interlocutors, repeatedly dispatched on sensitive regional missions.
“Riyadh is investing serious political capital in dialogue with Iran, seeking to contain escalation and create a credible diplomatic path out of the crisis,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst who is close to the government, posted on social media.
‘Don’t test us’
Recent comments have heightened speculation about renewed conflict.
US President Donald Trump said on Oct 23 that Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the US-Israeli campaign against Iran that began on Feb 28.
On Oct 25, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran may try to disrupt the Israeli elections, where he is in a neck-and-neck race to stay in power.

Wheelaroos out to 'send a message' in pursuit of breakthrough World Cup title
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:54:08 UTC
03:54:08 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Breakthrough moment beckons for Australia's Wheelaroos at home Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
Australian wheelchair rugby league is poised for a breakthrough moment this week, with Wollongong, south of Sydney, hosting the nation's first World Cup since 2008.
Bundled in as part of the larger Rugby League World Cup, which also includes the men's, women's and physical disability tournaments, the wheelchair competition will benefit from free-to-air coverage in prime-time slots.
It is the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of, and Australia's Wheelaroos are well aware of the gravity of the moment.
"I think it's going to bring a whole different experience for wheelchair rugby league in Australia," Australia captain Bayley McKenna told ABC Sport.
"It's gonna bring people together, it's gonna bring people in to support our sport."
The Wheelaroos are currently ranked fourth in the world and are yet to claim a world title, with their game generally taking a back seat to the likes of wheelchair basketball and wheelchair rugby at a grassroots level in Australia.
But coach Brett Clark has told ABC Sport his charges are ready to take the rough-and-tumble sport into living rooms across the country.
"We know this is a quality game for all to play and this is the opportunity for us to show it at its top level," Clark said.
A unique kind of inclusion
Wheelchair rugby league, not to be confused with Paralympic favourite wheelchair rugby, is played on a basketball-sized court and with five athletes per side.
The sport replaces tackles with tagging like in Oztag and uses AFL-style handballing instead of kicking, but otherwise, remains relatively faithful to the running game.
Played across full-length 40-minute halves, it is a game filled with exhilarating chair skills, hair-raising collisions and retains much of rugby league's trademark physicality.
For Wheelaroos captain McKenna — who played the running game for years before joining the wheelchair sport — wheelchair rugby league's physicality is one of its biggest drawcards.
"In hindsight, I've had more injuries playing wheelchair rugby league than I did in the running game," McKenna said.
"You can hit people as hard as you want as long as you're going for the tag."
At 26, McKenna is a Wheelaroos trailblazer, being both the youngest and first non-disabled national team skipper.
Wheelchair rugby league is unique among international wheelchair sports in allowing teams to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.
This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from the grassroots all the way to elite competition, allowing for both non-disabled and disabled friends and family to share the same court.
McKenna, who began playing wheelchair sports alongside his disabled father, has seen the benefits of that inclusiveness firsthand.
"Being a non-disabled athlete in this sport is one of the most unreal things you can ever be a part of," McKenna said.
"The sport's so big, it's so broad, you can travel all across the world … it's so inclusive, because for me it gave me an opportunity to play a sport underneath my dad as a coach."
Wheelaroos squad member Liam Luff, living with hereditary spastic paraplegia, told ABC Sport the policy was an "incredible benefit".
"It just opens the doors to more and more people in our sport, which is what we need to grow awareness, get more people in chairs and show how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
The importance of the moment
Beginning on Friday, the 2026 World Cup will be just the fifth edition of the wheelchair tournament, with France and England having split the first four titles evenly.
With the sport having been first designed in France in the early 2000s, the two northern hemisphere titans have benefited from close contact and regular meetings.
In England, the sport experienced an explosion in popularity after the nation hosted the 2022 World Cup, which was also held alongside the men's and women's competitions. Grassroots participation saw a sharp uptick in the year after the event, while standalone international games have attracted audiences in the thousands since.
The Wheelaroos are now optimistic the 2026 tournament will have a similar impact in Australia, and Luff believes the sport is well and truly ready for it.
"I think more people are going to stumble across the game and find out about how special wheelchair rugby league is," Luff said.
Finding a way past France and England will undoubtedly be an almighty task for the Wheelaroos, who will play three group-stage games before the knockouts.
But the team is bullish on its chances in the Illawarra, and Luff is convinced the Wheelaroos are finally ready to take a seat amongst the world's elite.
"This is our biggest opportunity to really prove where the Australian Wheelaroos are in wheelchair rugby league," Luff said.
"We are gonna make sure we can prove ourselves taking on those top dogs … I think we're gonna really send a message about where we stand."

Ukrainian forces evacuate 2 severely wounded soldiers from battlefield using drone, video shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:42:57 UTC
03:42:57 KST

Ukrainian forces evacuate 2 severely wounded soldiers from battlefield using drone, video shows
Ukraine's 475th Separate Assault Regiment Code 9.2 evacuated two severely wounded soldiers from the battlefield using a domestically developed aerial evacuation drone, StarGate, the unit reported on Oct. 26.
The two soldiers, 25-year-old Yevhen, call sign "Izium," and 24-year-old Artem, call sign "Kolobok," had suffered severe limb injuries and were stranded in a contested area about five kilometers (three miles) from the Russian border.
Ground evacuation was impossible due to difficult terrain, water obstacles, and the threat of Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones, the regiment said.
The two evacuation missions were carried out over the course of a week in cooperation with SkyFall, the Ukrainian company that developed and manufactures StarGate.
The operations required coordination between several units and fire support from heavy Vampire attack drones to suppress Russian positions.
During one mission, StarGate flew nearly 30 kilometers (20 miles) to reach a wounded soldier and approximately the same distance back with him aboard.
Russian electronic warfare systems attempted to jam satellite navigation signals in the area, but the drone completed the evacuation using its AI-based navigation system and the pilots' skills, according to the regiment.
Oleksandr Nastenko, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, said the unit plans to use the experience to train additional crews and make aerial evacuations a regular practice.
The operations come a week after Ukrainian forces reported what they described as a first-of-its-kind aerial evacuation of a severely wounded soldier who had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position, using a drone.

GENEVA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Israel continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave, a UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel dismissed as part of a “misinformation campaign”.
The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel examined violations against Palestinian children since the start of the war between Israel and Hamas on October 7, 2023 up to September this year.
It said Israeli authorities had kept committing “genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza”, and that the situation had also continued to deteriorate in the occupied West Bank.
Another report by the commission in September last year found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that top Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu incited these acts — accusations that Israel called scandalous.
The Israeli mission in Geneva said the latest report was part of a misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel.
“The attempt to destroy the Jewish state … continues today through efforts by actors such as the UN Commission of Inquiry to undermine Israel’s legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself,” Ambassador Daniel Meron said in a statement.
HEAVY MUNITIONS HIT POPULATED AREAS, COMMISSION SAYS
The commission found that Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire in Gaza.
It said the “Yellow Line” which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, was encroaching increasingly into Gaza, and becoming a de facto border, which the report said reflected Israel’s expanding territorial control of Gaza.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
In its report to the UN Security Council, the commission said the situation in the West Bank had also deteriorated sharply, with the number of Palestinians killed in airstrikes increasing from six between 2008 and October 6, 2023, to 254 between October 7, 2023 and September 30, 2026.
Commission Chair Srinivasan Muralidhar said the intentional killing of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank formed part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians.
Military operations since January 2025 have led to the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians remaining displaced as of August 2026, the report said.
The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority, saying it had targeted Palestinians who voice dissenting views and that journalists and human rights defenders had been killed and injured.
(Reporting by Olivia Le Poidevin, writing by Kirsti Knolle)

Australian billionaire James Packer paid at least $1.25 million – 1.78 million Australian dollars or 3.85 million shekels – to the law firm of Amit Hadad, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's attorney, the Australian newspaper The Age reported Monday.
Packer is also a witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial, in which Hadad represents the prime minister.
The investigation, published on the eve of Israel's election, uncovered a trail of monthly bank transfers of $50,000 over the past two years, from a bank account controlled by Packer's company to the account of the law firm representing Netanyahu.
On the same day the investigation was published, Hadad filed a motion on behalf of Netanyahu's defense team requesting that Packer and two of his employees be allowed to testify from abroad, with their testimony broadcast by video link to the judges in Israel.
According to the investigation, the first monthly payment was made on September 23, 2024, from a Citibank account belonging to Packer's legal firm to an account held by Hadad, Roth, Shenhar at Mizrahi Tefahot Bank. A source familiar with the details reportedly said the payments urgently needed to be investigated to determine whether Netanyahu had received an undisclosed benefit from Packer.
Packer insisted that the bank transfers to Netanyahu's lawyers were payments for work carried out on his behalf, including "deal finding" in Israel, where he has business interests, and that they were unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
The Australian newspaper also reported that a Netanyahu spokesperson asked for comment replied: "I couldn't give a monkey's about your questions. We are very busy. We have an election on right now."
Packer did not deny making the monthly payments but declined to comment. Hadad also declined to comment.
Packer's representatives responded that the law firm represents him in his "personal and business affairs." "Any claim that I paid even a single cent toward the legal defense of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is false. Anyone who claims otherwise risks being sued."
Packer was expected to testify as a key prosecution witness in Netanyahu's corruption trial in Case 1000, in which he and businessman Arnon Milchan are alleged to have provided Netanyahu and his wife with gifts and other benefits worth hundreds of thousands of shekels.
Packer gave a statement to police during the investigation, but in February 2024, prosecutors announced that they would not call him to testify at the trial. During the phase of the trial devoted to prosecution witnesses, prosecutors were unable to contact Packer to arrange for him to travel to Israel.
Meanwhile, attorney Amit Hadad filed a motion on Netanyahu's behalf Monday requesting that Packer and two of his employees, Ben Tilley and Guy Jolland, be questioned abroad. In the motion, Hadad stated that he represents Packer in Israel on matters unrelated to Netanyahu's trial.
In the letters, the two described their visits to Israel between 2013 and 2016, when they were members of Packer's staff. Tilley testified that he smoked a cigar every evening during each of the 83 days he spent in Israel, as did Ian Morris, another Packer employee.
Jolland described the hospitality at Packer's properties, including a suite at the Royal Beach Hotel in Tel Aviv and a villa he purchased in Caesarea. He claimed that the properties were always stocked with food and wine for entertaining guests, including a supply of rosé champagne, and that Packer himself regularly drank rosé champagne.

Hadad explained that the defense has no way to compel the witnesses, who live abroad, to testify in Israel because they refuse to travel there. However, they have indicated that they would comply with any lawful court order issued by the courts in their countries of residence.

Ukrainian Intelligence Reveals How Russia Targets Africa to Recruit Soldiers for Ukraine War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:40:48 UTC
03:40:48 KST

- Category
- World
Ukrainian Intelligence Reveals How Russia Targets Africa to Recruit Soldiers for Ukraine War
Russia has significantly expanded military recruitment across Africa, targeting poorer countries to replenish its forces amid heavy battlefield losses in Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 26.
The outlet cited a presentation by people familiar with Ukraine’s intelligence service detailing Moscow’s growing reliance on African recruits. The campaign aims to “offset massive losses and a shortage of people to mobilize,” the document stated.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the intelligence assessment, Russia has increasingly targeted countries with weak democratic institutions, limited press freedom, and inadequate judicial protections.
The recruitment campaign has expanded particularly rapidly in Burundi, Zimbabwe, and Sierra Leone, following efforts by Kenya and South Africa to prevent their citizens from joining Russian forces.
Between January 1 and September 30, 2026, Russia recruited 699 men from Burundi, compared with just 30 throughout 2025. In Zimbabwe, recruitment increased from 65 men in 2025 to 530 during the first nine months of 2026.
Significant increases were also recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Cameroon, and Sierra Leone.
Russia has also begun recruiting military personnel in Madagascar for the first time since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Following a military coup in 2025, Madagascar strengthened cooperation with Moscow, receiving Russian military equipment and food supplies.
Russian personnel have also provided military training to Malagasy forces.
Recruiters reportedly exploit economic hardship by promising high-paying civilian employment in Russia, including positions in catering and transportation.
Some prospective recruits are misled about the nature of their employment and subsequently deployed to the battlefield in Ukraine. Other incentives include substantial signing bonuses, high salaries, and the possibility of obtaining Russian citizenship.
The intelligence materials also described an online recruitment advertisement circulated in Zimbabwe, promoting a “program for specialists from Zimbabwe.” Applicants were directed to an online eligibility assessment, without explicit warnings that military contracts could lead to frontline deployment.
The surge in African recruitment is part of a far broader foreign-recruitment drive that has grown sharply since 2022, when only 94 such contracts were recorded. For 2026, Moscow set a target of 18,500 foreign recruits, and by mid-October, 16,168 had already signed contracts.
Russia has also used legal and administrative restrictions to pressure migrants living in the country without citizenship. This approach presents military service as one of the few routes to legal residency and a Russian passport, while circumventing opposition from countries across Asia, Africa, and Latin America that officially reject the recruitment of their citizens into foreign armed forces.

The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:40:14 UTC
03:40:14 KST

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s presidential election is a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress to extend presidential terms and pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.
Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married to controversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief from everyday costs and indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employed voters whom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration with student protests, mass demonstrations and a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.
Mr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for 27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even a prominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations of corruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.
After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run of seven rightwing presidential wins across Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump had claimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs to pressure Brazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.
Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded the Workers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.

‘Students Have Won’: Overwhelming Turnout Shatters Serbia’s Entrenched Regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:39:00 UTC
03:39:00 KST

When a handful of university students first spilled onto the streets two years ago to protest the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy, Serbia’s state-run media dismissed them as unruly kids merely looking for an excuse to cut class.
They were grieving the 16 people crushed to death and demanding accountability for what they condemned as lethal state corruption and crony contracting, bearing banners that read: “Corruption kills” and “Your hands are bloody.”
But those scattered demonstrations soon swelled into a generational revolt. Over two relentless years, the students slept in occupied lecture halls, barnstormed rural strongholds where state television branded them foreign mercenaries, and punctured a pervasive climate of fear with biting wit and viral banners.
On Sunday, the kids actually did it.
In a stunning ballot-box upset that shattered Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power, Serbia’s student-led movement defeated the Balkan country’s formidable ruling machine, clinching a triumph so historic that even its young architects were left reeling in disbelief.
“Fantastic. I can’t believe it,” Ilija Ratković, 30, told OCCRP. “A regime that ruled for 14 years, was corrupt, and killed people in Serbia is out.” He admitted he never expected Vučić to yield quietly: “I expected him to fight to the end.”
The movement’s slogan, “Students are winning” (Studenti pobeđuju), mobilized Serbians at home and abroad to vote for the “Students’ List”—a slate of candidates chosen by activists to replace Vučić’s state apparatus. Though convinced the regime would try to manipulate the count, organizers aimed to counter fraud through overwhelming turnout, operating on a simple premise: elections can be stolen, but not in a landslide.
“The higher the turnout, the less chance he has to steal it,” one voter who identified himself as David told OCCRP ahead of the poll.
Then came Sunday. Even after Serbia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs adjusted overseas polling hours to align with Belgrade’s time zone, thousands of diaspora Serbs lined up outside embassies and consulates in Australia and the United States in the dead of night. Some traveled thousands of kilometers from Brisbane to Sydney. In New York, voters showed up at 2:00 AM singing defiant songs, with several wearing pajamas, bathrobes, and sleep masks to mock a rule they viewed as blatant voter suppression.
Inside Serbia, queues at polling stations stretched around city blocks. Voters brought sandwiches and flasks of tea and coffee, waiting patiently for hours to cast their ballots.
A video circulating on social media on Monday perhaps best captured that determination: just one minute before polls were set to close, a man was filmed carrying a woman wearing house slippers toward a polling station entrance. “She delivered a baby two days ago!” he shouted to the people at the door, as another bystander rushed over to help carry her inside. She was the final voter admitted to the station.
“Change requires participation. Citizens who do not participate in the democratic process – not in the public square through protest and engaged debate, nor through the ballot box – will achieve nothing,” political analyst Jasmin Mujanovic wrote in a commentary.
With turnout approaching 70 percent—nearing a historic record—Vučić did the unthinkable roughly an hour and a half after polls closed at 8:00 PM. Preempting the official election commission tally, he conceded defeat from party headquarters, announcing that based on his party’s samples, the youth-led Students’ List had won decisively, projecting roughly 2.2 million votes for the “List” compared to 1.72 million for his party.
His admission unleashed an immediate explosion of jubilation across the country. Car horns blared, red flares illuminated squares, and crowds of weeping, laughing students spilled into the autumn night, dancing well past dawn.

The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:38:53 UTC
03:38:53 KST

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.
Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.
On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.
For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.
As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat Viktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority.
What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge towards the bottom of European corruption rankings.
Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.
As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’s Serbia, like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.

Authorities continued monitoring road conditions and warning motorists about sections where accumulated water made driving dangerous.

Putin’s schedule at the Russia-Africa summit will be incredibly busy: "I emphasize that they will be very grand, even a little chaotic (the events - TASS). But we will try to do everything, we will try to get everything in on time."

The Russia-Africa Summit organized so that Putin can hold talks with every visiting leader.

Childcare is undergoing a 'reckoning' but safety gaps remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:11 UTC
03:30:11 KST

Australian child care is undergoing a reckoning, but some centres remain unsafe
When Christina Spark toured Little Zak's Academy in the Sydney suburb of Gladesville early last year, it seemed like the perfect place to enrol her one-year-old.
"The playground was shiny, they had soccer and yoga and swimming," she said. "I was pretty blown away and amazed."
Within weeks, Spark started to notice hygiene issues, dietary instructions not being followed, her little boy's milk bottle coming home unused and babies sitting in soiled nappies.
"The underlying problem was just a lack of supervision … and not enough people," she said.
Then the incidents started to pile up. One bite turned into two and by October her child, now 19 months old, had been bitten five times.
After months of mounting concerns, Spark pulled her son out and used her skills as an auditor to dig into the centre and the chain behind it.
"If I [had] just looked up who owns the centre, done a little bit of digging, realised the number of enforcement actions, realised the level of profits being generated, I wouldn't have sent him there, but I just didn't know," she said.
Little Zak's is one of the country's fastest-growing childcare chains, generating $142 million in revenue and $17 million in profit in 2025.
The family-owned business also has the highest proportion of centres subject to enforcement action among the country's 26 largest long daycare operators.
'It's child abuse'
At the Little Zak's centre at Shellharbour, two hours south of Sydney, the warning signs had been building for months.
Leigh Cotter said he initially blew off the incidents as kids being kids, but when they started to escalate, he raised concerns.
"I said, 'Look, you guys really need to do something about the safety of kids, because if you don't, something serious is going to happen.'
"A month later, my son broke his leg in daycare, and I don't think they were completely honest about how it happened."
Cotter said the centre told him his son was wearing socks indoors and had slipped and hit his head and left ankle just before pick-up.
When he took him to the hospital, the doctors discovered a spiral fracture on the other leg, running from his ankle towards his knee.
Cotter said an educator later told him his son had been screaming in another room much earlier in the day, but staff had not realised he was seriously injured.
"Six hours of walking on a broken leg — it's child abuse," Cotter said.
Four Corners put the claims to Little Zak's but it did not comment for privacy reasons.
Since Cotter pulled his son from Little Zak's Shellharbour in May 2023, the centre has faced repeated parent complaints and regulatory action.
In the past two years alone, it has been subject to four enforcement actions, including an emergency action notice over staffing ratios, which is the minimum number of educators legally required for the children in care.
In August, regulators issued a further compliance notice.
The centre has also been downgraded from Meeting the National Quality Standard to Working Towards, which means it is no longer meeting the nationally agreed standards for child care.
Gabrielle Meagher, an emeritus professor at Macquarie University, has spent decades researching privatised social services including child care.
Her analysis of the country's 26 largest long-daycare providers found the proportion of Little Zak's centres subject to enforcement action was 10 percentage points higher than the next highest, Edge Early Learning, which entered voluntary administration in August.
Meagher says 56 per cent of Little Zak's centres are recorded on Starting Blocks as having been subject to enforcement action in the past two years.
She says the chain has experienced rapid expansion. The company grew from 16 centres in 2021 to about 43 today.
A deeper analysis of regulatory records reveals the regulator confirmed almost 600 breaches at Little Zak's centres between 2020 and September 2025.
Of these, 181 were linked to inadequate supervision, inappropriate discipline and failures to protect children from harm and hazards.
At September 2025 staff turnover was 79 per cent, which is equivalent to almost eight departures for every 10 employees in its average workforce over the year.
Childcare sector faces 'reckoning'
But the problems uncovered at Little Zak's are not isolated.
Four Corners has analysed thousands of regulatory records from across the sector, examined internal company documents, spoken to parents and educators and obtained CCTV as part of an investigation into child safety across Australia's $23 billion childcare sector.
It has uncovered serious failures at some major operators and examined the gaps that remain despite sweeping government reforms.
ABC Investigations has been uncovering systemic failures in child care for the past 18 months.
Early Childhood Education Minister Jess Walsh says those stories have had a profound impact on the sector.
"There has been a reckoning in this system over the past 12 months, and it is changing in no small part because of the way in which you have shone a light on the problems in early learning," she said.
The revelations have triggered a series of reforms including tougher penalties, mandatory child-safety training, a national worker register, tighter Working With Children Check requirements, greater powers for regulators and new powers to cut Commonwealth childcare subsidies to poorly performing providers.
"The reforms that we have put in place are the right reforms," Walsh told Four Corners.
"They are on track, and we are seeing the results of those reforms."
So far, 120 services with a history of failing to meet quality and safety standards have been put on notice to improve or risk losing access to Commonwealth subsidies. To date, funding has been withdrawn from 12.
More than 1,300 childcare services are currently failing to meet the national quality standards, accounting for around 48,000 childcare places. About 350 have failed twice in a row and can go on average more than three years between assessments.
"Around half of the services that we have put those conditions on have turned around and have met the quality standards," Walsh said.
"That is what we would like to see, but where they fail to do that or refuse to do that, we are clear that there is no place for those services in early learning."
But a year into the funding crackdown, some big operators with regulatory issues have not been caught by it.
None of Little Zak's centres are on the list, despite a regulatory record spanning dozens of centres and hundreds of confirmed breaches, including failures involving supervision, staffing ratios and protecting children from harm.
Little Zak's said it had restructured its executive management team, including replacing its CEO, and that its focus was the health, safety and wellbeing of children in its care.
It said notifiable incidents and compliance breaches were down following increased investment in staff training and more open communication with families.
"Our focus is on quality and safety in our existing services, not on growth," it said in a statement.
Only About Children (OAC), which is owned by US-listed Bright Horizons, isn't on the list either. In the past two years, more than one in four of OAC's centres have been subject to enforcement action, including for inadequate supervision of children.
In April, OAC's Mosman centre on Sydney's north shore entered into an enforceable undertaking after a child was subjected to inappropriate conduct.
In August, enforcement action was also taken against two OAC centres in Victoria. Brunswick West was cited for inadequate supervision and failing to protect children from harm and hazards.
Coonans Hill was cited for a much broader range of breaches, including inappropriate conduct, inadequate supervision, staffing arrangements, protecting children from harm and hazards, interactions with children, and safety and record-keeping requirements.
"They've got 78 services, and of them, 21 have had enforcement actions against them in the last two years, which is 27 per cent of them, more than a quarter of their services," Meagher said in September. One centre has since been closed.
"That's quite a high number, and it's more than twice as many as the largest not-for-profit."
The public record tells only part of the story.
Four Corners has seen previously secret regulatory records, parent complaints and internal documents detailing thousands of incidents across its centres, including children going missing, serious injuries, failures of supervision and allegations of children being grabbed, dragged and forcibly restrained.
OAC's Williamstown centre in Melbourne's inner west has its own troubling history. Alleged paedophile Joshua Brown, who was committed to trial on 156 charges, worked there in 2020 and 2021, and police have since identified alleged victims from his time at the centre.
In the past two years, Williamstown has also faced two enforcement actions. In July, it was breached for failing to protect children from harm and hazards, as well as breaches of health, hygiene and safe food practices. In September, its quality ratings were slashed from exceeding to "working towards", which means it failed to meet the national quality standards.
The Williamstown centre is slated to close next year and its website says it is not taking any new enrolments.
OAC said in a statement that child safety was its highest priority, that it had a strong reporting culture and acted quickly when problems were identified.
It said more than 97 per cent of services were meeting or exceeding the standards. Services facing enforcement action were down 20 per cent.
For-profit providers still dominate
The Commonwealth has begun using its new powers against some major operators. One is Edge, which has 59 centres across Australia.
"We had very serious safety concerns about that provider," Walsh said. "Since then, we know that Goodstart Early Learning, which is a large quality not-for-profit provider, is in discussions with the administrator to take over some of those services. We're supporting them in that," she said.
Walsh said the Commonwealth had also stopped two large providers from expanding until safety concerns were addressed. One was Edge. She would not name the other.
While experts and advocates say the reforms will make child care safer, they warn they won't fix the deeper structural problems in a sector dominated by for-profit operators.
Georgie Dent, from parent advocacy group The Parenthood, says until the funding model is addressed, little will change.
"I think if we look at the money that is being spent on early education and care from taxpayers via the childcare subsidy to the tune of $16 billion a year … and you look at the out-of-pocket costs that parents are contributing, which is billions and billions of dollars, and you think for the exponential increase in investment, what are we getting?" she said.
"Are we seeing better outcomes for children? Are we seeing better access? Are we seeing better quality services? The answer is no, we're not. Not at scale, not across the board."
She says the problem is not educators or every childcare service, but a funding model that she argues creates the wrong incentives.
"It means our system is not delivering on the objectives of best meeting the needs of children and enabling parents to participate in the workforce," she said.
"Providers have set up in areas where they can charge higher fees. They are far less likely to go and set up in a regional town."
The Commonwealth is trying to change that. Its $1 billion Building Early Education Fund will support up to 160 new or expanded services, with a focus on not-for-profit provision in areas where child care is scarce.
"We do want to see more quality not-for-profit services out there and we're backing that to happen," Walsh says.
But in a sector plagued by childcare deserts, with one in four Australians living in areas where demand outstrips supply, rolling out 160 new or expanded centres will hardly make a difference.
Dent argues a much bigger shift is needed.
"Over 70 per cent of long daycare in Australia is now delivered by for-profit organisations, and that has come at the expense of not-for-profit and community organisations, notwithstanding the fact we know that not-for-profit and community services tend to have higher quality ratings," she said.
In Melbourne's north, parents are fighting to save Merrilands Uniting Early Learning, a not-for-profit long daycare centre that signalled it would close before the end of the year after three for-profit centres opened in the area since April.
"There are [now] six for-profit centres in the area and another one being built that's due to open next year," said one mother, Erica. Another mother, Etta, said one of the reasons she sent her child to Merrilands was that staff had been there for a long time.
"A lot of them [have been there] decades," she said.
"It was just full of heart. There was a lot of warmth in all the staff," said Nikolas, the father of another child.
Non-profit childcare services operate under a different model with any surplus reinvested back into the centre. They are generally cheaper for families, employ more highly qualified staff and perform better on national quality standards. But they are losing ground as for-profit child care expands.
One of the parents who sends their child to Merrilands said the difference could be as much as $70 a day.
"The financial impact is … huge," said one mother, Eman.
For Eman, however, she chose a community-run centre mainly for reasons of safety.
"For me, the deciding factor … was about the lower incident rate. I'm a survivor of child sexual abuse myself, so it was really important to find somewhere where my daughter will be safe," she said.
Walsh says safety is the priority.
"The reforms that we're making are really putting children first. We have made child safety and wellbeing the paramount consideration in early learning as it should always have been," she said.
Putting children first may now be written into law. But in a sector dominated by large for-profit operators, including private equity-backed and listed companies, ensuring children come first will not be easy.

How a shocking death led to the downfall of To Catch a Predator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Explain The Internet: How To Catch a Predator trod the line between justice and entertainment
Welcome to Explain the Internet, where we break down the noise on the World Wide Web with the help of experts.
"Why don't you take a seat right over there?"
It's a question asked by journalist Chris Hansen of dozens of men caught with their metaphorical, and in some cases literal, pants down by the news reality show To Catch a Predator.
Running from 2004 to 2007, the hidden camera show became such a cultural touchstone that it was parodied in the cold open of the 2006 Emmys, with Conan O'Brien playing the part of a distressed accused sexual predator confronted by Hansen in a rented house masquerading as a family home.
A ratings juggernaut for US network NBC, the show ended following a high-profile suicide after one of the program's sting operations.
Almost 20 years later, the program and its host are being put under the microscope by documentarian Lance Oppenheim in his directorial narrative debut, Primetime.
The 30-year-old, whose next project is the highly anticipated Nathen Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, grew up watching To Catch a Predator.
"I'd never seen anything before that had mixed truth and fiction in the way the show had. Hiring adult actors pretending to be children … these houses that would be turned into sets," Oppenheim tells ABC News.
"All of this artifice would collide with the very real high-stakes situation of getting an attempted child predator into the house.
"There was something so odd about the mixture of real-life horror with this sort of surrealist absurdity that came from Hansen."
What is To Catch a Predator?
To Catch a Predator premiered in 2004, originally as a part of NBC's Dateline news program.
A typical segment would include production working with private investigation organisation Perverted-Justice, whose volunteer decoys would pose as children to chat with potential predators.
The decoys would then invite them to a house leased by production with the promise of meeting and sexual activity. After being initially greeted by hired actors playing tweens, Hansen would emerge, questioning the men and revealing the hidden cameras. The men would then be allowed to leave, only to be arrested by local law enforcement. All of which was recorded and broadcast.
To Catch a Predator soon outgrew Dateline, with episodes featuring the segment attracting 13 per cent more audience than those without. By 2006, the show was moved to its own prime time slot on US television, directly competing with ratings juggernaut Lost. This is also around the time To Catch a Predator brought law enforcement officers into the co-ordination of the stings.
Men caught by the program included firefighters, teachers, religious and government workers.
In 2006, a To Catch a Predator sting in Murphy, Texas netted 25 arrests from men arriving at their decoy house. Perverted-Justice volunteers had one more man marked, soon revealed to be local assistant district attorney Louis William "Bill" Conradt.
Production was unable to lure Conradt to their Murphy house, so in coordination with local law enforcement, the decision was made to confront Conradt at his home. After a multi-hour sting, local police sent in a SWAT team to arrest Conradt, who killed himself.
Following the incident, legal issues were found with all arrests made in Murphy, including insufficient evidence and lack of active warrants. In June 2007, a Texas district attorney refused to prosecute any of the 24 men arrested in the sting.
A month later, Conradt's sister brought a $US109 million wrongful death lawsuit against NBC Universal. Although the network initially announced to be fighting the claims, in June 2008 the suit was "amicably resolved" with an undisclosed settlement amount.
To Catch a Predator was cancelled shortly after.
What is Primetime about?
Primetime chronicles the period of time leading up to Conradt's death, loosely based on the 2007 Esquire article Tonight On Dateline, This Man Will Die.
Some characters, like Robert Pattinson's Chris Hansen and Perverted-Justice founder Xavier Von Erck (Matthew Maher), are based on real people. Some, like Merritt Wever's stern producer and Skyler Gisondo's starry-eyed "Decoy Dan" are an amalgamation of several real people involved in the story.
And some like Jeff Zucker, the former NBC Universal CEO who moved To Catch a Predator into its prime-time slot to compete with Lost, simply play themselves.
"I liked this idea of being able to mix truth and fiction in a way that almost was an homage to the show and the way the show created almost this reality-distortion field," Oppenheim says.
"When people would enter it, they would no longer be a part of the world we all exist in. They were a part of Chris Hansen's world."
Oppenheim paid particular care to the characters playing "predators": young men; older men; a rabbi who demands to know who gave Hansen permission to conduct the sting; a man with cerebral palsy.
"It was interesting to present the predators in a similar way to how Chris Hansen would experience it, to how his crew would experience it," Oppenheim says.
"The attempt to sort of deny any form of humanity to these people and see them as almost a form, a token of entertainment. They almost became commercial objects in this sort of space race against Lost."
How to keep children safe
Hansen has condemned Primetime as "detached from reality", going so far as to buy ad space before US screenings to promote his streaming service TruBlu, where he still conducts predator investigations.
In Australia, child safety in online spaces remains an issue, with a 2025 eSafety report revealing one in four girls experience online sexual solicitation by an adult before they turn 18.
Cybersecurity and privacy expert Joel Scanlan is the academic co-lead of the CSAM Deterrence Centre, working with the technology industry and other stakeholders to prevent the access and sharing of child sexual abuse material (CSAM).
"To Catch a Predator did raise awareness of this harm occurring, and that is great, because the awareness of the level of harm that's occurring online is actually pretty low," Scanlan says.
"However, it is doing it for entertainment. The motivations aren't there. So many of those cases got thrown out or overturned. What if it had just been law enforcement in the first place and not all those other elements?"
Scanlan says there needs to be a "generational shift" in how we view online safety for children and that the solution lies in robust prevention, including education, deterrence messages, legislation like Australia's social media delay and higher expectations of online companies.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $23.6 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial.
"To stop this kind of crime that's happening at this large a scale, we need five or 10 different approaches as there is no quick fix," he says.
Scanlan points towards the Stop It Now! Australia program, Australia's first national child sexual abuse offending prevention service, as an effective tool for harm prevention.
Launched locally in 2022 by Jesuit Social Services, the program includes a free phone helpline and resources for anyone concerned about their own sexual thoughts or behaviours toward children, or about the behaviour of someone else.
The program received federal funding in April 2026 as a part of the National Strategy to Prevent and Respond to Child Sexual Abuse 2021-2030.
"People ask, 'Why are you sympathising with them?' But I do work in this space. I see the horrific scale of the problem. We need to have less harm happen," Scanlan says.
"If that means we need to get people in therapy, let's do it. That's it. That's literally abuse prevention."
Primetime will be in Australian cinemas from October 29.

Why a big discount during Black Friday sales isn't necessarily a great deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Why a big discount during Black Friday sales isn’t necessarily a great deal
This year Black Friday falls on Friday, November 27.
Cyber Monday, which typically marks the end of the sale period, is on November 30.
It is becoming hard to miss in Australia, with competing offers vying for our attention in emails, texts, app notifications and shop windows.
Black Friday sales originated in the United States as a way for retailers to make money after Thanksgiving Day, says Sara Quach Thaichon, an associate professor in marketing at Griffith University on the Gold Coast/Yugambeh language region.
But it has now become part of the Australian retail calendar and November is "almost a whole sale season" with deals beginning weeks in advance, Dr Thaichon says.
You can expect retailers to promote offers of "up to 50 per cent off" and "up to 70 per cent off", but most discounts fall closer to 20 or 30 per cent off, she says.
Mark Serrels, the editorial director at consumer group Choice on Gadigal land in Sydney, says the Black Friday "behemoth" is expanding every year.
But before tapping a card or clicking "buy", Mr Serrels and Dr Thaichon recommend considering the value of the purchase to you, its quality and how much you're spending — rather than just how much you are saving.
Why percentage discounts can be deceiving
While there are savings to be made, Mr Serrels says, there are "a million different ways retailers are using Black Friday to their advantage".
"[For example], they're trying to get rid of stock. They're trying to get rid of older models. They're trying to get you hooked into giving your details so they can reach out and sell more things down the line."
Sometimes products are advertised as 50 per cent off the recommended retail price (RRP) during a promotion period, but it might normally be 40 per cent off anyway.
"You've got to be wary of those markdowns," Mr Serrels says.
Dr Thaichon says the percentage discount can make us feel like we've scored a bargain but "doesn't actually tell us whether the final price is good".
If it's an inferior product or something you simply don't need, you've wasted money buying it, even if it was 70 per cent off, she says.
Mr Serrels says that an expensive pre-sale RPP price does not equate to quality.
"Sometimes you might think, 'oh great, that TV is 50 per cent off', but it's a shit TV, so don't buy it," he says.
"We've had coffee machines that cost $200 that outperformed $2,000 [machines in testing]."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
Finding a good deal
Dr Thaichon recommends focusing on how much you're spending and what you're getting for that money.
"Instead of looking at percentage, compare the final price across different retailers, think about the quality of the product, how long it will last and how often [you will] actually use it," she says.
Research the product and compare prices before sales begin, particularly when it comes to white goods and electronics, Dr Thaichon says.
When we don't know much about "big ticket" products we tend to use price as an indicator of quality, she says.
Electronics and appliances tend to be the "most heavily promoted categories", Dr Thaichon says, and major retailers have previously offered discounts of as much as 70 per cent off on some specific products.
Mr Serrels says you should decide on the exact product you want to buy — such as the model of TV — beforehand.
This gives you the opportunity to check reviews and the product's historical pricing.
Recognising scams
Slowing down is "key", Dr Thaichon says.
Mr Serrels says to try to avoid the influence of time pressure when shopping during sales, such as "you've got four minutes to complete this transaction" or "this sale only lasts for 12 hours".
"Worst case scenario it's a scam. Best case scenario you're getting bullied into buying something you're not really 100 per cent sure you actually need."
A spokesperson for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission's Moneysmart program says to check who you are buying from.
"With an unfamiliar online retailer, look for independent reviews and make sure you are using the genuine website rather than a look-alike site," they say.
How to prepare and shop during Black Friday
Ahead of Black Friday, Moneysmart also suggests:
- Making a list before you start shopping
- Setting a spending limit
- Shopping around and comparing prices
- Checking the full cost of an item, factoring in additional costs such as delivery and international transaction fees.
- Being careful with buy now, pay later services and making sure you can afford repayments
Mr Serrels cautions against embracing sales with unbridled "consumer lust".
"Don't feel like you have to buy [a product] right now. There's always another sale around the corner," he says.

Trump faces private citizens lawsuit over limiting White House media access
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:29:26 UTC
03:29:26 KST

Trump faces private citizens lawsuit over limiting White House media access
The plaintiffs argue they are losing access to vital information media outlets covering Trump used to provide.
A group of private citizens has sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over its restrictions on news outlets covering the White House.
“All of the Plaintiffs rely on the White House press corps for independent reporting about the president and his administration, and all of them use that reporting in a variety of ways in their scholarship, teaching, journalism, or advocacy,” says the lawsuit, filed on Monday in a federal court in New York.
The lawsuit is the first lodged not by the news outlets being banned, but by those who consume the news and rely on it for their work.
The plaintiffs include a human rights advocate, a media watchdog, a university history professor, a high school teacher, a legal journalist and a student journalist.
Each argues they need unbiased, diverse media reporting from the White House to do their work.
“I’m gravely concerned that the Trump administration’s restrictions on White House reporters are cutting off access to crucial information,” Peter Schmidt-Nowara, a high school social studies teacher in New York City, said in a statement.
“I joined this lawsuit because my students deserve to know what’s happening in their government and to hear from a free and independent press.”
Trump already faces several legal challenges to his practice of banning journalists from outlets he dislikes from accessing the White House.
Last month, he banned journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from attending news conferences at the White House. A federal judge later ruled the order was unconstitutional, a violation of the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press, and ordered access be restored. However, the Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.
Last week, Trump dismissed reporting that he planned to evict journalists from the White House press briefing room and restore a swimming pool that was housed there starting in 1933. But he said he is still considering moving the press out of the briefing room.
“I am thinking about moving the Press, and putting them in a different location, but I will use that location for very badly needed space,” Trump said in a social media post.
Kenneth Roth, a senior fellow at Yale University and former executive director of Human Rights Watch, said the restrictions on press access were familiar postmarks in countries whose leaders have become authoritarian.
“Worldwide, I have seen how governmental leaders’ efforts to penalise independent journalists are a prelude to the rise of autocracy,” he said in a statement.

"Today's decisions confirm the EU's continued firm and unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders in the face of Russia's war of aggression," the EU Council said.

Przemyśl suspended its partnership with Lviv over a decision concerning the UPA
Kyiv • UNN
Przemyśl suspended cooperation with Lviv over the decision to declare 2027 the Year of the UPA, Shukhevych, and Olzhych. It may be restored after the decision is revoked.
The city council of Przemyśl, Poland, unanimously decided to suspend its partnership cooperation with Lviv, which had continued since 1995. The city’s mayor, Wojciech Bakun, announced this, UNN reports.
Details
The reason was the decision by the Lviv Regional Council to proclaim 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), Roman Shukhevych and Oleh Olzhych.
According to Bakun, after an extended discussion, the councillors agreed that joint activities with Lviv should be suspended until a clear position is received from the city authorities regarding the commemoration of historical figures and organizations whose activities are considered anti-Polish in Poland.
As PAP reports, Przemyśl councillors recognized that the decision of the Lviv Regional Council of October 20 insults the memory of Polish victims of crimes committed by the UPA and contradicts the establishment of relations based on historical truth and mutual respect.
The resolution obliges Przemyśl Mayor Wojciech Bakun to take legal measures aimed at terminating the 1995 cooperation agreement.
At the same time, it stipulates that cooperation between the cities will be restored if the Lviv Regional Council finally cancels or officially withdraws the resolution and the Lviv authorities clearly distance themselves from initiatives that "glorify structures responsible for crimes against the civilian population."
The mayor must inform Lviv’s local authorities of this position and provide the Przemyśl city councilors with information about the measures taken and the deadline for terminating the agreement.
"After a lengthy discussion of this issue, all the councillors unanimously decided that until the Lviv authorities clearly determine their position on promoting ideologies directed against Poland and Poles, we are suspending all joint activities. For my part, I thank the councillors for this position and for demonstrating that we will not remain indifferent to provocative and anti-Polish actions!" Bakun wrote.

MFA on UN Commission of Inquiry's report: As another winter approaches, these findings particularly important
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
20:06:26 EET
03:06:26 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA) welcomes the presentation of the report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on violations in Ukraine to the Third Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
"Ukraine highly values the independent and impartial work of the Commission, which consistently documents violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law. The Commission is establishing the circumstances of international crimes and gathering evidence to hold those responsible to account," the MFA said in a statement.
The ministry said the Commission's findings regarding Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure are of particular importance. The Commission has recognized such targeted attacks as war crimes, and the large-scale and systematic strikes that caused severe suffering to civilians as crimes against humanity.
Indeed, the Commission established that for over four years, Russian strikes on energy infrastructure deprived millions of Ukrainians of electricity, heat, and water.
"Of fundamental importance is the Commission's conclusion that these attacks were intentional and consistent with the state policy of the Russian Federation. The aim of this policy was to deprive civilians of vital energy supplies and to inflict suffering upon them. Russia has deliberately turned cold and darkness into weapons against Ukrainian civilians. As winter approaches, these findings are particularly important. They serve as a reminder to the international community that Russia continues to systematically destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We cannot allow the lives of millions of people to be threatened once again by cold and darkness," the MFA said.
The statement notes that the Commission's findings regarding how Russia recruits citizens of other states into its armed forces through deception and coercion warrant the strongest possible international response. The Commission found evidence of such practices involving citizens of 29 countries and classified the actions of the Russian authorities as human trafficking. People were lured to Russia with false promises of work and sent to fight in the war against Ukraine. Many of them were killed, wounded, or went missing.
"We call on the states whose citizens have been victimized by these criminal practices to strengthen cooperation in order to dismantle the recruitment networks and hold those responsible to account. We believe that the Commission's findings should be used to ensure that accountability for international crimes committed during Russia's aggression against Ukraine becomes inevitable," the statement reads.
The MFA also called on the international community to strengthen its support for Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, and to facilitate the effective investigation of crimes and the prosecution of those responsible.
"Behind every documented crime lie human lives and destinies. These crimes cannot go unpunished. Justice and accountability are essential conditions for a just and lasting peace," the ministry said.
Earlier, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine stated in its new report to the UN General Assembly that Russian authorities committed war crimes by deliberately targeting civilian objects, as well as crimes against humanity in the form of other inhumane acts, by carrying out continuous attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The Commission also concluded that Russian authorities recruited men who were victims of human trafficking in various countries into their armed forces, which constitutes a violation of international human rights law.
The Commission investigated the impact of the Russian armed forces' large-scale attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure on the civilian population, particularly during the difficult winter of 2025-2026, as well as the cumulative effects of these attacks since the fall of 2022.
