Russia has fallen from third to fourth place among the world’s largest exporters of non-coking coal, according to data from analytics firm BigMint. From January through September 2026, Russian exports in the category fell by 18.6% to 42.5 million metric tons, the steepest decline among large suppliers.
Russia ceded third place to South Africa, which increased shipments by 8% to 52.1 million metric tons. Based on BigMint’s published figures, The Insider calculated that Russian shipments fell by about 9.7 million metric tons from the same period in 2025.
Overall, global trade in non-coking coal declined by 3.2% to 602.5 million metric tons, a drop of about 19.9 million metric tons. That means the decline in Russian exports accounted for roughly 49% of the overall contraction in global trade in the category as tracked by BigMint. Russia’s share of that market fell from about 8.4% to 7.1%.
Indonesia remained the world’s largest exporter despite a 10% decline in shipments that lowered its output to 240.3 million metric tons. Australia ranked second after increasing exports by 2% to 151.2 million metric tons.
Among major suppliers, Mongolia recorded the strongest growth, with exports rising 73% to 24 million metric tons.
The biggest declines in Russian exports were to China and Turkey. Shipments to Turkey fell 32% to 15.7 million metric tons, while exports to China dropped 26% to 15.1 million metric tons.
India was the only major destination in where Russian companies managed to increase sales, rising by 63% to 9.6 million metric tons and surpassing the 7.4 million metric tons Russia shipped to India during all of 2025.
Analysts interviewed by the Kremlin-aligned newspaper Kommersant attributed the decline in Russian exports to weaker demand for power-station coal in Turkey, high fuel inventories in China, and growing competition from Mongolia. Russian suppliers also face additional pressure from the cost of rail transportation, shipping, and vessel insurance. Companies were able to increase sales in India by offering discounts, analysts said, although higher logistics costs could make Russian coal less attractive in that market as well.
BigMint’s figures should not, however, be treated as a measure of Russia’s entire coal export sector. According to data from Kpler, Russian seaborne exports of all types of coal rose 7.25% from January through September, reaching 135.86 million metric tons.
The two estimates cover different product categories and use different methodologies.
Nearly two-thirds of Russian coal companies are unprofitable
The deterioration in Russian exporters’ position comes amid a prolonged crisis in the country’s coal industry. According to official data from Russia’s state statistics agency Rosstat, coal-mining companies posted a combined net loss of 178.2 billion rubles ($2.2 billion) from January through July 2026. Profitable companies earned 45 billion rubles ($556.9 million), while total losses among the rest reached 223.2 billion rubles ($2.8 billion). Overall, 64.5% of companies in the sector were unprofitable.
The situation is particularly severe in Kuzbass, Russia’s largest coal-producing region. According to data from the regional Coal Industry Ministry, 20 of the region’s 93 underground mines and open-pit operations were not operating as of August 2026. Employment in the coal sector fell from 103,000 to 97,300 workers over the course of a year.
Russia’s Energy Ministry, however, says the industry has passed the worst stage of the crisis. Deputy Energy Minister Dmitry Islamov said recently that prices had begun to recover, although the situation remained difficult. The ministry estimates that the industry’s losses for all of 2026 will be as high as 310 billion rubles ($3.8 billion).
As The Insider previously reported, among suppliers to the Chinese market Russia fell from second to third after being displaced by Mongolia. In August, Mongolia exported 9.81 million metric tons of coal to China, compared with Russia’s 9.2 million metric tons.
Experts cited Chinese import duties of 3% to 6% on Russian coal — tariffs from which Russia’s main competitors are exempt — as well as rising transportation costs as being among the reasons for Russia’s declining position.
In June, The Insider also reported on a Green Think Tank study that concluded redirecting exports to China had failed to compensate Russian coal companies for the loss of the European market. The initiative’s researchers estimated that the industry’s combined financial losses during the years of the full-scale war exceeded 2.5 trillion rubles ($30.9 billion). For Russian coal companies, maintaining export volumes has become increasingly dependent on government benefits, tax deferrals, and state support for rail transportation, rather than on actual market mechanisms.

03:04:41 KST

NEW DELHI: In a major relief for local commuters, residents living within 20 km of a National Highway toll plaza can now opt for an annual concessional pass costing Rs 1,500 for plazas located outside municipal or local town limits and Rs 3,000 for those within such limits. Currently, eligible residents can obtain a monthly pass for Rs 360, amounting to Rs 4,320 annually.Road transport ministry notified the changes to NH Fee Rules on Monday. Under the provision, vehicle owners with valid and functional FASTags registered for personal use can choose either the existing monthly pass or the new concessional local pass for commuting through the specific toll plaza.
Govt will revise these rates every year on April 1. As per the notification, the concession will be applicable only to the specific toll plaza and will not be transferable for use at other plazas. However, the pass will not be issued for NHs or expressways where toll is collected under a closed user fee collection system.The rules also make the concession conditional on the non-availability of a service road or alternative road for the vehicle owner or driver. This means residents will not be eligible for the concessional pass if such an alternative route is available for their use .

Israel enters election silence period ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:49 UTC
02:56:49 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel entered an election silence period Monday ahead of Tuesday's parliamentary elections, with restrictions on campaign activities taking effect at 7 pm local time (1700GMT), an Anadolu correspondent reported.
Under Article 129 of the Knesset Elections Law, campaigning at gatherings and marches, through loudspeakers, and on radio and television is prohibited from 7 pm on the eve of the election and throughout polling day, according to the Knesset's official website.
Most polling stations will open at 7 am (0500GMT) Tuesday and close at 10 pm (2000GMT). In communities with no more than 350 eligible voters, voting will take place from 8 am (0600GMT) to 8 pm (1800GMT).
Vote counting will begin after polling stations close at 10 pm, when Israeli media outlets are also expected to release exit poll results, according to Israel's Channel 12.
Under Article 11 of the Basic Law: The Knesset, the Central Elections Committee has eight days after election day to publish the official results in the official gazette, setting a deadline of Nov. 4.
 
More than 7.3 million eligible voters
A total of 37 parties and electoral alliances are contesting seats in the 120-member Knesset, with 13 projected to secure parliamentary representation.
The main contenders include Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and Yashar, which is contesting its first election under former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Opinion polls suggest Yashar could emerge as the largest party, challenging years of Likud dominance.
According to the Central Elections Committee, 7,331,981 Israelis are eligible to vote in elections for the 26th Knesset.
Voting will take place at 12,018 polling stations, with approximately 18,000 ballot boxes deployed nationwide and around 100,000 personnel working on election day.
Of the polling stations, 6,209 will be accessible to people with disabilities.
Twenty regional election committees will oversee preparations and voting operations in their respective jurisdictions.
To facilitate access to polling stations, 660 intercity public transport routes and all Israel Railways services will operate free of charge on election day, according to the committee.
 
Netanyahu faces challenge from Eisenkot
Forming a government requires the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset.
The previous Knesset dissolved on July 17, paving the way for the Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has led the current government since December 2022, heading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel's history.
He is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
The International Criminal Court has also issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu over war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:56:31 UTC
02:56:31 KST

Paralelo Transversal organises Chilean house under cantilever roof
Chilean studio Paralelo Transversal has designed a rectangular house with a large hip roof and a terrace that cantilevers over a ravine in Puerto Varas, Chile.
Completed in 2025 on a 1.2-acre site near Lago Llanquihue, the 155-square-metre house, known as Casa Ensenada, was oriented around its roof.
“In southern Chile, rain is not an exception but part of everyday life, so we wanted the roof to become more than a protective element,” architect Sebastián Silva of Paralelo Transversal told Dezeen.
“It creates a place beneath the rain, extending daily life beyond the enclosed rooms while bringing the different parts of the project together under one continuous gesture.”
The roof serves as the organising element for the program, circulation, relationship to the landscape and the home’s structure.
“Its section thickens toward the center while remaining remarkably thin at its perimeter,” Silva said.
“This allows it to be perceived as a light, continuous sheet while providing the structural depth required for long-span trusses capable of resisting both Chile’s seismic conditions and the strong winds of Patagonia.”
The house sits on a sloped site with a stream. Residents and visitors approach along the stream before the access ramp turns towards the house, where they enter at the junction of public and private zones.
The narrower side of the plan contains a large, open kitchen, dining and living room that bleeds onto the cantilevered terrace.
Oriented toward the northeast to capture winter sunlight, the house opens its living spaces to the landscape – the valley of Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park on one side and Calbuco Volcano on the other – through floor-to-ceiling windows with thin black frames.
The other side of the house widens to hold three suites. On either side of the house, the perimeter wall pushes under the roof canopy to form a covered bench and a planted garden.
The warm, contemporary material palette continues across the exterior and interior with exposed concrete slabs, large spans of glazing, tongue-and-groove timber and standing-seam metal roofing.
The concealed joints allowed the roof to be precise while reducing the visual impact of construction tolerances. The team collaborated closely with engineers and local builders to achieve its long spans and thin edge.
“Looking back, we believe the project fulfilled its original ambition of integrating architecture and landscape without compromising comfort, construction logic or budget,” Silva said.
“More importantly, it reinforced our belief that a project becomes stronger when one clear architectural idea is capable of organizing structure, climate, materiality and space simultaneously.”
Previously, Paralelo Transversal created a sail-like skylight that brought sun, shadows and air into a home on the outskirts of Santiago.
Other homes recently completed in Chile include a mass timber forest hideaway by Iragüen Viñuela Arquitectos and a seaside home with stacked terraces by Croxatto and Opazo Architects.

How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:59 UTC
02:55:59 KST

Ricardo Contreras’s new leg rests on a wooden countertop.
More than four months after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the 24-year-old is still recovering from his injuries.
When he was trapped beneath the rubble on the night of June 24, he waited hours to be rescued. His left leg had been pinned beneath a fallen door frame, limiting its blood circulation. It had to be amputated.
“One of the biggest achievements is that we survived,” Ricardo said, glancing towards his 16-year-old brother, Andres Contreras. “At first, when I found out Andres was well, I didn’t care about my leg too much. I would have chosen a thousand times over for Andres to be OK.”
But now Ricardo is adapting to his new reality.
He and his brother are still undergoing physiotherapy for their injuries. On a scorching afternoon, he sits in a small workshop in the hills of northwestern Caracas, waiting to do rehabilitation exercises to prepare for his new prosthetic leg.
“Now it’s about regaining a little of the independence I had before the earthquake, because that’s what limits me most," Ricardo said.
But recovery is only part of the challenge he is facing. His parents died in the collapse.
Resources and aid have also grown scarcer, particularly as global attention faded and international donations dried up.
As of September, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said it had secured only $29.5m of the $65.7m needed to continue its earthquake support in Venezuela, a shortfall of 55 percent.
Separately, that same month, the International Red Cross said its Venezuela response effort was only 39.8 percent funded.
Not only are survivors like Contreras left to grapple with loss of limbs and family members, but they now face the prospect of lifelong health costs — with dwindling support.
From rescue to recovery
More than 6,500 people have been confirmed dead as a result of the earthquakes, according to government authorities.
At least 226,696 people have received hospital treatment for injuries. The government says it has compiled a census of amputees, but no details have been made public.
At Ortoprotecnica, a Caracas workshop that makes prosthetic limbs, director Bianca Damaso is helping survivors like Ricardo through the next stages of recovery.
For those who have lost limbs, it typically takes two to three months of physiotherapy, rehabilitation and preparation to be ready for a prosthesis — sometimes longer depending on how their wounds heal and any pre-existing health conditions.
“It’s a very individual process where you have to support each person from where they are, because some are very anxious to have the prosthesis already, but their skin hasn’t even healed yet,” Damaso explained.
She said there are more than 100 types of knees to choose from, as well as more than 200 skin shades.
But the process does not end with the first fitting. Children may need five or six replacement prostheses as they grow, while adults might require ongoing adjustments and repairs.
Then there are the psychological hurdles. Many earthquake survivors wonder about practical realities like whether they will walk again, whether they will need a wheelchair or whether they will be able to urinate independently.
Many, in Damaso's experience, also question whether they will find a partner who will love them.
"Right now, the challenges for them are going to be more than just physical. They’re mental battles," Damaso said.
There is one rule she is adamant about in her workshop: “We tell them that the only thing that’s forbidden here is saying, ‘I can’t.’”
Karina Bechara, who lost both her legs in the earthquakes, is hoping to stand on her new feet by December 1. For now, she relies on a wheelchair.
“That motivates me every morning to get up and say, 'One day less to go.' It's painful, yes, but we're getting closer to the goal,” Bechara told Al Jazeera.
Before the earthquake, Bechara ran her own business and had an active life, training regularly with high-intensity CrossFit workouts. Her children saw her as an independent mother who did not depend on anyone.
“Now I am the opposite, a mum who needs their help, a dependent mum,” Bechara said.
After the earthquakes struck, Bechara was stuck in the rubble for 23 hours, immobilised by a piece of heavy furniture that crushed her legs.
She describes her recovery as an “emotional rollercoaster”. She said she allows herself to cry on the harder days but tries to keep looking ahead.
“Because if I don’t see the future for myself, no one else will.”
More than just limbs
But readjusting to routines can be difficult for those who have sustained life-altering injuries — not to mention other losses.
So far, Ricardo is optimistic about his daily activities. He has resumed work at his family's truck parts business, as well as his university studies. A new semester of classes has started, and he uses crutches to get around.
“I was really quite nervous. I was even worried about where the classes will be because we have three floors and also the distances are long,” Ricardo said.
But his concerns quickly melted away. The professors even moved his lessons to ground-floor classrooms to make the courses more accessible.
“It was actually great going back," Ricardo explained. "My classmates have always been there, helping me.”
The most difficult adjustment, however, has been grappling with the loss of loved ones.
“If my leg hurts, I take a pill, but with that, there’s nothing I can do. There’s no cure, there’s no remedy, there’s nothing,” Ricardo told Al Jazeera.
His mum and dad both died from suffocation during the earthquakes while the family was waiting to be rescued. Their building was one of dozens in the state of La Guaira to collapse.
“I fell in the bathroom hugging my mother, and Andres fell near my father. She was telling me she was fine, but I saw that her head was covered with concrete, with a wall on top, and dust,” Ricardo said.
Before the earthquakes, he remembers his mother cooking, singing and spoiling the family dog, who also died in the destruction. He credits his father with teaching him and Andres the value of work and the importance of being strong.
The brothers often look through photographs of their parents on their phones. One shows their family home, overlooking the sea. Another has them by the pool.
“As time goes on, the crying is the same, but the reason is different. Instead of crying so much from sadness, it's more like remembering the good times,” Ricardo said.
Following his parents' death, Ricardo has taken on additional responsibilities beyond school and work.
He is now Andres's legal guardian, and he is hoping the pair can soon find a home of their own through a government housing programme for earthquake victims.
His university has also offered him a full scholarship to finish his studies, to help relieve the financial burden.
Money, however, is still expected to be tight. The average salary for a private-sector worker in Venezuela is not much more than $200 a month.
“Of course, I'm worried about my financial situation,” Ricardo said, explaining the family business has slowed since the earthquakes.
“Sometimes it's hard to cover all the expenses, given everything that's happened, but we find a way. I think that's what Venezuelans do: We’re always finding a way to make things work.”
The cost of recovery
The Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation, a Venezuelan nonprofit, is among the groups helping earthquake amputees. Its founder and namesake, Dos Santos, lost his legs in a car accident in 2019.
He remembers realising the scale of June's tragedy when, at the first hospital he visited, he encountered a ward with 12 children. All of them had either lost limbs or were facing amputation.
“It's very difficult for everyone in general but especially for children, who suddenly lost so much. They lost family members, their homes, their schools, their abilities, and on top of that, they're missing a part of their body,” he told Al Jazeera.
One of his priorities was to show them what their lives could look like after amputation, telling them of his own achievements as an athlete and model.
But alongside the physical and psychological challenges, he knew they would face another obstacle: the cost of prosthetics.
“A prosthesis for a below-knee amputation, which is a transtibial prosthesis, can cost between $3,000 and $5,000," Dos Santos said. "And a prosthesis for an above-knee amputation can cost between $7,000 and $12,000."
The price tag for artificial limbs with electronic components — that react to the body's muscles — can stretch even higher, into the tens of thousands of dollars.
Even before the earthquake, the foundation had a waiting list of hundreds of people who needed a prosthetic limb but could not afford one.
After the seismic disaster, some 200 people were added to its database, Dos Santos said.
He explained that the foundation focuses on functional prostheses rather than the most expensive technology, partly because patients also need to be able to afford adjustments, repairs and replacements.
For many families, the cost is simply beyond reach.
The foundation is now planning to set up a specialist orthotics and prosthetics centre in Venezuela, which it says is essential to provide ongoing support for amputees.
Navigating the healthcare system
Medical professionals also see continued care as fundamental to recovery.
“For patients who suffered serious injuries or amputations, being saved and discharged from hospital is only the beginning. The recovery can be long, and that’s where we encounter many limitations,” Ana Rosario, the president of the Caracas Nurses Association, told Al Jazeera.
She said the earthquake compounded problems in Venezuela’s health system, which was weakened by years of economic crisis.
There are often too few nurses for the number of patients. Hospitals sometimes relied on supplies donated by citizens and organisations to help meet their needs.
“Although healthcare is technically free, patients may still have to pay for medicines, medical supplies, tests, transport and rehabilitation,” Rosario said. “And these are costs that can continue for months.”
For families who cannot afford them, the consequences can be serious.
“We see it every day: Families ask for help through social media, look for donations, go into debt, or simply have to wait,” she said. “When a test, medication or procedure is delayed, recovery can also be delayed, and new complications can arise.”
For survivors like Ricardo, private donations through organisations such as the Juan Pablo Dos Santos Foundation are helping pay for prosthetic limbs and rehabilitation.
“A few days ago, I saw my leg being made, and that got me really excited,” Ricardo said.
Though Ricardo is his guardian, Andres explained they help care for one another as they each recover from their injuries.
“Just getting out of the wheelchair was already a big step," Andres said of his brother. "He’s getting better every day. Honestly, it makes me so happy that he’ll be able to walk again."
The brothers attend physiotherapy sessions together, with Andres encouraging his older brother as he learns to walk again.
“My brother makes me feel like a world champion,” Ricardo said, laughing as his younger brother breaks into a smile.

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:55:47 UTC
02:55:47 KST

Algeria’s president orders troop deployment to neighbouring Niger
Niger requested troops to secure shared energy interests in what would be Algeria’s first deployment abroad since 1973.
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy and economic interests shared by both countries.
The decision, announced by Algeria’s presidency on Monday, came after both chambers of parliament approved the deployment in an emergency session on Sunday.
The presidency said authorities in Niger had requested military assistance.
If carried out, it would be Algeria’s first overseas military deployment since 1973, when it sent soldiers to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.
The move marks a departure from Algeria’s longstanding reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
A 2020 constitutional reform allows the president to authorise overseas deployments with the approval of at least two-thirds of legislators in each parliamentary chamber.
Algeria sent fighter jets and support aircraft to Niger in August after what Algerian officials described as an attempt to destabilise its military government.
The presidency said the deployment decision was made under provisions of Algeria’s constitution allowing the military to operate abroad with parliamentary approval.
It has not been announced how many soldiers will be sent or when.
Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after Sunday’s parliamentary vote that the soldiers would protect economic infrastructure, particularly Algerian oil facilities in Niger.
He said Algeria was “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, describing the mission as a response to changing security conditions in the Sahel region.
Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach, has been working with Niger on the proposed Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline. It would carry natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria for export to European markets.
Niger and neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso have faced years of attacks by armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).
All three countries are governed by military leaders who seized power in coups and subsequently formed the Alliance of Sahel States, a regional political and security bloc.
The deployment follows an improvement in relations between Algeria and Niger, which has been led by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a 2023 military coup that Algeria initially condemned.
Tensions deepened in April last year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border, prompting the three alliance members to recall their ambassadors from Algiers.

Breadcrumb
Oil spill off UAE widens, satellite images show, prompting more beach closures
Satellite images show that an oil spill from a damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns.
Images from the European Union's Copernicus satellite observation network dated 24 October show the oil spill has widened over the last few days and is nearing the shores of northern Umm Al Quwain emirate, with dark layers of oil spreading at sea and along the coastline.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy think tank.
The UAE said on Friday that it was working to contain oil leaking from an offshore tanker, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill came from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished.
Images from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker.
Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas.
The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that it temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain, while authorities in neighbouring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution.
"The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed," Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi's Water Research Centre, told Reuters.
In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that they would close all beaches in the emirate until further notice.
The UAE's marine life "is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters," including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website.

02:53:48 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has published a resolution on updating the organization of deferments from conscription for those liable for military service during the period of mobilization and under martial law.
Specifically, in accordance with Resolution No. 1328 dated October 23, central executive authorities, other state bodies, public administration entities with jurisdiction covering the entire territory of Ukraine, as well as regional and Kyiv city state administrations (or military administrations, where established), are required within ten days of the resolution’s entry into force to ensure the review and harmonization of the criteria used to designate enterprises, institutions, and organizations as "critically important" for the functioning of the economy.
Following this review, an analysis must be conducted to determine whether enterprises still meet these criteria. If a criterion—on the basis of which an enterprise was originally designated as "critically important"—is removed, the decision designating that enterprise as "critically important" must be revoked.
The Government has established that decisions designating enterprises as "critically important"—in effect as of the date this resolution enters into force—shall remain valid for the duration for which they were originally issued, unless they have since been revoked.
It is noted that decisions by the Minister of Defense to increase the quotas for the deferment from military service ("reservation") of liable individual, adopted prior to the entry into force of Resolution No. 1608, shall remain in effect for the entire duration of the enterprise’s designation as "critically important," but no later than December 8, 2026. Decisions by the Ministry of Defense to increase such quotas, adopted after December 8, 2025, shall remain in effect for the duration of the enterprise’s "critically important" status, but not beyond the specific timeframe stipulated in the relevant Ministry decision.
Furthermore, the Cabinet of Ministers has established a Coordination Center for the organization of the deferment from military service for liable individuals during periods of mobilization and wartime.
Enterprises may be designated as "critically important" to the functioning of the economy and the provision of essential services to the population during special periods if they operate within the following sectors: the defense-industrial complex; the fuel and energy complex; housing and utility services; the extractive industry; the manufacturing (processing) industry; the agro-industrial sector (including the assurance of food security); retail trade; construction; transport and logistics; information technology; banking; healthcare; and communications. This also applies to entities engaged in emergency rescue and other urgent operations (emergency rescue services), as well as those operating in sectors approved by the Coordination Center, following a substantiated request from a central executive body or another state authority responsible for developing and/or implementing state policy in the relevant field. It has been established that the number of individuals liable for military service who are eligible for deferment (exemption from mobilization) may exceed 50%, subject to the recommendations and proposals of the Coordination Center.
Substantiated proposals to increase the number of deferments are to be submitted to the Coordination Center by the relevant government authority. Grounds for the Coordination Center to refuse to consider such proposals include, among other things, the documented, systematic violation of legal requirements regarding the organization and maintenance of military registration by the head of a critical institution, specifically, the occurrence of two or more such documented violations within the preceding 12 months, and/or the imposition of administrative liability upon the head for committing such violations.
Furthermore, it is established that for individuals liable for military service who hold positions within the representative offices of donor institutions or with entities implementing international technical assistance projects, the number of those eligible for deferment shall not exceed 50% of the total number of such employees directly engaged in the tasks of a single project, and in any case, shall not exceed 7 individuals.
Pursuant to a decision by the State Secretary of the Cabinet of Ministers, made in light of the Coordination Center’s recommendations, the number of individuals eligible for deferment may exceed 7, provided it does not exceed 50% of the total number of employees liable for military service.
For critical institutions, defined by the Ministry of Defense as critical within the defense-industrial complex, the fuel and energy sector (including their contractors), or as domestic manufacturers of transformer equipment for the energy sector, the number of employees liable for military service, who are eligible for deferment, may reach up to 95%. This applies to entities engaged in the construction, repair, restoration, manufacturing, and/or supply of equipment, the provision of services, or the execution of other engineering and technical activities aimed at ensuring the uninterrupted operation of the unified [energy/power] system.

Ukraine Hits Russian Drone Workshop and Control Post, Targeting Frontline Attack Capability
Ukrainian forces struck Russian military communications facilities, command posts, drone infrastructure, and supply depots across three regions on October 25 and overnight into October 26.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the strikes on its official Facebook page on October 26, identifying targets in the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This disrupts the enemy’s communications and command and control of its troops," the General Staff wrote, describing the strike on a Russian military communications hub near temporarily occupied Melitopol.
According to the military, Ukrainian forces targeted:
- a Russian military communications hub near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian command posts near Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region and Chervonohirka in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- a Russian UAV control post near Vyshneve and a drone workshop near Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- Russian military equipment and supply depots near Komisarivka and Katerynivka in the Luhansk region.
The General Staff explained that the strikes on command posts were intended to disrupt Russian battlefield coordination, while targeting drone infrastructure could reduce Moscow's ability to attack Ukrainian military positions and frontline communities.
The attacks on supply depots were also intended to undermine Russian logistics by destroying materiel needed to sustain military operations. The General Staff did not disclose the weapons used, the number of Russian casualties, or detailed damage assessments for the targeted facilities.
"Operations against the enemy’s key military targets will continue until Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine ends completely," the General Staff stated.
Days earlier, Ukrainian forces carried out a similar wave of strikes across the same three regions on October 19 and overnight into October 20.
Targets included a command post near Fedorivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a military repair unit near Kalmiuske in the Donetsk region, and logistics depots near Kripenskyi, Rivnopil, and Lahidne.
Russian troop concentrations were also hit near Horlivka, Selydove, Svatove, and several settlements in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Award-winning producer receives £400,000 payout from BBC over workplace antisemitism claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:52 UTC
02:39:52 KST

An Oscar- and Emmy-winning producer has received a payout of more than £400,000 from the BBC after claiming she was victimized and forced out of the corporation following the October 7 attacks.
Lucie Kon left the broadcaster in April, just 19 days after winning an Oscar for her work, following a dispute over antisemitism in the workplace. Having built a stellar career on major programs including Panorama, Today, BBC Breakfast, and Storyville, her commissioned and produced films have earned an Emmy, an Oscar, a BAFTA, and many other prestigious industry honors.
Speaking to The Telegraph on Sunday, Kon alleged that her professional treatment shifted rapidly after the October 7 attacks in Israel. As footage and news of the atrocities emerged, she had messaged a colleague on WhatsApp asking if they had seen what was happening in Israel and remarking that Hamas were evil. In response, the colleague told her that “Zionists” were evil.
“I was like, ‘What?’ And she went, ‘Evil Hamas, evil Zionists,’ a bit like it was a joke, like they were the same and they’re not the same, and that was a particularly tasteless thing to say at that particular moment in history,” Kon said.
Later, when Kon sought to raise concerns about the treatment of Jewish staff and insisted that staff should at least be able to describe Hamas as committing acts of terror, another colleague told her that if she wanted to refer to Hamas as terrorists, she was required to call Israel a terrorist state as well.
Kon helps set up WhatsApp group for Jewish BBC employees
Pushed by the worsening workplace environment, Kon helped set up an internal WhatsApp group for Jewish employees at the corporation and wrote to then-Director General Tim Davie to raise concerns.
Shortly afterward, as more footage of the atrocities emerged, Kon proposed producing a film about the events of October 7 to a colleague who had previously made inappropriate remarks. When she mentioned the idea, the colleague dismissed it, saying they had already made enough films about Israel, but Kon’s manager later called her over to discuss the project.
“She said, ‘Lucie, we probably will do the Nova film,’” Kon recounted. “And she said to me, ‘But if we do it, we need to contextualize why Hamas did what they did.’”
When Kon questioned this requirement, explaining that the project was intended as a straightforward account of what happened that day rather than a deep dive into the historical and political context of the region, her manager’s manager informed her that she could no longer oversee the film. When Kon asked why, the manager told her it was “because you’re Jewish” and stated she was partial.
Kon noted that the manager then stated the person who was going to look after the film instead was the very same colleague who had previously told her that if Hamas were terrorists, the Israelis were terrorists too. An arrangement was later reached where Kon could oversee the film, but only under the strict supervision of someone else to ensure she remained impartial.
Kon subsequently raised a formal grievance. News of the grievance quickly reached the colleague who had made the remarks about Zionists, and that colleague wanted nothing more to do with Kon. This meant the two could no longer attend meetings together, and Kon was instructed not to come into work.
Six months later, she received the outcome. “It wasn’t upheld,” Kon said. “I was told that a lot of the things that I’d said people didn’t remember saying. And I was told that I’d been told - that I hadn’t been told I couldn’t work on the Nova film because I was a Jew - that they were worried about my mental health.”
When she appealed the decision, that appeal was also unsuccessful. At the time of her appeal, the BBC moved her colleague away from the Strand to work elsewhere, while Kon was told she could no longer travel, commission, or speak on behalf of the BBC because it would be unfair to her colleague.
Kon continued working from home while her appeal was considered, but by December, the stress took a toll, and her health began to deteriorate. After submitting a doctor’s note for stress-related sick leave, she was called into a meeting where she was told her job was being put at risk of redundancy. Having returned from sick leave, she applied for a newly created position but was rejected and made redundant in April.
BBC refuses to apologize, call Kon victim of antisemitism
According to The Telegraph, she brought unfair dismissal proceedings against the BBC, which agreed to pay her substantial compensation, partly funded by the license fee, without admitting liability. The corporation refused to apologize or admit she was a victim of antisemitism.
The Telegraph noted that she is the first person known to have been given a settlement by the BBC after alleging antisemitic behavior among colleagues. Speaking about the broader climate for staff after her departure, Kon reportedly told The Telegraph that other Jewish colleagues are still being bullied and abused, adding, “I know that nothing has changed because I’ve spoken to quite a few people since I left. Friends who are still struggling, still suffering, who feel embarrassed to say that they’re Zionist or that they’re a Jew.”
“I went from being a journalist and commissioner at the BBC who was Jewish to being a Jewish journalist at the BBC,” Kon said. “It was like I had Jew stamped on my forehead. I think I became a problem. I think I made too much of a noise about being a Jew inside the BBC.”
Kon added, “A colleague of mine said to me a while ago that if you say you’re a Zionist at the BBC, you might as well say that you were the person who had their foot on the neck of George Floyd. You’re a murderer. You’re an evil colonialist. You are a racist, and I’m not any of those things, and neither are the other people I know who are Zionist.”
“I stood up for who I was,” Kon said. “I stood up for what I believed to be right. The BBC says, ‘Bring your authentic self to work.’ And I did, and I lost my job as a result.”
A BBC spokesperson said in a statement, “We are grateful that Ms. Kon acknowledges that the BBC is not institutionally antisemitic. The BBC processes did not uphold any of Ms. Kon’s allegations of antisemitism. However, the outcome acknowledged shortcomings and the personal impact on Ms. Kon. We would like to acknowledge that Ms. Kon was a valued member of staff with many years of dedicated service to the BBC.”

President Herzog receives credentials of five new ambassadors to Israel day before elections

President Isaac Herzog diverted from his efforts to promote a national unity government to receive the credentials of five new ambassadors to Israel on Monday.
Under the country’s current government, Maj.-Gen. Emmanuel Bayingana of Rwanda, Christophe Parisot of France, Arad Benko of Austria, Stella Ronner Grubacic of the Netherlands, and Evelyn Korantemaa Ofosu-Amable of Ghana were the last ambassadors to present their credentials.
They will serve out their terms under Israel’s next government.
Israel and Rwanda established relations in the early 1960s, but severed them in 1973. Decades later, in 1998, Israel and Rwanda renewed their relations, which have remained cordial. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Rwanda in 2016, and Rwanda President Paul Kagame visited Israel in July 2017 in return.
Since taking office in the immediate aftermath of the Rwandan genocide, Kagame has spent the past 26 years rebuilding his country and forming strong international partnerships. Israel and Rwanda cooperate on many levels, including innovation, technology, agriculture, and security. Rwanda and Israel signed several bilateral agreements earlier this year when Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe visited Israel.
Bayingana said that he would work to further expand the relationship between the two countries.
Neither Herzog nor Parisot tried to pretend that relations between France and Israel were rosy. However, Parisot noted that, despite their diplomatic challenges, the people-to-people relations and cultural ties between France and Israel remained strong.
Herzog and Parisot also discussed the chaos and unrest that have overtaken France in recent weeks. Herzog recalled how different Champs-Élysées had felt when he accompanied his late father, then-president Chaim Herzog, on a state visit to France in 1988.
Herzog recalls time of 'amazing' French-Israeli relations
Herzog also recalled a time when relations between France and Israel were so positive they were “amazing.”
Parisot later wrote in the guest book that he would devote all of his energy to improving relations between the two countries.
Benko previously said returning to Israel felt like coming home. Indeed, it was. He was born in Haifa; he left the country as a child, and returned some 20 years ago as a spokesman for the Austrian embassy. He said that when he left Israel, he had a hard time in school because the only language he spoke was Hebrew. Aside from the usual diplomatic subjects and antisemitism, Benko and Herzog also discussed the Jews of Austria.
Michal Herzog, the president's wife, seldom sits in on the presentation of diplomatic credentials. This time, however, she attended the meetings with both the French and Austrian ambassadors and joined the ensuing conversations.
While welcoming Rubacic, Herzog spoke of the “special relationship” between Israel and the Netherlands. But he also expressed concern over the discourse emanating from Holland and some of the government’s own negative comments. He warned that Israel and Holland’s relations were currently under strain. Rubacic replied that she was happy to be in Israel and stressed the importance of highlighting the good relations between the two countries, which are based on shared values.
The significance Israel attaches to its ties with the Netherlands was evident in the brief, closed-door tete-a-tete Herzog had with the ambassador after the formalities concluded.
Most African countries with which Israel has diplomatic ties are proud of their culture and heritage. Ghana is no exception. Ofosu-Amable and her entourage arrived at the President’s Residence in national dress. Herzog was struck by the swell of colors and commented on it. He also noted that Israel’s relations with Ghana span seven decades, dating back to when former premier Golda Meir made her historic visit to Africa.
Israel trained Ghanaian soldiers early in relationship
In the early years of their relationship, Israel helped to train soldiers in Ghana’s army. Ghana stands out for the confidence it places in its women. Many of the country’s diplomats and high-ranking officials are women, and the ambassador is among them.
Where Israel and Ghana differ is their stance on a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Ghana’s President John Mahama told Ofosu-Amable that she must remember that her mission is to uphold Ghana’s longstanding commitment to the two-state solution.

Form a government, you can hate each other on your own time - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:47 UTC
02:39:47 KST

Before casting his vote in Israel’s first national election, Rabbi Moshe Yekutiel Alpert told off the polling committee.
Its chairman was two minutes late.
On January 25, 1949, Alpert got up at 5:35 a.m., put on his Shabbat clothes, and headed for a Jerusalem polling station. His home in the Beit Yisrael neighborhood had been damaged by shelling; he was staying elsewhere while it was being repaired. He carried his Israeli identity card, he wrote, with the same joy of carrying a Torah scroll during Simchat Torah celebrations.
He arrived at 5:50. The chairman appeared at 6:02. Alpert reminded him that proceedings were supposed to begin at six. The man apologized.
As the oldest person present, Alpert was invited to vote first at that station. He received “voter number one,” said Shehecheyanu, the blessing of gratitude for reaching a special occasion, and cast his ballot.
His father and grandfather had never had the same opportunity.
I shared the story this week. The Jewish state was eight months old, and Alpert already expected it to run on time.
It’s a familiar mix of reverence and impatience. Israelis can be fiercely attached to their country and furious with it, often in the same conversation. People expect a great deal from a place their families have paid a great deal for. From abroad, the anger can be easier to hear than the attachment.
Today, Jewish and Arab Israelis will again choose the people who govern them. I hope we allow ourselves a little of Alpert’s pleasure before we begin arguing about the exit polls. The ability to vote a government out is worth appreciating, including when a government we favor loses.
Israel needs several years where its citizens can make plans again
What I want from this election is a few years in which Israelis can make plans again.
Three years after October 7, consider what that would mean for a reservist trying to keep a business alive. Someone has to cover the work while he is away. His spouse has to rearrange work and childcare. Eventually, decisions about next month become decisions about whether the business has a future.
Families rebuilding their homes need to know that funding and official attention will last until the work is finished. They should be able to plan around a budget that survives the next coalition dispute.
I believe only a broad Zionist government can give this country the political stability it needs for that work. Likud, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, and other Zionist parties should negotiate an agreement to govern together for several years.
That will require leaders to sit with people they have spent the campaign attacking and explain the arrangement to voters who believed those attacks.
Some will have to accept a job smaller than the one they wanted. They should tell us which demands they are prepared to set aside. I would find that interview considerably more useful than another account of why everything is someone else’s fault.
There is a reason these concessions are so hard. In Israel, a political allegiance often comes with a family history. It may include a grandparent’s experience of immigration, a parent’s sense of being looked down on, or a lasting belief that people like us were denied a fair hearing. Calling an entire camp ignorant or dangerous reaches well beyond the politician at its head.
An election settles who has the votes to govern. People still have to live together afterward. A citizen should be able to lose an election and feel at home in their country. Leaders who want a broad coalition will have to show they understand one another’s voters.
Start the negotiations by asking what 70 or 80 percent of Israelis could support. I would begin with security preparedness, restoring damaged communities, and arrangements that let reservists serve without ruining their livelihoods. Agree on what can be done, how much it will cost, and who is responsible. Give ministers enough time in office to be judged on whether they delivered.
A coalition agreement might even contain a deadline unrelated to the next leadership rotation.
Independent October 7 commission must be part of coalition agreement
An independent, credible examination of October 7 must be part of that agreement. Families deserve to know how the state failed them. Officials and commanders need to answer for their decisions. A coalition assembled to restore public trust will have to accept findings that may be uncomfortable for its own members.
Before accepting another promise, I want to know whom that candidate appointed, what improved while they were in office, and what they did when something went wrong. The politician I like deserves the same questions. Newcomers can be judged on their experience and the seriousness of their plans.
Theodor Herzl, the founder of modern political Zionism, described Zionism in 1904 as “a never-ending ideal.” Even after the Jewish people obtained a homeland, he wrote, the pursuit of “ethical and spiritual fulfillment” would continue.
In our time, that responsibility includes a government office being responsible for treating a bereaved family, the education available to a child far from the center of the country, and the willingness of a prime minister to accept scrutiny.
The late chief rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook approached the problem from another direction. He wrote about the religious, national, and universal human concerns within Jewish society, arguing that each had value and could restrain the others’ excesses. He also understood how hostility between camps could consume them.
A religious minister and a secular mayor can have different ideas about the purpose of Jewish sovereignty and still agree on how to get a school built. They can resume the philosophical argument after the classrooms open.
The Jewish Agency’s Board of Governors has been meeting in Israel this week. The gathering brings Israeli leaders and Jews from abroad into the same room on the eve of the election.
Having spent years covering Jewish life abroad, I wish more Israelis were interested in what those communities are trying to achieve.
A minister visiting a Jewish school should ask how it keeps tuition affordable and what its pupils know about Israel. There is a great deal to learn from people who have to persuade families to choose a Jewish education.
We Israelis often ask Diaspora Jews to understand the pressures we live under. We should also be equally willing to learn about the pressures they face. The government answers to Israel’s citizens; its decisions can still affect a Jewish family thousands of miles away.
The next prime minister should put regular consultations with Jewish communities abroad in the diary and give the relevant ministers responsibility for following up. The Jewish Agency and other communal bodies can bring in voices from beyond the familiar leadership circles. Publish the commitments, then report what happened to them.
I would put affordable opportunities to study and spend time in Israel high on that list. Help young immigrants find their feet here. Give young Israelis more chances to encounter Jewish life abroad. A friendship formed over a semester has time to develop beyond the positions people take in an argument about the news.
A Jewish child abroad should be able to cultivate a relationship with Israel that lasts through several changes of government. She ought to have friends here, places she wants to revisit, and enough knowledge to form her own opinions.
I want my own children to make their lives here, and I want them to be able to plan beyond the next emergency. They will have plenty to complain about. I would like them to grow up expecting a government to finish the work it starts.

The regime change we need for Thames Water | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:41 UTC
02:39:41 KST

Andy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question.
Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed.
Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name.
The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once.
The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like.
 
Terry Barker
 
Honorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East Anglia
Your report that Andy Burnham has instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest.
The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds.
We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors.
The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options.
No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest.
 
James Wallace
 
CEO, River Action
If Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers.
There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs.
 
Philip Clayton
 
London

Bigger does not always mean better in hospital care | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:39:24 UTC
02:39:24 KST

The closure of maternity units is always a temptation when the NHS runs into staffing problems, largely of its own making (Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns, 19 October).
In my area the quality of care has already been called into question at the largest local unit, and directing mothers to chance their luck there seems to be an undeserved reward. Likewise a nearby large trust has had the quality of its neonatal care called into question. Closing small units is unlikely to provide the quality gain that is sought.
The problem for the NHS is that there is a freedom of ability to employ consultant staff. If you have the money, get on and advertise. This means that the supposedly better, larger units will be able to hoover up all the people they want. The smaller units don’t get a chance.
The reason people want to work at big centres is because for the same pay they don’t have to work so hard, or have the same level of responsibility. Government policy has created specialist units in large centres with the belief, promulgated by the medical profession, that bigger means better.
When I was appointed as a consultant in 1988, before trusts were invented, the regional health authority made the appointments and made sure that senior medical staffing was fairly spread. You could not have 20 specialists in one district general hospital (DGH) and none in the next.
Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations. If a DGH loses its obstetrics department, paediatrics would be immediately under threat. It would mean more children would have to travel. Accident and emergency departments would lose specialist support from paediatricians and gynaecologists. Fine if you have a broken arm, not so fine if you have meningitis etc.
So, when reviewing the future of obstetrics and midwifery, how about considering the people who live in the area and not just the needs of professors?
How about planning to relatively overstaff small units to make sure that they can provide for the needs of the population they serve, and ensuring that the newly qualified are directed towards these posts? After all, the NHS is paid for by everyone, so everyone should get a decent quality of care, without having to travel 50 miles in the dead of night.
 
Dr Paul Godwin
 
Keighley, West Yorkshire

France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb | Letter

I’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed.
Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.
Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality.
If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion.
 
Muriel E Cockcroft
  
Duclair, Normandy, France

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:24:43 UTC
02:24:43 KST

Virginia Woolf’s 'Freshwater: A Comedy' published in Persian
TEHRAN – The Persian translation of the book “Freshwater: A Comedy” written by Virginia Woolf has been released in bookstores across Iran.
Yousef Najafi Jablou is the translator of the book that has been brought out by Tagh Publication, ISNA reported.
“Freshwater: A comedy” is a play written and produced by Virginia Woolf in 1935, and the only play she wrote. Although only performed once in her lifetime, it has been translated into many languages and produced in many countries since. Alfred Lord Tennyson appears as a character in this play.
Virginia Woolf researched the life of her great-aunt, the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, publishing her findings in an essay titled “Pattledom” (1925), and later in her introduction to her 1926 edition of Cameron's photographs.
The play is named after Freshwater, Isle of Wight, where Julia Margaret Cameron lived in a somewhat bohemian atmosphere at her home, Dimbola Lodge, surrounded by a number of artists and literary figures, including George Frederick Watts and Tennyson in the 1860s.
Tennyson's nearby home, Farringdon, was another artistic center. The plot revolves around the attempts by the young actress Ellen Terry to escape from her marriage to the much older Watts, partly family history, partly mocking the conventions of the Victorian times that the Bloomsbury group had fought to escape.
The Camerons are set to embark for India, while both Mrs. Cameron and Watts are intent on portraying Ellen in their respective media. Ellen, on the other hand, views a young naval lieutenant as her escape, with an offer to escape to Bloomsbury. This collapses a number of historic events into a single afternoon.
Although a slight work not intended for publication, and easily dismissed as frivolous, it has been given a larger meaning when placed in the broader context of Woolf's work and views. For beneath the comedic elements, there is an exploration of both generational change and artistic freedom. Both Cameron and Woolf fought against the class and gender dynamics of Victorianism, and the play shows links to both “To the Lighthouse” and “A Room of One's Own” that would follow.
Virginia Woolf (1882 – 1941) was an English writer and one of the most influential 20th-century modernist authors. She helped to pioneer the use of stream of consciousness narration as a literary device.
Woolf began publishing professionally in 1904 and rose to prominence during the interwar period with novels including “Mrs. Dalloway” (1925), “To the Lighthouse” (1927), and “Orlando” (1928). She also wrote the influential feminist essay “A Room of One's Own” (1929), followed by “Three Guineas” (1938), which explores the roots of fascism in society. Her work became central to 1970s feminist criticism and remains influential worldwide, having been translated into more than 50 languages.

Baran Auction to showcase Iranian calligraphy, miniatures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:24:18 UTC
02:24:18 KST

Baran Auction to showcase Iranian calligraphy, miniatures
TEHRAN – The fifth edition of Baran Auction, specializing in Iranian and Islamic art, will be held in Tehran on Friday, October 30, featuring works of traditional calligraphy and Persian miniature painting, including “The Third Feather” by the late Iranian master Mahmoud Farshchian.
The event will take place at 5 p.m. at the Raizan International Conference Center, IRNA reported on Monday.
A public exhibition of the selected works will be held at the same venue on October 28 and 29, offering art enthusiasts, researchers and collectors an opportunity to view the pieces before the sale, the report added.
The upcoming edition continues Baran Auction's focus on preserving and promoting Iran's calligraphic heritage while expanding its presentation of traditional visual arts. Alongside calligraphic works, this year's selection includes pieces from the country's miniature painting tradition, highlighting the historical connections between the two art forms.
Among the featured works is “The Third Feather” by Farshchian, whose paintings frequently draw on Persian literary, spiritual and mythological themes. According to the organizers, the work evokes the mysterious feather of the Simorgh, the legendary bird associated with wisdom and spiritual discovery in Persian literature. They describe it as a symbol of awareness, hope and renewal, reflecting the enduring power of Iranian cultural thought.
Calligraphy remains central to Baran Auction's identity. Previous editions have featured works associated with major figures in the history of Iranian calligraphy, including Mir Emad Hassani, Darvish Abdolmajid Taleqani and Mirza Gholamreza Esfahani, alongside works by contemporary artists.
The fourth edition of Baran Auction, held in 2019, demonstrated the market appeal of Iran's traditional arts, with five folios from a rare copy of Ferdowsi's “Shahnameh”, written in the nastaliq style during the Timurid period (1370–1507), selling for more than $2.1 million.
The auction, held at Tehran's Raizen International Conference Center, presented 94 works and generated more than $6 million in sales, although 25 lots failed to attract buyers.
Other notable sales included a miniature portrait of Princess Navab Akbari Beigom, created by an Indian artist during the Zand dynasty (1751–1794), which fetched more than $1.3 million, and a cylinder inscribed with a Persian translation of the Cyrus Cylinder by calligrapher Hossein Niktalab, which sold for approximately $930,000.
The results underscored the commercial potential of traditional Iranian and Islamic art within the country's art market.
By bringing together calligraphy and miniature painting, the fifth edition aims to present a broader view of Iran's artistic legacy while providing a platform for the appreciation and circulation of works rooted in its cultural traditions.
Founded by Mahbubeh Kazemi Dulabi in 2016, Baran Auction specializes in calligraphic paintings and works of calligraphy.

Source: Kernel's operations update
Details: Grain exports fell by 54% in the same period to 574,000 tonnes. Kernel redirected some shipments through Danube ports and Ukraine's western land border.

Iran-Pakistan border trade serves mutual interests: ambassador

Iran-Pakistan border trade serves mutual interests: ambassador
TEHRAN– Iran’s Ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri-Moghaddam, has stressed that cross-border trade is an integral part of high-level bilateral agreements and serves the mutual interests of both neighboring countries, while attributing the failure to implement the Islamabad understanding to 'US breaches of commitments.'
In remarks on Sunday, the ambassador addressed reports in Pakistani media about the status of trade across the shared border, emphasizing that disruptions to commercial exchanges under the current circumstances would serve neither country’s interests.
“There are currently no restrictions imposed by Iran on the export of Iranian goods, including liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), to Pakistan,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, adding that Iran’s borders with all its neighboring countries remain open.
He explained that difficulties affecting traders transporting goods from Iran to Pakistan stem from the implementation of an “E-Form” procedure by the Pakistani side for imports from Iran. Consultations are underway between the two sides to resolve the issue and facilitate the movement of goods.
The ambassador also acknowledged reports that several hundred LPG tankers had crossed the Gabd-Rimdan border into Pakistan but had yet to be unloaded or cleared. The situation, he said, had complicated the movement of goods and disrupted the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
Amiri-Moghaddam emphasized that Iran had consistently worked to facilitate and strengthen cross-border commerce and remained committed to cooperating with Pakistani counterparts to overcome existing obstacles and expand economic ties.
Border trade, he noted, is a vital component of economic cooperation between the two neighboring countries and benefits both nations and their peoples.
Pakistani media have meanwhile reported that the Gabd-Rimdan crossing has resumed operations, with commercial transport moving again on both sides of the border.
US breaches are behind stalled Islamabad understanding
Separately, Amiri-Moghaddam addressed speculation in Pakistani media about Tehran’s position on the future of negotiations with Washington, stressing that decisions and official announcements concerning whether talks will take place fall within the remit of Iran’s senior political authorities and Foreign Ministry.
Speaking to IRNA in Islamabad on Sunday evening, the ambassador said Iran remained committed to the Islamabad understanding, arguing that its implementation had been obstructed by the US side’s failure to honor its commitments.
He said that, during a recent meeting with think-tank figures and media representatives in Islamabad, he had reiterated Iran’s continued commitment to the understanding.
“The person who declared the Islamabad understanding over and violated it was US President Donald Trump,” Amiri-Moghaddam said, according to IRNA.
He added that Washington’s actions had created conditions in which understanding could not be implemented in practice.
The ambassador said Iran’s repeated emphasis on honoring the understanding reflected its respect for commitments and agreements undertaken within the framework of international law. He drew a parallel with Washington’s unilateral withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), arguing that Trump had similarly failed to implement the Islamabad understanding he had signed.
Amiri-Moghaddam stressed that any decision or announcement concerning the holding or cancellation of negotiations would be made by Iran’s senior political authorities and the Foreign Ministry in Tehran, with official information conveyed through the spokesperson for the Iranian negotiating team and official media outlets.
Tehran says diplomacy remains open as Iran stresses readiness to defend itself
The ambassador’s remarks come as Iranian officials have reiterated that diplomacy remains an option while emphasizing the country’s readiness to respond to any hostile action.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei, speaking to German public broadcaster ARD, said the United States continued to insist on unilateral demands in negotiations. He stressed that Iran was keeping the door to diplomacy open while remaining prepared to defend the country against any aggression and deal with every possible scenario.
Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, speaker of Iran’s Parliament and head of the Iranian negotiating team, also addressed the issue in remarks at the beginning of a parliamentary session held in person and online.
Qalibaf said Iran was prepared to deliver a response beyond its adversaries’ expectations to any act of aggression against the country’s territorial integrity. He added that threats of a wider war or assassination would not force the Iranian nation to abandon its rights and interests.
The statements underscore Tehran’s position that diplomatic engagement must be accompanied by respect for commitments and Iran’s national interests.
For Iran and Pakistan, maintaining the smooth operation of border crossings remains important to bilateral commerce and regional economic cooperation. Resolving the outstanding administrative obstacles would help restore the uninterrupted movement of goods and strengthen trade ties between the two neighboring countries.

Araghchi: Iran-Russia coop can strengthen global gas market stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:22:22 UTC
