Araghchi: Iran-Russia coop can strengthen global gas market stability
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for closer cooperation between Iran and Russia to diversify energy supply routes, strengthen global gas market stability and create new opportunities for investment and foreign-exchange earnings, warning that geopolitical tensions and military threats are disrupting international energy supplies.
In an opinion article published in Russia’s Vedomosti newspaper on Monday, Araghchi said energy security had become one of the world’s most pressing challenges, alongside food security, linking the situation to 'the coercive and arrogant actions of the United States in the region.'
Araghchi cited estimates by the International Energy Agency indicating that more than 112 billion cubic meters of liquefied natural gas passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, accounting for nearly one-fifth of global trade in the fuel.
He said the recent US-Israeli military aggression against Iran, together with continued military threats, had led to the closure of the strategic waterway and disrupted global gas supplies, particularly to Asian markets.
The disruption has also driven European gas prices sharply higher, while gas storage levels ahead of winter have fallen significantly below those recorded a year earlier, he added.
Araghchi noted that Asian markets consume around 90% of the gas transported through the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the waterway’s importance to global energy security and the economic interests of both producers and consumers.
He warned that instability in the region could have far-reaching consequences for international energy markets, calling for greater dialogue among gas-producing countries, diversification of supply routes and stronger protection for critical energy infrastructure.
The Iranian foreign minister also stressed the need to develop practical mechanisms to mitigate the impact of geopolitical shocks on energy supplies and market stability.
Iran and Russia see potential for deeper energy cooperation
Araghchi highlighted the potential for expanded energy cooperation between Tehran and Moscow, particularly in investment, technology, equipment, production, operational efficiency and energy exports.
He said closer bilateral cooperation could help diversify energy transportation routes and generate additional foreign-exchange revenue, while contributing to the stability of international gas markets.
The article also referred to the Global Gas Outlook 2055 published by the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), which projects that 86% of global gas production by 2055 will come from fields that are not currently producing.
Iran, which holds the world’s second-largest proven natural gas reserves after Russia, has significant potential to expand its role in the global gas sector, Araghchi said.
According to the outlook cited in the article, GECF member countries’ share of global gas production is projected to increase from 38% in 2024 to 44% by 2055, accounting for 65% of net growth in global production over that period.
Araghchi acknowledged that realizing the potential of Iran-Russia energy cooperation would require substantial investment, advanced technology and equipment, as well as solutions to challenges arising from unilateral coercive measures and the complexity of long-term energy contracts.
He described the GECF as an important multilateral platform for strengthening coordination among gas-producing countries and advancing cooperation in response to shared challenges. Political will and mutual trust, he said, would be essential to translating this potential into practical results.
Hormuz security central to global energy stability
Araghchi also addressed maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, saying Iran had proposed a seven-day plan to facilitate the waterway’s reopening and the resumption of normal maritime traffic, provided the necessary conditions were met and military threats were removed.
He said responsible dialogue and mutual commitments could help reduce tensions, strengthen sustainable maritime security and restore stability to global energy markets.
“Whether that path can be pursued ultimately depends on the choices made by the United States,” Araghchi wrote, concluding that cooperation and dialogue were essential to building greater stability in global gas and energy markets.

Gaza’s displaced families are struggling to keep the lights on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:09:05 UTC
02:09:05 KST

The sun is slowly setting earlier as winter approaches in Gaza. When night falls, Aseel Ayesh’s tent in the Nuseirat refugee camp goes dark. Last week, her private electricity provider cut her off after she couldn’t pay a bill of over 180 shekels (around $59).
“I need to use the light all night, so I can prepare milk and dinner for my daughter,” said Ayesh, 24, who shares the tent with her husband and their infant daughter. Her husband, Wassim Mohammed Ayesh, said he got bit by a rat that snuck into the dark tent, which resulted in an infection.
With Gaza’s power grid in ruins, private generators are now the only source of electricity for most people in the Strip, and the price has soared. Generator power costs about 30 shekels (around $9.80) per kilowatt-hour, compared to three or four shekels before the war, according to providers. Generator owners connect subscribers to their power lines, with a meter to measure energy consumption, and bills are collected every week. Anyone who doesn’t pay in time is cut off.
Gaza never had enough electricity in the past. Before October 2023, the Strip had about 212 megawatts of power, less than half of what it needed to function. Most of the electricity was supplied from Israeli power lines, with the remainder coming from Gaza’s only power plant. At best, homes got electricity in alternating eight-hour shifts. Around 350 private generators were already operating to cover the gaps.
On the night of October 7, 2023, Israel cut the power lines and stopped the fuel that ran the power plant. Since then, the bombardment has destroyed about 5,080 kilometres of power lines and 2,285 distribution transformers, according to Gaza’s government media office, which puts the sector’s losses at $1.4 billion. The generators that replaced the grid run on fuel, engine oil and spare parts, all of which Israel restricts from entering the besieged Strip.
Not far from Ayesh, Ashraf Mohammed, known as Abu Mohammed, lives with his family of nine in a hasil, a small storeroom once used as a shop or warehouse and now rented out as a home because so few houses are left standing. He lost his job in the war, and now every shekel counts.
“I lost my work because of the war, and now I need more than 2,000 shekels ($655) a month,” he said. “I sold my car during the war to provide for my family.”
Last month, the family’s weekly electricity bills added up to 582 shekels ($190). They now use power only to charge their phones, so two of his children can follow their university classes online, and to turn on a single light for a few hours at a time.
“We have to cut back on our basic expenses to pay for electricity,” said his wife, Umm Mohammed. “We don’t spend much on food, and we can’t pay the full university fees for our children.” Before the war, she explained, they had electricity for only about six hours a day, but the price was more reasonable.
The private generator economy
Abu Zayed Sons Trading and Import is one of the largest generator providers in central Gaza. Founded in 2017, the company moved into electricity when the war began, running its first lines in al-Zawayda, where it started, before expanding to ten branches across the Strip.
The private generators run about 20 hours a day, from 7:00am to 3:00am, and burn between 40 and 100 litres of fuel an hour, said general manager Aya Shaheen. “Our generators have very high capacity. They can’t be compared with competitors who own small generators.”
With fuel imports restricted, the company makes its own diesel in a private factory. It was among the first in Gaza to do so, Shaheen said, and that has allowed it to continue running. When asked about their running costs, Shaheen said that the figures change too often to provide an estimate.
The company has around 25,000 subscribers today. “The price per kilowatt is fixed at 30 shekels,” Shaheen said. “Each subscriber has an independent meter. They bring their own, and we connect it.” Bills are collected weekly so that debts don’t pile up as prices rise.
Abu Zayed doesn’t run lines to tents, because a single short circuit could start a fire and cause a catastrophe, Shaheen said. Its customers live in houses still standing and in hawasil like Abu Mohammed’s.
Mahmoud al-Baba, who owns a generator in the Central Governorate, does extend power lines to tents, including Ayesh’s. “Why, aren’t the people in the tents human beings, that I shouldn’t run lines to them?” he said.
He charges 29 shekels per kilowatt-hour and uses the same system of meters and weekly bills. “Payment is in cash or by bank transfer, and whoever doesn’t pay, we cut off the electricity.”
Opting out of electricity
Families who can’t keep up are canceling their subscriptions, choosing to live in the dark so they can cover food and rent. Some charge their phones at charging points set up across the Strip, which cost a few shekels a time but offer nothing more: no light, no heat, no way to cook.
Solar panels, which have eased electricity shortages in places like Lebanon, are too expensive and hard to find in Gaza, said economic analyst Ahmed Abu Qamar. High electricity prices have also raised production costs for small businesses by 10 to 15 percent, he said, and goods could be 15 percent cheaper if power were available at normal prices. If prices keep rising, he warned, families will drain their savings and sink into debt just to cover the basics.
They are likely to keep rising. On October 12, Gaza’s Energy and Natural Resources Authority capped the price of generator electricity at 29 shekels per kilowatt-hour. Shaheen said her company holds a permit from the authority but can’t bring its price down.
“There is a severe shortage of generator oil,” she said. “I expect the price to rise within days,”

Reacting to news that a prosecutor’s office in Moscow is about to initiate criminal proceedings on “extremism” charges against prisoners’ rights advocate Anna Karetnikova, from the Memorial Human Rights Centre, who is currently living in exile, Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director, said:
“Amnesty International has long warned of the danger that Russia’s vague and overly broad anti-extremism legislation would be used to criminalize lawful human rights work. Today, those fears are being realized with the criminal case against Anna Karetnikova – the first time such charges have been used against an individual solely because of their human rights work.”
“Although Anna Karetnikova is living in exile and can only be tried in absentia, the threat of prosecution sends a chilling message that is intended to silence human defenders in Russia and abroad, stop them from documenting violations and deter them from speaking up for the victims of these abuses. Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives.
Criminalizing the human rights work of a leading, Nobel Peace Prize-winning NGO is a harmful and shameful move that further exposes Russian authorities’ true motives
Marie Struthers, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Director
“The Russian authorities must drop these charges against Anna Karetnikova, close this case and stop abusing absurdly broad and vague ‘extremism’ legislation against their critics, whether they be human rights defenders, political opponents, LGBTI people or dissident religious groups. Russia’s repressive legislation must be brought into line with the country’s international human rights obligations.”
Background
On 26 October 2026, the Lefortovo Interdistrict Prosecutor’s Office in Moscow announced that it had gathered materials to initiate criminal proceedings against Anna Karetnikova on charges of “participation in activities of an extremist organization” (Article 282.2(2) of the Criminal Code) and “evasion of duties of a foreign agent” (Article 330.1(2)).
Although the prosecutors didn’t name the “extremist organization” in question directly, Anna Karetnikova has worked or collaborated since 2002 with Memorial Human Rights Centre, Russia’s oldest human rights group. Four years after it was awarded the 2022 Nobel Peace Prize, Memorial was arbitrarily designated as “extremist” by Russian authorities in April 2026.
Between 2008 and 2016, Karetnikova served on Moscow’s Public Monitoring Commission, an independent public body monitoring detention facilities. She later worked as a lead analyst for the Federal Penitentiary Service before being fired from her position in January 2023 and leaving Russia. In April 2025, she was arbitrarily designated as a “foreign agent” by the Ministry of Justice.

9/11 cost Americans their privacy. AI could take what’s left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:08:31 UTC
02:08:31 KST

9/11 cost Americans their privacy. AI could take what’s left
On October 26,2001, US President George W. Bush signed the USA PATRIOT Act into law, less than seven weeks after the September 11 attacks killed nearly 3,000 people in New York. The speed of its passage reflected the extraordinary political and social atmosphere in the United States. The tragedy had shattered the country’s sense of security, and fears of further terrorist activity continued to haunt the country in the months that followed.
In the weeks after 9/11, grief and anger were accompanied by an unprecedented surge of patriotism and national solidarity. President Bush’s approval rating reached 86 percent by late September, and public trust in the federal government rose to levels unseen in decades. A majority of Americans also expressed a willingness to sacrifice at least some civil liberties if doing so would help combat terrorism. Under intense pressure to prevent another catastrophe, Congress moved rapidly to expand federal investigative and surveillance powers.
The Patriot Act facilitated information sharing between intelligence and law enforcement agencies, broadened certain authorities to obtain records, and expanded investigative tools available in terrorism cases. Supporters argued that these measures were necessary to confront a transnational threat with legal instruments suited to a new security environment.
Yet national unity did not eliminate concerns about civil rights. Arab and Muslim Americans, as well as people perceived to belong to these communities, faced increased discrimination and violence. As the immediate shock of 9/11 receded, questions grew over how far the governments’ new powers should extend and what safeguards were needed to prevent abuse.
These tensions would shape the law’s legacy for decades. The debate intensified after Edward Snowden’s 2013 disclosures exposed the scale of certain US surveillance programs, helping spur the USA FREEDOM Act of 2015, which curtailed the government’s bulk collection of domestic telephone records. The controversy revealed that the challenge was not simply how to protect Americans from terrorism, but how to preserve privacy and civil liberties while doing so.
The Patriots Act’s legacy in the age of AI
The surveillance debate that follows 9/11 has evolved alongside technology. Today, governments can analyze enormous volumes of digital information, from communications metadata to online activity, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish targeted intelligence gathering from the broader collection of personal data.
However, not all modern US surveillance powers originate in the Patriot Act. One important distinction is between Section 215 of the Patriot Act, which became associated with the NSA’s bulk collection of domestic telephone records, and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), enacted in 2008.
Section 702 allows US intelligence agencies to target non-US persons reasonably believed to be outside the country for foreign intelligence purposes. Yet communications involving Americans may also be collected when they interact with foreign targets. A separate framework. Executive Order 12333 governs much of the intelligence community’s overseas surveillance activity.
These authorities raise questions that extend beyond the original post-9/11 debate. Artificial intelligence is adding a new dimension to the problem. Machine-learning systems can process vast quantities of communications, financial records, location data and other digital information, identifying patterns that human investigators might overlook. Such capabilities could help intelligence agencies detect terrorist networks and anticipate emerging threats. Yet they also raise the possibility of increasingly comprehensive surveillance, in which individuals can be assessed through their digital associations, behavior and inferred characteristics rather than through evidence of specific wrongdoings.
The risks are not limited to the amount of information collected. AI systems can produce false positives, reproduce biases present in their training data and generate conclusions that are difficult to explain or independently verify. If such assessments inform investigations or security decisions, errors may have serious consequences for individuals. The challenge for governments is therefore not simply to regulate access to data, but also to establish accountability for how algorithms analyze it, how their conclusions are used and whether affected individuals have meaningful avenues for redress.
Twenty-five years later: Has America found the balance?
Twenty-five years after the Patriot Act became law, the United States has neither abandoned its expanded national security apparatus nor settled the debate over its proper limits. The government’s ability to collect and analyze information remains an important instrument in counterterrorism and foreign intelligence. At the same time, experience has shown that powers introduced in response to an emergency can endure long after the circumstances that justified them have changed.
The law’s defenders argue that intelligence agencies need effective tools to identify threats before they result in violence. Critics counter that broad surveillance authorities, secret legal interpretations and insufficient oversight can undermine privacy and weaken public trust. Both concerns are fundamental to a democratic society: security is essential to protecting freedom, but security measures can also threaten it when they operate without adequate safeguards.
The central lesson of the Patriot Act is therefore not that national security and civil liberties are necessarily incompatible. It is that the balance between them cannot be established once and left untouched. It requires clear legal limits, meaningful judicial and congressional oversight, transparency wherever possible, and public debate about how surveillance powers are used.
Artificial intelligence makes this balance even harder to maintain. Surveillance systems are increasingly capable of drawing connections across datasets and generating assessments at a speed and scale that traditional oversight mechanisms were not designed to handle. Decisions may depend partly on algorithmic outputs that are difficult for the public, and sometimes even for officials, to scrutinize. Democratic oversight must therefore evolve alongside technology, requiring clear rules on the use of AI, independent testing, safeguards against discriminatory outcomes and human accountability for consequential decisions.
The digital age makes this task more urgent. As governments acquire increasingly sophisticated tools to monitor communications and analyze personal information, lawmakers must ensure that technological capabilities do not automatically translate into unlimited authority.
The question raised in October 2001 remains relevant today: how can a democracy protect its citizens without compromising the freedoms that give its political system legitimacy? Twenty-five years later, the United States continues to grapple with the answer.

Russia’s Sberbank links the crypto networks used by Moscow and Tehran to evade sanctions, Middle East Forum says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:07:42 UTC
02:07:42 KST

The U.S.-based think tank Middle East Forum has recommended that the U.S. Treasury Department treat cryptocurrency platforms used by Russia and Iran as a single interconnected system, according to a report published by the organization on Oct. 25. The report’s authors said Iran-linked Shelbit, Russia’s A7 network, and Kyrgyzstan-based crypto exchange TokenSpot all use shared infrastructure built around the USDT stablecoin, and that Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank, acts as the key link between the exchanges, as it “coordinates and legalizes” the final transactions.
The report outlined how Sberbank’s role expanded after Vladimir Putin signed Federal Law No. 282-FZ on Aug. 4, allowing Russian companies to settle foreign trade transactions using digital currencies. Kaplan Panesh, deputy chairman of the State Duma’s Budget Committee, said the law allows companies to pay foreign partners while “circumventing sanctions.”
Sberbank, which has been under full U.S. sanctions since 2022, began processing crypto payments of this kind immediately after Putin’s signature brought the law into effect. According to the report, that gave Russia access to state-backed payment channels operating in parallel with the A7 network.
Shelbit, which has companies in Georgia, Poland, and the United Arab Emirates, was sanctioned by the United States in August for transferring funds linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). TRM Labs estimates that $6.3 billion passed through Shelbit-linked wallets, including $318 million connected to A7. In September 2025, the platform transferred $2 million to a wallet that Israel later identified as being part of Hamas’ financial infrastructure. TRM Labs cautioned, however, that while blockchain data can show the path of funds, it does not establish what participants knew about the ultimate destination or purpose of the transactions.
TRM Labs also assessed that TokenSpot serves as a front for Grinex (the successor to the sanctioned Russian crypto exchange Garantex), and that it had transferred around $680 million to A7. The United Kingdom imposed sanctions on TokenSpot on Oct. 8. The United States has not yet done so, and as of Oct. 10, Kyrgyzstan’s financial regulator still listed the exchange as licensed.
The authors separately pointed to Putin’s August law allowing digital-currency settlements in foreign trade, after which Sberbank immediately began facilitating such payments.
The Middle East Forum recommended that the United States sanction TokenSpot and also proposed targeting Russian banks that process cryptocurrency payments for Iranian counterparties. Its authors suggested warning those banks that they could face the same treatment as VTB, which was sanctioned in September over its involvement in payment channels using rubles and Iranian rials.
The report also said the U.S. Treasury should seek to freeze USDT held in wallets linked to A7. According to a report by the Democratic minority in the U.S. Senate, 84% of 846 sanctioned crypto wallets linked to Iran used USDT.
On Oct. 1, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 as a transnational criminal organization, while the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed cutting the network’s subagents off from the U.S. financial system.
According to the Treasury Department, more than $17 billion passed through those intermediaries between January 2025 and June 2026. The network was used by Iran’s central bank, the IRGC, and Hamas.
A7 was created in late 2024 by Russia’s Promsvyazbank and fugitive Moldovan oligarch Ilan Shor.

Protesters kill longtime nurse treating Ebola patients in Congo

KINSHASA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Angry youths armed with machetes attacked two community health workers raising awareness about the Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo, killing one and wounding the other, according to officials and a memo seen by Reuters on Monday, in the latest in a series of attacks fueled by misinformation.
The worker who was killed was an experienced nurse who had worked at the general hospital in the town of Bafwasende in Tshopo province, and was recently tasked with helping to raise awareness about the deadly virus in the local community, where he was a well-known figure, a local official and the memo said.
“We are shocked at how the population turned against this nurse. It is impossible to believe that he was mistaken for a stranger,” a local health official told Reuters.
The attack took place on Friday afternoon, when the nurse and a colleague, a teacher also working on community outreach, stopped to check on a lot of land. A group of people building a home next door began to accuse them of spreading the disease by contaminating water.
“Here are the people that are spreading the Ebola virus through people’s toilets and rivers!” they shouted, according to the memo shared by a health official.
The angry group was joined by youths wielding machetes and batons, who attacked the pair. The nurse died on the spot before the hospital’s emergency services could reach them, the memo said, while the teacher survived.
MISINFORMATION FUELING ATTACK
Tshopo is among eight provinces in Congo that are battling a fast-spreading outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus. Congo’s public health institute on Friday reported 9,964 total confirmed cases with around a 48.6% fatality rate since the outbreak was declared in May.
Attacks on health workers have targeted hospitals, vehicles and staff involved in the Ebola response, underscoring the challenge of building trust among the population.
The local official said health workers in Bafwasende, where the latest attack took place, are sheltering at the general hospital under police guard, too afraid to go home, while the army also briefly deployed to the area.
“None of the nurses have slept at their homes because they fear for their security,” the official added.
Only days earlier, an angry mob attacked another community worker raising awareness about Ebola, and set his house on fire, the memo said.
Reuters previously reported on how the rapid spread of health misinformation posed a threat to healthcare workers in eastern Congo even before Ebola began to spread, with multiple health workers killed in Tshopo after they were accused of spreading an imaginary disease that caused male genitals to atrophy.
“The killing of a nurse yesterday in Bafwasende is a loss to the Ebola response and an even greater loss to patients,” Julien Harneis, the senior United Nations Ebola coordinator, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:00:09 CET
02:00:09 KST

By Edward McAllister and Aleksandar Vasovic
BELGRADE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing - something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.
The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
WINNERS, BUT CAN THEY STICK TOGETHER?
The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024 and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support, before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.
It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.
Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.”
REFORMING PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS
Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.
“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.
“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.
(Writing by Edward McAllister; Editing by Kirsten Donovan)

Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The ministry stressed that the measures are alternatives for political parties to consider, not an official programme of recommended cuts.
Finland faces an estimated adjustment requirement of €8–11 billion during the next parliamentary term. Government expenditure has exceeded revenue as a share of GDP every year since 2009, according to the ministry.
"Public finances are in a weak state," said Mika Niemelä, Director General of the ministry's Budget Department, calling for changes to public spending.
Abolishing child benefits would improve public finances by approximately €1.17 billion annually by 2031, although demand for other welfare payments would increase.
Other options include removing supplements for single parents and families with several children, ending child maintenance support and abolishing the guarantee pension for people with the lowest retirement incomes.
The ministry also examined replacing student grants with loans, potentially saving €537 million annually, and freezing inflation-linked increases to pensions, benefits and public funding. A broad freeze would generate estimated annual savings of €2.1 billion by 2031.
Healthcare measures include reducing the number of wellbeing services counties, restricting emergency care and ending publicly funded dental treatment for adults. The latter would reduce expenditure by an estimated €250 million annually, subject to corresponding reductions in operating costs.
Public sector employees also face possible changes to employment conditions. Options include halving holiday bonuses, shortening annual leave, extending working hours and reducing salaries.
Education measures include reversing the extension of compulsory schooling to age 18 and reducing vocational education funding.
The ministry also examined cancelling planned increases in research and development funding. Returning expenditure to 2023 levels would save approximately €1.84 billion annually by 2031 compared with current plans.
Tax measures include raising reduced VAT rates to the standard 25.5%, generating an estimated €3.9 billion annually. Increasing VAT on food and restaurant services from 13.5% to 18% would raise approximately €1.2 billion.
Other options include higher income and property taxes, changes to dividend taxation and new taxes on air and ferry tickets.
The proposals drew criticism from trade unions and opposition politicians.
Tom-Henrik Sirviö, an economist at trade union confederation STTK, accused the ministry of prioritising reductions in public services over maintaining their funding.
He argued that higher progressive taxation and changes to corporate dividend taxation deserved greater attention.
Left Alliance MP Pia Lohikoski criticised the potential cuts to education, research and family benefits, warning that they would increase inequality.
The ministry maintained that its surveys were intended to show the available options and their estimated financial effects. It also cautioned that some measures overlap, meaning their projected savings cannot simply be added together.
HT

German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

German police probe cruise ship captain after Bremerhaven collision
October 26, 2026
German police are investigating the captain of the Mein Schiff 3 cruise liner after it collided with two container ships in Bremerhaven.
The collision caused damage estimated to be in the millions of euros and forced the cancellation of a 20-day Canary Islands cruise, with further voyages potentially affected.
Why are police investigating the captain?
A police spokesperson said proceedings over a possible administrative offense had been opened to establish whether the captain breached his duty of care. Police have not specified the suspected lapse.
Broadcaster RTL reported that investigators spoke to the captains of all three vessels overnight into Monday.
How did the collision happen?
Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship leave the northern German port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.
The liner was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members. Nobody was injured, and none of the vessels took on water.
The larger container ship suffered substantial damage, with several meters of its port side torn open and container guides deformed. The smaller vessel sustained minor damage.
The cruise ship was also significantly damaged. Photographs showed damage to its lifeboats and bridge.
All damage was several meters above the waterline. The liner returned to the cruise terminal after the collision.
Could more cruises be canceled?
Technical experts boarded the ship shortly after the accident and determined that shipyard repairs were necessary, operator TUI Cruises said.
The company called canceling the Canary Islands voyage "the only responsible decision," saying passenger and crew safety had "highest priority." Passengers were initially allowed to remain aboard while the company arranged assistance.
It remained unclear whether other voyages planned for this year could go ahead.
The collision initially caused no disruption to other harbor traffic.

Vučić Out, Students In: Still, No Sanctions Against Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:52:31 UTC
01:52:31 KST

Serbia’s Student List won the Oct. 25 parliamentary election, ending 14 years of what many described as Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić’s dictatorship.
Tens of thousands of people in Serbia and abroad rallied behind the list, made up of students, professors and doctors, hoping to free the country from corruption and political pressure on its institutions. The country secured a historic win in its highest turnout of 70%, the biggest Serbia has seen in nearly three decades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Yet even as the result brings Serbia a step closer to the European, the list has said it will not impose sanctions on Russia, despite Vučić’s claims that it would do so within months.
Speaking to RT Balkan, a Serbian-language broadcaster run by the Russian state-owned network RT (formerly Russia Today), Professor Jovo Bakić of the Student List claimed that Belgrade respects Russia, “both as a great power and as our historically important partner, and in many cases even our protector,” adding that “there will be no changes.”
He claimed that sanctions from such a small country would essentially change nothing for Moscow, since even the entire EU had failed to harm it.
However, the move would damage bilateral relations, he said, adding that Serbia knows what “kind of misery that [sanctions] is,” having lived through UN sanctions during the 1990s.
“I said this during the election campaign, and I’m saying it after the elections,” Bakić said, echoing the Student List’s earlier position.
Putin Just Lost His Key Ally in Europe. Here’s What Happens Next
“The Republic of Serbia will retain its principled stance on not introducing restrictive measures toward the Russian Federation,” the list previously said in a statement on Sept. 30.
With the list holding an absolute majority of nearly 140 seats, the next step is a presidential election, which Serbia’s constitution requires by Dec. 26. Until then, Ana Brnabić of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), closely linked to Vučić, is serving as acting president.
Vučić concedes, but vows to fight back
Vučić conceded defeat, saying his coalition, United Serbia, won 105 seats.
The name of his coalition closely echoes United Russia, which won the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections, held in Russia and occupied territories of Ukraine, without the main election-monitoring body of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).
The same Duma elections that the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) deemed illegitimate earlier this month.
Vučić’s concession quickly proved to be anything but a surrender. He claimed that “you will see, in six months, no one will be happy and joyful anymore,” adding that “from tonight, we start preparing. We are going to defeat them.”
He also blamed foreign forces for his defeat, echoing Russia’s similar rhetoric towards the West.
“What brought us down is this verified revolution, which they carried out with direct support from various European countries, and the deep American state, the one against [US] President [Donald] Trump,” Vučić said.
“I congratulate them, even though they are just executors of work. Executors of dirty work, which someone else designed to bring down a sovereign country. For a moment you have succeeded. For how long, we shall see,” he continued, as if years of intense public frustration with corruption had not been enough to produce such a result.
From a collapsed canopy to a new regime
The Student List grew out of the Nov. 1, 2024, collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, north of Belgrade, which killed 16 people.
Four children were killed as well, with the youngest victim aged 5.
The tragedy sparked mass protests across Serbia, which escalated over Vučić’s refusal to accept responsibility and the use of a sound cannon against the students, a high-frequency weapon that causes disorientation, nausea and panic.
The movement eventually formed its own list, led by Novi Sad cardiologist Ilija Srdanović.
Its program, the “Student Plan,” has 11 points in three sections, aiming not just to change the people that hold power, but to dismantle decades of systemic corruption.
“Serbia or the Mafia” pledges an independent anti-corruption police unit, a purge of Interior Ministry officers tied to organized crime or the protest crackdowns, confiscation of illegally acquired assets, audits of opaque state projects and an end to political control over the media regulator and public broadcaster RTS.
“Knowledge Is Power” promises merit-based public hiring, free textbooks for all primary and secondary students and support for startups, entrepreneurs and farmers to move Serbia beyond a cheap-labor economy.
“Serbia Grows With Us” would cap fixed-term employment at 12 months instead of 24, curb the import lobby’s grip on food prices, offer affordable housing to young families and essential workers, lower medicine prices and reopen rural clinics.
Vučić informed Putin about his resignation
Vučić, first elected president in 2017 and re-elected in 2022, signed his resignation live on television on Sept. 26, cutting his final term short by eight months.
Following months of what could be described as world’s biggest anti-government protests, he stepped down to campaign “as an ordinary citizen,” planning to become prime minister if SNS won.
On the same day of his resignation, Vučić held a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which he emphasized Serbia’s energy partnership with Moscow, while also boasting their 14 year long friendship.
In a video address posted on social media, Vučić said that he secured a “good and low gas price” of €318 (roughly $361) per 1,000 cubic meters (264.172 gallons), far below the market rate of €868 ($987) at the time.
Currently, Serbia remains one of the few European countries that have not joined EU sanctions on Russia, and it continues to import discounted Russian gas and oil.
Vučić has long insisted no sanctions would be introduced while he was in power. On election night, he claimed the students would impose them by March or April, something the list had ruled out a month earlier.
A fresh choice ahead
Around the same time of Vučić’s resignation, Russian-state-owned media TASS reported that while analysts expected no major foreign policy shift, a student win could move Serbia closer to Western positions.
Polina Sokolova, a research fellow at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, said a Serbian turn against Russia under Western pressure “cannot be excluded.”
According to TASS, this is because European countries, “which have been Ukraine’s main sponsors, do not demonstrate any intention to enter substantive negotiations.” However, EU leaders consistently urge Russia to agree to a ceasefire; it is the Kremlin that has rebuffed every such proposal so far.
The argument mirrors Vučić’s own claim about “dirty work” designed abroad.
However, despite Vučić’s decades-long ties to Moscow, Serbia has backed Ukraine on several main issues, including territorial integrity on Crimea and Donbas. Belgrade has also provided Kyiv with non-military assistance throughout the war, which has drawn sharp criticism from Russia.
Similarly, Vučić showed support to Kyiv by attending the Carpathian Eight (C8) initiative, launched by President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 18 in Bukovel, western Ukraine.
“We have much to offer - from railway lines and roads to more open borders,” Vučić said, signaling openness to future cooperation with Ukraine across several sectors.
Results welcomed by European leaders
Several European leaders welcomed the result.
“This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine is ready to continue expanding cooperation with Belgrade.
In a telephone call with the Student List, Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar compared Serbia’s elections to its own, held earlier in the year. “I assured them of Hungary’s support,” he said. “I was delighted to hear how much strength our victory in April had given them during this difficult struggle.”
Meanwhile, President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen said that Europe stands “ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union.”
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos reiterated that Europe is ready to support the new government in progressing on its EU path, citing “their [Serbia’s] demands for the rule of law, the fight against corruption and free media.”
While cheap gas could keep Serbia close for now, should the EU membership ever demand a choice, the country may have to take a stronger stance towards Russia.
The question now is how the students, who campaigned for democracy and freedom, will steer Serbia toward European standards while still nurturing its friendship with Moscow and avoiding sanctions.
The Kremlin urged Serbia’s incoming leaders to maintain ties with Russia, claiming that cooperation “is in Serbia’s interests.”

Established Long-Term Relationship status for service personnel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:52:26 GMT
01:52:26 KST

Established Long-Term Relationship status for service personnel
The process for recording and approving a defence-recognised Established Long-Term Relationship (LTR(E)).
Established Long-Term Relationship (LTR(E))
An LTR(E) is a relationship between two people that has continued for a long time and has the intent of permanence, but does not have the legal recognition of marriage or civil partnership.
Having accurate data on LTR(E) relationships enables defence understand and meet the couple’s needs.
Benefits of LTR(E) status
Service personnel may seek LTR(E) status for:
- eligibility for service housing
- transfer of leave (for dual-serving LTR(E) couples)
- joint career management discussions (for dual-serving LTR(E) couples)
How to apply for LTR(E) status
Application form
Service personnel must complete the application form available from their HR admin team, or at Annex A within the and provide supporting evidence.
Only one service person within a dual-serving couple needs to apply for LTR(E) status. If approved, Joint Personnel Administration (JPA) will be updated for both partners.
The form must be signed by both the serving person and their partner, whether or not the couple is dual-serving.
Evidence requirements
To support an LTR(E) application, applicants must provide:
- one piece of evidence from Section A, or
- 3 pieces of evidence: two from Section B and one from Section C
Section A
Proof of shared children (e.g. joint birth certificates, adoption papers).
Section B (evidence must be more than 365 days old)
Evidence of long-term commitments, such as joint financial, domestic, legal, or child-related responsibilities.
Examples include but are not limited to:
- joint tenancy/mortgage agreements
- shared utility bills or financial accounts
- named beneficiary on life insurance or Armed Forces Pension Scheme
- having Recorded Long Term Relationship (LTR(R)) status - this is achieved when a service person’s partner is added to the ‘emergency contacts’ section on JPA for more than 365 days
Section C (evidence must be less than 90 days old)
Evidence that demonstrates ongoing commitment, such as utility bills or bank statements.
Exceptional circumstances
Where a service person cannot satisfy the qualifying criteria for LTR(E) they may submit casework to the Armed Forces Families and Safeguarding (AFFS) team via: People-AFFS-LTR-Casework@mod.gov.uk.
Submissions must include the application form, alternative supporting evidence and justification for the alternative evidence.
A service person may not meet the criteria if:
- HR cannot verify the provided evidence
- the evidence specified is unavailable
Contact
For queries or casework submissions, email: People-AFFS-LTR-Casework@mod.gov.uk

Pope says happy to return to South America after trip confirmed
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:52:12 CET
01:52:12 KST

Pope Leo XIV said Monday he was happy
to be able to return to the continent where he lived after his
November 6-17 trip to South America was confirmed after his
recent lung-cancer surgery including Peru, where he worked as a
missionary for many years before becoming a bishop there and
whose citizenship he holds along with his US one.
                                    
"I am happy to be able to return to the continent where I
experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a communiqué
from the Holy See Press Office, which confirmed that the Pope's
trip to South America will proceed as scheduled.
                                    
"May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one
another, to strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters,
and to renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy!
"The Pope," the statement reads, "is following medical
recommendations with scrupulous care and attention, while
remaining deeply determined to continue serving the Church.
                                    
"The Holy Father looks forward to this journey with great joy
and enthusiasm; it will offer an opportunity to strengthen the
bonds of communion with local Churches, encourage the faithful
in their mission, bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to
the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encounter their
faith, and share the hope and peace that Christ brings to our
world."
Leo's apostolic journey to South America his sixth international
trip.
                                    
He will be in Uruguay November 6-8, visiting Montevideo,
Paysandú and Florida, then travel to Argentina, where he will go
to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján November 8-11, and
subsequently stay in Peru until November 17.
                                    
The American pontiff spent large chunks of his life in Peru
after first going there as a missionary in the 1980s and served
as the bishop of Chiclayo between 2015 and 2023.
                                    
He also acquired Peruvian citizenship.
                                    
Chiclayo and the capital Lima are among the Peruvian cities he
will travel to.
                                    
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis never returned to his homeland of
Argentina during his 12-year pontificate.
                                    
Confirming the trip, the Holy See Press Office said: "Dr. Luigi
Carbone confirms that the Holy Father's post-operative recovery
continues to progress, and the latest medical examinations
confirm his good health.
                                    
"Given the current clinical picture and the results of the
diagnostic tests and laboratory analyses performed, there are no
contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking the
upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned.
                                    
"Accordingly, the Holy See Press Office confirms that the
Apostolic Journey of Pope Leo XIV to Uruguay, Argentina, and
Peru—scheduled for November 6-17, 2026—will take place according
to the previously published itinerary."

Russian government urges strategic data centers to move underground as Ukrainian drone attacks intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:51:22 UTC
01:51:22 KST

Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development has approved recommendations for protecting data centers from drone attacks, including a proposal to place particularly important strategic facilities underground or in bunkers, the Kremlin-aligned newspaper Kommersant reported on Oct. 25.
An industry task force under the ministry divided critical data centers into three categories, proposing different security requirements for each:
- K1 — strategic facilities whose damage would disrupt government functions for at least one hour;
- K2 — facilities that support economically or socially important systems at the regional or industry level;
- K3 — corporate data centers whose disruption would primarily affect the company rather than government agencies.
For existing data centers, the recommendations call for reducing their visibility from the air and building layered defenses around them. Strategically important data centers that are still under construction should be placed underground or in bunker-type facilities, and all protective structures should ensure the continued operation of server halls, cooling systems, and power supplies.
The recommendations also call for the creation of a centralized coordination center through which data center operators can communicate with emergency services, law enforcement agencies and the military. Industry representatives interviewed by Kommersant generally described the measures as effective.
Following a recent wave of attacks on data centers, with the latest targeting facilities run by Russia’s Federal Tax Service in the Nizhny Novgorod Region, operators have already begun installing anti-drone netting at their facilities. Implementing the new measures, however, could increase provider service prices by as much as 10%.

The Diesel Diversion: Trump’s Faulty Attempt to Blame Inflation on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:50:55 UTC
01:50:55 KST

The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States since 2022 is expected to arrive in New York within the next few weeks, but its 40,000-ton cargo amounts to less than two hours of American consumption. The shipment will barely register at the pump—and it answers the wrong question, since what drove American diesel past $6 a gallon was never a shortage of Russian supply, but historic bottlenecks from the war in the Middle East.
Recall what happened between May and July of this year, when Ukraine launched one of the most destructive phases of its energy war against Moscow, sending waves of drones attacking massive Russian refineries at Kirishi, Ryazan, Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, and Omsk one after another. If Russian refining capacity governed American fuel costs, prices at U.S. truck stops should have exploded. Instead, American diesel fell by $1.06 a gallon.
With the midterms days away and September’s consumer price index showing fuel oil up a staggering 74% on the year, President Donald Trump has cast Kyiv as the architect of American inflation. “What’s happened in Russia with Ukraine has been really the biggest problem for diesel,” he said in the Oval Office on September 30 before naming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the culprit, telling reporters that Zelenskyy “wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The charge is politically convenient but economically backward. Until this month’s waiver, Russian fuel had been barred from American ports since 2022, meaning Ukrainian strikes have reached U.S. pumps only through the gradual tightening of global supply. The real shockwave runs through the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran can choke off a fifth of the world’s seaborne crude overnight. Diesel was $3.48 a gallon in January and still under $4 the week American and Israeli bombs fell on Iran. When Tehran closed the Strait, the price jumped 96 cents in a single week.
From that moment, the U.S. price line has moved in lockstep with the Iran war—cresting at the April ceasefire, dipping only after the June truce, climbing after the pause in hostilities collapsed in July. By September, the tanker war had driven diesel to a record $6.53.
Ukraine’s unceasing drone campaign has at most modestly nudged up the global floor, while the Iran war has steered every spike and plunge.
By authorizing the sale of Russian diesel, Washington provided Moscow the relief that sanctions are meant to withhold. And when Zelenskyy refused to halt strikes on Russian refineries, Americans throttled the Starlink defenses only they can supply.
Now, Ukraine and its European backers are left with a narrowing set of options. Pulled with discipline, however, the levers they hold can still keep Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on a tightening clock.
A cure that feeds the disease
After an Oct. 9 phone call with Putin, President Trump directed the Treasury to reopen American ports to Russian diesel through April 2027. On paper, the deal promises 4.8 million tons of fuel. In reality, the promise amounts to roughly 10 days of U.S. demand, and analysts doubt that Moscow can ship even that much after months of Ukrainian strikes on the refineries that would fill the tankers.
Carnegie’s Sergey Vakulenko calls the arrangement “largely for show,” yet for a Kremlin watching its September oil and gas tax revenues plunge 22% year-over-year, the spectacle is the prize. What former U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul condemned as “absolutely deplorable,” and Zelenskyy called “a gift to Putin,” was followed a week later by a concession of far greater strategic weight. Two days before the Russia provisions of the Graham sanctions act were scheduled to bite, an executive order waived them. In a single stroke, the White House neutralized both the 100 and 500% tariffs and stripped out the clause locking existing sanctions in place.
While Moscow collected waivers, Kyiv got the vise. Washington announced an “energy ceasefire” the Kremlin never bothered to acknowledge. After Zelenskyy held his fire for three days, Russia pounded Ukrainian energy infrastructure 76 times in the week that followed. By the Ukrainian president’s account—one Secretary of State Marco Rubio denies—the American satellite alerts that warn Ukraine when a Russian missile is in the air went dark for a period of time. Procurement contracts required for the transfer of an allied-funded batch of Patriot interceptors reportedly sat unsigned on the desk of U.S. Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth.
Meanwhile, the speed of Starshield datalinks, the military-grade Starlink network that Ukraine’s drone units rely on, was throttled. Starshield datalinks need to operate at speeds up to 550 km/h (342 mph) to effectively intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed and Geran drones.
The 160 km/h (100 mph) cap was apparently instituted—simply insufficient to protect Ukrainian civilians from Russian ballistic missiles.
Trump and Elon Musk finger-pointed at each other for the restriction. Trump has reportedly since called Musk to lift the cap. U.S. officials say service is running more normally. Kyiv says the limit remained in place into this weekend, with President Zelenskyy tweeting on October 24 that service has now been restored.
The Trump Administration should also allow Ukraine to use the system in Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers. Take out the archer, not the arrows.
What Ukraine can still do
Washington’s squeeze rests on the premise that Kyiv is losing and must be forced to settle, but the front-line situation does not support that notion. Russian forces have made virtually no net territorial gains in 2026 despite suffering more than 40,000 casualties a month since July. At this year’s rate of advance, we estimate that Moscow would need 60 years to capture the rest of Donetsk Oblast.
In fact, the momentum has tilted the other way, with Ukrainian counteroffensives, such as the exceptionally innovative Operation Vivaldi. For months, Kyiv’s forces have killed or seriously wounded more Russian soldiers than the Kremlin can recruit. Closing that gap would require a mass mobilization Putin has been afraid to order, wary of unrest in a country reeling from the fuel shortages created by Ukraine’s refinery strikes. The myth of an inevitable Russian victory amounts to a Kremlin sales pitch aimed at Washington, and the very energy campaign the White House wants to shut down is what keeps Putin boxed in.
Nor can the White House physically switch that campaign off. For all the damage the administration’s freeze inflicted on Ukraine’s air shield, enough Ukrainian drones and missiles were able to reach their targets. Washington’s leverage is entirely defensive, whereas Ukraine’s offensive reach is built at home and in Europe. The 1,000-strong armada that struck St. Petersburg in mid-October was built around FP-1 drones, 90% of which are Ukrainian-made, flying into Russian airspace where Starlink does not function, and Starshield caps do not apply. The E.U.’s Kaja Kallas has rightly defended Ukraine’s actions as legitimate self-defense.
By Putin’s estimate, the wider Ukrainian campaign has cost Russia about 1% of GDP, more than a year of Russian growth, as the central bank’s fight against punishing inflation pushed interest rates to their highest level since the early 2000s. The true toll is almost certainly worse. As we have previously argued, even after Moscow blacked out mandatory economic data, the IMF continues to recycle unverified Kremlin figures to dub Russia the world’s fourth-largest economy at peak output, despite ranking just 51st in GDP per capita.
In 2022, hundreds of billions of dollars abandoned the Russian economy after our team helped spur the withdrawal of more than 1,000 major corporations following the invasion. Firms that curtailed operations outperformed those that did not, in terms of market performance.
Even where Kyiv chooses to look beyond oil, its domestic weapons require no American permission and offend no American farmer. Homegrown Long Neptune missiles have already crippled four of the Black Sea Fleet’s Kalibr missile carriers and recently destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, proving that Ukraine can systematically hunt the launchers, airfields, and factories that fire on its cities. The same freedom of action applies to striking Russian data centers, an asymmetric campaign that an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute judges lopsidedly in Kyiv’s favor because Ukraine’s critical data is already safely hosted abroad.
Holding an offensive campaign that Washington wants to stop but cannot physically block changes the terms of diplomacy. Toward the White House, Kyiv should act as a customer rather than a supplicant. Any pause in energy strikes should be treated strictly as an opportunity to make a deal—offered only in exchange for verified Russian reciprocity and binding, written guarantees from Washington on Patriot interceptors, satellite-based missile launch warnings, and uncapped Starshield access, a bargain of the kind legislators like Senator Roger Wicker and organizations like the Foundation for Defense of Democracies have urged.
What Europe must now do
Kyiv’s balancing act rests on a hard truth in Brussels. Europe can replace most of America’s financial support and much of its weaponry within two years, but it cannot replace Patriot-class interceptors, space-based ballistic-missile warning, or Starlink-scale connectivity this winter. The vulnerability is partly of Europe’s own making after three decades of over-reliance on American dominance, and it now collides with an American arsenal running dry.
The on-again, off-again war with Iran that drove U.S. diesel to $6.53 is also the conflict that emptied the Pentagon’s magazines. According to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the Gulf conflict consumed roughly two-thirds of America’s Patriot inventory and more than a third of its THAAD interceptors, leaving a rebuild measured in years at the exact moment Ukraine’s Patriot stockpiles are reportedly exhausted. Europe’s scramble to build sovereign air defenses—four SAMP/T NG batteries currently on order, a 10-nation FREYJA program aiming for a first intercept in mid-2027, and the diplomatic courtship of Japan, the sole non-American producer of PAC-3 interceptors—is real and necessary, but slow. Every euro spent on European interceptors is one less dollar earned in Washington, and one fewer armament President Trump can delay.
A similar bottleneck applies to space. While Europe’s radar and optical satellites could potentially replace American targeting imagery within weeks, OneWeb and the E.U.’s GovSatcom offer only a partial hedge against a Starlink slowdown. And a European satellite constellation capable of warning of a ballistic launch probably will not exist before the 2030s.
Because Europe cannot buy its way out of those technical bottlenecks overnight, it must lean aggressively into the financial and maritime levers it controls today. The E.U.’s €90 billion loan covers 2026 and much of 2027, and when the remaining €70 billion gap comes to a head at the December European Council, moving the €202 billion in frozen Russian assets out of Belgium offers the clearest route around Belgium’s objections. Better still, a full ban on shipping services for Russian crude, along with expanding the shadow-fleet boardings that European navies have already begun, could squeeze Moscow’s war chest at almost no cost to European taxpayers.
Ukraine’s most decisive advantage, though, is found on the factory floor. Domestic drone production has surged 370% this year, and the Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missile costs just under $600,000, less than a fifth of an American Tomahawk’s $3.5 million price tag. By guaranteeing a loan to the Flamingo’s manufacturer, Denmark has laid out a blueprint for surviving an erratic Washington: European capital behind Ukrainian weapons.
The lesson of the lever
A bitter paradox governs the current battlefield. The offensive campaign squeezing Moscow is the one Washington objects to, while the defenses faltering over Ukrainian cities are the ones only the U.S. can supply. By blaming Kyiv for an energy shock originating in the Persian Gulf, the White House has struck a bargain that lowers no prices at home, replenishes the aggressor’s coffers abroad, and teaches the Kremlin that American sanctions expire if Putin simply waits them out. Such a posture delivers neither peace nor strength.
Ukraine is akin to the Biblical hero David, who, through cunning, triumphed over the lumbering giant Goliath. Moscow's “card hand” is neither the colossus Trump believes it to be nor the colossus its propaganda advertises. Russia is not remotely an economic superpower. Beneath its vast map lies a concentrated population—over 80% of the population lives in the 20% not plagued by extreme cold, permafrost, and poor soil—and a brittle economy dependent on raw materials the world can increasingly buy elsewhere, backed by a military with a long history of failing to subdue smaller, more determined foes, from Japan in 1905 and Poland in 1920 to Finland in 1940 and the Afghan mujahideen in the 1980s. Sheer land mass has never guaranteed victory when the smaller side is fighting for its existence.
The silver lining is that Washington’s attempted coercion is forging the European autonomy it assumed would never materialize. If European leaders withstand Russian pressure over the next 18 months and resist the political disarray stoked by Kremlin disinformation, the continent will emerge a far more formidable power—proving the quip circulating in allied capitals that Europe has found no better unifier since Charlemagne than Donald Trump. Europe, Ukraine, and the world now know what an American guarantee is worth when the guarantor changes its mind, and Washington is about to learn that leverage, like interceptors, is a stock that depletes with every use.
As Mark Twain advised, “It’s not the size of the dog in the fight; it’s the size of the fight in the dog.”

Serbian longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in a snap vote, handing victory to a student-led movement that built mass support by pledging to fight graft and reverse democratic backsliding.
The Student List won 53 percent of the vote, according to nearly complete results released yesterday, compared with 39 percent for Vucic. The outcome marks a fall from power for a veteran politician who dominated the country for more than a decade and balanced close ties with Russia, China, the US and Europe.
However, it was a grassroots protest movement sparked by an outrage over a deadly construction disaster that became his undoing. By resigning as president last month and calling the election, Vucic hoped to return as prime minister. His plan, which mimicked his ally, Russian President Vladimir Putin, backfired amid the highest election turnout in 33 years.
Photo: AP
The nation is now headed for an unprecedented redrawing of its political spectrum with a pro-
European parliament, an extensive review of deals and policies, as well as potential probes into the ruling elite. It remains to be seen how that revamp would play out as the Students List has operated without a distinct leader and is yet to announce its candidate for prime minister.
“You can have a movement without a name to topple an autocrat, but you cannot run a country that way,” said Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European studies at the University of Graz. “Now it’s a different world for them, and that’s a big demand.”
On the election night, the movement was late with a victory speech, as its representatives could not decide who would speak on their behalf.
“This is the victory of the conviction that Serbia can and will do better,” said Radomir Saicic, one of the movement’s leaders.
“We call on all citizens to act peacefully and in dignified manner. We didn’t fight for months to lose it,” he added.
Vucic, 56, is the second longtime leader to lose power in eastern Europe this year, following the ouster of his ally, Viktor Orban, in Hungary six months ago.
The former president told his supporters 90 minutes after polls closed that the Student List won the ballot with the “direct support from some European countries and the American deep state, the one that is also against” US President Donald Trump.
He called the movement “just contractors doing some very dirty work,” without providing evidence for his claims.
Vucic pledged to make a comeback, saying: “I’ll defeat them much sooner than they think.”

A chorus of boos echoed through Rogers Arena as Quinn Hughes stepped on the ice for warm-ups on Sunday night. They never stopped.

Photo: Bob Frid-Imagn Images
Hughes scored off a rebound on a power player midway through the second period to make it 3-0, and set up Kirill Kaprizov’s NHL-leading 13th goal early in the third for a 4-0 advantage. In 13 games this season, Hughes has three goals and 13 assists.

Hundreds of people — many clad in Canucks jerseys emblazoned with Hughes’ name and No. 43 — stood around the glass ahead of warm-ups, hoping to get a glimpse of the star American defenseman.

As the video ended, Hughes skated out from the bench and raised his stick in salute as both his current and former teammates tapped their sticks on the boards.
