Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan’s defense buildup needs more than shiny new toys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:58 UTC
01:48:58 KST

On Oct. 2, after years of delays, Taiwan’s air force took delivery of the first two F-16V Block 70 fighter jets at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County. In a sign of how eagerly anticipated this arrival was, speculation and rumors had been flying as to why they had been sitting for weeks in Hawaii en route to Taiwan.
These are part of a total of 66 F-16V Block 70s on order. There are hopes the rest will arrive by the end of next year, but no one will be surprised if that extends into 2029 or even later. Worse, in the two that have already arrived, according to an Air Force briefing of the legislature on Oct. 12, the Viper Shield electronic warfare suite is only partly installed and its software is still in development
On Sept. 24, AIDC delivered the final two aircraft in the 66-aircraft Brave Eagle trainer program. One aircraft had previously been lost in a crash. In July, the last AT-3 jet training mission ended, and the F-5E/F jets are being phased out.
Photo: Peter Lo, Taipei Times
Taiwan’s armed forces — the Army, Navy, Air Force and Military Police — and Coast Guard are in the midst of a boom in (typically delayed) arrivals of shiny new weapons systems and kit. Far more is on order or planned. According to Taiwan Security Monitor’s September estimate, there is a US$29.72 billion (NT$968 billion) backlog in orders from the US.
Alongside the increased annual defense budget, lawmakers approved a special procurement framework authorizing up to NT$780 billion in US arms purchases over 2026–2033, subject to subsequent appropriations. Separately, the government is investing NT$44.2 billion over 2025–2030 in developing Taiwan’s drone industry.
In April, the Army received the final batch of the controversial 28 M1A2T Abrams tanks purchased from the US, bringing the total to 108. The Army is also planning to procure 178 domestically developed Cheetah armored vehicles between next year and 2033.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
According to a Taipei Times report last month citing a military expert, Taiwan’s first domestically built submarine, the Hai Kun (Narwhal, 海鯤), could be delivered to the Navy as early as this month. This is the first of eight planned submarines.
Both the Navy and Coast Guard have been taking delivery of various types of ships in recent years. On Oct. 2, the keel-laying ceremony was held to launch construction on the Coast Guard’s second 5000-tonnes high-latitude oceanic patrol vessel, out of a planned six total by 2031.
These examples highlight some of the flashier headline-grabbing additions currently flooding into system to defend Taiwan, but there are many, many more. There are smaller ships growing the Navy and Coast Guard fleets, mine-layers and missile systems for the Army and Air Force and hardly a day passes without some missile, unmanned vehicle or drone program being announced.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
Surely that is all good news, right? Maybe.
PEOPLE NEEDED
To illustrate the problem, imagine if you received a top-of-the-line Formula 1 racing car. No doubt for many fans, that would sound like a dream come true. But what would you do with it?
A first thought would be: how do I drive this thing? These are not for amateurs; you had better get some training.
On reflection, the challenge gets harder. They require pit crews, supply chains of highly specialized and very expensive parts, and specialists to keep them in top running condition. There are legal and insurance issues, never mind finding a place to simply park it.
The challenges would be enormous, but nothing compared to what is required to fly and maintain those two new F-16V fighters and the 64 more that are expected to arrive soon. They will join 139 older-version F-16s, 52 aging French Mirage 2000s, 129 indigenously developed F-CK-1 Ching-kuo fighters and the aforementioned Brave Eagles.
Despite the Hollywood glamor and prestige of flying a fighter jet, the Air Force is struggling to maintain enough pilots for its existing fleet. They may struggle to have enough pilots for the new jets as they arrive, or be required to ground existing ones.
It takes years of flight, simulator and operational training to prepare a fighter pilot. In a report to the legislature, the Ministry of National Defense proposed scrapping the maximum length of service for air force pilots amid a shortage of experienced pilots, many of whom leave the military to fly for civilian airlines. Reportedly, civilian pilots make about NT$100,000 to NT$200,000 more a month.
Under current law, pilots holding the rank of lieutenant colonel can serve a maximum of 26 years and colonels a maximum of 30 years, so pilots at these ranks must generally leave military service at about 48 and 52 years of age, respectively. The new proposal would extend their service to around age 58.
If the Cabinet approves the proposal and it takes effect, the ministry aims to retain 72 pilots ranked lieutenant colonel or colonel in service longer. Hopefully, the proposal is accepted and all those pilots are retained; they will be needed.
The problem is that may not be enough. Gray zone incursions by Chinese forces are in part designed to wear down the personnel and the jets themselves. Exhaustion may make those higher-paid civilian jobs, with their regular schedules, look even more appealing.
Now spare a thought for the equally critical, highly skilled crews needed to keep those planes flying. They face all the exhaustion and stress without the sexy job title of fighter jet pilot. Does the Air Force have enough of them?
‘GOOD AS DEAD’
Recently, gray zone incursions have increasingly been at sea. The brunt of handling those falls on the Coast Guard, and there the situation is dire.
A report by the National Audit Office found that at the end of June last year, of 108 vessels in service, only four had a full complement of sailors. That means that 96 percent were sailing without full crews. The same report found that the problem is getting worse, just as the Coast Guard is rapidly adding new vessels.
A report in Storm Media paints a grim picture. Because gray zone incursions can happen at any time, sailors can be forced to respond, regardless of holidays or personal plans. The Chinese can use their far larger navy and fishing boat militia to probe endlessly.
That report describes how in calmer times, a three-day tour meant exactly that. Now, sailors on vacation can be called to active duty for up to 15 days, put in dangerous standoffs with Chinese vessels and often called to duty sleep-deprived. With spotty cell phone service, one insider quoted in the report told Storm that some spouses complain that their husbands are “as good as dead.”
Unsurprisingly, despite offers of high salaries right out of police colleges, the Coast Guard is struggling to recruit sailors willing to take on this challenging, unglamorous and exhausting job that offers little personal freedom or control over their lives.
The government is acutely aware of all of this, and has actively been working to boost pay and benefits to make these jobs more appealing. They have also restored the one-year mandatory conscription, up from four months, which may help with some of the more mundane tasks.
Already struggling with personnel issues in both the military and Coast Guard, and with automation filling the gaps years away, the ability of the military to handle the influx of new platforms is a significant concern.
Though they disagree on how to go about it, both the administration and opposition parties agree that making these careers more attractive is a priority.
Faced with a demographic meltdown, they have their work cut out for them.

Nature cannot wait for calmer times to return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:48:58 UTC
01:48:58 KST

In times of war, geopolitical turmoil, and fiscal tightening, it is tempting to view the defense of nature as a desirable but non-urgent goal — an objective that can be pursued when calmer times return. But we embrace this view at our peril.
As world leaders gather for the UN biodiversity and climate-change conferences this fall, they must remember that over half of global GDP depends on nature and the services it provides. Healthy soils underpin a US$9.5 trillion global food industry, while forests support 1.5 billion livelihoods around the world. Healthy rivers help absorb floodwaters and sustain vital transportation networks. Nature is the backbone of the global economy, and protecting it must be a top national and international priority.
Nature-related crises will not wait until the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are over. This summer’s sweltering drought in Europe caused US$2 billion to US$3 billion in crop losses, a double blow for farmers after the war-induced closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused fertilizer prices to surge by 71 percent. The combined effects of conflict and extreme weather have helped push global food prices to their highest levels since 2022.
All told, scientists predict that a partial collapse of ecosystems could cost the global economy US$2.7 trillion annually. Despite intense geopolitical instability, we cannot afford to undermine the natural systems on which our economies depend. The global goal to protect and conserve at least 30 percent of the world’s land and ocean by 2030, known as 30x30, is more important than ever.
Protecting nature is an investment in resilience and solidarity. Resilience strengthens food and water security, and the capacity to weather climate shocks. It sustains livelihoods, public health, and long-term economic stability. The 30x30 goal, adopted by governments in 2022 under the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, recognizes that protecting nature is fundamental to providing these and other public goods.
For example, kelp beds, mangroves, and marshes absorb carbon dioxide, while coral reefs help protect against storms and provide natural habitats for some of the world’s most diverse ecosystems. On land, forests regulate rainfall and support the livelihoods of local communities, and healthy soils retain water and nutrients that are vital to global food security and flood protection.
Four years on, the world has made significant strides toward the 30x30 goal. New analysis from Campaign for Nature shows that 20 percent of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and that fully delivering on existing commitments could increase this share to approximately 27 percent by 2030, closing much of the remaining gap.
Progress at sea, however, has been much slower. Only 10 percent of the ocean is formally designated for conservation, and existing commitments would increase this to a mere 12 percent by 2030. Worse, Together for the Ocean’s latest Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that only 3.5 percent of the ocean is assessed as effectively protected, with harmful activities continuing in many areas that are supposed to be off limits.
With just four years remaining, the world still has a chance to achieve 30x30, which is one of the defining global commitments of this decade. But what will it take to make up for lost time?
For starters, governments must dramatically increase financing for nature. Delivering 30x30 will require approximately US$100 billion to US$180 billion annually, compared with current annual spending of US$24 billion. But, again, this spending represents an investment, not just a cost. Achieving 30x30 could add up to US$450 billion to annual global GDP by 2050 and support an estimated 4 million to 7 million jobs.
Policymakers at all levels urgently must move from talking about solutions to implementing them. As of May this year, 116 countries had submitted commitments to protect up to 27 percent of land and inland water areas. But many have yet to follow up with mapped, costed, and financed plans. Commitments alone will not protect nature.
Protecting more of the planet is only part of the challenge. Governments also must ensure that protected and conserved areas are well managed, deliver real benefits, and meaningfully preserve biodiversity. That requires long-term funding arrangements that can endure through changing economic and political cycles.
There is no denying that the global outlook is uncertain. The wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are spurring governments to increase spending on defense and focus more on economic growth. But it would be a mistake to put nature on the back burner. Protecting natural systems is not just for the bees. Investing in their future is an investment in our own.
Mary Robinson is a former president of Ireland and a former UN secretary-general’s special envoy for climate change.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

Agricultural losses from typhoon reach NT$221.63m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:48:57 KST

Agricultural losses caused by Typhoon Champi had reached NT$221.63 million (US$6.82 million) as of 11am yesterday, with garlic crops sustaining the heaviest damage, the Ministry of Agriculture said.
Crop losses accounted for NT$210.73 million, while livestock losses, primarily pigs, stood at NT$90,000, data compiled from local government reports by the ministry’s Agriculture and Food Agency and Department of Animal Industry showed.
Damage to private facilities reached NT$10.8 million, which included NT$8.57 million in livestock and poultry facilities and NT$2.23 million in agricultural infrastructure, such as horizontal trellises and plastic greenhouses, the ministry said.
Photo: Huang Shu-li, Taipei Times
Among crops, garlic sustained the most severe damage, with losses totaling NT$63.59 million.
Other heavily affected crops included peanuts (NT$15.91 million), onions (NT$11.65 million), tangerines (NT$11.51 million) and corn (NT$9.99 million).
By region, Yunlin County reported the heaviest agricultural losses at NT$137.07 million.
It was followed by Miaoli County (NT$24.83 million), Taichung (NT$20.42 million), New Taipei City (NT$16.18 million) and Yilan County (NT$9.38 million).
To mitigate the financial impact, the ministry announced cash relief and low-interest loans for nine municipalities: New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Taichung, as well as Changhua, Nantou, Yunlin, Yilan and Taitung counties.
The subsidies cover crops, forestry, fisheries and livestock, the ministry said, adding that all agricultural products in Yilan County are eligible for the relief program.
The relief package also includes items that did not strictly meet weather parameter thresholds, but were confirmed to have sustained severe damage during on-site inspections, it said.

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) yesterday proposed revitalizing the capital’s waterways before attending a Halloween event where parents expressed support for his childcare policies.
At a news conference at his campaign headquarters in Taipei’s Zhongzheng District (中正), Shen outlined a plan to revitalize the city’s waterways, drawing inspiration from Singapore’s approach to urban water management.
The plan focuses on five priorities -- Active, Beautiful, Clean, Detention and Ecosystem -- collectively known as "ABCDE," Shen said.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
Specific measures include improving waterfront facilities along the Tamsui and Keelung rivers to make them more accessible to the public, using wetlands and vegetation to improve water quality, and developing small-scale floodwater retention facilities in schools and parks to strengthen the city’s flood control capacity.
"We use water every day, but we are actually very far removed from the water in our city," Shen said, arguing that urban water management should incorporate education, culture and environmental protection rather than focus solely on engineering.
Shen said many of Taipei’s streams and irrigation channels had been covered, filled in or incorporated into underground drainage systems during urban development, distancing residents from the city’s waterways.
He said the initiative aimed to reconnect residents with these waterways and make water a central consideration in urban planning.
Later yesterday, Shen, dressed as a ship captain and wearing an Afro wig, handed out candy to children and other attendees at a Halloween event outside the Tianmu Baseball Stadium.
Among those at the event was Taipei resident surnamed Wu (吳), a 35-year-old designer who came with his wife and 2-year- old daughter.
Wu said he was not a staunch DPP supporter and had previously supported former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), but welcomed Shen’s childcare proposals.
One proposal that particularly appealed to him was Shen’s plan to provide up to four hours of free drop-in childcare per week for preschool children.
Taipei currently offers drop-in childcare at designated facilities, most of which charge NT$200 (US$6.13) per hour, according to the city government.
Wu said the proposed free childcare could provide much- needed relief, as he and his wife both work and their daughter spends around 12 hours a day with a nanny on weekdays.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva was re-elected against all expectations on Sunday, but his conservative rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to have the vote annulled.
Lula’s dramatic comeback meant Brazil had not followed Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Peru, all backed by US President Donald Trump, in swinging to the right.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed Lula’s re-election as a triumph for “democracy and multilateralism,” joining a slew of world leaders who welcomed the leftist figurehead’s return for an unprecedented fourth term.
Photo: AFP
Lula, who turns 81 today, defied projections to defeat Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, and win an unprecedented fourth term.
He won 51.8 percent of the votes to 48.2 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling about 4.4 million more votes, official results showed.
Lula was warmly congratulated by the leaders of left-wing governments across Central America, including Mexico, Cuba and Venezuela.
“Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on X.
Right-wing governments in Chile, Ecuador and Peru said they wanted to work toward common goals with the region’s economic powerhouse.
China echoed that sentiment, while Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi also offered his friend Lula his “heartiest congratulations.”
Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.
“People went to vote, because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country,” Lula said in his first comments after the win.
Sunday’s vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours, because some polling stations had already closed.
The move came at the request of Lula, who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as “unacceptable” and a “dirty trick.”
“It is impossible to recognize the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections,” he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia.
Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country’s last election in 2022.
No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the military dictatorship.

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) yesterday began a four-day meeting of its highest-ranking members, targeting concrete measures for “full and rigorous party self-governance,” as Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) seeks to reinforce his authority and enforce ideological uniformity.
Xi briefed the party’s Central Committee on a draft document that state news agency Xinhua said addressed the challenges the party faced, including growing its governing capacity, as well as guarding against complacency and combating corruption, the president’s signature campaign.
The implementation of major decisions and plans of the Central Committee, the largest of its top decisionmaking bodies, must not be empty rhetoric, the commentary wrote.
Photo: EPA
“It is essential to both refine institutional rules and regulations to close loopholes and strengthen safeguards, and ensure their effective implementation,” it said.
The Central Committee is hlding closed-door meetings until Thursday — the fifth since the current cohort was formed in 2022 and therefore known as the fifth plenum.
Analysts say this could be the last major party gathering before its leadership reshuffle next year, when Xi is expected to hold on to the top job for a fourth term.
“The plenum will present Xi as in control, and able to continue his command,” said Kerry Brown, director of King’s College London’s Lau China Institute. “It is likely everything will be centered on him, to dispel any rumors or doubts about his physical fitness and ability to continue in his role.”
With substantive policy issues already largely set in previous gatherings, “this will be a plenum where appearances will matter as much, if not more, than substance,” Brown added.
Xi has overseen a vast anti-corruption campaign in recent years, which has led to the purge of hundreds of senior officials and top generals, even his one-time allies.
While critics argue the purges — particularly those targeting the highest ranks of the armed forces — are destabilizing and undermine combat readiness, the party has portrayed the campaign as both necessary and regenerative, saying the military must undergo a phoenix-like rebirth and “bathe in flames and be forged anew.”
The Xinhua commentary propped up the anti-corruption drive as a demonstration of “sustained and systemic” self-governance to “ensure officials dare not, cannot and do not want to commit corruption.”
“For global investors and policymakers, this signals greater predictability,” it said, adding that China was creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation as merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery.

Chinese automakers outsold Japanese rivals in Europe for the first time over a full quarter, underscoring how quickly brands like BYD Co (比亞迪) and Chery Automobile Co (奇瑞汽車) are gaining ground in the region.
Registrations of Chinese-branded cars roughly doubled from a year earlier in the three months through September to make up 12.7 percent of total sales across the region, led by hybrids, according to market researcher Dataforce. That has put them ahead of Japanese manufacturers, including Toyota Motor Corp, at 11.9 percent.
The advance accelerated at the end of the quarter. Chinese brands’ European share jumped to a record 14.5 percent last month, according to Dataforce, almost three percentage points higher than in August.
Photo: Reuters
While European manufacturers like Volkswagen AG or Renault SA still dominate the region, the speed of China’s surge has been a surprise. Five years ago, Chinese brands accounted for barely 1 percent of European sales. Japanese automakers, by contrast, have spent decades building their position in Europe.
Toyota has sold cars in the region since 1963 and now operates factories across the continent, while Nissan Motor Co has produced vehicles at its Sunderland plant in the UK since 1986. China’s offering is especially successful in the UK, where Chery’s Jaecoo 7 SUV was the country’s best-selling model in March and last month.
Earlier this month, Chery, BYD and Geely Holding Group Co’s (吉利控股集團) Zeekr Intelligent Technology Co (極氪智能) showed off a range of new models at the Paris car show, offering well-priced cars like the BYD Dolphin G DM-i, a compact plug-in hybrid specifically developed for Europe. Bringing their electric vehicle lineups to Europe also positions them to benefit from a jump in demand as fuel prices hit record highs.
The EU is trying to temper an expansion that is partly fueled by state-backed subsidies. After adding extra tariffs on China-made battery-electric vehicles, the bloc this month agreed in principle to curb fast-growing imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU is also considering new rules that would favor locally made cars when granting subsidies and other incentives.
Chinese manufacturers have been preparing to produce locally already. Chery is preparing production in Barcelona and BYD is nearing the completion of a manufacturing site in Hungary. Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co (零跑科技) has started making its B10 SUV at Stellantis NV’s plant in Zaragoza, Spain, as part of the companies’ joint venture.

Russia has been awarded the right to host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships, the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Oct. 25. It is the first time since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 that the country has been awarded a major international competition in an Olympic sport.
The announcement is part of a larger trend. In January, the IWF allowed Russian athletes in the under-23 category to compete internationally under the Russian flag and anthem. In June, the federation lifted all remaining restrictions on athletes from Russia and Belarus. And in July, the International Olympic Committee reinstated the Russian Olympic Committee and recommended that international sports federations lift restrictions on Russian athletes’ participation in competitions.
On Oct. 25, the IWF selected the hosts of four world championships, scheduled to take place between 2028 and 2030. In 2028, the Youth World Weightlifting Championships will be held in Pristina, Kosovo, while the Junior World Championships will take place in Caracas, Venezuela. The Senior World Weightlifting Championships will be held in Ahmedabad, India, in 2029.

Lithuania expects an EU vote on ending seasonal clock changes in late June 2027, during its presidency of the Council of the European Union, public broadcaster LRT reported Monday.
Deputy Transport Minister Lukas Paskevicius said the issue would first be discussed at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers in February.
“In February 2027, we will discuss this issue at an informal meeting of EU transport ministers, and toward the end of Lithuania's presidency, in late June, a vote will be held. We will see what the decision will be,” he said.
Lithuania will hold the council’s rotating presidency during the first half of 2027. Ending twice-yearly clock changes has been included in its proposed presidency agenda, pending final approval by parliament.
Paskevicius said Lithuania had discussed the initiative with ministers from France, Spain, Germany and the Nordic countries, as well as members of the European Parliament.
The EU is awaiting a European Commission study, expected in February 2027, assessing the potential effects of ending seasonal time changes on the economy, agriculture, public health and other sectors.
Member states remain divided over whether to adopt summer or winter time permanently, according to the deputy minister.
Southern European countries tend to favor summer time for its brighter evenings, while Nordic countries have concerns over darker winter mornings, he said.
“Our goal is to abandon seasonal time changes altogether, regardless of whether summer or winter time is chosen. Surveys show that most Lithuanian residents prefer remaining on summer time,” Paskevicius said.
The commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes in 2018, and the European Parliament backed the proposal in 2019. Progress subsequently stalled amid disagreement among member states.

Key Israeli health committee faces tough choices as funding increase stays flat for fourth year

Israel's health basket committee began deliberations Monday on which drugs and medical technologies to add to the state-subsidized health care system in 2027, with an additional 650 million shekels ($211 million) allocated for new treatments – the same amount added to the basket's budget annually since 2023, despite advances in medical technology and an aging population driving increased health care needs.
When asked by Haaretz about the budget increase, Health Ministry Director General Moshe Bar Siman Tov said, "The healthcare system's needs don't start or end" with the committee's work, citing the system's "many diverse needs," including increasing the number of doctors and building infrastructure. At a press conference marking the committee's convening, Health Minister Haim Katz said, "I know that however much we give, it's never enough."
This year, the committee will consider innovative cancer drugs, expanding routine childhood vaccinations to include Bexsero, a vaccine against meningococcal disease, and widening access to contraceptives and mammography screenings. It will also examine expanding eligibility for diabetes medications, including drugs taken orally rather than by injection.
The committee's makeup for 2027 was approved only on Sunday, later than the usual schedule, under which it is appointed by the end of September and begins deliberations after the Jewish High Holy Days. Delays in appointing the committee over the past three years pushed the introduction of new treatments into the health basket to February and March.
Because of the delay in appointing the committee, its deliberations may extend into the beginning of next year, delaying the addition of new drugs to the health basket and potentially forcing patients who need them to incur significant out-of-pocket expenses.

Russia’s trade with African countries exceeded $27B in 2025: Kremlin aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

Kanyshai Butun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Russia's trade with African countries exceeded $27 billion in 2025, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, highlighting agriculture as a key area of cooperation, state media reported.
Russia exported 1.5 million tons of mineral fertilizers to Africa in 2025, with shipments exceeding 2.2 million tons in 2026, Ushakov said, according to the state-run news agency Tass.
Russia also supplied more than 18 million tons of grain to African countries in 2025 and exported another 13 million tons in the first nine months of 2026, he said.
Moscow is also expanding its diplomatic presence across the continent. Since 2022, Russia has opened three embassies, in South Sudan, Gambia, and the Union of the Comoros, while five other diplomatic missions have resumed operations in Burkina Faso, Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Togo, Ushakov said.
He added that Russia cooperates with African countries through international organizations, particularly the UN, on issues including counterterrorism, drug trafficking, and cybercrime.
His remarks came ahead of the Russia-Africa summit, scheduled for Oct. 28-29 in Moscow, with 48 African countries confirming participation, including 22 represented by their heads of state.
 
Gas Exporting Countries Forum
Ushakov also highlighted the role of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), saying global natural gas demand is projected to rise 28% by 2055, from 4.2 trillion cubic meters to 5.4 trillion cubic meters.
He said the global gas industry needs a platform for professional, depoliticized dialogue amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, attacks on Russia's Nord Stream pipelines and Western restrictions on gas purchases, equipment, and technology.
Russia considers reliable and stable gas supplies essential to meeting growing global demand, Ushakov said, describing Moscow as a responsible participant in the global gas market and a reliable supplier.
He added that Russia holds the world's largest natural gas reserves and ranks second globally in terms of production.
The GECF summit is scheduled for Tuesday in Russia, with participants expected to adopt the Moscow Declaration at the conclusion of the event, Ushakov said.

Everyone knows the schedule we have, and they ran the floor and dictated a fast pace. We shot 2-for-18 from 3-point range in the first half. You have days like that, and you can lose games because of them.”

“That’s the power of Maccabi Rishon and its fans. We just need to play hard. Basketball is secondary, and when you come in with the right energy and believe in yourselves, you can play good basketball and win. Credit to the fans for the atmosphere and to the players for their fighting spirit. We took a very painful hit on Monday, and I’m glad we’ve at least started to respond. We still have a lot to make up for.”

Clark scored 20 points, Colson added 19, and Yam Madar contributed 14 in the defeat. Campazzo led Real Madrid with 21 points, Feliz scored 18, and Luwawu-Cabarrot and Alberto Abalde each added 15.
Katash reflected on the defeat, pointing to his team’s inability to maintain its first-half momentum.
“We had a good first half, but in the second half we just ran out of steam and were tired, especially our guards. Playing against a team like Real is tough, and you have to pick your poison. But when their guards hit their shots and had good possessions, it was just very difficult for us. However, we can take some good things from this game.”
Hoard acknowledged that Maccabi needed to improve its ball movement and find ways to come up with wins without Lundberg.
“We stopped moving the ball, and anytime that happens, it puts us in a hole. It’s not the first time. I’m not sure what we can do to correct it. We have to do it the same way as we did against Valencia. We can’t use Iffe’s absence as an excuse, and we have to find ways to get wins. We have to stay together on the defensive side and share the ball on offense.”
Brissett: 'Not great to lose,' team has to 'be better'
Brissett also stressed the need to learn from the loss.
“Two completely different halves, and we have to learn from this. It’s not great to lose, and we have to be better when a team goes on a run. We let this slip away, and we’re not happy with the result. We have to get better.”
In other Israeli League action, Hapoel Holon eased past Hapoel Beersheba 91-75 after jumping out to a commanding 30-12 lead in the opening quarter and cruising to victory.
Claudell Harris led Holon with 22 points, Brandon Jones added 20, and Adama Sanogo scored 18. Tyreek Smith led Beersheba with 25 points, while Brian Cameron contributed 15 and MJ Walker added 14 in the loss.
“We played solid defense and also had a solid performance on offense,” Holon coach Predrag Krunic said. “It was really important to win this game as we have to integrate some new guys into the team, and we showed character to take this victory.”
Beersheba coach Doug Spradley was disappointed with his team’s lack of intensity.
“We had a lack of intensity at times. Our concentration on both sides of the ball wasn’t good enough. We had guys who didn’t show up for some reason. We showed no intensity and no heart. Holon was the more aggressive team. We have to learn from this and move forward.”

Pope says happy to be able to return to continent where he lived

01:42:09 KST

Pope Leo XIV said Monday he was happy
to be able to return to the continent where he lived after his
November 6-17 trip to South America was confirmed including
Peru, where he worked as a missionary for many years before
becoming papal representative there and whose citizenship he
holds along with his US one.
                                    
"I am happy to be able to return to the continent where I
experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a communiqué
from the Holy See Press Office, which confirmed that the Pope's
trip to South America will proceed as scheduled.
                                    
"May this journey be an occasion to open our hearts to one
another, to strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters,
and to renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy!
"The Pope," the statement reads, "is following medical
recommendations with scrupulous care and attention, while
remaining deeply determined to continue serving the Church.
                                    
"The Holy Father looks forward to this journey with great joy
and enthusiasm; it will offer an opportunity to strengthen the
bonds of communion with local Churches, encourage the faithful
in their mission, bring a message of faith, hope, and peace to
the peoples of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, encounter their
faith, and share the hope and peace that Christ brings to our
world."
Leo's apostolic journey to South America his sixth international
trip.
                                    
He will be in Uruguay November 6-8, visiting Montevideo,
Paysandú and Florida, then travel to Argentina, where he will go
to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Luján November 8-11, and
subsequently stay in Peru until November 17.
                                    
The American pontiff spent large chunks of his life in Peru
after first going there as a missionary in the 1980s and served
as the bishop of Chiclayo between 2015 and 2023.
                                    
He also acquired Peruvian citizenship.
                                    
Chiclayo and the capital Lima are among the Peruvian cities he
will travel to.
                                    
Leo's predecessor Pope Francis never returned to his homeland of
Argentina during his 12-year pontificate.

Russian oil refineries ramp up diesel production after deal with the US - Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:31:47 EET
01:31:47 KST

Russian oil refineries ramp up diesel production after deal with the US - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
In October, Russian oil refineries increased diesel production to 180,000 tonnes per day after export quotas were approved. The quotas were granted as part of a deal with the US.
Russian oil refineries increased diesel fuel production in October after the government granted export quotas as part of a supply deal the Kremlin concluded with the United States, two industry sources close to the situation told the publication. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Traders said that from October 1, the Russian government allowed exemptions to the existing ban on diesel fuel exports, allocating quotas that enable Russia to supply fuel under a deal with Trump.
Since Russia's ban on diesel fuel exports came into force in August, Russian oil companies have been forced to cut production to meet domestic demand, while also limiting supplies to Central Asian countries in accordance with intergovernmental agreements.
Industry sources said that diesel fuel production in Russia in the first half of October fell to approximately 160,000 tonnes per day from 175,000 tonnes per day in September. After the new export quotas were approved in the middle of the month, production began to rise to 180,000 tonnes per day.

Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care.

MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population.

Strikes are impacting people's access to healthcare in Yemen
Share
Crisis Update26 October 2026
Over the past few days, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams in Aden and Mocha have been exposed to a series of incidents that further restrict humanitarian access and the provision of medical care to people in Yemen.
This morning, on Monday 26 October, three strikes hit the coastal area of Mocha. One of them fell only 150 metres away from Mocha General hospital, where our teams are working in the maternity and paediatric wards. While all staff and patients are safe, the strike caused damages to the building that may weaken the structure in the longer-term — a building already weakened by years of regular blasts.
The strike also created panic among patients, medical staff, and civilians, further limiting their safe access to healthcare. Such incidents are preventing patients from coming to the hospital, fearing for their lives. With every strike around the hospital, there is a decrease in the number of patients coming to seek care.
A few days earlier, while an MSF plane was about to take off from Aden’s airport on a routine flight intended to carry humanitarian workers, a missile hit the vicinity of the airport. The plane was forced to stay on the ground, and the staff were asked not to board but to seek shelter inside the airport instead. Aden's airport is the main entry point for humanitarian workers, supplies, and medical equipment to the southern parts of Yemen, and accessing it safely is crucial.
These incidents, among others, are exposing MSF and other humanitarian organisations in Yemen to more threats, directly impacting the capacity to urgently operate and reach people, at a time where their needs are highest and the provision of humanitarian care is essential.
We reiterate to all parties to the conflict that humanitarian and medical workers, as well as medical facilities and patients, and access to care, must be protected.

. Out of the total acceptance of necessity (in-principle approval) given, around 82% of the procurements will be made from Indian Industry.

‘Cong Wants Bangladesh-Like Regime Change’: Rajnath Singh SLAMS Rahul Gandhi Over Anti-CEC Stir
While HMVs will enhance operational capabilities, logistical support and mobility in challenging terrains, the self-propelled tracked gun system will provide matching mobility and firepower to mechanised formations. LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and Indian Air Force for reconnaissance and surveillance, combat, search and rescue of troops, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.

While VSHORADS will engage new-generation small-size aerial threats, C-UAS will enhance the survivability of tanks in the modern battlefield. For the Indian Navy, approval was given for the procurement of an active offboard decoy system (AODS) and other major Naval platforms. AODS will enhance the credibility of anti-missile defence, especially against modern anti-ship missiles of adversaries. For the Indian Air Force, approval was accorded for the procurement of helicopters, air defence systems, weapons and a mobile X-Band Doppler weather radar system to enhance air defence and war-fighting capabilities. The procurement of special utility helicopters will help the IAF to meet the important air transport requirements. The Doppler radar system will provide high-resolution, localised weather surveillance in forward areas.

rima dain frames exterior living zones with custom architectural outdoor rugs

[FEATURED]
RIMA DAIN TREATS OUTDOOR TEXTILES AS ARCHITECTURAL ZONING TOOLS
Marbella-based studio Rima Dain develops technically engineered, flatwoven outdoor rugs designed to structure seating zones across Mediterranean residential and hospitality terraces. In exterior architecture and landscape design, outdoor rugs function as foundational spatial dividers, defining boundaries for lounge zones and anchoring furniture across stone, tile, and timber decks. When left unresolved, terraces often present proportion issues where seating groupings appear isolated on expansive paving. Rima Dain approaches exterior rug design through architectural proportion, geometric zoning, and technical textile performance, treating the ground plane as an integral component of the exterior furniture plan.
Caletta Rug in Bronze / Sand
PROPORTION AND GEOMETRIC SIZING CALIBRATE FURNITURE FOOTPRINTS
For Rima Dain studio, specifying an outdoor rug requires careful consideration of scale and layout geometry. In lounge zones, standard spatial planning dictates that front furniture legs rest on the textile, with full-perimeter coverage preferred for larger layouts to unite disparate pieces. In outdoor dining settings, extending the perimeter by 60 to 75 centimeters beyond the tabletop ensures that pulled-out dining chairs remain entirely on the woven surface. For linear or irregular architectural terraces, custom dimensions allow rugs to align with structural columns and boundary walls, establishing clear functional zones across open footprints.
Dune Rug in Olive / Sand
Synthetic FLATWEAVES WITHSTAND DEMANDING EXTERIOR settings
Material engineering and drainage determine an outdoor rug’s longevity across harsh climates and high-traffic hospitality environments. Synthetic flatweaves manufactured from UV-stabilized polypropylene or recycled PET yarns resist moisture absorption, staining, and fading while collecting less debris than high-pile alternatives. Permeable backings and non-slip outdoor underlays are essential on stone paving and timber decking to promote water evaporation, prevent surface mold, and eliminate slipping hazards in poolside and resort settings.

UK: Oxford Street pedestrianisation begins in central London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:29:06 UTC
01:29:06 KST

The British capital is turning almost a kilometre of Oxford Street into a pedestrian-only zone, banning cars, buses, taxis, bicycles and e-scooters between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street.
Shoppers took to the traffic-free road as buses were diverted. Mayor Sadiq Khan visited retailers to promote the changes, intended to make the street safer and more welcoming ahead of Christmas.
Black cab drivers, however, warn that the restrictions could make access harder for disabled passengers.
Paris pedestrianised much of Rue de Rivoli in 2020, attracting more than 20,000 cyclists daily and reducing nitrogen dioxide levels, although critics say congestion has shifted to nearby roads.
Brussels closed 800 metres of Boulevard Anspach to traffic in 2015. Some retailers initially reported sales falling by up to 20%, but 85% later supported the scheme despite criticism of its implementation.
Oxford Street now faces a familiar challenge: attracting more pedestrians while keeping shops accessible and surrounding traffic moving.

Europe is living in a new ‘era of darkness,’ Finland’s Stubb warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:16:52 UTC
01:16:52 KST

Alexander Stubb after a meeting with the President of the French Republic at the Élysée Palace in Paris. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Europe is living through an “era of darkness” as multiple wars and competition between the U.S. and China trample the rules-based global order, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Monday.
Speaking at the College of Europe in Bruges, Stubb said the post-Cold War age has ended and the world now faces a pivotal moment, like those at the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of communism in 1989.
While he tends towards optimism, there are now “unfortunately, plenty of reasons to be pessimistic,” he told an audience of students at the institution, which Stubb himself attended in the 1990s.
Advertisement
“In a sense, I began my studies during an era of light and you begin your studies in an era of darkness,” he said. “We used to be able to say that the three biggest killers of mankind, disease, famine and wars, have been defeated. That is not true anymore. The light has given way to darkness.”
Stubb, who has studied and written extensively on geopolitical upheaval, has been intimately involved in European efforts to navigate U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term — particularly when it comes to the question of a peace deal for Ukraine.
He told his audience they would graduate into “a dog-eat-dog world” in which there are, by some estimates, 65 conflicts or wars playing out — “more than at any time after the Second World War.”
Global security will “depend on what the big powers — namely the U.S. and China — end up doing. Will they choose co-operation or confrontation?” he said.
“The key question for all of us is to create a European security structure which makes sure that Russia does not attack its neighbors again,” he said. NATO will remain a vital security alliance but new processes should also be developed, he said, including “confidence building” measures between Russia and Europe to build “trust.”
Stubb urged the audience of future diplomats, politicians and officials not to be pessimistic, but to be ambitious for a new “era of light,” despite the challenges. He said that in 30 years’ time, the European Union could grow to 40 member countries from the current 27 — including the U.K. rejoining the bloc alongside Norway, Moldova and Ukraine.

electronic fibers weave touchscreen into sleeve that survives machine washing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:15:44 UTC
01:15:44 KST

electronic fibers weave touchscreen into sleeve that survives machine washing
the technology can display images and video, respond to finger presses, and connect wirelessly to digital devices, while retaining the breathability and flexibility of everyday fabric.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
electronic fibers turn fabric into a touchscreen
Researchers at the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed a touchscreen integrated directly into a garment using electronic fibers that combine light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and touch sensors. Led by Assistant Professor Tural Khudiyev, the team integrates 54 of these fibers into a sleeve to create a flexible display that shows images and video, responds to finger presses, and connects wirelessly to digital devices. The research introduces a textile interface that retains the breathability and flexibility of everyday clothing while withstanding machine washing.
Unlike conventional wearable technology, which typically attaches a screen or electronic device to the body, the NUS team’s approach builds display and touch functionality into the fibers themselves. Each thread contains interconnected microelectronic components within a structure just one millimeter thick, allowing the fabric to function as an interactive screen without a rigid display panel. The prototype measures 168 by 105 millimeters, refreshes at 30 frames per second, and retains nearly unchanged display and touch performance after 50 machine-washing cycles. The technology could eventually allow clothing to function as an interface for digital information, environmental sensing, and health monitoring.
how to turn a thread into a screen
Conventional electronic circuits are designed on flat surfaces, where components can be arranged and connected across two dimensions. A thread, by contrast, is narrow and cylindrical, leaving little room for the complex wiring needed to operate a display. In order to overcome this limitation, the researchers developed an interconnection architecture that allows thousands of microelectronic devices to be connected along a single fiber. The process begins with tiny, insulated wires. A laser exposes specific points along their surfaces, while controlled wetting directs molten solder to the designated locations, creating electrical connections without joining unintended areas. Using this method, the team integrated more than 5,000 chips through over 20,000 electrical connections.
The interconnected digital LEDs are then incorporated into a multilayer fiber using a thermal drawing process. The resulting thread measures approximately one millimeter in diameter and 10 meters in length, with separate layers responsible for displaying images and detecting touch. A touch-sensitive layer sits beneath the LEDs. When someone presses the fiber, the contact completes an electrical circuit, allowing the system to identify the location of the touch and illuminate the nearest pixel. Display and interaction therefore happen within the same thread, rather than through separate components attached to the fabric.
a device that behaves like fabric
For the prototype, the team threaded 54 pixel-bearing fibers into the forearm of a sleeve. Each fiber carries 96 LEDs, combining to form a 96-by-54-pixel display measuring 168 by 105 millimeters. The screen refreshes at 30 frames per second and supports 8-bit color depth. The display is still modest in resolution compared with a smartphone, but its capabilities extend beyond showing static images. It can play video, display photographs, run a calculator, and function as a compass. Users can also receive images over Bluetooth, interact through voice commands, and rotate the display or adjust its brightness automatically. The sleeve incorporates additional fibers that carry a microphone, a speaker, and sensors for movement, temperature, magnetic orientation, and ambient light. A temperature-sensing fiber positioned under the arm, for example, can measure body temperature and display the reading on the sleeve itself. Each pixel fiber also has its own control channel, meaning a fault in one line does not necessarily interrupt the others. The system can register multiple touches simultaneously, bringing it closer to the interactive behavior of a conventional touchscreen.
According to the researchers, the prototype retained nearly unchanged light output and touch response after 50 machine-washing cycles with detergent and 1,000 bends around a radius of five millimeters. The integrated display is also reported to be as breathable as cotton, polyester, and denim, while remaining within established skin-contact safety limits.
toward clothing that senses and responds
Healthcare is one potential application identified by the team. Fibers equipped with physiological sensors could collect information continuously and present it directly on a garment, allowing wearers to access measurements without consulting a separate device. Combined with artificial intelligence, the researchers suggest, such systems could eventually support personalized monitoring and feedback. That possibility remains a future direction rather than a demonstrated capability of the current prototype. The team’s next steps include improving resolution, integrating more sensing functions, and exploring on-device AI. The broader implication is a shift in how digital interfaces are designed. Smartphones and computers have accustomed us to accessing information through dedicated screens, while wearable technology has largely miniaturized existing devices or attached them to the body. The NUS research proposes a different relationship between electronics and everyday objects, one in which information can be displayed on the material already in contact with the wearer.
project info:
 research team: Tural Khudiyev, Heng Fu, Ziang Li, and Swetika Chaturvedi
institution:College of Design and Engineering, National University of Singapore (NUS)
lead researcher: Asst Prof. Tural Khudiyev, Department of Materials Science and Engineering

Volunteer urges residents to leave Oleshky in evacuation, as town may face greater destruction

Volunteer urges residents to leave Oleshky in evacuation, as town may face greater destruction
The Russian-occupied town of Oleshky may face even greater destruction after civilians leave as part of a recent U.S.-negotiated ceasefire, evacuation volunteer Kseniia Arkhipova told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 26.
"When television channels around the world show that dozens of buses full of people have left Oleshky, when it is reported that the evacuation has taken place and the town is practically deserted, we are very much afraid that, after that, Oleshky will simply be wiped off the face of the earth," Arkhipova said.
"Those who remain may find themselves in even more dreadful conditions," she added.
Her warning comes after U.S. first lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid. The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 3:00 a.m. on October 27th, Kyiv time, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Both Russia and Ukraine agreed to a local ceasefire during the evacuation, but the exact evacuation routes remain unclear, and the sides are still working on the arrangements.
Arkhipova urged local residents remaining in the town to consider evacuation. She acknowledged that leaving home is a difficult decision for residents who have spent their entire lives there, but staying could expose them to escalating danger, intensifying hostilities, and lacking access to help.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, it has faced a deepening humanitarian crisis, with residents struggling to access food, medicine, electricity, and other basic necessities.
Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank, including Oleshky, to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Amid possible Russian escalation in the area, Arkhipova highlighted the risk that residents who remain in the town could be overlooked if reports of mass evacuations make it seem as if no civilians remain behind.
"The worst thing would be if the whole world came to believe that everyone had been evacuated from Oleshky, whilst (people) were still there. And (they) would simply be forgotten."
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. But in recent months, dangers posed by drone attacks, artillery fire, and mined roads have made evacuation by road almost impossible.
Russian forces have also prevented Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had previously verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.

Ukrainian military rescues two wounded soldiers using aerial evacuation drone – video
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
18:13:00 EET
01:13:00 KST

Ukrainian military rescues two wounded soldiers using aerial evacuation drone – video
Fighters from Ukraine's 475th Separate Assault Regiment (also known as CODE 9.2) have rescued two wounded soldiers from the battlefield within a week using the StarGate drone designed for aerial medical evacuations.
Source: 475th Separate Assault Regiment; SkyFall, the drone's manufacturer, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The drone was used to evacuate two soldiers: 25-year-old Yevhen, alias Izium, and 24-year-old Artem, alias Kolobok.
"Both sustained severe limb injuries and were in the grey zone, approximately 5 km from the Russian border. Due to the difficult terrain, water obstacles and the threat posed by enemy FPV drones, ground evacuation was impossible. Aerial evacuation was the only available way to save them," the unit said.
The military spent a week preparing the complex evacuation missions in coordination with representatives of SkyFall, the company behind the casualty evacuation drone. The operations required fire support and coordination with other units of the Ukrainian defence forces. Heavy Vampire attack drones were used to suppress Russian positions.
"During one of the missions, StarGate travelled almost 30 km to reach a serviceman's position and approximately the same distance back, this time with the soldier on board. In the operational area, the enemy actively deployed electronic warfare systems in an attempt to completely suppress satellite navigation signals," CODE 9.2 explained.
The StarGate drone's flight was controlled using an AI-based navigation system, enabling the evacuation mission to be completed successfully despite the loss of satellite navigation.
The experience gained from using drones for aerial evacuation is expected to help the regiment establish a dedicated medical aviation unit, said Oleksandr "Flint" Nastenko, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment.
"It will specialise specifically in evacuating wounded soldiers from the battlefield by air," the commander explained.
SkyFall was previously reported to have developed the StarGate drone for the aerial evacuation of wounded personnel and handed it over to the military for frontline testing.
StarGate has a range of up to 30 km and can carry a payload of up to 150 kg. For casualty evacuation, it is fitted with a dedicated medical capsule equipped with a stretcher.
The SkyFall drone has a maximum speed of 105 km/h and is remotely operated. Its AI-powered systems allow it to function without GPS and in the face of electronic warfare interference.
On 19 October, a unique operation was also reported, in which the military evacuated a wounded soldier using an aerial drone for the first time. The operation was carried out using a drone manufactured by the Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence.

Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru to go ahead, Vatican says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:11:14 CET
01:11:14 KST

By Alvise Armellini
VATICAN CITY, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Pope Leo’s trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru will go ahead, the Vatican said on Monday, indicating that Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery was on track and that he was fit enough to make the November 6-17 journey.
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering from an October 13 surgery in which doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
“The Holy Father’s recovery after the surgery continues, and the latest medical examinations attest to his good health and favorable clinical condition,” the Vatican said in a statement, citing Leo’s personal physician Luigi Carbone.
“Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey,” the statement said.
POPE RETURNING TO FAMILIAR REGION
Leo’s South America tour is set to be one of the most intense foreign trips taken by a Catholic leader in decades. The pope is scheduled to travel some 31,000 km (19,300 miles) over the 10-city tour and give 36 speeches.
The Vatican said the trip would proceed with no changes to the previously published agenda.
Leo had spent decades as a missionary in Peru before his predecessor Francis called him back to Rome in 2023 and promoted him to Vatican positions, so the trip will mark a homecoming of sorts for the first US pontiff.
“I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I’ve experienced so many moments of my life,” he said in the Vatican message.
“May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy,” Leo said.
In its statement, the Vatican said Leo was “adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritize his recovery while continuing to fulfil the responsibilities of his ministry.”
On Sunday, the pope addressed the faithful in St Peter’s Square, but on doctors’ advice he cancelled a day visit to the central Italian town of Assisi, which had been scheduled for Tuesday.

====================================================================================================

Frequent cannabis use linked to higher odds of nighttime breathing problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:00:47 UTC
01:00:47 KST

Adults who use cannabis are more likely to report loud snoring and pauses in breathing during the night, according to new research published in Sleep Health: Journal of the National Sleep Foundation. The findings indicate that more frequent cannabis consumption corresponds with higher odds of experiencing these nocturnal breathing issues, even after accounting for factors like body weight and tobacco smoking. This relationship raises important questions for the growing number of people who turn to cannabis as a sleep aid.
Sleep-disordered breathing is an umbrella term for medical conditions characterized by abnormal respiratory patterns or insufficient ventilation during rest. The most common form is obstructive sleep apnea, a disorder in which the muscles in the back of the throat relax too much, causing the upper airway to narrow or collapse entirely. People with this condition require extra physical effort to breathe, often resulting in loud snoring, gasping, or brief, repeated stops in breathing known as apneas. Standard treatments like continuous positive airway pressure machines, oral appliances, and surgery can be effective, yet many patients find the devices uncomfortable or difficult to tolerate over the long term.
At the same time, cannabis has become increasingly accessible across the United States, and difficulty sleeping is one of the most common reasons people cite for using it. While users frequently report that the plant helps them rest, controlled clinical trials examining cannabinoids and sleep have produced mixed outcomes.
For example, a 2023 clinical trial covered by PsyPost found that consuming medicinal cannabis oil improved sleep duration and increased midnight melatonin levels in adults with insomnia, whereas a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that a cannabis compound called cannabinol reduced nighttime awakenings when taken alone but showed no benefit when combined with cannabidiol, another cannabis compound. Observational tracking also points to potential drawbacks, such as a 2026 longitudinal study of military service members that linked current cannabis use to worse overall sleep quality and longer times needed to fall asleep.
When it comes to breathing disorders specifically, tetrahydrocannabinol, the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, has shown some potential to stabilize breathing in animal experiments and small human trials using oral pills. However, the broader clinical evidence remains inconsistent, leading the American Academy of Sleep Medicine to formally advise against using cannabis to treat obstructive sleep apnea. Most everyday consumers inhale cannabis rather than taking standardized pills, exposing their airways to smoke and heat that could inflame the tissues of the throat.
The new research, led by Tyler J. Gallagher, a resident physician in the Caruso Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery at the Keck School of Medicine of the University of Southern California, and co-first author Matthew E. Lin of the David Geffen School of Medicine at the University of California, Los Angeles, sought to evaluate how everyday consumption relates to signs of breathing issues at night.
“While some studies have explored cannabinoids as potential treatments for obstructive sleep apnea, there has been relatively little population-level research examining whether real-world cannabis use is associated with common signs of sleep-disordered breathing, such as loud snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep,” Gallagher told PsyPost. “We sought to better understand this relationship using a nationally representative sample of US adults.”
To investigate this connection, the authors analyzed information from the 2017 to 2018 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, a state-based telephone survey coordinated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Although nearly 900,000 adults completed the main survey during those two years, only Minnesota and Tennessee included optional survey modules asking about both cannabis habits and sleep breathing symptoms. From the respondents in those two states who had complete data, the researchers selected a stratified random sample of 14,485 adults designed to match the demographic profile of the broader United States population.
Participants were asked how many days they had used marijuana or cannabis during the past 30 days, as well as their primary method of consumption and whether they used it for medical or recreational purposes. The researchers grouped the respondents into three categories: non-users (zero days in the past month), non-regular users (1 to 15 days), and regular users (16 to 30 days). Signs of sleep-disordered breathing were assessed using two yes-or-no questions asking if anyone had ever observed the respondent stop breathing during sleep, and if the respondent had ever been told that they snore loudly.
Of the participants, 13,461 reported no current cannabis use, 438 were classified as non-regular users, and 364 were regular users, meaning about 5.5 percent of the sample currently used cannabis. Smoking was by far the most common consumption method, reported by about 87 percent of both non-regular and regular consumers, followed by vaporizing and eating. Among non-regular users, 61.6 percent used cannabis strictly for recreational reasons, whereas 37.6 percent of regular users reported using it strictly for medical reasons and another 24.7 percent used it for both medical and recreational purposes.
Overall, signs of sleep-disordered breathing were common across the entire cohort, with 44.7 percent reporting either loud snoring or witnessed apneas. In the unadjusted raw numbers, 44.3 percent of non-users reported at least one of the two breathing signs, compared to 48.4 percent of non-regular users and 55.2 percent of regular users. Specifically, witnessed breathing pauses were reported by 15.3 percent of non-users, 17.1 percent of non-regular users, and 19.8 percent of regular users. Loud snoring was reported by 41.3 percent of non-users, 44.5 percent of non-regular users, and 50.0 percent of regular users.
To account for other differences between users and non-users, the researchers ran statistical models that applied national survey weights (statistical adjustments that make a sample better mirror the U.S. adult population) and controlled for a wide range of potentially confounding factors. These adjustments accounted for age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, income, health insurance status, diabetes, body mass index, alcohol consumption, traditional cigarette smoking, and electronic cigarette use. Even after factoring out the influence of tobacco smoking and body weight, cannabis use remained independently associated with higher odds of sleep-disordered breathing symptoms.
Compared to non-users, non-regular cannabis users had 41 percent higher odds of reporting witnessed apneas, 26 percent higher odds of reporting loud snoring, and 33 percent higher odds of experiencing either symptom. The association was more pronounced among regular consumers. Those who used cannabis 16 to 30 days per month had 73 percent higher odds of witnessed apneas, 68 percent higher odds of loud snoring, and 82 percent higher odds of reporting either sign compared to non-users. These figures describe odds rather than probabilities, so the absolute differences are smaller than the percentages might suggest; in the raw numbers, about 55 percent of regular users reported at least one sign, compared with about 44 percent of non-users.
“While the impact of infrequent use is relatively small, the odds of irregular breathing during sleep almost double with more frequent cannabis use, making this a strong association worthy of consideration before frequent cannabis utilization,” Gallagher explained.
The researchers also analyzed cannabis consumption as a continuous spectrum from zero to 30 days. In the weighted models, each additional day of cannabis use per month was associated with an approximate 2 percent increase in the odds of reporting witnessed apneas, loud snoring, or either sign, an estimate the authors note is clinically small and serves as a general summary across use levels rather than a strict per-day effect. When the authors repeated the analysis without the national survey weights, regular cannabis use remained linked to both breathing signs, though the estimates were smaller (for example, 36 percent higher odds of either sign rather than 82 percent). In that analysis, non-regular use was no longer linked to loud snoring or to either sign, and its link with witnessed breathing pauses sat right at the threshold of statistical significance.
“The strength of the association and its greater magnitude among more frequent users were notable, particularly given that some studies have investigated cannabinoids as potential treatments for sleep apnea,” Gallagher said. “These findings may reflect differences between isolated cannabinoids studied in clinical settings and real-world cannabis use, including differences in composition and method of consumption.”
The authors proposed two primary biological mechanisms that might explain why cannabis consumers report more signs of airway obstruction at night. Because roughly 87 percent of the consumers in the sample smoked their cannabis, physical irritation from smoke is one possible contributor. Unlike tobacco, cannabis smoke is typically inhaled through deeper breaths without a filter, and it burns at a higher temperature, which can cause thermal injury and inflammation in the throat tissues that narrow the upper airway.
A second potential mechanism involves the way cannabis interacts with the autonomic nervous system, which regulates involuntary body functions. While small doses of cannabis tend to stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, the body’s “fight or flight” system, higher doses activate the parasympathetic nervous system, which promotes physical relaxation. Frequent users may develop tolerance and consume larger quantities, and the resulting parasympathetic activity may cause the muscles that hold the upper airway open to relax excessively during sleep, making the throat more likely to collapse.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the survey captured information at a single point in time, the study cannot establish whether cannabis use causes sleep-disordered breathing or if the relationship works in the opposite direction. People who suffer from undiagnosed sleep apnea often experience fragmented, unrefreshing sleep, and it is possible that some of these individuals turn to cannabis in an attempt to self-medicate their exhaustion or insomnia. The researchers also could not account for factors such as sleeping pill or sedative use, heavy drinking, or psychiatric conditions, any of which might influence both cannabis use and nighttime breathing.
The reliance on self-reported telephone survey data also introduces constraints. Asking participants if they have been told they snore or stop breathing is less reliable than conducting an overnight medical sleep study, and people who sleep alone may be unaware of their nighttime breathing habits. Additionally, the survey only tracked how many days a person used cannabis over the past month, without measuring the exact dosage, potency, or ratio of specific compounds like tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol.
The data came from just two states, Minnesota and Tennessee, because they were the only ones to include both sets of questions, and roughly 98 percent of the original survey respondents were excluded for that reason or because of missing information. Survey weights help align the sample with national demographics, but the authors note that applying them to such a small subset is debated among statisticians. In addition, the breathing questions asked whether these symptoms had ever been observed, while the cannabis question covered only the past month, so some symptoms may have predated participants’ current cannabis habits.
Gallagher emphasized that reporting these symptoms is not the same as receiving a formal medical diagnosis. “While obstructive sleep apnea – a clinically defined and hazardous intermittent airway obstruction during sleep – is a type of sleep-disordered breathing, this study cannot make conclusions about the association between cannabis use and sleep apnea or other associated long-term risks,” he noted.
Future research will need to incorporate objective sleep testing, such as polysomnography, an overnight sleep study that monitors breathing, oxygen levels, and brain activity, to verify whether cannabis habits correspond with clinically diagnosed sleep apnea. Scientists also need to compare different delivery methods, such as edibles versus inhalation, to separate the chemical effects of cannabinoids on throat muscles from possible damage from inhaling hot smoke.
“Further research is required to examine the long-term effects of cannabis use on sleep and to determine the effects of cannabis dosage, different cannabis compositions, and different methods of consumption on sleep-disordered breathing,” Gallagher said. “Additionally, the long-term consequences of these impacts must be studied.”
Until those relationships are clarified, the authors suggest that physicians should counsel patients about the potential respiratory risks of using cannabis, particularly for individuals who already show signs of sleep-disordered breathing. “People experiencing persistent snoring, pauses in breathing, or other symptoms of sleep apnea should seek medical evaluation rather than trying to utilize cannabis to manage their sleep,” Gallagher advised.
“This study highlights the importance of evaluating the broader health effects of substances that people increasingly use for self-management,” Gallagher added. “Cannabis may have benefits for certain symptoms or conditions, but those potential benefits should be considered alongside possible risks. Sleep-disordered breathing is particularly important because it can go unrecognized for years while causing significantly worse quality-of-life. We hope these findings encourage further research and help clinicians have more informed conversations with patients who use cannabis for sleep-related concerns.”
The study, “Cannabis use and associated sleep-disordered breathing among US adults,” was authored by Tyler J. Gallagher, Matthew E. Lin, Ian Kim, Ziva D. Cooper, Sebastian M. Jara, and Eric J. Kezirian.
