EU set to miss 2030 marine protection targets, auditors warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:00:37 UTC
01:00:37 KST

Despite designating 14% of its waters as protected areas, the EU has placed less than 1% under strict protection, leaving marine ecosystems vulnerable to damaging fishing practices and putting its 2030 biodiversity targets at risk.
The EU is unlikely to meet its 2030 targets for protecting marine biodiversity, with many designated marine protected areas offering little meaningful protection against damaging activities such as commercial fishing, the European Court of Auditors (ECA) warned on Monday.
Around 14% of EU waters are currently designated as marine protected areas, but less than 1% are under strict protection, exposing a gulf between the bloc’s environmental ambitions and the reality at sea.
The EU aims to protect 30% of its marine waters by 2030, including 10% under strict protection. But auditors warn that simply expanding the network of protected areas will not be enough without tougher restrictions on activities that damage marine ecosystems.
“The EU has made some progress in designating marine protected areas, but our audit shows that the true challenge is turning designation into actual protection," said Iliana Ivanova, the ECA member in charge of the audit.
Imposing tougher restrictions could, however, prove politically contentious, particularly if fishing communities and other affected industries bear the costs without adequate consultation or support.
While countries such as France and Sweden have made progress through community involvement and new bans on bottom trawling, Ireland has been hampered by major data gaps and legal delays.
Protected on paper but not in practice
A chronic shortage of staff, inadequate funding and lengthy administrative procedures also hamper enforcement. Authorities may identify harmful or illegal activities but lack the resources or legal powers to stop them.
"Turning political ambition into tangible results for marine ecosystems will require faster action, applicable protective measures and a more coherent network across the EU’s seas,” Ivanova added.
Protected status does not necessarily mean that damaging activities are restricted. Fishing restrictions, for example, apply to only a small proportion of designated areas, despite the threat posed by commercial fishing and other activities that damage the seabed.
As a consequence, designating protected areas is politically easier than imposing the restrictions needed to make them effective.
Those restrictions could affect fishing fleets operating across national borders, creating tensions between biodiversity objectives and the economic interests of coastal communities.
The EU auditors are calling for the European Commission and EU countries to move beyond national approaches towards more harmonised and enforceable conservation rules.
“To ensure that marine protected areas function effectively, we need the European Commission and member states to join forces, as well as engagement with local stakeholders,” Ivanova said.
Funding gaps and local opposition hamper protection
Fragmented financing is also a barrier to effective protection, the ECA report warns.
Conservation efforts rely on national budgets and different EU funding instruments, leaving protected areas facing problems with staffing, resources and long-term planning.
Even if stricter rules are imposed, securing support from the communities affected by them can also be a challenge, according to the EU auditors.
"The process for adopting conservation measures affecting fishing fleets of several member states can be complex and lengthy because it may require negotiations between member states that have fishing interests, as well as with various stakeholders. It can take many years, and few conservation measures have been adopted since 2013," reads the ECA report.
Monica Verbeek, executive director at the NGO Seas At Risk, said Europe does not lack policies, solutions or scientific knowledge.
"Where measures are implemented consistently and at a sufficient scale, nature responds. But recovery at scale is still not happening. We cannot afford another decade of ambitious targets followed by insufficient implementation," Verbeek said.

Israel’s top court rejects bid to ban firearms at polling stations ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:56:52 UTC
00:56:52 KST

Abdel Ra'ouf Arnaout and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Israel’s Supreme Court has rejected a petition seeking to prohibit polling station officials and party representatives from carrying firearms inside voting facilities during Tuesday’s parliamentary elections, according to the Arab rights group Adalah.
In a statement Monday, Adalah said the court dismissed the petition, which it filed with the Joint List, on Sunday evening.
The petition followed announcements by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party that they planned to deploy around 2,000 observers to polling stations in Arab towns and cities with mixed Jewish and Arab populations.
Adalah said the plans raised concerns that armed observers could “intimidate Arab voters, which could also spark violent confrontations.”
The petitioners cited previous incidents in which voters had reportedly been intimidated by people brandishing firearms, warning that the presence of armed civilians could lead to the unlawful use of lethal force.
They argued that the risks were heightened when weapons were carried by untrained civilians sent to polling stations in Arab communities amid what they described as “a racist incitement campaign that portrays Arab citizens as a threat.”
 
Court defers to police judgement
According to Adalah, the state argued that there were no grounds for judicial intervention in the police’s professional assessment, which found no concrete threat or operational need to impose a firearms ban.
The state also said there were no indications of plans to disrupt voting or threaten voters.
The court accepted the state’s position and declined to intervene in decisions made by the police and the Central Elections Committee chair not to impose a ban, Adalah said.
According to the group, the court emphasized that police have broad discretion in matters of security and public order, with judicial intervention limited to exceptional circumstances. It also found that police had considered the petitioners’ concerns in their election preparations.
There was no immediate comment from the court on Adalah’s account.
 
Intimidation of voters
Responding to the ruling, Adalah said the state and the Central Elections Committee had ignored the petition’s central argument: that organized groups of armed right-wing activists inside polling stations could intimidate Arab voters.
The group said the committee chair’s decision to allow party representatives to carry firearms relied on a police security assessment conducted before Likud and Religious Zionism announced their election-day plans.
“The Court’s decision allows those taking part in Netanyahu and Smotrich’s provocation to show up at polling stations in Arab communities like armed militias,” Adalah said.
Israel holds parliamentary elections Tuesday amid a closely contested race between Netanyahu’s bloc and its opponents. Arab voter turnout could play a significant role in determining the balance of power in the 120-seat Knesset and the prospects for forming the next government.
Polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition parties will secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority, potentially leading to a unity government, another election or an alliance with Arab parties.
Both blocs have so far ruled out forming a governing coalition with Arab parties.

The advocacy groups Common Cause and the League of Women Voters, which previously sought to intervene in the DOJ's lawsuit, on Monday joined Peltola's motion seeking a quick briefing and dismissal by Alaska District Court Judge Sharon Gleason.
The Department of Justice filed the suit Thursday. Trump later that day said he ordered it.
The DOJ's suit asks a judge to bar Alaska from certifying the Senate race results if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voters mistakenly casting their ballots for another candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan.
The DOJ, in that case, would want an investigation to determine whether enough voters were confused by the men's names to swing the vote to another candidate, presumably the former Rep. Peltola. The DOJ claims that Daniel J. Sullivan's "sole purpose" of running "is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan."

"DOJ filed this lawsuit in the midst of the ongoing general election, less than two weeks before election day, raising issues governed exclusively by state law that were definitively resolved by the Alaska Supreme Court months ago," the filing says.
"DOJ seeks an unprecedented order precluding certification of the U.S. Senate election if the candidate the President favors loses narrowly," the filing said.
"As the proposed Motion to Dismiss reflects, DOJ's claims are utterly without legal basis," the filing said.
"The Court should not allow this lawsuit to hang like the Sword of Damocles over the ongoing election, lending false legitimacy to the President's and the Attorney General's ongoing efforts to spread false narratives about Alaska's elections as voting continues and as results begin to be tabulated next week."

"The Department of Justice does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska's election," Blanche had said. "This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner so that only Alaska's governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead."
"The lawsuit was written by Justice Department attorneys and the Department did not coordinate with any campaign or candidate, but rather relied solely on federal law," Blanche said.
The department has not said how any investigation before certification of the election could determine whether a voter was confused about which Sullivan they were voting for. The ballot for the election notes that Sen. Sullivan — whose name is listed as Dan S. Sullivan — is an incumbent and a Republican. There are no words next to the name of the other candidate, whose name is spelled out Daniel J. Sullivan.
Peltola on Friday night told MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace that the DOJ's suit "is exactly the kind of corruption that Alaskans are sick and tired of."
"This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power, using his allies in Washington, D.C., to rig the system even further," Peltola said.
Peltola's campaign on Sunday said that on Saturday night she and her family "sustained minor injuries" that required medical attention after a vehicle transporting them en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet was struck by another driver.
As a result, Peltola posted events in Fairbanks and Bethel on Sunday and Monday. The campaign said that those events would be rescheduled.

Egyptian parliament authorises military aid for Saudi Arabia
Legislators approve military support amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, but Cairo has ruled out strikes on Yemen.
Egypt’s parliament has authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis intensify.
The House of Representatives, chaired by Speaker Hisham Badawi, approved the mandate in a vote on Monday.
A parliamentary statement members shared with Reuters said el-Sisi had been authorised to “undertake necessary” measures to support Saudi Arabia in defending itself, should Riyadh request assistance.
The move raises the possibility of Egypt becoming more directly involved in a conflict which has consumed the Gulf and the Red Sea in recent weeks.
Nawaf Obaid, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Saudi officials wanted reassurances that Egypt would support the kingdom if asked.
The vote was Cairo’s way of saying “it will be there”, he said, but questions remain over what type of assistance Riyadh might request and how Egypt would provide it.
The decision follows Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s international airport and facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, Aramco, which have disrupted flights and oil exports.
The Houthi armed group that controls Yemen’s capital, Sanaa is fighting the Saudi-led coalition which backs the internationally recognised government.
Fighting has intensified in recent weeks, deepening the humanitarian crisis that has already devastated Yemen.
El-Sisi said on Wednesday that any Egyptian military action would be limited to protecting Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks on Yemen.
Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo continued to favour a diplomatic settlement after visiting Riyadh on Wednesday.
The vote followed closed-door parliamentary discussions and an earlier postponement of the military aid authorisation for Saudi Arabia, which is one of Egypt’s most important economic partners.
Egypt’s constitution requires approval from two-thirds of legislators before troops can be sent abroad on combat missions.
Egypt also has a direct stake in Red Sea security. Houthi attacks near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the key route to and from the Suez Canal, have disrupted shipping and reduced canal revenue.
Egypt joined a previous Saudi-led campaign in Yemen in 2015, largely helping secure shipping routes with naval forces.
Cairo has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Diplomacy
El-Sisi also met United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in Cairo on Monday to discuss regional tensions and peace efforts.
According to Egypt’s presidency, Guterres praised Cairo’s efforts to prevent escalation in the Gulf and said diplomacy could help address disputes over Iran’s nuclear programme and shipping.
In a post on X on Monday, Guterres urged “maximum restraint”, warning that further fighting could spiral out of control.

Captured Russian soldiers have a rule for one stretch of the Kupiansk front: go anywhere, but not there.
That stretch is the “safety corridor” the “Orion” unit of Ukraine’s Offensive Guard brigade “Pomsta” says it has built for its ground robots. The zone is so lethal that, by the unit’s count, 88% of attacking Russians are killed before they reach their positions, and Russian armor cannot get within 25 kilometers, the military outlet ArmyInform reports.
Behind that shield, the unit says its ground robots have run dozens of fully autonomous missions through the most dangerous ground on the axis, with a success rate of 99.57%. The results made Orion the top-ranked unit for effectiveness on the South-Kupiansk axis in September within Ukraine’s battlefield management system, DELTA.
“You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone”
The claim that the Russians now avoid the sector, the unit says, comes from them themselves.
“Prisoners admit in interviews: 'You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone.' Eighty-eight percent of the enemy is destroyed before reaching their positions, and Russian equipment cannot approach closer than 25 kilometers,” the unit says.
That is what opens the corridor. Where a human supply run would be a death sentence, a robot can cross, and cross again.
The quiet blood of the front
The point, the unit says, is to take the soldier out of the deadliest job on the front: carrying ammunition and the wounded across open fire.
“We broke the stereotype that supplying the army takes truck convoys and hundreds of soldiers under targeted fire. Our robotic systems are the ‘quiet blood’ of the front,” Vladyslav Zolotarov, an officer in the unit’s staff control group, says.
When Russia thinks our positions are depleted, a tracked platform quietly comes in at night and brings in a ton of ammunition.
In September alone, the unit says, its wheeled and tracked robots ran 85 of the hardest combat missions and hauled more than 30,000 kilograms of cargo. Its evacuation record is the line it is proudest of: four missions pulling wounded soldiers out by robot, all four successful, not one man lost.
Ukraine has bet heavily on this kind of machine, aiming to field 50,000 ground robots to keep its troops out of the drone-ruled kill zone.

Saudi Arabia to store oil in Singapore to bolster Asia supply security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:40:02 UTC
00:40:02 KST

SINGAPORE (Reuters) -- Saudi Arabia plans to store crude oil at Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027 to strengthen supply security in the region, energy ministers from both countries said on Monday.
The move comes after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran severely disrupted energy supplies to Asia shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, prompting countries to draw down inventories and raising concerns about stockpile levels globally. Asia imported two-thirds of its oil supplies from the Middle East before the war.
"Saudi Arabia and Singapore are announcing our joint intent to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027," Tan See Leng, minister for energy, trade and industry, told the Singapore International Energy Week conference.
"This arrangement enhances the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia, as well as contributes to Singapore's energy security and resilience in the event of supply disruptions."
Tan said Saudi Aramco will sign a memorandum of understanding with the Energy Market Authority and JTC Corp. on Monday and aimed to conclude negotiations in a few months' time.
"Bringing supply closer to key Asian markets would strengthen the flexibility of our supply network and support Singapore's security of supply and preparedness," Saudi Arabian Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al-Saud said in a video recording at the conference.
Located at a depth of 150 meters below the ground, the rock caverns at Jurong Island can store up to 1.47 million cubic meters, or roughly 9 million barrels of liquid hydrocarbons such as crude oil and condensate.
Saudi Aramco currently stores crude in Japan and South Korea, where local governments have priority to buy the supplies in the tanks in the event of an unexpected shortage.
The crude storage capacity in Okinawa was expanded to 8.2 million barrels in September 2017 in an agreement with Japan Oil, Gas and Metals National Corp. (JOGMEC), Aramco Japan said on its website.
In 2023, Aramco inked a deal with Korea National Oil Corp. to store 5.3 million barrels of oil in South Korea's reserve facilities in the port of Ulsan for five years.
Elsewhere, Japan is in talks with Asian countries to boost crude reserves across the region, part of the Partnership in Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia) initiative proposed earlier this year by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi backed by $10 billion in financial support.
While China, Japan and South Korea have built large oil stockpiles, most other Asian countries have less of a buffer in the event of supply shocks.

Iran's Greco-Roman team win 2026 World Championship

Unknown Publisher

Iran's Greco-Roman team win 2026 World Championship
TEHRAN – Iran have secured the Greco-Roman team title at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan, following an outstanding performance by their wrestlers on the international stage.
The Iranian squad clinched the championship ahead of the conclusion of the Greco-Roman competitions, underlining the country's dominance in one of its most successful sporting disciplines.
Iran made an impressive start to the tournament, collecting one gold, two silver and one bronze medal in the first four weight categories before securing additional places in the finals.
Gholamreza Farokhi delivered Iran's first gold medal in the 82kg division, defeating Turkey's Yuksel Saricicek 5-1 in the final.
At 55kg, Payam Ahmadi claimed silver after losing 3-1 to Azerbaijan's Eldaniz Azizli in the gold-medal contest.
Ali Ahmadi Vafa also earned silver in the 60kg category, narrowly missing out on gold after being pinned by Japan's Koto Gomi despite holding a 7-1 lead.
Iran's fourth medal came through Ali Oskou in the 77kg division. He secured bronze with a 4-3 victory over Uzbekistan's Nekibov.
The Iranian team's impressive campaign continued as Saeid Esmaeili and Alireza Mohmadi advanced to the finals in the 67kg and 87kg categories, respectively.
Esmaeili defeated Azerbaijan's Hasrat Jafarov in the semifinals, while Mohmadi booked his place in the final with a commanding 10-1 victory over Armenia's Gevorg Tadevosyan.
Danial Sohrabi at 72kg and Fardin Hedayati at 130kg also won two gold medals, while Olympic and world champion Mohammadhadi Saravi seized a bronze medal at 97kg.

Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 0191 239 4261 or the police.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas

Europe’s voters keep throwing leaders out. Who has the answers?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:38:22 UTC
00:38:22 KST

Europe’s voters keep throwing leaders out. Who has the answers?
This past election day did deliver one bombshell: Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections. Hardly anyone seems to have seriously expected that. Calling the election was a gamble, of course, but he still had reason to believe he could pull it off.
The reasons will take time to untangle. Vucic himself spoke of a “revolution” backed by Europe. Others, with some justification, see an “Orban scenario”: accumulated fatigue with one man’s prolonged rule, during which his personal traits and interests came to exert too much influence over national policy.
Clearly, more than one factor was at work. Just as clearly, Serbia is entering a new era. Vucic’s increasingly elaborate and convoluted balancing act will likely give way to an attempt to steer the country sharply toward the European Union. Hungary’s experience is telling in this respect. And Russia should expect little good to come of it.
Serbian society, however, is different from Hungary’s. There really is considerable sympathy for Russia. Whether that sentiment can rally a new opposition, this time against a firmly pro-EU course, should become clear soon enough. The EU will try to make the most of the defeat of yet another set of “pro-Russian forces.” Whether that will bring Serbia any closer to EU membership is another question entirely.
Whatever the outcome, if there is a common thread running through elections across Europe, it is probably this: people in different countries are disillusioned with the status quo and the establishment, whatever its political stripe – even when those establishments stand at opposite ends of the spectrum.

Rogue Claude AI tapped into US voter data – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:22:11 UTC
00:22:11 KST

Rogue Claude AI tapped into US voter data – Axios
Anthropic’s Claude AI model went rogue and broke past a paywall to obtain voter data in the US state of Georgia, Axios reported on Sunday. The intrusion heightens concerns about developers’ ability to control increasingly autonomous AI systems.
The incident occurred during an internal statistics project involving public information. Anthropic said the model obtained aggregate voter counts but did not access Georgia’s voter registration system, retrieve individual voter records or alter any data.
The company confirmed the incident on Sunday, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“Without being asked to, the model requested a token to query a dashboard that contained information normally available for a fee,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios. Claude had learned from an archived government webpage that the dashboard issued digital access keys to visitors. It was able to request a key and retrieve the information without paying.
Georgia Deputy Secretary of State Jordan Fuchs confirmed to Fox Business that the data came from a public information service but insisted that Claude “did not get into the voter registration system.”
Anthropic described the incident in an October 9 report but did not name Georgia. According to Axios, it notified state officials and the White House weeks ago. A source told the outlet that administration officials had urged Georgia to disclose the incident publicly sooner, but those requests went unheeded.
The case is among several instances Anthropic has disclosed of models finding unintended ways around restrictions instead of stopping. Other incidents included a false homicide tip submitted to Philadelphia police and incomplete applications filed on the US State Department’s visa website.
On Friday, Anthropic also revealed that a model had impersonated a human during a cybersecurity exercise, attempting to persuade an unrelated software developer to accept malicious code. The developer rejected the request and the attempt failed.
Other developers have tightened controls following similar incidents. OpenAI said Friday that it was keeping its most powerful models’ training offline after agents escaped restricted environments. In July, its agents bypassed safeguards and accessed systems belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets.
Anthropic said it has moved some evaluations offline, restricted internet tools and introduced systems to detect unauthorized actions. It said those systems blocked each of the disclosed cases when tested against them.

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.
The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.
Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.
In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.
For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.
John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.
"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.
Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.
Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.
Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.
Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

Ukraine opens 29 new export channels for agricultural products in 2026

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:19:27 EET
00:19:27 KST

Ukraine has agreed on 29 new export channels for agricultural products and animal feed in 13 countries and the European Union since the start of 2026, the highest annual total since at least 2022, the State Production and Consumer Service said on its website on Monday.
The new channels cover Europe, the Caucasus, the Middle East, Africa, Asia and Latin America, the agency said.
They include exports of flour to China, egg products to Vietnam and Egypt, milk and dairy products to Chile, and table eggs and fish products to Egypt.
Market access has also been agreed for meat and meat products, including beef to Iraq, Georgia and Côte d'Ivoire. Côte d'Ivoire has also approved imports of poultry meat. Algeria has opened its market to live cattle, while Egypt has approved imports of sheep. Moldova has authorized imports of live snails, snail caviar and certain categories of meat products.
For crop production, the European Union has approved imports of planting material for sour cherry and mahaleb cherry, their hybrids, and eight maple species.
In the animal feed sector, Ukraine has secured access for pet food to Egypt and South Korea, processed feed to Albania, and plant-based feed and animal by-products to Georgia.
The agency said it would continue working to expand access for Ukrainian products to international markets.
In 2025, Ukraine secured access to 22 new foreign markets for domestic exporters. China opened its market to peas and wild-caught seafood, India approved apple imports, and Canada approved imports of apples and table eggs. Albania opened its market to eggs for human consumption, Argentina to sunflower seeds, Kuwait to processed products, while Malaysia, Vietnam, Moldova and Chile approved imports of certain dairy products and animal feed.
Since 2022, Ukraine has opened 75 new markets, expanding access for agricultural products to 386 trade destinations, the agency said.

Ukraine restores civil service recruitment competitions, securing EUR 137 mln under Ukraine Facility
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
17:18:56 EET
00:18:56 KST

The Verkhovna Rada adopted bill No. 13478-1 on restoring competitive recruitment to the civil service in its second reading on Monday, fulfilling an indicator under the Ukraine Facility that provides for EUR 137 million in funding for Ukraine's state budget, Minister for Communities, Territories and Internally Displaced Persons Vitaliy Bezgin told Interfax-Ukraine.
"Martial law required quick and flexible decisions on staff appointments. But emergency decisions must not become permanent practice. Restoring competitions means returning to a system where professionalism and suitability for a position are decisive. A professional public service is first and foremost about open recruitment, integrity and clear rules," Bezgin said.
Open competitions for civil service and local government positions will resume once the law enters into force, he said. Transitional periods have been set for positions filled without competition. Continued employment without a competition will be possible by decision of the head of the service, subject to a positive annual performance assessment.
The bill gives war veterans priority in appointments and makes integrity a mandatory criterion for candidates and serving officials.
It also provides for the restructuring and depoliticization of the Commission on the Senior Civil Service. A repeat special background check will not be required if the previous check produced no adverse findings, service has been continuous, and the new appointment takes place within five working days of dismissal.
Transitional rules will also apply to local government employees appointed without competition. In areas of active hostilities and temporarily occupied territories where no end date has been established, certain managers may be appointed without competition.
Bill No. 13478-1 forms part of Ukraine's commitments under the Ukraine Plan for 2024-2027 within the Ukraine Facility and continues public administration reform.

Changes to animal protection are being prepared in Ukraine - will punishment for cruelty become more effective
Kyiv • UNN
The ministry has established a working group to bring animal protection in line with EU standards. Only 5% of those convicted of cruelty received actual prison sentences.
The Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine has established a working group tasked with preparing proposals to strengthen the protection of animals from cruel treatment. In Ukraine, animal abuse is punishable by up to eight years in prison, yet only a handful of offenders receive actual prison sentences.
UNN found out what the authorities are proposing and what animal-rights advocates are demanding.
What the Ministry of Economy decided
The ministry announced the creation of the working group on October 26. It consists of about 30 participants and is headed by Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Krasnolutskyi. The participants will identify problems and prepare proposals in the area of animal protection.
The issue concerns the protection of domestic, stray, and wild animals. The goal is to bring Ukrainian regulations closer to EU law and improve interaction between the authorities and the public
What the working group will focus on
The tasks include analyzing current legislation, preparing recommendations for its improvement, and reviewing the practice of responding to cruel treatment. They also plan to strengthen coordination between the police, local authorities, and animal-rights advocates, since even strict prohibitions do not protect animals when the police fail to respond to reports or collect evidence. It is not yet known whether the group will propose new sanctions or powers for oversight bodies.
Why the animal-protection system in Ukraine raises questions
According to estimates by Opendatabot based on prosecutor's office statistics, 386 proceedings under Article 299 of the Criminal Code were recorded in Ukraine from January to May 2025. This is 3.7 times more than during the same period in 2024. At the time of the study, approximately 80% of the cases had resulted in charges being brought, while about 4% had reached court.
UAnimals lawyer and analyst Anastasiia Hevchuk explained the increase in the number of registered cases as resulting from a more active stance by citizens.
This is not about an increase in violence, but about less silence
However, registering a case and punishing the perpetrator are different stages. In November 2025, NGL.media analyzed 148 guilty verdicts handed down after liability was strengthened in 2021. Actual imprisonment was imposed in only seven cases, or approximately 5%. In 129 cases, the convicted persons were released from serving their sentences on probation; in 11 cases, fines were imposed, and in one more case, community service was ordered.
What punishment for cruel treatment of animals is provided for by law
Under Article 89 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses, abuse that causes an animal pain or suffering but does not result in bodily injuries, mutilation, or death is punishable by a fine of 3,400 to 5,100 hryvnias. If the offense is repeated within a year, committed by a group of persons, or involves several animals, the fine ranges from 5,100 to 8,500 hryvnias. Administrative arrest for up to 15 days is also possible. If the owner poses a threat to the animal, confiscation is possible.
Article 299 of the Criminal Code establishes liability for cruel treatment of vertebrate animals under circumstances specified by law, in particular if the actions result in mutilation or death. The basic sanction is restriction of liberty for one to three years or imprisonment for two to three years. Such actions committed in the presence of children are punishable by three to five years in prison, while particular cruelty, repetition, or the commission of the crime by a group of persons carries a sentence of five to eight years.
European animal-protection rules: what is already in force and what still needs to be changed
Ukraine has already become a party to the Council of Europe's European Convention for the Protection of Pet Animals: it entered into force for the country in 2014. In January 2026, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 11328 at first reading. Among other things, it proposes clarifying the concepts of abandoning animals to their fate and proper conditions of keeping, as well as strengthening the role of communities in information and educational programs.
In August 2026, EU Regulation 2026/1818 on the welfare of dogs and cats and the ability to trace their origin entered into force. It establishes common requirements for breeders, shelters, the keeping, identification, and sale of animals. The main provisions will begin to apply in August 2028, while certain registration requirements will be introduced gradually at a later date.
What animal welfare advocates propose changing
The animal welfare organization UAnimals is already insisting on changes concerning stray and wild animals, the operating conditions of breeding facilities, the keeping of animals in captivity, and liability for cruelty. The law protects both domestic and stray animals equally.
UAnimals lawyer Alina Soroka emphasizes: photos and videos may constitute grounds for opening a case; however, for a person to be served with a notice of suspicion, there must be a body of material evidence. Therefore, the specialist advises witnesses to document the circumstances of the incident, record the contact details of eyewitnesses, and submit written statements to the police. This will help challenge possible inaction by law enforcement officers.
Some activists are calling for harsher sentences. In particular, at the beginning of 2026, the initiator of a petition to the government, Lyudmyla Tsaryova, advocated stricter criminal penalties, a ban on convicted individuals keeping animals, and a register of people punished for such crimes.
Stray animals in Ukraine and the challenges of war
The full-scale war has added evacuation, treatment of injured animals, and the search for foster homes and shelter places to the challenges of protecting animals. Because of hostilities and the evacuation of people, some animals are left without care.
According to a UAnimals report, in September 2026 alone, the organization evacuated 145 animals from 13 settlements in four regions, helped improve the conditions in which 550 animals were kept in shelters and rehabilitation centers, and sterilized 871 animals. Its team also contacted the police regarding 13 cases of possible cruel treatment. This is the data of just one organization.
For communities, sustainable programs for sterilizing, vaccinating, housing, and rehoming stray animals are particularly important. Rules are needed regarding the removal of animals, their transfer to shelters, and the financing of their care.
In addition, cases of cruel treatment of animals have increased because of internal migration and Ukrainians leaving for other countries. Within the country, animal owners leaving dangerous regions cannot find housing because landlords refuse to rent them apartments and houses. Even attempts to pay a large deposit and a willingness to compensate for material damage if it is caused by a pet do not help. Moreover, according to the OLX platform, where internally displaced persons most often try to search for housing, in some cities (such as Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, and Kryvyi Rih) there are no housing offers at all for pet owners. As a result, some owners leave their cats and dogs outside or even resort to killing the animal.
In situations involving leaving the country, matters are even more complicated. To legally take an animal out of the country, veterinary documents, a microchip, and valid vaccinations are required. All of this costs money and takes time (on average, from one month to several months). Far from everyone has the financial means and time to meet all the requirements. In addition, not all countries can accept people traveling with a pet. For example, red-eared turtles cannot be taken to France because the country's law prohibits it. Therefore, instead of looking for foster care or new owners for the animal, some people simply abandon it.
Animal protection in Ukraine: should we expect real changes
For now, the new working group has an advisory mandate: to prepare proposals that could become the basis for legislative decisions. The creation of the group itself does not change sanctions or owners' obligations. The transparency of its work will also matter: publicly available proposals will make it possible to assess which proposals officials supported and which were left without progress.
The result can be assessed by concrete steps: whether the amendment texts and timelines for their consideration will appear, whether the police and communities will receive clear response procedures, whether there will be more properly investigated cases and court decisions, and whether animal-keeping conditions will improve.

Swedish government blocks ChatGPT and Claude. Here’s why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:18:02 UTC
00:18:02 KST

The ban on employees using browser-based versions of ChatGPT and Claude took effect on Monday 26 October amid security concerns over data processing.
Swedish government employees can no longer use browser-based versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude on their work computers following security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data.
The decision comes following a review of AI tools used by workers at the Swedish Transport Administration earlier this year that found “problematic” uses of the AI platforms in carrying out government work.
Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training.
The use of platforms not regulated or protected by such agreements, also known as shadow IT, could bring “consequences for our information security”, said Mikael Wettercrantz, director of digitalisation at the Government Offices of Sweden.
Microsoft’s Copilot, which has passed a security screening process and is covered by a security agreement between the US company and the Swedish government, is being recommended as an alternative.
While government workers will still be able to use AI to help them carry out their tasks, they will do so under tighter security controls and with just a limited number of employees permitted to continue using ChatGPT and Claude but only through a special platform for AI assistants developed by Swedish authorities.
According to the Swedish public broadcaster Sveriges Radio, restrictions on the use of ChatGPT and Claude have also been put in place at the Swedish Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care. The Swedish Enforcement Authority is currently reviewing the issue.
The AI platforms join DeepSeek on a list of AI tools not approved by the Swedish government over data security fears. Last week, the US announced it was banning all products and services from the Chinese AI company.

How birds can quietly spread a severe form of pneumonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:17:59 UTC
00:17:59 KST

Birds are everywhere. They perch on rooftops and windowsills and sometimes share our homes as pets. But they can also carry dangerous germs, even when they appear healthy.
In a recent case report published in Frontiers in Medicine, a 43-year-old man presented with a persistent fever of 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius), fatigue and muscle pain but few respiratory symptoms. Several courses of antibiotics failed to bring down his fever.
Doctors detected abnormal breath sounds, and a scan revealed a round blotch in his right lung—a sign of blood, pus, fluid or tissue—but tests for common pathogens came back negative. Suspecting a more unusual infection, they tested samples from his lungs and identified the culprit: Chlamydia psittaci, a bird-borne bacterium.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The finding was key: the man switched antibiotics and recovered.
The likely source of the pathogen was a visit to a zoo, where the man had had direct contact with parrots about 10 days before his symptoms began. The infection, known as psittacosis, or parrot fever, can spread from many different birds, however, including poultry and pigeons.
Another case report describes a 16-year-old boy who developed pneumonia from a C. psittaci infection after he cleaned his dormitory, including by dusting windowsills and ventilation systems—despite the fact that he had no known direct contact with birds.
These cases show how everyday activities can expose people, sometimes unknowingly, to bird-borne diseases.
“Psittacosis is a respiratory disease mainly spread through inhaling the dust of bird droppings. You need to breathe in the bacteria to get infected,” says Brian Labus, an infectious disease epidemiologist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that there is no evidence that C. psittaci spreads through preparing or eating poultry products, though other case reports raise this possibility.
One, published in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases, described a chef who may have contracted psittacosis through handling poultry. Another, published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases, involved a man who developed fever and severe diarrhea after eating undercooked pigeon meat. The same bacterial strain was detected in the patient and in pigeons from the source of the meat, raising the possibility of foodborne transmission. But the exact routes of transmission in these cases remains unclear.
Psittacosis can be difficult to recognize because its symptoms resemble those of other respiratory illnesses.
“There are no unique symptoms that can make you suspect psittacosis as the cause of a respiratory illness, and doctors can’t tell without laboratory testing,” Labus says. He recommends that people with symptoms tell their doctor about any bird-related exposures, including caring for pet birds or cleaning up after wild birds.
According to the CDC, fewer than 10 cases of parrot fever are typically reported in the U.S. each year. Psittacosis may be more common than reported figures suggest.
“Many infections probably go undiagnosed and are simply classified as community-acquired pneumonia without identifying the underlying causative pathogen,” says Daisy Vanrompay, a professor at Ghent University in Belgium. She directs the country’s national reference laboratory for human C. psittaci infections.
While some infections are mild, others can cause severe pneumonia and, in rare cases, damage to organs such as the heart, liver and brain.
Severity depends on the amount of bacteria that’s inhaled, the strain that’s involved and individual susceptibility, Vanrompay says. Labus adds that young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems or underlying lung conditions may be at greater risk of severe illness.
To reduce exposure, both experts recommend wetting bird droppings before removal rather than dry sweeping or vacuuming them and wearing a well-fitting respirator when cleaning contaminated areas.

Disgusting or scary? What an aversion to clusters of holes tells us about the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:17:40 UTC
00:17:40 KST

Since childhood, clusters of circles have made me queasy—especially holes. Just thinking of honeycombs or lotus seed pods makes my stomach churn and skin crawl. My affliction has a name: trypophobia. By some estimates, trypophobia affects roughly one in six people. But its rise is sometimes put down to an online meme—an aversion to holes had a moment on the mid-2000s Internet. The condition is no joke, however: it can be debilitating, causing panic attacks and nausea—in extreme cases, people stop driving, miss work or avoid nature for fear of confronting upsetting stimuli.
Researchers first described trypophobia in a 2013 paper and argued that it may be a primitive fear response to venomous animals. Other, more recent theories include that it’s a disease-avoidance instinct that makes us recoil from anything resembling skin lesions or parasites, a form of cortical hyperexcitability where clusters of holes trigger a neural response—a visual equivalent to nails on a chalkboard—or simply a condition that caught on because it was a meme.
Now scientists may finally be closing in on an answer. Geoff Cole—the British scientist who originally pitched the evolutionary fear of venomous animals theory in 2013—recently looked back at the evidence and made a new conclusion. In a 2026 paper, Cole and his co-authors came down in favor of the disease-avoidance theory. Reviewing experiments that tested people’s reactions to triggering images, he concluded that trypophobia is primarily driven by disgust, not fear.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“Disgust is the mechanism with which we can detect things which carry disease,” says Cole, a researcher at the University of Essex’s Center for Brain Science in England. “It’s clear that the evidence, when you stack it up, is more in favor of the disease-avoidance hypothesis.”
In one experiment, for example, college students were shown trypophobic images, typical fear-inducing pictures—such as those of snakes and spiders—and control images. Participants’ pupils constricted more when they saw the trypophobic images than any of the others—a sign that the parasympathetic nervous system, which is linked to disgust, was activated. Fear, by contrast, is linked to the sympathetic nervous system, which dilates the pupils.
Other research suggests trypophobic people find hole clusters as unpleasant as pictures of skin disease and that people with a history of skin problems may find hole clusters particularly uncomfortable to look at.
That’s not to say fear has no role in trypophobia. Last year a French-led team concluded that while disgust is the “dominant emotion” for trypophobes, “fear is also not negligible.”
To fully settle the question, scientists would need more “hard evidence,” says Christopher DiMattina, a psychology professor at Florida Gulf Coast University. For example, people could be put in an fMRI machine to track their brain activity, then be shown trypophobic and control images. Amygdala activation would suggest fear, while responses in the insular cortex would suggest disgust, he says.
Clinically, phobias are considered anxiety disorders, but some researchers believe that everyone is a little trypophobic. Some people, like me, are bothered by such images but can mostly ignore them. Trypophobia isn’t an official diagnosis—but someone with it could be diagnosed under the term specific phobia if they have severe reactions that interfere with their daily life, according to Kevin Chapman, a clinical psychologist and director of the Kentucky Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders.
“You can technically be phobic of anything,” Chapman says. “There are certain phobias that load more with what we call disgust sensitivity, versus, say, anxiety sensitivity.”
There is little research on effective treatments for trypophobia, and scientists have called for more investment in potential therapies that target disgust. Most people with trypophobia are offered exposure therapy—a form of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) that aims to gradually desensitize someone to the phobic trigger by exposing them to low-level versions of it in controlled settings.
In a handful of published case reports, treatment, including CBT, seems to reduce people’s fear-related symptoms, but it hardly affects their disgust response. That could be because disgust is “generally more resistant to exposure than fear,” according to researchers at Macquarie University in Australia. Just as important as exposure, they argue, is counterconditioning, in which the upsetting stimulus is paired with something positive, such as a good experience or relaxation exercises.
The Australian team put that to the test in a small trial that aimed to alleviate both fear and disgust in nine trypophobic people. The participants underwent a one-session treatment that condensed key CBT principles into a single three-hour session—and was modified to include counterconditioning and other techniques to help them adjust their thinking. A month after the session, most participants reported significant improvements in both disgust and fear.
Chapman says treatment should be tailored to the trypophobic patient based on whether they experience more disgust, fear or anxiety. He recommends a combination of exposure therapy and cognitive restructuring, another CBT-based technique that aims to replace irrational thoughts with neutral, realistic alternatives.
“Particularly when disgust sensitivity is high, you’ve got to really identify what they’re concerned would happen if they encounter it,” he says.
If a person is worried about vomiting, for example, Chapman will work with them on applied muscle tension—a CBT-related technique—to tense up their core so they don’t actually puke. Applied tension is often used to help people with phobias related to needles or blood avoid fainting. Other individuals simply need help learning to tolerate the discomfort of seeing trypophobic images.
“Learning history does matter,” Chapman says.

A ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect at 0100GMT on Tuesday to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
An official press release was issued Friday by the White House confirming that the first lady had served as the "Exclusive Intermediary" to secure the localized agreement.
The development came amid worsening shortages of food, medicine and clean water in Oleshky, a frontline town located on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine's southern Kherson region. Residents must also contend with limited access to electricity, mined roads and recurring military attacks, according to the White House.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said. “It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”
Russian Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov said Moscow would implement a “regime of silence” in the Kherson direction from 4 am Moscow time on Oct. 27 to facilitate humanitarian operations.
“To ensure the safety of the population and the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted, and the safe passage of a humanitarian convoy to the settlement of Oleshky, Kherson Region, will be facilitated,” the Russian Defense Ministry quoted him as saying.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it would implement a localized ceasefire from 3 am Kyiv time the same day to deliver humanitarian aid to Oleshky’s residents and ensure the safe, unhindered evacuation of civilians.
Under the arrangement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will assess residents’ needs. Those wishing to leave will receive coordinated transportation to destinations in either country, while a US media organization will accompany the teams to document the process, according to the White House.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the duration of the operation remained uncertain but noted that it could last several days.
The truce comes as Moscow and Kyiv trade blame for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, a city that Russian forces captured in 2022.
Oleshky had a prewar population of around 24,000, but estimates suggest that only 1,700-2,000 people remain, many of them older residents unable to leave.
The collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in southern Ukraine in June 2023 triggered massive flooding in nearby communities, including Oleshky, that destroyed homes and forced thousands of people to flee, with Ukraine and Russia each accusing the other of deliberately destroying the dam.

Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana Timmerman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:11:10 UTC
00:11:10 KST

The impossible happened. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in Sunday’s runoff election in Brazil, overturning Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in a historic comeback. No candidate has ever lost the first round and won the second, until now. Grassroots mobilisation, alongside social welfare policies, helped turn the contest into a referendum on Brazilian democracy, rallying voters against a candidate seeking to restore the legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, imprisoned for plotting a coup after his 2022 defeat. Lula’s victory suggests that defending democracy can still be a powerful electoral argument against the ascendant right.
Having already consolidated most of the leftwing vote, Lula had limited room to attract supporters of other candidates after his first-round defeat. His best chance lay in mobilising abstainers and reconnecting with working-class voters. The Workers’ party intensified its grassroots and digital campaigns, using social media influencers and messaging networks to reach supporters. Nearly 3 million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, and Lula gained ground across the country, particularly in major cities and his north-eastern strongholds. He also appealed to voters’ immediate economic concerns, drawing on a record of reducing poverty and inequality, and increasing benefits under Bolsa Família, the landmark welfare programme he launched in 2003. Lula framed the election as a choice between protecting social gains and democratic institutions, or returning to the Bolsonaro family’s attacks on both, warning that his opponent would compromise Brazil’s sovereignty by aligning himself with Donald Trump.
The implications extend far beyond Brazil. Lula’s victory interrupts a regional trend: rightwing candidates have won seven presidential elections across Latin America in the past 18 months. Two decades ago, Lula was among the leaders of Latin America’s pink tide, a succession of leftwing governments that reshaped the region’s politics and sought greater autonomy from Washington. Today, he finds himself resisting a new regional wave moving in the opposite direction, without a comparable coalition of allies.
Lula’s victory is welcome, but we shouldn’t forget that Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 48% of valid votes, demonstrating the enduring strength of a movement with substantial representation in an increasingly rightwing congress. His proposals on security and the economy appealed to voters frustrated by high living costs, including working-class Brazilians who had traditionally supported Lula. This mirrors the success of authoritarian-leaning rightwing candidates across the continent. Frustration with crime, economic insecurity and established political parties has propelled a new right promising tougher security policies and attacking progressive social agendas. From Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, to Javier Milei in Argentina, to the recent election of Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia.
The emerging rightwing alliance is, in many ways, the mirror image of the pink tide, developing in close alignment with Trump and his ambitions to reassert US dominance over the hemisphere. The relationship is mutually reinforcing: rightwing leaders who gained ground through domestic discontent look to Washington to consolidate their power, while the US relies on those same governments and movements to advance its strategic interests. In his victory speech, Lula said the surge of street support in recent weeks “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s back yard”. His declaration directly challenges the so-called Donroe doctrine, which asserts an expanded US role in policing the region.
Since returning to office, Trump has used endorsements, sanctions, tariffs and financial assistance to reward allies and put pressure on opponents. He backed rightwing candidates in Honduras and Colombia. He has turned a blind eye to Salvadoran president Bukele’s negotiations with criminal organisations (Bukele denies having made an informal pact with these organisations). And ahead of Argentina’s 2025 legislative elections, he offered Milei a $20bn financial lifeline while warning that US generosity depended on the electoral outcome.
Security provides a particularly powerful instrument for this alignment. The Trump administration has invoked the fight against “narcoterrorism” to expand its military role and apply pressure on governments to accept Washington’s priorities. Terrorist designations have helped justify the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, threats of unilateral strikes against Mexican cartels and joint military operations in Ecuador. Washington has also discussed similar operations with Colombia. The designations do not themselves authorise military action, but they strengthen the administration’s justifications to intervene beyond US borders.
Brazil demonstrates how this strategy can also serve Washington’s allies outside government. The Bolsonaro family had itself sought Washington’s intervention against the Brazilian judiciary during Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazil and sanctions against supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes. Following lobbying from the Bolsonaros, Washington also designated Brazil’s two largest criminal organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, reinforcing Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign message that Lula was failing to confront organised crime.
The stakes extend beyond the Bolsonaro family’s political fortunes. Washington has pressed Lula for access to Brazil’s critical minerals as it seeks to reduce dependence on China. Lula has defended Brazil’s freedom to trade with other partners.
Brazil shows that Trump’s interventions can backfire. In 2025, Lula’s approval ratings rose after Washington threatened punitive tariffs over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The president turned the dispute into a defence of national sovereignty, making resistance to foreign interference a defining theme of his re-election campaign. The electoral effect of Trump’s involvement is difficult to isolate, but the backlash helped Lula mobilise support. Combined with grassroots organising, appeals to democracy and social welfare policies, it offers one possible response to the regional right’s advance.
Yet a defining feature of that resistance is that it has remained national. Brazil’s size gives it a capacity to resist Washington that none of its neighbours possess. Lula has also been pragmatic in keeping that resistance national, rather than attempting to forge a regional coalition against Trump’s hemispheric ambitions. He also faces a strengthened right at home. Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to concede, seeking to annul the election over a last-minute extension of voting hours that both campaigns had requested. Electoral authorities maintain that the extension did not affect the outcome.
The region’s rightward shift also obscures a fragmented political landscape. Across Latin America, deeply divided electorates have produced closely contested elections, complicating claims that either the left or the right has established a durable political hegemony. Brazil is a case in point: Lula’s victory interrupted the right’s advance, but nearly half of voters backed a candidate who embraced much of Trump’s agenda.
Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington. Brazil may have stopped the blue tide at its borders, but it has yet to emerge as a regional bulwark against it.
- Jordana Timerman is a journalist based in Buenos Aires. She is the managing editor of The Ideas Letter and compiles the Latin America Daily Briefing

Details
According to Russian media reports, a train carrying Moscow "Lokomotiv" football players was attacked by a drone as the team returned from its match against "Rostov" in the 12th round of the Russian Premier League.
"An attack was carried out on the train, and one carriage was damaged. But the football players and staff of "Lokomotiv" were not injured; they are currently traveling to Moscow by bus, and they are all fine," Russian media reports.
"Lokomotiv" itself stated that the team returned to its training base in full and began preparations for the Russian Cup and league matches.
It should be noted that the football club "Lokomotiv" is effectively owned by the Russian state-owned company JSC - "Russian Railways".
The club, like its owner, officially participates in public campaigns and events in support of Russia's military invasion of Ukraine.
In particular, the club regularly participates in campaigns supporting war participants and their families - providing free tickets to matches and inviting active-duty military personnel and veterans of the so-called "special military operation" to the stands.
Like other Russian clubs, "Lokomotiv" has been barred from participating in UEFA- and FIFA-organized European competitions.
