Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula's election victory
Brazil's Liberal Party has acknowledged President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election victory, breaking with its own candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede defeat.
"We recognize the presidential election results," party leader Valdemar Costa Neto said in a statement on Monday. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified."
The statement marks a clear break with Bolsonaro's position. The senator has vowed to seek the annulment of Sunday's runoff result, claiming that a two-hour extension of voting favored Lula.
The extension was ordered due to transport problems in several cities that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. Bolsonaro's own campaign had also requested more voting time in some regions because of heavy rainfall.
According to electoral officials, the extension did not change the outcome of the election.
Bolsonaro has yet to publicly respond to his party's statement.
Flavio Bolsonaro says he is banned from leaving Brazil after election defeat
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro says he has been ordered to surrender his passports and is banned from leaving the country.
The right-wing senator said federal police approached him after he visited his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.
"I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a video posted on social media.
He called the move "a clear attempt to intimidate me" and claimed the order came from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. Neither the court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported ruling.
Bolsonaro said the decision was based on comments by his brother Eduardo, who had suggested he should leave Brazil if he lost the election. He denied having any plans to flee the country and said he would comply with the order.
Trump says Brazil vote 'looked terrible to me' but adds, 'I like Lula'
Ask, and you shall receive — sometimes anyway! Now a senior US government representative has commented on Brazil's vote.
Leaving Washington for a midterm election campaign rally, President Donald Trump told reporters that it "looked terrible" to him.
"I didn't take sides but it looked like another rigged election frankly... it looked so corrupt, so terrible," he said.
Asked by a reporter if he wanted to "do something about the election," Trump seemed to suggest he did not, albeit repeating his criticism of the mechanics of the vote.
"Well, I'm not running Brazil. I'm running the USA. I just thought that the election was, uh — I like Lula, I get along with him very well — I just think it had a very bad look, the election. The way it was tabulated, you know? The extension given was very strange."
US yet to comment on Brazil election
As of 3:20 p.m. in Washington D.C. (1920 GMT), the upper echelons of US government were yet to respond to the election in Brazil on Sunday.
The only October 26 State Department press releases concerned Austria's national day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's planned trip to Georgia later in the week for a G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting.
Rubio had not opined on his social media channels and US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account — which only tends to pick up on stories with a tape delay unless they involve Trump directly — had remained inactive since Sunday night.
Lula and his Workers' Party often had strained relations with US governments, especially Republican ones, but this has been particularly pronounced in Trump's case.
Recap — Why is Bolsonaro crying foul after the voting extension?
Just joining us and wondering how Brazil's runoff vote had a considerably clearer margin of victory than predicted and yet still ended in controversy and the losing candidate refusing to concede defeat?
Challenger Flavio Bolsonaro's objections were focused around the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
The decisions by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice on Sunday followed a complaint over allegations of pro-Bolsonaro mayors being behind public transport irregularities that may have hampered people's plans to vote.
On election night, Bolsonaro then told journalists it was "impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded."
For now it's unclear whether, as the dust settles, Bolsonaro will continue to resist the outcome and try to encourage protests in the way his now-jailed father Jair Bolsonaro did four years ago.
But two factors in particular seem to speak against the prospects of a potential Bolsonaro challenge.
Firstly, his fairly sizeable margin of defeat — losing by slightly more than 4 million votes rather than just a few thousand — makes it much more unlikely that a two-hour extension at polling stations could have even the theoretical potential of swaying the result.
And beyond that, his camp appealed for and successfully secured permission to keep polling stations open in some of Bolsonaro's southern strongholds, after torrential rains interfered with would-be voters' travel plans.
African leaders congratulate Lula, seek to 'advance shared interests'
Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was one of several African leaders to congratulate Lula on Monday, saying that his renewed mandate offered an opportunity to strengthen bilateral ties.
"As two leading nations of the Global South, we can promote economic integration and advance our shared interests in a rapidly changing global order," Tinubu said online, saying he looked forward to expanding cooperation in a raft of areas.
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu also extended her "sincere congratulations" to Lula.
"Tanzania values its longstanding friendship with Brazil, and looks forward to continue building on this foundation to further strengthen bilateral relations and deepen cooperation, for the mutual benefit of our two nations," Suluhu said.
Seychelles President Patrick Herminie called the runoff election result "a powerful affirmation of the trust the Brazilian people have placed in President Lula's leadership," in comments published by his office online.
He said Lula's win was "a testament to his lifelong commitment to the dignity and well-being of ordinary men and women," saying the Seychelles shared Lula's values like "social justice, equality of opportunity, the protection of workers and the most vulnerable, and a model of development that places people at its center."
Herminie expressed a desire to deepen bilateral cooperation, particularly in tackling climate change, protecting the oceans and advancing the interests of the Global South.
Putin congratulates Lula, praising his 'personal contribution' to bilateral ties
Russian President Vladimir Putin offered congratulations to Lula in a telegram published by the Kremlin on Monday.
"It is difficult to overstate your personal contribution to strengthening the strategic partnership between Brazil and Russia," the telegram stated.
Putin, a leader of a fellow BRICS alliance member, is one of few world leaders to have worked with Lula across all of his presidential terms, starting in 2003.
Putin also congratulated Lula on his upcoming 81st birthday, which falls on Tuesday.
The Russian president's spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow earlier in the day that the Kremlin welcomed Lula's re-election.
WATCH: Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term after defeating far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff election.
It's a historic political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round.
DW reports from Rio de Janeiro.
Sao Paulo stock exchange halts trading over sharp drop after Lula win
Trading on the Sao Paulo stock exchange, the largest in Latin America, was suspended for 30 minutes on Monday after plummeting nearly 17% in the wake of the re-election of left-wing Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who defeated conservative Flavio Bolsonaro.
The sharp drop in the benchmark Ibovespa index triggered a 30-minute "circuit breaker" mechanism provided for "periods of sharp market decline," according to a stock exchange statement.
Meanwhile, the US dollar surged 12% against Brazil's currency, one of the real's biggest daily moves on record.
Prices of raw sugar, one of Brazil's most important exports, slid nearly 5% on the collapsing exchange rate.
Prediction markets had indicated a Bolsonaro win but the right-wing senator's refusal to concede defeat and his pledge to challenge the election result have added to investor uncertainty.
"Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," Chris Turner, a strategist at ING in London, told the Reuters news agency as attention turned to Lula's choice of finance minister — a clue as to his fiscal approach.
"The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Graham Stock told Reuters.
Germany's Merz wants to deepen 'the strategic partnership' with Brazil
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has joined the chorus of world leaders congratulating Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his re-election.
"I look forward to further deepening the strategic partnership between Germany and Brazil together," Merz said in a message posted on X.
Germany and Brazil held government consultations in Hannover in April of this year, at which Merz and Lula agreed to cooperate more closely on defense and raw materials, among other things.
Brazilian markets poised for sharp drop Monday after Lula win
Brazilian markets are bracing for heavy selling on Monday, with futures of Brazil's benchmark stock index Bovespa falling nearly 15% in early Monday trading
On global markets, the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF, which tracks a basket of major Brazilian stocks, plunged as much as 26% in premarket trading as investors unwind bets on a right-wing victory.
Brazilian Real November futures also fell 10% in Asian trading, while US-listed shares of Brazilian stocks dropped as well, with energy giant Petrobras plunging more than 20% and banking group Itau Unibanco cratering almost 30%.
Investors had seen election loser Flavio Bolsonaro as the candidate most likely to boost markets with fiscal austerity and deregulation, while Lula has pursued policies of redistribution and state-led development, including costly welfare programs.
Russia says it welcomes Lula's re-election
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.
"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
He said Russia hoped for more of the same.
Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.
However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.
Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.
It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

France, China, Spain congratulate Lula on victory
Messages of congratulations continue to rain in from around the world following Lula's unexpected win.
China's response was measured, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying that "China has noted that Brazil's Superior Electoral Court has announced President Lula has won the second round of the Brazilian general election, and expresses its congratulations."
Guo added that Beijing was "willing to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future."
French President Emmanuel Macron, after expressing his congratulations, said Brazil and France should work to "strengthen our strategic partnership."
"France and Brazil have much to build together," Macron said X, adding that the two countries should nurture their friendship "in the service of a fairer world."
Spain's prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, was more effusive, casting Lula's victory as evidence that the world is experiencing a backlash to its seeming rightwards political trajectory at present.
"A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The global progressive comeback has just begun," Sanchez, who has called snap elections in November, posted on X.
Big challenges face Lula's fourth term
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is likely to face several difficulties in enacting his agenda in a fourth-term.
Among other things, Brazil has elected its most conservative congress since the country's return to democracy in the 1980s.
Flavio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allies could control more than 280 seats in the 513-seat lower house and up to 50 seats in the 81-seat Senate following parliamentary elections three weeks ago.
This could lead to Lula's being forced to cede to congress on decisions about the budget, important legislation and key nominations.
Economic woes
Brazil is also in a period of weak economic growth, with his government forecasting just a 2.3% rise in GDP next year.
This is combined with public debt that surpasses 82% of GDP, the highest rate since the coronavirus pandemic.
Security concerns
Public security also remains a major concern in Brazil, with criminal organizations holding considerable influence in parts of the country.
Lula has said he plans to establish a Ministry of Public Security to combat the problem.
Environmental problems
There are also environmental challenges ahead.
Although deforestation in the Amazon — a major carbon sink and thus vital for the stability of the world climate — fell significantly during Lula's third term, Brazil is still a long way from its goal of ending deforestation by 2030.

From the Mecca defence pact to Tehran talks: Is the Middle East’s security landscape shifting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:07:28 UTC
00:07:28 KST

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.
A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.
During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.
Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.
A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

Economic pain collides with regulatory changes for small businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Economic pain collides with regulatory changes for small businesses
In short:
Small business operators are navigating tough economic conditions, changes to payday super, a ban on debit and credit surcharges, an increase in wages and changes to trusts.
According to CreditorWatch, one in 10 invoices were more than 60 days overdue in September.
What's next?
The Reserve Bank meets next week, with an interest rate hike increasingly expected.
Small businesses are unlikely to receive a reprieve from tough conditions, with another potential interest rate hike looming and fuel costs continuing to climb.
The unfavourable economic climate has collided with a string of policy changes facing operators, who say a growing regulatory burden has only increased their costs.
The changes include the introduction of payday super, a ban on debit and credit surcharges, an increase to minimum and award wages, and changes to how trusts will be taxed.
Industry associations have voiced concerns about the cumulative impact on small firms, creating additional red tape at a time businesses were already navigating higher costs.
"It's just killing us, killing our industry," builder Steve Bright told The Business.
He went into construction for the love of the trade, but running his own firm, a typical day at work now looks very different.
"Instead of getting out and building a house, we're spending more than half our time in an office doing paperwork," he said.
He is one of about 2.7 million small business owners navigating the current conditions.
Mr Bright has hired extra staff to help implement the policy changes in his business.
"We've got full-time people that do it now ... it's just another cost that we've got to wear."
Simon Croft from the Housing Industry Association said reforms have often been viewed in a "policy silo".
"It's that layering effect of simultaneous changes that then also … trickle down to their business operations."
Sunshine Coast designer and planner Debbie Johnson is rethinking her plans to pass her business onto her son after a tough year.
"I really don't know that as a mother, I would like to see [my son] coming in and taking this business over. It's not like you work 38 hours a week and you get your holiday pay and your sick pay," she said.
"It's very difficult when you want to deliver services for your clients and, I suppose, the regulations that you're working within keep changing because it's disruptive to your focus of what your core business is."
Cashflow crunch worsening
The data demonstrates the cashflow crunch facing businesses at the same time as they adapt to regulatory change. An increasing number have fallen behind on payments.
Credit reporting agency CreditorWatch found "serious arrears" hit an 8.5-year high in September.
Its latest Business Risk Index showed more than 50 per cent of invoices were not paid on time.
One in 10 invoices were more than 60 days overdue, which CreditorWatch chief executive Patrick Coghlan said was the highest level of "serious arrears" since April 2018.
"Even though we're at almost record insolvency levels, the indicators that we're seeing show that that's likely to increase,"
he said.
"It's rarely one decision that gets made or one event that takes place that knocks a business over.
"It's generally [the] cumulative effect of all of these changes that really just continues to put pressure on small businesses."
Inflation and interest rate squeeze
In a week, the Reserve Bank's interest rate-setting board will decide whether to increase borrowing costs for a fifth time this year.
Like households, many businesses have been squeezed by high inflation and rising rates.
"The biggest single factor that is squeezing small business and the economy in general is higher fuel costs and therefore higher transport costs," said Westpac's chief economist, Luci Ellis.
The costs have often been passed on to consumers, as with last month's ban on debit and credit surcharges, which had hospitality venues increase their pricing.
"There have been a few instances of firms, particularly cafes, where it seems prices have increased even more [than the surcharge price]," Dr Ellis said.
"These are often places that have been dealing with other cost pressures, and this has just given them permission to adjust their prices."
Economic concerns overshadow regulatory changes
A survey by small business accounting platform MYOB found 38 per cent of small businesses have seen a drop in revenue from a year ago.
Loading...
Sixty-five per cent reported being concerned about cashflow for the coming year, and 69 per cent were worried about attracting new customers.
MYOB's chief executive, Paul Robson, said the payday super and surcharge policy changes have required small businesses to adapt.
"These two shifts have taken place within a relatively short period," he said.
"However, for the most part, our research suggests that concerns around regulatory changes are still behind cost factors including fuel, energy and interest rates."
Charlie Sheppeard, from competing accounting platform Xero, said slow sales growth in certain sectors made it harder to adapt to changes such as the surcharge ban.
"That leaves little room to absorb additional costs,"
he said.
"It is particularly challenging for sectors like retail and hospitality, where customer card transactions are common, and margins are already thin."
In a statement to the ABC, Small Business Minister Anne Aly said the government knows businesses have been managing rising costs and adjusting to changes, and took the challenges seriously.
"That's why the Albanese Labor government is delivering billions in business tax relief," Dr Aly said, citing the $20,000 instant asset write-off being made permanent, and backing payment reforms, which the RBA has said will lower business costs by $910 million a year.

Will Donald Trump or AI blow up financial markets first?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

analysis
Will Donald Trump or AI blow up financial markets first?
It's an unpalatable choice.
But investors now must consider which poison will cause the least harm.
With civil unrest running rampant across the developed world and global investors desperately seeking exits from the great artificial intelligence boom, a double dose of debt worries has suddenly infected the world of finance.
One is a problem that has been decades in the making, as governments have spent their way out of various crises with nary a care about the cost.
The other has arisen in a frighteningly short time, driven by a manic investment boom that used trillions of dollars of borrowed cash to fund a technology with debatable benefits for society.
Over the past eight weeks, competing demands from those two piles of debt have coalesced into a dramatic repricing of borrowing costs.
Financial markets are perennially worried about the next crisis.
But they now find themselves debating whether a sovereign debt crisis would be worse than an undoing of a technology boom that has driven stock markets since before the pandemic.
The one thing over which there is no dispute is that, if there is a meltdown, interest rates will provide the trigger.
The US Federal Reserve meets tonight and tomorrow, and while there is little chance of an official US rate hike this time around, markets are convinced that December will likely see an increase.
Either way, it's academic.
The US government has seen the cost of its long-term borrowings soar in recent months as bond markets, concerned about the mounting cost of its war in Iran coupled with US President Donald Trump's massive tax cuts, have pushed debt costs higher.
America's debt is now equivalent to 126 per cent of its economic output, the highest it has been in the post-war era, with no plan to reverse the trend.
The annual interest cost on that $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) debt has topped $US1trillion, creating a snowballing budget deficit.
The great AI unravelling
They've been falling like bowling pins in recent weeks.
It began with the Firmus float flop, an audacious $44 billion grab for cash that may have gotten across the line just a few months earlier.
Last week, NextDC — a long-established Australian data centre builder with a strong track record — saw its share price plunge 42 per cent after Melbourne residents successfully delayed a monster computer shed in the suburbs.
A similar incident occurred in Sydney recently, when Goodman Group canned a data centre in the northern suburbs.
It's a story resonating across the developed world.
CoreWeave, a US neocloud like Firmus that rents out its chips and computing power to AI firms, has seen its stock drop 36 per cent in the past month on concern over its mounting debts.
The Nasdaq exchange, dominated by global technology firms, has just endured its worst fortnight since April as developed nations have collectively turned their backs on AI infrastructure.
The AI giant behind Claude, Anthropic, will be hoping the mood is different by the time it floats on Wall Street, which could be just weeks away.
But a recent Gallup poll in the US found 71 per cent of Americans opposed data centres. Of those questioned, only 53 per cent opposed nuclear power plants.
Continuing those delays will dramatically slow the expected rollout of AI technology to businesses and firms.
That, in turn, could undermine revenue for AI firms and destabilise those that have taken on huge debts to fund their investment.
Those concerns have escalated dramatically in the past two months.
ASIC takes a deep dive
It's not all bad news.
Unlike the global financial crisis, where debt problems emerged out of left field, monetary authorities and market regulators are warning and preparing for the worst this time around.
In Australia, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is taking a helicopter view of national financial markets to ensure they are operating for the interests of all.
From the deeply troubled Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) to private credit markets, fixed income, commodities and foreign exchange, it is holding round table talks to improve their operation and eliminate friction points.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says the watchdog has two key themes running across all markets: resilience and transparency.
"Resilience gives you strength, transparency gives you trust," she says.
And the corporate watchdog is aware of the growing risk facing Australian investors and institutions.
"Global markets are becoming more integrated and are open more hours than ever.
"Capital flows are going offshore as much as onshore because of the dominance of tech stocks.
"There's high and strategic risk … and giant pools of savings in Australia."
During the 2008 financial crisis, a complete absence of transparency from ratings agencies, auditors and little-known corners of debt markets trading instruments that were mostly unregulated created panic across the financial system.
No-one knew who owed what or which bank held a toxic pile of worthless IOUs. As trust evaporated, the system ground to a halt.
Loading...
ASIC's overview won't stop a market crash. But it will limit the potential for regulators to be blindsided.
"We're seeing movements in spreads and volatility that we haven't seen for a long time," Constant notes.
The view from the helicopter may improve market efficiencies, she adds, the benefits of which will flow through to Australian investors, including those exposed through their superannuation funds.
"We don't want to be a regulator that fears the risk of the challenges ahead.
"It's about adapting to it with that trust and with that strength, that resilience and transparency give."
The AI payday
The prospect of a simultaneous sovereign-debt crisis and a stock-market collapse of hugely indebted companies terrifies many investors.
But some argue that an implosion in one area may ease problems in the other, as interest rates would fall sharply.
Either way, it would still hurt.
Loading
In the early days, big tech companies funded their AI dreams through their enormous cash flows.
But as capital expenditures escalated and the boom expanded beyond the technology itself and into hardware like chips and then architecture like data centres, everyone turned to debt markets.
Even the giants, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, have raised more than $US200 billion between them this year alone.
Nvidia, the world's biggest company, has raised more than $US80 billion this year and routinely finances data centre firms like Australia's Firmus to roll out new data centres using its chips, making it a financier and supplier.
Then there are the "innovative" financing arrangements such as "Special Purpose Vehicles" financed by industry suppliers and investors, along with what is known as "chip financing" as well as debt guarantees and lease arrangements that cloud the boundaries between financing definitions.
And these figures barely scratch the surface. Private credit firms, pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and a host of financiers have gleefully handed over cash.
For years, technology and artificial intelligence have had investors enthralled and have driven stock markets to record levels.
Australia's superannuation funds have dived in with their ears pinned back, delivering double-digit returns to members.
But now comes the reckoning.
What if the rollout stalls because no-one wants a big humming data factory in their backyard?
What if China produces an ultra-cheap version of AI that undercuts Silicon Valley?
Or perhaps something more fundamental, like the pencilled-in sales revenue falls short and simply isn't enough to make the interest payments on the debt?
No wonder Wall Street is getting cold feet.

'Travesty of justice': SC flays UP Police for 'slipshod probe' in murder case, orders reparation for undertrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:58:39 UTC
23:58:39 KST

The verdict came on a plea challenging an Allahabad high court order in January that had denied the man bail. The Supreme Court had directed the trial court on March 23 to conclude the proceedings within three months. The trial was subsequently completed, and the accused was acquitted.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the Uttar Pradesh government to pay Rs 6 lakh in reparation to a man who spent six years in jail as an undertrial in a murder case before being acquitted. The apex court said that the years lost to a faulty investigation were a travesty of justice.Slamming the state police for a “slipshod investigation” and the prosecution for its haphazard handling of the case, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran called the man a “victim of the system”. It said six years of his life had been erased based on a “concocted story” built on mere surmises and conjectures.The man had been in custody since November 14, 2019, in a murder case registered in Agra.The Supreme Court noted that the trial court acquitted him after finding that none of the four circumstances cited by the prosecution, including electronic evidence, had been proved.“This is a classic case of how an investigation should not be proceeded with, resulting in the prosecution putting into jeopardy a person's life and liberty,” the bench said.The court directed the state to pay the compensation within one month, acknowledging that the amount was small compared with the years he had spent behind bars.
“We, hence, direct the state to pay an amount of Rs 6 lakh; though paltry in comparison to the years spent in custody, within a period of one month to the petitioner herein,” it said.The verdict came on a plea challenging an Allahabad High Court order in January that had denied the man bail. The Supreme Court had directed the trial court on March 23 to conclude the proceedings within three months. The trial was subsequently completed, and the accused was acquitted.The bench said the case highlighted the failure of investigating and prosecuting agencies to safeguard an individual's liberty despite the presumption of innocence.“The state cannot shirk from its responsibility to protect its citizens, especially when a person arraigned in a criminal case is presumed innocent until proven guilty,” it said.The court stressed that the role of investigating and prosecuting agencies was not simply to secure convictions, but to ensure justice for all parties, including the accused.“They should recognise themselves to be essential stakeholders in the justice delivery system, ensuring justice, not only to the victim, the de facto complainant and the injured, but also to the accused,” the bench said.The judges also expressed concern over the wider implications of such cases, saying they had encountered similar failures but that this one stood out for its severity.
“We come across such travesty of justice in many matters, but in some, so blatant and shocking, as in this case, which requires reparation to the accused, who in turn is a victim of the system,” it said.The bench directed that a copy of its verdict be sent to the Uttar Pradesh director general of police and the state's home secretary. It also urged the police to train officers in proper investigative procedures, criticising the manner in which the case had been handled.The court said the acquittal was fortunate, given the consequences of the flawed investigation and prosecution for the man's life and liberty.

Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:58:00 UTC
23:58:00 KST

Why Ukraine may be involved in Mali's conflict
October 26, 2026
Ukraine is fighting Russia — and the conflict may extend into Africa's Sahel region.
According to an investigation published by US media outlet CNN in September, around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are reportedly supporting Tuareg rebels in northern Mali. Their common enemy: the military government in Bamako and its Russian allies.
But how reliable is the information? And what price could Kyiv pay for engaging in Africa?
Marta Oliynyk-D'omochko, coordinator of the African Studies Program at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, sees a strategic motive. "Ukraine's main interest is to weaken Russia's influence around the world," she told DW. If Russia's military influence were rolled back, she added, the economic opportunities arising from it would also diminish.
Russian historian Irina Filatova, professor emeritus at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, also considers Ukrainian support for the Tuareg movement plausible. However, she said she has no independent evidence to confirm such involvement.
Kyiv's alleged partners are controversial. The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) cooperates with the Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimeen (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated with al-Qaeda.
Suspicions dating back to 2024
In July 2024, DW reported on possible involvement by the Ukrainian military intelligence service (HUR) in an ambush on Russian Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten in northern Mali.
At the time, HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov said the Tuareg rebels had received information they needed to carry out the attack. Ukraine denied direct involvement.
Paramilitaries from Russia's Wagner Group and Malian troops suffered heavy losses in the July 2024 attack.
CNN's investigation has reignited the question of whether the Russia-Ukraine war is also being fought on African soil.
Signals from Kyiv, but no confirmation
The suspicions were renewed by a post on X by Kyrylo Budanov. The former head of Ukraine's military intelligence, now chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on September 7 that Ukrainian intelligence protects the country's interests worldwide — "from Russia to Africa … in the burning desert sands and in the snows of icy Antarctica...".
Budanov did not explicitly mention Mali and his post does not confirm any specific operation. CNN reported that the Ukrainians provided drone training, operational planning and remote support for drone missions. DW has not independently verified those claims.
DW reached out to the HUR for comment. Among other things, DW wanted to know whether personnel had been deployed to Mali, whether the political leadership had approved such a mission, and what measures were in place to ensure that the JNIM — which cooperates with the FLA — does not indirectly benefit from Ukrainian support.
DW did not receive a specific response. An HUR spokesperson said the agency might provide information at a later date. The extent of any potential Ukrainian involvement therefore remains unclear.
Why Mali matters to Kyiv
Following military coups in 2020 and 2021, Mali increasingly turned away from Western partners and toward Russia. The Wagner Group was subsequently replaced by the Africa Corps in 2025 as Moscow reorganized its military presence.
Russia has sought to consolidate its influence in the Sahel region and present itself as a reliable security partner.
Ulf Laessing, former head of the Sahel program of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Mali and now head of its Syria and Iraq program, said Russia is continuing to expand its activities in Africa.
"I have received information that the Africa Corps still uses Syria and Libya as transit points for flights from Russia, including for refueling and loading, to support its operations on the continent," Laessing told DW.
From Ukraine's perspective, it could be attractive to exert pressure on Russian forces in Africa.
Filatova sees a strategic logic to this: "The Ukrainians regard Russian troops anywhere in the world as legitimate targets." Setbacks in Mali could tie up Russian resources and undermine Moscow's reputation as a security partner, she argued.
However, Oliynyk-D'omochko stressed that the relationship with the Tuareg is not a comprehensive alliance. The FLA is not seeking to replace the government in Bamako. Instead, it is focused on northern Mali and is pursuing self-determination or extensive autonomy.
Oliynyk-D'omochko describes the relationship as a tactical arrangement: "It is more of a situational alliance against a common enemy than a comprehensive partnership."
The alliance with jihadists
The FLA is fighting for an independent state in the north of Mali, a region predominantly inhabited by Tuaregs. JNIM, by contrast, aims to impose strict Islamic rule. Both groups oppose the military government and its Russian allies, but their objectives differ.
Any potential Ukrainian support for the FLA would not, in itself, prove that Kyiv is directly supporting JNIM. However, jihadists could benefit indirectly if they conduct joint operations with FLA or gain access to knowledge and equipment.
Cooperation between Tuareg and Islamist groups dates back more than a decade.
After the ousting and killing of Libya's longtime dictator Muammar al-Gaddafi during the Arab Spring in October 2011, heavily armed Tuareg fighters returned to Mali and took up the struggle for an independent state.
In the process, separatist ambitions became intertwined with Islamist movements. Iyad Ag Ghaly, the current leader of JNIM, was himself involved in the Tuareg rebellion before turning to jihadism.
According to Oliynyk-D'omochko, the cooperation is primarily tactical in nature. The two sides have collaborated during past uprisings but later fell out. It remains unclear how long the current alliance will last.
For Kyiv, this also poses a political risk. In many African countries, the Tuaregs are viewed as separatists. Cooperation with them could therefore create the impression that Ukraine is interfering in another country's internal affairs.
Claims of support for armed groups
Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso accuse Ukraine of supporting armed groups and threatening their territorial integrity. The three Sahel nations, all ruled by military governments, have severed diplomatic relations with Kyiv and deepened their cooperation with Russia.
In September, Mali's Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop accused Ukraine at the United Nations of "providing clear and open support to terrorist groups and other mafia-like groups to undermine our country's territorial integrity," reported Agence France-Presse. Diop did not provide evidence for his claim.
The three nations' governments have may have an interest in legitimizing their partnership with Moscow and portraying Kyiv as a destabilizing actor.
Oliynyk-D'omochko has found no definitive proof of the allegations, yet warned of the potential consequences for Ukraine's Africa policy. Kyiv advocates equal partnerships with African countries. Any alleged cooperation with separatists could undermine that message and affect how potential partners view Ukraine.
What price could Ukraine pay?
Engagement in Mali could offer Ukraine a relatively low-cost way to weaken Russian interests beyond Europe. A small team of specialists could train local fighters and improve their capabilities in the use of drones.
But a potential partnership with the FLA carries political risks. Because the Tuareg separatists cooperate with the JNIM, Kyiv could face accusations of indirectly supporting jihadist fighters. That could undermine Ukraine's efforts to strengthen its relations with African countries.

Russia-Ukraine war reaches orbit: What a close satellite encounter means for space operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:57:28 UTC
23:57:28 KST

In mid-October, a Russian military satellite in low-Earth orbit came dangerously close to a commercial US spacecraft reportedly serving Ukrainian military needs.
The approach was so extreme that the two spacecraft may have been “just a few meters” away from each other at one point.
Satellite trackers called the non-consensual manoeuvre a “worrisome cat-and-mouse game” in space between Russia and Ukraine, the two countries at war since February 2022.
Experts say the incident is an indication that space is increasingly turning into the final frontier for drawn-out geopolitical wars that countries can’t settle using conventional tools.
Russia’s Kosmos-2612 moved dangerously close to ICEYE-X36 equipped with a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) – a technology that can see through clouds during both day and night to create two-dimensional images of objects on Earth.
The satellite is owned by ICEYE US, an American subsidiary of Finland-based ICEYE. Analysts say ICEYE-X36 is likely used by Ukraine for satellite imagery. Kiev has formal access to data collected by the Finnish company’s constellation of SAR satellites.
ICEYE has been supplying satellite data and images to the Ukrainian armed forces since 2022.
Ukraine relies heavily on satellite networks such as Starlink, Starshield, and ICEYE to monitor Russian troop movements and run drones that both intercept missiles and strike targets.
Any disruption in the satellite network by Moscow would substantially degrade Kiev’s ability to launch precision weapons and execute interceptions.
Ukraine’s dependence on its so-called eyes-in-the-sky was on full display last week when Elon Musk’s SpaceX imposed speed restrictions on Starlink and its military-grade Starshield service.
US President Donald Trump had to intervene on Ukraine’s behalf as Musk restored internet speeds to previous levels.
Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in the department of space engineering at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands, tells TRT World that the encounter was unusual in its closeness.
“We have never seen two satellites coming so close without cooperation between the operators of both satellites,” says Langbroek, who first reported the close encounter.
Earlier uncooperative approaches in space had taken place at distances of tens of kilometres, rather than a few hundred metres, he says.
Langbroek links the episode to a broader pattern that includes Russian satellites approaching other countries’ satellites apparently for eavesdropping, reported hacks of satellite feeds, on-orbit exercises involving close approaches, and tests of anti-satellite weapons.
“Space is quickly developing into a potential battlefield,” he says.
No wonder the language around space operations has also become militaristic of late: the US Space Force now treats space as a “battle domain” and has acknowledged possessing “space weapons”, he says.
Modern military operations now depend heavily on space-based communications, live data streams, including from drones, and satellite intelligence.
In the same vein, civilian life has also grown equally dependent on space-based communications, Langbroek says.
The result is heightened vulnerability for everyone, he adds.
“This is not just a military threat. It is a threat to us all,” he says.
Langbroek notes that the traditional divide between military and civilian satellites has blurred of late.
Commercial systems, such as those operated by ICEYE and Starlink, now support military tasks, he says.
Russia already considers any commercial satellite used by Ukraine as a legitimate target.
Consequently, satellite systems that multiple countries and ordinary users rely upon can become targets, potentially harming states that are not parties to the conflict, he says.
Militarisation of Earth’s orbits
Mark J Sundahl, director of the Global Space Law Centre at Cleveland State University, tells TRT World the stalking of satellites in space is on the rise.
The phenomenon is fanning global concerns about the growing militarisation of Earth’s orbits, he says.
“All kinetic warfare that could result in the creation of massive debris clouds that will stay in orbit for hundreds of years must be prohibited,” he says.
Sundahl says such action is already inconsistent with Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, which requires states to exercise “due regard to the corresponding interests” of other countries.
Generating debris clouds that threaten civilian satellites would constitute a “clear violation” of that obligation, even though he notes that not everyone shares this interpretation of the law.
“The common orbital infrastructure that we all share for purposes of telecommunication, navigation, and other daily needs cannot be put into danger due to terrestrial conflicts,” Sundahl says.
Ilyas Golcuklu, head of the private international law department at Altinbas University in Istanbul, tells TRT World that the non-consensual close approach between a military and a commercial object in space is no longer a hypothetical exercise.
“Space has already become a new frontier for geopolitical conflict,” he says.
With the growing volume of objects in orbit, distinguishing commercial from military assets will become harder, he notes.
“The escalation of national rivalries into space is a justified concern for all humankind,” he says.
Lack of established norms
Clear and widely accepted norms for uncoordinated proximity operations in space remain mostly non-existent.
Langbroek attributes this mainly to the opposition by major space powers, which have resisted rules that might constrain their own extraterrestrial activities.
In wartime, rules of conduct are often the first to be broken, he says.
“Any form of uncooperative proximity should not be performed, because of the risks involved. Yet, it happens,” he says.
Golcuklu notes that space approaches conducted for peaceful purposes – such as refuelling, repairing a component, or removing space debris – rely on technologies that are essentially identical to those needed to spy on or disable a rival satellite.
Distinguishing legitimate activity from hostile intent – and closing the regulatory vacuum – has become increasingly challenging, he says.
“Minimum safe distances” or “keep-out zones” must be devised as quickly as possible by the UN before the risks become too big to handle, he adds.
For example, experts consider the risk of a minor miscalculation resulting in collisions and creating space debris as serious.
Langbroek notes that a kinetic attack – whether by collision or by a projectile – would generate large amounts of on-orbit debris that endangers satellites belonging to countries uninvolved in any conflict.
Even non-kinetic methods, such as disabling electronics with an electromagnetic pulse, would leave the targeted satellite itself as debris, adding to collision hazards, he says.
During close approaches, the risk of an unintended collision is real: if the operator of the approached satellite becomes nervous and attempts an evasive manoeuvre, the geometry can become hazardous, he says.
Even controlled approaches in space can go wrong.
“It really is a risky thing to bring your satellite so close to another satellite, especially without coordination with the owner of that satellite,” Langbroek says.

Humanitarian Aid From Russia to Cuba Directed to Most Vulnerable Citizens - Minister

Kenya releases first Ebola contacts from quarantine, milestone in containment efforts
NAIROBI, Oct 26 - Kenya on Monday released from quarantine the first group of people who came into contact with its index Ebola patient, a milestone in its efforts to contain cases to a single infection cluster.
The 20 people released completed 21 days of monitoring without developing Ebola symptoms and are in good health, the director-general in Kenya's health ministry, Patrick Amoth, said in a statement.
Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases so far, two of whom have died. The remaining seven patients are stable and receiving treatment, Amoth said, adding that 98 others still in quarantine would be released in four waves beginning on November 3.
"This is a milestone worth celebrating," Amoth said. "It is also a reminder that the work is not yet done."
Kenya's first case died in a hospital in Nairobi on October 5, after which eight others fell ill while in quarantine. It announced on Friday that a second person had died.
Ebola's spread from Congo, where the outbreak was declared in mid-May, to Kenya has raised concerns about lapses in border screening.
Nigeria has said its first Ebola case in more than a decade, which it reported last week, appears to be closely related to Kenya's index case, citing genomic analysis. The two cases both flew out of Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day in early October.
Amoth said those leaving quarantine posed no risk to their families or communities where they live and urged Kenyans to welcome them home. "We cannot afford to drop our vigilance," he said. REUTERS

Head of Mexico's electoral authority resigns amid corruption allegations
MEXICO CITY, Oct 26 - The head of Mexico's National Electoral Institute will resign amid allegations of corruption, a decision President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Monday that she supports.
INE chief Guadalupe Taddei's resignation is the most high-profile departure tied to alleged corruption in Sheinbaum's two-year-old presidency.
The move raises fresh questions over the credibility and leadership of the autonomous electoral authority as it prepares for the 2027 midterms and after lawmakers rejected Sheinbaum's broader attempt to reform Mexico's electoral system earlier this year. Lawmakers later supported a narrower package of electoral changes.
"There couldn't be this shadow of a conflict of interest. It's good that she made the decision to step aside," Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference, while rejecting the notion that the resignation pointed to a political crisis.
Mexico's Superior Audit Office is investigating alleged irregularities involving INE contracts, including possible conflicts of interest and the triangulation of public funds. Taddei, in local news outlets, has been accused of favoring an INE contractor, with whom she has a personal relationship, with contracts worth millions of dollars.
"Over the past few days, rumors, fabricated material, leaks, and versions of events have spread through the media and social networks, and as in all such cases, their authenticity, context, and purpose must be verified and corroborated," Taddei said in a Sunday statement announcing her planned resignation.
Taddei said her resignation aimed to protect the INE and allow it to fulfill its constitutional mission.
The 2027 elections are expected to be hotly contested, and the INE's credibility is essential to avoid conflict, said Antonio Ocaranza, a consultant who was a spokesman for former President Ernesto Zedillo. He called Taddei's exit "a necessary and timely correction."
Ocaranza said the case also poses a broader test for Sheinbaum, as there are already many cases of political families close to her political party, Morena, accused by local news outlets, and "the government has shown little desire to investigate and punish them."
Authorities are also investigating potential fraud linked to several contracts signed by other INE officials in which there may have been conflicts of interest.
Opposition party PRI's President Alejandro Moreno said Taddei's resignation should not be used to "impose another person close to Morena."
"Mexico cannot go into the 2027 elections with an electoral authority whose impartiality is in serious question," he added. REUTERS

Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:45:22 UTC
23:45:22 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous shipping route
Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine has turned the Black Sea into the world’s most dangerous waters for commercial shipping, the Financial Times reported. At least 40 sailors have died there since the start of 2026, compared with 24 who died in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war the United States and Israel are waging against Iran has complicated shipping.
More than 570 ships have come under attack in the Black Sea since the start of the year, according to the maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization. Some ships were hit by accident, while others were deliberately targeted. Both Russia and Ukraine try to disrupt each other’s maritime shipping to reduce export revenues.
War-risk insurance for the Black Sea now costs as much as 15% of a ship’s hull value, almost twice the rate for ships in the Persian Gulf. Nearly the entire Black Sea is now classified in the highest war-risk category, except for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey.
Shipping oil from the Middle East through the Strait of Hormuz is now cheaper and safer by comparison. As a result, shipping companies increasingly refuse to operate in the Black Sea or use older vessels that are cheaper to insure.
Crews are recruited from Syria, Egypt, and Azerbaijan. The FT found that Syrian sailors earn about $800 a month working in the Black Sea. They are promised double pay for each day spent in the combat zone, and their families are to receive $25,000 to $50,000 in compensation if a sailor is killed.
Ukrainian forces struck more than 300 Russian vessels over an 11-week period, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said in September. The targets included sanctioned tankers as well as cargo ships carrying grain.
Russia has responded by stepping up strikes on ships entering Ukrainian ports. Russian attacks accounted for about 90% of strikes on commercial vessels over the past 45 days, according to Ambrey’s estimates.
The strikes are affecting global fuel and food supplies. Russian wheat exports fell 52% in September compared with a year earlier, while Ukraine is exporting only half its projected volume of agricultural products. Russian diesel exports fell by 467,000 barrels a day in September compared with a year earlier, according to Kpler.
The global effects of the war in the Black Sea are difficult to separate from those of the conflict in the Persian Gulf, Bloomberg reported. High global wheat stocks have kept disruptions in grain supplies from significantly affecting prices, while diesel fuel grew more expensive even before Russian–Ukrainian attacks escalated, because of the war the United States is waging against Iran.
The war in photographs
A family from Oleshky starts a new life in the Kyiv region
Vitaliy and Iryna fled the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in September with their 13-year-old son, Vlad, and their cat, Marsik. By then, residents had been left in complete isolation, without food, water, electricity, or medical care.
A drone damaged Vitaliy and Iryna’s home, prompting them to leave Oleshky and walk more than 20 kilometers (12 miles) along a mined road. The family traveled through Russia and Belarus to reach Ukrainian-controlled territory and is now rebuilding its life in the Kyiv region.
Russia and Ukraine agreed last week to a ceasefire in Oleshky for the evacuation of residents. It is set to take effect at 4 a.m. on October 27.

17 public broadcasters mapped Russia’s hybrid war on Europe. Germany: four dots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:43:27 UTC
23:43:27 KST

Journalists from 17 European public service broadcasters, coordinated by the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) Eurovision News Spotlight network, published an interactive map on 23 October 2026. It documents hybrid incidents linked to Russia across 17 European countries between 1 April and 15 October. Journalists compiled a database of hundreds of reported incidents, categorizing each by type and the source and strength of its alleged links to Russia, then verifying them through open-source research.
The map comes as officials warn the campaign is growing. On 28 September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in Brussels that Russia was planning more acts of sabotage to divide societies and intimidate them into abandoning their support for Ukraine. The points on the map represent an incomplete list of publicly known cases attributed to Russia or suspected of being linked to it, the report states.
The map covers airspace violations, sabotage attempts, “disposable” agents with no formal intelligence training, migration used as a weapon, and Russian military activity near or across European borders. It excludes cyberattacks, influence operations, and espionage by trained intelligence officers.
The EBU calls the result a very conservative estimate, not an official tally. Russia has consistently denied responsibility for the incidents. Many single points represent several incidents of the same type in one area or in quick succession. In Moldova, for example, Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatîi said on 30 September that the government had recorded 84 drone incursions.
Four German incidents are on the map, out of many more
The map shows four incidents in Germany, according to BR.
- On 2 August, German authorities arrested a 33-year-old Ukrainian man in Thuringia on suspicion of photographing a Bavarian weapons manufacturer for a foreign intelligence service as part of an alleged sabotage plot.
- On 4 August, a drone carrying explosives and a detonator struck the wing of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport but failed to explode.
- On 3 September, attackers threw firebombs from a car onto a construction site next to defense firms in Munich, and German security authorities suspect Russian intelligence.
- On 14 September, investigators learned of a crashed drone found near the Bundeswehr’s Wunstorf air base.
Internal papers from the new Joint Hybrid Defense Center, seen by Correctiv, record 163 suspected sabotage cases in 2026 up to 19 August. The targets included rail lines, military facilities, substations, and radio masts. The same papers record 1,034 drone overflights of critical infrastructure, military sites, and defense companies, and 25 espionage investigations. The papers cover possible attacks by Russia, China, and Iran, and media did not report a breakdown of the sabotage cases by country.
European leaders sound the alarm over Russian hybrid attacks
On 15 April, Swedish civil defense minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin said pro-Russian groups had moved from denial-of-service attacks to attempts at destructive cyberattacks, including one on a Swedish power plant in 2025. On 1 September, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul named Russia as the perpetrator of the Leipzig attack and accused Moscow of “blatant hostility” toward Germany.
On 18 September, French President Emmanuel Macron said Russia’s hybrid attacks would not go unanswered and ordered a plan to protect France’s critical infrastructure. On 1 October, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany was preparing for new hybrid attacks, “including serious ones.” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on 14 October called the attacks a sign of Russian weakness at a press conference in Tallinn and said NATO would react where needed without being “rattled.”

Uzbekistan Wants Out of the Iran-US Social Media War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

On October 23, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Iranian ambassador in Tashkent in order to hand over a note of protest related to a recent slate of social media postings made by several Iranian diplomatic missions. The posts sniped at U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, using his recent visit to Samarkand as a touchstone.
“It’s great that you’re learning history! The place where you are standing is part of the Persian civilization and architecture. The same civilization you were babbling nonsense about last week at the Acropolis!” read a since-removed post on X from the Iranian embassy in Armenia.
In early October, Rubio delivered remarks during a visit to Greece that set off a history-based social media war that has now spilled over to Uzbekistan. With the ancient Acropolis as his backdrop, he mused on the meaning of Western civilization. Early in the speech he recounted the destruction of the Acropolis in 480 BCE by a Persian army.
“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon,” Rubio said before jumping ahead a 25 centuries to the modern era and the American obsession with antiquity.
Later in the speech, Rubio got the point: a rhetorical attack to match the physical war ongoing between the U.S. and Iran.
“It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country… This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.”
When Rubio landed in Uzbekistan two weeks later, Iran’s keyboard warriors were ready.
“At the Acropolis, you invoked civilizations. Samarkand invites you to a deeper conversation with history, in a city whose heritage is deeply interwoven with Iranian civilization,” the Iranian Permanent Mission to the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) stated in its post, which remains available as of publication.
On October 24, the Uzbek Foreign Ministry reported that it had summoned the Iranian ambassador, Mohammad Ali Eskandari, to complain about the posts, which it said in its own social media post, “interpret the historical and cultural heritage of the city of Samarkand for unilateral political purposes.”
“During the meeting,” the ministry said, “it was noted that the heritage of Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva, and other historical cities of Uzbekistan is an integral part of the rich and multifaceted historical and cultural development formed over many centuries.” The ministry demanded that the offending posts be taken down, and those posted the Iranian embassies in Armenia, China, and Zimbabwe have been.
“Uzbekistan values relations with Iran based on mutual respect and trust,” the Foreign Ministry stated. “At the same time, it maintains its principled position against one-sided interpretation of the historical and cultural heritage of our country.”
Of note: While a post regarding Tashkent’s summoning of the Iranian ambassador remains available on Instagram as of publication, there’s no trace of an earlier post on the Foreign Ministry’s website regarding the meeting – although a relic remains on Facebook.
Without recounting the entire history of Samarkand, it’s fair to say that the city’s history and culture is multilayered, with many empires having risen and fallen across (and from within) its territory. It has existed, in some form, since the 8th century BCE. In 329 BCE, Marakanda – as it was then known – was captured by Alexander the Great. It had been one of the most important cities for the Sogdian civilization; by the time of Alexander, Sogdiana was part of the greater Achaemenid Persian Empire.
The importance of Persian civilization to Central Asia is indisputable. What Tashkent took umbrage over, however, is the operationalization of the past into a weapon (albeit an online one) in a very modern, and very difficult, conflict.
To put it bluntly: Uzbekistan does not want to be invoked in the Iran-U.S. conflict, certainly not while it has tried to deepen relations with Washington while also maintaining ties with Iran.

A cargo ship became uncontrollable during a storm off the Netherlands; there are injuries
Kyiv • UNN
The UHL Freedom, with 25 crew members on board, became uncontrollable due to the storm, the loss of its anchor, and engine problems. Three people were injured.
In the North Sea off the coast of the Netherlands, the cargo ship UHL Freedom lost its anchor during a storm and effectively became uncontrollable. There were 25 crew members on board, three of whom were injured. Two of the injured were evacuated by helicopter. Bild reports, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred on Sunday approximately 30 kilometers west of the German island of Borkum, near the Dutch island of Schiermonnikoog. Due to a storm reaching up to nine on the Beaufort scale, the vessel began drifting under the influence of the wind and current. Engine problems created an additional hazard.
Dutch rescuers and the German rescue cruiser Hamburg came to the crew’s aid. A helicopter brought medical specialists on board, who provided assistance to the injured. Emergency tugboats were also dispatched to the site of the accident.
The 150-meter-long and 26-meter-wide cargo ship sails under the flag of Portugal and is owned by the Hamburg-based company United Heavy Lift. It was carrying, among other things, wind turbine blades and was heading to the port of Emden in northern Germany.

Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:42:27 UTC
23:42:27 KST

The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.
Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.
Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.
Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.
A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.
Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.
Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.
The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.
Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.
Its German factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.
Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.
The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:31:30 UTC
23:31:30 KST

Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of students electing to train as Frisian language teachers has doubled this year, amid a historic drive to strengthen and revive the Netherlands’ only officially recognised second language.
More than 34 students signed up to take a Frisian teacher training course at Leeuwarden’s hbo college NHL Stenden, either as a minor or part-time element of their studies, according to Omroep Fryslân.
The change signals a growing revival trend as Friesland, often ranked the Netherlands’ culturally proudest province, fights to protect its linguistic identity. Only 10 years ago, experts warned the language was on the verge of extinction.
Geert Driessen, of Radboud University in Nijmegen, said in a 2016 study that it was the “eleventh hour” for the province’s mother tongue – especially in urban areas, where Dutch speaking newcomers increasingly mix with locals.
Between 1994 and 2014, he found, Frisian spoken outside family homes had halved. This led to the founding of Taalplan Frysk 2030, a government-backed scheme to protect the language through education and social initiatives.
The plan has received millions of euros in funding, much of which has gone to NHL Stenden. Recent studies show Frisian comprehension is rising, and since this school year all primary and secondary school pupils in Friesland are actively taught the language.
In September, the University of Groningen also launched the first standalone Frisian language degree in 15 years.
