Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian
Iran’s anti-negotiation hardliners turn against President Pezeshkian over negotiations with the US.
As the threat of a new war with the United States looms, the Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, a hardline political faction also known as the Paydari Front, has asked the Iranian parliament and the Supreme National Security Council to initiate a withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
This move has been interpreted as a call for Iran to develop nuclear weapons, with the Paydari Front saying these military endeavours should happen “as quickly as possible”.
It is the latest bold and defiant message by Iran’s hardliners against Washington, after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28 on the pretext that Tehran was trying to develop nuclear weapons.
The war has seen the Strait of Hormuz largely closed to shipping, massive damage to Iranian and Arab infrastructure in missile and air strikes, and huge disruptions to global energy supplies.
The past eight months have also marked an ongoing existential power struggle between moderates and centrists, such as President Masoud Pezeshkian, who generally favour talks with the US, and hardliners in the Paydari Front who do not.
Ultimately, the moderate camp wants a swift end to the conflict to save Iran’s crumbling economy. Hardliners believe Washington only understands the language of force, so the war should continue until the US capitulates to Iran’s demands.
The domestic rivalry can be seen in the public squares of major Iranian cities, where for the past 200 days supporters of the hardline faction have rallied at night.
Initially, these gatherings were a way for people to express public support for the government and protest the unprovoked US war on Iran. Over time, they have evolved into highly organised political rallies where activists can publicly express their strong opposition to moderates’ efforts to end the war through diplomatic channels.
The hardliners’ slogans include “No compromise, no surrender – the fight against America” and “Negotiating with the enemy is a betrayal of the homeland”.
They also protested against President Pezeshkian’s return to Tehran from the UN General Assembly in September, where he condemned the US war but also extolled the virtues of diplomacy. The pickets were viewed as a way for their “anti-negotiation” message to be heard by the president.
This bloc has considerable power beyond these activist circles. Hardliners have a strong presence in Tehran’s municipal government, the parliament, among religious preachers and eulogists, and academia and the media.
Amirhossein Sabeti, a member of parliament aligned with the Paydari Front, said in a statement that negotiations with the US will not begin unless Washington’s siege on Iran’s southern ports or sanctions end.
“The enemy’s objective of destroying Iran has not changed. It is simply waiting for the right moment to launch another surprise attack. Those who thought negotiations could prevent war, or that the United States would lift sanctions through negotiations, did not understand how the world works and were deluding themselves,” he said. “The only language the world understands is the language of power.”
The political faction to which Sabeti belongs has filed a motion in the Iranian parliament to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, following his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Iran’s parliament is also considering a law to criminalise interviews with foreign media outlets, which would be another win for hardliners.
But as the impeachment motion against Iran’s foreign minister moves through parliament, the political camp supporting the government continues to advocate for a diplomatic solution to the current conflict.
Davood Heshmati, a journalist considered close to Pezeshkian, said there are signs that US forces have foregone the grand ambition of overthrowing the Iranian government and have instead opted for more modest aims, which makes a diplomatic solution more likely.
“There are several ways to achieve those other goals, one of which is war. But, in any case, to prevent a war, all alternatives to military action must first be tested. Negotiations and a diplomatic agreement are among those alternatives, and they should always take precedence over war,” Heshmati told Al Jazeera.
“Those who say the Strait of Hormuz must not be reopened are people who believe the war must not end. From the perspective of Iran’s anti-negotiation camp, the war between Iran and the United States has no end. What they do not explain is what outcome they expect from this war. They seem to believe that, after several rounds of fighting, the United States will simply walk away from the conflict. But that idea does not appear to be consistent with the logic of what we are witnessing.”
He indicated that for any war to end, there needs to be an understanding with the US that respects Iran’s territorial integrity.
“Those in Iran who support negotiations argue that a balance of power does not necessarily have to be achieved through war, although, given everything that has happened along the diplomatic path, the distrust that exists is understandable,” he said.
Political analyst Negar Mortazavi argues that hardline groups are a powerful domestic force, but they currently have limited influence over Iran’s foreign policy.
“Iran’s hardliners are not a marginal political force. They are a well-organised and deeply entrenched part of [Iran’s] political establishment. Their strength lies in their ability to mobilise supporters, shape political discourse, pressure the government, and raise the political cost of diplomacy,” she said.
“But political influence should not be confused with ultimate decision-making authority. Decisions about war, peace, and negotiations are made at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and national security establishment.”
Hardliners can continue to confront negotiators, threaten impeachments against those who propose talks with the US, and try to obstruct diplomatic endeavours, she said. But they cannot prevent an agreement being reached if it is backed by the country’s main powerholders, including Supreme Leader Mujtaba Khamenei and the Supreme National Security Council.
“The [hardliners] are powerful enough to complicate diplomacy, but not necessarily powerful enough to stop it. [They] are a highly visible and vocal political force, but they are not calling the shots,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.
“Throughout the war, Tehran has kept the door open to diplomacy, and the decision at the highest levels of leadership has been to pursue negotiations with the United States and seek an agreement. The hardliners have been unable to stop that. The real test of their power is that they could not stop the JCPOA [nuclear agreement] under [former President Barack] Obama, and they could not stop the more recent MoU [memorandum of understanding] with Trump. Ultimately, the decisions were made above their heads.”
Street rallies and television programmes opposing a peaceful solution to the US-Israeli war against Iran will continue. But the delay in scheduling the foreign minister’s impeachment hearing, alongside continued diplomatic engagement with mediators to end the war, suggests that the moderates are still a force to be reckoned with.

“Dynamo” is the winner of the Ukrainian Football Cup20.05.26, 20:33 • 81276 views

First international flight arrives at the new Western Sydney airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:27:11 UTC
23:27:11 KST

Sydney’s new 24-hour airport has welcomed its first international passengers with the opening described as a ‘milestone that has been decades in the making’.
Australia’s first major new international airport for 50 years is now fully operational.
Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport (WSI) welcomed its first international passengers on 26 October, with Air New Zealand flight NZ165 touching down from Auckland.
The arrival came a day after the airport officially opened, with Jetstar launching its first domestic passenger services.
Located at Badgerys Creek, about 60 kilometres west of central Sydney, the new airport operates around the clock. That gives airlines greater scheduling flexibility than at Sydney’s existing Kingsford Smith Airport, where a curfew restricts take-offs and landings between 11 pm and 6 am.
“WSI is the most transformational piece of infrastructure our nation has seen since the Sydney Harbour Bridge,” said WSI CEO Simon Hickey.
“WSI's passengers will be able to enjoy access to more than 250 destinations around the globe just over a year from now – a remarkable start for Sydney’s new 24-hour gateway.”
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the opening of the new airport a “milestone” that has been “decades in the making”.
“With the opening of Western Sydney International, this will help drive the next chapter for the region,” he said. “This isn’t just about a new runway or terminal. This is about jobs, investment and delivering for one of Australia’s fastest-growing regions.”
The airport is officially named after Nancy Bird Walton, who was Australia's first female commercial pilot.
What can passengers expect at Sydney’s new airport?
Domestic and international gates share a single terminal, with automated check-in and baggage technology designed to make journeys smoother.
WSI initially has capacity for 10 million passengers a year. The airport says it could eventually become Australia’s primary gateway, with capacity for more than 80 million passengers annually.
Transport options include public buses, taxis, rideshares and rental cars, while drivers can reach the airport via the toll-free M12.
Flights to and from WSI
Singapore Airlines will launch daily Singapore services on 23 November, followed by Vietjet flights to Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam in January 2027, and Fiji Airways services to Nadi in March. Qatar Airways will connect Doha and WSI from 15 December 2027.
Domestically, Jetstar’s network covers the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane, with daily Gold Coast services, up to 14 weekly return services to Melbourne and three to Brisbane.
Qantas will join on 28 March 2027, operating four weekly flights on each of its Melbourne and Brisbane routes through QantasLink.

Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
Unknown

Sugar rush: blood bank acts to stem flow of free iced biscuits
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch blood bank Sanquin has had to lock away the iced biscuits it hands out to donors after discovering it was haemorrhaging money through the heartwarming gesture.
A volunteer at the donation point in Delft told Omroep West the organisation had taken the drastic step because some visitors were abusing its generosity. “People were going out of here with their bags full,” they said.
Sanquin’s Instagram page promotes the pink-topped biscuits as a “well-earned tradition” to thank blood donors and restore their blood sugar levels.
But according to volunteers, the gesture is costing it around €1,000 a month in Delft alone, forcing it to put the biscuits behind the counter.
Instead there are now laminated menus in the café telling people they can ask for a biscuit after they have given blood.
Not all Sanquin donation points have withdrawn the biscuits. NOS found they were still on display in Utrecht and at a football club in Utrecht.
A spokesman for Sanquin’s head office said it was up to individual branches to decide, but confirmed that at some locations there were problems with “people taking more than we would reasonably expect.”
A volunteer in The Hague said: “We see people taking more than they should, but if they say they’re taking them home, should we be forbidding that?”

The government is relaunching the competition for the position of head of ARMA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
16:17:47 EET
23:17:47 KST

The government is relaunching the competition for the position of head of ARMA
Kyiv • UNN
Applications to participate in the new competition will be accepted from October 26 to November 26, 2026. The previous selection process ended without a winner.
The Cabinet of Ministers announced a competition for the position of head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets Derived from Corruption and Other Crimes (ARMA). Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, UNN reports.
Details
"We are announcing an open and transparent competition for the position of head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets Derived from Corruption and Other Crimes. The Agency needs a leader trusted by both society and its partners. I invite everyone with management experience, an impeccable reputation and a desire to be useful to their country to participate," Koretskyi wrote.
Background
In June 2025, on Wednesday, 18 June, the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine voted in full for Draft Law No. 12374-d, which provides for reform of the Asset Recovery and Management Agency.
Under the adopted law, the head of ARMA may be:
-  a citizen of Ukraine who has a higher legal or economic education at a level no lower than specialist (master’s); 
-  at least five years of professional experience in the relevant specialty; 
-  at least three years of experience in managerial positions in state authorities, enterprises, institutions or organizations, regardless of their form of ownership; 
-  fluent in the state language and proficient in a foreign language that is one of the official languages of the Council of Europe; 
-  of proven integrity and competent; 
-  capable, based on their professional and moral qualities and educational and professional level, of performing the relevant official duties. 
On 25 September last year, the Cabinet of Ministers formed the Selection Commission that will choose the new head of the National Agency for Finding, Tracing and Management of Assets (ARMA).
Ukrainian and international experts joined the commission. They include:
-  Wolf-Tilmann Baumert - a German prosecutor and specialist in investigating economic crimes; 
-  Serhii But - chairman of the board of JSC "Prozorro.Sale"; 
-  Anzhelika Krusian - academic secretary of the Institute of State and Law of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine; 
-  Valentyna Lukianets-Shakhova - a researcher at the National Academy of Internal Affairs; 
-  Kateryna Ryzhenko - a representative of Transparency International Ukraine, who has monitored ARMA’s activities and promoted legislative changes for many years; 
-  Rita Simoes - a Portuguese prosecutor and expert at the Basel Institute on Governance in the areas of financial crime and asset recovery. 
On 9 December 2025, the announcement was made regarding the submission of documents for the position of head of ARMA; they had to be submitted by 19 January. At that time, 20 candidates applied for the position of head of ARMA.
However, on 19 January this year, the commission selecting the head of ARMA decided to extend the deadline for submitting documents by three weeks for everyone wishing to participate in the competition. The reason was the small number of candidates.
We have already received a number of document packages from candidates, and we would like to discuss the next steps. At least 13 candidates applied. Unfortunately, this is not the number that we, as a commission, would like to see in order to ensure, in our view, the most competitive and professional selection possible. Therefore, at this meeting I would propose discussing whether we, as a commission, are ready to extend the deadline for submitting documents in order to provide more opportunities for everyone interested
The first stage of the competition – testing on knowledge of legislation – took place on 11 March. Fourteen of the 15 applicants passed it. The second stage of the competition - general aptitude testing - took place on 24 March. Only one candidate - Viktor Dubovyk - passed it.
On 16 April, the Selection Commission interviewed Dubovyk at an official meeting.
As a result, Dubovyk received 4 votes from members of the Selection Commission; however, the commission stated that "the candidate cannot be included by the Selection Commission in the proposal to the Cabinet of Ministers for appointment to the position of Head of the National Agency."
The Commission referred to the law under which a decision is considered adopted if it is supported by at least four members of the selection commission, including at least two members of the selection commission appointed by the Cabinet of Ministers based on proposals from development partners.
Dubovyk received only one vote from an international member. It should be noted that Kateryna Ryzhenko and Rita Simoes opposed his candidacy.
They explained their position by citing doubts about the origin of some of Dubovyk’s assets and the candidate’s "superficial answers."
On June 10, the selection commission decided to conduct a repeat selection after all candidates had been eliminated in the previous one.
"I propose putting the following motion to a vote: to conduct a repeat competitive selection for the position of Head of ARMA,"
The relevant decision was supported by all members of the selection commission.
"The Commission understands that we must make every effort to ensure that the next, repeat competition proceeds with candidates from among whom we can propose one or several candidates for appointment,"
On October 19, the selection commission for the position of Head of ARMA held a meeting at which it approved updated procedural documents and officially announced the start of a new competition to select the Head of the Asset Recovery and Management Agency.
Documents may be submitted from October 26 to November 26, 2026 (inclusive).
The selection commission also allowed applicants to submit a certificate of proficiency in the state language throughout the selection process, but no later than three days before the interview.
We would like to remind you
Yaroslava Maksymenko has been appointed acting Head of the National Agency for Asset Recovery and Management.

NATO Brigade in Latvia launches 'most extensive' deployment exercises, Latvian army says
The NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia has launched its most extensive force deployment exercises, the Latvian army said on Oct. 26, as the Baltic states bulk up their defensive capabilities amid growing threats from Russia.
The Resolute Reforger 2026 exercises, scheduled from Oct. 26 to Nov. 2, will involve about 3,000 soldiers and 1,000 units of equipment, moving on roads and railways, according to the Latvian army.
"The aim of the drill is to test the brigade's ability to move, supply, and guide units at long distances in cooperation with the National Armed Forces," the Latvian army said.
The units would clean up the exercise areas and return to their military bases from Nov. 4-8, according to Delfi, an online news portal network.
The training sites would feature soldiers and Canadian CH-146 Griffon military helicopters, according to the Latvian army.
The NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia is a Canadian-led defensive formation that has taken center stage in protecting the alliance's eastern flank, heavily utilizing operational insights and lessons learned from the war in Ukraine.
Security concerns continue to grow in the Baltic region. NATO officials have warned about Russian drone incursions, airspace violations, sabotage, and other hybrid threats, while countries in the region have been strengthening air defenses. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, NATO has reinforced the eastern flank by deploying additional troops and preparing a rapid-response plan.
In an interview with the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 22, Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said that NATO troops already stationed on the alliance's eastern flank would be ready immediately in the event of a Russian incursion.
"If someone plans something, we are not expecting two weeks' debate in Brussels," he said. "We are expecting a very, very swift response from NATO troops that are stationed in Eastern flank countries."

Bulgarian triple jumper Viktoria Angelova, 17, has become the first woman from her country to win the European Athletics Rising Star award, the Bulgarian Athletics Federation announced on Facebook.

Angelova beat two other finalists: Czech hurdler Linda Botkova, the European under-18 champion in the 400 metres hurdles, and Slovenia's Živa Remič, who won the European under-18 and world under-20 titles in the 800 metres this season.

Less than a month later, she won the world under-20 title in Eugene, United States, with a jump of 13.91 metres, claiming gold in an older age group at just 17.
Previous winners of the women's European Athletics Rising Star award include Olympic and world champions Nafissatou Thiam, Yaroslava Mahuchikh, Femke Bol and Jessica Ennis-Hill.

“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:17:12 UTC
23:17:12 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
The European Pariament Prize for Independent Journalism is named after Daphne Caruana Galizia
“Strasbourg Calling” Daphne Caruana Galizia’s son calls for a retrial
Impunity for attacks on journalists in Europe is a worrying sign
Interview with Interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia
Monday 26 October 2026 15:32
Monday, 26 October 2026, 15:32
Matthew Caruana Galizia
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
October brings back two names that Europe must not reduce to mere anniversaries: Anna Politkovskaya, the Russian journalist murdered in Moscow 20 years ago, in October, and Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese investigative journalist killed in Malta nine years ago, also in October.
This year, the European Parliament’s commemoration of Daphne Caruana Galizia has been overshadowed by a new twist in the legal proceedings. On 2 September, a jury acquitted Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech of charges of complicity in her murder and criminal conspiracy. On 22 September, the Attorney General appealed the verdict, while an investigation into possible misconduct by jury members has further undermined confidence in the trial.
What remains of justice when people have been convicted of carrying out the murder itself, but responsibility for commissioning it continues to be contested in court? And what does this case tell us about the protection of journalists in Europe?
Matthew Caruana Galizia is the son of the Maltese investigative journalist and chairs the foundation established in her memory. Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb planted in her car exploded.
“Our top priority at the moment is to fight for a retrial, because there were serious problems with the trial over the summer, particularly with the selection of the jury. So this is the most important issue for us right now. I see no reason why there should not be a retrial,” he told the BNR on the live "Strasbourg Calling" programme from the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He added:
Matthew Caruana Galizia and Irina Nedeva in Radio Studio 3 at the European Parliament on “Strasbourg Calling”, 21 October 2026
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova
“One of the most troubling aspects of our justice system is that jurors are not required to explain why they reached a particular verdict. This means they can base their decisions on corruption or prejudice without facing any consequences.”
According to him, Malta’s institutions remain crippled and unable to provide society with the democracy and freedom it needs.
“It is not enough for the Attorney General simply to bring charges. The justice system itself must deliver fair outcomes,” Matthew Caruana Galizia stressed, adding:
“And if we cannot obtain fair outcomes, then Parliament and the government should step in and amend the legislation so that fair outcomes become possible.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with Matthew Caruana Galizia was aired on the BNR's Horizon channel and can be heard HERE.

US President Donald Trump disparaged Jewish voters who support Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday.
“Any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves,” Trump told some 4,000 supporters in the city north of Detroit, where he stumped for Republican nominee Mike Rogers. “You should never speak to them again.”
Hundreds of Michigan Jews have pledged to vote for El-Sayed, who polls indicate is narrowly leading Rogers in a race key to determining control of the Senate. Another subset of Jews has pressured El-Sayed, a staunch critic of Israel, to defend “Jewish safety - including for Zionist Jews” and “Jewish sovereignty in Israel.” Still others have urged their community members to reject El-Sayed outright and back Rogers.
El-Sayed opposes US military aid to Israel, saying the country has committed genocide in Gaza and is “not an ally.” Those positions divided the Democratic Party during his primary campaign against pro-Israel US Rep. Haley Stevens, whom he narrowly bested in August.
A former public health official, El-Sayed has also emphasized affordable healthcare, housing, and education. He has made a concentrated push to reach undecided Jewish voters in the homestretch before the Nov. 3 midterm election, hiring a Jewish outreach director last week.
Trump previously disparaged Jewish Democrat voters as 'disloyal' to other Jews, Israel
Trump has in the past accused Jews who vote for Democrats of being “disloyal to Jewish people” and “disloyal to Israel.”
At the Port Huron rally, he said he is “polling at 99% in Israel,” which will hold national elections on Tuesday.
Trump did not cite evidence for the claim, and no publicly available surveys support it. While he has historically been popular among Israelis, a June poll by the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) found the Israeli public’s trust in him was declining. The poll said 12% of Israelis reported having a great deal of trust in Trump, down from 21% in May, while the share of Israelis who completely distrust him rose from 32% to 37%.
Trump joined his comments about Jews and Israel with anti-Muslim rhetoric about El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim in the Senate if he is elected.
El-Sayed 'on the side of the terrorists,' Trump says
Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member” who was “on the side of the terrorists,” adding that he would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”
He threatened that “if Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas.”
Trump claimed that El-Sayed’s half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, celebrated the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. On the first anniversary of the attack, Abdelhadi posted a video that said, “no matter how great the brutality, the oppression, the intensity of what we’re going through, the horizon of justice is just around the corner,” according to The New York Times. She did not directly mention or celebrate the violence.
Trump also said that El-Sayed’s mother had “worked for an organization that gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.” A Times investigation reported that El-Sayed’s mother worked as a nurse in Missouri for a Muslim aid group that was later designated by the US government as a supporter of terrorist groups. She was never accused of wrongdoing.
El-Sayed’s campaign has said that he “disagrees” with his sister on “a number of political positions and the rhetoric she’s chosen to use, including on foreign policy.” He was raised by his father and stepmother and has said that he had little relationship with his biological mother while growing up.
Former US president Barack Obama campaigned with El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday, praising his potential partnership with Democratic Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who has endorsed El-Sayed.
“Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa,” said Obama. “You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman, fighting for you in the United States Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of.”

Russia helps Africa become stronger – Nasser’s grandson
Russia is helping African nations strengthen their capabilities through cooperation that benefits both sides, Gamal Abdel Nasser Jr., chairman of the Nasser Foundation for Humanities and Development, has told RT.
Speaking on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Media Forum in Moscow, the grandson of former Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser said Russia’s growing appeal on the continent stems partly from the fact that it never took part in the colonization of the continent.
He contrasted Moscow’s approach with that of former European colonial powers, which he accused of denying African societies access to education and technological progress. “Now Russia is coming today and offering us a kind of situation where they are helping us become stronger,” Nasser Jr. said.
He acknowledged that Moscow has its own strategic interests in expanding cooperation with African countries, but argued that the relationship is beneficial to both parties.
“It’s a win-win situation, kind of. And we are happy with that,” he added.
Nasser Jr. also criticized the legacy of European colonialism, singling out Britain, France, the Netherlands and Belgium for their treatment of African populations.
Turning to Egypt’s membership in BRICS, Nasser Jr. said he had long advocated for Cairo to join the group, viewing it as an opportunity for developing countries to reduce their dependence on Western-dominated financial institutions.
He argued that the World Bank and International Monetary Fund emerged from a post-World War II system in which the US and Britain exercised disproportionate influence. BRICS, by contrast, is giving developing nations a greater role in shaping international economic arrangements, he said.
The foundation chairman also called for greater attention to colonial reparations, arguing that recovering historical artifacts taken from Egypt should be only part of a broader effort to address the consequences of foreign rule.
The remarks came at the four-day Russia-Africa Media Forum, which opened in Moscow on Monday. Organized by RT in cooperation with Sputnik and TASS, the event has brought together more than 200 media professionals and experts from 46 African countries.
The gathering comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum, scheduled for October 28-29 in Moscow.

A short guide to the linguicide of the Ukrainian language | Infographics (updated)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:06:37 UTC
23:06:37 KST

From the 17th to the 20th century, Ukrainian lands were split between empires and states. Their rulers tried to assimilate Ukrainians and block their self-determination by going after what set them apart: their language and culture.
Nobody has an exact count of the bans. Historian Pavlo Hai-Nyzhnyk says there were more than 100 and that the real number is likely higher, because governors issued local bans too.
These measures differed in purpose and reach. Some restricted publishing, schooling, or official use; others suppressed cultural institutions or pushed assimilation. Most served the forced Russification of Ukrainians in the Russian Empire and the USSR. The timeline below is a selection of documented events, not a count of bans.
Russia has not stopped. Since 2014, schooling in Ukrainian has collapsed in the territories it occupies, and in 2025 it removed Ukrainian from the federal school programs it imposes there.
Here are some of the most important restrictions on Ukrainian language and cultural life imposed by the regimes ruling over Ukraine.
17th century
1627: Muscovy. Moscow church authorities condemn Kyrylo Trankvilion-Stavrovetskyi’s Didactic Gospel, a collection of sermons printed in Ukraine in 1619, and order copies burned in Moscow.
1697: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. An act requires tribunal and court decisions in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania to be written in Polish, displacing Ruthenian in those courts.
18th century
1720: Russian Tsardom. Peter I’s decree restricts the Kyiv and Chernihiv presses to approved reprints of church books and requires them to conform to Russian editions, suppressing local textual and linguistic differences.
1728: Russian Empire. Under the Decisive Points (Reshytelni punkty), the legal texts used in the Hetmanate’s courts are to be translated into Russian and compiled into a single code.
1730s: Russian Empire. Under Empress Anna, Kyiv’s archbishop is instructed to replace older locally printed church books with Moscow editions.
1769: Russian Empire. The Holy Synod refuses the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra permission to print primers in the local language and tells it not to submit such requests again.
1775: Russian Empire. A Russian army destroys the Zaporozhian Sich, the Cossacks’ last stronghold and one of Ukraine’s own political institutions.
1780s: Russian Empire. Samuil Myslavskyi, metropolitan of Kyiv from 1783, insists on literary Russian as the only language of instruction at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.
1789: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Commission of National Education orders the Ukrainian parish schools of Right-Bank Ukraine Polonized.
19th century
1847: Russian Empire. After suppressing the Cyril and Methodius Brotherhood, a secret society that called for a federation of free Slavic peoples, the authorities ban and withdraw from sale specified works by Taras Shevchenko, Panteleimon Kulish, and Mykola Kostomarov.
1859: Austrian Empire. Austrian officials back a plan to replace the Cyrillic alphabet used for Ukrainian in Galicia with a Latin one. Ukrainian opposition defeats the plan in what became known as the “alphabet war.”
1862: Russian Empire. The authorities close the Sunday schools, free schools for working adults and young people, including Ukrainian ones. They begin reopening under tighter control in 1864.
1863: Russian Empire. Interior Minister Pyotr Valuev’s circular tells censors not to approve Ukrainian religious, school, and popular-reading books, while still allowing fiction under censorship. It claims that most Little Russians themselves argue that “there was not, is not, and cannot be any special Little Russian language.”
1864: Russian Empire. The 1864 statute requires Russian as the teaching language in the elementary schools it regulates.
1869: Austria-Hungary. Polish becomes the internal language of administration and the courts in Galicia. The 1867 school arrangements had already strengthened Polish dominance, while leaving limited room for Ukrainian-language schooling.
1876: Russian Empire. Alexander II’s secret Ems Ukaz severely restricts Ukrainian publishing and bans Ukrainian publications from abroad, Ukrainian stage performances and public readings, and Ukrainian lyrics printed with music. Exceptions allow historical documents in their original spelling and fiction in Russian spelling under censorship.
1881: Russian Empire. New rules ease parts of the Ems Ukaz: Ukrainian plays may be staged with a governor’s special permission. Theater troupes performing only in Ukrainian stay banned.
1883: Russian Empire. Kyiv Governor-General Aleksandr Drenteln bars Ukrainian theater troupes from performing in the Kyiv, Podillia, Volhynia, Poltava, and Chernihiv governorates.
1895: Russian Empire. The censorship authorities ban the publication of Ukrainian children’s books.
20th century
1910: Russian Empire. A circular from Pyotr Stolypin’s interior ministry tells governors to refuse registration to non-Russian national societies, Ukrainian ones included, and to review existing ones for closure. Kyiv’s Prosvita is dissolved the same year.
1914: Russian Empire. The authorities ban public celebrations of Taras Shevchenko’s centenary. After the empire enters World War I, they close most Ukrainian periodicals, including the Kyiv daily Rada.
1914–15, 1916–17: Russian Empire. Russian occupation authorities suppress Ukrainian institutions and publications in Galicia and Bukovyna. The first occupation brings mass arrests and deportations, the destruction of Ukrainian books, and the arrest of Metropolitan Andrei Sheptytskyi.
1923: Soviet Ukraine. Dmytro Lebid, second secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, sets out the “theory of the struggle of two cultures,” which holds that the Russian culture of the city is more advanced than the Ukrainian culture of the village. The party rejects it and adopts Ukrainization the same year.
1924: Poland. Three laws of 31 July make Polish the state language of administration and the courts, keep limited rights for minority languages, and set school rules that favor Polish-Ukrainian bilingual schools over separate Ukrainian ones.
1924: Romania. The primary education law requires citizens of Romanian origin who have “lost their mother tongue” to send their children to Romanian schools. Ukrainian historians say it was applied to Ukrainians in Bukovyna.
1925: Poland. The Lviv Underground Ukrainian University, which had taught clandestinely since 1921, stops teaching after police raids and the Polish state’s refusal to recognize it.
1926: USSR. In a letter to Kaganovich and the Ukrainian Politburo, Stalin attacks Oleksandr Shumskyi and Mykola Khvylovyi and rejects Ukrainizing Russian workers “from above,” while still backing controlled Ukrainization of official institutions.
1932–33: USSR. A secret resolution of 14 December 1932 orders the Ukrainian-language paperwork and press of the North Caucasus switched to Russian at once and its schools prepared for teaching in Russian. In Soviet Ukraine, it puts Ukrainization under tighter party control and demands purges of “nationalist” elements. The repression of 1933 dismantles Ukrainization.
1938: USSR. A decree of 13 March makes Russian a compulsory subject in the non-Russian schools of the national republics and regions.
1947: Poland. In Operation Vistula, Polish authorities forcibly resettle about 150,000 Ukrainians to northern and western Poland, under an assimilation policy that sought to keep them below 10% of any locality.
1958–59: USSR. The school reform expands parents’ choice of teaching language and makes the study of Ukrainian optional in Russian-language schools in Soviet Ukraine.
1960s–70s: Romania and Poland. Romania nearly eliminates Ukrainian-language schooling from the mid-1960s. In Poland, Ukrainian schools and Ukrainian classes shrink.
1972: USSR. The party’s resolution on the USSR’s 50th anniversary promotes the “new historical community, the Soviet people,” an idea first voiced in 1961. Soviet ethnographers wrote that the spread of Russian among non-Russian peoples played the paramount role in forming this community.
1978: USSR. The USSR Council of Ministers orders wider study of Russian in the union republics. Ukraine’s implementing resolution of 2 November requires Russian from first grade in Ukrainian-language schools from the 1980/81 school year.
1983: USSR. A resolution of 26 May gives specified teachers of Russian in non-Russian schools in villages and small towns a 15% pay raise from 1984.
1984: USSR. The school reform resolution of 12 April adds two to three hours of Russian a week in grades 2 to 11 of non-Russian schools.
1989: USSR. The Communist Party’s party platform of 20 September calls for making Russian, by law, the language of the whole country alongside the republics’ state languages.
1990: USSR. The April 1990 law on the languages of the peoples of the USSR makes Russian the official language of the Soviet Union, while letting the republics set their own state languages.
21st century
2014–18: Crimea. Under Russian occupation, schooling in Ukrainian collapses. In 2013/14, 12,694 children studied in Ukrainian in 7 schools and 829 classes; by 2017/18, 318 children did, in one school and 13 classes, the UN human rights office reports, noting the figures conflict in places.
2020: DNR and LNR. The so-called DNR votes to amend its “constitution” on 6 March, dropping Ukrainian as a “state language” and leaving only Russian. The so-called LNR does the same in June.
2022: Occupied Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. Russia’s Education Ministry says on 12 August that schools in newly occupied areas will teach in Russian, with Ukrainian allowed only as an optional “native” language. Occupation authorities then cap Ukrainian at three hours a week, Human Rights Watch reports.
2023: Occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts. Russia removes nearly all Ukrainian literature from local libraries, most likely destroying it, Ukraine’s National Resistance Center reports. The so-called LNR publishes a list of banned books.
2024: International Court of Justice. On 31 January, the court ruled, 13 votes to 2, that Russia violated the UN convention against racial discrimination in how it ran school education in Ukrainian in occupied Crimea.
2025: Russia. Education Ministry Order No. 729, in force since 15 December, removes Ukrainian language and literature from Russia’s federal primary and lower-secondary programs, the UN human rights office reports. Russia imposes these programs on schools in the occupied territories, where about 582,000 children study, the Almenda center says.
What we changed in October 2026
Editor’s note, 27 October 2026: We first published this timeline in 2017. Like many lists of bans on Ukrainian that circulate online, it repeated some claims that have no document behind them. In October 2026, we went back to historians’ work and to the decrees themselves.
We removed about fifteen entries. Most we could not confirm; a few were not about language. We corrected others where the documents say something different: some bans had exceptions, some dates were off by a year, and the end of Ukrainization came in 1932–33. We replaced the old count of 60 bans, which we could not trace, with a historian’s estimate. And we added what Russia has done to the Ukrainian language in the territories it has occupied since 2014.
If you have a document for something we left out, write to us.

- Russia banned the scholars documenting Stalin’s starvation of Ukraine. They put their course out anyway—as Moscow repeats the famine.
- Zelenskyy: In Kyiv, where Lenin fell, Mazepa will stand—a Cossack hetman Russia still curses

Lizard's secret of defense preserved in 100-million-year-old amber
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
14:05:13 UTC
23:05:13 KST

Almost 100 million years ago, a lizard in what is now Myanmar was in mortal danger.
We know this because the presumably terrified reptile did exactly what lizards do today in similar situations: It "voluntarily" shed its tail and the rest of it scuttled off.
The tail would have remained on the ground wriggling madly, which the lizard would have hoped would distract the hunter. How this scenario panned out and whether the lizard survived, we do not know.
But we do know that the tail did exactly what it shouldn't have: It survived – the decay process at least – and became embedded in tree resin. Over millions of years, the resin fossilized into amber and now, according to researchers at Tel Aviv University, we have the earliest known proof of the reptilian defensive mechanism known as autotomy – voluntarily shedding one's tail.
Theoretically it's possible that the lizard wasn't being hunted but some creature stepped on its tail, which it promptly shed. But close analysis of the tissue shows the hallmarks of voluntary discard, which is important, because it's no great defensive trick for the tail to simply get stomped.
The wonder is that now we know that the real defensive trick existed in lizards at least 100 million years ago, explain doctoral candidate Dolev Fabrikant and his supervisor, Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou, of Tel Aviv University's School of Zoology and its Steinhardt Museum of Natural History. They worked in collaboration with researchers from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and Israel's Volcani Institute, publishing in Palaeontologia Electronica.
Until now, we could only speculate that ancient lizards living with dinosaurs had this defensive ability, Davranoglou notes. Now we know they did because the paleontological team observed a clean ring of tissue resembling the structure seen in tails shed by living lizards – absent trauma damage.
In fact, the small piece of cloudy amber had been found years ago but only now did Fabrikant examine it, using micro-CT scanning, and realize that what looked like a twig or insect fragment was covered in scales.
"Micro-CT… allowed us to examine structures hidden by the amber without needing to cut this one-of-a-kind piece open," says Ahmed Nasser, head of the Volcani Institute's Inter-Institutional Analytical Unit.
Which lizard it was, we do not know because this amber contained only its tail, not its head. Could have been almost anything.
"Possible affinities include the groups containing today's wall lizards or, alternatively, slow worms and monitor lizards," says Apostolos Christopoulos, a student at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
Note that snakes aren't lizards, they're snakes, and almost none in travail shed tail. They can't regenerate it. But likely, the ability goes back an insanely long way – tuataras can defensively shed their tail, and they split from other reptiles a quarter billion years ago, in the Jurassic.
There is one other option beside being stepped on or attacked. The lizard may have been climbing a seeping tree, its tail got stuck in the sticky resin and it shed it and moved on. If that's so, the little reptile may have regrown its tail. That's a nice thought.

The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
15:57:55 EET
22:57:55 KST

The European Business Association records an increase in companies’ preparatory work for employing veterans
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian businesses are gradually developing practices for employing and adapting veterans — from preparing teams and retraining to creating specialized positions.
Ukrainian companies are gradually developing practices for employing and reintegrating veterans. Businesses are training teams to interact with colleagues who have combat experience, creating adaptation and retraining programs, while some companies are introducing dedicated positions to support veterans. At the same time, it is still too early to speak of mass employment. Tetiana Karelska, head of the HR and CSR division of the European Business Association, said this in a comment to UNN.
We are observing a moderate increase in engagement. We have not measured separate, precise statistics that would representatively demonstrate the dynamics of veterans’ employment in recent years—and objectively, such statistics do not currently exist because of the dynamics of the hostilities. However, we are tracking an increase in preparatory work within companies
According to her, among the Association’s member companies there are both businesses that already have systematic practices for engaging and adapting veterans and those that are only beginning to develop their own programs.
Tetiana Karelska noted that the Association is recording growing demand for team training, including specialized training—from basic communication etiquette and psychological literacy to the specifics of interacting with people who have combat experience, injuries, or experience of captivity. In addition, the EBA is recording positive dynamics in the creation of internal adaptation and retraining pathways.
Introducing a veterans’ affairs officer position—companies that have the necessary resources are creating dedicated positions (veterans’ affairs officer/CVO) responsible directly for veterans’ reintegration. On our side, we have a vision for creating a specialized training program for such professionals
Adapting workplaces and teams
Veterans’ adaptation involves both arranging a physical workplace in accordance with the employee’s individual needs and preparing the team for their return.
The first aspect—adapting the physical workplace—is always about additional funding. Not every employer is able to independently arrange a workplace according to the individual needs of an employee with a disability. The state provides substantial assistance here, in particular through compensation programs, but this sometimes remains a complicated process that requires time and knowledge
At the same time, team adaptation and psychological support depend on the company’s willingness to invest in employee training, engage external specialists, or develop its own educational programs. According to the EBA’s assessment, this does not always require substantial budgets, since free training programs developed as far back as 2014 are available publicly.
What obstacles remain
One of the key challenges for employers is the so-called "military-to-civilian translation."
Recruiters and HR professionals still find it difficult to properly assess candidates’ military experience and match it with civilian vacancies. This requires systematic cooperation with support services and directly with veterans
Other obstacles include insufficient staff preparedness, a lack of communication and management skills, as well as stereotypes about people with combat experience, experience of captivity, or disabilities.
We continue to work on stereotypes concerning interaction with people who have combat experience, experience of captivity, or a disability. This is a lengthy process, and it is not solely the responsibility of the employer or a matter of training within the company. It is a global task for the state and society to develop a culture of respect and gratitude toward every citizen, regardless of their experience
As noted by the EBA, more effective integration of veterans requires companies to have not only their own programs, but also coordinated state policy and access to the necessary support tools.
Businesses are currently creating numerous initiatives and programs at their own expense. The main expectation businesses have of the state is synergy instead of duplication, along with a reduction in the number of fragmented working groups. Instead, there is a demand for the creation of a single specialized structure (or coordination center) that would bring together all process participants and provide convenient access to analytics, methodological materials, grant programs, and state compensation in one place, so that employers would not have to collect information separately
Let us remind you
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine is also working to support veterans. According to the words of FPU Chairman Serhii Byzov, the Federation’s sanatoriums provide medical rehabilitation services to military personnel, while the organization itself, together with specialized ministries and the National Health Service of Ukraine, is developing programs to support, socially adapt, and employ veterans. According to the FPU, more than 32,800 military personnel have undergone medical rehabilitation at its sanatoriums.

A Movement’s Promise: The Making of Contemporary Palestinian Theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

When Palestinian negotiators returned from the Madrid peace talks in the early 1990s, they briefed the press at a theatre in East Jerusalem. It seems an odd setting for news of talks that held the world’s attention, until you discover the role theatre had played in Palestinian life since the Nakba.
A burned-out cinema until 1984, the Palestinian National Theatre was where the negotiator Hanan Ashrawi and the Jerusalem leader Faisal Al-Husseini accused Israel of ignoring its commitments. It also hosted a festival for local schools and a literary festival marking twenty years since Ghassan Kanafani’s assassination. In Al-Saber’s words, the theatre “stepped into the role of an acting ministry of culture”.
That a theatre could take on such a role says a great deal about what it had come to mean for Palestinians. The mass displacement of 1948 scattered the artists, troupes and audiences of pre-war Palestine. In the years that followed, Palestinian culture survived inside Israel under military rule, which lasted until 1966, and in the West Bank under Jordanian rule.
After the 1967 war and Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza, a generation of young people in Jerusalem and Ramallah turned to the stage.
Writing from exile in Lebanon, the Jerusalem writer Mahmoud Shqair observed that the theatre movement “became the most conspicuous artistic phenomenon on our occupied land. None of the other arts matched it in drawing and influencing the audiences.”
Al-Saber explains why. Under an occupation that restricted Palestinian assembly, attending a play was a social activity and a political act at once. In his words, theatre had become “a site for free thought and a battleground that did not require forbidden arms”.
Read: Theatre community slams Israel lobby attack on touring Palestinian play
A Movement’s Promise tells how that movement, known to its members as Al-Haraka Al-Masrahiyya (the theatre movement), came into being and grew into the theatre industry Palestinians have today.
Al-Saber assembled this history from scattered records and the recollections of the people who made it. “Due to the absence of a Palestinian state,” he writes, “Palestinian theater history has not been collected into a centralized archive.” During fieldwork between 2009 and 2023, he interviewed theatre artists and gathered material from their personal collections: reviews and interviews cut from period newspapers, posters, photographs, brochures and actors’ copies of scripts.
Further material came from the archive of El-Hakawati (The Storyteller), the Jerusalem company founded in 1977 whose theatre later became the Palestinian National Theatre, and from the papers of its founder, François Abu Salem. Records of the Israeli censorship board, held in the Israel State Archive, show how companies dealt with the censors.
El-Hakawati’s satire Mahjoub Mahjoub (1980), about a hapless Palestinian everyman under occupation, shows how artists slipped their plays past Israeli censors, and how censorship backfired.
To obtain a performance permit, El-Hakawati’s co-founder Jackie Lubeck sent the censors an English summary that made the play sound harmless. In one scene, Mahjoub is interrogated for wearing clothes in the colours of the Palestinian flag, which was then illegal. In Lubeck’s summary, this became simply: “Mahjoub is questioned about the outfit he wears to work one day.” The censors saw nothing political, and the play was approved in December 1980.
The following month, the authorities stopped a performance in Nazareth, claiming El-Hakawati had departed from the approved text. The audience turned the evening into a protest, and the actors improvised a new scene, sitting on stage tied to their chairs with their mouths taped. The novelist Emile Habibi condemned the ban, and the play went on to tour Europe.
Episodes like this lead Al-Saber to argue that Israel “inadvertently and unknowingly promoted Palestinian theater” through its efforts to suppress it. Censorship taught artists to say things indirectly, and every ban or arrest only drew more attention to their work.
Al-Saber concentrates on East Jerusalem and its close ties with Ramallah, from 1967 to the Oslo Accords. The two cities worked as a single cultural centre, linked by family, social and professional bonds, and most of the pioneering artists lived and worked in one or both.
Al-Saber wants readers to understand Palestinian theatre through the people who made it. Occupation shaped their working lives, but so did artistic ambition, friendships, rivalries and the effort to build an audience. As he explains, accounts centred on the “conflict” too often leave Palestine’s story existing only in relation to Israel. His approach stresses “the right of Palestinian theater makers to exist on their own merits, without being subsumed by crisis narratives or orientalist motifs”.
Balalin (The Balloons), the first independent Palestinian theatre company formed in the West Bank after the 1967 occupation, showed how theatre could rally an audience without saying a single forbidden word. In its best-known production, Al-‘atma (The Darkness, 1972), a young troupe sets out to perform a play, but the lights fail and the actors ask the audience to help repair them.
Many spectators believed the blackout was real, and electricians sometimes climbed onto the stage to offer help. As Al-Saber explains, “the struggle to end the darkness and perform the play represents the Palestinian struggle to fix its internal conflicts and end the occupation.” When the eager carpenter Adel dies at the lighting board, the cast carries him out on their shoulders as Palestinians carry their martyrs. “It was truly a call for an uprising, but using symbols,” recalls Emile Ashrawi, a founding member of the company.
Obliterated: Theatregoers’ dreams of seeing Palestinian play in London
Fifteen years later, El-Hakawati turned to the memory of the Nakba. By then it had become, in Al-Saber’s words, “a de facto representative of the Palestinian theater” in the international media. The Story of Kufur Shamma (1987) follows Walid, a young man who returns from studying abroad to find his village deserted. Kufur Shamma is fictional, but it stands in for the hundreds of Palestinian villages destroyed in 1948. With the village fool, Walid sets out to bring its scattered people home, tracking them across the diaspora, only to return and find the village erased.
Telling the story of 1948 met resistance well beyond the occupied territories. At a festival in Acre in 1987, a mixed Palestinian and Jewish city inside Israel, supporters of the Jewish extremist group Kahane Chai stood up in the front row, raised an Israeli flag and chanted “Death to Arabs”.
Two years later, Joseph Papp, one of America’s leading theatre producers, cancelled the play’s booking at New York’s Public Theater for fear of offending his audience, many of them Jewish and, in his words, “very sympathetic to Israel”. Each time, El-Hakawati performed anyway: the actors in Acre returned to the stage to applause, and weeks after Papp’s decision the play opened at another New York theatre to warm reviews.
The movement’s divisions run through the book as strongly as its achievements. Factional loyalties split ensembles, and the row over who controlled El-Hakawati’s theatre ended with its founders leaving the building they had rebuilt. Yet Al-Saber sees this constant breaking and re-forming as the movement’s strength: a “self-sacrificial” process that kept making way for new companies and artists.
After Oslo came new pressures. Foreign donor money professionalised the theatres but turned a collective movement into separate organisations competing for grants. At the same time, the Separation Wall, military checkpoints and expanding settlements cut East Jerusalem off from the West Bank.
Within a few years, most West Bank Palestinians could no longer enter Jerusalem without a permit. The Palestinian National Theatre lost its largest audience, and Jerusalem was separated from Ramallah, the city whose family, artistic and professional ties had given birth to the movement. Theatre-makers now had to tour to audiences trapped in their own cities, and artists with West Bank identity cards could rarely work across the new lines.
Al-Saber closes by asking whether the movement still exists. He believes it does, carried in the stories that two generations of theatre-makers still tell one another. “Even during war, genocide, and uncertainty,” he writes, “the movement is alive in its lore and lineage, promising and delivering a richly diverse theater industry.” If at times it seems dormant, “its history has shown that it may simply be under the radar”.

Von der Leyen’s big Commission shake-up moves a step closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:56:29 UTC
22:56:29 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives a press conference at the end of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ursula von der Leyen’s push for a sweeping overhaul of the European Commission moved closer to fruition on Monday, as a group of external advisers handed over a report that will help shape the institution’s biggest administrative shake-up in two decades.
The report, drawn up by a high-level group led by former Commission Secretary-General Catherine Day, marks a new stage in the so-called large-scale review — an exercise intended to make the Commission more efficient, streamline its sprawling bureaucracy and turn it into a more attractive employer.
“Now we’re reaching the second phase,” von der Leyen said at the handover, referring to the conclusion of an initial phase that involved 15 internal workstreams and contributions from thousands of Commission staff.
Advertisement
“We need to be able to act effectively and to act quickly,” she said about the needed changes in the EU Executive’s machinery. “That means simpler procedures, clearer structures, better cooperation across departments so that our colleagues can focus their efforts where it makes the greatest difference.”
The external group, consisting of Day and eight other experts with experience in national administrations and international organizations including the OECD and OSCE, put forward nine interrelated recommendations aimed at making the Commission more agile and better equipped to adapt to future challenges.
Among its main proposals is a shift away from working in siloed departments toward greater collaboration across directorates-general, including through cross-DG portfolios.
This part of the exercise is politically sensitive. Behind the push to modernize the Commission lies the prospect of a far-reaching reorganization of its departments, potentially redrawing the responsibilities of powerful directorates-general that oversee billions of euros in EU spending.
As POLITICO first reported, several major Commission departments face an uncertain future under plans to overhaul how the bloc manages and distributes EU funds, raising the prospect of mergers or other structural changes.
Among the departments potentially affected is the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO), which oversees cohesion policy funding, accounting for almost a third of EU spending. Other departments facing uncertainty include the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI), responsible for Common Agricultural Policy money; DG EMPL, which oversees employment and social funding; DG MARE, which handles fisheries funding; and DG RTD, responsible for research and innovation.
Advertisement
The group also called for a stronger Secretariat-General to act as a strategic center driving results, and for a human-centered approach to artificial intelligence to simplify administrative processes and modernize the institution’s operations.
But the release of the report on Monday does not mean that any restructuring decisions have been taken. Day’s report will feed into a wider review overseen by Budget and Public Administration Commissioner Piotr Serafin, who is tasked with presenting final recommendations to von der Leyen by the end of 2026.
Catherine Day, Chair of the High-Level Group on the Future of the Commission’s Civil Service gives a press statement in Brussels on October 26, 2026. | Dati Bendo/European Commission Audiovisual Service
Serafin said at the handover that the external assessment, combined with feedback from Commission staff, provided a “mandate to go for far reaching changes.”
Day, for her part, said the Commission had already demonstrated a willingness to reform, pointing to the wealth of ideas emerging from within the institution.
“The work done on the large scale review has shown that there is a broad coalition for change right across the Commission,” she added.
A separate internal process produced an initial set of recommendations in July, drawn up by Commission officials. Those proposals were intended to kick-start a broader discussion within the institution rather than serve as final decisions.
Advertisement
Any major reshuffling of the Commission’s structure, however, is likely to take considerably longer.
Speaking in July to a small group of journalists, including POLITICO, Serafin acknowledged that structural reforms would be closely tied to negotiations on the EU’s next long-term budget, known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, which will determine how EU spending is organized from 2028 to 2034.
He indicated at the time that he did not expect decisions on major structural changes before those budget negotiations are concluded.
For now, Day’s findings will provide another input into Serafin’s final proposals, bringing von der Leyen one step closer to deciding how far she wants to go in reshaping the institution she leads.

Geneva to offer free home delivery of groceries to elderly
Following a trial phase, the Swiss city of Geneva is making its free home grocery delivery service a permanent feature for people aged 65 and over. This service will now also be available to recipients of a care allowance.
These people can enjoy free delivery of their shopping once a week. Launched in the summer of 2025, the pilot scheme for free home delivery of groceries has been a resounding success, with an average of 260 deliveries made each month, the Department for Social Cohesion and Solidarity (DCSS) said on Monday.
The beneficiaries, currently numbering 300, have an average age of 79.
Building on this positive outcome, the DCSS has decided to make this initiative a permanent service, whilst expanding the group of beneficiaries. The aim remains the same: to promote independence, mobility and social connections, while making everyday shopping easier.

How the internet is reshaping global postal services
Deliveries are made by electric bicycle by the Genèveroule association. Purchases can be made at all food markets as well as in all Migros supermarkets located in the city. Deliveries are available from Monday to Saturday, limited to two bags weighing a maximum of 20 kilos.

With Regional Tensions High, Mecca Alliance Partners Meet In Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:43:05 UTC
22:43:05 KST

Iran and three members of a regional mutual-defense pact have agreed to continue talks after their first meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported.
Iranian officials met with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey, the signatories to the Mecca Defense Alliance on October 26, to defuse tensions in the region.
The sides “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation...including on regional peace and security,” state television said.
The meeting came as the US-Iran war and increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have left the region reeling and are impacting global flows of oil and other cargo.
'Last-Ditch Effort'
Ahead of the meeting, a senior security official in Islamabad told RFE/RL that one of the main points of the meeting was to try to convince Iran to use its influence over Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia. The official said the alliance countries were prepared to raise the prospect of closer Saudi-Israeli security cooperation as leverage.
“The key question is why Iran should comply? The answer is that Saudi Arabia may ask for support from Israel and that will potentially require them to join the Abraham Accords,” said the official.
The accords, signed in 2020, normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
“Since Turkey has already diplomatic relations with Israel, the trio might place this scenario on the table should Tehran refuse to rein in the Houthis,” said the official. While Iran may comply by using its influence over the Houthis, the official added that it is unlikely that the regime would soften its stance on negotiations with the United States over the war.
Islamabad-based analyst Azaz Syed said the US-Iran conflict would be just as important during the meeting amid fears Washington is preparing to renew its military attacks on Iran.
Pakistan's powerful army chief, Asim Munir, was in Tehran last week where he reportedly delivered a "last warning" to the Iranian government.
“Apparently, this was a last-ditch effort to convince the Iranians” to come to a negotiated settlement with the United States, Syed told RFE/RL.
“The three partners will ask for an end to Houthi attacks, of course, but the key message is the broader settlement.”
Hamidreza Azizi, senior analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, said that the meeting in Tehran was a last-minute attempt to prevent another escalation.
“The immediate priority seems to be finding a way to prevent the resumption of war between Iran and the United States,” Azizi told RFERL.
Azizi said the October 26 meeting was essentially a continuation of diplomatic efforts already under way, and the timing suggests that regional countries are increasingly concerned that these efforts may be running out of time.
The Houthis, allies of Tehran who primarily operate from Yemen, have intensified their missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil infrastructure at a time when energy transit in the Middle East has already been curtailed by the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that normally sees around one-fifth of the world's oil and gas flows transported through it.
Earlier this month, Houthi rebels attacked Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, killing 13 people and wounding more than 300. The rebels have also warned airlines against using Saudi airspace.
Saudi Arabia has in turn launched strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen.
The conflicts have shed light on the complex diplomatic relations between nations across the Middle and Near East.
The Mecca Alliance enshrines a collective security arrangement modeled on NATO's Article 5, stating that "any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all."
Iran-Pakistan Tensions
The meeting also came amid already heightened tensions between Iran and Pakistan after Islamabad closed two border crossings between its Balochistan Province and Iran’s Sistan-Baluchistan Province.
Pakistan has also introduced changes in its E-form procedure, a digital declaration authorizing the tracking of foreign currency remittances, for Iranian exports coming into the country.
Sources say Islamabad has also suspended operating clearance for Mahan Air, the Iranian airline believed to have links with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). Iranian and Pakistani authorities have neither admitted nor denied the reports.
The Iranian side, in reaction, stopped the export of Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) to Pakistan causing manifold increase in gas prices for domestic and commercial consumers. Pakistan imports around 7,000 metric tons of LPG every day from Iran.
"The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal," said Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly in a social media post.
Commenting on the closure of Iran-Pakistan border crossings, Tehran envoy to Islamabad Reza Amiri Moghadam said in a social media post that consultations with the Pakistani side are under way to address the issue of cross-border trade.
Moghadam said several hundred trucks carrying LPG have crossed the Rimdan border into Gabd on the Pakistani side. However, despite having remained there for several weeks, these trucks have yet to be unloaded or cleared up, further complicating the movement of goods and the smooth flow of bilateral trade.
Significant Step
Rabia Akhtar, a professor of international relations at the University of Lahore, said the immediate concern among the three partners was to prevent the current confrontation from escalating further.
“Nobody at that table really benefits from another regional war,” Akhtar told RFE/RL, who added that if the participants can establish some understanding on restraint -- particularly regarding Saudi security, the Houthis, and further escalation with Iran -- that would already be a meaningful outcome.
“So I would see this as an attempt at regional crisis management rather than the birth of a new security architecture. And in the present circumstances, even that would be quite consequential,” Akhtar said.
Azizi of the International Crisis Group said the meeting could help reduce tensions, at least temporarily, by keeping channels of communication open.
“But the main problem remains unresolved: Iran wants credible security guarantees against renewed attacks, while the regional mediators have limited ability to influence Washington's decisions.”

The data center in Sasovo housed two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which are used to train neural networks. The most powerful of the two, Chervonenkis, ranked 19th among the world’s top 500 supercomputers in 2021, according to the independent science-focused outlet T-invariant.

Minister: Defense plan decisions must be reviewed, light fighter jets eyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

Minister: Defense plan decisions must be reviewed, light fighter jets eyed
Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) told ERR that Estonia's 10-year defense development plan needs improvements in air and maritime defense.
This includes weighing up the procurement of light fighter jets for the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF).
The latest status of the national defense development plan was that it had reached the Government Office for approval, but you nonetheless found some changes needed to be made. Is that right?
As far as I know, the 10-year national defense development plan was issued by the Ministry of Defense back in the spring, if not early spring. And during that time, there have indeed been some changes in air defense, which had already begun to emerge in the war in Ukraine last year; the picture is now likely clearer, and for that reason alone. This is not a question of my having reviewed anything, but rather the Defense Forces as a whole have become better informed, and some things have also developed further based on the example of the war in Ukraine. So these changes stem from that.
The latest status of the national defense development plan was that it had reached the Government Office for approval, but you nonetheless found some changes needed to be made. Is that right? As I understand it, the plan was in fairly final form at the Government Office, awaiting approval alongside the state budget strategy (RES), and upon becoming minister, drawing on the commander's advice, you reopened it and saw things needed to be added and changed?
As far as I know, the 10-year national defense development plan was issued by the Ministry of Defense back in the spring, if not early spring. And during that time, there have indeed been some changes in air defense, which had already begun to emerge in the war in Ukraine last year; the picture is now likely clearer, and for that reason alone. This is not a question of my having reviewed anything, but rather the Defense Forces as a whole have become better informed, and some things have also developed further based on the example of the war in Ukraine. So these changes stem from that.
So, keeping the shipping lanes in the Gulf of Finland open and procuring additional air defense capabilities – most recently, you spoke about the need to acquire light fighter jets. Is that right?
For us this is not just the shipping lanes in the Gulf of Finland, but the sea routes toward the west as a whole. The Gulf of Finland is actually a secondary issue in that respect. But without these maritime connections, we would certainly die out very quickly – 80 percent of our trade currently takes place by sea, and the same is true for the Finns. So we must look at this as a whole together with our allies, to ensure that these connections remain under our control at all times.
Now, as for air defense and air-to-air defense, meaning those same jet aircraft, what Russia has come up with over the past year is essentially cheap cruise missiles, or jet-powered drones. And one of the most effective means currently in use against them is aircraft, jet aircraft. Whether we take the route of acquiring light jets such as the Hawk, L-39 or something similar, or instead look toward unmanned jets, is another matter. But I do think we should consider how to bring our air-to-air defense capability into play, so to speak. However, resources are limited, and we have to consider what we would have to sacrifice to do all of this.
In your assessment, is acquiring light fighter jets a genuinely realistic prospect at present? Are you proposing that this be added to the national defense development plan and that the necessary funding be found?
I think that this is realistic. But it is not only realistic, it may also be needed. How else are we to counter such threats? However, to do that, we will first need to review the broader air defense picture. What do we want to develop there, what do we have, and how would these aircraft, however many there might be, fit into it? It also depends on the circumstances: imagine that we are in a full-scale war. What airfields or runways would we be able to use for this? Maybe at some point we would no longer have them, so then the question arises of where the aircraft would take off from, or whether we would have to use something else, some other locations. And finally, how many of these aircraft should there be, at what point would we use them, and where would they operate? All of this is not yet entirely clear to me.
When did the commander of the Defense Forces provide his additional input on the national defense development plan?
I think it was a few weeks ago. I cannot say exactly right now. But it was during my time as minister, meaning within the past month. And it was sent to the minister of defense, not the Government Office.
And what did he recommend? Is that a matter between the two of you, or can you make it public?
That is actually where the issue of jets comes from, at least in part. But it also touched on other matters.
And now, as I understand it, you are due to give a presentation on this to the National Defense Council, which reports to the president?
Yes, I will be discussing these issues at the National Defense Council. Not in the form of proposals yet, but I will raise the issues we are working on. That said, I am not ready to present concrete proposals.
When might those concrete proposals be ready?
I really cannot say right now, but sometime this year.

The value of the new naval agreement was not disclosed in the ministry's statement, although Calcalist previously reported that the proposed package was worth approximately $100 million.
