Why do people with psychopathic traits enjoy fear? New psychology research offers a clue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

People with elevated psychopathic traits tend to find frightening scenes less distressing and more exciting than other people do, according to a new study published in Psychological Reports. The findings suggest that a heightened belief in one’s own invincibility helps explain why these individuals feel less afraid when watching scary footage, while a tendency to become easily bored does not appear to explain why they find it enjoyable.
Psychopathy is a personality profile characterized by two distinct sets of traits. The first dimension involves interpersonal and emotional features, such as superficial charm, manipulation, and a lack of empathy or guilt. The second dimension encompasses an impulsive lifestyle, sensation-seeking, and antisocial behavior. Early psychological theories proposed that individuals high in these traits take reckless risks simply because they have a fundamental deficit in the ability to feel fear.
More recent work has challenged the notion that psychopathic individuals are completely incapable of experiencing fear. While these individuals often show muted physical reactions to threat, a 2016 meta-analysis found little evidence that they lack the conscious, subjective feeling of fear. Psychological theories of emotion note that fear and excitement share nearly identical physical symptoms, such as a racing heart, meaning that how a person experiences a high-stakes moment depends heavily on how their mind interprets that physical arousal.
Building on this distinction, members of the team behind the new study developed the Fear Enjoyment Hypothesis, which proposes that people with psychopathic traits actually interpret frightening situations as pleasurable. Experiencing fear as enjoyable requires two simultaneous reactions: a dampened negative response, such as feeling less panicked, and a heightened positive response, such as feeling exhilarated.
In a 2020 experimental study by the same group, participants with higher psychopathy scores watched scary video game footage and reported fewer negative emotions and stronger positive emotions than their peers, and a 2026 study covered by PsyPost found that individuals higher in psychopathic traits interpret an elevated heart rate during scary moments as pleasurable excitement rather than distress.
What remains uncertain is why people with psychopathic traits evaluate threatening situations so positively. One possibility draws on horror filmmaker Alfred Hitchcock’s observation that audiences can enjoy suspense when they feel safe from actual threat. Psychopathic individuals may possess a strong sense of invincibility, defined as the belief that one is immune to danger and personal harm, which could make frightening scenarios feel safe enough to enjoy, much like riding a roller coaster.
Another possibility is boredom proneness, the tendency to become bored easily, which has been tied to sensation-seeking and was linked to sadistic behavior and bullying in research covered by PsyPost in 2023, and which might drive individuals with psychopathic traits to seek out fear for an emotional rush. To test whether invincibility and boredom proneness help explain the link between psychopathy and fear enjoyment, study author Angela Book, a professor and director of the forensic psychology and criminal justice program at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ontario, and her colleagues conducted two studies.
“Much of the research on psychopaths and fear has focused on a deficit in feeling fear, but we didn’t think this told the whole story,” Book told PsyPost. “Instead, we thought that people with psychopathic traits likely feel something, but maybe it is different from other people. More specifically, we think they actually enjoy fear-inducing situations. This particular study tried to examine why they might enjoy fear.”
In the first study, the researchers recruited 825 participants across two distinct groups to test the role of invincibility. The first group consisted of 425 undergraduate students from two Canadian universities, who had an average age of about 21 years and were predominantly female (75 percent). The second group included 400 adults from Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, an online crowdworking platform, who had an average age of about 38 years and were mostly male (59 percent).
All participants completed the 64-item Self-Report Psychopathy Scale, rating their agreement with statements such as “People sometimes say that I’m cold-hearted” on a five-point scale. They also completed the Invincibility Belief Index, which presents 20 hypothetical scenarios, such as being confronted by a vicious, angry dog, and asks respondents to rate the probability from 0 percent to 100 percent that they would escape unharmed.
Next, participants watched two three-minute first-person video clips in random order: a SeaWorld roller coaster ride designed to induce excitement, and a suspenseful sequence from the horror video game Outlast designed to induce fear. After each clip, participants rated how strongly they felt nine negative fear-related words, including “alarmed” and “panicked,” and nine positive excitement-related words, including “exhilarated” and “delighted,” on a scale from 1 to 5.
Across the combined sample, participants rated the roller coaster clip as more positive and less negative than the horror game clip, confirming that the videos triggered the intended emotions. Compared to the university students, the online adult group scored higher on perceived invincibility (averaging 6.08 versus 5.68 on an 11-point scale) and rated the horror video more positively (averaging 26.30 versus 24.36 out of a possible 45) and less negatively (averaging 28.99 versus 31.49 out of 45). Although statistical tests indicated that neither age nor biological sex altered the underlying links between personality traits and emotional reactions, the authors analyzed the student and adult groups separately to account for these baseline differences.
To evaluate why psychopathy relates to fear enjoyment, the researchers used mediation analysis, a statistical technique that tests whether an intermediate factor accounts for the connection between two variables. The analyses predicting negative reactions controlled for positive reactions, and vice versa.
In both groups, higher psychopathy scores were linked to a stronger sense of invincibility, which statistically accounted for the link between psychopathic traits and lower negative emotion during the scary clip. In the student sample, the direct link between psychopathy and reduced fear was no longer statistically significant once invincibility was considered; in the online sample, that link had not been statistically significant to begin with. By contrast, invincibility did not explain why participants with higher psychopathy scores reported heightened excitement during the horror clip.
The links were modest. Correlations between psychopathy scores and positive reactions to the horror clip were about 0.26 to 0.32, while the correlations with reduced negative reactions were about 0.07 to 0.10. On the usual scale, about 0.1 is small, 0.3 medium, and 0.5 large.
Because feeling invincible appeared to explain why individuals with psychopathic traits were unbothered by threat, but not why they found it actively thrilling, the researchers conducted a second study examining boredom proneness. They recruited a new sample of 425 undergraduate students from two Canadian universities, with an average age of 21 years and a majority of women (74 percent). These participants followed the exact same procedure as the first study, with the addition of the Boredom Proneness Scale, in which they rated items such as getting restless while waiting in line on a seven-point scale.
Across the sample, participants averaged 22.94 out of 45 on positive ratings of the horror clip and 29.99 on negative ratings. Psychopathic traits were positively correlated with both boredom proneness and a sense of invincibility (correlations of about 0.3), as well as with more positive and less negative ratings of the horror clip (correlations of about 0.2).
When both potential explanatory factors were tested together in a mediation model, invincibility again partially accounted for the link between higher psychopathy scores and reduced negative fear responses, and unexpectedly also partially accounted for the positive excitement response, though both effects were small and statistically borderline. Contrary to the authors’ expectations, the indirect pathway linking psychopathic traits to heightened positive reactions through boredom proneness was not statistically significant.
“First, we did find that people with psychopathic traits not only have less of a negative response to fear-inducing situations, they also have a larger positive reaction,” Book explained. “Essentially, they enjoy fear. Importantly, this appears to be due to a sense of invincibility. As Alfred Hitchcock famously pointed out, we only enjoy fear when we don’t feel like we are in danger.”
The researchers also broke the psychopathy scores down into the two main trait dimensions. Both were linked to fear enjoyment, though results for the impulsive-antisocial traits were less consistent, particularly in the online sample. In the second study, accounting for boredom proneness made their link to enjoying the scary clip stronger rather than weaker, a result the authors say may be a statistical fluke. Overall, the findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which similarly found that higher psychopathic traits, especially interpersonal and emotional features, were associated with more positive and fewer negative reactions to scary video clips.
“The relationship between psychopathic traits and fear enjoyment is of medium size, which is a relatively large effect in psychological research,” Book noted. “It has been found in multiple studies by multiple researchers and appears to be fairly robust.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because the studies measured personality traits and emotional reactions at a single point in time using self-report questionnaires, the data cannot establish that feeling invincible directly causes people to feel less fear. The researchers also did not publicly record their predictions before collecting data. In addition, the participants were university students and online workers rather than clinical patients or incarcerated offenders, meaning the findings reflect variations in psychopathic personality traits within the general population rather than a diagnosed personality disorder.
Another point to keep in mind is that the frightening stimulus was a three-minute video game clip rather than a real-life physical danger. Previous neurological research suggests that individuals high in psychopathic traits often fail to notice subtle threat cues in their environment, so their reduced distress might reflect inattention to danger rather than a conscious belief that they are invincible. Because boredom proneness failed to explain why scary situations feel exciting to people with elevated psychopathic traits, the authors suggest that future studies should investigate the brain’s dopamine-driven reward system, as the anticipation of a high-stakes situation may itself act as a powerful reward for these individuals.
Looking ahead, the researchers plan to test how people with elevated psychopathic traits respond to more immersive threats that go beyond standard video clips. “Our next step will be to use virtual reality horror games/scenarios to look at the relationship in more realistic situations,” Book said.
The study, “Psychopathy and Fear Enjoyment: The Role of Invincibility and Boredom Proneness,” was authored by Angela Book, Beth Visser, Tori Wattam, and Kirkland Johnston.

Japanese company to compensate users hit by cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:52:50 KST

GMO Internet, a Japanese internet infrastructure company, will compensate customers for losses from unauthorised trading linked to a cyberattack on its cloud service, and will make a ¥5,000 (€28) goodwill payment to every customer currently using the affected service.
A Japanese internet infrastructure company is compensating customers affected by unauthorised transactions following a cyberattack on its cloud service.
GMO Internet announced on Saturday that it would cover losses from unauthorised trading linked to the attack and issue a ¥5,000 (€28) goodwill payment to all customers currently using the affected service, regardless of whether they had suffered financial losses.
The attack targeted Onamae.com Desktop Cloud, a virtual private server service used by customers to access remote desktop environments. GMO said customer information had been taken and some users had reported transactions in their trading accounts they did not recognise.
According to the company’s founder and CEO, Masatoshi Kumagai, the incident potentially affected 26,739 servers and involved unauthorised operations on trading accounts held with more than 70 securities and foreign-exchange firms in Japan and overseas.
GMO shares fell almost 16% on Monday to a four-month low. The company had a market value of around $2.6 billion at Friday’s close.
The company began investigating on 19 October after receiving a customer inquiry. It confirmed the installation of a malicious programme on some customer server environments on 20 October, suspended new applications and access to the service’s control panel, and began shutting down all servers the following day to prevent further damage.
In a blog post on Sunday, Kumagai apologised for the company’s response and acknowledged that security issues had been identified by its security specialists before the incident, but that the response had been insufficient.
GMO said it had received a ransom demand from a party believed to be behind the attack. In an update to his blog post on Monday, Kumagai said the attackers had demanded $50 million in cryptocurrency and threatened to disclose company and customer information. The company has refused to pay and is cooperating with the police and other authorities.
GMO will offer customers who wish to continue using a Windows desktop environment an alternative service on independent cloud infrastructure, free for six months. It also plans to overhaul its security architecture and investigate the cause of the breach with external experts.
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to strengthen its active cyberdefence measures, arguing that private companies cannot tackle sophisticated cross-border cyberattacks alone.
GMO has asked the authorities to consider applying the framework to the incident and has offered to share evidence and technical information with investigators.
The attack comes amid wider concerns over cybersecurity following the disclosure last week of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites and applications.
Security authorities warned that the flaws could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, prompting organisations around the world to patch systems or temporarily take services offline.
However, GMO has not publicly confirmed a link between the PHP vulnerabilities and the attack on its cloud service.
Separately, a Google Cloud outage in the UK disrupted online services last week, including those operated by financial technology company Revolut, showing the potential knock-on effects when digital infrastructure fails.

In 2020, one of the special forces unit's companies was disbanded.

golem’s ariel andré on reimagining architecture beyond the human
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:50:57 UTC
20:50:57 KST

golem’s ariel andré on reimagining architecture beyond the human
in this guest essay for designboom, the architect explores how shifting perspectives toward animals, overlooked bodies, and other forms of life can reshape the way we design and inhabit space.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
IMAGINING AN ARCHITECTURE BEYOND THE HUMAN
As a child, whenever I woke from one of those recurring nightmares that haunt the little ones, I would close my eyes again and imagine myself as a bee asleep with its wet nose nestled among the pistils of a flower; a young bird huddled against its siblings in a nest of twigs lined with feathers from their father, tucked into the hollow of a tree trunk; a snake free of predators, slithering across a carpet of moss in a world it claimed as its own. To this day, no other thought experiment, glass of alcohol or pill, prescribed or otherwise, has ever given me that same intensity of pure pleasure and well-being, the kind that starts in the belly and spreads to the very tips of your hair.
Looking back, I am convinced that this was the beginning of my path towards architecture, a practice capable of giving physical form to a world of fantasy guided by pleasure. An alternative to the nightmare of the built world we are compelled to inhabit.
Indeed, from apartments designed to constrain souls according to the ideals of the society that builds them, to sofas that fix bodies in front of televisions and airports that process crowds as fluids to be channelled and travellers as commodities to be exploited, the built world dictates how we live, down to the dimensions that govern the standard furniture at which we eat and work and sleep. All this feels like a bad dream, a terror by night and day.
My escape-dream is that of a world built to adapt to those who inhabit it and not the other way around. Through architecture and design, I aspire to build the flower in which to fall asleep, the nest in which to huddle against one’s siblings, the carpet of lichen across which to slide. To give these imaginary realities physical form, where the widest possible range of beings can find pleasure and fulfilment.
The premise is simple: use architecture’s transformative potential to produce an alternative reality guided by pleasure. And the best path to somewhere else is to start from a different standpoint. Therefore, the strategy follows: change perspective to design a world beyond conventions, one shaped around the full expression of people’s lives in their singularities.
BROKEN HEARTS BAZAAR EXPLORES ARCHITECTURE THROUGH SCENT
Broken Hearts Bazaar offers a direct example of this approach. We designed and built it for the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, commissioned by Gayane Umerova and curated by Diana Campbell. Diana asked me to develop the Biennial’s entrance and the kiosks distributed across the city as a food market, making arrival a convivial experience pulling it away from the trade-show atmosphere that so usually greets visitors to traditional biennials.
Within Bukhara’s historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, I approached these kiosks from the perspective of those who do not see architecture: people who cannot see, and beings whose encounter with a building is free of our distinction between nature and culture (man-made) such as cats or wasps, of which the city is full. Smell became the starting point. An architecture to be discovered through the nose before it is seen.
The answer emerged from Uzbekistan’s Silk Road heritage: spice markets and their spice mounds. The conical timber kiosks echo these displays and their coloured finishes are made with actual spices: paprika for red, dill for green, black tea for dark tones and clover blossoms for pink.
The fruitfulness of this shift in perspective, made before even sketching, became tangible in the variety of visitors who enjoyed the kiosks. A blind passerby returned with fifteen companions to identify the cones by scent. A local guide used them to weave folk knowledge of medicinal herbs into her tours. Bees rested on clover blossoms. Cats waited for the visitors to leave at night to lick the paprika walls.
For GOLEM, this project gives concrete form to architecture’s capacity to expand who design is for. Starting from the standpoint of those usually overlooked opens up new forms and spaces, enriching the experience of life for everyone.
AMOREBA: FURNITURE INSPIRED BY MICROSCOPIC WORLDS
The same thought experiment extends to furniture. Amoreba is an organic surface that spreads through rigid interiors, transforming them into contemporary environments for non-conformists. In a curator’s apartment in Brussels, it takes the form of a conversation pit. Its design begins with a psychedelic fantasy: lounging among the soft, microscopic bumps of a forest mushroom colony. This time I imagined the surface from the perspective of a tiny creature slithering across this buoyant terrain.
Amoreba follows smooth curves, negotiates sharp angles and adapts to complex geometries. For each project, we shape its design around the interior and the social activities its future inhabitants imagine taking place in it, much as lichen spreads across stones and tree trunks on a forest bed. Again, starting from the standpoint of those usually overlooked, here, microscopic beings, allows us to create new forms and spaces that enrich the experience of life for everyone.
DESIGNING FOR DIFFERENT BODIES, CULTURES AND WAYS OF LIVING
Beyond these animal fantasies lies a necessary response to a broader condition: the world has been designed by a small minority whose imagination extends little beyond themselves. This calls for an architecture beyond the self. A practice of shifting perspectives and exercising empathy to create new forms that enrich the experience of being alive and together in shared spaces.
For the sofa inside the Public Program Building we designed for the Diriyah Biennale Foundation in Riyadh, commissioned by Aya Albakree and Sybel Vazquez, we documented a plethora of ways of positioning one’s body in public space across Saudi Arabia’s diverse communities. The result is a 24-metre-long sofa that operates as both furniture and public infrastructure. It brings different cultures, generations and bodily habits together, allowing each person to settle comfortably into their own posture and opening up conversations across ages and cultures.
Lamputée takes an aesthetic step sideways. Each lamp is unique, moulded from an amputated limb. When the form is literally turned upside down and abstracted from its familiar context, a shape that can provoke fear or discomfort from an unfamiliar viewer’s perspective, becomes a source of beauty and an asset as a collectible object.
Our responsibility as architects is to draw on the needs that bodies, in all their plurality, express in space. It falls to us to dream into existence the environments in which we can all flourish, nest, forage or slither.
Ariel André is an architect and founder of GOLEM, an architecture, design, and research studio based in Paris. His practice challenges standardized design conventions by drawing on overlooked perspectives, marginal aesthetics, and the narratives of underrepresented communities and non-human life. Before founding GOLEM, André worked at OMA in Rotterdam, where he led design teams across projects spanning retail, museums, offices, and urban development, and collaborated with architecture studios in Paris, Tokyo, Los Angeles, Amsterdam, and Rotterdam, as well as the government in Haiti. GOLEM’s work has been presented at international platforms including the Diriyah Biennale, the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah, and the Bukhara Biennial.
project info:
architect: Ariel André, GOLEM | @golem.digital

Ukraine Wants EU Representative at Russia Negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:40:38 UTC
20:40:38 KST

Ukraine is seeking to move up planned trilateral negotiations with the United States and Russia by at least a week and bring an EU representative into the talks, Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing sources close to the negotiation team.
The next round of discussions between Ukraine, the US and Russia is tentatively scheduled to begin in Abu Dhabi on November 10, after the US congressional midterm elections. Kyiv and Washington are working to persuade Moscow to agree to meet at least a week earlier.
A source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's team told Ukrainska Pravda that the timing was critical because of the coming winter. “in December, every week will be important. When you have no power, water or heating, every single day plays a role”, the source said.
As of the evening of October 25, Moscow had not provided final confirmation of a change to the date.
Kyiv does not anticipate a breakthrough at the initial meeting, believing that several rounds of negotiations will be needed to reach substantive agreements. A source from the President's Office said Moscow still believed it “will be able to break us this winter”.
A member of Zelensky's team who has taken part in similar negotiations said the delegations might change, meaning the first meeting would be used to familiarize the participants with one another. “We have a feeling that there will be updates to the composition of the groups. Therefore, at the first meeting, the new delegations will get used to each other. At the second, substantive work will begin. And somewhere around the third, there may already be some real decisions,” the source said.
Ukraine also wants the sides to begin by discussing what peace should look like after the war, rather than immediately negotiating which villages should belong to each side.
A source close to the negotiation team told Ukrainska Pravda that Kyiv wanted to outline a future security arrangement for the region, including how Ukraine would be protected and what cooperation with NATO or other partners might entail. The source also pointed to low public confidence in the US president. “In Ukraine trust in Trump is only 6% higher than trust in Putin. Nobody here is going to do anything purely on Trump's assurances,” the source said.
Kyiv continues to push for European partners to participate in the negotiations despite resistance from Russia and, frequently, the United States.
Sources in Zelensky's diplomatic team told Ukrainska Pravda that Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had conveyed to Russian President Vladimir Putin the idea of discussing a new security model, and that Putin had reportedly agreed.
Over the past two meetings, a potential EU representative has also emerged: Björn Seibert, head of cabinet and close aide to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
According to a source cited by Ukrainska Pravda, Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, told US officials that any final peace arrangement must be acceptable to people living in Kharkiv and Dnipro. “After Donbas, they are next, and if the residents of these regions look at our 'peace formula' and say, 'Okay, this suits us,' then that will truly be a work in progress,” the source said, relaying Arakhamiia's message.
US government sources have said the next round of talks involving American, Ukrainian and Russian delegations could take place in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Russian leader's aide Yuri Ushakov has said Moscow is ready to resume trilateral negotiations on ending the war after November 4.
Zelensky has said Ukraine will not accept restrictions on the size of its armed forces or neutral status under any potential peace agreement.

Ukrainian regulator stalling EBRD-backed capital market plan – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:40:21 EET
20:40:21 KST

Implementation of an integrated capital markets infrastructure model, developed jointly by the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), the Ministry of Economy and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), is currently being held up by the position of the head of the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC), NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"We are being asked what is happening with the capital markets. We explain the capital markets infrastructure model that has been developed jointly by the NBU, the Ministry of Economy and the EBRD. Unfortunately, its implementation is currently being held up by the position of the head of the NSSMC," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
In the NBU governor's view, the proposed model takes the state's interests into account in building a vertically integrated system, and therefore confidence in it should not be undermined.
"The key idea is to bring the entire capital markets infrastructure chain together under a single holding company. The strategic investor in this infrastructure holding company should be an entity trusted by global private capital: Deutsche Börse, Euroclear, Clearstream… Naturally, it should be selected through a competitive process. But in the current circumstances, national security requirements must also be taken into account. Our model provides for all of this. So why is the process being held up?" Pyshnyy concluded.
As reported, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso expressed hope at the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group that Ukraine would pay greater attention to the capital market development project.
"Despite all the short-term challenges, we have indeed managed to move this process forward, and I hope this issue will soon become a priority," she said.
In July last year, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Rome by the Ministry of Economy, the Ministry of Finance, the NBU, the NSSMC and the EBRD on supporting integrated capital markets infrastructure in Ukraine. Its signing was preceded by the Financial Stability Council's approval of a plan for the practical implementation of the target capital markets infrastructure model.
In early September 2025, the National Bank announced the launch of the memorandum's implementation. The first stage involved optimizing the ownership structure and corporate governance of the National Depository of Ukraine (NDU) by transferring management of the state-owned stake, previously managed by the NSSMC, to the NBU.
The next stage envisages the creation of a holding company involving a reputable international strategic investor selected through an open tender, an operator of trading and post-trading infrastructure, international financial institutions, local market participants, and the state and state-owned banks. The holding company, in turn, will establish a new stock exchange in Ukraine, which will become the majority owner of the Central Counterparty Clearing Institution, the Settlement Center (SC), replacing the National Bank in that role. In addition, the exchange will own a minority stake in the NDU, while the National Bank will hold a majority stake.
The final stage is to consolidate depository services under the NDU, which is to operate as a single central securities depository, by transferring to it the functions of recording and servicing the circulation of government bonds from the National Bank.
In early June this year, the Cabinet of Ministers approved a bill on establishing a capital markets infrastructure holding company with the participation of a foreign strategic investor. However, due to a change of government, the document was submitted to the Verkhovna Rada only on September 4. The NSSMC subsequently proposed substantial amendments to the government's bill, including tightening the conditions for attracting a foreign strategic investor.
In addition, an alternative bill (No. 16038-1) was registered on September 21. Its authors include 12 members of parliament, among them Serhiy Taruta, first deputy head of the Verkhovna Rada's economic committee; Andriy Nikolaienko, head of the capital markets subcommittee of the parliament's finance committee; Oleksandr Fediyenko, head of a subcommittee of the parliament's security committee; and Anton Yatsenko.

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:39:00 UTC
20:39:00 KST

Experts look to math teaching changes to ease Estonia's engineer shortage
Despite growing interest in engineering, Estonia faces a shortage of more than 800 young engineers in the next decade as 40 percent retire. Changes to math teaching may help.
Interest in engineering has grown sharply, but according to OSKA, the Estonian Qualifications Authority's labor market forecasting system, the sector will still be short more than 800 young engineers over the next decade as 40 percent retire. There are no quick solutions, but efforts are being made to alleviate the shortage by changing how mathematics is taught.
Interest in studying at Tallinn University of Technology's (TalTech) School of Engineering has increased by 25 percent over the past three years. According to Fjodor Sergejev, dean of the School of Engineering, students are enrolling in a variety of programs, from energy and construction to mechanical and industrial engineering, but there will not be enough graduates to fill the gap.
"We need replacement workers because many engineers from previous generations are retiring and need to be replaced, but we also need to ensure the development of the sector, and for that we need even more engineers. Even the substantial demographic support we currently have is unfortunately unable to meet all our needs, because the replacement demand is indeed very high, in some fields even numbering in the thousands."
Cathy-Liis Põlluveer, president of the Estonian association of engineers (Eesti Inseneride Liit), also acknowledged the shortage: "We currently have a situation where it depends somewhat on the field, but when an engineer, particularly an experienced engineer, is being sought and a recruitment competition is held, there is practically no queue of applicants or diversity among candidates. Instead, engineers are being sought like needles in a haystack."
According to Anneli Leemet, an analyst at OSKA, demand will grow most for electrical and energy engineers, mechanical engineers and electronics engineers. Leemet said the issue is not only meeting the numerical demand but ensuring engineers have a diverse range of skills.
One possible solution experts see is strengthening mathematics education in basic schools (grades 1–9) — making mathematics teaching more relevant to everyday life, more integrated with other subjects, and delivered in a way that supports all children's motivation to learn. According to Tiina Kraav, a lecturer in mathematics education at the University of Tartu, there are no quick solutions, but mathematics teaching is being continuously developed.
"Making mathematics more interesting to learn, making mathematics learning more visible, making mathematical thinking more visible to students, making mathematics learning more creative, improving how problem-solving skills are taught in the classroom, getting students to talk about what they think and how they think when solving mathematics problems – all of this will certainly help in the longer term," Kraav said.
Põlluveer believes subjects that help connect natural sciences and mathematics could be beneficial.
Priit Laats, a teacher of technology education, arts and technology at Tartu Raatuse School, confirmed that schools are increasingly moving toward theme-based learning: "For example, in the first stage of basic school, there is integrated learning. It is theme-based, with Estonian, mathematics, nature studies and creative subjects all together all the time. In fact, other grades should already be structured in a similar way. But again, who is going to develop all of this? It is a huge amount of work. If I take how I, in turn, support mathematics, we introduce 3D modeling as early as fourth grade: the spatial world, shapes, symbols, symmetry, reflection, all the faces and planes – it is all mathematics all the time, and we do this right through ninth grade."
OSKA will publish a new cross-sector study of labor and skills needs in engineering in early November, which will show that competition for hybrid competencies is increasing in the labor market. This means engineers must have in-depth specialist knowledge combined with digital, data analysis, artificial intelligence, business or management skills.

Italy sees progress in well-being indicators, but poverty remains above EU average
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:35 UTC
20:38:35 KST

Aysu Bicer
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Italy has made progress in several areas of equitable and sustainable well-being, including health and the environment, but continues to face challenges related to poverty, disposable income and households’ ability to make ends meet, according to the latest report by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT).
The report, which examines 132 indicators of equitable and sustainable well-being, found that 54 indicators improved, 55 remained stable and 23 deteriorated.
Despite the overall progress, Italy’s at-risk-of-poverty rate remains 2.3 percentage points above the EU average.
Compared with the EU, Italy performs better in health and safety, while significant challenges persist in education and training, employment, work-life balance, and innovation, research and creativity.
More than 5.4 million people were living in absolute poverty in Italy in 2025, with large families and households with at least one minor child facing particularly difficult conditions.
According to the report, 8% of households were living in absolute poverty, affecting 9.3% of the country’s population.
The incidence of individual absolute poverty remained highest in southern Italy, although it declined to 11.5% in 2025 from 12.5% in 2024.
In northern Italy, the rate fell to 8.5% from 8.8% a year earlier, while central Italy continued to record the lowest incidence, at 7.4%, down from 7.6% in 2024.

How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:32 UTC
20:38:32 KST

Article
Presidential election 2026
How far away is Bulgaria when you choose its president?
Monday 26 October 2026 14:05
Monday, 26 October 2026, 14:05
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The boundary between geographical distance and national identity often fades on election day. For our compatriots living thousands of kilometres from their homeland, presidential elections are not merely an administrative procedure, but an expression of belonging, hope and the desire to have their voices heard. How do Bulgarians around the world view the role of the head of state, and what makes them feel close to their homeland despite the physical distance?
Principles, Unity and International Standing: What matters most in a President
The question of whether the head of state should primarily uphold principles, unite the nation or defend the country’s standing on the international stage prompted a range of nuanced responses in our conversations with fellow Bulgarians on election day on October 25. For many, however, these three roles are inseparable.
40 thousand Bulgarians abroad register to vote in presidential election
“Personally, I think that if one person embodies all three of these qualities, that might sound a little utopian, but it would be the best possible outcome,” says Marina Tomova, who lives in Nettuno, Italy. “The president is the face of a country. We Bulgarians would identify with this representative figure in a number of ways: how they present themselves on the international stage and how they defend Bulgaria’s interests. At the same time, the president should serve as a unifying figure and a corrective force in both domestic and foreign policy.”
“People want to see a president who stands up for Bulgaria’s interests and is not afraid to take a position. They also want someone who protects their interests, is educated and well-informed, can speak eloquently at international events and is not afraid to express their views clearly and openly.”
Estela Encheva, from Munich, Germany, emphasises the importance of international law and domestic dialogue.
“For me, it is also important that the president respects international law and insists that our country abide by it, while also bringing the nation together. We live in a time when society is so divided that political measures alone can hardly bridge the divide. In our particular situation, it is important for the president to be able to act as a check on those in power.”
Marin Kachamakov, from Geneva, Switzerland, stresses that the head of state should unite people around moral principles and integrity, while also having the strength and voice to hold those in power to account.
“I believe the president should unite fellow Bulgarians around integrity and a shared moral compass, and help ensure that Bulgaria is not seen as a country that disregards principles, a country where anything goes and where signed treaties are not honoured. In short, the president should bring people together, set a moral example and ensure that the agreements and treaties signed by the state are respected.”
Milena Baeva, from Kuwait, says that, for her, it is equally important for the next presidential ticket to unite people in Bulgaria and defend the country’s interests:
“I imagine them as people whose actions, both at home and on the world stage, will make me proud to be Bulgarian.”
Viktoria Vlahovska, from Reading, United Kingdom, points out that Bulgarians abroad want a steady hand as commander-in-chief and a representative figure they can be proud of.
Adriana Dimitrova, from Berlin, Germany, sums up her expectations by saying she wants a competent leader who can hold their own with dignity on the world stage, someone Bulgarians will not be ashamed of.
When do Bulgarians abroad feel represented and heard?
For Bulgarians living outside the country to feel represented by the presidential institution, they need genuine attention, not merely formal gestures.
The role of the presidential ticket is to seek common ground and represent all Bulgarian citizens, regardless of their political beliefs or place of residence, stresses Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia:
“I would feel represented if the president regarded Bulgarians abroad as an integral part of the nation. This is not just about official visits or statements, but about genuinely understanding the problems faced by Bulgarian communities around the world and the contributions they make. What matters is that people abroad know their voices and experiences also count in shaping Bulgaria’s future,” says our compatriot from the other side of the world.
Martina Shopova-Yanev, from Vienna, Austria, is adamant that she has yet to see genuine concern from the presidential institution for the problems faced by Bulgarians abroad, and hopes this will change:
“I hope for a president and vice-president who will be present in the lives of Bulgarians abroad, not just on paper or during election campaigns, and who will help address our problems. These often concern the exercise of our right to vote and making voting easier. We hope the next presidential ticket will take a more active approach in this regard and demonstrate genuine interest, rather than merely campaigning for support.”
“I think the president should visit as many different countries as possible and make time for Bulgarians abroad,” suggests Marin Kachamakov from Geneva. “Although there are only 24 hours in a day, the president should also try to listen to the views of these Bulgarians. Let us not forget that some of them left Bulgaria not because they wanted to, but because they decided they could build a better life abroad, or because they were driven out of the country. I am referring to the period before 1989-1990.”
Marinela Koleva, from Kraków, Poland, proposes a concrete way to show support: the president could serve as patron of initiatives organised by Bulgarians abroad, demonstrating through action and policy that their concerns matter.
Ties to the Homeland and Faith in the Power of the Vote
Despite the distance and fluctuations in voter turnout, the bond with Bulgaria remains strong. In Melbourne, for example, 77 people voted, compared with 149 in the previous parliamentary elections in April 2026. Bulgarians abroad continue to express a desire for change in their homeland. This is reflected in the decisive victory of the Andrey Gyurov-Georgi Kandev presidential ticket among voters abroad, while in Bulgaria the advantage went to incumbent head of state Iliana Iotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev.
Gyurov wins 45.79% of overseas vote, well ahead of Iotova
“Wherever we live, we always feel close to our homeland,” says Mancho Manev, from Melbourne, Australia.
“We keep ourselves informed through social media and the news, and we watch Bulgarian television. We will always remain Bulgarians, no matter how far away we are from our homeland. Every one of us cares deeply about Bulgaria, which is why you see such strong engagement abroad. People vote, they take an interest and they are not indifferent to what is happening, because we all care about Bulgaria.”
The organisation of polling stations abroad demonstrates the strength of the community and its commitment to developments in the homeland. In this sense, voting is not simply a civic duty, but a powerful expression of an enduring connection with Bulgaria. This is also evident in a video sent to us by Nadia Ullman from the Bulgarian Centre in Boston, USA. Voter turnout in New England was lower than in the previous vote in April 2026, but for her, taking part in the electoral process is a personal mission.
“As the mother of two grown-up children who have attended Bulgarian school in Boston for years, I see it as my mission to raise them as informed and engaged Bulgarian citizens. I teach them to love Bulgaria and value their right to vote. By actively participating in the life of the Bulgarian community abroad, they are learning to preserve their roots and traditions. I believe that this is how we raise responsible individuals who will always carry Bulgaria in their hearts and contribute to its future.
For me, voting is not simply an obligation, but a way of helping shape a better and more prosperous Bulgaria. Every vote cast from abroad sends a clear message that Bulgarians living outside the country are not indifferent to what is happening at home. The organisation of polling stations demonstrates the strength of our community and our desire to make Bulgaria a more attractive place for us and our children to return to.”
The conversations conducted by the Radio Bulgaria team with Bulgarians living in different parts of the world make one thing clear: liviging at a distance from Bulgaria does not diminish their expectations of the country’s institutions. Bulgarians abroad want their president to act as a check on those in power, unite the nation and serve as an authoritative representative of the country on the international stage. They want a leader who shows genuine concern for Bulgarian communities around the world and makes them proud of their origins.

As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:38:27 UTC
20:38:27 KST

Breadcrumb
As a Palestinian, liberation is a right, not a plea for sympathy
It has become almost customary for Palestinians, whenever we speak about Palestine, to begin by telling the story of our suffering. We are expected to explain how we became refugees, how our parents and grandparents were displaced, and which members of our families were killed, imprisoned or disappeared under Israeli occupation.
We are expected to expose our deepest wounds, relive generations of trauma, and to offer our grief as evidence that our demands for justice deserve to be heard.
This is nothing but emotional labour.
And today, I refuse to audition for anyone’s sympathy.
I refuse to bare my wounds for the world to see, simply to validate the decisions and actions we take on the path towards our liberation.
Palestinian rights are not conditional upon our ability to move an audience to tears.
This is why when Green Party members voted to adopt the historic motion declaring Zionism to be racism and calling for a free Palestine from the river to the sea, it felt like a historic movement in UK solidarity efforts.
As a Palestinian and a Green Party member who co-authored and helped develop and advance this motion, I saw this as more than a political victory. It was also an affirmation that Palestinian voices could shape the policies of a major British political party without having to surrender their own understanding of their oppression or dilute their demands to be palatable.
Yet what should have been a moment of collective reflection and celebration quickly became overshadowed by opposition from several Green Party MPs and figures within the party leadership.
A democratic victory that some refuse to accept
The motion did not emerge overnight. Outsiders did not impose it, nor was it the product of some mysterious group of extremists, as some have suggested.
It was drafted and championed by ordinary Green Party members, including Palestinians and anti-Zionist Jews, who spent months organising workshops, seminars, discussions and fringe events to engage fellow members.
Even after the motion was denied a hearing following procedural delays and filibustering during the party’s spring conference, we continued organising, discussing and engaging.
We believed in the Green Party’s commitment to grassroots democracy, even when its procedures appeared to work against us.
Nevertheless, once the motion finally passed, some elected representatives responded not by acknowledging the democratic outcome, but by questioning the motivations of those who brought the motion forward, portraying our organisation and determination as something threatening.
MP Ellie Chowns called for protecting the party from extremists and entryists.
Ironically, only months earlier, party leadership was enthusiastically celebrating a remarkable surge in membership.
Apparently, welcoming new members is something to celebrate until those members organise, exercise their democratic rights and successfully influence party policy.
Even my own MP, Sian Berry, whom I personally contacted to engage with the motion and its arguments, did not respond. Yet, once the media attacks started, Berry weighed in by publicly distancing herself from the motion, describing it as seriously flawed and accusing its Palestinian proposers of being unwilling to compromise.
She has even called on the party to revisit a decision reached through its own democratic processes.
MP Adrian Ramsay, the party's former co-leader, has publicly encouraged Green council groups to distance themselves from the democratically adopted policy. In a recent public statement
Ramsay praised council groups that rejected the motion, described the conference decision as a distraction from their work, and said it did not reflect the views of most party members.
It is deeply disappointing to see a former party leader effectively encouraging a division between elected council groups and the democratic decisions of the party’s own membership.
Selective silencing
Whilst disagreement is a legitimate part of political life, actively encouraging local representatives to distance themselves from a policy adopted through the party’s highest democratic forum raises serious questions about whose voices are ultimately respected.
What message does this send to party members who invest their time, energy and conviction in the democratic process, only to see its outcome publicly undermined by those elected to represent them?
What makes this particularly painful is that these Green MPs are now among the most vocal opponents of a motion written by Palestinians, for Palestinians, and supported through the party’s democratic process.
Not long ago, Palestinians within the Green Party extended a gesture of solidarity and goodwill to those very MPs. After Israeli authorities imposed entry bans on them, we sent a letter replacing that exclusion with an invitation to visit a Free Palestine, to stand alongside us and to hear directly from Palestinians about our aspirations for freedom, dignity and self-determination.
It was an invitation to listen, to engage and to recognise that Palestinians are not merely subjects of political debate, but people with voices, histories and a right to determine their own future. Judging by some of the responses to the motion, it feels like the invitation was buried under a pile of political calculations and selective solidarity.
Palestinians are also not the only ones who’ve been silenced by opposing MPs and the subsequent media storm.
A leading accusation against the motion is that it threatens the safety of Jewish members of the Green Party. But Jewish safety is not at risk from a motion that defines and confronts Zionism as a settler colonial ideology, examining its historical and contemporary manifestations, and reaffirming the Palestinian struggle for liberation, including ending occupation and confronting the structures of displacement and dispossession.
Not only is this argument, which conflates Zionist views with Jewish identity, antisemitic in itself, but it also completely ignores anti-Zionist Jewish members. Many of those members participated in drafting the motion and organising discussions and public meetings in support of it, but opponents have shown they’re not interested in this part of the story.
No one’s safety should ever come at the expense of another people’s freedom, dignity or right to self-determination.
Amro Tabari is a British Palestinian renewable energy engineer, activist and writer. Born a refugee in Syria and raised in Jordan, his family originates from Tiberias, Palestine. He has lived in the UK since 2014 and is actively involved in grassroots campaigns for Palestinian liberation, social justice and environmental sustainability. A member of the Green Party and Greens for Palestine, he was recognised as one of The Big Issue’s 100 Changemakers in 2026 for his work in politics and activism.

Award-Winning Production Designer Dies at Moscow Hospital After Arrest for Treason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:37:46 UTC
20:37:46 KST

Alexander Kondratov, an award-winning production designer for the popular Russian TV series “Liquidation,” has died at a Moscow hospital after being transferred from a detention center where he was awaiting trial on treason charges, the rights NGO Perviy Otdel said Monday.
Kondratov, 52, was reportedly hospitalized at the Botkin hospital last Friday for an undisclosed ailment. The cause of his death has not been made public.
Russian law enforcement authorities charged Kondratov with treason on Aug. 5, though he had been held for more than 70 days under so-called “carousel arrests,” a practice of consecutive detentions on charges of disorderly conduct.
Born and raised in Moscow, Kondratov moved to Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2012, where his family currently resides.
Russian border guards at Vnukovo International Airport detained him on May 5, when he arrived to renew his international passport.
His defense attorney Natalia Tikhonova said the treason charges, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison for men, stemmed from “at least six” online posts Kondratov had made. The nature of those posts has not been disclosed.
Kondratov was best known for his work as an art and production designer for the 2007 post-World War II detective drama “Liquidation.” His work on the series earned him two of Russia’s highest honors in television production — the TEFI and Golden Eagle awards.
Perviy Otdel reported that Kondratov’s death marks at least the 11th known case of someone dying in Russian custody this year while standing trial on charges widely viewed as being politically motivated.

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:37:32 UTC
20:37:32 KST

AI uses sleep to predict heart problems up to 10 years ahead
The system analyzes heart activity recorded during overnight sleep studies. Researchers found that it could identify patterns linked to future health problems, including risks that standard medical checks might not fully capture.
The study, published in the journal Sleep, used data from more than 35,000 patients at three US medical centers. Researchers trained an AI model to analyze heart signals alongside information about patients' sleep stages.
The team then tested the system on two independent groups, including 9,810 patients at Emory University Hospital and 12,576 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
The model predicted 5 outcomes: atrial fibrillation, a condition that causes an irregular heartbeat; stroke; heart attack; heart failure; and death from any cause. Researchers tracked health outcomes for up to 10 years in one group and 7 years in the other.
The strongest results came from predictions of irregular heartbeat, heart failure and death. Adding the AI's analysis improved the accuracy of risk assessments for these outcomes beyond estimates based on established risk factors, such as age, smoking, high blood pressure and diabetes.
For heart failure, the researchers reported an improvement of about 8% to 9% in the model's ability to distinguish between people who later developed the condition and those who did not.
However, the AI did not significantly improve predictions of stroke or heart attack beyond existing risk factors. The researchers said these conditions may be harder to predict years in advance using heart signals alone.
The approach could make better use of information already collected during sleep studies, which doctors commonly use to diagnose sleep disorders. These studies typically record an electrical signal from the heart, but clinicians do not routinely use it to assess long-term cardiovascular risk.
The researchers said the system could eventually help doctors identify patients who need closer monitoring or preventive care. It is intended as a screening tool, not a stand-alone diagnosis, and any concerning prediction would require further medical assessment.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Brazil would develop an AI-based system to help monitor the condition of forests and other natural areas.

Israeli voters head to polls for pivotal election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:28:20 UTC
20:28:20 KST

A woman walks past a Likud Party campaign billboard featuring U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with a Hebrew message reading, "We have one opportunity to win," in Tel Aviv, Israel, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (AP Photo)
Israelis will vote on Oct. 27 in the first national elections since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack in what is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership.
The deadliest day in Israel’s history features prominently in the campaign, but not in the way many outsiders might expect.
There’s been almost no debate over Israel’s wartime conduct in Gaza, which led to an international arrest warrant against Netanyahu, its occupation of much of southern Lebanon and parts of Syria, or its two wars launched against Iran, all of which have broad support.
Instead, candidates have focused on Netanyahu’s leadership and moral character; his role in the security breakdown on Oct. 7, 2023,; his efforts to exempt ultra-Orthodox Jews from military service and a 2023 judicial overhaul seen by critics as an assault on Israel’s democratic institutions.
Both of the main electoral blocs are dominated by parties that support Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state, and no major candidate is advocating a return to the long-moribund peace process.
A poll published by public broadcaster KAN found that out of 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, 52 would go to Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with
Netanyahu and 50 to the Israeli premier, with the rest going to non-aligned parties, including Arab ones.
People heading to the polls will pass the faces of fallen soldiers peering from stickers on train station walls and faded yellow ribbons honoring the hostages, the last of whom were returned in a ceasefire deal last year.
Around 68 percent of Jewish Israelis say their attitudes toward the 2023 attack are a central factor in deciding which party to support, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. 
Among the Arab minority, just 32 percent said it factored prominently, with most citing crime as the main issue.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has sought to shift blame for the failures surrounding the attack to security officials while touting Israel’s military achievements against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and their patron, Iran.
Critics accuse him of evading responsibility by blocking an official inquiry into the attack, of not reaching a deal to bring back the hostages sooner, and of failing to win a decisive victory against any of Israel’s foes.
Netanyahu’s governing coalitions have long relied on ultra-Orthodox parties that demand exemptions from military conscription for young men engaged in religious studies. That policy has infuriated
Israel’s secular majority as reservists have been repeatedly called up in the various wars.
Israelis vote for parties, not specific candidates, and no single party is expected to win anywhere close to a 61-seat majority in parliament, known as the Knesset. Whoever can cobble together a majority coalition will become the next prime minister.
If no one is able to, Netanyahu’s government will continue to serve as caretaker until another round of elections in the coming months.

General Staff confirmed the striking of Russian facilities producing missile components
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Energia plant and facilities in Oryol, Donetsk, and Tolyatti. The strikes complicate the production of missiles and drones.
On October 26, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strike on the Energia plant in Yelets and the results of the strikes on Proton-Elektroteks and Tolyattikauchuk, UNN writes.
Details
According to the General Staff, "on October 25 and during the night of October 26, units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck":
-  "the workshop producing power sources for the enemy’s weapons at the Energia enterprise in the city of Yelets, Lipetsk region, rf. A fire broke out on the enterprise’s premises". 
The strike, as stated, complicates the rf army’s production of power sources for missiles, guided aerial bombs, and other weapons. "Energia" is the only manufacturer of batteries for guidance and correction modules for aerial bombs, and also produces batteries for Iskander-M operational-tactical missile systems and sea-launched cruise missiles.
Following the previous strikes, the General Staff reported that the following had been confirmed:
-  "the main microchip production workshop was destroyed, and the building and servers of the Proton-Elektroteks enterprise in the city of Orel, Orel region, rf, were damaged. The strike took place on October 23". 
This, as noted, complicates the enemy’s production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles with which it strikes Ukrainian cities.
-  "a storage, preparation, and launch site for attack UAVs in the Donetsk area, struck on October 23. Three buildings used for preparing and equipping attack UAVs and one launch rail were damaged". 
This, as noted, reduces the enemy’s capabilities to attack Ukraine and civilian infrastructure with drones of various modifications.
-  "the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the city of Tolyatti, Samara region, rf, struck on October 24. A process pipeline, two butyl rubber production units, and one rectification unit were damaged". 
This, as reported, strikes at the production chain for solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
"The Defense Forces of Ukraine are striking the enemy’s military facilities within the framework of the right to self-defense guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter," the General Staff emphasized.

Pakistani Mustafa Prize laureate explores nanotechnology in fight against breast cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:26:45 UTC
20:26:45 KST

Pakistani Mustafa Prize laureate explores nanotechnology in fight against breast cancer
TEHRAN - Nanotechnology is opening new avenues for breast cancer treatment by improving drug delivery, overcoming resistance to chemotherapy, and reducing damage to healthy cells. Pakistani medicinal chemist Muhammad Iqbal Choudhary, a 2021 Mustafa Prize laureate, is among the researchers exploring how advanced drug-delivery systems can make cancer therapies more precise and effective.
Breast cancer remains a major global health challenge, with patients often facing recurrence, drug resistance, and severe treatment-related side effects. Conventional chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells but can also damage healthy tissues, including hair follicles, the gastrointestinal lining, and bone marrow. Meanwhile, cancer cells can develop multidrug resistance (MDR) by activating molecular pumps that expel drugs before they can take effect.
“Cancers are very difficult, complex, and diverse diseases,” Choudhary said. He explained that chemotherapy drugs often affect both cancerous and healthy cells, making it challenging to target tumors without causing significant side effects.
Choudhary, who heads the International Center for Chemical and Biological Sciences (ICCBS) at the University of Karachi, serves as vice president of The World Academy of Sciences (TWAS) and coordinates the Standing Committee on Scientific and Technological Cooperation of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (COMSTECH).
Receiving the Mustafa Prize marked a turning point in his scientific career, providing renewed motivation and focus. Since then, his research group has increasingly concentrated on innovative breast cancer treatments and smarter drug-delivery technologies.
Nanocarriers offer one promising approach by encapsulating therapeutic compounds in microscopic particles that protect drugs from premature degradation and release them more effectively at tumor sites. These systems can use passive targeting, which exploits the increased permeability of tumor blood vessels, or active targeting, in which antibodies, peptides, or other molecules help nanoparticles bind to cancer-cell receptors.
According to Choudhary, nanoparticles can contribute both to drug discovery and to delivering existing medicines more precisely, potentially improving their effectiveness while limiting harmful side effects.
One promising strategy involves poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer widely investigated for controlled drug delivery. Adding vitamin E-derived TPGS may further help counter drug resistance by interfering with the energy-dependent mechanisms that cancer cells use to expel chemotherapy drugs.
Researchers are also investigating nanoparticles coated with natural cell membranes to help them evade immune clearance and accumulate more effectively in tumors. Platelet membranes are particularly promising because their surface proteins may support tumor targeting. A 2025 preclinical study reported greater uptake of platelet-membrane-coated, bufalin-loaded PLGA nanoparticles by tumor cells than that of uncoated particles.
These advances could be particularly valuable against triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype lacking estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors, which limits conventional targeted treatment options. Nanoparticle-based systems that respond to local tumor conditions may offer alternative ways to deliver drugs without relying on these receptors.
Despite the promise, significant challenges remain. Producing platelet-membrane-coated nanoparticles consistently at clinical scale is difficult, and incomplete membrane coverage remains a concern. Such technologies must overcome manufacturing and regulatory hurdles before routine clinical use becomes possible.
Choudhary emphasizes that, although increasingly selective therapies are available, no drug can yet deliver absolute disease-specific precision. Integrating molecular biology, nanotechnology, and medicinal chemistry could nevertheless bring researchers closer to safer, more effective treatments for cancers that have long resisted conventional therapies.

Koretsky urges business to plan for worst case, warns of $1.5 bln budget gap
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:26:04 EET
20:26:04 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky has called on the business community to prepare in advance for the most critical scenarios regarding enemy attacks and economic challenges.
"When we talk to founders and top management, I’ve sensed a certain attitude that 'it will somehow blow over.' Perhaps I won't be targeted by missiles or drones, perhaps my sector won't be touched. Therefore, first: I would strongly ask and recommend thinking according to the most critical scenario of events. Thinking ahead about alternative production sites: who you can cooperate with, where you can make a private label if we are talking about consumer goods, if your enterprise is hit. How to talk in advance with suppliers, perhaps even for imported goods, how to conclude framework contracts and be ready rather than doing it all later. Looking at alternative premises for relocation, for restoration. In other words, think in the most critical scenario. It is better to be ready for this and have it not happen than to find oneself in an unexpected situation," Koretsky said at the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) themed "People. Business. Economy. What's Next?" in Kyiv on Monday, as reported by an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to the Prime Minister, enemy strikes have already caused over $7.7 billion in losses, with more than 1 million square meters of various types of real estate, both state and private, destroyed or damaged. Significant destruction has hit energy, metallurgy, logistics, processing enterprises, retail, and other sectors.
"Considering these losses, considering the strikes, we already see that by the end of the year the state budget will underfulfill its plans and forecasts by about $1.5 billion. That is the baseline forecast we have today," he stated.
At the same time, he emphasized that despite all this, the country's economy continues to function.
"If we think in terms of PnL (Profit and Loss statement), allocating a lot of funds to support business is impossible. There is no such PnL, because we can only cover one-third of the budget. Even realizing, clearly realizing this, we live even on a cash flow principle and in a certain way go all-in, allocating certain funds to support programs, to various subsidies, to grant programs. Because we realize that without this support, business – small, medium, and large in particular – cannot be sufficiently resilient to counter enemy attacks. And this is the conscious logic and tactics of the government," Koretsky noted.
The Prime Minister stressed that the government will continue programs that have proven their effectiveness, notably the "Affordable Loans 5-7-9%" program. He noted that since the program's inception, UAH 580 billion has been issued, with the current loan portfolio principal standing at around UAH 200 billion. He recalled the recent decision allowing large businesses to receive about UAH 2 billion "in one hand per group of companies" at a preferential interest rate of around 10%.
"The 2026 budget allocated Hr 18 billion. We are expanding this program and see that by the end of the year it will be Hr 22 billion. We currently have a certain deficit on four billion, but one way or another we will cover it, because we consider this to be one of the fundamentally important, correct programs that genuinely supports business," the Prime Minister said.
He also pointed out the necessity of establishing a war risk insurance and damage compensation system. Koretsky recalled the proposal to create a special fund in the budget with an initial state contribution of $1 billion, which partners would double or triple.
"How will this work further? A simplified procedure. Compensation within 30 days after processing. And the tariff for this insurance risk must be very basic, symbolic, we are aiming at approximately 2%. And the maximum damage compensation will be about $5 million in one hand," the Prime Minister detailed.
Koretsky also stated that there is currently no consensus or support for increasing the Value Added Tax (VAT) from 20% to 21% to fund this special fund.
"There is no consensus among big and medium business, there is no support in parliament yet. We are looking for other mechanisms, we will see how the budgetary process proceeds in parliament and build from that. But we have no other path, we must find the instrument. Together we will see what we can contribute," Koretsky emphasized.

Iraqi security forces on Oct. 26 have taken control of key military positions held by the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS), a group affiliated with the PKK terrorist organization, as the group prepares to disarm and integrate into Iraq’s security institutions.
The handover is part of a broader process to bring the group’s members, weapons and military positions under state control, according to statements by Iraqi authorities.
Iraq’s Security Media Cell announced that the transfer of military positions in the Sinjar district began, confirming that Iraqi security forces took over several key sites previously held by the YBS. Additional positions were expected to be handed over later on Oct. 26.
A ceremony scheduled for Oct. 26 on Mount Sinjar will mark a new phase in the process, with around 2,000 YBS members expected to lay down their arms.
A further 3,000 to 4,000 members are expected to disarm in subsequent stages, while YBS personnel will be distributed among the Iraqi army, police and the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), also known as al-Hashd al-Shaabi, an Iraqi state-sponsored paramilitary umbrella organization.
Sabah al-Numan, military spokesman for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, said the process would also involve reorganizing the group’s military ties with Iraqi security forces and transferring responsibility for security on Mount Sinjar to the relevant federal authorities.
Al-Numan said the initiative was part of the government’s policy to bring all weapons under state control, adding that Iraq’s Constitution prohibits the formation of armed groups outside the country’s official armed forces.
The developments come amid broader efforts by Ankara and Baghdad to strengthen state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of unauthorized armed groups.
Türkiye and Iraq agreed on Sept. 23 to restore full state authority in Sinjar and end the presence of banned foreign armed groups, according to a joint statement issued after Turkish President Recep Tayyip 
Erdoğan met Iraqi al-Zaidi on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Under the agreement, Turkish forces are to gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan military compound to Iraq’s federal government, in line with progress on Baghdad’s security measures and an agreed mechanism and timetable.
The move also comes as Türkiye continues its “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, aimed at ending the PKK’s terror in the country. While the disarmament process is ongoing, Ankara has called for a broader regional approach, urging that all groups affiliated with the PKK across the region should lay down their arms.

The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) Executive Committee on Sunday firmly rejected any plans to lay off large numbers of staff at the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA), calling on donor countries to provide adequate and sustainable funding.
The committee discussed the issue at a meeting in Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, following remarks on Friday by Riyad Zeighan, head of the General Conference of Local Staff Unions at UNRWA, who said the agency planned to lay off large numbers of employees across its areas of operation due to a lack of funding.
The committee called for urgent international action to provide about $70 million to cover immediate funding needs and ensure UNRWA staff receive their salaries in November and December.
In a statement, the committee said the meeting had addressed the “existential challenges facing refugees” and UNRWA’s plans to lay off staff and cut services.
It strongly rejected any plans to lay off large numbers of UNRWA employees across its areas of operation and warned that the financial crisis could undermine the agency’s ability to continue providing services and fulfil its UN mandate.
The committee said UNRWA staff formed the backbone of the agency and that laying them off would not resolve the financial crisis. Instead, it would threaten the continuation of education, healthcare, relief and social protection services provided to millions of Palestinian refugees.
It warned that cuts to these services would increase the humanitarian and social burden on refugee camps, threatening regional stability.
