Frozen Russian assets key to covering Ukraine's 2027 financing needs – National Bank governor
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
13:13:04 EET
20:13:04 KST

The issue of immobilized Russian assets is being discussed in the context of the need to find confirmed sources of financing to cover the "gap" in the state budget for 2027, which Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky estimated at $32.6 billion at the Ukraine Ministerial Roundtable on October 14 during the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) Governor Andriy Pyshnyy said.
"Currently, the IMF chief [Kristalina Georgieva] has confirmed the need for assurances from partners regarding coverage of this 'gap,' which has been verified by the IMF. The IMF is also considering, in this context, the use of immobilized assets in a way that European partners would consider acceptable to them, in order to ensure that Ukraine receives the necessary amount of financing," Pyshnyy said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings.
According to him, the IMF always discusses this issue very cautiously, recognizing that its mandate and influence are limited.
"But the IMF is involved in discussions on the format for accessing immobilized assets. For example, the Fund may recommend paying attention to a factor such as debt sustainability, so that the use of immobilized assets does not create additional interest-rate pressure for Ukraine. As for how exactly this will be structured, that will be determined by the European bureaucracy," the NBU governor explained.
He said he was optimistic about the possibility of continuing to use immobilized Russian assets to finance Ukraine and mentioned the evolution of the IMF's and the European Central Bank's positions on the issue.
"This issue requires complex, comprehensive communication on the part of the president, the government and the National Bank. You have seen how many meetings I have had here: over these past few days, I have held dozens of discussions with partners. This issue remains one of our priorities," Pyshnyy said.
As reported, in 2024, the G7 established the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) mechanism, providing Ukraine with $50 billion in unconditional, non-repayable financing based on discounting future cash flows from the further investment of Russian assets immobilized in Europe, primarily at Euroclear, totaling approximately EUR 200 billion. Most of the $50 billion is scheduled to be disbursed in 2025–2026, while only $1.4 billion is allocated for 2027.
In addition, after the idea of a EUR 140 billion reparations loan for the EU backed by the same proceeds from frozen Russian assets fell through in autumn 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan (USL), a EUR 90 billion mechanism for 2026–2027 to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine. This is also non-repayable assistance to Ukraine; however, the allocation of part of the funding for budget financing is tied to Kyiv's fulfillment of reform conditions.
The 2027 state budget currently provides for $52.6 billion in external financing, of which only approximately $20 billion comes from confirmed sources. In mid-October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, taking defense spending into account, estimated Ukraine's total additional financing needs for 2027 at EUR 70 billion while in Brussels.
As part of efforts to secure these funds, according to available information, consideration is being given to launching ERA-2 and/or USL-2 mechanisms by continuing to discount future cash flows from Russian Federation assets immobilized for a longer period or investing them in higher-yielding assets.

Trump officials back Orbán bid for UN secretary-general, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:11:58 UTC
20:11:58 KST

Trump administration officials are reportedly floating former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for UN secretary-general, potentially backed by the US, Russia and China, though nothing is confirmed and his selection remains uncertain.
Officials in the Trump administration are advocating the nomination of former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for the post of UN secretary-general, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.
The newspaper reports that Orbán could be a joint American, Russian and Chinese candidate, and that sources in all three countries have confirmed the Trump administration is backing his bid.
Orbán lost power in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar’s Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of governing with an absolute majority.
His hard-right, fiercely anti-migration and eurosceptic policies, together with the rule of law backsliding in Hungary, strained relations with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. Nevertheless, Orbán maintained close ties with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Since the election, Hungarian authorities have launched fraud and corruption investigations into several members of Orbán’s former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary’s National Bank are under arrest, and authorities could also examine Orbán’s potential involvement in those cases.
According to the WSJ, no final decision has been taken on the plan. A US State Department official admitted that the idea sounds crazy at first, but said previous talks with Washington suggest Russia and China also support it. The aim is for Orbán to be the joint candidate of the three countries.
“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper. The second five-year term of the current secretary-general, António Guterres, ends on 31 December.
The White House, and Beijing have not confirmed the information.
According to Russian deputy foreign minister Aleksandr Alimov, the US, China or Russia will not nominate Orbán, as permanent members of the UN's Security Council can not do so.
"Neither Russia, the United States, nor China will nominate Orbán because we are permanent members of the UN Security Council and we do not nominate anyone for the position of UN Secretary-General," Alimov told the Interfax news agency, adding that if press reports are true, those behind the idea need to find a nominating country.
"We will discuss all the people officially nominated for the post of Secretary General" Alimov noted.
Euronews has contacted Orbán’s spokesperson for comment but has not yet received a response. The spokesperson previously dismissed press reports about Orbán’s candidacy for the post of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.
In May, the VSquare investigative newsletter reported that a UN position could be important for the former prime minister because of the diplomatic immunity attached to the role.
According to the WSJ, Orbán would only run if his victory were assured, a scenario that currently seems unlikely.
A candidate must secure the support of at least nine of the 15 Security Council members, while any of the five permanent members can veto the nomination. Besides the US, Russia and China, France and the United Kingdom are also permanent members.
Two European governments have already spoken out against the idea of putting forward Orbán as a potential candidate.
"I do not foresee Poland supporting Viktor Orbán's candidacy for UN Secretary-General," Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said in a social media post.
His Ukrainian counterpart, Andrij Sbyha, also posted on X, saying:
"Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions."

Israel, but not in Palestine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:11:49 UTC
20:11:49 KST

Argentina, 1896
In ‘The Jewish State’, Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, proposed Palestine and Argentina as possible locations for a Jewish state, citing Argentina’s fertile land and Palestine’s historical significance to Jews.
Cyprus, 1901–1902
Herzl and other Zionist leaders explored establishing a Jewish settlement in then British-controlled Cyprus, but the idea never became an approved proposal.
Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, 1902–1903
Herzl negotiated with British authorities to establish a settlement near El Arish. The plan depended on Nile water but failed to win Egyptian approval.
British East Africa, 1903
British Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain proposed territory in present-day Kenya. The Zionist Congress agreed to study the “Uganda Scheme”, but rejected it in 1905 after fierce divisions.
Angola, 1907–1913
The Jewish Territorialist Organisation, led by Israel Zangwill, explored alternatives to Palestine. Angola, then a Portuguese colony, was considered but the plan never materialised.
Palestine, 1947
UN Resolution 181 proposed dividing then British-ruled Palestine into Arab and Jewish states, with Jerusalem under international administration. Zionist leaders accepted the plan, while Palestinian Arab leaders and Arab states rejected it. Israel was declared a state in 1948.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:11:03 UTC
20:11:03 KST

Russia will not slow its offensive against Ukraine despite plans to resume US-brokered peace talks, but Moscow is open to localized humanitarian ceasefires, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday, Oct. 26.
Asked whether Russia would consider temporary truces along the front line, Peskov told reporters: “For humanitarian purposes, absolutely.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
His remarks come ahead of a localized ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region, intended to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The agreement, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, is scheduled to take effect on Oct. 29, according to the White House. Russian and Ukrainian officials are coordinating the operation.
However, Peskov made clear that the arrangement would not signal a broader halt to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“The decision to resume trilateral talks does not imply any restrictions on combat operations,” he said.
“Our armed forces continue to carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial complex,” he added.
Oleshky сeasefire aims to evacuate civilians
Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city on the left bank of the Dnipro River opposite Kherson, has faced a worsening humanitarian crisis, with residents reporting severe shortages of food, clean water, and medicine.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, the city had a population of about 24,000. The White House estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 people remain, including elderly residents and around 50 children.
It’s About Security, Stupid!
The temporary truce is intended to allow humanitarian supplies into the city and establish a safe passage for civilians who want to leave. Residents will be able to choose whether to evacuate to Ukrainian-controlled territory or Russia, according to the White House.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, who led Kyiv’s negotiating team, confirmed the agreement and said the operation would be implemented in stages.
Melania Trump said she worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to coordinate the arrangement. Her involvement builds on previous efforts to reunite Ukrainian children separated from their families during Russia’s war.
Russia intensifies attacks as talks approach
The latest diplomatic push follows meetings between US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
The envoys had held consultations with Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo the previous day.
On Sunday, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US after Nov. 4, following Russia’s National Unity Day holiday.
“After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations,” Ushakov said, according to Russian state media.
He cautioned against expecting an immediate breakthrough, describing the next round as an opportunity to explore the parties’ positions rather than reach a final agreement.
Working-level delegations could meet in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland to prepare for further discussions.
Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to bring the sides closer to a settlement. Moscow continues to demand additional Ukrainian territory and sweeping restrictions on Kyiv’s military and political independence.
Ukraine and its allies have rejected those demands as unacceptable, warning that concessions imposed under pressure could leave the country vulnerable to another Russian attack.

International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

International parcels drop by 32% after EU imposes surcharge
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of parcels sent from outside the EU dropped by one-third in the last three months, mainly as a result of tighter EU restrictions, postal service PostNL said in its latest quarterly report.
The company said the 32% drop mainly reflected a drop in packages being sent from Asia after the bloc imposed a €3 surcharge per product on July 1.
It follows a 15% dip in the second quarter of the year and PostNL expects the trend to continue after the import fees are raised by a further €2 from next month.
The impact was partly offset by a 40% increase in parcels within the EU compared to the third quarter last year as Asian websites lost trade to European rivals because of result of the new measures.
But PostNL said that growth was “more than wiped out” by the drop in deliveries from further afield.
Three-day deliveries
The company’s turnover increased in the third quarter by €6 million to €768 million after the government relaxed the rules on deliveries.
Since July PostNL has been required to deliver letters within two days rather than 24 hours and the deadline is due to be stretched to three days next July.
CEO Pim Berendsen said the move to three-day deliveries was an important “interim step” towards ensuring the postal service could survive in the long term, but also renewed his calls for the government to compensate the company’s losses in recent years.
“Until we have a future-proofed regulatory framework, the uncertainty for thousands of our postal workers, customers and consumers will continue,” he said. “This situation requires a structural solution.”

RSF drone strikes damage 5 power substations, cause blackout in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:10:15 UTC
20:10:15 KST

Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Sudan Electricity Holding Company said Monday that drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted five power substations, causing extensive damage and a complete blackout across the country’s southeast.
In a statement, the company said the strikes targeted substations in Singa, Al-Hawata, Al-Faw, Mashkur and Al-Junaid in central and southeastern Sudan.
“The attacks caused significant damage to components of the facilities and completely cut electricity from the southeastern grid, affecting Sennar, Gedaref, White Nile and Gezira states,” said the statement cited by local media.
It warned that the damage also threatened the stability of Sudan’s national electricity grid.
“Engineering and technical teams were dispatched to the affected substations to assess the damage and begin repairs aimed at restoring electricity and stabilizing the grid as soon as possible,” it added.
The daily Sudan Tribune said an RSF drone struck the Al-Junaid power substation in eastern Gezira state early Monday, knocking it out of service and cutting electricity to the area.
The outlet said RSF drones also attempted to strike strategic fuel depots in Umm Aliyla in eastern Gezira without causing damage. The facility had been targeted in September, when a drone attack sparked a fire at one of its storage units.
In Sennar, the state government said an RSF drone struck the Singa power substation, causing material damage and injuring members of the facility’s guard team.
Drones also targeted the Al-Faw and Al-Hawata substations in Gedaref state, cutting electricity supplies, while another drone struck the Mashkur substation in White Nile state, causing a local power outage.
The RSF has intensified drone attacks in recent days against fuel storage facilities and electricity infrastructure in North Kordofan, Gedaref, Gezira and White Nile states amid escalating fighting with army forces.
The army and the RSF have been at war since April 2023 following disputes over integrating the paramilitary group into the military. The conflict has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million people, fueling one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Source: broadcast of the Verkhovna Rada plenary session on 26 October

Without security guarantees, this war will not truly end; we will not be able to recognise that it has ended, because there would remain a risk of renewed aggression from such a neighbour."

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:54 UTC
20:01:54 KST

From army exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox to a stalled 7 October inquiry, the issues splitting voters have little to do with Gaza, Lebanon or Iran.
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday in the country’s first national election since Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack, a vote that is shaping up as a verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Yet for a country that has spent three years fighting on several fronts, the campaign has been strikingly quiet on how those wars were fought.
Israel’s conduct in Gaza, which led to an international arrest warrant for Netanyahu, has barely been debated. Nor have its occupation of much of southern Lebanon and parts of Syria, or the two wars it launched against Iran. All enjoy broad support among Jewish Israelis.
The main contenders have instead argued over Netanyahu himself: his character, his responsibility for the security failures of 7 October, military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men and his 2023 attempt to overhaul the judiciary.
There is also little to separate the two main blocs on the Palestinian question. Both are dominated by parties that back Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank and oppose a Palestinian state, and no leading candidate is calling for a revival of the peace process.
The shadow of 7 October
Reminders of the war are everywhere. Stickers bearing the faces of fallen soldiers line train stations, alongside fading yellow ribbons for the hostages, the last of whom came home under a ceasefire deal last year.
According to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), a Jerusalem-based think tank, around 68% of Jewish Israelis say their views on 7 October are central to how they will vote. Among Arab citizens, the figure is 32%, with most naming crime as their main concern.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has pointed to military gains against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran while placing blame for the 7 October failures on the security establishment.
His critics say he has dodged accountability by blocking an official state inquiry. They also accuse him of delaying a hostage deal and of failing to secure a decisive victory on any front.
Who serves in the army?
The issue that has stirred the most anger is conscription. Military service is compulsory for most Jewish Israelis, but Netanyahu’s coalitions have long depended on ultra-Orthodox parties that insist yeshiva students be exempt.
Resentment has grown as reservists have been called up repeatedly and the army struggles with a manpower shortage. Around 13,000 ultra-Orthodox men turn 18 each year, but fewer than one in ten enlist.
About a quarter of Jewish voters told the IDI the issue would weigh on their choice. IDI president Yohanan Plesner said it was “probably the number one issue” for the anti-Netanyahu camp.
The IDI’s Tamar Hermann said many Israelis see military service as a “kind of permit to citizenship”.
Netanyahu’s main challenger, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to end the de facto exemptions. Eisenkot, a centrist, lost his son and two nephews in the fighting in Gaza.
Judicial overhaul fades as an issue
The judicial overhaul brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets in 2023 and left Israel deeply divided when Hamas attacked. Netanyahu cast it as a check on unelected judges. Opponents saw a power grab by a leader under indictment on corruption charges, which he denies.
After 7 October, much of that protest movement turned its energy towards demanding the hostages’ release. Today, only 18% of Jewish Israelis say the overhaul will shape their vote, a sign of what Hermann described as “public fatigue”. It matters more on the left, where 22.5% cite it.
A law passed last year giving the government more say in judicial appointments will only take effect once the next Knesset is sworn in. The opposition bloc has promised to scrap it.
Coalition arithmetic
Israelis vote for party lists rather than individual candidates, and no party is expected to come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The next prime minister will be whoever can assemble a governing coalition. If no one can, Netanyahu will stay on as caretaker until yet another election.
More than a quarter of Jewish voters say the party leader is a decisive factor. Netanyahu’s backers see a seasoned statesman who has stood up to US presidents and refused concessions they believe would endanger Israel. His detractors see him as corrupt.
Eisenkot’s supporters cite his decades in uniform and his personal losses. The son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, he would become Israel’s first prime minister of non-European heritage, though he has not campaigned on it.
The missing economic debate
Living costs are a major concern but have barely featured. Research by Sarit Menahem-Carmi of Reichman University’s Aaron Institute for Economic Policy found that Israel is now more expensive than wealthy European countries such as Austria, Denmark and Sweden.
The IDI found 38% of Jewish Israelis rank the economy as their first or second priority, rising to 46% among Arab citizens. Netanyahu credits his policies with fuelling growth and a thriving tech sector, while opponents say many have been left behind.
None of the leading candidates has put the cost of the wars at the centre of their campaign. Joseph Zeira, an economics professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, warned that heavy military spending cannot be ignored. “The cost of the conflict is tremendous,” he said.

Kremlin Signals Desire to Maintain Ties With Serbia After Vučić Ousted by Student Movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:37 UTC
20:01:37 KST

The Kremlin said Monday that it wants to maintain and develop ties with Serbia despite the defeat of former President Aleksandar Vučić’s ruling coalition in this weekend’s parliamentary elections, while noting that building those relations will require effort from both sides.
“We deeply value the contribution that Mr. Vučić has made to the development of our bilateral relations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters at a daily briefing.
“We know that he will remain on the political stage, and we hope that even in opposition, he will continue to contribute to advancing our ties,” Peskov added.
Vučić, who dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade as prime minister and then later as president, conceded defeat on Sunday night following a historic snap election. The vote pitted his ruling coalition against a student-led movement that had spent months protesting against his government.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade.
The defeat followed Vučić’s resignation as president in September, a risky political maneuver intended to allow him to reclaim the prime minister post. It also came after nearly two years of anti-government demonstrations triggered by the November 2024 roof collapse at the Novi Sad railway station, an accident that killed 16 people and sparked widespread outrage over state corruption.
During his tenure, Vučić balanced Serbia’s candidacy for EU membership with a refusal to join Western sanctions against Russia over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. He had remained one of the few European leaders to maintain direct contact with the Kremlin and make official visits to Moscow.
Peskov said Monday that Moscow hopes the incoming government in Belgrade will work “constructively” to preserve bilateral relations since, in its view, doing so would bring “tangible benefits to Serbia itself.”
“For our part, we intend to continue doing everything possible to foster our relations with Belgrade. But as you know, it takes two to tango,” he said.
Jovo Bakić, a representative of the Student List, told the Kremlin-backed broadcaster RT Balkan that the incoming government would not impose sanctions on Moscow or abandon Russian gas supplies despite pressure from the European Union.
He argued that sanctions imposed by a country of Serbia’s size would change little but would send a negative signal symbolically.
“We respect Russia as a great power and as a historically important partner, and in many cases as a protector,” Bakić said. “There will be no changes on this issue.”
Reuters and AFP contributed reporting.

Poland eyes more cooperation with Germany in space, Polish minister says
WARSAW, Oct 26 - Poland sees a lot of room to deepen cooperation with Germany in the space sector, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said on Monday, underscoring the need to possess sovereign technology in order to bolster security in the face of external pressures.
• "We need to invest in technologies ... that are not available right now in Europe, but are absolutely critical for our joint security," Domanski said, naming the space industry, during a joint panel with Germany's Economy Minister Katherina Reiche.
• "Together with our German partners I see lots of room for cooperation, thanks to which we'll be more resilient from some external pressure that can appear one day," he said, answering a question on how Poland and Germany could respond to competition from China and the U.S. in global trade.
• Domanski said security started in space and questioned how countries could defend themselves not having their own satellites, without which they were "blind".
• Domanski also said that Poland had decided to double its investment in the space sector.
• "We believe it's not only a very efficient way of spending money – from each euro invested you get 6-7 euros back, but that's also about our security and resilience. And we see room for further cooperation with German counterparts," Domanski said. REUTERS

Gyurov Sweeps Sofia and Most of Europe as Yotova Dominates Bulgaria's Provinces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

Andrey Gyurov leads in Sofia and among Bulgarian voters across most of Europe, while presidential candidate Iliana Yotova dominates in most Bulgarian provinces and Kostadin Kostadinov tops the vote in Russia, according to Central Election Commission (CEC) results from Bulgaria’s October 25 presidential election.
With 98.99% of polling station protocols processed by Regional Election Commissions, the results show that Yotova and Gyurov will face each other in a runoff in a week, following low turnout in the first round.
Yotova and running mate Kiril Valchev lead in the provinces, except for the 16th Multi-Member Electoral District, which covers the municipality of Plovdiv, where Gyurov and Georgi Kandev are in first place. Support for the candidates varies considerably from one region to another.
Gyurov leads in all three electoral districts of Sofia-City, with a substantial advantage over Yotova. In the 23rd district, he received 88,681 votes against her 35,767, while in the 24th district he secured 52,493 compared with 24,764 for Yotova. All protocols in both districts have been processed.
In the 25th district, where 99.81% of protocols had been counted at the time of reporting, Gyurov was also ahead, with 37,762 votes to Yotova’s 28,273.
The contest was much closer in Varna, where Yotova received 33,199 votes and Gyurov 31,364. In Plovdiv Province, Yotova led with 22,073 votes against 13,184 for Gyurov. The result was reversed in the municipality of Plovdiv, where Gyurov won 30,306 votes and Yotova received 24,608.
Yotova recorded a much wider lead in several other provinces. In Haskovo, she won 20,039 votes, compared with 7,768 for Gyurov. In Kardzhali, her total was 9,896 against his 4,953, while in Vratsa she received 13,242 votes to Gyurov’s 5,835. In Pleven, Yotova secured 18,274 votes, compared with 9,414 for Gyurov.
In Yambol, Yotova led with 8,886 votes. The battle for second place between Gyurov, who received 3,934 votes, and Kostadinov, with 3,354, was separated by less than three percentage points.
Among Bulgarian voters abroad, Yotova led in Turkey, receiving 3,933 votes against Gyurov’s 1,893. Turnout there was exceptionally low: around 7,000 people voted, compared with more than 27,000 in the parliamentary election less than a year earlier.
Yotova also led in Moldova, where she received 402 votes to Gyurov’s 216. She came first in Kosovo, Albania and North Macedonia, and won in Montenegro, where fewer than 20 people voted. Gyurov, meanwhile, led in Serbia and Romania.
Across most of the rest of Europe, Gyurov held a strong advantage. In Germany, with 99.84% of polling station protocols processed, he received 6,376 votes, compared with 2,630 for Yotova. In Spain, he won 2,521 votes against her 1,903.
Gyurov, who was backed by PP-DB, also led in France, with 1,469 votes to Yotova’s 417, and in Italy, where he received 1,254 votes against 521. In the United Kingdom, Gyurov secured 5,178 votes, while Yotova received 2,771.
Russia was an exception to the broader European pattern, with Kostadin Kostadinov taking first place in a vote in which approximately 200 people participated.
In the United States, Gyurov won 3,207 votes, far ahead of Yotova’s 871. Kostadinov placed third with 647 votes. Gyurov also led in Canada, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, China, Japan, Singapore, Kuwait, New Zealand and Australia.
The overall overseas results showed Gyurov and Kandev in first place, with 36,681 votes, or 45.61%, followed by Yotova and Valchev with 18,402 votes, or 22.88%. Their difference was 18,279 votes, close to 23 percentage points.
Kostadinov and Petar Volgin ranked third among overseas voters, receiving 9,352 votes, or 11.63%. Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva followed with 5,220 votes, or 6.49%, while Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov received 3,015 votes, or 3.75%.
The CEC figures for the overseas vote were reported as of 8 a.m. on October 26, with 99.35% of protocols from polling stations abroad processed.

stefan sagmeister’s artworks turn global data into good news at la gaîté lyrique

stefan sagmeister’s artworks turn global data into good news at la gaîté lyrique
finally, something good reframes metrics across health, democracy, and equality, inviting visitors to look beyond prevalent cynicism and view our era through data-driven optimism.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
‘FINALLY, SOMETHING GOOD’ FRAMES HARD DATA TO DRIVE OPTIMISM
Thirteen years after ‘The Happy Show’, Stefan Sagmeister returns to Paris’ La Gaîté Lyrique with his solo exhibition, ‘Finally, Something Good’, on view through April 18, 2027. Arriving at a pivotal moment marked by global pandemics, environmental crises, and political instability, the showcase directly confronts the relentless stream of short-term negative news and algorithm-driven outrage. Stepping back to examine broad historical patterns, Sagmeister uses visual design to demonstrate that human progress becomes undeniable when viewed across extended timeframes.
His work draws on centuries of data from the United Nations, the World Bank, and global archives. The empirical evidence reveals a clear trend: across health, democracy, and equality, global conditions have improved dramatically over time. Converting these complex datasets into tangible visual experiences, the exhibition invites visitors to shift focus away from short-term headlines and consider our era with fresh eyes.
STEFAN SAGMEISTER AND LA GAÎTÉ LYRIQUE LINK BEAUTY WITH ACTION
A two-time Grammy Award winner, the designer has long bridged graphic design, fine art, and human philosophy through album covers, public installations, and research on happiness and beauty. Guided by the belief that design should either inform or delight, he asserts that pairing aesthetic beauty with empirical data makes abstract statistics emotionally resonant.
‘There’s something almost perverse about being an optimist right now—the culture has decided that pessimism is the serious position,’ Sagmeister reflects. ‘I embedded these facts into 18th-century paintings because I think beauty and evidence, rarely combined, are more devastatingly strong together than either is alone.’ Hosted within La Gaîté Lyrique as part of its Factory of Our Times project, the exhibition aligns with the institution’s mission to address urgent cultural, democratic, and climate challenges through creative activism.
MATERIAL SYNTHESIS TAKES OVER TWELVE CHAPTERS
Spanning eleven thematic chapters across every floor of La Gaîté Lyrique, spilling into hallways and infiltrating even the restrooms, where no visitor escapes data-driven optimism, the exhibition transforms the venue into an immersive spatial takeover designed for active reflection. Sagmeister overlays historical 18th- and 19th-century oil paintings with bold geometric color fields, visualizing long-term metrics across conflicts, nutrition, healthcare access, climate, migration, and happiness. The showcase offers an essential opportunity to step back from the often exhausting nature of daily news, reminding us that social and political movements do change society over time, even if progress feels slow and indirect.
Beyond two-dimensional canvases, complex indices like the Gini Index and carbon reduction strategies are translated into physical forms using arranged produce, 18th-century Alpine sculptures, and monumental dark figures. Combined with projections detailing centuries of unfulfilled apocalyptic predictions and an engagement program co-developed with makesense and Studio 13/16, the project turns statistical evidence into a compelling material presence. Paralleling this artistic approach, the initiative aligns directly with La Gaîté Lyrique’s daily commitment to empowering new creative talents, breaking down barriers between disciplines and audiences, and building transformative cultural perspectives across Europe.
project info:
name: Finally, Something Good
exhibitor: Stefan Sagmeister | @stefansagmeister
location: La Gaîté Lyrique, Paris
date: until April 18, 2027

‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:00:42 UTC
20:00:42 KST

US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.
In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”
Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.
These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.
Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.
Inflation
The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.
In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.
That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.
The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.
It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.
Gas prices
In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.
Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.
Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.
Monthly job figures
The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.
Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.
S&P 500
Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.
Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.
While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.
Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.
Interest rates
Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.
For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.
When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.
Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.
For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.
Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

Restrictions on demining introduced near the front line and the border with Russia

Restrictions on demining introduced near the front line and the border with Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Due to security risks, new operations near the front line and the border have been restricted in six regions. Ongoing demining will continue where possible.
Due to security risks, the planning of new humanitarian demining operations has been restricted in certain areas of six regions. This does not mean that demining has been halted. The Ministry of Defence stated this on October 26, UNN reports.
Details
"The decision of the National Mine Action Authority concerns certain areas in the Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv and Sumy regions within 20–50 km of the line of contact and the border with the aggressor state, where operations have not yet begun," the Ministry of Defence said.
According to the report, "where demining is already underway, the operations must be completed if the situation allows and they do not interfere with the tasks of the Defence Forces."
"Within the 50-kilometre zone, priority will be given to emergency response measures necessary for the evacuation of the population; emergency rescue operations; providing access to shelters; medical and humanitarian assistance; and responding to threats from explosive ordnance," the defence ministry said.
According to the ministry, the possibility of conducting unscheduled humanitarian demining also remains available upon justified requests.
"The decision will be reviewed depending on the security situation," the Ministry of Defence emphasised.
"Humanitarian demining remains a priority even in frontline areas. But we must act on the basis of a risk-oriented approach in order to find a balance between the safety of the people carrying out demining and the needs of communities in frontline areas," commented Vasyl Shkurakov, Deputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine .
The restrictions introduced do not provide for the cessation of humanitarian demining in frontline areas

Syria to launch first nationwide map of mine-contaminated areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:58:27 UTC
19:58:27 KST

Syria will soon launch its first map showing the distribution of mines across the country as part of a three-year strategy to address landmines and remnants of war, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al Saleh said on Monday.
“The National Mine Action Center is implementing the strategy to identify mine-contaminated areas and strengthen efforts to address the threat,” al Saleh said in comments carried by the ISNA news agency.
Mines and unexploded remnants of war remain among Syria’s most serious challenges because of their impact on civilians and children, as well as the obstacles they pose to reconstruction and the use of agricultural land, he said.
Al Saleh said his ministry continued to develop mine-clearance plans despite existing challenges, aiming to protect civilians and enable residents to use their farmland safely.
Syria is also working with Germany and Ukraine to exchange expertise and benefit from advanced demining technologies, he added.
Joint operations room with Türkiye
Separately, al Saleh said the ministry was working to establish a joint operations room with Türkiye to coordinate emergency response and disaster management on both sides of the border.
The mechanism is intended to speed up coordination and responses to fires, floods and other disasters, he said.
Syrian authorities regularly report deaths and injuries caused by explosions involving remnants of the war waged by the Bashar al Assad regime against civilians between 2011 and 2024.
The conflict killed and injured hundreds of thousands of people and caused widespread infrastructure damage before opposition fighters entered Damascus on December 8, 2024, bringing down the Assad regime.
Syrian authorities and international organisations, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, continue operations in several parts of the country to detect mines and unexploded ordnance left by the war.
According to Landmine Monitor data, unexploded ordnance in Syria has killed or injured more than 13,000 people since 2011.

Algeria to Deploy Troops Abroad for First Time Since 1973, Sending Forces to Niger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:58:27 UTC
19:58:27 KST

Algeria’s two parliamentary chambers approved on October 25 the deployment of the country’s armed forces to Niger to protect Algeria’s energy interests and honor bilateral agreements.
Algeria’s Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, made the announcement.
The decision was approved in closed-door sessions after President Abdelmadjid Tebboune submitted a request on October 22.
The lower house of parliament, the National People’s Assembly, also approved the troop deployment by an overwhelming majority.
According to an official statement by the Council of the Nation, the decision aims to protect Algeria’s energy interests and fulfill the terms of a bilateral agreement with Niger.
Algerian authorities have not yet disclosed the size of the military contingent, the exact deployment date, or the duration of the planned mission.
According to Reuters, one possible deployment site for Algerian troops is the Madama area in northern Niger, near the border with Libya.
Algeria has significant economic interests in Niger, particularly in oil production and the development of transcontinental energy projects.
The state-owned company Sonatrach is developing the Kafra oil project in northern Niger. In August 2026, its subsidiary ENAFOR was preparing to drill the Kafra Sud-Est 1 exploration well, approximately 85 km from the Algerian border.
Algeria, Niger, and Nigeria are also pursuing the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project, which aims to transport natural gas from Nigeria through Niger to Algeria.
In June 2026, Sonatrach announced the start of construction on the pipeline’s Algerian section.
In August, Militarnyi reported that Algeria had deployed four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger following an attempted military coup in the country’s capital, Niamey.

South Korean firm signs air defence deals with four Lithuanian companies
Unknown

10:58:00 UTC

South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace has signed memorandums of understanding with four Lithuanian companies to cooperate on producing and integrating air defence systems, the companies and the Lithuanian Defence and Security Industry Association said on Monday.
The memorandums cover four areas of cooperation related to the 40mm wheeled anti-aircraft gun (WAAG) system.
Potential vehicle integration will be explored with KMT, turret hull and cable production with Cosmos Construction and T&G Lithuania, and the integration of command and control systems into NATO networks with Nortal.
The WAAG is a mobile air defence system designed to counter low-flying targets, including drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles. It combines automated fire control and target-tracking technologies with 40mm ammunition.
Robert Park, senior vice president of Hanwha Aerospace, said in a press release the company aims to build “long-term industrial partnerships” with Lithuanian companies, focusing on technology transfer, joint solution development and system maintenance throughout their lifecycle.
Park added that the company also aims to support Lithuania's ambition to become a regional hub for defence industry manufacturing and maintenance in the Baltic region.

November 2026 travel guide: Where to go, what to see and the new hotels to book in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:57:33 UTC
19:57:33 KST

From early Christmas markets in Vienna to late-autumn sunshine in the Canary Islands, November offers plenty of reasons to plan a European escape before the festive rush.
November can sometimes be an awkward month for travel. The days are shorter, the weather is less predictable, and much of Europe is firmly between autumn and winter.
However, that all tends to equal fewer crowds, plenty of cultural events and, by the end of the month, the first signs of Christmas appearing across European cities.
From early festive markets in Vienna to food and wine in Portugal, a major marathon in Athens and winter sun in Fuerteventura, there are still plenty of reasons to get away.
Here’s Euronews Travel’s guide for where to go, what to see and where to stay this November.
Destinations
Vienna, Austria
If you want to get into the Christmas spirit without waiting until December, Vienna is one of the best places to start.
The Austrian capital's Christmas markets begin opening early in the month, with both the Schönbrunn Palace and Stephansplatz markets opening on 6 November. The most famous market, Rathausplatz, follows on 13 November.
When you’ve had your fill of mulled wine and Christmas lights, November is a great time to explore Vienna's museums, grand coffee houses and palaces without the summer crowds.
Make sure to check out both the Belvedere and Hofburg palaces and head to the Kunsthistorisches Museum, which is filled with European old masters and Habsburg art treasures.
Fuerteventura, Canary Islands, Spain
For those who would rather avoid the cold altogether, the Canary Islands remain one of Europe's safest bets for some late-autumn sunshine.
Fuerteventura is particularly appealing in November, when its beaches, volcanic landscapes and enormous dunes can be explored without the intensity of the summer heat – and it’s one of the most affordable islands in the Canaries, too.
For those who suffer from seasonal depression, the sun sets in the Canary Islands later than in most places in mainland Europe, so it’s ideal for staying cheerful as the winter sets in.
There's also a new reason to stay here. The Elba Corralejo Resort & Spa is opening on 1 November, bringing with it 478 rooms, a staggering 20 swimming pools, restaurants and extensive wellness and family facilities.
Hotel openings
Casa Verbena Madrid, Spain
Hilton's new Outset Collection is making its European debut in Madrid with Casa Verbena Madrid.
The 45-room hotel is set on Calle de Preciados, a pedestrianised shopping street in the heart of the Spanish capital, within walking distance of Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor and the Royal Palace.
It is designed by Spanish interior designer Lorenzo Castillo, with boutique rooms drawing on Spanish architecture and culture.
Hotel Maastricht-Maas, Netherlands
Maastricht is getting a new four-star-plus hotel this November, with the Van der Valk Exclusief Hotel Maastricht-Maas celebrating its grand opening on the banks of the River Maas.
The 113-room property has a contemporary design with South American influences, alongside a restaurant, bar, meeting spaces and a fifth-floor panoramic wellness area.
It is also within easy reach of Maastricht's historic centre, making it a useful base for exploring the buzzy Dutch city.
Events and attractions
Berlin Science Week, Berlin, Germany
Germany’s capital gets particularly cerebral in early November, when Berlin Science Week takes place from 1-10 November.
This year's theme is “In Touch”, exploring how science affects everyday life through exhibitions, workshops, talks, performances and events across the city.
A public weekend from 6-8 November is one of the highlights, making this a good option for anyone who wants something a little different from the usual museum-and-gallery city break.
Athens Marathon The Authentic, Athens, Greece
November is a particularly good month to visit Athens if you like your city breaks with a bit of sporting drama.
The 43rd Athens Marathon, the Authentic, takes place on 7 and 8 November, following the historic route from Marathon to the Panathenaic Stadium.
Even if you're not running, it's a chance to see one of the world's most famous marathon routes and enjoy Athens at a time when summer's heat has disappeared.
International Hot Air Balloon Festival, Alentejo, Portugal
The Alentejo region of Portugal is set to gain tonnes of popularity next year, thanks to its appearance in countless travel experts’ trend predictions.
To experience it for yourself before it blows up as a destination, why not visit the International Hot Air Balloon Festival taking place there from 7-12 November.
The festival, which has been running since 1997, will feature balloon flights, public displays and opportunities to see the colourful aircraft filling the skies over the Alentejo landscape.
While you’re there, you could head to Borba, which will host its annual Vine and Wine Festival from 11-15 November, bringing together wine tastings, regional food, entertainment, crafts and local producers.
Planning ahead: Christmas markets, skiing and winter sun
November is also the month when Christmas travel starts becoming a much more immediate prospect.
If you want to visit some of Europe's biggest markets without the crowds of December, the final week of November is worth considering. Vienna starts early, while cities including Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Prague move into full festive mode later in the month.
It's also worth booking winter-sun trips now, with the Canary Islands and Madeira remaining as popular choices as temperatures fall across northern Europe.
Travelling over Christmas and New Year is notoriously tricky and sometimes pricey, so it’s best to book ahead to secure the best possible deals.
Finally, if you're thinking about skiing, November is the time to start looking ahead. A number of new Alpine hotels and lodges are opening for the 2026-2027 season, including The First Cortina in Italy, The Ski Lodge in Verbier and new properties in Morzine and Les Menuires.

France prepares for further unrest during weekend demonstrations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:29 UTC
19:56:29 KST

French authorities are preparing for possible renewed violence during demonstrations planned for the coming weekend.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday would “definitely” be considered a high-risk day, according to Reuters.
He told French broadcaster BFM TV that curfews would probably remain in place in several areas to prevent vandalism and looting.
Trade unions and the Yellow Vest protest movement plan to continue street demonstrations during the coming weeks.
The protests began peacefully in late September over high living costs and conditions in French schools but have repeatedly developed into unrest.
More than 400,000 people participated in demonstrations Saturday.
Nuñez said 267 police officers were injured during the weekend, most of them lightly. Three officers sustained more serious injuries, while more than 250 protesters were estimated to have been injured.
The French government has blamed much of the violence on groups it describes as “ultra-left-wing.”
Education ministers will meet student leaders Monday to discuss their demands.
“We hope that the prime minister agrees to our demands,” said Louis Letoublon, a leader of high school student organization Les Lycéens!
Right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen promised Sunday to “restore law and order” if elected next year.
The next president will also inherit an economy in which public debt and the budget deficit exceed European Union limits.

====================================================================================================

German business sentiment improves in October on brighter outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:28 UTC
19:56:28 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Business sentiment in Germany improved in October, driven by more optimistic company expectations, the Munich-based ifo Institute said on Monday.
The ifo Business Climate Index rose to 90.2 points in October from 89.9 points in September, according to the institute's monthly survey of approximately 9,000 businesses.
While expectations climbed to 91.6 points from 90.4 points a month earlier, companies assessed their current business situation as slightly worse, with that subindex edging down to 88.8 points from 89.5 points.
"The economic recovery is continuing," said Clemens Fuest, president of the ifo Institute.
In the manufacturing sector, the index rose significantly to a seasonally adjusted balance of 1.2 points from minus 2.7 points in September.
Manufacturing companies rated both their current situation and expectations as substantially better, with both indicators returning to positive territory for the first time in more than three years.
Companies plan to expand production following an increase in incoming orders, the institute said.
In the service sector, the business climate suffered a setback, falling to minus 1.2 points in October from 0.7 points in September.
While service firms were less satisfied with their current performance, their expectations grew more positive, with IT service providers performing particularly well.
In the trade sector, the indicator remained unchanged at minus 17.2 points, as slightly improved expectations offset a more negative view of the current situation.
The wholesale sector outperformed retail, Fuest noted.
The construction sector index rose to minus 15.5 points from minus 17.0 points in September, as companies reported noticeably higher satisfaction with their current business situation alongside a slight improvement in expectations.

====================================================================================================

Power fault causes train delays and cancellations across Zealand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:56:23 UTC
19:56:23 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Fitch affirms Lithuania's A+ rating with stable outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

International credit rating agency Fitch Ratings has affirmed Lithuania's long-term foreign-currency issuer default rating at A+ with a stable outlook, the Finance Ministry said on Saturday.
The rating is currently the highest long-term debt rating assigned to Lithuania by the three major credit rating agencies.
According to Fitch, the rating is supported by a credible policy framework, membership of the European Union and eurozone, resilient economic growth, moderate government debt and high institutional quality.
It is constrained by heightened geopolitical risks and the small size of the Lithuanian economy.
The agency also said consistent fiscal policy should help consolidate public finances, although the budget deficit is projected to widen in the near term.
The government plans to run a deficit exceeding the Maastricht limit of 3 percent of gross domestic product.
Government debt is projected to reach 54.3 percent of gross domestic product in 2029, remaining below the 60 percent threshold set by the Maastricht criteria.

Iran, Turkey explore trade opportunities, export potential

2026-10-26
10:47:58 UTC
19:47:58 KST

Iran, Turkey explore trade opportunities, export potential
TEHRAN – Iran and Turkey should strengthen trade ties by identifying competitive Iranian export products, assessing market demand and verifying potential buyers, Iran’s commercial attaché in Turkey said at a seminar on bilateral trade opportunities and challenges.
Kamran Davari Niko, Iran’s commercial attaché in Istanbul, made the remarks at a seminar hosted by the Qazvin Chamber of Commerce and attended by its board members and business representatives, according to the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO).
Davari Niko said none of Turkey’s border crossings with Iran had been closed, expressing hope that trade between the two countries would continue. He stressed the need to monitor developments, identify suitable routes for maintaining trade flows and make better use of existing capacities to expand economic cooperation.
He also highlighted direct engagement and bilateral consultations as important tools for strengthening commercial relations, referring to a meeting between Qazvin Chamber of Commerce board members and Turkish counterparts in Istanbul.
The seminar examined Iranian goods with export potential in the Turkish market, as well as opportunities for imports from Turkey. Participants emphasized the importance of assessing market needs, evaluating products’ competitive advantages, calculating production costs and determining profitability before entering new business sectors.
Other topics included estimating operating costs, assessing mutual benefits, checking the commercial credibility of trading partners and understanding formal and customary contractual practices. Participants also discussed required regulations and permits, tariffs, transportation costs and payment methods as part of efforts to reduce trade risks.
Earlier in June, the representative of the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce Ibrahim Dogan Salman stated that in 2025, the trade between Iran and Turkey surpassed $5.6 billion.
During a meeting with members of the Board of Directors of the Yazd Chamber of Commerce, Doghan Salman added that the preferential trade agreement implemented between the two countries in 2015 has provided a solid foundation for the development of these cooperations.
Referring to the history of economic and cultural relations between Iran and Turkey, he said: "There are deep-rooted cooperations between the two countries, and we are interested in strengthening these relations more than ever."
Dogan Salman, stating that "we are not on two sides of the Silk Road, but rather walk side by side on this road," added: "Iran and Turkey have always been neighbors throughout history and have known and understood each other. What binds the two nations together is a shared history, culture, and civilization."
The Istanbul Chamber of Commerce representative, referring to the value of trade between the two countries, stated: "In 2025, the trade between Iran and Turkey exceeded $5.6 billion. Furthermore, the preferential trade agreement implemented between the two countries in 2015 has provided a solid foundation for the development of these cooperations."
He cited the active presence of entrepreneurs from both countries as the most tangible sign of this bond and said: "Currently, 7,288 companies with Iranian investment are operating in Turkey, and at the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce alone, the number of companies of Iranian origin has reached 2,040."
Dogan Salman also referred to the people-to-people ties between the two countries and added: "In 2025, more than three million Iranians visited Turkey, and this statistic shows that Iran and Turkey are not merely each other's markets, but are also true partners."
The Istanbul Chamber of Commerce representative emphasized: "To strengthen the bond between the chambers of commerce on both sides, we are prepared to hold joint meetings, bilateral talks, and specialized exhibitions."

Jordan unites as victims' families recount Karak church massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:46:41 UTC
19:46:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Victims' families recount Karak church massacre as tragedy unites Jordanians
Grief, anger and shock have consumed the village of Hammoud in Jordan's southern Karak governorate following the deadly attack on St George's Church on Friday 23 October which saw nine lose their lives.
Relatives recalled the moment gunfire erupted and desperate attempts to rescue the wounded, while stressing the deep-rooted relationship between Muslims and Christians in Karak and insisting the attack will not undermine social cohesion or national unity.
Jordan's Public Security Directorate announced early on Monday that the three gunmen who carried out the massacre had been arrested following an armed confrontation with security personnel.
Sultan al-Khitan, a Hammoud resident who witnessed the horrific scenes on Friday, told The New Arab that the incident began as people gathered in the church courtyard and exchanged greetings. Heavy gunfire suddenly rang out, sending people scrambling for cover.
The attackers continued firing from the street behind the church, while those present attempted to assist the wounded and get them out of the area.
Al-Khitan said he helped transport two people to safety, one wounded in the shoulder and the other in the neck. The gunfire continued for a while before gradually subsiding, and residents used their cars to take the injured to hospitals before returning to help evacuate others, he said.
He described seeing a blue Dyna pickup truck carrying two people, one of whom was armed with what looked like a Kalashnikov rifle.
Al-Khitan said the attack was unprecedented, with life in Hammoud characterised by close ties, regular visits and shared celebrations and condolences. To his knowledge, there had been no previous disputes or feuds that could explain the violence.
Waad al-Halsa, a relative of some of the victims, told The New Arab that those inside the church had been attending the funeral of their uncle's wife when the firing erupted without warning, leaving those present confused and initially unsure how to act.
He insisted that the massacre will not affect relations between Karak's Muslims and Christians, describing their bonds as strong and deeply rooted in everyday life.
Al-Halsa said one example was his friend Louay al-Halalmeh, who contacted him immediately after the attack to offer help transporting the injured—such gestures reflected the genuine solidarity between residents, which was demonstrated through practical action, particularly during times of hardship.
Khaled Barqan, a cousin of one of the victims, told The New Arab that Jordan had lost young people and skilled professionals in an immense tragedy without precedent in the country's history.
The victims were peaceful residents of Hammoud who had gone to a funeral, never expecting that a social obligation would turn into a scene of violence and bloodshed, he said.
Barqan described the attack as an act of terrorism that was difficult to comprehend, and condemned its violation of all laws, customs and human values.
Ehab Haddadin, another relative of a victim, said the tragedy extended far beyond the bereaved families to encompass the whole country.
"No matter how much a person tries to speak, there are no words that can express the scale of this tragedy," he told The New Arab.
He said relations between Muslims and Christians in Jordan were based on fraternity and solidarity, with no history of religious division, adding that he was shocked that such an attack had taken place.
Lina al-Halsa, whose cousins were among the dead and wounded, called for the harshest possible penalties against those responsible, so they would serve as a warning to anyone contemplating attacks on places of worship or peaceful civilians.
Sarah Haddadin said residents were still struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy. She saw the targeting of the church as an attempt to sow discord between Muslims and Christians, but believes it will fail to change the nature of relations between Jordanians.
The scenes of mourning and solidarity at the funerals in the village had demonstrated national unity and rejection of discrimination and division, she said, expressing confidence that security forces would pursue those responsible and bring them to justice.
Tribal figures in Karak also stressed that the attack had struck the entire country.
Firas Madallah Ali al-Assasfeh told The New Arab that Jordanians shared a commitment to national unity and social cohesion. He pointed to members of the Habashneh tribe, including Saed Mahmoud Ahmed Faleh al-Habashneh and Raji al-Aroud al-Habashneh, who were wounded alongside Christian victims outside the church church.
The scene embodied the shared fate of Jordanian communities and underscored the importance of safeguarding the country's security and stability.
Tribal figure Ismat al-Majali likewise called the attack a "painful tragedy" for Karak and Jordan as a whole, insisting that it would not damage the longstanding bonds between Muslims and Christians in the governorate.
Karak had historically been a unified community in which religious affiliation did not divide its residents, he said, pointing to the family and social ties reflected in shared celebrations, condolences and regular visits.
Some of the victims had worked in humanitarian professions, particularly medicine, and were accustomed to treating patients and helping those unable to afford healthcare, al-Majali added.

Trend: Gyurov Wins Young Voters, Yotova Dominates Among Over-70s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:46:11 UTC
19:46:11 KST

Andrey Gyurov attracted 12.3% of voters who backed Progressive Bulgaria in the April parliamentary elections, while 30% of that electorate did not support Iliana Yotova in the first round of the presidential election, according to exit poll data from Trend Agency.
Gyurov also won the support of 86.2% of voters who had backed PP-DB in April and 47.6% of those who voted for GERB-SDS. Yotova, meanwhile, received 71.2% of Progressive Bulgaria’s voters and 76.9% of those who supported BSP-United Left. She also secured 22.9% of the GERB-SDS electorate.
Trend’s analysis found clear socio-demographic differences between the leading candidates’ supporters, particularly in terms of age, education and place of residence.
Gyurov performed best among younger voters. In the 18-to-29 age group, he received 42.5% of the vote, compared with 27.1% for Yotova. Among voters aged 30 to 39, Gyurov led with 40.5%, against Yotova’s 27.8%.
The two candidates were almost evenly matched among people aged 40 to 49, with Yotova receiving 34% and Gyurov 34.1%. Support shifted increasingly toward Yotova among older voters, reaching 56.8% among those over 70, compared with 22.2% for Gyurov.
More than 40% of Yotova’s voters were over 60, while that age group accounted for 22.6% of Gyurov’s electorate. Conversely, voters under 40 made up 36.1% of Gyurov’s supporters, compared with 21.4% of Yotova’s.
Geography also divided the two electorates. Gyurov won decisively in Sofia, receiving more than twice as many votes as his rival. Yotova led in regional centers, with 34.8% against Gyurov’s 30.8%, and held a much stronger advantage in small towns and villages.
Sofia residents accounted for 31.8% of Gyurov’s voters, compared with 12.2% of Yotova’s. In contrast, 45.8% of Yotova’s electorate lived in small towns and villages, compared with 26% of Gyurov’s supporters. The figures point to a concentration of Gyurov’s support in the capital and major urban areas, while Yotova performed better in smaller settlements.
Education was another significant factor. Among voters with university degrees, Gyurov led with 39%, compared with 31.7% for Yotova. Among those with secondary education, Yotova received 41.3%, while Gyurov won 24.7%.
University graduates accounted for 65.5% of Gyurov’s electorate and 47.1% of Yotova’s.
The profile of Kostadin Kostadinov’s supporters differed from those of the two leading candidates. People aged 40 to 69 made up 65.9% of his electorate, while voters under 30 accounted for 9.1% and those over 70 for 10.2%.
Trend’s findings also showed differences in when supporters of the two leading tickets decided whom to vote for. Two-thirds, or 66.3%, of Yotova’s voters had made their choice before the campaign began, compared with 53.1% of Gyurov’s supporters.
During the campaign, 25.4% of Gyurov’s voters decided to support him, compared with 16.7% of Yotova’s electorate, suggesting that Gyurov gained relatively more support as the campaign progressed.
Across the electorate as a whole, 55.7% had decided whom to support before the campaign started, while 20.9% made their choice during the campaign. Another 10.4% decided in the final days before the vote, and 9.3% made their decision on election day.

Trade flows continue despite temporary border closures, higher logistics costs

Trade flows continue despite temporary border closures, higher logistics costs
TEHRAN – Goods continue to enter Iran despite restrictions on transport routes, with shipments being redirected through alternative corridors when individual routes are disrupted, a trade official said.
Seyed Ali Emami, director general of the Trade Logistics and Support Office at the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO), said maritime restrictions had prompted a shift toward alternative transport routes but had not halted seaborne shipments into the country.
The level of restrictions varies according to cargo type and vessel conditions, with some ships facing tighter controls than others, Emami said.
He said importers were increasingly using multimodal transport and changes to shipping documentation, including a practice known as “switching bills of lading.” Some goods are also entering Iran on smaller vessels or via rail and road networks.
Restrictions may temporarily affect land crossings with Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan, Emami said, adding that the psychological impact of reports about border closures can sometimes exceed their practical consequences.
A border may close for two days before operations gradually resume, he said. Such reports can trigger significant concern even when cargo movements restart after a short disruption.
Goods continue to enter Iran through various routes despite the restrictions, Emami said. When one border becomes inaccessible, shipments can be redirected through other crossings, although detours may lengthen transport distances and increase costs.
The main downside is higher logistics expenditure, he said, noting that the additional costs depend on the type of goods, country of origin and mode of transport.
Restrictions have affected road, rail and maritime transport, but they have not brought the country’s commercial logistics to a complete standstill, Emami said. Shipments are continuing, although they may take longer and cost more than before.
Regarding trucks held up at border crossings, he said such delays had occurred even before the current wartime conditions, though the situation could exacerbate existing constraints.
