GECF ministerial meeting opens in Moscow ahead of leaders' summit
TEHRAN – The 28th ministerial meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) opened in Moscow on Monday, bringing together representatives of member states to discuss gas market developments, energy security and ways to strengthen cooperation.
The meeting is being held a day before the forum's eighth leaders' summit, scheduled for Tuesday, with President Masoud Pezeshkian attending on behalf of Iran.
Hamid Bovard, Iran's acting oil minister, traveled to Moscow to participate in the ministerial meeting and accompany Pezeshkian at the summit.
Iran is also seeking to advance bilateral energy cooperation with Russia during the meetings. Bovard said the two countries had reached agreement on the general terms of a natural gas swap deal, with technical arrangements for implementation now nearing completion.
The agreement was discussed at a previous meeting between the Iranian and Russian presidents in Turkmenistan, Bovard said. He added that a pipeline project Russia is pursuing through Azerbaijan could enable gas exchanges between the two countries in the near future.
Cooperation in the oil sector is also continuing, with Russian companies involved in the development of four major Iranian oilfields. Bovard said the projects had made satisfactory progress and that discussions on advancing the contracts would continue during his visit.
Iran plans to use the GECF meetings to discuss production plans, expand cooperation with member states, particularly in the gas sector, and address international developments and damage to its energy infrastructure, Bovard said.
Ahead of the ministerial meeting and summit, the GECF executive board held an extraordinary session in Moscow on Sunday, chaired by Seyed Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, Iran's deputy oil minister for international affairs and trade. The session focused on coordinating the two gatherings and finalizing key documents, including the summit's closing declaration.
During his visit, Bovard also toured the monitoring center of Russian oil company Zarubezhneft and was briefed on its operations and technical capabilities.
He welcomed the participation of Russian companies in Iranian oil industry development projects, saying Iran's national oil and gas companies had also established a similar monitoring center to oversee operations across the country.
Zarubezhneft Chief Executive Sergei Kudryashov said the center consolidates data from the company's onshore and offshore operations, allowing production volumes and other operational parameters at individual wells to be monitored.
The GECF has 12 full members, including Iran and Russia, and represents countries that hold about 70 percent of the world's proven natural gas reserves, account for 38 percent of global marketed gas production and supply 42 percent of global gas exports. Member countries also account for an estimated 47 percent of global liquefied natural gas exports.
The forum holds its leaders' summit every two years. Previous meetings have been hosted by Doha, Moscow, Tehran, Santa Cruz in Bolivia, Malabo in Equatorial Guinea and Algiers, which hosted the seventh summit in 2024.

LG B6 OLED TV Review (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Low price for an OLED. Deep and rich blacks. Easy setup and install. Great refresh rate for video games. The skintone test was better than average.
TIRED
Did not perform as well as a Micro RGB for brightness and contrast.
It’s amazing what can happen in just one year. The LG B6 is the cheapest LG OLED model around (priced lower than the LG C6 and LG G6), but it also has some stiff competition. New art televisions like the Amazon Ember Artline (which costs under $1,000) use a matte display that renders masterpiece paintings in convincingly realistic glory. RGB televisions like the LG Micro RGB Evo and those from Samsung and Hisense have also burst onto the market, making a convincing argument for choosing an RGB screen over an OLED one.
Last year around this time, we reviewed the LG B5 and ranked it a solid 8/10, but there was less competition. The LG B6 is still a good budget OLED TV, it’s just beset on all sides by better, brighter options, including from LG’s own LG C6.
Sleek Angles, Less Sleek Remote
Photograph: John Brandon
The first thing that struck me while setting up the LG B6 is that it’s incredibly thin—just 1.8 inches at the base and about a quarter-inch at the top and around most of the bezel. The OLED panel doesn’t need any backlighting like most LED or RGB televisions, so it can be extra thin. The lower portion of the TV is thicker because of the four HDMI ports (all of which support a 120-Hz refresh rate), an optical audio out, two USB 2.0 ports, and one LAN port. The TV only supports Wi-Fi 5, certainly not the latest standard.
The B6 comes with two legs that are easy to install (two screws each), though I generally prefer a single pedestal stand design. The 65-inch model I tested fit comfortably on two 38-inch IKEA SPIKSMED TV benches set side by side that measure 76 inches long.
Like all LG TVs, setup involves LG’s own WebOS interface or ThinQ app, not built-in Google TV or Fire TV. It was easy to complete the setup using the LG ThinQ app on my iPhone—in minutes, I was loading my usual assortment of apps like Prime Video, Disney+ and Apple TV+.
The B6 is packed with features too. A few of my favorites include a gaming mode that helps improve low latency gaming, AI picture enhancements that actually work and make a discernible difference, an artwork mode called LG Gallery+ that costs $5 per month, and an LG music app in case you don’t like Spotify or other music apps. It also has settings for audio dialogue sync, similar to what you can do with powered speakers like the Klipsch The Fives II. A desktop mode means you can mirror your laptop screen and even run a Gmail app.
Photograph: John Brandon
I have mixed feelings about WebOS, though. My main gripe is that you cannot disable the pointer on the LG remote, and it jumps around a lot. When you press the center dial on the remote, it turns off temporarily as though LG user interface designers are admitting it isn’t that great. I also have mixed feelings about the remote—it’s hard to use in the dark by feel. The Home button is offset so it’s hard to find, and shortcuts for Netflix and other apps are situated at the bottom, but not backlit.
OLED Strengths, OLED Weaknesses
Based on the pricing, it’s obvious LG has positioned the B6 as the entry-level OLED in their line-up. That became crystal clear once I started testing movies and TV shows.
In the official specs, LG only lists “wide color gamut” and not a percentage for the specific BT.2020 spec, nor a specific brightness rating. This is where the benchmark testing comes in handy, and what I tested right away.
One win for the B6 is blacks and grays, which have great texture and clarity, a surprise given how many midrange televisions make dark, shadowy scenes look washed out. Scenes from Awake and The Creator, very dark movies, were clear and detailed, after tweaking a few picture quality settings (namely changing to Vivid mode).
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
Contrast and brightness are more of a mixed bag. I watched House of the Dragon and Game of Thrones (yes, the infamously dark season eight, episode three) to stress test these specs, and the B6 struggled. On better TVs (and home theater projectors), you can see trees in the background of a scene where a character emerges on a frozen lake. On the B6, they are completely black—e.g., a contrast problem.
Color saturation and luminance could be better too, especially compared to RGB TVs I’ve tested recently. The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, with its various blooming effects, wasn’t exactly terrible looking, but certainly not as crisp as on something like the LG Micro RGB Evo. (The less technicolor The End of Oak Street fared better.) During a demo reel benchmark, green grass by a fence in winter looked a bit too brown for my taste (again, color saturation issue), but skin tone variation was surprisingly good.
LG is not the first brand I think of for playing video games (it’s Sony), but the B6 deserves some extra credit here. The 120-Hz refresh rate screen does its job, and made all my movements playing Crimson Desert on PC crisp and responsive. Resident Evil: Requiem looked almost photo realistic, with gleaming statues and surprisingly good color quality, even zooming in on crumpled leaves.
Watching sports and news didn’t yield any surprises—a Baltimore Orioles baseball game looked rich and textured, but not very bright.
Affordable, But Outclassed
LG B6 may be an entry-level OLED, but, like an entry-level BMW, it has a lot of the bells and whistles of a flagship, with plenty of ports, features, and premium finishes. My main issue with it is brightness and contrast, both could be better. And LG’s WebOS is still not my favorite interface in the world.
The main issue might actually be price. At the time of writing, the LG B6 is on sale for $1,300. The superior midrange LG C6 is also on sale for $1,500. That’s only $200 more for a much better, brighter TV (both 65-inches). That’s not even discussing buying an older (but still brighter) model like the LG C5 (which I found on sale for less than the B6). It all depends on how much you want to spend.
John Brandon is a contributing writer for WIRED. He reviews televisions, projectors, speakers, and other AV staples. He started writing full-time in 2001 and has been featured in Forbes, Popular Mechanics, The Telegraph, Minnesota Monthly magazine, and many other publications. He lives in Minneapolis–Saint Paul. Exiled Opposition Leader María Corina Machado Returns to Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

“I am here. With you.”
Venezuela’s popular opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado posted the message on social media platform X Sunday morning local time, announcing her return to the country after more than 10 months in exile.
Machado, who was briefly detained in January 2025 following a protest against autocratic then-President Nicolás Maduro’s swearing-in despite a dubious election victory, went into hiding in Venezuela and emerged in December that year in Norway. Since then, she has been fighting for a return to democracy in her own country, demanding that, following the extraordinary American military operation that captured Maduro, Venezuelans get to have free and fair elections.
The social media accounts of her political movement, Vente Venezuela, as well as her campaign, posted images and videos of Venezuelans crowding the streets of Caracas to welcome her return. The New York Times reported that Machado entered Venezuela from Colombia, citing two anonymized government officials.
Edmundo González Urrutia, another key opposition figure, also posted on social media Sunday that Machado is “on Venezuelan soil” and that he would soon be with her “so that our country truly advances toward freedom.”
Machado’s return adds some urgency to the country’s democratic transition—which the interim Venezuelan government under acting President Delcy Rodríguez, as well as its apparent overseer, the U.S., have both promised. Rodríguez, who was formerly Maduro’s deputy, and U.S. President Donald Trump have both said that elections will be held in the country, but a date has yet to be finalized.
The 59-year-old Machado, meanwhile, has called for elections by July 2027, telling the Financial Times that there was “more than enough time” to prepare for one. She has also said she will contest the presidency. A majority of Venezuelans want her to be President, according to a poll from AtlasIntel and Bloomberg.
Following Maduro’s ouster, Venezuela’s highest court said Rodríguez’s interim presidential appointment could last for up to 90 days, with the National Assembly potentially extending her term for another 90. But the assembly, controlled by the ruling party, did not vote on extending her term, which officially expired in April.
It remains unclear how Machado could hasten elections, given the Venezuelan government is in talks with a different U.S.-backed faction of the opposition. A third round of talks ended this month without reaching a firm election schedule. Venezuelans have since grown impatient and have taken to the streets to protest the delays.
What the U.S. has said about Machado’s return
Asked about Machado’s return to Venezuela, Trump said Sunday he was unaware of it. “I think she's a very nice woman,” Trump told reporters. “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.”
Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal earlier this year in what appeared to be a push to hasten Venezuela's democratic transition. But since Maduro’s arrest and the U.S. elevation of a new Venezuelan government under Rodríguez, tensions between Trump’s Administration and Machado have increased.
The opposition leader has tried to return to the country multiple times, but she has claimed Venezuelan authorities have repeatedly blocked her. Machado has denied suggestions that the U.S. was blocking her return. But her insistence on returning reportedly roiled some in the White House who worry it could spark a political crisis.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X that the conditions that allowed Machado’s return to Venezuela were “the direct result of the U.S. supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile.”
But Rubio also hinted that the U.S. expects no further interference in the ongoing discussions: “The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected. Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”
Machado said earlier that, despite not being a part of the discussions between the Venezuelan government, legislative opposition, and the U.S., her movement will not hinder initiatives that “produce real progress.”
The U.S. has argued that Venezuela must ensure political and economic stability before it can hold elections. But critics and other observers have pointed out that the Trump Administration’s approach has instead prioritized doing business with Venezuela over facilitating democratic transition—with Washington announcing a major oil deal with Caracas amid the talks.
“She’s a very nice woman,” Trump said of Machado Sunday. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

One in three young adults use AI chatbots for drug and alcohol information, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:28:11 UTC
19:28:11 KST

Researchers warn that chatbots could spread misinformation about substance use, as a survey finds that one in three young adults in the United States are turning to AI for drug-related information.
One in three young adults has used generative artificial intelligence to seek information about drugs and alcohol, raising questions about the public health risks of chatbots becoming an increasingly common source of health advice.
A study published in JMIR Formative Research found that 32% of 995 US adults aged 18 to 29 had used tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Meta AI for substance-related information.
Among those who had done so, nearly half reported using AI for that purpose at least monthly, including 12% who used it weekly and 4% who did so daily or almost daily.
“Using these tools can lead to misinformed or otherwise risky substance-use behaviour among young people, who are the age group most affected by adverse effects of substance use,” Mireia Triguero Roura, a postdoctoral researcher at Rutgers University and lead author of the study, said in a press release.
Of those who used AI for substance-related queries, 93% had also used Google search for the same broad purpose, suggesting that chatbots are supplementing rather than necessarily replacing established online search tools.
Risks and consequences top the list
The survey, conducted online in April 2026, found that users primarily turned to chatbots to learn about the risks and consequences of substance use — nearly 93% of those who had used AI for substance-related purposes cited this as a reason.
Around half sought substance-specific information, including questions about dosage, while 35% used AI to explore topics related to substance use disorders, such as addiction.
Young adults in the survey generally rated AI highly for helpfulness, reliability and trustworthiness. Those who used it for substance-related queries gave it an average trustworthiness score of 3.66 out of five, compared with 3.51 for general use.
The study also found differences in substance-related AI use by race and sex.
Black respondents were more likely than white respondents to report using AI for substance-related information, with adjusted odds 2.52 times higher. Male respondents had approximately twice the adjusted odds of female respondents.
“The observed disparities in who chooses to use AI for drug-related inquiries could reflect differences in healthcare access, stigma, trust, and health information-seeking behaviors,” said Triguero Roura.
The researchers said future work should assess the accuracy of chatbot responses, investigate the reasons behind demographic differences in use and establish how the information influences decisions and behaviour.

INTERVIEW - Ex-Scottish first minister says sustainable peace in Palestine must be ‘locally led’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:28:09 UTC
19:28:09 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
- - Lord McConnell, former UK special representative for peacebuilding, tells Anadolu lasting peace in Palestine must reflect needs, identity and aspirations of Palestinians
- Ex-first minister cites Bangsamoro peace process as example of how inclusive agreements can help sustain peace
- 'If there's going to be a solution to internal conflict, it needs to be appropriate for that area,' he says, pointing to Scotland, Northern Ireland as examples
Sustainable peace in Palestine can only be achieved through a “locally led long-term solution,” said former First Minister of Scotland Lord Jack McConnell.
Speaking to Anadolu, McConnell, who has served as the UK special representative for peacebuilding, said that lasting peace cannot be achieved through top-down mandates from the outside. 
"If we try to impose solutions from outside, then these are never going to work in that area where the difference is so stark and the divide is so deep," he said on the sidelines of the 9th Mediation Conference in Istanbul which concluded last week.
Asked how the UK should navigate trade-offs between strategic foreign policy interests and human rights commitments, McConnell insisted that core principles must take priority.
"In principle, human rights are not negotiable."
"In my view the strategic interest of the UK is in maximizing our influence in the pursuit of democracy, the rule of law and human rights. Each situation is different but we must remember the basic principles." 
Bangsamoro blueprint
He credited successful peacebuilding models like the 2014 landmark agreement on Bangsamoro in the southern Philippines for ending years of conflict.
McConnell, who has served as an international advisor to the Bangsamoro peace, hailed the accord as a historic turning point that has preserved stability for 12 years through political transitions, pandemic disruptions, and localized security challenges.
Rooted in historical land loss, marginalization, and colonial grievances, the conflict in Mindanao saw the Muslim Moro population fight for self-determination for over 50 years.
A string of peace initiatives between 1976 and 2008 failed to stick, but the 2014 agreement changed the game.
The deal created the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), offering the Moro population autonomy.
The region held its first elections last month since the interim administration was launched in 2019.
"The really important thing … this was an inclusive peace agreement that was founded on a mutual respect and an understanding of the history and the grievances and the identity of the Moro people as a whole."
The agreement has sustained because it was “comprehensive, covering both the need for a political voice and administration for the Moro people,” allowing former rebels a way back into society, he said.
"They have managed to deal with any issues by sticking to the agreement, going back to principles, and not allowing an individual incident perhaps to knock them off course," McConnell added. 
'Solution needs to be appropriate for that area'
McConnell pointed to Scotland and Northern Ireland as examples of how different governance arrangements can accommodate regional aspirations and address deep-rooted divisions while maintaining ties with the wider UK.
Reflecting on Scotland's experience, he recalled the decades-long campaign to establish a Scottish parliament, describing it as a "very passionate" effort.
He said the country had ultimately achieved what he called "the best of both worlds."
"Our colleagues in Northern Ireland had a different history. Their history was of deep division and conflict and violence, but similar outcomes," he said.
While Scotland had found a “peaceful route” to autonomy while maintaining its relationship with the UK government, Northern Ireland’s model gave “both of the divided communities a seat at the table,” he said.
Referring to regions where significant minority communities seek greater political representation, McConnell said: "I think what this tells us is that around the world, particularly where conflicts are internal, where you have a significant minority that has either been violent or maybe not been violent, but has been demanding a voice, demanding some autonomy, if there's going to be a solution to that internal conflict, it needs to be appropriate for that area."
"It needs to reflect and respect the norms and the culture and the identity of those people who feel marginalized," he added.

Eesti 200 preparing for 2027 Riigikogu elections
Eesti 200 Chairman Kristina Kallas said the party is preparing for the upcoming national election despite its low ratings and some members saying there is little point.
Junion coalition party Eesti 200 has polled below the 5 percent threshold for months in popularity surveys. This means the party is unlikely to be included in the next Riigikogu.
Eesti 200 parliamentary group member Ando Kiviberg and group chairman Toomas Uibo told ERR in mid-October that Eesti 200 should not run in the elections and that it would be more sensible to prepare properly for the 2031 parliamentary elections.
But Kallas is not giving up.
"We are currently preparing for the parliamentary elections and putting together candidate lists. That is the goal we are working toward," she told ERR.
The party has not yet chosen an advertising agency to run its election campaign, unlike some of its rivals whose posters can already be seen around the country.
"We currently have a so-called brief ready for advertising agencies, which we will use to start looking at agencies. We have not yet selected an advertising agency," Kallas said.
The chairman said the brief includes everything Eesti 200 would like to get from an advertising agency.
"We also have another option, which is to develop the creative solutions [election slogans and other content – ed.] ourselves. Because there have always been two options. In the previous parliamentary elections, we developed the creative solutions ourselves and only commissioned the work from an advertising agency," she said.
Kallas was unwilling to say how Eesti 200 would select an advertising agency or whether the party would hold a competition to find one.
"Look, this is a normal thing that parties do. It's a bit like explaining what goes on behind the scenes. I'm not going to explain how agencies are selected and on what basis. It's also something of a trade secret. I do not think it makes sense to explain that publicly," Kallas said.
The chairman said the party's candidate lists would probably be finalized in early January, as the deadline for submitting candidate lists is at the end of January.
Kallas said the party's election manifesto will start to be made public in the near future: "We will probably hold the election board meeting in early December, when the election promises will also be announced."
For now, Kallas was unwilling to reveal any election promises. "No. Absolutely not," she said.

Snakes that cartwheel, vultures that groan, and a Martian moon full of mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:26:38 UTC
19:26:38 KST

Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
Let’s start with some space news. Last week, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA for short, successfully launched a half-a-billion-dollar mission to land on Phobos, the largest Martian moon.
The Martian Moons Exploration spacecraft, also known as MMX, is expected to reach the vicinity of Mars in August of 2027. Once there, it will spend three years circling Mars in a path similar to Phobos’s orbit. One of its objectives is to find an ideal spot for landing on Phobos. In 2028 or 2029, MMX will send a rover down to the surface to spend 100 days observing the moon. That data will come in handy later in 2029, when MMX itself will attempt one or even two landings. If all goes well, MMX will return back up to orbit with 10 grams, or one-third of an ounce, of material from Phobos. It’s expected to make it back to Earth sometime in 2031.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
So, why all this effort to check out a lumpy little moon? Phobos may be just 14 miles wide, but it’s got a lot to say. With an orbit of just over seven hours, it’s closer to its planet than any other moon in our solar system. That orbit is also gradually shrinking, bringing it on a slow-but-steady collision course with Mars.
Then there’s the unknown origin of Phobos and its little sibling, the Martian moon Deimos. Scientists aren’t sure whether these wee moons were once asteroids that got too close to Mars or if they formed from debris after something collided with the red planet. When the MMX sample comes home, researchers will compare its composition against Martian material and asteroids to try to solve that mystery.
Speaking of weird little guys with adorably tiny orbits, our next story features a little snake that uses cartwheels as a strange evasive maneuver.
Now, I don’t know about you, but I find cartwheels hard enough with two arms and legs to support me. But apparently there are tiny little snakes that put my acrobatic attempts to shame with nary a limb in sight. Scientists first showcased this ability with the dwarf reed snake in 2023, but now they’ve identified that same cartwheeling behavior in two additional species of the same genus, Pseudorabdion. And what’s even better is that they caught the bizarre locomotion on video.
The snakes start out by making a tight little curve, kind of like the letter “C,” with its head up top, facing the direction it wants to go, and something like the middle of its body touching the ground. Then it reels forward until its tail is the part touching the ground, which gives it the momentum to launch itself into the air. While it’s airborne, the snake twists around until it gets itself into the position of the starting point of the next roll, and it alternates which side of its body strikes the ground with each rotation. And did I mention these snakes are tiny and adorable? I’m definitely not doing the footage of their limbless leaping justice, so you really gotta check the video out for yourself. We’ll link to that in our show notes!
Those aren’t the only animal showoffs we saw making headlines last week. In a study published last Wednesday, researchers shared the surprisingly complex range of sounds made by birds not generally known for their gorgeous singing voices: vultures.
When you think of a vulture, you probably picture a relatively solitary and silent bird, maybe like a few of them flying around in an ominous circle but not much more than that. But the thing is that some species are quite social—and, as it turns out, those more gregarious species can also be quite vocal. Rüppell’s vultures, which nest in colonies hundreds of birds strong, are known to follow a literal pecking order when it comes time to pick a carcass clean. Some experts think that social complexity fuels the evolution of complex communication. So, the set hierarchy that these vultures live by made scientists wonder how they might use sound to communicate.
Researchers captured 150 hours of noise from two groups of vultures in captivity, which contained something like 2,500 calls. When they analyzed qualities like pitch and length, they were able to distinguish 16 distinct call types, which could be double the average for birds in general, based on previous research.
If you’re wondering what those calls sound like, well lucky for you we have some examples. The study authors dubbed the most common call the “metallic groan,” and it generally came from birds who were on the receiving end of some kind of aggression. There were also specific brays that came from vultures trying to bully other birds for food, hisses made in response, hoarse mating groans, and special calls made by parents as they lovingly puked food into their babies’ mouths.
For our next story, you know those tabloid stories that show celebrities, like, grocery shopping and stuff with the headline “they’re just like us?” Well slap some Japanese macaques onto those glossy pages. Because according to a study published last week in Royal Society Open Science, these monkeys have a lot in common with humans when it comes to responding to disease outbreaks.
Not unlike the human tendency to stock up on hand sanitizer and wipe down groceries in the wake of a pandemic, the researchers say, primates who have survived life-threatening disease outbreaks remain more cautious about potential food contamination than their peers. That’s especially interesting given the fact that, for a macaque, there’s no public health agency announcing where a deadly ailment has come from. But even with no empirical knowledge of disease transmission, like literally these guys do not have germ theory, this study suggests that a brush with contagion inspires habits that limit exposure to new bugs.
The study looked at Japanese macaques at a primate sanctuary in southern Texas, where they’re grouped into several distinct enclosures. Three groups experienced an outbreak of simian retrovirus Type II, which can cause a sickness similar to AIDS, back in 2020. A fourth enclosure was completely spared, which provided a natural control group.
To test how that experience impacted pathogen avoidance, the researchers offered macaques food from visibly clean surfaces as well as ones seemingly contaminated by monkey poop, though covered by epoxy to prevent any actual disease risk. Previous studies have shown that this species will avoid some food with fecal contamination, but will risk it all for a favorite treat like a peanut. And, indeed, in this new study, monkeys ate from a seemingly dirty surface in 79 percent of trials. But in the groups that had survived an outbreak, monkeys went for the poop food less than half of the time. Even individuals who had not personally been sick were less likely to risk contamination.
Simian retrovirus Type II doesn’t actually spread through food, but via scratches and bites. But we know that disgust and pathogen avoidance are complicated—and not always actually very useful—in humans, too.
We’ll wrap up with a story about the funnest little animals of them all: preschoolers. Researchers were curious about why people seem to think that kids are more creative than adults, despite scientific evidence showing the opposite. In a study published last week in PLOS One, they had 92 preschoolers and 70 adults tackle three creative tasks: spending eight minutes drawing freely on blank paper with colored pens and spending eight minutes inventing and drawing a made-up animal. The study subjects were all asked about how much they enjoyed those activities, how anxious the tasks made them feel, and how confident they felt about the quality of what they’d come up with. Then their results were evaluated by five people trained in a system for rating creative work.
It turns out that, at least in this case, adults were objectively more creative than preschoolers, coming up with more original and effective ideas—but they also enjoyed themselves way less and felt worse about their work. So if you often find yourself wishing you could recapture the boundless creativity of your youth, maybe you should actually just work on your self-confidence. One time a lady in my ceramic studio looked at what I was making and said, “Wow, I wish I gave myself that much freedom.” And I have to tell you, at the time, it did not feel good. But now, I think I might have changed my mind.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to see how science is showing up in the midterm elections.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Sushmita Pathak, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Emily Makowski, Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Austrian chancellor threatens veto in EU budget dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:34 UTC
19:25:34 KST

Timo Kirez
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker of the Austrian People's Party (OVP) threatened on Monday to veto the EU budget proposal.
Speaking to the German daily newspaper Die Welt, Stocker said, “There is a pain threshold for Austria. If this pain threshold is exceeded, I will not agree.”
Although Stocker did not specify exactly where Vienna’s “pain threshold” lies, he did point out that “a compromise will only be possible if the new proposal is realistic.”
Stocker specifically criticized the European Commission’s demand for 2,500 additional civil service positions as “completely unreasonable and out of touch with reality.”
“We are cutting 2,600 administrative positions in Austria,” the chancellor said. He expects EU institutions to do the same.
If bureaucracy is curtailed through future staff reductions, that would suit him just fine, Stocker continued.
Austria is currently subject to an EU deficit procedure and must consolidate its own budget. Therefore, Stocker said, he expects Brussels to exercise fiscal discipline and use its resources efficiently.
The EU's financial framework for 2028 through 2034 must be approved unanimously by the member states.
The European Commission had proposed a total budget of €1.985 trillion ($2.226 trillion) for the next seven years.
Opposition to this financial plan comes not only from Austria but also from Germany, the Netherlands, Finland, Sweden, and Denmark.

Japan indicts U.S. Marine on murder charge over woman's killing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:09 UTC
19:25:09 KST

U.S. Marine indicted on murder charge over woman's killing in Japan
Japanese prosecutors have indicted a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering a woman on Okinawa, a court spokesman told AFP on Monday, in a case that prompted public outrage.
The alleged killing of the 39-year-old Japanese woman caused Japan's premier to slam the "heinous crime" and reignited controversy over the heavy U.S. military presence on the southern island.
"The case was indicted on October 25," said the spokesman for the court in Naha, confirming media reports that the suspect had been indicted on charges of murder and robbery.
Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha.
The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that, according to the indictment document, the suspect allegedly strangled the woman from Naha in a hotel with a telephone cord on Oct. 3.
He is also accused of stealing a backpack containing the woman's wallet and other belongings, the newspaper said.
The Marine denied the allegations at the time of his arrest but has now made statements that imply some involvement in the case, the Yomiuri and other media said, citing investigative sources.
Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions in the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi has said that officials were reviewing the off-base code of conduct for U.S. troops in Japan following the alleged killing.
The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said.
"We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States.
The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on U.S. military personnel drinking in public off base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours.
The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a month-long curfew.
Previous incidents have strained relations
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
In Japan, once a suspect is formally indicted, the conviction rate stands at more than 99%.
The justice ministry says the near-perfect rates are because prosecutors only pursue airtight cases, they are confident about winning.
Why are so many bases concentrated in Okinawa?
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today Okinawa hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 54,000 U.S. troops based in Japan today, despite comprising just 0.6% of Japan's landmass.
In the wake of World War II, Japan regained its sovereignty under the San Francisco Peace Treaty of 1952, but Okinawa remained under American control, making it a hub of U.S. military build-up.
The 1972 return of Okinawa's sovereignty to Japan did little to diminish the number of U.S. bases on the island, leading to the disproportionate burden it is saddled with today.

North Korea ‘Reaches’ Seoul in South Korea–U.S. War Games Simulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:25:08 UTC
19:25:08 KST

During the South Korea–U.S. joint command post exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield, North Korean troops breached defensive lines and advanced to the outskirts of Seoul in a simulation.
According to Chosun Ilbo, citing its own sources in military circles, the involvement of combined South Korean and U.S. forces did not prevent North Korean units from posing a critical threat to the South Korean capital.
The scenario accounts for the deployment of reinforcements, the operation of air defense systems, and ground maneuvers by both countries’ forces.
South Korean military officials suggest several possible reasons for the simulation’s unfavorable outcome.
These include coordination issues within the combined command and the significant transformation of North Korea’s military capabilities in recent years.
A key feature of the August exercises was assigning the main command-and-control functions for ground operations to South Korea’s Ground Operations Command. The Commander of the Combined Forces provided overall leadership.
This division of responsibilities rehearsed a scenario involving the future transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) from the United States to South Korea.
The simulation results indicate that South Korean forces have not yet achieved the readiness required to independently command a combined force.
South Korea’s reliance on U.S. intelligence systems remains another outstanding issue.
Without the U.S. constellation of satellites and reconnaissance aircraft, South Korean forces are unable to independently track the movements of North Korea’s mobile launchers.
Despite the simulation’s negative results, South Korean government officials reaffirm their intention to complete the transfer of OPCON during President Lee Jae-myung’s term in office.
Previously, North Korean self-propelled artillery systems, likely of 122 mm caliber, were spotted near the border with South Korea along the western front.

Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:14:39 UTC
19:14:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agree to further talks
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey agreed on Monday to continue security consultations and strengthen regional cooperation following high-level talks in Tehran, amid fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
A joint statement issued after the first meeting between Iran and senior representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement confirmed that the four countries had agreed to maintain dialogue and consultations, particularly on regional peace, security and stability.
The meeting was hosted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
The statement said the participants had agreed to continue discussions aimed at strengthening cooperation between their countries, but did not announce any specific security agreement or new joint mechanism.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also received the three visiting officials earlier on Monday, calling on regional countries to overcome their differences and work together to address common security threats.
Pezeshkian said historical and religious ties between Muslim countries should provide the foundation for closer cooperation, expressing hope that the meeting would help establish mechanisms for regional security based on shared interests.
He accused Israel, with US support, of committing widespread crimes in Gaza, Lebanon and other countries before extending its attacks to Iranian territory, including strikes that killed military commanders, scientists and civilians.
The Iranian president argued that military and economic pressure had failed to weaken Iran or force it to surrender, instead strengthening domestic solidarity and determination to defend the country's sovereignty.
He also urged regional governments to turn political understandings into practical measures rather than limiting cooperation to statements and agreements that remain unimplemented.
Pezeshkian called for stronger economic, scientific and cultural ties, as well as easier movement and exchanges between neighbouring countries.
He warned against attempts to inflame sectarian and political divisions, accusing Washington and Israel of seeking to weaken Muslim countries and deal with them individually.
Iran calls for regional security without foreign interference
Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the talks formed part of efforts to establish a regional security framework led by Middle Eastern countries rather than external powers.
Speaking to Iranian state television earlier on Monday, Bagheri Kani said the initiative had emerged during Munir's visit to Tehran last week, when Iranian officials were informed of the three countries' intention to hold joint consultations.
He expressed hope that the discussions would contribute to regional stability and enable the participating countries to draw on one another's experience in addressing security threats.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the meeting would address developments in the occupied Palestinian territories and Lebanon, Israeli policies in the region and the consequences of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Baghaei described the talks as an opportunity to explore regional security arrangements based on the shared interests of neighbouring countries.
He said the initial consultations were intended to identify priorities and establish an agenda for further discussions.
Pezeshkian reiterates Iran's nuclear position
During his meeting with the visiting delegation, Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran was not seeking nuclear weapons and that its nuclear programme was intended for peaceful purposes.
He stressed Tehran's right to peaceful nuclear activities under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The Iranian president also criticised Washington's contradictory approach of expressing willingness to negotiate while threatening military strikes against Iranian facilities.
He argued that such threats undermined confidence in diplomacy and made it more difficult to reach lasting agreements.
Pezeshkian said Iran would continue defending its rights and interests under international law and urged regional countries to coordinate their positions to prevent further military attacks.
Saudi Arabia backs efforts to reduce tensions
Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry said the visit by Prince Khalid bin Salman and representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was part of continuing efforts to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
The ministry said the discussions supported mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan aimed at preventing another confrontation between Iran and the United States.
Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Raed Krimly also said the talks reflected the role the agreement's member states hoped to play in promoting regional stability through dialogue.
The diplomatic efforts come amid intensifying tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement, which has continued launching attacks against the kingdom.
The possibility of renewed US-Israeli military action against Iran has also raised concerns that another confrontation could spread across the region.
Qatar steps up mediation amid fears of renewed war
Monday's meeting followed the arrival of a Qatari delegation in Tehran on Sunday evening as part of Doha's efforts to prevent further escalation between Washington and Tehran.
A source familiar with regional mediation efforts told The New Arab that the visit was intended to build on continuing diplomatic contacts aimed at preventing the conflict from worsening.
The source said Iran had already communicated its positions and demands clearly to mediators.
Baghaei confirmed that the Qatari delegation's visit formed part of ongoing regional consultations, covering both bilateral cooperation and Doha's mediation efforts.
He said the exchange of messages and diplomatic initiatives between regional countries was important amid the current tensions.
Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States throughout the conflict.
Iran warns against another military confrontation
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday against renewed US military action, saying Tehran would maintain its regional policies regardless of whether another war broke out.
Araghchi said that although there was growing discussion of another conflict, he was already considering what would happen after it ended.
He argued that previous military confrontations had demonstrated the consequences of attempting to resolve disputes with Iran through force.
The foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's position that lasting regional security could only be achieved through cooperation between neighbouring countries without foreign interference.
He stressed that Iran remained prepared to work with Gulf states and other regional countries to establish a more stable security environment.

IN BRIEF: What is known about FSB’s thwarted attack on Moscow air defense site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:14:27 UTC
19:14:27 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) detained two men from the South Caucasus who, acting on orders from the Ukrainian State Security Service (SBU), were preparing an attack using FPV drones against one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility, the FSB press office reported.
TASS has compiled the key information known at this time.
Thwarting of terrorist attack
- The FSB thwarted the sabotage and terrorist activities of two men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, the press office reported.
- According to the Federal Security Service, the men were going to prepare attack drones obtained from hidden stashes, transport them to the Moscow Region for launch, and activate them before takeoff.
- It was specified that the drones were to be controlled remotely from Ukrainian territory.
- While preparing to carry out a terrorist attack on an electric power facility and one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system, the suspects were detained by FSB officers, the press office said.
- The FSB released a video showing the FPV drones that the two detainees, natives of the South Caucasus, were using, on orders from the SBU, to prepare an attack on one of the key components of Moscow’s air defense system and an electric power facility.
- A video provided by the FSB press office shows the suspects assembling the drones and getting them ready for use according to instructions from their handler.
- The video shows two drones, both disassembled and assembled, as well as the communication devices used by the agents and instructions for assembling the drones.
Recruitment
- According to the FSB, one of the detainees was recruited by an SBU officer. Acting on his orders and in exchange for a promised monetary reward, the detainee traveled to Russia to plan a terrorist attack.
- To this end, he enlisted the help of a close acquaintance. Together, they retrieved FPV drones and components for homemade explosive devices from hiding places in the Smolensk and Kaluga Regions.
- The FSB had prior intelligence indicating that individuals from the South Caucasus were preparing an FPV drone attack on air defense and energy facilities in Moscow on behalf of the SBU. These individuals were agents of the Ukrainian special services, just like their handler, an FSB officer reported.
- The operation involving the handlers is ongoing, he noted.
Investigation
- A criminal case has been initiated against the detainees under Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code (Participation in a Terrorist Organization).
- The court remanded them into custody.
- The Federal Security Service is conducting the necessary investigative and operational measures to establish all the circumstances of the suspects’ illegal activities and their possible connections, the press office noted.

Burnham wants UK back in EU within his lifetime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:13:20 UTC
19:13:20 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives to address a press conference with the German Chancellor at the Chancellery in Berlin on October 8, 2026. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images
LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated Monday his desire for the U.K. to rejoin the EU within his lifetime — but ruled out a move to reverse Brexit in the current parliament.
Asked by ITV's Good Morning Britain Monday whether he wanted to rejoin the EU, Burnham said: “I'm going to be honest and say, in my lifetime, I would like to see that happen but I am not going to move ahead of the public.
“I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here. You have to make sure that the public, the British public, are the bosses.”
Advertisement
At the ruling Labour Party's conference last month, Burnham called for closer links with the EU.
He has yet to spell out precise details of the relationship he would seek — but the party's 2024 election-winning manifesto under Keir Starmer ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or accepting freedom of movement with the bloc.
Burnham said Monday that the promises of the 2016 referendum that took Britain out of the EU have not been delivered.
“We got a harder Brexit than was proposed in the referendum campaign,” he said. “It's weakened our economy. It's also weakened our control of immigration and that might surprise people.”
But he said: “I'm not proposing rejoining in this Parliament. We're way, way away from that at this particular moment in time. What I am saying is we need to take some practical steps to make the arrangement work better than the arrangement we've got right now.”
The PM's remarks come after he told the Sunday Times that accepting freedom of movement with the bloc should not be off the table in future negotiations.
Advertisement
A U.K.-EU summit is scheduled for next month, although that is set to focus tightly on technical tweaks to the existing relationship rather than addressing bigger questions of Britain's future ties to the bloc.
Burnham's decision to reignite debate in Britain about the EU has already provoked a bullish response from some of Brexit's leading cheerleaders.
Speaking at a Westminster press conference Monday, Nigel Farage said rejoining the bloc would be “utterly moronic” and argued Brexiteers would win a referendum on reversing the result “very comfortably.”
“Listen, Brexit would not have happened if I had not been born — all right, simple as that," the Reform UK leader said Monday. "Yes, there were some Johnny-Come-Latelies. They came in at five minutes to midnight. Am I up for the fight again? You bet your blooming life I am.”

Syria to launch 1st nationwide mine map under 3-year clearance strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:12:36 UTC
19:12:36 KST

Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Syria will soon launch its first map showing the distribution of mines across the country as part of a three-year strategy to combat landmines and war remnants, Emergency and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Monday.
“The National Mine Action Center is implementing the strategy to identify mine-contaminated areas and strengthen efforts to address the threat,” al-Saleh said in comments carried by the ISNA news agency.
“Mines and unexploded remnants of war remain among the most serious challenges facing Syria because of their direct impact on civilians and children, as well as their obstruction of reconstruction efforts and the use of agricultural land,” he said.
Al-Saleh said his ministry continues to develop mine-clearance plans and strategies despite existing challenges, with the aim of achieving tangible results that protect civilians and allow residents to make use of their farmland.
“Syria is also working to exchange expertise and benefit from advanced demining technologies in cooperation with Germany and Ukraine,” he added.
Separately, the minister said the ministry is working to establish a joint operations room with Türkiye for emergency response and disaster management on both sides of the border.
The mechanism is intended to spee coordination and response to fires, floods and other disasters, he added.
Syrian authorities regularly report deaths and injuries caused by explosions from remnants of the war waged by the Bashar al-Assad regime against civilians from 2011 to 2024.
The war killed and injured hundreds of thousands of people and caused massive destruction to infrastructure before opposition fighters entered Damascus on Dec. 8, 2024, leading to the fall of the Assad regime.
Syrian authorities and international organizations, including the International Committee of the Red Cross, continue field operations in several parts of Syria to detect mines and unexploded ordnance left by the war.
According to Landmine Monitor data, unexploded ordnance in Syria has killed or injured more than 13,000 people since 2011.

Jordan: 3 arrested over deadly church attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria
October 26, 2026
Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.
Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.
Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.
But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.
A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.
Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province
Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.
Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.
"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."
He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.
"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.
Who carried out the attack in Jordan?
There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.
Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn and Wesley Dockery

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment in over 50 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:10:40 UTC
19:10:40 KST

Algeria to send troops to Niger in first foreign deployment in over 50 years
Algeria’s parliament on Sunday approved a resolution to send troops to Niger, making the first time Algerian soldiers will be deployed abroad since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including near its border with Algeria, and the deployment comes as Algiers and Niamey are building the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline after decades of delays.
Algeria on Sunday approved sending troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy facilities, according to statements from both houses of parliament, in what is the country's first foreign deployment of military forces since the 1970s.
The rare measure comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.
The overseas deployment will be a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The upper house approved the proposal, it said in a statement, with a legislator telling AFP it was approved by all 148 members in attendance.
The parliament's lower house said it also voted "by an absolute majority" to deploy the military unit in Niger, though it did not provide numbers.
Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre (600-mile) desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.
"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher, before the official confirmation.
"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.
The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.
Read moreTrans-Saharan Gas Pipeline: an African dream that could reshape world energy markets
'Strong signal'
Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" – two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.
Read moreAlgeria cuts diplomatic ties with United Arab Emirates over 'provocative and hostile actions'
Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".
Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means – dialogue, international law, multilateral forums", Porter told AFP.
"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved towards more tangible means – actual physical presence."
"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."
Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.
"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on October 3. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."
"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."
The deployment of troops outside Algeria's territory required the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.
Gifted warplanes
The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.
A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.
The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.
Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.
Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.
The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.
Niger has been run by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a July 2023 coup that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

France Tests HELMA-P Laser Anti-Drone System Aboard Charles de Gaulle Aircraft Carrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:10:30 UTC
19:10:30 KST

The French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle tested a laser anti-drone system during the La Fayette 26 mission.
The system was tested on the ship’s flight deck between June 4 and 8, according to the French Navy’s magazine Cols Bleus, as reported by Zone Militaire.
The experiment took place while the aircraft carrier was docked in the Gulf of Oman. A joint team of specialists from the Centre for Military Aviation Expertise (CEAM) and the ground-based air defense division was involved in deploying the system.
Installing the equipment aboard the ship took about four hours. The system comprises a camera turret, a LIDAR, a laser emitter, a cooling unit and a control console.
Although Cols Bleus described this as the system’s first shipboard test, the published photo shows the HELMA-P system in use.
In June 2023, the French military first tested the laser on the deck of the Forbin frigate. At the time, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces noted the laser’s high accuracy and effectiveness.
Development of the HELMA-P (High Energy Laser for Multiple Applications – Power) system began in 2017 by CILAS. The project is being carried out under the L2AD program to develop laser weapons for countering drones.
Before its sea trials, HELMA-P successfully completed ground tests in 2020 and 2021. The system was also deployed to provide security during the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris.
Technically, HELMA-P is a directed-energy weapon integrated with target detection and tracking systems. It is designed to neutralize small drones and other ‘asymmetric’ threats.
During operation, the laser uses a powerful beam to destroy the target’s structure within seconds.
The Charles de Gaulle is not the only aircraft carrier equipped with similar weaponry. In October 2025, the US aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush tested the LOCUST system and subsequently used it in the Gulf of Oman.

If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner Mueller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:28 UTC
19:00:28 KST

Whichever metaphor one prefers – landslide, earthquake, wave – it seems increasingly like the Democrats can expect a significant victory in the midterms.
As the joke goes, every gas station display of prices has become an ad for Democrats; what’s more, some of them have managed to connect the relatively abstract issue of corruption to the daily misery of many Americans.
But, in the end, no election outcome ever interprets itself; Democrats should not rest content with the conclusion that only what moderate leaders (and consultants) like to call kitchen table issues really mattered.
They have a historic opportunity to dislodge the image of the Republicans as the party of national security and the party best trusted with the economy.
After 2024, Republicans massively benefited from elite actors – Silicon Valley oligarchs, no less than many journalists – reading a globally important “vibe shift” into the presidential election outcome; we now know that what political scientists politely call “low-information voters” were simply fed up with inflation, as opposed to a large majority thirsting for a far-right agenda.
But Trumpists turned the perception to their advantage; and to be sure, successful politicians are entitled to interpret a vote as they see fit.
Democrats could stay relatively timid and read the outcome as simply a rejection of Donald Trump and the most egregious elements of his misrule since January 2025; they certainly should make the point that the spectacular cruelty of ICE and the incitement to hatred in which Stephen Miller and JD Vance regularly engage is deeply unpopular with the public. But it would be a mistake to see the outcome as only a referendum on Trumpism.
True, the US president’s catastrophic record in foreign policy is partly explained by conduct the old Republican establishment could never have imagined: recklessly alienating allies, with the result that the US may never be trusted by Nato countries again; massively destroying soft power by mistreating foreign students and undermining the capacity of American universities to attract talent internationally; blatant interference in elections to favor the global far right.
But the Iran war shows continuities with the George W Bush era that neoconservatives probably find uncomfortable to contemplate: an inability to think strategically and an apparent indifference to loss of human life. In fact, a line can be drawn from the torture memos to the murders at sea and the plans for a public execution under the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.
Yet the Republican party still lives off an image that the party of Ronald Reagan is supremely competent in matters of national security. The right response is not that Democrats should not enter a competition of how often they can use the word “lethality” in one sentence; they should simply point out how shameful it is that Republicans, some murmuring on the part of has-beens like Thom Tillis aside, have betrayed Ukraine; how damaging the loss of bases in the Middle East will turn out to be; and that, from the very beginning of Trump 2.0, it was a sign of deep unseriousness to put a second-rate TV host in charge of the world’s most powerful military force. There might be monuments to both Trump and Hegseth in Moscow and Beijing one day; after all, they effectively capitulated to the former and sped up the rise of the latter.
The Republican party has also long benefited from the notion that, as the party of business, they are best qualified to boost the economy (no doubt, some low-information voters still buy into the myth of Trump as the great entrepreneur).
The actual record has long shown something different: not just when it comes to Trump and his string of bankruptcies, but for the party as a whole. Since Trump engaged in policies so irrational and damaging that the old Republican establishment would never have contemplated them – tariffs being the obvious example – it is again easy to overlook continuities.
The party that claims to be deeply concerned about debt and deficits (one of Elon Musk’s disingenuous justifications for Doge’s chainsaw massacres) has given us Reagan, Bush and Trump – all of whom managed massively to increase the national debt. The reason is, of course, that they pushed through enormous tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy.
In the postwar period, economic growth, job creation and even stock market returns have on the whole been higher under Democratic administrations; it just seems that average gains are not enough for the uber-wealthy, who can buy themselves tax cuts by donating massively to Republicans.
Needless to say, as soon as Democrats are in charge, Republicans discover that the very debt they were instrumental in causing constitutes a national crisis and requires deep cuts to social security.
Conventional wisdom has it that the Biden administration overreached: too woke, too ambitious a Green New Deal, too harsh in its criticisms of Maga Republicans (with the next claim usually being that such overreach made a “backlash” inevitable and, so the implication goes, at least somewhat legitimate).
But what if the opposite is true? What if Joe Biden’s mistake was to assume that there were still many Republicans who cared about policy – as opposed to endless culture war performance a la Hegseth – and long-term success for the country?
What if Democrats seized the opportunity to discredit their opponents in the way Franklin D Roosevelt made the most of the Great Depression (as opposed to pining for bipartisanship); what if they showed people that all the Republicans who will soon be running away from Trump were not just complicit in the misrule, but that the misrule has been part of a larger story predating Trump?

If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:00:27 UTC
19:00:27 KST

After Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.
I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.
Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.
Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.
This kind of talk isn’t cheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.
But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownership and investing on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.
Many of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures to provide breathing room in the face of the cost of living crisis.
Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.
So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the time John Healey finishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.
We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such as equalising income and capital gains tax.
The decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.
So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.
- Andrea Egan is the general secretary of Unison

Carrying Iran’s flag at Youth Olympics a great honor, Faraji says

Faraji and national futsal player Hadis Yari have been selected as Iran’s flag-bearers for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
