From metalworker to Brazil's president: Lula da Silva's rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:18:13 UTC
18:18:13 KST

Lula broke with his unfavourable record since 1989, winning the runoff after losing the first round, crowning a career that took him from metalworker to Brazil's presidency.
After losing in the first round, Lula da Silva pulled off a historic comeback to be re-elected president of Brazil in the second round. Back in the Palácio do Planalto, which he had never left, the leader of the Workers' Party (PT) defied unfavourable precedent: since 1989, the year when Brazil returned to direct presidential elections and introduced the two-round system**,** no candidate trailing after the first round had ever gone on to win the second.
"I owe this to you. I have always thought that God has been very generous to me, because there are so many people better prepared than I am, so many people with more diplomas than I have, so many people who have read more books than I have, so many people who have studied more than I have," he said in his victory speech, his fourth after a presidential election.
It was a first for Lula, too. In 1989, he finished 13.3 points behind his rival Fernando Collor de Mello in the first round and failed to close the gap in the second.
From factory worker to trade unionist, from trade unionist to politician, from politician to president of Brazil. Nothing has ever seemed impossible for Lula, who once again showed with this election that adversity is not always insurmountable.
"I want to tell you that I am enormously proud. First, because I am the only president of the Republic, a metalworker without a university degree, elected four times, democratically, to call for peace," he told the crowd.
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, promised "the best term" in Brazilian history.
"The day after tomorrow, on the 27th, I will turn 81. And I want to make a pledge in front of the press and in front of you. I am going to deliver the best term any president has ever served in the history of this country," he vowed.
The seventh child of illiterate farmer parents, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was born on 27 October 1945 in the Brazilian city of Garanhuns, in the north-eastern state of Pernambuco. He was only seven when he moved with his family to São Paulo, and 14 when he was admitted to a technical course in metalworking. Before that, he had already worked as a street vendor, shoeshine boy, and dye-shop assistant. He went on to become a metalworker, a profession he later defended as a trade unionist.
"Lula" began as a nickname and was later officially incorporated into his name – he is the epitome of the worker who becomes a politician: it was as a union leader and organiser of metalworkers' strikes in the São Paulo region, during the military dictatorship, that he made his name. During his years as a metalworker, he lost a finger in a workplace accident, which later earned him the disparaging nickname “nine fingers” among opponents.
It was these strikes, which he led between 1978 and 1980, that paved the way for the founding of the Workers' Party (PT) in 1980. The party would go on to emerge as the main force on Brazil's left after the country's democratisation between 1985 and 1988, with Lula as its leading figure.
After losing the presidential elections of 1989, 1994 and 1998, he finally reached the presidency in 2002, where he remained for two terms. He was the first trade union leader and manual worker to enter the Palácio do Planalto.
Supporters of his political legacy point to the transformation of a country marked by extreme poverty and illiteracy into a more prosperous and more equal Brazil, through social policy measures such as the introduction of the "Bolsa Família" in 2003 and the creation of the "Zero Hunger" programme.
Lula ended his first term with an approval rating of 57% and was re-elected in 2006 with more than 58 million votes, the highest tally in Brazil's history.
The results would ultimately bolster Lula's narrative that the state can play a decisive role in reducing poverty and hunger. In 2014, under the government of Dilma Rousseff, Lula's political successor, Brazil left the United Nations' Hunger Map after a significant reduction in undernourishment in the country. The shift was linked to a package of social and economic policies.
Politically, he has always presented himself as a defender of multilateralism, diplomacy and an international order in which decisions are not determined solely by the power of the major powers.
"War is not the continuation of politics by other means. It is the total failure of politics. In an interdependent world, to lead is to reconcile the interests of the homeland with those of humanity. That is the reflection of someone who represents a nation that cherishes peace and freedom. Someone who fought against a military dictatorship and defended his country against an attempted coup. It is the conviction of a worker elected three times as president who took Brazil off the Hunger Map," he declared on 22 September 2026 in his speech to the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.
But the corruption scandals engulfing Lula and the PT would catch up with him, temporarily curtailing his political career.
The "Car Wash" investigation and subsequent trials led by judge Sérgio Moro (later Bolsonaro's justice minister) dominated the second half of the 2010s. It brought down numerous heavyweights and sent dozens of politicians from across the spectrum to prison. The investigation, which exposed a complex bribery and kickback scheme centred on the semi-state oil company Petrobras and the construction giant Odebrecht, was central to fuelling distrust of Brazil's political class and the rise of right-wing populism embodied by Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula was jailed in March 2018, after being sentenced to nine years in prison for allegedly receiving a flat in exchange for political favours. After 580 days in custody, Lula was released in November 2019, following a change in Supreme Federal Court case law on when a sentence may begin to be served.
In 2021, the Supreme Court went further and annulled the former president's convictions in the case, ruling that the court in Curitiba lacked jurisdiction to try him. This cleared the way for the PT founder to return to the presidential race, which he went on to win in 2022.
His victory in the 2026 election marks a new phase in a political story defined by his ability to return to power, even if the road ahead now appears somewhat steeper.
The Brazil Lula now governs is not the one he led in the 2000s: the country remains deeply polarised, Congress is dominated by the centre-right and Bolsonarism still commands significant electoral strength.

Radev Says Bulgaria’s Presidential Runoff Will be a Choice Between Peace and War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:17:26 UTC
18:17:26 KST

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the upcoming presidential runoff would be a choice between peace and war, democracy and corruption, urging voters to support Iliana Yotova and warning against complacency, this was reported from his remarks to journalists at the Sofia Economic Forum.
Radev blamed PP-DB, GERB and the DPS for low turnout, arguing that their constitutional amendments and political conduct had persuaded many people that voting would make no difference. He also congratulated Yotova on her victory in the previous vote, describing the turnout as unprecedentedly low and praising her for maintaining her dignity instead of joining the aggressive campaign against her.
“Let’s send the 'assembly' to oblivion this Sunday,” Radev said, calling on Bulgarians to vote for Yotova. He argued that the presidential election was a battle for the political survival of the architects of the so-called sglobka, or “assembly” (referring to the previous joint government of PP-DB and GERB) and accused them of seeking revenge through the presidency.
Radev also claimed that Andrey Gyurov had entered the political fray to defend Delyan Peevski after the arrests of DPS mayors the previous week. He said the runoff would offer voters a clear choice between peace and war, democracy and what he called the coalition’s corrupt model, as well as calm truth and the hysteria spread by internet trolls.
Asked whose support Yotova would rely on in the second round, Radev cautioned against treating the presidential race like a parliamentary election, saying that forecasts had made some voters complacent. He insisted that the outcome remained open and that the low turnout sent a deeply troubling signal about Bulgarian society.
The prime minister also said Bulgaria’s ports were safe and that NATO and allied countries were providing assistance following recent attacks on vessels in the Black Sea.
At the Sofia Economic Forum, Radev outlined the government's priorities for the 2027 budget, including stabilizing public finances, supporting economic growth, providing assistance to families and businesses, and raising defense spending. He also presented plans to expand transport and energy infrastructure and attract major international investment in artificial intelligence and robotics.
Radev said the cabinet was working amid a difficult economic and geopolitical climate shaped by the war in Ukraine, conflicts in the Middle East and growing security risks. He said the draft budget for next year, due to be presented next week, would need to balance higher incomes and investment support with reductions in the budget deficit and national debt.
The government had inherited what Radev described as an empty treasury burdened by debt, no budget, a delayed Recovery and Resilience Plan, rapidly rising social expenditure and insufficient capital investment. He also pointed to continuing declines in foreign direct investment, exports and industrial production.
“In the 2027 Budget, we are setting clear priorities. First and foremost is the restoration of sound public finances,” Radev said. He said the plan would provide greater social and family support, increase defense funding and expand investment in healthcare, education, culture and sports. The government also intends to encourage production through tax incentives, arguing that higher productivity and competitiveness are essential to meeting its budgetary goals.
Radev said Bulgaria needed to move away from an economic model based on consumption, wealth redistribution and cheap labor, and toward faster growth driven by investment, innovation and improved productivity.
On security in the Black Sea, the prime minister said Bulgarian institutions had responded quickly to recent attacks on vessels, deploying military capabilities and seeking help from NATO and European partners. He said rescue teams had reached the sites of the incidents in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone within minutes, despite darkness and severe weather.
“We demonstrated that Bulgaria, as a civilized nation, is capable of fulfilling its international obligations regarding emergency search and rescue,” Radev said.
He said talks had taken place with representatives of NATO, the European Commission, Romania and Turkey, and that allied aircraft were already helping monitor the Black Sea region.
Radev also addressed demands to identify those responsible for the attacks, saying he had summoned the Russian ambassador and clearly stated his position. He described himself as the only prime minister among the three NATO member states bordering the Black Sea to have done so, but said accusations required evidence.
“Before making an accusation, I must have clear evidence. I cannot do so based on mere slogans,” he said.
The prime minister assured that Bulgaria’s ports and territorial waters remained safe for navigation. According to the figures he presented, the incidents had not reduced traffic through the ports of Varna and Burgas.
Radev said the European Union and NATO remained the foundation of Bulgaria’s security, alongside a strong transatlantic partnership with the United States, while stressing that the country also needed to continue building its own defense capabilities.
The government is planning to change how strategic infrastructure projects are financed, Radev said, arguing that relying exclusively on public funds could leave Bulgaria waiting at least 50 years to complete the transport links it needs.
He said the proposed approach would mobilize private capital and involve setting up a national investment company to begin raising funds through different channels as soon as possible. The government's priorities include a tunnel under the Petrohan Pass, the Black Sea and Rila motorways, the Vidin-Botevgrad corridor, completion of the Hemus highway and a third lane on the Trakia highway between Sofia and Plovdiv. Another planned project would link the Greek port of Alexandroupolis with Bulgaria and Romania.
Radev said the government was in advanced discussions with international investors about building large-scale artificial intelligence centers in Bulgaria. He described the prospective investors as a major European-American consortium interested in establishing what they called the largest AI “factory” in the country.
He said he had asked why the consortium would not choose Germany or France, and that the investors had cited waits of five years for permits and grid connections in those countries. Bulgaria, he said, offered faster decisions and implementation, together with support at the highest political level.
Radev also pointed to the country’s substantial battery-based electricity storage capacity, saying it created opportunities for lower electricity prices and renewable energy development. The government plans to advance three pumped-storage hydropower projects to help balance the energy system.
The prime minister described the Burgas refinery as a strategic asset for both Bulgaria and Europe, arguing that shortages of certain fuels across the continent made greater European involvement necessary to determine the refinery’s future.
The proposed budget will also include measures to support businesses, such as tax incentives for research and development and technology transfer, a higher VAT registration threshold, less administrative red tape and easier access to investment support.
Radev said the government intended to lower the threshold for priority investment projects from 25 million to 15 million, making it possible for medium-sized Bulgarian companies to qualify. He said the aim was to encourage Bulgarians to invest capital currently held in bank accounts in the real economy.
Despite public finance constraints, the government would allocate more funding to education and healthcare, Radev said, including for the National Children’s Hospital and the pay of young doctors. It is also preparing stricter oversight of spending by the National Health Insurance Fund through new digital systems.
Planned social measures include tax relief for families with children and children with disabilities, along with incentives for spending on sports and cultural activities.
“We will not leave pensioners without a pension increase. There will also be an increase within the administration, albeit a minimal one,” Radev said.

FRANKFURT – The chief executive officer of VW’s Audi unit drew heavy criticism on Oct 26 for appearing alongside US President Donald Trump at a rally to announce a US$4 billion (S$5.1 billion) plant in Georgia, with the head of Germany’s top union saying it violated the automaker’s company guidelines.
The plan, which still requires approval from the supervisory board of parent Volkswagen, comes after years of considerations over a local plant to escape painful US tariffs that have dealt a massive blow to the company.
Audi CEO Gernot Dollner appeared alongside Trump on Oct 24 at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia, to announce the plans to build its first assembly plant in the US that will produce 200,000 sport utility vehicles (SUVs) annually.
“The way in which Gernot Dollner has presented himself and Audi in the US is deeply embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company,” IG Metall president Christiane Benner said in a statement, adding that the appearance had violated Audi’s corporate rules. She is also the deputy chair of VW’s supervisory board.
German automotive expert Ferdinand Dudenhoffer referred to Dollner as a “mini Elon Musk”, comparing him to the Tesla boss who has appeared on stage with Trump.
Audi’s code of conduct stipulates that no “public engagements with political parties or politicians standing for election, nor any sponsorship of such events” are to take place in the three months leading up to an election.
The US investment also coincides with VW’s biggest corporate restructuring in history, including massive job cuts as well as potential plant closures at home.
Trump has pressured automakers to move production to the US and has raised tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminium and parts.
In 2025, Trump’s tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion (S$1.72 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico.
Georgia has competitive election races for the US Senate and state governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. But critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Dollner said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
In Germany, meanwhile, there has been increasing tension between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker’s home market, including possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian competition.
“It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant,” said Benner earlier. “However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out.”
An opportunity if German workers gain
Olaf Lies, Premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, VW’s second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit.
“Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them,” he said.
Dollner defended Audi’s planned investment. “This decision was preceded by many months of careful planning and intense negotiations,” he told reporters on Oct 25.
“If the American President invites you, you accept the invitation. That is what respect for the office and for the country in which we invest demands.”
He declined to give full details on the investment deal with the US, including whether it involves tariff relief for the company.
The plan to set up the premium carmaker’s first US production presence was “not a decision against Germany”, Dollner added, arguing that it could protect jobs at home by strengthening Audi’s global business.
“The optics are not great, jobs are being created in the US while Audi is reducing the capacity globally,” Metzler analysts said of the US plan. “Still, we would argue the decision to produce in the US is right.” REUTERS

Lula wins Brazil election after cutting Amazon deforestation to record low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:15:46 UTC
18:15:46 KST

Lula’s victory in Brazil's presidential election brings hope for the Amazon – but far-right gains threaten progress.
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s election has been hailed as a win for democracy and the Amazon.
Since his return to office in 2023, deforestation in the Brazilian rainforest has hit a record low, dropping 42 per cent in the last year alone.
The left-wing President’s historic fourth-term reelection comes as a relief for environmentalists who feared a return to weakened nature and climate protections under right-wing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
During his presidency from 2019-2023, environmental policies were dismantled and deforestation surged by around 60 per cent, with more than 45,000 square kilometres cleared.
Under Lula, deforestation has fallen 71 per cent below its 2022 level.
Greenpeace Brazil said the 2026 election result “is a win for democracy and maintains the commitment to protecting the Amazon and fighting climate change”.
This optimism has been shared by environmentalists around the world: “Hurrah for the Amazon, the Cerrado, Pantanal and all Brazil’s nature!”, posted Glenn Hurowitz, founder and CEO of global nature advocacy organisation Mighty Earth. “Lula’s reelection is a much-needed relief for the rainforest and the country’s other extraordinary ecosystems.”
Why is Brazil's Amazon important to the world?
“Brazil is home to most of the world’s largest tropical rainforest and five other biomes, harbouring around 15 per cent of global biodiversity,” says Camila Jardim, International Political Expert at Greenpeace Brazil.
“Protecting these ecosystems matters far beyond Brazil’s borders and is essential to halting biodiversity loss worldwide.”
The rainforest also stores huge amounts of planet-heating carbon dioxide and generates atmospheric moisture that helps regulate weather far beyond South America.
Under Lula’s government, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since monitoring began in 1988.
How did Brazil cut deforestation to record lows?
The huge progress in cutting deforestation is thanks to the Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon (PPCDAm), which had been shelved under Bolsonaro.
The plan strengthened satellite monitoring of illegal forest clearing and enforcement of sanctions. It also uses regulations and financial incentives to curb deforestation and promote sustainable actions.
“Lula’s election keeps hope alive for nature finance that can make trees worth more alive than dead,” says Hurowitz. “Under Lula, the Brazilian government launched the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, an elegant system where investors reward countries for conservation, but which needs more capital.”
“This progress must be sustained, and efforts to protect and restore ecosystems across Brazil’s biomes must intensify, respecting the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities,” says Jardim.
Right-wing congress could dampen Lula’s power
Flávio Bolsonaro has said he does not recognise the 2026 election result and will challenge it in court, citing a last-minute Supreme Court ruling that extended voting by two hours. Lula won by about 4.4 million votes, receiving about 51.8 per cent versus Bolsonaro’s 48.2 per cent.
Despite Lula’s narrow win, his rival’s party made huge gains in the National Congress.
“These elections saw a significant surge of the far-right in the National Congress, which includes a large contingent of climate deniers and anti-environmentalists,” Greenpeace Brazil said in a statement.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will control 121 out of 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 28 out of 81 seats in the Senate from February 2027. Lula’s Workers’ Party federation will have 88 seats in the Chamber of Deputies. Centre-right parties will be decisive in whether legislation passes.
“Over the next four years, public mobilisation will be essential to defend rights and prevent potentially irreversible environmental setbacks,” said Greenpeace Brazil.
“Although the government faces a hostile Congress, it can enforce the law and designate new parks and Indigenous reserves – locking in progress,” says Hurowitz.
Threats also remain from wildfires, logging and drought, with this year’s strong El Niño expected to bring hotter, drier conditions conducive to fires.

Breadcrumb
Beirut's pricey $13 chicken sandwich becomes symbol of class divide in Lebanon
Seven years after Lebanon's devastating financial meltdown, a debate over a chicken sandwich has exposed an increasingly stark divide between those who can still spend freely and those struggling to get by.
A trendy health restaurant wanted to offer its calorie-conscious customers a healthier take on the beloved Levantine wrap known as the shish taouk. So, The Glow Paradise launched the "Chic Taouk," pricing it at around $13—nearly double what an un-chic chicken sandwich typically goes for in Beirut.
The pricy pun proved hard to swallow, with outraged critics accusing the restaurant of overcharging in a country where many households struggle to afford basic necessities.
Yet while the debate raged on social media, customers kept buying. The Glow Paradise sold more than 20,000 Chic Taouk sandwiches in just 11 days, according to managing partner Hrag Jeghalian, who described the online exchanges as "natural marketing".
The contrasting reactions touched a nerve in Lebanon, where years of financial turmoil, political dysfunction and conflict have reshaped the country's social landscape, hollowing out much of the middle class while leaving a smaller group of consumers able to sustain an affluent lifestyle.
Debate pulls focus away from urgent crises
Sami Nader, an economist at the Saint Joseph University of Beirut, said the throngs at The Glow Paradise belied another reality.
"So you see people in the restaurant, but what you don't see is that 22 restaurants closed last month," Nader told Reuters.
Lebanon's Instagram-active community was split between those accusing the restaurant of theft and others saying the sandwich was intended for those who could afford it.
Some questioned whether the dispute itself reflected misplaced priorities in a country grappling with urgent crises, from Israel’s occupation of large swaths of the country’s south to the endemic electricity and water crises.
Lebanon's 2019 financial collapse was prompted by decades of corruption and profligate spending by the ruling elite, and several rounds of conflict since then have worsened the country’s economic outlook.
GDP has declined by nearly 40% since 2019 and inflation is expected to rise to 17.5% due to rising global energy and shipping prices eating away at people’s purchasing power, according to the World Bank. The figure is more than quadruple the global headline inflation rate flagged by the International Monetary Fund in July.
Four in five households in Lebanon struggle to afford basic necessities, the UN children's agency said in September.
'People can't keep up'
The country’s middle class has "disappeared," Nader said, dismantled by a series of crises including the collapse of the financial system in 2019, the 2020 Beirut Port explosion and two wars in under two years.
Monthly bills from private generator operators, which provide electricity to many homes and businesses during outages on Lebanon's failing national grid, jumped by nearly 20% in August 2026 alone, bringing rates nearly 60% higher than they were in February of this year, according to the kilowatt-hour prices set by Lebanon's energy ministry.
For many, that means paying for 24/7 electricity now costs several hundred dollars a month, in a country where the minimum wage is set at $400.
"Everything has become expensive, and people can’t keep up," said Fouad Fakhreddine, a 53-year-old restaurant worker from nearby Hamra. "We are now getting paid, then getting in debt over that just to get by."
The years of economic instability, he said, have produced "a class that is living, and a class that is not dead and waiting to die from the unbearable situation it is in."

India-Russia trade jumps more than 20% this year – Duma chairman

Volodin met the speaker of the Lok Sabha, Om Birla, ahead of the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, which New Delhi is hosting on October 26-27. The discussions covered closer cooperation on trade, industry and agriculture, along with the strengthening of parliamentary ties.
Bilateral commerce reached $47.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 24.3% from a year earlier, according to data from the Indian Commerce Ministry, cited by Russian lender Sberbank.
India imported $44.9 billion of Russian goods during the period, including $36 billion in crude oil. Indian exports to Russia totaled $2.8 billion, with Moscow increasing purchases of chemicals, electrical goods, medical equipment, seafood, tea, and spices.

New power outages in six regions due to Russian attacks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
11:07:02 EET
18:07:02 KST

New power outages in six regions due to Russian attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Due to Russian attacks, new power outages were recorded in six regions. Hourly and industrial restrictions will remain in effect until the end of the day.
New power outages caused by Russian attacks have been recorded as of the morning of October 26 in six regions of Ukraine. The schedules remain in effect. This was reported by NEC "Ukrenergo" on Monday, UNN writes.
Enemy shelling
"Over the past day, the enemy continued to attack Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure. As a result, as of this morning, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Chernihiv, Kharkiv, and Sumy regions," Ukrenergo reported.
As stated, emergency restoration work is already underway wherever security conditions currently allow. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power to all consumers who have been disconnected as soon as possible.
Schedules
"To prevent overloading equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, in some regions today until the end of the day, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to 2.5 rounds) for all categories of consumers will be applied as a necessary measure," Ukrenergo noted.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has decreased. Today, October 26, as of 09:30, it was 5.8% lower than at the same time on the previous working day—Friday, October 23. The reason for the change is the necessary restrictions caused by enemy attacks.
Yesterday, October 25, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 4.8% higher than the maximum recorded on the previous Sunday—October 18. This was caused by a drop in air temperature, prompting consumers to use electric heaters in the evening hours.
"Given the consequences of Russian shelling and the weather conditions, the need for economical electricity consumption during the evening hours remains. Please limit the use of powerful electrical appliances from 16:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo urged.

Ambassador Lener in Melbourne for the Eureka Democracy Award ceremony
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
10:06:59 CET
18:06:59 KST

Nicola Lener, the ambassador to Canberra, spoke in Melbourne at the annual “Eureka Democracy” award ceremony, where this year’s prize was awarded to Antony Green, a former journalist with the public television network ABC who specializes in analyzing voter trends. The ambassador attended the event at the invitation of the “Stockade Australia” association, composed of descendants of the key figures in the failed Eureka Rebellion of December 3, 1854, remembered as one of the founding moments of Australian democracy.
                                    
In recent months, the embassy in Canberra had collaborated with the association to identify the location (the ossuary at the Verano Monumental Cemetery in Rome) where Raffaele Carboni is buried, a follower of Giuseppe Garibaldi who took part in the uprising and later recounted it in the book “The Eureka Stockade.” In his remarks, Ambassador Lener recalled the life story of Carboni, a follower of Mazzini and Garibaldi, who emigrated to Australia following the Roman Republic of 1849 and returned to Italy after being tried and acquitted for the Eureka Rebellion, and he highlighted the significance of the connection between the two countries centered on democratic ideals even before both achieved their independence. A deep connection, the ambassador emphasized, that predates the great waves of Italian migration to Australia and is being renewed today through the full alignment between Rome and Canberra on multilateralism and a rules-based international order.

China congratulates Brazil’s Lula on reelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:06:32 UTC
18:06:32 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
China on Monday congratulated Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva following his reelection to a historic fourth term and expressed readiness to strengthen bilateral ties.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters that Beijing has noted the outcome of Brazil's presidential election, won by Lula, and congratulated him on his victory.
China wished Brazil "even greater achievements in national development under the leadership" of Lula, Guo said.
"We are ready to promote the China-Brazil community with a shared future," he added.
Lula defeated Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff, winning 51.79% of valid votes, or more than 60 million ballots, compared with Bolsonaro's 48.21%.
"China respects the choice of the Brazilian people," Guo said when asked to comment on Bolsonaro's refusal to concede defeat.
Lula's victory in Sunday's election was historic, securing him a fourth term as president, a first for any Brazilian politician.

BELGRADE, October 26. /TASS/. The opposition Student List is leading in Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections with 52.57% of the vote, while the United Serbia list backed by former President Aleksandar Vucic has received 39.27%, the Republic Electoral Commission reported after counting 96.47% of the voting records.
The remaining parties failed to clear the 3% electoral threshold. The Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians will also be represented in the 250-seat National Assembly, Serbia’s unicameral parliament, as it is exempt from the requirement to reach that threshold.
On October 25, Vucic conceded defeat for his supporters in the election. He said the Student List would be able to form a parliamentary majority on its own.

Istanbul braces for new round of flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:06:16 UTC
18:06:16 KST

Istanbul is bracing for another round of heavy rainfall on Oct. 27, with Türkiye’s meteorological authority warning of possible flash floods and inundations in the city and other parts of western Türkiye, less than two weeks after torrential downpours killed eight people in Istanbul and the neighboring province of Kocaeli.
The Turkish State Meteorological Service forecast heavy showers and thunderstorms across western parts of the country throughout the week, with temperatures expected to fall below seasonal averages in some areas.
Abdullah Macit, a weather forecasting expert, said heavy rainfall was expected on Oct. 27 in the Marmara region, including Istanbul, Çanakkale, Tekirdağ and Bursa, as well as parts of the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts.
Rainfall is also expected to affect southern parts of İzmir, Antalya and Muğla, along with eastern areas of Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay.
Macit warned that the downpours could cause flooding and inundation, urging residents to take precautions. He said Istanbul was expected to remain dry on Oct. 26 and 28, but face heavy showers on Oct. 27.
Temperatures in Istanbul are forecast to drop to around 15 degrees Celsius on Oct. 27 before rising to approximately 19 degrees in the following days.
The meteorological service also expects heavy rainfall in parts of the Aegean and Mediterranean regions. Showers are forecast to be particularly intense in İzmir, Muğla, Aydın and western Antalya, with very heavy to torrential rain possible in parts of Muğla and Aydın.
The agency issued an orange-coded heavy rainfall warning, indicating a high risk of dangerous weather conditions for Aydın and Muğla, and a yellow-coded warning, signaling potentially hazardous conditions that require caution, for Antalya, Denizli and İzmir.
In the capital Ankara, showers and thunderstorms are expected from Oct. 27, accompanied by falling temperatures that could dip below seasonal norms in some areas.
The latest warnings come after torrential rainfall on Oct. 14 set an 84-year precipitation record in Istanbul, killing seven people in the city and one in neighboring Kocaeli. The downpours flooded roads, underpasses, homes and businesses, while vehicles were swept away by floodwaters.
Schools were closed from Oct. 15 as a precaution and reopened on Oct. 19, following the deadly flooding.
Authorities have advised residents in regions expected to see heavy rainfall to exercise caution against flash flooding and water pooling, especially in vulnerable urban zones.

Lula da Silva reelected Brazilian president: voting results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:05:47 UTC
18:05:47 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which carries out the functions of the Central Election Commission, has completed the vote count for the second round of the presidential election. According to the final results, with 100% of ballots counted, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has officially been reelected.
TASS has compiled the key information about the voting results.
Election results
According to the election authority’s final statistics, Lula da Silva, the candidate of the left-wing Workers’ Party, won with 51.79% of the vote, receiving 64,256,232 votes.
His rival, right-wing opposition Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, received 48.21%, with 59,826,041 people voting for him.
The total number of valid votes was 124,082,273.
Voter turnout in the second round stood at 80.78%, with 128,236,074 citizens taking part in the vote.
A total of 19.22% of the electorate, or 30,509,005 people, did not vote.
Invalid ballots accounted for 2.12%, or 2,723,305 ballots.
Another 1.12%, or 1,430,496 ballots, were blank.
A total of 158,745,502 people were eligible to vote in the election.
Records set
Lula da Silva set a new record by receiving the largest number of votes in the country’s history.
He also became the first politician in Brazilian history to hold the country’s highest office for a fourth time and set a record for the number of reelections since the rule allowing them was introduced in 1997. He has now been reelected twice.
In addition, Lula da Silva became the first candidate in the country’s history to win the election after finishing behind in the first round, when he received 45.16% of the vote against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 47.03%.
He will also become the oldest president in Brazil’s history.
According to CNN Brasil, the politician will be 81 years old when he takes office.
His fourth term as president will officially begin on January 5, 2027.
Flavio Bolsonaro’s position
Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing opposition candidate and senator who lost the second round of Brazil’s presidential election, refused to recognize the voting results and said they should be annulled.
He cited the judicial authorities’ decision to extend voting hours by two hours as the reason.
However, Bolsonaro’s campaign team, which refused to recognize the election results over the authorities’ decision to extend polling hours, had itself submitted a similar request, CNN Brasil reported.
According to the broadcaster, the campaign teams of both candidates had formally asked the courts to adjust voting hours.
Bolsonaro’s team requested an extension of voting in Sao Paulo state and several cities in the south of the country because of heavy rains that hit the region on the eve of and during the second round.
Meanwhile, the campaign team of incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s ruling left-wing Workers’ Party justified its request by citing a reduced bus fleet and transport problems in several states, including Sao Paulo and Bahia.
According to CNN Brasil, the Supreme Federal Court selectively considered the request submitted by the Workers’ Party’s campaign team.
The request was referred to Justice Cristiano Zanin, who ordered voting hours to be extended nationwide.

Türkiye services confidence falls in October, retail and construction sentiment improve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:05:24 UTC
18:05:24 KST

Türkiye’s seasonally adjusted confidence index fell in the services sector in October, while confidence improved in the retail trade and construction sectors compared with the previous month.
The services confidence index declined 2.4 percent month-on-month to 109.2 in October from 111.9 in September.
Readings above 100 indicate an optimistic outlook, while readings below 100 point to a pessimistic outlook.
Within the services sector, the business situation over the past three months index fell 3.1 percent to 106.8, while the demand-turnover over the past three months index declined 3.5 percent to 105.8. The demand-turnover expectation for the next three months edged down 0.7 percent to 115.0.
The retail trade confidence index increased 1.1 percent from the previous month to 112.5.
The business activity-sales over the past three months index rose 6.2 percent to 121.5, while the current volume of stock index increased 1.2 percent to 92.5. The business activity-sales expectation for the next three months, however, declined 3.4 percent to 123.6.
Meanwhile, the construction confidence index rose 0.4 percent month-on-month to 83.3 in October from 83.0 in September.
The current overall order books index increased 0.4 percent to 80.7, while the total employment expectation over the next three months index also rose 0.4 percent to 85.9.

Cruise liner hits container ship in Germany (VIDEO)
Unknown

Cruise liner hits container ship in Germany (VIDEO)
A cruise liner has collided with a container ship while departing Bremerhaven in northwestern Germany for a voyage to the Canary Islands.
The incident involving the Mein Schiff 3 occurred on Sunday in poor weather brought by storm Manja. Strong crosswinds appeared to overpower the tugboats assisting the 293-meter vessel down the Weser River. The collision was filmed from aboard the liner.
Hamburg-based operator TUI Cruises reported no injuries among the 2,428 guests and 922 crew members aboard the ship. The vessel was brought back to the pier for a damage assessment.
Media reports and footage indicate that at least three lifeboats were seriously damaged, potentially disrupting the voyage unless they can be replaced promptly. In similar cases, operators have negotiated cancellations with some guests to bring the number of people aboard into line with the remaining lifeboat capacity.
Die „Mein Schiff 3“ kollidiert beim Auslaufen in Bremerhaven mit einem Containerschiff. Aufnahmen zeigen die Wucht des Zusammenstoßes; mehrere Rettungsboote wurden offenbar beschädigt. Nach bisherigen Berichten gab es keine Verletzten. Die Unfallursache muss untersucht werden. Doch ich frage mich grundsätzlich: Wie lange wollen wir noch eine Kreuzfahrtindustrie fördern, deren Geschäftsmodell mit enormen Treibhausgasemissionen verbunden ist? Luxus auf See darf nicht bedeuten, dass die Umwelt die Rechnung bezahlt. Wir brauchen einen konsequenten Ausstieg aus besonders klimaschädlichen Kreuzfahrten. Klimaschutz ist keine freiwillige Zusatzleistung!
— Paro. Karl Kautabak (@KarlKautabak) October 25, 2026
The Mein Schiff 3 was beginning a 20-day ‘Timeless Canary Islands’ cruise, with its first stop scheduled for October 28 in the Spanish port of A Coruna.
The MSC Victorine, which the liner struck, also postponed its departure for Hamburg following the collision.
An initial police report mentioned a third vessel involved in the collision, although footage suggests the Mein Schiff 3 narrowly missed the smaller container ship MSC Anne F. before hitting the Victorine.
Some reports said two tugboats were also damaged. Shipping was temporarily suspended after the incident.

Criminal case opened against editor-in-chief of Russian border-region outlet Pepel on charges of justifying terrorism
The Belgorod branch of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has opened a criminal case against Nikita Parmenov, editor-in-chief of the outlet Pepel, on charges of justifying terrorism, Fonar reported, citing a statement from the security service.
According to the FSB, Parmenov voiced support for the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion, both designated terrorist organizations in Russia.
The FSB’s press release does not include the actual statements, when they were made, or links to them, Fonar said. The security service did not name Parmenov but said the person named in the case has been designated a “foreign agent” and “is located in one of the South Caucasus countries.”
Pepel itself suggested the case was likely triggered by a livestream on the YouTube channel Vremya Nakazhet “Time Will Punish.” Asked by the host during the stream about his attitude toward volunteer units fighting on Ukraine’s side, Parmenov said he could not condemn Russians who join them. In the same stream, he also said he “unequivocally condemns” the actions of units that have shelled civilians in the Belgorod region.
The outlet said the pro-war Telegram channel Zapiski Veterana “A Veteran’s Notes” had previously written that Parmenov allegedly supports the Russian Volunteer Corps and the “Freedom of Russia” Legion. According to Pepel, the channel’s authors had edited the stream, cutting out the part where Parmenov condemns the units for shelling Shebekino.
Pepel launched in the fall of 2022. Its Telegram channel now has 170,000 subscribers, and the outlet covers the war and its aftermath in the Belgorod border region without censorship.

7-year-old girl among 4 Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:54:53 UTC
17:54:53 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Lina Altawell
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Four Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl, were killed and 14 others injured in attacks by the Israeli army and Israel-backed gunmen in the Gaza Strip on Monday, amid daily violations of last year’s ceasefire agreement, a medical source said.
 
The source at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza told Anadolu that the bodies of two young men and a girl were brought to the hospital following an airstrike and gunfire in the Bir 19 area west of Khan Younis.
 
An Israeli drone carried out several strikes on Bir 19, an area housing tents for displaced Palestinians, killing a young man and moderately injuring four others, witnesses said.
 
Israeli military vehicles also opened heavy fire toward the displacement tents as Israeli-backed gunmen fired in the surrounding area, killing another young man and a 7-year-old girl, who was shot while inside her tent, they added.
 
Another Palestinian man was killed and four others were injured in an Israeli strike west of Khan Younis, the source said.
 
Local sources said an Israeli drone struck a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis.
 
Israeli artillery also shelled areas east of Khan Younis as military vehicles stationed east of the city opened heavy fire.
 
In central Gaza, a Palestinian woman sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire in the Ard al-Shawa area east of Deir al-Balah, another medical source said.
 
Israeli military vehicles made a limited advance east of Deir al-Balah amid heavy gunfire, witnesses said.
 
In northern Gaza, Israeli artillery shelled eastern Gaza City as tanks positioned behind the “Yellow Line” opened fire east of the Shujaiya and Tuffah neighborhoods, they added.
 
The “Yellow Line” marks the area to which Israeli forces withdrew during the first phase of the ceasefire agreement and separates territory under Israeli military control from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
 
Despite the ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
 
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Estonian musicians refuse to perform alongside Chinese orchestra with Russia links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Estonian musicians refuse to perform alongside Chinese orchestra with Russia links
The Estonian Festival Orchestra canceled a concert last week in China after it was revealed that the local symphony orchestra had close ties to Russia.
The Estonian Festival Orchestra, conducted by Paavo Järvi, is on tour in China and was scheduled to perform at Wuxi Symphony Hall, in eastern China, with the local orchestra on October 23.
The Wuxi orchestra toured Russia last year as part of an official China-Russia Years of Culture event and has performed with the Russian National Orchestra.
After learning about their partner's background, the Estonian musicians refused to take part in the joint concert.
The cancellation could cost the Estonian Festival Orchestra hundreds of thousands of euros, although the exact amount is not yet known.
According to the Estonian musicians, going ahead with the concert would have conflicted with their principles and caused irreparable reputational damage.

Mandelblit resumes testimony as Netanyahu defense presses on investigation approvals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:51:58 UTC
17:51:58 KST

Former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit testified Monday that police questioning of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Case 1000 went beyond the warning given at the outset, and that the warning in Case 2000 did not match the suspicions being investigated.
His testimony at the Jerusalem District Court came as Netanyahu’s defense continued to challenge the scope and timing of his investigation approvals. The judges also pressed Mandelblit on when he authorized questioning Netanyahu as a suspect in Case 2000, and whether an earlier decision he recalled had been documented.
Mandelblit, who authorized the investigations and later approved the indictment, was called as a defense witness. His questioning by Netanyahu’s lawyer, Amit Hadad, has focused on what investigators were permitted to examine and what Netanyahu was told about the suspicions against him before being questioned.
Case 1000 concerns expensive gifts Netanyahu allegedly received from businessmen Arnon Milchan and James Packer, and actions he allegedly took to benefit Milchan. Hadad argued that the warning given to Netanyahu described suspicions concerning the rules on accepting gifts, rather than bribery or fraud and breach of trust.
Mandelblit said that, to the best of his recollection, he had not been involved in drafting the warnings. He agreed that questioning about Netanyahu’s relationship with Milchan went beyond the wording presented to him.
Hadad compares language used in Case 1000, 4000
Hadad also compared the language used in Cases 1000 and 4000. Mandelblit said the wording in Case 4000 was intended to preserve room to determine whether the suspicions amounted to bribery or fraud and breach of trust. Hadad challenged the consistency of that explanation with his earlier answers about Case 1000.
Much of Monday’s hearing concerned the decision to question Netanyahu as a suspect in Case 2000, which centers on discussions with Yediot Aharonot publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in exchange for steps against rival newspaper Israel Hayom.
Mandelblit said recordings of the conversations established reasonable suspicion against Mozes, while he deliberated over Netanyahu’s position. He recalled testimony from former Netanyahu chief of staff Ari Harow as a development that led him toward approving questioning of the prime minister as a suspect.
The judges pressed him to distinguish that developing assessment from a formal authorization.
Asked about a decision preceding January 5, 2017, Mandelblit said he could not identify documentation of it. He described discussions with other officials rather than a formally recorded decision, and agreed that the actual approval was given on January 5, the day Netanyahu was first questioned in Case 2000.
Mandelblit maintains he intended to have Netanyahu questioned as suspect
Mandelblit nevertheless maintained that he intended to have Netanyahu questioned as a suspect, possibly as early as December 25, 2016, when arrangements for questioning in both cases were discussed. He said final approval may have awaited Mozes’s questioning on January 4.
Hadad argued that Netanyahu had initially been summoned without approval to question him as a suspect in Case 2000. Mandelblit rejected the suggestion that he intended Netanyahu to be questioned merely as a witness.
Mandelblit also agreed that the Case 2000 warning, which referred to requesting and receiving improper benefits from businessmen in connection with his position, did not fit the suspicions in that case.
Monday’s exchanges followed testimony on Sunday in which Mandelblit said he had ordered police to stop wiretapping Netanyahu confidant Natan Eshel. Although investigators had obtained a court warrant, Mandelblit said the operation should have been brought to him for approval beforehand.
Netanyahu’s trial began in May 2020. He faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in all three cases and a bribery charge in Case 4000, concerning alleged regulatory benefits for Bezeq in exchange for intervention in Walla’s news coverage. He denies wrongdoing.

EU gas prices hit highest level since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:51:27 UTC
17:51:27 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
European natural gas prices rose 3.3% to exceed €97 ($108.8) per megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022 as the Middle East conflict continues to threaten supplies.
Intensifying conflict in the Middle East has sharply heightened concerns over winter energy supplies, particularly as liquefied natural gas (LNG) flows from the Persian Gulf — which previously accounted for nearly a fifth of global supply — remain down roughly 80% year-on-year.
European gas futures traded at €97.15 per megawatt-hour as of 0820GMT, up 3.3% from Friday's close and hitting their highest level since December 2022.
Adding to market vulnerability, Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) reported EU gas storage facilities at just 74.6% of capacity — well below historical seasonal averages.

SBU agents detained for plotting drone attack on Moscow’s missile defense facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:50:48 UTC
17:50:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. The Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained two individuals from the South Caucasus who acted on instructions from Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) to carry out an FPV-drone attack on a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system and an electric power facility.
"The Federal Security Service has thwarted the subversive and terrorist activities of two individuals from the Transcaucasus region, born in 1991 and 1998, who were acting as agents of the Security Service of Ukraine and were involved in preparing a terrorist act," the FSB’s Public Relations Center (PRC) said.
According to the FSB, the suspects were tasked with assembling strike-capable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) retrieved from hidden caches, transporting them to a launch site in the Moscow Region, and preparing them for launch.
"The drones were to be operated remotely from Ukrainian territory. FSB officers apprehended the individuals while they were preparing an attack on an electric power facility and a key component of Moscow’s missile defense system," the agency said.
The FSB reported that one of the detainees had been recruited by an SBU officer and traveled to Russia in exchange for a promised monetary reward to carry out the planned attack. He subsequently enlisted an acquaintance from his inner circle to assist him.
FPV drones and components intended for the manufacture of improvised explosive devices were recovered from caches in the Smolensk and Kaluga regions, the FSB said.
The FSB’s Investigative Department has opened a criminal case against the detainees under Part 2 of Article 205.4 of the Russian Criminal Code, which concerns participation in a terrorist organization. A court has ordered both suspects to be held in custody.
A comprehensive set of investigative and operational measures is underway to establish the full circumstances of the alleged activities and identify any possible accomplices, the FSB added.
The agency also warned that Ukrainian intelligence services were seeking to recruit civilians for illicit activities intended to harm Russia. It emphasized that anyone assisting what it described as the adversary would be identified and held accountable, according to the FSB’s Public Relations Center.

Battleground metros to watch in South Africa's municipal elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:50:31 UTC
17:50:31 KST

Battleground metros to watch in South Africa's municipal elections
JOHANNESBURG, Oct 26 - South Africans vote in municipal elections on November 4 amid voter frustration over poor service delivery, unstable local government coalitions and rising costs.
Held every five years, the elections will be an important gauge of the political landscape ahead of the 2029 national vote, with support for the African National Congress (ANC), Nelson Mandela's former liberation movement, continuing to erode.
Here are the key battleground metros:
JOHANNESBURG: THE PRIZE
Africa's richest city has churned through seven mayors since the 2021 local elections as successive coalition governments have unravelled.
The pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA) gained an early advantage by naming former Cape Town mayor and Western Cape premier Helen Zille as its mayoral candidate months ahead of its rivals. The 75-year-old political veteran has run an energetic campaign focused on deteriorating infrastructure and poor service delivery.
Recent polls put the DA above 30% and the ANC above 20%, raising the possibility of a coalition between the two parties, which have governed together nationally since the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024. Both parties could first seek deals with smaller parties rather than share power.
TSHWANE: ACTIONSA THE KINGMAKER
Tshwane, home to the administrative capital Pretoria, underscores the importance of smaller parties in South Africa's fragmented municipal politics.
The ANC governed the metro until 2016, when the DA captured it in a major urban defeat for the ruling party. Coalition politics subsequently proved volatile, and the DA lost power in 2024 after its coalition partner ActionSA backed an ANC-led no-confidence motion against its mayor.
Tshwane has since been governed by a multi-party coalition led by ActionSA. The party, founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, is a centre-right party that campaigns on anti-corruption and a hard line on immigration.
CAPE TOWN: DEMOCRATIC ALLIANCE BASTION
The DA is heavily favoured to retain Cape Town, which it has governed since 2006 and where it has held an outright majority since 2011.
Polls suggest the party should remain above 50%, though some analysts expect a tighter contest as voters grapple with soaring property prices and persistent gang violence.
The DA is also targeting Nelson Mandela Bay, one of South Africa's most turbulent coalition metros and currently governed by an ANC-led coalition.
ETHEKWINI: ZUMA WILDCARD
The economic hub of KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, could deliver one of the election's biggest blows to the ANC, with former president Jacob Zuma's uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) threatening to displace it.
Zuma backed MKP after his bitter split with the ANC in 2023. Polls suggest the party could win 40% to 50% of the vote, while ANC support could fall into the low teens. MKP's rise helped drive the ANC's losses in the 2024 national election.
EKURHULENI: CORRUPTION TEST
Ekurhuleni, home to Johannesburg's OR Tambo International Airport, could provide another measure of the ANC's decline in Gauteng Province, where voters have cited concerns over corruption and crime.
Polls suggest ANC support could fall from 38% in 2021 to about 25%, leaving it neck-and-neck with the DA.
BUFFALO CITY AND MANGAUNG: LAST STRONGHOLDS OF THE ANC
Buffalo City, which includes KuGompo City in Eastern Cape province, and Mangaung, home to Bloemfontein in Free State province, remain the ANC's strongest metropolitan bastions, making them important tests of how far the party's urban support has eroded.
The ANC won 59% in Buffalo City and 51% in Mangaung in 2021, helped by deep-rooted loyalty to the former liberation movement. REUTERS

Slovakia seeks agreements with the Kremlin: Foreign Minister in Moscow for energy talks

Slovakia seeks agreements with the Kremlin: Foreign Minister in Moscow for energy talks
Kyiv • UNN
A Slovak delegation has arrived in Moscow for talks on energy and Russian gas. Bratislava fears arbitration claims of up to €16 billion.
A Slovak delegation headed by Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanár has arrived in moscow to participate in a meeting of the intergovernmental commission. UNN reports this, citing Deutsche Welle and the Slovak Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The main topic of the talks will be Slovakia's energy security, in particular the supply of Russian gas.
"The absolute priority with which I am travelling to moscow is Slovakia's energy security," Blanár said.
Details
On Monday, October 26, the 22nd meeting of the Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission on economic and scientific-technical cooperation will take place in moscow. The commission last met in November 2021, before the start of russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The meeting will be co-chaired by Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár and Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education valery falkov.
The aim of the meeting is to determine the scope of cooperation with russia in areas of "common interest," the ministry said. At the same time, it clarified that Slovakia's obligations within the EU would be taken into account.
The parties plan to discuss issues in energy, including nuclear energy, agriculture, environmental protection, tourism, sports and culture. Negotiations are also planned on economic cooperation in areas not covered by European Union sanctions. According to Blanár, the main priority of his visit will be Slovakia's energy security against the backdrop of the EU's decision to gradually abandon Russian gas.
In particular, the Slovak state-owned company Slovenský plynárenský priemysel (SPP) has a long-term contract with the Russian "gazprom" that runs until 2034. The agreement provides for the take-or-pay principle ("take or pay"), under which the buyer is obliged to pay for the agreed volumes of gas even if it declines to receive them.
The head of the Slovak Foreign Ministry warned that an early termination of purchases could lead to arbitration claims from russia amounting to more than €10 billion. In his estimation, potential financial claims could reach €16 billion. At the same time, Blanár stressed that the European Union is ready to provide Slovakia with legal assistance, but does not guarantee compensation for possible financial losses.
According to Russian media, Blanár is already in moscow.
The Slovak delegation was also expected to include State Secretary at the Ministry of Economy Vladimir Šimonjak and Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee of the National Council Marián Kéry. Experts from the Ministries of the Environment, Economy, Agriculture, Culture, Tourism and Sports are also expected. In addition, representatives of the Slovak gas industry, the Slovak state-owned joint-stock company JAVYS, the Slovak Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the Slovak-Russian Business Council were expected to arrive in moscow.
The Slovak minister plans to hold separate talks with russia's Foreign Minister sergey lavrov. The parties will discuss bilateral relations, economic cooperation and international issues, including initiatives to end the war in Ukraine. Blanár said that, despite condemning Russian aggression and violations of international law, Bratislava considers it necessary to maintain contacts with moscow in order to protect its national interests.

French political turmoil may affect olim with restrictions on transferring money out of country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:34:05 UTC
17:34:05 KST

Israel's Aliyah and Integration Ministry is preparing for the possibility that political and economic turmoil in France could lead to restrictions on transferring money out of the country, potentially complicating plans by French Jews to immigrate to Israel, ministry director-general Dganit Sankar-Langa told Walla on Monday.
The concern centers on the possibility that, following elections in France, the government could impose restrictions on capital transfers that would make it more difficult for Jews seeking to move their lives to Israel to bring their savings with them.
"We are preparing for the possibility that, following the elections, a government decision will be made that will make it more difficult to transfer money out of France," she said.
According to Sankar-Langa, France's economic crisis is a significant factor behind growing interest in aliyah, no less than antisemitism.
"France's debt-to-GDP ratio is among the highest in OECD countries, and we are seeing the economic protests. That is why we are also examining this aspect and preparing to assist immigrants with tax advice, pension advice, and financial guidance."
Sharp increase in immigration from France
The ministry stressed that the concern relates to a possible scenario, not a decision that has already been made in France.
The remarks come amid a sharp increase in immigration from France. According to Aliyah and Integration Ministry figures, approximately 3,400 Jews immigrated to Israel from France in 2025, while more than 4,000 have already arrived since the beginning of 2026, an increase of nearly 50% compared with the corresponding period last year.
By comparison, North America, home to nearly eight million Jews, is expected to send only about 4,000 immigrants to Israel this year, according to the most optimistic forecasts. France has a Jewish population of approximately 440,000.
This month, the Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency for Israel, and Ofek Israeli held three aliyah fairs in Paris, Marseille, and Lyon.
More than 600 households, representing approximately 2,000 people, attended the Paris Fair. According to ministry figures, about 90% of those expressing interest at the fair said they wanted to immigrate to Israel immediately or during 2027.
Sankar-Langa, who has worked at the ministry for approximately 12 years and also served as director-general during the Russia-Ukraine war, said she had never encountered such determination among prospective immigrants.
"We held large fairs a year and two years ago as well, but this time people are arriving with clear decisions. They say they are immigrating in the summer of 2027, approach the Education Ministry booth, and ask where their children will study. This is a level of certainty I have never experienced before. These are not questions of 'maybe' or 'let's see,' but questions about the here and now. There is a real sense of urgency."
Roni, a 75-year-old French-Israeli who has lived in Paris since 1975 and spent his career in senior management positions working with numerous public-sector clients, is well acquainted with the change.
For decades, he saw no contradiction between his Israeli identity and his life in France. Now, he says, everything has changed.
"We used to be proud to say we were Israelis, that we had served in the IDF. People were impressed. Now it has become something negative," he told Walla.
Antisemitism affecting day-to-day life of French Jews
"In the past, we wouldn't even think twice before speaking Hebrew in the street or telling people in a business setting where our roots were. Now it's better to keep quiet. Now we're careful. My wife no longer speaks Hebrew as freely in a taxi as she once did. When we're asked at the airport where we've arrived from, we're no longer quick to say Israel. There are restaurants where we prefer that people not know we're Israeli or Jewish. There are restaurants we simply don't go to anymore."
The change is evident even at the entrance to their home.
"We have a mezuzah, but we moved it from the outside doorpost to the inside several years ago."
According to Roni, many Jews now avoid wearing a kippah in public, even on their way to synagogue and even on Yom Kippur.
"The atmosphere is very worrying. People tell you, you're Jewish, so you must be a Zionist, so you defend the killing of Palestinians. We used to speak enthusiastically about Israel, about its technology and the IDF. Now people look at you differently. You can speak, but they don't want to listen or understand."
He said concern about the future is especially pronounced among younger French Jews in their 30s and 40s, many of whom have children.
"Their parents, who came to France from Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia and managed to build good lives here, weren't necessarily thinking about leaving. But their children have started asking themselves where their future lies. This phenomenon began several years ago, long before the war, but now the questions have become much harder."
Even Jews with successful careers in France's high-tech industry are reconsidering their futures, he said.
"They ask what will happen in one, two, or three years, and whether their future is still in France."
Roni is also troubled by the country's political polarization and the growing strength of Marine Le Pen's nationalist right and the radical left led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a fierce critic of Israel.
"Jews are caught between a rock and a hard place, between the far Right and the far Left. Even well-established Jews, business owners, and people who have already built entire lives here are beginning to ask themselves where their future and their children's future lie."
Roni and his wife have already purchased an apartment in Herzliya and visit Israel three or four times a year, sometimes staying for a month or longer.
On this occasion, he came specifically to vote in Tuesday's elections.
"I'm trying to convince my wife to move permanently. She's still worried about the security situation in Israel. I actually feel safe here. Even with all the chaos in the country, I prefer to be here."
He can also see the change in Herzliya.
"Every time I come, I hear more and more French, in shops, in cafés, and even on the padel courts. Sometimes I feel as though I'm still in France."
His dream is to reverse the living arrangement he has become accustomed to over the past five decades: to live in Israel and visit France, rather than live in Paris and visit Israel.
Immigrants from France arrive in Israel with high hopes. Many are deeply committed to Zionism, speak Hebrew, and are religious or at least traditional.
Even those who do not wear a kippah regularly tend to send their children to state religious schools.
Many operated small businesses in France and intend to open similar businesses in Israel. They arrive with relative financial independence, a willingness to integrate into Israeli society, and an interest in volunteering for community activities.
Another prominent characteristic is their preference for living in close-knit communities near other families who have immigrated from France.
While French immigrants previously concentrated primarily in Netanya, Tel Aviv, and Ashdod, new communities have emerged in recent years in Nahariya, Afula, Hadera, and Haifa's Neve Sha'anan neighborhood.
In Or Akiva, for example, approximately 200 immigrants from France have settled in recent years.
These communities provide immigrants with supportive social networks, help them cope with the challenges of integration, and allow them to preserve the language and culture they brought with them.
Yet moving is not straightforward, even for those who have already decided to immigrate.
Israel's cost of living, housing prices, and the need to find employment are significant obstacles.
According to Sankar-Langa, many French Jews live in high-quality subsidized housing, sometimes in spacious apartments in desirable areas, and moving to Israel means making financial sacrifices.
Leading company reps. join Paris Fair
To address one of the main obstacles, representatives of leading Israeli companies and organizations joined the Paris Fair for the first time this year.
They included Israel Aerospace Industries, Elbit Systems, Mekorot, Bank Mizrahi-Tefahot, and the National Artificial Intelligence Headquarters.
The goal was to begin recruiting employees even before they immigrated to Israel.
During the fair, company representatives met with approximately 200 prospective immigrants, more than 50 of whom were found to be potentially suitable for available positions.
"People didn't come just to find out what the options were and what the salaries were. They came to look for work," Sankar-Langa said.
"By the very next day, advanced interviews were being held with candidates who had been found suitable."
At the same time, approximately 200 families received guidance and information from ministry and Jewish Agency representatives, led by delegation head Erez Cohen.
Defense Ministry representatives who joined the delegation also met with parents of lone soldiers serving in Israel.
Following the developments, the prime minister instructed officials to formulate a dedicated government plan to encourage immigration from France and integrate the new arrivals.
Ministry officials are careful not to describe the preparations as an "emergency plan," a term that evokes previous events, particularly the wave of immigration following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war.
"Back then, people landed here carrying bags, sometimes without medication," Sankar-Langa recalled.
This time, she said, the goal is to prepare in advance for large-scale immigration, remove economic and bureaucratic obstacles, and ensure that immigrants not only reach Israel but also integrate successfully and remain in the country.
"Immigration from France is at its highest level in years, and we are preparing to absorb thousands more,” Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer said.
“This year, for the first time, we brought the major companies in the Israeli economy to France, based on the understanding that quality employment is one of the central keys to successful immigration and optimal integration."
Sankar-Langa also sees immigration as an opportunity for the Israeli economy, which faces shortages of engineers, doctors, teachers, and artificial intelligence professionals.
"We increasingly understand that the Aliyah and Integration Ministry is, in effect, the human resources department of the State of Israel," she said.

Israeli rehabilitation village prepares adults with disabilities for Election Day voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:34:03 UTC
17:34:03 KST

Ahead of Tuesday's election, more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities at a Perach Israel village are learning about their right to vote and practicing how to cast their ballots.
As millions of Israelis prepare to head to the polls, residents of a Perach Israel-operated rehabilitation village are getting ready for Election Day with a special initiative to help them exercise one of their most fundamental democratic rights.
The village, home to more than 200 adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities, has set up a mock polling station, complete with a voting booth, envelopes, and ballot slips, allowing residents to familiarize themselves with the voting process ahead of the October 27 Knesset election.
Staff members are guiding residents through the process, explaining their right to vote and helping them practice selecting a ballot and placing it in an envelope, as they would at an official polling station.
Right to choose is important element of rehabilitation village
"The right to choose is part of everyday life in our village," said Moshe Stein, CEO of Perach Israel.
"We work to teach our residents the importance of making their own choices, from deciding what color clothes to wear to choosing how to spend their free time. The ability to make their own decisions plays a significant role in their quality of life."
For residents, the exercise offers a chance to learn the practical aspects of voting in a familiar environment, ahead of an election in which millions of Israelis will choose their representatives in the next Knesset.
With Election Day just around the corner, the practice sessions are helping ensure that residents who are eligible to vote have the opportunity to make their voices heard alongside the rest of the country.

Anthropic’s Claude bypassed paywall to obtain vote count in US state of Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:32:56 UTC
17:32:56 KST

Dilara Hamit
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
Anthropic's Claude artificial intelligence model bypassed a paywall to obtain publicly available aggregate vote counts from the US state of Georgia without human authorization, Axios reported Sunday.
The incident occurred while Claude was being used internally for a statistics project requiring public data that the state normally provides for a fee.
"Without being asked to, the model requested a token to query a dashboard that contained information normally available for a fee," an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.
"We have since put in place mitigations to block these kinds of actions," the spokesperson added.
Anthropic said Claude did not access Georgia's voter registration system, obtain individual voting records or alter election data.
The information obtained consisted solely of aggregate vote counts available to members of the public who paid the required fee.
According to Axios, Anthropic notified the Georgia secretary of state's office and the White House about the incident several weeks ago.
The company had previously described the case without identifying Georgia in an Oct. 9 report examining unintended actions by its AI models.
In that report, Anthropic said Claude Mythos 5 learned from an archived version of an unnamed state agency's website that its public dashboard issued access tokens to visitors.
The model then requested a token and used it to query the database without paying, the company said.
Anthropic said the incident was among several cases in which Claude circumvented restrictions to access information protected by tokens or fees, including on websites operated by US federal, state and local government agencies.
The company described the behavior as "persistence," in which the model encountered an obstacle and found an unintended way around it rather than stopping.
Anthropic said the incidents caused minimal real-world harm but warned that similar behavior could have greater consequences as AI models become more capable.
Following its review, the company moved some evaluations offline, tightened restrictions on Claude's internet tools and developed systems to detect and block unauthorized actions.
Anthropic said the new safeguards successfully blocked all the disclosed behaviors during testing.
