‘The polls never counted us’: 67,000 Israelis abroad expected to fly home to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:32:01 UTC
17:32:01 KST

Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are returning home to vote in Tuesday's Knesset election, with some traveling thousands of miles and others arranging special flights after regular services were canceled. Among them are expatriates hoping to move back to Israel and others who say the country's political direction has changed how they feel about identifying as Israeli overseas.
According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, approximately 810,000 eligible Israeli voters live abroad. The Fly&Vote initiative, which encourages Israelis overseas to exercise their voting rights, estimates that roughly 67,000 will return to Israel to participate in the October 27 election, potentially representing the equivalent of about one and a half Knesset seats.
The figure is an estimate by the initiative, rather than a confirmed count of voters who have arrived. Most Israeli citizens living overseas cannot cast their ballots abroad and must travel to Israel to vote.
On Sunday, a special flight from Portugal landed at Ben Gurion Airport carrying dozens of Israelis determined to make their voices heard at the ballot box. Representatives of Fly&Vote were waiting to welcome them in the arrivals hall.
The flight was arranged after Portuguese airline TAP canceled its services to Israel, leaving hundreds of Israelis who had planned to travel home for the election without their original flight arrangements.
‘We want to return, so it's important to be part of what happens here’
"If you want to make a difference, you have to take action. You can't wait for someone else to do the work," said Gali Mazor Biton, a married mother of three who has lived in Cascais, Portugal, for the past five years.
Standing in the arrivals hall at Ben Gurion Airport, she explained that she had come to Israel for just three days, specifically to cast her ballot.
"We want to return to Israel, so it's important for us to be part of what's happening here and to influence our future," she said.
But not everyone making the journey plans to move back to Israel. For some, the motivation is closely connected to their experience of being Israeli abroad.
Itamar Tzahovel, a costume designer working in the film industry, has spent the past three decades living in Milan, Shanghai, Berlin and, most recently, Lisbon. He said Israel's policies have increasingly affected the way he is perceived overseas, prompting him to purchase a plane ticket and return to vote.
"Whenever I used to say I was Israeli, I said it with pride. That's no longer the case," he said.
"Today, when I say I'm from Israel, there's a certain defensiveness to it. I told myself, enough. I bought a ticket and came to make a difference. I want honest people running this country, so that every Jew in the Diaspora can stand tall and proudly say they're Israeli."
‘We could be the surprise of this election’
For Dana Levy, 51, originally from Jerusalem, the decision to travel from Lisbon, where she has lived for 23 years, came after an outpouring of encouragement from friends and former acquaintances.
"My friends convinced me to come especially because this time every vote matters," she said.
"The appeals came from everywhere. Friends in Israel, even my old group of friends from the Scouts in Jerusalem. They asked me to come and explained how important it was to vote in this election. They told me we must not end up again in a situation where there is no clear outcome."
Levy said the encouragement went beyond messages and phone calls. Israelis have established informal support networks to help people living abroad make the trip, including offering accommodation to those returning specifically to vote.
"I received so much support and assistance to make it here. There are even Facebook groups where people offer to host those arriving especially to vote. Everyone just wants me to come. It's incredibly moving," she said.
Her stay in Israel will be brief. She plans to vote and return immediately to Lisbon. But she believes overseas Israelis could have an impact that has not been fully reflected in election polling.
"I'm staying in Israel for a very short time. I'll vote and then go straight back to Lisbon," she said.
"I think the votes of Israelis living abroad will be the surprise of this election because nobody has counted us in the polls."
Ella Raz, 41, who has lived in Portugal for five years and works in tourism, expressed a similar sense of responsibility.
"It was absolutely clear to me that in this election I had to show up at the polling station and make a difference," she said.
"My entire family is in Israel, and I care deeply about what's happening in the country. Both for those who live here and for those of us who don't."
‘Israel is still our home’
The wave of returning voters is not limited to Europe. Israelis living in North America are also traveling to Israel to take part in the election.
Shay Eden, who works in human resources at a Jewish research institute in New York, spoke to ynet before boarding a flight with her husband, Josh Daryl.
"For us, Israel is our home," she said. "We're living in New York for a limited period, with the intention of returning. So even when we live abroad, we feel committed to the future of the country, its character and the values on which it will be built."
For Eden and her husband, the journey is about maintaining their connection to a country they still consider home, despite temporarily building their lives elsewhere.
"These elections are an opportunity to influence the direction Israel takes and the society we want to live in," she said.
"We believe that even two votes are part of our collective ability to make a difference, and that we shouldn't give up the opportunity to help shape the future."
She added: "This is our way of taking responsibility, making our voices heard and being part of the decision about the future of our home."
Whether the estimated tens of thousands of returning voters will materially affect the distribution of Knesset seats remains uncertain. Their political preferences and the number who will ultimately cast ballots cannot be determined from the travel estimates alone.
But for the Israelis arriving from Lisbon, New York and elsewhere, the motivation is already clear. They may have built lives far from Israel, but they are determined to participate in deciding its future.

Can EU Inc still make business easier? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:30:34 UTC
17:30:34 KST

EU Inc, Europe’s harmonised corporate form, is stalled after Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs failed to vote. Caught between furious founders and protesting workers, could EU Inc still change how you build a startup? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
The European Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) failed to agree on the draft report on EU Inc on 19 October, having already postponed the vote on 5 October. Disagreements among MEPs over workers' rights are driving the deadlock.
EU Inc is an EU-wide company structure that lets businesses register in one member state and operate across the bloc. It would follow a shared set of rules, the “28th corporate regime”, so founders wouldn’t have to navigate 27 different national frameworks.
Proposed by the European Commission in March 2026, EU Inc aims to make it easier and cheaper to set up a business in the EU. It tackles the fragmentation across Europe’s startup ecosystems and boosts collaboration, talent mobility, and access to funding.
Founders could set up a company fully online within 48 hours, with starting capital of €1 and no notary. Registration and documentation are handled in English, with no translation or local-language requirements when operating abroad.
While EU leaders agreed to finalise the law by year-end, pushback is coming from multiple fronts.
EU Inc founders argue that months of negotiations had weakened the proposal. On 15 October, in a public statement they accused the EU of reducing EU Inc to a fast-track registration process by stripping away its core features, including free choice of registration and a common-stock framework to attract talent.
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) warn that a proposal threatens workers’ rights. On 24 September and 20 October, trade unions from across the bloc protested in Brussels and Strasbourg, warning that it would let companies use lighter corporate rules to circumvent national labour laws and social standards.

Bulgaria heads to presidential runoff after close vote

SOFIA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Bulgaria will head to a runoff vote on November 1 after a tight race between the two leading presidential candidates failed to produce an outright winner in Sunday’s elections, which garnered record-low participation, official results showed.
With 95% of the votes counted, incumbent Iliana Iotova, 61, attracted 34.6% against 32% for ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, falling short of the 50% threshold for the largely ceremonial role in a race of 27 candidates.
Sunday’s vote took on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast that likely killed some two dozen international seafarers. However, only about 22% of the eligible voters showed up to cast their ballot, according to polling agencies.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
BOTH CANDIDATES CONDEMN DRONE STRIKES
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
“I want to share a certain worry and tell Bulgarians that it is an illusion if they think we can change something in this country without (them) voting,” Iotova said after polls closed at 8 p.m.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
(Reporting by Alex Lefkowitz; Writing by Angeliki Koutantou; Editing by David Holmes)

Layan Bsharat and Rania Abushamala
26 October 2026•Update: 26 October 2026
The Israeli army has forced more than 2,200 Palestinians from their homes and demolished five commercial and industrial facilities and a three-story residential building amid a large-scale military offensive in Hebron in the southern West Bank, the city’s mayor said.
Speaking in an interview with Anadolu, Yousef al-Jabari said the forced evacuations affected Deir Bahha and parts of Al-Jilda in western Hebron, an area that covers approximately 330 dunams (330,000 square meters), and contains more than 495 housing units.
He said Israeli forces surrounded Deir Bahha and Al-Jilda and used loudspeakers to order residents out of their homes.
“Those displaced include children, women, young men and older people,” he said. Some residents initially refused to leave before troops stormed their homes and forced them out.
On Saturday, Hebron municipality said that around 1,500 Palestinians from 250 families had been displaced, before the mayor updated the figure to over 2,200 people.
Al-Jabari did not specify where the displaced residents had gone, while witnesses said some families sought refuge in other West Bank towns and villages.
In a separate count covering three neighborhoods, Riyad Khamis, a media official with a local committee supporting affected families, told Anadolu that more than 380 Palestinian families had been forced from their homes in Deir Bahha, Al-Jilda and Khirbet al-Maghariba.
The Israeli army launched its offensive on Friday following a shooting that killed two Israeli soldiers in the Farsh al-Hawa area at the city’s northwestern entrance.
Khamis said the affected neighborhoods form a contiguous residential area within Area A, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to exercise civil and security control under the Oslo Accords.
The neighborhoods are “located far from settlements, outposts or settler roads,” he said.
 
Collective punishment
Al-Jabari said the Israeli army closed Hebron’s entrances, preventing Palestinians from entering or leaving.
Israeli forces also closed the Ibrahimi Mosque and prevented prayers, as troops and military vehicles deployed across the city, he said.
Streets have become largely deserted because of the siege and movement restrictions, the mayor said, describing the measures as a “policy of collective punishment.”
Al-Jabari accused Israeli authorities of using Friday’s attack to intensify measures against Hebron’s residents ahead of Tuesday’s Israeli elections.
He said the escalation aimed to bolster occupiers’ support for the far right.
Following Friday’s attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened a wider military operation in the occupied West Bank that he described as unprecedented since the 1967 war, including evacuating Palestinian neighborhoods and raiding homes.
The Israeli siege has forced hundreds of businesses in Hebron and neighboring villages to close because workers cannot reach their workplaces and goods cannot move in or out, al-Jabari said.
“Israeli forces have continued demolishing commercial and industrial facilities and residential buildings since Friday,” he added.
Al-Jabari said the municipality declared a state of emergency in the area and deployed teams to assist displaced residents.
“Municipal teams are working to secure shelter for displaced families, assess residents’ needs and address damage to roads, water networks and sewage infrastructure,” he said.
The offensive comes amid escalating Israeli army and occupier attacks across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings, arrests, demolitions of homes and other structures, destruction of agricultural land and displacement of Palestinian communities, alongside settlement expansion.

The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) has now suspended funding of CHF1.25 million ($1.52 million) to MSF.
The frozen amount represents one tranche of the CHF6.25 million pledged to MSF for the current year.
According to the newspaper NZZ Am Sonntag, an internal investigation by MSF revealed 59 reports of sexual violence and exploitation, particularly involving women and young girls who are refugees from neighbouring Sudan. Eighteen staff members have been dismissed, including six employees from the NGO’s Swiss branch.
The NZZ explains that this constitutes “widespread sexual exploitation”, adding: “Money, jobs or humanitarian aid in exchange for sex: staff members are alleged to have taken advantage of the distress of refugee women and girls”.
The German-language newspaper notes that “the Confederation’s aid workers were effectively operating in the dark”. Although the SDC received the first indications as early as November 2024, it only became aware of the true scale of the problem following articles published in the press in June 2026 by the AP news agency.
More
MSF in Sudan: ‘It’s very hard to reach people in need’
“Internal emails now reveal just how reluctant the Swiss Confederation was to act, even though it was already aware of the facts,” reports the NZZ.
Whilst fighting rages in Central Africa, which has been experiencing a major humanitarian crisis since 2023, hundreds of thousands of people are fleeing the civil war in Sudan to seek refuge in neighbouring Chad.
The first alert from MSF staff at the Geneva headquarters reached the SDC by email on a Friday in November 2024, “shortly before the end of the working day”. Three female refugees “are reported to have described cases of sexual exploitation in Chad; the allegations are reportedly already under investigation”, the NGO stated.
A very slow response
In mid-December 2024, it was agreed at the Swiss foreign ministry “that a meeting with MSF would take place in January”. But it was not until June and July 2025 that the department resumed discussions on how to handle the case.
+ Switzerland pledges CHF23 million more aid to war-torn Sudan
Meanwhile, dozens of allegations of abuse were brought to MSF’s attention and disciplinary measures were taken; however, the SDC was kept in the dark (see box).
It was not until February 2026 that representatives of the SDC and MSF “met to discuss protection against sexual exploitation; once again, the Confederation received no new information”.
Breach of contractual obligation to report
When the scandal broke in June 2026 following revelations by the AP news agency, the SDC “demanded documents” from MSF.
More
What is the cost for killing humanitarians?
According to the foreign ministry, MSF breached its contractual reporting obligation; mistrust of the NGO is “now immense within the Confederation”, the NZZ writes. MSF eventually acknowledged its mistakes.
The Confederation is considering the possibility of further sanctions and an external investigation. From 2027, reporting obligations will be tightened for all Swiss partner NGOs.

Photos: Serbia celebrates as ruling party loses grip on power

In Belgrade late on Sunday, drivers in cars draped in Serbian flags honked their horns through the streets as fireworks lit up the sky and crowds flooded central squares and the area around parliament. “I feel as though I am finally living in a free country,” student Mila Martic told reporters as people raised three fingers, the Student List ballot symbol and a traditional Serbian greeting.
Sunday’s elections capped nearly two years of student-led demonstrations triggered by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, a disaster widely blamed on corruption and cronyism. The movement grew into some of Serbia’s largest protests since the 2000 overthrow of strongman Slobodan Milosevic.
At the Student List headquarters, supporters hugged, cried and chanted, “Victory, victory!” Candidate Radomir Saicic, a university professor, declared: “Serbia has won as we promised. Never again a tyrant in this country,” while he urged peaceful, dignified celebrations and “serious, responsible hard work” from Monday.
Elsewhere, pro-government encampments near parliament were dismantled as riot police trucks withdrew to the sound of cheering crowds.

Chinese AI video-generation models have surpassed leading US rivals in visual quality, but several fall behind in safety precautions, according to researchers at the University of Hong Kong.
ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 Pro took top spot in a ranking of 12 leading artificial intelligence video-generation models, scoring 3.84 out of 5 for visual quality. Exploitation and misinformation hinder DRC Ebola response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Exploitation and misinformation hinder DRC Ebola response
Ebola is spreading through the rainforests and mining camps in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), fuelling one of the country’s most devastating epidemics. A doctor with the Swiss NGO Medair explains why the fight to contain the epidemic has so far failed.
It’s been five months since authorities in the DRC officially confirmed the latest Ebola epidemic, the seventeenth in the country’s history and one of the deadliest to date.
“You have to grasp the sheer scale of the affected area,” says Pierre-Oliver Ngadjole, a doctor and nutritionist with the Swiss aid organisation Medair. “The epidemic has spread across an area larger than Switzerland.”
The National Institute of Public Health has recorded more than 9,000 confirmed cases and over 4,300 deaths. In the eastern provinces of Ituri – the epicentre – as well as North Kivu and Haut-Uélé, the virus continues to spread unchecked among the population.
Seven river-crossings to the nearest hospital
At the Ebola treatment centre of Katwa in Butembo, the figures are just as grim. “Over 70 of the 252 patients admitted have died so far,” says Ngadjole.
For Ngadjole, the main reason for the high death toll is not the aggressiveness of the virus, but delays in treatment. Patients simply arrive at hospitals too late.
The profile of those infected also reflects the region’s social structure: the 15- to 49-year-old age group is the hardest hit, which can be put down to work in the mining camps. Young children are also quickly infected within their families.
Getting to a treatment centre is often an odyssey. “The roads are in a terrible state. During the rainy season, not even motorbikes can get through,” says Ngadjole. Some patients have to travel for days and cross several rivers to reach a hospital. With little transport, families often resort to home remedies, which means they lose precious time. The delays can be fatal.
The devastating effect of myths
At the start of the epidemic, geographical isolation was compounded by a fatal communication failure that delayed treatment. Rumours spread that there was neither a vaccine nor a cure for the current strain of the virus.
“This message seriously undermined the population’s willingness to seek treatment,” Ngadjole explains.
It is true that currently no approved vaccine is available for the Bundibugyo strain that caused this epidemic. However, early intensive care, including intravenous fluids containing electrolytes, can dramatically improve a patient’s chances of survival. Isolation in hospital also helps to break the chain of transmission.
Another compounding factor is the dire security situation in the country. People infected with Ebola fear being attacked by armed militias on their way to hospital. Religious communities also urge patients to pray rather than seek medical help. Aid organisations such as Medair are therefore increasingly involving survivors to help build trust. “We let survivors tell their stories,” says Ngadjole.
About the organisation: MedairExternal link is an international emergency relief organisation based in the Swiss canton of Vaud. It provides medical and infrastructure support in crisis zones. Founded in 1989 by two medical doctors and other volunteers, the organisation now has an annual operating income of around $91.6 million (CHF75.6 million) and employs more than 1,500 people worldwide. In Switzerland, it receives financial support from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), among others. According to its 2025 annual report, other donors include the EU’s humanitarian aid office (ECHO) and USAID. Congolese doctor Pierre-Olivier Ngadjole works for Medair on the ground.
The challenge of contact tracing
Paris-based infectious disease specialist Xavier Lescure believes that contact tracing is another obstacle to containing the epidemic.
“We have to trace every link in the chain of transmission,” says Lescure, who heads France’s coordination mission for epidemic risks and co-coordinates international research networks of the World Health Organization (WHO). Currently, contact tracing in the DRC reaches about 75% of all contacts.
“Given the circumstances, this is remarkable, but it is simply not enough to put out the fire – we would need more than 95%,” Lescure tells Swissinfo. He also blames the information crisis for the dire situation in the DRC. He calls it an “epidemic of post-truth” in which unfounded myths and mistrust undermine public health measures.
Hence, hope lies in medical research. According to Lescure, two approaches are being pursued. One involves testing vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo strain, while the other involves using the existing rVSV vaccine developed against the Zaire strain.
“Early scientific evidence points to possible cross-immunity. If this vaccine proved even partially effective and prevented severe cases, we would have an immediate weapon to fight the epidemic,” Lescure says.
>>For the health authorities, containing the outbreak of Ebola is a regional priority:
More
Ebola vaccine: ‘In an outbreak situation we’re racing against time’
Raw materials, uprooting and the trauma of war
It’s no surprise that the epidemic is hitting the mining camps in Ituri particularly hard. Hundreds of thousands of people work in informal mines in appalling hygienic conditions. Many of these sites lie deep in the rainforest, where workers have little choice but to rely on wild animals for food – known as bush meat, the primary source of virus transmission. The crammed conditions in the mines and camps for internally displaced persons provide ideal conditions for the virus to spread.
And then there are the psychological scars. The virus is hitting people who have endured three decades of war. “We deal with families who are deeply traumatised because their relatives were murdered while fleeing,” Ngadjole tells Swissinfo from Bunia.
An Ebola death is doubly devastating for families already struggling to survive. Traditional funeral rites are banned because of the risk of infection. The deceased must be buried immediately under strict safety precautions, while all their belongings, including clothes, mattresses and rubbish, must also be burnt. For families already living in extreme poverty, this means losing the last of their possessions. For this reason, Medair also provides material assistance to support them.
The price of digital consumption
For Ngadjole, the fight against Ebola must not end with emergency medical aid. “We need structural change across the entire production chain,” he says, pointing to the dismal hygienic conditions in the mining camps.
The outbreak, says Lescure, is also a reflection of our global consumption culture. “The minerals mined in the DRC are used in our smartphones, computers and numerous other everyday devices. Their extraction comes at a heavy cost: the overexploitation of natural resources, the destruction of ecosystems, geopolitical tensions and the suffering of local communities.”
Epidemics, he says, are never merely a natural phenomenon but also a reflection of economic and social choices: “Our consumption habits have global consequences.”
>>An analysis of the conflict minerals situation in DRC:
More
UN experts warn Congo’s conflict minerals slipping into global market
Switzerland’s response to Ebola in the DRC
In 2026, Switzerland increasedExternal link its support for the fight against Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to an annual amount of CHF4.6 million ($5.6 million). The funding is going primarily to the World Health Organization (WHO), the coordination of emergency medical teams, expanded laboratory capacity and epidemiological surveillance.
According to the foreign ministry, Switzerland also works closely with the DRC’s health authorities as well as with international partner organisations.
Switzerland support projects run by aid organisations such as Medair in the hardest hit provinces of Ituri and North Kivu.
Swiss institutions also cooperate with Congolese partners to monitor the virus’ genome. Basel-based pharmaceutical company Roche is providing lab equipment and testing methods to detect the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in collaboration with the Congolese National Institute of Public Health (INSP).
Donations from Switzerland also help to fund the fight against Ebola. In May 2026, Swiss SolidarityExternal link allocated CHF 1.2 million ($1.45 million) from its emergency relief fund.

Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries at the request of US President Donald Trump’s team, but only if one of three conditions was met, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with journalist Alla Mazur.
Speaking on the TSN.Tyzhden (TSN.The Week) program, Zelensky said that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries could not have a significant impact on global prices, noting that Russia accounts for only 2% of global diesel exports, while the remaining 98% comes from other exporters.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“How can one reach an ‘energy truce’ with the Russians? You might be hated, but you should at least be respected as an adversary. They must respect Ukraine – and our strength. He [Putin] inflicts great pain upon us, and we respond. It is a matter of justice,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine had proposed three possible ways to resolve the dispute to the American side. However, none of the proposals had been implemented, which is why Ukraine continues to strike Russian oil refineries, he said.
“I said: if you want us to stop hitting diesel facilities and refineries, then they [the Russians] must stop striking our power infrastructure. That is fair – an ‘energy truce.’ A second option: you enable Starlink coverage over Russia, and we show you the locations of their ballistic missile launchers. We want to destroy them.
Trump’s Big Lie About Ukraine
“The third option is this: if you won’t enable Starlink for us – which is entirely up to you – and you’ve said that Musk doesn’t want to, then give us something that doesn’t depend on Musk or Putin: missiles for the Patriot systems,” Zelensky said.
He added that Ukraine had received none of the three proposed forms of support.
“That is why the reaction is what it is – we are fighting for our lives,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky warns against lifting sanctions before negotiations
Zelensky also said that lifting sanctions against Russia should be considered only as part of the process of ending the war, rather than as a precondition for negotiations.
“I would not want us to approach the meeting of the three leaders – Ukraine, the United States, and Russia – having already lifted all sanctions against the Russian Federation. This is a crucial point. Sanctions were imposed in response to aggression, not as a price for the mere opportunity to talk.”
He said he had conveyed this position to the American delegation, cautioning that Russia could benefit from sanctions relief before any agreement on ending the war had been reached.
He warned that once sanctions were lifted, restoring them could prove difficult, requiring Ukraine and its partners to rebuild international support for a new round of restrictions.
“Without sanctions, we could reach a point in the trilateral dialogue where the future remains uncertain, yet the sanctions have already been removed,” Zelensky added.
He said that the international community had adopted more than 20 separate sanctions packages against Russia and questioned whether the same political resolve could be mobilized again if Moscow failed to follow through on its commitments.
“I do not want us to find ourselves without any leverage – lacking sanctions, funds, or frozen assets – when we sit down with Putin. Because then, as Mr. Trump put it, we would truly have very few cards left in our deck,” Zelensky added.
Ukraine, US, EU and NATO plan security talks in Brussels
Zelensky also said Ukraine, the United States, the European Union and NATO planned to hold a broad meeting in Brussels this week to discuss security issues, guarantees and European integration.
According to the president, the format of the discussions had expanded following a visit by the American delegation to St. Petersburg and a preliminary briefing to Ukraine.
The talks had initially been limited in scope, but the Americans were now seeking a broader discussion, Zelensky said.
“The Americans [after Oslo] went to St. Petersburg; we received a ‘brief’ from them, but now they want more than just a ‘brief’ – they want a broad discussion regarding security, guarantees, the EU, and involvement,” he added.
The meeting was expected to take place this week, tentatively on Tuesday or Wednesday. Zelensky said the participants would include representatives of Ukraine, the US and the EU at the presidential level, as well as NATO, represented by the alliance’s secretary-general.

====================================================================================================

MPs urged 'let light win' as cockatoo sits in for Helen Haines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:47:12 UTC
16:47:12 KST

A cardboard cockatoo sits in tribute for Helen Haines as MPs are urged to 'let light win over darkness'
Far from the gum trees of north-east Victoria where cockatoos gather in noisy flocks, an orange cardboard bird perched in the parliament on Monday, saving a seat for Helen Haines.
"How lonely it looks," Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said.
But cockatoos are not normally lonely birds, and Ms Haines has built her life in much the same way.
The Independent Member for Indi could be loud for those she cared about. She made sure her people were impossible to ignore, and was surrounded by her community, building her political career from a grassroots campaign run by locals.
And unlike the rest of parliament, loud and raucous, Ms Haines was calm.
A week ago, she was standing by the boot of her car outside her Wangaratta office when a man hit her with his own car in what police say was a targeted attack.
The injuries were so severe both of her legs were later amputated.
"This should not just shock us," Wentworth MP Allegra Spender said.
"It should change us."
As the parliament suspended normal business to make time for messages of support for Ms Haines and her family, it was hard to escape the feeling that something had shifted.
One after another, for hours, MPs stood up to speak in the House about Ms Haines's uncommon kindness, wisdom and respect for civility as a politician.
"These are the type of politicians we wish we had more of," friend and crossbench colleague Kate Chaney said.
Like a "trick the heart plays on the mind", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described finding himself looking across to where Ms Haines would normally sit, expecting to see her there.
"It is hard to think of anyone in this place with a more irrepressible twinkle in the eye," he said.
But the tributes were also threaded with another message: that the tenor of Australian politics must change, and that the country needed to find a better way to argue.
"And this is a moment for all of us to rise to the challenge," Speaker of the House Milton Dick said.
What Would Helen Do?
Members of the crossbench cried as they listened to messages of support for the woman they regard as the "matriarch" of Australia's independent movement.
Ms Haines was among the first wave of community-backed independents to reshape Australian politics, winning Indi after the retirement of fellow independent Cathy McGowan.
Community Strong MP Zali Steggall spoke of the role Ms Haines had played in helping shape the modern crossbench, guiding newly elected independents through the workings of parliament and teaching them how to advocate for their communities without the backing of a major party.
"There will be much discussion ahead about the need for better health and mental health services in the regions, our increasingly polarised political environment, harmful online debate and the need for greater civility in disagreement in parliament, in our media, online and in our communities," she said.
"So, Helen, I look forward to seeing you back here and getting on with the job. Let light win over darkness."
Independent MP Allegra Spender shared the first words Ms Haines spoke after the attack, as relayed by her husband, Phil Haines, who had met with parliamentarians earlier on Monday.
"Your first concerns were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders," she said.
"And that exactly speaks to the character of who you are."
But for all her decency, Ms Spender said, Ms Haines was not a "benign force wandering through the parliament".
"People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition," she said.
"What I will say is that you are also a force for change."
After winning Indi, voters have rewarded Ms Haines with two further terms, entrusting her with an electorate of mountains, rivers and fertile farmland, which was also acutely exposed to the effects of a warming climate.
After years of advocacy by Ms Haines, the federal government adopted temporary disaster roaming, an emergency system that allows mobile phones to switch to another carrier's network when their own service fails during a major disaster.
But few issues, her friends and colleagues said, animated her more than integrity in government.
Independent MP Andrew Gee was emotional speaking about the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which she is credited for establishing.
Several politicians chose to commit to a Civility Pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016. Ms Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge earlier this year.
MP Kate Chaney spoke about t-shirts printed for a Christmas party in her first year in parliament with the slogan: What Would Helen Do?
"I ask myself that question all the time," she said.
"Helen, please come back to us. We need you here more than ever".
The rage is getting worse, but we can get better
Mr Albanese said Australia had a proud tradition of disagreement but warned against confusing the vigour of democracy with "this rising tide of rage".
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop. We keep talking. We keep working towards something better," he said.
There was a shared disbelief in the chamber that someone like Helen Haines, among parliament's most respected and unassuming figures, had become a target.
She had been "so, so far down" his list of potential security concerns, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
Mr Burke said Phil Haines had earlier urged the parliament to think not only about the words they choose, but about who might hear them.
"It goes to not simply would I be capable of doing something horrific, but would my words, if heard by someone on the edge, potentially have an impact that I wouldn't want them to have,"
Mr Burke said.
A number of people also called for an honest conversation about mental health, including Liberal MP Dan Tehan.
Ms Haines is a former nurse and maternal health expert, and has long campaigned for additional support for regional services.
"We have to look at mental health services in and around regional and rural Victoria and across this nation," Mr Tehan said.
"We have to see whether we can do better."
As one man hurt Haines, others ran to help
Many MPs said they had spent the week hearing from Australians worried about a country growing more angry and more divided.
But in the same breath, they pointed to people like Ricky Jefferies, the local barber who ran towards danger when Haines needed help.
"One man drove at Helen, but others ran to her instinctively and courageously, and they saved her life," Independent MP Monique Ryan said.
"Our basic decency and our selflessness are there still, and we have to use those muscles, not the others."
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said Mr Jefferies knew most of the first responders because he cut their hair, "not because of social media networks".
"And there's something in that," he said.
"We thrive as a nation when we are in a community with our neighbours, when we are known by them and they are known by us."
He encouraged all politicians to behave better in parliament and online.
"We can all go better and we should strive to do better," he said.
"Lets play the ball, not the person and leave nasty personal politics of MAGA in the US."
Labor MP Ged Kearney broke down as she spoke about Ms Haines but said she had tried to honour her example by making herself as "visible as possible" over the weekend.
"I walked the streets amongst kids in Halloween costumes. I went to listen to music. I had lunch in a cafe, and visited a scouts party," she said.
"We all have fears and we do things differently now to assess risks … but at the end of the day, if I can't walk down High Street or Edward Street or Station Street and be with the people I represent, then well, what is this for?"
Parliament looks to the day it is made whole again
At a vigil held in Wangaratta to honour Ms Haines in the days after her attack, cockatoos wheeled overhead.
"They make a lot of noise, but they're very supportive of each other as a flock," former politician and friend Cathy McGowan told the ABC.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said when Ms Haines resumed her seat, it would be a "resounding moment for democracy".
"In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man's cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he said.
In her maiden speech, Ms Haines had reflected on the erosion of trust affecting democracies around the world.
Indi, she argued, offered a different lesson.
"Division and polarisation are not the inevitable outcome," she said then.

Singapore and Saudi Aramco plan to store Saudi crude oil in the underground Jurong Rock Caverns starting in 2027 to boost energy security amid global supply disruptions.  
Tan See Leng, Singapore's minister for energy, trade and industry, announced the joint intention during the Singapore Energy Lecture 2026 on Monday.  
Tan said the arrangement would enhance the resilience of the Saudi crude oil supply chain across Southeast Asia.
The minister noted that the initiative would also contribute to the city-state's energy security during supply emergencies.  
"Today, Saudi Arabia and Singapore are announcing our joint intent to establish an arrangement for Saudi crude oil to be stored at the Jurong Rock Caverns from the second half of 2027," the minister said.
Saudi Aramco, the Energy Market Authority and JTC signed a memorandum of understanding to finalize the storage agreement.
Officials aim to conclude negotiations within a few months.  
The global energy landscape has faced significant challenges this year following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabian airports and energy infrastructure have further escalated the international energy situation.
Tan emphasized that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would not be the last supply disruption.
Singapore has established multiple lines of defense to mitigate the economic impact of sudden supply chain crunches.
The government requires electricity-generating turbines to run on either gas or diesel to draw on reserve fuels.
The country also plans to expand its liquefied natural gas (LNG) capacity by 50% with a second terminal by 2030.

Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing its sources, as reported by European Pravda

One State Department official under the Trump administration admits that at first glance this sounds crazy. However, judging by previous talks with Washington, Russia and China are believed to support the idea, and the plan is for Orbán to become their joint candidate.
Officials from the US and another country emphasised that when the US, Russia and China pursue the same goal in the UN Security Council, they generally achieve it.

One American official stated that Orbán is "the dream MAGA-conservative candidate".

Furthermore, the WSJ notes that Orbán frequently clashed with the European Union while benefiting from it in the form of subsidies and his pro-China orientation never undermined his image as a defender of Western civilisation.
If Orbán puts forward his candidacy for the UN post, US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are expected to support him once again, although according to a source familiar with the process, the announcement is being held back until after the US midterm elections.
American officials primarily contacted Orbán to gauge his interest in the UN position. They found that he was positively inclined, albeit with caveats.
The remaining candidates for the position of secretary-general, according to a representative of the second country, are heavy on "secretary" – with experience in international bureaucracy or behind-the-scenes diplomacy. Orbán, on the other hand, would be a "general".
A State Department representative agreed with this, adding that Orbán adheres to the correct ideology, knows how to exercise power under hostile conditions and will not be intimidated by the establishment.
Background:

Secondary schools to be get new minimum targets: bar for Dutch and maths set high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:44:33 UTC
16:44:33 KST

After primary education, new minimum standards are also to be introduced in Flemish secondary education. The Flemish Government has approved the proposal put forward by Education Minister Zuhal Demir (Flemish nationalist N-VA). The new minimum standards will come into force in September 2029: by then, the first cohort of pupils to have completed primary education under the new minimum standards will be moving on to secondary school.
Secondary schools to get new minimum targets: bar for Dutch and maths set high
The revised minimum targets for secondary education will be set on a subject-by-subject basis and will no longer be organised around 16 broad, cross-curricular key competences. The so-called ‘overlapping target frameworks’ will be phased out.
New minimum targets have already been introduced in primary education. There, the emphasis is more on knowledge and clear expectations for pupils. Particular attention is being paid to Dutch and mathematics.
The same priorities are also being emphasised in the revised minimum objectives for secondary education. The aim is to raise the standard of education once again. “We want to achieve a knowledge-rich curriculum for all pupils whilst significantly simplifying the educational objectives,” the people behind the project say.
Education Minister Zuhal Demir: “Education must form a single, coherent whole. What you learn in one year must form the basis for the next. So, when the first pupils enter secondary school in September 2029 with their new knowledge, secondary schools must be ready to build on it.”
Raising the bar for Dutch and maths
As with the revised minimum targets for primary education, there will be a greater emphasis on knowledge in secondary education. The various subjects will once again take centre stage.
The educational objectives centred on 16 broad key competences will be phased out, to be replaced by specific objectives for each subject area, such as Dutch, maths, history and science.
In addition, some general objectives, such as citizenship and financial literacy, will be retained. However, the foundation of these objectives is the knowledge that pupils need to build up across various subjects.
“We have sometimes made education a little too complicated. We talk about 16 key competences, whilst ultimately, it is about something very simple: what do our children need to know and be able to do in various subjects such as history, maths or Dutch? We are simplifying the rules, without lowering the bar,” says Minister Demir.
“Knowledge is not an outdated concept. Those who know a lot can understand things better, think more critically and make independent choices. That is exactly what we want to equip our young people with.”
The bar is set particularly high for Dutch and maths. By the end of the first grade, every pupil must achieve the set minimum targets for these two subjects, although the class council still has the final say.
For other subjects, schools must ensure that their pupils, as a group, sufficiently meet the minimum targets.

Brazil heads back to the future as Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to recognize Lula win
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
08:34:09 CET
16:34:09 KST

By Oliver Griffin and Eduardo Simões
SAO PAULO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential vote ”looked like another rigged election,” although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result.
The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in Sunday’s presidential election, saying he would seek the annulment of Lula’s victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours.
Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party said it acknowledged the runoff result in a statement signed by the party’s head Valdemar Costa Neto.
“We recognize the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”
Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party’s statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil.
Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election,” Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. “It looked very bad to me.”
Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos.
“I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” Trump said. “The extension given was very strange.”
Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil’s electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump’s remarks were “totally wrong” and “unfounded.”
Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil’s former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula.
Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022.
MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN
World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with dismay by investors who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win.
Brazil’s real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020.
“The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure,” said Pantheon Macroeconomics’ chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia.
Lula’s victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved social media campaign helped power Lula to victory.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will face an uphill battle for his agenda in a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

Iran says Mecca pact states agree to boost cooperation
Iran and the three Mecca alliance countries have their first high-level contact since Houthi rebels escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Iran has said it will continue discussions with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye amid escalating tensions that have threatened regional stability and shaken the global economy.
The announcement came as top Iranian military officials met with senior Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials on Monday in what Iranian state television described as their first joint meeting.
Pakistan and Turkiye are strong allies of Saudi Arabia and have pledged military support to Riyadh as part of their new mutual defence pact, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The meeting in Tehran was held after Saudi Arabia faced weeks of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are fighting forces with the country’s internationally recognised and Saudi-backed government.
The meeting, which focused on “peace and security in the region”, was hosted by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.
A statement issued by Iranian officials after the meeting said participants “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation between the four regional countries”, according to Iran’s Fars news agency.
Saudi Arabia and its allies have not commented on the meeting or reported agreement.
Rayed Krimly, the Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy, said earlier today that the visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement allies “for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions in support of the mediation efforts carried out” by Qatar and Pakistan.
“The visit underscores the pivotal role of Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries in reinforcing regional security and stability and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he wrote on X.
Turkiye’s state news agency Anadolu reported that Kalin will attend the meeting in Tehran, citing Turkish security sources.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
The planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and the three members of the alliance since Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi armed group escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia last month.
Pakistan’s Field Marshal Munir last week visited Tehran, where he met President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials.
During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with the United States about ending the US-Israel war on Iran until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan has been a key intermediary between Washington and Tehran since the US and Israel launched the war in February.
Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an interim agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks later.
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the Houthis continued.
Ministers from the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli war on Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August. Under it, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
The agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and internationally recognised borders, according to the text publicised at the time.
Efforts by Turkiye’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

Report: Cost of living pressures driven up by high oil price
Phillip Inman
Pressure on John Healey to provide more support at the budget to the most vulnerable in society is only going to become more intense with the price of a barrel of Brent crude still above $110.
A new report from a longstanding study of the impact of cost of living pressures on low income families, shows that parents struggle to pay the costs of transporting disabled children to school and health appointments.
Those in employment are also affected getting to and from work in a car when petrol is above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre. It can mean that work doesn’t pay, says the report by RuthPatrick, a professor in social and public policy at the UniversityofGlasgow.
Patrick runs the changing realities project that follows 100 low income families.
Rosie L, who lives in a couple household in rural Scotland, said:
“... it’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car, we live rurally. Absolutely have to have a car and public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are ... Not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly, as my children are disabled.”
The latest report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants of which 67 shared strategies taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
It found:
“Nearly three-quarters (73%) had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold. More than two-thirds (68%) had gone without buying something they needed for their children, such as new shoes or a winter coat. Just over half (51%) had visited a food bank or used other forms of charitable food provision, while 40% had borrowed money from family and friends. Almost half of parents (49%) had also said no to their children’s requests for educational or after-school activities.”
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities, so far, did not match the scale of the problem.
“The Budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’. Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of Child Benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

On a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor may have dreamed of, pedestrians walked freely through the temporary bollards onto a green welcome banner rolled along the tarmac, declaring Oxford Street traffic-free.
SadiqKhan said it was a “momentous day”, with almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street now pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with the private car.
After decades of discussion, the closure to traffic has come into effect in time for the busy Christmas shopping period, although the bigger transformation of the street, a £150m project including trees, seating and level “plazas” for events, will start taking shape from spring 2027.
Speaking on Monday morning in the John Lewis department store, Khan said he was proud to be “finally unlocking a new era”, noting that the first action plans to pedestrianise the street started in 1971 “when I was literally in nappies”.
The mayor, whose first jobs were in retail in stores in the street, said:
“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street and the capital. We want high quality shops that will atrract people here but also culture, hospitality, leisure, and people going to and from the office having a good experience and I’m confident we’ll get that.”
He added:
“We’ve seen over the last couple of decades this street in decline… Pedestrianising the street with great public transport links, more greenery, more seating, will link to a better experience all round.”
The permanent plans will depend on feedback in the first phase and testing, and Khan said London “would be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”.
He added: “I want this to be a proof of concept – that investing in people rather than traffic leads to better footfall and spend.”
About half of the 1.2 mile street is now vehicle-free, roughly from Oxford Circus station to close to Marble Arch.
Many of London’s double-decker buses have traditionally run the length of the street and will now be diverted into neighbouring roads.
Claire Mann, chief operating officer at TransportforLondon, said there would still be “plenty of capacity for passengers” and it should not affect reliability. She said:
“People have said for some time it’s an unpleasanat environment to walk along, narrow and busy – the main movement through Oxford Street is pedestrians so this is us enabling people to make that journey in a nicer way. We’ll be monitoring to see if it does have an impact on ridership – but Bond Street and the Elizabeth Line does give you a way to arrive in style.”

South Korea bans missile maker LIG D&A from bids over bribery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:31:02 UTC
16:31:02 KST

- South Korea’s DAPA barred LIG D&A from government bidding for two years over a bribery and cost fraud case, the maximum penalty allowed.
- Prosecutors say a DAPA official received 460 million won in money and benefits, and LIG D&A has asked a court to suspend the ban.
South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA) has barred LIG Defense & Aerospace, the maker of the Cheongung air defense missile formerly known as LIG Nex1, from bidding on government contracts for two years after prosecutors accused the company of paying a DAPA official hundreds of millions of won in bribes during weapons development tenders, the maximum penalty allowed under the country’s State Contracts Act.
DAPA’s defense procurement contract review committee, a 20-member panel that includes outside experts, approved the 24-month ban at a meeting at the Government Complex in Gwacheon on Oct. 20, South Korean daily Kyunghyang Shinmun reported, citing the agency. The committee said it chose the harshest sanction because the case involves the largest bribe since DAPA was founded in 2006, deliberate misconduct including cost fraud carried out over a long period, and the damage such wrongdoing does to national security and public trust in defense procurement.
The ban takes effect five business days after the company is notified, and from Oct. 29 LIG D&A will be unable to take part in new bids by DAPA or other public institutions, The Asia Business Daily reported, keeping it out of new domestic tenders until October 2028. Existing contracts and export deals are not affected, but the company relies heavily on its home market, which accounted for 72.1% of its revenue in the first half of 2026.
The case stems from an investigation by the Suwon District Prosecutors’ Office, which said on Aug. 20 that a grade-five DAPA civil servant who sat on proposal evaluation panels for six defense projects worth a combined 91.5 billion won (about $69 million) between 2021 and late 2025 had received 460 million won (about $348,000) in money and benefits. Prosecutors said the official took 320 million won in cash, the right to recommend a subcontractor for a 2.2 billion won (about $1.7 million) service contract, and 140 million won in fees for selecting subcontractors, with the money allegedly routed through sham service and consulting contracts. The official and an LIG D&A executive were both detained and indicted, along with others accused of helping launder the money.
The sanction approved on Oct. 20 covers only one of the six projects, a counter-small-drone system, together with the cost fraud tied to that contract, and DAPA said the other five projects will also be reviewed, leaving open the possibility of further penalties. The agency weighed a two-year ban for the bribery and a six-month ban for the cost fraud and, under its rules, applied the heavier of the two.
LIG D&A said it regretted that DAPA had imposed an administrative sanction based only on an indictment while legal proceedings were still under way, and announced that it would seek a stay of enforcement and file a lawsuit to have the ban overturned, filing the request for a stay with a court on Oct. 22. The company has also said it will take every step to keep its programs on schedule.
Lawmaker Chun Ha-ram of the Reform Party responded that both the DAPA official who received the bribes and the subcontractor representative who passed them on have admitted the charges. At the first hearing of the case at the Suwon District Court on Sept. 29, four defendants, including the DAPA official, acknowledged the allegations in the indictment, while LIG D&A has disputed the prosecutors’ findings.
The ban could also affect major upcoming programs. LIG D&A was ranked first for system integration in the roughly 1.9 trillion won (about $1.44 billion) program to develop a long-range air-to-air missile for the KF-21 fighter, and industry observers have raised concerns that the sanction may leave the program to a single company. DAPA has also asked the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy to revoke LIG D&A’s designation as a defense contractor for the counter-small-drone system, a step that would limit its access to negotiated contracts as well.
