66th Brigade Commander Krot: I don't want some latte-swilling guy judging my actions in front of the whole country
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
09:30:00 EET
16:30:00 KST

66th Brigade Commander Krot: I don't want some latte-swilling guy judging my actions in front of the whole country
On 15 September, after several months of keeping it quiet, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps announced Operation Vivaldi, a major offensive operation on the Lyman front.
The operation involves mopping up Russian troops that have infiltrated deep into Ukrainian positions and cutting off a sizeable Russian salient west of the Chornyi Zherebets River.
The salient had been expanding for two years, gradually encircling Lyman and looming over Sviatohirsk. Allowing it to keep growing would have put several areas at risk – the town of Izium in Kharkiv Oblast and the Kramatorsk agglomeration, widely regarded as Ukraine's last "fortress belt" in Donetsk Oblast.
One of the brigades involved in the initial stages of Operation Vivaldi was the 66th Separate Mechanised Brigade named after Mstyslav the Brave.
The 66th advanced from west to east and liberated at least two settlements that have been publicly confirmed – Serednie and Shandryholove (we don't yet have the complete list).
Interestingly, the brigade did not simply storm the two villages head-on. Serednie was partially blockaded before being mopped up. Shandryholove was encircled and brought under complete fire control, and it was only after a period of siege had demoralised the Russian troops that Ukrainian forces moved in to mop it up.
A few days ago, Ukrainska Pravda had an exclusive opportunity to work on the Lyman front, where we spoke to Rostyslav "Krot" ("Mole") Sylivakin, commander of the 66th Brigade.
In this interview with Ukrainska Pravda, Sylivakin explains how his brigade managed to retake one settlement without suffering a single casualty, whether Operation Vivaldi is really changing the balance of forces in Donetsk Oblast, how the 3rd Army Corps treats his brigade despite it not being one of the corps' original units, and why he hates giving interviews, yet still spent two hours with Ukrainska Pravda journalists at his command post.
Secrets of Operation Vivaldi
Your brigade has been deployed on the Lyman front since 2022 – longer than any of the brigades currently operating here. Can you take us back a year or two and explain what was happening here before Operation Vivaldi? Where was the line of contact?
At the start of the operation, the official front line ran near Serednie – a village we later liberated. But Russian groups had penetrated even further. They had infiltrated as far as the outskirts of Korovii Yar [5 km north-west of Serednie – ed.]. So during the preparatory stage of the operation, we had to mop up those infiltrating groups, stabilise the situation, and prevent the Russians from capturing Korovii Yar. We succeeded.
We then seized the high ground overlooking Serednie, followed by the northern part of the village and then its centre, effectively encircling the Russian troops inside the settlement. That enabled us to eliminate all the Russian troops who had infiltrated onto our side of the Nitrius River.
We then began offensive operations to capture Shandryholove, which is across the river from Serednie. We crossed the Nitrius, established a bridgehead on the high ground north of Shandryholove and continued advancing through the strips of forest [the brigade continued advancing further east – ed.]. It was only after moving further forward that we began mopping up Shandryholove.
Why did you leave Shandryholove before it had been mopped up and continue advancing? Was that the plan?
It was. We had neither the time nor the personnel to mop up the village at that stage. We needed to wear the Russians down and demoralise them. And it worked: nine Russian soldiers surrendered, around 15 were killed, and another two, according to the POWs, died of starvation.
A few months ago I was working on a piece about an offensive operation by Ukraine's Air Assault Forces on the Oleksandrivka front, and I can tell you that they used similar tactics. But they ran into problems: Russian troops would emerge from their shelters and attack Ukrainian soldiers as they made their way through the forest strips that hadn't been mopped up yet…
I'm not saying this tactic would be effective on every part of the front. But storming well-fortified positions, and especially mopping up settlements, even small ones, requires far more forces, resources and personnel than simply blocking them and continuing to advance.
It was better for us to first block the enemy and cut them off from the rest of their units so they were unable to bring ammunition and supplies into Shandryholove, and then keep them under observation and fire on them with drones and artillery.
Every time the enemy came out from their cover, we were able to hit them, force them back, and make them feel their situation was hopeless. In time they realised that no one was coming for them – there would be no food or ammunition. We also dropped leaflets on them and played audio recordings over loudspeakers offering them the chance to surrender.
And it worked. An enemy that was prepared to defend their positions just a month earlier eventually breaks and becomes willing to surrender. Especially after eating nothing but roots, clay and worms for four or six weeks...
If we'd tried to mop up Shandryholove without blocking it first, we would have lost a lot of our people.
In your interview with Anna Kaliuzhna, you said you liberated one settlement without suffering a single casualty. Which settlement was that, and how did you manage it?
It was the village of Serednie. We were able to do it first and foremost because of the training our people had received. We were helped enormously by the fact that in February or March 2026 we were given permission to conduct basic combined military training at our own military unit. Because when we got people who'd done their basic training at training centres, they were just as strange to us as those who'd come straight from the enlistment offices. We had to spend time giving them additional training.
Do you remember when fair and regular replenishment of personnel was introduced at the end of 2025?
But they promised 50 people per brigade, didn't they? That's not many.
It isn't, but under those circumstances it was enough for us to prepare people for offensive operations. It gave us some certainty. Based on the battlefield situation and the fact that we would receive 50 people, we decided that we would conduct offensive operations [at the start of Operation Vivaldi – ed.] using small infantry groups of two or three people. A group like that is harder to detect and hit, and it's easier for them to find or dig shelter.
Groups of two or three assault troops? Wait, how many people did you actually have retaking Serednie?
Up to 30 people in total [an astonishingly small number for an offensive operation – UP]. But you can't say it was just those 30 people, because capturing a settlement involves a whole range of measures. To liberate Serednie, we had to capture the strongpoints overlooking the river, establish a safe route to the village, and so on.
We weren't able to block Serednie in the same way we later blocked Shandryholove because the Nitrius River runs along its eastern side. At the time we couldn't cross the river and seize the opposite bank, but we did manage, to some extent, to isolate the village using drones and minimise the number of enemy personnel that went into it.
Did the Russians not engage your men in small-arms combat in Serednie at all? Given that you suffered no casualties there.
Of course they did. There were about 20 enemy troops there. But when planning the operation, we were counting on the element of surprise. Basically our infantry shot the f**kers while they were asleep or resting in their dugouts and completely unaware of what was coming. Of course there were some cases where the enemy put up resistance, but thanks to our training, every small-arms engagement ended in our favour.
Am I right in thinking that this is the second time the Ukrainian army has liberated villages on the Lyman front? Didn't the first offensive operation sweep through here in 2022?
Yes. These territories were liberated, roughly all the way up to Ploshchanka, in autumn 2022. Then, from spring 2024 onwards, we began losing these territories. The enemy's 20th Army launched a large-scale offensive here, and our forces were weakened and stretched thin because everyone was fighting on higher-priority fronts – in Bakhmut, near Avdiivka.
Serednie and Shandryholove, the villages we're talking about, were lost in the autumn and winter of 2025.
A Ukrainian tank in a liberated village on the Lyman front in autumn 2022. Photo: Dmytro Larin
There was a whole combination of reasons why we lost those territories, ranging from incompetence on the part of individual officers at the commander level to decision-making at the group level.
In my view, another major factor was the mixing of units. In summer 2024, the 66th Brigade's sector was 38 km long [this is a huge sector – UP] and in addition to five of our own, 15 other attached battalions were fighting in it. For a single brigade, that's far too many attached units – untrained, understaffed, and originating from various structures ranging from Territorial Defence to border guards.
"I don't like it when every commander who gets an interview talks about how great he is"
You've emphasised several times that you aren't particularly keen to give interviews. I've heard a lot of military personnel say that. Why is that?
I don't like it when every commander who gets an interview talks about how great he is, giving expert assessments of what other commanders or other units have done without having the relevant experience to do so. And then there's the principle that the more frequently a person is interviewed, the faster they're made a Hero of Ukraine.
In normal armies in the rest of the world, it doesn't work like that. Press officers comment on events, not commanders. The commanders lead the troops.
From my point of view, I have to say that for us as journalists, it's an immense privilege to be able to speak with commanders directly and not just with press officers.
In our country and in our army, it's something we have to do, because service members and the Armed Forces as a whole have had a pretty poor reputation since 2014. There's a widespread stereotype that commanders are butchers, bribe-takers and incompetent fools and every other soldier is an alcoholic or a drug addict. So we need to promote the army and improve our reputation.
But some commanders exploit this carte blanche they have in terms of interviews and media exposure to satisfy their personal ambitions and become famous. From a professional standpoint, this is inappropriate. It leads to a situation where any young lad in this country can sit in front of a camera and deliver expert evaluations of decisions made by generals and colonels.
Personally, I don't want my actions and decisions to be judged later by some latte-swilling fella who's never been in my shoes.
I don't think that General Syrskyi deserves to have his decisions and actions judged by a generation this young, privileged and superficial – people who have experienced little beyond lattes, consumerism and sexual experimentation. Still less does he deserve to be judged publicly, before the whole of Ukraine.
Or even those colonels who've made sure they get interviews but have never served as group commanders – they sit there and criticise decisions made by Syrskyi or Zaluzhnyi, and in the future they'll criticise Drapatyi's decisions. Assessment and criticism should only come from people who have the necessary competence, relevant experience and level of training.
Remember Oleksandr "Henii" Shyrshyn – in the summer of 2025, when he was serving as a battalion commander in the 47th Brigade, he posted on Facebook saying the tasks set by the top leadership were "idiotic"...
Henii was criticising a specific situation and tasks in which he was directly involved. Henii was not criticising the commander-in-chief's overall activities across the Armed Forces or decisions made with regard to other sectors and other commanders.
So that form of criticism is acceptable?
The reason that criticism was expressed publicly was because it hadn't worked at the level where Henii initially raised his concerns and proposed alternative courses of action – it had been ignored.
I know Henii as a completely capable and effective commander.
Personnel audit, relationship with 3rd Army Corps and expectations of Drapatyi
When you took over in 2024, the 66th Brigade was in a pretty bad way: exhausted, understaffed and suffering losses. How did you handle that situation? What advice would you give to those in a similar situation today or in the future, especially considering that new brigades continue to be created, such as the 167th?
First of all we had to figure out what kind of personnel we actually had and what we didn't. Remember, we had 15 attached units at the time and only a handful of them were fighting independently. Most had minimal training, lacked proper combat experience, and were fundamentally unable to fight independently. So step one was to determine the true state of the personnel.
Then we did a huge amount of work to form a good, effective team with the right moral values. Some unit commanders had to be removed.
What are the right values to you?
First, zero tolerance for corruption. Second, openness and honesty. And third, you could be melodramatic and say the value of human life, but to be honest, it's the pursuit of efficiency.
In any interview you listen to these days, all the commanders talk about human life being the top priority. That is undoubtedly true. But if the command is incompetent, it doesn't matter how much they value human life – they're not going to preserve it.
The only way you can value human life in the conditions of our war is through high-quality training, high standards and discipline. There is no other way. If you're constantly shielding the lives of your own soldiers, your neighbours to the left and right of you are going to suffer. If you protect your own people all the time, someone else is going to get killed. If we run away from every danger, then I'm sorry, but tomorrow the front line is going to be beyond the Dnipro.
I think the very fact that we took the decision, as a society and as a country, to fight and not surrender in 2022 means we fundamentally agreed that for us, Ukraine's existence stands higher than any single human life.
Putin said in an interview that he does not see a world without Russia – the same must hold true for Ukraine, for Ukrainians. There are no Ukrainians without Ukraine.
So first you conducted a sort of personnel audit, then you assembled a team with the right values?
Assembling a team is a lengthy process – it can't be done in a week or two. That process continues to this day and will continue for as long as I am in this position. I found all the battalion commanders right here within the brigade – I didn't bring anyone in from outside or pull in any friends or acquaintances. I observed them for six months and found them, and we are learning here together and developing our brigade.
I get a sense from your words that you're a supporter of the corps reform, even though your 66th Brigade is fighting in another corps. I'd like to ask: how does the 3rd Army Corps treat you as an attached brigade?
The 3rd Corps treats our attached brigade as if we were their own (smiling).
To put it in simple terms and briefly, to start with, the 3rd Corps helped us to complete missions with their own personnel so that we had time to train our new recruits and non-commissioned officers. This ensured that we didn't deploy them chaotically, but according to plan – so that people could first gain combat experience in defence, and then we could train specialised groups to eliminate infiltrated enemy forces and conduct assault operations.
[According to UP's information, Andrii Biletskyi ordered the allocation of well over a thousand soldiers from the 3rd Assault Brigade to reinforce the brigades that joined the newly formed corps and its operational control.]
Prior to the corps reform, those types of decisions didn't happen. If any units were sent to reinforce us, they were mostly understrength. Firstly, they couldn't really reinforce us much, and secondly, they'd arrive when it was already too late.
The 3rd Corps also evaluated our brigade's capabilities very quickly and objectively. Their groups visited our units and observed the commanders and our supply levels. They provided training wherever possible, helping us restructure our command and control system.
I understand that this includes introducing a role known as a "battle captain" – a dedicated person who directs combat operations in real time from the command post? I saw some last year at 13th Khartiia Brigade command posts, and it looked very unusual.
Yes, the 3rd Army Corps helped us introduce this system. Before that, the entire burden of managing ongoing combat operations fell on the brigade commander and his deputies. As a result, we were falling behind in every area of our work, particularly when it came to planning future operations. Now we have time to plan, develop our capabilities and so on.
So if you didn't have a battle captain now, we wouldn't be sitting here recording this interview? Would you be next door in the main command room, watching a live drone feed on a big TV and shouting "Open fire!" into the radio?
Yes. When I took command of the 66th Brigade, what it boiled down to was that either I or one of my deputies would be sitting in front of a screen shouting orders about who should fire where, which drone should go where, where to put the mortar and where to put the machine gun. This is called hands-on control or micromanagement, and it has never been effective anywhere. I knew perfectly well even then that this wasn't how things should work.
I'd been a company commander and a battalion commander. For example, at the 93rd Brigade, I was taught that every commander must make decisions within their own remit. When I was a company commander, I didn't tell section commanders what to do – I expected them to make decisions themselves. If I wasn't happy with their decision, I'd adjust it and guide them towards a better one.
At the 66th Brigade, we had to start from scratch and teach commanders to make their own decisions. I spent a lot of time on that.
By 2025, when the corps reform began, my battalion commanders had become fairly independent. I no longer needed to sit in front of a screen all the time shouting orders. But I didn't have a dedicated officer who could take over that role.
The 3rd Army Corps showed us how battle captains should operate. It sent its own battle captains to our command posts to train us and share their experience. That had a positive effect. Now, other brigades are coming to us to learn.
How did you let go of the need for constant control? I've written more than one article about what micromanagement in the military was like under Oleksandr Syrskyi. And as someone who has managed at least something in life – even a tiny team working on a tiny task – I understand how difficult it can be.
It's not a question of how I let go. I never intended to hold on to that kind of control in the first place. I'd been a company commander and a battalion commander; I'd had my fill of directing small infantry groups. I don't want to be doing the same things as a brigade commander that I did when I was a company commander.
It's simple: any reasonably sensible person will be too lazy to do someone else's job.
My job is to appoint effective leaders, train them, hold them to high standards and give them the autonomy they need to make decisions. I will only make decisions on their behalf if those decisions contradict my intentions or if, based on my experience and training, I can see that they won't lead to the task being carried out effectively. That's how it works.
The system should work, not rely on one person.
On the subject of micromanagement, our sources say the new commander-in-chief is trying to move away from this kind of command system. Have you noticed any changes in the military since Mykhailo Drapatyi took over?
I'd put it this way: it's too soon for anyone at brigade level to have felt the effects of the change of commander-in-chief. The appointment can't be evaluated solely on the basis that I've asked the commander-in-chief about a few specific issues and he's agreed to help me. [Our sources say that Sylivakin has a fairly good relationship with Drapatyi – UP.]
But I believe that over time our defence forces will undergo major systemic changes, particularly when it comes to micromanagement. I know that General Drapatyi wants to build effective teams at every level, made up of competent people and officers, and root corruption out of the Armed Forces.
"There will be no wars without living people taking part"
How has Operation Vivaldi affected the defence of Donetsk Oblast as a whole? Has it really changed the situation fundamentally?
Operation Vivaldi will at the very least force the Russians to ease the pressure on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, because they will have to redeploy reserves from there [to the Lyman front] to stop us from advancing further.
Secondly, it's a massive blow to the Russians' illusion that they are already in the final stages of this war. Their media keeps claiming that Sviatohirsk has been captured, that Oskil [a village 10 km east of Izium] has been encircled, or that they are already storming Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. The successes of Operation Vivaldi are tearing their whole "victory" narrative to shreds.
It's unlikely, of course, but maybe some ordinary Russians will eventually realise that they are still a very long way from capturing Donbas.
They're a long way from capturing Donetsk Oblast at the moment, but could they still manage it?
We're fighting a huge country with an effectively inexhaustible pool of manpower for mobilisation. With those resources, the Russians can achieve anything they want. The question is whether they are capable of doing so with their current approach. I don't believe they are.
Personally, I don't think losing one territory or another would be a huge catastrophe for us. The war will go on for years, and the decisive factors in the final outcome will be things such as the combat effectiveness and technological development of the Armed Forces.
We may lose some territory, but if we preserve our combat effectiveness and develop faster than the Russians, we will be able to liberate that territory later.
Why are you confident that training and developing the Ukrainian Armed Forces can offset Russia's numerical superiority?
The clearest example is 2022, during this very war, when their numerical advantage was reduced to nothing because our units were more experienced. In 2022, Ukraine was technologically more advanced than Russia. Some of our companies already had Mavic drones and FPV drones, which had become available thanks to enthusiasts who had figured out how to use them on their own.
There will be many more technological innovations during this war. The question is which side will be quicker to adopt them and scale them up.
Like two-metre-tall humanoid robots?
That's possible too. When I was just beginning to gain combat experience, I couldn't have imagined that one day I'd be adjusting artillery fire with a drone and using that same drone for reconnaissance. Back then I had to go out on foot to see anything and gather information. And now warfare has changed so much…
There was a time when we couldn't even have imagined that you could kill an enemy by dropping a munition from a drone or evacuate a wounded soldier using a robot. Just six months ago our brigade wasn't using UGVs [unmanned ground vehicles] at all. Now we're consistently among the top 10 most effective units in terms of UGV use. And this month we even built our own UGV.
In the same way, five years from now, humanoid robots might be running through trenches and shooting. But the point is that they too are just a tool, a piece of technology, and they won't remain effective forever. As long as war exists, there will always be a place for ordinary infantry. There will be no wars without living people taking part.
Do you agree that the war has reached a stalemate?
In my opinion, the claim that the war has reached a stalemate is more political than military and isn't entirely accurate. From a military perspective, there are no dead ends in war. Sooner or later, one side will achieve a breakthrough.
If a ceasefire isn't reached politically, the war will continue until one side develops new technological solutions that give it a significant advantage. In the First World War it was chemical weapons and tanks. In the Second World War it was aircraft and new tactics for motorised and mechanised units. There will be something new in this war, too.
Olha Kyrylenko, Ukrainska Pravda

Planned Overflow: How Singapore Balances Floods, Canals, and Public Space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park in Singapore, a river does not occupy a fixed boundary. Under ordinary conditions, water moves through a naturalized channel bordered by grass, planting, and paths that bring visitors close to the river. During heavy rainfall, water spreads into the surrounding park, which is designed to accommodate flows beyond the capacity of the narrower channel. What appears to be a public landscape is also working infrastructure. Singapore's approach retains drainage engineering while assigning a wider role to the land around it.
For decades, Singapore's network of concrete canals has been central to managing stormwater in a densely developed city exposed to intense tropical rainfall. Their hard surfaces and defined channels were designed to convey water efficiently. These channels moved stormwater efficiently, but offered limited space for public access, planting, or other uses along the water's edge. Through its Active, Beautiful, Clean Waters (ABC Waters) Programme, launched in 2006, Singapore began integrating waterways with parks, ecological systems, and public spaces. The programme links stormwater management with the design of parks, waterways, and public spaces.
The transformation of the Kallang River at Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park offers one of the clearest examples of this approach. A 2.7-kilometer stretch of the former concrete canal was redesigned as a naturalized river, bringing the waterway into the surrounding park. The central design decision was to allow the park to function as a flood conveyance area. Under normal conditions, water occupies a narrower stream. During heavy rainfall, the flow can expand into the adjacent landscape. The park's ground is part of the flood conveyance system, not just the public space around it. Soil bioengineering and naturalized banks support this arrangement, combining hydraulic requirements with a more varied river edge.
Related Article
Rivers Before Roads: How Southeast Asia's Waterways Produced an Alternative Urbanism
At Bishan, the naturalized banks allow visitors to approach the water more closely. Compared with the former concrete canal, the naturalized river introduces gentler banks and stepping stones along the water's edge. PUB documents the park's dual role as a recreational landscape and a flood conveyance area. Sungei Tampines shows how naturalized banks can be introduced alongside measures to increase a canal's stormwater capacity.
In 2022, drainage improvements along a 1.4-kilometer section included widening the waterway by up to 4.5 metres and deepening it by 0.5 metres. These interventions increased its stormwater conveyance capacity by a reported 30 per cent. Approximately one kilometer of one bank was also naturalized using soil bioengineering techniques. A cantilevered park connector, lookout decks, and a bridge provide public access along the waterway.
A canal can be widened and deepened while sections of its banks are naturalized. The widened channel conveys stormwater, while selected sections of its banks accommodate planting, habitat, and public access. At Sungei Tampines, naturalisation is limited to sections of the bank while the main channel is enlarged to carry more stormwater. Channel dimensions, bank stability, water levels, and maintenance requirements continue to determine how these spaces operate.
At Sungei Ulu Pandan, the landscape also treats runoff before it reaches the canal. Here, the design incorporates features intended to treat runoff before it enters the waterway, making the landscape an active part of the drainage system rather than simply its visible setting. PUB's project documentation describes vegetated swales, sedimentation basins, cleansing biotopes, and habitat cells as components of this approach. Swales guide runoff while helping remove larger sediments. Sedimentation basins allow suspended particles to settle, while cleansing biotopes use plants and soil media to filter pollutants and absorb nutrients. Shallow, planted habitat cells along the canal edges provide shelter and feeding opportunities for wildlife.
The interventions were implemented in phases. An initial 600-metre section was completed in 2013, followed by works along a further 1.9 kilometers, completed in 2022. The phased works combined drainage improvements with runoff treatment and habitat features along the canal. The presence of these features alone does not establish their environmental performance. Research evaluating Singapore's ABC Waters Programme has found that some interventions perform well in removing suspended particles, while nutrient removal has been less consistent. Treatment performance varies with site conditions, including the characteristics of incoming runoff and the operation and maintenance of individual features.
At Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park, the river forms part of a larger recreational landscape. At Sungei Tampines, bridges, lookout decks, and a park connector establish points of access along a more linear drainage corridor. In both projects, access is provided along waterways that continue to serve drainage functions. When a canal is accessible from everyday routes, it can become part of how residents experience their neighborhood. Paths, bridges, and places to stop along the water's edge allow residents to encounter the canal as part of everyday public space.
Research on the non-market value of Singapore's ABC Waters Programme found that residents valued its environmental and amenity features, although preferences varied between groups. They do not, however, establish that every project increases social interaction or provides equal access to public space. Those outcomes depend on how spaces are connected, maintained, and used by different communities.
Public access must be maintained alongside the operational requirements of the waterway. These landscapes must accommodate fluctuating water levels and intense rainfall, while planted and engineered systems require ongoing maintenance. Paths and public amenities must therefore remain compatible with changing water levels and flood conditions.
Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park, Sungei Tampines, and Sungei Ulu Pandan extend the role of drainage infrastructure in different ways. One integrates the river with a floodable park; another combines increased conveyance capacity with naturalized banks and public access; the third incorporates runoff treatment and habitat features into the waterway's landscape. Across the three projects, drainage remains the primary hydraulic function, while the surrounding landscape also provides flood storage, runoff treatment, habitat, or public access.
The long-term performance of the ABC Waters Programme depends on how its projects are monitored and maintained after completion. Monitoring is needed to assess environmental performance, while ecological features require maintenance. The benefits of public access also need to be evaluated through how people use these spaces. A greener canal is not, by itself, proof of improved water quality, restored biodiversity, or reduced flood damage. These outcomes must be established through evidence over time.
Singapore's waterways show why drainage infrastructure needs to be evaluated beyond its hydraulic capacity. Hydraulic capacity and the appearance of a natural river are insufficient measures of a waterway's performance. The surrounding landscape can provide space for floodwater, habitat for other species, and public access to the waterway. The canal remains a drain. Its banks and surrounding ground determine how much more the waterway can do.

Ukraine war lessons show up on Chinese armor in Pakistan drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:15:54 UTC
16:15:54 KST

- Chinese Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles with anti-drone roof cages took part in Karakoram 2026, the first China-Pakistan joint army training, in Xinjiang.
- The drill included drone swarm strikes and robotic dogs scouting buildings, with all equipment supplied by China.
Chinese Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles fitted with anti-drone roof cages and side grilles carried assault troops during Karakoram 2026, the first joint army training between China and Pakistan, now under way in Korla in China’s northwestern Xinjiang region, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Oct. 21.
The exercise has moved into its main drill phase, in which mixed Chinese and Pakistani units rehearse a full raid on a mock terrorist camp, from reconnaissance and strikes to clearing buildings. Footage aired by CCTV also showed drone swarms carrying out suicide strikes and robotic dogs scouting building interiors ahead of the troops.
The drill opened with reconnaissance vehicles and drones watching the camp to track the mock enemy’s positions and movements. Snipers then took up firing positions, drone swarms struck exposed targets, and armored vehicles followed with direct fire. When the strikes ended, Type 08 vehicles carried the assault team forward, and more of them brought in clearance teams that dismounted and pushed deeper into the camp, with the robotic dogs going ahead to check buildings.
The Type 08 is an eight-wheeled armored vehicle family used by the People’s Liberation Army. The vehicles seen in the drill had a metal grille fitted over the roof and additional grilles on the sides, which CCTV said were designed specifically to counter drone attacks.
Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs commentator, told the Global Times that the roof cage was a rapid tactical adaptation to the drone threat, drawing on lessons from the war in Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East. He said that even in counterterrorism training, units in high-altitude areas rely on drones, and that the PLA needs ways to counter militant groups that might use drones for sabotage.
Such cages, often called “cope cages,” first spread widely on Russian armor during the war in Ukraine, where first-person-view drones have repeatedly hit the thinner roof, rear and engine areas of tanks and armored vehicles. Chinese forces have adopted them before: the PLA has fitted cages to ZBD-09 infantry fighting vehicles and showed Type 15 light tanks with anti-drone cages during a high-altitude exercise in October 2024.
Chinese soldiers said they had picked up tactics from their Pakistani counterparts, whose army has extensive counterinsurgency experience.
“What impressed me most about this joint training is that the Pakistani military has real combat experience, so many of their lessons are worth learning. When we enter a building and throw a grenade, we throw it far; they throw it at the ground so it bounces at speed, ricocheting two or three times instead of staying in one place. That effectively stops the enemy from picking it up and throwing it back,” said Pan Li, a member of a unit under the Xinjiang military command, CCTV reported.
China’s Ministry of National Defense announced the exercise on Oct. 10, saying it would focus on joint counterterrorism operations at high altitude and include training in drone operations, firing on the move and long-range sniping, as well as joint command and live-force drills. All weapons and equipment are being provided by China, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and drone and counter-drone systems, CCTV Military reported.

massimo dutti lands in new york with rare patti smith portraits by steven sebring and a soho flagship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:15:38 UTC
16:15:38 KST

massimo dutti lands in new york with rare patti smith portraits by steven sebring and a soho flagship
massimo dutti explores new york's cultural memory with ‘patti smith by steven sebring,’ an exhibition on bowery unveiling unseen archival photos alongside its multi-disciplinary soho debut.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
MASSIMO DUTTI ARRIVES IN SOHO
Before officially unlocking the doors at 575 Broadway, Massimo Dutti is making its New York entrance with an unexpected housewarming gift: a photo exhibition celebrating the godmother of punk. Running through October 25th at 260 Bowery, Patti Smith by Steven Sebring digs into the filmmaker’s personal vaults to reveal previously unseen portraits of the legendary artist. Instead of launching with a standard ribbon cutting, the brand serves up raw downtown culture first. Not confined to a single footprint, the project builds a network of creative partnerships across SoHo and Manhattan, ensuring its arrival echoes well beyond the main flagship.
Inside the restored SoHo landmark, local antiques blend with contemporary design across a sequence of interconnected rooms defined by high ceilings and visible original cast-iron columns. Bringing back the atmosphere of classic downtown interiors, the space bridges photography, publishing, fashion, and art to set an active stage for public programming and local collaborations.
PATTI SMITH’S NEW YORK IN UNSEEN ARCHIVAL PHOTOS BY STEVEN SEBRING
At the center of this project is a special commission by the brand, uniting a rare batch of unseen Patti Smith photographs captured by Steven Sebring over a multi-decade friendship. The exhibition dives deep into Sebring’s private archives to celebrate the city’s favorite poet-punk and the downtown scene she helped define. Following a private preview on October 16th, the showcase is currently open to the public at 260 Bowery Street through October 25th, anchored by a live talk between Sebring and The Theatre NYC on October 19th.

The cultural takeover spills directly onto Manhattan’s streetscape through a web of local creative partnerships. In collaboration with Apartamento, Massimo Dutti has launched an editorial city guide packed with insider recommendations from local creatives. Back inside the SoHo flagship, guests can experience tailored services in private Style Advisor fitting rooms and discover handpicked garments identified by special editorial labeling. The initiative culminates on October 26th with a public conversation hosted by Jessica Diehl on contemporary fashion and creation. Through this agenda, the opening turns into a full cultural program, inviting people to explore the city, discover new perspectives, and join an open dialogue.

Climate-driven farm losses push agricultural insurance payouts higher in Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:14:42 UTC
16:14:42 KST

Extreme weather events linked to climate change are taking an increasing toll on Türkiye’s agricultural sector, with crop damage reports and insurance payouts rising sharply in recent years, according to data from the Agricultural Insurance Pool (TARSİM).
The number of crop insurance damage notifications increased by 51.2 percent year-on-year in 2025, while compensation payments surged from 8 billion Turkish Liras in 2023 to 12 billion liras in 2024 and 35 billion liras in 2025. In the first 10 months of 2026, producers received 13 billion liras in compensation payments, bringing total payouts over the past four years to nearly 70 billion liras.
TARSİM data showed that damage notifications in crop insurance rose from 284,357 in 2024 to 430,076 in 2025. In the January-October period of this year, total damage notifications across all agricultural insurance branches reached 478,000, including 311,000 related to crop and greenhouse insurance.
The main causes of agricultural losses have changed over time. Hail, frost, wild boars, floods and storms were the leading sources of damage reports in 2023, while hail dominated in 2024. Agricultural frost became the primary cause in 2025, whereas floods and water inundation emerged as the most damaging events in 2026.
In crop insurance, hail accounted for 123,239 damage notifications, or 43.3 percent of the total in 2024. In 2025, frost-related claims rose to 171,558, representing 39.8 percent of all notifications. This year, floods and water inundation became the most significant source of losses, while frost damage remained more localized.
The provinces recording the highest number of claims in the January-October period were Malatya, Manisa, Diyarbakır, Amasya and Tokat. Hazelnut-producing areas in Samsun, Ordu and Giresun were affected by floods, water inundation and landslides, while reports of damage caused by wild animals and birds increased in corn- and sunflower-growing regions.
This year, lentils, wheat and barley were hit by floods, hail and storms, while peaches and nectarines suffered hail-related damage. Grapes and apricots were also affected by lighter hailstorms and frost.
Under the TARSİM system, insured agricultural land totaled 33 million decares in 2023, 35.6 million decares in 2024, 44.3 million decares in 2025, and 27 million decares as of October 2026. According to TARSİM, insurance coverage in crop and greenhouse insurance stood at around 30 percent at the end of 2025.

Elbit wins $200 million from unnamed Asia-Pacific country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:12:33 UTC
16:12:33 KST

- Elbit Systems won about $200 million in contracts from an unnamed Asia-Pacific country for helicopter targeting sensors, head-up displays and training system support.
- The deal includes Elbit’s new SPECTRO 12 compact surveillance and targeting payload, with work running up to five years.
Israel’s Elbit Systems has won contracts worth about $200 million from an unnamed country in the Asia-Pacific region to supply helicopter targeting sensors, cockpit head-up displays and support for airborne combat training systems, the company announced on Oct. 26.
The work will be carried out over up to five years. Elbit did not identify the customer, the aircraft types involved or how many systems it will deliver.
The largest element is the SPECTRO 12, a new multispectral surveillance and targeting payload that will be integrated on the customer’s helicopters. The turret-style sensor combines high-resolution imaging channels with a laser designator and artificial intelligence-based image processing, allowing crews to detect, identify and track targets at long range, at night and in bad weather, and to mark them for precision-guided weapons.
The SPECTRO 12 is the newest and smallest member of Elbit’s SPECTRO family. The company describes it as a 12-inch-class payload derived from its larger 15-inch-class systems, designed for aircraft where size, weight and power are tightly limited, such as light and medium helicopters.
The contracts also cover follow-on support and upgrades for airborne live training systems already installed on the customer’s aircraft. The systems let pilots fly realistic air-to-air and air-to-ground training sorties, including mixed live and simulated scenarios, with real-time combat simulation, weapon scoring and mission debriefing.
Elbit will also deliver head-up displays, the transparent screens in front of a pilot that project flight and targeting data so the pilot can keep looking outside the cockpit. The company said the new displays offer higher resolution, improved video and lower power consumption for day and night flying.
“Elbit Systems’ airborne solutions combine advanced technologies with extensive operational experience across a wide range of mission environments. We are proud to provide our customers with innovative capabilities that enhance mission effectiveness, situational awareness and operational readiness across a broad spectrum of airborne missions,” said Bezhalel Machlis, president and CEO of Elbit Systems.
The award follows a roughly $270 million deal for SPECTRO family payloads that Elbit signed with another unnamed international customer in September, covering systems that combine mid-wave infrared, visible and short-wave infrared channels with laser designation, along with the AMPS NG airborne surveillance payload. Earlier customers of the family include Romania, which ordered SPECTRO XR sensors for its IAR 330 Puma helicopters in 2023.
Elbit, based in Haifa, reported revenue of $2.29 billion for the quarter ended June 30 and an order backlog of $32 billion.

Brazil's Lula wins, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to concede
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:12:05 UTC
16:12:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Brazil's Lula wins, Flavio Bolsonaro refuses to recognise results
Brazilian right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has followed his imprisoned father's lead by refusing to concede defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won a historic fourth term in Sunday's presidential election.
Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for corruption charges and a coup attempt, called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities. He said he would ask for the result to be annulled.
"It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded," Bolsonaro told journalists.
Yet the scale of the loss, with Bolsonaro trailing Lula by over 4 million votes, makes it unlikely his efforts to annul the vote will succeed, analysts said. His petition is also undermined by the fact that his campaign also sought a voting extension due to heavy rains in the conservative-leaning south.
Still, Bolsonaro's refusal to concede could spark a wave of protests in a country where faith in the electoral system, and in judicial independence, has been strained in recent years, observers say.
Jair Bolsonaro plunged Brazil into a deep democratic crisis after the election in 2022, when his supporters stormed government buildings in protest against the result. He later received a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup.
Lula defies expectations
Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. The result will disappoint the administration of US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power.
Financial markets also expressed initial concerns at the shock result. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index dived nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory, while analysts expected the Brazilian real to fall against the US dollar.
Lula had trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff.
Speaking at a hotel in São Paulo late on Sunday, he took a conciliatory tone.
"I won’t speak of national unity, because that doesn’t always fit the reality of this country. No one is obliged to like the elected president, but he was put in place to govern for everyone," Lula said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging.
He will have to work alongside a Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies after a surge of right-wing voting recast Brazil's legislature in favor of the president's enemies.
"The challenges are countless," said Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper in São Paulo.

Chinese automotive brands, which have been among the main drivers of growth in the European market, suffered sharp declines in Türkiye amid additional customs duties and stricter import requirements.
Chinese brands sold a combined 36,245 vehicles in Türkiye in January-September 2026, down 43.8 percent year-on-year, according to data compiled from the Automotive Distributors and Mobility Association (ODMD). Their combined market share fell to 5.77 percent during the period.
Chery remained the largest Chinese brand in the Turkish market with 17,357 units sold, although its sales declined 23 percent from a year earlier. Omoda-Jaecoo followed with 9,717 units, posting a 64.4 percent increase, while BYD sold 6,886 vehicles, marking an 80 percent decline. MG recorded sales of 2,266 units, up 36.2 percent, and Hongqi sold 19 vehicles, an increase of 46.2 percent.
BYD’s steep sales decline played a significant role in the overall contraction, as the company was unable to import vehicles due to its investment plans in Türkiye. Chinese brands collectively sold around 30,000 fewer vehicles in Türkiye compared with the same period a year earlier, highlighting the slowdown in the local market.
Türkiye’s overall passenger car market contracted 15 percent in January-September from a year ago.
By contrast, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) showed that the European passenger car market expanded 6.3 percent in January-September, surpassing 10.5 million units. Car sales across Europe increased by 626,903 units from a year earlier.
Of that increase, 510,976 units came from five major Chinese-owned automotive groups. In other words, Chinese companies accounted for 81.5 percent of the growth in the European car market during the period.

North Korea deployed a howitzer on the border with South Korea amid escalating tensions

North Korea deployed a howitzer on the border with South Korea amid escalating tensions
Kyiv • UNN
Pyongyang accused Seoul of fabricating the landmine incident and threatened self-defense. A howitzer and North Korean troops were spotted near the border.
Tensions between North and South Korea escalated this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council reiterating its accusations that Seoul fabricated the September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted near the border. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
On Monday, October 26, a Reuters witness at an observation post in South Korea, located along the heavily fortified border, confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery gun positioned in plain view near the border.
South Korean news agency Yonhap on Sunday, October 25, identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border was a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as approximately 20–30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the demilitarized zone (DMZ).
"It is highly unusual for North Korea to put its self-propelled artillery on such prominent display," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
"By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signaling through actions rather than words that it intends to enforce its border policy by force, not through dialogue or negotiations," he added.
He also cautioned South Korea to be careful about escalating friction along the border in order to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in a letter sent on Sunday, October 25, the country's representative to the United Nations said Seoul was using the landmine incident to portray Pyongyang's construction of a border strip as a military invasion.
In the letter, North Korea warned that violations of its sovereignty could lead to self-defense measures, and that South Korea would be "fully responsible for all consequences."
The letter was a response to South Korea's letter to the UN Security Council last week, which said that the September 21 explosion in the demilitarized zone had been planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The United Nations Command, which oversees the demilitarized zone, said that a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang denies responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea's Ministry of Unification said on Monday that North Korea's letter appeared to repeat its existing position and was an attempt to justify its so-called work marking the border line.
The ministry had no separate comment on the deployment of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to ease tensions along the border.
North Korea's letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling this a violation of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity of another state.
Seoul said its military issues warnings and fires warning shots to force North Korean soldiers to return behind the line when they cross the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), which divides the DMZ.
A Yonhap report carries photographs taken at an observation post in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appear to show the howitzer, as well as North Korean troops conducting drills along the coast of Kaepung County, approximately 1.5 km from the observation post.
A similar incident occurred in 2015, when South Korean troops were wounded by North Korean mines. Seoul then resumed broadcasting anti-North Korean slogans across the demilitarized zone, leading to a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.

What will a pedestrianised Oxford Street mean for transport?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

Much of Britain’s most famous shopping street will be closed to traffic from Monday as the long-awaited pedestrianisation of London’s Oxford Street begins.
About half of the 1.2 mile street will initially be vehicle-free, after decades of planning and dispute over how to best use the street, an important transport thoroughfare and the home for flagship stores for big shopping chains.
Private cars have been barred for years but now all motorised traffic, including buses and black cabs, as well as bicycles, will be kept away.
For the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has targeted the switch as part of clean air plans throughout his tenure, it is a political victory, aided by the backing of central government to override local council objections.
While towns and cities around the UK have long pedestrianised their centres, the location, scale and notoriety of Oxford Street, attracting millions of foreign visitors each year, will make the £150m scheme’s outcome of interest to city planners around the world.
London has studied the pedestrianisation of central Sydney, and discussed the scheme with Barcelona, whose La Rambla is similarly viewed as shabbier than its renown deserves.
The big retailers, Transport for London and those who just want a pleasanter, green city centre will be hoping the changes live up to their promise. Here we unpack what is changing:
Where will be pedestrianised?
From 7am on 26 October, a stretch of nearly 0.6 miles (almost 1km) of Oxford Street, containing the most famous department stores including John Lewis and Selfridges, will be vehicle-free.
The junction with Orchard Street, near Marble Arch, to Great Portland Street, east of Oxford Circus Ikea, will be closed to all traffic between 7am and midnight on every day of the week.
Businesses will be able to make deliveries outside those hours via certain access routes, but vehicles will not be able to travel the length of Oxford Street.
What does this mean for transport?
Private vehicles, such as cars, are already forbidden to drive on the street between 7am and 7pm and this ban will now extended to 24 hours a day seven days a week and cover buses, black cabs and bikes too.
Vehicles will still be able to cross the pedestrianised stretch of street at several points including the major junction of Regent Street and Oxford Circus, and others including New Bond Street.
Bus routes including the numbers 7, 98 and 390 will now run along Wigmore Street, which runs parallel to Oxford Street.
There will be taxi ranks within 100m of the traffic-free area on Oxford Street and surrounding roads.
In contrast to some other traffic-free areas of London, cycles, e-bikes and e-scooters will not be allowed on the pedestrianised strip at any time.
What about disabled people and essential services?
Mobility scooters will still be allowed. Access for disabled people may prove easier than many other parts of London, with Bond Street and Tottenham Court Road stations, on the Underground and Elizabeth line, both step-free.
Emergency services will be able to access the entire area whenever required via the cross streets. Cargo e-bikes will be introduced to collect litter and enable street cleaning during pedestrianised hours.
What other plans are there for the street?
Khan has talked about making Oxford Street a public plaza with outdoor dining, and improved street furniture and lighting is coming.
Early next year, more trees and seating are due to be installed, while the road surface will be raised level with the pavements in places to create public squares and event spaces.
Will the rest of Oxford Street follow?
The pedestrianisation of this stretch of the landmark shopping street has repeatedly been described as the “first phase”, although plans for the rest of the thoroughfare are likely to depend on the success – or otherwise – of the scheme.

====================================================================================================

Stung with a parking fine for an 18-second airport stop to tackle a wasp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:26 UTC
16:00:26 KST

I had to stop my car for 18 seconds in a red zone at Leeds Bradford airport to deal with a wasp. It was buzzing in front of my face and making safe-driving impossible.
The result was a £100 parking charge notice (PCN) sent to my wife (the registered keeper) by Vehicle Control Services (VCS).
I’ve explained the circumstances to VCS, whose CCTV footage shows I only stopped for seconds and never left the car, but it won’t listen. 
 
AW, Hebden Bridge
Its hearing improved when I contacted the airport, which ordered VCS to refund the charge as “goodwill”. The airport tells me that if you had contacted it directly, it would have intervened. However, it is evidently worried that its actions in this case will open the floodgates to wasp-ridden drivers.
“Stopping in this area remains enforceable,” it says sternly. “And due to the safety-critical nature of the road, we would not be able to consider cancellation of any future penalty notices for stopping in this area.” VCS did not respond to a request for a comment.
Parking operators are infamously ruthless when enforcing airport no-stopping zones. Drivers have been charged for stopping at temporary lights, or waiting in traffic queues.
By remarkable coincidence, SM of Pontyclun in Wales also stopped for 18 seconds in an airport red zone. She was billed £100 by VCS, via her husband, who is the vehicle’s registered keeper.
In her case, the airport was Bristol, and she stopped to read the terms and conditions on a sign planted in the no-stopping area.
“I had prepaid £103.60 for three days in the short-stay car park,” she writes. “At the entrance was a prominent sign stating that payment was on exit, and including several lines of information. Confused, I wanted to make sure I was at the right place.”
Her appeal was rejected by VCS, which argued that it is “the motorist’s responsibility to ensure they are familiar with the terms and conditions displayed on the signage” – which is ironic given that SM was doing just that.
It was also rejected by the Independent Appeals Service, which concluded that red-route restrictions prohibit stopping under any circumstances.
“Is it reasonable to expect a motorist to read a substantial amount of car park information while their vehicle is moving, particularly when that information is relevant to determining whether they are entering the correct car park?” asks SM.
There are 24 lines of information, in varying sizes of font, on the sign SM was studying.
Drivers enter a contract when using a car park and are assumed to have agreed the terms and conditions, or else risk a PCN. It was therefore imperative SM read the notice, and not unreasonable she stopped to do so safely.
Bristol airport says: “The customer did not contact us to make us aware of the situation and that she had pre-booked parking. After the circumstances were reviewed, the penalty charge was refunded by the enforcement company.” VCS was contacted for a comment.
In fact, neither AW nor SM were obliged to pay the charge because of a loophole in the law. Airports are “statutory land” governed by bylaws, and are not subject to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012, which governs private parking enforcement in England and Wales.
The act allows private parking operators to pursue the registered keeper of a vehicle for charges. There is no such keeper liability on statutory land, so if the keeper declines to confirm who was driving, the parking operator is powerless. Operators don’t, of course, want you to know this.
The clue is in the small print of PCNs sent to the spouses of AW and SM which “invite” them to pay up or name the driver. Anyone else in this situation should reply stating that as an airport is statutory land, they are not liable as the vehicle keeper and not obliged to name the driver.
Motorists penalised for reasonable stops on land that does fall under the act may have a future get-out clause.
The government’s newly announced crackdown on private parking charges means that when the new official code of practice takes effect (we don’t have a date yet), charges will be cancelled on appeal for things such as stopping briefly because of a medical emergency (potential wasp stings, hopefully, included).

A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.
Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.
As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.
Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.
“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”
At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.
The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.
“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”
By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.
“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.
By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.
“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

The UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Over the past few years, you can plot the plunge into global instability not only through the unchecked assaults on international law and civilian life, but through the decline and undermining of the authority and credibility of international institutions. The latest level in this spiral is the proposed appointment of Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the UN secretary general. Her bid has been rapidly gaining momentum and endorsements. And it has been met with outrage among the Sudanese.
Nusseibeh is the minister of state at the UAE and a former UAE ambassador to the UN. For the past three years, the country has been connected to – bear with me, this will be a long sentence – supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia in Sudan, facilitating mercenaries to fight alongside the militia (which is accused of ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity and sexual violence), and appropriating international aid infrastructure to smuggle weapons into the country.
The war between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) is an ongoing calamity of historic proportions. It is grinding and brutal, and has already resulted in hunger, displacement and a humanitarian crisis. Although it has drawn in external actors, multiple investigations and reports point to the UAE as the country that has in essence fuelled the conflict by aggressively sponsoring one side from the start. The result has been intractable conflict, unfathomable losses and relentless momentum fed by external supply lines.
The UAE’s role in Sudan’s war has been the target of years of media investigations, human rights activism and political condemnation. There were calls from two US congressmen to American media and sports organisations to end all associations with the UAE in response to its “abetting genocide” by “arming one faction”. In the UK, a complaint was submitted to the government demanding an investigation into the Manchester City owner and deputy prime minister of the UAE, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, due to the “abundance of evidence” of UAE involvement. Attention has been called to the well-established violations associated with the vastly wealthy and hitherto immune power, which has used that wealth to try to secure a toehold in territories in Africa with geopolitical significance. Sudan’s Red Sea coastline, its bountiful gold reserves and strategic location within the continent seemingly drew the Gulf power’s predatory eye.
In the face of all efforts to highlight the gravity and high stakes of the situation, the UAE has behaved with arrogance, dissimulation and, according to reports, the use ofmisinformation and digital propaganda. Wherever such prevarications were made, there was Nusseibeh, affirming the denial of “baseless allegations”, undermining the work of the international media and, in one instance that should surely be disqualifying, disputing the findings of a UN panel of experts.
In one instance, Nusseibeh was confronted by an indignant Sudanese man in Chad who rejected her whitewashing visit to his refugee camp, imploring her delegation to keep their aid and insisting that if the UAE wants to help, it should stop interfering and stoking the war. Another enraged refugee refused aid, saying the UAE killed her brothers. Against this backdrop, the appointment of Nusseibeh, who has been the face of the UAE’s Sudan strategy, would be a slap in the face to the millions of people suffering the horrors of war, a dereliction of duty towards those thousands who have already been killed, and a green light to the prolonging of conflict.
It has been a lesson, or I should say another lesson, about the extent to which so many of the pleas from those who purport to care about Sudan are performative. How so much of the rhetoric about Sudan or even cursory interest in it is a sort of box-ticking, name-checking exercise. Something to be put on the record – here is the official statement of concern for civilians, here is the pundit with their once-and-that’s-enough treatment, here is the post on X. Going beyond that, making the necessary links that render the conflict not just a sad clash of armed groups but a war in which powerful external parties have been allowed to play abjectly immoral and accelerating roles, is a step too far.
It has also been a lesson in how much a certain kind of Arab politics and mien goes a long, long way to securing consent and licence. Nusseibeh is an operator, that’s for sure, but she is also a beneficiary of a branding exercise that the UAE has been working on for a long time to ingratiate itself with western establishments. One pillar of that strategy has been presenting itself as a “moderate” Muslim country that is alive to the dangers of radical Islam (up to and including being allegedly linked to the funding and support of hard-right groups in Europe). The other is in the cultivation of close financial ties with the UK and the US, particularly with the Trump family, conjoining itself with political and business elites.
And it has understood that between the allied, the gullible and the ignorant, Nusseibeh can easily be presented as the obvious choice for the position as a Muslim woman with liberal credentials and a western education, regardless of the dark politics she advances and represents. It is hard for some to see beyond the facts of her CV – Wycombe Abbey, Cambridge University and, on top of that, of Palestinian origin, serving a country that has normalised relations with Israel. A high identity-politics jackpot.
All which makes Nusseibeh and the country she represents far more relatable and knowable to the world than the vastly weaker, poorer and underrepresented Sudanese people who have been victimised. The UAE, to put it simply, is seen as one of the club, its offences the private business of a country that is too wealthy to antagonise and too solicitous to spurn. Its rise speaks to this moment. At a time of big regional wars, multipolarity, energy crises and fraying norms, who better to become a global anchor than a country that is offering value-free transactional politics, is backed with sovereign wealth, and is expert in the opulent backroom gangsterism of the new world order.
Appointing a representative widely seen as one of the authors of Sudan’s tragedy to such a prestigious and influential post, one that only entrenches the UAE’s position and secures it even more wriggle room vis-a-vis its actions in Sudan, is not just another small way in which the business of international affairs is changing. It is a new chapter, one in which a perpetrator and its tribunes are not just not held to account, but crowned. The contempt is exceptionally bewildering even in an era of outrages. Nusseibeh’s appointment can only be secured by stepping over the dead, and turning backs on the living.
- Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist
