‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Everyone had their reasons for joining the trip. Louisa from south London was putting her life back together after a split from her partner; first-timer Tim was strapping on ski boots following years of hesitation; and Lexi from Bristol had a classic case of the non-skiing boyfriend.
I was there because I needed a ski gang. None of my friends ski, and my brother was out of action with an injury. Not only that, I needed a good night’s sleep. I love my two-year-old son dearly, but I have somehow spawned an insomniac – still waking four times a night. Weary from bedtime battles, Holly, my partner, bluntly pointed out we could both benefit from “a temporary break from family life”. In other words: separate holidays.
Holly arranged a walking trip with friends; I opted for a week’s skiing in the French ski resort of Les Deux Alpes with Friendship Travel, a specialist operator in solo travel for more than 20 years. They find a chalet, fill it with solo skiers, provide travel, most meals and group ski lessons – that’s the basic service.
We were staying in a comfortable, largeish chalet just back from the resort’s mile-long drag. Entering a group holiday with strangers is a leap into the unknown. I was greeted by Sam and Mike, our (thankfully) low-key hosts, shown to my private room (you can save by bunking up with a same sex stranger), then introduced to my fellow holidaymakers. It turned out that there were 17 of us – nine women, eight men – and we were whisked into the lounge for a briefing and welcome drink. The atmosphere was upbeat and easy, and we gathered round one large table for an excellent three-course dinner.
Most Friendship Travel guests are aged between 35 and 65, and our group was at the top end of that range. There was Vivienne, a retired nurse from Cumbria who had just lost her partner, and Adriana, a “silver splitter” relishing retirement. For a few – myself included – it was the first such holiday, but many were inveterate solo travellers, with Ivyon, a former production operator from Bridgend, clocking up more than 90 trips.
The first morning, we set off to our ski lockers at the bottom of the slopes (tip: I booked my equipment hire in advance, saving €40). The group naturally fragmented, allowing small cliques to form – people relaxed as they started to identify potential après buddies.
I skied with Elaine, Clemmie, James and our guide, Luke, in the “level 4 advanced” group (we were asked to rate our ability beforehand). The backbone of Les Deux Alpes, the new Jandri 3S cable car, whisked us up to an altitude of 3,200 metres in 17 minutes – instead of the previous 40. Above broken clouds, we paused to admire the astonishing jagged peaks of the Écrins national park.
We blasted down a mixture of broad blue and red runs, plus some not overly challenging blacks. Although none of us had met before, we quickly settled into a rhythm, looking out for one another as the snow fell softly. There’s safety in numbers, especially on the off-piste sections. “I’d never have tried that alone,” said Clemmie.
Afternoons brought more skiing, followed by hands-in-the-air après at Skandal – reopened in 2025 following an extension – with a DJ on a packed terrace. Around sundown, the chalet WhatsApp group would start to ping. “Polar Bear Pub, anyone?” would be a typical message, often sent by Mícheál from Armagh, a dependable partner for a pint.
Solo travel has undergone a perception shift in recent decades, according to Colum McLornan, who founded Friendship Travel in 1999. “Travelling alone was often seen as unconventional, and for many it carried a stigma. But travellers are increasingly seeking independence, flexibility and personal growth. What was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industry,” he said.
At times, group etiquette could be a minefield: nobody likes waiting for latecomers (me); is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast? (probably); is it OK to peel away from the group and ski by oneself? (up to a point); will I look like a skinflint if I buy my own wine? (absolutely, but life’s too short for plonk).
Honourable mention to Steve, a jolly retired doctor from north London. I enjoyed his vivid stories of cruising the Yangtze River, and skiing with his father in Austria during the late 1950s. Despite our age gap, we struck up a bond that lasted all week. Naturally, not all guests are interesting and fun. One seemingly endless dinner conversation about printer cartridges had me dreaming of Netflix in my room.
Then, suddenly, I found myself hugging my ski gang goodbye, bound for the train. Would I go solo again? Yes. Our hosts were helpful without being intrusive, the skiing superb (especially the high-altitude stuff on Glacier de Mont-de-Lans) and I met people I will stay in touch with. Best of all, I finally got some sleep.
The trip was provided by Friendship Travel. A seven-night package with a private room in a shared chalet, daily breakfast and afternoon tea, dinner with wine on five evenings, and six days of group ski lessons in Les Deux Alpes, costs from £1,820pp. Return rail travel from London to Grenoble was provided by Eurostar

Anthropic AI model bypasses paywall to access Georgia voter counts without human authorization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:42 UTC
15:47:42 KST

AI model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available US state of Georgia aggregate voter counts without human authorization, Anthropic said in a statement on Sunday.
"Claude didn't access the state's voter registration system or change or pull any voting records," Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block these kinds of actions.
Anthropic said in a blog post earlier this month it found examples of Claude "working around a restriction to reach data that was gated by a token or a fee," and some of these cases involved websites run by US government agencies at the federal, state, and local levels.
The secretary of state's office in Georgia did not respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
Axios first reported the unauthorized action by Claude.
Anthropic AI passes itself as human during cybersecurity exercise
On Friday, Anthropic revealed that one of its artificial intelligence models passed itself off as human during a cybersecurity exercise to fool a human outside the exercise.
According to Anthropic, the model, which used Mythos 5, performed unsanctioned actions in nine out of 43 runs that impacted humans not participating in the exercise, with one of the cases even involving the AI pretending to be human.
The attack, which was described by the AI Security Institute (AISI) as a "supply chain attack," attempted to disrupt a public code repository on the GitHub platform by creating fake inquiries, introducing corrupted data, and even demanding changes by creating false accounts on the platform.
Tobias Holcman contributed to this report.

Will 70,000 Israelis returning from abroad for Election Day tip the political balance? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:23 UTC
15:47:23 KST

An estimated 70,000 Israelis living abroad have returned or are expected to return to Israel ahead of Tuesday's Knesset elections, potentially influencing the results if the race between the political blocs is close.
This begs the question: Could the Israelis arriving from abroad influence the election results?
In the 2022 elections, approximately 36,000 votes were needed to secure one Knesset seat. Given population growth and an expected increase in voter turnout, estimates suggest that the threshold for a seat could rise to approximately 38,000 to 39,000 votes.
It is difficult to determine which parties most of the Israelis arriving from abroad will support. Some estimates suggest that many will vote for the change bloc, but there is no reliable measure of their political preferences.
Even if, for example, 60% support the change bloc, this would add at most one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
These figures, however, remain estimates. The election results will reveal whether Israelis living abroad have tipped the balance in the event of a close race between the political blocs.
Election Day boosts hotel occupancy by 23%
The vast majority of Israelis arriving from overseas are combining family visits and vacations with Election Day. Most are staying with relatives or friends, or in apartments they own in Israel that are currently vacant.
However, some have chosen to stay in hotels.
Africa Israel Hotels reported an approximately 23% increase in hotel occupancy during election week. Although the comparison is with October of last year, when the security situation was more complicated, the increase appears significant.
"We are seeing an increase in occupancy at Africa Israel Hotels properties across the country ahead of Election Day. We are seeing more Israelis choosing to combine exercising their democratic right with a short vacation, taking advantage of the opportunity to break from their routine and enjoy a hotel stay," said Alex Eliyahu, marketing director of Africa Israel Hotels.
"Alongside the increase in demand, the chain is offering particularly attractive promotions and accommodation packages for Election Day, allowing guests to enjoy vacations at a variety of destinations across the country at affordable prices."
Fattal Hotels also reported an increase in room occupancy at its properties, particularly in central Israel.
"We are seeing an increase in bookings compared with October of last year, apparently due to the elections," said Maya Shalev, vice president of marketing and sales at Fattal Hotels.
"Many Israelis are taking advantage of the day off to combine voting with a vacation. Accordingly, we have offered promotions of up to 30% off, along with an additional 10% discount for members of the 'Fattal and Friends' club between October 25 and 29. At the same time, we are seeing bookings made from abroad for these dates, which may indicate that Israelis are coming to Israel to vote."
'I came from Miami to vote': Israelis returning to the ballot box
Among the tens of thousands who attended the October Council rally at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv on Saturday night were Israelis living abroad.
"I came from Miami to vote. I coordinated my vacation in Israel with Election Day, and I'm returning to the US at the beginning of November," said Judy, who has lived in the US for more than 50 years.
"Many Israelis living in Miami and Los Angeles tend to vote for the Right. I'm different, and I'm not alone."
Nurit, from the South Sharon area, attended the rally with her son-in-law and grandson, who had arrived from Canada.
"My grandson is voting for the first time. He's 18 years old. They're combining a family visit with voting in the elections. My daughter stayed in Canada to be with my younger grandson."
Ofer, who arrived from New York, also shared his experience.
"We came to Israel specifically to vote. We're returning to the US the day after the elections. We have family here, and it's an opportunity to see everyone."
Gidi, who arrived from Australia with his wife, is scheduled to fly out of Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday.
"We've already been here for three weeks. We've met with many family members and friends. And I'm going back on Wednesday because I have work commitments. My wife will stay here for another two weeks."
In contrast, Zehava, who arrived on a flight from New York, said: "I'm voting for Likud, and I came to visit family ahead of the elections. I planned it in advance."
Canceled flights leave some Israelis unable to vote
Some Israelis had hoped to travel to Israel but were left stranded abroad after flydubai canceled flights following an attempted terrorist attack.
"Flydubai's cancellation caused flight prices to the Far East to rise," explained a young man who had planned to travel to Israel ahead of the elections.
There are also Israelis who live in Israel but will be abroad on Election Day. However, their number appears to be lower than the number of Israelis arriving from overseas.
"I booked the flight tickets for a vacation with my husband in Vietnam almost a year ago, and we didn't know the elections would be held in October. This will be the first time I don't vote. It breaks my heart, but we're going ahead with the vacation we started planning a year ago," said Racheli from Ramat Gan.
"It's a shame that Israelis traveling abroad can't vote on Election Day."

Could Trump's allies push Netanyahu into unity gov't without his far-right partners? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:22 UTC
15:47:22 KST

Voices within US President Donald Trump's inner circle are advocating for the establishment of a broad and moderate Israeli unity government without National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, with some even floating the idea of a rotation agreement in which Benjamin Netanyahu would serve as prime minister first.
However, Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot and former prime minister Naftali Bennett remain opposed to serving under him, and American officials have yet to discuss the framework with them.
American billionaire Bill Ackman, a prominent supporter of Trump with close ties to his circle, publicly called on Sunday for the formation of a broad, moderate Israeli government that excludes Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In a social media post, Ackman argued that such a government would allow Israel to restore its international standing, expand the Abraham Accords, and improve relations with both major political parties in the United States.
Ackman, who heads the hedge fund Pershing Square, supported Trump in the presidential election and is considered an influential figure in US political and business circles. He criticized Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, stating that their presence harms Israel's global image and its ability to advance key diplomatic objectives. At the same time, he praised Netanyahu and his relationship with Trump. Ackman favors Netanyahu remaining in office, but with a different set of coalition partners.
Realizing Trump's Middle East ambitions requires a change in Israel's Knesset
Ackman is not the only figure in Trump's orbit holding this view. According to several sources, additional figures in Washington believe that over the remaining two years of the president's term, realizing his ambitious Middle East plans requires a change in the composition of Israel's government.
Foremost among these plans is the possibility of a historic normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia, a prospect difficult to envision advancing while Ben-Gvir and Smotrich sit at the cabinet table.
Several senior advisors to Trump believe an Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right partners would make it significantly easier to advance the president's regional policy.
This comes amid existing friction between Washington and Jerusalem: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are reportedly frustrated by the pace at which Netanyahu is advancing Trump's plan for Gaza; Special Envoy Tom Barrick disagrees with Israel's strategy regarding Syria; and officials around Secretary of State Marco Rubio seek to strengthen the Lebanese government while expressing frustration over insufficient action regarding Jewish violence in Judea and Samaria.
These officials place high importance on the composition of Israel's next government, which could impact Trump's chances of achieving major diplomatic breakthroughs before his term ends. A deal with Saudi Arabia, for instance, requires difficult Israeli decisions on the Palestinian issue and other regional matters.
A government reliant on Ben-Gvir and Smotrich could struggle to make such choices, even if Netanyahu himself were willing to do so. However, replacing coalition partners alone does not guarantee a deal: Riyadh maintains its own political demands, including tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
Trump's inner circles question viability of diplomacy with Netanyahu around
Some within Trump's circle even question whether a diplomatic breakthrough is achievable as long as Netanyahu serves as prime minister. Consequently, an idea has emerged within the president's team for a rotation-based unity government: Netanyahu would serve during the first year, after which another prime minister would replace him to lead negotiations with the Saudis before the conclusion of Trump's term.
Proponents of the idea believe this arrangement would maintain governance continuity in the first year while entrusting regional diplomatic efforts to a prime minister who is not dependent on Netanyahu's current partners. According to several Israeli and American sources, Netanyahu told Trump he wants to form a unity government and will work toward that goal after the election.
Israel's Ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, also publicly said Netanyahu wants a broad government. Leiter said Netanyahu prefers a national unity government over continuing with the current coalition makeup.
He also addressed Ben-Gvir's future, saying Netanyahu made it clear he would not serve as national security minister again. The comments drew a sharp reaction from Otzma Yehudit, whose officials fear Netanyahu is paving the way for a coalition with Eisenkot at the expense of his current partners. For his part, Ben-Gvir called on Netanyahu to form a right-wing government rather than one with Eisenkot.
Although the idea originated in his inner circle, Trump has not formally endorsed the initiative. The president publicly backed Netanyahu on October 18, even as several advisors expressed reservations. Vice President JD Vance did not join the public endorsement.
Furthermore, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee explicitly denied allegations of an American effort to push a unity government, clarifying that the administration does not intervene in Israeli elections or dictate actions to the prime minister.
Meanwhile, the proposals discussed in Washington remain far removed from Israel's political reality. American officials have not conducted a deep feasibility check with leaders of the change bloc, and no substantive talks have taken place with Eisenkot or other senior figures in the opposition regarding the proposed framework. Electoral scenarios also present obstacles for the initiative.
If Netanyahu's bloc secures 61 mandates, he is expected to receive the mandate to form a government, but it remains doubtful whether Eisenkot or Bennett would agree to join. Additionally, ultra-Orthodox parties demand the passage of the conscription bill as a precondition for coalition talks. Conversely, if the right-wing bloc fails to secure a majority, Netanyahu may not get the first chance to form a government.
Even in the event of a victory for the right-wing bloc, Netanyahu could find himself in a trap: his natural partners will demand the fulfillment of previous commitments, primarily the ultra-Orthodox demands regarding military draft legislation.
Reaching out to Eisenkot and Bennett would require offering them a partnership in a government they have pledged not to join. Even within the right-wing bloc, few believe Eisenkot or Bennett would consent to such a move.

Investors see economic upside for Israel if opposition beats Netanyahu in upcoming elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:47:14 UTC
15:47:14 KST

Israel's markets have soared despite three years of war and political turmoil, but some investors see further upside if the opposition defeats Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s election, potentially easing regional tensions and political risk.
Opinion polls point to a tight contest, with neither Netanyahu's ruling Likud bloc nor an opposition alliance centered on former military chief Gadi Eisenkot expected to secure the 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset needed to govern.
That raises the prospect of lengthy coalition negotiations or even another election, all at time when one of the key drivers of the Israeli market rally - the global frenzy around AI - has also started to splutter.
Since the October 7 Hamas attacks in 2023, the Tel Aviv stock market has soared 130%, far outpacing Wall Street's 80% gain, while the shekel has climbed 25%, one of the world's strongest currency performances.
Analysts attribute some of that strength to Israel's tech sector and the global AI boom, while defense spending, which has nearly doubled to around 8% of GDP, has also provided a boost.
With both Netanyahu and Eisenkot vowing to maintain pressure on Hamas and Iran, markets are focused on their broader policy differences. JPMorgan estimates the shekel could swing as much as 3% depending on the result.
Opposition victory could improve Israeli economic position
An opposition victory that improves relations with Western allies and halts a judicial overhaul that sparked mass protests in 2023 could strengthen the currency, JPMorgan said, while another Netanyahu-led government could weaken it.
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, while stopping short of backing a candidate, said a government without far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich would signal that Israel was "turning a new page," potentially helping rebuild its international credibility and expand the Abraham Accords with its neighbors.
IBI Investment House also expects an opposition victory to lift the markets. "From a capital markets perspective, this would likely be reflected in a decline in Israel's risk premium, appreciation pressure on the shekel, and a positive reaction in the local market," IBI's Chief Economist Rafi Gozlan said.
According to prediction market Polymarket, close to 60% are betting on Eisenkot becoming the next Israeli prime minister, compared with 27% for Netanyahu.
"The most significant issue is what the result will mean for the region," said Equity Bank's chief economic adviser Charlie Robertson. "If Netanyahu is reelected, it might increase the chances of further escalation with Iran, whereas a defeat might be seen as lessening the tensions."
But the prospect of gains under an opposition government does not mean investors expect Israeli assets to suffer if Netanyahu remains in power. Stocks and bonds have proved remarkably resilient through years of war and political upheaval, and some investors remain confident in the economy regardless of the election outcome.
Union Investment's Sergey Dergachev has been buying Israeli bonds ahead of the election, betting the economy and companies he favors will remain fundamentally strong. "We are very constructive on Israeli credits going into the election," Dergachev said, adding that bonds were less prone to major swings and the region's intertwined conflicts should eventually ease.
Tel Aviv shares were up around 1% in the final session ahead of Tuesday's vote, taking their year-to-date gain to about 12%.
However, both they and the shekel have pulled back some 10% since May. Analysts again point to the strong link to tech, given global AI indexes have also been dropping, although there has been one nagging issue throughout the last three years.
Despite the rally, foreign investors remain cautious. Copley Fund Research data show the share of global funds holding Israeli equities is at a record low, having fallen sharply since 2023.
TS Lombard's Christopher Granville cited central bank estimates that the war had cost the economy more than $55 billion by last year, equivalent to 8.6% in cumulative lost GDP growth.
Public debt, budget deficit high amid Iran war
Israel's fiscal position is another focus. Public debt has risen to nearly 70% of GDP, about 10 percentage points higher than in 2022, while the budget deficit is expected to remain around 4.5% of GDP, up from less than 2% before the conflict.
Central bank head Amir Yaron stressed last week the need to "preserve adequate fiscal policy space" given the Iran war.
Like stocks, Israeli government bonds have rallied, returning about 30% over the last two years, more than double the main emerging market indexes.
The main risk for investors is an inconclusive result that prolongs political uncertainty, delaying budgets, reforms and investment, some investors believe.
That uncertainty can produce sharp short-term swings. Tel Aviv Stock Exchange research covering the last 10 elections found volatility in leading share indexes rose by as much as 45% in the weeks after voting compared with a typical week. But initial losses were typically recovered within a month, with the indexes posting an average gain of about 1.7%.
Over a longer horizon, the TA-125 returned an average 16.4% in the year following elections, compared with a long-term annual average of 11.5%, the research found. Political deadlock often weighed on stocks before voting, but the effects typically faded within months, said Nissan Avraham, an analyst at the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's research unit.
Israeli businesses continue thriving despite political, regional upheaval
That record supports the view that elections matter less for Israeli companies than many investors assume.
Lior Yochpaz, chief investment officer at insurance company Menora Mivtachim, said businesses have continued to thrive despite years of political upheaval, judicial overhaul proposals, and regional conflict, helped by a relatively business-friendly environment.
For some investors, however, the more attractive election trade lies outside Israel. TT International's Jean-Charles Sambor said an opposition victory or weakened Netanyahu government could ease regional tensions and benefit Lebanese bonds.
"The best way to play it for us is through other Middle East countries, and for us Lebanon is a good proxy," Sambor said.

Appeals court skeptical over Trump administration lawsuit against California mail-in ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:46:46 UTC
15:46:46 KST

A federal appeals court appeared skeptical on Sunday of a lawsuit filed by US President Donald Trump's administration that seeks to force California officials to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots the administration says were sent to noncitizens ahead of midterm elections.
During a rare weekend oral argument, two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals sharply questioned a Justice Department lawyer about the lawsuit, a high-profile effort by the Trump administration to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms.
The Department of Justice's lawsuit signals the willingness of Trump's administration to contest midterm results that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
At the end of the two-hour oral argument, Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to rule as quickly as possible.
Trump's Justice Department has warned election officials across California that they could be targets of federal scrutiny if they refuse to help identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls. It has distributed to California officials a list of 20,000 people it says are likely aliens registered to vote in the state, a Democratic stronghold.
Data shows ineligible voting in US exceedingly rare
California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and, in a court filing, stated that the Justice Department's assertions relied on suspect data.
All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation this year found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department filed its lawsuit in federal court in Los Angeles on October 15. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration's list from the rest of the ballots and not count them until it verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens.
The department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case.
Bennett, a Trump-appointed judge, said during Sunday's oral argument that the lawsuit could not be reconciled with a provision of the US Constitution known as the Elections Clause, which gives states the authority to set election processes.
"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," Bennett told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly. "How can we do that?"
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
California focal point of Trump's anti-immigration crackdown
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold, with 52 seats in the House of Representatives — more than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump's fellow Republicans in the midterms.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through so-called sanctuary state policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has also long asserted that California's immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud.
Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of former president Joe Biden, said on Sunday that he was confused by the question of why the appeals court should have jurisdiction to rule at this juncture, noting that the lower court judge assigned to the case had already set a hearing for Tuesday.

Green light shining on Mount Olympos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:43:27 UTC
15:43:27 KST

The U.N. climate conference (COP31), which will be held in Antalya this November, has been making headlines lately. I’ve been spending more time in Antalya due to a small assignment I’ve taken on. While the climate summit may not be on many people’s radar, climate change inevitably affects everyone. Recent flood disasters have turned our lives upside down. I don’t know if COP31 decisions are as binding on governments as they used to be, but it’s important from our perspective that the summit is being held in Antalya. Antalya and its surrounding areas are among our leading agricultural regions. At the same time, the Bey Mountains, which form the city’s backdrop, are a unique natural treasure. Mount Olympos, just west of the Antalya Gulf, is particularly special because at the top of its Çıralı hill is an ever-burning flame called Yanar Taş, which simply means “The Burning Stone.” The local name of the hill indicates its never-dying spark of light, as “Çıralı” means “with kindling firewood.” According to mythology, the flames came from the mouth of the monster Chimera.
Çıralı Hill is rocky, but further inland, you will find yourself in a wonderland of amazing flavors and aromas. Deep in the woods, you can find wild honey and mushrooms, and the air in the forest is healing. Down from the village of Beycik is a small retreat called the Olympos Mountain Lodge. It has only a few rooms, all of which face the woods. When Mehmet Ali Börtücene, the chef at The Rabbit Hole at Olympos Mountain Lodge, called me and offered me the chance to escape to Olympos, I put all my plans on hold for a night.
My reason for escaping wasn’t just my love for Olympos, though. It was mostly curiosity. I was eager to meet the trio of chefs — three nature-loving chefs whose cuisine has intrigued me and whose work I’ve followed from afar: Mehmet Ali Börtücene of The Rabbit Hole, the host; Bahtiyar Büyükduman of Telezzüz in Istanbul; and Daniel Vidal of Baldío in Mexico City. I wanted to witness what they would create when they came together.
Arca Tierra-Baldío: Mexico’s green star
The concept of “zero waste” has been rising in popularity in recent years. Mexico City, one of the world’s most populous cities, is likely a prime candidate for this concept. Baldío, the city’s first and only restaurant with a Green Michelin Star, is an Arca Tierra project. The core idea is simple: Source all ingredients from small-scale farmers, waste nothing and use fermentation to transform materials destined for the trash into delicious meals. Of course, achieving this in a bustling urban environment is no easy feat. The collaboration between Baldío chef Daniel Vidal and Arca Tierra founder Pablo Usobiaga has made it possible to bring this mission to life. The source of the food is key to the endeavor’s success. The starting point is the chinampas, agricultural islands dating back two thousand years. These man-made, floating gardens are essentially islands. The restaurant sources its fresh ingredients from these islands. They also apply the zero-waste concept to the full, that’s why they are nicknamed the restaurant without a trash bin. This is precisely how Baldío earned its Green Michelin Star.
Different landscapes, shared mindset
How did this green connection stretching from Mexico to a mountain village in Antalya, Türkiye, come about? Thanks to Mehmet Ali Börtücene, who is well known in Ankara and is affectionately called “Mali” by his friends. His “rabbit hole,” an escape from Ankara, is the Olympos Mountain Lodge in Beycik village. The lodge offers a tasting menu that changes every night, providing a surprising adventure where you never know what you’ll encounter — just like falling down the rabbit hole in Alice in Wonderland. After Mali’s exploratory trip to Mexico, his like-minded Mexican friends followed him into this rabbit hole. Bahtiyar Büyükduman, the chef at Telezzüz — Istanbul’s go-to spot for plant-based cuisine and recipient of the Michelin Green Star — also joined them, contributing with finding a sponsor for the whole mission. His totally vegan restaurant is the only vegan fine/dining venue in Istanbul and as he is an archaeologist in origin, he likes to dig deep down in the history of dishes and ingredients.
These three like-minded chefs have prepared a special nine-course tasting menu. They are all committed to sustainability. They find joy in even the smallest things they forage and gather in nature. They don’t want to waste anything. Bahtiyar’s Ajo Blanco dish used zucchini stems and was inspired by the Mediterranean tradition of repurposing stale bread.
Daniel’s amazing white mole dish was straight out of the woods, featuring local wild mushrooms and pine nuts foraged from the forest and served with white mole sauce. Mali’s crispy chicken was blended with forest herbs, his butter spread was cedar-smoked and the olive explosion was straight from the olive tree in the garden, only a few meters away from the kitchen. Each flavor was a new discovery and an exciting surprise.
This culinary collaboration, shaped around the gastronomic heritage of Anatolia and Mexico, as well as a focus on sustainability and a zero-waste approach, brought together three different chefs not only at a shared table but also with a shared vision and a common goal. And that was what truly mattered. While Antalya was bustling with preparations for COP31, a quiet yet powerful voice emerged from the Olympos Mountain. The ever-burning flame of Yanat Taş, the burning stone, seemed to shine even brighter. The shared vision of these three eco-conscious chefs lit a green light for the future.

TTK to host 20th Turkish History Congress in Ankara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26

AA Photo
The capital Ankara is set to host the 20th Turkish History Congress from Oct. 26 to 30 at the Atatürk Supreme Council for Culture, Language and History campus, Turkish Historical Society (TTK) President Professor Dr. Haluk Selvi has announced.
Established in 1932, the landmark congress continues to illuminate research on Turkish history. It gained international prominence during its second edition in 1937, attracting scholars and participants from across the globe.
TTK President Selvi noted that they began preparations for the 20th conference approximately two years ago. He mentioned they have invited academics from both Türkiye and abroad to Ankara and have finalized the conference topics.
“The 230 papers selected through the academic selection process will be presented by 300 scholars from 30 different countries. At the conference, a wide range of topics related to Turkish history — from the earliest times to the present — across a broad geographical area stretching from Central Asia to the Balkans and from Crimea to Qatar will be addressed by an international audience,” he said.
Selvi explained that the purpose of the Turkish History Congress is to demonstrate the Turkish contribution to civilization through historical data in response to Western-centric claims, and announced that the papers presented will be published in a book.
As the conference runs through Oct. 29, a special panel will be held to observe Republic Day, Selvi announced. He also revealed that another special panel at the conference will focus on the role of institutes in historical writing, featuring the participation of scholars from the Turkic states and Italy.
Selvi stated their great honor in hosting the congress as the TTK approaches its 100th anniversary. “Throughout the five-day congress, sessions and special exhibitions will be held in five different halls. We invite history enthusiasts and history students from all over to our conference,” Selvi said.

Netanyahu denies clash with IDF chief over Iran as mystery Iraq strikes raise tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:29:11 UTC
15:29:11 KST

The heightened military alert declared by IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir roughly a week and a half ago was driven by fears of a dangerous miscalculation involving Iran. His message to Israel's political leadership was clear: The military wants to avoid inflammatory statements and provocative operations that could trigger an Iranian response or convince Tehran that a U.S.-Israeli attack is imminent.
Such a misunderstanding could lead Iran to launch a preemptive strike, even if Israel and the United States had not yet decided to attack.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have continued issuing warnings to Tehran, raising concerns that Iranian leaders could conclude a joint U.S.-Israeli operation is approaching, potentially before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
The tensions between Israel's political and military leadership have now surfaced publicly, alongside reports of mysterious attacks on Iranian-supplied military equipment in Iraq.
The reported confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir
On Sunday, Channel 12 reported details of a serious confrontation between Netanyahu and Zamir over an undisclosed military operation connected to Iran.
According to the report, Zamir recently received instructions from the political leadership but requested an extensive discussion before implementing them. He also sought formal, signed legal authorization from the political echelon for the proposed action.
A security source said the operation could trigger a rapid confrontation with Iran at an exceptionally sensitive moment, potentially resulting in precisely the kind of miscalculation the IDF chief has been seeking to prevent.
Two sources said the atmosphere at a meeting held Sunday at Palmachim Airbase was extremely tense.
Netanyahu denied that any confrontation had occurred.
"There is no clash," he told Channel 14. "Someone is trying to obscure the fact that the chief of staff himself said Iran is trying to interfere in the elections."
The prime minister's remarks referred to warnings by Israeli security officials about possible Iranian attempts to disrupt the Israeli election, scheduled for Tuesday.
The precise nature of the military directive at the center of the reported dispute has not been disclosed.
The mysterious attacks in Iraq
A separate development may help explain the broader strategic tensions surrounding Iran and Israel's military activities.
According to a report published Saturday by the Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat, Iraqi authorities suspect that two facilities storing air defense systems supplied by Iran to pro-Iranian militias were targeted in airstrikes last week.
The weapons reportedly included portable antiaircraft missile systems intended to provide an additional defensive layer in eastern Iraq.
The militias were apparently preparing to use these systems as a forward line of defense against Israeli Air Force fighter jets and drones in the event of another Israeli attack on Iran.
That would potentially complicate Israeli air operations by placing air defense assets outside Iranian territory, along routes that Israeli aircraft might use in a future operation.
According to the assessment presented here, an Israeli Air Force attack against such targets has already taken place in recent days, possibly using drones or precision-guided weapons launched from a distance.
Reports of the suspected operation appeared in a limited number of Arab media outlets. However, Israel has not officially acknowledged carrying out the strike, and the Iraqi government has neither confirmed nor denied Israeli involvement.
The identity of those responsible and the precise circumstances of the reported attacks therefore remain unconfirmed.
Why Netanyahu and Zamir see the risks differently
Netanyahu has sought to assist Saudi Arabia and Iranian Kurdish groups operating in northern Iraq through operations against the militias threatening them.
Both have come under attack from Iran-aligned armed groups, making the militias a concern not only for Israel but also for other regional actors.
Zamir, however, is understood to believe that Israel has already accomplished enough through previous operations, some conducted in cooperation with the Americans.
His concern is that further operations, or even public reports about them, could put pressure on Tehran to respond.
Iran's leadership may feel compelled to defend the Iraqi Shiite militias that remain loyal to it, particularly given the financial and operational support those groups have received from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Quds Force.
Iran has provided money to these militias, including funding that enabled the Quds Force to pay their personnel.
Any Iranian intervention on behalf of the militias could expand an otherwise limited confrontation into a wider conflict.
Iran's strategy after the US withdrawal
The regional situation has become more complicated since U.S. forces completed their withdrawal from Iraq at the end of September.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps is now attempting to exploit the new circumstances by positioning Iraqi Shiite militias as an additional defensive shield for Iran.
This involves developing air defense capabilities on Iraqi soil that could threaten aircraft approaching Iranian airspace.
The militias also serve another strategic purpose for Tehran: They can operate against Saudi Arabia in support of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
In this way, the Iraqi militias are becoming increasingly important to Iran's regional military posture, both as an additional layer of defense and as a means of applying pressure on neighboring countries.
The Asharq Al-Awsat report suggested that officials in Baghdad were examining intelligence assessments raising an even more consequential possibility: that the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran may already have resumed, not through direct attacks on Iranian territory but through operations targeting Iranian military assets and allied forces inside Iraq.
The October 17 explosion and unanswered questions
One incident being examined took place on October 17, when Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces, known in Arabic as Hashd al-Shaabi, reported an explosion at an ammunition storage facility at one of its bases in the Baghdad area.
The organization said a fire had broken out following an explosion in an ammunition depot and that its personnel had brought the blaze under control. Five people sustained minor injuries.
The Iran-aligned militia umbrella organization announced that an investigation was underway to determine the circumstances of the incident.
More than a week later, however, no findings had been publicly released.
The Saudi report raised questions about whether the incident could be connected to the suspected attacks on weapons facilities storing Iranian-supplied air defense systems. No confirmed evidence establishing such a connection has been made public.
The uncertainty surrounding the Iraq incidents illustrates the challenge confronting Israel's military and political leadership. Operations intended to weaken Iran's regional defenses may carry limited immediate risks, but the cumulative effect of military action, public threats and Iranian fears of an imminent attack could prove much harder to control.
For Zamir, that possibility appears to be the central concern: An operation intended to strengthen Israel's security could instead produce the rapid escalation that the military is trying to avoid, particularly in the politically sensitive days surrounding Israel's election.

Caribbean presses Britain for reparations ahead of King Charles tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:28:24 UTC
15:28:24 KST

King Charles III and Queen Camilla begin a nine-day Caribbean tour this week, arriving to demands for slavery reparations, a formal British apology and greater independence from London.
The Bahamas National Reparations Committee says it knows what the royal couple will find. It expects “schools emptied of children who will stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling.”
Charles is expected to visit the Bahamas on Tuesday to begin the nine-day trip to the Caribbean. His last official visit to the archipelago was in July 1973 as a prince who granted the Bahamas independence, ending 300 years of British rule. But the Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, along with six other Caribbean nations that recognise Charles as their king and head of state.
While in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to visit Clifford Park, where the archipelago’s black, turquoise and yellow flag was raised for the first time more than half a century ago.
His visit will raise important questions, said Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said.
A psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, Campbell-Dean said she recently mentioned Charles’ upcoming visit to her students, and they were not excited. She responded: “I know y’all might not care about this man who is coming, but here’s why this is of importance.”
Reparations push gains legal momentum
Caribbean leaders have long demanded an apology and reparations from Britain, which has consistently rejected both.
In early September, Jamaica took its reparations case to Charles. It has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the island, a move AP describes as unprecedented.
After three days in the Bahamas, Charles flies to Guyana, where thousands of enslaved people rose up in the 1823 Demerara rebellion, one of the region’s biggest slave revolts. It took place on a plantation owned by the father of former British Prime Minister William Gladstone. More than 200 people were killed, and several were decapitated, with their heads placed on poles.
President Irfaan Ali told ITV News that Charles has “rightfully recognised slavery as the darkest days in human history”. “Moving to the apology is the next step,” he said.
Reparations set to test Commonwealth summit
After two days in Guyana, Charles flies to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where he meets leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders say slavery reparations should dominate.
Jamaica, a regular stop for British royals, is not on Charles’s itinerary this time.
Steven Bennett, a 51-year-old Rastafarian, says that is for the best. “Until the British monarchy is ready to stand on Jamaican soil, look us in the eye, apologise, and talk about actual repair and restitution, he has no business here. We want justice, not a parade,” he says.
Hermine Reid, a 68-year-old retired civil servant, fondly remembers Queen Elizabeth II’s visits but accepts the change. “Jamaica is growing up and charting its own course, and the king clearly recognises that,” she says.

Milena Baeva

The situation in the Persian Gulf in March 2026, amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, necessitated the timely evacuation of dozens of Bulgarians from Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain. Those events also prevented a polling station from being opened in Kuwait City for Bulgaria’s parliamentary elections in April 2026. Bulgaria remembers the revolt of 1185 on St Demetrius’ Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:27:18 UTC
15:27:18 KST

Author
Ivo Ivanov
Bulgaria remembers the revolt of 1185 on St Demetrius’ Day
Led by brothers Peter and Asen, the uprising ended nearly two centuries of Byzantine rule
Monday 26 October 2026 07:10
Monday, 26 October 2026, 07:10
The Church of St Demetrius of Thessaloniki in Veliko Tarnovo, where historical accounts place the proclamation of the uprising led by the brothers Peter and Asen.
PHOTO BTA
Font size
In 1018, after half a century of warfare, the First Bulgarian Empire was conquered by Byzantium. Despite repeated Bulgarian uprisings, Byzantine rule lasted more than a century and a half. In the autumn of 1185 or early 1186, the local nobles Peter and Asen launched a new uprising in Tarnovgrad. After three years of fighting, Bulgarian independence was restored.
In 1185, the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos sought a marriage alliance with his strongest European neighbour, marrying the ten-year-old daughter of King Béla III of Hungary. Her dowry included the regions of Braničevo, Belgrade and the Morava valley, then inhabited by Bulgarians. But, as the senior imperial official Niketas Choniates writes in his chronicle, “being reluctant to pay for the wedding celebrations from the state treasury, he extracted the money from his subjects… and stirred up hostility among the barbarians around Mount Haemus, chiefly against himself and the Romans, who were formerly called Moesians and are now known as Vlachs and Bulgarians”.
“The Uprising of Asen and Peter” by Georgi Bogdanov, 1961.
PHOTO museumvt.com
“The instigators of this evil, who stirred up the entire people, were a certain Peter and Asen, two brothers,” Choniates continues. “What words could convey what these godless and impious men did to the Romans? What account could encompass these Iliads of misfortune?” he exclaims dramatically.
Bulgarian historian Professor Plamen Pavlov, citing fellow historians, points out that Bulgarians commonly call it the “uprising of Asen and Peter”, although the correct order is “Peter and Asen”. Until 1194, the leading figure was the elder brother, Theodore, who took the royal name Peter and provided the ideas behind the movement.
The uprising was proclaimed at the consecration of a church the brothers had built in Tarnovo, dedicated to St Demetrius of Thessaloniki. His feast day, 26 October, is therefore traditionally regarded as the date the uprising began.
PHOTO BGNES
“They persuaded these fervent people to proclaim that God had decreed freedom for the Bulgarian and Vlach peoples and had consented to their deliverance from the long yoke. That was why Demetrius, the martyr of Christ, had left Thessaloniki and his church there, abandoning the Romans, and had come to help and protect them in their undertaking,” the chronicler recounts.
Even after Bulgarian independence was restored, the first tsars of the Asen dynasty – the brothers Peter, Asen and Kaloyan – continued to fight Byzantium. Their struggle was long and hard, with many setbacks. It continued until the Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople in 1204, forcing the remnants of the once-great Eastern Roman Empire into exile. The Latin Empire established by the crusaders then attempted to conquer Bulgaria, but suffered a crushing defeat at Adrianople, present-day Edirne. The victory of Tsar Kaloyan, who ruled Bulgaria from 1197 to 1207, proved enough to deter the Latins for good.
Editor: Elena Karkalanova

Presidential Election 2026
Estela Encheva from Munich: We are voting with sceptical hope
The president should act as a check on those in power and unite a divided society
Monday 26 October 2026 07:33
Monday, 26 October 2026, 07:33
PHOTO Facbook /Estela Encheva
Font size
There are nearly 420,000 Bulgarians living in Germany, and Munich is home to one of the country's largest Bulgarian communities. According to the city's official statistics office, more than 14,500 Bulgarians live and work in Munich.
By early afternoon on Sunday, around 550 people had cast their ballots at one of the three polling stations outside Bulgaria's Consulate General in Munich, our compatriot Estela Encheva told Radio Bulgaria in an interview. Voters were heading to the polls with a range of emotions:
“Some are quite desperate, but still hope that things will change. The prevailing emotion is one of sceptical hope for change. Many people are also angry, probably because of the situation in Bulgaria, but this sense of sceptical hope is what dominates overall.”
Encheva is studying law and has been living in Munich for nearly seven years. Her time in Germany has changed the way she sees Bulgaria:
“I came to Germany when I was very young. I had not even finished school, and when I moved here, I had a somewhat idealistic feeling about and view of the place I was going to. Once I arrived, I realised that both Bulgaria and Germany have their advantages and disadvantages, which made me look at things more realistically. Back then, I seemed to have greater hope that something would change in Bulgaria in the near future. Now, after all these years, although I still want change, I do not know whether it will happen.”
PHOTO Private archive
For Estela, it is important that the president stands by their principles, brings people together and safeguards Bulgaria's international standing.
“It is also important to me that the president respects international law and insists that our country abide by it, as well as bringing the people together. We live in a time when society is so divided that it is almost impossible to unite it through political measures.”
Last but not least, the president must also act as a check on those in power, our compatriot insists.

Who are the leading candidates in Israel’s election on Oct 27?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
06:05:48 UTC
15:05:48 KST

Who are the leading candidates in Israel’s election on Oct 27?
- Israel’s Oct 27 election is tighter than expected, but Benjamin Netanyahu still has a path to power. The vote follows the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
- Netanyahu is under pressure from ICC war crimes claims and corruption charges, while his Likud party has fallen in polls. He wants a “broad national” government, but a deadlock could keep him as caretaker prime minister.
- Main rivals include Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett with Yair Lapid, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan. Far-right allies Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, plus ultra-Orthodox parties, may still help Netanyahu, while Arab and swing parties could decide the result.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long looked on course to lose power in Israel’s election, but the race has narrowed as the vote approaches and his rivals have no clear path to power.
Votes will be cast on Oct 27 for parties, and seats in Parliament will be allocated to individuals on party lists according to proportional representation.
Here are details of some of the leading candidates in Israel's first parliamentary election since the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, that plunged the Middle East into turmoil, with Israel going to war in Lebanon and Gaza and launching air strikes against Iran.
Benjamin Netanyahu
In power for much of the time since 2009, after a first stint as prime minister in the 1990s, Netanyahu has become the face of Israel abroad and a polarising figure at home.
Supporters hail Netanyahu as “King Bibi” and see him as the strong leader Israel needs to defend itself in a hostile region.
But, wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes in Gaza which he rejects and on trial in Israel on corruption charges which he denies, he is fighting for his political life.
Opinion polls have pointed to a sharp drop for his Likud party since the Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel, which shattered Netanyahu’s security credentials.
His government’s policies on matters of religion and state have also been unpopular among many Israelis.
But Netanyahu, 77, is a consummate political survivor. He has said he wants to form a “broad national” government after the election, if he wins. In the event of a stalemate, he could remain a caretaker prime minister for many months.
Netanyahu’s top rivals
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who lost a son in Gaza combat, heads a new centrist party called Yashar, Hebrew for “straight” or “honest”.
Eisenkot, 66, has projected an image as a political outsider, soldier and security hawk whose humble background and family sacrifices stand in vivid contrast to Netanyahu’s decades in high office and lingering corruption cases.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, 54, a right-wing former commando, former Netanyahu aide and high-tech millionaire, has joined forces with centrist former premier Yair Lapid.
Their new party is called Together and its messages have focused on healing a traumatised nation and getting the country back on track. Their alliance, despite being on opposite ends of the political spectrum, ousted Netanyahu in a 2021 election.
Former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman, 68, was once a close ally of Netanyahu.
Even more hawkish than his former boss, Lieberman quit Netanyahu’s government in 2018, accusing the prime minister of being too soft on Palestinian militants in Gaza, and has become one of Netanyahu’s sharpest critics.
His party, Israel Our Home, draws much of its support from the country’s ex-Soviet immigrant community.
Former general Yair Golan, 64, hailed for his rescue of people from one of the Hamas Oct 7 attack sites, leads the Democrats, founded on the moribund remnants of Israel’s historical Labour party and smaller left-wing Meretz.
Candidates on Netanyahu’s side
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, 46, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50, have both drawn intense international scrutiny for their far-right policies towards the Palestinians.
Smotrich has spearheaded Israel’s rapid expansion of West Bank settlements, voicing his hope that it would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state.
Ben-Gvir, who was convicted in 2007 of racist incitement against Arabs, has promoted capital punishment for convicted Palestinian militants, toughened prison conditions for jailed Palestinians and easier gun ownership for Israelis.
Both men have advocated for the expulsion of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip and Israel resettling the enclave.
Ultra-Orthodox allies
Netanyahu has relied on two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, for his political survival for years.
Their demands for their community to be mostly exempt from compulsory military service, along with their low participation in the workforce and reliance on state benefits, have angered many Israelis, all the more so at a time of war.
Potential key players
Parties which are not clearly aligned with either side could tip the balance in favour of Netanyahu or his rivals.
They include Raam and the Joint List, the two parties that represent Israel’s 20% Arab minority.
Along with them are a new right-wing party called People of Israel and a centre-right party called The Reservists, both of which have been wavering in opinion polls. REUTERS

ADB approves 72 mln USD package to boost Cambodia's rural farming resilience

15:05:47 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved a 72-million-U.S.-dollar financing package to help Cambodia strengthen rural farming and increase women's participation in agriculture, according to its press release on Monday.
The financing consists of a 57-million-dollar concessional loan and a 15-million-dollar grant, the press release said, adding that the Smallholder Resilient Economic Development Sector Project will enhance the resilience of about 200,000 smallholder farmers in disaster-prone communes.
"Investing in smallholder farmers, particularly women, is essential for boosting the rural economy and supporting poor communities that are most vulnerable to extreme weather events," said ADB Country Director for Cambodia Yasmin Siddiqi.
"By helping women lead and participate in local decision-making and development programs, this project will scale up inclusive agricultural value chains and strengthen food systems, while driving women-led businesses and supporting families to build healthier, more secure, and resilient futures," she added.
Overlapping natural hazards such as heatwaves, drought, and flooding acutely impact Cambodia's agriculture and food systems, damaging infrastructure, limiting market access, and exacerbating food insecurity, particularly in rural areas where 59 percent of the country's population lives, the press release said.
Women, representing 51 percent of Cambodia's agricultural labor force, remain among the most vulnerable as they face limited access to economic opportunities, support, and financing, it added.
The project will upgrade agricultural infrastructure and services across 186 communes in seven provinces severely vulnerable to natural hazards, it said, adding that it will modernize irrigation systems to serve an additional 7,000 hectares of farmland and rehabilitate 190 kilometers of access roads to connect farmers to markets, jobs, and opportunities.
"The project will provide farmers with technical support and training to upgrade their skills and adopt resilient practices in crop production, horticulture, poultry, insect farming, and aquaculture," the press release said. "It will offer grants to help farmers reduce dependence on imported fuel and fertilizers and boost their resilience to disasters and global shocks." ■

France's deteriorating public finances will take center stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.
The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Oct. 29’s meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fueled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading — but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded, "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at the Oct. 29 meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5 percent.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the U.S. central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, although closely watched core inflation — excluding volatile energy and food prices — hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task."
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.
