How purchases of sanctioned Iranian jet fuel were disguised by Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:41:20 UTC
13:41:20 KST

In December 2025, the US-sanctioned tanker Reef arrived in Myanmar waters with some 113,000 barrels of fuel backed by sham paperwork.
Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave ordered the shipment, agreeing in a sales contract inked with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel. But the $15.8 million agreement, which Reuters viewed, was a charade: there was no such trade between South Africa and Myanmar in 2025, according to data from the United Nations and Vortexa, a shipping and energy data provider.
In reality, Reef carried jet fuel from Iran to Myanmar, according to records of fuel shipments to Myanmar, as well as satellite images and analysis by SynMax Intelligence, which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.
The deception was needed because the US in 2023 imposed targeted sanctions on Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry. The US did so citing the deadly bombing campaign waged by the Southeast Asian country’s military on civilian targets as part of an effort to crush a rebel-led insurgency. All purchasers of Iranian oil and fuel are also exposed to sweeping American sanctions.
Details of how Myanmar disguised purchases of Iranian jet fuel, as well as the entities involved in the transactions, are reported here for the first time.
Myanmar’s military junta was involved in the ruse. Days before Reef arrived, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel,” according to a copy of the agency’s November 30 letter seen by Reuters. The document, which was provided to Reuters by the activist group Justice for Myanmar, did not explain the purpose of the mislabeling.
The letter from the regulator also authorized Dynamic Wave and its client, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Company, to pay Tawan for the shipment.
Neither Dynamic Wave nor its client, which is part-owned by Myanmar’s military-backed government, responded to questions about the fuel shipment.
Spokespeople for Myanmar’s military-backed government and foreign exchange regulator, as well as the Iranian foreign ministry, also did not return requests for comment.
Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025, with much of the trade carried out by the tankers Reef – since renamed Maris – and Noble, a Reuters report revealed in January.
The scheme uncovered by Reuters underscores both the reach and limits of Washington’s power. The lengths taken to disguise the trade suggest US sanctions are biting. But Iranian jet fuel has continued to flow, earning Tehran valuable foreign currency and providing Myanmar with the means to conduct both commercial aviation and air raids.
The US Treasury did not respond to questions about jet-fuel shipments between Iran and Myanmar.
Jet fuel, airstrikes, and civilian casualties
Myanmar’s generals seized power in 2021 from the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The coup sparked a civil war, during which the military has killed thousands – including many civilians – in aerial assaults, the United Nations said in August.
Myanmar’s foreign ministry said in response to the UN allegations that the military “exercises maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.”
Justice for Myanmar, which also shared the fuel sales contract with Reuters, published a report on Monday concluding that Myanmar’s junta was importing jet fuel mislabeled as diesel.
The organization, which supports further sanctions on Myanmar's jet fuel imports, said it obtained the documents from a junta-run server that was briefly publicly accessible.
Reuters found a dead link to one of the documents on the DuckDuckGo search engine, indicating it had once been hosted on that server. Delivery dates and fuel quantities in the documents also match Iranian jet fuel shipment records that were separately reviewed by the news agency.
Thai bank connection
The sales contract for Dynamic Wave's fuel shipment stipulated that the payment be transferred into Tawan’s account at Siam Commercial Bank (SCB), Thailand’s oldest bank.
Tawan was identified by UN experts in a 2024 report as a jet-fuel supplier to Myanmar’s military. The firm has not commented on those allegations.
SCB was described as a major facilitator of Myanmar military procurement in that report.
The bank said after the report’s release that it adheres to anti-money-laundering laws and that its Myanmar-related transactions were legitimate and not connected to the arms trade.
Reuters could not determine whether SCB was aware of the nature of Tawan’s business.
Thai regulators in 2024 ordered banks to closely scrutinize transactions involving Myanmar in order to comply with sanctions and anti-money-laundering laws.
SCB did not respond to repeated requests for comment about its commercial relationship with Tawan.
Tawan and the Bank of Thailand, which supervises the kingdom's financial industry, also did not respond to questions.
The December shipment was not the first time jet fuel arrived in Myanmar disguised as diesel.
Dynamic Wave in May 2025 agreed to buy from Tawan 202,000 barrels of what a second contract, also obtained from the junta server, described as South African diesel. The agreement stipulated that the diesel should arrive at Yangon within a month and that Dynamic Wave would pay $26 million into Tawan’s SCB account.
The invoice for that contract contained discrepancies suggesting the tanker actually contained jet fuel.
The density of the fuel listed in the document matched the specifications for jet fuel rather than diesel sold in Southeast Asia, according to Joshua Heyne, a jet-fuel expert at Washington State University, and data from Platts, the energy-industry information provider. In addition, the price of the fuel was more than 50% higher than a global diesel benchmark.
Noble called at Yangon on June 17 carrying just under 200,000 barrels of jet fuel earmarked for Dynamic Wave, shipment records show.
Like Reef's December shipment, Noble’s cargo was loaded at Iran’s Bandar Abbas according to SynMax’s analysis of satellite imagery. As it made its way to Myanmar’s commercial capital, Noble transmitted location signals that made it appear as though its destination was the port of Chittagong in Bangladesh, according to SynMax.
The manager of the Reef and Noble tankers did not respond to questions sent via its listed website.
Shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued this year, Reuters reported in October, citing SynMax analysis and satellite imagery.

Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported.

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:40:10 UTC
13:40:10 KST

For Russia’s sanctions-busting A7 payment service, international transfers start with bags of cash at Moscow markets. At its peak, it processed at least 58 metric tons in a single month.
What A7 is and how it became the largest player in the shadow payments market
Sanctions against Russian banks and payment systems, along with their disconnection from SWIFT after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, gave rise to shadow intermediaries offering Russians cross-border money transfers. Many have offices in the capital’s Moscow City business district, the investigative outlet Proekt reported in spring 2026.
The largest is A7, a company owned by Moldovan businessman Ilan Shor, who was convicted of fraud and embezzlement in Moldova. Shor owns a controlling stake; the remaining 49% belongs to Russia’s state-owned Promsvyazbank (PSB). In late 2019, PSB officially became the designated bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry and defense industry.
The state development corporation VEB.RF, headed by Igor Shuvalov, “provides support” to A7. Proekt’s journalists suggest that Roman Abramovich may play “an important but secret role in the company.” A source in the cross-border payments business described Abramovich to Proekt as A7’s “protector and sponsor.” In the source’s view, Abramovich began working with Shor because he valued Shor’s ability to “devise financial schemes.” Abramovich’s representatives deny that he is involved in A7.
How Abramovich is connected to A7
According to Proekt, Shor’s first flight to Russia after a Moldovan court ordered his arrest in absentia was aboard Abramovich’s plane, suggesting that the two knew each other well.
Igor Shuvalov, the head of VEB.RF, the state corporation that “provides support” to A7, is a longtime acquaintance of Abramovich’s.
In 2024, A7 rented offices in Abramovich’s Belye Sady and Skolkovo Park business centers. Two A7 subsidiaries still occupy offices owned by Abramovich.
“Another indication of the oligarch’s involvement is the enormous financial support A7 receives from businessman Viktor Kharitonin, whom the press has long called ‘Abramovich’s protégé,’” Proekt reported.
A business partner of Abramovich’s, who spoke to Proekt on condition of anonymity, estimated that A7 handles about 15% of all cross-border transfers in Russia. The company puts its share even higher, at 19%. “No one else even comes close to A7,” a source working in the market told Proekt. The outlet’s other sources agreed that A7 is the largest player in the industry.
Proekt obtained a list of all of A7’s clients. They included at least 25 Russian companies already under U.S. and EU sanctions. Five manufacture or supply combat drones used by the Russian army in its war against Ukraine.
Other A7 clients include Arkady Rotenberg’s tour operator Biblioglobus, the online marketplace Wildberries, cigarette manufacturer International Tobacco Group, the Sunlight jewelry chain, and industrial companies including Leonid Mikhelson’s natural gas producer Arctic LNG 2, AAEM Turbine Technologies, and S7 Engineering.
In late October, journalists from the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) expanded on Proekt’s investigation. After reviewing internal company documents and speaking with sources, they found that most payments entering A7’s network are funded by hundreds of metric tons of rubles in cash collected from individuals and companies at several Moscow wholesale and retail markets, including the largest, Sadovod.
Sadovod is known as a market where most transactions are conducted in cash, and many of its shop employees and owners are migrant workers from countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. “Sadovod is simply a big client base,” a source familiar with the situation told ICIJ, explaining A7’s choice of location.
How the scheme works
Before 2022, intermediaries at Sadovod were already converting cash into ordinary bank transfers or into cryptocurrency, which most often went to China. Western sanctions later disrupted this system by cutting Russian companies off from SWIFT.
A7’s improved system allowed a group of brokers at Sadovod to keep operating. They now accept bags of cash brought in by vendors and count the money, according to the documents. A7’s records refer to these initial cash collection points as “departments”; there are at least eight.
The brokers then pack the rubles into numbered bags. The bags are loaded into vans along with customers’ payment orders and sent to an A7 payment processing center elsewhere in Moscow. About 50 cashiers work there, recording the cash in A7’s counting system. The cash is then delivered to Promsvyazbank, which places it in a vault and credits A7’s accounts.
A7 then uses its shell companies registered abroad. Intermediary companies in Kyrgyzstan buy cryptocurrency through Grinex, a crypto exchange linked to A7. By this point, the money is no longer identified as originating in Russia, thanks to Kyrgyzstan’s permissive policies on cryptocurrency transactions.
PSB provides the banking infrastructure for transferring money to Kyrgyzstan, along with loans and guarantees when needed. From Kyrgyzstan, the money goes to intermediary companies linked to A7 in third countries, most often in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. They convert the cryptocurrency into local currencies and send the money to the end recipient.
“By the time [an A7 payment] is received, nobody in the chain, from the U.S. clearing bank to the Chinese supplier, knows where it came from,” said illicit finance expert Zachary Tvarozna, who co-authored an investigation into A7 conducted with the British nonprofit Open Source Centre. “Washington essentially created a market for A7 [by restricting legitimate transactions] and then did nothing about it,” he concluded.
The risks this scheme poses to the global financial system
From November 2024 to July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 metric tons of rubles in cash worth more than $14 billion, ICIJ and Proekt reported. The journalists were unable to trace the cash’s origins, but it is clear that most of it went to China, as before.
A registry of A7 promissory notes that leaked online and was reviewed by ICIJ shows that A7’s cash deposits at PSB rose in 2025, reaching 195 billion rubles ($2.3 billion) a month by April and 250 billion rubles ($3.1 billion) in June. At its peak, A7 processed at least 58 metric tons of cash a month.
On October 1, 2026, the U.S. Treasury Department designated A7 a “significant transnational criminal organization.” This means U.S. financial institutions will no longer be able to process transfers involving A7’s “Sub-Agents” — foreign shell companies through which the network routes payments for clients in Russia.
A7 “uses a modern, multilayered system of controls” and “was established to ensure uninterrupted payments in the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures,” the company said in a press release issued after the Treasury Department’s announcement. “All clients are screened to identify risks and prevent us from serving individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” the company insisted.
Just two years earlier, when it launched, A7 presented itself as a “sanctions-proof payment system.”
George Voloshin, a financial crime expert at the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists, told ICIJ that A7 “not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls” but “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime.”
International intermediary banks and beneficiaries effectively become complicit in these activities even though they do not know where the money comes from. The reason lies in the cash itself, Voloshin added:
Cash is considered one of the highest-risk payment methods because it is anonymous, can move across borders, and is not tied to a specific person or company.
The entire scheme “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” said Ilya Shumanov, managing partner of TriTrace Investigations, a Russian company specializing in financial market due diligence. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
According to documents reviewed by ICIJ, A7 received 314 payment requests totaling $76 million from brokers working at Sadovod in late 2024. All of the money was intended for the Hong Kong export company Yiton Trading Ltd.
A7 representatives did not respond to ICIJ’s request for comment.

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:32:48 UTC
13:32:48 KST

US appeals court sceptical of Trump’s lawsuit over California voter rolls
Judge questions the Trump administration’s efforts to exert greater influence over elections process ahead of the upcoming midterm vote.
A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.
“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.
It asked the federal court system to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots that the government says were sent to “likely noncitizens”.
The lawsuit indicates the Trump administration sent California officials a list of 20,000 names it believes are not eligible to vote, based on citizenship.
Trump has often pushed the discredited claim that the Democratic Party is benefitting from widespread voting by noncitizens.
California has long been one of the targets of his election misinformation.
Earlier this year, Trump denounced the state’s primaries after right-wing candidates like Los Angeles mayoral hopeful Spencer Pratt felt short of his expectations.
“There’s BIG cheating by the Dumocrats in California,” he wrote on social media at the time.
He then announced that the state would be under investigation by the US Attorneys’ Office.
Trump’s efforts have caused alarm, with critics accusing him of seeking to dampen voter turnout through intimidation and confusion.
The midterms will decide which party controls the US Congress, as well as key state and local positions.
Polls, however, predict steep odds for Republican candidates, given Trump’s souring approval ratings and dissatisfaction with issues like the cost of living and the US-Israel war on Iran.
Voting rights advocates have warned that the Trump administration has not publicly revealed how it has compiled its list of noncitizen voters, and whistleblower reports have cast doubt on the accuracy of such lists.
In response to the October 15 lawsuit, California has countered that it has strong safeguards to prevent noncitizens from voting.
It also said the Justice Department’s claims are based on dubious data.
“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement earlier this month.
“We will continue to carry out free and fair elections in the Golden State — and call out this authoritarian as he tries every play in the dictator’s playbook.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked six Chinese naval vessels, nine official ships, and three military aircraft between 6 a.m. on Sunday and the same time Monday.

Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

"As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."
This is not a quote from a famous figure. Rather, it was something a friend’s father said to us during the Iran-Iraq war, while on leave behind the front lines, in a discussion about Saddam. We, the sons of his friends, found it so striking that for a long time, we used to jokingly write it in beautiful Persian calligraphy and mount it on a wooden plaque in our bunkers before returning to the front.
Years after the war, when I had written an open letter to Trump warning him against going to war with Iran, Noam Chomsky gave me a fascinating response. He essentially said that while my letter was excellent, the problem was that Trump was too foolish to understand such advice. I later realized that Professor Chomsky’s brief observation was, in essence, a different translation of what my friend’s father had said during the war:
As long as there is a God to be God and a world to be the world, foolish people will remain foolish."

Richard Nixon once wrote in his book, War and Peace and Beyond [Note: referring to his concept of ‘Victory without War’], that one should always present the enemy with a dilemma where both choices lead to defeat. The current global narrative regarding this illegal aggression by these two narcissists against Iran follows this pattern. One of those paths, the results of which are already visible on the horizon, is the total collapse of American military prestige—a result I hold no concern for.
Instead, I wish to address a question that might sound strange coming from an Iranian: What will be the definitive and catastrophic consequences of the fall of the Islamic Republic for the world and the West?

1-The Emotional Domestic Opposition: Most domestic opponents of the Islamic Republic lack a true understanding of their country’s lack of independence following a collapse. Even the taboo of seeking nuclear weapons will be cast aside, as the West has effectively proven to them that tolerance toward Western predators leads only to ruin. In short: be as narcissistic as they are.

France works with 10 European nations to increase strength as nuclear deterrent - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:06:16 UTC
13:06:16 KST

France is working with 10 other European nations to expand its capacity as a nuclear weapons power on the continent and a deterrent to Russian aggression as Europe's faith in the US's commitment to its security wanes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday morning.
The 'forward deterrence' plan involves the creation of new infrastructure, communications, early-warning and intelligence-sharing links with France's allies as well as deployments of French nuclear-enabled Rafale jet fighters across Europe.
The UK, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have all joined the project with varying degrees of involvement since French President Emmanuel Macron announced it in March.
“We don’t have any plans to put nuclear weapons on Finnish soil in peacetime. But we do have plans for creating a strategic dilemma for Russia,” said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
“We felt it would be useful for our security to get information, to be involved in it. We don’t know where this is going to end, it’s probably a 10- to 15-years process.”
Instead of the countries all gathering together to work on the plan, France has been holding individual talks, leading European partner nations to constantly communicate with each other to compare what the French have told them, WSJ cited senior defense officials as saying.
European countries doubt US reliability
The plan comes as faith in the US's willingness to defend Europe wanes. Doubts over if the US would risk nuclear war over the defense of a European ally have increased as US President Donald Trump strikes energy deals with Russian President Vladimir Putin and puts increasing pressure on Ukraine, WSJ wrote.
France claims that the French program is more credible as the safety of European countries is of far more direct importance.
“There is one difference between France and the US–we share the same geography, we are part and parcel of the same continent, we have economic and sociological continuity with our neighbors writ large,” Chatel, Macron’s adviser, said at the Warsaw Security Conference.
In his speech announcing the initiative in March, Macron emphasized that France's vital interests were directly affected by its allies.
“Could we consider that the survival of our closest partners may be put at risk without it affecting our vital interests?” Macron said.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said that the plan was not intended to "replace anything. It supplements the nuclear guarantees that were already there" from the US.
Program under French control
Macron also announced that France would resume making nuclear devices for the first time in decades and that the size of its stockpile would become confidential. Despite the involvement of other countries, the nuclear force will be entirely under French control, WSJ wrote.
“The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” one government minister of another European nation said.
According to the WSJ report, the decision was made to make the forward deterrence strategy acceptable across the political spectrum, including to the far-right party of Marine LePen who is polling ahead in the race for the presidency in next spring's elections.

The FBI is investigating whether to pursue economic espionage charges against former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested earlier this month for allegedly planting a recording device in a restricted conference room at the artificial intelligence company, the Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
Investigators are examining whether Alfozan obtained confidential information to offer to the Saudi government, even without being recruited to do so, according to a law enforcement official cited by the WSJ.
Authorities are also considering potential trade secret theft charges, although the investigation may not result in additional prosecution.
Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and US permanent resident, allegedly concealed a small circuit board and microphone behind a television in a conference room primarily used by OpenAI executives.
He currently faces a federal charge of unlawfully intercepting communications, punishable by up to five years in prison. His next court appearance is scheduled for November 6.
His attorney, William Pernik, said he had received no indication that additional charges were being considered.
“We made it very clear that Mr. Alfozan will fight these charges and allegations in court, not in the press,” Pernik said.
Prosecutors examine ties to Saudi royal family
Prosecutors say Alfozan exchanged frequent WhatsApp messages with an unidentified member of the Saudi royal family in 2025 and 2026.
The royal family member allegedly sought to recruit him for a Saudi artificial intelligence initiative, writing, “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!”
Alfozan reportedly responded, “100,” but indicated he intended to remain at OpenAI until his company shares had vested.
Prosecutors said their last known exchange occurred on October 5, the same day Alfozan allegedly returned to the conference room to retrieve the recording device. OpenAI security personnel had already discovered and removed it, subsequently notifying the FBI.
Planned departure, Saudi consulate involvement raise concerns
Prosecutors also disclosed that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for himself, his wife, and their three-month-old son. He was arrested three days before their planned departure.
His wife and son subsequently traveled to Qatar on business-class tickets purchased by a Saudi military official, according to prosecutors.
Defense attorneys said the official was the wife's brother-in-law, that no military funds were used, and that Alfozan frequently booked one-way flights.
During an October 19 detention hearing, US Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse questioned a letter from the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles offering to cover Alfozan's entire bail bond.
“Even if I set it at $10 million?” the judge asked. “I find that problematic. Seems like a blank check. ‘We’re gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out.’ ”
Alfozan was denied bail after the judge determined he posed a significant flight risk.
OpenAI is examining what information the recording device may have captured and whether the incident involved corporate espionage or potential state-sponsored intelligence gathering, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

US military says it helped Gulf states export 1.5 billion barrels of oil
US Central Command says more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support.
US military forces have helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of oil since June, despite Iran’s efforts to control the critical waterway, according to US Central Command (COMMAND).
The US military command said on Sunday that more than 3,000 commercial vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz with its support over the past six months.
It added that more than 95 percent of ships navigating the channel had sailed through safely in recent months despite Iranian threats, “clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway”.
CENTCOM announced the figures as Commander Admiral Brad Cooper made a visit to the region, during which he observed the “current operational environment” in the strait while flying in a US Army helicopter.
“We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry,” Cooper said in a statement.
“This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Cooper said the primary transit routes for vessels in the strait were free of Iranian mines due to the “incredible efforts” of personnel who conduct mine clearance operations.
“We remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the US interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry,” he said.
Crude oil flows have largely returned to levels seen before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in late February, despite the ongoing threat of attacks on commercial vessels by Iranian forces.
At least 16.5 million barrels of oil per day left the region in September, equal to the pre-war average, excluding Iran, according to market intelligence firm Kpler.
Analysts have attributed the rebound to a combination of offshore ship-to-ship transfers, US military escorts, and increased use of oil pipelines.
However, oil prices remain far higher than before the start of the war.
Brent crude futures stood at about $114.50 a barrel on Sunday, after easing about 2 percent from last week’s nearly six-month high.
Brent settled at $72.48 per barrel on February 27, the day before the US and Israel began strikes on Iran.

The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was part of efforts to "de-escalate" and "promote dialogue and diplomatic solutions." It stressed the need to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation."
Saudi Arabia was being represented by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.
They were due to consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, its deputy secretary, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV.
Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. On Sunday, Qatari mediators were in Tehran, an official told Reuters.
Earlier efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June but fighting between Iran and the United States soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-backed Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front.
US, Iran threaten renewed attacks
The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, pushed up global oil and gas prices, left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new humanitarian crisis in Yemen.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. US President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran. Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again.
The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, has weighed on Trump's approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections that decide control of Congress.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's discussions would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran".
Baghaei said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus of Monday's meeting was to build a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, the official said.
Iranian officials told Munir during that visit that there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands - which include ending the US blockade and lifting sanctions on Iranian its oil exports - were met, according to Iranian media.
Pakistan's military media wing and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Houthis strike Saudi airport, energy infrastructure
Saudi Arabia has intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. Houthi attacks have targeted Saudi airports, ports and oil installations.
On Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked East-West crude oil pumping stations in Saudi Arabia as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had resumed operations at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreementsays signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognized borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still underway, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

By Hongji Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are running high this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council, repeating accusations that Seoul fabricated a September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted close to the border.
A Reuters witness at an observatory in South Korea overlooking the heavily armed border on Monday confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery piece positioned in clear view near the frontier.
South Korea’s Yonhap news agency on Sunday identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122-mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border marked a rare public display of such artillery.
Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as about 20 to 30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ).
“It is highly unusual (for North Korea) to expose its self-propelled artillery so conspicuously,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
“By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signalling through action, not words, that it intends to enforce its border policy through force rather than dialogue or negotiation.”
It is also warning South Korea to exercise caution about escalating border friction, with the intention to prevent an accidental clash, he added.
North Korean state media KCNA reported that in the letter sent on Sunday, the country’s UN representative said Seoul was using the landmine incident to depict Pyongyang’s border construction as a military incursion.
North Korea warned in the letter that violations of its sovereignty could trigger self-defence measures and that South Korea would be “wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences.”
PHOTOS ALSO SHOW NORTH KOREAN DRILLS
The letter is a response to a South Korean letter to the Security Council last week, which said a September 21 blast in the DMZ was planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.
The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang has denied responsibility.
A spokesperson for South Korea’s Unification Ministry said on Monday that the North Korean letter appears to repeat North Korea’s existing position and seeks to justify its so-called border line marking work.
The ministry had no separate comment on the placement of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to defuse border tensions.
North Korea’s letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling that a violation of the UN Charter, which bars the threat or use of force against another state’s territorial integrity.
Seoul has said its military issues warning broadcasts and fires warning shots to send North Korean soldiers back across the line when they cross the military demarcation line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ.
North Korean troops have been building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the MDL in recent years.
The Yonhap report cited photographs taken from an observatory in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appeared to show the howitzer as well as North Korean troops conducting drills on the coast of Kaepung county, about 1.5 km (1 mile) from the observatory.
In 2015, there was a similar incident in which South Korean troops were injured by North Korean mines. Then, Seoul resumed anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts across the DMZ, triggering a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.

Trump dials up Islamophobia at Michigan Senate rally against Abdul El-Sayed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
04:03:28 UTC
13:03:28 KST

Trump dials up Islamophobia against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan Senate rally
Al Jazeera looks at the key takeaways from the US president’s campaign event in Michigan ahead of the midterm vote.
Port Huron, Michigan – United States President Donald Trump has sharpened his anti-Muslim attacks against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, going so far as to suggest that Christmas would be cancelled if the progressive doctor won.
Trump visited Michigan on Sunday to shore up support for Republican candidates in the Midwestern state ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.
But from his podium, he levelled unfounded allegations against El-Sayed, including calling him a “jihadist”.
“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said of El-Sayed.
“I want him to have a metal detector.”
The president, whose popularity has been slipping in part due to the US-Israel war on Iran, spoke for nearly two hours to hundreds of supporters.
His remarks largely focused on Michigan’s Senate election, which is one of only about seven toss-up races for the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed faces Republican candidate Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat, and the race is considered crucial for Republicans to retain control of the 100-member Senate.
If Rogers wins, he would flip a seat currently held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, leaving Democrats with the difficult task of flipping five other seats to regain control of the chamber.
Currently, Republicans have a 53-seat majority in the Senate. Only 35 Senate positions are up for election in 2026.
Here are five key takeaways from the Republican event.
Trump doubles down on anti-Muslim attacks
While Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed’s Muslim identity in recent weeks, including by misrepresenting the Democrat’s name as “Mohammed”, the US president took his rhetoric to new heights on Sunday.
Throughout the speech, Trump returned to themes related to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, falsely accusing the candidate of wanting to impose Islamic law in the US.
“So Abdul… also wants our country to go to Sharia law, and if he ever pulls that off, he should be the first one that’s tried. I’ll be a witness,” Trump said, apparently imagining El-Sayed being tried in a religious court.
Several times during the rally, some attendees blurted out “traitor” when El-Sayed’s name was mentioned.
“I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said.
El-Sayed is a US-born citizen and former public health official who has pledged to uphold the Constitution. There is no evidence that he was ever a member of the Muslim Brotherhood or any foreign organisation.
Since Trump first ran for president during the 2016 election cycle, he has weaponised anti-Muslim bigotry for political gain.
In 2015, for instance – near the beginning of his first successful campaign – Trump said he would support “a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States”.
Less than two years later, Trump used the presidency to sign a short-lived executive order barring travel from multiple Muslim-majority countries, what became known as the “Muslim ban”.
In Sunday’s speech, Trump appealed once more to fears of Muslim immigration.
“If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump said.
El-Sayed has previously largely dismissed the anti-Muslim rhetoric against him as an attempt to create “distractions”, saying he is focused more on domestic issues, including lowering the cost of living and expanding access to healthcare.
Rogers embraces Trump
With Trump’s approval ratings plummeting, some Republican candidates in tight races have kept their distance from the president.
Rogers has previously called for an end to the Iran war and expressed reservations about Trump’s tariff campaign, urging an end to the trade war with Canada, which borders Michigan.
But Rogers attended Sunday’s rally and took the stage alongside Trump in a display of mutual support.
A survey by the research firm Marketing Resource Group suggested earlier this month that only 35 percent of voters in Michigan view Trump positively.
Rogers set the tone for the anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed earlier in the rally, also claiming the Democrat is connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, a political movement in Egypt designated as a “terrorist” group by the US this year.
As a congressman, however, Rogers voted in 2012 to continue US aid to Egypt under Muslim Brotherhood President Mohamed Morsi.
In Sunday’s speech, Rogers also tried to paint El-Sayed as part of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), but unlike other progressives, El-Sayed is not a member of the left-wing group.
“This DSA-affiliated candidate is also taking a lot of money from organizations that support the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah,” Rogers said, without offering evidence.
All three groups are designated as “terrorist” organisations in the US, making it illegal to provide any material support to them.
Trump unapologetic about Iran
On Sunday, the average price of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol in Michigan was $4.83, up from $2.91 before the start of the war on Iran.
Tehran has restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz in response to the war, sending energy prices soaring.
Trump initially promised the conflict would only last four to six weeks.
But nearly eight months after the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, the conflict is showing no signs of concluding.
On Sunday, Trump said he has no regrets about the war.
“I made that decision, and I have no second guess,” Trump told the crowd.
He added that he thought petrol prices would have increased by much more than they had. He also defended his decision by referencing the threat of nuclear warfare.
“The number one state sponsor of terror is Iran by far, and we had to make sure they didn’t have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
Iran has denied seeking a nuclear weapon. It has long argued its uranium enrichment programme is for civilian energy production.
Before the war, Trump also argued that US strikes against Iran’s uranium enrichment facilities in June 2025 had completely “obliterated” the country’s nuclear programme.
‘We’re making a freaking fortune’
Despite the economic anxiety related to the cost of living and skyrocketing petrol prices, Trump bragged about the amount of profit US oil companies are making from the war.
Demand for energy products has increased globally in recent months, as supply chains tighten.
“Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what’s happened in the Middle East, because they’re coming to Texas, and they’re coming to Oklahoma, and they’re coming to Louisiana, and they’re taking that oil,” Trump said. “They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars.”
Trump added that his advisers asked him not to bring up this issue because “people are paying a little higher” for petrol and gas.
“I could just see the fake headline: ‘President Trump is talking about all the money they’re making while people are suffering at the pump.’ That’ll be the headline. I said, ‘I don’t give a damn. I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune,'” the US president said.
Trump can still mobilise Republican base
A line of Trump supporters stretched several blocks outside the rally on Sunday.
Attendees, dressed in Make America Great Again (MAGA) gear, filled the hockey arena where Trump spoke.
The crowd roared and laughed with Trump, with attendees frequently blurting out expressions of admiration for the president and insults against his opponents, especially El-Sayed.
Trump may appear politically on the back foot amid dwindling popularity and mounting anger over inflation and the Iran war.
But the president has highlighted his continued ability to mobilise his core MAGA base, often pointing to his crowd size as a metric for his success as a campaigner.
The audience remained engaged and seated throughout the speech on Sunday.
At one point, the address took a bizarre turn as the president spoke about the backside of Jon Husted, a Republican incumbent from Ohio competing in another tight Senate race.
“I looked at his a**, and I’ve never done that with a man before. Women? Yes. Men? No,” Trump said.
The US president also complimented the derriere of the rapper Nicki Minaj, one of his prominent supporters in attendance.
“By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful a** before: Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss,” Trump said.
The crowd cheered.

RLWC quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:28:38 UTC
12:28:38 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Rugby League World Cup quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
The second week of the Rugby League World Cup was short on genuine contests as the tournament's haves and have-nots collided.
Aside from Australia's win over Fiji, where the gallant Bati gave the Kangaroos a hell of a scare, it was big scorelines across the board.
But with fans across three Australian states and two other counties voting with their feet, there are still plenty of quick hits from the second round of matches.
1. Tongan wall holds yet again
For the second week in a row, Tonga's opponent enjoyed plenty of field position and for the second week in a row Tonga's scrambling defence proved more than up to the challenge.
After holding England to 12 points last week, despite the English enjoying 34 tackles inside the red zone to Tonga's 18, they repeated the dose against Lebanon on Friday night.
The Cedars came in with an offload-heavy game plan and had some success moving the ball up the field. By the end, they had 29 tackles inside the attacking 20 to Tonga's 30, but that was where they stalled.
Some of it was due to a lack of creativity but there were plenty of last-gasp Tongan efforts to deny Lebanese players who looked tryline bound, and it means Tonga carry a strong form line into Sunday's blockbuster against Samoa.
2. Samoa running riot over PNG is a sign of the times
Rarely will you see two halves of a single game more different than what Samoa and Papua New Guinea dished up in Port Moresby.
The Kumuls held the gloves up well through the opening 40, trailing just 14-6 at the break and could have been even closer had Robert Derby successfully grounded the ball for their second try.
But what followed was a procession: Samoa scored 50 unanswered points in the second half, as their size and athleticism totally overwhelmed PNG, who had just four sets in the entire stanza.
Of all the blowout results this weekend, this more than any other was a sign of the times. Rugby league's embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of the game makes it almost impossible for an underdog team to stay in the fight beyond a certain point and when things break they can break badly.
Samoa only had to make 36 tackles through the entire second and the Kumuls only got over halfway for two tackles.
They finished the game conceding six tries in 15 minutes against a side they had held their own against for the whole first half.
There were plenty of less-extreme examples of the same through this year's NRL season, most notably when a top eight side conceded the third-most points in a game ever, but it's been turned up to greater levels through this World Cup given the talent and fitness disparity and it stacks the deck even further against the underdogs.
3. France's woes continue in England smash-up
England beat the clock against their old rivals in Perth, running out 82-0 winners in a result that means France have conceded 160 points in as many minutes through their two matches.
It's hard to find any silver lining for Les Chanticleers and ahead of their tournament finale against Lebanon, the French game finds itself in a strange position.
The potential for growth or a return to the glory days when France were one of Test football's true powers is always the dream, and with two Super League clubs in Catalans Dragons and Toulouse — giving France more professional teams than New Zealand — they seemingly have the ingredients and infrastructure for improvement.
All but two of this year's squad were home-grown players and since 2020 they have won nine of the 16 Tests they have played, with all seven losses coming against England or Samoa.
Problem is, across those seven games they have been outscored by a cumulative total of 394-44, with this England loss the worst of them.
There's greater pathways to the top for French talent than ever before but they can't seem to close the gap between them and the big dogs.
If anything, the gap has become wider. Nine years ago, in the 2017 World Cup, they played England at the same ground and lost 36-6 a week after losing to Australia 52-6.
Those scorelines aren't exactly a good time, but they're not a point-a-minute for two straight weeks either.
The Southern Hemisphere racing ahead of the north is a wider issue for the sport, but France are the collateral damage and they don't have a contingent of heritage NRL players to paper over the cracks.
4. Christchurch puts its best foot forward
Despite Esom Ioka's first-half hat-trick that briefly gave the Cook Islands the lead, few would have ever expected the Aitu to trouble New Zealand for long in their match at Te Kaha in Christchurch.
That didn't stop a sell-out crowd of 26,800 coming through the gates, marking the fifth biggest Test attendance of the past century in New Zealand and the highest ever for a game outside of Auckland.
It was a strong week of crowds throughout the tournament — Tonga and Lebanon pulled in more than 25,000 and Australia topped 40,000 for the second week in a row despite taking on Fiji.
But with the NRL expansion race heating up as the league prepares to hand out a licence for a 20th team, Christchurch showing up in droves did their chances of winning the bid no harm at all.
5. Fiji take Australia to the brink
Speaking of that Australian-Fiji crowd, the 41,108 punters who packed into Lang Park didn't just push the attendance past that of the 2017 World Cup final at the same venue, they were treated to easily the best clash of the weekend.
On the back of an inspired display by five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe and a hat-trick to Castleford winger Semi Valemei, Fiji pushed Australia all the way before a late Jacob Preston try wrapped up a 36-22 win for the green and golds.
Consider the previous margins between the two (42-8, 54-6 and 64-0 in their last three meetings) and it's a measure of how far the Bati have come and how this World Cup is more up for grabs than one might think.
A couple of contentious calls and some killer instinct in key moments got the Kangaroos home.
But on what they've shown through two weeks, Samoa, Tonga and New Zealand will all fancy their chances of springing an upset should they meet Australia, who have wrapped up a semi-final berth in surprisingly shaky fashion.

The Strategic Logic Behind Pakistan’s Defense Pacts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:28:00 UTC
12:28:00 KST

On October 21, Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia signed the Badr Pact, a quadrilateral defense cooperation framework. As per the joint statement issued after the signing of the memorandum of understanding in Doha, the pact is aimed at deepening cooperation in defense manufacturing, joint research and development, technical training, and industrial capacity building among the signatory countries.
The pact is expected to pave the way for deeper technological integration and joint production by leveraging the complementary strengths of the defense sectors of the four countries.
This agreement is the latest addition to Pakistan’s expanding security partnerships. Over the past year, Islamabad has concluded multiple defense pacts with numerous countries in West Asia and neighboring regions.
In September 2025, Pakistan signed the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, under which aggression against one will be treated as aggression against the other. In August 2026, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia concluded the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, which contains an explicit collective defense commitment. The same month, Pakistan signed a Protocol Agreement with Kuwait, which has expanded military cooperation in training, capacity building and related areas between the two countries.
The Badr agreement has now added a multilateral industrial cooperation framework with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia.
There are three interconnected reasons for Pakistan’s participation in these agreements, which highlight the strategic trajectory Islamabad is now pursuing in terms of its defense partnerships.
First, these agreements reflect Islamabad’s growing strategic engagement with key Muslim countries amid rapidly shifting regional security alignments in West Asia. It is important to note that Pakistan’s military performance during last year’s clashes with India demonstrated credible conventional capabilities and helped restore a measure of international strategic credibility. At the same time, Pakistan has played an important and visible mediating role between Iran and the United States, and has helped in keeping channels of communication open at a time when many other actors found themselves constrained by their own alignments.
Arguably, these developments have reinforced perceptions of Pakistan as a useful middle power, which is capable of engaging competing power blocs. In a tumultuous region like West Asia, traditional security umbrellas have shown their limits amid the U.S.-Iran war. Against this backdrop, countries are increasingly seeing value in deepening ties with a state like Pakistan that has maintained working relationships across multiple camps and has proven operational military capabilities in recent years.
Second, Pakistan has long pursued the idea of joint defense production and investment in its defense industry to elevate its security partnerships beyond transactional procurement of weapons. This vision has benefited Pakistan in many ways. For instance, cooperation with China has produced notable results, including the JF-17 fighter program and related industrial capacity. Similarly, ties with Türkiye have expanded into naval shipbuilding along with other technology and production initiatives.
A recent analysis published in Dawn newspaper observed that each of the recent defense agreements signed by Pakistan carried an explicit provision for joint defense production and investment in the defense industry. “This clause in every defense pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region,” it noted.
This essentially means that such opportunities can help Pakistan accelerate its defense modernization and help sustain credible conventional deterrence in a difficult neighborhood.
Third, Pakistan has been working to develop a more competitive defense industry, which is capable of supporting meaningful arms exports to a level where it could compete with major international players. In recent months, there has been a noticeable increase in reporting of export discussions and deals involving countries in Africa, West Asia and other regions, including substantial packages linked to platforms such as the JF-17 and related systems.
Moreover, Pakistan has long participated actively in international defense exhibitions, where it has showcased both domestically developed and jointly produced equipment with partners such as China. In this regard, the new agreements offer Pakistan a way to build on the idea of expanding arms exports, attract investment into the sector, and raise the competitiveness of Pakistani offerings. One can argue that over time these defense deals may also support the further development of Pakistan’s local production capacity, creating a direct link between increased industrial strength, export earnings, and operational self-reliance.
Taken together, the Badr agreement and Pakistan’s recent defense pacts reflect Islamabad’s growing role in shaping an emerging security architecture in West Asia. Arguably, through these frameworks, Pakistan is not only going to play a role in enhancing the security of its partners through military training, operational expertise, and joint manufacturing, but it will also likely benefit by securing foreign investment, technology transfer, and building defense industrial self-reliance.
It will be interesting to watch how Pakistan will navigate the opportunities these arrangements will bring, while also managing the constraints that will inevitably accompany a growing list of commitments.

During the visit, Iranian officials told him there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran’s demands were met, according to Iranian media.
Earlier mediation efforts involving both Pakistan and Qatar helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but the deal quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the United States resumed weeks later.
The deputy secretary of Iran’s top security body, Ali Baqeri-Kani, told state TV that Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid, Pakistan’s Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin would visit Tehran for consultations with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on regional security.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the meeting is part of ongoing efforts by the Mecca Pact countries to de-escalate the current crisis, promote diplomatic solutions, and support mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan.
“The visit also underscores the pivotal role of the Mecca Pact states in fostering regional security and stability, and their commitment to working with all nations in the region toward achieving this goal,” Krimly posted on X.
Pakistan’s military media wing and Turkey’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Tensions rising
Saudi Arabia intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Oct 25 as fighting with the Houthis continued unabated.
Ministers from the Mecca Pact countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier in October and agreed to ensure the “rapid deployment” of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi attacks have become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Oct 23 the US may carry out another military operation against Iran and Iran’s leaders have said that a renewed US military campaign would be met with a stronger response than before.
Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. A US intelligence memo this week warned that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached “advanced stages”.
The war, now nearly eight months old, has weighed on President Donald Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the midterms.
The Mecca agreement’s first article says the parties shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.
Efforts by Turkey’s Parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week. REUTERS

Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection on Oct. 25, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term in office, as his opponent, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede defeat and vowed to challenge the election results.
The election ended with Lula receiving 51.79% of votes compared with Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to Brazil's electoral authorities.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election, calling a decision by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting by two hours "unacceptable."
The extension was introduced following transportation disruptions and severe weather that affected voting in parts of the country, according to the Associated Press.
The electoral court has recognized Lula's victory, and Bolsonaro's refusal to concede does not invalidate the result.
Lula had expressed the view in 2024 that Brazil should remain neutral and not interfere in Russia's war against Ukraine, but in the years that followed had been engaging in diplomacy, including efforts to position Brazil as a potential mediator between Kyiv and Moscow.
In June of this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky accepted Lula's offer to assist efforts to negotiate an end to the war, Ukrainian presidential communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said, according to Reuters.
The leaders held a bilateral meeting on during the G7 summit in France on June 17, discussing ways to revive stalled diplomatic negotiations, including potential outreach to permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
While Ukraine maintains close diplomatic ties with three of the five permanent members — France, the United Kingdom and the United States — Brazil has maintained diplomatic relations with Russia and China.
Lula spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone in August, discussing the war in Ukraine and bilateral relations, CNN Brasil reported.
Brazil has maintained diplomatic and economic ties with Russia since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, opting out of Western sanctions and expressing a wish to have a role in a negotiated settlement to the war.
Lula has also rejected suggestions that Brazil supports Russia's invasion, saying in an April interview that his government has never recognized Moscow's right to occupy Ukrainian territory.
The Brazilian president's victory comes after a closely fought campaign against Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a prison sentence for his role in an attempted coup following his 2022 election defeat.
The elder Bolsonaro also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. He was subsequently convicted for his role in a plot to overturn that election.
The victory makes Lula, 80, the first Brazilian president to win four terms and the first candidate since the country's return to democracy to win a presidential runoff after finishing second in the opening round.
While Bolsonaro refused to concede and asked for the vote to be annulled, election officials have expressed "absolute" confidence in the proceedings and the result, as reported by Reuters.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama announced plans Sunday for new legal measures targeting protests as demonstrations by university students demanding improved education conditions continued in the capital Tirana.
The protests, which began on Oct. 13, entered their 13th day, drawing support from high school students, citizens, faculty members from several universities and various trade unions. Some demonstrations turned violent.
Protesters marched through streets and squares across the capital, first gathering outside the Education Ministry, where they threw stones at the building. They later moved to the prime minister's office, where tensions escalated between demonstrators and security forces.

Rama reiterated his calls for dialogue, as he had in previous days, but protesters rejected the appeals. Students said they would continue their demonstrations.
Rama said the current law governing demonstrations dates back to 2001 and contains no provisions addressing digital technology tools, which have become a fundamental part of protests today.
The proposed legislative package includes compensation for businesses affected by demonstrations, fines for participants in violent protests, measures to address calls for violence on social media and amendments to the Criminal Code.
The planned regulations would introduce fines for organizing unauthorized demonstrations, failing to comply with orders to disperse, wearing masks during protests and obstructing traffic.
The package also aims to require the removal of social media posts calling for violence and initiate legal proceedings against those responsible.

First time voters could determine as many as 12 Knesset seats with high turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-26
03:16:37 UTC
12:16:37 KST

On Oct. 27, Yael Chernyvsky, 18, from Ramat Hasharon in central Israel, plans to cast her ballot for the first time.
“I’m voting so we can change the future of this country,” the teen told Jewish Telegraphic Agency earlier this month. She was entering a Tel Aviv auditorium where some of Israel’s top politicians were about to address more than 1,000 first-time voters, including many in pre-military programs.
Chernyvsky, who is studying in an army preparation program in the Negev, blames the current right-wing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the country’s problems.
So she said she will vote for one of the opposition parties in the “change bloc,” which seeks to oust Netanyahu, who has been in office since 2009 except for a brief period in 2021-2022.
Chernyvsky had not decided which party she will vote for, but she said it will “probably” be either the Democrats led by Yair Golan or Yashar led by Gadi Eisenkot.
“We’ve basically had the same government for 20 years, and I genuinely think it’s corrupt. Why has this war been going on for three years? Why did it take two years to return the hostages? Why does the government give so much money to haredi Jews who don’t work and don’t serve in the army?”
Chernyvsky is one of the estimated 640,000 Israelis aged 18 to 22 eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI). Comprising nearly 10% of the electorate, their votes could determine as many as 12 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
High voter turnout expected
“Israel is a young country with a high birth rate,” said Tammy Hoffman, head of the education policy program at the IDI, which co-sponsored the young voter event with the Yigal Allon Center. “If their turnout is high, as our research suggests, first-time voters will make a difference.”
In May, Hoffman and her colleagues surveyed potential young first-time Jewish and Arab voters about their attitudes and political engagement. Across Israel’s population groups, 80% to 95% said they would “definitely” or be likely to vote. Secular Jewish youth expressed the highest level of certainty regarding participation, while 87% of Arabs said they intend to vote.
It’s a higher percentage than in the US, where the youth turnout in the 2024 presidential election was only 47%, according to the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement.
More than four-fifths of respondents to the IDI survey described the opportunity to vote as either “fairly meaningful” or “very meaningful,” with particularly strong responses among traditional and religious Jewish youth.
A separate poll of 18-year-old to 22-year-old potential first-time voters for the Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth news outlets also revealed high motivation: 67% of respondents said they were certain they would vote, while another 19% thought they would.
National security, cost of living highest priorities
In both polls, national security and the cost of living were top priorities for both Jews and Arabs. Hoffman wasn’t surprised.
"For the past several years, they’ve lived in an unstable environment during their adolescence. They were in junior high during COVID, they witnessed the judicial reform protests, and of course Oct. 7. They are worried about their future.”
While the Hamas attack affected every Israeli, the fact that so many first-time voters are either serving in the Israel Defense Forces or will do so in the near future could influence how they vote.
Jewish Israeli voters of all ages have moved rightward politically over the past couple of decades, Hoffman noted.
“But military service doesn’t necessarily lead you to a nationalist stance,” Hoffman emphasized. “It can do the opposite: It can bring up questions about the war and its goals.”
Arab Israelis, meanwhile, haven’t shifted rightward, but they are more eager to vote in this election than previous elections, reflecting their growing engagement in Israeli society, Hoffman said.
In a Sept. 23 N12 poll, 74% of young people described their political views as right-wing or center-right, while 23% identified as left-wing or center-left. If the election were held at the time the poll was taken, 16% of respondents would vote for Eisenkot’s Yashar party and 14% would vote for Netanyahu’s Likud party.
Despite the assumption that the majority of Jewish youth will vote for right-wing and far-right parties, Hoffman said, mock elections at high schools around the country show a different picture.
She said the majority of students voted for Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Beyachad, led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid from the opposition Change bloc, and “some for Netanyahu’s [right-wing] Likud, but not a lot for [Itamar] Ben-Gvir,” who heads a far-right party.
Omer Gross from Jerusalem, who graduated from high school in June and is now in an army-prep program in the Golan, plans to vote for the Religious Zionist party led by far-right politicians Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin.
“I don’t really agree with what Smotrich has been doing in Gaza,” he said, referring to Smotrich’s objective to reestablish the uprooted Jewish settlements in Gaza and incentivize Palestinian emigration from the strip, “but I support what he does in the territories” – the West Bank. “We need a strong, secure Israel.”
Tomer Shiloh from Herziliyah, who attends the same Golan Heights program as his friend Omer, has different plans.
“I’m voting for the ‘Change’ bloc, for Gadi Eisenkot or Naftali Bennett,” the 18-year-old said.
If it were up to Shiloh, the next government would require Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, young men to serve in the IDF, as he will do next year. He wants the next government to lower Israel’s high cost of living.
“I want the people who run this country to have good values and to do what’s best for the country and not for themselves,” the teen said.
Sgt. M is a 22-year-old office worker doing his first stint of reserve duty following the conclusion of his mandatory army service. He says ensuring that all Israelis serve the country either in the IDF or through National Service is at the top of his election priority list. But he will be voting for the left-of-center Democrats party mostly for economic reasons.
“Did you know that most university students have to work while they study to pay for tuition, books, food and housing?” the reservist, who requested anonymity due to IDF regulations, said as he traveled home by train from his army base. “I wanted to start studying right after finishing the army, but between the cost and reserve duty, that’s impossible,” he said.
Speaking from his home in the northern Israeli city of Shef-Amra, Khalel Alaa Sabeh, 18, said he plans to vote for an Arab party that will prioritize addressing resource gaps in the Arab community.
“I want to see more money allocated to the Arab community,” he said, noting that historically, Arab municipalities have received less government funding than Jewish municipalities. “But most of all, I want our families to be safe. There’s a lot of crime in the Arab sector and the Netanyahu government isn’t doing enough to stop it.”
Sabeh, who plans to start university next year, said he is urging his friends to show up to vote on Oct. 27.
“I want to see change in this country, and if Netanyahu wins we’ll have four more bad years.” Yet whatever the outcome on Election Day, he said, “I won’t leave the country. This is my land, this is my home.”
